## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III**

A chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and thoroughly corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each Father on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the texts of each book of Scripture and in what passages of their works they did so.

The most accurate edition, and one easily preferred to all others if the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceptionally convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there—but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form—are properly considered.

### Second Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Lives of the Fathers, or History of the Hermits: Continuation

## Book Nine of the Lives of the Fathers, Called *Philotheus*, or *Theophilus*

By Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus; translated by Gentianus Hervetus.

[Col. 0009]

## Prelude

We cited certain testimonies concerning this book above, in the general prolegomenon, section 11. In addition to those, now take the following.

## Testimonies Concerning the Author and This Book

[Col. 0009A] John of Damascus, Oration 3, *On Images*.

793. [Greek:] From the *Philothean History* of Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, in the Life of Saint Simeon the Stylite: “For it is superfluous even to speak of Italy. For they say that in Rome, the greatest city, this man became so celebrated that in all the entrances to workshops they set up small images of him, thereby obtaining for themselves some protection and security.” [Latin translation:] “From the *Philotheus* of Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, in the Life of Saint Simeon who lived on a column: for what need is there to speak of Italy? For they say that this man became so famous and celebrated in the greatest city of Rome that people set up small images of him even in all the vestibules of workshops, thereby procuring for themselves some protection and security.”

[Col. 0010A] The Seventh General Synod, that is, the Second Council of Nicaea, October 4.

[Greek:] From Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, from the Life of Simeon the Stylite, whose beginning is: “Simeon, the great wonder of the inhabited world.” And further on: “For they say that in Rome, the greatest city, this man became so celebrated that in all the entrances to workshops they set up small images of him, thereby obtaining for themselves some protection and security.” [Latin translation:] “Of Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, on the Life of Simeon the Stylite, whose beginning is: ‘Simeon, who was a very great wonder of the world.’ And further on: ‘For they say that this man was most famous in the greatest Rome, and that in all the doors of workshops they set up small icons of him, obtaining from this for themselves some protection and safeguard.’”

[Col. 0009]

# Author’s Prologue

794. It is a beautiful thing to behold the contests of excellent men who have exercised themselves nobly in virtue, and to draw profit through the eyes. For things that are praised while they are being observed appear worthy of possession, embrace, and love, and they move spectators to acquire them. Yet narratives of such deeds, rightly and virtuously performed, offer no less considerable benefit when they are presented to the ears of those who do not know them by people who do.

Some say that sight is more trustworthy than hearing; yet hearing also becomes trustworthy when it judges what is said by the truthfulness of those who speak. Just as the tongue and palate are entrusted with judging sweetness, bitterness, and qualities of that kind, and people pronounce their judgment concerning them, so the discernment of speeches is entrusted to hearing, which knows how to separate from harmful accounts those that offer some benefit.

If the memory of useful narratives remained whole and uncorrupted, and if no stain—like a kind of fog of forgetfulness—caused it to fade, it would certainly be superfluous to write about them, since the benefit gained from them would readily reach posterity. But while time brings destruction to bodies, introducing old age and death, it also, as I think, brings forgetfulness upon things rightly and virtuously done and obscures their memory. No one, therefore, could rightly blame us for undertaking to write the lives and disciplines of devout men who loved God.

Just as those entrusted with the care of bodies prepare medicines, waging war against disease and bringing help to the afflicted, so the diligence devoted to writing these accounts becomes a kind of saving medicine: it attacks forgetfulness and assists memory.

How could it not be absurd for poets and historians to record the brave and noble deeds performed in war; for tragedians to bring into public view calamities that were rightly hidden and to preserve their memory in writing; and for others to spend their speeches on comedies and ridiculous matters, while we allowed men who, in mortal and suffering bodies, displayed freedom from suffering and imitated incorporeal nature to be handed over to oblivion?

What punishments would we not rightly deserve if we treated the preservation of the memory of contests worthy of admiration as worthless? If philosophers who imitated the supreme philosophy of the saints of former times did not engrave their memory in bronze and letters, but, expressing all their virtue, made themselves into living images and statues of them, what pardon would rightly be granted to us if we did not honor their illustrious life even in writing?

This is especially so when athletes and pancratiasts who compete at the Olympic games are honored with statues, and when charioteers who appear to be victorious in horse races receive the same reward. Nor is this all: men who are womanish and effeminate, and of whom one might doubt whether they are men or women, are inscribed on tablets by those who delight in such spectacles, as they strive to preserve their memory for the longest possible time—although such remembrance brings harm rather than benefit to the soul.

Yet these honor the lovers of such things with such paintings, and those others honor those others with those paintings, even though they cause harm. Since death plunders mortal nature, they mix colors and place their likenesses on panels, devising a means by which their memory may live much longer than they themselves.

We, however, write of philosophy, the teacher of life, which has imitated the manner of life conducted in heaven. We do not describe the shapes or features of bodies, nor do we display things represented for those who do not know them; rather, we sketch the forms of souls, which do not fall under the senses, and we set forth wars that cannot be seen and conflicts that do not appear.

With such armor the commander and leader of their army, Paul, clothed them for battle: “Take,” he says, “the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand” (Ephesians 6). And again: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in readiness for the gospel of peace; in all things take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. And receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (ibid.).

Having clothed them in this armor, he led them into battle. Such is the nature of their enemies also: incorporeal, wholly invisible, attacking obscurely, lying in ambush secretly, and suddenly rushing upon them unexpectedly. Teaching this very thing, the commander also said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (ibid.).

Yet although this company of saints had such enemies—or, rather, although each of them was surrounded by so many and such great enemies—for they did not all attack at once but assaulted some at one time and others at another, they achieved so glorious a victory that their adversaries fled, while the saints, having routed and overthrown them, raised a trophy, since nothing impeded them.

Nature did not give them the victory, for nature is mortal and full of countless passions; rather, it was the mind that drew down divine grace. Since they were ardent lovers of divine beauty and had willingly resolved both to do and to suffer everything for what they loved, they endured the attacks of their passions and disturbances with brave and noble spirit. They vigorously repelled the tempests raised by the devil’s weapon.

To speak apostolically (1 Corinthians 9), when they disciplined their bodies and brought them into subjection, they stilled the heat of anger and compelled the frenzy of desires to rest. By fasting and sleeping on the ground, they put the movements of the soul to sleep and restrained their exultations. They compelled the body to enter into an alliance with the soul and dissolved the war implanted in them by nature.

When peace had thus been made between them, they drove out the entire host of their adversaries. For since the enemies lacked thoughts that would betray what was within, and were deprived of the aid of human limbs, they could not wage war.

The devil uses our own members as weapons against us. If the eyes are not enticed, the ears not charmed, the sense of touch not tickled by some pleasant sensation, and the mind does not admit wicked counsels, those who prepare ambushes labor in vain.

Just as no enemy could capture a city built on high ground, fortified with strong defenses, and surrounded on every side by deep ditches, if no one inside betrayed it and opened some of the gates, so demons waging war from outside cannot overcome a soul enclosed by divine grace unless the negligence of some thought opens a window of our senses and admits the enemy within through it.

Those whose praises we celebrate had plainly learned this from divine Scripture. They had heard God say through the prophet, “Death has come up through the windows” (Jeremiah 9). Having closed their senses with divine laws as with barriers and bars, they entrusted their keys to the mind.

They did not open their lips and tongue unless the mind commanded it. The pupils of their eyes were not permitted to extend beyond their eyelashes. Hearing, blocking access to harmful sounds, rejected foolish and useless speech and admitted only those things in which the mind delighted.

Thus they taught the sense of smell not to desire things that emit a pleasant fragrance, since such things are naturally disposed to soften and relax. Thus they drove satiety from the belly and taught it to take what would not bring pleasure but would fulfill necessity, and no more than was sufficient to prevent death from hunger.

Thus they dissolved the sweet tyranny of sleep. Having freed the eyelashes from its servitude, they taught them to exercise mastery over it, admitting sleep not when it invaded but when they summoned it, as a brief aid to nature.

Having thus guarded the walls and gates and reconciled the inner thoughts to concord, they mocked the enemies attacking from outside. The enemies could not enter by force because of the protection of divine grace, and they found no traitor willing to admit them.

Since the enemies were by nature invisible, they could not overcome the body, which is visible and subject to the necessities of nature. Its charioteer, musician, and helmsman, holding the reins skillfully, persuaded its horses to proceed correctly and in order. Striking the string of the senses rhythmically, he caused them to produce a sound harmonious and consonant in every respect. Skillfully moving the rudder, he broke the attacks of the waves and the force of the winds.

Who would not rightly admire those who entered upon the path of life through innumerable labors, subdued the body with sweat and affliction, knew nothing of laughter, and spent their whole life in mourning and tears; who counted Sybaritic pleasures as fasting; sweet sleep as laborious vigils; a soft bed as hard ground; and immense, insatiable pleasure as their way of life in prayer and the singing of psalms?

[Note: [Col. 0115B] Sybaritic pleasures. Below, chapter 5: “as those who enjoyed Sybaritic pleasures.” On these, see the *Adagia*.]

I mean those who embraced every kind of virtue. Who would not admire them, or rather, who could praise them as their worth deserves?

I understand well enough that no speech can attain their virtue, yet the attempt must be made. It would not be right that, because they loved true philosophy perfectly, they should therefore receive not even lesser praises.

I shall not write one common praise for all of them, for different gifts were divinely given to them. Teaching this, blessed Paul said: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in the same Spirit, to another workings of powers, to another prophecy, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12).

Showing the source of all these gifts, he added: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing separately to each one as he wills.”

Since, therefore, they received different gifts, we shall rightly give a separate account of each. We shall not pursue everything they did—for not even a whole lifetime would suffice to write it all—but after narrating a few things about each one’s manner of life and deeds, and showing in a few words the character and form of his entire life, we shall pass to another.

Nor shall we attempt to commit to writing the lives of all the saints who were illustrious everywhere. We do not know all those who were famous everywhere, and it is impossible for one person to write about them all.

I shall therefore describe only the lives of those who shone like lights in the East and embraced the ends of the earth with their rays. The account will proceed by narrative, not following the rules of encomia, but reporting a few things truthfully.

I ask those who encounter this religious history, or this account of monastic discipline—for let each person call the work what he wishes—not to believe less in what is said if they hear something exceeding their powers. Let them not measure the virtue of those men by themselves, but let them know clearly that God measures out from above the gifts of the most holy Spirit to devout souls and gives greater gifts to those who are more perfect.

I have said this for those who are not thoroughly initiated into the mysteries of divine matters. The initiates of the Spirit’s sanctuaries know the glory of the Spirit and what miracles he performs through human beings, drawing unbelievers to the knowledge of God.

But whoever will not believe what I am about to say clearly does not regard as true even the miracles performed through Moses, Jesus, Elijah, and Elisha, and counts as fables the miracles performed by the holy apostles. If he testifies that those things are true, let him also believe that these accounts are free from falsehood; for the grace that worked in those earlier figures performed through these men also what it performed.

Grace is everlasting. Choosing those who are worthy, it pours out the streams of its activity through them as through channels or fountains.

Of the events that are to be related, I myself saw some. Those I did not see, I heard from men who had seen them—men who loved virtue and were considered worthy both to see those saints and to enjoy their teaching.

The writers of the gospel teaching are trustworthy not only Matthew and John, great and foremost among the evangelists, who saw the Lord’s miracles, but also Luke and Mark. Those who saw the events from the beginning and were ministers of the Word taught them accurately not only what the Lord suffered and did, but also what he continually taught.

Indeed, although blessed Luke himself had not seen these events, at the beginning of his work he says that he is recounting what he had learned with certainty.

Even if we hear that he did not see what he narrates but received this teaching from others, we believe him and Mark no less than Matthew and John. Each is trustworthy in his narrative, having learned from those who saw.

We, therefore, shall relate some things as having been seen by us, and others as believed by us on the testimony of men who saw them and imitated their lives.

I have used a more extended speech concerning these matters because I wish to persuade the reader that I shall narrate the truth. From this point onward I shall begin the narrative.

[Col. 0015]

# Philotheus, or Theophilus

[Note: [Col. 0115A] First observe that this book had two translators: Albericus Longus of Salento and Gentianus Hervetus. See what was said in the general prolegomenon, section 14. Here I have given Theodoret’s *Philotheus* according to Hervetus’s translation, which is better known among the public and was printed among his works. Laurentius de la Barre also inserted it, with certain marginal notes, into his *Christian History of the Ancient Fathers*, published at Paris in 1583.

Second, observe that this book may be divided into three parts. The first treats of the Fathers who lived before Theodoret’s time, from chapter 1 to chapter 21; the second of those who lived in his own time, from chapter 21 to chapter 29; the third of illustrious women, from chapter 29 to the end, that is, the final two chapters.]

## Chapter One: Jacob of Nisibis

[Note: [Col. 0115B] Jacob of Nisibis. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on July 15, and the Greek Menologion on October 31. He is also mentioned in the *Menaea*, both on January 13 and on October 31. Theodoret also mentions him in Book II, chapter 30, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and again in Book I, chapter 7, where he says that Jacob attended the Council of Nicaea and raised the dead. Concerning this miracle and the others, he refers the reader to this *Philotheus* of his. He is also mentioned by Nicephorus in Book VIII, chapter 14, and Book IX, chapter 28. He also attended the Council of Antioch, as recorded in the Acts of Saint Alexander, Bishop of Constantinople.]

[Col. 0015A]

That divine Moses, the lawgiver, who opened the bottom of the sea, covered the dry land with an inundation of waters, and performed all his other miracles, wrote the deeds of the saints who lived in ancient times—not using the wisdom he had received from the Egyptians, but the splendor of grace received from above.

From where else could he have learned of Abel’s virtue, Enoch’s devotion to virtue, Noah’s righteousness, Melchizedek’s devout priesthood, Abraham’s calling, faith, courage, and hospitality, which was his great concern; the widely reported sacrifice of his son; and the catalogue of his other noble deeds? To speak briefly, from where could he have learned of the contests, victories, and praises of divine men unless he had received the rays of the intelligent and divine Spirit?

798 I too now need this help, since I am attempting to write the lives of the saints who shone shortly before our time and in our own days, and whom I wish to set forth as laws for those who desire to imitate them.

Their prayers, therefore, must be invoked, and the narrative must begin.

Nisibis is a city on the border of the Roman and Persian kingdoms. Formerly it paid tribute to the Romans and obeyed their rule. From this city came the great Jacob, who embraced a solitary and quiet life. Taking possession of the summits of the highest mountains, he lived there.

In spring, summer, and autumn he used the forests and had the sky for a roof. In winter, however, he took shelter in a cave, which provided him with a small covering.

His food was not what grows and is cultivated through labor, but what grows spontaneously. He gathered from the trees wild fruits that grew of themselves, and from the herbs those that were edible and served as vegetables. From these he gave his body what was sufficient for life, refusing the use of fire.

The use of wool was also unnecessary to him. The extremely rough hair of goats served his purpose; from it he made for himself both a tunic and a simple cloak.

Thus, while afflicting his body, he continually supplied it with spiritual nourishment. Purifying the faculty of thought and making it a clear mirror contemplating the divine Spirit, he contemplated the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, according to the saying of the divine Apostle, and was transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (1 Corinthians 3).

From this his confidence toward God increased daily. Asking God for what he ought to ask, he received it immediately. Moreover, he prophetically foresaw things to come and received from the grace of the most holy Spirit the power to perform miracles.

I shall narrate a few of these things and reveal to those who do not know it a ray of his apostolic splendor.

At that time madness for human images prevailed. Lifeless statues claimed divine worship for themselves, while the worship of God was neglected by many. Those who refused to share in the people’s drunkenness and who, endowed with perfect virtue, discerned what truly existed were held in contempt. They laughed at the weakness of the idols and worshiped the Maker of all things.

At that time Jacob had come into Persia to see the shoots of true religion and to give them the care they deserved. As he was crossing a spring, certain girls were washing cloths and cleaning garments with their feet.

[Note: [Col. 0115B] Girls. Nicephorus, Book XV, chapter 22, attributes to another, younger Jacob what should be attributed to this Jacob of Nisibis. He also calls that other man a Nisibene; Theodoret discusses him below, in chapter 22. Perhaps Nicephorus posited two Nisibenes because Jacob of Nisibis appears twice in the *Menaea*. Yet the same man is intended in both places, as will be clear to anyone consulting the *Menaea*—unless this younger man too was a Nisibene. Certainly this is how the matter is presented in the Catalogue of illustrious persons to whom the Emperor Leo wrote concerning the Council of Chalcedon. See volume II of the Councils.]

They did not even show respect for his novel and dignified appearance, but, having cast off modesty, hardened their faces, and looked at the divine man with shameless eyes. They neither covered their heads nor lowered the garments they had girded up.

[Col. 0016B]

The man of God was distressed by this and wished to reveal God’s power at the proper time, so that by a miracle he might free them from their impiety. He cursed the spring, and its stream immediately vanished.

He also cursed the girls and chastised their shameless youth: before its time he caused their hair to turn gray. The word was followed by the deed; the blackness of their hair changed, and they became like newly planted trees that in autumn are entirely covered with leaves.

When they experienced this punishment—for the spring’s waters had fled, and, looking at one another’s heads, they saw the sudden change—they hurried toward the city to report what had happened.

When they came running and encountered the great Jacob, they begged him to restrain his anger and remit the punishment.

[Col. 0016C]

He did not delay long. He offered prayers to the Lord and ordered the waters to flow again. At once they streamed once more from their hidden sources, channeled according to the just man’s command.

After obtaining this, the girls’ relatives asked that the natural color also be restored to their daughters’ hair. They say that he granted this request as well, but asked for the girls who had received the discipline. Since they did not come, he allowed the punishment to remain—a lesson in temperance, an example of moderation, and a perpetual and evident memorial of divine power.

Such was the miracle of this new Moses. It was not accomplished by striking with a rod, but received its efficacy through the sign of the cross.

Besides the miracle, I greatly admire his gentleness. He did not, like the great Elisha, hand those shameless girls over to savage bears; rather, by using a harmless discipline that involved little disgrace, he taught both piety and moderation.

I have said this not to accuse the prophet of cruelty—for far be such madness from me—but to show that, possessing the same power, Jacob did what was suited to the greatness of Christ and to the New Testament.

Once, seeing a Persian judge deliver an unjust verdict, he cursed a huge stone lying nearby and ordered it to be crushed and scattered.

[Note: [Col. 0115C] He ordered it to be crushed and scattered. In the *Menaea* the Greek reads, “he crushed this,” which our Rader translated, “and struck down the judge,” referring “this” to “judge,” not to “stone.” But since the judge survived and changed his sentence, it is clear from Theodoret that the *Menaea* should be translated, “he crushed that stone,” namely, by a mere curse, as the preceding account states.]

And he reproved the judge’s unjust sentence. When the stone was immediately pulverized into innumerable fragments, those present were terrified. The judge, filled with horror, withdrew his former sentence and pronounced another, just one.

The Greek reads: “When he saw a Persian judge using an unjust verdict, he cursed a very great stone that happened to lie there, and crushed it.”

Here too Jacob imitated his Lord. When Christ wished to show that he willingly and voluntarily underwent his passion, and could easily have punished the wicked had he wished, he did not inflict punishment upon them, but with a word caused a lifeless fig tree to wither and displayed his power (Matthew 21).

Imitating this clemency himself, Jacob did not punish the unjust judge; he taught him justice by means of the stone’s destruction.

When he had become distinguished by these deeds, beloved by all, and the subject of everyone’s conversation, he was drawn into the office of the episcopate and placed over his native city.

[Col. 0017B]

Although he changed his mountainous way of life and entered upon the civil manner of living, he did not do so according to his own inclination. He did not change either his food or his clothing. Only his surroundings were changed; his manner of life underwent no alteration.

His labors increased and became far greater than before. In addition to fasting, a bed spread on the ground, and the sackcloth he wore, there was now the entire care of those in need: he was concerned for widows, provided for orphans, reproved those who committed injustice, and brought just aid to those who suffered it.

Why enumerate everything to those who know what belongs to men who have undertaken this ministry? He embraced such labors with distinction, as one who both greatly loved and greatly feared the Lord of the sheep.

[Col. 0017C]

The more he gathered the riches of virtue, the more abundantly he enjoyed the grace of the most holy Spirit.

Once, while traveling to some village or town—I do not remember the place precisely—certain poor people approached him. They laid before him one of their companions as though he were dead and humbly asked him for what was necessary to bury him.

He granted their request and offered prayers to God as for a dead man, asking that God forgive him the sins he had committed in life and deem him worthy to enter the choir of the righteous.

[Note: [Col. 0115C] He offered prayers to God as for a dead man. I think Theodoret alludes to this story in Book I, chapter 7; Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 14, discusses the raising of the dead.]

[Col. 0115D] Sozomen has a similar trick involving a man who pretended to be dead, in Book VII, chapter 26; Cassiodorus drew on him in Book IX, chapter 48; Nicephorus, Book XII, chapter 46.]

While these things were being said, the soul of the man who had been pretending to die departed. Coverings for the body were supplied.

After the holy man had gone a little farther, those who had contrived the deed ordered the man lying there to rise. When they saw that he did not answer, that what had been pretended had become real, and that the person had changed into a genuine corpse, they went to the great Jacob.

They humbly entreated him, fell at his feet, and said that poverty had been the reason for the deed they had rashly undertaken. They begged him to forgive their offense and restore the soul that had been taken from the man lying there.

Imitating the Lord’s clemency, Jacob heard their prayers and displayed a miracle: having taken away life through prayer, he restored it through prayer to the man lying there.

This seems to me similar to the great miracle of Peter, who handed Ananias and Sapphira over to death after they had stolen and lied (Acts 5). For here too he took away the soul of one who had stolen the truth and practiced deceit.

Peter, however, recognized the theft—for grace had revealed it—and inflicted punishment. Jacob, not knowing the trick, offered prayers and halted the course of life for the man who had pretended to be dead.

The divine Apostle did not rescue the dead from their calamity, for the beginnings of the saving preaching required fear. Jacob, however, being filled with apostolic grace, both punished temporarily and soon remitted the punishment.

That was the work required of one who would win those who had offended.

But we must proceed to other matters and set them forth briefly.

After Arius, the father and author of curses and blasphemies against the Only-Begotten and the most holy Spirit, had raised his tongue against the one who had made him and filled Egypt with tumult and confusion, the greatest emperor Constantine—

[Note: [Col. 0115D] Constantine. See Eusebius’s four books *On the Life* and his *Oration in Praise of Constantine*. Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 55, records that various miracles were performed at Constantine’s tomb. The pagan author Eunapius complains that under Constantine the temples of the gods were turned into monasteries.]

—our own flock’s Zerubbabel—for he led the entire captivity of the devout back from exile, and raised and rebuilt the divine temples that had been cast down to the ground—after he had summoned all the leaders of the churches of that time to Nicaea, the great Jacob also came with the others to fight for the true decrees, as a brave man and commander of the entire phalanx.

At that time Nisibis was subject to the Roman Empire. When that sacred assembly had been dismissed and each man had returned to his own place, Jacob too returned like a brave man who had obtained victory, rejoicing because of the trophies of piety.

When some time had passed, that great and admirable emperor departed this life with the crowns of piety; his sons inherited the empire of the world. Then the king of the Persians, whose name was Sapor, despising the sons because their power was not equal to their father’s, made war against Nisibis with great forces of cavalry and infantry. He also brought a very large number of elephants, and, dividing his army for the siege of the city, surrounded it, constructed siege-engines, and built towers. Planting stakes and obstructing the space between them with branches woven together like hurdles, he ordered the soldiers to raise an embankment and towers opposite the towers of the city. Then, stationing archers there and ordering them to shoot missiles at those who were [Col. 0018D] on the walls—800 in number—he ordered others to dig below and undermine the walls.

But when all his efforts had proved futile and vain, since the prayers of the man of God dissolved them, he finally, relying on the multitude of men, blocked the flow of the river that ran past the city. Having built dams and made barriers for retaining it, he collected a great quantity of the river and discharged it all at once against the fortifications, using it as an exceedingly powerful siege-engine. The walls, however, could not withstand the assault of the water; shaken by its force, they collapsed utterly in that section.

The Persians raised a great shout, since the city now seemed easy to capture. They did not know about the great inner wall of the inhabitants. Nevertheless, they postponed their assault when they saw that the city could not be approached because of the waters. When they had withdrawn some distance, expecting that their labor would soon cease, they rested and tended their horses. But the inhabitants of the city had turned wholeheartedly to supplication, having the great James as their intercessor.

All who were still strong in body rebuilt the wall with the greatest energy they could muster [Col. 0019A] [Note: [Col. 0115D] “They rebuilt.” Theodoret, Book II, chapter 30, and Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 27, maintain that the walls were rebuilt through James’s prayers and exhortation.]—without any concern for beauty or orderly construction, but putting everything together at random: stones, bricks, and whatever each person happened to carry. In a single night the work advanced so far and rose to such a height that it was sufficient both to keep back the horses and to prevent men from climbing it without ladders.

Then they all earnestly begged the man of God to show himself upon the walls and hurl the weapons of his curses [Col. 0019B] against the enemies. He was persuaded to do so, climbed up, and, observing their many thousands, humbly asked God to send against them a cloud of gnats and mosquitoes [Note: [Col. 0115D] “A cloud of gnats and mosquitoes.” In the Menaea, 13 January, the Greek reads: “clouds of gnats and mosquitoes.” Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 28; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, Book II, chapter 30; and below, chapter 21, in the account of another, younger James, where he has “an army of flies and mosquitoes.”].

He spoke, and God sent them, being entreated by him as by Moses. The men were wounded by the divine missiles, while the horses and elephants, breaking their bonds, fled, scattered here and there, unable to endure those stings.

When the impious king saw that his siege-engines had been of no use, that the inundation of water had proved fruitless—for the wall that had fallen had been rebuilt—and that his whole army was both worn down by labor, suffering in the open air, and tormented by the plague sent from heaven; when he also saw the man of God walking upon the walls and concluded that the emperor himself was directing the work [Col. 0019C]—for he seemed to him to be wearing purple and crowned with a diadem—he became angry with those who had deceived him, persuaded him to make war, and told him that the emperor was not present. After condemning them to death, he dismissed the army and returned as quickly as possible to his own royal residence.

In this case also God performed miracles through this Hezekiah, no less than those, and in my view even greater. For what greater miracle could there be than that, although the wall had collapsed, the city was not captured? Besides this, I greatly admire the fact that, when he used curses, he did not ask that flashes and thunderbolts be sent from heaven, as the great Elijah did when the two captains of fifty came to him, each with his fifty men. For he had heard the Lord openly say to James and John, who were attempting to do this very thing: “You do not know of what spirit you are” (Luke 9).

Therefore he did not ask that the earth open up beneath them, nor did he pray that the army be consumed by fire. Instead, he asked that they be wounded by those little creatures, so that, having recognized God’s power, they might at last change and learn piety and the true worship of God.

Such confidence did this man of God possess before God, and such grace did he obtain from heaven. While he was continually engaged in these things and daily increasing in divine matters, he laid down this life with the greatest glory [Note: [Col. 0116A] “He laid down this life.” Laurentius de la Barre is incorrect in asserting here that Theodoret had a stone coffin prepared for this James. He did this for another James the anchorite, as he himself testifies below in the *Philotheus*, chapter 21, as does Nicephorus, Book XV, chapter 22; this can be inferred from the chronology in Nicephorus, although he also calls this later James a Nisibenian. For he says that the former James lived in the time of Constantius, and the later in the time of Leo.], and departed from this world.

After some time had passed, when this town had been handed over by the reigning ruler to the kingdom of Persia, all who lived there came out. They carried the body of their defender and ruler, grieving deeply and sorrowfully that they were being forced to migrate, but singing and celebrating the power of the mighty victor. For if he had been alive, they would certainly not have fallen into the power of the barbarians.

Having related these things about the man of God, I shall proceed to another narrative, asking that I may obtain his blessing.

## CHAPTER II. JULIAN SABAS

[Note: [Col. 0116A] “Julian Sabas.” The Roman Martyrology, 14 January: “In Syria, Saint Julian Sabas the Elder, who, in the time of the emperor Valens, restored the Catholic faith, which had almost collapsed at Antioch, through the power of miracles.” I do not find his commemoration in the Greek Menologion. Concerning him, see Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 19, and Book IV, chapter 25; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 25. Saint Chrysostom celebrates him in an encomium, Homily 21 on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians.]

Julian, whom the inhabitants honorably called by the surname Sabas—while the Greek word *presbytēs*, that is, “elder,” signifies this name—established his monastic hut in a region that was formerly Parthian but is now called Osroene.

This region extends westward as far as the bank of the river called the Euphrates; toward the rising sun, its boundary is the Roman Empire. Assyria borders the Persians; the western limit of the Persian kingdom was later called Adiabene by those who came afterward.

In this country there are many large and populous cities, while much of the region is inhabited and much is uninhabitable and desert. When this man of God reached the farthest parts of this wilderness, he found a cave that was neither made by human hands nor properly or skillfully excavated, but could provide some slight shelter for those who fled to him. He willingly took up residence there, considering it more magnificent than royal dwellings glittering with gold and silver.

There he lived, taking food once a week. His food was barley bread, and that bread contained the bran; his relish was salt; his most delightful drink was water flowing naturally from the earth. He did not measure it according to satiety, but determined its amount beforehand according to need.

His delights and sumptuous, most elegant banquet were the chanting of David’s hymns and continual communion with God. Since he enjoyed these things without ever becoming satiated, he never wished to have his fill of them. Rather, he was always filled and always cried out: “How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118).

Again he heard blessed David say: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified altogether, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 18). Again he heard him say: “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 36). And again: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Psalm 104). And: “Gladden my heart, that it may fear your name.” And: “Taste and see that the Lord is gracious” (Psalm 33). And: “My soul thirsted for the strong and living God” (Psalm 41). And: “My soul clung after you.”

He transferred into himself the love of the one who had spoken these words. For this reason, when the great David sang these things, he taught them so that he might establish many companions and rivals in the love of God. Nor was he disappointed in his hope; he wounded this man of God, and countless others, with divine love.

For this man was so inflamed by the fire of love that he was intoxicated with desire and saw nothing earthly. He dreamed of the beloved alone at night and grasped him in vision by day.

When many had learned this summit of his philosophy—some living nearby, others at a greater distance—the report spread everywhere. They came running, begging to share his training ground and to live thereafter under his direction as under a trainer and athletic instructor.

For birds do not merely hunt while singing and call birds of the same kind to themselves, entangling them in snares; human beings also hunt those of their own nature, some for destruction and others for salvation.

Thus ten were soon gathered, then twice and three times as many. Although they were so numerous, the cave received them all. From the old man they had learned to disregard care for the body, and they too ate like their trainer: barley bread seasoned with salt.

After some time, they also gathered vegetables that grew spontaneously. Then, filling jars and mixing in as much brine as was sufficient, they used this as a relish when they needed nourishment.

But damp dwellings are especially hostile to such vegetables, since by their nature they cause mold and decay in them. When this happened to their relish—for the cave was extremely damp on every side—the companions begged the old man to allow them to build a small hut sufficient to hold the vessels containing the relish.

At first he absolutely refused their request. At last, however, he was persuaded—for he had learned from the great Paul not to seek what was his own [1 Corinthians 13], but to yield something and accommodate himself to the lowly. He granted the hut a short and very small measurement, then went far away from the cave to offer his customary supplications to God.

For he often used to travel fifty stadia into the desert, and sometimes twice that distance, separating himself from all human company and returning to himself, meeting and conversing alone with God, and contemplating that divine and ineffable beauty.

While those who had been deemed worthy to have him care for them had this free time, they built a hut that corresponded to the proper proportion for its use, but was larger than he had ordered.

On the tenth day, like Moses returning from the mountain and from a contemplation that cannot be expressed in words, he saw that the building was larger than he had wished. “I fear, men,” he said, “that while we enlarge our earthly dwellings, we may diminish our heavenly ones. These are temporary and will serve us only briefly, whereas the heavenly dwellings are eternal and can have no end.”

He said this while teaching the community what was more perfect. Nevertheless, when he heard the apostolic declaration, “I do not seek what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10), he tolerated the building.

He also taught them to offer common hymnody to God inside the cave, and after dawn to go out into the desert in pairs. One of them was to kneel and offer the worship due to the Lord, while the other, standing, sang fifteen Psalms of David. [Col. 0022A] Then they were to exchange their tasks: one rising to sing, the other prostrating himself on the ground to worship. They did this continually from morning until dusk.

Before sunset, they rested briefly in the cave—some on one side, others on the other—and then all gathered into the cave from every direction and offered the evening hymns to the Lord together. The old man himself also used to choose one of the more distinguished members as his companion in the service.

A certain man more frequently followed him, Persian by birth, large and admirable in bodily stature, but possessing a soul still more admirable in appearance. His name was James [Note: [Col. 0116B] “James the Persian.” A monk in Syria who lived 104 years, as stated here, distinct from James the Persian surnamed “the Cut,” who was a martyr and is commemorated in the Menologion on 27 November.].

He too shone afterward in every virtue, not only in the philosophical training grounds or monasteries that were there, but also in those throughout Syria, in which he ended his life after, as is reported, living 104 years.

As the great old man’s companion on the road to the desert, he followed at a distance. The teacher did not allow him to come nearer, lest the opportunity for conversation arise; conversation would draw his mind away from contemplation of God.

While following, he saw an enormous dragon on the road. When he observed it, he did not dare proceed. Although he often wished to avoid it out of fear, he again strengthened his courage. Then, bending down, he picked up a stone and threw it. He saw that the dragon remained in the same position and was entirely unable to move.

When he realized that it was dead, he thought that the old man had accomplished the death of the beast. When the journey was completed and the office of hymns had been finished, the time for rest arrived. The old man sat down and ordered James also to give his body a little rest. At first James sat silently, but when the old man gently began a conversation with a slight smile, James asked him to explain what he did not know.

When the old man allowed him to ask, James said: “On the road I saw an enormous dragon lying there. At first I was afraid, thinking that it was alive; but when I saw it was dead, I proceeded on my way without fear. Tell me, father, who killed it? You were going ahead, and no one else passed this way.”

The old man replied: “Stop inquisitively asking about matters that can bring no benefit to those who inquire about them.”

Nevertheless, the admirable James persisted, desiring to know the truth. The old man tried for a long time to conceal it, but could not bear to distress his friend any longer.

“I will tell you,” he said, “if you desire to know it. But I command you that, while I am alive, no one else learn from you what I am about to say. Such things must be concealed, since they often provoke arrogance and pride. But if I depart from this life and am freed from disturbances of that kind, I do not forbid you to speak and proclaim the power of divine grace.

“Know, then,” said the great Julian, “that as I was traveling along the road, the beast attacked me and opened its mouth, wishing to devour me. But when I called upon Jesus and showed the trophy of the cross with my finger, I shook off all fear. Immediately I saw the beast fall to the ground. After praising our common Savior, I continued onward.”

When he had finished the story, he went to the cave.

On one occasion a young man, born of noble family but brought up delicately, and displaying greater readiness and eagerness of spirit than his strength could bear, humbly asked the old man to allow him to accompany him on a journey into the desert—not the journey that everyone made daily, but a very long one, during which they often had to travel for eighteen days.

This was the famous Asterius. When the man of God tried to prevent the young man from coming, saying that the desert was dry and without water, the youth persisted, begging him to grant him this favor.

Overcome by his pleas, the old man yielded. The youth followed, at first cheerfully. But when the first, second, and third days had passed, and he was scorched by the sun’s rays—for it was summer, and in the height of summer the sun’s heat is naturally more intense—he suffered continually from thirst.

At first he was ashamed to reveal his condition, remembering what his teacher had foretold. At last, overcome and completely exhausted, he begged the old man to have pity on him.

The old man recalled what he had predicted and ordered him to turn back. The youth replied that he did not know the road leading to the cave and, even if he did know it, could not travel it because his strength had been consumed by thirst.

The man of God pitied the youth’s plight and forgave the weakness of his body. Kneeling, he prayed to the Lord and watered the ground with hot tears [Col. 0023C], asking for the road of salvation for the youth.

He who fulfills the desire of those who fear him and hears their prayer turned the drops of tears that had touched the dust into a spring of water. Having filled the youth with its flowing stream, he ordered him to depart at once.

The spring remained until the present day, bearing witness to the divine old man’s Mosaic prayer. For just as Moses once struck that barren rock with his staff and caused it to produce overflowing river waters to satisfy the thirst of those many thousands of people, so this man, having watered that driest sand with his tears, caused fountain streams to flow—not to relieve the thirst of many myriads, but to provide relief for one youth.

Illuminated in soul by divine grace, he clearly foresaw the youth’s future perfection. For many years later, moved by divine grace to train many others also in that same grace, he established a monastic training ground in the region around Gendarum [Alternative reading: Gidarum]—a very large village under Antioch—and drew many other athletes of philosophy to himself.

He also attracted the great Acacius [Note: [Col. 0116B] “The great Acacius as well.” As stated here, he was bishop of Beroea. Theodoret calls him a vigorous athlete of virtue, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 25; see also Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 25, and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 25, and Book XII, chapter 47.], that distinguished and renowned man. He was outstanding in monastic life and sent forth brilliant rays of virtue, so that he was deemed worthy to become a bishop and was assigned to shepherd Beroea.

After the care of the flock had been entrusted to him for fifty-eight years, he did not abandon the pattern of monastic life. Rather, he blended monastic and civic virtue together, taking from the former its exact perfection and from the latter its administration and stewardship, and bringing together what had been separated.

But the hunter and cultivator of this virtue was that Asterius, who was always held by so great a love for the great old man that he often traveled to him twice a year, and sometimes three times.

When he came, he used to bring figs for the companions, loading three or four beasts. Gathering two *medimni* [Note: [Col. 0116B] A *medimnus* is a kind of measure for dry goods. See the *Onomasticon*.]—enough, as he believed, to supply the old man for the whole year—he placed the burden on his own shoulders, calling himself and showing himself to be his teacher’s beast of burden.

He carried that load not for ten or twenty stadia, but over a journey of seven days.

Once, when the old man saw him carrying a load of figs on his shoulders, he was distressed and said that such provisions ought not to be brought for him. It was not right, he said, for the one man to undergo so much labor while the other delicately enjoyed the fruits of his sweat.

But when Asterius swore that he would not take the burden from his shoulders unless the old man consented to share the food that had been brought, the old man said: “I will do as you command, provided that you put down the basket as quickly as possible.”

In this too he imitated the chief of the apostles. When the Lord wished to wash his feet, Peter first refused, openly declaring that this would never happen (John 13). But after he heard that he would be cut off from communion with the Lord unless he permitted it, he asked that not only his feet but also his hands and head be washed.

So also the excellent John, when commanded to baptize the Savior, first confessed his own servitude and acknowledged the Lord. Later, he carried out the command, not behaving harshly but obeying the Lord.

In the same way this man of God was troubled that he should enjoy food while another labored; but when he saw the ardent eagerness of his devoted servant, he placed the latter’s service before his own preference.

Perhaps someone who takes great pleasure in criticizing others, and has learned only to mock what is honorable, might say that this story is not worthy of being recorded.

I have added it, however, to the other miracles of this man, wishing not only to show the piety of great men toward him, but also to make clear the gentleness and moderation of his character, believing this to be useful.

For although he possessed such great and remarkable virtue, he did not consider himself worthy of even the slightest honor. He rejected it as something that did not belong to him at all, yet again accepted it in order to benefit those who conferred it.

Fleeing—for he had become known to all and drew to himself, through the reputation of his good and honorable deeds, those who loved them—he came with a few of his close companions to Mount Sinai. He did not enter a town or village, but set out through an inaccessible wilderness.

He also carried on his shoulders the necessary provisions: bread and salt, a flask and a wooden cup, and a sponge tied to a cord, so that whenever they found deeper water, they could draw it up with the sponge, squeeze it into the cup, and drink it.

When they had completed a journey of many days, they reached the desired mountain. After worshiping their Lord, they remained there for a long time, considering the solitude of the place and the greatest quiet of the soul to be supreme delight.

When he had built a church upon that rock beneath which Moses, the chief of the prophets, lay hidden and was deemed worthy to see God as far as he could be seen, and had consecrated a divine altar—which has remained until the present day—he returned to his training ground.

When he learned of the threats of the one who bore the same name as himself but was an impious emperor—for the emperor had departed against the Persians, threatening to destroy the pious completely, while those who shared his views eagerly awaited the abominable man’s return—he offered prayer to God with great devotion and ardent longing. He continued it until the tenth day, when he heard a voice saying [Note: [Col. 0116B] “He heard a voice saying.” The death of Julian the Apostate was divinely announced to Didymus and to Julian Sabas; Nicephorus, Book X, chapter 35.] that the accursed and foul pig had been removed from the midst of men.

Yet, although he had reached the end of his prayer, he did not immediately bring the prayer to an end. Instead, he changed his petition into the chanting of a hymn, giving thanks to the Savior of his own people and to the merciful and powerful punisher of the enemies of others.

For a very long time God had been merciful and patient with the impious man. But when his mercy and patience had provoked the criminal to greater madness, he inflicted punishment at the proper time.

When he had completed the prayer and turned back to his companions, it was clear that he was joyful and peaceful in spirit; the liveliness of his soul showed itself in his cheerful face.

Those who lived with him were amazed at the unusual sight—for although he always appeared sad, he now seemed to be smiling—and when they asked the cause of his joy, he said:

“The present moment, brothers, is one of rejoicing. For the impious man has ceased to be, as Isaiah says (Isaiah 24), and has suffered the punishment deserved by his audacious enterprises. He who exercised tyranny against the God who made and preserved him has rightly been struck down by the hand of the one who ruled under his authority.

“Therefore I rejoice when I see the Churches that he attacked exulting, and when I perceive that the criminal obtained no assistance from the demons whom he worshiped.”

Such foreknowledge did he possess of the death of this impious man.

When Valens [Note: [Col. 0116C] “859 Valens.” Concerning his persecution against the Church, see Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 22, and others.]—who took up the reins of the Roman Empire after him—had abandoned the truth of the evangelical doctrines and adopted the deception of Arius’s error, a greater storm then arose against the Church. The governors were expelled from every side, while certain plunderers and enemies were appointed in their place.

But so as not to recount the entire tragedy at present, I shall pass over the rest and mention only one incident, which clearly shows the grace of the divine Spirit flourishing in this old man.

The great Meletius had been expelled from the church of Antioch, which had been entrusted to him by the God of all to shepherd. Those who had been enrolled in the clergy and worshiped the one divine essence of the Trinity had also been expelled from the divine temples, together with the people who shared their faith.

Now they would gather in some cave on the mountain and celebrate sacred assemblies there; now they would make an oratory on the bank of a river; sometimes they would use as a place of worship the military training ground situated before the northern gate. Those conducting the war did not allow the pious to remain in one place.

The fosterlings of falsehood had spread a rumor throughout the city that this great old man embraced communion with the religious doctrines they themselves held. This particularly distressed the pious, lest the rumor deceive the less educated and simpler people and entangle them in the snares of the heretics.

The divine and blessed men Flavian and Diodorus, who had been deemed worthy to serve as priests and preside over the pious people, together with Aphraates [Note: [Col. 0115D] Concerning Aphraates, see below, chapter 8.]—whose life, if God permits, I shall add separately for you—persuaded the great Acacius, whom we have mentioned, to take as his companion on the journey his own teacher and the holy old man’s disciple, the distinguished Asterius.

They urged him to hasten to the common glory of piety and the support of evangelical teaching, and to persuade the old man to abandon his manner of living in the wilderness, come to their aid, and extinguish with the dew of his arrival the Arian flame that was destroying so many thousands through deception.

The divine Acacius hastened forth and, taking with him the great Asterius as he had been ordered [Note: [Col. 0116C] “Asterius.” The printed editions read “Acacius,” incorrectly. I have restored “Asterius” according to the sense. Longus does the same.], approached the great light of the Church.

After greeting him, he said: “Tell me, father, why do you so willingly endure all this labor?”

When the old man replied, “In body, soul, life, and everything that belongs to life, the worship of God is more precious to me. I strive, insofar as I am able, to offer him a service stripped of defilement and to please him continually,” Acacius said:

“I will show you a way by which you will serve him more than you do now. I shall say this not relying merely on reasoning, but as one who has learned it from his teaching.

“When the Lord once asked Peter whether he loved him more than the others, and learned what he already knew even before Peter’s answer—‘You know, Lord, that I love you’ (John 21)—he showed him how he might honor him more.

“‘If you love me,’ he said, ‘feed my sheep and feed my lambs.’

“You too, father, must do this. There is a danger that the sheep may perish among wolves; and the one who is greatly loved by you loves them greatly. It is characteristic of those who love to do the things that, when done, are pleasing to those they love.

“Besides, there is no small danger, and the loss of many great labors, if you are able to neglect and silently pass over the grave assault upon the truth, while those who adhere to it are being hunted. Your name is being used as bait to hunt them.

“For the governors of the abomination of Arius boast and proclaim that you are their partner in impiety.”

When the old man first heard this, he ordered solitude to take leave for a time. He did not shrink from the noise of the city, to which he was unaccustomed, but hurried to Antioch.

After traveling for two or three days through the wilderness, he came by night to a certain estate. A wealthy little woman, hearing that the sacred company was approaching, ran out to receive their blessing. Falling at their feet, she begged them to make her house their lodging.

The old man consented, although he had been separated from such a spectacle for more than forty years.

While that admirable woman was occupied in serving the holy men, her seven-year-old boy—the woman’s only child, and she herself an imitator of Sarah’s hospitality—fell into a well. It was evening and darkness had come.

When, as was natural, an uproar arose, the mother realized what had happened. She ordered everyone to remain quiet, placed a cover over the well, and continued her service.

When the table had been set for the men of God, the holy old man ordered the woman’s child to be summoned and receive his blessing.

The admirable woman said that he was unwell, but the old man persisted in ordering that he be brought.

After the woman told him what had happened, the old man left the table and hurried to the well. He ordered the cover removed and a light brought. He saw the boy sitting upon the surface of the water, striking it with his childish hand and, though counted among the dead, treating the event as a game.

They tied some ropes together and lowered them into the well; then they brought the boy out. The child immediately ran to the old man’s feet and said that he had seen the old man himself carrying him in the water and preventing him from drowning.

Such was the reward that the woman received from the blessed old man for her hospitality.

To pass over the other events that occurred on the journey, they arrived at Antioch. Everyone flocked together from all sides, eager to see the man of God, and each person wishing to receive healing for his illness.

He lived in the caves on the side of the mountain where, they say, the divine apostle Paul had also lived and hidden.

As soon as everyone learned that he was there, however, he was seized by a most severe fever. When the great Acacius saw the multitude gathered together and was distressed by the illness that had occurred—for he thought that those who had assembled would be disturbed if they learned that the man from whose hand they hoped to obtain healing was ill—the old man said:

“Do not be troubled in spirit. If health is necessary, the Lord will grant it immediately.”

At once, therefore, after these words, he turned to prayer. As was his custom, he pressed both his knees and his forehead to the ground and asked to obtain healing, if healing would bring some benefit to those who had assembled.

He had not yet finished praying when suddenly a great sweat poured forth and extinguished the fever’s flame.

After he had healed many people there from illnesses of every kind, he went to the assembly of the pious.

As he passed through the gates of the royal palace, a beggar who used his buttocks as feet and dragged himself along the ground stretched out his hand and touched the old man’s cloak. By faith he drove away his illness, then leaped up and showed that he could run as well as before his illness, doing the same thing as the lame man whom Peter and John raised up (Acts 3).

When this had happened, the whole population of the city streamed together, and the military training ground was filled with those who came running. The slanderers and fabricators of falsehood were covered with shame, while the fosterlings of truth were joyful and tranquil in spirit.

From that point onward, those who needed healing carried the light of truth into their homes.

A certain man who had been entrusted with the highest magistracy, and to whose care the key of the East had been committed, sent to him, asking him to come and free him from the illness that was afflicting him.

The old man came without hesitation. After pouring out prayers to the common Lord, he dissolved the illness by his word and ordered the man to give thanks to God.

When he had done these and similar things, he decided thereafter to return to the hut of his monastic discipline. As he was traveling through Cyrus [Al.: Gyrrhus, or Cyrrhus] [Col. 0028B] (this city is a two days’ journey from Antioch), he turned aside to the church of the illustrious martyr Dionysius. Those who presided there over the worship of the true God and orthodox religion gathered together and begged him to bring aid to them as they awaited the impending destruction. For they said that Asterius, who had been trained in sophistry [Note: [Col. 0116C] Asterius, who was trained in sophistry.] [Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 53, mentions Asterius the Sophist.] and the false art of argument, had thrust himself into the church of the heretics and attained episcopal office; that he was vigorously defending falsehood and employing unscrupulous artifices against the truth; and, they said, “We fear that, by concealing falsehood beneath eloquence as beneath some bait, and spreading out the connections of syllogisms like nets, he may capture many of the simpler people. For this reason he was summoned by his opponents.”

The old man replied: “Be of good courage, and pray to God with us [Col. 0028C], joining bodily affliction to your prayers.” While they were thus entreating God, one day before the festival and solemn occasion on which the defender of falsehood and enemy of truth was to speak, that man received a blow inflicted by God; and after being sick for only one day, he departed this life, hearing, as is likely, that saying: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you” (Luke XII). “But the nets and snares that you have prepared—you yourself will be caught in them, and not others.”

The same thing also happened to Balaam, who likewise had been summoned against the people of God. When he had given Balaak certain impious counsels against them, he paid the penalty, being struck down by the Israelite hand (Numbers XXIV). So this man too, having devised certain cunning plans against the people of God, was deprived of life by God through the people [Col. 0028D]. Thus Cyrus also obtained deliverance through this man’s prayer.

The account I have related was handed down to me by that divine head, the great Acacius, who knew accurately everything that had been done by him. After he had departed from there, returned to his companions, and spent a considerable time with them, he passed very readily and eagerly into a life free from old age and suffering, having practiced insensibility to suffering in mortal nature and awaiting the immortality of the body. Here I shall bring my discourse about him to a close and pass to another, asking the saints who enter into this narrative to secure for me, through their intercession, heavenly favor.

## CHAPTER III. MARCIANUS

[Note: [Col. 0116C] Marcianus.] Roman Martyrology, 2 November: “At Cyrus in Syria, Saint Marcianus the confessor.” Greek Menologion, on the same day: “Our holy Father Marcianus, from the city of Cyrus, a man distinguished for piety, who admirably lived the monastic life.” Menaea, on the same day and on 18 January. Concerning him, Theodoretus, book IV of the *History*, chapter 26; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 41.]

[Col. 0029A]

How shall we admire the celebrated Marcianus of old in a manner worthy of his excellence (Theodoretus, book IV of the *History*, chapter 26)? Should we not join him with Elijah, John, and others like them, who wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, tormented—men of whom the world was not worthy (Hebrews XI)—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the earth?

In former times he had Cyrus as his homeland, of which we have previously spoken; afterward, the desert; but, having left both that place and the other, he now has heaven. The first gave him birth, the second nourished him and made him victorious, while heaven received him crowned, [Col. 0029B] after he had despised the splendor of his lineage. For he traced his descent from patricians and royal magnificence. In that sphere he flourished, possessing bodily beauty and stature received from the craftsman of nature, and a mind adorned with intellectual sharpness. But he transferred all his love to God and the things belonging to God. Bidding farewell to everything else, he occupied the center of the desert. After constructing a small hut—one whose proportions scarcely corresponded even to his body—and surrounding it with another small enclosure, he remained shut up there continually, separated from all human society, conversing with the Lord of all and hearing that sweet voice. For, as he occupied himself with the divine utterances, he thought that he enjoyed the divine voice. While praying and offering supplications, he himself spoke with the Lord; and although he continually enjoyed such delights, he was never satisfied.

For he heard the divine Spirit singing through the great David [Col. 0029C]: “He who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall” (Psalm I). Desiring these fruits, he embraced this most delightful labor. Prayer was followed by psalmody, psalmody by prayer, and both again by reading the divine utterances.

His only food was bread, and even that was supplied in a fixed measure. The measure was such that it would not have been enough even for a recently weaned child. They say that one pound of bread was divided into four portions, distributed over four days, one portion being assigned to each day. [Col. 0029D] For he had decided to eat every evening, never to be satisfied, but always to remain hungry and always thirsty, giving the body only what was sufficient for life. He said that anyone who takes food after fasting for many days performs the offices of the Lord more weakly during the days of fasting. But on the day when he again takes food, naturally taking in more, he burdens the stomach; and when it is burdened, it makes the soul slower for keeping vigil. He therefore said that it was better to eat every day but never to await satiety. True fasting is perpetual want.

That divine man observed this rule almost continually. Although his body was both very large [Col. 0030A] and, among all the men of his time, the largest and most handsome, he nourished it with this small amount of food. After some time had passed, he admitted two companions: Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0029D] Concerning Eusebius, below, chapter 4.] who became heir to that sacred hut, and Agapetus [Note: [Col. 0116C] Agapetus.] who, on account of his merits, became bishop of the Apameans; Theodoretus, book V of the *History*, chapter 27], who carried these rules to Apamea.

There is a very large and populous village called Nicerte. In it he constructed [Col. 0030B] two great schools of ascetic discipline. One was named after him, while the other was named after the admirable Simeon, who shone for fifty years in this discipline. To this day more than four hundred men live in them: athletes of virtue, lovers of religion and of the worship of the true God, purchasing heaven through their labors. The legislators of this community were Agapetus and the Simeons, who received their rules from the great Marcianus. It would be difficult to count the many habitations of ascetics planted by these men, all governed by the same rules and institutions. Yet the planter of all these was that divine man; for whoever provided the most excellent seed may rightly be called the author of the good things that grow from it.

At first, as I said, he alone occupied that voluntary prison. Then, after admitting two companions, they did not live in the same house as he did; indeed, the hut was not sufficient even for him, being very small and causing him great difficulty both when he stood and when he reclined. When standing, he could not stand upright, since the roof touched his head and neck; when reclining, [Col. 0030C] he could not stretch out his feet, since the house was not as long as his body.

When he permitted them to build another dwelling, he ordered them to live in it and to sing hymns, pray, and read the divine utterances on their own. When it became necessary for more people to share in this benefit, he ordered another dwelling to be built at a distance, and commanded those who wished to do so to live there. Their leader was Eusebius, who transmitted the teaching of the great Marcianus.

That divine Agapetus, properly instructed and trained, and thoroughly educated in this athletic art, returned, as I said, and sowed the seeds that he had received from that divine soul. He became so renowned and illustrious that he was judged worthy of an episcopal see; pastoral care was entrusted to him, and the care of his homeland was committed to his faith [Col. 0030D]. The admirable Eusebius, meanwhile, had been appointed overseer of the gathered flock and had assumed the care of his master. He alone was considered worthy to visit him from time to time and ask whether he wanted anything.

Once, wishing to see at night what he was doing, he dared to approach the window—it was extremely small—and, bending down to look through it, saw a light, not from a lamp or anything made by human hands, but given by God. It shone around the head of his teacher by heavenly grace and revealed the meaning of the divine utterances in Scripture. Marcianus was holding a book and searching out the most sacred treasure of the divine will. When the admirable Eusebius had witnessed this, he was seized by great fear and trembling. He learned the grace spread abroad upon the servant of God and understood God’s benevolence toward his servants.

[Col. 0031A]

On one occasion, while Marcianus was praying in the vestibule, a dragon that had crawled over the wall facing east looked down from above the wall. It was hissing, gazing terribly, and indicating that it was about to attack. Eusebius, standing at a distance, was terrified by the dreadful spectacle and suspected that his teacher was unaware of it. He pointed it out to him, shouting and urging him to flee.

Marcianus rebuked him and ordered him to drive away his fear—for fear too is a deadly vice. First, with his finger, he traced the sign of the cross; then he blew upon the creature with his mouth and displayed the ancient enmity. Dried up by the breath of his mouth as though by fire, and as if cut to pieces, the dragon was dissolved into many parts like burned straw [Col. 0031B]. See, then, whether he imitated the Lord as a gracious servant. For when the sea once raged against the disciples’ boat, and he saw them anxious and troubled, the Lord did not calm the storm of the sea until, by rebuking the disciples, he had restrained their unbelief (Matthew VIII). Thus this admirable man first expelled the disciple’s fear and then punished the beast.

Such were the wisdom, miraculous power, and trust in God of the great Marcianus. Yet although he was judged worthy of such great grace and could perform great miracles, he nevertheless strove to conceal his virtue, suspecting the devices of the robber of virtue. For the vice of arrogance plants its seed beneath one’s labors and attempts to snatch away the fruits gathered through toil [Col. 0031C]. Although he wished to conceal the grace given to him, he came unwillingly to perform miracles whenever the radiance of his righteous deeds shone forth and revealed the virtue that was being hidden.

Indeed, something of this kind once happened. A man of honorable birth, who had often been entrusted with military commands, was traveling from the Syrian city of Berhoea. His daughter had long been raging and, tormented by an evil demon, was insane. He came into the desert, being an acquaintance of the great Marcianus and hoping, on account of their former association, to meet him and make his request. But disappointed in his hope, since he was not permitted to see the servant of God, he asked an old man, who at that time had been entrusted with the service of the divine man, to take a small flask filled with oil and place it at the door of the hut [Col. 0031D].

The old man repeatedly refused to do this, but, repeatedly asked again, he was overcome by the entreaties. When the great Marcianus perceived the noise, he asked who it was and for what purpose he had come. The man concealed the true reason but pretended that he had come to learn whether Marcianus wanted anything. Saying this, he was dismissed [Col. 0032A].

Toward dawn, the girl’s father again asked that the flask be returned to him. Though afraid, the old man went with as much silence as he could manage. He reached out his hand, received the flask, and wished to leave. Marcianus again asked what he wanted and why he had come. When he gave the same reason that he had offered in the evening, the man of God was displeased, since his visit had been contrary to the usual custom, and ordered him to speak the truth. The man, afraid and trembling, since he could not hide anything from one who was full of God’s grace, told him who the suppliant was, described the tragedy of the girl’s illness, and showed him the flask.

Marcianus became angry, as was natural, because he did not wish to display his power. Nevertheless, threatening that if he dared to do such a thing again he would be deprived both of this association and of his service—for those who knew how to profit from it would suffer a very great loss—he relented and ordered him to return the flask to the person who had given it.
