Marcianus gave these orders, but the demon, although four days’ journey away, cried out about the power of the one who was driving him out. Marcianus acted as judge at Berhoea, employing certain executioners against the demon, expelling the wicked creature, and restoring the girl cleansed from her affliction [Col. 0032B].

The girl’s father learned this precisely. When he was returning and was only a few stadia from the city, a servant sent by his mistress into the countryside met him. Seeing his master, the servant announced the miracle, saying that it had occurred four days earlier. By counting the days and carefully examining the time, the father learned that it had occurred at the very time when the old man had brought the flask.

I am led to wonder what that great man would have done if he had wished to perform miracles. If, while striving to conceal the power he had received, he displayed such brilliance, what miracle would he not have performed had he wished to do so?

In the same way he did not display his spiritual wisdom to everyone [Col. 0032C]. Thus, when at last, after the feast of the saving Passion and the Lord’s resurrection, he permitted those who wished to do so to enter to him, everyone was eager to see him at that particular time. The leading bishops came to him: the great Flavianus, to whose care the feeding of Antioch had been entrusted; the divine Acacius, whom we previously mentioned; Eusebius, bishop of Chalcis; and Isidorus, who at that time had been entrusted with governing Cyrus. All were distinguished for virtue.

With them was also Theodotus, who held the reins of the church of the Hierapolitans, renowned for monastic discipline and gentleness. Some magistrates were also present, inflamed by the ardor of faith.

When all were sitting in silence and awaiting that sacred voice [Col. 0032D], Marcianus himself also sat silent for a long time, his tongue inactive but his ears attentive. Then one of those seated, who was familiar with him because of his care for the soul and otherwise distinguished in authority and dignity, said:

“All these divine Fathers, O Father, thirstingly await the sweetest streams of your teaching. Therefore grant all those present some benefit, and do not close the channels of your benevolence.”

He, after groaning deeply, replied:

“God, the Lord of all, speaks daily through the creatures and, through the divine Scriptures, teaches and admonishes us concerning what we ought to do and introduces what is beneficial. He terrifies us with threats and encourages us with promises. Yet we derive no benefit from any of these things. How, then, could Marcianus benefit others by speaking, when he himself loses so great a benefit and refuses to derive advantage from these things?” [Col. 0033A]

As a result, the Fathers engaged in many discussions, which I have judged it superfluous to insert into this narrative. When they had risen and prayed, and wished to lay hands upon him in order to confer the priesthood, they again hesitated to place their hands upon him. Each ordered the other to do it, and when all alike refused, they returned.

Nevertheless, I wish to add another account, through which his divine prudence may be recognized.

### Avitus

[Note: [Col. 0116C] Avitus.] Concerning him, Suidas should be consulted: Ἄβιτος, ὄνομα κύριον. Ἄβιτος τὴν ἀσκητικὴν καλύβην ἐπήξατο. “Avitus, a proper name. Avitus was the first to construct a hut suitable for practicing ascetic discipline, so that he might exercise himself while living a solitary life.” This was certainly taken from this passage of Theodoretus. In Suidas, πρῶτοι (“first”) seems to be missing before τὴν. For so Theodoretus reads.]

A certain Avitus had been the first to establish a hut in the desert for the sake of monastic discipline. His dwelling lay farther toward the north than this one and somewhat toward the east; it faced the north wind, Aparctias [Col. 0033B], which is close to the east wind, Subsolanus. He was older than the great Marcianus both in time and in ascetic labor, a philosophical man trained in a hard and austere life.

When he heard everywhere of the virtue of this man, he considered such a spectacle more useful than silence and quiet. He hastened, eager to see the man he desired to meet. When the great Marcianus learned of his arrival, he opened the door and admitted him.

He ordered the admirable Eusebius to cook legumes and greens, if he had any. When the two men had satisfied their mutual desire to converse and had learned one another’s virtue, they performed the office of the ninth hour together. Eusebius then came carrying the table and bringing bread [Col. 0033C].

The great Marcianus said to the divine Avitus:

“Come, my dearest friend of all, and let us share this meal together.”

Avitus replied:

“I do not know that I have ever eaten before evening. Often I remain fasting for two or three days at a time.”

The great Marcianus said:

“Then let the custom be changed today for my sake” [Note: [Col. 0116D] “Let the custom be changed today for my sake.” Daily fasts undertaken from devotion of mind may rightly be interrupted by the arrival of guests. Cassianus, book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 24, and *Conferences* II, chapter 26.]: “for, since my body is weak, I cannot wait until evening.”

When these words failed to persuade the admirable Avitus, Marcianus is said to have groaned and said:

“But I am distressed in spirit and deeply tormented because you have undertaken so great a labor to see a hardworking and philosophical man, yet, deceived in your hope, you have seen some innkeeper living extravagantly and luxuriously.”

Avitus was troubled by these words and said that he would rather eat meat than hear such things. The great Marcianus replied:

“We too, my friend, pursue the same life as you [Col. 0033D], embrace the same manner of living, and prefer labors to ease. We desire fasting more than food and take food only as night approaches. But we know that love is superior to fasting. The work of love is commanded by the divine law, whereas fasting lies within our power and choice. We must consider the divine laws far superior to our own.”

After they had discussed these matters with one another, eaten a little food, praised God, and spent three days together, they again separated, seeing one another in spirit. Who, then, would not admire this man’s wisdom? Guided by it, he knew the time for fasting, but he also knew the time for brotherly love [Col. 0034A]. He knew the distinction among the parts of virtue, what should yield to what, and to which virtue victory should be granted at the proper time.

I can also relate another event through which his perfection in divine matters may be recognized. His sister came to him from his homeland with her son, who was a grown man and easily one of the leading citizens of Cyrus, bringing in abundance whatever he thought would be useful to him. Marcianus did not permit himself to see his sister, but he admitted her son, since the appointed time had arrived when he could meet with him.

When they urged him to accept the things that had been brought, he said:

“Through how many monasteries have you passed, and to how many of them have you distributed some of these things?”

When the young man replied that he had given nothing to anyone, Marcianus said:

“Go away with what you have brought. We have no need of any of these things; and even if we did need them, we would not accept them. You are exercising this benevolence toward us because you care for natural kinship, not for divine piety and service [Col. 0034B]. If you did not honor mere kinship of blood, you would not have distributed what you brought to us alone.”

Saying this, he dismissed his sister’s son together with his sister and ordered that nothing of what they had brought should be accepted.

Thus he was beyond nature and had migrated to a heavenly manner of life. For what other example could be offered more clearly worthy of God and in agreement with God’s own voice? “Whoever does not leave father and mother, brothers and sisters, wife and children, is not worthy of me” (Matthew X). If the one who does not leave them is unworthy, then it is clear that the one who leaves them and practices such exact and complete perfection was supremely worthy.

Beyond these things, I also admire his complete perfection concerning divine decrees [Col. 0034C]. He recoiled from the madness of Arius [Note: [Col. 0116D] Arius, etc.] Epiphanius discusses the heresies of this period in the *Panarion*]. He also abhorred the insanity of Apollinaris. He fought vigorously and energetically against those who agreed with Sabellius and forced the three hypostases, or persons, into one. He strongly detested those called Euchites, who, under monastic dress, suffered from the disease of the Manichaeans.

His zeal for ecclesiastical decrees burned so fiercely that he even undertook a righteous struggle against an admirable and divine man. There was a certain elder named Abraames in that desert, a man gray-haired but even grayer in prudence, distinguished in every virtue and continually pouring forth abundant tears of compunction. At first, led by a certain simplicity, he had persisted in celebrating the first Pascha [Col. 0034D] [Note: [Col. 0116D] “Had persisted in celebrating the first Pascha.” Concerning the ancient variation in the manner of observing Easter and Lent, Nicephorus, book XII, chapters 33 and 34.], evidently unaware of what the Fathers at Nicaea had decreed concerning it, and preferring to serve the ancient custom. Many others at that time suffered from the same ignorance.

But the great Marcianus, often using many words, attempted to persuade the elder Abraames—for that was what those living in that region called him—to agree with the Church. When he saw that Abraames would not comply, he openly ceased to communicate with him.

As time passed, however, that divine man too, having cast off the stain, embraced the Church’s agreement concerning the celebration of the feast and truly sang in psalmody:

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Psalm CXVIII).

This was brought about by the teaching of the great Marcianus.

Many people everywhere were building oratories for him [Col. 0035A]: in Cyrus, Alypius, the son of his sister; and in Chalcis, a certain Zenobia, distinguished both by birth and virtue and possessing great wealth. Many others did the same, striving, after victory had been won, to carry off that illustrious athlete.

When the man of God learned of this, he asked the admirable Eusebius—offering him an oath full of every terror—to bury his body in that place, so that no one should recognize the tomb except the two who lived with him most closely, until many years had passed. That admirable man fulfilled the oath.

For after the end of that illustrious victor had come [Col. 0035B], and the choir of angels had carried that sacred and divine soul to the heavenly dwellings, Eusebius did not announce his death until, with the two closest companions, he had dug a grave, deposited the body, and leveled the surface of the earth. Even after fifty years or more had passed, when innumerable people had gathered and searched for the body, the tomb remained unknown.

Later, when one of the aforementioned oratories received the relics of apostles and another those of martyrs, the heirs of that tabernacle and teaching, now secure, had a stone coffin constructed two years earlier and placed the relics of the precious body in it, once one of them had revealed the tomb—for he alone of the three was still alive.

The admirable Eusebius, who had imitated his virtue [Col. 0035C], continually afflicted his body for a long time. For while he had one hundred and twenty pounds of iron placed upon his body, he also imposed upon himself another fifty belonging to the divine Agapetus; he added another eighty belonging to the great Marcianus. He had an oratory and a certain basin in which no water remained. He spent three uninterrupted years living in this manner.

I have digressed to relate these matters because I wished to show how many and how great were the accomplishments of Marcianus, performed rightly and virtuously, and how he was their author and overseer.

The admirable Basil also received the fruit of this discipline. Much later, at Seleucobelus—which is a city of Syria—he constructed a monastic dwelling. He was distinguished in many kinds of virtue, but especially [Col. 0035D] in that possession most pleasing to God, love, and in the divine work of hospitality.

Who could easily count how many laborers for God he too produced, handling the word of truth without shame, as the Apostle says? To pass over others for the present—men worthy of praise, but who would make the narrative too long—I shall mention one man alone.

There was someone who repeatedly visited him, called Sabinus, who consumed his body in innumerable labors. He took no part either in bread or in any prepared dish; his food was flour moistened with water. He was accustomed to mix together the entire month’s supply of food, so that it would become stale and emit a foul odor [Col. 0036A]. By this kind of nourishment he wished to dull the appetites of his body and cause the pleasure of food to wither through the stench of the nourishment.

Although he lived in this way by himself, if one of his companions approached him, he ate simply and without discrimination whatever was set before him. He had received such great grace from God that a certain Antiochene woman—whose lineage and enormous wealth made her proud—ran to him and begged him to aid her daughter, who was tormented by a demon.

“For in a dream,” she said, “I saw someone ordering me to hurry here and secure the child’s salvation through the prayers of the head of the monastery.”

The one who gave the oracle, she said, told her that the head of the monastery did not usually speak with women. When the woman persisted, weeping, wailing, and crying out bitterly, the head of the monastery came out [Col. 0036B]. But the woman said that he was not the man she had seen. She had been shown another man, reddish in complexion, who had certain pustules on his cheeks.

When they discovered the person she was seeking—it was the monastery’s third man, not the first—they persuaded him to come to the woman. She immediately recognized his face, and the evil demon, crying out, left the girl.

These glorious deeds were performed by disciples of the disciples of the great Marcianus. Such plants did the excellent planter plant everywhere. Bringing this narrative once more to an end, I ask and entreat that through the intercession of all these men I may obtain divine assistance.

## CHAPTER IV. EUSEBIUS

[Note: [Col. 0116D] Eusebius.] Concerning him, Theodoretus, book IV of the *History*, chapter 26; Sozomenus, book VI, chapter 3; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 41. Concerning him, I think, the Menaea, 23 January, [Col. 0117A] in two verses. He is mentioned in the Menaea, 2 November, in the Life of Saint Marcianus.]

[Col. 0036C]

What fruits the barren desert offered to God—beautiful and ripe, pleasing to the one who planted them, and dear and greatly desired by people of understanding—we have shown in the narratives already written. But lest anyone suppose that virtue is confined by place, and that only the desert is suitable for producing such returns, let us now proceed in our account to the inhabited land and show that it is in no way an obstacle to practicing this discipline.

There is a high mountain situated east of Antioch and west of Beroea, surpassing all the nearby mountains. At its highest summit it resembles a cone in shape; from its height it received its name. For κορυφήν, that is, “summit,” is what the inhabitants commonly call it. Formerly, on its highest peak, there was a temple of demons, held in great honor by the neighboring people. Below it, toward the south, there extends a plain presenting the shape of a bay, bounded on both sides by arms of land that are not very high. These extend as far as the road along which riders travel; on both sides they run from south to north, receiving smaller paths. Villas, both large and small, have been built there, containing the people who live on either side of the mountains. Near the lofty ridges of the mountain there is a very large village, densely populated; they call it Teleda, after the region.

[Note: Teled. I. This village also occurs below, in chapter 26, in the account of Simeon Stylites.]

On the upper part of the mountain’s side there is a grove that is not very steep but slopes gently, facing that plain and the south wind. In it a certain Ammianus established a training-ground for philosophy. He was a man distinguished by many other virtues, but he surpassed the others especially in the greatest modesty. This is sufficient evidence of it. Although he could have sufficed as a teacher not only for his own companions but even for twice as many others, he often hurried to the great Eusebius, asking and entreating him to be the assistant, trainer, and teacher of the school he had founded. Eusebius was shut away twenty-five stadia distant, in a very small dwelling that did not even have windows.

Marcianus, his uncle and a faithful servant of God, had led him to this virtue. It is enough to say this, since the Lord also honored the great Moses with that name. When this Marcianus had tasted divine love, he did not wish to enjoy the blessings alone, but made many others his companions in love. He pursued the great Eusebius, as well as his brother, who was truly his brother in life also. He did not think it reasonable to pursue strangers for virtue while leaving his own brothers untouched. So, after shutting both of them in a small house, he taught them the evangelical way of life.

The brother, however, was attacked by illness, and that course was interrupted; death followed the illness. For after leaving that place, he lived only a few days before reaching the end of his life. The great Eusebius remained throughout the lifetime of his uncle, speaking with no one and looking upon no light, shut up continually. After his uncle’s death he embraced this life, until that admirable Ammianus, after softening him with many entreaties, persuaded him.

“Tell me,” Ammianus said to him, “excellent man, for whom do you suppose you have pursued this laborious, filthy, and squalid life?” When Eusebius, as was natural, replied that it was for God, the lawgiver and teacher of virtue, Ammianus said: “Since you love him, I will show you a way by which you may both kindle your love more greatly and serve the one whom you love. For, as I see it, the fact that all your care and industry are directed toward yourself will not escape the charge of excessive self-love. The divine law commands us to love our neighbor as ourselves (Romans 13). To make many people share in one’s possessions is the proper work of true charity. Divine Paul called this ‘the fulfillment of the law’ (Galatians 5). Again he cries out: ‘The whole law and the prophets are summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Moreover, the Lord himself, in the holy Gospels, commanded Peter, who confessed that he loved him more than the others, to feed his sheep (John 21). Rebuking those who did not do this, he cries out through the prophet: ‘O shepherds, do shepherds feed themselves rather than the sheep?’ (Ezekiel 34).

“For this reason he also commanded the great Elijah, who pursued this life, to live among the impious; and after Elijah, he sent John, so greatly celebrated, who embraced solitude, to the banks of the Jordan, ordering him there to baptize and preach. Since you too are an ardent lover of the God who made you, make many others lovers together with you. For this is highly pleasing to the common Lord. Therefore he also called Ezekiel a watchman and ordered him to testify to sinners (Ezekiel 3); and he commanded Jonah to run to Nineveh, sending him there in chains when he was unwilling (Jonah 1).”

As he said these and similar things, he tamed the divine man. After he had dug out that voluntary prison, he brought him out and took him away, entrusting him with the care of his companions. I do not know whether I admire more the moderation of the one or the obedience of the other, and the fact that he was persuaded by him. Eusebius fled from authority and preferred to be among those who obeyed, fearing the danger of office. Yet the great Eusebius, although he shunned association with many people, yielded; caught in the nets of charity, he accepted responsibility for the flock and led the choir. He needed few words for teaching. His mere appearance was enough to make even the slowest person quick in running—quick in running the race of virtue.

Those who saw him say that he always had a grave expression, one capable of inspiring fear in those who looked upon him.

He himself took food on the third day, and sometimes on the fourth; to those who lived with him he ordered that they eat on alternate days. He commanded them to converse continually with God.

[Note: “To converse continually with God.” That is, to pray. For when we pray, we address God; when we read the holy Scriptures, God speaks with us. Chrysostom, *On Praying to God*, book I. *The Life of Barlaam and Josaphat*, chapter 20: “Through prayer we converse with God.”]

They were to leave no time vacant from this practice, but to carry out together the duties appointed for them. During the intervening portions of the day, each one separately—under some shade of a tree, beside some rock, wherever anyone happened to rest, whether standing or lying on the ground—was to entreat the Lord and seek salvation.

He trained every part of the body in virtue, so that each part would do what reason alone permits. To make this clear to everyone, I shall mention one of his stories.

He and that admirable Ammianus were sitting on a certain rock. One of them was reading the account of the divine Gospels, while the other explained the meaning of the more obscure passages. When some farmers were cultivating the soil in the plain below, the great Eusebius was drawn toward this sight. After the divine Ammianus had read the Gospel passage and asked for its interpretation, the great Eusebius ordered him to repeat the reading. He then said, “Perhaps, delighted by those who plow, you did not hear it, as is likely”—the reading *lis qui arant* is materially uncertain.

Thereafter he imposed a law upon his own eyes: they were never again to look upon that plain, nor to enjoy the beauty of the heavens and the sight of the choir of the stars. He was not permitted to leave a very narrow path, said to have been one palm in width, which led to the oratory. He is said to have lived more than forty years after imposing this law.

To draw him by some necessity toward these things as well, in accordance with his own purpose, he bound his loins with an iron belt and placed a very heavy collar around his neck. He fastened the belt to the collar with another piece of iron, so that, bent forward in this fashion, he might continually strive to look down at the ground. He imposed these punishments upon himself because he had looked upon those farmers.

Many others who knew him and were thoroughly acquainted with his practices taught me this; the great old man Acacius also related it, the same Acacius whom we mentioned earlier in other accounts. He said that he too had once asked Eusebius, when he saw him bent in this way, what benefit he gained from not allowing himself to look at the sky, to behold the plain below, or to leave that narrow path. Eusebius replied that he was devising these measures against the schemes of the evil demon:

“So that he may not wage war over great matters—attempting to take away temperance and justice, arming anger, kindling desire, causing me to be carried away by arrogance and swollen with pride, and plotting whatever else against my soul—I try to divert the enemy toward these small matters. Even if he conquers in them, he causes no great harm; and if he is defeated, he becomes more ridiculous, since he cannot prevail even in small things.

“Because I know that this battle is less dangerous—for one who suffers some loss in these matters is not greatly injured—I have transferred myself to this kind of combat. What harm is there in seeing a field or raising one’s eyes to heaven? In this battle he can neither strike nor kill me, for these are not deadly arrows, since they lack those iron points.

“This is what the great Acacius said he had heard, and he said that he had marveled at his wisdom, his skill in spiritual warfare, and his experience. For this reason he also related it to those who desired to learn such things, as something marvelous and worthy of being entrusted to memory.

As his fame spread everywhere in all directions, it drew to him all lovers of virtue. The most divine successors of the old man Julian also came—[Longus adds: “James the Persian and Agrippa”]—men who had been leaders of an excellent flock. For after that divine man had completed his life and departed to the heavenly life, they hurried to the great Eusebius, judging it better to be rightly governed than to govern and preside.

As for James, whom I have already mentioned and whose virtue I previously displayed in outline, I shall now offer clear evidence of his supreme philosophy. After the divine Eusebius had departed this life and ordered him to preside over the flock, James refused the charge. When he failed to persuade those who wished him to accept it, he went away to another flock, preferring to be fed rather than to feed. After living on for a long time, he ended his life in this manner.

Agrippa then undertook that office. He was adorned with many other good qualities, but especially with purity of soul. Through this purity he continually apprehended the vision of divine beauty; kindled by the fire of that love, he watered his cheeks with perpetual tears.

After he had rightly shepherded that chosen and divine flock for a long time, and then departed this life, the divine David, whose appearance I too was privileged to enjoy, undertook the office. He was a man who, in truth, according to the saying of the divine Apostle, had put to death the members that are upon the earth (Colossians 3).

He had gained such fruit from the teaching of the great Eusebius that he spent forty-five years in that monastery and lived throughout that time without anger or irritation. No one ever saw him overcome by this disturbance of soul after assuming the office, even though, as is likely, there were innumerable occasions that might have compelled it.

One hundred and fifty men were fed by his hand. Some possessed the highest and most excellent virtue and imitated the way of life that is in heaven; others were only then beginning to grow wings and were being taught to leap over and soar above the earth. Yet although so many were being taught divine things and, as is likely, some were doing wrong—for it is not easy for one who has only just begun to conduct himself properly in everything—nevertheless that divine man remained unmoved like one incorporeal. Nothing ever gave him occasion for anger.

I learned this not only by hearsay but also through experience. For once, desiring to see that flock, I approached, bringing with me other companions on the journey who had embraced the same way of life as I. After spending an entire week with that divine man, we saw that his face underwent no change: it was not at one moment spread with cheerfulness and at another contracted by sadness. His eyes likewise were never at one time fierce and stern and at another joyful, but always remained in the same condition of propriety and dignity. These things are sufficient to demonstrate tranquility of soul.

Someone might suppose that he appeared such because no occasion moved him. I must therefore relate something of the kind that occurred while we were there.

That divine man was sitting among us, discussing matters of philosophy and seeking the highest point of the discipline of evangelical life. While such conversations were taking place, a certain Publius, Roman by descent but himself also admirable in conduct, and possessing the dignity of the priesthood and the second rank in that administration, came to us shouting against the divine David. He called that gentleness a common misfortune, said that his mildness brought ruin upon everyone, and called that supreme philosophy madness rather than moderation.

But his soul was like adamant. He listened to the accusations but was not stung by what naturally causes pain. He did not change his expression or abandon the conversation he had begun. In a gentle voice and with words that expressed serenity of soul, he dismissed the old man, asking him to take care of whatever matters he wished.

“As you see,” he said, “I am speaking with those who have come to us, since I consider this duty necessary.”

Could anyone better demonstrate gentleness of soul? The man entrusted with that office received such insults from the holder of the second rank, especially in the presence of guests who heard the abuse, yet underwent no storm or disturbance of anger. What virtue and strength of a great and lofty soul could surpass this?

The divine Apostle, considering the weakness of human nature and measuring his law according to what nature permits, says: “Be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4); “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4). Since he knew that the movement of anger belonged to nature and not to our choice, he did not establish by law requirements that would be laborious and perhaps impossible to fulfill. Instead, he set a measure for the natural movement and storm of anger: a day. He ordered reason to restrain it, hold it back as with a bridle, and not allow it to advance beyond its limits.

But this divine man strove beyond the laws that had been laid down and leaped beyond their boundaries. He did not merely refuse to allow anger to move until evening; he did not permit it to move at all. Such was the fruit he received from his association with the great Eusebius.

I saw many others in that hut who were lovers and imitators of this philosophy, some in the flower of their bodily strength, others already in deep old age. Although they had lived more than ninety years, they did not wish to abandon their laborious life. They remained distinguished by youthful exertions to the end, praising God day and night and performing those sacred duties, while eating their wretched food only every other day.

To pass over others who are not indeed worthy to be silenced but deserve the highest praise and celebration—for fear that the account should become longer than is fitting—there was in this divine place a certain man whom they call the abbot.

[Note: Longus reads *Abban* or *Amman*, so that it may be a proper name.]

He sprang from an Ishmaelite root, but was not expelled from Abraham’s household, as was the ancestor from whom he derived his lineage. Rather, he became a sharer in the paternal inheritance with Isaac—or, better, he himself seized the kingdom of heaven.

He immediately undertook the discipline of this monastic exercise under a certain man who was then living in the wilderness and who trained his disciples excellently. His name was Marosas.

[Note: Marosas. On him, Sozomen, book VI, chapter 34, and Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 41. Barreus wrongly confuses him here, at chapter 16, with Maron.]

After this man too ceased to preside over others, he came with the abbot to this flock. He did not live for a short time, but after having fought splendidly and become eminent, he departed from this life.

He remained there for thirty-eight continuous years. Yet he desired to labor as though he had only just begun to labor; even to the present day he has never covered his feet with shoes. When it is cold, he sits in the shade; in the heat, he receives the sun, accepting its flame as though it were a breeze from the West Wind, Zephyr, proceeding from it.

Throughout all this time he did not permit himself to drink water—not by eating the foods given to those who train themselves not to drink, for such people generally use more liquid foods, but by using the same foods as the others. Eating little and foods that supplied him only modest strength, he considered the use of water superfluous.

With heavy iron girding his loins, he rarely sat. At night and for most of the day, either standing or bending his knees, he offered the service of prayer to the Lord. He entirely deprived himself of the use of lying down; no one to this day has ever seen him recline.

Moreover, when he was appointed leader of the choir and it fell to him to preside, he bore all this labor with a ready and cheerful spirit, presenting himself as a model of philosophy to those who obeyed his command.

Such fighters, distinguished by victory, did the divine Eusebius, the trainer and instructor of these contests, present to the Lord. After producing many others like them, he sent them as teachers to other training-grounds. They filled that entire holy mountain with these divine meadows, giving forth a sweet fragrance.

Since the hut of that monastic exercise had been situated from the beginning in the east, one could see the offspring of its philosophy in the west and south, like stars leading choirs around the moon. Some praised the Creator in Greek, others in the language of the region in which they lived.

Yet I am undertaking what cannot be done, wishing to pursue everything that was rightly accomplished by that divine soul.

An end must therefore be set to this account, and the narrative must turn to another subject. We must again add the benefit gained from that place, after asking to share in the blessing of these great men.

## CHAPTER V. PUBLIUS

[Note: Publius. Theodoretus, book IV of the *History*, chapter 26; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 41; and the *Greek Menologion*, 4 April: “Commemoration of Publius and Plato, abbot of the Studite monastery.” I do not know whether this is our Publius.]

At the same time there was a certain Publius, worthy of admiration in appearance and endowed with a soul corresponding to his appearance—or rather, one who made his bodily appearance more admirable through his soul.

He was descended from the senatorial order and was born in a city near which that Xerxes, whose fame is celebrated everywhere, while waging war against Greece and wishing to lead his army across the Euphrates, gathered a multitude of ships, joined them together, and in this way constructed a bridge over the river. He called the place Zeugma, that is, “joining,” and gave the city a name derived from the event.

Born there and descended from such a lineage, Publius occupied a high place situated no more than thirty stadia from the city. After building a small house there, he sold everything he had received from his father: the house, I mean, and the properties, the flocks, the clothing, the silver and bronze vessels, and whatever else there was along with these things.

After distributing them according to the divine law among those to whom this was appropriate, and freeing himself from every earthly concern, he undertook one concern in place of all the others: to serve the one who had called him. He continually revolved this purpose in his mind, considering and examining day and night how he might increase it.

For this reason his labor grew daily, becoming each day greater and more intense. It was sweet and full of delight, driving satiety far away. No one ever saw him resting, even for the smallest part of the day. Prayer followed psalmody, psalmody followed prayer, and both were followed by reading the divine utterances. Then came care for visiting guests, and afterward some necessary work.

Following this course of life, and set forth as a model of virtue for those who wished to imitate him, he compelled many of his own kind, like a melodious bird, into these saving nets.

At first he allowed no one to live with him. Instead, he built small houses near the doors and ordered each of those who came to live separately. He often visited and inspected the little houses to see whether anything had been stored there beyond what was necessary.

They say that he also approached the scales and carefully weighed the measure of bread. If he ever found more than had been prescribed, he was distressed and called those who had done this gluttons. For he ordered them neither to eat nor to drink until they were satisfied, but to take only as much as was sufficient to preserve the life of the body.

If he saw flour covered with bran, he attacked those who had done this with curses, as people who were enjoying Sybaritic delicacies. Moreover, he would come unexpectedly at night to the door of each person. If he found someone awake and praising God, he departed silently; but if he sensed that someone was sleeping, he knocked on the door with his hand and attacked the one lying there with his tongue, as one who cared for his body more than he ought.

When some people of like mind and purpose considered his labor, they proposed to him that he build one dwelling for all. They said that those who were now scattered would live more exactly and carefully, and that he would be freed from a great part of his anxiety.

The most wise man approved the proposal. After gathering them all together and destroying those little houses, he built one dwelling for those who had assembled and asked them to live together and encourage one another: one should imitate the gentleness of this man, another should temper that man’s gentleness with zeal, and another, sharing in the vigils, should receive the discipline of fasting.

“For in this way,” he said, “taking from one another what is lacking, we shall produce the most perfect virtue. Just as at the gates of cities one man sells bread, another vegetables, another has clothing for sale, and another is a shoemaker, and by obtaining from one another what they need they live more pleasantly—the one who gives a garment receives shoes in return, and the one who buys a vegetable sells bread—so we ought to exchange among ourselves the most precious parts of virtue.”

While those who spoke the same language were being trained and competing in this way, and praising God in the Greek tongue, love for this way of life also seized those who used the language of that region. Some of them came running and begged to be admitted into their flock and to share in his sacred teaching.

He granted what they requested, remembering the Lord’s command given to the holy apostles: “Go and teach all nations” (Matthew 28). He built another dwelling beside the first and ordered them to live there. He also constructed a divine temple, commanding both groups to assemble there at the beginning and end of the day, so that they might offer evening and morning hymns to God together. They were divided into two groups, each using its own language, but producing the hymn in alternation.

The form of this institution has remained to the present day. Neither time, which strives mightily to change such things, nor those who succeeded to its administration, have brought themselves to overturn anything of the boundaries he established. This was so even though not two or three but many men undertook that office.

When he had completed his contest and departed from this life, migrating to that life free from every trouble, Theotecnus of the Greek language and Aphthonius of the Syrian received the administration. Both were living statutes and images of his virtue. They did not allow either those who assembled together or those who came from outside to feel his death, since they showed themselves to be exact images of his way of life.

The divine Theotecnus, however, did not live long, and handed the administration over to Theodotus. Aphthonius, while caring for the flock and governing it according to the laws already established, remained for a very long time.

This Theodotus, who was from Armenia, had seen the order of monastic discipline. At first he was among those who obeyed the great governor Theotecnus. After Theotecnus, as I have said, departed and Theodotus himself assumed the administration, he adorned it with so many virtues that he nearly obscured his predecessors by his reputation.

For divine longing so affected him and wounded him with so many and such arrows that he poured forth tears of compunction by night and by day. He was so full of spiritual grace that when he prayed, all who were present fell silent and heard only those sacred words, regarding the hearing itself as a good prayer.

Who could be so adamant that, when those words were spoken so sincerely and genuinely, his soul would not be soothed, his hardness softened, his disobedience removed, and he not be led to serve God?

As he increased his riches daily and displayed sacred treasures full of such blessings, after shepherding the flock for twenty-five years he was gathered to his fathers, as divine Scripture says (Genesis 15), brought to a good old age. He handed over the reins to Theotecnus, who was his nephew by birth but his brother in character.

The divine Aphthonius, after presiding over the choir for more than forty years, received an episcopal see. He did not change his monastic hair shirt or his tunic woven from goatskins, and he ate the same foods as before he became a bishop.

Even after accepting this office, he nevertheless continued to care for that flock, spending many days there. Sometimes he settled disputes among those who were fighting one another; sometimes he gave counsel to those who had suffered some injury; and at other times he offered his companions divine admonition.

He did each of these things while sewing the garments of his fellow residents, cleaning lentils, washing grain, or handling some other task of that kind. Having thus adorned the episcopate and increased his virtue, he reached the divine harbor with his burdens.

And why should I speak of Theotecnus and of Gregory, who followed him? The former gathered every kind of virtue from his youth and surpassed the glory of his ancestors; the latter, even to this day, labors in deep old age as though he were in the flower of youth.

He continued constantly to refuse the fruit of the vine, eating neither vinegar nor raisins, and drinking neither milk, whether fresh or curdled. For the great Publius established this way of life. Although they acknowledge the use of oil during the season of Pentecost, they again refuse to partake of it afterward.

This is what I learned about the great Publius: some of it I received by hearsay, and some from his own disciples whom I saw. In them I recognized their teacher, and through the athletes I learned about their trainer.

I therefore judged it wrong, and unworthy of a pure man, to consign such great benefit to silence. I have set this account before those who did not know it, both seeking to ensure that they receive benefit from it and gaining from it a treasure for memory.

For I heard the Lord say: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10). I know clearly that if I commemorate them among men, they too will remember me before the God of all.

## CHAPTER VI. SIMEON THE ELDER

[Note: Simeon the Elder. On him, the *Menaea*, 26 January, translated by our Raderus in part I of the *Greenery of the Saints*; Theodoretus, book IV of the *History*, chapter 26.]

If anyone deliberately passes over the old Simeon (Theodoretus, book IV of the *History*, chapter 26) and consigns the memory of his philosophy to oblivion, he may rightly be accused of injustice and envy, as one who neither wishes to praise what deserves praise nor offers to those who wish to be helped what is most desirable.

I, however, not fearing accusation but wishing to honor him with praise, shall relate the discipline of his life.

For a very long time he continually embraced a solitary life. Living in a small cave, he enjoyed no human company, for he had determined to live alone. Yet he conversed continually with the God of all, and prepared edible herbs as his food; his labor was spent in this activity.

He had been endowed from above with such abundant grace that he could command even the strongest and most savage beasts. This became evident not only to the pious but also to unbelieving Jews.

On one occasion, while traveling abroad on some business of theirs to a certain fortress situated beyond the region inhabited by the people of our empire, a violent rain arose and a storm descended. They went astray from the road because they could not see what lay ahead. They wandered through the wilderness, finding neither a village, nor a cave, nor any traveler.

When they were tossed about in the middle of the land like those sailing in the midst of waves, they noticed the cave of the divine Simeon as though it were a harbor. They saw a filthy and squalid man wearing on his shoulders a small piece of cloth woven from goatskin.

As soon as he saw them, he greeted them—for he was affable—and asked the reason for their arrival. After they had related what had happened and asked him to show them the road leading to the fortress, he said:

“Stay here. I shall immediately give you guides who will show you the road you desire.”

They obeyed and rested there for the moment. While they were sitting, two lions came—not looking at them with a grim or savage gaze, but fawning upon them as upon a master and signifying their servitude.

Simeon nodded to them and ordered them to lead the guests and bring them back to the road from which they had strayed.

Let no one regard this account as a fable, since it has common enemies of the truth bearing witness to its truth. For those who received the benefit continually sang of it. The great Jacob related it to me here, saying that he was present when they told the blessed Maron this miracle.

Therefore, whoever does not believe Jews when they bear witness to the miracles of Christians, how will he not rightly be called more unbelieving than the Jews? For although they are hostile toward us, they are nevertheless overcome and yield to the rays of truth. But these men, who are considered benevolent and fellow believers, do not even believe enemies when they testify to the power of grace.

When that divine man had become distinguished by such miracles and had attracted many people from the neighboring barbarians—for those who boast of Ishmael as the founder of their race inhabit that wilderness—his love of solitude made it necessary for him to leave the cave.

After traveling a considerable distance, he reached the mountain called Amanus. What had formerly been filled with the madness of the worship of many gods he adorned with many miracles of every kind, and he planted there the piety and true religion that are practiced in it now.

To relate everything, however, would be very laborious and perhaps beyond my ability. After mentioning one event and adding it as a kind of pattern and representation of an apostolic and prophetic miracle, I shall leave it to my readers to consider what power of grace he had received.

It was summer and harvest time, and sheaves were being carried into the threshing floors. A certain man, who was not content with the labors belonging to him but coveted what belonged to others, had taken several sheaves from his neighbor and was trying by this means to increase his own heap.

Immediately divine judgment fell upon his theft: lightning struck, and the threshing floor was burned. The unfortunate man approached the man of God, who had pitched his tent not far from the village. He related the calamity that had befallen him but tried to conceal the theft.

When ordered to speak the truth, he confessed the theft—for the disaster forced him to accuse himself. The divine man ordered him to correct the wrong so that he might be freed from the punishment.

“For if you restore those sheaves,” he said, “the fire sent by God will be extinguished.”

It was therefore possible to see the man running and offering the stolen ears of grain to the one who had been wronged, while the pyre was extinguished without water through the prayer and intercession of the divine old man.

This filled not only the inhabitants with terror but also compelled the entire city—Antioch, I mean, for the estate was under its jurisdiction—to run there. One person came asking to be freed from demonic madness, another that his fever might cease, and another that he might obtain a remedy for one of the afflictions that tormented him.

To those who dwelt there, he supplied the streams of grace abundantly.

But again, being a lover of solitude, he wished to reach Mount Sinai. When many excellent men who pursued the same philosophy learned of this, they hastened together, wishing to become companions of his pilgrimage. After they had completed a journey of many days, when they had entered the wilderness of Sodom, they saw from a distance a man’s hands stretched upward from the depths. At first they thought it was a demonic deception; but when they had prayed with greater earnestness and had seen the same thing again, they went to the place. They saw a small pit, such as foxes usually make when they devise hiding places into which they may retreat; but they saw no one appearing there. For when the man whose hands had been extended sensed the sound of approaching feet, he had hidden himself inside the cave. The old man remained there for a long time, earnestly asking him to show himself if he possessed human nature and was not some demonic impostor who had transformed himself into these shapes.

“For we too,” he said, “who pursue the life of monastic discipline and love solitude, are wandering through this wilderness, desiring to worship the God of all on Mount Sinai, where, when he appeared to Moses his servant, he gave the tablets of the laws—not because we suppose that God is confined to a place, for we hear him say, ‘I fill heaven and earth,’ says the Lord (Jeremiah XXIII), and that he contains the circuit of the earth and those who inhabit it as locusts; but because those who love ardently desire not only the persons they love, but also find the places pleasing and delightful where those beloved ones were present and where they lived.”

As the old man said these and similar things, the man who had been hiding in the cave revealed himself. In appearance he was wild: his hair was filthy and unkempt, his face wrinkled, and all the members of his body dried out and utterly bloodless. He was clothed in certain dirty rags sewn together from palm shoots. After greeting them and giving them the word of peace, he asked who they were, where they came from, and where they were going. The old man answered his questions and in turn asked where he had come from and why he had chosen this way of life.

“The same desire,” he replied, “had begun to draw me toward the place to which you are now going. I had taken as my companion in this life a certain kinsman of mine, who was of the same mind and purpose and whose goal and discipline were the same as mine. We had bound one another by oath never to separate our fellowship, not even by death. It happened, then, that he met the end of his life here during the pilgrimage. Bound by my oath, I dug a pit as best I could and committed his body to burial. Then, having dug another grave for myself beside this memorial, I await the end of my life here and offer the Lord my customary service. I eat dates, which a certain brother, appointed by the one who cares for me, has been ordered to bring me.”

As these things were being said, a lion appeared in the distance. When those who were with the old man fell into anguish and fear, the one lying in the cave, realizing what had happened, rose and beckoned to the lion to go to the other side. It immediately obeyed and came carrying a cluster of dates. Then, after permission had been given, it departed again and lay down at a distance from the men and fell asleep. After he had divided the dates among them, shared in their prayers and psalmody, and greeted them at the end of the morning office, he dismissed them, astonished at the unprecedented spectacle.

[Col. 0047B–0048A]

If anyone does not believe what has been related, let him recall the distinguished life of Elijah and the service of the ravens, which continually brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening. For the Maker of all things easily provides for his own and finds every means of doing so. Thus he preserved Jonah in the belly of the sea creature for three days and nights, and caused the lions in the den to be astonished at Daniel, and caused lifeless fire to act as though endowed with reason: it illuminated those who were inside, but burned those who were outside. Yet I am doing something unnecessary by bringing forward arguments to prove God’s power.

[Col. 0048A–B]

After he had reached the mountain he desired, they say that the admirable old man knelt in the place where Moses was deemed worthy to see God—he saw him insofar as human nature could see—and did not rise before he heard a divine voice indicating to him the Lord’s benevolence. Since he had remained bent over in this manner throughout the entire week and had taken no food at all, the voice addressed to him ordered him to take what had been set before him and to eat with a willing and cheerful spirit. When he stretched out his hand, found three apples, and ate them as the one who had given them commanded, his full strength was restored, and with the cheerful spirit appropriate to the occasion he greeted those who lived with him. Thus he returned joyful and glad, having both heard the divine voice and again eaten food given by God.

[Col. 0048B–C]

After his return, he established two training grounds of philosophy: one on the summit of the mountain, of which we spoke earlier, and the other below, beside the very slopes of the mountain. Having gathered athletes of virtue in both places, he was the trainer and instructor of these and of those. Teaching them to withstand the attacks of their adversaries, promising benevolence to the presiding judges of the contest, commanding them to be courageous rather than degenerate and faint-hearted, and instructing them to exercise moderation toward their own people but greatness of spirit toward the enemy, he taught these things, lived in this manner, performed these miracles, and radiated every kind of splendor. He brought this laborious life to an end and departed into that old age which is free from suffering, leaving behind glory that cannot be extinguished and a memory that endures forever.

My blessed—indeed, thrice-blessed—mother obtained his blessing while he was still alive, and she often told me many things about him.

I now pray that I may obtain the intercession he is able to give, and I know that I shall obtain it: he will certainly grant my request, imitating the Lord’s kindness.

## CHAPTER VII. PALLADIUS

[Note: Palladius. Theodoretus, Book IV of the History, chapter 26; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 41.]

[Col. 0049A]

Palladius, who was celebrated in the speech of many (Theodoretus, Book IV of the History, chapter 26), was his contemporary, equal to him in character, and known and intimate with him. For, as they say, they continually visited one another, deriving benefit from one another, mutually provoking one another and inciting one another to zeal for God.

He was enclosed in a small dwelling near a very large village and one exceedingly crowded with people. Its name is Lemme [Long: Imme]. I think it unnecessary to speak of the man’s extraordinary abstinence from food—or fasting and hunger—his vigils, and his continual prayer. In these matters he bore the same yoke as the blessed Symeon. But I thought it worthwhile to relate the miracle that is celebrated in song even to this day and that was performed through his voice and hand.

[Col. 0049A–B]

In the village mentioned above there is a highly celebrated gathering, which draws merchants from every direction and a crowd larger than can be counted. A certain merchant, having sold what he had brought and gathered his gold, wished to depart by night. But a murderer who had seen the gold collected there, seized by a kind of frenzy and madness, drove sleep from his eyelids and watched for the time when the man would depart. After the cockcrow, the merchant went away unsuspecting. The murderer, however, having occupied a place suitable for an ambush, suddenly attacked him, struck him, and killed him.

[Col. 0049B–C]

To his accursed crime he added another impious deed. After taking the gold, he threw the dead body at Palladius’s door. When day came, the news spread, and the entire gathering of people was speaking everywhere about what had happened, they all ran together and broke down the door, wishing to exact punishment for the murder from the divine Palladius. One of those taking part in this was the very man who had committed the murder with his own hand.

When the holy man was surrounded by such a great multitude, he looked toward heaven and, rising above heaven in his mind, supplicated the Lord to refute the lie of the accusation and reveal the truth that lay concealed. After he had prayed in this way and taken hold of the dead man’s hand, he said:

“Tell me, young man, who inflicted this wound upon you. Show who committed this accursed deed, and free the innocent man from this wicked accusation.”

Word was indeed followed by word. The man, even while sitting up, looked around at those who were approaching and pointed with his finger to the murderer.

[Note: He pointed with his finger to the murderer. Thus thieves were apprehended by a miracle. Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 42.]

A cry rose from everyone: they were astonished at the miracle and lamented the accusation that had been brought. They stripped the criminal and found the sword still stained with blood, as well as the gold that had provided the motive for the murder. The divine Palladius, who had already been admirable, thereby became deservedly far more admirable. The miracle was sufficient to display the man’s confidence before God.

[Col. 0049D–0050A]

From the same order was the admirable Abraames, who built what is called Paratomon and sent forth the splendors of virtue in every direction. How illustrious his life was is demonstrated by the miracles that occur after his death. From his tomb, cures for every kind of disease gush forth even to this day. Those who abundantly draw them from that place through faith are wealthy witnesses of this. May I too be granted the help of one whose memory I have sanctified with my tongue.

## CHAPTER VIII. APHRAATES

[Note: Aphraates. Theodoretus, Book IV of the History, chapter 24; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 25.]

[Col. 0050A–B]

That the nature of all human beings is one and that it is easy for those who wish to philosophize, whether they are Greeks or barbarians, can readily be learned from many other examples as well. But for demonstrating this clearly, Aphraates alone is sufficient (Theodoretus, Book IV of the History, chapter 24).

He was born and raised among the Persians, who are exceedingly unjust; he was descended from such parents and trained in their laws. Yet he attained such virtue that he surpassed those who had been born of pious parents and had received pious instruction from childhood.

First, despising his lineage—for it was distinguished and illustrious—he hastened to worship the Lord, imitating the magi, his ancestors. Then, abhorring the impiety of the people of his own race, he preferred a foreign land to his own. When he came to Edessa, a very large city crowded with people and conspicuously adorned by piety, he found a small dwelling outside its boundaries and shut himself inside it. There he cared for his soul like an excellent farmer, cutting out the thorns of vice by the roots, cleansing the divine field, and offering mature fruits of the Gospel to the Lord.

[Col. 0050B–C]

From there he came to Antioch, which was being sorely besieged by the storm of heresy. When he had withdrawn to a certain training ground of philosophy outside the city and had learned a few words of the Greek language, he drew many people to hear divine discourses. Using a language mixed with barbarisms, he produced the fruits of intelligence and understanding, receiving these streams from the grace of the divine Spirit.

For who among those who boast of their eloquence, who draw together their brows and speak proudly and grandly, and who exult like young men over the snares of syllogisms, was ever superior to him in that uneducated and barbarous speech? He defeated arguments with arguments and the reasoning of philosophers with divine utterances, crying out with the great Paul: “Even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (II Corinthians XI). In this way, continually following the Apostle’s judgment, he humbled arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and he took captive every understanding into obedience to Christ (II Corinthians X).

[Col. 0050C–D]

It was possible to see those who held public offices, those enrolled in various military units, and those who earned their livelihood with their hands; in short, civilians and soldiers, educated and unlearned, poor and rich. Some silently received what was offered; others asked questions and made inquiries, supplying an opportunity for discourse.

Although he undertook so much labor, he never allowed anyone to remain with him as a resident. Indeed, he preferred his own labor to the service and ministry offered him by others. Since his meetings and conversations took place at the gate of the courtyard, he himself opened it to those entering and escorted and dismissed those departing. He never accepted anything whatsoever from anyone—not bread, not relish, not clothing—but one single person known to him supplied him with bread. When he had reached an advanced old age, he ate vegetables after sunset.

[Col. 0051A]

They say that Anthemius, who later became both prefect and consul, when he had been chosen as ambassador and departed for the Persians, brought him a tunic woven in Persia and said:

“Knowing that everyone finds his own homeland dear, and that the fruits born there are especially delightful, I have brought you this tunic from your homeland. I ask you to accept it, while I may share in your blessing.”

At first Aphraates ordered it to be placed on a bench. Then, after many words had passed between them, he said that he was troubled in mind because his thoughts were divided in two. When Anthemius asked the reason, he replied:

“I have always decided to have only one person living with me, and I have imposed this rule upon myself: that I must absolutely refuse the cohabitation of two people at once. Now, after one person has lived with me for sixteen years and has become dear to me, one of my fellow countrymen has come wishing to live with me and asking that this be permitted. This distracts my mind, for I will not tolerate having two at once. I embrace my fellow countryman as a fellow countryman; but I consider it both harsh and unjust to expel the former, who has become dear to me.”

Anthemius replied: “Rightly so, Father. It is not proper to love a man who has served you for so long as though he were unsuitable, while admitting someone whose character you have not yet tested merely because he comes from your homeland.”

To this the divine Aphraates said: “Then I shall not accept this tunic, admirable man, for I will not tolerate having two. In my judgment, the one you have brought is more pleasing; but in yours, the one that has served me for so long is better.”

Having thus outwitted Anthemius by this clever contrivance and displayed an extraordinary feat of ingenuity, he persuaded him never thereafter to speak to him about the tunic.

I have related this because I wished to show two things at once: both that he received from only one person what was sufficient for the care of his body, and that his wisdom was so great that he caused the man who was asking him to accept the tunic to decide that he ought not to accept it. But leaving these and similar matters aside, I shall relate greater things.

[Col. 0051D–0052A]

When Julian, hostile to God, had paid the penalty of his impiety in the land of the barbarians, circumstances became somewhat more peaceful for the followers of piety when Jovian took up the helm of the Roman Empire. But after Jovian too had ruled for a short time and then met the end of his life, and Valens had assumed the imperial power, storms and tempests once again churned our sea, a heavy swell arose, and enormous waves struck the vessel from every side.

The absence of capable pilots made the storm more severe. The emperor, who exercised his boldness only against the true religion, forced its leaders to live in exile. Although he practiced such injustice, he was not satisfied with his impiety; instead, he scattered and dispersed the entire assembly of the pious, trying, like a savage beast, to tear the flock apart. For this reason he not only expelled them from every church, but also from the mountainside, the riverbank, and the military training ground. They continually changed these places, so that an armed force might unexpectedly rage against them wherever it encountered them.

The Scythians and other barbarians were ravaging all Thrace safely, from the Danube to the Propontis; but the emperor could not receive news of this even with his ears raised, as the saying goes. Instead, he used weapons against those of his own race and under his own authority, who were distinguished by piety and religion.

[Col. 0052A–B]

The divine people lamented the oppressive nature of these evils, singing the Davidic song:

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down; and we wept when we remembered you, Zion” (Psalm CXXXVI).

The remaining words of the song, however, did not suit them. For Aphraates, Flavian, and Diodore did not allow the instruments of instruction to be hung upon the willows, nor did they permit themselves to say, “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm CXXXVI). Rather, in the mountains, in the plains, in the city, in the suburbs, in houses, and in the marketplaces, they continually sang the Lord’s song.

They had learned from David: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Psalm XXIII). Again they had heard the same Prophet cry out: “Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion” (Psalm CII). They had also heard the divine Paul command men to pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger or dispute (I Timothy II).

Moreover, the Lord himself, speaking with the Samaritan woman, had predicted this more clearly:

“Truly, I say to you, woman, the hour is coming, and now is, when they will worship the Father neither in this place nor in Jerusalem, but in every place” (John V).

[Col. 0052B–C]

Having learned these things, they continually bore witness both at home and in the marketplace, and, to speak in apostolic terms, publicly and from house to house (Acts XX). Like outstanding commanders, they armed their own forces and struck down their adversaries.

That the great Flavian and the divine Theodore, who at that time were being shepherded under another and were deemed worthy of the second chair, did these things I have described is both admirable and deserving of praise. Yet they did these things when they had been appointed commanders of an army and were subject to imperial laws.

The exceedingly wise Aphraates, however, sprang of his own accord into these struggles. He had been raised in quiet and had made it his discipline to live by himself; he sat, as the saying goes, beyond the range of a missile. But when he saw the violence of the war, he was not pleased to remain secure. Ordering solitude to stand aside for a time, he became the leader in battle of the phalanx of the pious, striking through life, speech, and miracles, while never himself being struck.

[Col. 0052D–0053A]

Once, when the emperor, utterly foolish in every respect, saw him going out toward the military training ground—for it happened that those who rightly venerated the Trinity had gathered there—someone pointed him out to the emperor as he was walking along the riverbank. The emperor asked him where he was going.

When Aphraates replied that he was going to pray for the inhabited world and for the empire, the emperor again said:

“And for what reason, since you profess the monastic life, do you enter the marketplace openly?”

[Note: “You enter the marketplace openly.” Monks may leave the enclosure when the Church’s distress requires it. See Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 25, concerning Julian and Aphraates, who abandoned the monastic life for the sake of Christ’s flock.]

“Leaving behind silence and quiet?”

Aphraates replied—for he was accustomed to imitate the Lord by reasoning in parables:

“Tell me, emperor: if I were a secluded virgin in a bridal chamber, and I saw someone setting fire to my father’s house, what would you advise me to do when I saw the flames burning and the house being consumed? Would you advise me to remain inside, ignoring the house that was burning? But in that case I too would be consumed by the fire.

“If instead you say that I must hurry, bring water, run back and forth, and extinguish the flames, then do not reproach me, emperor, if I am doing precisely that. For what you would advise a virgin in her bridal chamber to do, that I am compelled to do, having professed the monastic life.

“If you reproach me for having abandoned quiet, reproach yourself, who cast this fire into the divine house, and not me, who am trying to extinguish it. You yourself will admit that one must bring help to the paternal house while it is burning. And that God is a more genuine and true Father than those who are on earth is evident to everyone, even to one who has not been fully initiated into divine matters.

“Therefore, emperor, we are doing nothing absurd or contrary to our undertaking and discipline when we gather and nourish the followers of the true religion and provide them with divine pasture.”

After he had said this, the emperor silently assented, recognizing the justice of his defense.

[Col. 0053C–D]

One of those who are counted neither among men nor among women, because the capacity ever to become fathers has been taken from them, and who for this reason are thought to favor the emperor and speak to him confidently, insulted the divine man from an elevated position and threatened him with death. But not long afterward he paid the penalty for his audacity.

For when the emperor wished to bathe, the wretched man approached as though to see whether the bath was properly tempered. Out of his mind, however, he leapt into the tub, which contained excessively hot and insufficiently tempered water. Since no one was present inside—for he had entered alone to see whether it was ready—he remained there, cooked and dissolved.

After some time had passed, the emperor sent another man to summon him. When that man found no one in the building, he reported this to the emperor. Then several others hurried there, searched all the baths, and finally came to that one. They saw him lying there, deprived of life.

When a commotion arose and everyone lamented, some drained the hot water, while others lifted out the wretched body. As a result, fear seized the emperor and all who were arming themselves against piety. The report spread throughout the entire city of the punishment that unfortunate man had suffered for the insult he had inflicted on Aphraates, and everyone continually celebrated the God of Aphraates with praises.

[Col. 0053D–0054A]

This prevented the man of God from being sent into exile, even though his adversaries were pressing for it. The emperor, terrified, turned away from those who were giving such advice and revered the holy man.

He also learned of Aphraates’ virtue from another event. A horse of excellent breed, highly trained to carry riders, was especially dear to the emperor. A disease that had afflicted it distressed the emperor: the discharge of its bodily fluids was obstructed. Those trained in this art were summoned to cure it. But since their skill was inferior even to the disease, the emperor was troubled, while the man entrusted with the care of the horses lamented.

Since he was pious and firm in faith, at midday he came with the horse to the dwelling of the great Aphraates. After describing the disease and declaring his faith, he prayed that Aphraates would release the illness by his prayers.

Aphraates did not hesitate. He immediately prayed to God and ordered water to be drawn from a well. After making over it the sign of the saving cross, he ordered that it be brought to the horse. The horse drank more than usual. Then, after filling oil with a blessing through the invocation of God, he anointed the horse’s belly; and at once, by the touch of his hands, the illness was removed.

[Col. 0054A–B]

The man rejoiced, took the horse, and ran to the stable. In the evening—for the emperor was accustomed to come to the stable at that time—the emperor arrived and asked how the horse was doing. The man indicated that it was well, brought out the horse healthy, vigorous, leaping, neighing, and proudly raising its neck, and was asked the reason for its recovery.

After hesitating for a long time—for he feared to identify the physician, knowing that the emperor who was asking was hostile to him—he was finally compelled to speak the truth and explained the method of the cure.

The emperor was astonished and admitted that Aphraates was an admirable man. Yet he did not abandon his former madness. He continued to rage against the Only-Begotten until he was consumed by barbarian fire, not even deemed worthy of burial, such as is granted to servants and beggars.

The divine Aphraates also displayed his virtue in that crisis and, when tranquility had been restored, performed other similar deeds. He performed countless other miracles as well, of one or two of which I shall preserve the memory.

[Col. 0054C–D]

A woman of noble birth, yoked in marriage to an intemperate husband, came to that blessed man lamenting her own calamity. She said that her husband, captivated by his attachment to a concubine, had been enchanted by certain magical spells and hated her, the woman joined to him in lawful marriage.

The woman said this while standing at the gate of the courtyard, for he customarily conversed with women in this manner and never admitted any woman inside the doors. Taking pity on the grieving woman, he abolished the effect of the spell by prayer. After sanctifying, through divine invocation, a drop of oil brought by the woman herself, he ordered her to anoint herself with it.

When the woman had obeyed these instructions, she transferred her husband’s love to herself and persuaded him to choose the lawful marriage bed instead of the unlawful one.

[Col. 0054D–0055A]

They also say that, when locusts suddenly invaded the region and consumed everything like fire—crops, trees, meadows, and woods—a pious man came to him and asked him to bring help to a man who possessed one field, from which he supported himself, his wife, his children, and his household, and from which the imperial tax was also collected.

Again imitating the Lord’s kindness, Aphraates ordered a vessel of water to be brought to him. After the petitioner had brought the vessel of water, Aphraates laid his hand upon it and prayed to God to fill the water with divine power. When the prayer was finished, he ordered the water to be sprinkled along the boundaries of the estate.

The man who had brought it did as he had been ordered, and it became for those fields a sacred and unconquerable rampart. For when the locusts, crawling and flying like an army, reached those boundaries, they again retreated, terrified of the blessing that had been placed there, as though strangled by a kind of bridle and prevented from advancing farther.

[Col. 0055A–B]

Why need I relate everything that was done by that blessed soul? These things are sufficient to demonstrate the splendor of the grace that dwelt in him.

I saw him and received the blessing of his holy right hand when I was still a young man and had accompanied my mother on her journey to him. As was his custom, he opened the door, honored her with his speech and blessing, and, when I had been brought inside, bestowed upon me the riches of his intercession.

May I now also enjoy that intercession, since I believe that he lives, leads the choirs together with the angels, and possesses greater confidence before God than he formerly did. At that time, mortal flesh measured his confidence, lest it become an occasion of arrogance if it were greater than was fitting. Now, having laid aside the burden of the soul’s disturbances, like an athlete who has won the victory, he uses confidence and freedom of speech before the judge of the contest. For this reason I also pray that I may obtain his intercession.

## CHAPTER IX. PETER

[Note: Peter the hermit. Theodoretus, Book IV of the History, chapter 26; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 41.]

[Col. 0055C–D]

We hear about the Gauls who are in Europe toward the West (Theodoretus, Book IV of the History, chapter 26). We also know those in Asia, who descended from people who settled near the Pontus Euxinus. From these people sprang the blessed Peter—indeed, thrice and four times blessed.

They say that, after being raised by his parents for seven years from the time of his birth, he spent all the rest of his life in the contests of philosophy. He is said to have died after living ninety-nine years.

Who could praise adequately one who contended for ninety-two years and always emerged victorious, by day and by night? What tongue would suffice to recount his deeds, nobly and virtuously accomplished in childhood, adolescence, manhood, advancing age, and extreme old age? Who could measure his sweat? Who could enumerate the struggles that took place over so long a period? What discourse could encompass even the seeds he cast or the sheaves he gathered? Who possesses a mind so great and lofty that he could fully contemplate the resources and wealth gathered from such an excellent commerce?

I know the vast sea of his achievements and therefore fear approaching their history, lest discourse be overwhelmed. Accordingly, I shall walk along the shore and admire and recount what was done on land before the sea; but I shall leave the depths to him who, as divine Scripture says, searches the deep things and knows what is hidden (I Corinthians II; Daniel II).

[Col. 0055D–0056A]

At first he contended in Galatia. From there he came to Palestine in order to see the places that had received the saving sufferings and, after seeing them, to worship in them the God who had saved us—not as though God were confined to a place, for he knew that God’s nature cannot be confined, but so that he might nourish his eyes with the spectacle of what he desired and might not enjoy spiritual nourishment through faith only by the soul’s contemplative sight, without bodily vision.
