For those who love someone have by nature an instinct not to derive pleasure only from seeing the beloved, but also to behold the beloved’s house, clothing, and shoes with great joy. The bride who possessed such love for the bridegroom and desired him in the Song of Songs cried out:

“As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. I desired and sat in his shadow, and his fruit is sweet in my throat” (Song of Songs II).

Therefore this divine man did nothing absurd or foreign to the matter when he received the same love for the Bridegroom and used the words with which the bride had spoken:

“I am wounded,” he cried, “by love” (Song of Songs IV).

When he desired to contemplate something like a shadow of the Bridegroom, he departed to see the places from which springs flowed forth, bringing salvation to all human beings.

[Col. 0056A–B]

After he had been permitted to enjoy what he desired, he departed for Antioch. When he saw the city’s piety and religious devotion, he preferred that foreign land to his own homeland, considering his fellow citizens not to be his kinsmen and relatives, but those who shared his convictions, were companions with him in faith, and bore the same yoke of piety and religion.

When he decided to remain there, he did not pitch a tent, establish a hut, or build a small dwelling. Instead, he spent the entire time in someone else’s tomb. A certain upper platform had been constructed in it, with a staircase attached by which those who wished to ascend could enter. He remained enclosed there for a very long time, using warm water and eating only bread—not every day, but fasting for one day and taking food on the next.

When a certain man, raging and frenzied and filled with the activity of an evil demon, came to him, he cleansed him through prayer and freed him from that demonic madness. But when the man refused to leave and begged him to grant him his service in return for that healing, he admitted him to live with him.

I both knew this man and remember the miracle; I saw the reward of the healing and heard the conversation they had about me. For Daniel—for that was his name—said that I too would one day become a companion in this excellent ministry. But that divine man did not consent to this, considering my parents’ affection for me. Often he would set me upon his knees and feed me grapes and bread. When my mother had tested his spiritual grace, he ordered me to receive his blessing once a week.

She came to know him for the following reason. A disease had settled upon one of his eyes and seemed to surpass the skill of medicine. Nothing written by the ancients or discovered by later physicians had been left untried upon the disease. After he had tested everything and shown that nothing was of any use, one of her acquaintances came to her, pointed out the divine man, and told her of a miracle performed by him. She said that the wife of the man who at that time held the command of the East—for he was a Pergamenian—had contracted this disease and that he had cured her by prayer and the sign of the cross.

My mother heard this and immediately ran to the divine man. She was wearing earrings, chains, necklaces, and other gold ornaments with which she had adorned herself, as well as a variegated garment woven from silk threads. For she had not yet tasted the more perfect virtue; she was in the bloom of her years [Read: “years”], and wore women’s finery like a young girl.

When the divine head saw these things, he first cured her of the disease of excessive adornment, using words such as these:

“Tell me, daughter”—for I shall use his own expression and shall not alter a word of his holy language—“if a painter, well trained in his art, had painted an image according to the requirements of the artistic law and had displayed it for those who wished to see it, and then someone else, who did not fully and accurately understand the art, came and rashly and thoughtlessly, as it seemed to him, wished to paint over it; and, criticizing the skillfully executed picture, lengthened the lines of the eyebrows and eyelashes, made the face whiter, and added red color to the cheeks—would you not think that the first painter would rightly be angry, because his art had been dishonored and insulted, and because his work had received additions that were unnecessary from an untrained hand?

“Therefore, believe that the Maker of all things, the Fashioner and Painter of our nature, is also rightly angry because you accuse of incompetence that nature and wisdom which cannot be expressed in words. You would not pour red, white, and black color upon yourselves if you did not think that you needed this addition. In thinking that the body requires these things, you condemn its Creator.

“You must understand that he possesses power corresponding to his will in due proportion. For, as David says, ‘The Lord has done all that he willed’ (Ps. 113, 134). Caring for what will be useful to all, he does not give what causes harm. Therefore do not corrupt God’s image, do not attempt to add what he wisely did not give, and do not devise this adulterous beauty, which brings destruction even to the chaste by lying in ambush for those who look upon it.”

The most excellent woman, good in every respect, heard this, and immediately became entangled in Peter’s net—for he too was a fisherman, like the one who bore the same name as himself. Touching his feet and crying aloud, she begged him to heal her eye.

But he said that he was merely a human being and possessed the same nature as she; that he carried a great burden of sins and was therefore deprived of the confidence that belongs toward God. When my mother wept and prayed and said that she would not leave him unless she obtained healing, he said that God was the healer of these things and that he always granted requests to those who believe.

“He will grant it now as well,” he said, “not by giving grace to me, but by looking upon your faith. If, then, you possess faith that is sincere and true, pure and free from every doubt, dismissing physicians and medicines, receive from God this medicine.”

When he had said this, he placed his hand upon the eye and, making the sign of the saving cross, drove out the disease.

Returning home from there, she washed away the medicine and discarded all the adornment she had applied externally. She ordered her life according to the rules laid down by the physician, wearing neither a variegated garment nor golden ornaments, although she was still very young. She was in her twenty-third year and had not yet become a mother; after living seven more years, she gave birth to me, her first and only child.

Such was the fruit she gained from the teaching of the great Peter: she received a twofold healing. While seeking medicine for her body, she also prepared for herself a good disposition of soul.

By saying such things, he worked these deeds; and he was so powerful in prayer.

On one occasion she brought to him a servant who was a cook and was tormented by an evil demon, and she begged him not to refuse the man his aid. After the divine man had prayed, he ordered the demon to state why it had power over God’s creature.

The demon, standing before the judge like some murderer, wall-breaker, or robber, and ordered to say what it had done, recounted everything as one compelled, contrary to its nature, to tell the truth. It said that at Heliopolis the servant’s master had fallen ill; that the mistress had sat beside her husband because he was sick; and that the maidservants had told the mistress of the house where they were staying about the life of the monks who practiced philosophy at Antioch and about the great power they possessed against demons.

The girls, being young and delighting in play, had acted demonically and madly; but the servant himself, dressed in a monastic garment made of goatskin, had adjured them in the monastic manner.

“When these things were happening,” it said, “I was standing by the doors. Unable to endure those proud and glorious claims that were being made about the monks, I wished to test the power which they boastfully claimed, in youthful fashion, that they possessed. For that reason, leaving the maidservants, I entered this man, wishing to discover how I would be expelled by the monks. Now I have learned it, and I need no further experience; at your command I shall immediately depart.”

Saying this, it fled, and the servant was freed.

On another occasion, when my mother’s mother—my maternal aunt—had brought another peasant, she begged the adversary of vice to help him. [Note: [Col. 0057D] Alternatively, “grandmother.” I think the Greek has μητρομήτωρ, “mother’s mother.”]

He again asked him where he was from and from whom he had received power over God’s creature. But when the demon remained silent and gave no answer, Peter prayed on bended knees, asking God to display to that accursed demon the power of his servants.

Then he rose again. The demon, still resisting, remained silent. This continued until the ninth hour. After he had offered the Lord a prayer with greater zeal and greater fervor, he rose and said to the wicked demon:

“Peter does not command you, but Peter’s God. Answer, then, since you are compelled by his power.”

Though shameless and destructive, the demon respected the saint’s gentleness and moderation. In a loud voice it cried out that it dwelt on Mount Amanus.

“When I saw him on the road,” it said, “drawing water from a spring and drinking it, I resolved to make this man my dwelling place.”

“But depart,” said the man of God, “by the one who was crucified for the whole world, who commands you to do so.”

The demon heard him and fled, and the peasant was restored to my maternal aunt, freed from his madness.

Although I could tell countless other such things about that blessed soul, I shall omit many of them, fearing the weakness of the crowd. For people, looking at themselves, have no faith in the miracles of holy men. After recounting one or two, I shall pass to another athlete.

There was a lustful man who had formerly been a military commander. A certain unmarried but marriageable girl, subject to his authority, left her mother and family and fled to a women’s house in which there was a community of athletes. Women too contend in the same way as men and descend into the stadium of virtue.

When the military commander learned of her flight, he beat her mother with whips and bound her. He did not release her from her chains until she showed him the dwelling of the religious women. Then, giving free rein to his rage, he dragged the girl away from there and brought her back to his house. The wretched man hoped to satisfy his lust.

But the one who, through great and evil temptations, tested Pharaoh concerning Sarah, Abraham’s wife, and preserved the chaste woman undefiled; and the one who struck the Sodomites with blindness when they had attacked incorporeal beings—who were present as guests—with insults and abuse: when he had struck this man blind regarding the girl’s virtuous way of life, he caused the prey to escape from his hands.

The man himself had entered the bedchamber, but she who was being guarded within immediately went out, vanished from his sight, and reached the dwelling she most desired. When the fool learned that he could not overcome one who had chosen God as her bridegroom, he was compelled to desist and no longer seek the woman who had been captured but had escaped by divine power.

As time passed, she fell into a severe illness. The disease was cancer, and as the breast became swollen, the pain also increased. Yet she called for the great Peter whenever the pain was most intense. She said that when that sacred voice was admitted into her ears, all the pain was lulled and she no longer felt any sensation of suffering. For this reason, whenever she summoned him, she received consolation more frequently. She said that throughout the entire time of his presence the pains completely withdrew.

But after she had contended in this way, someone escorted her from this life with praises signifying victory.

Again, when my mother, after giving birth to me, stood at death’s very doors, he came at the request of my maternal aunt and snatched her from the hands of death. She lay, as they say, with the physicians despairing, her relatives lamenting and awaiting the end, her eyes closed, suffering from a violent fever and recognizing none of those she knew.

When the man who had been endowed with apostolic speech and grace arrived, he said, “Peace to you, daughter”—for this was his greeting. At once, they say, she raised her eyelashes, looked at him with fixed eyes, and announced the fruit of his blessing.

When the chorus of women raised a howl—for anguish and joy of soul were mingled together and caused that outcry—the divine man ordered them all to become participants in her prayer. For he also said that Tabitha had recovered when the widows were lamenting and the great Peter offered their tears to God (Acts 9).

They prayed as he commanded, and they received what he had foretold. For when the prayer reached its end, the illness also reached its end. Sweat suddenly poured from her whole body, the fever was extinguished, and signs of health appeared.

God has performed such miracles in our own times as well through his benevolent servants.

The surface of his garments also worked in the same way as those of the most divine Paul. I have stated this without exaggeration, having truth in agreement with my words. For he divided his own belt into two parts—it was broad and long, woven from thick linen—and with one half he girded his own loins, while with the other he girded mine.

When my mother often placed it upon me while I was ill, and often upon my father as well, it drove away the disease. Indeed, she herself also often used this remedy for healing. When many of our acquaintances learned of this, they continually took the belt in order to bring help to the sick, and everywhere it displayed the working of his grace.

When a certain man had received it in this way, he deprived those who had given it of it, showing himself ungrateful toward those who had benefited him. Thus we were stripped of that gift.

When he had shone forth in this manner and illumined Antioch with his rays, he was taken away from the contests, awaiting the crown laid up for the victorious.

And I, who received his blessing while he was still alive, praying that I may enjoy it even now, shall bring this narrative to an end.

## CHAPTER X. THEODOSIUS

[Note: [Col. 0117B] Theodosius the hermit. His memory is recorded in the Menologion on 11 January, when the commemoration of another man’s natal day also occurs. That one is called the Coenobiarch, whereas this one is Antiochene. Laurentius de la Barre incorrectly wrote Nicephorus in the margin here; he is dealing with the other Theodosius, the Coenobiarch, who was younger and died during the reign of the emperor Justinian.]

Rosus is a town of Cilicia, on the right hand of one sailing into the Cilician Sea. To its east and south lies a high, spacious, shady mountain, which nourishes wild animals in its forests.

When the great and widely celebrated Theodosius found there a grove sloping toward the sea, he built a small dwelling and alone embraced the evangelical way of life. He was born in Antioch and distinguished by the nobility of his family; nevertheless, abandoning home, kindred, and everything else, he bought the most precious pearl, as I may say in evangelical language (Matt. 13).

It is unnecessary to speak to those who see his disciples and companions, and observe in them the same way of life, about his abstinence from food, his sleeping on the ground, or his wearing of sackcloth. Yet he pursued these practices with distinction, setting himself before those who were contending as an example.

To these practices he added an iron burden worn upon his neck, loins, and both hands. He also wore dirty hair that reached all the way to his feet and extended even farther; for that reason it was tied around his loins.

Using prayer and hymnody continually, he put to sleep desire, anger, arrogance, and the other beasts of the soul. Always increasing labor upon labor, he also pursued manual work: sometimes weaving the baskets and wickerwork known by those names; sometimes making small fields in the woodland [Note: [Col. 0117C] “Sometimes making small fields in the woodland.” The Menologion has: εἰργάζετο μικρὰς ἀρούρας ἐν τῇ νάπῃ, “he worked small plowed fields in the wooded valley.” Longus: “At times he prepared little gardens on the rock.” An arura is a definite measure of land. See the remarks on the Life of Saint Antony, chap. 2, no. 10, and the Onomasticon.], sowing seed and gathering from there as much as was sufficient for food.

As time passed, his fame spread everywhere. Many people hurried from many places, wishing to become companions of his dwelling, labor, and discipline. Receiving them, he led them into the same way of life.

It was possible to see some weaving sails, others making cloaks from skins, others fastening together wickerwork or baskets, and others cultivating the earth. Since the place was maritime, they also used a certain little boat which had been built for crossing over—called a *pontos*—to transport what had to be brought in and to export the work of those who lived together, while importing what was necessary.

He remembered the apostolic saying: “Working night and day, so that we might not be a burden to any of you” (2 Thess. 3); and: “These hands have supplied my needs and those of my companions” (Acts 20).

He himself worked and urged his companions to join bodily labor to the labors of the soul. For it is absurd that those who are nourished in secular life should support their sons and wives through toil and labor, and in addition pay taxes and have tribute exacted from them, offer first fruits to God, and, as far as they are able, relieve the poverty of beggars; while we should not seek through our labors what is necessary, even though we use cheap and modest food and cheap clothing, but should sit with folded hands and enjoy the labors of others.

Saying these and similar things, he urged them to work. At the appointed times he performed the divine offices prescribed everywhere; the intervening time he devoted to work.

He did not neglect the care of guests. He entrusted their provision to men adorned with gentleness and mildness of character and endowed with love toward their neighbor; he himself visited and inspected everything, examining whether each person was performing his duty according to the established rules.

As a result, his fame became so remarkable and celebrated that those who sailed, even when they were more than a thousand stadia away, invoked the God of Theodosius in danger and calmed the storm by calling upon Theodosius.

Even the bold and savage enemies who ravaged most of the East respected him. Who among those living in our inhabited world has not heard by report what was done at that time by those who were once called Solymi but are now called Isaurians?

Yet those who spared neither city nor village, and plundered and committed to the flames whatever they could seize, respected that philosophy. When they had asked only for bread and indicated that they wished him to pray for them, they left the monastery unharmed—not once only, but did this twice.

Nevertheless, the leaders of the churches feared that, through a love of money sent into those barbarians by the devil, that great light might be carried away captive. For it was likely that a great quantity of money would be sent from all who honored divine things in order to ransom him. They therefore persuaded him to withdraw to Antioch.

The barbarians had already captured two leaders of churches. They treated them with every kind of courtesy, but after receiving fourteen thousand gold pieces for both, they allowed them to return wherever they wished.

When he reached Antioch, he lived in a dwelling that he found near the river, and drew to himself all who knew how to gather such things.

While the impulse of my narrative carried me onward, I neglected to relate a miracle performed by that divine man—a miracle that many may perhaps regard as incredible, yet which remains to this very day, bearing witness through prayer and showing what grace and confidence before God this admirable man had attained.

A steep rock overhangs the monastery that he himself built. At first it was dry and completely without moisture. Upon it he made a water channel that descends from the summit to the monastery, as though he had power over the movement of the waters.

Filled with confidence in God and, as is likely, firmly believing that the Lord was well disposed toward him, possessing a faith upon which no doubt could fall, he climbed to the highest point of what is now the water channel before his companions had risen for their customary prayers. He prayed to God and, trusting in the one “who fulfills the desire of those who fear him” (Ps. 144), struck the rock with the staff upon which he leaned.

When it split open, water gushed forth like a river. Entering the monastery through the channel, abundantly supplying as much as was sufficient for every use, it flowed into the nearby sea. To this very day it is shown to be operating, through the Mosaic grace of the great Theodosius. This alone is sufficient to demonstrate the man’s confidence toward God.

After living in Antioch for a short time, he departed to the choirs of angels. His sacred body was carried through the middle of the city, adorned as though with golden crowns by that bier, while all the commanders and those holding the great offices entrusted to their faith came running together.

There was a great struggle over the bier, as everyone tried to carry it away and desired to receive blessing and benefit from it. Thus he was carried and placed in the church of the holy martyrs, where Julian, the illustrious athlete in piety, had also lived and competed and had used the same roof. The same tomb received him that had also received the divine and blessed Aphraates.

The admirable Helladius received the leadership of the flock. He had remained for sixty continuous years in those places and was then divinely chosen as bishop of the Cilicians, without abandoning his former philosophy and adding daily the labors of his episcopate to those earlier toils.

The blessed Romulus had also been his hearer, and was appointed leader of the great flock.

His community has remained to this very day, preserving the same way of life. Near the monastery there is a village called in Syriac Maratus.

Having brought this narrative to an end, I pray that I too may obtain his blessing.

## CHAPTER XI. ROMANUS

[Note: [Col. 0117C] Romanus. Theodoretus, book 4, chapter 26; and Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 41.]

The great Theodosius therefore departed from Antioch, competed in the mountains of Rosus, and returned to Antioch, where he ended his life in this manner (Theodoretus, *History*, book 4, chapter 26).

The divine Romanus, born and first raised at Rosus, displayed the first contests of virtue at Antioch. He pitched his tent outside the circuit of the city beside the mountain and lived throughout the whole period in another, very small dwelling.

Until old age he never used fire or the light of a lamp. His food was bread and salt, and his drink was water from a spring. His hair resembled that of the great Theodosius, and his garment was likewise iron.

He excelled in simplicity of character, gentleness, and moderation, and therefore emitted the radiance of divine grace. “Upon whom shall I look,” he says, “except upon the meek and quiet one, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). And again he said to his disciples: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). Again: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5).

This was also especially the distinction of Moses the lawgiver. “Moses was very meek,” it says, “more than all the men who were upon the earth” (Num. 12). The most holy Spirit also testified this concerning the prophet David: “Remember, O Lord, David, and all his meekness” (Ps. 131).

We have also learned concerning the patriarch Jacob that he was not pretentious, dwelling in a house (Gen. 25). Having gathered these virtues, as a bee gathers honey from divine meadows, he produced the honey of true philosophy.

Streams of great sweetness also flowed from him toward outsiders. Using a gentle and sweet voice with those who came to him, he offered many admonitions concerning love for the brethren, concord, and peace. By his mere appearance he made many people lovers of divine things.

Who would not have been extraordinarily amazed on seeing him physically afflicted, wearing long hair, carrying of his own will an enormous weight of iron, using a garment woven from hair, and taking only as much food as was sufficient to keep him from dying of hunger?

Alongside the magnitude and multitude of his labors there flourished in him a grace by which everyone was persuaded to admire and honor him. He often drove away difficult diseases from many people, and obtained children for many barren women.

Although he had received such power from the divine Spirit, he called himself poor and a beggar. All who continually came to him he filled, throughout his entire life, with benefit both by his appearance and by his speech.

When he too departed from here and was transferred to the angelic choir, he left behind a memory that was not buried with his body, but remains vigorous, blossoms, and bears fruit; it cannot be extinguished but endures forever, and is sufficient to help those who wish to be helped.

When I have thereby secured his blessing for myself, I shall recount the deeds of other athletes as I am able.

## CHAPTER XII. ZENO

[Note: [Col. 0117C] Zeno. This is the same man whose memory is recorded in the Menologion on 10 February. Theodoretus also writes about him in book 4 of the *History*, chapter 26; and Nicephorus in book 11, chapter 41.]

Not many people know the admirable Zeno; but those who know him cannot admire him according to his worth (Theodoretus, *History*, book 4, chapter 26).

After leaving behind great wealth in his homeland—which was Pontus—he drank, as he himself said, from the streams of the great Basil, who was his neighbor and irrigated the region of Cappadocia; and by that irrigation he produced worthy fruits.

As soon as the emperor Valens had been removed from the world, he laid aside his military belt. He had been enrolled among those who rapidly carried the emperor’s letters.

When he had come from the imperial court to a certain tomb—there are many on the mountain—situated near Antioch, he lived there alone, cleansing his soul, continually purifying its capacity for contemplation, continually grasping divine contemplation in vision, arranging the ascents of God in his heart, and desiring to receive wings like a dove and fly away into divine rest (Ps. 83; Ps. 54).

For this reason he possessed no bed, lamp, fire, pot, pitcher, little chest, book, or anything else. He was dressed in old rags. His shoes were of such a kind that they required straps, for the leather of their soles was torn and shredded.

He received the food he needed from one of his acquaintances. It was a single loaf, which supplied him for two days. He drew water from far away and carried it himself.

When someone once saw him carrying a load, he asked to relieve him of the labor. At first Zeno resisted, saying that he could not bring himself to drink water carried by another. When the man did not yield, Zeno gave him the jars—for he carried two in both hands. But after he had entered through the courtyard gate, he poured out and scattered the water, then ran back to the spring, confirming in deed what he had said.

When I too first climbed the mountain, desiring to see him [Note: [Col. 0117C] “Desiring to see him.” Sozomen also saw him, says Barreus, book 7, chapter 27. But that was another Zeno, ruler of the church of Majuma.], I saw him holding the jars in his hands.

Then I asked him where the dwelling of the admirable Zeno was. He said that he knew no monk called by that name. But when I conjectured that he himself was the man, I followed him, inferring this from the modesty of his speech.

After I entered through the doorway, I saw a couch made of hay and another mat spread over stones in such a way that those sitting upon it were not harmed by them.

After we had spoken at length about philosophy—for I asked questions, while he explained to us what we sought to know—and it became necessary for me to return home, I begged him to give me provisions for the journey in the form of a blessing.

He resisted, saying that it was right for us to fulfill the office of prayer and calling himself deprived, while calling us soldiers—for at that time I was reading the sacred books to the people of God.

When we pleaded our youth and immaturity—for at that time we were only beginning to grow a little down—and swore that we would not come again if compelled to do this, he was at last bent by our many entreaties. He did indeed offer an intercession to God, but then excused himself at length for having done so, saying that he had acted out of love and obedience. For, as we approached, we heard him praying.

Who could sufficiently admire, in proportion to the greatness of the matter, the modesty and moderation of this old man amid such profound philosophy? He had spent forty continuous years in monastic discipline. What praises could anyone offer equal to the magnitude of his achievement?

Although he possessed such riches of virtue, he came with the people to the church of God on Sunday as though he were in extreme poverty, listening to the divine discourses and lending his ears to the teachers. After sharing in the mystical table, he returned to that new dwelling, possessing no key or lock and leaving no guard.

It was completely inaccessible to sorcerers and sacred, since it contained only that single mat. He would receive one book from his acquaintances, read it completely, return it, and then receive another.

Although he had neither locks nor bars, he was guarded by heavenly grace. We learned this plainly through experience itself. When the Isaurians seized the fortress by ambush at night and then, in the morning, made raids as far as the side of the mountain, they cruelly stabbed many men and many women who were practicing the monastic life.

At that time, therefore, the divine man, seeing the slaughter of the others, caused their eyes to grow dim through prayer. Entering through the doorway, they did not see the entrance. As he said, calling truth to witness, he also clearly saw three young men driving away the entire band, while God openly displayed his grace toward him.

This is sufficient to teach what sort of life this divine man led and what sort of grace he obtained from God. Yet it is necessary to add this as well.

He was greatly distressed and troubled that his possessions had remained and had not been sold and distributed according to the evangelical law. The reason was the immaturity of his brothers. Since their money and property were held in common, he himself did not wish to return to his homeland for the purpose of division. The others, however, were afraid to sell their share of the possessions, lest buyers, moved by greed and cheating the brothers, bring disgrace upon them.

Turning these matters over in his mind, he postponed the sale for a long time. Later, after selling everything to one of his acquaintances, he distributed most of it. In the meantime, an illness that came upon him forced him to make arrangements concerning what remained.

He therefore summoned the bishop of the city—who was the great Alexander, the splendor of true religion, an exemplar of virtue, and an exact and accurate image of philosophy—and said:

“Come here, divine master. Be for me the best steward of these funds, distributing them according to divine ordinance, as though you were going to render an account of them to that Judge. I distributed the others with my own hand, assigning them as seemed best to me. I wished to administer the remainder in the same way; but since I am ordered to depart from this life, I appoint you their steward, since you are both a bishop and rightly govern the episcopate according to its laws.”

Thus he handed over the money as to God’s treasurer.

He himself lived no more than a year afterward [Note: [Col. 0117C] “Lived.” Sozomenus is an eyewitness who says that Zeno lived one hundred years, Barreus states above. But he is mistaken; as I have said, that was another Zeno.]. Then, like an Olympic victor, he withdrew from the barriers, having obtained glory not only from human beings but also from angels.

After I have prayed that he intercede with the Lord for me, I shall turn to another narrative.

## CHAPTER XIII. MACEDONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0117C] Macedonius the Barley-eater. His celebrated memory is recorded in the Greek Menologion on 24 January; translated into Latin, it can be found in Part 1 of the *Garden of the Saints* by our Raderus. Theodoretus writes about him in book 5 of the *History*, chapter 19; Nicephorus in book 12, chapter 43; and Damascenus in *Against Those Who Revile the Images*.]

Everyone in Phoenicia, Syria, and Cilicia knows Macedonius, surnamed Κριθοφάγος, that is, “barley-eater”—for this food gave him his surname. His neighbors and those living nearby also know him: some saw the miracles themselves, while others heard of them through the fame that celebrated them.

Yet not everyone knows everything. When some have learned one thing and others another, each rightly admires only what he knows.

Since I know more perfectly than others about this divine man—for many things moved me to go to him and to spend much time with him—I shall recount each matter as I am able.

I have followed this order in his case and placed his narrative after those of many others, not because he was inferior to them in virtue—for he was equal to the greatest and foremost—but because, having lived for a very long time, he reached the end of his life after those whom I have already mentioned.

Here, then, he had the mountain peaks as his wrestling ground and stadium—not settled in one place, but now laboring in this spot and now moving to another. He did this not because he found the places disagreeable, but because he avoided the crowds of those who came to him and flocked together from every direction. For forty-five continuous years he lived in this manner, using neither tent nor hut, but standing in a deep pit; hence some also called him Goubba. That name, if transferred from the Syriac language into Greek, signifies λάκκον, that is, “a pit” or “pond.” After that period, when he had grown old, he yielded to the entreaties of others and established a hut. Later, at the request of his companions, he also used little dwellings, though not his own but belonging to others. He spent twenty-five years continuously in a hut and in little dwellings, so that the period of his struggles amounted altogether to seventy years.

For food he used neither bread nor vegetables, but cleaned barley, moistened with water alone. My mother, [Col. 0067B] who was his close associate, supplied him with this food for a very long time. Once, when he had come to her while she was ill and had learned that she refused to be persuaded to take food appropriate to her illness—for she too had by then embraced the monastic discipline—he advised her to yield to the physicians and to regard that nourishment as medicine. “For,” he said, “it is taken not for indulgence but out of necessity. I too, as you know, have used barley alone for forty years; but when an illness came upon me on the day before yesterday, I ordered the man who lived with me to seek and bring me a little bread. For it came to my mind that, if I were to die, I would have to give an account of my death before the just Judge, as one who had fled from the contests and shrunk from the labors of service. Since death could be prevented by a little food, and I could thus remain in this life, laboring and afflicting myself and gathering the riches acquired through these things, I judged it preferable to die of hunger than to live in philosophy.”

Filled, therefore, with fear on this account, and wishing to dull the goads of his thought, he ordered bread to be requested, and ate what was brought. “And I instruct you,” he said, “to give me barley no longer, but bread.” From that tongue, therefore, wholly free from falsehood, we heard that he had eaten barley for forty years. These things are sufficient to show how vigorous the man was in monastic discipline and how laborious.

His integrity and simplicity of character we shall demonstrate by other examples. After the great Flavian had been ordained to shepherd God’s great flock, and had learned of the man’s virtue—for it was proclaimed and on everyone’s lips—he brought him down from the mountain’s summit, as though a charge concerning him had been brought before him. When the mystical sacrifice was about to be offered, he brought him to the altar and enrolled him among the priests. After the sacred service had ended, someone informed him of this—for he was entirely unaware of what had been done. At first he assailed everyone with curses and insults; then, taking his staff—for, owing to his old age, he usually walked leaning upon it—he pursued the bishop himself and all the others who were present. He thought that his ordination would deprive him both of the mountain’s summit and of the manner of life he desired. At that time some of his companions could scarcely calm him in his anger.

When the week had ended and the Lord’s festival day came again, the great Flavian again summoned him, asking him to share in the celebration with them. But he said to those who had come: “Were what happened not enough for you? Do you want to make me a presbyter again?” When they told him that the same ordination could not take place twice, he did not yield or come until the passage of time and his companions had taught him the truth. I know that many will think this story not especially remarkable; I have included it because I consider it worthy of remembrance, since from it one may sufficiently infer both the simplicity of his mind and the purity of his soul. To such people the Lord promised the kingdom of heaven: “Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like these children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVIII). Since, then, we have briefly shown the form and character of his soul, let us also display his confidence arising from virtue.

A certain military commander who delighted in hunting climbed the mountain to hunt. Dogs, soldiers, and everything suitable for the hunt followed him. When he saw a man at a distance and learned from those who were with him who he was, he immediately leapt down from his horse, approached him, addressed him, and asked what he was doing there. The other in turn asked him: “And what have you come here to do?”

When the commander replied, “To hunt,” he said: “And I am hunting my God: I desire to capture him and contemplate him, and I shall not cease this beautiful hunt.” When the commander heard this and, as was fitting, marveled, he withdrew.

Once, when a city had been driven into a frenzy by some evil demon and was raging against the emperor’s statues, certain men of the highest rank among the commanders arrived, carrying a sentence of destruction against the city. When he came down from the mountain, he detained both commanders as they approached in the marketplace. When they learned who he was, they leapt from their horses, grasped his hands and knees, and greeted him. But he ordered them to tell the emperor that he was a human being and possessed the same nature as those who had insulted him; that although anger ought to be measured according to nature, he had used anger without measure; and that, for the sake of his statues, he was killing images of God, and, for the bronze of statues, delivering bodies over to death. “For us,” he said, “to cast and fashion bronze figures again is easy and readily within our power; but you, even though you are emperor, cannot bring murdered bodies back to life. And why do I say bodies? You cannot even fashion a single hair.”

He said these things in the Syriac language. They heard them through an interpreter translating them into Greek, were terrified, and declared that they would convey the message to the emperor. I believe that everyone will acknowledge that these words were a gift of the divine Spirit. How else could a man who was entirely without learning, brought up in the countryside, living on mountain peaks, and displaying complete simplicity—one who had not even devoted himself to the divine utterances—have spoken in this way? Since I have thus shown both his spiritual wisdom and the confidence proper to the righteous—for “the righteous is bold as a lion” (Proverbs XXVIII)—I shall pass to his miracles.

The wife of a wealthy and noble man had fallen into a disease of gluttony. Some called the illness a demonic activity or affliction; others thought it a bodily weakness. Whatever the cause, it was as follows. They said that, although she ate thirty chickens in a day, she could not extinguish her appetite by satiety but desired still more. As her resources were thus being consumed, those concerned for her took pity on her and entreated that divine man. He came and prayed; after placing his right hand upon water, making the saving sign, and ordering her to drink, he cured the illness and so blunted that excessive appetite that thereafter a small portion of a chicken each day satisfied the amount she needed to eat. Thus that illness was cured.

When a certain girl was still confined to her bridal chamber and suddenly began to be tormented by an evil demon, her father ran to the divine man, praying, crying out, and asking that his daughter be healed. After praying, he ordered the demon to leave the girl immediately. The demon said that he had not entered her of his own accord but had been compelled by magical spells. He also named the person who had compelled him and said that the girl’s habit was the cause of the incantation. But when he had [lacuna] said this, the father could not restrain the force of his anger or wait for the girl to be healed. He went to the highest of all the magistrates, namely, the governor who ruled over several peoples, accused the man, and related the affair.

The accused was brought to trial. He denied the matter and called the accusation slander. The father cited no other witness than the demon who had served the incantation, and begged the judge to hasten to that divine man and receive his testimony. When the judge said that it was neither lawful nor just to hold an inquiry in a place of monastic discipline, the girl’s father declared that he would bring Macedonius to court; running to him, he persuaded him and led him there. The judge sat outside the court and was not a judge but a spectator. For the great Macedonius [Col. 0069D] performed the office of judge, exercising the power that dwelt within him.

When he ordered the demon to utter his customary lie, but instead to recount the entire tragedy with complete truth, the demon, compelled by the greatest necessity, pointed out both the man who had used magical incantations to inflict this power upon him and the maidservant through whom that potion had been given to the girl. When, compelled by others, he was preparing to tell of other deeds he had committed—burning one man’s house, killing another’s animals, and injuring someone else in another way—the man of God ordered him to be silent and immediately to withdraw far from the girl and the city. Like one obeying the law of the Lord, he did what he had been ordered to do and quickly fled.

Thus, while the divine man had freed the girl from her frenzy, he also rescued that wretched man from the accusation and prevented the judge from imposing the death penalty upon him. He said that it was not lawful for him to be sentenced to death on account of the things proved through the demon, but that salvation should instead be granted to him through repentance. These things are sufficient to show the abundance of divine power that had been given to him, but I shall relate other examples as well.

A woman born of noble family and exceedingly wealthy—her name was Assyria—was deranged in mind and recognized no one among her household; she could not bear to take food or drink. For a very long time she was constantly delirious. Some said that this was a demonic affliction and activity; physicians said that it was a disease of the brain. When every medical skill had been exhausted and no help came from it, her husband, Abrodianus, a man who belonged to the magistrates and possessed great dignity, ran to that divine man, described his wife’s illness, and begged that she might obtain healing.

The divine man yielded, came to the house, and offered fervent and intense prayer to God. When the prayer was complete, he ordered water to be brought, made the figure of the saving sign, and ordered her to drink. The physicians objected, on the grounds that drinking cold water would worsen the illness. But once the whole group of them had been expelled, he offered the woman the drink. As soon as she drank, she returned to herself, was entirely freed from the illness, recognized the divine man, asked to take his right hand, placed it upon her eyes, brought it to her mouth, and thereafter always remained in possession of her senses.

While he was embracing that manner of life in the mountains, a shepherd searching for lost sheep came to the place where the man of God was. It was deep night, and much snow had fallen. He saw, as he himself said, a pyre burning around him and two men dressed in white supplying fuel to the fire. For, bringing him courage of spirit, divine assistance attended him.

He also shared in the prophetic gift. And when a certain commander came to him, distinguished for piety and true religion—for who does not know the virtue of Lupicianus?—he said that he was worried about certain men who were bringing necessities to him by sea from the royal city. More than fifty [Col. 0070D] days had passed since they had set out from the harbor, and they had heard nothing about them. Without hesitation he said: “One ship, my friend, has perished; the other will enter the harbor of Seleucia tomorrow.” He had heard this divine voice speak; experience then taught him the truth of what had been said.

To omit other matters, I shall relate what concerns us ourselves. When my mother had lived together with my father for thirteen years, she had not become the mother of children; she was barren, being prevented by nature from bearing fruit. She herself did not take this very hard, for, being instructed in divine matters, she believed that it was beneficial. My father, however, was greatly distressed because he lacked children, and running about everywhere, he asked the servants of God to request children for him from God. Others promised that they would pray to God and ordered him to be content with God’s will.

This divine man openly declared that he would ask one thing from the Maker of all and promised that he would receive what he requested. When three years had passed and the promise had not been fulfilled, my father again approached him, demanding the promised gift. He ordered that his wife be sent to him. When my mother came, the divine man said that he would indeed make the request, that she would receive a son, and that he must be dedicated to the one who had given him. When my mother asked only that he receive salvation of soul and be freed from Gehenna, he said: “In addition to this, the generous and munificent God will give you a son. For to those who ask purely and sincerely, he grants their requests twofold.”

My mother returned from there bearing the blessing of the promise. In the fourth year after the promise she conceived and carried a child in her womb, and she came to the divine man, displaying the sheaves of the blessing. In the fifth month after conception, there was danger of miscarriage. She again sent to her new Elisha—for illness prevented her from coming to him—and reminded him that she had not wished to become the mother of children, and brought his promises forward.

When he saw her approaching from a distance, he recognized her and indicated the reason for her coming; for during the night the Lord had shown him both the illness and the cure. Taking his staff, he came, leaning upon it. When he had entered the house and, as was his custom, had offered the greeting of peace, he said: “Take courage and do not fear. The one who gave the gift will not take it away unless you break the agreement. You promised that you would return to him the one who would be given and consecrate him to the divine ministry.”

“My wish and desire,” my mother replied, “are indeed as you say. For I consider even the most imperfect fetus preferable to raising a son estranged from God.”

When he had taken water and blessed it, the divine man said: “Drink this water, then, and you will feel divine assistance.” She drank as he had ordered and escaped the danger of miscarriage. These are the miracles of our Elisha.

I often received his blessing and instruction. When he encouraged me, he would frequently say: “You were born, my son, amid many labors. For many nights I continually asked God for this one thing: that your parents might become what they were called when you were born. See, therefore, that you live a life worthy of these labors, since, before you were born, you were dedicated through promises. What is dedicated to God is revered by everyone and must not be handled by the common crowd. It is therefore fitting that you also admit no evil impulses of the soul, but do and think only those things that please God, the lawgiver of virtue.”

The divine man continually urged these things upon me. I remember what he told me, and I have been taught the divine gift. Since I do not demonstrate by my deeds the things he urged upon me, I ask that through his prayers I may obtain divine assistance and spend the remainder of my life according to his instructions. What sort of man he was, then, and through what labors he drew divine grace, these things too are sufficient for instruction.

Even in this world his death received an honor worthy of his labors. All alike—citizens and foreigners, and those entrusted with the administration of the great magistracies—carried that sacred bier upon their shoulders and conveyed it to the church of the martyrs renowned for victory. Together with the holy men Aphraates and Theodosius, they laid down that holy and God-beloved body. His glory remained such that it could not be extinguished. Now, bringing our narrative to an end, we receive from it the good fragrance that can be drawn from the story.

## CHAPTER XIV. MAESYMAS

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Maesimas. I find mention of him only in the Greek Menaea, 23 January, where he is called Μαυσιμᾶς Σύρος, “Mausimas the Syrian,” which our Rader translated from the Greek in Part I of the *Garden of the Saints*.]

We know that many other lights of piety and true religion also shone in the city of Antioch—Severus the Great, Peter the Egyptian, Eutyches, Cyril, Moses, and Malchus [Note: [Col. 0117D] Malchus. Theodoret also mentions him, *History*, Book IV, chapter 26; perhaps the Menaea, 23 November.]—and that many others entered upon the same path. But if we attempted to write down all the deeds performed by everyone during their lives, all our time would not suffice, especially since the reading of the lives of very many people brings satiety to many. From those whose lives have been written, therefore, let them form an understanding of the lives of those who have been omitted, and pursue them with praise, imitate them, and derive benefit. I shall now pass to the meadows of Cyrus and, as far as I can, display the beauty of the fragrant and lovely flowers that were in them.

There was a certain Maesymas in the times before ours, Syrian in speech, brought up in the countryside, and one who displayed every kind of virtue. When he had become renowned in the solitary life, he was entrusted with the care of a certain village. Offering sacrifice and shepherding God’s sheep, he both said and did what the divine law commanded.

They say that he often changed neither tunic nor hair shirt, but by sewing a few patches over the tears that appeared in them, he provided this remedy for his old age. He cared for guests and the poor with such eager goodwill that he opened his doors to everyone who came. For he is said to have had two jars, one of grain and the other of oil. From these he continually supplied all who were in need; yet he always had them full, through the blessing given to the widow of Zarephath and poured into those jars. The Lord himself pours out all riches upon all who call upon him. Just as he commanded her jar and her measure to overflow, providing handfuls of seed for hospitality, so he also supplied this admirable man with provision corresponding equally to the eagerness of his spirit.

Moreover, he received from God, the ruler of all, great grace for performing miracles as well. I shall mention one or two miracles and omit the rest, since I am eager to come to others.

A woman distinguished both by birth and by faith presented her son, who had fallen gravely ill—he was still very young—to many physicians. When medical skill was overcome, and the physicians had despaired and openly declared that the boy would die, the woman did not abandon the better hope. Imitating the Shunammite woman, she placed a litter upon mules. After placing herself and the boy upon it, she reached the divine man. Lamenting and displaying a mother’s natural affection, she begged him to bring help.

He took the boy in his hands, brought him near the base of the altar, and lay prostrate, asking the physician of souls and bodies. Having received her petition, he restored her son to her in good health. I heard this from the woman who had witnessed the miracle and received the boy’s healing.

They also say that the lord of that village came to him. He was Latoius, who held the leading position in the Antiochene senate but was held in the darkness of impiety. He demanded the produce from the farmers more harshly than was proper. The divine man advised him to show clemency and spoke to him about mercy. But he remained unmoved, and learned through experience the harm that followed from his disobedience.

When he had to depart, and the carriage was ready, he sat down and ordered the driver to urge on the mules. They pulled with all their strength, straining and attempting to carry away the carriage pole; but the wheels appeared to be fastened with iron and lead. When a crowd of peasants also tried to move the wheels with levers and accomplished nothing, one of Latoius’s friends who sat beside him explained the cause, saying that the old priest had cursed him and that he ought to appease him and make him favorable.

Leaping down from the carriage, he became a suppliant before the man whom he had previously rejected. Falling at his feet and embracing his filthy rags, he begged him to restrain his anger. When the divine man accepted his prayers and offered them to the Lord, he loosened the unseen bonds of the wheels and caused the vehicle to be carried along as usual.

Many other things of this kind are also related about that divine man. From these things too it may be understood that dwelling in towns and villages causes no harm to those who wish to practice philosophy. For he, and those like him who care for the worship of God, showed that even those who live amid the midst of human crowds can attain the very summit of virtue.

[Col. 0073D] Would that I might be lifted up at least a little toward that summit, assisted by their prayers.

## CHAPTER XV. ACEPSIMAS

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Acepsimas. Greek Menologion, 3 November: “The nativity of Saint Acepsimas, who under Theodosius the Great shut himself up in a cell, where he spent sixty years, seeing and speaking with no one, but devoting himself to himself and to God, and finding all consolation. After performing many miracles, he rested in peace.” Concerning him, the Menaea also give a fuller account on the same day. Theodoretus, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 26; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 41.]

Acepsimas lived at the same time, and his fame spread widely throughout the East (Theodoretus, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 26). After shutting himself up in a little dwelling, he spent sixty years there, neither seeing nor speaking, but turned inward upon himself and apprehending God in contemplation. From there he received all consolation, in accordance with the prophecy that says: “Delight in the Lord, and pray to him, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Psalm XXXVI).

Extending his hand through a small opening, he received the nourishment that was brought to him. The opening had not been dug so that it ran directly inward—for it was not to be opposite those who wished to see him—but was oblique and constructed like a curved line. The food brought to him was lentils moistened with water. Once a week, at night, he went out and drew from a nearby spring as much water as was sufficient.

On one occasion, a shepherd who was grazing sheep at a distance saw him moving in the darkness and supposed that he was a wolf. For the man walked bent over, as though weighed down by a heavy iron burden. The shepherd swung his sling as if he were about to hurl a stone. When his hand remained motionless for a long time and he could not release the stone until the divine man had returned after drawing water, he recognized his error. After dawn he came to the gymnasium of virtue, related what had happened, and asked forgiveness. He received remission of his offense—not through an audible voice, but by understanding from the movement of the hands that reconciliation had been granted.

Another man, indulging in a malicious desire to investigate and wishing to know what Acepsimas did throughout the whole of his life, dared to climb a plane tree situated beside the opening. He immediately experienced the fruits of his boldness. The middle part of his body down to his feet dried up, and he became a suppliant, accusing himself of his sin. Acepsimas, however, having the plane tree cut down, first indicated that healing would follow. So that no one else who did the same thing might suffer similar punishment, he ordered the tree to be cut down; and the cutting of the tree was followed also by the removal of the punishment. Such was the courage and endurance of this divine man; from the contest-master, however, he received such grace.

[Col. 0074C] When he was preparing to depart from this life, he foretold that he would meet the end of his life after fifty days. He received everyone who wished to see him. When the bishop of the church also came, he urged him to accept the yoke of the presbyterate.

“I know,” he said, “father, both the height of your philosophy and how great my poverty is. But since the administration of the episcopate has been entrusted to me, I ordain by laying on hands from this office, not from that of philosophy. Accept, therefore,” he said, “the gift of the priesthood, with my right hand ministering and the grace of the most holy Spirit supplying it.”

A few days later, Acepsimas, who was about to depart from this life, is said to have replied: “I shall not contend about this. If I were going to live longer, I would certainly have fled this heavy and terrible burden of the priesthood, fearing the account that must be rendered for the deposit entrusted to me. But since I shall depart from here so soon, leaving behind the things that are here, I obey the commands without reluctance.”

Immediately, with no one leading him, he knelt and awaited grace, while the other laid his hand upon him and ministered the Spirit. After receiving the priesthood, he lived only a few days; then he exchanged this life for life, receiving, in place of a life subject to many cares, one free from old age and anxiety.

When everyone wanted to seize the body, each intending to carry it away to his own village, someone ended the dispute by invoking an oath sworn by the saint. He said that the saint had bound him by oath to bury him in that place. Thus, even after death, the citizens of heaven cared for frugality and simplicity. When alive, they never allowed anything to make them high-minded; when dead, they did not embrace human honor, but transferred all their love to the bridegroom, like chaste women who strive to be loved and praised by their husbands alone and disdain the praise of others.

For this reason the bridegroom makes them famous and distinguished even against their will, and from his overflowing abundance bestows upon them the glory of men. For when someone pursues divine things and seeks heavenly things, he adds many other things to them as well, granting requests in multiplied measure. He also said this when laying down laws: “Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke XII). And again: “Whoever has left father and mother, brother and children for the sake of my Gospel will receive a hundredfold even in this age, and in the future will be heir to eternal life.” He both said and did these things (Matthew XIX).

May he also assist us, instructed by their word and deed and relying upon their prayers, to reach, as our goal, the prize of the heavenly calling that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## CHAPTER XVI. MARO

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Maro. Concerning him in the Greek Menaea, 14 February; later, in chapter 24, he is called Marum. Concerning him also, says de la Barre, Sozomenus, Book VI, chapter 34, and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 41, call him Marosas. But that man is different from Maron. Here you have Marosa in chapter 4, in Eusebius.]

After this I shall remember Maron, for he too adorned the divine choir of the saints. Embracing the life lived under the open sky, he occupied a certain summit that had once been honored by those who were impious. After consecrating to God the temple of demons that stood there, he remained in that place, fixing there a small tent, though he rarely used it.

He did not merely employ the customary labors but devised others as well, accumulating the riches of philosophy. The contest-master measured out grace to him according to his labors. For the generous and munificent God gave him the gift of healing in such abundance that his fame spread to every region, drew everyone to him from all directions, [Col. 0075D] and demonstrated by experience that the report was true. One could see fevers extinguished by the dew of blessing, chills cease, demons flee, and diseases of every kind cured by a single remedy. Physicians provide each illness with an appropriate medicine, but the prayer of the saints is a common remedy for every disease.

He not only healed bodily illnesses but also supplied appropriate treatment for souls: curing one man’s avarice, another’s anger; giving one instruction in moderation and another discipline in justice; chastening one person’s intemperance and awakening another’s dullness. By practicing this agriculture, he produced many plants of philosophy and planted for God the garden that now flourishes in the region of Cyrus. The great James is the work of this planting, to whom someone might apply the prophetic utterance: “He shall multiply like the cedar that is in Lebanon” (Psalm XCI); [Col. 0076A] and so too all the others, whom, God willing, I shall mention individually.

While thus caring for divine agriculture and treating souls and bodies alike, he suffered a slight illness, so that we might learn both the weakness of nature and the strength of his spirit, and then departed this life.

A fierce dispute arose among the neighboring people over his body. A certain nearby village [Note: [Col. 0118A] “A certain nearby village.” Theodoretus here, chapter 24: “He asked to be placed in the same tomb also; but those who seized that sacred body did not permit it.”], crowded with people, arrived with its entire population assembled, routed and scattered the others, and seized that greatly desired treasure. They built a magnificent church and to this day enjoy the benefit received from him, honoring the illustrious victor with a public and celebrated festival.

Even while absent, we too enjoy his blessing, [Col. 0076B] for his memory is sufficient for us in place of a monument.

## CHAPTER XVII. ABRAAMES

[Note: [Col. 0118A] Abraames. The Menaea, 14 February, briefly recount his deeds. Concerning him also, Theodoretus, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 26; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 41.]

It is not lawful to omit the memory of the admirable Abraames on the pretext that, after the monastic life, he became an ornament to the episcopal see (Theodoretus, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 26). Indeed, he is certainly all the more worthy of remembrance for this reason: although compelled to change his mode of life, he did not change the life itself. After passing from the hardship of monastic discipline and being surrounded at once by monastic labors and episcopal cares, he completed the course of his life.

He too was a fruit of the region of Cyrus. Born and raised there, he gathered the riches of monastic virtue. Those who lived with him say that, by keeping vigil, standing, and fasting, he so subdued his body that for a very long time he remained immobile, utterly unable to walk. But when divine providence freed him from that weakness, he wished to endure grave dangers for the sake of divine grace.

He came to Lebanon after learning that a certain village was held in the great darkness of impiety. Concealing his identity and adopting the appearance of a merchant, he arrived with those who accompanied him, carrying baskets as though he intended to buy nuts—for this was the village’s principal produce. After renting a house and advancing its owners a certain sum of money, he rested for three or four days. Then, little by little, he undertook his divine ministry, using a moderate voice.

When they sensed the psalmody, the herald shouted and summoned everyone. Men, boys, and women gathered together; then, breaking through the outer doors, they piled up a great quantity of dust from above and cast it down upon them. When they saw that the monks were being suffocated and buried, and that they neither wished to do nor say anything else but only offer prayers to God, they abandoned their madness at the elders’ urging.

Afterward, when the doors had been opened and they had dragged the monks out from beneath the heap, they ordered them to leave immediately. At that very time, however, tax collectors arrived, compelling them to pay their taxes. They bound some of them and subjected others to insulting beatings. But that holy man, remembering none of the things that had been done to them, imitating the Lord who, while affixed to the cross, cared for those who had done this [Col. 0077A], prayed that the tax collectors would exact the payment with moderation and clemency.

When they demanded guarantors, he voluntarily undertook the guarantee and promised that within a few days he would pay one hundred gold pieces. The men who had inflicted those grievous acts upon them, greatly astonished at his kindness, asked pardon for what they had dared to do and begged him to become their governor. For the village had no master: they themselves were both farmers and landowners.

When he had come to the city—for its name is Emesa—and had found some acquaintances, he borrowed the one hundred gold pieces. Then he returned to the village and, on the appointed day, fulfilled his promise. When they saw his zeal in this matter, they pressed him still more earnestly. He promised that he would do so if they would promise to build a church. They asked him to begin at once and led the blessed man about, pointing out the more suitable locations. One praised this place, another that one. When he had chosen the better site and laid the foundations, he placed a roof upon it in a short time. When the building was completed, he ordered them to admit a priest.

When they replied that they would choose no one else and begged him to be both their father and their shepherd, he accepted the grace of priesthood. After living among them for three years and guiding them nobly toward divine things, he arranged for one of those who had been with them to be appointed in his place, and returned to his monastic dwelling.

And lest, by recounting everything about him, I should make my narrative too long: after he had shone forth in these matters, he became bishop of Carrhae. [Col. 0077C] That city had been surrounded by the drunkenness of impiety and had given itself over to the revelry of demons. But when it was deemed worthy of this man’s cultivation and received the fire of his teaching, it remained free from its former thorns and now produces an abundant harvest of the Spirit, offering God sheaves of ripened grain.

Yet the holy man did not cultivate this field without labor. Employing countless exertions and imitating the art of those who treat bodies, he brought about this healing: at times applying sweet encouragement, at times using harsh medicines, and sometimes even cauterizing and cutting. The lights of his life, together with his teaching and his other diligence, also supported him; enlightened by these, the people both listened to what was said and willingly accepted what was done. [Col. 0077D]

Throughout the entire time that he was bishop, bread was superfluous to him, water also unnecessary, a bed useless, and the use of fire needless. At night he completed forty hymns, which they recite by speaking and answering one another, doubling the number of the intervening prayers. He spent the rest of the night sitting on his seat, allowing his eyelids a little rest.

Now, “man does not live by bread alone,” said Moses, the beholder of God (Deut. VIII); and the Lord also remembered this village when he rejected the devil’s temptation (Matt. IV). But we learn from no passage of divine Scripture that one can live without water. [Col. 0078A] Indeed, that great Elijah first drank water from the brook, and afterward, when he had gone to the widow of Zarephath, he ordered water to be brought to him first, and then bread.

But this admirable man, throughout the whole time of his episcopate, ate neither bread, nor pulses, nor vegetables that had been brought near to fire. Nor did he drink water, which those who seemed knowledgeable about such matters considered, because of its use, to be the foremost of the elements. Instead, he regarded lettuces, endives, celery, and similar things as both food and drink, showing the arts of bakers and cooks to be superfluous. In autumn, fruits supplied him with the same nourishment. He took these after the evening office.

Although he consumed his body with such labors, he was insatiable in caring for others. When guests arrived, he was entirely prepared for them: excellent and choice bread was offered, together with fragrant wine, fish, vegetables, and whatever accompanies these foods. Moreover, at midday he himself sat beside those who were dining, offering each person portions of what had been set out, giving each one cups, and ordering them to drink. In this he imitated the patriarch of the same name as himself, who served his guests but did not dine with them.

During the day he attended the tribunals of those who quarreled and disputed with one another. He persuaded some to be reconciled among themselves, while he compelled others who did not obey gentle and mild instruction. No unjust man withdrew after gaining victory through his audacity over a just man. For he always added a portion to the one who had been wronged, making him unassailable and superior to the one who wished to commit the wrong. He was like an excellent physician who constantly restrains those humors that overflow and ensures equality among the constituent elements. [Col. 0078C]

The emperor also desired to see him—for report, which readily conveys everything good and bad, had brought news of him—and summoned him to his presence. When he came, the emperor greeted and received him, and considered that rustic cilicium more excellent than his own purple. The whole chorus of queens even took his hand and embraced his knees, begging the man who could not even understand the Greek language. So evidently philosophy appears to kings and to all human beings to be a thing worthy of honor and reverence. [Col. 0078D]

Indeed, when those who love and follow him have died, they attain even greater glory. This can be learned from many others as well, but especially from what happened to this holy man. After he died and the emperor learned of it, he wished to place him in some sacred church. But when he understood that it was pious and honorable for the shepherd’s body to be restored to the flocks, he himself led the procession, with the chorus of queens following, together with all the magistrates, the people governed by them, the soldiers, and the private citizens.

The city of Antioch received him with such eagerness, as did the cities that lay along the route, until the procession reached that great river. At the bank of the Euphrates [Col. 0079A], citizens came running, as did visitors and peasants; even those from neighboring regions hastened to partake of the blessing.

Many lictors followed the bier, frightening and beating those who tried to uncover the body and take pieces of cloth from it. One could hear some singing psalms and others lamenting. One woman, mourning him, called him governor; another, nourisher; another, shepherd and teacher. One, weeping, named him father; another, helper and guardian. Amid such praises and lamentations, they committed that holy and sacred body to the grave.

I, however, admiring the fact that, although he had changed the discipline of his life, he had not changed his life itself in any respect, and that, while he was bishop, he had not embraced a relaxed and unrestrained manner of living but had increased the labors of monastic discipline, included him in my History of the Monks. Nor did I depart from the order that pleased him, desiring also to receive a blessing from him.

## CHAPTER XVIII. EUSEBIUS

[Note: Eusebius. Concerning him, see the Menaea, 15 February. Theodoret and Nicephorus refer to him in the place already cited. De la Barre writes in the margin here, “Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 33.” But that author is speaking of Eusebius, who lived at Carrhae, whereas here the subject is the man who lived at Asicha.]

After the holy men already mentioned, I shall add the great Eusebius, who died not long ago (Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, Book IV, chapter 26). Having lived many years, he endured a labor equal to the time, and at the same time chose a virtue equal to the labor. He derived manifold profit from it, for the distributor of prizes surpasses the contests in the greatness of his rewards.

At first, then, he entrusted his care to the faith of others and was led wherever they led him. They too were holy men, athletes of virtue and practitioners of ascetic discipline. After spending some time with them and receiving a sound and proper knowledge of philosophy, he embraced the monastic life. Having taken possession of a ridge of a mountain—for a very large village called Asicha lies beneath it—he merely dug a trench, using stones not even joined with mud [Col. 0079C].

[Note: Stones not even joined with mud. That is, dry-stone construction (*xerolithoi*). See the Life of Simeon Stylites, chapter 5, no. 8.]

He spent the rest of his life in the open air, afflicting himself, clothed in a garment of skins and nourishing himself on chickpeas and beans soaked in water. At times he also ate dried figs, thus making some sort of effort to sustain the weakness of his body.

When he reached extreme old age and had lost most of his teeth, he changed neither his food nor his dwelling. Even when he was frozen in winter and scorched in summer, he bravely endured the contrary conditions of the air. His face was wrinkled and all the members of his body dried up.

He so consumed his body with countless labors that not even a belt remained around his waist; it fell downward, since there was nothing to prevent it. His buttocks and hips had been worn away, and so they offered the belt an easy descent toward the lower parts. He therefore sewed the belt to his tunic, devising this means of keeping it in place.

He found it burdensome to associate with many people. Since he continually grasped divine contemplation through vision, he did not wish to withdraw his mind from it. Yet, although he possessed such intense love, he allowed some acquaintances to remove what blocked the doorway [Col. 0080A] and enter. After giving them instruction from the divine utterances, he ordered them, when they departed, to replace the mud on the door.

But when he considered it altogether preferable to avoid intercourse even with a few people, he blocked the entrance entirely by placing a very large stone against the door. Through a certain trench he spoke with a few close associates, though he himself was not seen. He had arranged matters in this way. From there he also received that small amount of nourishment.

When he had again denied conversation with everyone else, he alone honored me with that sweet and God-pleasing voice, and often detained me when I wished to leave, discussing heavenly matters with me. When many people came to him seeking the blessing they desired, and he found their tumult burdensome, he considered neither his old age nor the weakness that pressed upon him [Col. 0080B]. He leapt across the trench, which even the strong could not easily cross if they wished to do so, and, arriving at a nearby community of monks, dug another small trench beside the corner of the wall and continued his customary contests.

The superior of this community, a man filled with every virtue, said that after eating fifteen dried figs Eusebius spent seven weeks in holy fasting. He undertook this contest when he had lived more than ninety years and was afflicted with indescribable weakness. But the eagerness of his spirit overcame his weakness, and love of God made everything easy and manageable. Surrounded by such streams of sweat, he reached the finish of his course, seeing the distributor of prizes and longing for the crown.

[Col. 0080C] I pray that I may obtain the intercession that I have enjoyed up to this point, while he was still alive. For I believe that he lives and possesses a purer confidence before God.

## CHAPTER XIX. SALAMANUS

[Note: Salamanus. He is mentioned in the Menaea on 17 February, where he is said to have originated from the village of Persana, which here is Capersana. The same Menaea, on 23 January, also mention him, with the addition *ἡσυχιαστοῦ* (*hesychastou*), “of the peaceful” or “of the quiet”; you will find this translated into Latin in the first part of our Rader’s *Garden of the Saints*.
