I consider him a different Salamanus from the one who lived in Palestine, concerning whom Sozomen speaks in Book VI, chapter 32, and Nicephorus in Book XI, chapter 39. Nor was the testimony of these authors correctly written in the margin here by Laurent de la Barre.]

Judging that I would do violence to virtue if I failed to make the life of the admirable Salamanus known to posterity and neglected it by burying it in oblivion, I shall give the account in summary. There is a village west of the Euphrates, overlooking the riverbank itself, called Capersana. Born there, and embracing a life of quiet, he found a small house in the village opposite and shut himself inside it, leaving neither door nor window.

Once a year he dug the earth and obtained nourishment for the entire year, never speaking to anyone. He persisted in doing this not for a short time but for a very long period.

The bishop of the city to which the village belonged, having learned of the man’s virtue, approached him, wishing to confer the priesthood upon him. He dug through part of the little house and entered; he laid his hand upon him, performed a prayer, and repeatedly spoke to him, announcing the grace that had come to him. When he heard no voice, he departed, ordering that the opening be built up again.

At another time, the inhabitants of the village from which Salamanus had come crossed the river by night and broke through the house. They took him—he neither resisted nor gave orders—and carried him away to their village. After constructing a similar little house for him in the east, they immediately shut him inside it. There likewise he practiced quiet, speaking with no one.

A few days later, the inhabitants of the village opposite again attacked by night and broke through the house. They took him away to their own village, although he neither opposed them nor urged them to let him remain, and did not depart with any particular eagerness or cheerfulness.

Thus he made himself wholly dead to the world, truly speaking that apostolic saying: “I have been crucified with Christ. Yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in Christ, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Gal. II). Such was this man also. These details are sufficient to display the whole discipline of his life.

[Col. 0081B] Now, after receiving a blessing from him also, I shall move on to another.

## CHAPTER XX. MARIS

[Note: Maris. I find nothing concerning him. There is another Mares in the Menaea, on 27 March, together with the martyrs Baraches and Jonah. There is also another bishop in Sozomen and Nicephorus.]

There is a village of Homeros that we call Netis. The holy Maris built a small house there and remained shut inside it for thirty-seven years. From the nearby mountain it received a great deal of dampness, and in winter certain drops of water also seeped into it.

The extent of the harm this causes to bodies is known both to townspeople and to peasants, for even those who live in the fields plainly experience the illnesses that arise from it. Yet not even this persuaded that sacred head to change his little house. He remained there courageously [Col. 0081C] and steadfastly until he completed his course.

Moreover, he had spent his earlier life in the labors of virtue. Thus he preserved chastity in both body and soul. He himself clearly disclosed this to me, teaching that his body had remained whole and undefiled, as it had emerged from his mother’s womb. This was despite the fact that, when he was a young man, he had celebrated many martyr feasts and had charmed the people with the excellence of his voice. For he persisted in singing psalms for a very long time and possessed remarkable bodily beauty.

Yet neither his physical appearance, nor the brilliance of his voice, nor the association he had with many people caused any harm to the beauty of his soul. While living, he cared for his soul in the same manner as those who are enclosed. He also increased his virtue through the labors he endured in confinement. [Col. 0081D]

I often enjoyed his company. He ordered the door to be opened for me; indeed, he embraced me when I came and spoke at length and expansively about philosophy.

He was also distinguished by simplicity and utterly avoided varied and elaborate ways of life. He loved poverty more than the greatest abundance. At ninety years of age he wore garments woven from goat’s wool. Bread and a little salt supplied his nourishment.

After longing for a long time to see the spiritual and mystical sacrifice offered, he asked that the divine gift be celebrated there. I gladly complied. I ordered the sacred vessels to be brought—for the village was not far away—and, using the deacons’ hands in place of an altar, I offered the mystical, divine, and saving sacrifice.

He was filled with every spiritual delight and said that he believed he was seeing heaven; he declared that he had never experienced such joy.

Since I was greatly loved by him, I thought I would wrong both him, if I failed to praise him even after his death, and others, if I did not present this excellent philosophy to them for imitation. Now, after praying that I may obtain his help, I shall bring my narrative to an end.

## CHAPTER XXI. JACOBUS

[Note: Jacobus. Concerning him, see the *Menologion*, 26 November; also the *Menaea*, 26 November, at considerable length, translated by our Rader in the first part of the *Garden of the Saints*. Nicephorus also speaks of him in Book XV, chapter 22, and calls him Nisibenus. I fear that he is mistaken, as he is mistaken regarding the punishment inflicted on the shameless girls, which he says was inflicted by this man, although, as we saw above in chapter 1, it was inflicted by the elder Nisibenus. He may be called Hypaethrius—“the Open-Air One”—to distinguish him from Nisibenus and from another Jacobus the hermit, discussed below in chapter 25; for the text says that he lived in the open air. Evagrius also speaks of him in Book II, chapter 9, where he calls him Jacobus the Syrian and asserts that the emperor Leo sent him letters. Baronius places this event in the second year of Leo, that is, in the year of Christ 458.]

Since we have reviewed the contests of those athletes of virtue who have already been declared victors, recounting in summary both the labors they undertook in meditation and the exertions they endured in their contests, as well as their victories, far the most renowned and distinguished [Col. 0082B], let us now write down the disciplines of those who are still alive, who are contending magnificently and striving to surpass their predecessors in exertion, and let us leave posterity a useful memorial. For just as the discipline of the lives of the holy men who formerly shone forth brought the greatest benefit to posterity, so their narratives will become examples for those who come after us.

I shall begin with the great Jacobus. He is prior to the others both in time and in labor, and those who have imitated him perform things admirable and beyond expectation. Somehow, I do not know how, it has happened that this is the first name both among those who have departed this life and among those who are still alive.

For when I narrated their manner of life, I began with that divine Jacobus who routed the Persian army by his prayers. When the circuit of the city walls had fallen, he did not allow the city to be captured but forced the enemy to flee, having sent against them an army of flies and gnats [Col. 0082C].

[Note: An army of flies and gnats. Above, chapter 1, in the account of Jacobus Nisibenus: “a cloud of gnats and mosquitoes.”]

Since the man who bears a similar name is also similar in character, let him be first in the order of those athletes who are still alive—not because he shares the same name, but because he imitated that man’s virtue and himself became an example of philosophy to others.

After spending time with the renowned Maron and sharing in his divine teaching, he surpassed his teacher through greater labors. Maron had a temple of the former error as a shelter of walls and had fixed up a tent woven from skins; using it, he escaped the assaults of rain and snow. But this man, dismissing all these things—the tent, the hut, and the shelter of walls—has the sky for his roof and endures every contrary assault of the air.

At one time he is overwhelmed by heavy rain; at another he is frozen by ice and snow; sometimes he is scorched and burned by the sun’s rays. He conducts himself bravely and steadfastly in every circumstance, as though competing in another’s body and striving through the eagerness of his spirit to conquer the nature of his body.

Clothed in this mortal and suffering body, he lives as though he were incapable of suffering. Meditating upon an incorporeal life within the body, he cries out with blessed Paul: “Though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For our weapons are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds; we destroy arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and we take every understanding captive to the obedience of God” (2 Cor. X).

He practiced these contests, which transcend nature, by exercising himself in lesser labors. For after first shutting himself in a small house, freeing his soul from external disturbances, and fastening his mind upon the remembrance of God, he meditated upon virtue in its perfection and completeness.

When he had trained himself thoroughly and accustomed his soul to good labors, he dared to undertake greater contests [Col. 0083B]. Coming to this mountain, which is thirty stadia from this city, he made it illustrious and venerable, though formerly it had been obscure and utterly barren.

Now it is believed to have received such a blessing that the earth spread upon it is consumed by all who come from every direction, carrying it away for their benefit. He is seen living there by everyone who approaches. As I said, he has no cave, no tent, no hut, no trench, and no enclosure surrounding and protecting him. He is seen praying and resting, standing and sitting, in health and when held by some illness—so much so that he continually contests before the spectators present and expels the necessities of nature.

For even other people who have been moderately well brought up do not easily discharge their bodily waste in the presence of outsiders, much less a man trained in the highest philosophy. I say this not because I learned it from others, but because I saw it myself.

Fourteen years ago, when he had fallen into a serious illness, it affected him, as was natural, since he possessed a mortal body. The heat was intense, and the flame of the sun’s rays burned fiercely, while the winds were still and the air remained motionless.

His illness was an inundation of yellow bile, which flowed downward, gnawed and constricted the intestine, and forced him to go outside to evacuate. Then I witnessed great endurance. People had gathered from many villages to salute this glorious body, but he sat divided between two necessities. Nature compelled him to go out to relieve himself, but shame before the crowd that was present forced him to remain in the same position and condition.

Knowing this, I addressed some of those assembled with many exhortations and others with threats, ordering them to leave. Finally, I bound them by the bonds of priestly authority and, only after the greatest effort, managed to send them away at evening. But even when they had departed, that holy man was not overcome by nature; he continued to endure until the deepening night compelled everyone to return home. [Col. 0083D]

The following day, when I came to him again, I saw that the intense heat had grown stronger and that the fever from which he was suffering was being nourished and increased by the externally supplied fire. Pretending to have a headache, I said that I was distressed by the force of the sun’s rays and asked him to spread some modest shade for me.

After he gave the order, we devised a shade by fixing three reeds in the ground and laying two cilicia over them. When he ordered me to enter, I said: “It is shameful, Father, that I, who am both young and strong, should obtain this consolation, while you, who are held by a severe fever and need such consolation, sit outside receiving the sun’s rays.

“If you wish me to enjoy the shade,” I continued, “be my companion in this little tent. I wish to remain with you, but the sun’s rays prevent me.”

He yielded when he heard these words and accepted my remedy. Since we were enjoying the shade together, I began another conversation and said: “I need to lie down, because my hip cannot sit without discomfort.” Again he asked me to lie down, but I replied that it was intolerable for me to recline while seeing him sitting.

“If you wish me also to enjoy this rest,” I said, “let us recline together, Father; I shall not be ashamed to lie down alone.”

Having deceived his endurance with such words, I offered him the comfort of reclining. While he lay alone, I entertained him with pleasant conversation, turning his thoughts toward cheerfulness. Inserting my hand beneath his garment, I tried gently to wipe his back. Then I saw a great weight of iron, which bound both his loins and his neck.

There were also other chains extending from the ring around his neck: two ran in front and two behind, slanting downward toward a lower ring and forming the shape of the letter X. In front and behind, they joined the two rings. His hands also had similar bonds inside, around the elbows.

When I saw the burden, weighing many talents, I begged him to aid his suffering body, which could not bear at once both voluntary weights and involuntary illness.

“Now, Father,” I said, “the fever is performing the function of the iron. When it ceases, we shall again impose upon the body the labor taken from the iron.”

He granted this request, softened by such persuasive songs. At that time, although he had been ill for only a few days, he recovered easily.

Later, when he fell into a more serious illness and many people had gathered from various places to carry away his body, the citizens heard of it and all rushed there—soldiers and private citizens alike. The soldiers took military weapons, while the others used whatever weapons they had. They formed a dense and ordered battle line and began to fight, shooting arrows and hurling stones with slings, not to strike but merely to frighten.

After driving away the neighboring inhabitants, they placed the victorious athlete, distinguished by his victories, upon a bed. He was unaware of everything that was happening—for he had not even felt it when the peasants pulled out his hair—and they came into the city. When they reached a prophetic church, they set down the bed in the monastery adjoining it.

A man came from Beroea—for I was there at the time—reporting what had happened and bringing news of his death. When I immediately ran there and spent the entire night on the road, I encountered the man after dawn, neither speaking nor capable of recognizing anyone present.

When I addressed him and greeted him in the name of the great Acacius, he immediately opened his eyes, asked how I was, and inquired when I had arrived. When I answered these questions, he closed his eyes again.

After three days had passed, in the evening he asked where he was. When he learned, he was distressed and asked to be carried back immediately to the mountain. Since I wished to watch over him continually and serve him, I ordered that the bed be brought at once and carried to the place he desired.

Then I saw how completely the venerable head was estranged from ambition and the desire for glory. The following day I offered him a bowl of barley broth after cooling it, for he would not take anything hot at all, having forbidden himself the use of fire.

When he refused to take it, I said: “Grant us this, Father. We all regard your health as a common benefit. You have been set before us not only as an example of usefulness, but even while praying you provide assistance and secure God’s favor for us.

“If it troubles you that you are unaccustomed to this, then, Father, endure this firmly as well; this too is a kind of philosophy. For just as, when you were healthy and desired food, you overcame your appetite through endurance, so now, though you have no appetite, show endurance in eating.”

As I was saying this, the man of God Polychronius was present [Col. 0085B].

[Note: Polychronius. Concerning him, see below, chapter 24.]

Defending what I had said, he declared that he wished to take it first himself, although it was morning, even though he often nourished his body only after an interval of seven days.

Thus overcome by the argument, Jacobus swallowed one cup of the broth with his eyes closed, as we customarily do when drinking bitter potions.

Since we also persuaded him to wash his feet, which through weakness had lost the ability to walk [Col. 0085C], I consider it worthwhile to disclose this aspect of his soul’s philosophy as well, since a basin was nearby.

One of those who were serving him wished to cover the basin with a basket, so that it would not be seen by those who came to see him. But he said: “Why are you covering the basin?”

When the man replied, “So that it may not be seen by those who come to look at you,” he said: “Far be it, my son, that you should conceal from people what is open to the God of all.” [Note: “Do not conceal from people.” Nicephorus reports the terrible death of a hypocritical monk in Book XIV, chapter 52.]

“For I wish to live for him alone and have no concern for human glory. What benefit would it be to me if these people knew that I had labored more and practiced greater exertion, while God knew that I had done less? They are not the givers of recompense for labors; God is the provider.”

Who, then, would not greatly admire both his words and the mind that produced them—a mind so far above all human glory?

I also remember something similar happening on another occasion. It was evening, late evening, and the time for eating. Taking an earthen dish that had been set out, he ate soaked lentils; this was his nourishment.

A certain man came from the city, entrusted with some military levy. When Jacobus saw him from a distance, he did not put down the lentils but took food as usual. Taking the sight to be a demon, he assailed him with words as an enemy; and, showing that he was not afraid, he meanwhile brought the lentils to his mouth.

The man who was being assailed with curses pleaded, saying that he was a human being and that, having earlier been compelled by a certain oath to leave the city before evening, he had arrived at that hour.

“Be of good courage,” Jacobus said, “and do not be afraid. But after you have prayed, depart. Be my guest and share my food.”

As he said this, he filled his right hand and gave the man some lentils. Thus he expelled the disease of vain glory from that man’s soul, along with the others.

It is superfluous to speak of his endurance, since sight itself bears witness to it. Often he was so buried beneath snow that had fallen for three days and as many nights that, lying face down and praying to God, he could scarcely be seen at all beneath the rags with which he was clothed. His neighbors repeatedly removed the snow that had accumulated over him with mattocks and hoes, pulling him out and raising him while he was still lying there.

From these labors he gathered the gifts of divine grace, in which everyone wishes to share. Through his blessing, many fevers have been and are extinguished, many illnesses have ceased and disappeared altogether, many demons have been compelled to flee, and water blessed by his right hand becomes a saving remedy.

Who does not know that a dead boy was restored to life through his prayer? His parents lived in the suburbs of the city; they had indeed fathered many children, but had sent them all immature to the grave. When, therefore, this last son was born, the father ran to the man of God, asking that the child might have a long life and promising that, if he lived, he would dedicate him to God. After he had lived four years, however, he came to the end of his life; his father was away. On returning, he suddenly saw him being carried out. Snatching him from the bed, he said: “I must fulfill my promise and give him back to the man of God, even if he is dead.” He carried him there, as he had said, and placed him at the holy man’s feet, saying the same things he had also told his household. The divine man, when the boy had been placed before him, bent his knees and prayed prostrate, entreating the Lord of life and death. In the evening the boy uttered a sound and called for his father. When the holy man perceived that the Lord had accepted his prayers and supplied life to the child, he rose, worshiped him who does the will of those who fear him and hears their prayers (Psalm 144), finished his prayer, and returned the son to his father. I too saw this and heard the father recount it; he related the apostolic miracle to many others, knowing that it would prove beneficial to many who heard it.

Moreover, I too obtained his assistance. I shall mention one or two instances, thinking it ungrateful to pass them over in silence and not to make known the kinds of benefit involved. The accursed Marcion sowed many thorns of impiety throughout the region of Cyrrhus. As I tried to uproot them completely, I undertook every labor and continually employed every device. Those who enjoyed my cultivation, although for that reason they ought to have loved me, “slandered me,” as I may say prophetically (Psalm 108:34); but I prayed, and “they returned evil for good and hatred for my love” (Psalm 108:34). Using magical tricks and relying on the aid of wicked demons, they attempted to wage a war that could not be seen. At night a destructive demon came, shouting and speaking in the Syrian language:

“Why are you waging war against Marcion? Why are you undertaking this struggle against him? What harm has he ever done you? Stop making war; cease from your malevolence, or you will learn by experience how good rest is. Know that I would long ago have stabbed you, had I not seen the choir of martyrs guarding you together with James.”

I heard this and said to one of my companions who was sleeping near me: “Do you hear what is being said?” He replied: “I heard everything. When I wanted to rise, look around, and learn who was speaking, I remained still for your sake, since I thought you were at rest.” We therefore both rose and looked around, but saw no one moving and heard no one speaking. Other people who lived with us also heard those words.

He understood, therefore, that by the “choir of martyrs” the demon meant a flask of martyrs’ oil, which, containing a blessing gathered from many martyrs, hung from my bed. Beneath my head was an old mantle of the great James, which had been stronger protection for me than any adamantine enclosure.

Furthermore, when I was about to enter their largest village, and many obstacles intervened to prevent my departure, I sent to my Isaiah, asking that I might obtain divine assistance. He said: “Be of good courage; all those obstacles have been dissolved like a spider’s web.” The Lord had shown this to him at night—not by presenting a shadowy image in a dream, but by displaying it truly. “I saw,” he said, “when I had begun the hymn, in the direction where those places lie, a certain serpent resembling fire, crawling from west to east and moving through the middle of the air. When I had completed three prayers, I saw it again, bent into a circle, with its tail joined to its head. When I had completed another eight prayers, I saw it cut into two parts and dissolved into smoke.”

He had thus foreseen these things, while we saw the outcome that agreed with his prediction. In the morning, obeying the command of the demon who had caused the evil, the inhabitants—formerly adherents of Marcion but now belonging to the apostolic party—came from the west and displayed naked swords to us. At the third hour, however, they all gathered together and concerned themselves only with guarding themselves, like a serpent that covers its head with its tail. At the eighth hour they dispersed and gave us room to enter the village. Immediately we found a serpent made of bronze, which they worshiped. Since they had openly undertaken war against the Maker and Creator of all things, they attempted to honor the accursed serpent as his enemy. Such benefits have I received from the head whom I venerate.

Since my narrative has now entered upon divine revelations, come, let me recount what I heard from that tongue entirely free from falsehood. He did not tell it because he was led by any desire for glory—for his divine soul was furthest removed from that vice—but because a certain circumstance compelled him to say what he wished to conceal.

I earnestly begged him to pray to the God of all, so that he might return to me a harvest pure of weeds and free it entirely from heretical seeds; for I was greatly distressed by the error of the detestable Marcion, which had gained very great strength. In response to my entreaty he said:

“You need neither me nor anyone else as an intercessor with God. You have that illustrious John, the voice of the Word and the Lord’s forerunner, continually offering these prayers on your behalf.”

When I said that I believed both in his prayers and in those of the other holy apostles and prophets, whose relics had recently been brought to us, he replied: “Be of good courage; you have John the Baptist.”

Even then I did not allow him to remain silent, but pressed him still more, questioning him and wishing to know why he had remembered John in particular. He said:

“I would wish to embrace and kiss his beloved relics.”

When I replied, “I shall not bring them unless you promise to tell me what you see,” he made the promise. The next day I brought him what he desired, and when he had ordered everyone else to withdraw, he related the following to me alone:

“When you received these patrons of the city, who had come from Phoenicia and Palestine, with a Davidic dance, it occurred to me to consider whether these might be the relics of that illustrious John, rather than those of another martyr who bore the same name. One day afterward I was standing to sing the hymns, and I saw someone dressed in white saying: ‘Brother James, why did you not come out to meet us when we arrived?’ When I asked who they were, he replied: ‘We are those who recently came from Phoenicia and Palestine. Although all of you welcomed us with ready and cheerful hearts—the shepherd, the people, the citizens, and the countryfolk—you alone did not share in their honor.’ He was indicating the doubt I had entertained.

“To this I said: ‘Although both you and the others are absent, I honor you and worship the God of all.’

“Again, on the following day and at the same hour, when the same person had appeared, he said: ‘Do you see that man standing there? His garment resembles the color of snow, and beside him a furnace of fire has been placed.’ When I turned my eyes in that direction and surmised that he was John the Baptist—for he was dressed accordingly and held his hand as one baptizing—he said: ‘That is the man whom you have surmised.’

“Moreover,” he said, “when you once went out at night to the first village to instruct those rebellious people, and had ordered me to offer prayer to God with greater and more intense zeal, I kept vigil throughout the whole night, beseeching the Lord. Then I heard a voice saying: ‘Do not be afraid, O James, for the great John the Baptist is praying throughout the whole night to the God of all. A great slaughter would have taken place if the boldness of the devil had not been extinguished by his intercessions.’”

After he had related these things to me, he ordered me alone to know them and not to take others into my confidence. For the sake of their benefit, however, I have related them not only to many people but have also committed them to writing.

[Col. 0089A] He also said that he himself had seen the patriarch Joseph, whose head and beard were gray, who radiated splendor in his old age, and who, at the summit of virtue, called himself the last of the saints. “For when I,” he said, “first called him the foremost of those who share the same bier with him, he called himself the last.”

He also told me of the various and manifold assaults of demons directed against him. “When I had first entered this way of life,” he said, “a certain naked Ethiopian appeared to me, emitting fire from his eyes. When I saw him, I was seized with fear and turned to prayer; I could not bring myself to take food, for at that time he appeared to me. When seven, eight, and ten days had passed and I remained fasting, at last, scorning that insolent attack, I sat down and ate. Since he could not bear this courage of mine, he threatened to strike me with a rod.

“I said to him: ‘If the God of all has permitted you to do so, strike me, and I shall gladly receive the blow, since I shall be struck by him. But if you have not been permitted, you will not strike me, even if you rage a thousand times.’ When he heard this, he fled.”

“But again he secretly afflicted me with continual trouble. Meeting the man who brought the water to me from below twice a week and imitating my appearance, the demon received it; then, ordering the bearer to depart, he poured out the water. When he had done this not only twice but even three times, he attacked me severely through the suffering of thirst.

“When I was therefore greatly distressed, I asked the man who used to bring the water to me why he had not brought it for fifteen days. He said that he had already brought it three or four times and that I had received it. ‘And where,’ I asked, ‘did I receive it from you when you brought it?’ He pointed out the place. ‘Even if you see me approaching that place a thousand times,’ I said, ‘do not hand over the vessel until you have come to this spot.’”

When these open and frustrated plots of his had likewise failed, he undertook others. At night he shouted:

“I shall fill you with such a foul odor and imprint such a disgrace upon you that no one will look at you in any respect.”

“To this,” he said, “I replied: ‘I shall thank you. Unwillingly you will benefit your enemy, since you will cause me to dwell more deeply upon the remembrance of God. For the more leisure I have, the more I am occupied with continually contemplating the divine beauty.’”

When a few days had passed, while at midday I was performing my customary office, I saw, he said, two women descending from the mountain. Since I was distressed that this happened contrary to custom and was beginning to pelt them with stones, I remembered the threats of the wicked demon and concluded that this was the disgrace of which he had spoken. I therefore said aloud that, even if they were sitting upon my shoulders, I would neither strike them with stones nor pursue them, but would use only entreaty. I said this, and they vanished; thus the vision came to an end.

“After this,” he said, “I was again praying at night. The noise of a vehicle was heard, together with the cry of a driver and the neighing of horses. The novelty of the event disturbed me, for I considered that there was then no ruler in the city, that this was not a road for vehicles, and that the time was not suitable for vehicles.

“While I was reflecting upon these matters, a noise of an approaching multitude was heard. Some lictors going before shouted, whistled, drove the crowd aside, and prepared a way for the one in command. When they seemed to be very near, I said: ‘Who are you, and from where do you come? What business brings you here at this hour? How long will you mock me, wretched one, and despise divine patience?’ I said this while turning toward the east and offering prayers to God. He pushed against me, but could not throw me down, for divine grace resisted him; and immediately all those things vanished.

“He also said that during the time of those destructive brigands, when they had come from Isauria, burning most of the East and carrying off plunder, he had been exceedingly afraid—not that he might be killed, for he was not held by such a great love of the body, but that he might be carried into slavery and captivity and be forced to witness a spectacle of impiety and injustice.

“When the devil perceived this fear—for he had often heard him reveal it to his acquaintances—he imitated at night the howling of women. ‘I seemed to hear,’ he said, ‘that the enemy was coming and that they were setting fire to the villages. Immediately I parted my hair into two sections, moving one part to my right breast and the other to my left, and prepared my neck so that the sword might cut it off more easily; after receiving a brief stroke, I would thus be freed from that detestable spectacle.

“Having passed the whole night in this way and continually expecting their incursion, when day came and some people arrived, I asked what they had heard concerning the Isaurians. They said that they knew nothing of such events in those days. Thus,” he said, “I recognized that this too had been a demonic vision.”

“Sometimes, taking the form of a vigorous and lively young man, handsome in appearance and adorned with blond hair, he approached me smiling and playing at the same time. I, armed with anger, drove him away, pursuing him with curses. He remained, however, with a harlot’s appearance, enticing me to pleasure by his laughter and speech.

“Then, inflamed with still greater anger, I said: ‘How can you travel over the whole earth and prepare such plots for everyone?’ He replied that he was not alone, but that a multitude of demons was dispersed throughout the whole world, who in this manner both play and act in earnest; for, in the apparent play, they at the same time strive to destroy the whole human race.

“‘But you,’ I said, ‘go away, since Christ commands you to do so—he who sent the whole legion into the abyss through the pigs.’ He heard this and fled, unable to endure either the power of the Lord’s name or the splendor of the philosophy of his servant.”

Moreover, although I know many other things that I could relate, I do not wish to write them down, lest their multitude become a cause of disbelief for the weaker. To those who behold the man of God, nothing of this kind appears incredible, since the virtue that is seen confirms what is reported. But since written accounts of these narratives will be handed down to posterity—and many ears are more incredulous than eyes—we shall measure our narrative according to the weakness of our hearers.

Others also built for him a very large church in a neighboring village, which is not many stadia distant. I too constructed a small tomb in the church of the apostles distinguished by victory. When the divine man learned of this, he often asked me that his body be buried on that mountain. I often replied that one who had cared nothing for the present life ought not to concern himself with a grave. When I saw that this matter was dear to him, however, I agreed and consented, and arranged for the sarcophagus to be cut out and carried up.

When I saw that the stone was being damaged by frost, I asked him to allow a small house to be built for the sarcophagus. When he gave the order and, after the building was completed, we had placed a roof upon it, he said:

“I shall not allow this to be called the tomb of James. I wish it to become a church of the martyrs distinguished by victory, and I myself to be placed like some tenant in another tomb, as one judged worthy to dwell among them.”

Nor did he merely say this; he also acted upon it. After gathering from every direction many prophets, many apostles, and especially very many martyrs, he placed them in one sarcophagus, wishing to dwell together with the people of the saints, desiring to rise again with them and to be deemed worthy of the contemplation of God.

This is sufficient to indicate how great was his modesty. He who had gathered such great riches desired to dwell as a stranger among wealthy merchants, as though he were in extreme poverty. What the labors of this venerable head were, what struggles he undertook, how great a grace he received from God, how many victories he won, and with how many crowns he was adorned—these facts are sufficient for demonstration.

Since some criticize his harsh and difficult manner and resent the fact that he takes such delight in solitude and quiet, I shall say a little about him and then bring my narrative to an end. As I have already said, he is set out for all to see; he is surrounded neither by a ditch nor covered by any hut or tent. Anyone who comes, prevented by no enclosure, approaches immediately and says whatever he wishes.

Other lovers of this philosophy have both ditches and doors, and they are able to enjoy quiet. The one who is enclosed opens when he wishes, delays as long as he wishes, and is filled as much as he wishes with divine contemplation. Here there is none of this. Consequently, he bears with extreme difficulty those who disturb him during the time of prayer. If, when he orders them, they withdraw immediately, he resumes his prayer. But if they continue to cause disturbance, and after he has ordered them once or twice they do not obey, then, distressed and rebuking them, he sends them away.

I once spoke with him about this matter also. I said that some people resented being expelled and not sharing in his blessing, and that those who came for this reason and completed a journey of many days ought to depart not indignant but filled with joy of heart, so that they might be able to welcome, at the banquet of philosophical narratives, those who were ignorant.

He replied:

“I came to the mountain not for the sake of anyone else, but for my own sake. Since I abound in many ulcers of sin, I need very much medicine; for that reason I pray to the merciful Lord to provide remedies that may cure my faults.

“How, then, would it not be highly blameworthy and extremely foolish both to interrupt the sequence of prayer and meanwhile converse with human beings? If I were a servant of a human master, one of the same nature as myself, and at the time when I ought to minister to my master I left off bringing food or drink at the proper time and chatted with one of my fellow servants, how many blows would I justly receive? If, moreover, I had approached a governor and, while recounting an injury inflicted upon me by someone, interrupted my speech midway and said other words to one of those present, would you not think that the judge would resent this, refuse me assistance, beat me in addition with whips, and drive me from the tribunal?

“How, then, is it proper that a servant toward his master, and one who pleads toward a judge, should conduct himself as he ought, while I, approaching God, the eternal Lord, the most just Judge, and King of all, should not approach him in the same manner? Instead, while praying, should I turn toward those around me and engage them in a lengthy conversation?”

I heard these things and passed them on to those who resented his conduct; and it seems to me that he spoke rightly and beautifully. Besides what has been said, it is also characteristic of lovers to despise everyone else and cling only to the one whom they love and cherish, dreaming of him at night and grasping him in vision by day. For this reason, it seems to me that he resents being prevented, while engaged in the contemplation he desires, from being filled with the beauty that he seeks and that is most worthy of love.

We have written these things as narrators, not praising him in the manner of a panegyric, taking great care for brevity lest we burden our readers with length. If he survives this account, he will add innumerable other splendid deeds to those already mentioned; others will also write about them. We greatly desire to withdraw from here. May the agonothete—the director of the contests of piety—bring his contests to a worthy end, grant that the remainder of his course may correspond to what came before, so that he may reach the finish as a victor, and sustain and strengthen our weakness by his prayers, so that, strengthened, we may wrest from them the many victories that others have won against us and depart from life as victors.

## CHAPTER XXII. THALASSIUS AND LIMNAEUS

[Note: [Col. 0118C] Thalassius and Limnaeus. Their memory is preserved in the Greek Menaea, 22 February, where their life is reviewed in summary. This entire chapter concerns chiefly Limnaeus, except for a few lines at the beginning, as we learn from the Menaea. He is also mentioned in the Menaea, 23 February, on the occasion of John, who was his disciple.]

Helimna [Note: [Col. 0118D] Helimna. Longus reads Tillina.] is a village in our region which formerly received the seeds of Marcion’s impiety but now enjoys evangelical cultivation. South of it there is a hill, neither very rugged nor especially steep. On it Thalassius, an admirable man, built a monastic dwelling. He was adorned with many other virtues, but surpassed all the people of his time in simplicity, gentleness, and moderation of character. I say this not as one who merely trusts hearsay, but as one who tested him personally. I often visited the man and often enjoyed his gracious companionship.

In this place the now universally celebrated Limnaeus was initiated by him. When he came to that training ground while still very young, he was beautifully instructed in this supreme philosophy. First, knowing that the tongue is slippery, while still an adolescent he imposed upon himself this silence [Note: [Col. 0118D] Silence. John, known for religiously observing silence, surnamed the Silent, 13 May.] and remained for a very long time speaking with no one.

After he had sufficiently shared in the teaching of that divine old man and shown himself to be an exact image of his virtue, he went to the great Maron, whom we mentioned earlier (above, chapter 16). He came at the same time as the divine James. After gaining great benefit from him also and imitating the life lived under the open sky, he occupied another summit of the mountain overlooking a village called Targallam [Note: [Col. 0118D] Targallam. Longus: Targalam. The Menaea has Γάλγαλα, “Galgal[a],” and on the 23rd of the same month Τάργαλα, “Targala.”].

He has lived there to the present day, possessing neither a little house, nor a tent, nor a hut, but confined only by an enclosure built of stones [Note: [Col. 0118D] Stones. The Menaea has ξηρολίθοις, “dry stones,” which is translated in the Life of Simeon Stylites, chapter 5 of Book I of the Lives of the Fathers, as “dry stone.” Here too, chapter 18, “stones not even cemented with clay.” See the note on Simeon Stylites.]. He has a small doorway that is continually blocked with mud. He never opens it to other visitors, but allows me alone to do so when I approach. For this reason, whenever they sense my arrival, many gather from every direction, wishing to share in my entrance.

Speaking with those who sometimes come to him through a small window, he gives them his blessing, and through it grants healing to very many. Using the name of our Savior, he makes diseases cease, drives out demons, and imitates the miracles of the apostles.

He supplies healing not only to those who come to him, but has often provided it also for his own body. He had long been afflicted by a colic. Those who have experienced them know very well how sharp are the pains and tortures that arise from it; those who witnessed them know this as well. Such sufferers roll about like people driven mad, turning this way and that, repeatedly extending and contracting their feet. Sometimes they sit, rise, and walk, seeking some means of relief; for this reason they sit beside baths, often receiving some consolation from them. Why should I use a longer account to enumerate things obvious and manifest to all?

While struggling with this disease and with pains and tortures so great and so numerous, he accepted no medical assistance, did not consent to enter a bed, and was restored neither by medicines nor by food. Sitting upon a board lying on the ground, he was healed by prayer and the sign of the cross, and by invoking the divine name he put the pains to sleep.

Moreover, when he was once walking at night, he stepped upon a viper that was sleeping. It seized the sole of his foot and sank its teeth into it. When he tried to help his foot, he bent down and brought his hand toward it; the animal turned its mouth toward that hand. When he again used his left hand to assist himself, he drew the beast’s anger upon that hand as well. After its fury had been satisfied—for it inflicted more than ten bites upon him—it withdrew and returned to its cave.

He was tormented by the most severe pains throughout his body. Even then, however, he did not consent to use medical skill, but applied to the wounds only the remedies of faith: the sign of the cross, prayer, and invocation of God. For this reason, I think, the God of all permitted that creature to rage against that sacred body, so that he might display openly to all the endurance of that divine soul. For we see that the same was also the purpose concerning Job, who possessed a noble and courageous spirit. God allowed him to be tossed by waves of every kind and of the greatest magnitude, because he wished to display to all the wisdom of the helmsman. For how else would we have known either his courage or this man’s endurance, unless the enemy of piety had been given the opportunity to cast every kind of missile against them?

These things suffice to demonstrate the man’s endurance. We shall show his gentleness and kindness from another source. After gathering many people who had been deprived of sight and forced to beg, he built dwellings for them on both sides, toward the east and the west, ordered them to live there, and instructed that the food they needed be supplied by those who came to him. He himself, enclosed in the midst of them, incites both groups to hymn-singing, and one can hear them continually praising God. So great is his constant kindness toward people of his own kind.

The period of their contests under the open sky is the same as that of the great James. They have now completed thirty-eight years.

## CHAPTER XXIII. JOHN, MOSES, ANTIOCHUS, ANTONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0118D] John, Moses, Antiochus, Antonius. Greek Menaea, 24 February.]

John also imitated this way of life, a man distinguished among other things for gentleness and meekness. After taking possession of a certain very rugged rock, exposed to storms and facing north, he has now spent twenty-five years there, receiving the contrary blasts of the elements. In all other respects—not to pursue every detail—his food, clothing, and weights of iron are like those of the men mentioned earlier. He is so far above all human things that he enjoys none of their consolation whatsoever.

I shall offer clear evidence of this. A good man planted an almond tree because of his grassy bed. In time it grew into a tree, so that it gave him shade and delighted his eyes. He ordered it to be cut down, so that he might receive no refreshment from it.

Moses also embraced this way of life, striving on a certain lofty peak of the mountain overlooking the village of Roma.

And the old man Antiochus built a small enclosure on a very deserted mountain.

And Antonius, whose body has been worn out by old age, struggles just as the young do.

They have the same clothing, food, posture, prayer, and labors by night and by day. Neither length of time, nor old age, nor the weakness of nature overcomes their endurance; rather, their zeal for labor flourishes and remains vigorous. God, the agonothete of virtue, has many other athletes in the mountains and countryside, whom it is not easy to enumerate, much less to write the life of each one.

Since I have added enough benefit from these men for those who wish to profit, I shall turn to another kind of narrative, asking that I too may share in their blessing.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ZEBINAS AND POLYCHRONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0118D] Zebinas and Polychronius, Moses, Damianus. Greek Menaea, 23 February, concerning these four.]

They praise Zebinas to this day—those, that is, who were deemed worthy to see him. They say that, when he had reached extreme old age, he continued to practice the same labors until the end and, although weighed down by the greatest old age, changed nothing of the contests of his youth. As they said, he surpassed all the people of his time in constancy of prayer. For while he devoted himself to it by day and night, he was not only never satisfied but made his desire more intense.

Even when conversing briefly with those who came to him, he could not bring himself to draw his mind down from heaven. As soon as he had been released from them, without being separated even slightly from the things belonging to God of all, he again offered his supplication. When old age no longer allowed him to stand continually without discomfort, a staff served as his support; leaning upon it, he both praised and prayed to the Lord.

Since, besides his other virtues, he was adorned with love for guests, he ordered many of those who came to him to wait until evening. Fearing that they would have to remain there all night, however, they withdrew from these labors under various pretexts concerning their own affairs.

The great Maron also admired him and ordered everyone who came to him to go to Zebinas and receive his blessing, calling him father and teacher and naming him a model of every virtue. Maron asked to be placed in the same tomb, but those who seized that sacred body did not permit it [Note: [Col. 0118D] Those who seized that sacred body. Above, chapter 16: “A fierce conflict arose among the neighboring communities over the body.”] and carried him to the place we mentioned [Note: [Col. 0119A] And carried him to the place we mentioned. Above, chapter 16: “A neighboring village, crowded with people, came with its entire assembled population; they routed and scattered the others, but seized that most desirable treasure.”].

Since the divine Zebinas had died before him, in the neighboring village called Cirtica, he received the funeral rites due to him. They built a very large church over his tomb; for those who approach with faith, it pours forth varied and manifold healing. Even now it shelters under the same roof martyrs who contended among the Persians but whom we honor in annual and customary festivals.

The great Polychronius received his teaching. Indeed, the most divine James used to say that Zebinas had first given him, James, a tunic woven of hair. I, however, never saw Zebinas—for he had ended his life before my arrival—but in this excellent Polychronius I see the philosophy of the divine Zebinas. Wax does not reproduce the figures of seals as exactly as this man reproduces Zebinas’ form and character.

I know this clearly, comparing what is reported about Zebinas with what Polychronius does. He is similarly inflamed with divine desire, superior to all earthly things, and, though bound to the body, has a mind with wings. His mind rises aloft, traverses the air and the ether, becomes higher than the heavens, and continually apprehends the divine vision in contemplation; he cannot ever draw his mind away from it. Even while conversing with those who come, he travels through the heights in his mind.

I learned of his vigil and standing throughout the entire night in the following way. Seeing him struggling simultaneously with old age and weakness and taking absolutely no care for his body, I repeatedly urged him to take two companions who might live with him and from whom he might receive some consolation. Since he asked for men distinguished in virtue who were living by themselves in another monastery, I also persuaded those admirable men to place care for the divine man above everything.

After they had lived with him for a short time, they tried to flee, unable to endure standing through that night. When I begged the divine man to measure his labor according to the weakness of his body, he said:

“I not only do not compel them to stand continually with me; I often even order them to lie down.”

They replied: “How could we lie down while one who has grown old in labors stands and despises the weakness of his body, when we are healthy and in the prime of life?”

Thus I learned of the nightly labors of this venerable head. In time, however, those men acquired such great virtue for themselves that they pursued the same philosophy together with this great man.

[Col. 0096C] Moses—for that is his name—remained to the present day, rendering him every service as to a father and master, and carefully and perfectly expressing the virtue that shines forth from that sacred soul.

Damianus—for that was the other man’s name—when he had reached a certain village situated not far away, called Niara, and had found there, among other dwellings, a small house, took up residence in it, pursuing the same way of life. Thus those who know both men well, when they look at him, think they are seeing the soul of blessed Polychronius in another body. For there are the same simplicity, gentleness, self-control, mildness of speech, sweetness in companionship, vigilance of soul, understanding of God, manner of life, labor, wakefulness, and food; and the same poverty prescribed by divine law, possessing nothing. For apart from a single basket containing soaked lentils, there is nothing in his dwelling. Such benefit did he derive from association with the great Polychronius.

I shall leave the disciple and return to the master; for the streams of a river flow from its source. This man, then, having expelled from his soul the love of glory along with the other vices and having trampled underfoot the tyranny of empty glory, always took pains to conceal his labors. He would not bring himself to carry iron, fearing that he might suffer some harm from it if his soul should derive from it an inflammation of arrogance. But when he had ordered a very heavy oak root to be brought to him—for he needed it, of course, for some other purpose—he would place it on his shoulders at night and pray with it so placed; and likewise during the day, whenever he had leisure. Whenever someone came and knocked at the door, he would hide it somewhere. When a certain man saw this, he reported it to me; and when I wished to learn how heavy it was, I could scarcely lift it with both hands. When he saw me, he ordered me to put it down. I begged him to allow me to take it, so that I might relieve him of the opportunity for such labor. But when I saw that he took the matter badly, I yielded to his desire for victory.

From these labors, grace granted by God also blossoms forth in him, and many miracles are performed through his prayers. When that severe drought which afflicted the people stirred them to prayer, a multitude of priests came to him. [Col. 0097B] Among them was a man to whom many villages in the region of Antioch had been entrusted for pastoral care. He asked the elders who were present to persuade the holy man to place his right hand upon a flask. When they told him that he would not do this, while the prayers were subsequently being offered and the venerable man was praying, the visitor, standing behind him, held out the flask with both hands. It immediately began to gush forth so abundantly that two or three of those present extended their hands and received them full of oil.

Although he pours forth the rays of divine grace, is full of upright services and glorious deeds of virtue, and daily gathers the riches of philosophy, he nevertheless possesses such modesty and self-control that he embraces both feet of everyone who comes to him and places his forehead upon the ground, whether the visitor is a soldier, an artisan, or a peasant.

I shall relate something that can demonstrate his simplicity and self-control. A good man, who had obtained the governorship of this people, came to Cyrus and wished to enjoy with me the sight of these great athletes. After visiting the others, we approached this man also, whose virtue we are now recounting. When I said that the governor who had come with me was a lover of equity and justice, the holy man immediately stretched out both hands, grasped both of the governor’s feet, and said: “I want you to promise me one request.” The governor was distressed, begged him to rise, and promised that he would do whatever he commanded—for he supposed that the holy man intended to ask something on behalf of one of those under his authority. “Since, then,” said the holy man, “you have promised and confirmed your promise by oath, offer prayers to God for me with earnest and vehement zeal.” The governor struck his forehead and begged him to release him from his oath, since he was unworthy to offer prayers to the Lord on the holy man’s behalf. What speech could worthily attain the praises of a man who, in such lofty philosophy, possesses such modesty and self-control?

His zeal in undertaking labors was not restrained even by the various and numerous illnesses that afflicted him; although beset by many diseases, he endures the same labors. After we had often pleaded with him at length, we scarcely managed to build this little house, thereby providing a little warmth for his thoroughly chilled body. Many who are still alive have often offered him gold, and those who have died left it to him; but he never accepted anything from anyone, ordering them instead to be stewards of what was offered. Moreover, the great Jacob sent him a hair shirt that someone had brought to him; but he returned that as well when he saw that it was too thick and elegant. For he always used cheap garments of the lowest value. He considered poverty so much more desirable than any kingdom that he did not even always possess the food necessary for his sustenance. I know that I often came and asked for his blessing, finding nothing there except two figs. The honey of this man is greatly desired by those who see him, and is sweet and most delightful to those who hear him. For I have never seen anyone—not even among those who are witty and given to jesting—besmirch him with any stain of reproach; rather, everyone praises and celebrates him, and those who come to him are most unwilling to depart.

## CHAPTER XXV. ASCLEPIUS AND JACOBUS THE HERMIT

[Note: [Col. 0119A] “Asclepius and Jacobus the hermit.” I find nothing about them.]

The admirable Asclepius also belongs to this order. He is ten stades away, but has imitated the same way of life. He has the same food, clothing, moderation of conduct, charity toward guests and brothers, gentleness and meekness, communion with God, extreme poverty, abundance of the highest virtue, riches of philosophy, and everything else that we have listed concerning that holy man. They say that, while he too was among the brothers who live in the village, he embraced a monastic and temperate life and contracted no stain from his association with the many. Since, therefore, he conducted himself excellently in both ways of life—the civic and the solitary—he will rightly be deemed worthy of a double crown.

Moreover, many others have also imitated their virtue; and not only our cities but also those nearby, as well as the villages, are full of this philosophy. One of these is the holy Jacobus, enclosed in a little house near the village called Duzan. Although he is already at the very end of life—for he is more than ninety years old—he is enclosed alone. Through a small opening made like a curved line, he gives answers, but is not seen; and he uses neither fire nor lamplight. When I had twice knocked upon the door, he ordered me to be admitted, honoring me in this way and showing how well disposed he was toward me.

Those who are still alive do not need my writings; if they wish, they themselves can behold their philosophy. For posterity, however, and for those who did not witness this spectacle, these accounts are sufficient for practical use, since they display the character of their philosophy. Having thus completed my account of these men and received the recompense of the blessing I had requested, I shall pass to another narrative.

## CHAPTER XXVI. THE SIMEONS

[Note: [Col. 0119A] “Simeon Stylites.” See the notes on him in Book I, *Lives of the Holy Fathers*.]

Everyone who is subject to the Roman Empire knows that illustrious Simeon, that great marvel of the world; but the Persians, Indians, and Ethiopians know him as well. His fame has even reached the nomadic Scythians, teaching them of his diligence and philosophy in undertaking labors. Although, as I have said, I have all mankind as witnesses, I nevertheless fear recounting his contests, which surpass all speech, lest posterity regard the story as a bare fable devoid of truth. For what happens is beyond human nature, while people habitually measure what is said by nature. If something is reported that exceeds its limits, the account appears false to those who have not been initiated into the divine mysteries. Since, however, earth and sea are full of pious people endowed with true religion, and since those instructed in divine matters have received the grace of the most holy Spirit, they are far from disbelieving what must be told; rather, they will place great confidence in it. I shall therefore approach the narrative with a willing and eager mind. I shall begin from the point at which he was also deemed worthy of a heavenly calling.

There is a village situated on the border of our region and Cilicia, called Sesam. Born there, he was first taught by his parents to pasture sheep, so that in this respect he might be compared with the great men Jacob the patriarch, Joseph the temperate, Moses the lawgiver, David the king and prophet, the prophet Micah, and the holy men who resembled them. Once, when it had snowed very heavily and the sheep were compelled to remain indoors, he was given permission to rest and went with his parents to the divine temple.

[Note: [Col. 0099D] Earlier misprinted: *navigasset* (“had sailed”).] I heard him recount these things in the sacred language. He said that he heard the evangelical voice which pronounces blessed those who weep and mourn, calls wretched those who laugh, and names happy those who are pure in heart, along with the other sayings connected with these (Matthew 5). Then he asked one of those present what a person had done to attain each of these conditions; and that man described a solitary life and displayed that highest philosophy.

When he had received these seeds of the divine word and had carefully hidden them in the deep furrows of his soul, he said that he went to a nearby shrine of the holy martyrs. There he fixed both his knees and his forehead upon the ground and asked him who desires all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2) to lead him to the perfect path of piety and true religion. After he had remained there for a long time in this manner, a sweet sleep came upon him, and he saw the following dream:

“I seemed,” he said, “to be digging foundations. Then I heard someone standing nearby say that I ought to make the trench deeper. When I had added to its depth as he commanded, I again tried to rest; but once more he ordered me to dig and not cease from the labor. After he had commanded me to do this three or four times, he finally said that the depth was sufficient and ordered me thereafter to build without labor, since, once the labor had ceased, the construction too would proceed without labor.”

Events bear witness to this prediction, for the things that take place surpass human nature.

When he had risen from there, he came to the dwelling of certain nearby monks. After spending two years with them and being seized by a love of more perfect virtue, he came to the village of Teleda, which we mentioned earlier, where the great and holy men Ammianus and Eusebius established a training ground for monastic life. The holy Simeon did not enter this one, however, but another that sprang from it. For Eusebonas and Abiton, after sufficiently absorbing the teaching of the great Eusebius, built this gymnasium of philosophy.

[Note: [Col. 0119A] “Eusebonas and Abiton.” I do not recall reading of these elsewhere.] Since throughout their lives they were united in mind and character and displayed, as it were, one soul in two bodies, they attracted many who were held by the love of the same way of life.

When they had gloriously departed this life, the admirable Heliodorus received the leadership of his companions.

[Note: [Col. 0119A] “Heliodorus.” Sozomen, Book VI, chapters 33 and 34, mentions Heliodorus, a monk in Syria.] He lived to be sixty-five years old, sixty-two of which he spent enclosed inside. After being raised for three years by his parents, he entered this flock without ever having seen any of the things that occur in the world. He said that he did not even know the appearance of pigs, roosters, or other such creatures. I often saw him, admired the simplicity of his character, and embraced with extraordinary affection the purity of his soul.

When this outstanding athlete of piety came to him, he struggled continuously for ten years. Although he had eighty companions in the same contest, he surpassed them all by a wide margin. While the others ate after a period of two days, he remained fasting for an entire week. The superiors were displeased, contended with him, and called the practice a disturbance of the order, but they could neither persuade him to abandon what he was doing nor restrain the eagerness of his spirit.

I heard the present leader of this flock himself relate that, on one occasion, he took a woven cord made from palm leaves—for it was extremely rough—and fastened it around his hands. With it he girded his loins, placing it not outside his clothing but directly against the skin; and he tightened it so firmly that the entire area around which it had been placed became ulcerated. After he had spent more than ten days in this condition, and the ulcer, growing worse, began to emit drops of blood, someone who had seen it asked what was causing the bleeding. When he replied that nothing was troubling him, his companion forced his hand beneath the garment, discovered the cause, and reported it to the superior. The superior immediately rebuked him, pleaded with him, and condemned the cruelty of the act; with difficulty he loosened the bond, but even then could not persuade him to apply any medicine to the ulcer. When they saw him undertaking other practices of this sort, they ordered him to leave that training ground, lest those whose bodies were weaker should try to imitate practices beyond their strength and thereby come to harm.

After leaving, he came to more secluded places in the mountains. When he found a shallow pool without water, he lowered himself into it and offered hymns to God there. The leaders of the training ground, repenting, sent two men and permitted them to search for him and bring him back. After they had gone around the mountain, they asked some shepherds who were grazing livestock there whether they had seen anyone of such a complexion and dressed in such clothing. When the shepherds pointed out the pool, the searchers cried out loudly at once; then, bringing a rope, they pulled him out with great difficulty, for the ascent is no easier than the descent.

After spending a short time with them, he went to the village of Telanessus, situated beneath the summit of the mountain where he now lives. There, having found a small house, he spent three years enclosed.

As he sought to increase the riches of virtue, he desired, like the holy men Moses and Elijah, to remain fasting for forty days. He tried to persuade the admirable Bassus, who at that time visited many villages and presided over the priests in the countryside, to leave nothing inside and seal the door with mud. When Bassus explained the difficulty of the undertaking and warned him not to regard a violent death as virtue—for that is both the greatest and the first of crimes—Simeon said: “But, Father, place ten loaves and a jar of water inside for me; and if I see that my body needs nourishment, I shall partake of them.”

It was done as he commanded: the provisions were placed inside, and the door was sealed with mud. When the days had ended, that admirable man and man of God, Bassus, came. After removing the mud and entering, he found the loaves still there; he also found the jar full of water, but Simeon lying there, not breathing and unable either to speak or to move. He therefore asked for a sponge, moistened and washed his mouth with it, and offered him the symbols of the divine Sacraments. Strengthened by these, Simeon rose and took a little food, gradually chewing and swallowing lettuce, chicory, and similar vegetables.

The great Bassus was astonished and returned to his flock, recounting this great miracle. He had more than two hundred companions, and he permitted them neither to possess a beast of burden nor a mill, neither to accept gold offered by anyone nor to go outside the doors to purchase any necessities or see any of their acquaintances; they were to remain inside and receive the food sent by divine grace. The companions continue to observe this rule to the present day, and although their number has increased, they have not transgressed the commands given to them. I shall now pass to the great Simeon.

From that time until the present day—twenty-eight years have now passed—he has remained fasting for forty days. Time and habituation have greatly reduced the labor. In the early days he used to stand and praise God; then, when his body could no longer endure standing because of hunger, he would sit and perform the divine office; in the final days he would even lie down. As his strength was gradually consumed and extinguished, he was forced to lie there half-dead. After he stood upon the column, he did not consider descending, but devised another means of remaining upright. He fastened a beam to the column and again attached himself to the beam with ropes; in this way he spent forty continuous days. Later, after receiving greater grace from above, he no longer needed even this assistance. He stood for forty days without taking food, strengthened by the eagerness of his spirit and divine grace.

After spending those three continuous years, as I said, in that little house, he came to the summit so widely proclaimed and celebrated in speech. He ordered an enclosure to be constructed around it and obtained an iron chain twenty cubits long. He fastened one end to an enormous rock and fitted the other to his right foot, so that he could not leave those boundaries even if he wished. There he lived, continually grasping heaven in contemplation and forcing himself to behold what lies above the heavens; for the bond of iron did not impede the flight of his mind.

After the admirable Meletius—who at that time had been entrusted with the episcopal administration of the region of the city of Antioch, a resolute man, distinguished for prudence and adorned with intellectual ability—had said that the iron was superfluous, since the mind was sufficient to impose the bonds of reason upon the body, Simeon yielded and submitted to his persuasion. Meletius ordered a metalworker to be summoned and instructed him to loosen the bond. Since a piece of leather had also been fitted around the shin so that the iron would not injure the body, and since it had to be torn apart—for it had been sewn together—they said that they saw more than twenty enormous bugs hiding in it as in a cave. The admirable Meletius said that he too had seen this. I remember the incident, thereby also demonstrating the man’s great endurance: although he could have squeezed the leather with his hand and easily killed them all, he patiently endured their troublesome bites, willingly training himself through small hardships for greater ones.

[Note: [Col. 0119A] “Meletius.” Hervetus translated as though this were the Meletius who was then bishop of Antioch: “To whom at that time the administration of the episcopate of the region of the city of Antioch had been entrusted.” Longus translated: “But when Meletius, who at that time was governor of the Antiochene region....” Certainly, if this is understood of that famous Meletius, bishop of Antioch, he must have been an old man to have dealt with these matters together with Simeon, as I briefly mentioned above in Book I, in the *Life of Simeon Stylites*.]

When his fame spread through all the regions, everyone flocked to him—not only those nearby, but also those who were many days’ journey away. Some brought paralytics, others sought health for the sick, and others asked to become fathers, wishing to receive from him what they had not received from nature. When they received what they asked for and obtained their requests, they returned joyfully, proclaiming the benefits they had gained, and sent many more to seek the same things. As everyone came from every direction and streamed along the entire road like a river, one could see a sea of people assembled in that place, receiving streams from all sides. For not only did those who inhabit our region converge there, but also the Ishmaelites, Persians, Armenians subject to them, Iberians, Homerites, and those who live farther within their territories. Many also came from the far ends of the West: Spaniards, Britons, and Gauls, who occupy the lands in between. It is unnecessary to speak of Italy, for they say that in Rome, which is by far the greatest city, he became so celebrated in everyone’s speech that they placed small images of him in all the vestibules and porticoes of their workshops, thereby preparing for themselves a protection and safeguard.

[Note: [Col. 0119B] “They placed images.” This passage is cited in the Seventh Council, act 4.]

When innumerable people came—and all tried to touch him and receive some blessing from those leather garments—he first considered it absurd and inappropriate that such extraordinary honor should be shown him, and then found the matter burdensome because it was excessively laborious. He therefore devised standing upon a column: at first ordering one six cubits high to be built, then one twelve cubits high, afterward one twenty-two cubits high, and now one thirty-six cubits high.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] Codrenus has this verbatim, in the fifty-second year of Theodosius.]

For he desires to fly up into heaven and be freed from this earthly manner of life.

I do not think that this station was established without divine counsel. Therefore I urge those who delight in the zeal for criticism to restrain their tongues and not allow them to rush recklessly onward, but rather to consider that the Lord has often devised such things for the benefit of those who are more sluggish. He commanded Isaiah to walk naked and barefoot (Isaiah 20); Jeremiah to put a belt around his loins and in this manner present the prophecy to unbelievers (Jeremiah 13), and at another time to place wooden yokes and iron upon his neck (Jeremiah 27); he also commanded Hosea to take a prostitute as his wife, and again to love a woman who was a prostitute and an adulteress (Hosea 1); and Ezekiel to lie on his right side for forty days and on his left for one hundred and fifty (Ezekiel 4), and again to break through a wall, go out as a fugitive, and depict the captivity for himself (Ezekiel 12). At another time he commanded him to sharpen a sword, shave his head with it, divide the hair into four parts, and distribute some to this person and some to that one (Ezekiel 5), not to list everything.

The Ruler of all commanded each of these things to be done, drawing those who did not heed the word or resolve to listen to the prophecies by the wonder of the spectacle and causing them to hear the divine responses. For who was not astonished when he saw the holy man entering naked?

[Note: [Col. 0119B] “Entering naked.” Barraeus thinks that Theodoretus is referring to Simeon Salus, concerning whom Evagrius, Book IV, chapter 33, relates that, because he brought bread to a hungry prostitute, he endured the accusation of fornication. But he is mistaken, for Simeon Salus lived after Theodoretus. Theodoretus is referring to Isaiah, whose nakedness he had mentioned earlier.]

Who did not desire to know why this was happening? Who did not ask why the prophet allowed a prostitute to dwell with him?

Just as the God of all commanded each of those things to be done, caring for those who lived negligently and sluggishly, so he also arranged this new and wondrous spectacle, drawing everyone to look by the novelty and marvel of the event and making the admonition credible to those who came. The novelty of the spectacle is a sufficient pledge of instruction; and whoever comes to the spectacle, after being taught divine things, departs instructed.

Just as those who happen to be kings of men, after some passage of time, change the images on their coins—sometimes stamping images of lions, sometimes of stars, and sometimes of angels, attempting through a new design to make the gold more precious—so also the supreme King of all, adding these new and various ways of life as figures and designs to piety and true religion, arouses the tongues not only of the children of faith but also of those afflicted with the disease of unbelief to praise.

That this is so is testified not only by words, but is also proclaimed by the events themselves. Innumerable thousands of Ishmaelites who had served the darkness of impiety were enlightened by that station upon the column. For, like an exceedingly bright lamp placed upon a lampstand, it sent rays in every direction like the sun. And, as I said, one can see Iberians, Persians, and Armenians coming and receiving divine baptism. The Ishmaelites came in groups—two hundred, three hundred at a time, and sometimes even a thousand—renouncing their ancestral error with loud cries, crushing before that great light the images they had worshiped, and renouncing the rites of Venus, whose worship they had inherited from ancient times. They receive the divine Sacraments, accepting laws from that divine tongue, dismissing their ancestral rites, and rejecting the eating of wild asses and camels. I myself saw and heard them renouncing their ancestral impiety and consenting to the evangelical teaching.

On one occasion I myself incurred the greatest danger. Simeon told them to approach me and receive a priestly blessing, saying that they would thereby receive great benefit. When they rushed toward me somewhat more barbarously, some pulling from the front, others from behind, and others from the side, those who were farther away charged forward and stretched out their hands. Some pulled my beard, while others seized my clothing. I would have been suffocated by the violence of their approach had he not uttered a shout and dispersed them all. Such benefit did the column, which men given to jesting ridicule, pour forth, and such a ray of knowledge of God did it send into the minds of the barbarians.

I know of another similar event involving him. One tribe implored the holy man to send a prayer and blessing to the leader of its tribe.
