Another tribe that was present objected, saying that the blessing ought not to be sent to him but to the one who presided over its own tribe: the former, they said, was supremely unjust, whereas the latter was free from injustice. When a great dispute and barbarian contest had arisen between them, they finally rushed against one another. I used an extended speech to persuade them to be quiet, since the holy man was sufficient to give a blessing both to one and to the other. But they continued to say that the first should not receive it, and the others tried to deprive him of it. When Simeon threatened them from above and called them dogs, he scarcely managed to calm the dispute. I have related this to show how great was their faith of soul. They would not have behaved so insanely toward one another unless they had believed that the blessing of the holy man possessed the greatest power.

I also witnessed another much-celebrated miracle. A certain man entered—he too was the leader of one of the Saracen tribes—and humbly begged the holy man to help someone whose bodily limbs had been paralyzed on the road. He said that the disease had befallen the man at Callinicus, which is a very large fortress. When the afflicted man had been brought into their midst, Simeon caused him to renounce the impiety of his ancestors. Once he willingly obeyed and fulfilled what he had been commanded, Simeon asked whether he believed in the Father, the Only-Begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit. When the man confessed that he did believe, Simeon said: “Believing in these names, rise.”

After he had risen, Simeon ordered him to carry the tribal leader on his shoulders all the way to the holy man’s tent—for the leader had a very large body—and the man, taking him up, immediately departed. Those who were present raised their voices in praise of God.

Simeon gave this command in imitation of the Lord, who commanded the paralytic to carry his bed (Matthew 9). Let no one call imitation of God tyranny. For his word is: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14). We have indeed seen the fulfillment of this promise. For although the shadow of the Lord never performed a miracle, the shadow of the great Peter both broke the power of death, drove away diseases, and expelled demons. The Lord performed these miracles through his servants; and now as well, using the Lord’s name, the holy Simeon performs countless miracles.

Another miracle also occurred, in no way inferior to the first. One of the Ishmaelites who had believed in the saving name of the Lord Christ, a man born into a distinguished station, had made a vow to God in the presence of this holy man. He had promised that thereafter he would permanently abstain from eating anything living. Somehow, at a certain time, he transgressed this promise and dared to eat a slaughtered bird. When God wished to lead him to repentance by rebuking him, and to honor his servant who had witnessed the promise that the man had violated, the flesh of the bird was changed into the nature of stone, so that he could not thereafter eat it even if he wished. For how could he have done so, when the body taken as food had become stone?

Struck with astonishment at this marvelous and incredible spectacle, the barbarian came as quickly as possible to the holy man, bringing the hidden sin into the light, proclaiming his transgression to everyone, asking God’s forgiveness for his offense, and invoking the saint’s help, so that by his all-powerful prayers he might release him from the bond of sin. Many people saw this miracle: they saw in the bird’s breast a piece consisting of bone and stone.

I was not merely a spectator of miracles but also a hearer of predictions concerning the future. He foretold two years in advance the drought that occurred, the great barrenness of that year, and the famine and pestilence that followed together. He said that he had foreseen the rod inflicted upon human beings and the scourges threatened through it. On another occasion he also announced the invasion of what is called the locust or grasshopper, and said that it would cause no great damage, since divine mercy would soon follow the punishment. After thirty days had passed, an innumerable multitude stood above, so numerous that they even cut off the sunlight and cast a shadow; we all saw this clearly and completely. It damaged only the pastures of animals and in no way harmed human food.

He also told me, when I was being attacked by someone, that the war would end within fifteen days; I learned the truth of his prediction by experience.

[Note: [Col. 0119B] “Of the prediction.” Thus the other Simeon Stylites predicted many things concerning Maurice; see Evagrius, Book V, chapter 21.]

On another occasion he saw two rods being carried from heaven and falling upon the eastern and western earth. The holy man interpreted this as signifying the uprising of the Persian and Scythian peoples against the Roman Empire, and he disclosed the vision to those who were present. Through many tears and continual prayers he restrained the blows whose threats hung over the world. The Persian people were already armed and prepared to invade the Romans, but, divine will opposing them, they were held back from their undertaking and became occupied with their own internal troubles. Although I know many other things of this kind, I shall pass them over to avoid prolonging the account. These things are certainly sufficient to display the spiritual contemplation of his mind.

He was also highly renowned among the Persian king. For, as the envoys who came to him related, the king carefully inquired what his way of life was and what miracles he performed. They say that the king’s wife too requested oil honored by his blessing and received it as a very great gift. Moreover, all the king’s attendants, moved by his fame and hearing many accusations devised against him by the magi, made careful inquiries; and when they understood the facts, they called him a holy man. The rest of the crowd—including muleteers, servants, and soldiers—offered money and asked to share in the blessed oil.

The queen of the Ishmaelites was barren and desired children. First, through someone who possessed rank and authority, she implored him to make her a mother. When she obtained her request and gave birth as she wished, she took the child who had been born and went to the holy old man. Since women were not permitted to approach him, she sent the infant to him and asked that she might obtain his blessing. “This deed is yours,” she said. “For I offered, with tears, the seed of prayer; but you made the seed into a sheaf by drawing down the rain of divine grace through your supplication.”

[Note: [Col. 0119B] “This deed is yours.” Thus Euthymius made barren women fruitful; Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 52.]

But how long shall I try to measure the depth of the Atlantic Sea [Note: “I try to measure the depth of the Atlantic Sea.” Thus: “To drain the Atlantic Sea with a cup.”]? For just as human beings cannot measure it, so the deeds performed by him each day surpass all account. Before all these things, however, I admire his endurance; for night and day he stands in such a way that he is visible to everyone. With the doors removed and no small part of the surrounding structure dismantled, he is presented to all as a new and marvelous spectacle: now standing for a long time, now frequently [853] bending himself [Col. 0107A] and offering worship to God. Indeed, many of those standing nearby also count these acts of worship. Once, one of those who were with me, after counting one thousand two hundred and forty-four, then stumbled and stopped counting. He always bends himself so that he brings his forehead near the toes of his feet. Since his stomach receives food only once a week, and only a little—about as much as participation in the divine mysteries—his back permits him to bend easily. They say that, from standing on one foot, an ulcer called *chironium* arose, and that from it a great quantity of pus is continually discharged. Yet nothing that happens to him suppresses his philosophical discipline; with a brave and noble spirit he endures both voluntary and involuntary sufferings, overcoming each through the cheerfulness of his soul.

[Col. 0107B] Once he was even compelled to show this ulcer to someone [Note: “To show it to someone.” Thus he displayed to the Fathers his ready obedience; Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 51.]. I shall state the reason. A good man, honored for his service to Christ, came from Arabena. When he had reached that summit, he said: “Tell me, by the very truth that converts the human race to itself: are you a human being, or incorporeal by nature?” Those who were present were distressed by the question, but he ordered them all to be silent and said to the man: “Why did you put this question to me?” He replied: “Because I hear everyone commonly claiming that you neither eat nor sleep; yet both are proper to human beings, for no one endowed with this nature could live without food and sleep.” Then he ordered a ladder to be brought to the column and told the man to climb up: first to look at his hands, and then to put his hand inside the leather garment with which he was clothed and see not only his feet but also that very serious ulcer. When the man had seen it, marveled at the size of the ulcer, and learned from it how he took nourishment, he descended and came to me, relating everything.

During the public festivals he also displayed another form of endurance. For after sunset, until the sun again reached the western horizon, he stands all night with his hands extended toward heaven [Note: “He stands all night.” Nicephorus wrote that there were monks called Ἀκοιμήτους, “sleepless,” who passed the night praying and singing psalms; Book XV, chapter 23. Concerning their monastery, see the Menaea, September 15, under John Calybita; and December 29, in the Acts of Marcellus, abbot of the Acoemetae, in Metaphrastes; and in the Acts of Daniel the Stylite, December 11.], neither lulled by sleep nor overcome by labor. Yet amid such great labors, such magnitude of achievement, and such a multitude of miracles, he possesses such modesty and self-restraint that he seems the least distinguished of all human beings. Besides his modesty, access to him is easy, and he is approachable and gracious; he answers each person who speaks to him, whether craftsman, beggar, or peasant. From the munificent and generous Lord he also received the gift of teaching. Twice each day he gives exhortations, watering the ears of those who listen, speaking with great beauty and displaying the instruction of the divine Spirit; commanding them to look up to heaven and soar away, to depart from the earth and grasp by contemplation the kingdom that is awaited, to fear the threats of Gehenna, to despise earthly things, and to await the things to come. One may also see him acting as a judge and delivering upright and just decisions. These matters and others like them take place after the ninth hour [Col. 0108A]. For he prays continually throughout the whole night and day until the ninth hour. After the ninth hour, he first offers divine teaching to those present; then, after hearing each person’s request and performing some cures, he settles the disputes of those who are at odds. Around sunset he then begins to commune with the Lord. Although he is occupied with these things and does all of them, he does not abandon concern and providence for the holy churches: sometimes combating the impiety of the nations, sometimes breaking the audacity of the Jews [Note: “Breaking the audacity of the Jews.” It refers to what Epiphanius has in Book I of his History, chapter 13, from which Baronius drew material under the year 432. See also Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 51.], sometimes pouring out and routing the ranks of heretics; sometimes writing about these matters to the emperor, sometimes rousing governors and magistrates to divine zeal, and sometimes commanding the pastors of the churches themselves to take greater care of the flock.

I have pursued these matters, trying to show the rain from a drop [Note: “Rain from a drop.” A similar proverb is “The lion from its claw.” Thus also, “The salt sea from a drop.”], and offering those who read this account a taste of the sweetness of honey, as though through a sample. Yet what is sung and celebrated by everyone is far more extensive than this. I did not promise to write everything, but only to display briefly the pattern and character of his way of life. Others, as is fitting, will write much more about him.

After this, when he had lived for a long time [Note: “After this, when he had lived for a long time.” Barraeus notes that this does not belong to Theodoret but was added by someone after Simeon’s death; when Theodoret wrote, Simeon was still alive.], and when, through many miracles and labors, the heat of the sun, winter frost, the violent assaults of the winds, and the weakness of human nature, he alone among all who had ever lived had remained unconquerable, the time came when he had to be with Christ and receive the crowns of his immeasurable contests. His death confirmed to those who did not believe that he was human. Yet even after death he remained unmoved: his soul had indeed reached heaven, but his body would not even then consent to fall. It [854] stood upright at the place of combat, like an undefeated athlete, unwilling that any part of its limbs should touch the ground. Thus the victory of Christ’s athletes remains with them even after death.

The cures of various diseases, miracles, and the power of divine works continue to occur now just as they did while he was alive—not only at the reliquaries of the holy remains, but also at the monument of his supreme virtue and long struggle: that great and celebrated column of this righteous and praiseworthy Simeon [Col. 0108D].

By whose holy intercessions I pray that, aided by him, I may persevere in these holy labors. And I beseech God, who is the common adornment and the splendor of piety and true religion, that my life may be corrected and directed toward the evangelical form of life.

## CHAPTER XXVII. BARADATUS

[Note: “Baradatus.” Concerning him, see the Greek Menaea, February 22; Evagrius, Book II, chapter 9. In Nicephorus, Book XV, chapter 22, he is called Varadatus.]

The common enemy of humanity has discovered many paths of vice, striving utterly to destroy the whole human race; and the followers of true piety and religion have devised many different ladders by which one might ascend to heaven. Some, contending in companies—for these assemblies are innumerable—enjoy incorruptible crowns and attain the desired ascent. Others, embracing the monastic life and practicing conversation with God alone, sharing in no human consolation, are thus publicly proclaimed victors. Others live in tents, and others in huts, celebrating God with praises. Still others embrace life in caves and caverns. Many, among whom we have remembered some, determined to possess neither cave, tent, cavern, nor hut, but to entrust their bodies to the open air, enduring contrary conditions: sometimes frozen by the most severe cold, sometimes scorched by the fire of the sun’s rays. Their manner of life, too, differs. Some stand continually; others divide the day between sitting and standing. Some, enclosed within certain fences, avoid the company of many; others, using no such covering, are set before all who wish to behold them. Since I wished to write the life of the admirable Baradatus, I have necessarily pursued each of these matters here. For he devised new methods of practicing endurance.

At first, after enclosing himself for a long time in a little house, he enjoyed only divine contemplation. Later, when he had occupied an overhanging rock and constructed from wood a small chest, not proportioned to the dimensions of his body, he lived in it, compelled constantly to bend downward. For its height did not correspond in proper proportion to his length. It was not assembled from boards fitted together but was open, like a lattice; it resembled windows that have wider openings for the entrance of light. Consequently it was neither free from the force of the rain nor sheltered from the sun’s flame; it admitted both no less than other things under the open sky. In this one respect it surpassed them: it added the labor of confinement.

After spending a long time in this manner, he later came out, yielding to the prayers of the divine Theodotus, who had obtained the episcopal see of Antioch. He now stands continually, extending his hands toward heaven and praising the God of all. His entire body is covered by a tunic of leather; only around his nose and mouth has he left a small opening for breath, receiving the common air, since human nature could not live otherwise. He endures all this labor although his body is not robust but sickly and subject to many diseases. Yet the fervent eagerness of his soul, kindled by divine love, compels him to labor though he cannot physically labor.

He is also adorned with wisdom and understanding, and he asks questions, answers, and reasons extremely well—sometimes better and more powerfully than those who read the labyrinths of Aristotle. Although he stands at the very summit of virtue, he does not allow arrogance to raise his spirit along with him; rather, he commands it to crawl downward [Col. 0110A] around the very side of the mountain. For this is how much harm a mind brings upon itself when it swells and burns with insolence. This, in summary, is his philosophy.

May he be granted, as he grows, to reach the goal of his course. For he is the common joy of the pious, the glory of those who have won the victory. May I, supported by their prayers, not remain far from this mountain, but gradually climb it and satisfy myself with the delight of contemplating them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. THALELAEUS

[Note: “Thalelaeus.” The Menaea mention him on February 27. Moschus, chapter 59, mentions Thalelaeus of Cilicia; Raderus thinks it possible that he is the same man, since both were Cilicians and confessors. I accept the identification. But the man in the Menaea on May 20 is entirely different, since he is said to have lived in the time of Numerian and to have suffered martyrdom. Another Thallelaeus appears in Moschus, chapter 91, who was a sailor.]

I shall not be silent about the story of Thalelaeus, for it is a spectacle full of wonder. I have not merely heard others recount it; I myself also saw a marvelous and extraordinary spectacle. When he had occupied a mound twenty stades from Gabala—for this is a small and elegant city—there was on it a temple dedicated to demons, long honored with many sacrifices by those who had been impious from ancient times. He fixed there a small hut. Those wicked and accursed beings, as they said, were continually worshiped, in an effort to appease their great cruelty through worship. For they brought destruction upon many, both those who approached and those who lived nearby—not only upon human beings but also upon asses, mules, oxen, and sheep. They did not wage war against the animals, but through them also laid snares for human beings.

When they saw him arrive, they tried to terrify him, but could not, since faith protected him and grace fought on his behalf. Filled with rage [Col. 0110C] and fury, they attacked the trees that had then been planted there. There were many flourishing fig trees and olive trees on that mound. They say that more than five hundred of them were suddenly torn up. I heard several neighboring country people recount this, men who had once been held in the darkness of impiety but through his teaching and miracles had received the light of knowledge of God. Since the destructive and wicked demons were not able to terrify the athlete of philosophy by doing this, they prepared other stratagems against him. At night, howling and displaying lamps, they tried to frighten him and disturb his reason. When he laughed at all their assaults, they later abandoned the place and fled.

He constructed two wheels, each two cubits in diameter. Their boards were not joined to one another but were separate and apart, and he joined the two wheels together. Then, after sitting inside and fastening the separated boards with wedges and nails, he hung the wheel under the open sky, using three other tall pieces of wood fixed into the ground, their upper ends joined by other timbers, with the double wheel fastened in their midst and raised aloft. The inner space of this structure is two cubits high and one cubit wide. Sitting—or rather hanging—in it, he has now spent ten uninterrupted years. Though he has a very large body, even while seated he cannot raise his neck; he always sits bent over, with his face resting upon his knees.

When I came to him, I found him drawing instruction from the Gospels. I asked him, wishing to know the reason for this new way of life. He replied in Greek, for he was Cilician by birth:

“I am burdened with many sins, and I believe in the punishments whose threats have been declared. Therefore I devised this way of life, treating the body with moderate penalties so that I might be delivered from the magnitude of the punishments that await me. Those punishments are more severe not only in quantity but also in their very nature, for they are involuntary. What is done unwillingly is very painful; what is voluntary, even if laborious, brings less pain. It is undertaken willingly, and the labor is not forced. If, therefore, by these small hardships I lessen the punishments that await me, I shall gain a great profit.”

When I heard this, I greatly admired the ingenuity of his mind: he not only leaped beyond the fences already established but also devised contests for himself; and he not only contended but understood the reasons for his contests and taught them to others.

The inhabitants also said that many miracles occurred through his prayers, and that he obtained cures not only for human beings but also for camels, asses, and mules. Thus the entire population that had been held in impiety renounced the error inherited from its fathers and received the splendor of divine light. Using these instruments, he both demolished the temple of the demons and raised a great church, setting victorious martyrs—dead men called divine—against those falsely called gods.

May he be granted, through the intercession of these saints, to reach the goal of his contests with the same victory; and may we, aided by them and by him, become ardent lovers of the contests of philosophy.

## CHAPTER XXIX. MARANA AND CYRA

[Note: “Marana and Cyra.” Roman Martyrology, August 3: “At Beroea in Syria, Saints Marana and Cyra.” Concerning the same women, see the Menaea, February 28.]

After writing the way of life of the best and most distinguished men, I consider it worthwhile to remember women also, who contended no less—and perhaps even more. They are more worthy of praise because, although they received a weaker nature, they displayed the same eagerness of spirit as men and freed their sex from the disgrace received from its first parent. I shall now recall Marana and Cyra, who surpassed all others in the contests of endurance.

Their homeland was Beroea, their family distinguished, and their upbringing suited to their lineage. Yet, despising all these things, they took possession of a small place outside the city and, having entered it, blocked the entrance with mud and stones [Note: “With mud and stones.” The Menaea has πηλῷ καὶ λίθοις, “with mud and stones.” Compare Book I, here, in the Life of Simeon the Stylite, chapter 5, where the opposite is found: dry stone, or ξηρόλιθος.]. They ordered the servant women who wished to share their way of life to live in a dwelling constructed outside the enclosure. Through a small window they themselves watched what those women did, frequently urged them to prayer, and inflamed them with divine love. The two women themselves, possessing neither house nor hut, voluntarily lived under the open sky. In place of a door, a small window had been constructed for them, through which they received the necessary food and conversed with the women who came to them. A fixed time for such meetings was Pentecost; at other times they embraced a quiet life. Only Marana spoke with visitors; no one ever heard the other speak. They also wore iron and carried so heavy a burden that Cyra, whose body was the weaker, bent all the way to the ground and could scarcely raise herself. They had very large veils, which dragged behind them and completely covered their feet, while in front they descended to the belt, entirely concealing the face, neck, breast, and hands.

I often saw them, having been admitted inside the entrance; for they ordered it to be opened for me, honoring the dignity of my priesthood. I saw the weight of iron, which not even a strong and robust man could carry, and only after earnestly begging them was I able to remove it. When we had withdrawn, they placed it again upon their limbs: a collar around the neck, a belt around the loins, and upon their hands and feet the objects assigned to them. They have lived in this manner not merely for five or ten years, but for forty-two. Though they have contended for so long, they delight in their sweats as though they had only just entered the contest. For, grasping through contemplation the beauty of the Bridegroom, they easily endure the labor of the course and hasten to reach the contest’s end, seeing the Beloved standing there and displaying the crown of victory. Therefore, enduring the assaults of rain, snow, and sun, they feel neither torment nor pain; from things that appear troublesome they receive joy of soul. Emulating the fast of the divine Moses, they endured abstinence for three times as long: for forty days they partook of only a little food. They also emulated the abstinence from food of the divine Daniel three times over, completing three weeks and supplying nourishment to the body.

Once, when they had desired to behold the holy places of Christ’s saving Passion, they came to Aelia without taking any food along the way. After they had entered the city and completed their worship, they ate and returned, again completing the journey fasting. The journey is no fewer than twenty days.

Moreover, when they wished to see the church of the celebrated Thecla in Isauria, so that they might kindle the flame of their love for God from every direction, they set out in this manner and returned fasting. Such was the effect of divine love upon them: it drove them to rave with a kind of divine madness. Such insanity did their divine love for the Bridegroom arouse in them.

These women, who adorned their sex by such a way of life and became examples to others, will be crowned by the Lord with victorious crowns. As for me, having gathered the blessing that comes from the benefit set before us, I shall pass to another narrative.

## CHAPTER XXX. DOMNINA

[Note: “Domnina.” Greek Menologion, March 1. A somewhat fuller account appears in the Menaea on the same day. Our Raderus translated it in Part I of the *Garden of the Saints*.]

[Col. 0113A]

The admirable Domnina, emulating the life of the divine Maron, whom we mentioned earlier, fixed a small hut in the garden of her mother’s house. The hut was made of stalks of millet. With continual tears she waters not only her cheeks but also her garment, for she covers her body with such clothing. Around the time of the cockcrow she goes with other women and men to the divine temple, which is not far away, and offers praises to the Lord of all. She does this not only at the beginning of the day but also at its end, judging and teaching others that a place consecrated to God is more venerable than any other place. For this reason she also took great care of it, persuading her mother and brothers [Col. 0113B] to spend their resources on it.

Her nourishment is lentils soaked in water. She endures all this labor although her body is completely dried out and half-dead. Her skin is exceedingly thin, like a membrane, stretched over slender bones; fat and flesh have been consumed by her labors. She presents herself to all who wish to see her, men and women alike, neither looking upon anyone’s face nor allowing anyone else to look upon hers [Note: “Nor allowing anyone else to look upon her face.” See Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 78, concerning a dead virgin who severely rebuked the violator of her tomb for stripping her of her clothing, although while alive no one outside her household had seen her face.]. She is completely covered by her garment and bent down as far as her knees. She speaks in a very thin and indistinct voice, always uttering it with tears. Often, when she took my right hand and placed it upon her eyes, she released it so thoroughly soaked that tears dripped from the hand itself [Col. 0113C].

What speech could praise in a manner worthy of her such wealth of philosophical discipline, while she weeps, laments, and groans like women in the utmost poverty? For vehement love of God produces those tears, inflaming her to divine contemplation, pricking her with goads, and urging her toward the departure that will come from this life.

Moreover, although she is occupied with these matters day and night, she does not neglect the other kinds of virtue. To the best of her ability she cares for the excellent athletes whom we have mentioned and those whom we have omitted. She also cares for those who come to her, ordering them to stay with the village pastor while she herself sends everything necessary. The resources of her mother and brothers have been placed at her disposal for expenses, by which they receive a blessing. Indeed, when I too come to that region—for it lies south of our region—she sends me bread, fruit, and soaked lentils.

But why should I continue at such length, striving to recount all her virtue, when I ought also to present the lives of others who imitated both her and those whom we mentioned earlier? Many other women have partly embraced a solitary life and partly chosen to live with others, so that two hundred and fifty, or more, or fewer live together, eating one common food, sleeping by rule only on mats, assigning their hands to wool [Col. 0114A], and consecrating their tongues to hymns. There are countless such schools of wisdom not only in our region but throughout the East. Palestine, Egypt, Asia, Pontus, and all Europe are also full of them. Ever since Christ the Lord honored virginity, he who was born of virginity caused the meadows of virginity to blossom by nature and offers the Creator these sweet-smelling and unfading flowers. He does not distinguish virtue between male and female or divide philosophy into two classes. There is a difference between bodies, but not between souls. For, as the divine Apostle says, in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female (Galatians 3). One faith has been supplied to women and men alike. For there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all (Ephesians 4). Indeed, the contest’s presiding judge has set before victors one kingdom of heaven, defining this common reward for their contests.

Thus, as I said, there are many arenas of piety for men and women, not only among us but throughout Syria, Palestine, Cilicia, and the region lying between the two rivers. In Egypt, they say, there are monasteries containing more than five thousand men, who work while praising the Lord and celebrating him with hymns. They obtain from their labor not only the food they need but also provide assistance to visiting guests and the needy.

Yet neither I nor all writers together could recount everything; and even if it were possible, I consider it superfluous and an ambition for honor that offers no benefit. For those who wish to gain some profit, what has been said is sufficient to provide what they seek.

For this reason we have mentioned the lives of different people and added the narratives of women to those of men: so that old men, young men, and women might have examples of philosophy; and so that each person, reproducing the life suited to his or her heart, might possess a rule and measuring rod for life, set out in the narrative. Just as painters look to a model and imitate the eyes, nose, mouth, cheeks, ears, forehead, and the hairs of the head and beard, as well as posture and stance—and even the gaze of the eyes, whether cheerful and lively or severe and fierce—so each reader of these writings who wishes to imitate a particular life ought to conform his or her own life to the one chosen. And just as craftsmen straighten boards with a red marking line, removing the excess until, when the rule is applied, they see that the board is even, so anyone who wishes to imitate a particular life ought to set it before himself as a rule, cut away the excesses of vice, and fill in what virtue lacks. For this reason we undertook the labor of writing, setting before those who wish it an opportunity for benefit.

I ask those who will read this work that, since they take pleasure without labor from the labors of others, they repay those labors with their prayers. I also beseech those whose lives I have written not to despise me, who live far away from their spiritual choir, but to draw me, lying below, upward to the height of virtue and join me to their choir, so that I may not merely praise the riches of others but may myself also possess some occasion for praise, glorifying the Savior of all in deed, word, and thought. With him be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

# THE TENTH BOOK OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR THE SPIRITUAL MEADOW, BY JOHN MOSCHUS. TRANSLATED BY AMBROSIUS OF CAMALDOLI

[Col. 0119]

## AUTHOR’S EULOGY

[Note: See more eulogies in General Prolegomena 12. This one is now added from the Greek, from the Vatican manuscripts and from the manuscript of the illustrious Franciscus Olivarius.]

[861] This book, the *Meadow*, or *Lives of the Saints*, was composed by John, a presbyter of holy memory and a monk surnamed Moschus. It contains the lives of holy Fathers distinguished by virtue and pleasing to God, together with other exceedingly useful spiritual narratives and the wise sayings of holy, righteous, and Christ-loving Fathers and brothers. At the outset he renounced the world in the monastery of our holy Father Theodosius, abbot and archimandrite of all the coenobitic communities or monasteries in Jerusalem [Col. 0121]. After spending a considerable time in the desert near the holy Jordan with the holy Fathers who live there, and collecting their virtues, he inserted them into this work.

While he was living in the monastery called the New Monastery, which had been built by our holy and great Father Sabas and his disciples and remains to this day, he heard how the Persians had oppressed the Romans with tyranny on the occasion of the murder of the emperor Maurice and his children. He withdrew from the New Monastery and went to the region of great Antioch. When he saw the foreign people gaining strength there as well, he went on to Alexandria. After traversing the entire desert around it—for at the beginning of the reign of Tiberius he had already been sent to Egypt to carry out a ministry—and reaching the Oasis and the desert nearest to it, he visited the Fathers who lived there. Then, hearing again that the holy places had been occupied and that the Romans had been seized with fear, he left Alexandria and sailed to the great city of the Romans together with his beloved disciple Sophronius. While they were traveling, they visited various islands.

The blessed man had received such grace from the Lord that, if he heard or saw anything concerning the life and deeds of men distinguished in virtue, he would commit it to writing. Thus, when he was in Rome, he followed the same practice.

[862] When the blessed man foresaw the time of his departure to God, he composed this book—not according to the order of the things he had heard or seen, but joining together in writing those matters that were comparable, whether heard or seen.

When he was about to withdraw from these earthly disturbances and pass into a tranquil and peaceful life, he summoned his beloved disciple and handed him this book, which contains the lives and God-pleasing deeds of the holy Fathers. He commanded him not to leave his remains in Rome but to try, insofar as it depended on him, to transport them, enclosed in a wooden chest, to Mount Sinai, so that they might be placed there with the holy Fathers who dwell there. If some barbarian disturbance should arise and prevent this from being done, he ordered that the remains be deposited in the monastery of Saint Theodosius, where at the outset he had renounced the world.

While the beloved disciple was striving to fulfill this command, he took with him John and his fellow disciples—there were twelve of them—and imitated the great Joseph, who, taking Israel with his brothers, transported him from Egypt to his fathers, just as his father had commanded him.

When he had landed at Ascalon and learned that he could not reach the holy mountain of Sinai because of the tyrannical incursions of those called Hagarenes, he took the remains of blessed John and, at the beginning of the eighth indiction, came to Jerusalem. There he found George the presbyter, superior of the great monastery of our holy Father Theodosius. After reporting to him everything that the old man had commanded, he and the brothers of the monastery who happened to be in the city at that time, together with the monks who lived with him, carried blessed John away and, as he had ordered, buried him in the cemetery of Saint Theodosius, together with the holy Fathers who lie there. He spent the remainder of his life in the same coenobium.

The cemetery is a cave in which the Magi, after deceiving Herod according to the Gospel account, lodged as they returned to their homeland. In this cave our holy Father Theodosius, after completing the contests of the religious life, was granted the power to expel demons. He expels them not only in this temporary and brief life but also after death, even to this day, to the glory and praise of Christ, the true God and our Savior, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0121]

## Prologue

John Moschus to his beloved in Christ, Sophronius the Sophist.

The face of meadows is plainly most delightful, dearest son, especially in springtime. Their pleasing variety of flowers of every kind attracts the gaze of those who look upon them, holds back passers-by, and nourishes them in diverse ways; for it smiles upon the eyes and soothes the sense of smell. One part of this meadow blooms with the redness of roses; another, whitening with lilies, readily draws observers to itself by its rosy appearance. Another [p. 863] part glows with violets and, by its color, imitates royal purple. Everywhere, the varied and diverse appearance and fragrance of countless flowers pours forth grace.

Consider this present work likewise to be such a meadow, holy and most faithful son Sophronius; for in it you will find the virtues of holy men who shone forth in our own times and, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying, were planted beside streams of water (Ps. 1). Although all of them were especially acceptable and pleasing to God, one is adorned more than another with a different kind of virtue; and from this sweet variety of virtues arises a pleasing beauty and an agreeable appearance. Plucking the fairest flowers from these, I have woven for you, most faithful son, a crown from an unfading and everlasting meadow, and I offer it to you and, through you, to everyone.

For this reason I have also chosen to call the present work *The Meadow*, on account of the delight, fragrance, and usefulness which readers will derive from it [Col. 0123]. Virtue is uprightness of life and conduct; to it one is led not only by meditation upon divine matters and right faith, but also by the association of others and by a life full of virtue handed down in writing. Therefore I have undertaken this task, trusting in the Lord, dearest son, and wishing your charity to be persuaded of this: like a bee, pursuing everything useful and true, I have written down the worthy deeds of the holy Fathers for the profit of souls.

[Col. 0123]

# THE SPIRITUAL MEADOW

## CHAPTER I. The life of the holy elder John, and concerning the cave of Sapsas

[Col. 0123A]

There was an elder named John living in the monastery of Abbot Eustorgius. The holy Elias, archbishop of Jerusalem, wished to appoint him superior of the monastery. But he would not agree, saying: “I wish to go to Mount Sinai for the sake of prayer.” The archbishop urged him first to become abbot and afterward to go wherever he wished. Since the elder would not consent, he let him go, after he had promised that, when he returned, he would undertake the responsibility of governance.

Having therefore taken leave of the archbishop, he set out to travel to Mount Sinai, taking his disciple with him. When they had crossed the Jordan River and proceeded scarcely one stone’s throw, the elder began to be seized by a chill, and [Col. 0123B] shortly afterward fever attacked him. When the fever’s heat increased so greatly that he could not walk, they found a small cave and entered it to rest. When the fever grew so severe that he could scarcely move, they remained in that cave for three days.

Then, in a dream, the elder saw someone standing beside him and saying: “Tell me, elder, where do you wish to go?” He replied: “To Mount Sinai.” The other said to him: “Please do not depart from here.” When he could not persuade the elder, he went away. The fever, however, afflicted the elder still more fiercely.

The following night the same figure appeared again to the elder in the same form and said: “Why do you wish to suffer, elder? Listen to me, and never depart from here.” The elder said to him: “Who are you?” The one who had appeared replied: “I am John the Baptist. For this reason I command you never to depart, [Col. 0123C] because this little cave is greater than Mount Sinai. Indeed, our Lord Jesus often entered it when he visited me. Promise me, then, that you will dwell here, and I will immediately restore your health.”

Hearing this, the elder willingly promised that he would remain in the same cave. At once he became well and continued there for the rest of his life. He made the cave into a church and gathered brothers there. The place is called Sapsas. Beside it, on the left, lies the torrent of Chorath, to which Elijah was sent during the drought, across from the Jordan.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the elder who fed lions in his own cave

In the same place, Sapsa, there lived another elder in a cave [Col. 0123D], a man of such virtue that he received lions into the same cave with him and gave them food from his own bosom; so full was this man of divine grace.

## CHAPTER III. The life of Conon, priest of the monastery of Penthucula

[Col. 0124A]

When we had gone to the monastery of our holy Father Sabas, to Abbot Athanasius, the elder told us:

“When I was in the monastery of Penthucula, there was a certain priest assigned to the ministry of baptism, named Conon, an Alexandrian by birth. Because of his manner of life, the Fathers had ordered him to baptize those who came for this purpose. He therefore anointed with holy chrism and baptized those who came to be baptized.

“Whenever he anointed a woman, he was scandalized, and for this reason wished to leave the monastery. Whenever he was troubled by this thought, Saint John the Baptist stood beside him and said: ‘Endure and persevere, and I will deliver you from this struggle.’ [p. 864]

“One day [Col. 0124B] a girl from Persia came to be baptized. She was so beautiful and of such great loveliness that the priest could not anoint her naked with holy oil [Note: [Col. 0239B] ‘To anoint her naked with holy oil.’ In former times both men and women were baptized naked in body, and thus anointed. See the *Onomasticon*.]. When the girl had remained there for two days, Archbishop Peter heard of it and was greatly astonished at the elder. He wished to assign a deaconess to this task, but did not do so, lest he appear to have acted contrary to the canons.

“Conon the priest, taking his sheepskin cloak, departed, saying: ‘I will no longer remain in this place.’ When he had gone out toward the hills, behold, Saint John the Baptist met him and addressed him in a gentle voice: ‘Return to your monastery, and I will relieve you of this struggle.’

“But Abbot Conon said to him angrily: ‘I certainly will not return. For behold, you have already promised me this so many times, and you have not done it.’

“Then Saint [Col. 0124C] John made him sit down, removed his clothing, signed him three times with the sign of the cross below the navel, and said to him: ‘Believe me, Priest Conon, I wanted you to be rewarded for this struggle; but since you do not wish it, behold, I have taken this struggle away from you, and you will lack the reward for this work.’

“The priest returned to the monastery where he had been accustomed to baptize. On the following day he baptized the girl whom he had anointed, and did not perceive at all that she was female by nature. He continued another twelve years in the ministry of baptism with such tranquility of soul and body that he no longer felt any movement of the flesh and did not see a woman as female by nature. Thus he completed his life in peace.”

## CHAPTER IV. The vision of Abbot Leontius

[Col. 0124D]

Abbot Leontius, superior of the monastery of our holy Father Theodosius, told us:

“After the monks had been driven out by the unbelievers, [Col. 0125A] having suffered persecution on account of the new monastery called the Laura, I went there and remained in that Laura. One Sunday I went down to the church to receive the holy Mysteries. When I entered, I saw an angel standing at the right horn of the altar. Seized with great fear, I returned to my cell.

“Then a voice came to me from heaven, saying: ‘Ever since this altar was sanctified, I have been commanded to stand beside it continually’” [Note: [Col. 0125D] Similar below, chapter 10.].

## CHAPTER V. Abbot Polychronius’ account of three monks

Abbot Polychronius, priest of that same new Laura, told me:

“Once, while I was sitting in the monastery of the Towers of the Jordan, I noticed that one of the brothers there was neglectful of himself and never fulfilled the canon of the holy Lord’s Day. [Col. 0125B] After a short time, however, I saw the same man exercising himself with complete zeal and eagerness.

“Then I said to him: ‘You are doing very well now, brother, taking care of yourself.’

“He said to me: ‘Lord Father, I am about to die.’” Three days later he died.

Again the same Abbot Polychronius told me:

“When one of the brothers had died in that same monastery of the Towers, the steward said to me: ‘Do me this kindness and come, so that we may carry the brother’s vessels to the place of administration.’

“When we had begun carrying them, I saw the steward weeping. I said to him: ‘Why, please, are you weeping so, Abba?’

“He replied: ‘Today I am carrying the brother’s vessels, and after two days others will carry mine.’

“On the third day that man rested, just as he had foretold, when the Lord [Col. 0125C] had placed him individually in hope.”

## CHAPTER VI. The same man’s account

The same Abbot Polychronius the priest also related this:

“When I was in the monastery of Abbot Constantine, superior of the monastery of Saint Mary the Mother of God, which is called New, I heard that one of the brothers had died in the hospice at Jericho. The brothers took him to carry him to the monastery of the Towers and bury him. From the moment they began traveling with the body, a star continued to appear above the dead man’s head like a companion on the journey, until they delivered him to burial.”

## CHAPTER VII. The life and death of an elder who refused to become abbot in the monastery of the Towers

[Col. 0125D]

Another elder lived in the same monastery of the Towers. The Fathers of that monastery wished to appoint him abbot, since he was a great man renowned for his virtues. But the elder prayed, saying:

“Forgive me, Fathers, and allow me to mourn my sins. I am not of such merit that I can care for souls. This is the work of great and excellent Fathers—Anthony, Pachomius, and Saint Theodore.”

When the brothers would not consent and prayed to him every day, he saw that they were pressing him too hard and said to them:

“Allow me to pray for three days, and whatever God commands me to do, I will do.”

[Col. 0126A]

It was the day of Preparation. On Sunday morning he died.

## CHAPTER VIII. The life of Abbot Myrogenes, who suffered from dropsy

There was an elder in the same monastery of the Towers named Myrogenes, who [p. 865] had become dropsical because of his excessive austerity of life. He continually said to the elders who came to visit him:

“Pray for me, Fathers, that the inner man may not become dropsical. For my part, I pray God that I may remain longer in this illness.”

When Eustochius, archbishop of Jerusalem, heard about this Abbot Myrogenes, he wished to send him whatever was necessary, but the elder never consented to accept anything from him. He communicated only this to him:

“Pray for me, Father, that I may be delivered [Col. 0126B] from eternal torment.”

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the wondrous charity of a certain holy Father

In that same monastery of the Towers there was an elder who was an ardent lover of holy nakedness and almsgiving. One day a poor man came to his cell asking for alms. Since the elder had nothing but one loaf of bread, he brought it out and gave it to the poor man.

Then the poor man said to him: “I do not want bread, but clothing.”

Wishing to help him, the elder took him by the hand and brought him into his cell. When the poor man found absolutely nothing there except the clothing the elder himself was wearing, he was so moved by the elder’s virtue that he untied his sack, emptied everything he had into the middle of the cell [Col. 0126C], and said:

“Take these, excellent elder, and I will seek elsewhere what I need.”

## CHAPTER X. The life of Barnabas the anchorite

There was an anchorite in the caves of the holy Jordan named Barnabas. One day, when he went down to drink water from the Jordan, a splinter from a reed pierced his foot. It remained lodged there, continually pricking his foot, and he did not allow a physician to see it. Thus his foot became putrid.

He was forced to go up to the monastery of the Towers and take a cell for himself. His foot continued to decay more each day. He would say to those who came to him:

“The more the outer man suffers, the more the inner man flourishes.”

[Col. 0126D]

After Abbot Barnabas had gone up from his cave to the Towers and had spent some time there, another anchorite went to his cave. When he entered, he saw an angel of God standing above the altar which the elder had built and consecrated.

The anchorite said to the angel: “What are you doing here?”

The angel replied: “Ever since these things were sanctified, they have been entrusted to me by God himself” [Note: [Col. 0126D] Similar above, chapter 4.].

## CHAPTER XI. The life of Abbot Agiodulus

[Col. 0127A]

Abbot Peter, priest of the monastery of our holy Father Sabas, told us about Abbot Agiodulus as follows:

“When he was superior and leader of the monastery of the blessed Gerasimus, it happened that one of the brothers living there died. The elder did not know this. When the prefect of the canon struck the wooden signal for the brothers to assemble and carry out the dead man, the elder saw the corpse lying in the middle of the church and was deeply grieved that he had not greeted him before he departed from this world.

“He went to the bed where the dead man lay and said to him: ‘Rise, brother, and give me a kiss.’

“The man immediately rose and kissed the elder.

“Then the elder said: ‘Sleep now, until Christ, the Son of God, comes and raises you.’”

The same Abbot Agiodulus, when passing along the banks of the Jordan, was considering in his mind and thoughts what had become of the stones which Joshua son of Nun had placed in place of those he had taken from there. While he was thinking about this, the waters immediately divided on both sides [Col. 0127B]. Then he saw those twelve stones, prostrated himself on the ground, gave thanks to God, and departed.

## CHAPTER XII. A saying of Abbot Olympius

A brother asked Abbot Olympius, priest of the monastery of Saint Gerasimus:

“Tell me a word.”

He said to him:

“Do not sit with heretics, restrain your tongue and your stomach; and wherever you sit, say continually: ‘I am a stranger.’”

## CHAPTER XIII. The life of Abbot Mark the anchorite

They said of Abbot Mark the anchorite, who lived near the monastery of Penthucula for sixty-three years, that he possessed the virtue of fasting for entire weeks [Col. 0127C], so that some thought he had no flesh. He worked day and night and distributed everything to the poor, accepting nothing from anyone.

Faithful men, hearing about him, came to offer him an *agape*, and he said to them:

“I do not accept it, because my hands feed me and those who come to me for God’s sake.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the brother who was attacked by the spirit of fornication and became a leper

Abbot Polychronius again told us that in the coenobium of Penthucula there was a brother who was very attentive to himself and continent. When he was once attacked by the spirit of fornication and could not withstand the struggle, he left the monastery and went to Jericho to satisfy his [p. 866] desire [Col. 0127D].

As soon as he entered the prostitute’s cell, he became completely leprous. When he saw the leprosy, he immediately returned to the monastery, giving thanks to God and saying:

“For this reason God struck me with this chastisement, so that my soul might be saved.”

And he glorified God exceedingly.

## CHAPTER XV. The marvelous deed of Abbot Conon

They said of Abbot Conon, superior of the monastery of Penthucula, that one day, as he was going to Betamarim, he encountered Hebrews. When they wished to kill him, they rushed against the elder with drawn swords. When they had approached and brandished their swords against him [Col. 0128A], their hands remained suspended aloft and motionless.

After he had prayed, the elder released them and let them go. They departed giving thanks to God.

## CHAPTER XVI. Abbot Nicholas’ account of himself and his companions

An elder named Nicholas lived in the monastery of Abbot Peter beside the holy Jordan. He told us:

“Once, when I was at Raithu, three of us brothers were sent on an assignment to the Thebaid. As we were traveling through the desert, we lost our way and were carried through the vast expanse of the wilderness. When our water ran out after several days, we began to dry up from thirst.

“When, exhausted by thirst and heat, we could no longer go farther, we found tamarisk trees in the desert. Each of us threw himself [Col. 0128B] beneath the shade of a tree, expecting to die of thirst.

“Lying down in the shade, I fell into ecstasy and saw a pool full of water, with water flowing around it, and two men standing above the rim of the pool, with one wooden vessel. I began to entreat one of them, saying: ‘Do me this kindness, lord, and give me a little water, for I am failing.’

“But he did not wish to do so.

“Then the other said to him: ‘Give him a little.’

“He replied: ‘Let us not give him any, for he is very lazy and neglectful of himself.’

“But the other said: ‘Indeed, he is neglectful and lazy; nevertheless, because of hospitality, let us give him some.’

“Thus they gave water to me and to those who were with me. As soon as we had drunk, we recovered our strength, and, traveling for another three days without drink, [Col. 0128C] we reached inhabited places.”

## CHAPTER XVII. The life of the elder Macnus

They said of an elder named Macnus, who lived in the same monastery of Abbot Peter, that he had spent fifty years in his cave, neither drinking wine nor eating bread, except bran. He received Communion three times each week.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The life of another elder of the Laura who slept with lions

Abbot Polychronius the priest told us about another elder who lived in that same Laura of Abbot Peter. He would often go away and remain on the bank of the Jordan, and wherever he found a lion’s lair, he slept there.

[Col. 0128D]

One day he took two lion cubs beneath his cloak into the church and said to the brothers:

“If we kept the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ, these animals would certainly fear us. But because we have become servants on account of sin, we are shown to fear them.”

Greatly edified by this, the brothers withdrew to their dwellings.

## CHAPTER XIX. Abbot Elias’ account of himself

Abbot Elias told us:

“Once I was living in the region of the holy Jordan, in a cave near the monastery of the Eunuchs, because I did not communicate with Macarius, archbishop of Jerusalem. One day, around the sixth hour, while the most intense heat was scorching from above [Col. 0129A]—for it was the month of August—someone knocked at the door of my cave.

“When I went out, I saw a woman and said to her: ‘What are you doing here?’

“She replied to me: ‘I too, my father, belong to the same way of life as you, and my cave is scarcely a stone’s throw from yours.’ She pointed to a place toward the south and said: ‘I have traversed this wilderness and am exhausted from thirst because of the great heat. Therefore, father, do me this kindness and give me a little water.’

“I brought out a pitcher and gave it to her. After she had taken it and drunk, I dismissed her.

“When she had gone away, the devil began to attack me, casting filthy thoughts about her into my mind. Overcome and unable to bear the heat of lust, I took my staff, left my cell in the scorching heat, while the stones were glowing, and went toward her [Col. 0129B] to fulfill my shameful desire.

“When I was still about one stade from her cave, burning fiercely with the heat of lust, I suddenly fell into ecstasy. I saw the earth opened, and myself swallowed by the earth’s chasm. I saw there decaying and disintegrating corpses filled with an unbelievable stench, and a man of venerable appearance showing them to me and saying:

“‘Behold, this one belonged to a woman, this one to a man, this one to a child. Now enjoy them as you wish and as much as your desire allows. Yet, for the sake of this pleasure, see how many labors you wished to cast away. See on account of what sin you wish to deprive [p. 867] yourselves of the kingdom of heaven. Woe to human misery! For the pleasure of a single hour you are deprived of the reward of so great a labor.’

“I fell to the ground from the excessive stench. Then the venerable man [Col. 0129C] who had appeared to me came near and raised me up. Giving thanks to God, I returned to my cell.”

## CHAPTER XX. The conversion of a soldier through the miracle God worked in him; his life also described briefly

One of the Fathers told us that he had learned the following from a soldier:

“When the Romans were waging war in Africa against the Moors, and, defeated, were being driven into flight by the barbarians, while many of them were being slaughtered here and there, one of the barbarians also caught up with this soldier and began to brandish a spear in order to strike him.

“When he saw this, he began to pray to God and say:

“‘Lord God, who appeared to your servant Thecla and rescued her from the hands of the wicked, deliver me also from this danger and save me from [Col. 0129D] this bitter death. I will immediately go into the wilderness and lead a solitary life.’

“But when he turned around, he saw none of the barbarians. He therefore immediately came to this Laura of Cupatha and had already spent thirty-five years in a cave, while the grace of God protected him.”

## CHAPTER XXI. The death of an anchorite and of his killer

Abbot Gerontius, superior of the monastery of our holy Father Euthymius, told me and Sophronius the Sophist:

“There were three of us together beyond the Dead Sea. As we were walking toward the mountain, another anchorite was walking about near the shore of the sea. It happened that Saracens [Note: [Col. 0239B] “Saracens.” Concerning the monks killed by the Saracens, the *Roman Martyrology*, February 19, says: “In Palestine, the commemoration of the holy monks and other martyrs who, under Alamundarus as leader, were most cruelly slaughtered by the Saracens for the faith of Christ.” Baronius notes: “These men were killed in the same incursions of the Saracens mentioned in the deeds of Saint John the Silent, which Metaphrastes recounts on May 13, and likewise in the Life of Saint Sabas the abbot, in the same author, on December 5, as well as in the Acts of [Col. 0239C] Saint Euthymius the abbot, which he likewise recounts on January 20. The same accounts agree with what is found in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 21 and 99. One and the same persecution by the Saracens killed 935 holy monks on different days, so it should not surprise you if below there is frequent mention of monks slaughtered by the Saracens. Thus far Baronius.”] came through those regions and encountered him.

“When they had passed him, [Col. 0130A] one of them turned back and cut off the anchorite’s head, while we watched from a distance; for we had already climbed the mountain. As we were weeping sadly over the anchorite’s death, suddenly we saw a bird come from above, seize the Saracen, carry him aloft, and then drop him to the ground. The Saracen died from the fall.”

## CHAPTER XXII. The life of another elder named Conon

There was an elder in the coenobium of our holy Father Theodosius named Conon, a Cilician by birth, who observed this rule of life for thirty years: once a week he ate bread and water, worked without interruption, and never left the church.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The life of Theodulus the monk

[Col. 0130B]

We saw another elder in the same monastery, named Theodulus, who had formerly been a soldier. He fasted every day and never slept on his side.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The life of a certain elder living in the cells of Cuziba

There was an elder living in the cells of Cuziba. The elders of that place told us that, when he was in his village, he had this custom: if he saw someone in the village unable, through poverty, to sow his field, he would go by night, unknown to the owner of the field, carrying seed with him, and sow the poor man’s field.

When he came into the wilderness and lived in the cells of Cuziba, he performed the same works of compassion. [Col. 0130C] He would travel along the road leading from the Jordan to the holy city, carrying bread and water. Whenever he saw someone exhausted, he carried his burden and climbed as far as the holy Mount of Olives; then he returned by the same road with the others, carrying their burdens as far as Jericho.

You might sometimes have seen the elder carrying a great load and sweating beneath the burden; sometimes carrying a little boy on his shoulders, often two. At times he would sit and mend the torn footwear of a man or woman; he carried with him everything necessary for this purpose. He gave some to drink from the water he carried, supplied bread to others, and, if he found anyone naked, gave him the cloak he was carrying.

It was a pleasant sight to see the elder laboring every day. Whenever he found a dead person on the road, [Col. 0130D] after completing over him the customary psalms and prayers, he buried him.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning a brother of the monastery of Cuziba, the words of the holy oblation, and Abbot John

There was a brother in the coenobium of Cuziba who had learned the words and rite of the holy oblation, as Abbot Gregory *ex Scholaribus* told us [Note: [Col. 0239C] *Ex scholaribus.* In Greek it is ἀπὸ Σχολαρίων. Hervetus translated it as *scholasticus*. The *scholares* belong to the military order. See the *Onomasticon*.].

One day he was sent to carry the offerings. As he was returning to the monastery, he recited the words of the holy oblation [Note: [Col. 0239C] “The words of the holy oblation.” Below, chapter 196, there are likewise the words of the oblation spoken by a boy, and the bread, together with the stone that served as an altar, consumed by heavenly fire. I believe this was done out of reverence, lest so holy a mystery be exposed to childish games.], as though he were singing some verses.

The deacons placed these same offerings upon the holy altar. When Abbot John the priest, who later became bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, offered them, he did not see, as he usually did, [Col. 0131A] the descent of the Holy Spirit. He was greatly saddened and wondered whether he had perhaps sinned in his mind, and whether for that reason the Holy [p. 868] Spirit had turned away from him. He entered the sacristy weeping and fell on his face.

An angel of the Lord appeared to him and said:

“Because the brother who brought the offerings spoke the words of the holy oblation on the road, they have already been sanctified and completed.”

From that time the elder decided that no one should henceforth learn the words of the holy oblation except one ordained for this purpose, and that no one should recite them casually, at any time, outside a consecrated place.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The life of Brother Theophanes, his wondrous vision, and communion with heretics

[Col. 0131B]

An elder named Cyriacus lived in the Laura of Calamon beside the Jordan River. He was a man of great merit before God. A pilgrim brother from the region of Dora, named Theophanes, went to him to question the elder about thoughts of fornication. The elder began to encourage and exhort him with words concerning modesty and chastity.

The brother, being greatly edified, said to the elder:

“Truly, my Father, if I did not communicate with the Nestorians in my own region, I would remain with you.”

When the elder heard the name of Nestorius, he was distressed over the brother’s destruction. He rebuked him and urged him to withdraw from this most evil and destructive heresy and to approach the holy catholic and apostolic Church. He said that there was no other hope of salvation unless we think and believe rightly—that, as is indeed the case, holy Mary is the Mother of God.

The brother said to the elder:

[Col. 0131C]

“Certainly, Father, all the heresies say the same thing: ‘Unless you communicate with us, you cannot be saved.’ What shall I do, then, wretched man that I am? I do not know. Therefore, entreat the Lord to make me certain in reality which faith is true.”

The elder joyfully received the brother’s words and said to him:

“Remain in the cave with me and place your hope entirely in God, for his goodness will reveal to you which faith is true.”

Leaving the brother in his cave, the elder went out near the Dead Sea, praying to God for him. Around the ninth hour of the following day, the brother saw someone of terrifying appearance standing beside him and saying:

“Come and see the truth.”

Taking him, he led him to a dark and foul-smelling place, exhaling fire. In those fires he saw Nestorius, Eutyches, Apollinaris, [Col. 0131D] Dioscorus [the source reads *Diocorum*], Severus, Arius, Origen, and certain others.

The one who had appeared said to him:

“This place has been prepared for heretics, blasphemers, and those who follow their doctrines. If you like this place, persist in your doctrine; but if you do not wish to experience this punishment, approach the holy catholic and apostolic Church, as the elder teaches you. For I tell you that even if a man practices every virtue but does not believe rightly, he will be tormented in this place.”

At these words the brother came to himself. When the elder returned, he told him everything he had seen and approached communion with the holy catholic Church. He remained with the elder, and after completing four years with him, he fell asleep in peace.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The life of the priest of the village of Mardandos

[Col. 0132A]

About ten miles from the Cilician city of Aegina there is a village named Mardandos, in which there is a church of Saint John the Baptist. An elder priest of the highest merit before God and possessing great virtues lived there.

One day the inhabitants of the village went to the bishop accusing the elder and saying:

“Take this elder away from us, for he is troublesome to us.”

The bishop said to them:

“What does he do to you?”

They replied:

“He comes to celebrate the Mass on Sunday, sometimes at the third hour, sometimes at the ninth hour, whenever it seems right to him, and he does not observe the solemn and lawful order of the holy oblation.”

When the bishop had learned this, [Col. 0132B] he took the elder aside and said to him:

“Why do you do this, elder? Do you not know the regulations of the holy Church?”

The elder replied:

“What you pursue is true, and you speak rightly; but I do not know what to do. On Sunday, after the nocturnal hymns, I sit near the holy altar and do not begin the solemn rites of the Mass until I see the Holy Spirit overshadowing the altar. When I see that the Holy Spirit has arrived, then I complete the sacred offices.”

Hearing this, the bishop admired the elder’s virtue, summoned the inhabitants of the village, satisfied them, and dismissed them in peace.

Abbot Julian the Stylite sent greetings to this elder and also sent him a wrapped cloth containing three burning coals. The elder received the greeting and the burning coals, and sent the same abbot [Col. 0132C] the wrapped cloth filled with water. They were nearly twenty miles apart.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The wondrous deed of Abbot Julian the Stylite

[Col. 0132C]

Abbot Cyriacus, a disciple of the aforementioned Abbot Julian the Stylite, related:

“My father, my brother, and I came from our region to Abbot Julian after hearing of his reputation. I was suffering from an incurable illness which no [p. 869] human being had been able to cure. As soon as the elder saw me coming, he healed me through prayer.

“We all remained with him and renounced the world. The elder appointed my father over the grain. One day my father came and said to Abbot Julian:

“‘We have no [Col. 0132D] grain.’

“The elder, answering from his pillar, said:

“‘Go, brother, gather today whatever you find and grind it, and tomorrow God will take care of us.’

“Disturbed by these words—for he knew that he had left nothing—my father went to his cell. But when necessity pressed, the elder sent for him, saying:

“‘Come here.’

“When he had scarcely agreed to come, the elder said to him:

“‘Brother Conon, go and make whatever you find into food for the brothers.’

“Angrily taking the keys of the granary, he went away, intending to bring back dust from the ground. When he removed the bolts and wished to open the doors, he could not. The entire granary was full of grain.

“When he saw this, he was terrified and, prostrating himself, asked the elder’s forgiveness.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. The miracle of the most holy Eucharist

[Col. 0133A]

About thirty miles from the Cilician city of Aegina there were two Stylites, separated from one another by six miles. One of them communicated with the holy catholic and apostolic Church; the other, who had spent even more time upon his pillar, belonged to the Severian impiety and accused the Catholic in various ways of being a heretic.

The Catholic, divinely inspired, asked him to send him a portion of his Communion. The other was delighted, thinking that he had somehow deceived him, and immediately sent it without hesitation.

The Catholic received the Mass-particle sent to him by the heretic, a follower of Severus, and threw it into a boiling pot. It immediately dissolved. He then took a portion of the holy Communion of the catholic Church and [Col. 0133B] placed it in the pot; at once the boiling pot became cool, and the holy Communion remained whole and was not moistened. He carefully preserved it and showed it to us when we came to him.

## CHAPTER XXX. The life of Isidore, a Melitene monk, and another miracle concerning the most holy Eucharist

Dade is a commercial town of Cyprus, and in it there is a monastery called Philoxene. When we came there, we found a monk born in Melitene named Isidore. We saw him weeping continuously with lamentation.

When everyone urged him to rest a little and cease from weeping, he would not agree at all, saying to everyone:

[Col. 0133C]

“I am an excessive sinner, beyond all who have existed since the beginning of the world.”

When we said to him:

“Certainly no one is without sin except God alone,”

he replied:

“Truly, brothers, I have found no sinner among human beings like myself, nor any offense greater than mine. And so that you may know that I am speaking the truth, hear my sin, so that you too may pray for me.”

When I was still in the world, I had a wife; we were both adherents of Severus’s doctrine. One day, when I came home, I did not find my wife. I heard that she had gone to a neighboring woman to receive communion from her—for that woman belonged to the Catholic religion and faith—and I immediately ran there, intending to prevent it. When I reached the house, I found that she had already received communion. [Col. 0133D] Enraged, I seized her by the throat and made her vomit up the holy communion. I then tossed the sacred particle here and there until it fell into the mud. At once I saw a flash of light take up the holy communion at that very spot. Two days later I saw a man resembling an Ethiopian, dressed in a loincloth, saying to me: “You and I have been condemned together to one punishment.” And I said to him: “Who are you?” He replied: “I am the one who struck the Creator and Lord Jesus Christ on the cheek at the time of his Passion.” For this reason I cannot restrain my weeping.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Conversion and Life of Mary the Prostitute

[Col. 0134A]

Two old men went from Aegae to Tarsus. When they entered an inn to rest—for it was hot—by God’s providence they found there three young men with a prostitute. The old men sat apart, and one of them, taking up the holy Gospel, began to read. When the prostitute who was with the young men saw the old man reading, she left them, approached him, and sat beside him. The old man pushed her away and said: “You are exceedingly shameless, unhappy woman, not being ashamed to approach us and sit down.”

But she replied: “Please, Father, do not abhor me or drive me away. Although I am filled with every sin, the Lord and our Savior Christ God did not reject the prostitute who came to him.” [Col. 0134B]

The old man answered her: “But that prostitute did not remain a prostitute.”

Then she said: “I hope in the Son of the living God, because from this day onward I too shall not remain in this sin.”

She therefore left the young men and all that belonged to her, and followed those old men. They sent her to a monastery near the city of Aegae. I myself saw her there as an old woman, a woman of great wisdom, and I learned this account from her own mouth. Her name was Mary. 870

## CHAPTER XXXII. The Conversion and Life of Babylas the Mime, and Also of Cometa and Nicosa, His Concubines

[Note: [Col. 0239C] Babylas. When he enters a church here and is converted to a better way of life after hearing an incidental sentence from the Gospel, the same thing happened to several others. See what is said in *The Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 2, no. 9. [Col. 0239D]]

There was a certain mime in Tarsus of Cilicia, named Babylas. He had two concubines: the name of one was Cometa, and that of the other Nicosa. He lived dissolutely, doing everything that the devil suggested to him.

One day he entered a church and, by God’s providence, heard the holy Gospel being read. The reading was this: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew III). Struck with remorse, he began to groan with tears and to call himself wretched because of the sins he had committed.

Immediately, then, he went out of the church, summoned his two companions, and said to them: “You know how dissolutely I have lived with you, and that I have never loved one more than the other. Therefore, all that I have acquired belongs to you; take my remaining possessions as well and divide them between yourselves. For from this moment I renounce the world and become a monk.”

But they both answered him with one voice and with tears: [Col. 0134D] “We shared in your lust and in the destruction of our souls; now, when you wish to perform this deed pleasing to God, will you abandon us and do it alone? Surely this will not happen. We too shall share with you in what is good.”

Thus the mime shut himself up in one of the city’s towers. They, having sold all their possessions and distributed them to the poor, themselves took the religious habit, built a cell near the tower, and shut themselves up there as well.

I myself saw this man and was greatly edified by him. He is an exceedingly humble, gentle, and compassionate man. I have written this also for the benefit of those who read it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The Life of Saint Theodotus, Bishop

[Col. 0135A]

One of the Fathers told us that there was a certain bishop in the holy city named Theodotus, so kind that, when on one occasion he had invited some of his clergy to a feast and one of them did not wish to come or accept the invitation, the patriarch at that time remained silent; but on another occasion he went to him in person, asking him to come and share in the common table.

He also said of this Bishop Theodotus that he was so gentle and humble that, when he was once traveling with a cleric—he himself being carried in a litter while the cleric rode a horse—the patriarch said to his cleric: “Let us exchange our vehicles. You ride in the litter, while I shall go on horseback.”

When the cleric absolutely refused to do this, saying that it would disgrace the patriarch if a cleric were carried in a litter while the bishop entered on horseback, the holy and humble Theodotus did not desist until he persuaded the attendant that the matter was not insulting, and compelled him to do it.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Life of the Blessed Alexander, Patriarch of Jerusalem

The same city had another patriarch, named Alexander, so devout and compassionate that, when one of his notaries stole gold from him and, terrified by fear, fled to the Thebaid of Egypt, where he fell in with robbers while wandering about and was led by them as a captive to the remotest parts of Egypt, the blessed Alexander, upon learning this, redeemed him—bound and captive—for eighty-five coins. When the man returned, Alexander treated him with such pious mercy that one of the city’s inhabitants once said that nothing was more advantageous than to sin against Alexander.

On another occasion one of his deacons insulted the blessed Alexander in the presence of all the clergy. He immediately fell prostrate on the ground and asked forgiveness, saying: “Forgive me, my lord and brother.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Life of Elias, Archbishop of Jerusalem, and of Flavian, Patriarch of Antioch
