[Note: [Col. 0239D] Elias. There is a reference to Elias, who was sent into exile, in *The Life of Saint Sabas*, by Cyril, 5 December. See Baronius, volume VI, in the year of Christ 513, the fifteenth year of Pope Symmachus, the twenty-third of the Emperor Anastasius, and the twenty-first of King Theodoric. As for the statement here that it happened “after two days,” Baronius, in the same volume, under the year of Christ 518, the fifth year of Pope Hormisdas, the twenty-eighth of Emperor Anastasius, and the twenty-sixth of King Theodoric, notes that the two days must be counted from the writing of the letter, not from the death of Anastasius. Certainly, in *The Life of Saint Sabas* written by the monk Cyril, on 5 December Elias himself says, on the basis of a vision and revelation, that he would follow Anastasius, who had died on the tenth day at that hour.]

Abba Polychronius said of Saint Elias, Archbishop of Jerusalem, that just as he did not drink wine when he was a monk, so, when he became patriarch, he did not drink it either, but preserved the same rule.

They said of this Archbishop Elias and of Flavian, Archbishop of Antioch, that both had been banished into exile by the Emperor Anastasius because of the holy Council of Chalcedon: Elias to Haila, and Flavian to Petra. One day the two patriarchs signaled to each other, saying mutually: “Anastasius has died today; therefore let us go as well, so that we may be judged together with him.” And after two days both departed to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Life of Ephraem, Patriarch of Antioch, and How He Converted a Stylite Monk from the Impiety of the Severian Heresy

871 One of the Fathers told us about Saint Ephraem, Patriarch of Antioch, that he was exceedingly zealous and fervent concerning the faith. When he heard about a certain Stylite who was in the region of Hierapolis, that he belonged to the Severian heresy, he went to him to dissuade him from his impiety.

The blessed Ephraem began to rebuke the Stylite and to urge him to approach the holy apostolic throne and enter into communion with the holy and apostolic Church. But the Stylite replied: “I absolutely do not communicate with a synod.”

Saint Ephraem said to him: “Then how do you wish me to heal you and make satisfaction for the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ? The holy Church is free from every stain of heretical wickedness.”

The Stylite said to him: “Let us light a fire, my lord patriarch, and enter it together; the one whom the flame does not harm will be orthodox, [Col. 0136B] and we must follow him.”

He said this in order to frighten the patriarch.

Saint Ephraem replied to the Stylite: “It would indeed have been proper for you, my son, to obey as a son obeys his father and to ask nothing further of us. But since you have requested something that exceeds the powers of my wretchedness, I nevertheless trust in the mercies of the Son of God, and for the sake of your salvation I shall do this as well.”

Then the blessed Ephraem said to all who were present: “Blessed is the Lord; bring wood here.”

When the wood had been brought, the patriarch set it alight before the column and said to the Stylite: “Now come down, so that according to your decree we may both enter.”

Struck with amazement at the patriarch’s steadfastness, the Stylite refused to come down. Then the patriarch said to him: “Did you not ask that this be done? Why, then, are you now unwilling to do it?”

The patriarch then removed the stole with which he was clothed and, approaching the fire, prayed, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, our God, who for our sake deigned to become incarnate and to be born from our holy Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, show us the truth.”

When he had finished praying, he threw his stole into the midst of the flames. When the fire had continued for about three hours and the wood had already been consumed by it, they took out the stole intact, so that no trace of fire could be detected on it.

When the Stylite saw what had happened, he became convinced of the truth, anathematized Severus and his heresy, approached the holy Catholic Church, received communion from the hands of Saint Ephraem, and glorified God.

[Note: [Col. 0239D] “Let us light a fire.” This appeal to fire occurs frequently in matters of faith. I have collected several examples in my dissertation *On the Faith to Be Kept with Heretics*, chapter 12. [Col. 0240B]]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The Life of a Bishop Who Left His See, Came to the Holy City, and, Having Changed His Clothing, Served the Builders

[Col. 0136D]

One of the Fathers related to us the story of a certain bishop who left his bishopric and went to the holy city. There he put on a laborer’s clothing and served the builders.

At that time Ephraemius, a compassionate man devoted to works of mercy, was Count of the East, and public buildings were being repaired under his direction, for the city had fallen in an earthquake.

One day Ephraemius saw in a vision a bishop asleep, with a column of fire rising above him and reaching to heaven. When he saw this not once or twice but repeatedly, Euphremius was astonished—for the vision itself was terrifying and filled with wonder—and he kept wondering to himself what it could mean. He did not know who the laborer was, seeing him with unkempt hair, filthy clothing, and a cheap and wretched appearance, afflicted by excessive exertion, abstinence, and the fatigue of constant labor, his whole body covered in squalor. [Col. 0137A]

Ephraemius summoned such a laborer and asked who he was. He began privately to question him about his name and the city from which he came. The man said to him: “I am one of the poor of this city. Since I have no means by which I can support myself, I work as best I can, and God feeds me through my labors.”

Moved by God, Ephraemius answered him: “Believe me, I will not let you go until you have truthfully told me everything about yourself.”

When the man was pressed in this way and could no longer conceal himself, he said to him: “Promise me that, as long as I live this life, you will tell no one what concerns me; and I, with my name suppressed, will tell you the truth about myself.”

The count swore to him that he would tell no one while he was alive.

Then the man said to him: “I am a bishop. For God’s sake I abandoned my bishopric and came here as though to an unknown place. By afflicting my flesh and working, I earn a little bread from my labor. You, however, add as much as you can to my almsgiving.

“In these days God will raise you to the apostolic throne of this city, so that you may feed his people, whom Christ, our true God, acquired with his own blood. Therefore, as I have said, persist in almsgiving, and continually stand and contend for the true faith. For God is especially pleased by such sacrifices.”

It happened just as he had foretold. When the blessed Ephraemius heard this, he glorified God, saying: “How many hidden servants God has, known to him alone!” 872

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Death of Anastasius, the Impious Emperor

[Note: [Col. 0240B] Anastasius. Baronius, volume VI, under the year of Christ 495, the fourth year of Pope Gelasius, the fifth of Emperor Anastasius, and the third of King Theodoric, discusses Euphemius, who was sent into exile by Anastasius; and under the year of Christ 511, the thirteenth year of Pope Symmachus, the twenty-first of Anastasius, and the nineteenth of King Theodoric, Macedonius, who was driven into exile by the same Anastasius. What is stated here about “fourteen erased” should be understood as referring to years.

Zonaras, volume III, in his account of Anastasius, says:

“Again, it is said that this emperor saw in a dream a terrifying man holding a book and saying to him: ‘Behold, because of the perversity of your faith, I erase fourteen years from your life.’”

The Greek reads: Καὶ αὖθις ὄναρ ἰδεῖν λέγεται ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐκεῖνος, ἄνδρα τινὰ φοβερὸν, τόμον κατέχοντα, καὶ λέγοντα πρὸς αὐτόν· Ἰδοὺ διὰ τὴν κακοπιστίαν σου, ἀπαλείφω τῆς ζοῆς σου ἔτη τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα.

See Baronius, volume VI, under the year of Christ 518, the fifth year of Pope Hormisdas, the twenty-eighth of Emperor Anastasius, and the twenty-sixth of King Theodoric.]

A certain faithful man told us about the Emperor Anastasius. After he had expelled Euphemius and Macedonius, patriarchs of the Church of Constantinople, and because of the holy Council of Chalcedon had sent them into exile at Gaita in Pontus, the emperor saw in a dream a distinguished man standing before him, dressed in a white garment, carrying and reading a written codex.

The man turned five leaves of the codex, read the emperor’s name, and said to him: “Behold, because of your perfidy, I erase fourteen [years].” With his finger he erased them.

After two days, amid a great flash of lightning and thunder, Anastasius, overcome with terror, gave up his spirit in extreme distress, because he had been impious toward the holy Church of Christ our God and had condemned its pastors with assistance. [Col. 0137D]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Life of a Monk of the Monastery of Abba Severianus, and How He Was Prudently Turned Back by a Peasant Girl from Sinning with Her

When I came to Antioch, I heard one of the church’s presbyters recounting the following:

“Patriarch Anastasius said that, when a certain monk from the monastery of Abba Severianus had been sent on service to the region of Eleutheropolis and had lodged with a certain faithful peasant who had one daughter—the girl’s mother had already died—and had stayed in his house for several days, the devil, who always attacks human beings, injected the brother with impure thoughts. He was assailed by desire for the girl and sought an opportunity to violate her.

“The demon who attacked him also provided him with the opportunity. When the girl’s father departed for Ascalon on necessary business, the brother, knowing that no one was in the house except himself and the girl, approached in order to assault her by force.

“When she saw him entirely agitated and rushing toward the wicked act, she said to him: ‘Do not be disturbed, and do not attempt anything shameful against me. My father will not come today or tomorrow. First listen to what I have to say. For, God knows, I shall readily do whatever you wish.’

“She began to address him as follows: ‘How long, brother, have you been in the monastery?’

“The brother said to her: ‘Seventeen years.’

“She asked him again: ‘Have you had experience with a woman?’

“He replied: ‘No.’

“Then the girl said: ‘Do you therefore wish to lose the labor of so many years for the sake of one hour? How many tears have you shed in order to preserve your flesh pure and undefiled for Christ the Lord? And now do you wish to let all that labor perish for the sake of a moment’s pleasure?

“‘Nevertheless, let it be as you wish. If I listen to you and you sin with me, do you have the means to take me and support me?’

“The brother said to her: ‘No.’

“Then she said: ‘I am not lying when I say that, if you humiliate me, you will become the cause of many evils.’

“The monk said to her: ‘How so?’

“The girl replied: ‘First, because you destroy your own soul; second, because my soul too will be required of you. I declare this to you under oath by him who said, “Do not make me a liar” (John I). For if you humiliate me, I shall immediately take my own life by hanging myself, and you will be found guilty of murder and judged as a murderer at the tribunal.

“‘Therefore, before you become the cause of so many evils, return in peace to your monastery and pray for me.’”

The brother then came to his senses, turned back at once to his monastery, prostrated himself before the abbot, asked forgiveness, and begged that he never again be allowed to leave the monastery. After spending three months in heartfelt contrition, he departed to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XL. The Life of Abba Cosmas the Eunuch

[Col. 0138D]

Abba Basil, presbyter of the Bicantian district, told us:

“When I was in Theopolis with Patriarch Gregory, Abba Cosmas, the eunuch of the Laura of Pharan, came from Jerusalem. He was a man of extraordinary piety, exceedingly firm and zealous for the faith and correct doctrines, and by no means untrained in knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

“After he had been there only a few days, he died. The patriarch ordered his precious remains to be buried in his monastery, where a certain bishop had also been buried.

“One day I went to venerate the old man’s tomb. A poor man was lying above his grave, asking alms from those entering the church. When the poor man saw me prostrating myself for the third time and praying to the old man, he said to me: ‘Abba, that old man whom you buried here two months ago was certainly a great man.’

“Then I said to him: ‘How do you know this?’

“He replied: ‘Truly, lord abba, I had been paralyzed for twelve years, and through him God healed me. Whenever I am in distress, he comes to me, bringing consolation and granting me relief.’ 873

“Listen also to another miracle concerning him. From the day on which you buried him until today, I have heard him crying out every night and saying to the bishop: ‘Do not touch me, heretic; do not come near me, enemy of the holy Catholic Church of God.’”

[Col. 0139B]

When I heard this from the man who had been healed, I went and reported everything in order to the patriarch. I begged the most holy patriarch to have the old man’s body removed from that place and reburied in another tomb.

Then Abba Gregory the patriarch said: “Believe me, my son, Abba Cosmas is not harmed at all by the heretic. But all this happened so that the old man’s virtue and zeal for the faith might become known to us—what he was like and what he is even after the body’s falling asleep—and so that the bishop’s opinion might be exposed, lest we suppose him to have been orthodox and Catholic.”

Abba Basil also said the following about the same old man. When he had gone to see him living in the Laura of Pharan, the old man said to him:

“An occasional thought came to me concerning what the Lord says to his disciples: ‘He who has a garment, let him sell it and buy a sword’ (Luke XXII). When they said to him, ‘Behold, here are two swords,’ he replied, ‘It is enough.’ I was perplexed by this saying and did not understand what it meant.

“So, pondering this, I left my cell in the heat of the midday sun to go to the Laura of the Towers, to Abba Theophilus, and ask him. As I was traveling through the desert and was near Calamon, I saw a dragon of extraordinary size descending from the mountain into Calamon. It was so immense that when it moved it curved like a vault, and it left footprints deeply impressed in the earth.

“Following its tracks, I entered unharmed, and I recognized that the devil had wanted to hinder my purpose; but the old man’s prayers helped me.

“When I reached Abba Theophilus, I explained my perplexity to him. He said to me: ‘The two swords signify two lives, the active and the contemplative. Whoever possesses these two virtues will be perfect.’”

I myself went to this same Abba Cosmas while he was in the Laura of Pharan; I remained there for ten years. When he was speaking to me about the salvation of the soul and cited something from the writings of Saint Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria, the old man said to me:

“When you find something in the little works of Saint Athanasius and have no paper on which to write it, write it on your clothing.”

Such was the zeal and devotion with which this holy elder burned toward our holy Fathers and teachers.

Abba Cosmas also said this about himself: On the night of the Lord’s Day, from evening until morning, he would stand singing psalms and reading, both in his cell and in the church, and would not sit at all. At sunrise, when he had completed the rule, he would sit and read the holy Gospels until the dismissal.

## CHAPTER XLI. The Life of Abba Paul of Nazarbus

We also saw another old man in the same Laura, namely Abba Paul, a holy man devoted to God, exceedingly gentle and temperate. I do not remember ever having seen anyone so adorned with the grace of consolation and tears; tears continually flowed from his eyes.

This holy elder spent almost fifty years in the solitary life, content with the single loaf of alms that the church gave him, [Col. 0140B] and speaking to no one at all. He was from Nazarbus.

## CHAPTER XLII. The Life of Abba Anaxanontes, Servant of God

In the same place we saw Abba Anaxanontes, a compassionate and exceedingly abstinent man who lived the solitary life in his cell with such strictness that for four days he ate only one oblation worth twenty small coins.

[Note: [Col. 0240C] Twenty minute coins. I think the Greek had λεπτῶν or φολεῶν, for the text is lacking here. Below, chapter 134: “And he received a daily allowance of nine minute coins.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

Often he ate only that one portion for an entire week. Near the end of his life this venerable man contracted an illness of the stomach and intestines. We therefore carried him to the holy city, to the house for the sick that was under the patriarch’s care.

One day, when we were near him, Abba Conon, superior of the Laura of our holy Father Sabas, sent him a handkerchief containing one blessing and six coins, signifying to him: “Forgive me, for illness does not permit me to ascend and visit you.”

The old man kept the blessing but returned the money, saying: “If God wills, Father, that I remain in this life, I have ten coins. When I have spent them, I shall let you know, and you may send these.”

Then he added: “But so that you may know, Father, I shall leave this world after two days.”

And so it happened. We carried him back to the same Laura of Pharan and buried him there. This blessed man had been the companion of the blessed Eustochius; after leaving both of them behind, he completed his life in the desert. He was from the city of Ancyra in Galatia.

## CHAPTER XLIII. The Detestable Death of Thalelaeus, the Wicked Archbishop of Thessalonica

[Col. 0140D]

There was a certain archbishop of Thessalonica named Thalelaeus. He neither feared God nor dreaded the retribution that awaited him. Trampling upon Christian doctrine and despising priestly honor and dignity, he was found to be a wolf instead of a shepherd.

For the wretched man denied the holy and consubstantial Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and worshiped idols. Those who then presided over the Churches condemned him by common decree and drove him from his see.

A short time later that wicked man, full of every crime and impiety, wished to return to priestly dignity. Since, according to the wisest Solomon, “everything obeys gold” (Ecclesiastes X), he was recalled to his own region. He had been in Constantinople, where the rulers dwell—those who, according to the prophet, “justify the wicked for gifts, and take away the righteousness of the righteous” (Isaiah V). [Col. 0141A]

But almighty God did not disregard his holy Church. Rather, he once again condemned as unacceptable to himself the sentence issued on Thalelaeus, contrary to the canons of the apostles.

One day, when he was about to go forth in proud attire to approach the emperors and resume the priesthood by their decrees, his stomach seized him, so that he went to relieve nature. When he had entered a secluded place for this purpose and had remained inside for two or three hours without returning to his attendants, some of those who served him entered to tell him that he ought now to proceed. They found the wretched man headfirst, plunged into the place where excrement was discharged, with his feet raised upward.

When they lifted him out, they found that he had died the same horrible and eternal death as the impious Arius, the enemy of God.

[For when Arius, relying on the support of rulers, hoped tyrannically to enter the Church of God, the angel of the holy Church of God, wondrous and full of great counsel, burst apart in the privy his bowels, which were bringing forth that unholy crime. Likewise, when this man, relying on the support of rulers, hoped to perpetrate worse things than before, the angel of the Church of Thessalonica, together with the great martyr Demetrius, anticipated him and, in the very place where he sat and trafficked with an impure demon while plotting his schemes against the holy Church of God, left the feet of this useless servant—who refused to walk rightly—hanging, nailed in place. In them were displayed signs of the judgment by which he was to be punished, and of how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews X).]

[Note: [Col. 0141D] The material enclosed in brackets has been supplied from the Greek.]

## CHAPTER XLIV. The Life of an Old Monk Living near the City of Antinous, and Concerning Prayer for the Dead

When we came to the Thebaid, an old man told us that another old man lived outside the city of Antinous. He was a man of great virtue who had spent seventy years in his cell. He had ten disciples, one of whom was exceedingly negligent concerning himself.

The old man frequently rebuked him and exhorted him, saying: “Brother, take care for your soul. You are destined to die, and unless you reform yourself, you will go toward punishment.”

But that brother was always disobedient to the old man and did not accept what was said to him. After some time, it happened that he died.

The elder was greatly grieved over him—for he knew that the man had departed this world in great indolence and negligence—and began to pray, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, reveal to me what concerns the brother’s soul.”

Then, being brought into an ecstasy of mind, he saw a river of fire, a vast multitude in the fire, and the brother himself submerged in its midst up to his neck.

The elder then said to him: “Was it not on account of this punishment that I urged you to care for your soul, my son?”

The brother answered the elder: “I give thanks to God, Father, that at least my head has rest; for through your prayers I stand above the head of a bishop.”

## CHAPTER XLV. The Life of a Monk Shut Up on the Mount of Olives, and Concerning the Veneration of the Most Holy Image of Mary, the Mother of God

[Note: [Col. 0240C] And concerning veneration. The Seventh Ecumenical Council, which is the Second Council of Nicaea, cites this example in Greek from this book, sessions 4 and 5.]

Abba Theodore the Aeliote said that there was a certain monk shut up on the Mount of Olives, a most powerful spiritual athlete. The spirit of fornication attacked him.

One day, when the spirit was pressing him violently, the old man began to lament and say to the demon: “How long will you not leave me? Go away from me now—you who have grown old with me.”

The demon appeared to him visibly and said: “Swear to me that you will tell no one what I am about to say to you, and I shall not attack you again.”

The old man swore, saying: “By him who dwells in the highest places, I shall tell no one what you say to me.”

Then the demon said to him: “Do not venerate this image, and I shall not attack you any longer.”

The image bore the likeness of our holy Lady, Mary the Mother of God, carrying our Lord Jesus Christ.

The recluse said to the demon: “Leave me so that I may deliberate.”

The next day he reported this to Abba Theodore the Aeliote, who at that time lived in the Laura of Pharan, and told him everything.

The old man said to the recluse: “Truly, lord abba, you have been deceived, because you swore to the demon. Nevertheless, you have done well to reveal it. It would be better for you to fail to leave any brothel in that city unentered than to deny that you venerate God and our Lord Jesus Christ together with his mother.”

Having strengthened and encouraged him with many words, he left him in his place.

The demon therefore appeared to the recluse again, saying: “What is this, most wicked old man? Did you not swear to me that you would tell no one? And why did you say to the one who came to you: ‘I tell you that you will be judged as a perjurer on the day of judgment’?”

The recluse replied: “I know that I swore and that I broke my oath. Yet I broke my oath to the Lord and Creator; I shall not obey you. For from you, as the author both of the evil counsel and of the perjury, inevitable punishments will be demanded.”

## CHAPTER XLVI. The Wonderful Vision of Abba Cyriacus of the Laura of Calamon, and Concerning the Two Books of the Impious Nestorius

We approached Abba Cyriacus, presbyter of the Laura of Calamon near the holy Jordan, and he told us the following:

“One day I saw in a dream a woman of dignified appearance, dressed in purple, and with her two men, themselves also of venerable bearing and splendid appearance. I supposed the woman to be our holy Lady, the Mother of God, and the two men who were with her to be Saint John the Theologian and Saint John the Baptist.

“I came out of my cell and begged them to enter and pray in my cell, but she did not consent. I therefore continued for some time praying and pleading, saying: ‘Please, let the humble and confounded man not be turned away’ (Psalm LXXIII), and many other things of this kind.

“When she saw me persisting in my prayers and repeating the same request, she answered me more severely, saying: ‘You have my enemy inside your cell, and you want me to enter?’

“After saying this, she departed.

“When I awoke, I began to suffer and wondered whether I had committed some sin in my thoughts against her. For there was no one else in my cell except me alone.

“After examining myself for a long time, I found nothing by which I had sinned against her. But when I saw myself overwhelmed by excessive grief, I arose and took a book to read, so that through such reading I might drive away both the pain and my thoughts.

“I had borrowed the book from the blessed Isychus, presbyter of the Church of Jerusalem. When I opened it, I found two books of the impious Nestorius written at the end of the volume. At once I recognized that this was the enemy of our holy Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary.

“I then arose, went to the man who had lent me the book, and returned it to him, saying: ‘Take your book, brother; I have gained from it not as much benefit as harm.’

“When he asked me the cause of the harm, I related the entire sequence of events to him. Inflamed with zeal for God, he immediately cut those two books of Nestorius out of the volume and committed them to the fire, saying: ‘The enemy of our holy Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, shall not remain in my cell.’”

## CHAPTER XLVII. The Miracle of the Holy Mother of God against Gaianus the Mime, Who Blasphemed Her in the Theater

Heliopolis is a city of Phoenicia Libanensis. There was a certain mime there named Gaianus who blasphemed the holy Mother of God in the theater and offered the people a spectacle of blasphemy.

The holy Mother of God appeared to him and said: “What evil have I done to you, that you insult and blaspheme me before such a great multitude?”

But he rose and not only failed to reform, but blasphemed even more.

The holy Mother of God therefore appeared to him again, rebuking him and saying: “Please, do not, do not thus injure your soul.”

But again he blasphemed her still more wickedly.

Therefore, when she appeared to him a third time, she repeated the same words. But when he did not reform and even added further blasphemies, she appeared to him while he was sleeping at midday and, saying nothing, merely marked his hands and feet with her finger.

When he awoke, he found that his hands and feet had been amputated. Thus the wretched man lay helpless like a useless trunk, confessing to everyone why it had happened and how he had suffered this fate, and that because of his blasphemies he had been mercifully chastised.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Another Miracle of the Holy Mother of God, by Which Cosmiana, the Wife of the Patrician Germanus, Was Compelled to Return from the Severian Heresy to the True Faith of Christ
Anastasius the presbyter, guardian of the furnishings of the holy Resurrection of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, told us that Cosmiana, the wife of the patrician Germanus, having come there, wished one night to worship the holy life-giving tomb of our Lord Jesus Christ by herself. As she approached the door of the shrine, our Lady, the holy Mother of God, visibly appeared to her together with some other women and said: “How do you dare to enter here when you are not one of ours?” And she prevented her, saying: “You are not one of ours.” For she belonged to the heresy of Severus the Acephalous.

But Cosmiana pleaded earnestly that she might be allowed to enter. The holy Mother of God answered her: “Believe me, woman: you will not enter here unless you enter into communion with us.” When she understood that she was being prevented from entering because she was a heretic, and that she would not be permitted to enter unless she joined the holy catholic and apostolic Church of Christ our Lord and God, she immediately summoned a deacon. When the holy chalice arrived, she received the sacred body and the precious blood of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. Thus, without any further prohibition, she was deemed worthy to worship the holy and venerable tomb of the Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The miraculous vision of the governor of Palestine, by which he too was compelled to renounce the aforesaid heresy and enter into communion with the Church of Christ

The same presbyter Anastasius also told us this, saying that Gevemer, the governor of Palestine, once came to worship the holy Resurrection of Christ our Lord. When he began to enter the holy tomb, he saw a ram rushing violently toward him and attacking him with its horns. Seized with fear, he retreated. Azarias, the guardian of the holy cross, and the attendants who were present [Note: [Col. 0240C] “The attendants who were present.” In Greek, φραγγελισαί. He means the governor’s attendants. Hervetus translated it “and the others who were present.” See the *Onomasticon*.], moved by fear, said to him: “What is the matter, lord? What troubles you? Why do you not enter?”

He said to them: “Why have you brought this ram in here?” Astonished, they inspected the holy tomb, saw nothing, and said to him: “Enter; there is nothing of the sort inside.” He began to enter again, but once more saw the ram coming against him and preventing him from entering. When this had happened repeatedly, and while the others saw nothing but he alone perceived the ram, the guardian of the cross said to him: “Believe me, lord, you have something in your soul that prevents you from worshiping the holy, venerable, and life-giving tomb of our Savior. Therefore I advise you to confess your sins to the Lord. Since he is merciful and most compassionate, and wishes to have pity on you, he has shown you this kind of miracle.”

But he said to him with tears: “Truly, I am guilty of many great crimes.” Prostrating himself face-down, he remained for many hours weeping and confessing to the Lord. Then he rose and wished to enter again, but once more he was not permitted to do so by the ram. Then the guardian of the holy cross said to him: “Truly, there is something else that prevents you from entering.”

He said: “Could it perhaps be because I do not belong to the holy catholic Church, but am in communion with Severus, and for that reason I am forbidden to enter?” Then he asked the guardian that the holy and life-giving mysteries of Christ our God be brought to him. When the holy chalice had been brought, he received communion. Thus he entered and worshiped, suffering no further impediment and seeing nothing else that frightened him away.

## CHAPTER L. The vision and saying of Abba George the recluse

Scythopolis is the second metropolis of Palestine. There we met Abba Anastasius, who told us about Abba George the recluse, saying:

“One night, when I had risen to strike the signal—for, as canonarch, I had been entrusted with waking the brothers for the assembly—I heard an old man weeping. I went to him and began to ask him, saying: ‘What troubles you, Father, that you are weeping like this?’

“He answered me nothing. When I asked him again to disclose to me the reason for his weeping, he groaned and sighed from the depths of his heart, saying: ‘How can I restrain myself from weeping, when our Lord Jesus Christ does not wish to be reconciled with us? For, my son, I seemed to be standing before someone seated upon a lofty throne. Many thousands were around him, praying and entreating him about some matter, but he was not moved by their prayers. Afterward a certain woman dressed in purple approached him, fell before him, and said: “Be reconciled, my son, at least for my sake.” But he nevertheless remained implacable. For this reason I weep and lament, fearing what is to come.’

“Abba George told me this as Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Supper, was dawning. On the following day, that is, Good Friday, at the ninth hour, the coastal cities of Phoenicia collapsed in a sudden and great earthquake.”

The same Abba Anastasius also related this about the same old man: after some time had passed, when he was standing at the window, the old man began to weep and said to him: “Woe to us, brother, because we have no compunction, but live in negligence. I fear that when the wrath of God overtakes us, we shall be at the doors, ready to be judged.” On the following day, fire appeared in the sky.

## CHAPTER LI. The life of Julian, an old man of the monastery of the Egyptians

Anazarbus is the second metropolis of the province of Cilicia. About twelve miles from it lies the monastery called “of the Egyptians.” The Fathers of that place told us that five years earlier an old man named Julian had died there. He had lived for approximately seventy years in a small cave, possessing absolutely nothing of this world except a hair shirt, a cloak, a little wooden vessel, and a book.

They also told us this about him: throughout his entire life he never lit the light of a lamp. Rather, during the nights a light from heaven illuminated him, so that he could read clearly.

## CHAPTER LII. A saying of Abba Elias the solitary

[877] A certain brother came to Abba Elias the solitary in the coenobium of the ancient Father Sabas and said to him: “Tell me a word, Father.”

The old man said to the brother: “In the days of our Fathers, these three virtues were held in love and esteem among the monks: the renunciation of all possessions, gentleness, and self-control. Now there are greed, gluttony, and boldness. Choose whichever of these pleases you.”

## CHAPTER LIII. The life of the old man Cyriacus from the monastery of Saint Sabas

Abba Stephen told us about an old man named Cyriacus who lived in the monastery of our holy Father Sabas. One day he had gone down to Tuthela [in Greek, Κοθυλάν], stayed for a short time near the Dead Sea, and then returned to his cell.

Since the heat was extremely severe, so that the old man was almost fainting, he stretched out his hands toward heaven to God and prayed, saying: “Lord, you know that I can no longer walk because of thirst.” Immediately a cloud formed around him and did not leave him until he had returned to his cell. The distance from his cell was about twelve miles.

The same Abba Stephen also told us this about the same old man: one day his relatives came to see him. When they arrived at the place, they asked where his cell was. After learning this from some people who pointed it out, they approached and knocked at the door. When the old man recognized them, he prayed to God that they might not see him. He opened the door, came out of his cell, and was completely invisible to them. He went into the desert and refused to return until he knew that they had departed.

## CHAPTER LIV. The life of the monks of Scetis, and the old man Ammonius

Later we came to Terenuthis, to Abba Theodore of Alexandria. The old man said to us:

“My little sons, the monks of Scetis have truly declined greatly, in accordance with the prediction of the old men. Believe me, children: great charity, great abstinence, and great discernment once existed among the Scetiotes. I saw old men there who never took food unless someone came to them. Among them was a certain old man named Ammonius, who lived near me. Knowing his custom, I came to him every Saturday so that he would take food because of my arrival.

“They all had this general practice: whenever anyone approached them, at whatever hour, they allowed him to pray. While he was praying, they set the table and immediately took food.”

## CHAPTER LV. The vision of an old man living in Scetis, and Abba Irenaeus

Abba Irenaeus told us about an old man living in Scetis that he had seen the devil at night offering the brothers hoes, rakes, and baskets. The old man said to the devil: “What are these?”

The devil answered: “I am preparing distractions for the brothers, so that, occupied with these things, they may become more negligent in praying and glorifying God.”

The same Abba Irenaeus told us again:

“When the barbarians came into Scetis, I withdrew from there and went into the region of Gaza, where I took a cell for myself in a monastery. That very day the abbot gave me a book to read in which the deeds of the old men were written [Note: [Col. 0240D] “The deeds of the old men.” In Greek it says βιβλίον Γεροντικόν, “a Gerontikon book.” That was what the book was called. From the Gerontikon manuscript our Raderus translated certain passages in part III of his *Viridarium*. The sayings that those Fathers wisely uttered were called *Verba Seniorum*. See the first general prolegomenon.].

“As soon as I opened the book, this chapter caught my eye: a certain brother had come to an old man and said to him, ‘Pray for me, Father.’ The old man had answered him: ‘When you were with us, I prayed for you; but now, since you have gone off to your own place, I no longer pray for you.’

“When I read this chapter, I closed the book and said to myself: ‘Woe to you, poor wretch, because you have come to your own place, and the Fathers no longer pray for you.’ Immediately I returned the book to the abbot, withdrew, and came to this region. This was the reason, my little sons, why I came to this place.”

## CHAPTER LVI. The life of John, disciple of a great old man who lived in the village of Caparasima

Ptolemais is a city of Phoenicia. In it there is a village called Caparasima [in Greek, Παράσημα]. A certain great old man lived in that village, and he had a disciple named John, himself also a great man and one of singular obedience.

One day the old man sent his disciple on an errand, giving him a few loaves for his sustenance. The disciple went away, completed the errand, returned, and brought back the loaves. When the elder saw the loaves, he said to him: “Son, why did you not eat the loaves I gave you?”

The disciple prostrated himself before the old man and said to him: “Forgive me, Father, because you did not bless me when you sent me, nor did you order me to take food; therefore I did not take any.” Astonished at the brother’s discernment, the old man blessed him.

After the old man’s falling asleep, when this brother had fasted for forty days, a voice came to him from heaven, saying: “Upon whomever you lay your hands, he will be healed.”

In the morning, by God’s providence, a certain man came with his wife. A cancerous disease was consuming her breast. Her husband begged him to heal his wife. Though John declared himself a sinner and unworthy to attempt such a deed, the man persisted in asking him to consent and have mercy on his wife. When he laid his hand upon her and made the sign over her breast, she was immediately healed. From that time onward God worked many signs through him, not only during his life but also after his death.

## CHAPTER LVII. The death of Simeon the Stylite, and concerning Abba Julian, also a Stylite

About forty miles from the city of Aegae in Cilicia there was a Stylite named Simeon. He was struck by lightning and died.

Abba Julian the Stylite, a presbyter, contrary to his custom and at an unusual time, said to his disciples: “Put incense into the censer” [Note: [Col. 0240D] “Put incense into the censer.” Incense was formerly accustomed to be burned in honor of the saints. See the *Onomasticon*.]

They said to him: “Tell us the reason, Father,” and begged him to explain. The old man said: “Because my brother Simeon has just been struck down and killed by lightning, and behold, his soul is passing over with rejoicing and exultation.”

They were about twenty-four miles apart.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Again concerning Julian

Abba Stephen Trichinas, overseer of the monastery of our holy Father Sabas, also related this about the aforementioned Abba Julian the Stylite: a lion had appeared near the place where he lived and had become accustomed to killing many travelers and inhabitants.

One day the old man summoned his disciple, named Pancratius, and said to him: “Go about two thousand paces southward, and there you will find a lion lying down. Say to it: ‘The humble Julian, in the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of God who gives life to all things, commands you to depart from this province.’”

The brother went and found the lion lying down. When he had spoken the old man’s words to it, the lion immediately departed.

## CHAPTER LIX. The life of Abba Thalelaeus the Cilician

[Note: [Col. 0240D] “Thalelaeus.” Our Raderus, in part I of his *Viridarium*, thinks that this is the same man as Thalelaeus the martyr under Numerian, mentioned in the *Menæa* on 20 May. But I fear that the chronology suggests otherwise: Moschus heard from Peter what is recorded here about this man, whereas Peter lived a hundred years after the reign of Numerian. Another reason for the opinion may have been that this man is called a Cilician, while the other is said in the *Menæa* to have been hidden at Azarbi in Cilicia. But there he is said to have come from Lebanon; therefore he is a Lebanese. It is more likely that this is the same Thalelaeus as the one described by Theodoret in chapter 28 of the *Philotheus*, since both are Cilicians and both have the same saying about repentance. Theodoret saw him, while Moschus heard the account from Peter. Thus the chronology can be reconciled.]

Abba Peter, a presbyter of the same monastery, told us about Abba Thalelaeus the Cilician, who had spent sixty years in the monastic life, never ceasing to weep and continually saying: “This time has been granted to us for repentance, and it will be strictly required of us if we neglect it.”

## CHAPTER LX. The remarkable deed of a holy woman, by which her young admirer was moved to compunction and became a monk

[Col. 0148B] A certain faithful man told us the following when we were in Alexandria:

“A certain holy woman was living in her house, leading a solitary life. Very concerned for her salvation, she constantly devoted herself to fasts and vigils and gave many alms. But the devil, always envious of every good thing and unable to endure such virtues in the virgin, stirred up dust against her. He implanted in a certain young man a shameful and diabolical desire for her.

“The young man remained outside her threshold. Whenever the virgin wished to leave her house and go to church for prayer, the shameless and impure youth thrust himself before her eyes and would not let her leave, whispering amorous words to her with insolent gestures. At last, because of the young man’s excessive harassment, the virgin was forced never to go anywhere outside her house.

“One day the virgin sent her servant to him to say: ‘Come; my mistress is calling you.’ He went to her joyfully, eager to commit fornication. The holy woman was sitting in her room. When the young man entered, she said to him: ‘Sit down.’

“When he had sat down, she said: ‘Tell me, brother, I beg you, why are you so troublesome to me and do not allow me to leave my house?’

“The young man answered: ‘Truly, mistress, I love you greatly, and whenever I look at you, I am wholly inflamed with desire for you.’

“She said to him: ‘What have you seen beautiful in me, that you love me so?’

“The young man said: ‘Your eyes; they have ensnared me.’

“When the virgin heard that her eyes had ensnared him, she immediately took a weaver’s rod and gouged out her eyes. When the young man saw this—namely, that the virgin had torn out her own eyes—he was moved to compunction in his heart, went away to Scetis, renounced the world there, and became a highly approved monk.

## CHAPTER LXI. The life of Abba Leontius the Cilician

Some of the Fathers said about Abba Leontius the Cilician that he was exceedingly fervent in the service of our Lady, the holy Mother of God, and that for forty years he never left her church. He was always of extraordinary gravity and constantly attentive to himself.

They also said this about him: if he saw a poor person coming to him, then, if the man was blind, he placed the alms in his hand; but if he could see, he set them before him—on the base of a column, on a bench, or on the steps of the shrine. The poor man then picked them up.

An old man asked him: “Why, Father, do you not give the alms directly into their hands?”

He replied: “Forgive me, Father. I am not the one who gives them; rather, my Lady, the holy Mother of God, gives them, and she nourishes both me and them.”

## CHAPTER LXII. The life of Abba Stephen, presbyter of the monastery of the Aeliotae

One of the old men told us about Abba Stephen, presbyter of the monastery of the Aeliotae: while he was sitting in his cell, the demon sent thoughts into him, saying: “Leave; you are accomplishing nothing here.”

The old man said to the demon: “I do not listen to you. I know who you are: you cannot bear that anyone should be saved. But Christ, the Son of the living God, will himself crush you.”

## CHAPTER LXIII. Concerning the same man

They said about the same Abba Stephen that, while he was sitting in his cell and reading, the devil again came visibly and said to him: “Leave; you are accomplishing nothing here.”

Then he said to the demon: “If you want me to leave, make the thing on which I am sitting walk.” He was sitting on a wicker chair. When he heard this, the demon immediately made the chair walk throughout the cell.

The old man, observing the demon’s cleverness, said to him: “Since you are so swift and cunning, I am certainly not leaving this place.” After he had prayed, the demon vanished.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Concerning the same man

[Col. 0149C] Three old men came to Abba Stephen the presbyter. While they continued speaking about the benefit of the soul, the elder remained silent. The old men said to him: “Are you giving us no answer, Father? We have come to you for our benefit.”

Then he said to them: “Forgive me; until now I had not noticed what you were saying. Nevertheless, I will tell you what I have: day and night I see nothing other than our Lord Jesus Christ hanging upon the cross.”

When they heard this, they departed greatly edified.

## CHAPTER LXV. Concerning the same man

Abba John, surnamed Molybas, told us about this venerable old man, the blessed presbyter Stephen. When his liver became seriously diseased—for from this illness that holy soul departed from the body—the physicians compelled him to eat meat.

He had a certain secular brother who nevertheless lived very religiously and according to God. While the presbyter was eating meat, his secular brother arrived. Seeing him eating meat, he was scandalized and greatly saddened that, after such abstinence and self-control, he had at the end of his life resorted to eating meat.

Immediately he fell into an ecstasy and saw someone saying to him: “Why were you scandalized at the presbyter when you saw him eating meat? Do you not know that he did it under compulsion of necessity and out of obedience? Therefore you should not have been scandalized. If you wish to see your brother’s merits and glory, turn around and look.”

When he turned, he saw his brother crucified with the Lord. The one who had appeared to him said: “Behold the glory in which your brother is. Therefore glorify him who glorifies those who love him in truth.”

## CHAPTER LXVI. The life of Abba Theodosius the solitary

Abba Antony, superior of the monastery of the Aeliotae, who also built it, told us about Abba Theodosius. The old man himself used to relate this about himself:

“Before I entered the solitary life, I fell into an ecstasy and saw a man whose appearance surpassed the brightness of the sun. Holding my hand, he said: ‘Come, for it is fitting that you fight and wrestle.’ He led me into a theater of infinite size.

“I saw the theater filled with men, dressed in white on one side and in black on the other. When he had brought me into the theater, I saw a man of extraordinary size, an Ethiopian, whose exceedingly ugly head pierced the clouds.

“Then the young man who had appeared to me said: ‘You must wrestle with this one.’

“I was terrified at the sight of that tall man. I began to tremble and fear, and I pleaded with the radiant young man who had led me into the theater, saying: ‘What human being, surrounded by mortal condition and weakness, could wrestle with this one? Even if the whole human race were gathered together, it could not prevail against him.’

“But that illustrious young man said to me: ‘You must indeed wrestle with him. Enter, therefore, with complete eagerness and confidence. As soon as you attack him, I will be there to help you and will place the crown of victory upon you.’

“When I had entered the contest and we had begun wrestling with one another, that glorious judge of our contest immediately appeared and gave me a crown. The dark crowd and the immense multitude of Ethiopians vanished, lamenting, while the remaining company of those dressed in white gave thanks and praise to the one who had helped me and granted me a splendid victory.”

## CHAPTER LXVII. Concerning the same man

[880] Abba Cyriacus, his disciple, told us about this Abba Theodosius the solitary: he had spent thirty-five years in solitude, always eating after two days, constantly observing silence, and speaking to no one. If he wished to speak, he used a sign rather than a word.

I also witnessed this. For I lived in the same monastery of the Aeliotae for ten years.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Concerning the same man

When Abram, bishop of New Saint Mary’s, heard about Abba Theodosius that he had no cloak to use in winter, he bought one for him. After the elder had received it, one day, while he was sleeping—for the old man slept in his cell—thieves climbed up, stripped the cloak from him, and carried it away with them. After this, the old man said absolutely nothing.

## CHAPTER LXIX. The life of Abba Palladius and of David, an enclosed old man from Thessalonica

[Col. 0151A] Before he renounced the world, I and the lord Sophronius the Sophist went together to Alexandria, to Abba Palladius, a holy man and true servant of God, who had his monastery at Thelazomenus [in Greek, Λιθασόμενον].

When we both begged him to give us a word for our edification, the old man began to speak to us as follows:

“My little sons, the time has already been shortened. Let us struggle here for a little while and labor so that we may enjoy immortal goods forever. Look at the martyrs; look at the heavenly combatants, how manfully and bravely they overcame everything. Though past time has received them, they live forever in our memory, and we can scarcely admire their endurance enough.

“Each of those who hear bears witness, astonished at the patience of the blessed martyrs, which truly surpasses human nature. Some had their eyes gouged out; others had their legs cut off; some had their hands amputated; others had their feet severed. Fire suddenly consumed some, while others were slowly burned and tortured for a long time.

“Some were received by the depths of the sea; others were swallowed by rivers. Others were taken alive by the teeth of wild beasts, as though they were evildoers and criminals. Others, already half-dead from various and elaborate tortures, were taken as food. We cannot recount all the kinds of torments devised against those warriors of God by the enemy of the human race, the demon, who was wasting away with envy and spite toward the martyrs themselves.

“O how bravely they endured! With what ardor of faith they fought, overcoming the weakness of the body by the strength of the soul and receiving the rewards they hoped for—rewards more worthy and far more excellent than their present labors. All these things clearly displayed the firmness of their faith in both respects: on the one hand, because after suffering briefly they enjoy extraordinary goods forever; on the other, because they endured with the greatest courage the dreadful punishments inflicted upon their bodies by our enemy, the devil.

“If, therefore, we endure tribulations and conquer with the grace of God, we are truly shown to be lovers of God. God is with us, himself fighting and conquering in us, and by the grace of his favor lightening our labors and sweats.

“Knowing, then, my little sons, what kind of activity and expectation the time requires, let us come to know ourselves through quiet and silence. In this time granted to us, we must make good and noble use of repentance, so that we may deserve to be temples of God. For it is no small and brief honor that will be repaid to us in the age to come.”

He said again: “Let us always remember the one who had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8).”

Again the elder said: “Since, according to the apostle Paul, tribulation produces patience (Romans 5), let us make our mind capable of the kingdom of heaven.”

Again he said: “My little sons, let us not love the world or the things that are in the world (1 John 2).”

[Col. 0152A] He said again: “Let us watch over our thoughts, for this is a medicine of salvation.”

The same Abba Palladius, when we asked him to tell us for our edification by what reasoning and through what thoughts he had entered the monastic state—for he was the old man from Thessalonica—related the following to us:

“In my region, a certain old man from Mesopotamia was enclosed outside the walls of the city, about three stadia away. His name was David. He was richly adorned with virtues, merciful, and continent. He spent nearly eighty years enclosed in a cell [elsewhere, seventy].

“Because, out of fear of the barbarians, the city walls were guarded by soldiers at night, those who watched the section of the wall facing the old man’s cell saw one night that fire was coming out of the windows of the cell. The soldiers thought that the barbarians had set fire to the old man’s cell.

“When morning came, the soldiers entered and found both the old man unharmed and the cell entirely unburned, and they were astonished. Again, on the following night, when they saw the same fire, they marveled. The fire appeared in the old man’s cell not only on the following night but for a long time, so that it became known throughout the entire city, and many people often kept watch on the wall at night in order to observe the fire. That fire continued to be seen until the old man’s death.

“After I had witnessed this miracle not once or twice but many times, I said to myself: ‘If God grants such great glory to his servants in this world, how much do you think he has reserved for them in the future, when their faces too will shine like the sun?’

“This, my little sons, was the reason why I took up the monastic habit and chose this way of life.”

## CHAPTER LXX. The life of Addas, an enclosed Mesopotamian monk

The old man also told us this: after Abba David, another monk named Addas came, himself also from Mesopotamia. He enclosed himself in another part of the city, in a large plane tree, and made a window for himself through which he could also converse with visitors.

When the barbarians came and plundered the entire province, it happened that they passed through that place. One of them, seeing the old man, drew his sword to kill him. Although he raised his hand on high to strike, he could not bring it down; it remained suspended and motionless.

When the other barbarians saw this, they were astonished and begged the old man to heal their companion. The old man prayed, healed him, and dismissed him in peace.

## CHAPTER LXXI. A beautiful saying of a murderer to a monk who followed him as he was being led to execution

Abba Palladius again told us the following:

“In Arsinoe, which is a city of the Thebaid, a certain man accused of murder was arrested. After he had long been tortured, he finally received the sentence of beheading.

“As he was being led six miles outside the city—for he had also committed the murder there—a certain monk followed behind in order to see him beheaded. When the man being led to execution saw the monk following, he said to him: ‘Do you not have a cell, Abba, and manual labor?’

“The monk answered: ‘Pardon me, brother; I have both a cell and work.’

“The condemned man replied: ‘Why, then, do you not remain in your cell and weep over your sins?’

“The monk said to him: ‘Truly, my brother, I greatly neglect myself, and my soul has no compunction. Therefore I have come to watch you die, so that at least by this means I may come to compunction.’

“Then the condemned man said to him: ‘Go, brother, by the Lord; sit in your cell and give thanks to the Savior Jesus Christ. Since he became human and died for us sinners, no human being now dies an eternal death.’”

## CHAPTER LXXII. Abba Palladius’s account of the murderer who falsely accused a young man of the same crime

[Col. 0153B] Abba Palladius himself also related the following to us:

“A certain secular old man who had committed murder was arrested by the authorities in Alexandria. While he was being tortured, he said that another man had been his accomplice in that killing. The man whom the old man accused was a young man of about twenty years.

“Both were subjected to many tortures. The old man said: ‘You were with me when I committed the murder.’ But the young man denied it, asserting that he knew nothing of the murder and had not been with him.

“After they had been tortured, both received the sentence that they should be hanged on gallows. They went five miles outside the city, for it was customary to punish such criminals there. About one stadion from that place stood a ruined temple of Saturn.

“When the people and soldiers had arrived at the place, they first wished to hang the young man on the wood. But the young man prostrated himself on the ground and begged the soldiers, saying: ‘For the Lord’s sake, show mercy, and hang me facing east, so that I may see it when I am hanging.’

“The soldiers said to him: ‘For what reason?’

“The young man answered: ‘Truly, my lords, poor as I am, it has been no more than seven months since I received holy baptism and became a Christian.’

“When the soldiers heard this, they wept over the young man. But when the old man heard it, he growled angrily and said to the soldiers: ‘By Serapis, do it, so that I may look toward Saturn’ [Note: [Col. 0241A] “By Serapis, do it.” This passage has now been restored from the Greek. Previously it made no sense: “Serapis, do it.”].

“When the soldiers heard the old man’s blasphemy, they left the young man and hanged the old man first. As they were hanging him on the wood, behold, a horseman swiftly sent by the Augustal arrived and said to the soldiers: ‘Do not kill the young man; bring him back.’

“There was immense joy among the soldiers and all who were present. They brought the young man back and led him into the praetorium, and the Augustal acquitted him. The young man, saved beyond all hope, went away and became a monk.

“We have written this for our benefit and that of our readers, so that we may know that the Lord knows how to deliver the devout from temptation.”

## CHAPTER LXXIII. The life of John, an Alexandrian soldier

[882] The same Abba Palladius also told us this:

“There was in Alexandria a certain soldier named John, whose way of life was as follows. Every day, from morning until the ninth hour, he sat alone in the monastery beside the steps of Saint Peter, dressed in a hair shirt and weaving baskets. He was completely silent and spoke to no one. He sat in the oratory, laboring with his hands, and sang sweetly only this: ‘Lord, cleanse me from my hidden faults’ (Psalm 18), so that I may not be put to shame while praying.

“After saying this verse, he remained silent for about an hour, then resumed the same verse and repeated it seven times throughout the day, saying absolutely nothing else. At the ninth hour he removed the hair shirt, put on his military habit—that is, his own clothing—and went to his proper standards.

“I remained there for eight years and was greatly edified by his silence and discipline.”

## CHAPTER LXXIV. A truthful saying of the same Palladius concerning heresies

Once, when the old man was reproving us, he said to us:

“Believe me, my little sons: nothing else introduced schisms and heresies into the holy Church except that we do not greatly love God and one another.”

## CHAPTER LXXV. The miracle of our Lady concerning the wife and daughter of a faithful man who was accustomed to receive monks as guests
The same Abbot Palladius, when we had come to him on another occasion, related the following to us:

“There was,” he said, “in Alexandria a certain faithful man, very devout and merciful, who habitually received monks as guests. He had a wife, herself very humble and fasting every day. They also had a little daughter, about six years old [Col. 0154C].

“Now one day that pious man set out for Constantinople, for he was a merchant. Leaving his wife, daughter, and a single servant at home, he went away to board a ship. As he was going to the ship, his wife said to him: ‘To whose care are you entrusting us, my lord?’ Her husband replied: ‘To our Lady, the holy Mother of God.’

“One day, while his wife was sitting and working, with the little girl beside her, that servant, at the devil’s instigation, wished to kill his mistress and her daughter, seize everything they possessed, and flee. Taking a knife from the kitchen, he went toward the dining room where the two women were. When he reached the doorway, he was struck blind, so that he could neither enter the dining room [Col. 0154D] nor return to the kitchen.

“After remaining there for nearly an hour and trying unsuccessfully to enter, he began calling his mistress, saying: ‘Come here.’ Astonished that he remained standing in the middle of the doorway without entering to her but instead calling out, she said to him: ‘You come here instead,’ not knowing that he was being held by blindness.

“The servant boy began to entreat her to go near him, but she swore that she would not go. Then he said to her: ‘Send even the little girl.’ She refused and said: ‘If you want something, come here yourself.’

“When the servant saw that he could accomplish nothing, he struck himself with the sword and fell. His mistress, seeing what he had done, cried out, and the neighbors immediately came running. Some officials from the praetorium also entered [Col. 0155A], and, finding the boy still alive, learned everything from him. They glorified the Lord, who had displayed miracles and saved the mother together with her daughter.”

## CHAPTER LXXVI  
### The Submersion of Mary, a Sinful Woman

Palladius himself also related the following to us:

“I heard,” he said, “a shipmaster recounting something of this kind. One day, while he was sailing with men and women as passengers, he reached the open sea. Although everyone else was sailing successfully—some toward Constantinople, others toward Alexandria, and others elsewhere—and a favorable wind was blowing for them, he alone was unable to sail.

“‘We remained,’ he said, ‘for about fifteen days without moving from the place where we were. We were therefore in great sadness and despair, not knowing what this meant. As shipmaster, responsible for the vessel and everything in it, I began to pray to God about the matter.

“‘One day a voice came to me, saying: “Send Mary out, and you will sail successfully.” I began to consider what this might mean and who Mary was. While I was perplexed about it, the voice came again, saying: “I have told you: Send Mary out, and you will be saved.”

“‘Then, wondering what this meant, I immediately cried out: “O Mary!” For I did not know which woman was Mary. Lying in her place, she heard me and replied: “What do you command, my lord?”

“‘I said to her: “Do me this kindness; come here.” She immediately arose and came. When she had reached me, I took her aside and said to her: “Do you see, sister Mary, that my sins are such that, because of me, all of you are perishing?”

“‘She sighed deeply and said: “Truly, my lord shipmaster, I am a sinner.”

“‘I said to her: “What sins do you have, woman?”

“‘She replied: “Woe is me, for there is no sin that I have not committed, and because of my sins all of you are in danger.”

“‘Then the woman told me what had happened to her, saying: “Indeed, my lord shipmaster, unhappy that I am, I had a husband, by whom I bore two sons. When they had reached the age of nine and five, my husband died, and I was left a widow.

“‘“A certain soldier lived near me, and I wished to take him as my husband. I sent some people to him, but he refused, saying: ‘I will not take as a wife a woman who has sons by another man.’

“‘“When I saw that he refused to marry me because of my children, and having been led on by love for him, I killed my two sons. I told him, saying: ‘Look, now I have no son.’

“‘“When the soldier heard what I had done to the children, he said: ‘As the Lord who dwells in heaven lives, I will not take you.’ Therefore, fearing that this would become known and that I would be put to death, I fled.”

“‘When I heard this from the woman’s mouth, I still did not wish to throw her into the sea. Instead I delayed and said to her again: “Look, I am going up into the carabus [Note: [Col. 0241A] Carabus. From what follows it is clear what a carabus is. For it is said: “Bring out the skiff.” See the Onomasticon.], and if the ship moves, know that my sins are at work in the ship.”

“I immediately called the skiff-man and said: ‘Bring out the skiff.’ When I had boarded it, neither the ship nor the skiff moved any more than before. Then [Col. 0156A], going aboard the ship, I said to the woman: ‘You too, descend into the skiff.’

“As soon as she descended, the skiff immediately spun around five times and sank into the depths with the woman. After this the ship proceeded with such speed that we completed in three and a half days the voyage which we had expected to complete in fifteen days.”

## CHAPTER LXXVII  
### The Account of Three Blind Poor Men: How They Had Been Blinded

My lord Sophronius and I went to the house of the philosopher Stephen for instruction; it was midday. He lived beside the church of the holy Mother of God called Dorothea, which blessed Pope Eulogius had built eastward, near the Great Tetrapylon [Note: [Col. 0241A] Tetrapylon. A portico or temple consisting of four rows of columns. In the Greek, “eastward, near the Tetrapylon” is omitted; in its place stands τὴν ἐπονομαζομένην τῆς Δωροθέας, “which was called Dorothea,” referring to the church of the Blessed Virgin. Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem, mentions the Alexandrian Tetrapylon in his account of the miracles of the martyrs John and Cyrus: Εἴσελθε γοῦν εἰς Ἀλεξάνδρειαν, καὶ ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ Τετραπύλῳ νήστης καθεύδησον, “Enter therefore into Alexandria, and sleep fasting in the Great Tetrapylon.” These words are cited in the Seventh Synod, session 4.].

When we knocked at the philosopher’s door, a girl looked out and said to us: “He is asleep; you must wait a little.” Then I said to my lord Sophronius: “Let us go to the Tetrapylon and remain there.” That place is held in reverence by the Alexandrians, for they say that the bones of the prophet Jeremiah, brought from Egypt by Alexander, the founder of the city, were deposited there.

When we had come there, we found no one except three blind men; it was midday. We quietly and silently went near the blind men and sat down, carrying our books. The blind men were speaking at length with one another.

One said to the other: “How did you become blind?”

He replied: “I was a sailor when I was a young man. As we were sailing from Africa, I was suddenly struck in the eyes at sea, and, unable to walk, I developed a film over my eyes.”

This man said to another blind man: “And how did you become blind?”

He also replied: “I was a craftsman who melted glass for various uses. Through the fire I lost both my eyes and became blind.”

Then both of those who had been questioned said to the third: “Tell us also how you became blind.”

He replied: “Indeed, I will tell you. When I was a young man, I hated work intensely and refused it; I became lustful. Since I did not have the necessities of life, I began to steal.

“One day, after I had committed many crimes, I was standing in a certain place and saw a dead man being carried out, dressed in excellent clothing. I followed the funeral to see where he would be placed. They came behind Saint John and laid him there in a tomb. After completing the rites, they withdrew.

“As soon as I saw that they had gone, I entered the tomb, stripped him, and left him nothing except a single linen cloth. When I began to leave the tomb, laden with the garments, my wicked thought said to me: ‘Take the linen cloth too, for it is good.’

“I, wretched man, turned back so that, after taking the linen cloth as well, I might leave him naked. Then the dead man sat up before me, stretched out his hands over me, and with his fingers tore out my eyes.

“Thus, miserable as I was, I abandoned everything and left the tomb in great distress and danger. There—I have told you how I became blind.”

When we had heard this, my lord Sophronius signaled to me, and we withdrew. He said to me: “Truly, Abba John, let us study no further today; we have been sufficiently edified.”

We have therefore written this down so that you too may be edified together with us. Truly, no evildoer can remain hidden from God. We heard this account from the man who had suffered it.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII  
### The Astonishing Miracle of a Dead Girl Who Detained a Robber and Would Not Release Him Until He Promised to Become a Monk

Abba John, Father of the Monastery of the Giants, related another story similar to this when he had come to Theopolis. He said:

“A short time ago a certain young man came to me and said: ‘For the love of God, receive me, for I greatly desire to repent.’ He said this with many tears and sobs.

“When I saw that he was deeply contrite and in great sorrow, I said to him: ‘Tell me the reason for such repentance, and hide nothing from me; God is able to help you.’

“He said to me: ‘Truly, lord abba, I am a great sinner.’

“I replied to him: ‘Believe me: just as wounds are many and varied, so also are there very many and varied medicines. But if you wish to be healed, tell me truthfully your deeds, so that I may apply appropriate epitimia [Note: [Col. 0241B] Epitimia. I have retained the Greek word ἐπιτίμια, that is, “penalties.” Certain ecclesiastical Latin writers use this word. See the Onomasticon.] to them. A fornicator is healed in one way, a murderer in another; the remedy for a greedy man is one thing, and the medicine for a liar another. The angry man, the thief, and the adulterer are each healed by a different remedy. And not to enumerate your many vices, just as we observe that different remedies are applied to different bodily illnesses, so medicine also comes to the aid of the soul’s vices, which are many, in different ways.’

“He, sighing deeply and beating his breast, was overwhelmed with tears and sobs. Because of his excessive agitation and grief, he was fainting in spirit and unable to utter a clear voice.

“When I noticed that he had fallen into intolerable despair and sadness, and that he could neither say what he had suffered nor what evil he had done nor recount his misery, I said to him: ‘My son, listen to me. Exert some force upon your thoughts, and tell me what you have done; our Lord is able to grant you his help. For he who, because of his unspeakable mercy and immense compassion, suffered everything for our salvation, who associated with tax collectors, did not reject the prostitute who came to him, received the robber, and was called the friend of sinners (Matt. 9; Luke 7; Luke 23; Matt. 11)—he, my son, will gladly receive you also, if you repent and turn back, in his own hands. For he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 18, 33).’

“Then, forcing himself and restraining his sobs and tears somewhat, he said to me:

“‘I, my lord abba, am full of every crime and worthy neither of heaven nor of earth. Two days ago I heard that the virgin daughter of one of the leading wealthy men of this city had died and had been buried in a tomb outside the city, dressed in many costly garments. Following my usual practice in this most wicked occupation, I went by night to the tomb and entered it. I began to strip her.

“‘When I had removed all the garments with which she was clothed, sparing not even her undergarment but taking that from her as well, and leaving her naked as she had been born, I wished to leave the tomb.

“‘Then she sat up before me, stretched out her left hand, seized my right hand, and said to me: “Most wicked of men, was it fitting for you to strip me naked in this way? Do you not fear God, nor dread the judgment of the final retribution? Should you not at least have pitied a dead woman? Yet, being a Christian, did you judge it honorable for me to stand naked before Christ? Did you not respect the female sex? Was it not this sex that gave birth to you? Have you not also violated your mother through this outrage against me? What account, most wretched of men, will you render to Christ for the crime committed against me before his terrible tribunal—when, while I was alive, no stranger ever saw my face, but after my death and burial you stripped me and looked upon my naked body?

“‘“Woe to human misery! To what wretchedness has it fallen! With what heart, man, and with what hands [Note: [Col. 0241B] With what hands. In former times men and women received and partook of the Eucharist in a linen cloth. See the Onomasticon.] do you approach and receive the holy and precious body of our Lord Jesus Christ?”’

“When I saw and heard these things, I was wholly seized by terror and dread. Trembling and afraid, I could scarcely say to her: ‘Release me, and I will never do such a thing again.’

“She said: ‘It certainly will not be so. You entered here as you wished, but you will not leave here as you wish. This tomb will be shared by both of us. Do not think that you will die at once; after being tortured here for many days, you will perish and give up your wretched soul in an evil manner.’

“I begged her with tears to release me, repeatedly adjuring her by the almighty Lord, promising and confirming by oath that I would never again commit this wicked and abominable deed.

“At last, after many prayers and tears and my frequent sobs, she answered me: ‘If you wish to live and be freed from this necessity, promise me that, if I release you, you will not merely abandon these wicked and profane deeds of yours, but will immediately go, renounce the world, become a monk, do penance for the evils you have committed, and serve Christ.’

“I swore to her, saying: ‘By God, who is to receive my soul, I will do not only what you have said, but from this day I will not enter my own house. I will leave here and go to a monastery.’

“Then the girl said to me: ‘Dress me as you found me dressed before.’

“When I had dressed her, she lay down again and died.

“When I heard this from the young man, I restored and strengthened him with words and urged him to repentance and continence. I tonsured him, clothed him in the monastic habit, and shut him in a cave on the mountain. He gave magnificent thanks to God and fought manfully for his soul.” 885

## CHAPTER LXXIX  
### The Greatest and Astonishing Miracle of the Most Sacred Eucharist under Dionysius, Bishop of Seleucia

When we came to Seleucia, we met Abbot Theodore, bishop of that city. He related the following to us:

“Under Dionysius of holy memory, bishop of this city and my predecessor, the following occurred. There was in this city a very devout and wealthy merchant, but he was a heretic, for he was one of the followers of Severus.

“He had a certain faithful servant who was in communion with the holy and apostolic Church. According to the custom of the province, on the holy day of the Lord’s Supper he wrapped the communion he had received in a very clean linen cloth and placed it in a cabinet.

“It happened that after holy Easter this faithful man was sent to Constantinople on some business. Through forgetfulness he left the holy communion in the cabinet, but he gave its key to his master.

“One day the master opened the cabinet and found the linen cloth, with the holy portions of the communion wrapped inside it. He was troubled by this and hesitated about what he should do with them, for he did not wish to communicate from them because they belonged to the holy catholic Church, whereas he himself belonged to the Severian heresy.

“For the time being he left them in the cabinet as they were, thinking that the servant would return and take them. When the Lord’s Supper came and that faithful servant had still not returned, his master wished to burn them, so that they would not again be kept until the following year.

“When he opened the cabinet, he saw that all the holy portions had sprouted into stalks and ears of grain. Seized by immense fear and trembling at this new and wondrous sight, he took the holy portions and, crying ‘Kyrie eleison’ with his entire household [Col. 0159C], ran to the holy church, to the most holy and venerable Bishop Dionysius.

“This great and terrible miracle, surpassing every reason, every understanding, and every thought, was seen not by one or two or three, nor by only a few, but by the entire church: citizens and country people, natives and visitors, those who traveled on land and those who sailed the sea, men and women, old men and children, young and older, masters and servants, rich and poor, rulers and subjects, wise and simple, virgins and monks, widows and married women, those who held positions of authority and those governed by their command.

“Some cried ‘Kyrie eleison’; others praised God in different words; but all alike gave thanks to God for his unspeakable wonders. Many, as a result of this miracle [Col. 0159D], were added in faith to the holy catholic and apostolic Church.”

## LXXX  
### The Spring Granted by God to the Brothers of the Monastery at Scopulus through the Prayers of Their Abbot Theodosius

We came to the monastery of Abbot Theodosius at Scopulus. It is a mountain between Seleucia and Rhosus in Cilicia. The fathers of that place led us above the monastery, about the distance of an arrow’s shot, and showed us a very large and beautiful spring. They said to us:
