“This spring, brothers, is not natural; it has been granted to us by God. Our holy father Theodosius fasted greatly, shed many tears, and by many prayers and prostrations obtained that God should graciously provide us with the consolation and use of this water.

“Previously our fathers drew water from a torrent. But God, who fulfills the desire of those who fear him (Ps. 144), in his infinite goodness granted us the blessing of this water through the prayers of our holy father.

“About two years ago, however, some of the brothers asked the father of the monastery to build a bathhouse in the monastery. The abbot was deeply distressed by this, but nevertheless yielded, accommodating the weakness of the brothers.

“A bathhouse was therefore built in the monastery, and it was used for washing only once. Immediately this great and abundant spring, which God had granted us, dried up.

“Truly we tell you, Christians, we fasted greatly, prayed greatly, and made many prostrations in order to recover the water, but we achieved nothing. A whole year passed without the spring’s water, and we were in great distress.

“As soon as our good and gentle father demolished the bathhouse, God restored the water to us.”

## CHAPTER LXXXI  
### The Well Filled with Water after an Image of the Same Abbot Theodosius Was Lowered into It

The fathers themselves also related this to us, saying:

“A faithful woman in the region of Apamea dug a well in those days. Although she had spent a great deal and endured immense labor, after the well had been dug to a great depth she found no water. She was in great sorrow and distress, both because of the labor and because of the expense.

“While she was in this affliction, a woman appeared to her in a dream and said: ‘Send to Scopulus and have an image of Abbot Theodosius brought to you; through it God will provide you with water.’

“The woman immediately sent two of her people and obtained the holy man’s image. When she had lowered it into the well, water immediately flowed, so that half the well was filled.

“They brought us some of that same water; we drank it and glorified God.” 886

## CHAPTER LXXXII  
### The Life of John, an Elder of the Monastery of Scopulus

We saw a certain elder named John in the same monastery. The fathers of that place told us about him:

“Truly, Christians, the elder is great and terrible to demons. Whoever comes here troubled by an unclean spirit is immediately healed by the elder.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIII  
### Concerning the Same Elder

The fathers of that place also told us the following about him:

“Twenty-four miles from the monastery there is a trading station called Exile Promontory. At that trading station a certain shipmaster built a ship of thirty thousand modii. Wishing to launch it into the sea, he spent two weeks with a great many workers—he had three hundred workers every day—but he could neither move it from its place nor launch it into the sea.

“The ship had been bewitched by wicked men. Its master was therefore in great distress and anxiety, completely at a loss as to what he should do.

“By God’s providence the elder went to that region. When the shipmaster saw the elder and recognized him as a holy man, he said to him: ‘Pray, lord abba, for this ship, for it cannot descend into the sea because of magical arts.’

“The elder said to him: ‘Go and arrange for me to eat, and God will help you.’ The elder said this so that the shipmaster would return home.

“When he had gone, the elder approached the ship alone. He prostrated himself on the ground three times and prayed to God, and three times he signed the ship with the sign of the holy cross in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Then the elder came to the shipmaster’s house and said to him: ‘Go to your ship and launch it into the sea.’

“The shipmaster believed the elder’s words and went with a few men. As they pulled it, the ship was immediately launched into the sea.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIV  
### The Life and Death of an Anchorite, a Servant of God, from the Same Monastery

The fathers of the same monastery related the following to us:

“There was an anchorite in these mountains, a man very great before God, who had lived a solitary life for many years. He died in a small cave without our knowledge, for we all supposed that he had moved to another desert.

“One night he came in a dream and appeared to our present father, the good and excellent shepherd, Abbot Julian. He said to him: ‘Take some men with you and come, removing me from the place where I lie, on the mountain called the Deer.’

“Our father therefore took some of us and climbed the mountain he had named. After searching for many hours, we did not find the anchorite’s remains [Col. 0161C], for the entrance to the cave was temporarily covered with snow and branches.

“When we had not found him, the elder said: ‘Come, let us descend, children.’

“As we began to descend, behold, a doe came and stood not far from us. It began digging the earth with its feet.

“When our father saw this, he said to us: ‘Believe me, children, the servant of God is buried there.’

“We dug and found his body intact. We carried it to the monastery and buried it with honor.”

## CHAPTER LXXXV  
### How the Grain of the Same Monastery Sprouted because the Customary Almsgiving Had Ceased

They related this to us again, saying:

“It was customary for all the poor and orphans of this region to gather here on the Lord’s Supper and to receive, for each person, half a sextarius of grain, thirteen blessings, a sextarius of wine, and half a sextarius of honey.

“Three years ago there was a great failure of the grain harvest, and grain was being sold in this region at twelve sextarii for one coin.

“When the days of the fast came, one of the fathers said to our abbot: ‘Do not, lord father, give grain to the poor according to custom, lest the monastery lack it. Grain cannot be found.’

“The abbot began to say to the brothers: ‘Let us not violate the blessing of our father, children. See: it is the elder’s command, and it is not expedient for us to transgress it. Truly, he is the one who cares for us.’

“The brothers persisted in their opinion and said to the abbot: ‘We do not have enough to give.’

“Then the abbot, saddened, said to them: ‘Go and do as you wish.’

“Thus, contrary to custom, they did not give the blessing on the holy day of the Lord’s Supper and the Parasceve. Later the man in charge of the granaries went and opened the doors and found that all the grain had sprouted. We were consequently forced to throw it into the sea.

“Then our abbot began to say to the brothers: ‘This is what happens to one who makes our father’s admonitions fruitless; now reap the labors of disobedience. We were going to give five hundred modii and please our father Theodosius through obedience, and we would have comforted our poor brothers. But now we have lost nearly five thousand modii of grain. What have we gained, children? How much harm have we done to ourselves?

“‘We have certainly committed two evils. One is that we disregarded the command of our father; the other is that we did not place our hope in God, but in our granary.

“‘Let us learn from this, brothers, that God is the one who orders all human affairs, and that Saint Theodosius invisibly and anxiously cares for us, his children.’”

## CHAPTER LXXXVI  
### Concerning Another Anchorite of the Same Monastery, Who Was Immediately Completed after Receiving His Holy Communion

Abbot Egiarus related the following to us:

“When I had left Aegeae after the solemnity, and a harsher winter had set in, I came to the monastery of Scopulus. While I was there, the following occurred.

“There was an anchorite living alone in that region. On the holy Lord’s Day he used to come and receive the venerable Mysteries. Once, however, the anchorite took offense and remained away for nearly five weeks, never coming to the monastery as usual. The brothers of the monastery were therefore saddened.

“When I was in that monastery, he came on the Lord’s Day. When the brothers saw him, they rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and asked forgiveness. He likewise prostrated himself and asked forgiveness, and they exchanged charity.

“After the anchorite had received the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he placed himself in the middle of the church and immediately completed his course, although he had previously suffered no illness.

“The fathers of the monastery understood that the anchorite had foreknown the day of his death and had therefore come, so that, bearing nothing against anyone, he might depart to the Lord.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVII  
### The Discovery of the Body of John the Anchorite, Called the Humble

We came to a village six miles from Rhosus, and two secular elders received us as guests in the church on their estate. The village lay at the foot of a mountain.

In that church they showed us a marble slab and said: “Christians, a great anchorite lies in this tomb.”

We said to them: “How do you know this?”

They replied:

“Seven years ago we, the inhabitants of this village, saw during the night, on the summit of the mountain, a light like fire. We supposed that someone had lit a fire there.

“After seeing this for many days, we climbed up one day but found no sign of fire—neither fire nor anything in the forest burned by fire.

“On the following night we again saw the same lights. For three continuous months we saw this fire.

“One night we took some men from the village, armed because of wild beasts, and climbed the mountain toward the light that had appeared. We remained where the light was until the following day.

“When morning came, we saw a small cave at the place where we had seen the lights. We entered and found an anchorite who had died.

“He was clothed in a hair shirt and a cloak, and he held a silver cross in his hands. We also found a written tablet bearing these words:

“‘I, John the Humble, died in the fifteenth indiction.’

“When we calculated the years, we found that he had died seven years earlier. Yet he was intact, as though he had died that very day.

“We carried him to the church and buried him with honor.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII  
### The Life of Abbot Thomas, Apocrisiarius [Note: [Col. 0241B] Apocrisiarius. Below, chapter 145, one of his own apocrisiarii is sent. An apocrisiarius is approximately what the Greeks call ἀποκρισιάριος: an ecclesiastical legate who conducts church business. See the Onomasticon.] of the Coenobium of Apamea, and the Miracle of His Body after Death

When we came to Theopolis, a certain presbyter of that church related to us the following about Abbot Thomas: he had been apocrisiarius of the coenobium in the region of Apamea.

The elder therefore came to Theopolis for the benefit of the monastery. While he was staying there, he died at Daphne, in the church of Saint Euphemia.

The clergy of that place buried him as though he were a stranger among the tombs of strangers. On the following day they buried a woman there also and placed her above him. It was the second hour; around the sixth hour, however, the earth vomited her out.

The inhabitants of that place saw what had happened and were amazed. Then, again in the evening, they buried her in the same tomb, and on the following day they found the body above the tomb.

They therefore took the body and placed it in another monument. After a few days they again buried another woman above Abbot Thomas, the clergy of the place not considering that he did not permit anyone to be buried above him.

The earth again vomited her out. Then they understood that the elder did not permit a woman to be buried above him. They went away and reported this to Patriarch Domninus.

He caused the entire city to ascend to Daphne with candles, and with psalmody to carry the holy man’s relics into the city [Col. 0163D]. They placed the holy body in the cemetery where many bodies of martyrs had been buried, and they built a small oratory over it. 888

## CHAPTER LXXXIX  
### The Discovery of the Body of a Holy Anchorite on Mount Amanus

One of the fathers related to us, while we were in Theopolis, that he had climbed Mount Amanus one day for some necessary purpose and had found a cave.

When he entered it, he found an anchorite kneeling, with his hands extended toward heaven. The hair of his head reached to the floor.

Thinking that he was alive, he prostrated himself before him and said: “Pray for me, Father.”

When the man gave no reply, he arose, approached him, and wished to greet and embrace him. But when he took hold of him, he found that he was dead. He therefore left him and went out.

After he had gone a short distance, he saw another cave. He entered and found an elder. The elder said to him: “Welcome, brother. Did you enter another cave?”

He replied: “Yes, Father.”

Again the elder said to him: “Did you take anything from there?”

He answered: “No.”

The elder said: “Truly, brother, fifteen years have already passed since he completed his course.”

Yet the dead man was so intact that he seemed to have fallen asleep only an hour earlier. After the elder had prayed for him, I glorified God and departed.

## CHAPTER XC  
### The Death of Two Anchorites of Mount Phterigius

There were two anchorites above Rhosus on a mountain called Phterigius, near the Piapen River and beside the monastery of Abbot Theodosius at Scopulus. One of them was an elder, the other a younger man and the elder’s disciple.

When the elder died, the disciple prayed and buried him on the mountain. A few days later, the disciple descended from the mountain of the anchorites and came near inhabited places. He found a man cultivating the land and said to him:

“Do me this kindness, brother: take a spade and a hoe and come with me.”

The farmer immediately followed him. When he had come to the mountain, the anchorite showed the secular man his elder’s tomb and said to him: “Dig here.”

When he had dug out the tomb, the anchorite stood in prayer. After completing his prayer, he kissed the secular man and said: “Pray for me, brother.”

Then he descended and placed himself upon his elder, and immediately gave up his spirit. The secular man covered the tomb again and gave thanks to God.

When he had descended from the mountain about a stone’s throw, he said to himself: “Truly, I ought to have received the blessing of the saints.” He turned back, but he could not find their tomb.

## CHAPTER XCI  
### The Life of Abbot Gregory the Anchorite, and of Thalelaeus, His Disciple

Some of the fathers said of Abbot Gregory the anchorite that for thirty-five years he went about naked, wandering through the deserts.

They also said of him that, when he was in the mountains of the monastery of Abba Theodosius at Scopulus, he had a disciple. When the disciple died, and the old man had no tools with which to dig the earth and bury his brother’s body, he descended from the mountain toward the sea, where he found a ship lying at anchor. He asked the shipmaster and the sailors to climb the mountain with him and bury his brother. They readily obeyed the old man; taking the necessary tools, they climbed up with him, dug, and buried the brother’s body. One of the sailors, named Thalelaeus, moved by the old man’s virtue, begged him to let him remain with him. The old man said to him, “You cannot bear the labor of repentance.” He replied, “Indeed, I can endure it.” He remained with the old man for one year, laboring exceedingly in sacred discipline. After the year had been completed, Brother Thalelaeus prostrated himself before the old man, saying, “Pray for me, Father; for through your prayers God has taken the labor away from me. I am no longer weary, nor am I troubled by the severity of the air; I am not burned by the heat, nor frozen by the winter, but am in great repose.” The old man blessed him. After he had spent another two and a half years with the old man, Brother Thalelaeus foresaw his own death and begged the old man, saying, “Take me, I pray you, to Jerusalem, so that I may adore the holy cross and the holy resurrection of Christ the Lord and my God; for during these days the Lord will take me.” The old man therefore took him and departed for the holy city. When they had adored the sacred and venerable places, and had descended to the holy Jordan and bathed there, Brother Thalelaeus fell asleep in the Lord three days later. The old man buried him in the monastery of Copratha. After some time, Abba Gregory the anchorite also entered into rest, and the Fathers of that same monastery buried him in the church.

## CHAPTER XCII. The Life of Brother Gregory the Cappadocian, and the Discovery of the Body of Peter, the Solitary of the Holy Jordan

889 Our venerable Father Abba Gregory, archimandrite of the monastery of our holy Father Theodosius, which is situated in the wilderness of the holy city of Christ our Lord, told me—that is, me and Brother Sophronius the sophist—saying:

“I had here a brother named Gregory the Cappadocian; his ministry, however, was at Phaselide. One day, when the brothers were making bread, Brother Gregory was heating the oven. But when he had heated it, he found nothing with which he could wipe out the oven; for the brothers had hidden the cloth in order to test him. He therefore entered the oven and wiped it with his garment, suffering no injury at all from the fire.” When I heard this, I rebuked the brothers for having tested him in that way.

The same Abba Gregory, our Father, also told us this about the same Brother Gregory, saying: “One day he was feeding pigs at Phaselide. Two lions came to seize a pig. But he took his staff and pursued them as far as the holy Jordan.”

Again our same Father told us, saying:

“When I began to build the church of Saint Quiricus [Note: [Col. 0241B] The church of Saint Quiricus. It should be examined whether this is the same person who is called Saint Quiriacus in the Roman Martyrology, 29 September: ‘In Palestine, Saint Quiriacus the anchorite,’ whose Life, written by Metaphrastes, is found for that month in Laurentius Surius.] at Phaselide, while I was digging the foundations of the church, a monk appeared to me in a dream, apparently of great ascetic discipline, clothed in palm fibers and carrying on his shoulders a small cloak made of a mat. He said to me in a very gentle voice, ‘Tell me, Abba Gregory, after so many labors and so great an abstinence, ought you to have left me outside the church that you are building?’

“I, reverencing the old man’s voice and appearance, answered him, ‘No, Lord; far be it from me to do this.’

“And he said, ‘Indeed, you have done so.’

“I said to him, ‘Who, then, are you, Lord?’

“He replied, ‘I am Peter, the solitary of the holy Jordan.’

“So I rose in the morning, went there, and began digging around the church. As I dug, I found his body lying just as I had seen him in the dream. After building an oratory, I made a splendid tomb on the right side of the church and laid him there.”

## CHAPTER XCIII. The Life of Abba Sisinius, Who Renounced the Episcopate, and of His Disciple

Our same Father Gregory told us, saying:

“One day I went to Abba Sisinius the anchorite. This old man, having abandoned his episcopate for Christ, had come near a fortress called Bethabara, about six miles from the holy Jordan, and was living there a solitary life. When I arrived at the old man’s dwelling and had knocked for a long time, his disciple opened after a considerable interval and said to me, ‘Indeed, Lord Abba, the old man has fallen sick unto death, and he prayed to God that he might not depart from this world until he heard that you had arrived in this region.’ For I had gone to Constantinople on business for the coenobium, to the most pious Emperor Tiberius.

“When he had gone to the old man and announced my arrival, after a long interval he came down and said to me, ‘Come up, Father.’ When we went up, we found that the old man had fallen asleep in peace. I understood, therefore, that as soon as he learned that I was the person who had knocked, he had departed to the Lord. As he embraced him, the deceased said to me in a gentle and mild voice, ‘My abba has come well,’ and again fell asleep.

“I therefore sent word throughout those places that they should come and bury the old man. When they had arrived and were digging the tomb, the old man’s disciple said to those digging the grave, ‘Do me the kindness of digging it somewhat wider, so that it may hold two.’ While they were digging, he placed himself on a mat and entered into rest in peace. Thus we buried the two together, the old man and his disciple.”

## CHAPTER XCIV. The Life of Abba Julian, Bishop of Bostra

Our same Father Gregory the archimandrite told us about Abba Julian, bishop of Bostra, that after he had left the coenobium and become bishop of Bostra, certain inhabitants of that city, out of hatred for the name of Christ, wanted to kill him with poison. They corrupted with money the servant who handed him his cup and instructed him to put poison into the chalice when he presented it to the metropolitan. The boy did exactly as he had been told and gave the poison-infected chalice to Saint Julian.

The holy man received it and divinely recognized the plot. He placed the cup before him without saying anything to the boy, then sent for and summoned all the leading men of the city, including those who had plotted against him. The most blessed man, unwilling to expose those who had done this, said to all in a very gentle voice:

“If you think that you can kill the humble Julian with poison, behold, before you I drink the deadly cup.”

Making the sign of the cross over the cup three times with his finger and saying, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I drink this cup,” he drank the entire cup before them all and remained unharmed. When they saw this, they prostrated themselves and asked forgiveness.

## CHAPTER XCV. The Life of Patricius, an Old Man of the Monastery at Scopulus

There was an old man in the same coenobium of our holy Father Abba Theodosius, a native of Sebaste, whose name was Patricius. He was very old—for he said that he was one hundred and thirteen years old—gentle and quiet. The Fathers of that place told us about him that he had been superior of the monastery of Abazanus, but had abandoned the office, fearing its danger and judgment. For he used to say that feeding rational sheep was the task of great men. He had come there in order to live under obedience, judging that this was more beneficial for the soul.

## CHAPTER XCVI. Concerning the Same Man, and Julian the Blind Arab

They also told us this about him:

“When another old man was there, an Arab by birth named Julian, who was afflicted in his eyes, he once took offense at Macarius, archbishop of Jerusalem, and refused to communicate with him. One day, therefore, Abba Julian sent word to Abba Simeon, who was on the wondrous mountain—which lies nine miles from Theopolis—saying:

“‘I am blind and do not know where to go; nor do I have anyone who can help me, and I refuse to communicate with Macarius. Tell me, Father, what should I do concerning the brother who has fornicated and the man who has bound himself to him by an oath?’

“Abba Simeon answered Abba Julian, saying:

“‘Do not depart, and do not separate yourself from the holy Church; for she is not sick, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Know this also, brother: if anyone should fall into heresy, in your coenobium you have a great old man named Patricius. This old man dwells below the sacristy, among all the others, near the western wall of the church. He too offers the holy prayer of oblation for everyone, and his oblation is regarded as holy.’”

## CHAPTER XCVII. The Life and Death of Two Brother Monks Who Swore Never to Be Separated from One Another

Abba John the anchorite, surnamed Rufus, said that he had heard from Abba Stephen the Moabite, who related that when he was in the coenobium of the holy Abba Theodosius, the great leader of monks, there were two brothers who had sworn to one another that neither in life nor in death would they be separated from each other.

When they were edifying everyone in the coenobium, one of them was attacked by fornication and said to his brother, “Leave me, brother, because I am being attacked by fornication and, since I cannot endure it, I want to return to the world.”

His brother began to beg him, saying, “Do not, I pray you, my brother; do not destroy your labor.”

Then the other said to him, “Either let me go, or come with me, so that I may satisfy my desire.”

Since the brother did not want to let him go, he went with him into the city. The one who was being attacked entered a prostitute’s lodging; but the other, standing outside, threw dust from the ground upon his head and afflicted himself. When the first had completed his shameful act and came out of the brothel, his brother said to him, “What have you gained from your sin, my brother? How much harm have you suffered because of it? Let us return to the coenobium.”

He replied, “I can no longer return to the desert. Leave me; I am remaining in the world.”

Although he begged him at length and accomplished nothing, and although the other no longer wished to follow him into the desert, he too remained with him in the world. Both worked with their hands in order to live.

At that time Abba Abramius, who later became bishop of Ephesus and had recently built in Constantinople the monastery called that of the Abramitans, a good and gentle shepherd, was building his monastery, which was called the Byzantine monastery. The two brothers went there and worked, assisting the masons.

The brother who had fallen into fornication took the wages earned by both of them and went into the city every day, spending them in luxury. The other, fasting and chanting psalms every day, performed his work with complete quietness, saying nothing to anyone.

The craftsmen observed that he neither ate nor spoke on any day, but always appeared to be deep in thought. They therefore reported to holy Abba Abramius about him and his way of life. The truly great Abramius summoned the laborer to his cell and asked him, saying, “Where are you from, brother, and what is your work?”

He confessed everything to him in order, including that he endured everything for the sake of his brother, “so that,” he said, “when God sees my affliction, he may save my brother.”

When Abramius heard this, he said to the brother, “The Lord has granted you the soul of your brother.”

When holy Abramius had dismissed him and he had left the cell, behold, the other brother arrived, crying out, “My brother, take me into the desert, so that I may be saved.”

Immediately he took him, and they went to a cave near the holy Jordan and shut themselves in. After a short time, when the brother who had fallen into fornication had made great spiritual progress according to God, he departed to the Lord. The surviving brother remained in the same cave, in accordance with his oath, until he too died.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. Concerning the Same Surviving Brother

After the death of the other brother, an old man from the monastery of Calamon came to this brother and said to him, “Tell me, brother, after so much time in the solitary life and spiritual discipline, what have you gained?”

The brother said to him, “Go, and come back to me after ten days; I will tell you.”

The old man departed. After ten days he returned and found that the brother had departed to Christ, together with a potsherd on which was written:

“Forgive me, Father, because, while I was performing the work of God and chanting at the appointed hours, I never allowed my mind to descend to earthly things.”

## CHAPTER XCIX. The Life of Antony, an Old Man of the Monastery at Scopulus

The Fathers of the same monastery of our holy Father Theodosius told us, saying:

“A few years ago an old man died here, named Antony. During his life he devoted himself especially to fasting and went to a place called Cotulas. One day, while he was in the desert, behold, Saracens [Note: [Col. 0241C] Saracens. See what is said above, in chapter 21, about the incursions of the Saracens and the martyrs who suffered under them.] came into those parts and saw the old man. One of them drew his sword and came against the old man, wishing to kill him.

“When the old man saw the Saracen coming against him, he looked toward heaven and said, ‘Lord Jesus Christ, may your will be done.’

“Immediately the earth opened and swallowed that Saracen, while the old man was saved. He entered the monastery glorifying God.”

## CHAPTER C. The Life of Peter the Pontic Monk

Again the Fathers of the aforesaid place told us that there had been there an old man named Peter, a Pontic by birth, adorned with many splendid virtues.

Theodorus, who had been bishop of Rosus, told us about this old man that one day he met him at the Jordan, in the monastery of the Towers, where Theodorus himself was staying. Peter said to him, “Do me the kindness, Brother Theodore, of coming with me to Mount Sinai, for I have vowed to make that journey.”

Since he did not wish to refuse obedience, Theodorus said to him, “Let us go.”

When he had crossed the Jordan, the old man said to Theodorus, “Come, Brother Theodore; let us pray that neither of us eat until we reach Mount Sinai.”

The other replied, “Indeed, Father, I cannot do this.”

The old man prostrated himself and prayed, and he ate nothing until Sinai. When they had received the holy mysteries there, he then also took food.

Likewise, from Sinai they reached Alexandria, to Saint Menas, with the old man eating absolutely nothing. There he communicated again, and after communion he took food.

From Saint Menas they came to the holy city, while the old man had tasted nothing at all along the way. When he had received the venerable mysteries at the holy resurrection of Christ our God, only then did he take food.

Thus, throughout that entire long journey, the old man ate only three times: once on Mount Sinai, once in Alexandria, and once in the holy city.

## CHAPTER CI. The Life of Pardus, a Roman Monk

The Fathers of the same monastery also told us about another old man, saying:

“There was here an old man who died a short time ago, named Pardus, a Roman by birth. When he was younger, he had been a muleteer. One day he went to Jericho with mules. While he was in a hospice, a little boy was found there whom, through the agency of the devil, a mule kicked and killed, while Abba Pardus did not know of it.

“Greatly afflicted by this, Abba Pardus went to the Arnon and became an anchorite, always mourning and saying, ‘I have committed murder, and as a murderer I have been condemned in judgment.’

“There was a lion there near the torrent. Every day Abba Pardus went to the lion’s den, provoking and challenging the lion to rise and devour him; but the lion did not harm him at all.

“When the old man saw that he was accomplishing nothing, he said to himself, ‘I will sleep on the road by which the lion goes to the river; when he passes on his way to drink, he will devour me.’

“When he was lying there, behold, after a short time the lion came. As though endowed with reason, it calmly leaped over the old man and did not touch him at all.

“Then the old man became certain that God had forgiven his sin. He returned to his monastery and lived in great continence, edifying everyone by the example of his life until the day of his death.”

## CHAPTER CII. Sophronius the Sophist’s Account of What Happened to Him on the Road

When my brother Abba Sophronius the sophist was questioned, I, Abba John the scholastic, Abba Quiricus, and certain other Fathers were standing near him. He said to us:

“I was just going along the road, and young women were dancing in front of me, leaping and saying, ‘May Sophronius come well; Sophronius has been crowned.’”

## CHAPTER CIII. The Life and Virtues of Abba Stratigius

The Fathers of the monastery of our holy Father Theodosius, that distinguished monastery, said about Abba Stratigius that he possessed three virtues beyond the monks of our time: fasting, vigils, and continual labor.

## CHAPTER CIV. The Life of Abba Nonnus the Presbyter

In the coenobium of our holy Father Theodosius, Abba Theodosius, who had been bishop of Capitolius, told us about Abba Nonnus the presbyter:

“One night, before the signal for the night office had sounded, while he himself was lying on his little bed, he heard someone saying in a gentle voice, ‘Kyrie eleison’ (‘Lord, have mercy’). When this had been repeated fifty times, he wanted to know who was saying it. Looking, he said, through the window of my cell toward the church, I saw an old man prostrate on his knees, and a very bright star above his head, revealing to me who the old man was.”

Another of the old men of that coenobium told us about the same Abba Nonnus, saying:

“One night, before the signal sounded, I came out of my cell and was going to the church. I saw an old man standing before the church and praying with his hands extended toward heaven. His hands shone like lamps of fire. Terrified by fear, I withdrew.”

## CHAPTER CV. The Life of Saint Christopher, a Roman by Birth

When we were in Alexandria, we visited Abba Theodorus, who was at Saint Sophia near the Pharos. The old man told us:

“In the coenobium of our holy Father Theodosius, which is in the wilderness of the holy city of our Lord Jesus Christ, I renounced the world. There I found a very great old man named Christopher, a Roman by birth.

“One day I prostrated myself before him and said, ‘Do me the kindness, Father, to tell me what you did in your youth.’

“After I had begged the old man at length, and he had recognized that I was asking for the benefit of my soul, he told me:

“‘When I renounced the world, my son, I possessed great fervor and the highest eagerness of desire for the monastic life. By day I occupied myself with the appointed psalmody; at night I went to the cave in which Saint Theodosius and the other holy Fathers were accustomed to pray.

“‘Descending into the cave, I bent my knees one hundred times and prostrated myself before God at each step. There are eighteen steps in all. When I had descended all the steps, I remained there until the signal sounded. Then I went with the Fathers to the synaxis.

“‘After I had done this work for eleven years without interruption, together with much fasting, continence, renunciation of all possessions, obedience, and bodily labor, one night I came as usual to descend into the cave. When I had completed the prostrations at each step and was about to reach the floor of the cave, I fell into ecstasy. I saw the entire floor of the cave filled with candles. Some of them were lit, while others were not.

“‘I also saw two men dressed in cloaks and clad in white garments, preparing those same candles. I said to them, “Why have you placed these candles here and do not allow us to descend and pray?”

“‘They answered me, “They are the candles of the Fathers.”

“‘I said to them again, “Why are some of them burning and others not?”

“‘They answered, “Those who wished lit their candles, and those who did not wish to light them did not.”

“‘I said to them again, “Do me the kindness of telling me whether my candle is burning or not.”

“‘They said, “Pray, and we will light it.”

“‘Then I said to them, “I am still praying. And what have I been doing until now?”

“‘At these words I returned to myself, and when I turned again I saw no one. Then I said within myself, “Christopher, greater labor is required.”

“‘When morning came, I left the monastery and went to Mount Sinai, carrying nothing with me except what I wore. After I had spent fifty years there, a voice came to me, saying, “Christopher, Christopher, return to your coenobium, where you also contended well, so that there you may finish your life with your Fathers.”

“‘A short time after he had said these things to me, his holy soul entered into rest in peace.’”

The same Theodorus again told us about the same Abba Christopher. “The old man said,” he related:

“One day I went up to the holy city to adore the holy cross. After I had adored it and was already leaving, I saw a certain brother at the threshold of the courtyard of the Precious Cross, neither entering nor leaving. I also saw two ravens flying shamelessly before his face and persistently striking at his eyes with their wings, preventing him from entering.

“I understood that they were demons and said to him, ‘Tell me, brother, why are you standing in the middle of the doorway and not entering?’

“He replied, ‘Forgive me, my Father. I have thoughts, one of which says to me, “Enter and adore the precious cross,” while another says, “No, but go and perform the responsum [Note: [Col. 0241C] Responsum. You may well hesitate over what responsum means here. I suspect that the Greek had προσφωνάριον, which the translator rendered responsum in its first and most obvious sense. It should nevertheless be considered whether it ought here to be translated “basket,” or something similar. The thought was apparently suggesting to the monk that he should not adore the cross, but return to his cell and weave baskets. See what is said above, Book V, Little Book X, no. 18. If responsum is understood in its ordinary sense, take this brother to have been sent for the responses of the coenobium. So below, chapter 205: “Someone remaining in the coenobium was sent for the responses of the coenobium.”], and another time you will adore it.”’

“When I heard this, I took him by the hand and led him into the church; and immediately the ravens fled. After I had made him adore the holy cross and the holy resurrection of Christ the Lord, I dismissed him in peace.

“Theodorus said that the old man had told him this because he saw that he was greatly distracted by his duties and negligent in prayer.”

## CHAPTER CVI. Abba Theodorus’s Account of Severianus, a Syrian Monk

Our same Abba Theodorus told us again:

“There is a hospice here near the Pharos, between Saint Sophia and Saint Faustus. One day its superior asked me to go to the hospice and remain there for a few days. When I went there, I found a certain monk lodging there, a Syrian by birth, possessing nothing except a hair shirt, a cloak, and a few loaves of bread. He stood in one corner, always chanting psalms day and night and speaking to no one.

“When the holy Lord’s Day arrived, I went to him and said, ‘Come, brother, to Saint Sophia, so that you may communicate in the holy and venerable mysteries.’

“He said, ‘I am not coming.’

“I asked him, ‘Why, I pray you?’

“He said to me, ‘Because I am a Severian and do not communicate with the Church.’

“When I heard that he did not communicate with the holy and apostolic Church, and at the same time saw his excellent conduct and life full of virtues, I went away mourning to my cell. I shut the door, prostrated myself before the Lord, and for three days prayed to him with many tears, saying:

“‘Sovereign Christ our God, who, on account of your ineffable and immeasurable mercy, bowed the heavens and descended for our salvation, who were incarnate from our holy Lady Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, reveal to me who are the ones who believe well and rightly: are we, who are joined to the holy Church, or those who agree with Severus?’

“On the third day a voice came to me invisibly, saying, ‘Go, Theodore, and examine his faith.’

“The next day I went and sat before him, waiting to see something corresponding to what the voice had told me. When I had remained seated for about an hour, looking at him as he stood and chanted in the Syrian language, I saw—God is my witness, my children—a sooty dove standing above his head, as though it had come from a kitchen, filthy and foul-smelling.

“Then I understood that the dark and foul-smelling dove that had appeared to me was his faith.”

His holy soul told us this truthfully, with many tears and sobs.

## CHAPTER CVII. The Life of Abba Gerasimus

A monastery called that of Abba Gerasimus lies about one mile from the Jordan. When we arrived at this monastery, the old men who lived there told us about Abba Gerasimus:

“One day, as he was walking along the bank of the Jordan, he met a lion roaring loudly, with one paw held up. A thorn from a reed had pierced it, so that the paw had swollen and become filled with pus.

“When the lion saw the old man, it showed him the wounded paw pierced by the thorn, weeping, as it were, and begging him to care for it. When the old man saw that it was in such distress, he sat down, took hold of its paw, opened the wound, and extracted the thorn that had pierced it, together with a great amount of corruption. After carefully cleaning the wound and binding it with a cloth, he released the lion.

“When the lion saw that it had been healed, it did not want to leave the old man. Like a beloved disciple, wherever he went it followed its master, so that the old man marveled at the beast’s great gratitude. From then on, the old man fed it, placing bread and soaked legumes before it.

“The monastery itself had one donkey, used to carry water from the Jordan for the needs of the brothers. The old man had made it the lion’s duty to care for the donkey’s grazing. He therefore went with it along the banks of the Jordan and watched it as it grazed.

“One day, while the donkey was grazing, the lion moved some distance away from it. Just then a camel-driver coming from Arabia found the donkey, seized it, and led it away with him.

“The lion, having lost the donkey, returned to the monastery very sad, with its face and neck lowered, and came to its abba. Abba Gerasimus thought that the lion had eaten the donkey and said to it, ‘Where is the donkey?’

“The lion stood silent like a human being and looked down.

“The old man said to it, ‘You have eaten it. Blessed be the Lord. Whatever the donkey did, you shall do from now on.’

“From that time onward, at the old man’s command, the lion carried the canthelium [Note: [Col. 0241C] Canthelium. Canthelia, κανθήλια, are loads customarily placed upon donkeys.] holding four jars and carried water to the monastery.

“One day a soldier came to the old man to receive a blessing. When he saw the lion carrying water and learned the reason, he took pity on it. He brought out three coins and gave them to the old men, so that they might buy a donkey for this service of carrying water and free the lion from that necessity.

“After a short time, when the lion had been freed from the work, the camel-driver who had taken the donkey came carrying wheat to sell in the holy city, and had the donkey with him. When he had crossed the Jordan, it happened that he encountered the lion. When he saw it, he abandoned the camels and fled.

“The lion, recognizing the donkey, ran to it and, biting its halter with its mouth as it used to do, dragged it along with the three camels. Rejoicing and roaring because it had found the little ass that had been lost, it came to the old man.

“The old man, who had previously thought that the lion had eaten the donkey, then learned that the lion had suffered an attack. He gave the lion the name Jordan.

“The lion therefore lived in the monastery with the brothers for more than five years, never leaving the old man.

“When Abba Gerasimus departed to the Lord and had been buried by the Fathers, the lion, by God’s dispensation, was not then in the monastery. After a short time, however, the lion came to the monastery and looked for its old man.

“Abba Sabbatius the Cilician, who had also been Abba Gerasimus’s disciple, saw it and said to it, ‘Jordan, our old man has left us orphans and departed to the Lord; but come, take food and eat.’

“But the lion did not want to eat. It continually turned this way and that, looking around and seeking to see its old man, and indicated by its great roaring that it could not bear his absence.

“Abba Sabbatius and the other old men stroked its neck and said to it, ‘The old man has departed to the Lord and left us.’ But although they said this, they could not calm its cries and wailings. The more they thought they were comforting and consoling it with their words, the more it wailed and roared, adding lamentations and showing by its voice, face, and eyes the grief it felt because it could not see the old man.

“Then Abba Sabbatius said to it, ‘Come with me. Since you do not believe us, I will show you where our old man has been laid.’

“He took it to the place where they had buried him. It was about five paces from the church. Abba Sabbatius stood over the tomb of Abba Gerasimus and said to the lion, ‘Behold, our old man is buried here.’

“Abba Sabbatius bent his knees over the old man’s grave. When the lion heard this and saw Abba Sabbatius prostrate over the tomb and weeping, it too prostrated itself, violently striking its head against the ground and roaring. Thus it immediately died over the old man’s grave.

“All this happened not because one should think that the lion possessed a rational soul, but because God wished to glorify those who glorify him, not only in this life but also after death, and to show us the kind of subjection the beasts had to the first man before he disobeyed the commandment and before he was cast out of the paradise of delights.”

## CHAPTER CVIII. The Life of a Virgin Presbyter and His Wife, Likewise a Virgin

When we came to the island of Samos, we visited in the coenobium called Charixeni Abba Isidore, the superior of that monastery, a man of outstanding virtue, greatly adorned by charity toward all, simplicity, and humility. We also know that after some time he was appointed bishop in the same region. He told us:

“There is a village eight miles from this city, and it also has a church. A certain presbyter lived there who was very remarkable. His parents compelled him, against his will and resistance, to take a wife.

“Yet he was not captured by the allurements of pleasure, although he was young and joined to a lawful wife; rather, he also led her to live chastely and modestly with him. Thus they both learned the Psalter, and together they chanted in the church, preserving themselves as virgins until the end.

“One day this presbyter was falsely accused before the bishop. The bishop, unaware of his manner of life, summoned him from the village and sent him to the prison in which sinful clerics were accustomed to be confined and guarded.

“While he was in prison, when the holy Lord’s Day arrived, a very handsome young man appeared to him and said, ‘Rise, presbyter, and go to your church to offer the holy oblation.’

“The presbyter said to him, ‘I cannot, because I am confined.’

“The one who had appeared said to him, ‘I will open the prison for you; come, follow me.’

“He opened the door and went out before him. When they had gone out, he walked until he was about one thousand paces from the presbyter’s village.

“When day came, the man guarding the prison entered and looked for the place where he had been confined. Not finding him, he went to the bishop and said, ‘The presbyter has escaped while I had the key.’

“The bishop, thinking that he had escaped, sent one of the servants of the episcopal household, saying, ‘Go and see whether the presbyter is in his village, but say nothing to him for the time being.’

“The boy went and found him in the church offering the holy oblation. When he returned, he told the bishop that the presbyter was there and that he had found him offering the sacrifice.

“But the bishop became increasingly angry with him and swore that on the following day he would bring him back with the greatest disgrace.

On the following night, the one who had first appeared to the presbyter appeared to him again, saying: “Come, let us go where the bishop had imprisoned you in the city.” Taking him with him, he brought him back and replaced him in the prison, without the prison guard’s knowledge. On the following morning the bishop learned from the prison guard that the presbyter had been found in custody without his knowledge. The bishop sent to ask the presbyter how he had escaped from prison and how he had entered it again without the guard’s knowledge. He replied:

“A very handsome and excellently dressed young man, who said that he was a servant of your episcopal residence, opened the door for me and went before me as far as a mile near the village on the Lord’s Day night; and when he came again on the following night, he brought me back.”

The bishop therefore summoned all the servants of the episcopal residence, but the presbyter recognized none of them. Then the bishop understood that it had been an angel of God who had done this, so that the presbyter’s virtue might not remain wholly concealed, but that all might learn of it and glorify God, who glorifies those who glorify him. Greatly edified by him, he dismissed him in peace, loudly denouncing those who had falsely accused him.

## CHAPTER CIX. The Life of Abba George, Who Was Never Troubled

[Col. 0175C]

Concerning Abba George, the father of the monastery of Abba Theodosius, Abba Theodosius—his good, gentle, and humble disciple, who became bishop of Capitolius—told us that he had observed him for twelve years to see whether he would ever be troubled even once, and that he had never seen him troubled, even in this present age, when every kind of laziness, negligence, softness, and disobedience reigns.

“But who,” he used to say, “bridled his eye as our holy Father George did? Who put such a door upon his ears as that blessed man did? Who restrained his tongue as our Father did? What ray of the sun has ever illuminated the earth as our Father illumined the hearts of us all?” [Col. 0175D]

## CHAPTER CX. Excellent Sayings of a Certain Egyptian Elder

I took my lord Sophronius with me, and we went to a monastery eighteen miles from Alexandria, to a certain elder of great virtue, Egyptian by birth. I said to the elder: “Tell us a word, Father, about how we ought to live together, since my lord Sophista intends to renounce the world.”

The elder said: “You are doing well, my son, in renouncing the world and saving your soul. Sit, therefore, in whatever cell you wish, soberly and watchfully, preserving quiet and silence, and praying without interruption. And I have hope in God, my children, that he will send you his knowledge to enlighten your souls.” [Col. 0176A]

He said again: “If you wish to be saved, my children, flee from people. For today we do not cease wearing down everyone’s thresholds and going around every city and region, seeking wherever possible to obtain for ourselves the wages of greed or empty glory, and to fill our souls with vanity.”

The elder said again: “Let us flee now, my children, for the time is drawing near.”

He said again: “Woe, woe! How greatly we shall weep and how deeply we shall repent for what we now refuse to repent of.”

He said again: “When we are praised, we do not restrain ourselves in humility; and when we are criticized, we do not endure it. One thing suggests empty glory to us, another brings sorrow upon us poor wretches; but wherever sadness and empty glory are found, no good is discovered.” [Col. 0176B]

He said again: “Our fathers, being great and wondrous, fed many; but I, being humble, cannot manage even one sheep, and am continually exposed to the bites of wild beasts.”

He said again: “This is the work of demons: after they have cast the soul into sin, then to hurl us into despair, so that they may destroy us completely. For the demons always say to the soul: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’ But if the soul is sober, it will cry out against them in turn and say: ‘I shall not die, but live, and I shall recount the works of the Lord’ (Psalm 117).” [Col. 0176C]

“Because the demons have great shamelessness, they cry out again, saying: ‘Flee to your mountain like a sparrow’ (Psalm 10). Therefore we too ought to say to them: ‘For my God, my Savior, and my helper himself is with me; I shall not depart’ (Psalm 61).”

The elder said again: “Be the doorkeeper of your heart, lest a stranger enter and say: ‘Are you one of ours or one of the adversaries?’”

## CHAPTER CXI. The Deed of a Certain Bald Man Dressed in a Sackcloth Garment

I and my companion Sophronius were in Alexandria. One day we went to the church of Theodosius, and in the village we encountered a certain bald man dressed in sackcloth down to his knees. He appeared to be foolish and insane. Abba Sophronius said to me: “Give me some coins, and you will see the virtue of the one who is coming.”

So I gave him five coins. He took them and gave them to the man who appeared to be insane. That man accepted them without saying anything at all. We secretly followed him immediately. When he had turned away from the road, he stretched his right hand, which held the coins, toward heaven; then he prostrated himself before God, placed the coins on the ground, and went away.

## CHAPTER CXII. The Life and Death of Leo the Monk, a Cappadocian by Birth

During the reign of the most faithful Emperor Tiberius, we went up to the Oasis and saw there a great monk in divine matters, a Cappadocian by birth, named Leo. Many people told us many things about him worthy of admiration. When we attained familiar conversation with him and gained great experience of this holy man, we were greatly edified, especially by his humility, his silence, his renunciation of all possessions, and the love he showed toward everyone.

This venerable elder always said: “Believe me, children, I am destined to reign.”

We said to him: “Believe us, Abba Leo, no one from Cappadocia has ever reigned; you therefore have an unreasonable thought.”

But he replied again: “Truly, children, I am destined to reign.” No one, however, could remove this thought from him.

[Col. 0177B]

When the Mazices came and devastated and plundered that entire province, they also came to the Oasis. They killed many monks and led very many away as captives. Among them they seized Abba John—who was a reader of the Great Church of Constantinople—as well as Abba Eustathius the Roman and Abba Theodore the Cilician. These three were ill.

When they had been bound, Abba John said to the barbarians: “Take me into the city, and I will arrange for the bishop to give twenty-four coins on our behalf.”

One of the barbarians took him and led him near the city, and Abba John entered to see the bishop. Abba Leo and some other Fathers were also found in the city, and for that reason they had not been captured. Abba John entered and began to ask the bishop to give coins to the barbarian. But the bishop was found to possess no more than eight coins.

They therefore wanted to give the barbarian eight coins, but he refused to accept them, saying: “Either give me twenty-four coins, or give me a monk.”

Thus those who were in the city were forced to hand Abba John over again to the barbarian, weeping and lamenting. The barbarian brought him to his tents.

After three days, Abba Leo took the eight coins and went out into the desert where the barbarians were. He entreated them, saying: “Take me together with the eight coins and release these three, who are ill and cannot travel through the desert; otherwise you will kill them and suffer loss. I, however, am healthy and will serve you.”

Then the barbarians took Abba Leo and the eight coins and released the other three. Abba Leo went with them as far as a certain place, but when he could no longer proceed because of weakness, the barbarians beheaded him.

Thus Abba Leo fulfilled the Scripture that says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). Then we too understood what he had meant when he said, “I am destined to reign.” For he truly reigned who laid down his life for his friends.

## CHAPTER CXIII. Abba John of Petra’s Admonition

I went to Abba John of Petra, taking my companion Sophronius with me, and we asked him, saying: “Tell us a word.”

The elder said: “Love the renunciation of all possessions and self-control. Believe me when I tell you that, while I was a young man living in Scetis, one of the elders suffered pain in his spleen. A small quantity of vinegar was sought in the four monasteries of that place, but none was found. Such was their poverty, renunciation, and self-control. There were about three thousand five hundred Fathers there.”

## CHAPTER CXIV. The Life of Abba Daniel the Egyptian

The holy elder told us about Abba Daniel the Egyptian, saying: “One day the elder went up to Terenuthis to sell the work of his hands. A certain young man pleaded with the elder, saying: ‘For God’s sake, elder, come to my house and pray over my wife, because she is barren.’

“The elder, compelled by the young man, went with him to his house and prayed over his wife. By God’s will, the woman conceived.

“Some men who did not fear God began to slander the elder, saying: ‘Truly this young man is impotent, but the woman has become pregnant by the elder.’

“This report reached the elder’s ears, and he wrote to the woman’s husband, saying: ‘When your wife gives birth, inform me.’

“When his wife had given birth, the young man informed the elder, saying: ‘By God and through your prayers, Father, my wife has given birth.’

“Then Abba Daniel entered and said to the young man: ‘Prepare a meal and invite your relatives and friends.’

“When they were dining, the elder took the little child in his arms and, in front of everyone, said to the infant: ‘Who is your father, child?’

“The infant replied, pointing with his finger at the young man: ‘This one.’ The infant was twenty-five days old.”

## CHAPTER CXV. Admonitions of Abba John the Cilician

Abba John the Cilician, superior of Raythu, used to say to the brothers: “Children, just as we have fled from the world, let us flee from the desires of the flesh” (1 John 2).

He said again: “Let us imitate our Fathers, who sat in this place with such austerity of life and silence.”

He said again: “Let us not defile this place, children, which our fathers cleansed of demons.”

He said again: “This place belongs to monks, not to merchants.” [Col. 0178D]

He said again: “I found elders here who had spent seventy years in this same place, living only on herbs and the fruit of palm trees.”

The elder said again: “I have spent seventy-six years in this place, suffering many grievous and dreadful things from demons.”

## CHAPTER CXVI. Concerning a Brother Falsely Accused of Taking a Coin

Abba Andrew of Messenia told us, while we were in Raythu: “When I was a young man, my abba and I left Raythu and came to Palestine. We stayed with a certain elder.

“The elder who received us had one coin. Having forgotten where he had put it, through an error, he suspected that I, the younger man, had stolen it. The elder therefore told the Fathers of that place that Brother Andrew had taken the coin.

“When my abba heard this, he called me and said: ‘Tell me, Andrew, did you take the elder’s coin?’

“I replied: ‘Forgive me, Abba; I took nothing.’

“I had a cloak, however, which I sold as I was leaving, for a coin. Taking the coin, I went to the elder, prostrated myself before him, asked his forgiveness, and said: ‘Forgive me, Abba, for Satan deceived me, and I took your coin.’

“A certain layman was there as well. The elder said to me: ‘Go, my son; I have lost nothing.’

“Again I prostrated myself and asked forgiveness, saying: ‘By the Lord, Abba, accept the coin; here it is. And pray for me, because Satan prompted me to steal it and distress you.’

“The elder said again: ‘My son, I have lost nothing.’

“When I would not accept his words, that layman said to me: ‘Truly, brother, yesterday when I came here I found the elder weeping and prostrate, asking forgiveness in great anguish of spirit. I said to him: “Show charity; what troubles you?” And the elder said to me: “I unjustly harassed a brother with slander, saying that he had stolen the coin—and behold, I have found it.”’

“Then the elder was edified by me, because although I had not taken the coin, I had brought it to him, saying: ‘Accept the coin, for I took it.’”

## CHAPTER CXVII. Concerning a Demoniac Brother Healed by Abba Andrew

[Col. 0179C]

A certain brother who had a demon came to Abba Simeon Stylites on the Wonderful Mountain, asking him to pray for him and drive the demon out of him.

Abba Simeon said to him: “Where do you live?”

He replied: “In Raythu.”

The elder said to him: “I am astonished, brother, that you have wearied yourself with so much labor and traveled such a distance to come to me, a sinful man, when you have such great Fathers in your own monastery. Go, therefore, to Abba Andrew and ask him to pray for you, and he will heal you immediately.”

The brother therefore came to Raythu. As the blessed Simeon had instructed him, he prostrated himself before Abba Andrew, asking and saying: “Pray for me, Father.”

Abba Andrew said to him: “Abba Simeon has received the grace of this healing.”

When he had prayed, the brother was immediately cleansed, and he gave thanks to God.

## CHAPTER CXVIII. The Life of Mena the Deacon and Monk in Raythu

[Col. 0179D]

Abba Sergius told us in Raythu about a certain brother there, a deacon named Mena. He said:

“Once, when Mena had gone out to perform a service, he returned to the world. What happened to him we do not know, except that he abandoned the monastic habit and became a layman.

“After a long time he went to Theopolis. On his return to Seleucia, he saw from a distance the monastery of the holy Abba Simeon Stylites and said to himself: ‘I will go up and see the great Simeon,’ for he had never seen him.

“As he was going and had already drawn near the column, Abba Simeon saw him and, divinely recognizing that he was a monk and had been ordained a deacon, called his servant and said: ‘Bring scissors here.’

“When he had brought them, he said to him: ‘Blessed be the Lord; tonsure him,’ pointing at him with his finger, for there were many people around the column.

“The servant was astonished at the elder’s command and was seized with great fear. He received the tonsure without saying anything at all, for he understood that God had revealed to the elder what concerned him.

“When the servant had tonsured him, the great Simeon said to him: ‘Perform the deacon’s prayer.’

“When he had prayed, he said to him again: ‘Go to Raythu, from which you also came.’

“When Mena said that he was ashamed and could not endure the sight of the Fathers, Abba Simeon again said to him: ‘Believe me, my son, you have no reason at all to be ashamed. The Fathers will receive you with cheerful faces and grateful hearts, and your conversion will be a joy and an exultation to them.

“‘Know this also, my son: God will perform a sign in you, so that you may recognize that his immense and ineffable goodness has forgiven you this sin.’”

When he came to Raythu, the Fathers received him with uplifted hands and placed him in the holy sanctuary.

One Sunday, when he was carrying the holy and life-giving blood of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, one of his eyes immediately came out. From this sign the Fathers understood that God had forgiven him this sin, according to the word of the great Simeon.

## CHAPTER CXIX. Concerning the Demon Who Went in a Monk’s Habit to the Cell of an Elder in Raythu

Abba Eusebius, a presbyter of that same monastery of Raythu, told us, when we had come to him, that a demon in the habit of a monk went to an elder’s cell. When he knocked at the door, the elder opened it and said to him: “Pray.”

The demon replied: “Now and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”

The elder again said: “Pray.”

The demon likewise replied: “Now and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”

Then the elder said: “Pray, and say: ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.’”

When the elder had said this, the demon, as though overcome by fire, vanished.

## CHAPTER CXX. Concerning Three Monks Found Dead by Fishermen from Pharon

Fishermen from Pharon told us:

“One day we went to Buchrin, across the Red Sea. After catching a great many fish, we turned back and came near Pereleum. Wishing to cross over to Raythu, we were prevented by contrary winds and detained by a storm at sea for ninety days.

“Coming to a very great desert, we found beneath a rock three dead anchorites, dressed in colobia made of sibinum [Note: [Col. 0241D] Sibinum. The same term occurs below in chapter 123: 936, ‘dressed in a colobium of sibinum.’ What sibinum is has not yet been read by me.] Their melotes were lying beside them.

“We took them and brought them to the ship. Immediately the sea, which had been stormy, became calm, and the contrary winds changed into favorable ones. We crossed with favorable winds and came to Raythu. The Fathers buried them with the ancient elders.”

## CHAPTER CXXI. The Life and Death of Abba Gregory the Byzantine and His Disciple, the Other Gregory of Pharon

[Col. 0181A]

The Fathers of that place told us about Abba Gregory the Byzantine and his disciple, Abba Gregory of Pharon: they had lived on a certain island in the Red Sea. The island had no water, but they brought water to themselves from the mainland for their needs. They had a raft with which they went out and brought water.

One day they left the raft in the sea, tying it to a certain rock. That night a violent wave arose, and when the rope broke, the raft was lost. The Fathers remained there without any means of bringing water to themselves.

After eight months, monks came from Raythu and found both men dead. [Col. 0181B] They also found the following written on the back of a tortoise:

“Abba Gregory of Pharon died after drinking no water for twenty-eight days. I, however, have spent thirty-seven days since I drank.”

We found both bodies intact, took them, and buried them in Raythu.

## CHAPTER CXXII. Concerning Two Monks Who Entered the Church Naked to Receive Communion, but Were Seen by No One Except Abba Stephen

We came to Abba Stephen the Cappadocian on Mount Sinai, and he told us:

“When I was in Raythu some years ago, on Holy Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, I was in the church. When the holy oblation was being completed and all the Fathers were standing present, behold, I saw two anchorites enter the church. They were naked, but none of the other Fathers noticed that they were naked except me alone.

“When they had received communion of the Lord’s body and blood, they went out of the church and departed. I went out with them. When we had gone outside, I prostrated myself before them, saying: ‘Show charity; take me with you.’

“They understood that I had seen them naked and said to me: ‘You are well settled; remain.’

“Again I asked them to take me with them. Then they said to me: ‘You cannot be with us. Remain; you have a good dwelling.’

“After they had prayed for me, I watched them enter the waters of the Red Sea on foot, and they departed across the sea.”

## CHAPTER CXXIII. The Life of Abba Zosimus the Cilician

[Col. 0181D]

We went to Abba Zosimus the Cilician on Mount Sinai, where he lived. The elder had refused the episcopate and had returned to his cell. He was a man of great abstinence, and he told us:

“When I was younger, I left Sinai and went to Ammoniacus to live there. I found there an elder dressed in a colobium of sibinum.

“When the elder saw me, before I had greeted him, he said to me: ‘Why have you come here, Zosimus? Go away, for you cannot remain here.’

“Thinking that he had recognized me, I prostrated myself before him, saying: ‘Show charity, Father. How do you know me?’

“The elder said to me: ‘Two days ago someone appeared to me and said: “Behold, a monk named Zosimus will come to you. Do not permit him to remain here, for I wish to entrust to him the church of Babylon, which is in Egypt.”’

“The elder fell silent and, after dismissing me, went away from me about a stone’s throw. When he had completed two hours in prayer, he came to me, kissed my face, and said to me: ‘My dearest son, you have come well; for God brought you here so that you might commit my body to the earth.’

“I said to him: ‘How many years have you spent in this place, Abba?’

“He said to me: ‘I am completing forty-five years.’

“His face appeared to me like fire. He said to me: ‘Peace to you, my son, and pray for me.’ Having said this, he lay down and rested.

“I dug a grave, buried him, and after two days departed, glorifying God.”

## CHAPTER CXXIV. The Same Elder’s Further Account

[Col. 0182B]

The elder also told us this:

“Twenty-two years ago I went up to Porphyrites, wishing to live there. I also took my disciple John with me. When we arrived there, we found two anchorites and stayed near them.

“One of them was a Galatian named Paul; the other was a Melitene named Theodore, who had belonged to the monastery of Abba Euthymius. They wore colobia made from the skins of buffaloes.

“I stayed there for nearly two years, and we were about two stadia apart from one another.

“One day, while my disciple John was sitting, a serpent struck him, and he immediately died, pouring out blood from every part of his body.

“Being in great distress, I went to the anchorites. As soon as they saw me troubled and afflicted, before I had said anything to them, they said to me: ‘What is it, Abba Zosimus? Has the brother died?’

“I said to them: ‘Yes indeed, he has died.’

“They came with me, and when they saw him lying on the ground, they said to me: ‘Do not grieve, Abba Zosimus; divine help is present.’

“Calling the brother, they said: ‘Brother John, rise, for the elder needs you.’

“Immediately the brother rose from the ground.

“They searched for the beast and, when they found it, seized it and tore it into two pieces in our presence.

“Then they said to me: ‘Abba Zosimus, go to Sinai, for God wishes to entrust the church of Babylon to you.’

“So we departed immediately.

“When we had come to Sinai, after a few days the abbot sent me and two others on a service to Alexandria. The most blessed Pope Apollinaris of Alexandria detained us and ordained all three of us bishops: one bishop of Heliopolis, another of Leontopolis, and he sent me to Babylon.”

## CHAPTER CXXV. The Remarkable Deed of Abba Sergius the Anchorite

Some of the Fathers on Sinai told us about Abba Sergius the anchorite. While he was living on Sinai, they appointed him steward over the pack animals [Note: [Col. 0241D] Pack animals. See the notes on the Life of Simeon Stylites, chapter 20, no. 24. Consult also the *Onomasticon*.].

One day, as he was hurrying along, behold, a lion was lying in the road. When the muleteers and the pack animals saw the lion, they were seized with fear and withdrew.

Then Abba Sergius took one eulogia from his bag, went to the lion, and said to it: “Take the Fathers’ eulogia and move off the road, so that we may pass.”

The lion took the eulogia and withdrew.

## CHAPTER CXXVI. The Excellent Reply of Abba Orentius of Mount Sinai

The holy Fathers of that place told us about Abba Orentius:

“One Sunday the elder entered the church with his cloak turned inside out, so that its hairy side was on the outside. While he was standing in the choir, some of the stewards of the place came and said to the elder: ‘Why, Father, did you enter the church with your cloak turned inside out, to mock us before the pilgrims?’

“The elder replied to him: ‘You have overturned Sinai, and no one said anything to you; but because I turned my cloak inside out, you say to me: “Why have you turned your cloak inside out?” Go and correct what you have overturned, and I will correct what I have overturned.’”

## CHAPTER CXXVII. The Life of Abba George of Holy Mount Sinai and of a Certain Old Woman from Galatia of Phrygia

[Col. 0183B]

The solitary abbess Damiana, mother of Abba Athenogenes, bishop of Petra, told us:

“There was a certain abba on holy Mount Sinai named George, a man of great virtue and abstinence. On the day of Great Saturday, while this Abba George was sitting in his cell, he felt a desire to celebrate the holy day of the Resurrection in the holy city and to receive the venerable Mysteries at the holy Resurrection of Christ our God [Note: [Col. 0241D] ‘At the holy Resurrection of Christ our God.’ Here ‘Resurrection’ is the name of a church dedicated to Christ’s resurrection. See the *Onomasticon*.].

“All day long the elder was troubled by this thought and prayed. When evening came, his disciple approached him and said: ‘Give the command, Father, that we go to the synaxis.’

“The elder replied: ‘Go, and at the time of holy communion come to me, and I will go.’

“The elder remained in his cell. When the time of holy communion arrived at the Holy Resurrection, the elder was found near the blessed archbishop Peter, who gave him holy communion with the presbyters.

“When the patriarch saw him, he said to Mena, his syncellus or assistant [Note: [Col. 0241D] ‘His syncellus or assistant.’ I have retained the Greek term *syncellus*, which among the Greeks is the person next to the patriarch. See the *Onomasticon*.]: ‘When did the abba of Mount Sinai arrive?’

“He replied: ‘Through your prayers, lord, I did not see him until just now.’

“Then the patriarch said: ‘Tell him not to depart, for I wish him to eat with me.’

“Mena went and said this to the elder. The elder replied: ‘Let the will of God be done.’

“When the elder had left the synaxis and venerated the holy tomb, he was found in his cell. Behold, his disciple knocked and said: ‘Father, come, so that you may receive communion.’

“The elder went to the church with his disciple and again received the venerable Mysteries.

“Archbishop Peter was grieved because the elder had disobeyed him. After the solemnity, he sent to Bishop Photinus of Pharan and to the Fathers of Sinai, asking them to send the abba to him.

“When the messenger who carried the letter arrived and delivered it, the elder sent three presbyters to the patriarch: Abba Stephen the Cappadocian, that great man whom we also mentioned above (chapter 122); Abba Zosimus, whom we likewise mentioned earlier (chapter 123); and Abba Dulcitius the Roman.

“The elder cleared himself in writing, saying: ‘Far be it from me, my most holy lord, that I should have despised your holy angel.’ He also wrote this to him: ‘So that your Beatitude may know, six months from now we shall meet together before Christ the Lord and our God, and there I shall worship you.’

“The presbyters departed and delivered the letter to the patriarch. They also told him that the elder had been many years without coming to Palestine. They showed him the letter of the bishop of Pharan as well, likewise testifying that for nearly seventy years the elder had not left holy Mount Sinai.

“But the holy and most gentle Peter brought forward as witnesses the bishops and clerics who had been present at that time, saying: ‘We truly saw the elder, and we all greeted him with the holy kiss.’

“When the six months had been completed, the elder and the patriarch rested in peace, precisely according to the elder’s prophecy.”

[Col. 0184B]

The same abbess Damiana also told us this:

“On Holy Friday, before I was enclosed, I went to Saint Cosmas and Damian and spent the entire night there.

“Late in the day a certain old woman from Galatia of Phrygia came and gave two *minuta* to everyone who was in the church.

“One day my niece, the daughter of the most faithful Emperor Maurice, came to the holy city for the sake of prayer and spent a full year there. I took her and brought her to Saints Cosmas and Damian.

“When we were in the oratory, I said to my relative: ‘Look, daughter, a certain old woman is coming, giving two *minuta*—she has often given them to me. Take them, so that you may not become proud.’

“But she, indignant, said: ‘Am I under orders to accept them?’

“Then I said to her: ‘Yes, take them. The woman is holy and of great virtue: she fasts throughout the entire week, and whatever she earns by working during the week, she distributes to those who are found in the church. She is a widow of about eighty years. Take the two *minuta*, and you too give them to someone else; only do not reject this old woman’s offering.’

“While we were speaking, behold, the old woman came, distributing two *minuta*. She came and gave them to me in complete silence; she also gave some to my niece, saying: ‘Take these and eat.’

“When she had gone away, we understood that God had revealed to her what I had said to my niece: that she should accept them and give them to another poor person.

“She therefore sent one of her servants, bought lupins with the two *minuta*, and ate them. She solemnly affirmed before God that they had been as sweet as honey, so that she marveled and glorified God, who gives grace to his servants.”

## CHAPTER CXXVIII. The Life of Adelphius, Bishop of Arabessus, and Concerning Blessed John Chrysostom

We went to Abba Athanasius in the monastery of our holy Father Saba, and he told us:

“I heard Abba Athenogenes, bishop of Petra, the son of the abbess Damiana, relate the following:

“My grandmother Joanna had a brother named Adelphius, bishop of Arabessus, and also a sister who was abbess of a women’s monastery.

“One day the bishop went to the monastery to visit his sister. As he entered the monastery courtyard, he saw one of the sisters seized by a demon and thrown onto the floor.

“The bishop summoned his sister and said to her: ‘Are you content that this sister should be troubled by a demon and dishonored? Or do you not know that, as abbess, you bear responsibility for all the sisters?’

“She said to him: ‘What can I do against a demon?’

“The bishop replied again: ‘Then what have you been doing here all these years?’

“After praying, the bishop cleansed that sister of the demon.”

Again the same Abba Athanasius told us about the same Bishop Adelphius, saying that he had heard his venerable sister Joanna relate the following:

“When the most holy bishop of Constantinople, John Chrysostom, was sent into exile at Cucusus, he stayed in our house. From this we acquired great confidence and love toward God.

“My brother Adelphius used to say: ‘When the most blessed John died in exile, I suffered inconceivable grief, because such a great man, the teacher of the world, bringing joy to the Church of God, died in exile, away from his throne.

“‘I therefore besought God with many tears to deem me worthy of seeing in what condition he was and whether he had been numbered among the patriarchs.

“‘After I had prayed for a long time, I fell into ecstasy and saw a very handsome man. Taking my right hand, he led me to a certain bright and most glorious place, and showed me the teachers of the Church.

“‘I looked around, seeking to see the one I desired, my beloved great John. When he had shown me all of them and stated each one’s proper name, he again took me by the hand and led me outside.

“‘I followed him sadly, because I had not seen blessed John among the Fathers and teachers of the Church.

“‘As I was going out, the one who guarded the door seized me and said: “What is the matter with you? Why are you sad? No one who has ever entered here has left sad.”

“‘Then I said to him: “This is the cause of my sorrow: I did not see my beloved John, the bishop of Constantinople, together with the other teachers.”

“‘He said to me again: “Do you mean John, the leader of repentance?”

“‘I replied: “That very man.”

“‘He answered me: “No human being living in the flesh can see him. For he stands there where the Lord’s throne is.”’”

## CHAPTER CXXIX. The Life of a Certain Stylite

[Col. 0185D]
