The same Abba Athanasius told us that he had heard Abba Athenogenes, bishop of Petra, relate that there was in his province a certain Stylite. All who came to him spoke while standing below, because he had no ladder.

Whenever a brother said to him, “I want to tell you my thoughts,” he would say to him in a gentle voice: “Come to the steps of the column.” He himself would go to the other side of the column, and thus they spoke with one another: the Stylite standing above and the brother below. None of the others who were standing nearby could hear what was said.

Abba Athenogenes also said this about the same Stylite:

“Two laymen who loved one another very much used to go together to him for many years, and they never traveled separately. One day, without his companion’s knowledge, one of them came to him. Although he knocked at the door for several hours, the elder refused to open it to him, until the man, overcome by weariness, returned.

“On his way back he encountered his friend, who was himself going to the Stylite. The friend brought him back with him so that they might both enter together to see the elder.

“When they knocked at the door, the elder ordered that the one who had arrived later should enter alone. Once inside, the latter began to ask the elder to allow the other to enter as well.

“But the elder told him that he could not receive him. When the man persisted and pleaded for a long time, the elder said: ‘God rejects him, my son, and I cannot receive him.’

“When they had returned to their homes, that man died two days later.”

## CHAPTER CXXX. Admonitions of Abba Athanasius and His Wonderful Vision

[Col. 0186B]

The same Abba Athanasius used to say:

“Our fathers preserved self-control, poverty, and renunciation of all possessions until death; but we have enlarged our bellies and our purses.”

The old man said again: “In the time of our Fathers, it was their concern to avoid distractions of mind; in our own times, the cooking pot and manual labor have prevailed.”

Abba Athanasius also told us this about himself. “At one time,” he said, “a thought came to me saying: ‘What, do you suppose, will be the fate of those who strive and of those who do not strive?’ And when I had fallen into ecstasy, someone came to me and said: ‘Follow me.’ He led me to a place full of light and glory and set me beside a door whose appearance cannot be described. Inside, we heard what seemed to be an innumerable multitude praising God. When we knocked, someone inside heard us and said: ‘What do you want?’ My guide said: ‘We want to enter.’ He replied: ‘No one living negligently will enter here. But if you want to enter, go away, strive, and regard the vanities of the world as nothing.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXI. The Life of Abba Zachaeus of Holy Zion

Procopius the scholasticus of Porphyreon told us about Abba Zachaeus, saying:

“My two sons were living in Caesarea. A great pestilence arose in Caesarea, and I was distressed on account of my sons, lest they should die; I did not know what to do. I said within myself: ‘If I send for them and bring them away from there, it is impossible to flee from the wrath of God; but if I leave them there, they will die, and I shall not see them.’ Since I did not know what I ought to do, I said: ‘I shall go to Abba Zachaeus, and whatever he tells me, I shall do.’

“I therefore went to Holy Zion—for he always lived there—but I did not find him. I came to the courtyard of Holy Mary, the Mother of God, and found him standing in a corner of the courtyard. I told him about my sons. When he had heard me, he turned toward the east and gazed into heaven for about two hours, saying absolutely nothing. Then he turned to me and said: ‘Take courage and do not be distressed. Your sons will not die in this pestilence, and after two days the pestilence in Caesarea will cease.’”

And so it happened, according to the old man’s word. This, as I have said, was related to us by Procopius the scholasticus.

## CHAPTER CXXXII. Concerning the Same

Abba Cyprian, surnamed Cuculas, whose monastery is outside the gate of Caesarea, told us the following when we came to him:

“When that savage and dreadful pestilence was ravaging this city, I shut myself in my cell, entreating the Lord’s mercy, that he might have pity on us and avert the impending wrath. Then a voice came to me saying: ‘Abba Zachaeus has received this grace.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. Concerning the Holy Monk Who Rendered a Saracen Hunter Motionless for Two Days

A pagan Saracen, one of those who lived in Clysma, related this to us:

“When I had gone to the mountain of Abba Antony in order to hunt, I proceeded and saw a monk sitting on the mountain, holding a book and reading. I therefore climbed up to him, intending to beat him and perhaps even kill him. When I had come near him, he stretched out his right hand toward me and said: ‘Stand still.’ And I remained there for two days and two nights, completely unable to move from the place where I was.

“Then I said to him: ‘By the God whom you worship, release me.’ He said to me: ‘Go in peace.’ And so I was able to leave the place where I was.”

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. The Life of Theodore the Anchorite

There was an anchorite in the region of the holy Jordan named Theodore. He came to my cell and said: “Do me a kindness, Abba John, and find me a book containing the entire New Testament.”

When I searched, I discovered that Abba Peter—who later became bishop of Chalcedon—possessed such a book. I went and told him, and he showed it to me on very beautiful parchment.  
[Note: “On very beautiful parchment.” In Greek: ἐν σώματι πολὺ καλῷ, “in a very beautiful manuscript/codex.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

I asked him: “How much is it worth?” He replied: “Three coins.” He said to me again: “Do you want to buy it, or does someone else?” I answered him: “Believe me, Father, the anchorite wants it.”

Then Abba Peter said to me: “If the anchorite wants it, take it free of charge. Take these three coins as well; if the book pleases him, let him keep it. But if he does not like it, behold, you have three coins: buy him one according to his desire.”

I took the book and brought it to the anchorite. After receiving the book, he went away into the desert. When he had spent nearly two months there, the anchorite returned to my cell and said: “Know, Abba John, that my thought troubles me because I have the book for nothing.”

I replied: “Do not be distressed about this. Abba Peter is rich and good, and he rejoices in this.”

The anchorite said to me again: “Truly, I cannot rest unless I pay the price.”

I asked him: “Do you have the price to pay?”

He said to me: “No; but give me a sack so that I may clothe myself,” for he was naked.

So I gave him a sack and a little cloak, and he went away. He became a laborer at the lake that John, patriarch of Jerusalem, had made at Sigma [Greek: Sina]. He received a daily wage of nine *minutae*. He came near me at the monastery of the Aeliotae, ate only ten lupin beans, and worked all day.

When he had saved from his wages the small sum of three coins, he said to me: “Take the price, the book, and go to its owner. If he wants the *minutae*, give them to him; but if he does not want them, return the book to him.”

I therefore went and reported this to Abba Peter. He did not want to accept either the price or the book. Nevertheless, I persuaded him to accept the money and not reject the anchorite’s labor; and at last he accepted it.

I went and gave the book to the anchorite, who returned joyfully to the desert.

## CHAPTER CXXXV. Concerning the Five Virgins Who Wanted to Leave the Monastery and Were Seized by a Demon

[Col. 0188B]

We came—my brother Sophronius and I—to the Monastery of the Eunuchs near the holy Jordan. Abba Nicholas, the priest of that monastery, related the following to us:

“In my region—which was in Lycia—there is a monastery of about forty virgins. In this monastery, five virgins agreed among themselves to flee from the monastery by night and take husbands.

“One night, while all the nuns were asleep and these five were discussing taking their garments and fleeing, all five were immediately seized by a demon. After this they did not leave the monastery again. Rather, having confessed their sins, they gave thanks to God, saying: ‘We give thanks to God, the giver of great gifts, who has brought this scourge upon us so that our souls might not perish.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. Concerning the Charity of Abba Sisinus toward a Saracen Woman

Abba John, the priest of the same monastery, also told us:

“I heard Abba Sisinus the anchorite relate and say: ‘One day I was in my cave near the holy Jordan, and while I was singing Terce, a certain Saracen woman entered my cave. She placed herself before me and stripped herself naked. I was not disturbed; but after completing my psalmody with complete calm and fear of God, I said to her in Syriac: “Sit down, so that I may speak with you, and then I shall do what you want.”

“‘When she had sat down, I said to her: “Are you a Christian or a pagan?” She said: “A Christian.” I said to her again: “Do you not know that those who fornicate go to punishment?” She said: “I know that very well.” Then I said to her: “Why, then, do you want to fornicate?” She replied: “Because I am hungry.”

“‘I said to her: “Do not fornicate, but come every day, and, as God provides, I shall give you your food.” From that day onward she came to me every day, and whatever God sent me, I gave her as food, until I left those places.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. Abba John’s Account of Abba Callinicus

The same Abba John said again:

“When I was younger, I desired to go to the great and famous Fathers, so that I might receive their blessing and be spiritually strengthened by them. Hearing about the great Abba Callinicus, who was enclosed in the monastery of Abba Sabas, I asked one of his acquaintances to take me to him.

“I therefore went to him. The brother who had brought me sat beside the old man’s window and spoke with him for a long time. I was thinking to myself that the elder had never seen me, and perhaps would not receive me graciously.

“When that brother was leaving, he allowed me to enter, greet the old man, and receive his blessing, saying to him: ‘Father, pray also for this servant of yours, because he has come here among the first.’

“But the old man said: ‘I know him, my son. Twenty days ago I went down to the holy Jordan, and I met him on the road. He said to me: “Pray for me.” I asked him: “What is your name?” He said to me: “John.” From that time I have known him.’

“When I heard this, I understood that when I had thought of approaching him, God had revealed to him both my name and who I was.”

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. Concerning Abba Sergius the Anchorite and the Pagan Monk Who Was Baptized

The same old man also related this to us:

“When Abba Sergius the anchorite was at Roban, after he had departed from Sinai, he sent a certain young monk here to the monastery to be baptized.

“When we asked the reason why he was now being baptized, the servant of Abba Sergius told us: ‘When Abba Sergius came to us, intending to remain with us in the desert, he entrusted this man to me for instruction. I repeatedly warned him not to commit himself rashly and without testing to this way of life.

“When I had observed him and his steadfastness, I took him and went to the old man. As soon as the old man saw him, before I had said anything to him, he said to me privately: “What does this brother want?” I answered him: “He is asking to remain with us.”

“‘Then he said to me: “Believe me, brother, this man has not been baptized. Take him to the Monastery of the Eunuchs and have him baptized in the holy Jordan.”

“‘I was astonished at the old man’s words and asked the brother who he was and where he came from. He said that he was from the West, that his parents were pagans, and that he did not know whether he had been baptized or not.

“‘We therefore catechized him, had him baptized in the Jordan, and he remained in the monastery, giving thanks to God.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. Abba Sergius’ Prophecy concerning Gregory, Superior of the Monastery of Pharan

[Col. 0189D]

Abba Sergius the Armenian, his disciple, told us about this Abba Sergius the anchorite. He said that Abba Gregory, who was superior of the monastery of Pharan, had repeatedly urged him to take him to the old man.

“One day, therefore, he brought him to the old man. At that time the old man was in the region of the Dead Sea. When the old man saw him, he greeted him most warmly, brought water, and washed his feet. He spoke with him throughout the entire day about the edification of the soul, and on the following day he sent him away.

“After Abba Gregory had departed,” he continued, “I said to the old man: ‘Do you know, Father, that I was scandalized because, although I have brought many bishops, priests, and others to you, you never washed the feet of any of them except Abba Gregory?’

“Then the old man said to me: ‘My son, I do not know who Abba Gregory is. I know only that I received a patriarch into my cave. For I saw him carrying the holy pallium and the Gospel.’

“And this came to pass: six years later, by God’s arrangement, we saw that same Abba Gregory become patriarch of Theopolis, just as the old man had foretold.”

## CHAPTER CXL. The Life of the Same Gregory, Patriarch of Theopolis

Some of the old men said concerning Gregory, the patriarch of Theopolis, that he had been especially distinguished by these virtues: almsgiving, forgetfulness of injuries, and tears. He also had the greatest compassion for those who sinned. We ourselves often experienced all these qualities.

## CHAPTER CXLI. The Wise Reply of Abba Olympius

A brother came to Abba Olympius in the monastery of Abba Gerasimus near the Jordan and said to him:

“Abba, how can you sit in this cave because of the intensity of the heat and the gnats?”

The old man replied:

“My son, I endure these things in order to be freed from future torments. I suffer the gnats in order to escape the immortal worm. Likewise, I endure this heat because I fear the punishment of everlasting fire. These things are temporary; those have no end.”

## CHAPTER CXLII. Another Wise Reply of Abba Alexander

Another brother went to Abba Alexander, the abbot and superior of the monastery of Abba Gerasimus, and said to him:

“Abba, I want to leave the place where I live, for I am suffering greatly from acedia and weariness of spirit.”

Abba Alexander replied:

“My son, this is a sign that you have in mind neither the kingdom of heaven nor eternal torment. For if you considered these things with attentive concern, you would feel no acedia in your cell.”

## CHAPTER CXLIII. The Life of David, Chief of Robbers, Who Later Became a Monk

When we came to the Thebaid, we met the sophist Phibamon in the city of Antinoe. For our benefit he told us about a certain robber named David, who plundered many people near Hermopolis, killed even more, and committed countless evils, so that no one could be compared with him in these works of cruelty. He was the most notorious of them all.

One day, while he was carrying out robberies with more than thirty companions, he came to himself and, pierced with remorse for the crimes he had committed, left his companions and went to a monastery.

When he knocked at the monastery gate, the gatekeeper came out and said to him: “What do you want?”

The chief of the robbers replied: “I want to become a monk.”

The gatekeeper entered and informed the abbot about him. The abbot came out to him, and seeing that he was already an old man, said to him:

“You cannot remain here. The brothers endure much labor, and the ascetic discipline is severe. Since you have been accustomed to another way of life, you will not be able to bear the monastery’s rigor.”

But the man pleaded, saying: “I shall certainly do everything; only receive me.”

The abbot, however, persisted in his judgment, saying: “You cannot endure it.”

Then the chief of the robbers said to him:

“To let you know, I am David, the chief of the robbers. For this reason I have come here, to mourn my sins. But if you refuse to receive me, I solemnly declare to you, by him who dwells in heaven, that I shall return to my former way of life, take my companions with me, kill every one of you, and overthrow the entire monastery.”

When the abbot heard this, he received him into the monastery, tonsured him, and gave him the monastic habit.

Thus the veteran began to fight in the spiritual army as a recruit. Through his devotion to abstinence, obedience, and humility, he surpassed everyone in the monastery—there were about seventy monks—edifying them all and becoming for everyone a model of virtue and an example of holiness.

One day, while he was sitting in his cell, an angel of God was sent to him and said:

“David, David, God has forgiven you your sins, and from now on you will work signs.”

He replied:

“I cannot believe that God has forgiven me in so short a time all my sins, which are more numerous than the sand of the sea and more grievous.”

[Note: “Zachariah.” If the priest Zachariah did not fully believe the angel when the angel promised him a son, Luke testifies to this in chapter 1. Zachariah did not doubt God’s power, for he knew that Isaac had been born from barren Sarah and Abraham, but he doubted God’s will. Therefore, as punishment for his doubt, silence was imposed upon him.

“Augustine, *Book 50 of the Homilies*, Homily 44: ‘Zachariah received the punishment of silence deservedly for his unbelief: because he did not believe, he was silent. For it is rightly said in Psalm 115: “I believed, therefore I spoke”; because Zachariah did not believe, he deserved not to speak.’

“Ambrose, *Book II on Luke*: ‘Zachariah’s unbelief had taken away his speech and hearing.’”

Baronius, volume VI, under the year of Christ 449, the tenth year of Pope Leo, and the forty-second of Theodosius and twenty-fifth of Valentinian, emperors, commenting on this vision concerning Leo’s encyclical—which is the tenth among Leo’s letters—writes: “But it is better, he says, to hear Peter’s judgment rather than Peter’s vision, when he says: ‘We possess the prophetic word, made more firm than any vision’ (2 Peter 1), and so forth. For that letter claims greater authority for itself from the divine Scriptures, the traditions of the holy Church, and the common agreement of the holy Fathers than from the vision just related.” Thus far Baronius.

“What does he add concerning the vision in the following chapter about Saint Eulogius, defender of Saint Leo’s letter? ‘But in my judgment the public assertion and proclamation of the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon concerning Saint Leo’s letter possesses more certain faith and more certain testimony than any private vision of this kind.’ Thus Baronius. See in the same author further praise of this encyclical of Leo.

“Concerning the following chapter, 149, Baronius notes this about Leo under the year 461, the first year of Pope Hilary, the fifth of Leo, and the first of Severus, emperors: ‘But what does this mean: “All your sins are forgiven you, except for the laying on of hands”? Can sins be forgiven in part? Certainly not, if this refers to guilt. But with respect to punishment, it must be said that Saint Leo’s sins had been forgiven. For the holy Apostle rightly warns Timothy how easy it is even for a prudent bishop to err in these matters: “Lay hands hastily on no one, neither share in other men’s sins” (1 Timothy 5). Saint Leo therefore remained bound by the penalties for the offenses committed by those whom he had improperly promoted to orders. For bishops are then said to share in the sins of others when they confer honors and ministries upon the unworthy. Hence the prophet-king, fearing for himself, says: “Spare your servant from the foreign” (Psalm 18). And if these things are done in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke 23). Who was holier and wiser than Leo, that he should pass safely over so great a danger?]

The angel said to him: “I did not spare Zachariah, who did not believe me when I promised him a son; instead, I bound his tongue, teaching him that he ought not to disbelieve what I said. Nor will I spare you. Therefore from now on you will not speak.”

David fell prostrate on the ground and said:

“When I was in the world, committing unspeakable crimes and shedding human blood, I spoke. Now, when I want to serve God and offer him praises, do you bind my tongue so that I cannot speak?”

The angel replied:

“When you complete the appointed psalmody, you may speak; outside the appointed psalmody, remain entirely silent.”

And so it happened. Through him God displayed many miracles. He sang the psalms, but he could not speak a single other word. The man who related these things to us asserted that he had seen him and glorified God.

## CHAPTER CXLIV. Admonitions of One of the Old Men Who Were in the Cells

One of the old brothers who were in the Cells said:

“Let us not desire to serve the pleasures of the Egyptians, which make people subject to the pernicious tyrant Pharaoh.”

He said again:

“If only people had as much zeal concerning good things as they have concerning evil things, and if they transferred to the love of piety the great zeal they devote to spectacles and to vain and shameful festivals, as well as to greed, empty glory, and injustice. We would certainly never have been ignorant of how greatly we are honored by God and of what we are able to do against the demons.”

The old man said again:

“Nothing is greater than God, nor equal to him, nor anything that is not far inferior to him. What, then, is stronger and more blessed than those who have God as their helper?”

He said again:

“God is indeed everywhere, but he draws near to the pious and to those who labor in spiritual discipline—not to those who are honored by profession alone, but to those who are enlightened by their works. And where God is, who can lie in wait or inflict harm?”

He said again:

“Human virtue does not consist in nature, for nature is changeable, but in the purpose of piety and in God’s help. Therefore, my children, let us care for our soul just as we care for the body.”

Again the old man said:

“Let us gather together the remedies of the soul—that is, piety, justice, humility, and submission. For Christ our God, the greatest physician of souls, is near and wants to heal us. Let us not therefore neglect or despise him.”

He said again:

“The Lord teaches us to be sober and frugal, but we wretched people, through luxuries, dissolve into pleasures.”

The old man said again:

“Let us commend ourselves to God, as Paul says (Romans 6), as living from the dead; and, not fixing our attention on what lies behind, let us forget the former things and press on according to our purpose toward the prize of the heavenly calling (Philippians 3).”

A certain brother asked this old man why he was constantly judging the brothers. He replied:

“Because you have not yet come to know yourself. For the person who knows himself does not look at the faults of the brothers.”

## CHAPTER CXLV. The Life of Blessed Gennadius, Patriarch of Constantinople, and His Lector Charisius

We came to a coenobium called Salama, nine miles from Alexandria, and there we found two elderly priests. They told us that they were priests of the Church of Constantinople, and they related to us the following about blessed Gennadius, patriarch of Constantinople: he was exceedingly gentle, pure in body, and very continent.

They also told us this about him. When many people complained to him about a certain excessively wicked cleric named Charisius, the patriarch summoned him and tried to reform him. When he accomplished nothing by rebuking him, he allowed him to be scourged with paternal and ecclesiastical discipline.

After he learned that the man was in no way improving, either through words or through scourging—for he occupied himself with murders and magical arts—he sent one of his representatives and ordered him to say to the holy martyr Eleutherius—for Charisius was a lector in his oratory:

“Your soldier, holy Eleutherius of God, is a great sinner. Either reform him or cut him off.”

The representative came to the oratory, stood before the altar, gazed toward the martyr’s tomb, stretched out his hand, and said to the martyr:

“Patriarch Gennadius signifies to you, holy martyr of Christ Eleutherius, through me, a sinner, that your soldier is greatly sinning. Either reform him or cut him off.”

On the following day, the perpetrator of crimes, Charisius, was found dead, and everyone was astounded and glorified God.

## CHAPTER CXLVI. The Vision of Eulogius, Patriarch of Alexandria

While we were in the same coenobium, Abba Menas, the Father of that coenobium, told us about the holy Alexandrian pope Eulogius:

“One night, while he was celebrating the morning praise in the oratory of the episcopal residence, he saw Julian the archdeacon standing near him. When he saw him, he was troubled as to how he had dared to enter; yet he said nothing to him. When he had completed the psalm, he prostrated himself on the ground. The one who had appeared in the form of Julian the archdeacon did the same.

“Then, after the patriarch had risen following the prayer, the other still lay on the floor. The bishop turned and said to him: ‘How long will you not rise?’ He replied: ‘Unless you yourself extend your hand to me and raise me up, I cannot rise.’

“Then Eulogius extended his hand, took hold of him, and raised him. He began to sing the psalms again. After a little while he turned, but saw no one.

“When he had completed the morning praises, he summoned his chamberlain and said to him: ‘Why did you not announce the entrance of the archdeacon to me? How did he enter me here tonight without being announced?’ But the chamberlain insisted that he had neither seen anyone nor seen anyone enter.

“The patriarch did not believe him, but said: ‘Call the gatekeeper here.’ When he came, he said to him: ‘Did Julian the archdeacon not enter here?’ The man solemnly affirmed that he had neither entered nor departed.

“The patriarch was silent then. But when morning came, the archdeacon Julian went up to pay his respects. The bishop said to him: ‘Why did you not observe the proper order, Julian the archdeacon, but come up to me this night without being announced?’ He replied: ‘By the prayers of my lord, I neither came up here nor went down from my house, except just now.’

“Then the great Eulogius understood that he had seen Julian as a martyr, urging him to restore his church, which had nearly collapsed and grown old with time and threatened to fall into ruin. With great eagerness, and because he loved the martyr exceedingly, he stretched out his hands, restored his church from its foundations, and adorned it with every kind of ornament, as befitted the holy martyr.”

## CHAPTER CXLVII. The Astonishing Correction of the Letter Written by Blessed Leo, Bishop of Rome, to Flavian

Abba Menas, the Father of the same coenobium, also told us that he had heard Abba Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, say:

“When I had gone to Constantinople, I enjoyed the companionship of Lord Gregory, the Roman archdeacon, a great and exceptional man. He told me about the most holy and blessed Leo, the Roman bishop, saying that it is recorded in the Roman Church that, when he had written a letter to Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, against the impious Eutyches and Nestorius, he placed it upon the tomb of the chief of the apostles, Peter. Devoting himself to prayers, vigils, and fasts, he prayed to the supreme apostle:

“‘If, as a human being, I have written anything less carefully or have omitted anything, you—to whom the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, has entrusted both this seat and this Church—correct it.’

“After forty days, the apostle appeared to him while he was praying and said to him: ‘I have read it and corrected it.’ Leo took the letter from the tomb of blessed Peter, opened it, and found it corrected by the apostolic hand.”

## CHAPTER CXLVIII. The Vision of Theodore, Bishop of Darnae, Concerning the Same Most Blessed Leo

[Col. 0194A]

The most holy Theodore, bishop of the city of Darnae in Libya, related the following to us:

“When I was chamberlain of the holy pope Eulogius, I saw in a dream a man of venerable appearance, tall in stature, who said to me: ‘Announce my arrival to Pope Eulogius.’

“I said to him: ‘Who are you, lord, who command me to announce you?’

“He replied: ‘I am Leo, the Roman bishop.’

“I entered and announced him, saying: ‘The most holy and blessed Pope Leo, bishop of the Roman see, wishes to meet you.’

“When Pope Eulogius heard this, he rose quickly and ran to meet him. After greeting one another and praying, they sat down.

“Then the divine and eminent Leo said to Saint Eulogius: ‘Do you know why I have come to you?’

“He replied: ‘No.’

“Leo said to him: ‘I have come to thank you, because you responded properly and magnificently concerning my letter, which I had written to my brother Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople. You made my meaning and judgment clear and closed the mouths of the heretics.

“‘Know, brother, that through your divine labor and zeal you have served not only me, but also the supreme summit of the apostles, Peter, and above all the truth itself that we proclaim, which is Christ our God.’

“I saw this not once only, but two and three times, and, being confirmed by the threefold apparition, I related it to the holy Pope Eulogius. When he heard it, he wept, stretched out his hands toward heaven, and gave thanks to God, saying:

“‘I give you thanks, Lord Christ our God and ruler, because although I am unworthy, you have deigned to make me a herald of your truth. Through the prayers of your servants Peter and Leo, you have deigned, in your supreme and ineffable goodness, to receive our small and modest zeal like the two mites of the widow.’”

## CHAPTER CXLIX. The Astonishing Account of Amos, Patriarch of Jerusalem, Concerning the Most Holy Leo, Roman Bishop

When Abba Ammos had gone down to Jerusalem and had been ordained patriarch, all the abbots of the monasteries of the desert came to pay their respects to him. I too was present with my abbot.

The patriarch began to say to the Fathers:

“Pray for me, Fathers, for a great and unbearable burden has been laid upon me, and the dignity of the priesthood terrifies me exceedingly. Governing rational souls belongs to Peter and Paul and those like them; but I am an unfortunate sinner.

“Yet I fear the burden of ordinations more than anything else. For I found it written that the most blessed and angel-like Pope Leo, who presided over the Church of the Romans, remained for forty days at the tomb of the apostle Peter, devoted to vigils and prayers and asking the apostle to intercede for him with God, so that his sins might be forgiven.

“When the forty days had been completed, the apostle Peter appeared to him and said: ‘I have prayed for you, and all your sins have been forgiven, except for the laying on of hands. For this alone you will be required to give account, whether you have done it well or perhaps otherwise.’”

## CHAPTER CL. The Life and Holiness of the Bishop of the City of Rumella

Abba Theodore the Roman related the following to us:

“There is a small town not far from the city of Rome called Rumella. Its bishop was a man of great virtue and merit.

“One day the inhabitants of the town entered before the most blessed Roman bishop Agapetus, accusing their bishop and saying: ‘He eats from a consecrated vessel.’

“The bishop, shocked merely by hearing this, sent two of his clerics to bring the bishop to Rome in chains and on foot. When the bishop arrived, Agapetus immediately sent him to prison.

“After the bishop had spent three days in prison, the Lord’s Day came. As the pope slept, when Sunday was dawning he saw in a dream someone standing before him and saying:

“‘On this Sunday, neither you nor any other bishop who is in this city is to offer the saving sacrifice, except the bishop whom you have confined in prison. For I want him to offer today.’

“The pope awoke, troubled by the vision he had seen, and said to himself: ‘I accepted such an accusation against him, and he is to offer?’

“Then a voice came to him a second time in the vision, saying: ‘I told you that only the bishop who is in prison is to offer.’

“While he was still uncertain, the same figure appeared to him a third time and repeated the same words.

“The pope awoke, sent to the prison, and summoned the bishop before him. He questioned him, saying: ‘What is your occupation?’

“The bishop answered him nothing other than: ‘I am a sinner.’

“When the bishop could not persuade him to say anything else, the pope said to him: ‘Today you are to offer.’

“When he was standing at the holy altar, with the pope standing beside him and the deacons surrounding the altar, the bishop began the sacred rites of the Mass. When he had completed the prayer of offering, before concluding it he began it a second time, and then a third and a fourth time.

“When everyone was displeased by this delay, the pope said to him: ‘What is this? You have now said this prayer four times and have not concluded it.’

“Then the bishop replied: ‘Forgive me, holy Father. Because I did not see the descent of the Holy Spirit according to custom, I did not finish the prayer. But, my holy lord, remove from the altar that deacon standing near me who holds the fan.’  
[Note: “Fan.” In Greek, ῥιπίδιον (*rhipidion*), used in the sacred rite and carried by a deacon. See the *Onomasticon*.]

“For I do not dare tell him myself.”

Then, at the command of the blessed Agapetus, the deacon withdrew, and immediately the bishop and the pope saw the coming of the Holy Spirit. The veil that had been placed over the altar was also lifted of its own accord, and it covered the pope, the bishop, and all the deacons who were standing at the holy altar, for about three hours.

Then the venerable Agapetus, recognizing the bishop’s holiness from the miracle he had witnessed and understanding what a false accusation he had suffered, regretted that he had troubled him. He resolved never again to act on the basis of a misrepresentation, but to proceed with mature and considered judgment and with great patience.

## CHAPTER CLI. Abba John the Persian’s Account of the Most Blessed Gregory, Bishop of the City of Rome

We went to Abba John the Persian, and he told us about the great and most blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome:

“When I had gone to Rome to pay my respects at the tomb of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, I was standing one day in the middle of the city. I heard that Pope Gregory would be passing through that place, and I thought of paying my respects to him.

“When the pope was near me and saw me moving forward to pay my respects to him—I speak before God as witness, brothers—he himself first prostrated himself on the ground before me. He did not rise until he saw that I had risen first.

“Then, greeting me with great humility, he handed me three coins with his own hand and ordered me to buy whatever was necessary.”

Thus I glorified God, who had bestowed upon him such humility, mercy, and charity toward everyone.

## CHAPTER CLII. The Life and Sayings of Marcellus of Scetis, Abbot of the Monastery of Monidion

We came to Abba Marcellus of Scetis at the monastery of Monidion. The old man, wishing to benefit us, related the following:

“When I was in my own province—which was in Apamia—there was a charioteer named Phileremus. One day, when he had been defeated, those who were on his side rose up and shouted to him: ‘Phileremus does not receive the crown in the city.’

“Later, when I came to Scetis, whenever a thought arose in me urging me to return to a city or village, I immediately said within myself: ‘Marcellus, Phileremus does not receive the crown in the city.’

“By Christ’s grace, this thought caused me not to leave Scetis for thirty-five years, until the barbarians came, seized me, and sold me in the Pentapolis, while they laid Scetis waste.”

The same abbot Marcellus, speaking as though about another old man living in Scetis (although it was he himself), related that one night he had risen to chant psalms according to custom. When he had begun to chant, he heard the sound of a trumpet, as though it were sounding a battle call. The old man, greatly disturbed, thought to himself: “From where is the sound of a trumpet resounding in this place? There are no soldiers here; war is far from here.” While he was turning these thoughts over in his mind, a demon came near him and said: “Indeed, there is a war. If, therefore, you do not wish to be attacked and to fight back, go and sleep, and you will not be attacked.”

The old man said again: “Believe me, little sons, nothing so disturbs, excites, irritates, wounds, destroys, and grieves the demons, and causes Satan himself, the author of destruction, to move against us, as continual meditation on the psalms. For all divine Scripture is indeed useful to us and greatly grieves the demons, but not in the same way as the Psalter. Just as, among the populace, if one faction praises the emperor, the other faction is not thereby grieved or moved against those who praise him; but when they turn to insults and reproaches against those who do not praise him, then the others are aroused against them—so the demons are neither moved nor grieved by the other Scriptures in the same way as by the psalms. For when we meditate on the psalms, in part we pray by praising God for ourselves, and in part we pursue the demons with curses.

“Thus, when we say: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity’ (Psalm 50 [51]); and again: ‘Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me’ (ibid.); and: ‘Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not abandon me’ (Psalm 70 [71]), we are praying for ourselves. But we pursue the demons when we say (Psalm 67 [68]): ‘Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee from his presence.’ And again: ‘I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was gone; I sought him, and his place was not found’ (Psalm 36 [37]). And this: ‘Let their sword enter their own hearts’ (ibid.). And again: ‘He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit which he made. May his pain return upon his own head, and may his iniquity descend upon his own crown’ (Psalm 7).”

The old man said again: “Believe me, my sons, when I tell you: Just as there is great praise, great glory, and a kingdom for one who renounces the world and embraces the monastic way of life—for intellectual realities are more precious than sensible ones—so there is great shame and disgrace for a monk who abandons the monastic habit, even if he should become emperor.”

He said again: “From the beginning man was the likeness of God, but after he fell away from God he became the likeness of a beast (Genesis 1).”

Again he said: “Nature also arouses desires, brothers, but constant and attentive abstinence extinguishes them as well.”

The old man said again: “Learn the good life by experience, and do not now be afraid as though you were weak.”

Again he said: “Do not marvel that, although you are human, you can become an angel. For a glory equal to that of the angels has been set before you, and our contest-master promises it to those who contend.”

The old man said again: “Nothing makes monks so familiar with God as beautiful, honorable, and most pleasing chastity, which, as the holy and divine Spirit testifies through blessed Paul, grants honor and perseverance in continually attending upon the Lord without distraction (1 Corinthians 7).”

He said again: “My sons, let us leave marriage and the begetting of children to those who look toward earthly things, desire the present, do not contemplate the future, and do not attend to the acquisition of eternal goods, nor can they be rescued from temporal and momentary things.”

He said again: “Let us hasten to depart from the carnal life, just as carnal Israel departed from Egyptian slavery (Exodus 14).”

Again he said: “Splendid and sweet gifts of God have been set before us, brothers, in place of the burdensome pleasure of the world.”

[Col. 0198A] The old man said again: “Let us flee avarice, the mother of all evils (1 Timothy 6).”

## CHAPTER 153. A monk of the monastery of Raithu’s reply to a secular brother

909 There were two secular brothers in Constantinople, very religious and very given to fasting. One of them, therefore, coming to Raithu, renounced the world and became a monk. After some time, his secular brother also came to Raithu to see his brother the monk. While he was staying with him, the secular man saw his monk-brother taking refreshment at the ninth hour, and, scandalized, said to him: “Brother, when you were living in the world, you never ate before sunset.”

Then the monk said to him: [Col. 0198B] “Indeed, brother, when I was in the world, my ears nourished me; for the empty glory and praise of men refreshed me greatly and made the labor of fasting lighter.”

## CHAPTER 154. The life of Theodore the secular man, a man of God

Abbot Jordan the solitary said: “Three of us anchorites went together to Abbot Nicholas at the torrent of Betasimus—for he lived in a cave between Saint Elpidius and the monastery called of the Pilgrims—and we found a certain secular man with him. While we were speaking about the salvation of the soul, Abbot Nicholas said to the secular man: ‘Tell us something too.’

“The secular man replied: ‘What can I do for your benefit? If only I were able to benefit even myself.’

“The old man said to him: ‘You will certainly say something.’

“Then the secular man said: ‘For twenty-two years now, except on Saturday and Sunday, the sun has never seen me eating. I was a hired laborer on the estate of a rich man, unjust and greedy, with whom I remained for fifteen years, working day and night. He did not want to pay me my wages, but year after year afflicted me greatly. So I said to myself: “Theodore, if you endure this man, he will prepare the kingdom of heaven for you in place of the wages he owes you.” I have also kept my body pure from a woman to this very day.’”

When we heard this, we were greatly edified.

## CHAPTER 155. Abbot Jordan’s account of three Saracens who killed one another

[Col. 0198D]

Abbot Jordan also told us this about Abbot Nicholas: “The old man related,” he said, “that when the most faithful Emperor Maurice was ruling, at the time when Namanes, leader of the Saracen nation, was conducting a raid, as I was going around near Arnon and Aidan, I saw three Saracens who had with them a very handsome young man, about twenty years old, bound and captive.

“When the young man saw me, he began to weep and beg me to take him from them. I began asking the Saracens to release him. One of them answered in Greek and said: ‘We will not release him.’

“I said to them again: ‘Take me and release this man, because he cannot endure the fatigue.’

“He answered me again: ‘We will not release him.’

“I said to them a third time: ‘Will you not even accept a price for him? Give him to me, and whatever you ask, I will bring you.’

“He replied: ‘We cannot give him to you, for we have promised him to our priest: if we capture anything beautiful, we will offer it to him so that he may offer it as a sacrifice. But go now; for if you delay, I will throw your head to the ground.’

“Then I prostrated myself on the ground and said: ‘Our Savior, Christ God, save your servant.’ Immediately the three Saracens, filled with a demon, drew their swords and cut one another to pieces. I took the young man to my cave, nursed him back to health, and he no longer wished to leave me. Renouncing the world, he completed seven years in the monastic habit and then fell asleep. He was a Tyrian by birth.”

## CHAPTER 156. A certain old man’s reply to two philosophers

[Col. 0199B]

Two philosophers once came to an old man and begged him to say a word for their edification. But the old man remained silent. Again the philosophers said: “Father, do you give us no answer?”

Then the old man said to them: “I know that you are diligent in eloquence; but I affirm that you are not true philosophers. For as long as you are learning to speak, why do you behave as though you did not know how to speak? Let the work of your philosophy, then, always be to meditate on death, and accustom yourselves to silence and quiet.”

## CHAPTER 157. An account by two monks of the monastery of the Syrian Subevorites concerning a dog that showed a brother the way

[Col. 0199C]

The sophist Sophronius and I went to the monastery of Calamon, near the Jordan, to Abbot Alexander, and found with him two monks of the monastery of the Syrian Subevorites. They related the following to us:

“Ten days ago a certain host of pilgrims came distributing alms. When he came to Subiba of the Besorites, he gave a blessing-gift. He then asked the abbot of the monastery, saying: ‘Show charity, and send someone to the neighboring monastery of the Syrians, so that they too may come and receive a blessing-gift, and so that they may inform the monastery of Charembe to come as well.’

“Then the abbot sent a brother to the abbot of the Syrian Subevorites. The brother set out and said to him: ‘Come as far as the monastery of the Besorites; inform the monastery of Charembe also, so that they too may come.’

“The old man replied: [Col. 0199D] ‘Brother, forgive me, for I have no one whom I can send. But show perfect charity: go yourself and inform them.’

“The brother said: ‘I have never gone there, nor do I know the way.’

“Then the old man said to his puppy: ‘Go with this brother as far as the monastery of Charembe, so that he may inform them of what is wanted.’

“The dog went with the brother until it set him down beside the monastery gate. The men who related this to us also showed us the dog itself, for they had it with them.”

## CHAPTER 158. Concerning the ass that served the monastery called Mardes

There is a very high mountain near the Dead Sea called Mardes. Anchorites live on this mountain. They also have a garden at the foot of the mountain, situated about six miles from them near the shore of the sea; therefore the anchorites have a servant there as well.

Whenever they wish to send to the garden for vegetables, they saddle the ass and say to it: “Go to the garden, to the servant, and bring us vegetables.” It immediately goes alone to the gardener and, standing before the door, knocks with its head. The gardener at once comes out, loads it with vegetables, and sends it away laden. One may see the ass going up and down alone every day and serving only the old men, obeying no one else.

## CHAPTER 159. The life of Abbot Sophronius the solitary, and the admonitions of Menas, head of the coenobium of Severianus

Abbot Menas, head of the coenobium of Abbot Severianus, said concerning Abbot Sophronius the solitary that he had lived naked near the Dead Sea for about seventy years, taking herbs as food.

He said this about him as well: he had heard the old man relate and say: “I prayed to the Lord that the demons would not come near my cave. I saw the demons coming and standing at a distance of about three stadia, unable to approach any nearer.”

The same Abbot Menas said to the brothers of the coenobium: “Let us flee, my sons, the conversations of secular people; for they usually harm younger monks.”

The old man said again: “Every age ought to practice repentance, the young together with the old, so that we may deserve to enjoy eternal life with glory and praise. The young, because in the flower of their age, while desire is burning, they have placed their neck beneath the yoke of chastity; the old, because they have been able to transfer to better things the expectation of evils that had grown familiar to them over many years.”

## CHAPTER 160. How a demon appeared to a certain old man in the form of an extremely black boy

Abbot Paul, head of the coenobium of Abbot Theognostus, related to us that a certain old man had said:

“One day, as I was sitting in my cell and working with my hands—for I was weaving a basket while reciting psalms—behold, a kind of Ethiopian boy entered through the window. Standing before me, he began to dance, and said to me while I was chanting: ‘Old man, am I not dancing well?’

“I gave him no answer. Again he said to me: ‘Does this dancing of mine not please you?’ When I still gave him no answer, he said to me: ‘There you are—you think, wretched old man, that you are doing something great. I tell you that you have gone astray in the sixty-fifth, sixty-sixth, and sixty-seventh psalms.’

“Then I rose and prostrated myself in worship before God, and he vanished.”

## CHAPTER 161. The life of Abbot Isaac the Theban, and how a demon also appeared to him in the form of a young man

Lycos is a city of the Thebaid. About six miles from it there is a mountain on which monks live, some in caves and others in cells. We went there and met Abbot Isaac, a Theban by birth. The old man related the following to us:

“Fifty-two years ago, while I was making a mosquito net [Col. 0201A] [Note: *Conopionem.* The translator preserved the Greek inflection, which is now called *κωνωπεῖον* and now *κωνωπεών*, with *conopeum* being the customary Latin term, for a woven tent-like covering made to keep away mosquitoes.], I made a mistake in the work and was distressed because I could neither find nor correct the error. I therefore spent the entire day wearing myself out in vain, not knowing what to do.

“When I was almost in despair, behold, a young man entered through the window and said to me: ‘You have made a mistake; but give me the work so that I may correct it.’

“I said to him: ‘Go away from here; let this be far from me.’

“He answered me: ‘Certainly it is a loss to you if you do the work badly.’

“Then I said to him: ‘Do not concern yourself with this.’

“He said to me again: ‘I pity you, because you are wasting your labor.’

“I replied to him: ‘You have come here for an evil purpose, both you and those who brought you.’

“But he said to me: ‘In truth, you brought me here, and you are mine.’

“I said to him: ‘Why is that?’

“He answered me: ‘Because on three Sundays you received communion while you were at enmity with your neighbor. I am the one who presides over anger and the remembrance of injuries. From now on you are mine.’

“After hearing this, I immediately left my cell, went to my brother, prostrated myself before him, and asked his forgiveness; and we were reconciled. When I returned, I found that he had destroyed both the mosquito net and the mat on which I had prostrated myself, because he envied our charity.”

## CHAPTER 162. Abbot Theodore of Pentapolis’s reply concerning the relaxation of abstinence from wine

Fifteen miles from Alexandria there is a monastery called Calamon, between Octavum and Maphora. There we saw Abbot Theodore of Pentapolis—for the sophist Sophronius was with us—and asked him:

“Father, is it good, whenever we ourselves go to someone or someone comes to us, to relax our abstinence from wine?”

The old man answered us: “No.”

I said to him: “How, then, did the ancient Fathers relax it?”

The old man replied: “The ancient Fathers, being great and powerful, could both loosen and bind again. But our generation, my sons, is not sufficient either to loosen or to bind; for if we loosen the rule of our abstinence, we no longer retain the austerity of our religious life.”

## CHAPTER 163. The life of Abbot Paul of Hellas

Abbot Alexander of the monastery of Calamon, which is near the Jordan, said:

“One day, while I was with Abbot Paul of Hellas in his cave, behold, someone came and knocked. The old man went out and opened to him; then he brought out bread and soaked chickpeas, set them before him, and the lion ate. I thought that the visitor was a man, but when I looked through the window, I saw that it was a lion.

“I said to the old man: ‘Why, Father, do you give him food? Tell me the reason.’

“He said to me: ‘Because I warned him not to harm anyone, neither human being nor animal, saying: “Come every day, and I will give you your food.” And now this is already the seventh month since he has come twice each day, and I give him food.’

“Again, after a few days, I went to him, wishing to buy from him a wine vessel—for that was the old man’s trade—and I said to him: ‘What is it, Father? How is the lion?’

“He said to me: ‘Badly.’

“I said to him: ‘Why?’

“He replied: ‘The previous day he came here for me to give him food. But when I saw that his chin was stained with blood, I said to him: “What is this? You have disobeyed me and eaten meat. Blessed be the Lord; I will no longer give you food to eat from the food of the Fathers, you devourer of flesh. Go away.”’

“But he did not want to leave. Then I took a cord, folded it three times, struck him three blows with it, and he departed.”

## CHAPTER 164. Abbot Victor the solitary’s reply to a fainthearted monk

A brother came to Abbot Victor the solitary at the monastery of Elusa and said to him: “What shall I do, Father, since the passion of faintheartedness dominates me?”

The old man answered: “It is a disease of the soul. Just as those whose eyes are afflicted—for perhaps the text should read ‘the sick’—seem to themselves to see more light when they suffer more, while one who has healthy eyes sees only a little, so the fainthearted are quickly disturbed by a small temptation and think it great; but those who are healthy in soul rejoice more in temptations.”

## CHAPTER 165. The life of the brigand called Cyriacus

A faithful man related concerning a certain brigand named Cyriacus, who practiced brigandage around Emmaus, which is Nicopolis. He was so savage and monstrous that he was called “the wolf.” He had other partners in brigandage with him, not only Christians but also Jews and Samaritans.

One day some people from the district of Nicopolis went to the holy city during Holy Week to illuminate their children through baptism. After they had done this and were returning to their own district to celebrate the holy day of the Resurrection, brigands met them while their leader was absent. The men escaped by flight, but the women, after throwing down their newly baptized children, were seized by the Hebrews and Samaritans, who took possession of them.

As the men fled, they encountered the leader of the brigands, who said to them: “Why are you fleeing?”

They told him what had happened. He took them with him and went to his companions. When he found the infants thrown on the ground, he asked who had done this, beheaded the perpetrators of the crime, and returned the children to the men—for they did not permit the men to take back their wives, since they had been defiled. Thus the leader of the brigands saved them and led them back to their district.

After a short time, however, the leader of the brigands was captured and spent ten years in prison. None of the rulers killed him; at last he was even released. He always said: “Because of those children I escaped a bitter death. I often saw them in dreams saying to me: ‘Do not be afraid; we are making satisfaction for you.’”

Later Abbot John, presbyter of the monastery of the Eunuchs, and I spoke with him, and he himself related these same things to us, glorifying God.

## CHAPTER 166. The life of a brigand who became a monk and was later beheaded in secular clothing

912 Abbot Sabbatius said:

“When I was staying in the monastery of Abbot Firminus, a certain brigand came to Abbot Zosimus the Cilician and begged the old man, saying: ‘Show me charity, I beseech you by God, because I am guilty of many murders. Make me a monk, so that at last I may cease from my crimes.’

“The old man encouraged him, made him a monk, and gave him the holy habit. After a short time, however, the old man said to him: ‘Believe me, son, you cannot remain here. For if the ruler hears of you, he will seize you, and your enemies likewise will kill you. But listen to me, and I will take you to the coenobium of Abbot Dorotheus near Gaza and Majuma.’

“He went there. After he had lived there for nine years, learned the Psalter, and mastered the whole monastic discipline, he returned again to Firminus’s monastery, to the old man, and said to him: ‘Show me mercy, Father, and give me my secular clothing and take back the monastic habit.’

“The old man, becoming sad, said to him: ‘Why, son?’

“He replied: ‘Behold, Father, as you know, I have spent nine years in the coenobium; I fasted as much as I could, lived continently, remained in obedience with all quietness and fear of God, and I know that his boundless goodness has forgiven me many sins. Nevertheless, I very often see a little child standing before me and saying: “Why did you kill me?” I see him in dreams, in church, when I go to communion, and in the refectory, saying the same thing to me; he does not allow me to rest even for one hour. Therefore, Father, I want to leave so that I may die for the child. For I killed that child for no reason and without any cause.’

“After taking his secular clothing, he went out. As he was traveling in this clothing to Diospolis, he was captured and beheaded the following day.”

## CHAPTER 167. The life and death of Abbot Poemen the solitary

Abbot Agathonicus, head of the coenobium of the castle of our holy Father Sabas, said:

“One day I went down to Ruba to visit Abbot Poemen the solitary. When I had found him and told him my thoughts, he dismissed me late into a cave. It was winter, and that night there was extreme cold; I became stiff with the excessive force of the frost.

“In the morning the old man came to me and said: ‘What is it, son?’

“I said to him: ‘Forgive me, Father; I endured a difficult night because of the cold.’

“He said to me: ‘I felt no cold, son.’

“I was greatly astonished to hear this, for he was naked. I said to him: ‘Show charity; how did you not feel such severe cold?’

“He said to me: ‘A lion came and fell asleep beside me, and it warmed me. Nevertheless, I tell you, brother, that I shall be devoured by wild beasts.’

“I said to him: ‘Why, I ask?’

“He said to me: ‘When I was in our province—for we were both Galatians—I was a shepherd of sheep. I disregarded a passing stranger, and he was eaten by dogs. Although I could have saved him, I did not; I abandoned him, and he was torn apart by dogs. I know that I too must die in this way.’

“And so it happened. For after three years he too was torn apart by wild beasts, as he had said.”

## CHAPTER 168. Sayings of the old man Abbot Alexander

[Col. 0204A]

The old man Abbot Alexander said to the brothers: “Our Fathers pursued deserts and tribulations, but we pursue cities and rest.”

The old man said again: “In the time of our Fathers, these virtues flourished: nakedness and humility. In us, however, avarice and pride reign.”

Again he said: “Our Fathers never washed their faces, but we frequent public washing places and baths.”

The old man said again: “Woe to me, my sons, because we have destroyed the truly angelic way of life.”

Abbot Vincent, his disciple, said to him: “We are certainly weak, Father.”

The old man said to him: “What do you mean, Vincent, by saying that we are weak? Believe me, son, we are Olympian in body and robust, but our soul is feeble.”

He said again: “We are able to eat and drink much and to dress well, but we cannot abstain and humble ourselves.”

Again he said: “Woe to you, Alexander, woe to you! How great will your shame be when the others are crowned?”

## CHAPTER 169. The life of a certain old man blind in the monastery of Abbot Siscius

There was a certain old man blind in Scetis, in the monastery of Abbot Siscius. His cell was about a thousand paces from the well, and he never allowed another person to bring him water. Instead, he made a rope, tied one end of it to the well and the other in his cell. The rope lay on the ground.

Whenever he went to draw water for himself, he walked along the rope. The old man did this so that he could find the well. When the sand covered the rope because of the wind, he held it in his hand, shook it free, placed it on the ground again, and walked along it.

A certain brother begged the old man to allow him to bring him water. The old man answered him: “Son, it is already twenty-two years since I have always drawn water for myself in this way, and now you want to take away my labor?”

## CHAPTER 170. The life of a certain holy woman who died in the desert

A certain monastery called Samson’s was about twenty miles from Jerusalem. Two Fathers from this monastery went to Mount Sinai for the sake of prayer. When they returned to the monastery, they related the following to us:

“When we had worshiped on the holy mountain and were already returning, it happened that we followed the desert paths in error. We were carried, as though across the sea, through the middle of the wilderness for many days.

“One day we saw from a distance a small cave. As we made our way toward it and were already approaching, we saw a little spring, a few herbs around the spring, and human footprints. We said to ourselves: ‘Truly, there is a servant of God in this place.’

“We entered and saw no one, but we heard only the voice of someone whimpering. After searching for a long time, we found something like a manger, and someone lying in it. We approached the servant of God and asked him to speak to us. When he gave us no answer, we approached, took hold of him, and found that his body was still warm but that his soul had departed to the Lord.

“Then we realized that he had fallen asleep at the moment we entered the cave. We dug there, and one of us took the cloak in which he was dressed, so that he could wrap the old man’s body in it. When we took the body from the place where it lay and tended to it according to custom, we found that it was a woman, and we glorified God. After completing the service over her, we buried her.”

## CHAPTER 171. The life of two remarkable men, the philosopher Theodore and the lector Zoilus

[Col. 0205B]

There were two remarkable men in Alexandria, men of great virtue: Abbot Theodore the philosopher and Zoilus the lector. We had the greatest familiarity with both of them, with one because of instruction and study, and with the other because we shared the same homeland and upbringing.

Abbot Theodore possessed nothing except a cloak and a few books. He slept on a stool and entered whatever church he happened to visit. At last he also renounced the world in the coenobium of Salcime, and there brought his life to a glorious conclusion.

The lector Zoilus likewise embraced equal poverty. He too possessed nothing except an old cloak and a few books; he occupied himself with copying books. He too, perfected in the Lord, was buried in the monastery of Abbot Palladius.

Concerning these two, Theodore the philosopher and Zoilus the lector, certain Fathers went to Dom Cosmas the scholastic and asked him: “Which of them labored more in spiritual discipline?”

He said to them: “The food, bedding, clothing, and abstinence from every superfluous possession of both were similar, as were their nakedness, humility, and frugality. But Abbot Theodore the philosopher, barefoot and suffering from great weakness of the eyes, learned the whole Old and New Testament. Yet he had the consolation of the brothers, their companionship, and visits from friends, as well as much diversion while teaching and working.

“But the hospitality of the lector Zoilus is not the only thing worthy of praise; his solitude, immense toil, and guardianship of his mouth also deserve commendation. For without the companionship or intercourse of friends and relatives, free from every activity involving worldly affairs, he permitted himself no refreshment or amusement, accepting not even the smallest service from anyone. He cooked for himself, washed for himself, and received no comfort from reading. He was always ready to serve others and took no account of heat, cold, or bodily illness. He was always free from laughter, sadness, dissipation, and distress; besides the harshness of his clothing, he was continually consumed by a multitude of lice.

“Yet he too had considerably more relief than the former from his outings, since he had the freedom to go wherever he wished, day or night—although the magnitude of his labor restrained this freedom, and his infrequent outings excluded familiarity with secular people.

“Therefore each one will receive his own reward, according to his own labors, and in proportion to the measures of the resurrection, intellectual and spiritual purity, service, fear of God, love, compunction, continual psalmody, prayer, most intense faith, and virtue hidden and concealed from human beings.”

## CHAPTER 172. The life of the aforementioned Cosmas the scholastic

Many people told us many things about this Dom Cosmas the scholastic, each person different things and many people many things. But we write down only what we saw and what we carefully learned, for the benefit of those who read.

He was a humble, merciful, abstinent, virgin, quiet, angerless, sociable man, a host to pilgrims, and a lover of the poor. This remarkable man brought us great benefit, not only through his appearance but also through his teaching, and because he possessed a great abundance of books, more than anyone else in Alexandria, which he readily and willingly lent to those who wished to use them.

He possessed nothing else. For throughout his entire house one would have seen nothing except books, stools, a little bed, and a table. Everyone was allowed to enter, ask questions concerning what was useful, and read.

Every day I myself went in to him, and, in truth, I never entered without finding him either reading or writing against the Jews. He burned with great zeal to convert that people to the truth. For this reason he often sent me to certain Hebrews, so that I might converse with them by letter. He himself did not readily leave his house.

One day I went to this Dom Cosmas the scholastic. Since I had great confidence in him, I asked him: “Show charity and tell me how long you have been in this way of life.”

When he remained silent and gave no answer, I said to him again: “By the Lord, tell me.”

After he had remained silent for a little while, he said to me: “I have been at it for thirty-three years.”

When I heard this, I glorified God.

On another occasion I went to him again and asked him: “Show perfect charity, knowing that I question you for the benefit of my soul. Tell me, I ask, after so long a time in your way of life, in quietness and continence, what have you attained?”

He sighed and groaned from the depths of his heart and said to me: “What virtue can a secular man attain, especially one who remains sitting in his house?”

I asked him again: “By the Lord, tell me, so that I too may progress.”

Then, after I had pressed him greatly, he said: “Forgive me. I have attained these three things: not to swear, not to lie, and not to laugh.”

## CHAPTER 173. The remarkable deed of Theodore the anchorite, who by his prayer made sweet water in the sea

There was an anchorite in the region of the Jordan named Theodore, a eunuch. Compelled by a certain necessity, he had to travel to Constantinople, and he boarded a ship.

When the ship was detained at sea for a long time, the water ran out, and the sailors and passengers were in great anxiety and despair. The anchorite rose, stretched out his hands toward heaven to God, who saves our souls from death, prayed, and then signed the sea with the sign of the cross. He said to the sailors: “Blessed be the Lord; draw as much water as you need.”

They filled all their vessels with fresh water from the sea, and everyone glorified God.

## CHAPTER 174. The deed of a pious shipmaster who obtained rain from the Lord

Abbot Gregory the anchorite related to us the following:

“When I was sailing down from Byzantium, I boarded a ship. A certain secretary also entered with his wife, intending to go to the holy city for the sake of prayer. The shipmaster was extremely religious and devoted greatly to fasting.

“As we sailed, the secretary’s servants used up the water recklessly. When we had reached the open sea, our water ran out, and we were in great sorrow. It was a pitiable sight to see women, boys, and infants drying up with thirst and lying as though dead.

“After we had spent three days in this distress, the secretary himself, unable to endure the tribulation, drew his sword and wanted to kill both the sailors and the shipmaster. For he said: ‘These are the authors of our destruction, because they did not take on enough water.’

“But I begged the secretary, saying: ‘Do not do this. Rather, let us beseech our Lord Jesus, the true God, who does great and marvelous things beyond number. For behold, as you see, the shipmaster has now spent this third day devoted to fasting and prayer.’

“When the secretary had consented, on the fourth day, about the sixth hour, the shipmaster rose and cried out in a loud voice, saying: ‘Glory to you, Christ our God!’—so that we were all amazed at his voice.

“He said to the sailors: ‘Spread out the membranes.’ [Note: *Membranas.* Here they spread out membranes to catch rainwater, just as other sailors expose fleeces and skins both to collect rain and to gather dew.] When they had spread them out, behold, a cloud came over the ship and poured down so much water that they filled the vessels needed for our necessities. It was a great and fearful miracle: although the ship was under sail, that cloud followed us, and it did not rain outside the ship.”

## CHAPTER 175. An account of the almsgiving Emperor Zeno
[Col. 0207D] One of the Fathers told us about the emperor Zeno, saying that he had treated a certain woman outrageously in the person of his daughter. She, however, spent her time in the temple of our holy Lady, the Mother of God, praying to her and beseeching her, and saying with tears: “Avenge me against the emperor Zeno.” When she had done this for many days, the holy Mother of God appeared to her and said: “Believe me, woman, I have often wished to exact vengeance for you, but his hand prevents me.” For he was exceedingly merciful and gave alms.

### CHAPTER CLXXVI. A beautiful account by Abbot Andrew of ten pilgrims, among whom was a Hebrew youth

Abbot Andrew of the Octavi Decimi [“the eighteenth”; sic], when we were in [Col. 0208A] Alexandria, told us, saying:

When I was young, I was extremely undisciplined and restless. One day, having suffered persecution because of our restlessness, I and nine others fled to Palestine. Among them there was one industrious man, and another was a Hebrew.

When we had come into the desert, the Hebrew became ill, even unto death. God is my witness that we were in great distress, not knowing what to do for him. Nevertheless, as social charity requires, we did not abandon him. Each of us carried him as best he could, wishing to bring him either to a city or to a market town, so that he would not die in the desert.

But when the youth, from hunger, a most violent fever, excessive labor, and thirst caused by the sun’s heat, had almost entirely wasted away and was failing, [Col. 0208B] approaching death and no longer able to be carried, we decided, with many tears, to leave him in the desert and depart, fearing that we ourselves too would fail from thirst.

When, therefore, we had laid him down on the sand, weeping, and he saw that we intended to leave, he began to adjure us, saying:

“By the God who made heaven and earth; by the God who bowed the heavens and descended for the salvation of the human race; by the God who will judge the living and the dead: do not allow me to die a Hebrew, but, as Christians, show mercy to me and baptize me, so that I may leave this life as a Christian and go to the Lord.”

We replied to him:

“Truly, brother, we are not permitted to do this. We are laymen; this is the work of bishops and priests. Besides, there is no water here.”

But he persisted, [Col. 0208C] adjuring us in the same way and adding still more with tears, saying:

“Do not, Christians, deprive me of this gift granted by God.”

When we were in great perplexity, that industrious man, inspired by God, said to us:

“Raise him up and strip him.”

So, with great effort, we raised him, and while holding him upright, stripped him. Then the industrious man, filling both his hands with sand [Note: [Col. 0242C] Sand. Neither sand from the shore nor sand moistened in any manner whatsoever can be the matter of baptism, since the matter of baptism must be water, by which a person can be washed. See the Scholastics on the third part of Saint Thomas, and especially our Franciscan, Francisco Suárez, volume III, on the third part, question 66, article 4, disputation 20, section 1.], poured it three times over his head, saying:

“Theodore is baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

When we responded “Amen” to each name of the holy, consubstantial, and adorable Trinity—for the Lord God is my witness, brothers—Christ our God immediately healed and strengthened him, so that no sign of his former illness, [Col. 0208D] or of any affliction whatsoever, remained in him. Healthy and vigorous, with complete cheerfulness and a radiant appearance, he walked through the desert for the remainder of the journey, always going ahead of us.

All of us, therefore, marveling at such a sudden and complete transformation, praised and glorified the ineffable majesty and goodness of Christ our God.

When we came to Ascalon, we brought him to the blessed and holy Dionysius, bishop of that city, and told him what had happened to our brother on the road. When he had heard this, the holy and admirable Dionysius, astonished at so new and unheard-of a miracle, summoned the clergy and explained the whole matter to them, so that they might decide whether that pouring of sand was to be regarded as baptism for the brother or not.

Some said [Col. 0209A] that it ought to be regarded as baptism because of the unprecedented greatness of the miracle; others, however, said no.

For the theologian Gregory counts all the baptisms (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 39, which is *On the Holy Lights*):

> “Moses baptized,” he says, “but in water, and previously in the cloud, and in the sea. John also baptized—not indeed in the Jewish manner, for not in water alone, but also in repentance. Jesus too baptizes, but in the Holy Spirit. This is perfection. I know also a fourth baptism, by martyrdom and blood. I know a fifth as well, namely, that of tears.”

Thus, they said, by which of these was this man baptized, so that we might also confirm his baptism—especially since the Lord says to Nicodemus: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God” (John [Col. 0209B] 3)?

Others contradicted them as follows:

“What then? Since it is not written of the apostles that they were baptized, do they therefore not enter the kingdom of God?”

Still others, on the contrary, argued, saying:

“Indeed they were baptized, just as Clement of Alexandria recalls in the fifth book of the *Hypotyposeis* [Note: [Col. 0209] Clement of Alexandria, Book V of the *Hypotyposeis*, is no longer extant. See Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 3, from Evodius; Baronius, volume I, year of Christ 31]. For, explaining that apostolic saying in which it is written, ‘I give thanks to God that I baptized none of you’ (1 Corinthians 1), he says that Christ is said to have baptized Peter alone; Peter baptized Andrew, James, and John; and they baptized the rest.”

When these and many other things had been said, it seemed good to the blessed Dionysius to send that brother to the holy Jordan, where he was to be baptized. As for the industrious man, he ordained him deacon.

### CHAPTER CLXXVII. The evil death of an Egyptian monk who wished to live in the cell of the heretic Evagrius

[Col. 0209C]

916 Abbot John the Cilician said to us while we were staying at the Ninth district of Alexandria:

An Egyptian monk came to us and told us this:

“A brother from a distant region arrived at the monastery of the Cells, wishing to live there. He prostrated himself before the presbyter and begged to stay in Evagrius’s cell.

“The presbyter said that he could not live there. As the presbyter was departing, he said to the brother:

“‘My son, a most savage demon lives there—the one who deceived Evagrius, removed him from the true faith, and implanted wicked doctrines in him. That demon does not allow anyone to stay there.’

“But the brother persisted, saying:

“‘Certainly, if I remain here, I shall remain in that cell.’

“Then the presbyter, compelled, said to him:

“‘Go according to your own judgment and take it.’

“The brother therefore stayed in the cell for a week. When Sunday came, he went to the holy church. The presbyter, seeing him, was comforted, for he had been concerned about him.

“When another Sunday came, he did not come to the church. Since the presbyter did not see him, he sent two brothers to find out why he had not come to church. They came to the cell and found that the brother had hanged and strangled himself with a rope.”

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII. The life of an unassuming elder of the coenobium of the Scholarii

Abbot Gregory, presbyter of the coenobium of the Scholarii, told us that a great elder of very great ascetic discipline had lived there. He was simple concerning the faith, [Col. 0210A] and wherever he happened to be, he communicated indiscriminately.

One day an angel of God appeared and said:

“Tell me, elder: if you die, how do you wish us to bury you—as the Egyptian monks do, or as the Jerusalemites?”

The elder answered him:

“I do not know.”

Then the angel said:

“Consider and decide. After three weeks I shall come, and you will tell me.”

The elder went to another elder and told him what the angel had said to him. When that elder heard it, he was astonished. After looking at him intently for a long time, and being divinely inspired, he said to him:

“Where do you receive the holy mysteries?”

He replied:

“Wherever I find them.”

Then the elder said to him:

“May it never again happen that you communicate outside the holy catholic and apostolic Church, where the four holy councils are named: the Council of Nicaea, of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers; the Council of Constantinople, of the one hundred and fifty; the First Council of Ephesus, of the two hundred; and the Council of Chalcedon, of the six hundred and thirty.

“When the angel comes, say to him: ‘I wish to be buried as the Jerusalemites are.’”

After three weeks, therefore, the angel came and said to the elder:

“What is it, elder? Have you decided?”

The elder said to him:

“I wish to be buried as the Jerusalemites are.”

The angel said to him:

“Good, good.”

And immediately he gave up his spirit.

All this happened so that he would not lose his labors and be condemned together with the heretics.

### CHAPTER CLXXIX. The life of a devout woman who came from the holy city

We went to Abbot John the anchorite, who was called Rutilus, and he told us this. He said:

“I heard Abbot John the Moabite telling the following:
