“‘There was a certain devout woman in the holy city, very religious and making progress according to God. The devil envied the virgin and instilled in a certain young man an impure and devilish love for her.

“When that remarkable virgin perceived the devil’s snares, she pitied the young man’s destruction. Taking one hair shirt and a few soaked provisions, she went into the desert, thereby preparing quiet from temptation and salvation for the young man through her withdrawal, and security and an increase of merit for herself through solitude.

“After a long time, by God’s providence, lest her excellent way of life remain unknown, an anchorite saw her in the wilderness of the Jordan and said to her:

“‘What are you doing in this desert, mother?’

“Wishing to conceal herself from the anchorite, she said to him:

“‘Forgive me, for I have lost my way. But, by the Lord, Father, show me charity and point it out to me.’

“Having been divinely informed about her, he said to her:

“‘Believe me, mother: you have not lost your way, nor are you seeking the road. Therefore, knowing that lying is from the devil (John 8), tell me the truth about the reason for which you have come here.’

“Then the virgin said to him:

“‘Forgive me, abba. A certain young man was scandalized because of me, and for that reason I came into this desert, thinking it better to die here than to become an occasion of offense to anyone, according to the Apostle’s saying (2 Corinthians 6).’

“Again the elder said to her:

“‘How long have you been here?’

“She answered him:

“‘By the grace of Christ, I have been here seventeen years.’

“Again the anchorite said to her:

“‘And how do you nourish yourself?’ [Col. 0211A]

“She, bringing out the hair shirt and the soaked provisions [Note: [Col. 0242D] Soaked provisions. It is difficult to determine what these soaked provisions were. Various foods can be soaked and softened. Above, it says, “a few soaked provisions.” In Theodoret above, there is sometimes “a lentil softened in water.” Below, in chapter 184: “He soaked the *paximatia*, or softened them.”], said to the anchorite:

“‘Behold this hair shirt, which you see. It left the city with me, together with these few soaked provisions. God has shown such providence toward me, humble as I am, that I have been nourished by these things for so long, and they have not diminished.

“‘Know this also, Father: his goodness so protected me that during these seventeen years no man has seen me except you today, whereas I have seen everyone.’

“When the anchorite heard this, he glorified God greatly.”

### CHAPTER CLXXX. The life of John [Note: [Col. 0242D] John. This story is cited in the seventh ecumenical council, which is the Second Council of Nicaea, session 5, where *Araphas* is given instead of *Saraphas.] the anchorite who lived in a cave near the village of Sochus

The most holy Dionysius, presbyter of the holy church of the Ascalonites and custodian of the sacred vessels, told us about Abbot John the anchorite, saying:

“He was truly great in this generation. To commend the greatness of his merits before God, he told this miracle about him:

“An elder lived in a cave in the region of a village called Sochus, about twenty miles from Jerusalem. In the cave the elder had an image of our spotless Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, carrying in her arms Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior.

“Whenever he wished to go somewhere—whether through the vast wilderness, or to Jerusalem to worship the holy cross and the venerable places, or to Mount Sinai for the sake of prayer, or to martyrs far distant from Jerusalem by long and considerable intervals—for the elder was extraordinarily devoted to the martyrs—sometimes he went to Ephesus to Saint John, sometimes to Euchaita to Saint Theodore, sometimes to Saint Thecla at Seleucia in Isauria, sometimes to Saint Sergius at Saraphas, and now to one saint, now to another.

“He would trim the lamp and light it, as was his custom, and, standing for prayer and beseeching God to direct his journey, would say to the Lady while gazing at her image:

“‘Our holy Lady, Mother of God, since I am about to undertake a long journey, to be completed over many days, take care of your lamp and preserve it, according to my intention, so that it may not go out. For, with your help accompanying me, I am undertaking the journey.’

“Having said this to the image, he would depart. When he had completed his intended journey, he would return—sometimes after a month, often after two or three months, and occasionally after five or six months—and would find the lamp intact and burning, just as he had left it when he began the journey. He never saw it go out by itself, whether he rose from sleep, returned from his pilgrimage, or went from the desert to the cave.”

### CHAPTER CLXXXI. The same subject

The same venerable Dionysius the presbyter also told us this about him:

“One day the elder was walking within the boundaries of the village of Sochus, where his cave was. As he walked, he saw a huge lion approaching from the opposite direction.

“He was proceeding along a very narrow path situated between two hedges, with which farmers customarily enclose their fields by planting thorny bushes. The path was so narrowed by the thorns that it could scarcely accommodate one person walking freely, and it would not even allow him to pass without obstruction.

“When the elder and the lion had approached one another, the elder did not turn back to give the lion free passage; nor could the lion retreat because of the excessive narrowness of the path; nor was it at all possible for both to pass at once.

“When the lion saw the servant of God wishing to proceed and by no means willing to turn back, it rose on its hind legs. Standing upright to the elder’s left, it pushed back the hedge with the weight and strength of its body, making a little room for the elder and providing the righteous man a passage without obstruction. The elder then passed, rubbing the lion’s back. After he had passed, the lion rose from the hedge and continued on its own way.”

A certain brother went to this Abbot John. When he found nothing in his cave, he said to the elder:

“How do you live here, Father, having none of the necessities?”

The elder replied:

“This cave, my son, is a place of spiritual commerce: it gives and receives.”

### CHAPTER CLXXXII. The life of Abbot Alexander the Cilician, who was seized by a demon near death

Near holy Bethlehem there is the monastery of Saint Sergius, about two miles away, called Xeropotamus. Its abbot was a very devout man named Eugenius, who later became bishop of Hermopolis in Egypt, which is situated in the region [Col. 0212C] of the Thebaid.

When we came to him, he told us about Abbot Alexander the Cilician. After he had grown old among the caves of the holy Jordan, Eugenius received him into his monastery. Near the end of his life, Alexander lay on a bed for about three months. Ten days before he departed to the Lord, he was seized by a demon.

The elder began to say to the demon:

“Wretch, you have come at evening; this is no great thing, since I am bound to my bed and cannot move. You have shown, most miserable one, your weakness. For if you were powerful and strong, you ought to have approached me fifty or sixty years ago. I, through Christ who strengthens me, would have shown you your weakness, cast down your roar, and crushed that rigid and unbending neck of yours.

“Now, however, it is not my weakness, but an illness that oppresses me. Nevertheless, I give thanks to God, to whom I am departing, and to whom I shall make known the injury I have suffered from you, because after so many years of labor and exhaustion, near the end you have attacked me so savagely.”

Saying these and many other things at every hour, on the tenth day he gave up his spirit in peace to the Lord Christ.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIII. The marvelous deed of an Egyptian elder named David

Abbot Theodore the Cilician said:

“When I was still living in Scetis, there was there an Egyptian elder named David, who one day went out to reap. The people of Scetis have the custom of going to the villages and reaping.

“The elder therefore went up to a village and worked for wages. A certain farmer hired him. While the elder was reaping, one day around the seventh hour a great heat arose. The elder went into a hut and sat down.

“The farmer came and, seeing the elder sitting, said to him angrily:

“‘Why are you not reaping, elder? Do you not know that I am paying you wages?’

“He said to him:

“‘Certainly; but because the heat is great and the grains of wheat are falling from the ears, I am waiting a little until the heat passes, so that you do not suffer loss.’

“The farmer said to him:

“‘Rise, work, and let everything burn.’

“The elder replied:

“‘And do you wish it to burn?’

“The farmer said angrily:

“‘Indeed I do.’

“Then the elder arose, and immediately the field began to burn.

“The farmer ran to the other elders who were working in another part of the field and begged them to come and entreat the elder to pray and extinguish the fire.

“The elders came and prostrated themselves on the ground. But he said to them:

“‘He himself said that it should burn.’

“Nevertheless, he was persuaded by them. He went and stood between what had burned and what had not burned, prayed, and immediately the fire was extinguished, while the remaining part of the field was saved.”

### CHAPTER CLXXXIV. The life of Abbot John the Eunuch, and also of a young monk who had resolved never to drink, and of another elder greatly devoted to prayer

We were at the Ninth district of Alexandria when, for the sake of instruction, we visited the monastery of Abbot John the Eunuch. We found the elder himself, who had spent eighty years in the monastic habit, so merciful that we had never seen anyone like him. He was merciful not only toward human beings but also toward brute animals.

What, then, did the elder do? He had no other work than this: rising in the morning, he went to all the dogs in the monastery and gave them food. Likewise, he put flour before the little ants and wheat before the larger ants. He also soaked *paximatia* and threw them onto the roofs for the birds to eat.

Living continually in this way, when he died he left nothing in his monastery—not a door, not a window, not a *spetlum* [Note: [Col. 0242D] *Spetlum*. I have restored from the Greek text the word σπέτλον, which the translator omitted. It appears to mean a window, from *speculari lapide* (“window stone”). See the *Onomasticon*.], not a lamp, not a table; and, not to prolong the account by dwelling on each item, he left behind absolutely nothing earthly.

He never kept for even one hour a book, money, or clothing, but gave everything to the needy, transferring all his care to the things to come.

[Col. 0213D] They also told this about him, wishing to commend his mercy and compassion.

One day a certain farmer came to him and asked him to lend him a gold coin. Since the elder did not have one—for he never possessed gold—he immediately went and borrowed a coin from the monastery, giving it to the man who had requested it, who promised to return it to him after one month.

When two years had passed and the farmer had not returned it, Abbot John summoned him and said:

“Give me the coin, brother.”

The man said:

“God knows that I do not have it.”

Then the elder said to him:

“Understand, brother, that I have found a way for you to be able to repay it.”

The man said [Col. 0214A] to the elder:

“Command whatever you wish, and I shall do it,”

thinking that the elder intended to impose some task on him.

Then Abbot John said:

“When you have free time and have nothing to do, come here, make thirty genuflections for me, and I will give you one silver coin.”

He gladly agreed. Whenever he was free from work, he went to the elder, and after completing the appointed number of prayers, the elder gave him a silver coin as agreed. He also gave him food and drink, and additionally provided *paximatia* for his entire household.

When he had thus accumulated twenty-four silver coins—that is, the value of the gold coin—the elder accepted them from him and dismissed him, giving him blessings as well.

The same Abbot John the Eunuch told us this:

“We went up into the Thebaid to the coenobium of Abbot Apollo, and there we saw a younger brother who also had a natural father, himself a monk.

“The young man resolved never to drink water, wine, or any other beverage throughout his life. He ate certain edible vegetables that could refresh him from thirst. He also had the duty of baking bread.

“When he had continued this manner of abstinence for three years, he fell into a very serious illness, from which he also died. While he was burning with fever and tormented by immense thirst, everyone urged him to taste at least a little drink, but that brother absolutely refused to do so.

“The abbot therefore summoned a physician and begged him to help the sick man, if he could, by whatever means. When the physician came and saw the brother in such a condition, he began to ask him to take a little of some beverage.

“But when he would not agree, the physician said to the abbot:

“‘Bring me a large vessel.’

“When it had been brought, he poured four jars of tepid water into it and had the brother placed inside up to his thighs for one hour.

“Abbot John—who was present there—assured us that when they took him out of the water, the physician measured the water and found that a large part of it had diminished.

“Behold what strength the monks who practice abstinence exerted upon themselves, subjecting themselves to such necessities for God’s sake, so that they might enjoy eternal goods.”

He told us again:

“I entered the cell of a certain elder in the same coenobium and saw that, where he used to stand for prayer, a board had been placed underneath. Where he planted his knees and hands, there was a hollow more than four fingers deep, for the board had been worn away by the frequency and practice of continual prayer.”

### CHAPTER CLXXXV. The life of a faithful woman who converted her pagan husband to the faith through marvelous wisdom

When we were on the island of Samos, the venerable Maria, benefactress of the poor and mother of Lord Paul the *candidatus*, told us this:

“When I was in the city of Nisibis, there was a Christian woman there who had a pagan husband. They were poor, but they possessed fifty *miliarisia* [Note: [Col. 0242D] *Miliarisia*. I retained the Greek word μιλιαρίσια, which denotes a certain type of coin. The translator had rendered it simply as ‘coins.’ See the *Onomasticon*.].

“One day the husband said to his wife:

“‘Let us give these coins to a moneylender, so that we may derive some relief from them; for we are consuming them one by one, and they are running out.’

“The good wife replied to her husband:

“‘If you wish to lend them at interest, come, let us lend them at interest to the God of the Christians.’

“Her husband said to her:

“‘And where is the God of the Christians, so that we may lend them to him?’

“She said:

“‘I shall show him to you. If you give them to him, you will not only fail to lose them, but he will pay you interest and return double the principal.’

“He said to her:

“‘Let us go; show him to me, and let us give them to him.’

“She took her husband and led him to the holy church. That church had five large doors. When she had brought him into the portico of the church, she showed him the poor and said:

“‘If you give to these people, the God of the Christians himself receives it, for they all belong to him.’

“He immediately began joyfully distributing the coins to the poor, and they returned to their home.

“After three months, when they were pressed by their need for expenses, the husband said to his wife:

“‘Sister, as I see it, the God of the Christians is not going to give us anything from that debt, and now we are in distress through poverty.’

“The woman answered him:

“‘Certainly he will give it. Go where you gave the coins, and he will display them to you with complete readiness.’

“Hearing this, he ran to the holy church. When he came to the place where he had distributed the coins to the poor and went around the entire church, he saw no one who would repay his debt except the poor themselves, sitting there again.

“As he considered to whom he should say something or from whom he should demand payment, he saw one of the coins he had distributed to the poor lying on the marble before his feet. He bent down, picked it up, went home, and said to his wife:

“‘Behold, I went to the church. Believe me, woman, I did not see the God of the Christians, as you said, and no one gave me anything—except that I saw this coin lying there, where I had earlier distributed them.’

“Then that marvelous woman said to him:

“‘He is the one who invisibly provided this for you. By the invisible power of his hand he orders this world. But go, my lord, buy something for us to eat today, and he himself will provide for us again.’

“He went and bought bread, wine, and a fish, and, coming home, gave them to his wife. She took the fish and began to clean it. When she eviscerated it, she found in its entrails a very remarkable stone, so beautiful that the woman marveled at it; she did not know what it was.

“She kept it and showed it to her returning husband, saying:

“‘Behold, I found this stone in the fish.’

“He too, seeing it, marveled at its beauty, but he did not know what it was.

“When he had eaten, he said to his wife:

“‘Give me the stone, so that I may go and sell it, if perhaps I can obtain some price for it.’

“For, as I said, he himself did not know what it was, being simple and inexperienced.

“He took the stone and went to a moneychanger, whose business it was to buy and sell such things. He found him already leaving, with everything closed—for it was already evening—and said to him:

“‘Do you wish to buy this stone?’

“The moneychanger examined the stone and said to him:

“‘What do you want me to pay you for it?’

“He replied:

“‘Give whatever you wish.’

“The moneychanger said to him:

“‘Take five coins.’

“Thinking that the seller was making fun of him, the man said:

“‘And do you really wish to pay so much for it?’

“The moneychanger, supposing that he was speaking ironically, said to him:

“‘Take ten coins for it.’

“Believing again that he was being mocked, the seller was silent.

“The moneychanger said to him:

“‘Take twenty coins.’

“But he remained silent and answered nothing. When the buyer increased his offer to thirty, forty, and fifty coins, and swore that he would give that amount, the seller began to value the stone more highly.

“Gradually the buyer increased his offer until he reached three hundred coins, which he gave to the seller. The latter therefore handed over the stone, accepted the money, and came joyfully to his wife.

“When she saw him rejoicing, she said:

“‘For how much did you sell it?’

“She supposed that he had sold it for five or ten small coins (*minutis*).

“Then he brought out the three hundred coins and gave them to his wife, saying that he had sold it for that amount. Astonished at the greatness of divine goodness and mercy, she said to him:

“‘Behold what the God of the Christians is like—how good, gracious, and rich! You see that he has not merely returned to you the fifty coins that you lent him, but within a few days he has restored them to you sixfold.

“‘Recognize, therefore, that there is no other God, either on earth or in heaven, except him alone.’

“Having been instructed by the miracle, and having himself learned the truth through experience, he suddenly became a Christian. He glorified God and our Savior Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and gave very great thanks to his exceedingly prudent wife, through whom the true knowledge of God had truly been granted to him.”

### CHAPTER CLXXXVI. The life of Moschus, a merchant of Tyre

We went to the coenobium of the cave of Abbot Sabas, to Eustachius, the abbot and superior of that coenobium. He told us this:

“There was a certain merchant of Tyre named Moschus. When we came to Tyre, he recounted the following to us:

“‘While I was engaged in commerce, late in the evening I went to bathe and found a woman standing in the darkness along the road. When I approached her, she agreed to follow me.

“‘Because of my devilish pleasure, I did not bathe but hurried to supper. I urged her repeatedly to eat, but she would not taste anything. At last we rose, and when we had come to bed and I wished to embrace her, she cried out in a loud voice with tears:

“‘“Woe to me, wretched woman!”

“‘Terrified, I asked the reason for her tears. Wailing even more, she said:

“‘“My husband is a merchant. He suffered shipwreck, lost both his own property and that of others, and for that reason has been imprisoned. I have no means by which even to provide him with bread. Therefore, in my extreme poverty, I resolved to expose my body so that I might find bread for him, since everything has been lost.”

“‘I said to her:

“‘“How much is the debt?”

“‘She replied:

“‘“Five pounds of gold.”

“‘I brought out the gold and gave it to her, saying:

“‘“Behold, by God’s will I have not touched you. Take the gold, redeem your husband, and pray for me.”

[Col. 0217A] “After some time, a false accusation was brought against me before the emperor—that I had squandered all the goods involved in my commerce. The emperor sent men, who plundered all my property, dragged me naked to Constantinople, and put me in prison.

“‘After I had spent a very long time there, wearing only one garment besides my shirt, one day I heard that the emperor intended to kill me. Despairing of my life, I wept.

“‘As I was weeping and lamenting, sleep overtook me. In a dream I saw what seemed to be that woman who had once had a husband in prison, saying to me:

“‘“What is the matter with you, Lord Moschus? Why are you imprisoned here?”

“‘When I replied, “I have suffered a false accusation, and I think the emperor will kill me,” she said to me:

“‘“Do you wish me to speak to the emperor on your behalf, and he will release you?”

“‘I said to her:

“‘“Does he know you?”

“‘She said:

“‘“Certainly; he knows me.”

“‘When I awoke, I was uncertain what this meant. She appeared to me a second and a third time, repeating the same things and saying:

“‘“Do not be afraid. Tomorrow I shall set you free.”

“‘At dawn, by order of the emperor, they brought me to the palace. When I entered, he looked at me wearing a filthy and torn tunic and said:

“‘“See: I have now taken pity on you. Go, and reform your conduct henceforth.”

“‘I saw that woman standing at the emperor’s right hand, saying to me:

“‘“Take courage and do not be afraid.”

“‘The emperor ordered all my possessions to be restored to me, added many further goods, restored me to my former position, and moreover made me a deputy (locum tenens).

[Col. 0217C] “‘That very night the same woman appeared to me again and said:

“‘“Do you know who I am? I am the woman toward whom you showed mercy and whose body you did not touch for God’s sake. Behold, I too have delivered you from danger.

“‘“Do you see God’s mercy, how through me, toward whom you showed mercy, the Merciful One appeared to you, as though saying: ‘You did this for my sake, and I have magnified my mercy toward you’?”’”

### CHAPTER CLXXXVII. The teaching of Abbot John of Cyzicus on acquiring the virtues

As we were going up from holy Gethsemane to the holy Mount of Olives, we came upon the monastery of Abbot Abramius. The father of this monastery was Abbot John of Cyzicus.

One day we questioned him, saying:

“How does someone acquire virtue?”

The elder replied:

“Whoever wishes to possess virtue cannot acquire and possess it unless he first hates the vice that is diametrically opposed to virtue.

“If, therefore, you wish to have mourning, always hate laughter.

“If you desire humility, always abhor pride.

“If you wish to be temperate, hate gluttony.

“If you wish to be chaste, detest lust.

“If you wish to be naked, flee material possessions.

“Whoever wishes to be merciful must beware of greed.

“Whoever desires to live in the desert must hate the crowds of the city.

“Whoever wishes to find quiet must hate confidence.

“Whoever wishes to be a pilgrim must hate display [Note: [Col. 0243A] *Display*. In Greek, φανητία, that is, the desire to show oneself off.]—that is, the desire to exhibit himself.

“Whoever desires to restrain anger must avoid the company of many people.

“Whoever wishes to forget injuries must detest insults.

“Whoever longs to be without distraction must remain alone.

“Whoever wishes to restrain his tongue must close his ears so that he may not hear much.

“Whoever always desires to possess the fear of God must hate bodily repose and love affliction and distress.”

### CHAPTER CLXXXVIII. The life of two Syrian brothers who were moneychangers
Abbot Theodore, superior of an ancient monastery, told us:

There were two Syrian brothers in Constantinople who were bankers. The elder said to the younger: “Come, let us go down to Syria and take possession of our ancestral house.” The younger replied: “Why should we both abandon our ministry here? You go down, and I shall remain here; or I shall go down, and you remain here.” They therefore agreed that the younger should go down.

When he had departed, after a short time the one who had remained in Constantinople saw in a dream a handsome and most venerable old man saying to him: “Do you know that your brother has fornicated with the tavernkeeper’s wife?” Rising from sleep, he began to grieve and say to himself: “I was the cause of his fall. Why did I leave him alone?” Then he saw the same man a second time saying to him: “Do you know that your brother has fallen with the tavernkeeper’s wife?” At this he was again saddened. A third time he saw the same man saying to him: “Do you not know that your brother has ruined a free woman and has given himself to the tavernkeeper’s wife?”

He therefore wrote to him from Constantinople, telling him to leave everything immediately and come to Byzantium. When the brother received his letter, he at once abandoned everything and came to his brother. As soon as the elder saw him, he led him into the principal church and began sadly to reproach him, saying: “Well done, brother: you have committed adultery with the tavernkeeper’s wife?”

When the younger heard this, he began to swear by almighty God that he had neither committed adultery nor known any woman except his lawful wife. When the elder brother heard this, he said to him: “Have you committed some other and more serious sin?” The younger insisted, saying: “Truly, I am conscious of having committed no wrongdoing, except that I found monks of the Severian sect in our village and, not knowing whether it was evil, communicated with them. I do not know that I have done anything else.”

Then the elder brother understood that this was what had been signified to him: namely, that his brother had fornic­ated because, abandoning the holy catholic and apostolic Church, he had fallen into the heresy of Severus the Acephalian—who is truly a tavernkeeper—and, in his confusion, had defiled the nobility of the true faith.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIX. The Life of a Woman Who Kept Faith with Her Merchant Husband, and How Both Were Helped by God

We came to Ascalon, to the Fathers’ hospice, and Abbot Eusebius the presbyter told us that a certain merchant, while sailing, had lost everything belonging both to himself and to others, although he himself had escaped the shipwreck. When he came here, his creditors seized him and threw him into prison; everything he had at home was confiscated, including his wife’s clothing.

Because of her great anxiety, grief, and poverty, she could not even feed her husband. One day, while she was sitting in the prison and lamenting, a certain eminent man entered to distribute alms to the prisoners. Seeing the free woman sitting with her husband, he was wounded by love for her—for she was exceedingly beautiful—and sent word through the jailer that she should come to him. Seeing that she was going to receive an agape, she went willingly.

Taking her aside, he said to her: “What has happened to you, and why are you here?” She related everything to him. He then said: “If I pay the debt, will you sleep with me this night?”

But she, truly most beautiful and most chaste [922], said to him: “I have heard, lord, the Apostle say that a woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does (1 Cor. 7). Permit me, therefore, lord, to ask my husband, and whatever he commands I shall do.”

She came and reported everything to her husband. He, being most prudent and deeply devoted to his wife, was not carried away by the hope and desire of escaping the hardships of prison. Rather, sighing with tears, he said to his wife: “Go, go, sister; reject the man. For I hope in our Lord Jesus Christ that he will not abandon us to the end.”

She rose and dismissed the man, saying: “I told my husband, and he does not consent.”

Meanwhile, a certain thief had been thrown into that same prison before the merchant was confined. He observed everything and heard the words of the man and woman. He groaned within himself, saying:

“See the circumstances in which these people find themselves, and yet they did not betray their freedom in order to receive money and be released. They valued chastity more highly than money, and they despised the advantages of this life rather than violate her beauty. But what shall I do, wretched man that I am? I never considered that God existed, and for that reason I have been the author of murders.”

Calling them to himself through the window of the cell in which he was confined, he said to them: “I am a thief and a perpetrator of killings; therefore, whenever the governor comes, I shall be led to death as a murderer. But when I considered your chaste resolve, I was moved to repentance. Go, then, and dig in that place in the city, and take whatever money you find there. When you have paid the debt, many blessings will still remain for you. Pray for me, that I too may find mercy.”

After a few days, the governor entered the city and ordered the thief to be brought out and beheaded. The next day the woman said to her husband: “If you command me, my lord, I shall go to the place indicated by the thief, in case what he said is true.”

He replied: “Do as you think best.”

Taking a small hoe, she went in the evening to the place. As she dug, she found a pot carefully covered; she took it and departed. Acting prudently, she gradually repaid the creditors, so that they would think she had borrowed money from others. She completed the repayment of the entire debt and brought her husband out of prison.

The narrator said: “See how, because these people kept the commandment of our Lord Jesus Christ, he himself magnified his mercy in them.”

## CHAPTER CXC. The Miracle of the Wood Given to Abbot Brocha the Egyptian

Athanasius of Antioch told us about the Egyptian Abbot Brocha:

When that man came from Egypt to Seleucia, which is near Antioch, he found a deserted place outside the city and sought to build a small cell there for himself. After he had built it, since he had no means of roofing it, he entered the city one day and found Anatolius, surnamed the Hunchback, one of the leading men of Seleucia and Antioch, sitting outside the threshold of his house. He said to him: “Do me a kindness, lord, and give me a little wood with which to roof my cell.”

But Anatolius, greatly angered, said to him: “There is wood—take it and go away.” He pointed to a very large beam lying before his house, from which a mast for a cargo ship of fifty thousand [units] could have been made.

Abbot Brocha said to him: “Bless it, and I shall take it.”

Anatolius, still irritated, said to him again: “The Lord be blessed.”

Brocha seized the beam, lifted it alone from the ground, placed it upon his shoulders, and carried it to his cell. Anatolius was struck with astonishment at what had happened, an extraordinary and splendid miracle. He gave him the wood, from which Brocha not only roofed his cell, as he had requested, but also carried out many other works.

## CHAPTER CXCI. A Brief Life of Saint John Chrysostom, Patriarch of Constantinople

[Col. 0220C]

They said of Saint John, archbishop of Constantinople, who was justly and most worthily called Chrysostom—“Golden-Mouthed”—because of the purity of his doctrine and the brilliance of his exceedingly beautiful eloquence:

From the time he received saving baptism, he never swore at all, never compelled anyone to swear, never lied, never cursed anyone, never spoke obscenely, and never permitted frivolous joking.

[Note: “Chrysostom.” Henry Savilius, in his notes to volume VIII of the Greek Chrysostom edited by him, considers it worthy of notice that the surname Chrysostom was unknown between the Fifth Council, held in 553, and the Sixth, held in 680—the period in which, he says, George, the author of the Life of Chrysostom, probably lived. But John Moschus, or Sophronius, refutes him here: they lived at the time of that George and mention Chrysostom by this surname.]

## CHAPTER CXCII. The Account of a Certain Monk of the Monastery of Saint Gregory, the Pope, and How He Was Released from Excommunication after Death

[Note: “Gregory.” This account is found in the Life of Saint Gregory, book II, chapter 45, written by John the Deacon, who cites it from a book called by the Greeks *Leimōn* (Λειμών), and understood by the Latins as *Campus* or *Pratum*—“Field” or “Meadow.” This is the very book that we have before us. He cites it from the translation of his teacher, where the reading here is “I do not have a tunic,” but he renders it, “I do not have a cloak.” Likewise, in book IV, chapter 63: “And he ordered a cloak to be given to me, together with all my necessities.” Here our translator, Ambrose of Camaldoli, in chapter 181, abbreviates this as: “Ordering whatever was necessary to be given to me.” For he omitted the reference to the cloak or tunic.]

A certain holy presbyter named Peter, coming from the city of Rome, told us about the most blessed Gregory, bishop of that same city. When Gregory was supreme pontiff, he built a very large monastery for men and ordered that none of the monks should possess anything of his own—not even a single obol.

A monk of the monastery had a brother living in the world, from whom he asked: “I do not have a tunic. Therefore, do me a kindness and buy one for me.”

His secular brother said to him: “Here are these three coins; take them and use me as you please.” The monk took the three coins and kept them with him. When another monk saw this, he went and reported it to the abbot. Upon hearing it, the abbot reported it in turn to the most holy Pope Gregory.

Blessed Gregory, hearing this, ordered that the monk, because he had transgressed the rules of the monastery, be separated from communion. After a short time, that brother died while still separated, without Pope Gregory’s knowledge.

Two or three days later the abbot went and reported it to him, saying: “That brother has died.” When Gregory heard this, he was deeply saddened that the man had departed from the world before being released from the bond of excommunication. He wrote a prayer in the form of a letter and gave it to one of the archdeacons, ordering him to go and read it over the brother’s grave. Through that letter he released the dead man from the bonds of excommunication.

The archdeacon went, as he had been ordered, and read the short document over the brother’s grave. That same night the abbot saw the deceased brother and said to him: “Are you not dead, brother?”

He replied: “Indeed I am.”

The abbot again asked him: “Where have you been until today?”

The brother said to him: “Truly, lord, I was in prison until yesterday; yesterday, however, I was released.”

It became known to everyone that at the very hour when the archdeacon had read the words of absolution over the brother, he had been released from excommunication, and his soul had been freed from judgment and condemnation.

## CHAPTER CXCIII. The Remarkable Act of Charity of Saint Abbot Apollinaris, Patriarch of Alexandria, toward a Rich Young Man Reduced to Poverty

They told us about Saint Abbot Apollinaris, patriarch of Alexandria, that he was exceedingly merciful and rich in the depths of compassion. They offered the following as evidence of this.

There was, they said, in Alexandria a certain young man who had been the son of one of the city’s leading and most illustrious wealthy men. When his parents died, leaving him immense possessions both in gold and in maritime commerce, he did not manage them with sufficient good fortune or success. He lost everything and was reduced to the utmost poverty—not because he had devoted himself to gluttony or debauchery, which commonly exhaust the estates of the rich, but because he fell into various misfortunes and shipwrecks.

Thus, from being exceedingly wealthy he became exceedingly poor, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “They rise up to the heavens, and they go down to the depths” (Ps. 106). For the higher the young man had been raised by his wealth, the lower he became through poverty.

When blessed Apollinaris heard this and saw how deeply the young man had fallen into misery and poverty, although his parents had been exceedingly rich, he pitied his misfortune and wished to show him a small kindness by supplying him with food, but he was embarrassed to do so. Whenever he saw him, he was inwardly distressed, observing his filthy clothing and sallow face, signs of extreme poverty.

While the bishop was troubled by such concerns, one day, divinely inspired, he found a truly remarkable plan, one entirely suited to his holiness.

He therefore summoned the *Nomikos* [Note: “Nomikos,” or steward. The Greek term *Nomikos* (Νομικός), as it appears here in the Greek text, has several meanings. Here it signifies a steward. See the *Onomasticon*.], or steward, of the most holy church. Taking him aside, he said: “Can you keep a secret for me, lord steward?”

He replied: “I hope in the Son of God that whatever you command me I shall tell no one, and that no one will ever learn from me what you reveal to me, your servant.”

Then Bishop Apollinaris said to him: “Go, draw up a bond for a debt of fifty pounds of gold that this most holy church owed to Macarius, the father of that wretched young man. Add witnesses, a stipulation, and ratification, and bring it to me.”

The steward immediately carried out what the bishop had ordered with complete haste. He brought the bond and gave it to him.

Since the young man’s father had died ten years earlier and the document appeared new, the bishop said to him: “Go, lord steward, hide this bond either in wheat or in barley, and bring it back to me after a few days.”

When he had done so, on the appointed day he returned the bond as though it were somewhat weathered and old, and gave it to the bishop.

Then the bishop said: “Now go, lord steward, and say to the young man: ‘What will you give me if I give you a bond for a large sum of money owed to you?’ Take care not to accept more than three coins from him, and give him the bond.”

The steward replied: “Truly, my lord, if you command it, I shall accept nothing.”

The bishop said to him: “I absolutely want you to accept three coins.”

The steward went to the young man as he had been ordered and said to him: “Will you give me three coins if I show you something of great advantage to you?”

The young man promised that he would give him whatever he wished.

The steward then pretended and said to him: “Five or six days ago, while going through the church’s documents, I found this bond. I remembered that your father Macarius, placing great confidence in me, entrusted it to me for several days. After his death it happened to remain with me until today; it had slipped from my memory, and it never occurred to me to return it to you.”

The young man said to him: “Do you know whether the person who owes the money is wealthy?”

The steward replied: “Indeed, he is wealthy and well disposed, and you can recover the debt from him without difficulty.”

The young man said to him: “God knows that I now possess nothing. But if I recover what is mine, I shall give you whatever you have asked—and more than three coins.”

Then the steward gave him the document for fifty pounds of gold.

Having received the bond, the young man went to the most holy bishop. He prostrated himself before him and handed him the document. When the bishop had received and read it, he began to pretend that he was greatly troubled and said to him: “Where have you been until now? Your father died ten years ago. Go away; I do not wish to answer you now.”

The young man replied: “Truly, my lord, I did not have it; the steward had it, and I did not know. But may God have mercy on him, for he has now returned it to me, saying that he found it among his papers at home.”

The bishop dismissed him for the moment, saying: “I shall consider the matter. Leave the bond with me.”

After a week the young man returned to the bishop and again pleaded with him. The bishop, as though unwilling to give him anything, said: “Why did you delay so long before producing the bond?”

The young man replied: “My lord, God knows that I have no means of feeding my household. Therefore, if God inspires you, have mercy on me.”

Then Saint Apollinaris, pretending to yield to his entreaties, said to him: “I shall indeed return the entire sum to you. But this I beg of you, my lord brother: do not demand interest from this holy church.”

The young man fell down before him and said: “Whatever my lord wishes and commands me, I shall do. If it pleases you to reduce something from the principal sum, reduce it.”

The bishop said to him: “Not that; it is enough if you remit the interest owed to us.”

Then he brought out the fifty pounds of gold, gave them to him, and dismissed him, asking him to remit the interest.

Such was the work of the great Apollinaris: such was his holy craft and mercy. God so cooperated with the young man through the saint’s blessing that he emerged from such poverty, returned to his former condition and standing, and even surpassed his parents in wealth and possessions. Moreover, he gained great spiritual profit.

## CHAPTER CXCIV. The Admonition of an Elder Living in Scetis to a Certain Monk Not to Enter Taverns

A certain elder lived in Scetis. One day he came to Alexandria to sell the work of his hands, and there he saw a younger monk enter a tavern. Deeply distressed by this, the elder remained outside waiting to speak with the young man when he came out.

This happened. As soon as the young man emerged, the elder took him by the hands, led him aside, and said to him:

“Do you not know, lord brother, that you bear an angelic habit? Do you not know that you are young? Do you not know that there are many snares laid by our enemies? Do you not know that monks in cities are harmed through their eyes, their ears, and various images and forms of dress?

“Yet you enter taverns without fear, hear what you do not wish to hear, see what is harmful, and associate improperly with men and women. Do not, then, my son—do not, I beg you, act in this way. Flee to the desert, where, with God’s help, you can be saved.”

The young man replied: “Go on, elder. God seeks nothing but a pure heart.”

Then the elder stretched both hands toward heaven and said: “Glory to you, God! Behold, I have been in Scetis for fifty-five years, and I do not have a pure heart; yet this man, who frequents taverns, possesses purity of heart.”

Turning to the brother, he said: “May God preserve you, and may he not put me to shame in my hope.”

## CHAPTER CXCV. The Life of Evagrius the Philosopher, Converted to the Faith of Christ by Synesius, Bishop of Cyrene

When we were in Alexandria, Leontius of Apamea, a religious and most faithful man, came from the Pentapolis. He had lived in Cyrene for many years. He came during the days of Eulogius, the holy patriarch of Alexandria, who was destined to become bishop of that same city of Cyrene.

While we were engaged in familiar conversation, he told us:

“In the time of Theophilus, the most blessed patriarch of Alexandria, Synesius the philosopher was bishop of Cyrene. When he came to Cyrene, he found there a certain philosopher named Evagrius, who had been his companion in liberal studies and his dearest friend, but who was a pagan in religion and exceedingly devoted to the worship of idols.

“Bishop Synesius strove to turn him from idolatry to the worship of Christ, and because of the love he had borne him from the beginning, he took upon himself a great concern for this. But Evagrius would not tolerate it and did not wish to accept his teaching. The bishop, however, overcome by his immense love for him, did not cease, even then, to exhort him every day, instruct him, and persuade him to believe in Christ and receive his sacraments.

“When he persisted in giving him these admonitions daily, the philosopher said to him one day:

“‘Truly, my lord bishop, among the other things I dislike about Christians is this: they say that the end of this world will come; that after its end all human beings who have existed from the beginning of the world will rise again in this body; that they will receive this flesh incorruptible and immortal and will live forever; and that they will thereby receive rewards for what they did in the body.

“‘They also say that the one who shows mercy to the poor lends to God; that the one who distributes among the poor and needy stores up treasures for himself in heaven; and that whatever he gives will be returned to him a hundredfold in the regeneration, together with eternal life from Christ.

“‘When all this is said, it seems to me deception, mockery, and a fable.’”

Bishop Synesius, however, insisted that everything taught by Christians was true and contained nothing false or contrary to truth. He supported this with many proofs and strove to persuade him.

After a long time, when he had persuaded him to become a Christian, he baptized him, his children, and all his household. Not long after his baptism, Evagrius gave the bishop three hundredweights of gold for the use of the poor, saying: “Take this gold, distribute it to the poor, and give me a written acknowledgment in your own hand that Christ will repay it to me in the future age.”

Having received the gold, the bishop promptly wrote the acknowledgment for him, as he requested.

The philosopher lived several years after his baptism and finally fell ill unto death. When he was near death, he said to his sons: “When you prepare my funeral, place this document in my hands and bury me with it.”

When he died, his sons did as he had commanded and buried him with the bond. On the third day after his burial, he appeared by night to Bishop Synesius while he was sleeping and said:

“Come to the tomb where I lie and take your bond. I have received the debt, and it has been paid to me. And so that you may be more certain of this, I have signed it with my own hand.”

The bishop did not know that they had buried the bond with him.

When morning came, he summoned the philosopher’s sons and said: “Did you place anything in the tomb with your father?”

Thinking that he was asking them about money, they replied: “Nothing, lord, except the customary cloths.”

“What, then? Did you perhaps bury any document with him?”

Then they remembered—for they did not know that he was referring to the bond—and said to him: “Indeed, lord. When he was dying, he gave us a certain document and said: ‘When you bury me, place this document in my hands, without anyone knowing.’”

The bishop then told them the dream he had seen that night. Taking them with the clergy and the leading men of the city, he went to the philosopher’s tomb. When it was opened, they found the philosopher lying there, holding in his hands the bond written by the bishop.

They took the document from his hands and opened it. They found that the philosopher had recently added the following in his own hand:

> “I, Evagrius the philosopher, send greetings to you, my most holy lord Synesius the bishop. I have received the debt written in your hand in this document, and it has been paid to me. I have no claim whatsoever against you on account of the gold that I gave you, and through you gave to Christ our God and Savior.”

Those who had gathered, seeing this, were astonished and cried for many hours, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), glorifying God, who works wonders and grants his servants such clear and great evidence of his promises.

The same lord Leontius also affirmed that the acknowledgment, signed by the philosopher’s hand, was preserved to this day and kept in the treasury of the holy church of Cyrene. Whenever a new custodian of the treasury entered office, this document was entrusted to him, together with the other sacred vessels, to be guarded with every diligence; thereafter he was to hand it over intact and inviolate to his successor.

## CHAPTER CXCVI. The Miracle That Happened to the Children of Apamea, Who Recited the Words of the Holy Consecration in Play

[Col. 0225C]

Gregory, governor of the African province, a faithful man who loved monks and the poor and always rejoiced in every good thing, told us:

“In my province”—for he was an Apamean of the Second Province of Syria, from the town called Thorax—“there is a field about forty miles from the city called Gonagus. In this field, or in its vicinity, some boys were tending livestock. As commonly happens with boys, they wished to play according to a childish custom.

“While they were playing, they said to one another: ‘Come, let us celebrate Mass, offer the sacrifice, and receive communion, just as the presbyter always does in the holy church.’

“When everyone agreed, they appointed one of themselves to the office of presbyter and two other boys to serve as ministers. They went to a certain rock—for they were in a plain—and placed bread upon the rock, in the manner of an altar, together with an earthen vessel containing wine.

“They stood there: one in front of the altar, acting in the role of presbyter, and the other two on either side, like ministers. The one acting as presbyter recited the words of the holy offering; the others used the little cloths they had brought as fans and made a breeze.

“The boy acting as presbyter knew the words of the holy offering because it was customary in the church for boys to stand before the sanctuary during Mass and to receive communion immediately after the clergy in the holy and venerable mysteries of Christ our God. Since in some places presbyters were accustomed to pronounce the prayers of the holy sacrifice aloud, the boys had learned them by hearing them repeatedly while standing nearby.

“When they had done everything according to ecclesiastical custom, before they broke the bread and received communion, fire descended from heaven and consumed everything that had been set out. It also burned the entire rock, so that absolutely nothing remained—not of the rock nor of the objects placed upon it.

“When the boys suddenly saw what had happened, they all fell to the ground out of fear and remained there for a long time half-dead, unable either to utter a sound or to rise from the earth.

“When they did not return home at the hour when they were accustomed to come back, but lay terrified on the ground, their parents came out from the village to see why they had not returned at the proper customary time. When they went out, they found all the boys lying on the ground, unable either to recognize anyone or to speak to those addressing them.

“The parents, seeing them half-dead, each took up his own son and carried him home. When they saw the boys remain for so long in such a state of collapse, they were exceedingly astonished. They knew nothing at all of the cause of their stupor and could not discern what had happened. They questioned them repeatedly throughout the day but could receive no answer and could not learn what had befallen them until that day and the entire night had passed.

“Only then did the boys gradually return to their senses and tell their parents everything that had happened and what they had experienced. Their parents, together with all the inhabitants of the place, went out, and the boys showed them the place where these marvelous events had occurred, pointing out certain traces left by the fire that had descended.

“When the people heard what had happened and were warned by these visible signs, they ran to the city and reported everything to the city’s bishop. Struck by the greatness and novelty of the miracle, he hurried there with all the clergy. After seeing the boys, hearing again from them what had happened, and observing the traces of the heavenly fire, he immediately placed all the boys in a monastery. He made the site a very extensive monastery, built a church over the place touched by the fire, and erected a holy altar.

“The most faithful man Gregory himself said that he had seen one of these boys and had known him as a monk of the monastery where the miracle occurred. This truly great, divine, and astonishing miracle, Gregory the venerable man told us had happened in our own time.”

## CHAPTER CXCVII. Ruffinus’s Account of Saint Athanasius and His Fellow Children

Rufinus, who wrote the ecclesiastical history, relates that something similar had happened in an earlier age among children at play. In writing about the childhood of Athanasius, the most holy, the great champion and herald of the truth, bishop of the great city of Alexandria and renowned teacher of the whole world, he explains how his elevation to the episcopate began through divine foreknowledge.

It seems appropriate to recall briefly the man’s early life and to remember what kind of life and character he had as a boy, as we learned from those who lived with him in the closest familiarity (Rufinus, *History*, book I, chapter 14).

At the time when the most holy Alexander presided over the Church of Alexandria after Achillas, in accordance with the prophecy of Saint Peter, archbishop and martyr, who condemned the impious Arius, Alexander was one day looking out to sea from an elevated place. He saw boys playing on the shore, as boys do, imitating the bishop and all the ecclesiastical rites.

When he had watched the boys for some time, he saw them undertake certain greater and more sacred mysteries. Immediately disturbed, he summoned the clergy, showed them what he had observed, and ordered them to go, seize all the boys, and bring them to him.

When they arrived, he asked them what their game had been and what they had done and how they had done it. The boys, being frightened, initially began to deny everything; afterward, however, they explained the entire sequence and confessed that, through Athanasius—whom they had made their bishop—they had baptized certain catechumens.

Alexander then carefully questioned them about who had been baptized, what had been done, how the questions had been asked, and what answers had been given. When he had learned everything from the boy who had conducted the questioning and discovered that they had performed all things according to the rite of our religion, he discussed the matter with the clergy and, as they say, decreed that those who had been consecrated through baptism should not be baptized a second time, since everything had been solemnly performed around them through questions and responses; rather, those things should be completed that priests ordinarily perform.

As for Athanasius and the others whom he had treated as priests and deacons in the ministry, Alexander summoned their parents and, with God as witness, entrusted the boys to the Church, so that they might be brought up there.

After a short time had passed, when Athanasius had been thoroughly instructed by the elementary teacher and sufficiently by the grammarian [Note: “Thoroughly by the elementary teacher and sufficiently by the grammarian.” The *notarius* here is the person who oversees boys as they learn the first elements and form their letters. See the *Onomasticon*.], his parents immediately handed him over to the priest as a trustworthy deposit of God, and he was nourished in the temple like Samuel.

Whenever Alexander, in his old age, went to the bishops, Athanasius followed him, carrying the priestly vestment called in Hebrew the *ephod*.

Athanasius’s struggles against the heretics in the holy Church were so numerous and illustrious that what was written about him seems to have been fulfilled: “I shall show him how much he must suffer for my name.” For the whole world conspired against his persecution; the kings and nations of the earth were stirred up, and kingdoms and armies gathered against him.

He himself fulfilled in deed that divine saying: “Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; though battle rise against me, even then I shall hope” (Ps. 26).

Indeed, such great and remarkable deeds are reported of him that the magnitude of his achievements persuades me to omit nothing, while the multitude of his acts compels me to leave much unsaid. My mind therefore wavers in uncertainty and cannot clearly discern what it ought to record and what it ought to omit. For that reason we shall recall only a few matters relevant to the subject; the rest will be told by fame, which will certainly state them as lesser than the truth, since it can add nothing to the truth.

## CHAPTER CXCVIII. The Reply of Saint Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, Whether Anyone Can Be Baptized without Faith
They once asked the aforesaid holy Athanasius, after he had been appointed bishop of Alexandria, whether anyone could be baptized without faith, according to the rite and preaching of the Christians; or, if someone had been baptized on some other occasion while pretending to believe, what judgment should be formed concerning him, or how God would receive him. He replied:

“I once heard from our elders that, when a plague had occurred and many people were fleeing to baptism through fear of death, an angel appeared to blessed Peter, bishop and martyr, in human form, saying: ‘How long will you keep sending here these little purses, sealed indeed, but utterly empty and void, containing nothing within?’ Thus, as may be inferred from the angel’s words, they had the outward sign of baptism, since they thought they would obtain some benefit if they received baptism, and for that reason were baptized [Note: [Col. 0244A] ‘For that reason they were baptized.’ Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 310, § 13. This evidently signifies that they obtained such a sacrament, but not, as they say, the reality of the sacrament itself—the grace that washes away sins.].”

## CHAPTER CXCIX. Account of a Certain Simple Old Man Who Saw Angels When He Offered the Sacrament

[Col. 0228C] One of the Fathers related that a certain old man, pure and holy, saw angels standing beside him on his right and left whenever he offered the sacrament. This man had received the rite of consecration from heretics; and, being simple and inexperienced in divine doctrines, whenever he offered the sacrament he innocently uttered things that were not in accord with the true faith, unaware that he was being deceived.

By divine providence, therefore, a deacon highly skilled in divine doctrine came to him. It happened that, in the deacon’s presence, the holy old man offered the sacrifice. The deacon said to him: “The words you uttered in offering the sacrifice are not words of the true faith, but of heretics and men of false opinion.”

But the old man, confident because he saw the angels while offering, paid no attention to what the deacon said, but dismissed it. The deacon persisted, saying: “You are mistaken, Abba. The catholic faith does not admit what you are saying, nor does Mother Church.”

When the old man saw the deacon’s steadfastness in reproving him, and while he was looking, as usual, upon the holy angels during the saving offering, he said to them: “This deacon tells me this and that. How does the truth stand?” The angels said to him: “Listen to him, for he speaks the truth and explains these matters correctly.”

The old man said to them: “Why did you not tell me?” The angels replied: “God has ordained that human beings should be corrected by human beings.”

From that time onward he was corrected, giving thanks to God and to the brother.

## CHAPTER CC. How a Patrician Adopted a Young Goldsmith as His Son

[Col. 0229A]

One of the holy Fathers related that a gifted young man went to a goldsmith to learn the craft. While he was diligently learning it, one of the patricians ordered them to make a golden cross adorned with precious stones, so that he might offer it to a church. Since the young man was very gifted, his master assigned this work to him.

The young man began to think within himself and say: “If this man is offering so much money to Christ, why should I not also contribute my wages to this cross, so that Christ may count them for me as the widow’s two small coins?” Thinking, therefore, about the amount of wages he would receive, he borrowed the money [and] put it into the cross.

The patrician came and weighed the cross before the stones were set into it. He found that it weighed more than he had specified, and began angrily threatening and pressuring the young man, as though he had committed fraud and adulterated the gold.

Then the young man said to him: “He who alone searches the secrets of hearts knows that I have done nothing of the kind. But when I saw that you had offered so much money to Christ the Lord, I thought of putting in my wages, so that I too might have a share with you, and so that Christ might receive me, just as He accepted the widow’s two small coins.”

Astounded, the patrician said to the young man: “Is that truly what you thought, my son?” He replied: “Indeed it is.”

The patrician said to him: “Since you thought this way and offered your entire intention to Christ, wishing to have a share with me, behold, from this day I receive you as my son and appoint you my heir.”

He took him with him and made him his heir.

## CHAPTER CCI. Life of a Most Noble Constantinopolitan Whose Dying Father Left the Lord Jesus Christ as His Guardian

One of the Fathers related, saying:

“Once I went up to Constantinople on account of a certain necessity. While I was sitting in a church, a certain layman entered, a man of great distinction and profound faith. When he saw me, he approached and greeted me with every expression of charity. After the greeting he sat beside me and began to ask about matters pertaining to the salvation of the soul.

“When I told him that those who rightly order earthly things are also granted heavenly things, he said: ‘You have spoken well, Father. Truly blessed is the one who places his hope in God and entrusts himself wholly to God.’

“He continued: ‘I was the son of a layman of the highest worldly distinction. My father was deeply devoted to almsgiving and distributed very much to the poor. One day he called me and showed me all his money, saying: “My son, what would you prefer: that I leave you this money, or Christ as your guardian?”

“‘Since I was pleased with what he was doing, I replied that I preferred Christ. “For all these things pass away: they exist today and will not exist tomorrow. Christ, however, remains forever.”

“‘When he heard this, he began distributing everything freely and generously to the poor, so that when he died he left me very little. Having now become poor, I went about humbly, placing my hope in Christ, to whom my father had entrusted me.’

[Col. 0230A] “There was another man, very rich and prominent, who had a wife faithful to Christ and fearing the Lord. They had one only daughter.

“‘She said to her husband: “We have only this daughter, and God has bestowed such abundance upon us. What, then, does she lack? If we seek to give her to some prominent and wealthy man who is not of good character, he will always distress her. Let us seek for her a humble man who fears the Lord, one who will love and cherish her according to God’s will.”

“‘He said to her: “You have spoken rightly. Go, then, to the church, pray most earnestly, and remain there; the first man who enters will be the bridegroom whom the Lord has sent for her.”

“‘She did as her husband had commanded. When she had prayed and was sitting there, I entered first. She sent her servant and immediately summoned me, then began asking me: “Where are you from?”

“‘I replied: “I am from this city; I am the son of such-and-such a man.”

“‘She said to me: “The son of that almsgiver?”

“‘I replied: “Yes, I am his son.”

“‘Then she said to me: “Do you have a wife?”

“‘I replied: “No.”

“‘I told her what my father had said to me and what I had answered him. Glorifying the Lord, she said: “Behold, your good guardian has sent you a wife and money, so that you may use both with the fear of God.”

“She gave me her daughter and her money. I pray that I may follow my father’s way to the end.”

## CHAPTER CCII. The Life of Abiba, Son of a Layman, a Servant of God

[929] One of the Fathers related that a certain layman had a pious and devout son, a virgin accustomed from his earliest years to complete self-restraint, so much so that he no longer drank wine. He desired to live in solitude, but his father wanted to bind him to worldly business, and could not do so, for the young man would not tolerate it.

He had other brothers, but he was the eldest of them all. Since his way of life was utterly contrary to his father’s wishes, his father constantly rebuked him, reproaching him for this very abstinence and saying: “Why are you not like your brothers, and why do you not devote yourself to business?”

The young man endured this in silence. Everyone loved him because of his devotion and modesty.

When his father was about to die, certain members of his family and others who were extremely fond of Abiba—for that was the son’s name—thinking that his father hated him because of his constant reproaches, gathered together and said: “Perhaps his father will deprive the servant of God of his inheritance. Let us plead with him on his behalf.” For the father was very rich.

They went to him and said: “We have come to ask you for something.”

He said to them: “What do you wish to ask of me?”

They replied: “We plead on behalf of our lord Abiba: do not neglect him.”

Then the father said: “You are asking me on his behalf?”

They answered: “Indeed.”

He said: “Call him here.”

They thought that, as usual, he intended to rebuke him. When Abiba entered, his father said to him: “Come near me.”

When he had approached, the father grasped his feet, weeping and saying: “Forgive me, my son, and pray to God that He may not hold it against me that I afflicted you. You were seeking Christ, while I was moved by worldly considerations.”

Then he called his other sons and said to them: “This man is your lord and father. Whatever he tells you, do it; and whatever he wishes you to have will be under his authority.”

They were all amazed. As soon as their father had died, Abiba distributed portions to his brothers. Taking his own portion, he gave it to the poor, reserving nothing at all for himself. He made himself a small cell so that he might live as a solitary. As soon as he had completed the cell, he fell ill and came to the end of his life.

His brother was with him, and he said to him: “Go, brother, and make some preparation for your household.” For the celebration of the holy apostles was at hand.

His brother said to him: “How can I leave you and go away?”

He replied: “Go, and when my hour comes, I will call you.”

When the hour came, Abiba rose to the window and knocked. His brother looked toward him. Abiba beckoned to him, saying: “Come.”

As soon as his brother came, he gave up his spirit to the Lord. Everyone was amazed and glorified God, saying: “Through the extraordinary love with which he loved Christ, he was found worthy of such an end.”

## CHAPTER CCIII. Account of a Certain Jeweler Who Preserved His Life at Sea by Wise Counsel

One of the Fathers related that a certain jeweler, possessing very precious stones, gems, and pearls, boarded a ship with his sons, wishing to travel abroad and engage in trade.

By God’s providence, it happened that he came to love a certain boy who was on the ship. The boy served him there and was himself sustained by the man, eating what the man ate.

One day the boy heard the sailors whispering among themselves and deciding to throw the jeweler into the sea because of his precious stones. The boy came sorrowfully to the aforesaid man, as was his custom, to serve him.

The man said to him: “Why are you so sad today, my son?”

The boy concealed his grief and remained silent. Again the man questioned him, saying: “Tell me truthfully what troubles you.”

Then the boy burst into tears and said to him: “The sailors have made such-and-such a plan concerning you.”

The man said to him: “Are you certain of this?”

He replied: “Certainly. They have decided this among themselves concerning you.”

Then the man called his sons and said to them: “Whatever I tell you, carry it out promptly and without any dispute.”

He unfolded a linen cloth and began to say to them: “Bring the small chests.”

When they had brought them, he opened them and began taking out the stones. After he had unfolded everything and placed it before everyone, he began to say:

“Is this life? For these things am I in danger? Do I struggle with the sea? Do I die shortly afterward? And do I take nothing from this world with me?”

Then he said to his sons: “Throw all these things into the sea.”

Immediately, as soon as he had spoken, they took them and threw them into the sea. The sailors were astonished when they realized that their plan had been frustrated.

## CHAPTER CCIV. How a Religious Woman Who Feared God Restrained a Monk from a Shameful Desire

One of the Fathers said:

“A certain brother was bitten by a serpent and entered a city to be treated. A religious woman who feared the Lord received him and cared for him.

“When he had begun to be relieved somewhat from his pains, the devil began to send shameful thoughts into him, and he wanted to touch her hand.

“She said to him: ‘Not so, Father. Fear Christ. Recall the sorrow and pain of repentance that you will have to endure in your cell; remember the groans and tears that you will pour forth.’

“When he heard these and similar words from her, the struggle caused by the devil fled from him. Ashamed, he wished to flee from there, but because of embarrassment he could not look her in the face.

“Again, taking pity on him from the depths of Christ’s compassion, she said to him: ‘Do not leave, Father; you still need treatment. That thought did not come from your pure soul, but from the suggestion of the ruined and corrupting devil.’

“Thus she treated him without scandal and sent him away with provisions for the journey.”

## CHAPTER CCV. Concerning Another Wise Woman Who Rejected a Monk Who Attacked Her by Means of Wise Counsel

[Col. 0232B]

Someone related to us that a man living in a coenobium was sent out on the business of the coenobium. There was a certain religious layman living in a village, with whom the man stayed whenever he came to the village.

That man had a daughter who had recently been left a widow and had lived with her husband for one or two years. Whenever the brother entered and left their house, he began to be tempted concerning her.

She, being prudent, recognized this and took care not to come into his sight. One day her father entered a nearby city on account of some necessity, leaving her alone in the house.

The brother came as usual, found her alone, and said to her: “Where is your father?”

She replied: “He has gone into the city.”

He began to be disturbed by the temptation and wanted to assault her. She said to him with complete prudence: “Do not be disturbed. My father will not return until evening. We are both here alone. I know that you monks do nothing without prayer. Rise, then, and pray to God, and whatever He puts into our hearts, let us do that.”

But he did not comply; rather, he became more agitated. When she noticed this, she said to him: “Have you ever known a woman?”

He replied: “No, but I want to know what it is.”

She said to him: “That is why you are disturbed: because you do not know the stench of wretched women.” Wishing to lessen his passion, she said: “I am menstruating now, and no one can come near me or even smell me because of the stench.”

When he had heard these and many other things from her, he was pierced with remorse and came to his senses.

When the girl saw that he had returned to himself, she said to him: “Suppose I had listened to you and yielded to you, and we had committed the sin. With what face and with what eyes would you then have been able to look upon my father, or return to your monastery and hear the psalmody of the holy choir?

“Therefore I beg you to be sober and watchful. Do not now wish, for the sake of a brief pleasure, to lose all the labors you have endured and to be deprived of eternal blessings.”

When the brother who had suffered the temptation—and who related these events—heard her words, he gave thanks to God, who had rescued him through the woman’s prudence and modesty, lest he perish utterly. He returned to the monastery and did penance for his sin.

## CHAPTER CCVI. By What Method a Certain Distinguished Woman Was Taught Gentleness

[Note: [Col. 0244A] “Woman.” John Cassian, *Collation* XVIII, chapter 14, relates a similar example of a religious woman who was intent on acquiring patience.]

One of the Fathers related that a distinguished woman of senatorial rank came to venerate the holy places. When she had come down to Caesarea, she decided to rest there and asked the bishop, saying: “Give me a virgin to guide and teach me the fear of God.”

The bishop chose a humble virgin and gave her to the woman. After some time the bishop met her and said: “How is the virgin whom I assigned to you behaving?”

She replied: “She is good, certainly, but she does not greatly benefit my soul, for, being humble, she allows me to do as I wish.”

The bishop then took a harsher virgin and gave her to the woman. This virgin rebuked her, calling her a foolish rich woman and reproaching her with similar expressions.

After some time the bishop again asked her: “How is the other virgin?”

She replied: “In truth, she benefits my soul.”

And thus she acquired great gentleness.

## CHAPTER CCVII. The Life of an Alexandrian Girl Who Was Lifted from the Sacred Font by Holy Angels

Abba Theonas and Theodore related to us that, in Alexandria, under Patriarch Paul, a certain girl had been left an orphan by parents who were very wealthy. She was still unbaptized.

One day she entered an orchard that her parents had left her—for there are orchards in the middle of the city—and saw a man preparing a noose for himself so that he might strangle himself.

She ran up and said to him: “What are you doing, man?”

He said to her: “Leave me, woman, for I am in great distress.”

She said to him: “Tell me the reason, and perhaps I shall be able to help you.”

He replied: “I am oppressed by heavy debts and greatly suffocated by creditors. I have chosen to end my life once and for all rather than live in such misery.”

She said to him: “I beg you, accept everything I possess and repay them; only do not destroy yourself.”

He took it and repaid everything.

The girl, however, began to be distressed, having no one to care for her. Deprived of the support of her parents, she began to commit fornication and to seek her livelihood from it.

[Col. 0233D] The men who knew her said, recalling the condition of her parents: “Who knows these things except God alone?—namely, how a soul may be permitted to fall for some reason known only to Him and be abandoned for a time.”

After some time the girl fell ill. Coming to herself and pierced with remorse, she prayed to her neighbors, saying: “For the Lord’s sake, show mercy to my soul and speak to the bishop, so that he may make me a Christian.”

But they all rejected her, saying: “Who would receive this woman, who is a prostitute?” She was deeply distressed.

While she was in this anguish, an angel appeared beside her in the form of the man toward whom she had shown mercy. She said to him: “I desire to become a Christian, but no one is willing to speak on my behalf.”

He said: “Do you truly desire this?”

She replied: “Indeed, my lord, and I beg you to obtain this for me.”

He said: “Do not be sad. I will bring some others who will receive you.”

He brought two others, who were also holy angels, and they led her into the church. Then, again transforming themselves into certain distinguished persons known from the order of the Augustales, they summoned the clerics—namely, the priest and deacon appointed for this purpose—and said to them: “Does your charity vouch for her?”

They replied: “Yes, we too vouch for her.”

They took her and baptized her. Then, dressed in the newly baptized’s white garments, she was again carried away by them. When they had set her down, they vanished.

[Col. 0234B] When the neighbors saw her dressed in white in this way, after the men had departed they said to her: “Who baptized you?”

She told them the entire matter, saying: “Certain men came and took me to the church. They spoke with the clerics and baptized me.”

They said to her: “Who were they?”

When she could not say who they were, they went away and reported the matter to the bishop.

The bishop said to those appointed to baptize: “Did you baptize her?”

They confessed that they had baptized her after being asked to do so by this and that Augustalis.

The bishop summoned from the prefect’s court the men whom the clerics had named and said: “Did you stand surety for this woman?”

They replied: “We neither know anything about it nor are we conscious of having done this.”

Then the bishop recognized that this was the work of God. He summoned the girl and said to her: “Tell me, daughter, what good have you done?”

She replied: “Being a prostitute and a poor little woman, what good could I have done?”

The bishop said to her: “Have you done absolutely nothing good?”

She replied: “No, except that when I saw a man oppressed by creditors and wishing to strangle himself, I gave him all my possessions and freed him.”

After saying these things, she immediately fell asleep in the Lord, freed from sins both voluntary and involuntary.

Then the bishop glorified the Lord and said: “You are just, O Lord, and upright is your judgment” (Psalm 118).

## CHAPTER CCVIII. A Beautiful Reply of an Old Man to a Brother Who Was Attacked by Sorrow

A brother who was attacked by sorrow questioned an old man, saying: “What shall I do? My thoughts rise up against me and say: ‘You have renounced everything uselessly and inopportunely; you cannot be saved.’”

The elder said to him: “Do you know, brother, that even if we cannot enter the promised land, it is better for us to fall in the wilderness than to return to Egypt?”

## CHAPTER CCIX. A Beautiful Admonition of a Certain Holy Man Concerning the Words of the Lord’s Prayer: “And Do Not Lead Us into Temptation”

One of the saints said:
