“When we pray to the Lord, saying, ‘Do not lead us into temptation’ (Matthew 6), we are not praying that we may not be tempted—for that is impossible—but that we may not be overwhelmed by temptation if we do something displeasing to Christ. This is what it means not to enter into temptation.

“For the holy martyrs, tempted through tortures but not overcome, did not enter into temptation. So too does one who fights with a beast remain outside temptation so long as he is not devoured by it; but when he has been devoured, then he has entered into temptation.

“So it is with every passion: we do not enter into temptation unless we are overcome by the passion.”

## CHAPTER CCX. How a Holy Bishop Overcame Another Bishop Who Was Quarrelling with Him by Humility

One of the Fathers related concerning two neighboring bishops that a quarrel once arose between them. One of them was rich and shrewd, while the other was very humble; and the shrewd one sought to harm the other.

When the latter learned of this, he said to his clergy: “By Christ’s grace we can prevail.” They said to him: “Who, lord, could prevail against this man?” He said to them: “Wait a little, and you will see God’s mercy.”

He observed the day on which the other was celebrating a feast of the martyrs, and, taking his clergy, said to them: “Follow me, and whatever you see me do, do likewise, and we shall be entirely victorious.” They said: “What do you suppose he will do?”

He came to the bishop, and, while the litany was passing and the people of the whole city were assembled, he fell at his feet with all his clergy, saying: “Forgive us, lord; we are your servants.”

The other, astonished and compunct at such humility in the bishop, as God changed his heart, took hold of his feet, saying: “You are my lord and father.” From that day great charity and concord arose between them.

The humble bishop said to his clergy: “Did we not prevail by Christ’s grace? Therefore, whenever you have an enemy, do likewise, and you will be victorious.”

The old man said again: “The humble man has greater glory than a king; for the king is praised only to his face, but the humble man is praised and called blessed always and everywhere.”

## CHAPTER CCXI. Concerning an Old Man of Great Virtue Who Freed from Prison a Brother Who Had Stolen from Him

A certain abbot related to us, saying: “Near our coenobium there was an old man of most gentle disposition and great virtue. Near his cell he had a brother who, at the instigation [of the devil], one day while the old man was absent entered his cell and carried off his books and vessels.

“When the old man returned and, opening the door, saw that the vessels and all the furnishings had been taken away, he went to the brother to tell him what had happened to him. He found the vessels still set out in the middle, for the brother had not yet put them away. But the elder, unwilling to shame or accuse the brother, feigned a need and immediately went out to attend to nature; and he remained there for a long while, until the brother had removed the vessels from the middle and put them away.

“When the elder returned afterward, he began to speak with him about another matter and did not accuse him at all.

“A few days later the brother’s theft was discovered by some people, and he was sent to prison, the old man knowing absolutely nothing of it. When the elder learned that the brother had been cast into prison, not knowing the reason, he came to our monastery, which he often used to visit, and said to me: ‘Show charity and give me some food.’

“I said to him: ‘Do you have a guest?’ He replied: ‘Indeed I do.’ The elder took the food to go to the brother in prison, to comfort and refresh him.

“When he entered the prison, the brother fell at his feet, saying: ‘It is because of you that I am held here, Abba; for I am the one who stole all your things. But behold, your book is with such-and-such a person, and your cloak and the rest are in such-and-such a place.’

“The elder said to him: ‘Be assured, my son, and hold firmly to this: I did not come to you for that reason, for I did not know at all that you were here because of me. Rather, when I learned that you were held here in confinement, I was grieved and came in order to comfort you; for behold, I have brought these things for your refreshment. I will do everything to free you from prison.’

“He went and pleaded for him with some of the rulers. Since the man’s virtue was known to them, they sent and brought that brother out of custody.”

## CHAPTER CCXII. Concerning Two Old Men Who Showed Wonderful Patience toward Robbers

One of the elders said: “An old man of great virtue came to us. As we were reading the Lives and Sayings of the Fathers—for that old man especially delighted in such reading, so that it was always on his lips and in his heart, and from it he acquired a very great fruit of virtue—we came in our reading to the old man to whom robbers had come and said: ‘We have come to take everything that you have in your cell’ (in Pelagius, booklet XVI, no. 13).

“He said to them: ‘Take, children, whatever seems good to you.’ They took everything and went away. When they had left only the purse that was hanging there, the old man took it and followed after them, crying out and saying: ‘Take from me, children, what you forgot to take from our cell.’

“Because of this, amazed at the old man’s forbearance, they returned everything to its places in the cell, saying to one another: ‘Truly this is a man of God.’

“When we had read this, the elder said to me: ‘This example greatly benefited me, Abba.’ I said to him: ‘How, Father?’ He said to me: ‘When I was once staying near the regions of the Jordan, I read this and marveled at that elder, saying: “Lord God, who deigned to call me to this habit, make me worthy to follow in his footsteps.”

“‘As I burned with the strongest desire to imitate him, two days later robbers came and knocked at the door. Recognizing that they were robbers, I said to myself: “Thanks be to God; it is time to show the fruit of my desire.” Opening the door, I received them cheerfully, lit a lamp, and began to show them everything, saying: “Do not be troubled; I trust in the Lord that I will conceal nothing from you.”

“‘They said to me: “Do you have gold?” I replied: “Yes, I have three coins,” and I placed them before them. Taking them, they departed in peace.’

“After hearing this, I said jokingly to the old man: ‘Did these men return to you, as they did to that elder?’ He immediately said to me: ‘No; may God avert that! For I would not have wished them to return.’”

## CHAPTER CCXIII. Why Signs and Wonders Are Divinely Performed in the Holy Church

A certain old man said: “Signs and wonders are divinely performed in the Church even to this day because of the impious heresies that have sprung up and daily spring up, and especially because of the pernicious schisms of the acephali of Severus and of others: they are for the protection and strengthening of weak souls, and for the conversion of those very people, if they so desire. Therefore wonders have been performed in the holy catholic and apostolic Church by the holy Fathers and most blessed martyrs from the beginning of the faith until this day.”

## CHAPTER CCXIV. Miracle of the Baptismal Font in the City of the Caeanenses

Soruba is a village at the foot of the mountain on which the city of the Coeanenses is situated. In it is a baptistery which sweats at the holy Epiphany; this moisture increases continuously for three hours, and after the baptism has been performed it begins to diminish and gradually fails over another three hours.

## CHAPTER CCXV. Another Miracle of the Baptistery in the Fortress of Cedebrates

[Col. 0237C] There is also in the fortress of Cedebrates, situated beneath the mountain of the city of Aenoandron, a baptistery which, at the Paschal feast of the holy Resurrection, although it is a single stone, is filled continuously from itself. The water lasts until Pentecost, and immediately after Pentecost has passed it disappears. Both these miracles occur in the province of Lycia. If anyone does not believe that these things are so, let him go to Lycia—it is not a long journey—so that the truth of the matter may produce faith in him.

## CHAPTER CCXVI. Wise Counsel against Rashly Making Decisions and against Keeping What Has Been Rashly Decided

When I was once in the holy city, a faithful man came to me and said: “Because some resentment has arisen between my brother and me, and he does not wish to be reconciled to me, speak with him and exhort him to reconciliation.” I readily undertook this and met his brother, speaking with him about matters that seemed to concern charity and concord. For the moment he seemed to comply with me, but afterward he said: “I cannot be reconciled, because I have sworn by the cross never again to be reconciled with him.”

Hearing this, I smiled and said to him: “Your oath has the same force as if you had said: ‘By your precious cross, Christ, I shall not keep your commandments, but I shall do the will of your enemy the devil.’ For we ought not only not to keep things that we have decided most wrongly, but also to do the utmost penance and afflict ourselves over what we have wrongly decided against our salvation. For if Herod had repented, he would neither have kept the oath he foolishly uttered nor ever committed that greatest crime, of beheading Christ’s forerunner.

“This is also confirmed by Basil’s judgment, which he drew from the Gospel, when the Lord wished to wash the feet of the blessed apostle Peter: Peter at first obstinately resisted, but afterward changed his mind.”

## CHAPTER CCXVII. An Excellent Old Man’s Counsel That a Monk Should Not Approach a Woman

A certain elder said: “Little children, salt comes from water, and if it approaches water, it is immediately dissolved and ceases to exist. A monk likewise comes from woman; therefore, if he approaches a woman, he too is dissolved and comes to the point of no longer being a monk.”

## CHAPTER CCXVIII. How Abba Sergius Put to Shame an Insulting Farmer by Patience

Abba Sergius, superior of the monastery of Abba Constantine, related to us, saying: “When we were once travelling with a certain holy old man, we lost our way and, without knowing or wishing it, found ourselves among crops, trampling some of them whether we wished or not. When the farmer—who was working there—saw this, he began angrily to heap many insults upon us, saying: ‘Are you monks? Do you fear God? If you had had the fear of God before your eyes, you certainly would not have done this.’

“Then the holy elder said to us: ‘By the Lord, let no one answer him.’ Turning to the farmer, he said: ‘You have spoken rightly, my son; for if we had had the fear of God, we would not have acted so.’ The man again raged and assailed us with abuse.

“The elder again said to him: ‘You speak truly, my son; for if we were true monks, we would not have done this. But by the Lord, forgive us, for we have sinned.’

“Astonished at such humility in the elder, the farmer came nearer, prostrated himself at the elder’s feet, and said: ‘I have sinned; forgive me, and by the Lord take me with you.’ Blessed Sergius said that the peasant followed them and received the habit.”

## CHAPTER CCXIX. How a Certain Brother Was Reconciled by Humility to a Deacon Who Complained about Him
[Col. 0238D] A certain elder told us about himself, saying:

“Once, when I was staying for a short time in the monastery of Abbot Gerasimus, I had as my companion a brother whom I loved and cherished exceedingly. One day, as we were sitting together and speaking about the profit of the soul, I mentioned a saying of Abba Poemen. He said to me: ‘I have learned by experience the force, tranquility, and great effectiveness of those words.

‘For I once had a certain deacon of the monastery who was exceedingly dear to me and loved me very much. For some reason, a suspicion came to him concerning me about something that caused him sorrow, and he began to grieve and no longer look at me as he usually did. Seeing him sad, I began to ask him the cause of his sorrow. He said to me: “Because you did this thing.”

‘Since I was entirely unconscious of having done anything of the kind, I began to reassure him, saying that I had no awareness whatsoever of that matter. He said to me: “Forgive me, brother, but I am not satisfied.”

‘So I went away from him to my cell and began to examine my heart, asking whether I had committed anything of the sort, but I found nothing. When he was holding the holy chalice in his hands and distributing it to the brothers, I approached him and swore by that very chalice that I had done nothing of the kind. Even so, he was not satisfied.

‘Returning once more to myself, and recalling these words of the holy Fathers in my mind and believing them, I turned my thoughts aside for a little while and said within myself: “This deacon loves me exceedingly, [Col. 0239B] and, moved by charity, has told me what was in his heart concerning me, so that I may be sober and watchful, guard myself hereafter, and not do this again. But you, wretched soul, while saying, ‘I did not do this thing,’ have committed countless evils, and they remain hidden from you. Where are the things you did yesterday, or the day before yesterday, or ten days ago? Recall them, if you can. You did this thing as well as those others, and it is hidden from you in the same way as they are.”

‘Thus disposed in mind, as though I had truly done it but had forgotten it among my other deeds, I began to give thanks to God and to the deacon, because through him the Lord had deemed me worthy to recognize my sin and do penance for it.

‘I therefore rose and went to the deacon to do penance and give him thanks. When I knocked at his door, he immediately opened it and was the first to prostrate himself before me, saying: “Forgive me, for a demon suggested to me that I falsely suspect you of that matter. In truth, God made me certain of your innocence and did not allow me to be satisfied at all, saying to me: ‘There is no need.’”

‘I, then, being greatly edified, glorified the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the unchangeable and undivided Trinity, to whom belong honor, dominion, magnificence, and glory for ever and ever. Amen.’

## APPENDIX TO THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS

[Col. 0243]

### TO THE READER

Lest anyone devoted to antiquity should miss anything concerning the *Lives of the Fathers*, I have thought it appropriate to append here the *Paradise of Heraclides* from the old translation, since it treats the same material as Palladius. It was formerly published at Paris in 1503, under the care of Jacob Faber Stapulensis, from the Bellovisian press. Lipomanus later inserted it in the third volume of his *Lives of the Saints* under Palladius’s name, in an edition published at Venice in 1554, with a few additions and alterations, of which I give notice.

I also add Palladius as it formerly appeared from the old translation, in the early days of printing. There can be no doubt that this old Palladius, Heraclides’ *Paradise*, and Hervetus’s Palladius, since they treat precisely the same material, may be regarded as the work of one and the same author. Nevertheless, I have wished to append these versions at the end, so that one translation may occasionally shed light upon the obscurities of another, since one text will often be found to be more genuine and fuller than the other. See what we have said about these three versions and editions in the fourteenth chapter of the general prolegomena.

I have also added the *Sayings of the Egyptian Fathers*, translated from Greek into Latin by Martin, bishop of Dumium. Christopher a Castro, a theologian of our Society and professor of sacred letters at Salamanca, sent them to me from the Toledo library. I found the same work in a manuscript of Saint Florian, following the *Lives of the Fathers* translated from Greek into Latin by Paschasius. Certainly Paschasius inscribes and dedicates to the same Martin his book on the *Lives of the Fathers*, which above is seventh in order.

[Col. 0243]

### HERACLIDES

[Note: [Col. 0393D] The first edition adds “formerly bishop of Palestine.” I do not know where this was taken from. Certainly it is absent from my manuscript, which I obtained from the abbey of Saint-Amand: it is by an ancient hand, but very mutilated. The Moretian, Vezelian, and Insulensis manuscripts make Paschasius, or Palladius the deacon, the author of this book. The same first edition, at the end of the book, makes Heraclides bishop of Bithynia. Peter of Natalibus mentions him in the *Catalog of the Saints*, book XI, chapter 87, and what he relates there about him is taken from this book; therefore I do not transcribe it.]

### THE PARADISE OF THE HERMITS, BY AN UNKNOWN BUT ANCIENT TRANSLATOR

### HERACLIDES OF ALEXANDRIA TO LAUSUS THE PREFECT

[Note: [Col. 0243] Thus it is entitled in Faber’s first edition; in Lipomanus’s second, “The same to the same,” namely, Palladius to Lausus. In Hervetus’s third edition, it appears in place of a preface without any name.]

In this book, which we are about to write concerning the life of the holy Fathers, there is described the noble continence and the account of the wondrous way of life of coenobites and anchorites alike. Desiring to live in the desert in emulation and imitation of the heavenly beings, they undertook the road to the heavenly kingdom. There is also remembrance of eminent and honorable women, spiritual mothers who, with manly and perfect understanding, completed their contests with notable abstinence, as an example and for the love of God, for those who desire to be crowned with the crowns of continence and chastity.

Therefore, at the command of a man most gentle in character, most learned in understanding, peaceful in spirit, and most devout in heart; a man who loves God, shares in the needs of the needy, and by the goodness of his conscience is preferable to many eloquent men in the height of his dignities; a man fortified in all things by the virtue of the divine Spirit—indeed, what must truthfully be said, one who rouses sluggish minds to the higher contemplation by the example of his diligence—we endeavor to describe the abstinence of the holy and spiritual Fathers. They, living in accordance with God’s good pleasure, crucified the softness of the flesh in an unconquerable struggle; and he himself never ceases to proclaim their virtues, nobly completed.

The excellent Lausus is the instigator of this spiritual desire. After God’s protection, he is shown to have been appointed guardian of the most devout empire.

I, then, unskilled in speech, having tasted spiritual knowledge only faintly, and altogether unworthy of the spiritual company of the holy Fathers, saw that the greatness of the command exceeded my measure. I tried to resist such an order, which requires both literary wisdom and understanding of divine teaching. But when I considered first the noble zeal of the one giving the command, then the usefulness of the readers, and finally the grave danger of disobedience, I entrusted the burden of so great a command to the heavenly dispensation. Strengthening my powers more attentively through the intercession of the holy Fathers, I entered the arena of the contest, intending to write of the glorious signs and struggles of strong men and also of women whom I either had the privilege of seeing with my own eyes or whom I remember hearing about from holy Fathers who knew their virtues.

For I carefully traversed on foot, by God’s mercy and through the labor of walking, very many cities and villages, and almost all the caves and shelters of the desert where monks dwell. I have included in this little book, as far as my smallness permits, the names, lineage, homeland, and dwelling-place both of the men whom I saw with my own eyes and of the women who, because of the hope placed before us in Christ, overcame the female sex by the strength of their spirit. I have sent this account to you, Lausus, lover of Christ, servant of God, and illustrious ornament of the devout empire. I have also recalled how some of both sexes completed their struggles to the highest point, yet, because of the mother of pride called *Cenodoxia*, were miserably dragged at the end into the abyss and the depth of hell. Their palms of abstinence, acquired through long periods and labors, were prematurely withered by a sudden moment of exaltation and conceit; but by the grace of our Savior, the providence of the holy Fathers, the compassion of spiritual hearts, and the prayers of venerable elders, they were snatched from the snares of the devil and returned to the recovery of a nobler life.

Farewell.

## Preface to Lausus

Many people at various times have left various books to this age. Some, through heavenly inspiration and divinely given grace, have built up and fortified those who follow, with faithful purpose, the institutions and footsteps of the Savior. Others, desiring only to please human beings, with a corrupted and depraved disposition of mind, have comforted those who labor under the desire for glory, as though deranged by some confusion of things [Ms.: “aerum”]. Still others, blinded by some unknown frenzy and by the prompting of the demon who is hostile to good things, have seized the minds of foolish mortals with rabid arrogance, to the ruin of human frivolity and the disgrace of the divine and Catholic Church, in order to overthrow the discipline of praiseworthy conduct.

I too, the humblest of men, have decided—because I was ashamed not to obey the commands of your greatness, which I know to be a lover of learning, and by which souls are summoned to better things—to describe for you, who desire to know the deeds of our Fathers, not only men but also women whom I myself have seen or learned about from others. I am in my thirty-third year, reckoned among the brotherhood and the monastic life; in the twentieth year of my episcopate; and in the fifty-third year of my whole life. I have traveled with these people through the deserts of Egypt, Libya, the Thebaid, and Syene, where those called Tabennesiots also dwell; through the regions around the borders of Mesopotamia, Syria, and Palestine; and in the western lands, Rome and Campania, as well as other places near them.

I have set down and related in this little book, as I have already indicated, the lives from the beginning of all those regions, as an honorable memorial beneficial to the soul—that is, as a perpetual medicine of truth. May you reject every sleep of forgetfulness arising from irrational desire, exclude every deceit of a divided mind from the faith necessary for these matters, together with all sluggishness in good conduct and every shameful failing of the soul. May you, by avoiding through these examples anger, disturbance, sadness, and irrational fear, as well as the vain distraction of the world, shine with perpetual love around your purpose of devout religion, becoming a guide to blessed life for yourself, for those who are with you, for those under your rule, and for future most devout emperors.

For by such deeds and merits those who burn with love for Christ hasten to be joined to God. Yet await each day the rendering of the soul, which is unquestionably owed and will necessarily come, according to what is written: “I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is much better” (Phil. I). And again: “Prepare your works for perfection, and be a worker in the field” (Prov. XXIV). For whoever is always mindful of death, which will certainly and necessarily come without delay, will never commit grave and great sins, according to what is written: “In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII).

Above all, do not despise what has been commended to your understanding in salutary report; nor reject the humility of expression and rusticity of words. For this work of divine teaching does not consist in speaking eloquently, but in instructing everyone’s understanding in the knowledge of truth, according to what is said: “Open your mouth with the word of God” (Prov. XXXI). And again: “Do not neglect the narration of the elders, for they too learned from their fathers” (Ecclus. VIII).

I, then, a man of God and one astonishingly eager to learn, desiring to imitate, even in part, what is divinely commanded, remember seeing very many holy men. I did not do this casually or superficially, but spent thirty days on the journey and then as many more, completing the entire route on foot—as I shall say before God—and becoming acquainted by walking with almost the whole Roman land. I gladly embraced the hardships of the journey so that I might enjoy the sight of a holy man and lover of God, which I certainly could not otherwise have had.

For if the Apostle Paul, who is incomparably better than I, who far surpasses and excels the whole world in knowledge of affairs and the secure faith of his conscience, walked from Tarsus to the homeland of the Jews in order to see Peter, James, and John—and if, reporting this almost with a kind of boasting, he makes his own labors known while inflaming those who appear to grow dull through idleness and sluggishness, saying, “I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter” (Gal. II), since the mere report of his virtue was not enough for him unless he also desired to behold that man’s face and appearance—how much more ought I, a debtor of ten thousand talents, to have done this? Not in order to benefit those holy men in any way, but to provide in every way for myself, a sinner.

Those who wrote the lives of the Fathers before our own—of the holy Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of those who followed them, Moses, Elijah, John, and the rest—did not relate them in order to add anything to their glory, but for the benefit of their readers.

Therefore, knowing this, most faithful and greatly venerable servant of Christ, Lausus, and advising you for your own good by persuasion, embrace also my loquacity, so that you may preserve within yourself your purpose of devout good will. That purpose is beaten, as it were, by the various waves of visible and invisible vices, which we cannot calm except through frequent prayer and diligent withdrawal of the soul to God.

Many of the brothers, abounding both in the labors of abstinence and in good deeds toward the poor; others rejoicing in chaste widowhood; others exalted by virginity; and others greatly priding themselves on their readings and writings of divine letters—have strayed from the road of their right purpose. Indifferently, as though under the appearance of a certain religion, they languished through love of curiosity, from which a manifold anxiety of mind is generated. After this, concern for other affairs follows, and from it they incur even the name of “slanderer,” by which name they are prevented from administering good works. Nor do those who devote themselves exclusively to the affairs of the soul enjoy this condition as a mother.

Stand firm, then, courageously, I beg you. Do not increase your wealth—though you should always diminish it more—but distribute it sufficiently among all whom you know to be in need, using what advances you in the ministries and nourishment of virtue. Do not let some impulse anticipate you through irrational precommitment, so that, while you hurry to please human beings, you bind the will of your honorable purpose with the chains of an oath.

We have known many who suffered this. Through rivalry for empty glory, by abstaining from foods or drinks, they in a certain way reduced to servitude that free will which God had created in them, through the necessity of an oath. Bound by their own oaths, when they cannot fulfill their promises and are shamefully held back by their love of life and pleasure, they incur the crime of perjury through necessity, to which they are subject by their own fault.

If, therefore, you abstain from these things by reason alone, and again take them by reason alone whenever you wish, you will certainly never sin. For God, who is reason, supports by hidden aids the impulses that move within us, condemning what harms and embracing and accepting what benefits; for, as he says, “the law is not laid down for the just” (I Tim. I).

It is better to drink wine with reason than water with arrogance and disdain. If you wish to see this, observe that those who drank wine reasonably were holy men, whereas those who drank water without reason were vicious and profane. Do not therefore think that the thing itself, which God made, should ever be condemned or praised on this account; rather, judge those who use these things well or badly to be either blessed or wretched according to their purpose.

Joseph once drank wine among the Egyptians, yet he did not harm his wisdom, because he had first fortified the purpose of his mind. Pythagoras, however, Diogenes, and Plato—and among them the Manichaeans and the whole crowd of those who seemed wise to themselves—advanced so far in their desire for empty glory that they fell into condemnation, to the point of being ignorant even of God, the maker of all things, and worshiping the idols they themselves had made.

The Apostle Peter also used wine with the rest of the company of the disciples. Hence their own Savior and teacher appears to have been reproached by the Jews, who said: “Why do your disciples not fast as John’s disciples do?” (Matt. XI). They also taunted the disciples themselves, saying: “Your teacher eats and drinks with tax collectors” (Mark II; Luke V).

It can be made clear that they would never have been reproached merely for bread and water, but for wine or meat, by those who irrationally despise people who drink wine while admiring those who are accustomed to drink water.

The Savior therefore said: “John came in the way of righteousness, neither eating nor drinking” (he certainly meant meat and wine, for without other kinds of food he could not have lived), “and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’” (Matt. XI), because he ate and drank with them.

What, then, shall we do? Let us follow neither those who condemn nor those who praise, but either keep the fast with John in accordance with reason, even if we are said to have a demon, or drink wine wisely with Jesus Christ when bodily necessity requires it, even if some should at times reproach us, like the Jews reproached him, for eating meat and drinking wine.

Do not therefore consider either the use of these things or abstinence from them, in itself, to have any significance according to the truth of the matter. Rather, recognize that only faith, extended through love and works, has very great power. Therefore, because faith is always seen to cling to the deeds of the person, he will be blameless because of it, whether he eats or drinks the things mentioned. For “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XVI).

But since every sinner says that he acts from faith, even when he does something through foolish persuasion and a corrupt and vicious conscience, our Savior distinguished the matter by saying: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII).

It is entirely clear that the fruit of those who live reasonably and wisely according to the Apostle is love, joy, peace, patience, gentleness, goodness, faith, self-control, and simplicity. For Paul said: “The fruit of the Spirit is this and this” (Gal. V).

Moreover, the one who hastens to possess such fruits does not eat meat or drink wine at an unsuitable time or without consideration. Nor does he live with someone whose conscience he knows to be more malicious. Paul himself again said: “Everyone who prepares for the contest abstains from everything” (I Cor. IX). Thus, in order to appear sound in body, he abstains from things that make the body heavier. But when he is troubled by some illness or pain, or bitten by sadness or various temptations, he should use foods and drinks as medicines capable of healing those who are anxious. He should drive away from himself the things by which the soul is wounded: anger, envy, love of empty glory, abandonment of right purpose, whispering, and irrational suspicions, while giving everlasting thanks to the Lord.

Having sufficiently discussed this matter, I now add another admonition to your teachable spirit: [942] flee with all the strength of your mind from the sight and conversation of those whose purpose is contrary to a good life, who are entirely unable to benefit, and whose concern is to polish the body’s skin in various ways, even if they are reputed to be worshipers of the true faith. They are, so to speak, people of a perverse sect, who overthrow souls under the appearance of holiness, even if by their gray hair, complexion, and display of wrinkles they seem somehow to accumulate a number of years.

For even if, being fortified by upright conduct, you are not stained by any injury from them, you will nevertheless either be slightly relaxed into greater security or lifted up into considering yourself better; and you will condemn and mock such people. You will recognize that you have not done this without harm to yourself.

Follow the presence of holy men and women, like the light of a shining window, so that through their venerable conversations you may carefully inspect, as though in a book written in tiny letters, their actions and the secrets of their hearts. By comparison with them, you may discern and examine more carefully either your diligence or your negligence.

For even the color of religious people—the color by which praiseworthy conduct is covered as by a flower—their manner of dress, their composed mind, their spirit without any raised eyebrow or inflated speech, the modest reverence even of their syllables, and the pleasing arrangement of their meanings and words will be sufficient to encourage you, even if you are wearied by the tedium of some anxiety.

“The clothing of a man, the movement of his feet, and the laughter of his teeth” signify what is seen in him, as the proverbial speech of Holy Scripture bears witness (Eccles. X).

Beginning, then, the opening of the narrative I promised, I have not allowed any of these people to remain unknown to you, whether in cities, villages, or solitudes. For it is not location alone that is sought, where such men may have lived, but also the purpose of a righteous life and praiseworthy conduct.

[Col. 0249]

## LETTER

[Note: [Col. 0249] This letter is absent from the first edition of Heraclides. It is also absent from the Moretian manuscript. Lipomanus supplied it from the book of Cardinal Bessarion, translated by Brother Torres. In Hervetus’s Palladius it appears under the name of Heraclides, in Hervetus’s translation.]

### OF PALLADIUS, BISHOP OF CAPPADOCIA, TO LAUSUS THE PREFECT

I greatly praise your decision—for it is rightly with praise that my letter must begin—that while nearly everyone pursues frivolous things utterly useless to themselves, you strive to be taught what pertains to the salvation of the soul.

There is only one being who does not need teaching: God, the parent and creator of the universe, since, being the most ancient of all, he has no author of his origin except himself.

Apart from him, all other things, inasmuch as they have been made and created, can be formed by teaching. Even the first orders of heavenly beings have as their teacher the supreme Trinity itself; the second are taught by the first, the third by the second, and the rest similarly thereafter. For those who excel others in knowledge and virtue instruct those who are beneath them.

Therefore, those who think they have no need of teachers must be considered to suffer from the disease of ignorance, which is the mother of pride. Those are the ones who do not place faith in their teachers with charity. In this matter they imitate the demons who fly through the air, since those demons too, corrupted by the same plague, once fled from their heavenly seats and fell headlong from heaven into destruction.

Teaching does not consist in words or syllables, but in the rightly performed deeds of a well-formed soul. It consists in a soul free from every illness, entirely fearless and present to itself, ruled by no anger, and not afraid to express freely what it thinks in every matter. Hence, without doubt, speech bursts forth like a flame of fire.

For if this were not so, that great Teacher would never have said to his disciples: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). He did not instruct his hearers through corrupted eloquence, but was himself such that he offended no one by his conduct, except those alone who, of their own accord, hated teaching itself together with its teachers.

The soul that exercises itself in the course of Christian life must either learn elsewhere, through faith, what it does not know, or openly teach others what it knows. Otherwise, whoever neglects to do either of these two things should rightly be considered insane. For satiety with teaching and disgust with discipline are the beginning of defection, whereas the mind of a devout person has always been accustomed to hunger continually for them.

Be strong and farewell. And—what is a great thing—may God grant you knowledge of Christ.

[Col. 0251]

# THE PARADISE OF HERACLIDES

## CHAPTER ONE

### The Life of Isidore, Presbyter of Alexandria; Dorotheus, Monk of the Thebaid; Potamiaena the Martyr; Didymus the Blind; and Alexandra the Woman

[Col. 0251A]

When I first reached the city of Alexandria (Palladius, chapter 1), in the second consulship of the elder Emperor Theodosius, who now dwells with the angels because of the faith in Christ that he embraced, I came to know in that city an admirable man, distinguished in every virtue and learned, Isidore the presbyter. In the Alexandrian Church he was the receiver and provider for the poor brothers. It was reported that at the beginning of his youth he had won outstanding palms of abstinence in the desert; I also saw his cell on the mountain called Nitria.

He was then an old man in the seventieth year of his age. After completing fifteen further years of life, he died in peace. Until the end of his life he used no linen except that with which he covered his head; he did not enter baths; he did not eat meat; and he did not remain at table until satisfied.

His body was nevertheless so well nourished by the grace of spiritual nourishment that everyone who did not know his way of life attributed its condition to feasting and pleasures. If I wished to recount one by one the virtues of his soul, time would certainly fail me.

He was a man of such great goodness and humanity, and so peaceful, that even those who appeared to be his most obstinate enemies were ashamed of his very shadow because of his life, so venerable was it. He is also said to have possessed such knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and divine doctrine [Col. 0251C] that even during the brothers’ meals he would suddenly become astonished, and, with his mind changed and his spiritual senses occupied, would seem to have departed elsewhere. When later asked the reason for his astonishment, he would say that he had been transported to another thought and carried away by the wonder of a certain contemplation.

I myself also know that this man often wept while taking food. When I wondered why he was weeping, I heard this from his mouth: “I am ashamed,” he said, “to take irrational food, when, having been made rational by God, I ought to dwell in the delight of paradise and be nourished with divine food, because of the power that Christ has granted us.”

This same man was known to the Roman senate and to distinguished women. When he first traveled to Rome with Bishop Athanasius, and later with Bishop Demetrius, he abounded in wealth and material abundance without provoking envy. Yet at his death he made no will, left not even a single solidus, and gave no part of his property to his virgin sisters, but commended them to Christ, saying: “He who made you will also order your life as he ordered mine.”

There were seventy other virgins with his sisters.

[Col. 0252B]

When I came to him at the beginning of my youth and asked him to instruct me in the conduct and life of monks, since I was still in the first ardor of youth—a time when I needed not so much instruction in words as continual labor and bodily exertion—he, like a good horse-trainer, led me out from the inner part of the city to the fifth milestone, to the places called the solitudes, and entrusted me to a certain Dorotheus, a Theban monk (Palladius, chapter 2), who was living in the sixtieth year of his life in a cave.

He ordered me to remain with him for three years, in order to crush and break the unlawful passions of vice—for he knew the elder’s exceedingly harsh and laborious life—and instructed me then to return to him for knowledge and teaching in spiritual matters.

But when I was unable to complete the three years there as he had commanded, having been seized by a serious illness, I was taken away from him before the three-year term had ended.

[Col. 0252C]

For his life was a struggle with immense dryness and aridity. Every day, in the fiercest heat and in the solitude near the seashore, he gathered stones. Each year, completing the construction of a cell, he offered it to those who could not build one themselves.

When one day I said to him: “What are you doing, Father, killing your little body in such extreme old age amid these savage heats?” he replied: “It kills me, and I kill it.”

He ate an ounce of bread and one small bundle of the cheapest greens, drinking a small quantity of water. Yet, with God as my witness, I never saw him stretch out his legs, never saw him rest on a mat or on a bed. Throughout the entire night, sitting, he would weave a rope from a date palm, and he used its price to buy food.

Thinking that he did only what I saw him do when I was present, I questioned more carefully some of his other disciples, who lived separately, and learned that he had lived in this way from his earliest age. He never willingly slept except from the greatest necessity: either when exhausted by work, or while eating, if sleep happened to overwhelm him so completely that his eyes closed for a little while. Indeed, while eating, he frequently nodded his head under the excessive force of sleep, and the bread fell from his very lips.

Once, when I somehow compelled him to lie down on the mat even for a moment, he said sadly: “If you can persuade angels to rest, you will also persuade one who hastens to please God.”

One day he sent me to his well at about the ninth hour, so that I might draw water when the time for refreshment was approaching. When I arrived, I happened to see an asp at the bottom of the well and was terrified. I brought back the empty vessel and explained the reason for my fear, saying: “Abba, we are dead! I saw an asp in the well to which you sent me.”

He merely smiled, looked at me for a long time, shook his head, and said: “If it pleases the devil to turn himself into a serpent or a tortoise in every well, or into the rest of the poisonous animals, and to leap into the waters of the springs, will you be able to live without drinking?” Then he went out, drew water from the well while fasting, and, after first making the sign of the cross over it, tasted it, saying: “Where the cross is present, there the devil’s wickedness has no power.”

This holy Isidore, who once saw the blessed Antony, related to me a worthy account, which he said he had heard from Antony himself (Palladius, chapter 3).

A certain girl named Potamiaena, very beautiful, was a slave during the persecution of Maximian. Her master repeatedly tempted her with many different promises, but was unable to violate her. Finally, driven headlong by passion and madness, he handed her over to the man who then governed Alexandria, so that, claiming that she was a Christian and had cursed the emperors for the savagery of the persecution, he might promise the governor money on the condition that, if she consented to his will, he would spare her without any punishment and return her to him. But if she persisted in her resolve to refuse, he asked that she be worn down by tortures, lest, if she survived, she should seem to have despised her master’s lust.

When she had been brought before the tribunal and the judge desired to conquer her devoted will through various tortures and torments, he also had an immense bronze vessel filled with boiling pitch and kindled with a fierce flame. The cruel prefect then placed before her a double alternative: “Go,” he said, “and obey your master’s will, or know that you will be thrown into this boiling pitch.”

The girl replied: “May there never be another such counselor, who commands chastity to be delivered over to lust.”

Struck by enormous fury at this, he ordered her to be stripped and thrown into the boiling vessel. Her words were: “By the head of your emperor, whom you fear, I beg you: if you have decided to kill me with these torments, do not order me to be thrown all at once, but gradually into the boiling pitch, so that you may see how much patience Christ, whom you do not know, has given me.”

For the space of one hour she was gradually lowered into the glowing cauldron and died when the pitch, first boiling up, reached her neck.

[Col. 0254B] At that time many men worthy of the dwelling of the blessed, and women also, died in the city of the Alexandrian church. Among them was Didymus [Note: [Col. 0253D] He was an Origenist.], deprived indeed of the light of his eyes, but distinguished by his knowledge of the divine Scriptures. I remember having seen him four times at different periods within ten years, since he completed the term of his life after eighty-five years (Palladius, ch. 4). He told me that he had been deprived of his sight when he was in his fourth year. He had never been handed over to teachers of letters, nor had he ever learned even the first rudiments; nevertheless, he possessed an innate goodness that always remained unimpaired, his natural teacher being his conscience. Such grace of spiritual knowledge adorned him that in him it was most plainly fulfilled which is written: “The Lord makes the blind wise” [Col. 0254C] (Psalm 145).

He interpreted the Old and New Testaments word for word. He also expounded all the sects with such subtlety and firmness, discussing the reasoning behind them, that he surpassed the learning and knowledge of all the ancients. Once he compelled me to pray in his cell, but when I did not comply with his command, he said in explanation: “The thrice-blessed Antony, when he deigned to visit me, entered this lodging. When I asked him to bend his knee here and offer a prayer, he did so at once and did not wish to be asked a second time, teaching me by his very actions to obey the wishes of the saints. Therefore, if you follow his footsteps,” he said, “and live as a monk and as a pilgrim for the acquisition of virtues, I do not want you to argue.”

[Col. 0254D] He also reported the following to me: “When I was being worn down by a certain great anxiety and sadness on account of the most wretched life of the emperor Julian, so that one day, overcome by distress, I did not touch bread until the evening hours of deep night, it happened by chance that I was sitting down and was seized by sleep. In a kind of translation of the soul I saw this revelation: Four horsemen on white horses were running about in different directions and shouting, ‘Tell Didymus: Today, at the seventh hour, Julian died.’ ‘Rise, then, and eat, and send to the house of Bishop Athanasius, so that he too may learn this.’”

Thus, as he himself said, he noted the month, the week, the day, and the hour, and found that everything was confirmed just as he had heard it.

He also told me about a certain girl named Alexandra (Palladius, ch. 5), who had left the city in which she lived and settled inside a tomb, receiving the food necessary for life through a small opening and never seeing either men or women for ten years. In the tenth year, when she was about to depart in her final sleep, she prepared herself. The woman who customarily brought her food reported this to us, saying that at that time she had received no answer. When we heard this, we opened the door, which had been sealed and closed, entered, and found the woman’s body dead.

Concerning her and the most blessed Melania, a Roman woman about whom I shall speak shortly, she said the following: She had not been able to see the girl’s face, but, standing at the opening of the tomb, had asked her to tell her the reason for which she had shut herself up in that tomb. Speaking through the opening, she replied: “Once I had wounded a certain man’s feelings, and, lest I seem either to distress or destroy him, I preferred to shut myself alive in a tomb rather than harm a soul made in the likeness of God.”

When she had said this, she asked again: “How, then, can you endure, O handmaid of Christ, to see absolutely no one, but to maintain such a continual struggle in this solitude against acedia or thoughts?”

She answered: “From the beginning of the day until the ninth hour I devote myself to prayer, doing linen work hour by hour. During the remaining time I roam in thought through the holy prophets, apostles, [Col. 0255C] martyrs, and patriarchs. During the other hours I take bread for food; as evening approaches, I glorify my Lord in the greatest tranquillity and patiently await the end of my life with good hope.”

But I will not pass over in silence those whose whole life was spent in a certain contempt of their own salvation, so that we may proclaim them worthy of praise for this also and provide the readers with a safeguard by way of warning.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning a Certain Virgin and the Nitrian Monks: Ammon, Or, Pambo, Ammonius, and Benjamin

There was a certain woman in Alexandria who was a virgin in name only (Palladius, ch. 6). As far as appearance was concerned, she seemed humble; but as far as her purpose was concerned, she had a more inflated soul. She was sufficiently rich in various possessions, more a lover of gold than of Christ. She never went out and gave not even a small contribution to a stranger, a virgin, one suffering violence, a monk, the church, or a poor person. Despite the frequent admonitions of the holy Fathers, she had never cast off from herself this burden, so useless to the soul.

She also had several relatives, among them a daughter of her sister whom she had adopted for herself and with whom alone she enjoyed herself by day and night, abandoning and despising the love of heavenly things. Sometimes even this appearance, which the devil introduces, is an error: under the guise of affection apparently owed to relatives, avarice and greed are fostered. That the demon cares nothing for either greed or kinship is clearly demonstrated by this: he is the one who compels human beings to become murderers of mothers, brothers, and fathers. And even if he sometimes seems to pretend a concern for family relationship, he does not do this in order to benefit them, but to heap upon their souls the crime of injustice, since he is not unaware of the divine sentence that excludes the unjust from the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom (1 Corinthians 6).

Certainly a person moved by spiritual knowledge and divine love may avoid despising the salvation of his own soul and may piously supply the necessities of life to his relatives if they perhaps appear to be in need. But if he utterly tramples upon and despises his own soul, being occupied solely with concern for kinship, he incurs the sentence of the divine law, counting his soul, as I have said, as vanity. The sacred composer of the Psalms sings of those who care for their souls with the greatest fear, saying: [Col. 0256B] “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” [945]—that is, it is sufficiently rare. “Or who shall stand in his holy place?” The one “innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain” (Psalm 23).

For they receive their soul in vain who think that it is dispersed and dissolved together with the body—those, namely, who despise spiritual virtues.

The holy presbyter Isidore [Read: Macarius, according to Palladius], wishing to make this virgin in name only somewhat lighter from the burden of greed by “drawing blood,” as the proverb puts it, used the following stratagem against her. As I said earlier, he presided over the cells of poor and infirm brothers, and, in the earliest years of his youth, he had appeared to be skilled in testing stones and pearls.

He therefore approached her and said: “Necessary and precious stones—emeralds and hyacinths—have suddenly come to me. Whether someone found them or stole them, I cannot know. I cannot fix their price, because their value exceeds any individual sum: all of them together are being sold for five hundred solidi. If you should wish to buy them, you can sell one of them for five hundred solidi and assign the rest to necklaces for your niece.”

The woman who was called a virgin was utterly captivated by affection for the girl. She was deceived by such an ornament, embraced the man’s feet, and begged him not to let anyone else receive the stones mentioned. While eagerly encouraging her, the holy man said: “Come to my house, so that you may see the things I have described.”

She did not agree to this, but instead poured five hundred solidi into his lap and said: “As you wish; take those same stones yourself. I do not want to see the person who is selling them.” He took the five hundred solidi and immediately distributed them among the poor and infirm.

After some time, because his reputation was very great among everyone in Alexandria—since he was merciful, distinguished in the worship of God, and an elder who had already reached the course of his hundredth year, as I myself, who had long been with him, knew very well—the woman was ashamed to remind him about the solidi.

At last, when she happened to find him in the church, she addressed him: “What,” she said, “do you command, I ask, concerning those stones for which we gave five hundred solidi?”

He replied: “Since you gave me the gold, I gave it as the price of those stones. If you wish to come and see them in my lodging—for they are lying there—come and see whether they can please you. If not, you shall receive back the gold you gave.”

Having gladly heard this, she went to the presbyter’s house. In the upper part, infirm women were kept; in the lower part, men. When he had entered with her through the first doors, he said to her: “What do you wish to see first, hyacinths or emeralds?”

She replied: “Whatever you command.”

He led her to the upper parts of the house and showed her women with mutilated limbs and faces entirely lacerated by various diseases, saying to her: “These are the hyacinths.” Then, going down, he showed her similar men in the lower part and said: “These are the emeralds. If they please you, consider them; if not, take back the gold you gave.”

And so she left the house, overwhelmed by immense shame and very sad, because she saw that she had wished to do what could not please God. As soon as she returned, she fell ill; for she had not done this according to the will of God, but had been compelled by the ingenious necessity imposed by the most holy man. Shortly afterward she gave the presbyter the greatest thanks because the girl for whom she had shown such excessive concern, though married, died without rearing children.

After I had spent three years in the monasteries situated around Alexandria (Palladius, ch. 7), and had seen there as many as two thousand excellent men, adorned with the virtues of abstinence and most holy, I descended from there and came to the mountain called Nitria.

Between this mountain and the city of Alexandria lies a lake called Maria, extending over a distance of seventy thousand paces. After crossing it in a day and a half, I reached the southern side of the mountain mentioned above. Entirely deserted regions adjoin this mountain, extending as far as Ethiopia and as far as Mazicum, toward the land of Mauretania.

About five thousand men, as I think, lived on this mountain. They followed different rules of life and lived as they wished and were able: one was permitted to remain if he desired; another, if he wished, could live with only one brother; another could live with a multitude, if he desired this. On this mountain, both for the men already mentioned and for those who had withdrawn to the remotest solitudes—six hundred men—food was supplied by seven bakeries.

I spent the whole year making use of the hospitality of this mountain, and was greatly instructed and taught by the blessed Fathers: by the elder Arsisius, Putubastus, Agio, Serapion, and Chronius. I was also stirred by the reports of many spiritual elders concerning those who had lived before them, and proceeded as far as other, more remote places of solitude.

On the mountain of Nitria itself I saw one very large church, in which there were three date palms, from each of which hung a whip: with one, monks who sinned were beaten; with another, thieves, if any happened to fall into their hands, were struck; with the third, those whose offenses had been convicted anywhere and who deserved to be beaten for their sin were dismissed after embracing the trees mentioned and receiving a prescribed number of blows upon their backs.

There is also near the church a cell that receives travelers and poor brothers. Whenever they receive any newcomer, they support him there for as long as he wishes to remain, not preventing anyone from staying there for two or three years if he desires. For the first week after his arrival they also gave him leisure; during the remaining days they compelled him to perform some task, assigning him either to the bakeries, the gardens, or the kitchens. If someone appeared more respectable and less suited to such tasks, they gave him a book to read, and prohibited everyone from coming into his sight or conversing with him until the sixth hour.

On this mountain there are also pastry cooks and physicians. They use wine as well, for wine is sold there. All these men make linen cloth by hand, and from the proceeds of this work none of them lacks what is necessary for life.

It is a source of the greatest pleasure, around evening, to hear from each dwelling of the monks various voices singing psalms to Christ. If someone stands there at that time and pays careful attention, he will think that he has suddenly been lifted up and placed in paradise. They customarily assemble at the church itself only on Saturday and Sunday.

There are eight presbyters there. As long as the first presbyter lives, no one other than him offers sacred worship to God, preaches [Note: [Col. 0393D] “Or preaches.” The translator renders literally what in Hervetus is “he has a sermon.” In Greek, οὐχ ὁμιλεῖ. Hence the words “tractatus” and “tractatores” often occur in the writings of the Fathers. See the Onomasticon.], or judges; [946] they always remain silent, content with the honor of sitting together [Col. 0258C]. The elder Arsisius and many other most holy elders who were with him, whom I myself saw at that time, belonged to the same period as the blessed Antony. They also told us that they had known the holy Ammon of Nitria—the one whose soul Antony saw being carried to heaven by angels.

This Arsisius reported that he had once seen Pachomius of Tabennisi, a man renowned for prophetic grace who governed three thousand monks in a monastery. I shall speak shortly of his virtues.

He said that Ammon himself lived in the following manner: “When he was a boy, abandoned by his parents, and had reached the age of twenty-two, he was unwillingly bound by his uncle in the bonds of marriage” (Palladius, ch. 8). Since he could not resist the necessity imposed upon him by his relative, he was ordered to be crowned at the wedding, compelled to sit in the bridal chamber, and forced to endure patiently all the customary ceremonies of the wedding.

After everyone had departed from the bridal chamber and the newlyweds had been placed upon the bed, holy Ammon rose from the bed, shut the door, summoned the blessed woman, and, sitting beside her, called her his truly like-minded wife. He said: “Come, my lady, so that I may explain to you the very reason for this union. Our marriage extends only this far and contains nothing more. We shall therefore do well if from now on each of us rests separately, so that we may please Christ if we live with our virginity intact.”

He brought from his bosom a small book and read to the girl, who was ignorant of the holy Scriptures, words spoken in the person of the Apostle and the Savior. Adding to the reading many more things according to his own understanding, he explained to her the practice of chastity and virginity. After she had been satisfied, and by a sudden grace of divine power had been filled with understanding, she said: “You may know, my lord, that I too am persuaded to embrace a chaste life willingly. What more you wish to command, I await.”

He replied: “This is what I command and ask: that from this day each of us remain separately.”

She did not agree, saying: “We ought to remain in the same cell, but in separate beds.”

When this pleased them both, they lived for eighteen years in this way: she remained in the cell all day, while he devoted himself to work in the garden he cultivated and prepared balsam by the craft in which he was skilled. This balsam, however, is planted, cultivated, and pruned with much labor, after the manner of vines.

In the evening he returned home, offered prayers, ate food with her, and again performed the customary nighttime prayers. Early in the morning he went back to his usual work.

Meanwhile, while their life was such and all bodily enticement and passion had been utterly excluded from both of them [Note: [Col. 0259D] Read this cautiously against those who assert impassibility.], they began, through prayer, to obtain what they had at some time desired.

At last the blessed woman said to him: “My lord, I have something to say. If you listen to me in this matter, it will be proved to me that you love me according to God.”

He encouraged her to say whatever she wished. She replied: “This seems just to me. You are of the male sex and wholly devoted to righteousness, while I too imitate the path of your purpose, so that we may be separated into different dwellings for the edification of many. For I consider it unsuitable and unfitting that, because of me, you should possess such virtue in secret and that no one should know that we live and remain together in this chastity and purity for the love of the Lord.”

He gave her thanks and glorified God, replying: “You have made a good decision, my lady and sister. Keep this cell, then; I shall try to make another for myself.”

He left her and soon penetrated into the more remote parts of Nitria—for at that time there was not yet a multitude of monasteries there—and built two cells for himself. Thus, after spending twenty-two years in solitude, he died; or rather, he rested in sleep, having completed sixty-two years of age. Each year, however, he saw his blessed wife twice.

The blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, related the following miracle concerning him in the work in which he wrote Antony’s life. Once, when he wished to cross the river called Lycus together with his disciple Theodore, he was ashamed to remove his clothing, lest he should ever see his own naked body. Suddenly, without a boat and carried by an angel, he was transferred to the opposite bank of the river.

Thus Ammon lived and died in such a way that the holy Antony saw his soul being carried to heaven by angels. I myself crossed the river mentioned above by boat, with fear. For there is a branch there of that great river, the Nile.

On this mountain also, which is called Nitria, there was a certain monk named Hor (Palladius, ch. 9), whose virtue was praised by the testimony of many brothers [Note: [Col. 0260D] Hor was an Origenist.], but especially by the handmaid of God Melania, who had reached that mountain before me. I could not see the man mentioned above alive.

She therefore reported the following about the virtues of his manner of life: He had never lied, sworn, or cursed anyone, nor had he spoken without some necessity.

The blessed Pambo was also an inhabitant of this mountain. Dioscorus the bishop and the brothers Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, as well as Origenes, the nephew of Dracontius, an admirable man, had Pambo as their teacher. [Note: [Col. 0394D] “And nephew.” I do not see what “nephew” is doing here. Is Nepos a proper name? There is no trace of him either in the older Palladius or in Hervetus’s Palladius. The older Palladius, ch. 5, has “the brothers of Dracontius, an admirable man.” Hervetus’s Palladius has: “And John, the son of the brother of Dracontius, an admirable man.” The Greek in the Venetian manuscript is: Καὶ Ἰωάννου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ Δρακοντίου ἀνδρὸς θαυμαστοῦ, “And John, the brother of Dracontius, an admirable man.” I fear, therefore, that instead of ἀδελφοῦ, “brother,” the translator of Heraclides may have read ἀδελφιδοῦ, “nephew.” Alternatively, one might suspect that Ἀδελφίου should be read. Certainly, Adelphius also occurs below, in ch. 33, among the monks with Ammonius, Pambo, and others. In the first edition, feeling my way in the dark, I wrote or conjectured this. Now, in this second edition, since a more complete Greek text of Palladius has appeared, correct the whole passage as follows: “And Origenes, the nephew of Dracontius, an admirable man.” The Paris Greek manuscript has: Ὠριγένους τοῦ ἀδελφιδοῦ Δρακοντίου ἀνδρὸς ἐνδόξου καὶ θαυμαστοῦ, “Origenes, the nephew of Dracontius, a renowned and admirable man.”]

Pambo, who excelled with many and varied distinctions of virtue and with palms of victory, is remembered as having possessed this particular excellence among others: he was so contemptuous of gold and silver that he seemed to fulfill the Lord’s command.

The venerable Melania herself reported to me that, after setting out from the city of Rome, she first entered Alexandria. Having learned many things about the man’s virtues from the presbyter and keeper of the hospice Isidore, and having reached him in the desert under Isidore’s guidance, she offered him three hundred pounds of silver and begged him to accept something from her possessions.

“He was sitting,” she said, “and weaving palm fiber. He blessed me with words alone and said: ‘May God give you your reward.’ Then he said to his steward: ‘Receive this carefully and distribute it among all the brothers who are in Libya and on the islands; for these monasteries appear to be in greater need than the others.’ He also instructed him not to give any of this money to those living in Egypt, because he knew that those regions were more abundantly supplied with provisions.”

When the woman stood there, as she told me, waiting for a blessing or praise in return for the gift, and heard nothing from him, she said to him further: “Know, my lord, that there are three hundred pounds in this silver.”

He again did not even look up, but replied: “To whom have you offered these things, daughter? He does not need you to make him know the measure, for he who weighed the mountains in a balance (Isaiah 40:12) knows much more fully how great the weight of this silver is. If you were offering this to me, you would say this appropriately. But since you are offering it not to me but to that God whom we recognize as not having despised, but rather honored more greatly, those two coins (Mark 12:42), be silent and rest.”

He said that the Lord had arranged matters in such a way that, after a short time, once he had come to that mountain, that servant of God would rest. He was not afflicted by illness or any fever, but, while sewing a small basket, he rested in peace in the seventieth year of his age.

Before the hour in which he was to leave the world and commend his spirit to God, he called me and, at the final completion of his work, confidently said: “Take this basket from my hands, because I have nothing else to leave you, so that you may remember me.”

After his body had been wrapped in linen and given over to burial, I departed from the desert regions and continued onward toward my own end, carrying with me the inheritance of that holy man.

This same Pambo, at the end of his life and at the very hour when he was about to leave the world, with the presbyter Paul, the steward Ammonius—men renowned for holiness—and the other brothers standing around him, is remembered to have said the following:

“Since I came to this place of solitude and lived in the cell that I built with my own hands, I do not remember having eaten bread given freely by anyone, nor have I spoken, up to this present hour, a word for which I ought to do penance. Yet I go to my Lord as though I had not even begun to attain the worship of divine service.”

Paul and Ammonius, servants of Christ, reported this to us and confirmed it by their own testimony: Whenever he was questioned about either spiritual or secular writings, he never quickly gave an answer to those asking. He always said that he had not yet found what he should answer. Often, even after months had passed, he still gave no answer to those seeking one, maintaining that he had not yet reached knowledge of the truth.

He uttered judgments so careful and cautious according to God that they all received them as though they had been spoken by God himself. They say that the great Antony also possessed this virtue in his discourses.

Among other things, the following deed of Pambo is also reported (Palladius, ch. 11). When the monk Pior had come to him carrying his own bread, Pambo reproved him for this. When asked why he had done it, Pior replied: “So that a guest would not be burdened by his host.” Pambo then dismissed him immediately, having reproved him only by silence.

After some time, the aforementioned Pambo approached Pior and offered him bread soaked in water, as such bread was eaten by them. When asked why he had done this, he replied: “For this reason I added water, so that I would not be burdensome to you.”

The aforementioned Ammonius, his disciple [Note: [Col. 0261D] This Ammonius was an Origenist.], and three other brothers and two sisters, burning with the highest devotion and love of God, reached the desert regions and made separate dwellings for themselves, so that they were separated from one another by a great distance.

Because this Ammonius devoted himself beyond measure to reading the Scriptures, a certain city requested that he be made its bishop. When its citizens had asked this of a certain blessed Timothy, and he had said, “Bring him to me, and I shall make him do as you wish,” they entered with a large crowd, so that he might be taken away more easily. Realizing that he had been captured, he began to beg them and to bind himself by oaths, saying that he absolutely could not agree to leave the solitude that he occupied.

When he saw that he was not being allowed to do what he asked, he cut off his left ear at the root with a knife, in the sight of everyone, saying: “Now at least it will be proved to you that what you desire cannot be fulfilled, since divine law commands that no one with a severed ear may be made a priest.” At last they left him and returned to their own people.

When they had returned and told the bishop these things, he replied: “This law is observed by the Jews. But if you bring me someone even mutilated in the nose, provided that he is upright in character, I shall not hesitate to make him a bishop.”

When they heard this, they went to him most insistently, asking him again. When he did not agree, they also tried to use force against him. He replied to them under oath: “If you try to compel me any further, I shall even cut out my tongue—for it is because of it that you are troubling me.” Only then, since they accomplished nothing in this matter, did they leave him.

The following miracle is reported of this Ammonius. When a certain carnal desire tormented his little body without any interruption, he tore his own limbs with glowing iron, so that he was always completely covered with ulcers.

His food was of the following kind: From his youth until his death he used uncooked foods, sometimes even eating nothing besides bread. Retaining the Old and New Testaments by heart, he also surpassed six hundred thousand lines in reading the books of the most eloquent men, Didymus, Pierius, and Stephen [Palladius: Athanasius and Basil].

The most holy Fathers living in the desert also testify to these things about him. His prophetic power likewise became known to many. Among the brothers who loved the hidden places of the desert, no one surpassed him in the ministry of consolation.

The blessed Evagrius, a spiritual man and especially distinguished for the virtue of discernment, expressed the following judgment concerning him, saying that he had never seen a man who had so overcome bodily passions. (Read this cautiously.)

[This same most holy man, when he had been summoned by Rufinus [Note: [Col. 0395A] “This same most holy man when summoned by Rufinus.”]—Baronius, volume 4, under the year of Christ 394, the tenth year of Pope Siricius and the sixteenth of the emperor Theodosius, discussing the Constantinopolitan synod at the dedication, says: “For this reason I think that such an assembly of bishops was convened neither on account of ecclesiastical doctrines nor with the aim of settling ecclesiastical discipline, but for the purpose that those same bishops should dedicate a new basilica erected in the name of the apostles Peter and Paul by Rufinus, the prefect of the praetorium, who possessed the highest authority in the entire Eastern Empire. I also think that this was the assembly of bishops mentioned by Palladius [Baronius understands our Heraclides here, as I noted in the General Prolegomenon 4, § 3], when, writing the events of his own time, he speaks of Evagrius Ponticus, who, together with Ammonius and others from Egypt, was summoned by Rufinus and came to Constantinople for that reason.

“‘This same most holy man,’ he says, ‘when summoned by Rufinus’ (Palladius, in the Lausiac History, ch. 2),” adding that Ammonius died there and was buried in the same basilica, called the Rufiniana. Certainly, the statements made above concerning the custom of summoning bishops even from the most remote regions to basilica dedications show that this was done. Sozomen also mentions the basilica erected by Rufinus in book 8, chapter 17, and says that it was built across the sea near Chalcedon, in a place called Ad Quercus, where Rufinus had constructed a lavish villa and royal buildings. The basilica itself was dedicated in honor of the chief apostles Peter and Paul and was also called by the more common name Apostoleum. Later, a synod was assembled there by Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, against John Chrysostom, as will be said in its proper place. Thus far Baronius.]

The prefect of the praetorium of that time had repeatedly begged him to come, since the great Ammonius was arriving at Constantinople on account of necessary affairs of the desert. The holy bishops of various provinces and many other hermits, who had gathered for the dedication of the basilica that Rufinus himself had founded, urged him strongly to come as well. He received the aforementioned Rufinus with his own hands after Rufinus had been cleansed in the sacred font.

Rufinus greatly venerated him because of the merit of his manner of life and wished to obey holy Ammonius in everything. Ammonius shortly afterward fell asleep in the Lord and was buried in the basilica called the Rufiniana. At his tomb, all those suffering from various fevers are said to have been cured.]

[Note: [Col. 0262D] The material enclosed here is absent from Palladius.]

On the mountain of Nitria, about which we spoke above (Palladius, ch. 13), there was a remarkable man named Benjamin, who, through eighty years of the virtues of abstinence, attained the highest grace of spiritual gifts. Whether he laid hands upon someone or gave a blessing of oil, the person was freed from every affliction of illness.

This man, who excelled in such gifts of divine grace, was seized by a watery disease eight months before his death and swelled with such pitiable fatness of flesh [Col. 0263A] that in our time he was considered a second Job.

Dioscorus the bishop, who at that time was a presbyter of Nitria, took me and the blessed Evagrius with him and addressed us in this way: “Come and see the new Job, possessing exceptional patience amid such a swelling of the body and incurable suffering.”

We went and saw a man so distended by the swelling of his body that the joined fingers of both our hands could not encompass the little finger of his hand. Since we could not long look upon the severity of his suffering, we turned our eyes away from him.

Then the blessed Benjamin said to us: “Pray, children, that my inner man may be freed from this illness. For this body has neither exalted me by its health nor cast me down by its pain.”

During those eight months a very broad chair was made for him, in which he sat continually, since he could no longer rest on a bed because of the remaining needs of his body. Yet while afflicted by this condition of his body, he regularly healed others suffering from any illness by the grace of God.

I therefore considered it necessary to report the suffering of this most holy man, so that we may not be astonished whenever certain bodily afflictions befall the most just men. After the very strong man died, the doorposts of the doorway were removed—for his body, so greatly swollen, could not have been carried out otherwise.

## CHAPTER II. The Life of Abbot Apollonius, Called “From the Merchants,” and of Two Other Converted Brothers

[Col. 0263C]

A certain man named Apollonius (Palladius, ch. 14), one of the merchants who renounced the world and lived on the mountain of Nitria, was no longer able, being hindered by the weakness of old age, either to learn a craft or to practice the abstinence prescribed by spiritual Scripture. He is known to have established the following form of self-restraint.

From his own money and labor, he purchased every kind of medicine and provisions in the city of Alexandria and supplied what was necessary to all the sick brothers. You could see him from the beginning of the day until the ninth hour traversing all the monasteries of both men and women, visiting the sick at the door of each one and carrying with him raisins, pomegranates, eggs, and fine wheat flour—things that seemed especially necessary for the sick.

This servant of Christ had ordered his old age according to such a life, the only one suited to him. Before his death, however, when he found someone resembling himself, he handed over to him all the equipment of this ministry and begged him to provide such care to the brothers. Since five thousand monks reside on the mountain mentioned above, such concern and consolation are especially necessary; without them, life cannot be maintained in those desert regions.
