Two other brothers also lived [Note: [Col. 0263D] Palladius, chapters 15 and 16, calls them Paesius and Isaiah, and this manuscript likewise has these names.], whose father, occupied with buying and exchanging merchandise, continually traveled as far as Spain in pursuit of trade. When he died, they divided his property between them, which consisted only of movable goods: five thousand solidi in gold, and, in slaves, clothing, or whatever else they could find. These men, therefore, began to deliberate together with one mind and common agreement, saying to one another: “What way of life shall we choose, brother? If we take up the commerce in which our father lived, we too shall leave our labors to others, while we ourselves, perhaps traveling into dangers, will be destroyed either by precipitate falls, by the waves of the sea—as commonly happens—or by the weapons of robbers. Let us rather pursue, brother, the desert and the life of monks, so that we may both profit from our father’s inheritance and not destroy our souls through contact with any evil things.” When this resolve had pleased them both, each took a different path in choosing the solitary life.

After dividing the goods they had left equally, they both had the same purpose: to please God. Yet they did not both please him by living under the same rule. One of them distributed all his possessions among monasteries, churches, and prisons, and found for himself a certain craft by which he earned his daily bread; he devoted himself to the life he had chosen and to prayer. The other, however, gave nothing from his own property to anyone, but built a monastery for himself. There, having settled a few brothers with him, he received every visitor, every old person, every poor person, and every sick person, and on the Lord’s Day and the Sabbath he provided three or four tables for those in need. He spent his entire property in these ways for as long as he lived. When both men had died, both were celebrated as blessed, having completed lives worthy of approval, though in different ways. This one pleased some people, and that one pleased others.

When a dispute arose among the brothers from their praises—since both seemed to have been perfect—they went to the holy Pambo to learn the truth from him. They told him that they had chosen him as judge and asked him to explain which of the two had acted better. He replied that both were perfect before God. One of them, he said, had lived according to the character of Abraham, the other according to that of Elijah. When they continued their unresolved dispute, asking how they could be considered equal, and why the man who had fulfilled the evangelical commandments should not take precedence—the man who had sold everything, given it to the poor, and, carrying the Lord’s cross through every hour, every day, and every night, accompanied the Savior in perpetual prayer—others argued from the opposite side, saying: “This man whom we praise more showed such affection toward the needy that he sat beside the public embankments, gathered together those afflicted from every direction, and did not care only for his own soul, but saved many people by treating the illnesses of many and supplying what they needed.”

Thus the blessed Pambo answered them both: “I tell you again: both are equal before the Lord, and I think I shall satisfy both sides. If this man had not been such a perfect monk, he would certainly not have been worthy for me to compare him with that man’s goodness. But the other, in refreshing the needy and strangers, received some consolation from that very fellowship. For although his labors seemed to be a great burden, he also had some rest amid his labor. Wait,” he said, “until I learn about this from God’s revelation; when you come to me afterward, you will hear.” After a few days, when they asked him again, that blessed man replied: “I speak to you before God: I saw both of them standing together in paradise.”

## CHAPTER IV. The Life of Macarius the Monk Who Had Committed Homicide

A certain young man named Macarius (Palladius, chapter 17), eighteen years old, was playing beside a lake called Maria while pasturing sheep with his companions of the same age. Against his will he committed a homicide. Telling no one anything, he went away into the desert, so terrified by fear of both human beings and God that he seemed to have become deranged while remaining for three years in the wilderness without shelter. For that land is always without rain. All who are learned through reading the Scriptures and through experience know that what I am saying is true. The blessed man of whom I speak built himself a small cell in the desert. Living there for another twenty-five years of his life, he merited such divine grace that, rejoicing in his solitary life, he mocked and despised demons.

When I asked him—for I spent a long time with him—what thoughts his mind had concerning the homicide he had committed, he said that he was not at all sad about it; rather, he continually gave thanks to God for the homicide he had committed unknowingly. For from it, he said, an occasion of salvation had come to him. Producing testimonies from Scripture, he said that the great servant of God Moses would never have been granted the vision of the divine majesty, nor would he have received so great a gift from God that he could write down the heavenly and holy mysteries, unless, because of fear of King Pharaoh on account of the homicide he had committed in Egypt, he had fled into the deserts of Mount Sinai (Exodus 2).

I say this not so that anyone may seem to be encouraged toward homicide, but rather to show that from evil circumstances, when we fall into them unwillingly, we sometimes reach the glory of virtue through God’s hidden providence. For some kinds of virtue we ascribe to necessity, and others to the will.

## CHAPTER V. The Life of the Blessed Abbot Nathanael

There was another among the ancient men, a most noble spiritual athlete named Nathanael (Palladius, chapter 18). I could not see him alive, for he had rested fifteen years before my arrival. Nevertheless, I diligently inquired about the virtue of this man from the monks who had lived with him for a long time. They also showed me his cell, where he had been accustomed to live; no one had inhabited it after him, because people lived in the neighborhood of that place. At that time the blessed man had built his cell, when only a few people were still withdrawing into the hidden places of the deserts.

From them I learned this great virtue of continence concerning the aforesaid man: he possessed such patience in his cell that he never wavered at all from his purpose, from the time when he was first mocked and tempted by the demon who deceives and misleads everyone. Through that demon’s fraud he had previously suffered acedia and is said to have withdrawn from his cell and begun to build another near a certain village. But when he had completed the second dwelling and had begun to live in it, after three or four months the demon came to him at night in the appearance of a soldier, taking on the form of an executioner. He seemed to be covered with rags, hideously filthy, and making a sound as of whips.

The blessed Nathanael said to him: “Who are you,” he said, “who are trying to do such things in my lodging?”

He replied: “I am the one who drove you from your former cell, and I have now come to drive you from this dwelling also.”

When he heard this, and saw that he had been deceived by the demon, he immediately returned to his former habitation and completed thirty-seven years in the same dwelling, not even leaving its threshold, contending with the demon whom he desired to overcome. The demon harassed him with so many schemes, seeking by every means to compel him to leave his cell, that I cannot recount them all individually.

Among these attacks, that unclean spirit also attempted to turn him aside from the rule of his purpose. On one occasion, seven holy bishops came to visit him, whether by God’s providence or through a demonic temptation. After the bishops had prayed and were leaving, he did not accompany them even a single step. The bishops’ deacons said to him: “You are acting very arrogantly, abba, by not escorting the holy bishops.”

He answered them: “I revere my lords the bishops, and I follow the entire clergy with the honor they deserve. I do not doubt that I am the least of all people. But I am dead both to these men and to the entire world. God knows the hidden purpose and secret of my heart, and for that reason I do not escort the holy men.”

The demon was thus deceived and lost hope of succeeding through his present device. Nine months before Nathanael’s death, he devised another strategy against him.

Suddenly he took the form of a little boy, about ten years old, driving a donkey that was carrying loaves in a chest. When he had come to the cell late at night, he pretended that the donkey had fallen to the ground and made the child cry out. “Abba Nathanael,” he said, “have pity on me and give me your hand.”

When he heard this in what seemed to be the voice of a little child, Nathanael stood inside the doorway, part of which he had opened, and said to him: “Who are you, and what do you want me to do for you?”

“I am the boy of that monk,” he replied, “and I am carrying bread to him, because your brother is going to prepare an agape. When the Sabbath day dawns tomorrow, this spiritual offering will be necessary. Therefore, I ask you not to despise me as I lie here and to hand me over to the bites of wild beasts, for many such animals are known to be in these deserts.”

The holy Nathanael stood there like bronze. Astonished and deeply disturbed by uncertain thoughts, he considered these matters within himself: “I must either fail to show mercy, which is the greatest of the divine commandments, or depart from my purpose.” Finally, strengthened by sound reasoning, he judged that it would be better if the devil were put to shame and the merit of so many years were not lost.

After praying to God, he answered the one who was speaking like a child: “Listen, child. I believe in the one whom I serve, who rules over every spirit, that if you need someone’s help, he himself will provide it and will not allow either wild beasts or anyone else to harm you. But if this is some kind of temptation, let my Lord now look upon it and, doing his will, not allow me to suffer further harm from it.”

Then he closed the door and withdrew. The confused and defeated demon dissolved into a whirlwind of wind and into wild pigs [manuscript: onagers], gamboling about with noise and commotion. Such was the life of the blessed Nathanael; such was its end and its crown.

## CHAPTER VI. The Life of the Two Great Macarii, One Egyptian and the Other Alexandrian, and Also of the Monk Mark

I hesitate to relate or write the things reported about the two renowned and blessed men named Macarius (Palladius, chapters 19–20), because they are innumerable and unbelievable to unbelievers, lest I perhaps incur the name of liar as well. But the judgment of the Holy Spirit has declared that all who speak lies perish before God (Psalm 5). Therefore, most faithful of men, Lausus, by the grace of the Lord who does not lie, may you too not be unbelieving regarding the triumphs of the saints.

Of these two Macarii, one was Egyptian by birth, while the other, surpassing the vigor of a younger age by his virtues, was an Alexandrian merchant [manuscript adds: “who sold fruit, vegetables, and nuts”]. I shall speak first about the Egyptian, who lived all ninety years in total. Of these, he spent sixty in the deserts, having entered them as a young man in the thirtieth year of his age. Within ten years he lived with such a struggle of monastic abstinence that, already fortified by the wisdom of discretion, he was then called “the boy of an old man,” because he climbed more quickly to mature contests. When he first began to be forty years old, he merited divine grace both against the aerial spirits, in healings of people, and in announcements of future events. Finally, as he deserved, he also received the title of priest.

He had two disciples with him in the more remote deserts called Scetis. One was his attendant and never left his side, because of those who were accustomed to visit him for healing; the other lived separately in his own cell. After some time, while he was looking ahead with eyes that perceived the future, he said to his attendant named John—who afterward also merited attaining the priesthood in his place:

“Listen to me, brother John, and accept what I urge upon you for your benefit. You are being tempted, for the spirit of desire and greed troubles you. Thus I have seen, and I know, that if you listen to me, you will be perfected in this place which you have attained, you will glory, and the scourge will not approach your dwelling” (Psalm 90). “But if you refuse to listen to me, the end of Gehazi will come upon you, whose disease you also suffer from” (2 Kings 5).

It happened, therefore, that after the blessed man’s death, fifteen or twenty years later, John despised such salutary words. Hence that accursed disease seized him so completely—for he had committed the crime of theft against the poor brothers in the manner of Judas—that no sound part of his body could be found, not even one occupying the space of a single finger. This too is among the things that the holy Macarius had foretold long before.

I consider it superfluous to relate his food and drink, especially since we see even more negligent monks observing such practices, lest they be said to resemble either the luxurious or the worldly—especially in those places where barely enough food is available for their necessities, and where there are so many examples of saints whom they strive to imitate. I shall therefore speak of his other merits.

He was always thought to exist without interruption in a kind of translation of the soul; rather, he spent most of his life with God and was more occupied with heavenly than earthly affairs. In this connection, certain divine miracles are also reported.

For a certain Egyptian, burning with insane love for another man’s wife, could not bring such a criminal desire to fulfillment because she was devoted to chastity and loved her husband of her virginity [that is, her own husband] exceedingly. He entreated a magician either to make her love him or somehow to cause her to be rejected by her own husband. The magician, enticed by many gifts, using the customary skill of his own art, made her appear to be a mare rather than a woman.

When her husband returned home and saw her in that condition, he was disturbed by such a monstrous novelty—he saw a mare lying in his little bed—and groaned and wept, since, although he addressed the animal, he could hear no response from anyone speaking. He therefore called for the presbyters of the village, brought them home, and showed them what she was suffering. Even then he did not recognize the cause of so great a calamity. For three days she had taken neither hay like a mare nor bread like a human being, deprived of nourishment from either kind of food.

Finally, so that the glory of God might be magnified and the virtue of that holy Macarius might become known to all who were present, the husband suddenly conceived the idea of taking her into the desert. He bound her as beasts of burden are accustomed to be tied and led her into the desert. When he had already approached the cell of the holy Macarius, near which the monks were standing, they began to rebuke her husband, asking why he wished to come to the monastery with a mare.

He answered them: “I have come here so that I may obtain the holy man’s mercy through his prayers.”

When they asked what evil she suffered, he replied: “This is my wife, but she seems to have been changed into a mare. Today is the third day since she has taken absolutely no food.”

When the aforesaid brothers had reported this to the holy Macarius as he was praying—for God had already made this matter known to him—and he had prayed earnestly for her, he said to the brothers:

“You are the horses, because you have the eyes of horses. She is a woman, and she has not been transformed into another nature; she merely appears so to the eyes of those deceived by the emptiness of an illusion.”

Immediately, after completing his prayer, he poured blessed water upon her uncovered head. At once he made her appear to everyone as a woman. He ordered her to be restored and commanded her to return home with her husband, giving thanks to God. He said:

“She must never be separated from participation in the holy mysteries, and she must never withdraw from the prayer of the church. She suffered this because for five weeks she had not approached the divine mysteries.”

I shall relate another deed of his. Over a long period of time, he dug a tunnel from his cell beneath the hidden depths of the earth, extending half a stadium to the surface of another hill. There he made a cave for himself by his own labor, so that whenever he could not bear the disturbance caused by visitors, he could leave his cell by the secret passage and withdraw into the cave’s hiding place, since he never wanted to be seen by anyone.

One of his more devoted disciples once reported to us that whenever he went from his little dwelling to the cave, he said twenty-four prayers while going and the same number while returning.

Rumor also spread about him that he had raised a dead man, wishing to teach a certain heretic who denied that there would be a resurrection of bodies. This report remained in those desert regions because it was true.

Once a mother brought to him a young son suffering from a demon, lamenting, while two men held him bound, one on each side. They said that this was what the demon did: after forcing the unfortunate man to eat three modii of bread and drink a bottle containing one amphora [manuscript: or a bottle of Cilician water], he would belch out everything he had devoured and turn it into a sort of smoke in the air. Thus he would consume everything eaten or drunk as though with the heat of fire. There is also a legion of demons called “fiery.” For among them, as among human beings, there is much difference—not in natural substance, but in diverse and discordant will.

Since the young man’s mother could not prepare such enormous quantities of food for him, he often ate the excrement of his own body and drank it. Therefore his wretched mother, weeping over her son’s intolerable calamity, begged that holy man to cure the pitiable youth. After she had poured out many continuous prayers before him, and the most holy man prayed over him and entreated God, the remedy for so great an evil began to appear after a day or two.

He said to the boy’s mother: “How much do you want your son to eat?”

“Ten loaves,” she replied.

The holy man rebuked her for this: “What have you said?”

He then fasted and prayed for him for seven days and ordered him to receive three pounds of bread, but in such a way that he had to work with his own hands. Having been cured in this manner by the grace of God and restored to his former health, the young man was returned to his mother.

God also performed this miracle through his holy servant. I could not see that man in the body, for one year before I entered those solitudes, that great spiritual athlete had rested in the Lord.

As for the Macarius who was a presbyter in Alexandria, I saw him in the region called the Cells, where I myself lived for nine years. I lived with him there for three years. Some miracles he performed before my eyes; others I learned from his own mouth; still others I learned from the reports of others.

He had established this purpose for his life: whenever he learned that some great thing had been accomplished by any saint in abstinence, he would fervently fulfill it himself. When he learned from certain people that the Tabennesiots were said to eat no cooked food throughout the whole of Lent, he decided within himself that for seven years he would taste nothing that had been cooked by fire, but would be content merely to smell raw food. Even if he happened to find some legume, he would not taste it.

When he had imitated this for longer than he intended, he afterward despised it as though it were nothing difficult.

Again, he heard about another man who ate only one pound of bread. This outstanding monk, wishing to imitate him, placed bread broken into small pieces in bottles [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Buccellatum.* This is the reading from the manuscript; the earlier reading was *buccellatim*. See the Onomasticon.] and decided to eat only as much as he could bring out with one hand. He later happily reported this to me, saying:

“I could enclose more pieces of bread inside the bottle, but whatever I might have been able to hold within, I could not bring out, because of the narrowness of the small opening. For my publican [that is, my appetite] did not allow me to eat nothing at all.”

He lived for three years under this discipline, taking only four or five ounces of bread and drinking the same amount of water, while using one sextarius of oil, which lasted him throughout the entire year.

Recognize once more another virtue of his purpose. This strongest of men once decided to conquer sleep. He himself said that for twenty days he did not enter under any roof even once, so as to overcome sleep: burning during the day in the heat of the sun, trembling at night in the cold. As he himself related, he would have returned under a roof more quickly and fallen asleep, for he understood that his brain had already become so dry that he was almost thought to be without sensation.

“Thus,” he said, “I conquered sleep as far as I was concerned; but I yielded to nature the due use that it required.”

One day, while he was sitting in his cell in the morning, he felt a gnat. It wounded him on the foot, and he killed it painfully with his hand; dying, it shed a great deal of blood. Rebuking his own deed because he had avenged a personal injury, he wished to condemn himself in this way: he sat naked for six months in the meadows of the region called Scetis, situated in the most remote deserts, where gnats, like hornets, pierce even the skin of wild boars.

There he became entirely ulcerated, with swellings rising over all his limbs, so that he was thought to be one of those called elephantiasis sufferers. After six months he returned to his cell, and it was revealed that he was Macarius only by his voice.

This same man once desired, as he used to relate, to see the garden where the magicians Jannes and Jambres were buried. They are said to have possessed great power under Pharaoh. [The source reads: Jannes and Mambres.] Over a long period and with the great power of their art, they had built the aforesaid structure with squared stones. Above it they had placed a memorial to those men, where they had also hidden gold and filled the place with various little trees. They had also made a well, since the place seemed to be without any moisture.

They are said to have done all this because they believed that after death they would remain in that same place as though in paradise. The servant of Christ Macarius did not know what road would lead him to the aforesaid place. Therefore, as he walked through the deserts, he followed only the stars of heaven by a kind of inward calculation, as sailors do at sea. He carried with him a bundle of reeds, so that he could plant one every thousand paces and thus more easily recognize his own markers on the return journey.

After completing the journey in nine days, he approached the places mentioned above. Then the fiercest demon, who was always accustomed to fight against the athletes of Christ, gathered up all the reeds from their separate places and suddenly placed them at the head of the memorial where Macarius was resting a thousand paces away.

When the holy Macarius awoke from sleep, he recognized the reeds he had left elsewhere. I believe that this too occurred with God’s permission, as a test of the man, so that he would place no hope in reeds but rather in God’s grace, who showed the people of Israel their way through the desert for forty years in a pillar of cloud.

He said that seventy demons sprang forth from the aforesaid garden at his arrival, shouting and flying around his eyes and face like ravens, saying:

“What do you want, Macarius? What do you want, tempting monk? Why have you come to our places, where you will not be able to remain? Have we ever tempted any of your monks? You have your own desert with those like you, from which you hasten to drive out even our neighbors. We have nothing in common with you. Why do you enter our regions? If you are an inhabitant of the desert, let your solitude be sufficient for you. The founders gave this place to us to inhabit. Why do you seek to break into this possession, into which no human being has ever entered alive since it was handed over to us by our brothers, who were buried here by our own hands?”

While the demons continued to repeat many such things and lament, the most blessed man replied: “I will enter only to look, and immediately I shall depart.”

The demons said: “Promise us this faithfully by your conscience.”

The servant of Christ answered simply: “I shall do this.”

Immediately the demons withdrew from his sight.

He said that he entered and found there, near the well, a suspended bronze vessel with an iron chain, already consumed by the great age of time, and empty pomegranates, dried by the excessive heat of the sun.

After departing from there, he returned to his cell over twenty full days. When the water he had carried with the bread began to run out, and he was suffering greatly from scarcity and was almost perishing, a girl appeared to him, as he himself related, covered with a clean linen cloth and carrying a little bottle of dripping water. She was a stadium away from him.

For three days, as he walked, he saw her showing him the vessel; she seemed to be standing nearer and inviting him, so that he thought he could reach her, yet he was unable to do so. He said that, hoping to drink, he patiently endured the labor of three days.

A large herd of buffalo suddenly appeared—for there are many such herds in that region. Among them one female buffalo stood with her calf, as he himself related, and milk flowed from her udder onto the ground.

“I therefore lay down,” he said, “and placed my lips upon the animal’s wild udder to draw the milk from it, until I was refreshed to satiety.” He said that this was sufficient for him until he reached his cell. The very animal followed him and offered him her udders, no longer accepting her own offspring because of her regard for that holy man.

At another time, while he was making a well for the monks’ rest, he was bitten among the shrubs by the tooth of an asp, and death necessarily follows such a bite immediately. He seized it, pulled it apart from its mouth with both hands, and tore it in half, saying to it:

“Since my God did not send you, why did you dare to come here?”

He had various cells in the desert regions, in which he performed remarkable works of virtue: one in the inner desert called Scetis; another in Libya, where the Cells are called [manuscript: “another in Libya, another in the Cells”]; and another on Mount Nitria. Some of them had no windows, and it was said that this most blessed man sat in darkness there throughout the whole of Lent. One cell was narrower, so that he could not stretch out his feet. Another was wider, and he was accustomed to receive visitors there.

He cured such great crowds of people afflicted by demons that no number could be assigned to them, even while we were living there.

A noble and wealthy virgin was brought to him from Thessalonica. She had suffered from paralysis for many years. When she had been presented to him and thrown down before the blessed man’s cell, he was moved with compassion. For twenty days he anointed her with holy oil using his own hands and poured out prayers to the Lord for her. He restored her unharmed to her city. Later, after she had returned on her own feet, she sent many gifts to the deserts.

When this same man heard that the Tabennesiots had a rigorous manner of life, he changed his clothing to resemble that of a laborer, put on secular dress, and traveled through the deserts for fifteen days until he reached the Thebaid. When he arrived at the monastery of those men, he first sought out the man whom they called the archimandrite, a certain Pachomius, a thoroughly admirable man who possessed the spiritual gift of prophecy, although nothing about Macarius had been revealed to him.

When he came to him, Macarius said: “I ask you to receive me into your monastery, for I desire to be a monk.”

The great Pachomius said to him: “You are weighed down by old age, and you can no longer be a monk. You cannot live among the other brothers who learned this way of life from adolescence, because you cannot endure their customs and labor. If, unable to bear the trials of abstinence, you leave them in resentment, you will begin to curse those whom you could not imitate and follow.”

He therefore refused to receive him on the first day, or the second, or throughout the entire week. But when Macarius persisted continually in his request while fasting, he finally said:

“Receive me, abba, and if you discover that I am inferior to them in fasting or work, drive me from your monastery immediately.”

When he heard this, Pachomius persuaded the brothers that he should be received into the monastery. There was a single habitation there, containing even to the present day about fourteen hundred men.

When the holy Macarius had entered it, and after a short time the days of Lent arrived, he saw the various ways in which the men lived: one breaking his fast in the evening, another after two days, others tasting food only after five days, another standing throughout the nights, sitting during the day, and working.

Macarius, holding many soaked date-palm fibers, stood in one corner until the end of Lent and the beginning of Easter. He tasted neither bread nor water, did not bend his knees, and did not lie on the ground. He took only a few raw leaves of vegetables on the Lord’s Day, so that he would appear to the others to be eating.

Whenever he went out for a bodily necessity, he immediately returned and stood there, not opening his mouth or speaking to anyone, but remaining in complete silence, continually praying only in his heart and performing the one task he held in his hands.

When all the monks observed that his life was so rigorous and inimitable, they were stirred as though by a kind of revolt against their superior. “Where have you brought this man from?” they asked. “He lives as though he were not human flesh, to the condemnation of us all. Listen, then: either remove him from us, or know that we shall all leave this monastery today.”

When Pachomius heard of his manner of life and virtue, he entreated the Lord to reveal who he was. As soon as this was done, he took Macarius by the hand and led him to his oratory, where the divine altar was. He kissed him and said:

“Come, excellent old man. You are that Macarius, and you were trying to hide yourself from me. For many years I have desired to see you, hearing of your great miracles. I give you thanks because you have struck our little children on the cheek, so that they would not imagine themselves capable of accomplishing something great in their manner of life. Return now to the places from which you came, for you have sufficiently edified us all, and pray for us.”

At the request of everyone, he departed from there.

At another time he told us this, saying:

“Whatever kind of life and whatever practices of spiritual abstinence I desired, I imitated and fulfilled.”

He said again:

“On one occasion a desire for a new thought seized my mind, so that I wished to make the perception of my heart inseparable from God for five continuous days. I formed this intention in my mind and closed the doors of my cell and vestibule so that no one could receive an answer from me. At the beginning of the week I began to persist, saying to my understanding:

“‘Take care that you do not wish to descend from heaven to earth. There you have angels and archangels, the highest powers, cherubim and seraphim, and, above all, God the Creator. Remain there; reject every dwelling that seems to be below the heavens, lest you fall into carnal thoughts.’

“Persisting in this for two days and two nights,” he said, “I felt that I had provoked and goaded the demon to such a degree that he suddenly turned into a flame of fire and burned everything that seemed to be inside me. He even burned the mat on which I was accustomed to stand [Note: [Col. 0395C] 1008 *mattam* [‘mat’]. Thus the translator renders the word; in Palladius’s Greek it is ψίαθος. See the Onomasticon.] so that I thought I myself was already entirely on fire.

“Finally, struck by such fear, I withdrew from this purpose on the third day, when I saw that I could not keep my mind so continually and indivisibly with God. I therefore descended again to worldly thoughts, lest some kind of arrogance arise in me from the perpetual contemplation of the divine nature.”

When I once came to this same Macarius, I found before the door of his cell a certain presbyter [Col. 0274C] whose entire head had been so eaten away and consumed by that disease called *carcinus* [Note: [Col. 0395C] *Carcinus.* The translator retained the Greek word καρκίνος, which in Latin is *cancer*.] that even the bone of the crown could be seen. He had come there to be cured, yet up to that day he had neither been received nor seen by Saint Macarius. I therefore begged him to take pity on the man and at least give him an answer. To this the holy man said to me:

“This man is not worthy to be cured, for he received this punishment by the command of God. But if you wish him to be cured, first persuade him to withdraw from offering the holy sacrifices.”

When I said, “Why, I beg you, do you command this?” he replied: “Because, polluted by the uncleanness of fornication, he was accustomed to profane the Lord’s ministries; for this he is tormented by the severity of such punishment. But, as I said, if he never again, as a priest, touches the divine sacrifices, he will be able, with God’s help, to receive healing.”

When, therefore, I had told the man suffering from this disease that he should bind himself by an oath with me not to approach the priestly office again, only then was he summoned by that holy man. Macarius addressed him in these words:

“Do you believe that God exists, for whom nothing is hidden?”

He replied, “I believe.”

“Could you not escape,” he said, “the power of his divinity?”

He replied, “I could not, my lord.”

Then that great Macarius said: “If you acknowledge your sin and wish to escape the punishment which the Lord has inflicted upon you because of it, amend your life from now on.”

When he heard this, the man confessed his own crime and promised that thereafter he would never sin again, nor perform the office of a priest, but would henceforth live among the laity. Only then did the holy man lay his hand upon him. Within a few days he was cured, including by the restoration of his hair; and, glorifying God and giving thanks also to the holy man, he returned to his own home in our presence.

After this, in my presence, a certain boy was brought to him who was suffering from the spirit of a most savage demon. When Macarius had placed one hand upon the boy’s head and the other upon his heart, he prayed to God until he caused the boy to be suspended in the air. The boy, swollen throughout like a wineskin, grew so greatly that no one could estimate his size; then suddenly he discharged water from every part of his body with a tremendous cry. Thus, as all that swelling gradually subsided, he returned to the former health of his body. The saint anointed him with holy oil, poured blessed water over him, and restored him to his father, commanding that for forty days he should neither allow him to eat meat nor drink wine. In this way he restored him to perfect health.

At one time this same holy Macarius was harassed by thoughts of vainglory, which wished to draw him away from the very cell in which he lived. They persuaded him and displayed to him a certain appearance of good work, so that he might go to Rome for its sake, supposedly to heal those who there were tormented by the most wicked demons. For this most blessed man exercised great grace of divine power against unclean spirits.

When he had resisted for a long time such inducements, by which the demon wished to drive him away, and saw himself being pressed with great force, he suddenly threw himself across the threshold of his cell, leaving his feet outside the cell, and said:

“Drag me away, demons, if you can, and pull me along. I will not go on my own feet where you wish. If, therefore, you can carry me in this way, behold, I shall set out,” confirming this with an oath that he would not rise from that place until evening. “If you do not move me,” he said, “know that you will never again be heard by me.”

Thus he lay motionless for a long time, and finally rose when deep evening was approaching. But during the night that followed, the demons again began to trouble him. He filled a basket capable of holding two bushels with sand, placed it upon his shoulders, and walked about in the desert places.

A certain Theosebius, an Antiochene by birth, encountered him; he was also surnamed Cosmetur. He said to him:

“Abba, why are you carrying such a heavy burden? Transfer to me what you are carrying instead, and do not weary your shoulders.”

But he replied: “I am troubling the one who troubles me. While enjoying idleness, he compels me to undertake some journey.”

After he had walked for a long time under this burden and exhausted his little body with its weight, he returned to his cell.

This same holy man related another miracle to us—for he was a presbyter. “I observed,” he said, “that at the time when I was giving the holy mysteries to the brothers, I never gave them to the monk Marcus; rather, an angel always gave the holy gifts from the altar to him. Yet I saw only the hand of the giver.”

This Marcus was a man of extraordinary intellect. While still young, he retained the New and Old Testaments by heart. He was exceedingly gentle and quiet, and singular in his commitment to chastity (Palladius, ch. 21).

One day, since I had nothing else to do, I went to him in the extreme old age of his life. Sitting beside his door like a new and inexperienced monk, and considering him to be above ordinary men—as indeed he was—I wished to hear what he said and observe what he did. He was alone inside, about one hundred years old, and had also lost his teeth through the extreme length of his life.

He was therefore arguing with himself and with the demon, saying:

“What more do you seek, decrepit [Col. 0276B] old man? Look, you have tasted oil and wine. What more do you desire at the end of your life, devourer and worshiper of your belly?”

He spoke abusively to himself in such words. Then he said to the demon:

“Do I still owe you something that you might steal? Can you find nothing else? Now depart from me, enemy of mankind.”

And, as though taunting himself, he said:

“Come, most wicked old man; how long shall I remain with you?”

A certain Paphnutius, a disciple of this blessed man, reported to us that at one time a certain beast [Note: [Col. 0395C] *A certain beast.* Here Palladius has *hyaena*. Is *belua* here therefore a corruption of *belba*, that is, *hyaena*? Certainly *b* and *u* frequently interchange. Thus in book 1, ch. 11, where our text has *ferae*, Palladius has *hyaenae*. Capitolinus, in *Gordian III*, has “ten *belbi*, that is, hyaenas.” Yet *belua* is also written for *hyaena*. Gloss: ὕαινα ζῶον, “a beast.” Certainly among authors *belua* is taken sometimes for an elephant, sometimes for a hyaena, and sometimes for a whale. It seems to mean *hyaena* here also, above, ch. 5, in the story of Nathanael: “For many beasts are known to be in those deserts.” There Hervetus translates from his Greek text: [Col. 0395D] “For there are hyaenas in those places.”] brought its blind cub to Saint Marcus. It struck the threshold of his door with its head, entered to him while he was sitting outside in the courtyard, and threw its cub before his feet [Note: [Col. 0275D] Palladius, ch. 20, relates this of Macarius.].

He took the cub, spat into its eyes, and prayed. Immediately it saw the light which it had lost, and its mother took it away, having nourished it with her own milk. On the following day the same beast brought the holy and most blessed man a sheepskin. The servant of Christ mentioned above left it to Saint Athanasius the bishop; and Saint Melania later said that she had received it from the most blessed Athanasius.

And what wonder is it if he who caused the lions to become tame for Daniel also gave such wisdom to this beast?

It was also said of the blessed Marcus that from the time when he had received the grace of spiritual washing, he had never spat upon the ground—not even when he was sixty years old after baptism, although he had been forty years old before baptism.

The bodily appearance of this athlete of Christ was as follows—for I ought also to tell you this, servant of God Lause, since my insignificance lived with him for a long time and came to know him carefully. He was short in stature. His face was not covered by a full beard, but only around his lips; and a little hair could be seen around his chin. Because of his excessive abstinence and almost continual fasting, his face appeared bare, unlike the faces of other men.

Once, when I came to him in great sadness, I said to him:

“Abba Macarius, what do you command me to do? Various thoughts are disturbing my mind, saying to me, ‘Depart from here, because you see that you are accomplishing nothing.’”

He replied: “Say to your thoughts: ‘For Christ’s sake I guard the walls of this cell.’”

These few things, most learned lover and servant of God, I have indicated to you from among the many deeds and sayings of Saint Macarius.

## CHAPTER VII. The Life of Moses the Ethiopian, a Monk of Egypt

A certain Moses, an Ethiopian by birth (Palladius, ch. 22), was black in bodily complexion and was a slave of a certain official [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Official.* Hervetus, in ch. 22 of Palladius, has: “He was the slave of a certain man who governed the state”; οἰκέτης ὑπῆρχεν πολιτευομένου τινός. See *Onomasticon*.]. His master had cast him away because of his detestable behavior. For he was said both to commit robberies openly and to perpetrate murders. It is necessary for me also to recount his wickedness, so that I may more clearly display the greatness of his repentance.

Some reported, therefore, that he had been the leader of certain robbers. Among his robberies, the following deed of his was also remembered. A certain shepherd, who was staying in a particular region with his dogs, had obstructed him one night as he was going out on a criminal undertaking. Moses became so angry that he wished to kill him.

He therefore watched the place where the shepherd enclosed his sheep. When he was informed that the shepherd was across the Nile with his flock, and that the river had risen so greatly that it extended a thousand paces beyond its channel, Moses held his sword firmly in his teeth, placed his garment over his head, and swam across the entire river until he reached the sheepfold.

When the shepherd, seeing him swimming, hid submerged in the sand, Moses took four selected rams, slaughtered them, tied them together with a rope, and swam back in the same way. Finding a small and hidden place, he stripped the sheep of their skins, devoured the meat that seemed best, and sold the remainder, exchanging it for wine. He alone drank eighteen Italic measures [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Italic measures.* The Moretianus and Insulensis manuscripts have *cyathi*. In the Greek of Palladius, ch. 22, it is Σαΐτιν πιὼν ὡς Ἰταλικῶν δέκα καὶ ὀκτώ: “having drunk about eighteen Italic measures at least.”] of the wine, and then hurried back for fifty miles to the places where he had left his companions.

Such, then, was the man of whom I speak. At last, moved by some danger or necessity, he came to the monastery of the brothers. He seized the life of repentance with such force that he even placed Clemon, a partner in his wickedness [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Clemon, a partner in his wickedness.* In the Greek of Palladius preserved in the Paris manuscript: συμπαίκτην αὐτοῦ, “his companion in play” or “his accomplice.” In the Palatine manuscript it was συμπράκτης. In both Greek manuscripts, however, the reading was δαίμονα rather than Κλήμονα. Palladius should be corrected from Heraclides. On the same story, see Sozomen, book VI, ch. 29.], who had sinned with him from their earliest years, at a distance so that he might come to know the power of Christ [Note: [Col. 0277D] This is absent from Hervetus’s Palladius.].

The following deed of his is also reported. Four robbers had attacked his cell. Not knowing who the man living there was, they were asking about him. Moses seized them, bound them all together, and, placing them on his back like a sack of straw, brought them to the brothers, where they were all living together, saying:

“Since I can no longer harm anyone, what do you command concerning these men?”

Then even those whom he had carried away began to come to repentance, confessing their sins to God—especially because they loved Moses, who had formerly been called the leader of all the robbers. Glorifying the Lord, they too were converted because of his way of life and became excellent monks. They reasoned as follows:

“If this man, who was so powerful that he was considered invincible among robbers, has come to know and fear God in this way, why do we delay the salvation of our souls?”

[Col. 0278A] The demons once began to press this blessed Moses—for he must now be called by this title—to return to his former habit of impurity and fornication. He himself reported that he was tempted in so many and such great ways that they almost turned him away from his resolve to pursue a life of salvation.

He therefore went to that holy and blessed man Isidore, who lived in the places called Scetis, and reported to him the ways in which he was being attacked. But Isidore replied:

“I do not want you to be sad. These are still your beginnings, and for that reason such thoughts rise up violently against you, seeking your former habit. For just as a dog does not leave the butcher’s shop to which it is accustomed to go for food, but if it is shut up and no one remains there from whom the dog may hope to receive something, it departs; so also, if you persevere in your resolve of abstinence, mortifying your members that are upon the earth and excluding the entrance of gluttony—which is an incentive to fornication [Colossians 3]—the weary and defeated demon, to whom you provide no nourishment through food, will cease troubling you.”

Having heard this, the servant of Christ Moses returned to his cell and diligently cared for himself. Above all, he abstained from food, taking nothing except twelve dry ounces of bread, while nevertheless undertaking very heavy labor and performing fifty prayers during the day. Although he consumed his little body by these practices, even then his vain dreams did not cease.

Again, therefore, he went to another of the saints, a man of proven excellence, and said to him:

“What shall I do? Because of my former habit, my mind is continually darkened in dreams, my senses are disturbed, and my memory, familiar with carnal pleasures, does not withdraw from them.”

He replied:

“You still suffer this because you have not separated your mind from such thoughts. If, therefore, you are willing to occupy yourself for a while with vigils and to persist diligently in pure prayers, you will easily be able to free yourself from this affliction.”

Moses accepted this advice as a remedy from a man who had learned it through experience. He returned to his cell and determined throughout the entire night neither to bend his knees to the ground nor to give sleep to his eyes. Thus for six years he was accustomed to stand every night in the middle of his cell, always with his eyes open, and to pray; yet even then he could not be freed from the evil with which he struggled.

Again he undertook another and harsher kind of life, hoping in this way to overcome the demon. In the evening hours he would go out and make the rounds throughout the night of the dwellings of the aged monks who lived with long-continued vigilance. He often took their jars, which they call water vessels, filled them with water, and returned them full without anyone knowing. For they themselves sometimes fetched their water from places two miles away, and often from five.

One night, as he was coming, the demon lay in wait for him. Unable any longer to endure the contests of so great an athlete, while Moses was bent over and drawing water from the well, the demon struck his loins from above with a heavy club and left him half dead [Col. 0279A], without his perceiving what he had suffered or from whom.

On the following day, when a monk came there to draw water and saw the aforementioned Moses lying there, he reported it to the great Isidore the Scetian presbyter. Isidore himself went out with some others and immediately had Moses carried to the church of his monastery. There he suffered from such an illness for an entire year that only with difficulty could his body at last be restored to its former strength.

Then Saint Isidore said to him:

“Cease, Moses, provoking the demons so greatly and striving against them with such obstinacy. There is a definite measure even within the very purpose of the monastic life, within which it is proper for us to exercise our virtues.”

He replied:

“I will not withdraw from this intention of my mind so long as I see dreams and vain thoughts being separated from me.”

Then Isidore said to him:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, the shameful dreams have now departed from you. Therefore approach the communion of the holy mysteries with confidence. Know, however, that the demon appeared stronger than you for a time so that you could not boast that you had easily overcome so great a temptation; thus the event itself might contribute more to your salvation.”

Hearing this, Moses returned again to his cell, thereafter carefully observing moderation in his ascetic practice. Later—that is, after two months—Saint Isidore asked him whether the aforementioned spirit had continued to trouble him. He replied that he had suffered nothing of the kind from the hour when the servant of God had prayed for him.

Moses himself obtained such great grace from God against the demons that we were more frightened by flies than he was by demons.

We learned that this was the life of Moses the Ethiopian, who himself was counted among those great men. He died at the age of seventy-five at Scetis, where he had also become a presbyter and left seventy disciples at his death.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Life of Paul, a Monk from Mount Pherme

There is a mountain in Egypt that extends toward the immense solitude of the region of Scetis. Its name is Pherme (Palladius, ch. 23). Nearly five hundred highly ascetic monks live on this mountain. Among them was a certain man named Paul, an excellent monk, who lived in the following manner:

He never engaged in commerce of any kind, never performed any work, and accepted nothing from anyone except what he needed for food. He did nothing else except pray without ceasing. He had a fixed and clearly stated number of prayers—three hundred in all—and carried an equal number of pebbles gathered in the fold of his garment. Whenever he had completed a prayer, he would throw one pebble from his fold.

Once this man came to that holy Macarius who was surnamed Urbanus, because of his way of life. He said to him:

“Abba Macarius, I am very sad” (Palladius, ch. 24).

When Macarius compelled him to explain the cause of his sadness, Paul replied:

“It is said that in some village there is a virgin who has spent thirty years in a monastery. I learned that she fasts and passes entire weeks continually, tasting food only after every five days, and that each day she performs seven hundred prayers. When I learned this, I said that I was lost, because although I am a man and in sound bodily health, I cannot pray more than three hundred times.”

To this Saint Macarius replied:

“I, at sixty years of age, perform one hundred prayers each day and carry out as much work as can suffice for my life. I also reserve a definite time in which I offer greeting and conversation to the brothers, and my thoughts do not accuse or rebuke me as negligent on this account. But if you, who perform three hundred prayers, say that your conscience nevertheless reproves you, it is clear either that you do not perform these without some reproach, or that you do not wish to perform more although you are able.”

## CHAPTER IX. The Life of Chronius the Presbyter and Eulogius the Scholastic

Chronius, a presbyter of Nitria, once related to me:

“When I was still young and, wearied by the spirit of acedia, was languishing somewhat in mind, I fled from the monastery of my archimandrite and wandered as far as the mountain of Antony” (Palladius, ch. 25).

Antony was sitting at the farthest end of the desert, among places called Babylon and Hercules, from which one travels toward the Red Sea; the places were separated from the river by nearly thirty miles. When I came to his monastery, which was near the river, where his disciples Macarius and Amatus were sitting in the place called Pispir—and they buried the man mentioned above after his death—I waited there for five days to see Saint Antony.

It was said that he came to the monastery very frequently: sometimes after ten days, sometimes after twenty, and sometimes after five, according as God brought him there to benefit the many who flocked to that monastery.

Many brothers who were suffering from various needs had gathered there at that time. Among them was a certain Alexandrian monk named Eulogius (Palladius, ch. 26), together with another man who was afflicted by elephantiasis. They were said to have come there for this reason.

This Eulogius was a scholasticus [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Scholasticus.* In the Greek of Palladius, ch. 26, σχολαστικὸς ὑπῆρχεν ἐκ τῶν ἐγκυκλίων παιδευμάτων: “he was a scholasticus learned in the liberal disciplines.” See *Onomasticon*.], educated in secular literature. Seized by the desire for immortality, he had renounced the world. After selling and distributing all his possessions, he had kept a small amount of money for himself, with which he could live, since he was unable to work.

When a certain weakness of spirit was troubling him, and he could neither live patiently among many in a monastery nor endure a solitary life, he found a man lying in public in the street, so afflicted by the disease mentioned above that he seemed to be without hands and feet. Only his tongue was free from such torments, so that by it he might more effectively obtain a remedy for his sufferings from those who saw him.

When Eulogius saw him lying there, he prayed to God and made a certain pact with the Lord. Then he addressed him in these words:

“Lord God, in your name I receive this man afflicted by so terrible a disease, and refresh him [Col. 0281A] until the day of his death, so that through him I too may be saved. Therefore assist me, Christ, and grant me patience for such a ministry.”

Immediately he said to the man lying there:

“Brother, do you wish me to receive you into my house and support you by whatever means I can?”

When the sick man said that he would gladly accept this if Eulogius would be willing, Eulogius replied:

“Then I shall go and bring a donkey on which you may ride.”

The sick man consented with great joy. Eulogius did what he had said and carried him without delay to his lodging.

For fifteen years he served him with continual care and unceasing solicitude. Throughout all that time, the man to whom such service was rendered endured everything with thanksgiving and great patience. He was cared for by the hands of Eulogius, with medicines, food, and baths, according as his illness required.

After fifteen years, however, through the instigation of the demon, the sick man, forgetting all Eulogius’s labors and so many of his merits, began to wish to leave him and assail him with many insults and reproaches, saying:

“Runaway, you who have devoured your own household and stolen another man’s property! Do you think you have found in me an opportunity for your salvation?”

Eulogius begged him and, trying to appease his mind, said:

“No, my lord, please do not speak this way. Rather, tell me what I have done to grieve you, and I shall make amends.”

The man with elephantiasis said angrily:

“Go away; I do not want your flattering words. Throw me out into the street. I have no need of your relief.”

Eulogius replied:

“I beg you, be appeased, or tell me, venerable old man, what I have done to grieve you.”

But the elephantiasis sufferer, still harsher, said to him in anger:

“I can no longer endure your deceitful mockery. I will not tolerate your flattery and derision. Nor is this dry and meager life pleasing to me; I want to be filled with meat.”

When meats were brought to him by the most patient Eulogius, he began to shout again:

“You cannot satisfy my will, nor can I endure living in solitude with you. I want to see people and go into public.”

Eulogius said to him:

“I will bring you a multitude of brothers.”

The sick man, now more ferocious and almost blasphemous, replied:

“Woe to miserable me! I do not want to see your face, and you bring me others like yourself. You are merely a devourer of bread!”

Shaking himself, he shouted in an agitated voice:

“No, no! I want to go into public. O violence! Throw me into the place from which you took me.”

Such was his madness, and so completely had the demon turned his senses into something resembling the cries of wild beasts, that he would perhaps have hanged himself with a noose if he had possessed hands with which to do it.

Eulogius therefore went to the neighboring monks and said to them:

“What shall I do? This man with elephantiasis has driven me entirely to despair.”

They said to him:

“For what reason?”

He replied:

“Because what he is trying to inflict upon me is hard, and I do not know what to do. Shall I throw him out? But otherwise I have given my right hand to God, and I am very much afraid [Note: [Col. 0396A] *I am very much afraid.* That is, “I am exceedingly afraid.” The expression is often used in the sacred writings and in other authors.]. Shall I not throw him out? Yet I cannot again endure so many and such great evils day and night. I do not know what I should do with him.”

They addressed him in these words:

“While that great Antony still lives—for this was what he was called—go up to him. Place the sick man on a boat and take him to his monastery, waiting there until he comes out of his cave. When you see him, tell him what you are suffering and ask him for advice. Whatever he tells you to do, do it, and obey his instructions, knowing that whatever he commands you is commanded to you by God.”

Immediately, gladly instructed by the words of the brothers, Eulogius overcame the aforementioned sick man with gentle entreaties, placed him in a small coastal boat, carried him out of the city during the night, and brought him to the dwelling of Saint Antony’s disciples.

It happened that Saint Antony arrived there the following day in the evening hours. Chronius reported to me that he came dressed in a cloak made of skins. Whenever he came to the monastery of the brothers, he used to call for Macarius and ask him:

“Have any brothers come here?”

Macarius would say that some had come.

“Are they from Egypt,” Antony would ask, “or from Jerusalem?”

He had instructed them to give this sign: whenever people who were not sufficiently worthy of his conversation arrived, they were to say that Egyptians had come. Whenever certain men appeared to be holy and spiritual, they were to report that men from Jerusalem had come.

When Antony came, therefore, according to his custom, he asked whether the brothers there were from Jerusalem or Egypt. Macarius replied that he had seen some of both kinds.

When Antony learned that Egyptians had come, he said to Macarius:

“Prepare a little lentil porridge [Note: [Col. 0396A] *Lentil porridge.* In Palladius, ch. 26, the Greek is φακόν, “lentils.” I think that it was a porridge made from lentils, as occurs elsewhere in these books.]. I shall eat with them.”

After completing his prayer, he ordered them to leave. But when he learned that men from Jerusalem had come, he sat with them throughout the entire night, speaking to them about matters that would benefit their salvation. Chronius reported that Antony sat with them that night and summoned each of those who had gathered to him individually.

When Antony heard that no one was calling for Eulogius there, he himself called him three times in the darkness in his own voice, using his name. When the aforementioned scholasticus did not answer, thinking that another Eulogius was being called, Antony said to him again:

“I am calling you, Eulogius, who have come from the city of Alexandria.”

Eulogius replied:

“What, I beg you, do you command?”

Antony said:

“Why have you come here?”

Eulogius replied:

“He who was willing to reveal my name to you has doubtless also revealed the reason for my coming.”

Then Antony said:

“I know why you have come, but tell it before all these brothers, so that all may hear.”

Thus commanded by the great Antony, the servant of Christ Eulogius related before them all:

“I found this man with elephantiasis cast out in the public street, where no human being cared for him. I promised God that I would serve his illness, so that through him I might be saved, and he through me. It is now fifteen years since we came together, just as I believe your holiness has learned everything. Since, after so many years, he has suffered no harm from me, yet now he troubles me with various storms and tempests, I have considered throwing him out. For this reason I have come to your holiness, so that you may teach me by your counsel what I should do and assist me with your prayers. I am completely wearied and tormented by the worst impulses.”

Antony then replied in a stern and angry voice:

“You are throwing him away, Eulogius? But he does not throw away the one who knows that he was made by God. You are throwing him away? He will find someone better than you, and God will choose someone to gather up the abandoned.”

When Eulogius fell silent in terror at these words, Saint Antony left him and began again to strike the sick man with his own words. He addressed him with a very loud cry:

“You elephantiasis sufferer, hideous with filth and mud, worthy neither of earth nor heaven, do you never cease crying out in insult against God? Do you not know that Christ is the one who ministers to you? How have you dared to speak such things against Christ? For Christ’s sake this man has subjected himself to such service and attendance.”

He left the sick man wounded by this biting speech. Then, turning his words to the other brothers and addressing each according to his particular condition, he returned again to Eulogius and the sick man and said to them:

“Let neither of you, my sons, turn elsewhere or separate from the other. Return in peace to your cell, in which you have lived for so long, putting aside all sadness. For now my Lord will send something to you. This trial has happened to you because both of you have come to the end of your lives, and now each of you will deserve to be crowned.

“Therefore do nothing differently, lest perhaps the angel who comes be unable to find you in the place I have mentioned, and you be deprived of your crowns.”

When they had quickly returned to their cell and arrived there with their peace restored, Eulogius died first within forty days. After another three days, the aforementioned sick man also died, with his mind entirely sound.

Chronius, after spending a long time in the Thebaid, went down to the Alexandrian monasteries. It happened that he arrived on the day that the brothers were then observing as the fortieth day of one man and the third day of the other.

When Chronius learned this, he was astonished. He took the holy Gospel, placed it in the midst of the brothers, and, binding himself by an oath, explained everything to them in order, saying:

“I myself interpreted the words of all those whom I have mentioned, because Saint Antony did not know how to speak Greek. I knew both languages and spoke between them, answering the one group in Greek and the other in Egyptian.”

Chronius himself also related this to us (Palladius, ch. 27): on that very night [Col. 0283D] when Antony sent the blessed Eulogius away, Saint Antony had said that he had prayed to God throughout an entire year that the places of sinners and righteous people might be shown to him by revelation.

He said that he had seen a certain giant, tall enough to reach the clouds, of a gloomy color, with his hands stretched out toward heaven; beneath his feet a lake had spread out like the sea. There, Antony said, he saw souls flying like birds. All those that flew above the giant’s hands and head were preserved; but any that were struck by his hands were plunged into the lake.

He reported that a voice then came to him, saying:

“All these souls whom you see flying are the souls of the righteous, who rest in the dwelling of paradise. But those souls are sent to the underworld: all who have obeyed the carnal will, and all who, retaining anger, have attempted to repay evil with evil.”

Both Chronius and Saint Hierax, as well as many other brothers living nearby, reported to us the things I shall now relate.

## CHAPTER X. The Life of Paul the Simple, a Disciple of the Blessed Antony
Paul by name (Palladius, chapter 28), a certain rustic devoted to agriculture, exceptionally good and quite simple, was married to a wife who was very beautiful in appearance but morally corrupt. After he had for a long time known that she was sinning by secret deceit, he one day returned from the fields and disgracefully found her, suddenly catching her lying with another man—although divine providence was thereby directing the aforesaid Paul toward a better way of life—he smiled somewhat bashfully and addressed them both in these words:

“Good, good,” he said. “Know for certain that this has absolutely nothing to do with me; and I swear by Jesus, who sees these things, that I shall have her no longer. Go, then: she will be yours, together with her children. For my part,” he said, “I shall go, and from now on I profess myself a monk.”

After this, without saying anything to anyone, he climbed the eight intervening stages and went to Saint Antony. When his door was struck by Paul, Antony came out; and when he asked what Paul wanted, Paul said to him: “I wish to become a monk.”

Antony replied: “Since you are very old—sixty years of age—you cannot become a monk here. Rather, go back to your village and devote yourself to the work of a cultivator, so that you may both live by the life of laborers and give thanks to God. Know that you are unequal to the hardships and labor of the deserts.”

The old man replied: “Whatever you teach me, I shall do.”

Antony again said: “I have told you that you are very old and cannot fulfill what you seek. Depart; and if you desire to be a monk, go instead to less rigorous monasteries, to brothers who can patiently bear with the weakness of your body. For I sit here alone, taking food only after five days, and even then in the greatest poverty.”

Antony wished to drive Paul away by these and similar words. But when Paul would not yield, Antony shut himself inside the doorway of his cell because of him and remained there continuously for three days, without coming out even when bodily necessity pressed him. Yet Paul, though excluded from the door for so long, did not leave.

On the fourth day, when Saint Antony was compelled by natural necessity, he came out and said to him again: “Go away, old man. Why are you troubling me? You cannot live with me.”

Paul replied: “Nothing else can happen except that I live and die here.”

Saint Antony then looked around in every direction and saw that Paul had brought nothing with him for the nourishment of life—not bread, not water, nor anything else—and yet that on the fourth day he continued in unbroken fasting. Fearing that, being unaccustomed to a prolonged fast, he might die from excessive exhaustion and thereby leave Antony with some blame, he finally accepted him.

Antony then began to spend all his days in a manner of life such as he did not know himself to have experienced, not even when he still appeared to be young. He offered him date-palm fibers and said: “Take these, and weave ropes as you see me doing.”

When the old man had taken them and, with the greatest labor, had made fifteen of what they call orgyias up to the ninth hour [Note: Hervetus, in Palladius, chapter 28, translates Greek ὀργυίας (*orgyias*) as *ulnas* (“ells” or “cubit-lengths”).], Antony said to him: “You have woven badly. Undo what has been done and weave it again.”

He imposed this heavy burden upon the old man, who had been fasting for four days, so that, seeing himself unequal to such labor, Paul would finally be compelled by necessity to depart from Antony and abandon the life of the monks. But Paul, on the contrary, rose more vigorously to the task, unwove those same ropes, and wove them again. The labor of repeating the work was especially difficult, since a rope that had once been twisted first had to be untwisted and restored to its former shape, and then woven anew in another manner.

[Col. 0284B–C]

When Antony saw that the old man had listened willingly and patiently to these commands, had undertaken the repeated labor without resentment, and had not shown even for a moment a sorrowful expression or murmured against him, his heart was moved with compunction. As the sun was already setting, he addressed the old man:

“Tell me, old man: shall we eat a portion of bread?”

Paul replied: “As you wish, abba.”

This reply also moved Antony: at the mention of food, Paul did not rush forward at once, but placed everything in the power of the one who was giving the order.

“Set the table, then,” Antony said, “and bring the loaves.”

When Paul had obediently done so, Saint Antony placed before him the loaves that the Egyptians call paximates, each weighing six ounces. He sprinkled water over his own portion, for the paximates were dry; before Paul he placed three portions.

Saint Antony recited the psalm he was accustomed to recite and offered forty prayers, in order to test Paul in this way also. Paul again prayed with him patiently and willingly. For, as I suppose, he preferred to be among scorpions rather than live with an adulteress.

After twelve prayers, they finally sat down to eat, at an hour deep in the night. Saint Antony took one paximas and did not touch another. The old man ate more slowly; while he still had a little of one paximas left, Antony waited for him until he had consumed everything he was eating.

Then Antony said to him again: “Eat, old man, and take another paximas.”

Paul replied: “I shall eat this second one too, if I see you doing the same. If you do not eat, I shall not eat.”

Antony said: “This is enough for me; I am a monk.”

Paul replied: “It is enough for me too, for I also desire to be a monk.”

After this Antony rose, recited twelve psalms, offered an equal number of prayers, and rested briefly at the beginning of the night. Rising again at midnight, he kept vigil until daylight by singing psalms and praying. Paul did the same.

When Saint Antony saw that the old man was so ready for everything, he said to him: “Behold, brother: if you can live in this manner every day, you shall remain with me.”

Paul replied: “I do not know whether you might perhaps command something more. But I am confident that I shall easily fulfill what I have now seen.”

The following day Antony said to him: “Behold, in the name of the Lord, you have now become a monk.”

After Saint Antony had thus come to trust that Paul had satisfied him in every respect, and after some months—when he had established that Paul’s soul was already perfected, since true and complete simplicity dwelt in him—he built him a small cell three or four miles away, with the help of divine grace, and said to him:

“Behold: since you have now become a monk, remain alone, so that you may also test the demons.”

After Paul had lived there for one year, he received divine grace against human illnesses and against the power of demons.

[Col. 0286A–B]

One day a certain man was brought to Saint Antony, a man whom a most wicked demon tormented cruelly. The demon held authority over the other unclean spirits and even hurled blasphemous words against heaven itself. When Saint Antony saw him, he said to those who had brought the man:

“This is not my work; for I have not yet received divine grace against the prince of the demonic host. This is what is sought from Simple Paul.”

Saint Antony then went with those who had arrived to the aforesaid Paul and said to him: “Abba Paul, drive this demon from the soul of this man, so that he may return safely to his own people and bless the Lord.”

Paul replied: “What, then, of you?”

Antony said: “I have no time; I am engaged in another work.”

Saint Antony left him and returned to his own cell.

The old man then rose and, praying with the utmost concentration, said to the man who was suffering from the demon: “Abba Antony has commanded you to depart from this man’s soul, so that he may glorify the Lord.”

The demon shouted many things in insult to the divine nature: “I will not leave, detestable old man.”

Paul seized the hide with which he covered his shoulders and beat the demon, repeating: “Come out, because abba Antony has commanded it.”

The demon uttered insulting words against Saint Antony as well and heaped even harsher abuse upon Paul, shouting:

“Detestable old men—what our forgetfulness has overlooked! Insatiable men, who are not content with what belongs to you! What have you in common with us? Why do you exercise your tyranny against us?”

Finally Paul said to him: “You will come out of this man, or I shall go, and Christ will hear this from me. By Jesus, if you refuse to come out, I shall go at once and tell Christ this, and woe will be yours.”

Again the demon began to shout more fiercely against the divine nature and said: “I will not come out.”

Paul then became angry with the resisting demon and left his cell in the very midst of the flames of day. Such is the heat of Egypt that it is believed to surpass the burning of Babylon’s furnace. Upon the very crag of the mountain Paul stood immovable like a heavenly column and addressed these words to Jesus in his prayer:

“You see, Jesus Christ, who were crucified under Pontius Pilate, that I shall not descend from this rock, nor take food or drink, but shall surely die, until you drive the unclean spirit from this man and deign to make him free from such death.”

While he was saying these things, before he had completed the words of his own mouth, the demon cried out in a very loud voice:

“Go, go! I am coming out; I am being forced. Behold, I am leaving the man and will approach him no further. The simplicity of Paul presses and pursues me, and I do not know where it comes from.”

At once the unclean spirit came out of the man and was transformed into an enormous dragon seventy cubits long; it immediately rolled away into the Red Sea, so that what had been spoken by the Holy Spirit might be fulfilled: “The righteous makes faith manifest” (Proverbs 12).

And again, in another place: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66).

For the most wretched and contemptible demons are commonly driven away from great men by the mere strength of faith, while the great demons are driven away by the simple and humble.

[Col. 0287B]

These are the miracles of the simple and humble Paul, and many others like them and even greater ones [supply: he performed], who was called Simple by men.

## CHAPTER XI. The Life of Abba Pachomius [or Pachonius]

A certain man named Pachomius [Note: Palladius, chapter 29, calls him Pachon], who was seventy years old, lived in the region called Scetis.

It happened that, when a powerful desire for sexual intercourse began to press upon me and I endured the struggle against filthy thoughts and nocturnal insomnia with great difficulty and distress, the force of this condition compelled me to leave the desert where I was. I told none of my neighbors about this plague and such burning, nor did I confess anything of the kind to my teacher Evagrius. Secretly, however, I went into the inner and more desolate parts of the desert, where, during fifteen days in the place called Scetis, I saw many venerable Fathers who had grown old there. Among them I was also able to converse with the aforementioned Pachomius.

Because I found that he held nearly first place among the other monks, I confidently laid before him the anxiety of my heart. He spoke to me as follows:

“Let what you are suffering not seem strange to you. The fact that you have fallen into this disturbance not through negligence of mind or sloth is sufficiently demonstrated by the nature of the place, the lack of all things, and, as no one can doubt, the absence of women. Rather, you are suffering this temptation because of your zeal for and desire of chastity.

“For a threefold struggle arises from the onset of fornication. Sometimes our flesh grows wanton if it is excessively healthy within us; often this illness proceeds from empty thoughts; and sometimes the demon fights against us because he envies us. I have frequently examined these matters and have always found them to be so.

“For, as you yourself see, although I am very old and have lived forty years in this cell, exercising the greatest care for my salvation, I am still troubled by such a temptation even to the present day.”

With an oath the saint himself said this:

“For twelve years after my fiftieth year, neither by night nor by day did this illness ever depart from me. I came to suspect that I had been deprived of God’s help and therefore rightly thought that I was being overcome by the demon’s power. Yet at that time I preferred to perish by some irrational death rather than surrender to such a bodily disease with so obscene a deformity.”

He then went out and traversed the whole desert. He found a cave belonging to some wild beast [Palladius: hyena], and threw himself into it naked during the day, so that—as he was certain would happen—he might be devoured by the beasts emerging from it.
