When he had lain there until the evening hours—according to what is written, “The sun knows its setting; you have appointed darkness, and it is night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The young lions roar, seeking to seize and seek their food from God” (Psalm 103)—a female beast and a male came out and, led by his scent, approached him. Licking him with their tongues from his head all the way to his feet, they left him untouched and unharmed, although he thought that he was about to be devoured by them. Lying there through the entire night, he suffered nothing at all.

Thinking and believing that the Lord had altogether spared me, I soon returned to my cell. For a few days the demon was quiet; then again he attacked me much more violently than usual, so that he nearly compelled me to sin with a blasphemous mouth.

For the demon was transformed into a certain Ethiopian girl whom I remembered having seen in my youth gathering stalks during harvest. When she suddenly began to sit upon my knees, she stirred all my limbs so powerfully that I thought I had nearly committed the crime with her.

In anger and fury I struck her with my right hand, and immediately—as it seemed—she vanished. And if you believe what I say, for two whole years I could not bear the stench of her on the hand with which I had struck her.

Terrified by the greatest anxiety and despair of soul, I wandered into the innermost and most desolate desert. There I found a small asp. In anger I took it in my hand and applied it to my genitals, hoping that its bite would bring me death. I even rubbed down the serpent’s head, crushing it against my private parts, as though the cause of my temptation proceeded from them.

Yet even then the snake did not bite me, because, as I believe, divine grace watched over me. At that moment, when a voice descended into my consciousness, I heard it say:

“Go, Pachomius; persist in your contest. For this reason I allowed you to be overcome by the demon’s power: lest you begin to grow proud as though you were stronger, but so that, recognizing your weakness and placing no confidence in your manner of life, you might always flee to divine assistance.”

After I had been satisfied by this answer, I returned to my own retreat. From then on I sat with confidence, no longer suffering any anxiety or distress from the struggle, but living out the remaining days of my life with a mind at peace. When my enemy saw that he had been so despised by me and could no longer trouble me, he departed in confusion.

By these words Saint Pachomius strengthened me and made me more courageous against the battles with ambushing demons, and sufficiently encouraged me to endure, by divine grace, the contest against the spirit of fornication. He then sent me back to my cell.

## CHAPTER XII. The Life of the Monk Stephen

A certain Stephen, a native of Libya (Palladius, chapter 30), lived for sixty years in the part of that region called Marmarica and Mareotis. He became so perfect a monk and possessed such judgment in discerning ambiguities that he merited this divine grace: whoever came to him saddened for any reason at all departed joyful after seeing him and hearing his words.

He was also known to the holy man Antony, and he survived even into the days of our own time. I myself was unable to see him, because long distances of land separated us.

Saint Ammonius and Evagrius, together with those who were with them, once told me the following. They said that they had found him at a certain time suffering from such an illness that he was tormented by an ulcer on the very private parts of his body—an ulcer that some call a phagedaena [Note: Greek φαγέδαινα; Latin *phagedaena*. The term has three senses: ulcers generally that continually become larger and worse; a particular swollen, deep ulcer extending into neighboring parts; or an excessive appetite for food. See Joannes Gorraeus, *Definitiones medicae*.].

While he was being treated by a certain physician, they said, “we found him working with his hands, twisting ropes from palm fibers, and conversing with us, while he presented the remaining parts of his body to the physician and the knife. He was so remote from bodily sensation through the grace of patience that he seemed to believe that the limbs of another man were being cut apart.”

[Col. 0289B–C]

When all the private parts had been cut away, he felt absolutely nothing. His mind had been so separated from human affairs and occupied solely with heavenly thoughts.

We, however, were filled with sadness and confounded by the horror of his illness. We were thinking that the life of such a man had fallen into a disease of this kind, so that he had to be cut in such a manner. Perceiving this, that blessed servant of God, Stephen, said:

“My sons, see to it that your minds are not harmed by contemplating this illness [Note: *valetudo* here means illness or infirmity.]. Nothing that God does proceeds from any malice; rather, everything looks toward a good end and a desired outcome. Perhaps even that part of the body deserved to be handed over to such punishments; and it was better for him to receive his due here than to be reserved for eternal torments after this age.”

The contemplation of his words therefore sent us away edified and strengthened in the pursuit of patience. For this reason I have related these things, lest anyone perhaps wonder if we see—or later see—one of the saints suffering from an illness of this kind.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Valens

There was again a certain man named Valens, a Palestinian by birth but Corinthian in mind, and therefore puffed up in his understanding (Palladius, chapter 31). For in the minds of the Corinthians there is always a certain swelling and inflation of spirit, just as blessed the Apostle Paul reproaches them for this vice when he writes to them, saying: “And you are puffed up” (1 Corinthians 4).

After this same Valens came to the desert, where he lived with us for many years and attained to the discipline of a difficult life, he rose to such a peak of pride that he was overcome by diabolical mockeries and deceptions. For, gradually deceiving him through his conceit in teaching, the demon brought him to the point where he thought himself to be some great person, as though every day he enjoyed the sight and ministry of angels.

His closest acquaintances reported that one day, while he was working in the darkness, the needle with which he used to make a basket fell from his hands. Since he could not find it—because he could not see in the dark—a lamp was lit for him through the demon’s agency, and in this way he found the needle he had lost. Renewed by this very inflation, he was raised to such swelling pride that he even despised participation in the sacred mysteries of Christ.

It happened that certain travelers came there and brought various kinds of vegetables, nuts, and fruits to the church for the brothers. When our priest, Saint Macarius, had received them and sent to each man as much as one hand could hold, he also sent Valens a portion along with the others. Valens beat and abused the man who had brought the portion, saying to him:

“Go and tell Macarius that I am not worse than he is, so that he should send blessings to me.”

When Saint Macarius heard of this error of his and came to him on another day to console and advise him, saying, “You have been deceived, brother Valens; cease from this in future and pray to the Lord,” he could not persuade him. When Valens refused entirely to listen to him, Macarius left sorrowful at his downfall.

The demon then became certain that Valens would yield to its deceptions and schemes as it wished. Secure in his destruction, the demon immediately devised the following plan.

It was transformed into the image of the Savior and came to Valens by night with a chorus of a thousand angels—as it pretended—holding lighted lamps. A fiery wheel preceded them, on which it pretended that the Savior was seated. One of the angels went before him and said:

“Christ has been pleased with your way of life and the commendable character of your conduct, and he has come, desiring to see you. Therefore, come out of your cell and do nothing except, when you see him approaching from a distance, hasten to bow down and worship him. Then return to your dwelling.”

Valens came out of his cell, believing that he saw the divine offices of heavenly ministry, with everything shining in the radiance of the lamps. He saw the Antichrist himself standing no more than a stadium away, fell prostrate upon the ground, and worshiped the one whom he believed to be God.

His mind was so gravely injured that, when he entered the church the following day, he said to the brothers assembled together:

“I no longer need communion, for today I have seen Christ himself.”

The venerable Fathers then bound him in iron chains and spent an entire year treating him with their prayers. The form of the remedy was this: they gave him over to the manner of life of secular people, so that, because he had nothing in common with the saints, the inflation and swelling of his spirit might cease. As the saying goes, contrary things must be cured by contrary remedies.

I believe this also to be very necessary and useful for readers: that we have inserted into the pages of this little book the lives of such men as well, just as we know that the tree by which good and evil are known was planted among the holy trees of paradise (Genesis 2). Thus, if someone should at some time accomplish something great in his life, he will not boast of it as a display of his own virtue.

For frequently the very victory of great virtues becomes an occasion and cause of some ruin for us, unless we hasten by the straight road toward the glory of our purpose. For it is written: “I saw the righteous perishing in his righteousness, and this too is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 7).

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Heron [in Lipomanius, Neron]

There was a certain man named Heron (Palladius, chapter 32), who lived near me. He was Alexandrian by birth, urban in manner, young, intelligent in mind, and of a pure and commendable life. After many labors, excessive exertions, and a life filled with virtues to the highest degree, he nevertheless fell through some swelling of his soul into such ruin that he thought himself superior to the holy and venerable Fathers. He uttered such insulting words against Saint Evagrius [Palladius: Macarius] that he said to him:

“They are deceived by a very great error who believe your teaching. One ought to use no teacher other than Christ.”

He also abused a holy testimony to strengthen the purpose of his own folly, saying that the Savior himself had said: “Call no one on earth your teacher” (Matthew 25).

He himself fell into such blindness and dullness of heart that afterward it became necessary to bind him with chains and iron, because he no longer wished to approach even the holy mysteries.

Yet, as the truth of the matter stands, he had possessed immense virtue and an austere life, so that many who had lived with him reported that for three months he frequently received no food, being content solely with participation in the holy mysteries and with wild herbs, if he could find any.

I seem also to have encountered him at the time when I was traveling to Scetis with blessed Alban [Palladius: Albino]. Scetis itself was forty miles from us. During the journey we ate twice and drank water three times; he, however, took no food at all. Traveling on foot, he first recited fifteen psalms. Then he recited what is called the Great Psalm; afterward he recited the Epistle to the Hebrews, Isaiah, part of Jeremiah, and the Gospel of Luke, as well as Solomon’s Proverbs. He recited them from memory while walking, and hurried along so swiftly that we could not keep up with him.

In the end, driven as though by a kind of fire through the deceit of the evil demon, he did not return to his cell.

He went instead to the city of Alexandria and, as the saying goes, drove out one nail with another. For by his own choice he fell among those with whom people live in this manner. Yet from this he later found, unwillingly, a remedy for his salvation.

He attended the spectacles of the circus and the theater and remained in taverns day and night. When he had wholly surrendered himself in these places to gluttony and drunkenness, he also fell into the mire of feminine desire. While he was planning to sin, he began to speak with a mime and disclosed his own wound to her.

For a pustule called a carbuncle arose on his private parts, and he suffered such an illness for six months that his natural organs rotted and fell away from the root.

Afterward, when he had recovered his health except for that part of his body which he had lost, he returned to divine wisdom and confessed to the holy Fathers everything that had happened to him. Yet he could not fulfill his repentance through deeds, because after a few days he died his appointed death.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Ptolemy

There was yet another man named Ptolemy (Palladius, chapter 33), who lived in such a manner that it is difficult to relate it, since it appears indescribable.

He lived in the outer reaches beyond those places we have often mentioned as Scetis, in the region called Clima. Yet no monk could live in that place, because a well of water seemed to be eighteen miles away.

Ptolemy therefore carried several Cilician vessels [Note: “Cilician vessels”: perhaps amphorae or flasks from Cilicia? See the *Onomasticon*] there with him. During December and January he filled them by gathering dew from the rocks with a sponge, for a great deal of dew falls in those regions at that time. This sufficed for him to drink during the fifteen years he lived there.

Entirely cut off from spiritual instruction, from conversation with holy men whose words might have benefited him, and from frequent participation in the mysteries of Christ, he suddenly became almost alienated from himself and strayed so far from the right path that he said there was no providence governing things, but that everything was carried along by its own movements.

The enemy of human life therefore persuaded him, entering completely into his soul and saying:

“If matters stand thus, why do you wear yourself out in vain, Ptolemy? For what reward do you labor, since there is no recompense for merits? And even if there were a recompense, what reward would be sufficient for you in return for such labors? What judgment do the Scriptures threaten, when everything is slipping away without providence?”

Broken by these demonic thoughts, wretched Ptolemy is said to have gone mad and departed from natural prudence. Even to the present day he is said to remain in Egypt in this error, devoted solely to gluttony and drunkenness. He habitually has no good conversation at all with anyone, but returns from public places mute and stunned (*eneus*) [Note: Fabri’s edition has *Eneus*, Lipomanius *Aeneus*, as though an allusion to a proper name were intended. The translator retained the Greek-derived term *eneus*, from ἐνεός or ἐννεός, meaning “struck senseless, mute.” See the note above, Book I, Life of Abraham, chapter 5, note 10, and the *Onomasticon*], presented before the eyes of Christians as a pitiable spectacle filled with tears; he is an object of mockery and deception to all who do not understand the grace of our way of life.

Ptolemy fell into this madness through a kind of irrational presumption. Deceived by the author of crimes, he thought that he surpassed all the holy Fathers in the power of knowledge. Having thereby become the enemy’s own, he fell into this pit of destruction and never deigned to speak with men who had used the rudders of spiritual wisdom.

Thus neglected and negligent, he descended into the depths of death, like a tree rich in leaves that is suddenly shown, in a single moment, to be bare and dry, according to what is written: “Those who have no rudders fall like leaves” (Proverbs 11).

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning a Virgin of Jerusalem

I knew a certain virgin from Jerusalem (Palladius, chapter 34), clothed in a hair shirt and continually enclosed for six years, tasting nothing that could provide any pleasure. At last, deprived of divine assistance, she was overcome by a disease of such immense pride that she suffered the kind of ruin of which we speak.

For she suddenly opened the window of her little cell and admitted the man who used to supply her with the necessities of life; she lay with him.

This evil arose because she had not entered the monastic life according to a spiritual purpose or because of love of God, but through the lure of human vanity, which is generated by the desire for empty glory and by the weak and unstable will of the mind.

While she occupied all her thoughts with malicious criticisms of another person’s life, the angel of holiness departed from her, and she left herself no guardian at all of her own chastity.

For this reason we describe both kinds of life among deeply religious people: the lives of those who, after excessive labors and long periods of time, fell from the highest summit through neglect. We do this so that each person, considering the enemy’s snares from his own manner of life, may be able to escape his hidden traps.

Yet there are very many great men and women who began their renunciation with virtue and were afterward struck down by the enemy of all humanity. From among the many—some of whose lives I also shared—I enumerate a few, because I can neither recall those people to virtue nor benefit myself by praising the great athletes of Christ without imitating them.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Life of Abba Elias and Dorotheus

A certain man named Elias, an excellent monk, took great care of the consecrated virgins of the weaker sex (Palladius, chapter 35). There are indeed souls of this kind whose purpose is confirmed by the testimony of their final end.

Inflamed by love of virtue and compassion for the female sex, he built a vast monastery in the city called Atrivis [Palladius: Athribe], from funds supplied to him. To this place he gathered a great many women who had been accustomed to wander and go astray, and he cared for all of them as necessity required. He provided them with everything that contributed to the comfort of life, including gardens, tools, the necessary equipment for various household tasks, and whatever else human use demands.

These women, gathered within the enclosure of one dwelling from different ways of life, disturbed one another through frequent quarrels. Consequently, necessity sometimes required Elias himself to investigate the causes of such hostilities between them and restore peace.

He had gathered there as many as three hundred women, and without his mediation their community could not be organized. After he had done this for two years, while he still appeared almost young—for he was thirty or forty years old—he was suddenly tempted by bodily desire for pleasure.

He left the monastery and wandered fasting continuously for two days through the entire desert. Then he poured out this prayer to the Lord:

“Lord,” he said, “either kill me, so that I may not see them suffering in sorrow, or remove from me the temptation of this desire, so that I may care for them as I ought and as is fitting.”

Toward evening, sleep suddenly overcame him in the midst of his desire, and he saw three angels come to him, as he himself related. They seized him and said:

“Why did you leave the monastery of women?”

When he explained to them the reason for his departure and said that he had feared harming either himself or them, they replied:

“If, then, you are freed by us from this kind of temptation, will you go back and resume your care of them?”

He willingly consented. They began to demand from him an oath of the following kind, as he himself related:

“Swear,” they said, “in these words: ‘By him who cares for me, I swear that I shall care for them.’”

When he had sworn these words to them, one of the angels took hold of his hands, another of his feet, and the third seemed to seize a razor and emasculate him—not that he actually did this, but that he appeared to do it. For Elias believed that he was in a kind of mental stupor at that time and felt that he had been healed in this manner.

The angels then asked him whether he sensed that what had been done to him had benefited him.

He replied: “I understand very clearly that a certain burden has been removed from me, and I believe that I have been freed from all the trouble I feared.”

They said to him: “Then go now to your monastery.”

After returning five days later and entering the monastery of the women in mourning, he thereafter remained in the same place, in a cell situated directly opposite their dwelling. Since he thus seemed to be closer to them, he corrected them as far as he could through frequent admonitions.

He lived another forty years, assuring the holy Fathers that never again had any such thought entered his heart. Thus that blessed Elias obtained from God the grace to govern the women’s monastery while personally supervising it.

He was succeeded by the most blessed Dorotheus, who grew old in an admirable manner of life. He was not, indeed, able to live in the monastery itself as his predecessor had done; but he confined himself in a cell above it, where he made a window through which he could observe the women in his monastery. He was accustomed both to open and to close this window, and he was constantly seated beside it, instructing the sisters in concord and peace. Thus he grew old in that upper part of the monastery, since neither could the women ascend to him nor he descend to them, for no stairs had ever been placed there by which such access might be possible. Such was the perfection of blessed Dorotheus in the virtue of abstinence, and such was the end of this matter.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### The Life of the Virgin Piamon

There was a certain virgin named Piamon who lived all the years of her life with her mother, constantly working at linen and always taking food toward evening every other day (Palladius, chapter 37). From God she merited the knowledge of future events.

Once in Egypt, as one village was coming upstream on the Nile against the destruction of another village—for they divide the turns of irrigation with such fierce contention that they even proceed to wounds and deaths—a stronger population came against the inhabitants of the lower village, where this woman lived. Trusting in the size of its multitude and equipped with both military and rustic weapons, it was advancing to overthrow the aforesaid settlement.

Then an angel stood before her and announced the arrival of the enemy, an event which no one there could have suspected. The virgin therefore summoned the priests of the village and said:

“Go out and meet those who are hastening from that village to destroy you. Do not allow them and yourselves alike to perish in slaughter, together with your little dwellings; beg them to withdraw from the preparations for this battle.”

The priests were exceedingly frightened by these words. They fell prostrate at her feet and said:

“We do not dare to meet them, for we know both their drunkenness and their intolerable boldness. But add this also to your mercy, over this whole trembling village and over this little house of yours: go forth yourself and meet those who are coming, and restore peace to this place.”

She refused to do this, but immediately went up to the upper part of her house and remained there throughout the night in continuous prayer, without even bending her knees. She poured out this prayer to the Lord:

“Lord God, who judge all the earth, to whom nothing unjust has ever been pleasing, let my prayer rise to you, and let your power come down—the power that will hold those rushing upon our destruction fixed in the very place where it meets them, as though fastened there by nails.”

When this speech and prayer had been completed, their enemies—already stationed at the third milestone from the village—became so fixed in that place around the first hour of the day that they could not move from it at all. It was also disclosed to them by revelation that the virgin’s prayers had impeded their undertaking.

They therefore promptly sent some of their own men to her village and asked for peace, sending this message:

“Give thanks to God, who through the prayers of the virgin Piamon has turned you away from the destruction of your settlement.”

## CHAPTER XIX  
### The Life of Pachomius, the Abbot

In the province of Thebaid there is said to be a place called Tabennesis, where there was a certain Pachomius (Palladius, chapter 38), a man so righteous that by divine grace he knew future events and also enjoyed angelic visions.

He was perfectly merciful and humane, and loved the brothers with an immeasurable affection. While he was sitting in a cave, an angel of the Lord came to him and said:

“Know that in all matters pertaining to your purpose you are perfect. Therefore you now sit uselessly in the cave. Come, then, leave this place, gather all the younger monks, live with them, and instruct them according to the rule of life that you will learn from me.”

The angel gave him bronze tablets on which this was written:

“You shall permit each person to take as much food and drink as he requests, and you shall subject them to equal tasks according to the strength of those who eat and drink. You shall neither forbid anyone to fast nor prevent anyone from eating. Nevertheless, always assign more difficult work to the stronger and heavier eaters; the weak and genuine monks, however, shall be urged to lighter work.

“Within the courtyard of the house you shall make separate cells, and command three men to live in each. Their food, however, shall be prepared in one place for all. Let them sleep not lying down, but seated upon chairs that have been prepared and slightly reclined, resting while seated and covered with their cloaks.

“At night let them wear linen garments—called *levitons*—with belts, and let each one be covered with well-prepared goatskins. They shall not remove these skins even when they wish to eat or sleep. When they enter for Communion on Saturday or Sunday, each shall loosen his belt, remove his skin, and enter wearing only his hood.

“Make the hoods themselves small and woolen, as he prescribed for infants, and have certain signs woven into them in purple. Let there be twenty-four ranks of brothers, corresponding to the number of the twenty-four letters; and place over each rank a Greek letter, beginning with Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and the rest through Omega.”

When the holy Pachomius questioned them and sought to learn the life of each individual in such a multitude, he would say to the second man, who was prior in his rank: “How is Alpha?” or “How is Beta?” Again he would say: “Greet Zeta,” or “Lambda.” He questioned each person by his particular sign and the name of his letter.

The angel said:

“For the simpler and perfected monks, impose the name of the letter Iota; for the harsher and more difficult men, impose the name of the letter Xi. Thus you shall impress such names upon each rank that their characters may signify the dispositions of their souls. Only spiritual men, however, understood what sort of life the letters assigned to their rank appeared to indicate.”

This also was written on the tablets:

“If anyone arrives from another monastery as a stranger, following a different rule, he shall neither eat nor drink with them, nor be brought into their dwelling, unless he has happened to join them while traveling. Whoever has entered them in order to remain with them shall not be admitted into the more secluded parts of the monastery until he has completed a period of three years. But after he has first performed more laborious and harder work for the whole three years, then you shall permit him, once received, to enter the interior.”

While eating, let them cover their heads with their hoods, so that one brother may not see another eating. No one may speak while eating, or look toward any other place except the single dish and the table upon which it is set.

He also ordained and commanded that they offer twelve prayers throughout the day, and another twelve when they came to the evening light. During the nocturnal vigils they were likewise to pour forth the same number of prayers, but only three at the ninth hour of the day. When the whole multitude gathered to eat, he appointed that each rank should have a psalm sung before every prayer.

Then the holy Pachomius seemed inclined to contradict the angel, saying:

“These prayers are few.”

The angel answered:

“I commanded these prayers to be made so that the weaker members might be able to fulfill the rule of life imposed upon them without any sadness. Those who live with stronger and more perfected minds do not need to be bound by another’s law; for they have wholly devoted themselves, within their cells and throughout their entire lives, to the vision and worship of God.

“I gave these commands for those who can neither discover nor fulfill what is beneficial, so that, when compelled by a kind of servile necessity, they have demonstrated in themselves a discipline worthy of their vocation, they may finally become capable of attaining confidence in the knowledge of God.”

After these arrangements had been made and his ministry completed, the angel departed from the holy Pachomius.

There are therefore very many monasteries in which as many as seven thousand men preserve institutions of this kind. But the greatest and first is the one in which Pachomius himself lived; from it the other monasteries seem to have proceeded, and these are known to contain as many as fourteen hundred brothers.

Among them there is also a certain servant of God named Aphthonius, joined to me by a very close bond of friendship, who holds the second position in that monastery (Palladius, chapter 39). Since they trusted his life and conduct, they often sent him to Alexandria, so that he might sell there what they had made in the monastery, buy whatever necessities he knew were required, and bring them back.

There are also other monasteries containing two hundred or three hundred brothers, in a city called Panos. I entered one of them and found four hundred men there. Among them I found fifteen tailors, seven blacksmiths, four carpenters, twelve camel-drivers, and fifteen fullers, each laboring at his own craft.

From what could remain after their daily sustenance, they also supplied whatever was necessary to the neighboring women’s monasteries and prisons,

“and there were also those who kept pigs. When I thought this ought to be censured, they said that they had received this practice from the tradition of their forefathers, because pigs had to be kept in the monasteries so that neither the refuse of sifted grain nor the leaves of cleaned vegetables, nor anything else that would cause harm if thrown away, might perish. They therefore ordered the pigs themselves to be slaughtered, selling their flesh to purchasers, but assigning their hooves and smallest portions to the meals of the sick and elderly, since that region appeared to suffer from great scarcity of resources and a large population. They have the Blemmyes as neighbors along their borders.”

[Note: The material enclosed in brackets is absent from Hervetus’s Latin version of Palladius. It is present in the Greek.]

Rising before dawn, those who served the others in rotation prepared the food, while others arranged the tables. They usually set them out around the third hour of the day. Once all their work was finished, they placed upon them loaves and certain herbs prepared in their customary manner, which they call *lapsanas*.

[Note: *Lapsanas*: that is, wild vegetables. See the *Onomasticon*.]

They also served olives and cheese besides meat, as well as chopped vegetables of various kinds. After these had been arranged in this manner, some entered at the sixth hour of the day and took food; others at the seventh, others at the eighth, others at the ninth, others at the tenth, others at the eleventh, and others were accustomed to eat deep into the night. Some took food only after two days. The hour of each person could nevertheless be recognized from his particular letter.

Their occupations were likewise divided. One served agriculture; another cultivated the garden; one worked in the workshop; another at the baker’s trade; another as a carpenter; another excelled in the craft of the fuller; another labored in preparing skins; another in preparing leather; one took pleasure in reading or copying books; another was accustomed to weave large baskets; another, smaller ones. Yet all together held the spiritual books in memory.

## CHAPTER XX  
### The Life of the Tabennesiot Women, and of the Virgin against Whom False Testimony Had Been Given

Among these people there is a monastery of four hundred women, living according to the same customs and the same arrangement, except for the single matter of wearing skins (Palladius, chapter 39). The women live across the river, while the men live on this side of it.

When one of the virgins dies, the others carry her out clothed as usual and place her above the riverbank. The men then cross in a little boat with olive branches and palm branches, singing psalms; they transfer her to their side and bury her in the tomb assigned to her with the others. No one crosses to the women’s monastery except the priest and deacon, and even they do so only on Sunday.

In this women’s dwelling the following event occurred. A certain tailor of secular clothing crossed the river and, out of ignorance, asked them to undertake some work for him (Palladius, chapter 40). When one of the younger women came forward—for she seemed safe in doing so because of the solitude of the place and the desolation of the region—she suddenly saw him unwillingly and gave him this answer:

“We have our own craftsmen to mend our garments.”

Another of the women noticed them during the encounter I have described. Some time afterward, when a quarrel arose among them, she began, through diabolical suspicion, the wickedness of her own heart, and the heat of anger, to accuse the aforementioned virgin before the other sisters. Some of them agreed with her, though not with great malice.

The virgin became exceedingly sad. Unable to bear such an obvious slander—for she knew that she had not even thought of anything of the kind within her own mind—she secretly threw herself into the river and ended her life there.

When the woman who had slandered her heard this, she could not bear the horror of so great a crime and likewise ended her life by hanging herself.

The other sisters reported the matter when the priest came to them. He then ordered that no offering should be made to God in the name of either of those who had killed themselves by such a death. But those who appeared to have been divided by the whispering of that statement, as though conscious of sin because they had believed the slander, he ordered to be deprived of communion in the holy mysteries for seven years.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### The Life of the Holy Virgin Who Pretended Madness among Them

There was another virgin in this monastery (Palladius, chapter 41) who pretended, for Christ’s sake, to be foolish and to have a demon, so that she might fulfill the virtue of her purpose.

She humbled and abased herself so completely that she was an object of horror to all the others, to such an extent that they would not even eat with her. She had gladly chosen this way of life. Never leaving the kitchen, she fulfilled all its duties as a servant, obeying everyone; according to the common proverb, she was the sponge of the whole household.

By her actions she fulfilled what we read written in the holy Gospel: “If anyone among you wishes to be greater, let him be the servant and minister of all” (Matthew 20; Mark 10). And the blessed Apostle says: “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this world, let him become foolish, so that he may become wise” (1 Corinthians 3).

She kept her head wrapped in rags and served everyone in this way, while the other virgins, having been tonsured, covered themselves with hoods. Of the four hundred women, no one ever saw her eating. Throughout her entire life she never sat at table and never received even a small portion of bread from anyone. She merely wiped away the crumbs from the tables and washed the pots, living content with these alone as nourishment.

She never used shoes and never wronged anyone. No one ever heard a complaint from her, nor did she ever speak either little or much to anyone—yet everyone beat her, everyone hated her, and she endured everyone’s curses.

Concerning this most holy woman, the blessed and highly esteemed man Piterius [Note: In Palladius, chapter 42, he is called Pitirum]—for that was his name—who always lived among the deserts, an angel once appeared to him while he was sitting in the place called Porphyrite. The angel addressed him in these words:

“Why do you think that you are something great in your vocation, while living in such a place? Do you wish to see a woman holier than yourself? Go to the women’s monastery of the Tabennesiots. There you will find one of them with a torn cloth on her head. Know that she is better than you. While she alone struggles day and night against so many things, her heart has never departed from God; but you, sitting in one place and never going anywhere, wander in mind and thought through all the cities.”

He immediately went to the monastery mentioned above and asked the superiors of the brothers to transport him to the women’s dwelling. Since he was a man of celebrated life and already advanced in age, they soon ferried him across the river with great confidence.

After entering and praying, he wished to see all the sisters. Among them he did not see the one for whom he had come. Finally he said:

“Bring them all to me; one appears to be missing.”

They said to him:

“We are all here.”

He answered:

“One is missing—the one whom the angel showed me.”

They said to him:

“We have one foolish woman inside in the kitchen.”

For that is what they call a woman afflicted by a demon.

He said:

“Bring her to me also, so that I may see her.”

When they heard this, they began to call the woman. She refused to listen, sensing, I suppose, something or perhaps already recognizing it through divine revelation. They said to her:

“Saint Piterius wishes to see you.”

For he was a man of great reputation and renown. When she had been brought to him and he saw that her forehead was wrapped in cloth, he threw himself at her feet and said:

“Bless me, Amma.”

Then she too fell at his feet and said:

“You bless me, lord.”

All the sisters were astonished and said together:

“Do not endure such an insult, abba; this woman whom you see is mad.”

Then the holy Piterius said to them all:

“You are the madwomen. For although she is better than you and me, she is your Amma”—for that is what they call their spiritual mothers—“and I pray God that I may be found worthy of her on the day of judgment.”

When they heard this, all of them fell together at the feet of the holy Piterius, each confessing her own various sins by which she had saddened that most holy woman.

One said: “I mocked her.”

Another: “I ridiculed her shabby clothing.”

Another: “Because she was silent, I afflicted her with insults.”

Another, while washing the dirt from a dish, said that she had poured it over her.

Another often recalled that she had beaten her with blows.

Another lamented that she had filled her nostrils with mustard.

The others likewise reported that they had inflicted various injuries upon her.

For all these things the holy man, together with the aforementioned most holy virgin, offered prayers to God and then departed.

After a few days, unable to bear so much glory for herself and unwilling to be loaded with such honor by the sisters, while believing herself oppressed by the individual acts of repentance, she left the monastery. Where she went, at what place she stayed, or by what death she ended her life, no one has ever since been able to discover.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### The Life of John, the Abbot Who Lived at Lycus, and of the Virgin Poemenia

There was a certain John in a town called Lycus (Palladius, chapter 43). While still a boy he learned the craft of carpentry, and he had a brother who was a dyer. Later, when he was twenty-five years old, he renounced this world.

After spending five years in various monasteries, he finally withdrew alone to the mountain of Lycus. At its summit he made himself cells of three domes [Palladius: *tholoi*].

[Note: “He made himself cells of three domes”: that is, three domes, or three *tholoi*, τρεῖς θόλους, as in Palladius, chapter 43. See the *Onomasticon*.]

After entering there, he enclosed himself so completely that he also blocked the very entrance by which he had gone in. One dome was therefore assigned to bodily necessities, another was where he was accustomed to work and eat, and the third was where he prayed.

After he had completed thirty years enclosed in this way, always receiving through a single window the necessities of life from the person who served him, he merited such grace from God that he possessed knowledge of future events.

He frequently foretold to the emperor Theodosius of holy memory various things that were to happen. First, concerning the tyrant Maximus, he foretold both that Theodosius would overcome him and that he would return from the regions of Gaul. Later he foretold to him what followed concerning the tyrant Eugenius: that Theodosius would overcome him, but would himself end his life there and leave his son as successor to the empire.

His reputation consequently grew strong among everyone. For this reason the emperor Theodosius was accustomed to honor him with prophetic reverence, declaring that he possessed great virtue.

When we—myself, the blessed Evagrius, Ammonius, and Albinus—were living near the deserts of Nitria, we wished to learn carefully about the virtue of this man.

Then the holy Evagrius said to us:

“I would gladly hear from someone who knows how to examine a mind and speech what sort of man this is of whom we are speaking. If I do not first learn about him from someone else, I shall have to climb up to his mountain.”

When I heard this, I said nothing of the kind to anyone. After staying only one day, on the following day I closed my cell, commended myself and it to God, and went as far as Thebaid. I completed the entire journey in eighteen days, partly traveling on foot and partly sailing along the river.

This occurred at the time when the river usually rose, when many people were accustomed to fall ill—a condition which I myself also endured.

When I arrived there, I found the enclosure closed [Manuscript: *membrum*], which stood before the entrance to his rooms; afterward the brothers had built up that place. The building was so large that it could accommodate nearly one hundred men. They always kept the place closed, customarily opening it only on Saturday and Sunday.

When I learned why it was closed, I remained at rest, waiting for Saturday. When that day came, I entered around the second hour to see the man mentioned above. I found him seated beside a window through which he was accustomed to speak to those entering.

After the first greeting, he said to me through an interpreter:

“Where are you from, and why have you come? For I suspect that you are one of Evagrius’s companions.”

I replied that I was a stranger, that I came from the regions of Galatia, and confessed that I was one of Evagrius’s brothers.

While we were speaking, the governor of that province, named Alipius, suddenly entered. John left the conversation he had been having with me and went to him.

I withdrew from them for a short time, giving way and standing at a distance. I found their prolonged conversation burdensome and irritating, and within myself I reproached the good old man because, having disregarded my conversation, he had honored the governor instead.

Since I had found this displeasing, I considered leaving and abandoning him. He therefore called his interpreter, named Theodore, and said:

“Go to that brother and tell him: ‘Do not be discouraged; I shall dismiss the governor immediately and speak with you.’”

From this I recognized that he was a spiritual man who foresaw everything, and I therefore began all the more to remain.

When the governor had soon departed, John called me and addressed me in these words:

“Why have you wounded your soul by reproaching me? What fault had you found in me, that you should think within yourself what I do not recognize in myself and do not know to befit your character?

“Do you not know what is written—that it is not the healthy and strong, but those who are sick, who always need a physician (Matthew 9; Mark 2; Luke 5)? You can find me whenever you wish, and I can likewise find you; and if you cannot obtain some consolation from me, you can nevertheless receive it from other brothers and Fathers.

“But this man, wholly devoted to secular affairs and given over to the power of the devil, could scarcely breathe for the space of a brief hour. Now, like a servant fleeing from his harsh master, he has come seeking saving help here. It would therefore be an inconsiderate and ill-timed thing if I were to abandon him and remain with you, who are accustomed continually to devote yourself to the benefits of your own salvation.”

I earnestly begged him to deign to pray for me. This convinced me most certainly that he was a spiritual man.

Then, becoming more cheerful, he gently struck me on the left side of my face with his right hand and said:

“Many tribulations await you. You have endured much in order to leave the desert, and, fearing this very thing, you delayed doing it for a while. The demon tries to shake you by presenting pious and apparently reasonable arguments. He has reminded you of your father’s desire, and of the way in which your brother and sister ought to be converted and lead their lives in the desert.

“Now I announce this to you: know that both have been saved. For both have renounced secular affairs. Your father, moreover, will live another seven years. Therefore remain steadfast and live in the desert places as you began, and do not hasten to return to your homeland because of your parents. For it is written: ‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven’ (Luke 9).”

Thus instructed and taught by these words, which wounded me deeply, I gave thanks to God, especially after I learned that the circumstances compelling me to leave the desert had been fulfilled according to my desire.

Again, with a gentle laugh and in jest, he said to me:

“Do you wish to become a bishop?”

I replied that I already was one.

He asked: “Where?”

I said:

“In kitchens, at tables, in taverns, and in potters’ workshops. I carefully inspect all these things. If the wine is sour, I exclude it from my meal; but if it is good, I drink it. I likewise inspect the cooks’ pots, and if I see that salt or some kind of seasoning is lacking, I add it and eat the better-seasoned food.

“This is my episcopate; for my greed has made me such a bishop.”

The holy man smiled at me and said:

“Put aside your jokes. You will become a bishop, and you will have a great many tribulations and labors. If you wish to avoid them, do not leave our deserts; no one will make you a bishop while you live in the wilderness.”

I then descended from that man and returned to the deserts in which I had been accustomed to live, reporting to those venerable Fathers what I had learned there about that spiritual and divine man. Two months later they came to him by boat.

But I, most wretched man, forgot his words.

After three years I fell ill with an ailment of the stomach and spleen. The brothers sent me from the aforementioned place as far as Alexandria, where I was treated for dropsy. From Alexandria, at the urging of physicians, I went to Palestine because of the favorable breezes they thought existed there; my illness required the thinner air.

From Palestine I went to the province of Bithynia. There, I do not know how—whether through human ambition or by divine will, God knows—I was made a bishop beyond my merit.

I experienced the troubles of the disturbance that arose under Saint John. For ten months I was hidden in a very dark cell, and I began to remember the words of that holy man, since I was enduring there what he had foretold.

Perhaps that great athlete of Christ had said these things to me in order to urge me, by such predictions, to endure life in the deserts. For he said that he had lived forty-eight years in the same cell, affirming that he had never seen the face of any woman—not even his sister—and that no one had ever seen him eating or drinking.

The handmaid of Christ, Poemenia, also came to see him (Palladius, chapter 47). To her, though she had not yet been seen by him, he sent certain secret instructions through another person and warned her not to stop at Alexandria when departing from the region of Thebaid. If she refused to heed him, he said, she would necessarily fall into a certain temptation.

But whether through negligence or forgetfulness, she did not act as that holy man had commanded. She came to Alexandria in order to see a city unknown to her.

While she was traveling near a town called Nicius, her ships put in to shore so that they might relieve the weariness of the long voyage. The boys went ashore and, driven by a certain insolence against the peasants of that place—whose pride and boldness no one can endure—began to provoke quarrels.

The group in question cut off and seized one eunuch’s finger, killed another, and nearly drowned the holy Dionysius in the river, although the common people did not know that he was a bishop. They also overwhelmed Poemenia herself with insults and terror, while all the other boys were wounded.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### The Life of the Blessed Possidonius, a Thebaid Monk

Many extraordinary and innumerable things are related about Possidonius of Thebaid, a man of great distinction and patience (Palladius, chapter 77). I have never seen another man so gentle, so truly a monk, and so free from every kind of malice. For I lived with him for an entire year at Bethlehem, at the time when he was residing in the region called Poemenion, and I know that I saw many more virtues in him.

Among them he himself once recounted the following to me:

“For one year, while I was living in the place called Porphyrites, I saw no human being during the time I was there, heard no one’s voice, and did not touch bread. I lived only on a few dates and on wild herbs, if I could find any.

“Once, when the food by which I could sustain myself had completely run out, I left my cave in order to approach the regions inhabited by human beings. After walking all day, I discovered that my dwelling was scarcely two miles away.

“Looking around, I thought I saw a kind of horseman, bearing the appearance of a soldier and wearing a helmet on his head, from which a crest rose in the manner of a tiara. Since I truly thought him a soldier, I hurried back to my cave.

“When I returned, I immediately found there a little basket containing freshly gathered grapes and figs. I seized it at once and entered my cave joyfully. For two months that food provided me with the greatest consolation.”

The most holy Possidonius is also said to have performed the following miracle near Bethlehem.

A certain pregnant woman was tormented by an unclean spirit and gave birth with the greatest difficulty when the time of delivery came; the spirit was afflicting her. When the unfortunate woman was thus tormented by the demon, her husband ran to the holy Possidonius and begged him to deign to come and pray for her.

We entered together for prayer. As Possidonius stood and began to pray, having touched the ground with his knees only twice, he immediately drove away the unclean spirit.

Rising from the ground, he said to us:

“Pray, I beg you. For now, while that spirit is being expelled, a certain sign will be shown to us.”

To confirm this for us, after the holy man had spoken these words, the demon tore the entire vestibule wall from its foundations and cast it down.

The woman herself had remained mute for seven full years. But after she had been visited by that holy man who freed her from the demon, she immediately gave birth and was granted the ability to speak.

I also once came to know this man’s prediction—which they call prophecy (Palladius, chapter 82)—and afterward I knew Simon, an admirable man, whom I remember having noticed and known for a time.

The most blessed and abstinent Possidonius also told me that from the fortieth year of his life he had no use of bread in his diet, and that he had never retained anger against anyone until the middle of the day.

These are the miracles and signs of Possidonius, that mighty man in Christ, which divine grace worked through him; by these he merited to complete his celebrated life.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### The Life of the Monk Serapion, of Cleomon, and of a Certain Virgin

There was another man named Serapion (Palladius, chapter 83), who had acquired the surname Sindonius because he used no garment other than a single linen sheet. Everyone knew well that he had never possessed or owned anything. For this reason he was also called *apathes*, that is, “impassible,” because he suffered no desire to possess anything.

He was exceedingly learned in letters and retained all the Scriptures firmly in his memory. Through his extreme abstinence from everything and his continual meditation on the divine books, he could not be content with the quiet of a single cell; rather, his mind was continually drawn through various places.

Thus he traveled throughout the whole world and rose to the virtue of such glory. For this was the disposition of his mind—that is, of his will.

[Note: “That is, of his will” is absent from Moret’s manuscript.]

Therefore we call these differences differences of wills and affections, not of substances.

This, however, the holy Fathers used sometimes to relate about him: that, through a certain monk who acted as his accomplice [Note: “His accomplice” [Col. 0396B]. In Palladius, chapter 83, the Greek is συμπαίκτην ἀσκητήν, “an ascetic fellow-player.” Hervetus translates it as “an exercitator who played with him.” Understand that he had arranged for a certain monk to distract him with mimes.], in a certain town he sold himself to pagan mimes for the price of twenty solidi, retaining for himself the stamped solidi that he had received for his person. He therefore remained in such servitude with the aforementioned mimes who had bought him until he had made them Christians and withdrawn them from theatrical performances.

He used no other food besides bread and water, and never ceased reading the holy Scriptures. Meanwhile, after a long period of time, the husband of the female mime was first pierced by remorse, then his wife as well, and finally the entire household [Col. 0305D]. It was said that, before anyone knew his manner of life, he even washed their feet, as though they were his masters. But after both husband and wife had received spiritual cleansing, both withdrew from theatrical performance and turned together to a chaste and pious life.

They loved and revered the man with great affection, saying to him: “Come, brother; we now grant you your freedom, because you first freed us from shameful servitude.”

To them that great Serapion replied: “I am no longer necessary to you. God has accomplished through me his work in you, and the soul of each of you has been saved. Therefore I disclose to you my secret, and what I have concealed until now. Moved by compassion for your souls, which I saw entangled in great error, although I was a free monk, an Egyptian by birth, I wished to sell myself so that you might be free from your great sins. Since God has accomplished this fully through my humility, I rejoice. Therefore take the gold that you gave for me, so that I may find others whom I can help.”

Although they repeatedly and earnestly begged him, declaring truthfully that they would regard him as the lord and father of their souls if he would deign to remain and live with them, they could not persuade him in any way. Then they said to him: “You yourself, then, shall give that gold to the poor, since we acknowledge that we gave it as a kind of pledge for our salvation.”

[Col. 0306B] He answered them: “You give it yourselves, because it is yours; for I do not give other people’s money to the poor.”

They therefore said to him: “At least we earnestly beg you to visit us at Athens after a year has passed.”

This most holy servant of Christ, traveling frequently, reached Greece and, after remaining at Athens for three days, received from no one any bread to eat. He had neither money, nor a cloak, nor a bag, nor anything else with him besides the linen garment with which he was clothed. When he had reached the fourth day without eating anything at all, he began to feel severe hunger. There is no fast worse than one forced upon a person against his will, from whose necessity treachery often arises.

He therefore stood upon a certain hill of the city, where the leading men of that town [Col. 0306C] were accustomed to hold council. There he even struck his hands together and cried out that he was suffering the greatest violence, saying: “Men of Athens, come to my aid!”

All ran together—both those whom we see clothed in cloaks and those in coarse mantles—and asked him what he had, where he had come from, and what suffering he claimed to be enduring.

Then he replied: “I am Egyptian by birth and a monk by manner of life. Yet after I departed from my homeland, which was truly mine, I fell into the hands of three moneylenders. Of these, I have been able to escape two, somehow paying what I owed and thus evading the claims they brought against me. But the third still holds me, and I have no means by which I can satisfy him.”

When they asked him about the moneylenders to whom he said he was indebted—who they were, where they lived, and who this troublesome creditor might be—and promised that, if he showed him to them, they would help him in every way, he said:

“From the beginning of my youth these three have always troubled me: the desire for money, the longing for pleasures, and the voracity of the belly. Of these, I now seem to have escaped two, namely the desire for money and the longing for pleasures; they no longer trouble me. But I cannot endure the third, which I called voracity. For now that I have been fasting from necessity for four days, it presses upon me like the harshest moneylender, demanding and continually claiming its customary debt; and unless I repay it, it threatens me with death.”

[Col. 0307A] Then, thinking that he was telling some contrived and fictitious story, one of the philosophers offered him a solidus. He took it, gave it to a man who sold bread, accepted from him only a single loaf, and immediately departed from that city; nor did he ever return to it afterward. When those philosophers came to know him and perceived the truth of the whole matter, affirming that he was some great man, they repaid the price of the single loaf and recovered from the bread-seller the solidus that he had received.

When that most blessed man had come into the region of Lacedaemon, he discovered that one of the city’s leading men, otherwise a good man, and everyone in his household were Manichaeans. In that household, following the earlier example, he again sold himself; and within two years [Col. 0307B] he drew both the master of the household from the accursed sect, as well as his wife and entire family, and handed them over to the Church. They no longer loved him as a servant, but regarded him rather as a brother or father, truly blessing God.

After a short time, when this spiritual diamond Serapion had departed from them, he too boarded a ship with many others, first returning the price he had received from his masters, as though he intended to sail to Rome. The sailors, however, supposing that he had money for expenses and that he had brought some sort of gold with him, took him aboard, asking nothing at all from him and not doubting that one of them would have placed his belongings, as he did those of the others, in a part of the ship.

As they sailed, and seemed already to be five hundred stadia from Alexandria, all those who had boarded with him began, around sunset, to eat, as the sailors themselves had already done. When they did not see him eating on the first day, they thought that some discomfort of the voyage was the cause. But when he took no food on the third or fourth day either, they themselves, dining on the fifth day, addressed him as he continued in complete tranquillity:

“Why, man,” they said, “do you alone not eat here?”

He replied that he had nothing. On hearing this, the sailors began asking one another who had taken responsibility for his belongings and expenses aboard ship. When they discovered that he had given none of them anything, they rebuked him, saying:

“How did you board the ship without provisions? From where will you pay us our wages? From where will you yourself live?”

That most patient of men replied: “It is no concern of mine. Put me ashore and throw me back at the place where you found me.”

The sailors, angered, said: “What rage! Even if you were to give a hundred solidi, we would never willingly do that, now that the voyage is progressing so favorably. Therefore we shall carry out the plan of the voyage we have begun.”

Thus he remained safely on the ship, and all the sailors supplied him with food all the way to Rome.

When that most courageous athlete of Christ reached Rome (Palladius, chapter 84), he began to inquire carefully who was said to be a great monk there, or which virgin of God was praised by everyone. Meanwhile he became known to a certain Domnion, a most courageous and exceedingly abstemious man, famous for his miracles [Col. 0308A], whose little bed after his death was accustomed to cure the sick. When Domnion saw him, Serapion was both strengthened and instructed to perfection. For Domnion was an educated man, well trained in knowledge and good conduct.

When Serapion happened to ask him which other monk or which devout virgin was said to live in that city (Palladius, chapter 85), he learned that there was there a certain virgin who had separated herself from everyone and shut herself inside her cell, remaining there in quiet and never seeing any human being.

He immediately asked for her house. When he had found it, he approached an old woman who served the aforementioned virgin and said to her: “Go and tell the virgin that I urgently desire to see her.”

She returned [Col. 0308B] the answer that she had seen no one for many years.

He said to her: “Go and tell her; God has sent me to speak with her.”

But even then she refused to deliver the message. After he had kept watch there for two or three days, and had at last been received by the virgin, he said to her: “Why are you sitting here?”

She replied: “I am not sitting; I am walking.”

He said: “Where are you walking?”

She answered: “To the Lord.”

He said: “Are you alive or dead?”

She replied: “I believe in my God that I am dead to the world; for those who live according to the flesh cannot go to the Lord.”

He said: “If you therefore wish to persuade me of this very thing, do what I am doing.”

She replied: “If you command only what is possible, I shall do it.”

Then he answered: “Everything is possible for a person who is dead to this world, except impiety.”

Then he said: “Come out and proceed.”

[Col. 0308C] She replied: “I have completed twenty-five years during which I have never gone out from this place. Why, then, do you wish me to go out today?”

He said: “Ah! Did you not say that you are dead to the world? It is therefore clear that the world is dead to you also. If this is true, and a dead person feels nothing, then it is all one whether you go out or do not go out. Therefore proceed.”

Hearing this, the virgin came out.

After she had left her cell and arrived at a certain basilica, that most holy man again addressed her:

“If you wish to persuade me with complete certainty that you are dead and no longer live in a way that pleases human beings, do what I am doing, and then I shall know that you are truly dead to the world.”

The virgin said: “What more do you want me to do?”

“Take off your clothes,” he said, “and place all the possessions you use, just as I do, upon your shoulder. Then cross through the middle of the city, naked as I am, untroubled by any shame, and follow behind me as I lead.” [Note: This is astonishing, not to be imitated.]

She answered: “But I shall wound the souls of many who see me walking in such a disgraceful manner, and everyone will think that I am insane or will say that I am possessed by a demon.”

He said: “What is that to you, if you are believed to be possessed or called insane? You are dead to those who say these things about you, as you yourself claim. But a dead person never cares whether someone insults or mocks him; he cannot feel any of these things.”

Then the virgin said to him: “I beg you, command anything else you wish concerning my purpose, and I shall do it. For I have not yet reached this measure of life [Col. 0309A]; but I pray that someday I may reach it.”

Then that servant of Christ said: “See, sister, that you do not already think yourself great, and boast that you are holier than all human beings and dead to worldly affairs. You have learned that you are alive and still please human beings. For I am much more dead than you: by myself I demonstrate to everyone through my actions that what I say is true, doing what you cannot do. I do not suppose that anything can affect me or that I can be disfigured in any way.”

Having instructed her by such words in the pursuit of humility and brought her down from a certain citadel of pride and conceit, he left her and departed.

There are many other great and admirable things that he did, by which he proved that he did not perceive himself to be in the world [Col. 0309B]. He ended this life in his sixtieth year and was buried in those very deserts.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Life of Evagrius, Deacon and Monk

It would not be right to remain silent about Evagrius the deacon (Palladius, chapter 86), a man who is remembered everywhere [Note: Evagrius was an Origenist], who lived according to the manner of the apostles. Rather, we ought to entrust his deeds to written memorials, since they will undoubtedly benefit all who read them and acknowledge the glory of the goodness of our Savior.

I therefore think it appropriate to begin at the beginning of his life, carefully explaining how he reached such a calling and how, established in those very solitudes, he came to the end of a life so wondrous and renowned, dying at the age of fifty-four. Concerning him Holy Scripture [Col. 0309C] proved true when it said: “Having lived for a short time, he fulfilled many years; for his soul was pleasing to the Lord” (Wisdom 4).

He was Pontic by birth, from a town called Iberia, the son of a presbyter who had charge of many churches; such men are called Periodeutae [Note: “Periodeutae.” He himself explains it as “a presbyter who has charge of many churches.” This is absent from Palladius. See the Onomasticon.].

He was first made a lector by Saint Basil, bishop of the Church of Caesarea, in the region of Mount Argaeus. After the death of Saint Basil, the blessed and venerable Gregory, bishop of the city of Nazianzus [Nyssa in Palladius and Hervetus], seeing him to be especially suited to spiritual matters—the man distinguished for remarkable prudence and renowned for learning, who proved himself untouched by any passion of the human race—made the aforementioned Evagrius a deacon.

Thus, when Saint Gregory [Col. 0309D] had been summoned to Constantinople for the great assembly of bishops, he handed Evagrius over to Saint Nectarius, the bishop, and left him there, since Evagrius was destroying the ravings of all heretics by his profound knowledge of the Scriptures.

When he was flourishing in that city, vigorously attacking the vanity and error of perverse sects and enjoying the greatest honor from everyone, he was first—as he later related to us himself—entangled in the snares of desire for a woman. Yet he was soon freed from them, and the woman whom he had loved began to love him. She was the wife of a certain illustrious and high-ranking man.

Evagrius, therefore, fearing God above all, and then ashamed of his own conscience, placing before his eyes the magnitude of the detestable disgrace, and considering the joy and delight of all heretics in the sins of others, prayed most earnestly that God, who alone could do so, would prevent such great attempts.

When the aforementioned woman pressed him, and he could not easily separate himself from the frenzy of her passion because he was already entangled in her by many obligations and varied services, and because, as she pressed him, danger was at hand, God shortly afterward answered the prayer he had made. Before he experienced the burning of the evil with which he had begun to blaze, a vision appeared to him of angels bearing the appearance of soldiers, belonging to the office of a prefect.

He suddenly saw himself seized by them, sent to prison bound with iron throughout his body, and yet heard from no one the reason for which he was being subjected to such punishments.

Reflecting upon his conscience, he understood and saw that he was suffering this because of what he knew. He supposed that the woman’s husband had reported everything to the prefect. While he trembled under such fear before the judge’s doors, the judge seemed to be occupied with another case and to be inflicting various tortures upon certain men seized for a similar crime.

While he was intensely afraid and felt himself breathing with excessive difficulty, that angel who had terrified him in the vision suddenly took the form of one of his friends. He addressed Evagrius, whom he saw bound among forty other defendants:

“What is this, master deacon? Why are you being held in this way?”

He replied: “As to the actual matter, I do not know. I suspect, however, that someone from the prefect’s office has accused me, believing that I was plotting against his marriage. I fear that the judge, perhaps corrupted by his money, may condemn me to death.”

Then the other said: “If you accept the counsel of your friend, it is not good for you to remain any longer in this city.”

Evagrius answered: “If God frees me from these evils, and you see me again in the city of Constantinople, know that I justly deserve to suffer punishments of this kind and to be tortured with even greater ones.”

Then the other said: “If this is true, I shall bring you a Gospel. If you swear to me in it that you will leave this city and henceforth care for your soul, I shall arrange for you to be freed from this danger of necessity.”

When the Gospel had been produced and he had sworn upon it that, apart from a single day during which he would carry his little boxes to the ship, he would not remain in Constantinople, he began to see that the oath he had given had benefited him and that he had been completely released from the judicial inquiry he had feared that very night.

Rising from sleep, he thought to himself, saying: “Although I swore in a dream, I nevertheless remember that I swore.”

He therefore immediately boarded a ship with his little boxes and sailed to Jerusalem.

When he had been carried there and had been received by Saint Melania the Roman woman, his heart again became hardened by a demon, as Pharaoh’s once had. And [Col. 0311A] because he was still in the ardors of youthful age, another temptation again seized his senses there. Without revealing anything of the kind to anyone, he began again to change his clothing and, by conversing with many people, to pursue the enticements of vain glory.

But God, who always frustrates our destruction, struck him with a most severe fever. By this long illness he subdued him, and for six months weakened his body and consumed his flesh, from which he had been accustomed to obtain fuel for his particular vice.

When the skill of many physicians had tried everything but could discover no form of treatment that would contribute to his recovery, Saint Melania spoke to him:

“I am deeply troubled,” she said, “by the length of this illness of yours [Col. 0311B]. Tell me, then, what are the secrets of your heart. This illness has not come without God’s will and judgment.”

Then he confessed the whole matter to the holy woman. She replied:

“Promise me before God that you will return to the calling of the monks who dwell in the desert, and I, although I myself appear entangled in sins, shall nevertheless pray the Lord to grant you the means of life.”

When he promised that he would do this, he recovered his health within a few days. Rising from his bed, he immediately began to think about the departure he had promised.

Then, through the efforts of the blessed Melania, he changed his clothing, left that place, and set out for the Egyptian mountain of Nitria. After living there for two years, in the third year he proceeded to the more remote solitudes [Col. 0311C]. He lived for fourteen years in the places called Cells, eating one pound of bread each day and consuming one sextarius of oil over three months—he who had always lived amid great abundance and luxuries with the greatest pleasure.

He made one hundred prayers every day, writing each year only as much as could provide him, from the wages of his labor, with sustenance for a more disciplined life. For he wrote in a very fine hand, which the Greeks call Oxyrincham [Note: “Oxyrincham.” Palladius and Hervetus, chapter 86, have “a swift hand.” Did Hervetus therefore find in the Greek ὀξὺν χεῖρα, “a swift hand,” where the translator of Heraclides read a transposition of letters, ὀξυρίνχα? The Greek text of Palladius in the Venetian manuscript has ὀξύρογχον χαρακτῆρα, “a sharp character”; the Paris manuscript has ὀξύρυγχον. See the Onomasticon.].

Within fifteen years, therefore, he merited divine grace, having been purified in mind to perfection, so that he possessed both spiritual knowledge and wisdom and knew the distinctions between good and evil spirits.

He wrote books, which he named by these titles: one Epea, another Nonaxon, and a third Antiphyron [Note: “One Epeta, another Nonaxon, a third Antiphyron.” Here I am at a loss and do not see how to extricate myself. Palladius and Hervetus, chapter 86, have only this: “He composed three sacred books for monks, called Ἀντιῤῥητικά, that is, Contradictoria, or Contradictions.” I find in the Venetian manuscript: Συντάττων οὖν τρία βιβλία ἱερομοναχικὰ, ἀτιρητικὰ λεγόμενα, “Accordingly, composing three sacred monastic books, called atiretika, that is, ‘Refutations.’” I shall here add the authors who discuss the works of Evagrius, so that perhaps from them we may be able to extract the truth.

“First, Socrates relates the following about the writings of Evagrius, in book IV, chapter 23 according to the Greeks, or chapter 18 according to the Latins:

‘He also composed extremely serious books, of which one is entitled Monachus, or On the Practical Life; another Gnosticus, or The One Deemed Worthy of Knowledge. It contains fifty chapters. The third is Antirrheticus, drawn from the divine Scriptures against the demons who tempt us, divided into eight parts according to the number of the eight thoughts. He also composed six hundred predictive problems. In addition, there are two books of verses: one for monks who live in coenobia or communities, and one for the virgin. Those who read them will know how remarkable they are.’

“‘Likewise, books accurately composed by him: one entitled Monachus, or On the manner of life that is expressed in action; another Gnosticus, or The One Who Possesses Knowledge, in which there are fifty chapters; and another, Antirrheticus, that is, a refutation of the demons who tempt us, collected from the sacred Scriptures and divided into eight parts, corresponding appropriately to the number of the eight thoughts of our mind. In addition, six hundred problems concerning foreknowledge of future things. These are joined by two books of poems: one for monks who spend their lives in coenobia and communities, and another for the virgin. Those who read them completely will readily understand how excellent they are.’

“The same account occurs in the same words in Suidas under Μακάριος, and in Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 42.

“Gennadius, however, in *On Illustrious Church Writers*, chapter 11, reports the following:

“‘Evagrius the monk, the familiar disciple of the aforementioned Macarius of Egypt, distinguished in divine and human learning, whose book entitled *The Life of the Fathers* also mentions him as a man of the greatest self-control and learning, wrote many things necessary for monks. Among these are the following: against the suggestions of the eight principal vices, which he either first noticed or learned among the first, he opposed eight books drawn from testimonies of the holy Scriptures, after the likeness of the Lord, who always answered his tempter with testimonies from Scripture, so that each kind of suggestion, whether from the devil or from corrupted nature, would have testimonies directed against it. I translated this work into Latin, as I found it in Greek, with the same simplicity.

“‘He also composed for anchorites living a simple life a book of one hundred sayings arranged by chapters, and for the learned and studious a book of fifty sayings. I was the first to render it into Latin. For when I saw that the earlier translation had become corrupted and confused over time, I restored it to the author’s truth, partly by retranslating it and partly by correcting it.

“‘He also composed a teaching suited to the common life for coenobites and members of communities, and for virgins consecrated to God a little book appropriate to their religious commitment and sex. He also published a few very obscure little sayings, which, as he himself says in them, are intelligible only to the hearts of monks; these too I published in Latin. He lived to an advanced age, distinguished by signs and wonders.’”

Hitherto Gennadius.

“Of these works of Evagrius, three points now require clarification or correction. Since he is said to have written στιχηρά, which Christophorsonus translates in Socrates as ‘books of poems’ and Langus in Nicephorus as ‘books of verses,’ should Epea be read instead of Epeta, from the Greek ἔπεα, ‘words’ or ‘sayings’? Certainly the old Moret manuscript clearly has Epea. Although others translate στιχηρά as ‘elementary works,’ as Palthenius does in his preface to the *Homilies of Saint Macarius*. Unless someone suspects that Epea arose from the Greek ΙΕΡΑ, which is part of the word ἱερομοναχικά. Indeed, scribes often took the Greek Ρ for the Latin P, and copied Greek words written in Greek letters as though they had been written in Latin letters.
