I shall suggest a similar conjecture shortly in the notes on Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 9, note 4.

“The explanation of the remaining two words is easier. Instead of Nonaxon, Monachon should apparently be read, for authorities attest that Evagrius wrote a book under that name. Instead of Antiphyron, I shall read Antirrheticon. Thus, in the Venetian Greek text also, ἀτιρητικά should be restored to Ἀντιῤῥητικά.’]

He also taught arts by which demons could be subdued.

The spirit of fornication always assailed him with great force. For, as he himself related to us, during winter he would stand naked throughout the entire night in a well, so that even frost would stiffen his flesh.

On another occasion the spirit of blasphemy began to press him and compel him to utter sacrilegious words against God. For this reason he remained without shelter for forty consecutive days, as he himself said, to such an extent that all over his body there appeared certain pustules of the sort we have often seen on human bodies.

One day three demons stood before him [Col. 0312A] in the form of clerics, wishing to discuss the faith with him. One said that he was an Arian, another an Eunomian, and the third an Apollinarian. He defeated them all by arguing wisely and briefly.

On another day, when the keys of the church had been lost, he invoked the name of Christ, marked the part of the door where the key was, and opened it by striking the door with his hand.

He experienced demons with such intensity and was beaten by them so many times that their number cannot be counted.

To one of his disciples he foretold, prophesying each matter individually, everything that would happen to him after eighteen years.

[Col. 0312B] He used to say: “Since I came to the solitudes, I have eaten neither lettuce nor wild greens; I have touched no green vegetable, no grapes, no fruit, no meat, and I have seen no baths.”

Finally, in the sixteenth year of such a life, during which he ate nothing cooked, when his body’s stomach ailment made it necessary for him to take cooked food, he never touched bread, but for two years tasted only vegetables, posca (a vinegar-and-water drink) [Note: “Posca.” Palladius and Hervetus have “ptisana,” where the Greek has πτισάνη. An old Greek-Latin lexicon gives ὀξύκρατον, “posca.” Below, in chapter 42: “For the rest of her life she lived content with posca and dry bread.” I restore posca there instead of the common reading postea, “afterward.” For Palladius and Hervetus, chapter 145, have oxycraton in the same matter. The Greek is ὀξύκραμα, which properly means posca. The Moret and Insular manuscripts have aqua, “water,” instead of posca.] and lentils. Thus he departed from the world, communicating only in the church on the holy feast of Epiphany.

Toward the end of his life, therefore, he used to say that it was now the third year since he had understood himself to be freed from carnal desire—and this after such a life, after such great sweat, after such great [Col. 0312C] labors, and after those unceasing prayers.

Once the death of his father was announced to him. He said to the man who had announced it: “Why do you blaspheme, man? I know that my father is immortal.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Life of Pior, Monk

A certain Egyptian youth named Pior (Palladius, chapter 87), after renouncing this world and leaving his father’s house, possessed such devotion toward religion that he determined before God never again to see any of his family.

After forty years, when his sister, now extremely advanced in age, discovered that her brother was alive, she began to burn with longing like a madwoman until she could come into his presence. Since she could not approach those vast deserts, she asked the bishop of that region [Col. 0312D] to write to the holy Fathers who customarily lived in the solitudes, asking them to send her brother to be seen by his sister.

Compelled by the Fathers with great force to come, he arrived at his sister’s house with another companion for the journey. He announced that he had come, saying: “Pior, your brother, has come and is standing outside the door.”

When the sound was given at the door, thinking that the old woman herself would come out to meet her brother, he called to her by name with his eyes closed and said: “I am Pior, your brother; I am, I say. Enjoy looking at me as much as you wish.”

When he believed that he had satisfied her senses, he threw himself into prayer. Although she could not persuade him in any way to rise, she blessed the glory of God [Col. 0313A] and entered her dwelling, while he, after praying at the threshold of the house, returned to the secrecy of the solitudes.

This miracle of his is also reported: when he had dug a well for himself in the place where he lived and found the water there exceedingly bitter, he lived in that same place until the very end, content with the bitterness of the water he had found, so that he might show everyone the patience of his own virtue.

Many monks afterward, desiring with obstinate determination to live in his cell after his death, were nevertheless unable to remain there for even one year. For that place always has the greatest terror and no consolation at all.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Life of Moses of Libya

A certain Moses was born in Libya, a man of the greatest gentleness and boundless love, who by heavenly grace merited the ability to cure the sick (Palladius, chapter 88).

He related the following to me. When he was still a young man in his monastery and was digging a well of enormous capacity—twenty feet wide and one hundred feet deep—and saw no sign of water at such a depth, especially since no indications appeared even below that point where moisture might be expected, they dug nearly another hundred feet and still could not find any water.

“We became very sad,” he said, “and were considering abandoning such useless work.”

But suddenly Saint Pior appeared to us from the remotest parts of the solitudes [Col. 0313C], in the great heat of summer, at the sixth hour of the day, almost entirely covered with a skin. Finally he addressed us in these words:

“Why, people of little faith, are you distressed and wishing to despair? From yesterday until now you have been swallowed up by sadness.”

He descended into the depths by the stairs they had made. After praying there with everyone, he struck the bottom of the well three times with the iron he held in his hand, saying:

“God of the holy patriarchs, we pray and beseech you: do not allow the labor of so many brothers to have been expended without cause, but grant them the use of the water they desire.”

Immediately, bubbling up from the depths of the earth, streams poured over those who were praying. After praying again, he began to wish to return to his own place. When they detained him so that he might eat with them, he said to them: “The reason for which I was sent has been accomplished; no one sent me to eat.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Life of Ephraem, Deacon of Edessa

I have no doubt that you have heard much about Ephraem, deacon of the Church of Edessa (Palladius, chapter 101), for he was worthy to be spoken of by the saints. Since he completed the journey of the spiritual path as he ought and never deviated from the straight way, he merited, by God’s grace, knowledge of natural things. Divine blessing followed him, as did the blessedness that arises from it.

Always living a quiet life and teaching for many years all who came to see him, he eventually left his cell because of the following necessity.

When a very severe famine was raging in the city of Edessa, he took pity on the rural multitude who were perishing. He approached the rich and said to them:

“Why are you not moved by any compassion for human nature, which is wasting away before your eyes, but keep what is rotting within you for the condemnation of your souls?”

They replied: “We have no one to whom we can entrust money to distribute to the needy for the purchase of food. Everyone wishes to trade for his own advantage.”

To them, as they said this, he replied: “Do I seem such a person to you?”

That man had a great reputation [Col. 0314B] among all people. They therefore answered him truthfully:

“We know that you are a man of God.”

He replied: “Then entrust your money to me. Even now, for your sake, I appoint myself to undertake the service of strangers and the poor.”

After receiving the money, he enclosed the city porticoes with solid walls and placed three hundred beds inside them. There he restored those who were wasting away from hunger. He buried those who were dying, while caring for those who still had some hope of life amid their distress. To all who were perishing from hunger and had gathered there from every direction, he provided daily service for their necessary care, using what each of the rich brought to him.

[Col. 0314C] When the year in question had been completed and there was an abundant supply of grain, everyone returned to his own home. Since he no longer had anyone with whom or for whom he should remain, he immediately returned to his cell, where he died after one month.

Divine piety had provided such an opportunity toward the end of his life, after the example of Stephen. He left behind many writings, which he himself composed, several of which are celebrated with great praise.

It is also, I think, very necessary that we provide a page in our little book for the everlasting memory of women who, as we have said, possessed manly and honorable character—women to whom our God granted struggles and rewards no less than those granted to the male sex, so as to remove every excuse [Col. 0314D] from others who are negligent. Since these women appear to belong to the inferior sex, they say that they cannot attain the glory of virtue’s commendation.

[Note: [Col. 0313] Here Lipomanus inserted the Testament of Saint Ephraem, which is found neither in Heraclides nor in Palladius; you have it among the works of Ephraem.]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Paula, Eustochium, Veneria, Theodora, Usia, Adolia, Bassianilla, Photina, Sabiniana, Asella, and Avita

I saw many women and came to know very many, both widows and virgins. Among them was Paula the Roman (Palladius, ch. 125), mother of Toxotius.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] “Among whom also Paula by name, a certain Roman woman, mother of Toxotius.” Heraclides manuscript: “Among them I remember having seen also a certain woman named Paula, a Roman woman, mother of Toxotius, prudent and spiritual. Her daughter, named Eustochium, continues to live in her monastery at Bethlehem to the present day. I myself do not know her, but I have heard from many that she is exceedingly chaste and has fifty virgins with her.” Heraclides of Faber has the same, except that instead of Toxotius he reads Eustochius.]

She was a woman of exceptionally able mind for the manner of life that is according to the spirit. [The reason she did not give herself to it was a certain Jerome, a Dalmatian by birth, who [Col. 0315A], although he seemed able to leave behind him by a very long interval many—not to say all—of those who were pursuing the perfect manner of life, nevertheless, moved by envy, drew this woman of excellent natural disposition into his own particular way of living.]

[Note: [Col. 0315D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from Heraclides of Faber.]

Her daughter, named Eustochium, still practices the monastic life at Bethlehem (Palladius, ch. 126). I never spoke with her myself; nevertheless, she is said to be distinguished for chastity and to govern a community of fifty virgins.

I also came to know a certain woman named Veneria (Palladius, ch. 127), the widow of Count Vallacinus. She divided and scattered the camel’s burden well, and freed herself from the wounds ordinarily caused by the excessive weight of riches.

I also learned that Theodora, formerly the wife of a certain tribune (Palladius, ch. 128), had left herself so little of her own [Col. 0315B] possessions that, before her death, the compassion of others provided her with an allowance for food.

At the monastery called Escyca [Palladius: Hesycha], near the sea, a woman named Usia [Palladius: Usia] had died, always upright [Note: [Col. 0397D] “Always upright.” Palladius, ch. 129, has Usia as a proper name. Heraclides appears to make “upright” an epithet of Theodora.] and in every respect exemplary in her way of life (Palladius, ch. 129). I also knew her sister Adolia (Palladius, ch. 130). Although she could not be compared with her sister’s merits, she is nevertheless said to have possessed a reputation and a life worthy of the measure of her own virtue.

I also saw a woman named Bassianilla (Palladius, ch. 131), the widow of the former Master of Soldiers Candidianus, who even to the present time labored earnestly with a ready mind and holy conduct in the discipline and toil of the monastic life.

There is also another woman named Photina (Palladius, ch. 132), a virgin and daughter of the presbyter [Col. 0315C] Theoctistus, who is regarded as highly honorable and holy.

[At Antioch I also saw a most honorable deaconess named Sabiniana. She was thought to converse with God himself, and she was the aunt of blessed John the bishop.]

[Note: [Col. 0316D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from Palladius.]

At Rome I also came to know a very good virgin of Christ named Asella, who grew old in a monastery (Palladius, ch. 133). She was a gentle and meek woman, caring there for many people. There I also saw men with their wives learning, at that time, the lives and practices of the monks.

I saw an Avita worthy of God, together with a certain Apronianus, her husband, and their daughter Eunomia (Palladius, ch. 134). They pleased God so greatly that they deserved to be transferred to the heavenly life in his presence. They too [Col. 0315D] now rest in Christ, having reached the final limit of nature; for they were freed from every bond of sin and always possessed knowledge and understanding of divine things.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Life of the Blessed Monks Julian and Adolius

I heard about a certain man named Julian, dwelling in the region of the province of Edessa (he was truly called a monk) (Palladius, ch. 102), that he had reduced all the flesh of his body to nothing, so that he displayed only skin and bones. For this he earned from God, at the end of his life, the reward of the grace of healings.

I also saw at Jerusalem another man named Adolius [Col. 0316A] (Palladius, ch. 104), who traced his origin to the town of Tarsus. When he came there, he entered upon a path worn by scarcely anyone; and he did not follow a course such as most of us follow [p. 972], but discovered for himself a new manner of life, beyond ordinary human practice.

His austerity caused even demons to tremble, and they fled from his immense abstinence and his unbroken periods of great vigils, so that he was almost thought to be what they call a phantasm—that is, not a real being but some kind of image.

During Lent he ate only every fifth day; during the rest of the year he always took food after a two-day interval. But this was especially remarkable in him: from the evening hours until the morning time when the other brothers gathered again for the oratory [Col. 0316B], he customarily spent the night standing on the Mount of Olives, at the place from which the Savior was taken up, singing psalms and praying. Whether under clouds, rain, or frost, he remained motionless.

After he had completed the customary period in this manner, he struck the doors of all the cells with the mallet-sign by which he awakened the other brothers and led them to their respective oratories. In each oratory, singing with each man one or two psalms in antiphons and offering an equal number of prayers with each, he would still return to his cell before dawn.

The brothers—indeed, I speak under God—often clothed him after stripping off his garments, which were dripping with water, until they dried. Thus, after being refreshed by a little sleep until the third hour, he tried once more, singing psalms, to continue until the evening of [Col. 0316C] the following day.

Such was the virtue of Adolius of Tarsus. He lived at Jerusalem with a life perfected in endurance and there completed the final course of his life.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Life of the Presbyter Innocentius

You have heard from many distinguished men about the most blessed Innocentius (Palladius, ch. 103), who was presbyter in the church situated at the Olive. Nevertheless, you will learn a few things from us also, who lived with him for three years. Whatever escaped the notice of others could not remain hidden from us.

He was the simplest of all. Although, under the emperor Constantius, at the beginning of that emperor’s reign, he had served among [Col. 0316D] the ranks of distinguished men, and although he had lived with his own wife until that time and had a son named Paul, serving among the Domestici, he eventually renounced worldly affairs.

His father cursed his own son because he had violated the daughter of a certain presbyter. He prayed to the Lord, saying: “Give him, Lord, such a spirit that he may never again find an opportunity for sinning in his flesh.” He believed it better for him to struggle against the violence of a demon than against the impurity of bodily pleasure. What he said came to pass: even to the present day Paul himself, bound with iron chains, remains on the Mount of Olives [Col. 0317A] and is tormented by an unclean spirit as punishment for his crime.

If I should wish to report truthfully how merciful this same Innocentius was, someone might perhaps judge that I am rambling in certain matters because of his simplicity. I know that he frequently took food secretly from his brothers and gave it to the needy. He was extraordinarily simple, and his heart knew nothing evil. For this reason he also obtained divine grace against demons.

On one occasion, while we were watching, a certain young man was brought to him. An unclean spirit had filled him and had loosened all his limbs, so completely that, when I saw him from a distance in such a state and had no doubt that he could not be cured, I ordered his mother [Col. 0317B] and the others who had brought him to be driven away.

Meanwhile the old man arrived and saw the mother standing there, weeping and lamenting over her son’s indescribable illness. Immediately that venerable man was overcome by her tears; moved by the affection of his holy heart, he groaned, took the young man by the hand, and led him into his own oratory, which he had built and in which he had placed relics of Saint John the Baptist. There he prayed for him from the third hour until the ninth hour of the day, and that very day restored him whole—cleansed of the demon and with all his limbs bound together. They had been so completely dislocated that whenever the wretched boy tried to spit, he cast his saliva backward over his own back. The demon had distorted him in this way.

[Col. 0317C] An old woman came to the man mentioned above, seeking a sheep whose loss she lamented. He said to her: “Show me the very place where you lost it.” When the woman led him to the places called Lazarion, he stood there and prayed earnestly.

The young men who had stolen the sheep had already killed it. While he was therefore offering his prayer, though no one confessed anything, and while the flesh of the animal was hidden inside the adjoining vineyard, suddenly a raven flew above it and came to rest there. It carried away a piece of the flesh and departed again. When the venerable old man saw this, he discovered the theft that had been concealed. Soon the young men themselves confessed their guilt and fell at his feet. Afterwards he exacted from them what appeared to be a fair price and returned it to the woman.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The Life of the Presbyter Philoromus

[Col. 0317D] I came to know a certain presbyter named Philoromus in the region of Galatia (Palladius, ch. 113), with whom I also spent a considerable length of time. I found this man to possess the virtue of the greatest endurance and to be a monk perfect in every respect. His mother was a slave, but his father was freeborn.

His manner of life and the freedom that belongs to Christ were so great that even those who appeared unsurpassed in nobility of birth were ashamed and astonished at his conduct and virtues.

[Col. 0318A] At the time when the wretched Julian held the imperial power, he renounced worldly affairs. When questioned by Julian, he answered him with great authority. Julian then, after first having Philoromus’s head shaved, ordered him to be beaten by the boys. He endured the punishment of the blows with the greatest patience and gave Julian immense thanks, as he himself later reported to us.

At the beginning, however, he had a very serious struggle with fornication and gluttony. He overcame these diseases of soul and body as though someone were extinguishing an immense fire with the strongest waters. He shut himself in a certain cell, constantly burdened himself with iron, refused to eat bread made from wheat, and took no food cooked by fire.

At last, after eighteen years, having subdued these passions [Col. 0318B], he sang to God a hymn worthy of such a victory, saying: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me and have not made my enemies rejoice over me” (Psalm 29).

He also endured frequent and varied conflicts with unclean spirits for forty years, living with the greatest patience within the enclosure of a single monastery.

[p. 973] He also used to tell us that for forty-two years he had tasted no kind of fruit. When fear of death once troubled him, he shut himself for six years among the tombs, so that by dwelling in sepulchers he might overcome the demon whom he felt to be terrifying because of his fear of burial.

Saint Basil the bishop gladly kept him in mind, because of the strict and simple character he always displayed and because he directed his purpose [Col. 0318C] toward God. Even to the present day, although he is eighty years old, he does not cease writing books with his own hand.

The most blessed man also said that, from the time he received the washing of regeneration and the grace of the spiritual mystery, he did not know himself ever to have used another person’s bread without cause. Rather, as he used to assure us before God, from his own labors he had given two hundred and fifty solidi to people suffering from elephantiasis, and he had supplied this money not from even the slightest loss suffered by anyone else, but from the work of his own hands.

He completed the entire journey on foot and reached Rome. After offering prayers in the church of Saints Peter and Paul, he returned on foot to Alexandria [Col. 0318D], where he again prayed in the basilica of the martyr and Evangelist Mark. He also went to Jerusalem a second time, in honor of the holy places, and always honored the holy martyrs sufficiently, at his own expense and on foot.

He also often said, for our edification, that he did not remember ever having been separated from God in his senses.

These are the struggles of the most blessed Philoromus, by which he appeared unconquered; and by them an unfading crown of glory of the holy Fathers was given to him.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The Life of Melania the Elder

That holy and greatly blessed woman Melania (Palladius, ch. 117), descended from Spanish or Roman stock, was the daughter [Col. 0319A] of a certain Marcellinus, a former consul, and the wife of an honorable man whose name I cannot remember.

Reduced to widowhood in the twenty-second year of her age, she deserved, through love of divinity, to be joined to the eternal Bridegroom, whom she loved until the end of her life. Revealing the secrets of her heart to no one—for this was forbidden at the beginning of Valens’ reign—and having appointed her son as administrator, she sent what she appeared to possess in movable property onto a ship with certain boys and girls, and hastened by sea to Alexandria.

After she had sold everything there and converted it all into money and gold, she reached the mountain of Nitria. There she saw the venerable fathers: the most blessed Pambo, Arsisius the servant of Christ, the elder Serapion [Col. 0319B], Paphnutius the Scythian, Isidore the confessor and bishop of the city called Hermopolis, and the holy Dioscorus.

She remained with them in the desert places for only six months, visiting and seeing all the holy men who were there.

Afterwards, when the Augustal prefect of Alexandria condemned Isidore, Pithymus, Adelphius, Paphnutius, Pambo, and a certain old man named Ammonius, who had only one ear, together with twelve bishops and presbyters and certain others—112 persons in all—to exile around Palestine and Diocaesarea, this most blessed woman followed all of them and provided them with her service from her own resources.

When those who guarded the exiles prevented her from doing this [Col. 0319C]—as they themselves often told me, for I also saw the holy Pithymus, Isidore, and Paphnutius—that blessed woman then put on a child’s clothing and, toward evening, carried them everything necessary for life.

When the consular governor of Palestine learned of this, he thought that he could fill his own coffers with some smoke and terror arising from her money. He ordered her—she was unknown to them—to be seized and handed over to prison.

From that place the holy woman sent him this message through certain intermediaries: “I was the daughter of this man and the wife of that man; now, however, I am a handmaid of Christ. Therefore do not suppose that I should be despised because of my present clothing, since, if I wished, I could easily exalt myself. You cannot therefore terrify me in any way, nor can you take anything [Col. 0319D] away from my possessions.

“For this reason, lest, through ignorance of these things, you incur some danger or crime, I have sent you this message.”

It was as though she were saying: “Sometimes such measures must be taken against the imprudent, and arrogance must be used against them like a hawk or a dog, released at the proper time to seize the proud.”

Terrified immediately by such words, the judge excused himself to her for what he had done and honored her as she deserved. He also ordered that she might visit those men whenever she wished.

After the men mentioned above had been recalled from exile, she established a monastery for herself at Jerusalem, where she completed twenty-seven years, having fifty virgin sisters with her [Col. 0320A].

There was also with her a certain man named Rufinus, an Italian citizen from the town of Aquileia, a man of noble birth and notably firm character in his religious profession. He later also deserved to attain the presbyterate.

No one of the male sex could be found more gentle, more steadfast, or more peaceful than he, as though he knew everything. For twenty-seven years, therefore, these two were accustomed, at their own expense, to receive and support at Jerusalem all the holy and foreign bishops, monks, and virgins—for this they had vowed to God—and they made all who came to them better through contemplation of such great and such worthy things.

They also restored to the holy Church the four hundred monks who were separating themselves from the Church on account of Paulinus. In addition, by persuading them of the truth and teaching them all continually, they recalled to our Church all the other members of perverse sects, including those who fought with sacrilegious speech against [Col. 0320B] the Holy Spirit. They honored and frequently fed the clergy of that place.

Doing these things together, they completed their lives in devout zeal, giving no one even the slightest suspicion of scandal, and leaving the whole world filled with spiritual edification.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Life of the Presbyter Chronius

A certain man named Chronius (Palladius, ch. 89), originally from a village called Phoenice, which was close to the desert, measured fifteen thousand paces from his own village to a certain boundary of the desert, counting by the right foot.

[Note: [Col. 0398A] “Counting by the right foot.” Why should it be counted by the right foot? I believe it means that Chronius went from his cell toward the right, into the desert, and dug a well there. That is, the place where the well was dug was fifteen thousand paces from the village of Phoenice, where Chronius originated, the paces being counted by the right foot—that is, proceeding from his cell toward the right. In Palladius, chapter 89, the Greek reads: Ἀπομετρήσας ἀπὸ τῆς ἰδίας κώμης πλησίον οὔσης τῆς ἐρήμου μύρια πεντακισχίλια βήματα, τῷ δεξιῷ ποδὶ ἀριθμούμενα — “Having measured from his own village, which was near the desert, fifteen thousand paces, counted by the right foot.”]

There, after praying [Col. 0320C], he dug a well for himself and found a vein of excellent water, descending only seven fathoms (orgyai, as they call them) to the bottom of the well. He also built a small cell for himself beside it. [p. 974]

From the day he established himself in that dwelling, he prayed to God with the greatest earnestness that he might never again approach places inhabited by human beings. After a few years he deserved to become a presbyter, and he gathered around himself as many as two hundred men from various brothers.

They say that his great virtue was this: for sixty years he served God at the altar and carried out the priestly office, yet never left the desert places and never touched bread except what he had obtained by his own work and sweat.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Life of the Monk Jacob, Paphnutius Cephalas, and Certain Others Who Died Suddenly or Fell

[Col. 0320D] A certain man named Jacob, who had acquired the name Clodus (Palladius, ch. 90), joined Chronius from neighboring places. The two lived together a perfect monastic life. Blessed Antony knew them both.

One day, the holy Paphnutius, whom they called Cephalas (Palladius, ch. 91), was living with them also. By God’s gift, he possessed great knowledge of the Scriptures and was accustomed to interpret both the entire Old Testament and the New, although he himself had never read anything from the sacred Scriptures.

He was so gentle and peaceful that he could surpass even prophetic [Col. 0321A] virtue in the meekness of his life. The following praise is reported about him: for eighty years he never possessed two tunics at the same time.

When I and the holy deacons Evagrius and Albinus had seen these men, we asked them together, wishing to know what cause made some of the brothers go astray, sometimes fall into a sin, or depart entirely from their intention to follow the right path.

For in those very days it had happened that a monk named Cheremon (Palladius, ch. 92), sitting in his chair, suddenly died, and other brothers suddenly saw him dead in it, still holding in his hands the work he had been doing.

[Col. 0321B] It had also happened that one of the brothers, while trying to dig a well, perished, buried beneath the mound of earth (Palladius, ch. 93).

And another man, coming from the regions of Scetis, died on the journey itself because he could not endure his thirst (Palladius, ch. 94).

Among these men, at that very time, a certain Stephen had also abandoned the monastery of the brothers and descended into secular life because of lust (Palladius, ch. 95). Reports were also given concerning Eucarpus; Heron of Alexandria; Valens of Palestine; and Ptolemy of Egypt, who lived in the regions of Scetis—reports of whatever misfortunes had befallen them.

Because of all this, we begged those holy men to explain to us the causes of the events that compelled men of such exemplary life, living in desert places [Col. 0321C], either to change their minds, to be carried away into shameful and lustful behavior, or to be deceived and perish in other ways.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Answers to the Questions Just Mentioned

They gave us the following answer (Palladius, ch. 95), and Paphnutius himself, in whom there was the greatest knowledge of all things, answered together with them: everything that happens in this world is divided in two ways, into the will of God and the permission of God.

Whatever proceeds from virtue of soul and is done for the glory of God proceeds from the will of God. But whatever we experience as dangerous and harmful, in which we detect some perversity or ruin, happens by God’s permission.

This permission [Col. 0321D] itself proceeds from a cause—namely, some sin or unbelief gradually creeping in. For it cannot happen that a person whose wisdom and life have been tested should fall into a sinful disgrace or be thrown by the tricks of demons into snares of error.

Those, therefore, who depart from the path of virtue with a corrupted purpose of mind or reckless will easily become accustomed to sinning. They are abandoned by divine assistance so that they cannot understand what is beneficial. When they realize that they have been abandoned by God and recognize the collapse brought about by their perverse change, they begin to correct either their purpose or their deed.

Sometimes our very action is a crime, [Col. 0322A] when we do something neither from a right purpose nor in the manner that is appropriate. We know that this frequently happens.

For example, if a man who lives shamefully appears, from a disgraceful intention of soul, to show mercy toward a young girl, his purpose is shameful, though his action is reasonable insofar as he appears to offer protection to a girl who is alone.

Again, someone may, from a right intention, show mercy to a sick person or an old man and make himself poor out of his wealth, but with a parsimonious hand and with a certain sorrow of unwillingness. His intention may appear right, while the action itself is judged unworthy of that intention. For a merciful person ought to show mercy with joy and generosity.

Moreover, those men said that certain advantages exist in the faculties of many people. [Col. 0322B] They declared that some men, whose souls are naturally disposed and keen for virtue, possess excellent character in their intention and in the practices of the monks.

But when something is not done for the sake of that which we know to be good, neither the deed, nor the natural ability of the human mind, nor those very advantages implanted in the minds of many are credited to God, the giver of all good things. Rather, everything is attributed to the power of one’s own will.

Then, when such men have necessarily been abandoned by God, they fall into some disgrace. There they either suffer or commit many shameful things through the very person who has fallen into the act of a disgraceful life.

When, gradually warned by sobriety of mind, they withdraw from that swelling of spirit which they had thought to be a great virtue, they are compelled, once they recognize the giver, to condemn it.

[Col. 0322C] For when someone is puffed up by the arrogance of his eloquence or by the ability and keenness of his mind, he does not first attribute to God the origin and nourishment of those good qualities, which descend only from God’s own fountain. Instead, he considers them the product of his own study and nature.

Then God removes from him the angel of his providence. Once deprived of this, the man who had begun to grow proud while taking pleasure in gifts that were not his own is attacked and conquered by his enemy, the demon, and falls into some shameful crime.

From there he descends, raging like an irrational animal or a dog, even to that diabolical persuasion which is pride. Once the witness of his chaste and exemplary life has been removed, whatever [p. 975] such men may say, of whatever kind it may be, can neither be believed nor accepted by anyone.

[Col. 0322D] For those holy people who had been accustomed to listen to them teaching begin to flee from them, cursing the doctrine of their disgraceful mind and character, just as one must avoid a spring full of leeches, even when thirsty, so that the saying of divine Scripture may be proved true: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justice and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Psalm 49).

And truly, you might think the minds of sinners resemble polluted springs. Those who devote themselves to gluttony and drunkenness are compared with muddy places; those who are greedy for money or rapacious are compared with places filled with frogs; but those who are envious or proud, while nevertheless possessing some knowledge and expertise, are judged equal to springs [Col. 0323A] that nourish serpents among their waters.

Their speech always flows forth eloquently like useful water, but no one can willingly drink from them because of the bitterness of their character. Therefore holy David asked God to give him these three gifts: goodness, discipline, and knowledge (Psalm 118).

Without goodness and discipline, knowledge is exceedingly useless. But if such a man hastens to correct himself, abandons the cause for which God abandoned him—I mean pride—and wishes to recognize his own measure, so that from then on he neither exalts himself over others as better or greater, but always gives thanks to God, knowledge will surely return to him, glorious once more through the testimony of good deeds.

For spiritual eloquence, unless it agrees with honorable conduct and a chaste life [Col. 0323B], will resemble ears of grain spoiled by the corruption of the winds: they bear only the appearance of ears of grain, but do not possess what can help or nourish a person.

Every fall of a human being, whether produced by a fault of the tongue or of the mind, and whether proceeding from anyone’s actions or from any part of our body, even to the height of pride, usually occurs because we are stripped of God’s favor.

Yet God does this in order to spare more fully those whom he abandons. For if, together with that damnable perversity of character which they possess, he had also supplied their minds with the nourishment of eloquence, the Lord would, as though by his own testimony, have encouraged them. Without doubt they would have become perfect demons, if they had understood themselves to be ascending to lofty things while polluted by the filth of their life [Col. 0323C].

Those most holy and excellent men also used to tell us this: “When you see someone whose life is exceedingly bad but whose eloquence is great, you should remember that demon whom we read of speaking with Christ in the sacred Scriptures” (Matthew 4).

“You should also remember the passage in which we read: ‘The serpent was the wisest of all the beasts on earth’ (Genesis 2). That wisdom harmed it all the more because it possessed within itself no assistance from any other virtue.

“For a good and prudent man ought to understand what God has given him, to speak what he understands, and to do what he speaks. For if truth does not accompany eloquence, together with the virtues of life and honorable character, it will certainly appear to be bread without salt [Col. 0323D], insipid, which, according to the words of Job, cannot be eaten (Job 6), or which will be the cause of death to those who eat it.

“For if bread without salt can be eaten, then there may also be some good taste in empty words that are not confirmed by the testimony of good deeds.”

God sometimes abandons his servants in different ways.

At one time he abandons someone because of a hidden virtue, so that it may be revealed and made known to others, as in the case of that holy athlete Job. God revealed his secrets to him and said (Job 40): “Do not refuse to enter judgment with me, and do not suppose that I have given you these answers for any other reason than that you may be shown righteous to all. I, for whom nothing can be hidden [Col. 0324A], knew you very well; but because other people did not know you, and thought that you worshiped me because of the riches you had received, I therefore permitted such a temptation to come upon you. I therefore took away all your possessions, so that I might show everyone your wisdom, which could give thanks even in that condition.”

God appears to abandon people in another way when he wishes to turn them away from the evil of pride. We know this in the case of the holy Paul. Paul was then thought to have been abandoned by God, when he was oppressed on every side by so many and such great blows and was wearied by the various tribulations that Scripture enumerates: “There was given me,” he says, “an angel of Satan to buffet me, so that I might not be exalted” (2 Corinthians 11).

For perhaps, if together with the things he did by divine grace that were worthy of wonder he had also possessed some [Col. 0324B] ease or abundance of circumstances, the devil might have caressed him with the great honor that people bestowed upon him, softened him through many good things, and raised him up in a new swelling of pride.

A paralytic was once abandoned by God because of his own offenses. Jesus said to him: “Behold, you have been made well; do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5).

Judas was also abandoned. He preferred silver to the word of God, and for this reason he hanged himself and perished (Acts 1).

Esau was abandoned and fell into the crime of sin; for he preferred the filth of his entrails to his father’s blessings (Genesis 27).

Considering all these things, the most blessed Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke of those who are abandoned by God: “And as they did not approve [Col. 0324C] of having God in their knowledge, God delivered them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things that are not fitting” (Romans 1).

Of certain others who thought they possessed divine knowledge but whose minds were corrupt and proud, he said: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,” joined to the demon of arrogance and swelling.

Therefore it follows: “For this reason God delivered them over to dishonorable passions, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves.”

We must therefore understand that no one can fall into the crime of some great sin unless divine providence has first abandoned him because of his evil character.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The Life of Abbot Elpidius and His Companions Ennesius, Eustathius, and Sisinnius, Elpidius’s Disciple

[Col. 0324D] Elpidius was a certain man who traced his origin to Cappadocia (Palladius, ch. 106) and later deserved to attain the honor of the presbyterate. He belonged to the monastery of Timothy, a certain Cappadocian chorepiscopus.

[Note: [Col. 0398A] “Chorepiscopus.” Formerly the word was *coepiscopus*, “fellow-bishop,” but Palladius, chapter 106, has χωρεπίσκοπον, “chorepiscopus.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

Timothy was a very distinguished man. Elpidius made his dwelling in one of the caves mentioned above.

He displayed such zeal for abstinence in himself [p. 976] that he surpassed everyone. For the twenty-five years of his life, he took food only on the Lord’s Day and on the Sabbath, and throughout entire nights he sang psalms while standing [Col. 0325A] and praying.

An innumerable multitude of brothers followed him as bees follow their king, making the caves and desert places themselves appear to form a city. It was exceedingly delightful to observe the astonishing variety of their life and manner of living.

One night, while this same Elpidius was singing psalms with us, rejoicing in the glory of true hope and enduring the dangers of tribulation for Christ, a scorpion wounded him. He trod on it and did not even leave the spot where he had resolved to stand. Thus he disregarded the pain inflicted by the scorpion’s bite.

One day, when one of the brothers was holding a small piece of a branch from a dry vine, Elpidius took it from him while sitting at the summit of the mountain and buried it in the ground as though planting it. Although it was entirely the wrong season [Col. 0325B] for planting, it grew to an immense size, and a vine became so large that, spreading upward, it covered the roofs of the entire church.

With this athlete of Christ there was also Ennesius, a great and honorable man, and his brother Eustathius. They shared one life of continence and the same completion in Christ (Palladius, chs. 107–108).

So completely was the aforementioned Elpidius free from all passions of mind or body, his limbs having been wasted away by various exertions of abstinence, that the framework of his bones shone like the sun.

Some of his devoted disciples report that for twenty-five years he never turned toward the west (and indeed a mountain rose steeply above the entrance to the cave), and that he never saw the sun after the sixth hour, when it declined from the summit of the heavens toward the western regions, nor did he behold the stars rising in the west. From the time he entered the cave just mentioned, he never descended from its mountain until his body was buried.

One of this Elpidius’s disciples was named Sisinnius, born in Cappadocia. He traced his lineage to a servile origin, but possessed in God the freedom of confidence (Palladius, chapter 109). For we ought also to record the very lowly origin of certain people, so that the greater glory of the nobility bestowed by Christ may become apparent—the nobility through which people are recalled to true and heavenly dignity and freedom. After remaining with his master for six or seven years, Sisinnius finally shut himself inside a certain tomb, where for three years he stood continually in prayer. During that time he neither walked, sat, nor lay down, by night or by day. He also obtained spiritual power against demons. Now he has returned to his homeland, become a presbyter, and gathered brothers and sisters together in one community. He lived so free from every fault of mind and body that he demonstrated that there was no distinction of sex between males and females, so that the saying of Holy Scripture might be fulfilled: “For in Christ Jesus we are neither male nor female” (Galatians 3). He is also hospitable to all strangers, although it is well known that he possesses absolutely nothing—an object of reproach and punishment to those who, though rich, never give anything to the needy.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Life of Gaddan, Servant of God

I knew in Palestine an old man named Gaddan (Palladius, chapter 110), who always lived without a roof in the regions around the Jordan River. While he was dwelling in the districts of the Dead Sea, certain Jews, driven headlong by the madness of envy, once came against him armed with swords. When one of them wished to strike him, God worked the following miracle: his right hand, which he had raised to deliver the blow, withered, and the sword fell from the fingers with which he had been holding it.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Life of the Monk Elijah

[Col. 0326B]

A certain monk named Elijah (Palladius, chapter 111), accustomed to live inside a cave in those same regions, was a man disciplined to the perfect rule of conduct, hospitable, and full of charity. One day a crowd of brothers came to him—for it was a public thoroughfare there—and suddenly he ran out of bread. He faithfully told us himself that, when he had begun to feel extremely sad and had entered his cave, he suddenly found there three large, freshly baked loaves. Twenty brothers were nourished from them together, to complete satisfaction. He also recalled that one loaf remained, and that it afterward sufficed for his own food for twenty-five days.

## CHAPTER XL. The Life of Sabas, Servant of God

[Col. 0326C]

There was a certain man named Sabas [Note: In Palladius, chapter 112, he is called Sabbatius.], a native of Jericho, a layman with a wife, who loved all the monks so greatly that at night he would travel through the wilderness visiting all their cells. Before each dwelling he would place a single measure of dates and as many vegetables as he thought would suffice, since the monks who live in the regions of the Jordan do not use bread. One day a lion attacked him, caught and threw him down after pursuing him for the distance of one stone’s throw, but turned aside from him and seized only his donkey.

## CHAPTER XLI. The Life of the Monk Abraham

A certain man named Abraham existed (Palladius, chapter 105), an Egyptian by birth, who led a sufficiently harsh and austere life in the desert regions. At one point, however, he became deranged in mind through a certain presumption. He came to the church and began to quarrel with the presbyters, saying: “I have been made a presbyter by Christ this very night, and he received me as I performed the divine rites.” The holy Fathers afterward separated him from the desert and handed him over to ordinary secular human society. They restored him to his former soundness of mind, healed him, and freed him from all the pride by which the demon had deceived him, recalling him to knowledge of his own humility and weakness.

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning Melania the Elder and the Younger, Pinianus, Albina, Silvia, and Jovinius

[Col. 0327A]

[Above I gave a brief account of that holy and admirable Melania (Palladius, chapter 118); nevertheless, I shall also include in this narrative the remaining details that are lacking. [Note: The material enclosed in brackets is absent from Heraclides or Palladius of Lipomani.]] How much wealth she scattered, inflamed by an immense love of God like a flame of fire, is hardly within my ability to recount, or even that of those who live in the regions of Persia [977]. All four quarters of heaven knew and experienced her memorable good deeds. For thirty-seven years she continually received and fed the wretched and strangers, supplying food and every necessity at her own expense to churches, monasteries, prisons, and travelers. Her parents also, and her sons, acting as her agents, supplied much from their own resources. She persevered so continually and so completely in receiving and cherishing everyone that she did not wish to possess even a palm’s breadth of ground. She was never so captivated by the desire for, or love of, her only son that she could at any time be torn away from the love of Christ. Through her prayers, which were especially constant, that young man himself also grew in commendable education, good morals, and even secular honors, and attained a noble marriage, from which he had two sons.

After a long time, when she heard that her granddaughter Melania had married a man, and learned that after the wedding she wished to renounce this world, she feared that people of evil life, or of an evil sect and perverse teaching, might attach themselves to her. For this reason, although already very old—that is, sixty years of age—she sailed from the city of Caesarea to the city of Rome within twenty days. When she had seen those for whom she had come, she earnestly instructed and immediately converted to Christianity the blessed husband of her granddaughter, a respectable and noble man named Pinianus, who was nevertheless a pagan. She was able to persuade him spiritually also to abstain from intercourse with his own wife.

After confirming these two—her granddaughter Melania and her husband Pinianus—she likewise instructed Albina, her daughter-in-law, that is, her son’s wife, in all things. Thus she persuaded them all that, after selling whatever possessions they had in the city, they should come to the chaste and tranquil harbor of life. Against all the other men and matrons of the Roman people she fought daily as against wild beasts. They tried to prevent her from approaching anyone else, fearing that by her teaching and speech she might convert others to such a purpose. But she said to them: “It was written four hundred years ago: ‘For the final hour has already come’ (1 John 2). Why, then, do you so gladly linger in the vanity of this life? You ought to fear that the time of Antichrist may arrive, and that you may no longer be permitted to enjoy your riches and your parents’ possessions.” [Col. 0328A] Thus she freed all these people from secular snares and brought them to a life in the desert. By her counsel she also instructed her very young son as she wished and brought him as far as Sicily. After selling all his possessions there and collecting gold from the valuation of his estates, she transported him back to Jerusalem. There, after dividing all her wealth according to her own will, the best and gentlest of women rested in a blessed death within forty days, leaving a monastery at Jerusalem and assigning it sufficient funds.

But when all these people had departed from Rome, a certain barbarian storm and tempest suddenly overwhelmed the city itself. It invaded and seized everything to such an extent that it did not even leave the bronze objects that had customarily stood in public. The hostile attack overturned and destroyed everything as plunder, so that Rome—the city that had continually grown and continually been adorned for a thousand two hundred years—suddenly appeared as one enormous ruin and desolation. Then those who had obeyed the most salutary teaching rejoiced that they had been withdrawn from intolerable evils, whose mother is always siege. Those who had refused to obey were astonished at the power and glory of God, who by such a reversal of circumstances persuaded unbelievers to believe: for when everyone else had been placed under the yoke of captivity, only the houses mentioned above escaped and were preserved—those which, through the devotion of holy Melania, had been reserved by God like that sacrifice called a whole burnt offering—while the others in the city who had opposed their salvation were shut up in belated and fruitless repentance.

It happened afterward that we traveled together from Aelia to Egypt, escorting the holy Silvia [Note: In Palladius, chapter 142, she is called Silvania.], a virgin of God and the sister of the former prefect Rufinus.

Jovinius was also with us at that time a deacon, but now bishop of the city of Ascalon [Note: In Palladius, chapter 143, he is called Jubinus.], a very holy man and a devoted lover and most diligent reader of literature. When we were overtaken on the journey by an exceedingly oppressive heat and had entered the town of Pelusium, the holy Jovinius, exhausted by the excessive heat, began to cool his hands and feet by pouring very cold water over them. When he had done this as he wished, he threw himself upon a feather mattress spread on the ground. That holy woman Silvia approached him like a wise mother approaching her true son, and, reproving his softness and luxury, said: “How have you dared, at your age—when your blood is still alive—to care for and pamper your body in this way? Do you not understand what injuries to the soul ordinarily arise from this? Believe me, speaking confidently: although I am now sixty years old, except for the tips of my fingers I have washed neither my face, nor my feet, nor any part of my body with water. I did this even though I was always afflicted with various illnesses and was sometimes compelled by the physicians themselves to use bathing. Yet I never wished to indulge the ancient habit of my body; I have never rested in bed, nor traveled reclining in a litter.”

This woman was herself highly eloquent and possessed a great love of literature, so that by reading she turned nights into days. She knew all the books of the ancient interpreters exceedingly well. Among them she had read three hundred thousand verses—those of Gregory, Pierius, Stephen, and Basil—and two hundred thousand verses by other most learned men. Yet she did not run through them superficially; she went back over each author seven times. Thus, completely freed by her knowledge from the deceitfulness of names and sects, she was able, on the heavenly wings supplied by literary learning, to fly toward the eternal hope of the Savior, becoming a spiritual hen, destined to receive immortal rewards from him.

## CHAPTER XLIII. The Life of Olympias the Widow

[Col. 0329B]

Following in her footsteps, a woman named Olympias, of most chaste conduct and burning with the love of God (Palladius, chapter 144), displayed a life equal to hers, following in all things the counsel of the divine Scriptures. She was the daughter, in the flesh, of Seleucius, who had been a comes; the granddaughter of the prefect Ablavius; and the daughter-in-law, for only a few days, of Nebridius, who had been prefect of Constantinople. But she was the wife of no one at all: they say that she died a virgin, glorying rather in the marriage of the Word of truth. She scattered and distributed all her resources among the poor. Her struggle in defense of the truth was never small. She also taught many other women and honored many presbyters and bishops, as was proper. For the truth she revered, she was worthy to attain the palm of the confessors. Those living in Constantinople strive to compare her name and life with those very confessors, as I have said. For such was also the end of her life in this world: at the last she exposed herself to every danger for the name of God.

## CHAPTER XLIV. The Life of Candida the Widow and of Gelasia

Another blessed woman, similar in character, followed her: Candida by name (Palladius, chapter 145), daughter of Trajan, master of the soldiers, a great ornament to the Christian name and an outstanding cultivator of chastity, admirable in her manner of life, honoring the holy churches and bishops. She sent her own daughter on ahead to Christ, united to her by the order of her teaching in virginity, as the greatest gift of her body and virtues. Later, after completing the duty of chastity and holiness and distributing all her goods and possessions appropriately, she too followed her daughter.

I knew her as one who labored at night and always ground grain with her own hands in order to weaken the strength of her body. I often heard her say that, since fasting alone was not sufficient for her, she had also added laborious vigils, which, together with fasting, fought against incorporeal powers so that she might lay aside the pride and swelling of the mind. [Col. 0330A] She always abstained from the flesh of animals; on feast days and holy days she was accustomed to eat fish and vegetables with oil. For the rest of her life she lived content with vinegar-water and dry bread.

A most chaste woman named Gelasia afterward imitated her footsteps and approached the yoke of virginity with devout sentiments (Palladius, chapter 146). She was the daughter of a certain tribune. Her memorable virtue is reported as follows: the setting sun never saw her anger, whether she had been angry with a male servant, a female servant, or anyone else. This blessed woman fled from the memory of wrongdoing, knowing that its path led to eternal death.

## CHAPTER XLV. The Life of the Anchorite Solomon

[Col. 0330B]

I spent four continuous years in Antinoopolis, a city of the Thebaid province, and during that entire period I came to know all the monasteries there (Palladius, chapter 96). One thousand two hundred highly exemplary men lived in the territory of that city, supporting themselves by the sweat of their own hands. Many of them—those whom they call anchorites—had withdrawn into caves among the rocks and in the wilderness.

Among them was a monk named Solomon, most chaste and gentle, who had received from divine grace an exceptional gift of patience. He said that he had spent fifty years in his cave, always supplying himself abundantly with what was sufficient for his food by the work of his hands. He also appeared to have learned all the Holy Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XLVI. The Life of Abbot Dorotheus and Diocles

[Col. 0330C]

A certain presbyter named Dorotheus, living in another cave, was a man of immeasurable goodness (Palladius, chapter 97), and he himself led an irreproachable life. Because he had been found worthy of the priestly office, he ministered the holy mysteries there to all the brothers.

Once the younger Melania—the granddaughter of the elder Melania, of whom I shall speak below (below, chapter 49)—sent him five hundred solidi, asking him to distribute them among the brothers living there. He took only three for himself and ordered that the rest be given to a certain solitary monk named Diocles, a man endowed with knowledge of all things. Dorotheus said that Diocles was much wiser than he, since he could divide everything without injury to the soul, knowing how much more and more reasonably ought to be distributed to each person. He said that the three solidi would be enough for him.

This Diocles had first been a grammarian (Palladius, chapter 98), but afterward devoted himself to philosophy. As time went on, when he was twenty-eight years old, divine grace persuaded him to renounce secular studies and devote himself to the discipline of Christ and the knowledge of heavenly philosophy. Having himself then spent thirty-five years in the caves, he said to us: “When the human mind withdraws from the thought of God, it becomes either like a demon or comparable to mute animals.”

When we wished to learn from him the reasoning behind this statement, he said: “If someone withdraws from God, it is necessary that he fall either into some desire or into some anger. He said that desire belongs to irrational animals, and anger to demons.” When I objected and asked how it could be possible for the human mind to remain continually with God, he then said: “Whatever the thought or action in which the soul of a person who lives according to God may be engaged, if it is devout and hastens to please him, it is evident that the person is with God.”

## CHAPTER XLVII. The Life of Abbot Capito

[Col. 0331B]

There was a certain young man named Capito (Palladius, chapter 99), who in the earlier period of his life had been a robber. After completing fifty years in his cave, he never wished to approach within the fourth milestone of the town of Antinoopolis, nor even as far as the nearby river Nile. He said that he could not yet expose himself to the society and conversation of many people, because the common enemy was still resisting him vigorously.

With him we saw another man from among those solitaries (Palladius, chapter 100), likewise living in the secrecy of his cave. Deceived and led astray by the goads of vainglory under the guise of dreams, he in turn was accustomed to deceive in a similar way those whom he led astray. He seemed, in a manner, to be a foolish shepherd of winds and a pursuer of shadows (Ecclesiasticus 34:2), possessing bodily chastity indeed, undoubtedly because of his old age, the great length of time he had spent in the desert, and perhaps the very vanity of empty glory, which had corrupted his heart and mind—as it commonly does—with thoughts of perverse things and had made him a stranger to the life with God.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The Life of Amala [Note: Amata.] and Taor, and of Another Virgin

[Note: I think there is an error in Heraclides’ translator; for in Palladius, chapter 137, she is called Amma Talida. Now you see where Amata came from. In these books Amma sometimes occurs as a common noun, not a proper name.]

There are twelve monasteries of women in the same city of Antinoopolis, inhabited by virgins living a perfect life (Palladius, chapter 137). In one of them I saw an old servant of Christ named Amata, who, according to her neighbors’ own report, had already spent eighty years in her monastery. Sixty women lived with her and, through her teaching, lived in the purity of abstinence. They all loved her so greatly that it was not even necessary to fasten a key to the monastery door, as was customary elsewhere. The old woman’s immense love and teaching alone kept them all there, preserving their bodies and minds for the glory of incorruption.

This old woman, whom I have mentioned, was so pure in mind and body, free from the thought and passion of sin, that when I entered to see her and sat down, she sat beside me without hesitation and even placed her hands upon my shoulders. Astonishingly great was the confidence in Christ arising from her chastity.

In this same monastery there was a certain virgin named Taor (Palladius, chapter 138), her disciple, who had spent thirty years in the monastery. She never wished to wear a tunic, a *mavorte* [Note: *Mavorte.* Immediately below, chapter 49: “whatever silk garments she had in *mavortia*.” It is now written *mavorte*, formerly *maforte*, from the Greek μαφόριον (*maphórion*).], or new footwear, saying: “I desire nothing of that sort, lest because of it I should be compelled to go outside.” All the others were accustomed to go to church only on the Lord’s Day, for the sake of divine Communion; but that holy woman, dressed in the most ragged garments, remained alone in the monastery, continually doing her work. She was of such elegant appearance that her face and beauty could have attracted even the most chaste and steadfast man, had she not been so adorned with good character that she possessed within herself an inestimable guardian of her own chastity. This guardian would also have driven the eyes of anyone who desired her shamefully to immense modesty and fear.

Another woman lived nearby (Palladius, chapter 139), whose face I was unable to see. For, from the time she renounced this world, she is said never to have left the monastery, where she reportedly completed sixty years living together with her mother. When she was finally about to depart from this world, a martyr named Colothus, who was venerated in those same regions, appeared to her in a vision [Note: “The martyr named Colothus, who was venerated in those same regions.” This is how Palladius is to be explained through Hervetus. The common annotator of the margins had written in the margin: “He is here called a martyr who presides over a martyr-shrine”; but Hervetus’ unclear translation misled him.], saying to her: “Today you will go to your Lord, where you will also see all the saints. Come, therefore, to the basilica of my martyr-shrine, so that you may dine there with me.”

When she heard this, she rose at once at first light and, dressed as usual, took with her in a small basket bread, olives, and chopped vegetables. Then, for the first time after so many years, she went out and came to the shrine of the holy martyr. After properly completing her prayers, she began to wait for that time of day when everyone would have entirely departed from the place mentioned. When she saw that this had happened, she sat down and invoked the holy martyr, saying: “Holy Colothus, bless my food, and by your intercession deign to journey with me.” After eating and praying again, she returned to her monastery around sunset. There she gave her mother a little book of Clement, who was called Stromateus, written on the sayings of the prophet Amos, saying to her: “Give this to the bishop who is in exile, and tell him to pray for me, for I am departing to my Lord.” That very night she passed away. She felt neither any pain in her head nor any bodily fever, but prepared herself as she was to be buried, commending her spirit into the hands of God.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The Life of Melania the Younger, Her Husband Pinianus, and Her Mother Albina

Since above I promised that I would speak of the younger Melania, I shall now discharge the duty I owe (Palladius, chapter 119; above, chapter 46). For it is not right to pass over, as though in haste, the admirable youth of her embodied life, nor to let such virtue pass without mention—virtue for which she is now rightly preferred to old women and to women most devoted to God.

[Col. 0333A]

Her parents compelled her to marry, using very great force, first to a certain man of the Roman people. Yet she was continually urged on by the constant teaching of her grandmother, and advanced so far spiritually in the city that she did not remain long in the married state. For after she had borne two children and both had died, she came to hate marriage so greatly for Christ’s sake that she said to her husband Pinianus, the son of the former prefect Severus: “If you love chastity and wish to become a monk with me, I shall acknowledge you as the lord of my life. But if this seems burdensome to you as a young man, take whatever possessions I have and leave my body free to me, so that, living thereafter according to God’s will, I may fulfill what I desire. And by following her virtue, I may acknowledge myself to be the heir of my grandmother, whose name I also bear. For if God had wished us to enjoy this world, he would never have taken from me by premature death both children whom I bore.”

After the dispute between them had long disturbed the marriage yoke, God at last had mercy on the young man, inspiring his soul also to despise secular and earthly desires. Thus the holy saying could be fulfilled through the Apostle: “How do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? How do you know, man, whether you will save your wife?” (1 Corinthians 7). She had married the man when she was thirteen years old, lived with him for seven years, and renounced the world in her twentieth year.

First, whatever silk garments she had in *mavortia*, she gave to the holy altars; we know that the blessed Olympias did the same. She distributed her remaining silk garments among various church ornaments. She sent her silver and gold through a certain Dalmatian citizen named Paul, a monk and presbyter, by ship as far as the East. She divided everything in this way: she assigned ten thousand solidi to Egypt and the Thebaid; ten thousand to the city of Antioch and the regions surrounding it; fifteen thousand solidi to the province of Palestine; ten thousand to the churches throughout the individual islands, together with those condemned to exile and banishment; and to the churches, monasteries, hospices, and all the needy under the western sky, she personally supplied everything she knew they required.

[Col. 0333D]

All this, and much more besides than we have mentioned, as God knows, she snatched from the hands of Alaric, as though from the mouth of a lion, through her own faithful action (2 Timothy 4:17). She freed all the slaves of either sex who wished to be manumitted, as many as eight thousand. As for the rest, who preferred to serve her brother, she granted them to him, distributing three solidi for each one. She sold all the estates she had in Aquitania, Gaul, Tarraconensis, Spain, and the Gallic regions. She kept only the lands she possessed in Sicily, Campania, and Africa, so that she might afterward support and care for the monasteries from their proceeds. Such was this woman’s wisdom in distributing the burden of wealth.

[Col. 0334A]

Her life according to her chosen purpose was as follows. She was accustomed always to take food every other day; at the very beginning, however, she ate only every fifth day, and she observed this practice while also carrying out, with her maidservants, the daily turns of service that she kept with them as with sisters in a monastery.

Her mother Albina was also with her (Palladius, chapter 120), leading an equal life and likewise distributing her own wealth separately. They always lived on their estates and sometimes stayed in Sicily, sometimes in Campania, with fifteen eunuchs, sixty virgins, and other freeborn women or maidservants.

Her husband Pinianus likewise led an equal life with thirty monks (Palladius, chapter 121). He either devoted himself to reading the Holy Scriptures, took pleasure in the beauty of gardens, or enjoyed the company and conversation of the most honorable men. He was no less generous to us—for there were certainly very many of us traveling to Rome together on account of the blessed bishop John. While we were staying in those regions, they received us with the most attentive hospitality and honored us with the greatest expenditure when we departed from there.

## CHAPTER L. The Life of Pammachius, Macarius, and Constantius

[Note: *Parens.* Take care not to understand *parentem* here as “father.” In the later period *parens* is often used for a relative or relation by marriage. Thus above, chapter 2: “He also had several relatives, among whom he had adopted his sister’s daughter for himself.” And in the following chapter, chapter 51: “He entrusted and committed himself neither to a friend, nor to a cleric, nor to a relative, nor to anyone else.” The old translator of Palladius, chapter 12: “We offer these things not as to a relative, but as to a servant of God and a monk.” The speaker is Marciana’s sister addressing her brother. See the *Onomasticon.*]

A certain relative of theirs named Pammachius (Palladius, chapter 122), a proconsular man, likewise renounced secular pomp and lived with highly commendable conduct. He dispersed part of all his possessions himself while still in the world, and left the rest to brothers and the poor when, dying, he departed to the Lord.

Another man, named Macarius, formerly a *vicarius*, did the same (Palladius, chapter 123).

There was also a certain Constantius, who had been an adviser to the prefects in the regions of Italy (Palladius, chapter 124): highly noble and learned men, exalted by a great love of God. I believe they are still alive, living according to the excellent discipline of monks.

## CHAPTER LI. The Life of the Alexandrian Virgin Who Hid the Great Athanasius for Six Years

I knew a certain virgin in the city of Alexandria. I remember seeing her when she was seventy years old (Palladius, chapter 136). Almost all the clergy there bore witness to her, saying that when she still appeared young—perhaps twenty years old—and possessed great beauty, she was accustomed to avoid everyone’s gaze, lest, because of the wonder of her appearance, some stain of suspicion be attached to her.

At that time the Arians, under the emperor Constantius, through his deputy Eusebius, formed a conspiracy against the blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and stirred up against him detestable accusations of crime.

The venerable man, therefore, avoiding a corrupted and polluted judgment, entrusted and committed himself neither to a friend, nor to a cleric, nor to a relative, nor to anyone else. When certain officers of the prefecture suddenly entered his house in search of him, he fled in the middle of the night wearing only his tunic and cloak and came to this virgin.

The holy bishop spoke these words to her, terrified by the novelty of such an unexpected event: “I am being sought intensely by the Arians and accused with calumnious charges. Therefore, so that I might not be disfigured by an irrational stigma and so that those who are unjustly prepared to punish me might not fall into sin because of me, I thought it better to flee. But tonight God deigned to reveal this to me, saying: ‘Know that you can be saved with no one as you can with her.’”

She, raised up with the joy of spiritual gladness and casting away empty thoughts, began to be wholly with God in all her senses. She hid that holy man for six years in the secrecy of her cell, for as long as the aforementioned Constantius lived. She herself washed his feet; she alone prepared and supplied everything he needed; and she borrowed and provided the books he requested to read. Yet for the entire six years no one in the city of Alexandria was able to discover where the holy Athanasius was living.

When the death of Constantius was first announced and the news reached Athanasius, he again went out at night, as he had done before, dressed in his proper clothing, and suddenly appeared in the church while everyone stood amazed and astonished. They all thought they were seeing him raised from the dead. To his close friends he offered this explanation: “I did not come to your hiding places so that you could safely swear that you did not know where I was living. Since it was necessary that I be sought everywhere, I hid in that virgin’s cell, where there could be no suspicion that I was concealed, since she appeared both beautiful and young. I rejoice doubly in this plan of mine, because I gained both myself and her salvation; for I benefited her as well as my own reputation and honor.”

## CHAPTER LII. The Life of the Virgin Juliana

There was another virgin named Juliana in the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia, said to be exceptionally learned and faithful (Palladius, chapter 147). She received and concealed for two full years that Origen who wrote many works, when he had fled in fear of the uprisings of the pagans. She supplied him at her own expense with everything necessary and refreshed him by her service.

I read this account written in verse in a very ancient manuscript. It contained the following note in Origen’s own hand: “I found this little book with a certain virgin named Juliana in the city of Caesarea, while I was hiding with her. She said that she had received it from Symmachus, the Jewish translator.”

I have not recounted the virtues of these women without reason, so that we may know that, if we wish, we can benefit others in many ways.

## CHAPTER LIII. Concerning the Young Man Who Preferred to Die Rather Than Violate a Virgin of Christ

In another very old manuscript, whose title bore the written name of Hippolytus, the man whom the apostles knew, I found the following historical account (Palladius, chapter 148):

“There was,” it says, “a most noble and beautiful girl [981] living in the city of Corinth, devoted to virginity and to the life of virginity. At that time, when a mad persecution was raging under a certain pagan judge, certain people brought charges against her as though she were insulting their gods and their sacrilegious emperors. They were plotting against her beauty, and those accustomed to traffic in such merchandise wanted to profit from her.”

The mad judge, seized by lust for the woman, immediately accepted the opportunity desired by her accusers, as though by some [uncertain] ear of a four-footed animal. But after he had been unable, by various schemes and devices, to persuade her to do what he wished, he raged against her with renewed fury. He did not consign her to some punishment or to death, but—what was more grievous and cruel—ordered her to be prostituted in a brothel, and instructed the procurer of such disgrace that he should bring him three solidi from her intercourse each day. Since the procurer undoubtedly understood that this money was to be demanded from her, he placed her at the disposal of all who wished.

When the hawks of such prey learned that this was true, they went and watched the workshop of perdition. Having paid the price of their miserable hope, they spoke with her about the beginnings of pleasures they desired. But she, earnestly entreating each one, said that she had a certain wound in the inner parts of her body; if those who came to her were to perceive its stench, they would necessarily always flee in horror at the contagion. For this reason she pitifully begged them all to grant her a few days, after which they would have her at their disposal as they wished and without payment.

Meanwhile, while she spoke thus to these men and offered continual and most fervent prayers to the Lord (Palladius, ch. 149), God, guardian of human salvation, seeing the chastity of the holy virgin in those very days, moved the mind of a certain young man, an *agens in rebus* (imperial agent) [Note: [Col. 0398B] *Agens in rebus.* Palladius calls him Magistrianus.
