Do not take this there as his proper name. I have spoken elsewhere about the name Magistrianus, in the *Martyrology of Ado*, 2 July. See also above, on Pelagius, book VI, no. 24. See the *Onomasticon*.], good both in appearance and character, so that, kindled by divine love, he desired to die for her. Under the pretext of committing the intended disgrace, he came at the dead of night to the procurer of the brothel, offering him five solidi and asking that he be permitted to remain with her that night. Entering the more secluded part of the house, he addressed the virgin as follows:

“Rise; save and free yourself.”

He stripped off his own clothing—that is, his shirt, cloak, and all the other garments proper to a man—and clothed the girl in them, saying: “Draw the upper part of the cloak over your head, veil yourself, and depart.”

After she had signed herself in the name of the Lord, she went out as he had instructed. The Lord thus preserved her untouched and undefiled.

On the following day, when everyone learned of what had happened, that imperial agent was handed over to the judge and torn apart with the ferocity of beasts. Thus, in this matter also, the demon was put to shame and blushed when he saw the man crowned with a double martyrdom, both for his own salvation and on account of the blessed woman’s name.

## CHAPTER LIV. The Life of Excomites and Bosphoria, His Wife, Servants of God

[Col. 0337A]

In the city of Ancyra, in the province of Galatia, I saw a certain most distinguished man named Excomites [Palladius: Severianus], together with Bosphoria, his wife (Palladius, ch. 114). Their manner of life is so sustained by good hope that, by anticipating and providing for future wealth, they even disdain the present gains of their children. For they distribute the revenues of all their possessions to the poor and needy. They have four sons and two daughters, to none of whom—not even an ounce, except to those who were already married—did they hand over anything, saying that after the death of their parents everything would necessarily belong to the children. They themselves gather the produce of their fields and distribute it throughout the churches, monasteries, hospitals, and among all the needy of the cities and villages.

We know this further outstanding and admirable fact about them. When they were at one time afflicted by such severe famine that people did not even spare their own affections [Note: [Col. 0398C] “Did not even spare their own affections.” He seems to indicate that the famine was so great that people did not even spare their affections—that is, their children. Palladius, in Greek, ch. 114, has: Λιμοῦ γενομένου μεγάλου καὶ κατὰ σπλάγχνων χωροῦντος πάντων ἀνθρώπων, “When there was a great famine that penetrated the inward parts of all human beings.” Authors often use *affectiones* for children. See the *Onomasticon*.], they themselves, by their generous beneficence, caused a flock of heretics to pass over to the right way and true glory of the Catholic faith, storing great quantities of grain on their estates and distributing all of it to the poor and those suffering from hunger. The appearance of their manner and clothing is so respectable and frugal that they seem, even from their own garments, humble and despised; their food is very meager and plain, and their whole life is exceedingly chaste and approved by God.

[Col. 0337C]

They live chiefly on their own estates, avoiding the social life and enticements of the cities, and fearing that, through communication with them in such matters and conversations, they might share in some stain of their vices and be compelled to deviate from the path of their purpose.

## CHAPTER LV. The Life of Magna

In this same city of Galatia there are also many other virgins—up to two thousand or even more—who live with great abstinence and with highly honorable and virtuous conduct (Palladius, ch. 135).

Among them a certain woman named Magna seems deservedly to excel in holiness. She is a woman of great proven worth. I do not know whether to call her a virgin or a widow, for her mother compelled her with the utmost force to marry. But she, always pretending in various ways to be ill, deceived her husband and postponed the matter, so that she might remain pure and untouched, as they say.

After a very short time her husband died, and she at once became mistress of all his possessions. She devoted herself wholly to God, adopting the purpose and life of monks while maintaining the honorable administration of her own household. Whenever reason or necessity required it, her speech and appearance before everyone were chaste, so that, because of the immense merit of her holiness, even bishops were always accustomed to revere her and feel ashamed in her presence.

She was accustomed to divide and distribute all the surplus of her own possessions among strangers, the weak, and bishops passing through. She never ceased from such work, carrying it out cheerfully and secretly both in person and through little servants whom she knew to be completely trustworthy. Yet she never withdrew from the church during the night prayers, pursuing and fulfilling in all things the discipline of abstinence in hope of the life to come.

## CHAPTER LVI. The Life of the Merciful Monk

In this same city we likewise found a certain monk [Note: [Col. 0337D] Palladius, ch. 115, calls him Eleemon], who came to such a purpose after a short period of military service. Although he was repeatedly compelled, he always refused to become a priest. Nevertheless, he spent twenty years in a monastery, following this way of life.

He never left the holy man who was bishop of that city. He was so humble and so merciful that, even throughout the nights, he went around to every place, extending a hand to those who asked. He never denied his help, insofar as he ought or was able, to prisoners, to those exhausted by illness, to the poor, or to the rich. Instead, he always advised and benefited everyone: provoking some harsh and cruel people to mercy; protecting others, when he understood that this ought to be done; reconciling some through peaceful agreement; and also ministering to the bodily needs of the rest, whatever their circumstances of food and clothing required.

There is there, as is usually the case in the larger cities: in the portico of the church a multitude of poor and sick people lie, some of them married and others known to be without spouses.

One winter night it happened that a certain woman was pressed by the pains of a difficult childbirth. Agitated by the excessive difficulty and crying out from the pains, she had no one to assist her. The most blessed man, moved by great compassion, abandoned the prayer he was solemnly celebrating in the church and went out. Setting aside for a little while the horror that customarily accompanies women in labor, he himself undertook the work of a midwife, lest he fail to perform an act of mercy.

The clothing with which this man is dressed is exceedingly shabby and worthless; his food is extremely restricted and meager. He is held by such a love of humanity that, out of his eagerness for this work, he has no interest in reading. If one of the brothers gives him a book, he immediately makes a practice of selling it. When someone asked him why he did this, he replied:

“How can I prove to my teacher that I have diligently learned his craft, unless, by selling his books, I hasten to provide myself with the necessities of the craft?”

This most holy man continues to carry out such works even today, leaving the memory of his name unfading throughout all those regions. For what he expends on the needy, he is assured of an eternal recompense and of the joys of heaven.

At that time, a certain virgin, a handmaid of God, lived together with two other virgins and observed abstinence for nine or ten years. She was seduced and corrupted by a certain singer (Palladius, ch. 140). Immediately conceiving, and after giving birth, she developed such hatred for her seducer that, in the intensity of her remorse for the sin, she undertook a degree of penitential continence beyond measure. She wished to kill herself by starvation, continually appealing to the Lord with tearful prayers and saying:

“You great God, who are accustomed to bear the sins of all of us and the boundless wickedness of the whole world; who do not desire the death of sinners nor delight in the destruction of the guilty (Ezek. 33), but are shown to be merciful toward all your creation, since it is your will that everything be saved—show this also in me, who am lost. If you restore me to salvation, let what has been brought forth from the destruction of my sin be swiftly removed from this life, once you have displayed over wretched me your customary miracles, lest perhaps, if I am heard too little, I be compelled to perish either by a noose or by a precipice.””

The outcome showed that her prayers had been heard: immediately, what she had borne was taken from her by death.

From that day onward she was no longer seen by her former captor, but she devoted herself to the most severe hardships of penitence and continence. Wishing to make the Godhead favorable to her, she served women suffering from elephantiasis for thirty years. The merciful Lord did not disappoint her humble prayers. He revealed the following to a certain holy presbyter:

“That virgin has pleased me more in her penitence than in her virginity.”

I say this now so that no one may think that those who have truly practiced repentance are to be despised.

## CHAPTER LVII. The Life of Eustathius the Lector

[Col. 0339C]

There was in the city of Caesarea, in the province of Palestine, the daughter of a certain presbyter. Although she seemed to be committed to a life of virginity, she fell headlong (Palladius, ch. 141). The man by whom she had been led astray and corrupted persuaded her to transfer the blame for what had happened to another by lying, and to bring a slanderous charge against a certain lector of the city. When she already appeared to be pregnant, and her father compelled her to reveal the author of so great a crime, she said that she had been violated by the aforementioned lector. The presbyter, believing that he had discovered the truth, brought the matter to the bishop. The bishop had the lector summoned before the assembly of all the clergy.

The inquiry was conducted. When the bishop questioned him, the lector could confess to nothing of the kind. For how could a confession follow where no crime had preceded? The bishop, extremely angry with his lector, as though he were shamelessly denying the charge, said to him:

“Unhappy and wretched man, filled with the filth of impurity—will you not confess?”

The lector replied:

“I have said what was in my conscience: that I have had nothing to do with this woman and acknowledge no sin of mine concerning the virgin in question. But if you wish to hear what is not true, I admit this crime.”

As soon as he had said this, the bishop deposed him from the rank of lector.

Then he went to the aforementioned priest and begged him, saying:

“Since I acknowledge that I have sinned, order her to be given to me in marriage; for she is no longer a virgin, and I can no longer be a cleric.”

The bishop gave her into his power, thinking that the young man himself loved her and could not in any way be separated from her.

The young man accepted her, and, having received her from both the bishop and her father, entrusted her to a women’s monastery. He begged its abbess to support her there until she gave birth. He himself, leaving her in that monastery, shut himself in a narrow cell and undertook an exceedingly difficult abstinence. With a contrite heart, tears, and groans, he appealed to Christ, saying:

“You, Lord, to whom all things are known, also know my deeds. No place is hidden from the eyes of your omnipotence, for you know everything before it happens. You alone see the depths of thoughts, whose most sincere and penetrating judge you have always been. You are the helper of those who suffer injustice and the comforter of those who undergo slander. Nothing unjust pleases you; with you the measure of justice is always clear in inaccessible light, and every human work lies before you. It therefore belongs to your equity and unchangeable judgment that my case also be made known by a divine verdict.”

Thus, while the young man prayed to the Lord without fatigue and devoted himself diligently and attentively to fasting and vigils, a short time passed. When the girl had completed her term, the hour of childbirth came upon her, and God’s just judgment arrived with it. For when groans and pains pressed upon her violently, and the wretched slanderer herself already saw the torments of hell, she could not free herself from the difficulties of the birth. She endured such torture from the first through the seventh day. Compelled by unbearable pain, and now plainly seeing that she would die—unable any longer to eat, drink, or obtain sleep for her eyes—she proclaimed in the loudest voice:

“Woe to me, wretched woman, who have come to this danger in two ways: first, because I lost my virginity; and second, because I brought a false charge against that lector.”

This was immediately reported to her father. But her father, fearing that others might accuse him of having slandered the man, remained silent and at rest as though he did not believe it. For another two days, while the divine judgment hung over her, the girl neither died nor gave birth.

[Col. 0340D]

Since the sisters around her could no longer bear her cries and groans, they quickly reported to the bishop what they had heard. They said that, in her distress, she had also confessed what had happened earlier: that she had slandered the aforementioned lector and for that reason was unable to give birth.

The bishop then sent deacons to him with this message:

“Pray that your slanderer may give birth.”

He gave them no reply and did not open the door of his dwelling, in which, from the moment he had entered it, he had continually prayed to the Lord with fasts and vigils. Her father therefore went to the bishop. Prayers were again offered at great length in the church, but even then she felt no relief.

Then the bishop himself went to the lector. He knocked at the door and, entering, said:

“Rise, brother Eustathius, and loose what you have bound.”

At that very moment, when the lector knelt together with the bishop, the woman gave birth. The prayer of unbroken innocence had such power that the slander was destroyed, the slanderer was corrected through her punishments, and we were enabled to recognize how persistently we ought to devote ourselves to prayer, whose power we know to be so great.

## CHAPTER LVIII. The Life of a Brother, Companion of Heraclides

I shall now speak briefly about a certain brother who lived with me from the beginning of my youth until the present day, and with this I shall bring my little book to an end (Palladius, ch. 151).

I knew him very well for a very long time. He was overcome by no desire of mind or body: he did not wish to please people by fasting, nor was he conquered by the allurements of the flesh so as to eat. I believe that he had overcome, for the most part, the desire for both riches and empty glory, considering it sufficient for himself to have what he held in his hands. He took no pleasure in ornamental clothing. Even for contempt shown to him, he was always accustomed to give thanks; and for true friends he was willing even to face danger.

He also experienced the powers of demons a thousand times, and perhaps more. Once the devil wished to make a bargain with him and said:

“Promise me just once that you will sin, and I will bring you whatever woman in this world you desire.”

At another time, a demon fought with him for fourteen nights (as he himself told me). Dragging him by the feet at night from his cell, it said to him in a human voice:

“Do not worship Christ, and I will never again approach you.”

He replied:

“For that very reason I worship him all the more, and I shall worship him continually; I shall admire his glory beyond measure and be struck with awe, because you are greatly angered and tormented by the very thing I do.”

He himself knew one hundred and six cities, and he stayed for a long time in many of them. By the favor and mercy of Christ, he never had dealings with a woman, not even in dreams, except in visions of combat and struggle.

I also know that he received food from angels three times. On one day, in the vastest wilderness, when he did not have even a crumb of bread, he found three warm *paximates* (twice-baked loaves) in his leather bag. At another time he likewise found wine and bread. I remember that one day he told someone that he had heard the following from an angel:

“I have learned that you do not have the food necessary for life. Go; from that man you will be given grain and oil.”

When he himself came to the man to whom he had been sent, that man said to him:

“Are you that certain person—I do not know who?”

He replied that he was.

The other then said to him:

“Someone ordered me to give you thirty *modii* of grain and ten *sextarii* of oil.”

Of this man, therefore, who was such a person, I shall glory especially. I often saw him weep bitterly when he observed some people suffering from the most grievous necessity and poverty, and give them, apart from his own body, whatever he was able to possess. I also know that, for a certain monk who had fallen into the ruin of sin, he poured out so many tears in his prayers that, by praying and weeping, he recalled him to great repentance.

This same man once swore to me, saying:

“I begged the Lord never to accept from a sinner or a rich person anything that might seem necessary for my sustenance or use.”

For me, however, it is enough that I have been worthy to remember so many saints and to commit them to the memory of writing. For your mind was not kindled toward this without God’s prompting, so that you wished these things to be written down for you by me and ordered that the lives of all these people be contained in this little book.

But you, most fortunate servant of Christ, Lausus, recall these things gladly, recognizing in them the greatest image of the resurrection. Read the blessed lives of holy men, their unbearable labors, and their admirable endurance; follow them with an awakened mind, and nourish yourself with the hope of good and heavenly things, knowing that few will be those who follow those who have gone before in these days.

For me, pray, I beg you, and show yourself to me and to everyone as I have known you to be from the consulship of Titianus until the present day, and as I later found you when you were chief chamberlain of the sacred palace. For wealth, rank, and power have in no way made you less devoted to the love and fear of God. You belong wholly to Christ—to him to whom the devil once said:

“I will give you all these things if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4).

[But the Lord confounded him when he said: “Get behind me.” May you also imitate him, rejecting the fleeting riches and shadowy glory of this life, and loving that heavenly and immortal life, the eternal kingdom, the glory that endures forever, and those good things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). May he make us heirs of them together with all his holy patriarchs and prophets, apostles and martyrs, and those whose memory we have celebrated in this book, through the grace of our Savior Jesus Christ. [Col. 0342D] [Note: [Col. 0341] The passages enclosed in brackets are absent from Fabri’s edition.]]

[Note: [Col. 0341] In Fabri’s edition, the following peroration came here. It is identical with the prologue above.]

[Col. 0343]

# THE LAUSIAC HISTORY OF PALLADIUS, BY AN UNCERTAIN BUT ANCIENT TRANSLATOR

[Note: [Col. 0398] These notes occur at columns 398–400, but the callout numbers have not been printed in the text.]

1. **Brunum.** He understands this to mean stench. Hence *brumosus*, “foul-smelling.” See what was said above, on book III, note 39.9.

2. **Tauream.** Hervetus wrongly understood this as a bull’s hide, as though an executioner were clothed in a bull’s hide. Palladius means an executioner equipped with a *taurea*, that is, a whip.

3. **Grutaria.** Heraclides, ch. 6, simply calls it “commerce.”

[Col. 0398D]

4. **Neapoteponta.** Approaching these letters by conjecture, I thought the reading might be *νεαρογέροντα* or *νεογέροντα*. In fact, P—that is, the Greek rho—seemed to the earliest editors to be P, that is, the Latin *p*. In Palladius, ch. 19, the word is *παιδαριογέρων* (“boy-old-man”).

5. **Nebulae.** Heraclides, ch. 6, has “hornets.” I believe that Palladius’ ancient translator came upon a corrupt manuscript and, instead of *σκνίφες* (“gnats”), read *νέφος* or *νεφέλην*—“cloud,” “cloudy,” “mist,” or some similar related Greek word.

6. **Dehabent.** A rarer verb, and not easily encountered. The translator of Heraclides, ch. 2, expresses this as: “if they should perhaps seem to be in need.” Hervetus, in Palladius, ch. 6: “if anything should be lacking to them.” Jerome, *Letter* 22, to Eustochium, “On the custody of virginity”: “so that no one asks for anything, no one is in want.”

1010. 7. **Zabernam.** The translator of Heraclides, ch. 7, has “a sack.” So too Hervetus, the newer translator of Palladius, ch. 22. In Greek, Palladius in the Venetian edition has *ζάβερνον*; in others, *σάκκον*. See the *Onomasticon*.

8. **Praefectiani.** I corrected this conjecturally, lacking manuscript support; previously it read *praefaciani*. *Praefectiani* are known in later centuries as the attendants of the prefect of the praetorium. The matter itself here shows that it must be understood in this way.

9. **An Italic measure of oil (*Italicum olei*).** So Heraclides, ch. 8: “he alone emptied eighteen Italic measures of his wine.” See the *Onomasticon*.

10. **Libralem manum.** Heraclides, ch. 25, has “Oxyrhynchus.” Hervetus’ Palladius, ch. 86, has “a swift hand.” He means that Evagrius was a copyist, either a *ταχυγράφος* (shorthand writer) or a *καλλιγράφος* (calligrapher). See the *Onomasticon*.

11. **Rhinocerotis duceret.** Hervetus’ Palladius, ch. 86, previously had: “so that his body, no less than the bodies of wild animals, swarmed with flies.” I have now corrected it to “swarmed with ticks.” Heraclides, ch. 25: “so that across his entire body there emerged certain swellings of the kind we have often seen on bodies.” In Greek: *Ὡστε τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ καθύπερ τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων κροτῶνας ἐκβρᾶσαι* (“so that his body, like those of irrational animals, should break out in ticks”). Among the Greeks, *κρότων* now means a tick—that is, a worm harmful to dogs—now a shrub, now a disease of the olive, [Col. 0399B] and now the cartilaginous bronchial tube of the lung.

But what is the sense here, and what is the construction? “So that his body, like that of an irrational animal, should produce rhinoceroses”? If *rhinocerotis* is joined with *animalis*, something is lacking to the sense, and I do not know whether one should supply “wrinkles” or something similar. I do not see what the huge animal, the rhinoceros, is doing here, if we consult the other translators. *Ricinus* corresponds to the Greek word *κρότων*. Should we therefore read *ricinos duceret*, that is, “should be covered with ticks,” whether ticks or insects? Or should we read *cynorrhaistas duceret*, since *κρότων*, or *ricinus*, is also called by the Greeks *κυνοῤῥαϊστὴς*, from its infestation of dogs? In this way *ricinus*, or *cynorrhaistes*, may have degenerated into *rhinocerotis*.

I would still like to append one conjecture: that we should read *duresceret* instead of *duceret*. In this way both the sense and the construction will be sound. It is well known that the rhinoceros has an extremely hard hide. See the *Onomasticon*.

Among the Greeks, *κρότων* is also used for an ulcer, in Pollux, book 5, ch. 15. Was he therefore completely ulcerated from standing outdoors by day and night? This is how he understood *κροτῶνας*. The translator of Heraclides translates it as “swellings.”

12. **Pisper.** The name of this river is absent from Hervetus’ translation. From its proximity, the mountain of Antony was also called by this name. Rufinus, *History*, book II, ch. 8: “Poemen and Joseph at Pispir, which is called the mountain of Antony.”

13. **Chindii vini.** I have not yet encountered *Chindian wine* elsewhere. Chian wine is well known. But I do not think that Chian wine is meant, as though its use had existed among the Egyptian hermits. I prefer to read *Chydaeum*. Chydaean wine is known among manufactured wines, made from Chydaean dates. Pliny, book 14, ch. 16. See the *Onomasticon*.

## Prologue

[Col. 0343] 984

Many and varied accounts, written at different times by different authors, exist concerning those who, abandoning the enticements of the world, took refuge in Christ. The good desire of their hearts and the devotion of their religious minds were nourished by the inspiration of heavenly grace, like oil added to a flame, for the edification of those who voluntarily remain steadfast in the teaching of our Savior Christ with undivided faith.

Considering how pleasing to God is the sacrifice that consists in gaining souls, I too thought that, with humble reverence and according to my ability, I should contribute to the salvation of my brothers, display the conduct and lives not only of illustrious men but also of women, reveal their virtues, and declare their miracles—namely, those whom I saw and about whom I heard, with whom I lived both in the solitude of Egypt, and also in Libya and the Thebaid, and in Syene [Old Edition: Sirene. Or is it Cyrene?] as well; among those who are called the Tabennesiots; then in Mesopotamia, Palestine, and Syria; and among those who dwell in the western regions, at Rome and in Campania.

Out of a desire for humility and obedience, I became a hearer of monastic discipline. In my thirty-third year, I lived in a community of brothers, and nevertheless also spent time in the solitary life, where I learned many things both to imitate and to avoid. These I shall set forth in this book as briefly as I can, so that, instructed in a saving summary, we may receive unfailing medicine for the soul: that is, so that through these examples we may banish all sloth, drowsiness of mind, and carnal desire; drive away every dissension of spirit, agitation of anger, sadness, and irrational fear; despise empty glory and worldly ambition; and advance in faith in the truth and in desire for eternity.

Hearing, therefore, the courageous deeds of the saints, let us also gird ourselves. Let faith increase within us; let charity grow warm through the hope of victory; and let us be certain that Christ will help his warriors and crown them as victors.

## CHAPTER I. The Way of Life of Isidore and Dorotheus, and the Suffering of a Certain Virgin

[Col. 0343A]

When I first went to the city of Alexandria, I found a remarkable man, adorned on every side with virtue of conduct, way of life, and knowledge: Isidore the presbyter, who had been appointed to the hospital of the Alexandrian church (Heraclides, ch. 1). He was said to have disciplined the enticements of his early youth in the desert; we also saw his cell on Mount Nitria.

I found him an old man of seventy years. He died in peace fifteen years later. Until the end of his life he used neither linen nor a bath. Yet his body was so filled [another reading: refreshed] by the grace of God that all who did not know his way of life thought that he lived in luxury.

If I wished to set forth the virtues of his soul, I would run out of time while telling them. Among his other virtues, he was exceedingly merciful and kind, so that even his enemies and unbelieving pagans revered him. Through instruction in the divine Scriptures and in books, he possessed such knowledge that, even during the brothers’ meals, his mind would be carried away into spiritual visions. When he was asked to explain what this ecstasy of mind was, he said with tears:

“My mind has been carried away in a certain spiritual vision.”

I myself often saw him weeping at table while taking food. When we asked the reason, we heard him say:

“I am ashamed to receive bodily food like irrational animals, since I am a rational human being created by God, and ought to enjoy the delights of paradise.”

He was known to the Roman senate and to all the matrons of magnificent and distinguished men. He came to Rome with Bishop Athanasius on account of the faith, and afterward also with Bishop Demetrius. Although he was rich in the resources of the hospital and had sufficient means, when he died he made no will. Nor did he leave even a single coin as support for his sisters, who were committed to a life of virginity. Instead, he entrusted them to Christ the Lord, saying:

“He who created you will govern your life, just as he governs mine.”

There was a community of seventy virgins among his own sisters.

When I, still a young man, came to him and begged him to instruct me and establish me in a monastic life fervent in the vigor of youth, he did not comfort me with words but instead imposed bodily labor on me. He led me outside the city to the place called the more secluded region, at the fifth mile, and handed me over to a certain Dorotheus, an exceedingly austere man from the Thebaid, who had reached the age of sixty and lived in a cave. He ordered me to spend three years with him, for the disciplining of the passions of the body; for he knew that the old man lived with great strictness. He instructed me to return to him afterward for spiritual instruction.

But I was unable to complete the three years, having been held back by illness, and so returned to him before the three years were finished.

[Col. 0345A]

His life was hard and arduous. Every day, in the heat and solitude beside the sea, he gathered stones, built with them, and made cells. He gave these to people who were unable to build for themselves, completing one cell each year.

I begged him and said:

“What are you doing, Father, killing your body at such an old age?”

He replied:

“It kills me, so I kill it.”

His food consisted of six ounces of bread and a small bundle of vegetables seasoned with a little relish. He drank only a little water. I never saw him stretch out his feet; I never saw him rest on a mat or a bed. Instead, he sat and worked throughout every night, weaving baskets from palm leaves as the equivalent of his food.

Thinking that perhaps he did this only because of me, I made careful inquiries among his other disciples who had remained separately. I learned that from his youth he had always lived in this manner, never sleeping except when occupied with work; and even when eating, he would close his eyes in drowsiness, so that often, during the meal, bread would fall from his mouth because of excessive sleepiness.

When I once compelled him to recline briefly on a mat, he said sadly:

“If you persuade angels to sleep, you also persuade the fervent spirit.”

Once, however, when I was with him around the ninth hour, he sent me to fill a vessel with water for our meal. As I went away, I happened to see an asp at the bottom of the well. I threw down the vessel without filling it and said to him:

“We are dead, Father, for I saw an asp in the well.”

He smiled, gazed at the ground for a long time, and, shaking his head, said:

“If it pleases the devil to put snakes in every well—or some other beast—are we never to drink?”

Then he went out and drew water himself. He drank first, while still fasting, and said:

“Where the cross of Christ is brought upon a thing, the malice of the devil will not prevail.”

Blessed Isidore used to tell us that, when he had seen blessed Antony, a man of God, he related to me a story worthy of being written down, which he had heard from Antony himself: During the persecution of Maximian, there was a very beautiful girl who was the slave of a certain man [Note: [Col. 0345D] Heraclides, ch. 1, calls this virgin Potamiana.]. Her master tried to seduce her with many promises, but could not deceive her. Finally, burning with anger, he handed her over to the prefect then appointed over Alexandria [Col. 0345D], to be put to death as a Christian who blasphemed both the times and the emperor. During the persecutions themselves, he sent some people to her with money and said: “If you consent to my will, I will protect you from punishment. But if you persist in your obstinacy, I will ask the judge to torture you to death, so that, while still alive, you may not mock my desire.”

When she was brought before the judge’s tribunal, she bravely despised the various tortures of punishment, fortified by a good conscience. Among these tortures, the judge ordered a large cauldron full of boiling pitch to be heated. When the pitch was boiling and blazing fiercely, the judge proposed this to her, saying: “Go away, either submit to the will of your master, or know that I shall order you to be thrown into this cauldron.” She replied: “May there never be judges of such a kind, who order submission to lust.” Raging, he ordered her to be stripped and thrown into the cauldron of boiling pitch.

She raised her voice and said: “By the head of your emperor, whom you worship, I adjure you: if you have decided to torture me in this way, order me to be lowered gradually into the cauldron, so that you may see how much patience Christ, whom you do not know, has granted me.” She was then lowered gradually into the prepared boiling vessel, and at that same moment the pitch cooled when it reached her neck. Many who saw this miracle were strengthened in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Alexandrian church; they were made worthy of the land of the meek, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5).

## CHAPTER II. On Pasco, and how he overcame the assaults of the flesh

A certain man named Pasco [Note: [Col. 0345D] Heraclides, ch. 11, calls him Pachomius; Palladius, ch. 29, calls him Pachon.] was living in Scetis at the age of seventy. Now, when the spirit of fornication was grievously tempting me, and thoughts concerning womanly desire were agitating me, I almost left the desert, driven by the intensity of my suffering. I did not disclose the reason to the monks living near me; secretly, however, I went into the wilderness and visited the holy Fathers for fifteen days, those who had grown old in Scetis. Among them I found Pasco, whom all the Fathers living in that desert revered.

I therefore took courage and, entreating him with tears, confessed to him the passion that attacked me so violently and continually without ceasing. He said to me: “Let this matter not trouble you; for you are not suffering this through negligence. The place itself and the difficulty of circumstances testify on your behalf, as does the fact that in those regions women never visit. Rather, it is the envy of the devil, who is always lying in wait and hastening to deceive human souls.

“Behold, as you see me now an old man, I have spent forty years in this cell, and, with the help of Christ’s grace, I have been concerned for the salvation of my soul; nevertheless, I still endure temptation. For he said to me under oath: ‘For more than twelve years after my fiftieth year, he spared me neither by night nor by day,’ so much so that I thought perhaps God had abandoned me, and that this was why I was suffering the distress of this passion continually and without respite.

“I therefore chose rather to die irrationally than to endure such bodily suffering. I went out, then, and wandered through almost the whole wilderness. I found a lioness’s cave and lay down there naked for the entire day, so that the wild beasts entering might eat me. When evening came, as it is written, ‘He appointed darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through’ (Ps. 103), the male and female beasts came out, smelled me from head to foot, licked me all over, and withdrew from me. I thought they would devour me. I lay there throughout the night, but they did not approach me.”

I therefore thought that God had spared me, and I returned to my cell. After a few days, however, the same temptation rose up again with greater force, so that I almost reached the point of blasphemy. The demon, assuming the form of an Ethiopian girl whom I had seen in my youth gathering ears of grain, sat upon my knees and violently stirred me. In the fury of my passion I struck her with my fists and slapped her cheeks, and immediately that phantom disappeared. For two years, however, my hands—the hands with which I had struck what seemed to be her face—endured an unbearable stench and cold. I therefore despaired of the salvation of my soul; excessive sadness afflicted me with faintness of spirit, and I wasted away in profound grief.

Then I heard a voice within my consciousness saying: “Go, Pasco, fight! For this reason I permitted you to suffer these things: so that you may not think highly of yourself or exalt yourself as though because of your own virtues (Rom. 11), but may recognize your weakness. Do not trust in your way of life; rather, be submissive and humble, trusting in God’s help.” Thus assured of the saving Lord’s assisting mercy, I passed the rest of my days in peace.

## CHAPTER III. On Didymus, and the blessed virgins Alexandria and Melania

Among the holy Fathers there was Didymus [Note: [Col. 0347D] Didymus was an Origenist.], an expounder of the sacred books, who explained many books of the divine Scriptures (Heraclides, ch. 1). He was without eyes, and I knew him personally. He died at the age of seventy-five.

Although he was blind, he told me that he had lost his sight at the age of four, in infancy. He had never learned letters and had never attended teachers. But he had a very powerful natural teacher: his own conscience. He was adorned with such a great grace of knowledge that he interpreted the Old and New Testaments word for word. He pursued liberal studies with such subtlety, explaining speech in the smallest detail, that in knowledge he surpassed all the ancients.

He urged me to pray in his cell. When I did not consent, he told me: “Blessed Antony entered this little cell three times to visit me. When I asked him to pray, he immediately bent his knees in this dwelling and did not compel me to repeat the request, thereby teaching me obedience.”

He also told me this: “When I was anxious about the life of the wretched emperor Julian and was deeply saddened, one day I did not taste bread until the following evening because of my anxiety. It happened that, while I was sitting in my chair and had been overcome by sleep, I saw in a vision white horses running about, with riders saying: ‘Tell Didymus that Julian died today at the seventh hour. Rise, eat, and send word to Bishop Athanasius, so that he too may know.’ I immediately noted the hour, month, week, and day; and it was found to have happened just as it had appeared to me in my sleep.”

He also told me about a certain servant girl named Alexandria [Col. 0348A], who, after leaving the city, shut herself up in a tomb. Through a small opening she received the bread necessary for her sustenance for twelve years. In the twelfth year she arranged herself as though sleeping. When the person who customarily ministered to her had gone and received no answer, he informed us. We broke down the door and entered, and found her dead.

He also spoke of the blessed Melania herself, about whom we shall speak later. He said that he had not seen her face to face, but, standing at the opening, had asked her to tell him why, leaving the city, she had entered a tomb. Through the opening she replied:

“Because a certain man had conceived an improper thought concerning me. So that I would not accuse him, I chose rather to shut myself up alive in this tomb than to scandalize a soul made in the image of God.”

I said to her: “How do you persevere now, seeing no one, and suffering under such great and especially oppressive inactivity?” She said to me:

“From morning until the ninth hour I pray at each hour while spinning flax. I spend the remaining hours fasting; at the proper hour I eat my food and rest, and in dreams I see patriarchs, prophets, and apostles together with martyrs. I persevere while awaiting the end, with the sweetest hope in God.”

## CHAPTER IV. On Ammonius, his brothers, and his three religious sisters

Blessed Ammonius had two full brothers who lived together with him in the holy way of life (Heraclides, ch. 2). The elder of them, Dioscorus [Col. 0348C], was elected to the episcopate. They also had three sisters serving the Lord in virginity, living no less than their brothers in every spiritual discipline and abstinence. Thus there were seven of them—four men and their three sisters—all virgins from their mother’s womb.

They say that the eldest of the sisters possessed such knowledge of the divine Scriptures that her brothers marveled at her. In the evening she devoted herself intensely to reading; after reading, when she took a little sleep, she meditated in her sleep upon the very words of the reading. She also had with her three other foreign handmaids of Christ. Likewise, their brothers had three men who were highly learned and most eloquent; they too imitated their way of life and were held distinguished in Christ.

All of them, burning exceedingly with the love of Christ, went into the desert. They made a small monastic dwelling for their sisters apart, and made one for themselves separately, so that there would be a considerable interval between them and their sisters. They established for themselves that neither their brothers would receive other women for visits, nor would the women receive other men.

Since Ammonius was exceedingly learned in every respect, both in knowledge of the Scriptures and in eloquence, when the bishop of a certain city died, Ammonius’s admirers made a proposal to the bishop of Alexandria, asking that he ordain Ammonius their bishop. The archbishop said to them: “Bring him to me, so that he may be ordained bishop.”

They hurried to him with assistance. When Ammonius saw that he had been taken by surprise, he entreated them and affirmed under oath that he would not accept the episcopal order and would not leave the desert. Since they did not yield but pressed him violently, he took scissors in their presence and cut off his left ear from the bottom, saying: “Now at least be certain that it is impossible for me to become a bishop, because the law forbids a person defective in any limb to become a priest.” Then they left him and withdrew. They went away and reported this to the bishop.

The bishop said to them: “That law was observed among the Jews. But if you bring me even a man whose nose has been cut off, provided that he is so adorned with good morals that he is worthy of the priesthood, I will ordain him.” They therefore went back and entreated him again. But he swore, saying: “If you force me, I will cut off my tongue as well.” So they left him and withdrew.

A miracle of this Ammonius is also reported. Whenever carnal desire arose and stirred his limbs toward lust, he never spared his flesh; instead, he applied heated iron to his limbs, so that he would always be wounded. In this way the intensity of the pain restrained the desire of passion. Such was his abstinence from youth until death. He ate nothing that had passed through fire, except bread.

Once, while he was building his cell in the desert, a brother came to him and said: “Why do you afflict yourself in such burning heat, Abba?” Blessed Ammonius replied:

“Believe me, brother: by God’s grace I have committed the holy Scriptures to memory. From early youth I have fully learned both the Old and New Testaments. I have also read six hundred myriads (six million) of explanations of the divine law written by the holy ancient orthodox Fathers and priests of the Lord” (almost all the Fathers in the desert testified to this concerning him). “Yet if I am satisfied with bread for one day and do not exercise myself in work, my mind becomes exalted and becomes like that of irrational animals.”

Once blessed Evagrius came to holy Ammonius [Note: [Col. 0349D] Both Evagrius and Ammonius were Origenists.] for spiritual visitation. While they discussed many matters from the holy Scriptures and rejoiced together spiritually in the Lord, Evagrius later said to Ammonius, as though reproaching him for having cut off his ear:

“Do you not fear a grave sin? To avoid accepting the priesthood, you cut off your ear.”

Ammonius replied: “I ask you to pray for me to the Lord, so that I may deserve to receive forgiveness for my other sins; for this deed does not greatly trouble my spirit. Yet you ought rather to fear and be anxious, since you are learned according to the wisdom of the world and possess such great knowledge of the divine Scriptures, which God’s grace has bestowed upon you, so that you could teach many peoples, and you have chosen instead to live in the solitude of the desert. I cut off my little ear, but you have cut off your tongue, which could have taught many peoples.”

Holy Abba Dioscorus the presbyter, who lived in the desert of Scetis, used to say: “A monk ought not to pursue the desires of the palate and the belly. For how does he differ from worldly people if he satisfies his pleasures? Indeed, we often see worldly people abstaining from delicacies and pleasures because of illness, in order to attain bodily health. How much more carefully ought a monk to strive, for the salvation and soundness of his soul, to reach those true and eternal delights of paradise and the glory of the heavenly kingdom?”

## CHAPTER V. On Hor, Pambo, and Melania the Roman

[Col. 0350B] On this mountain of Nitria there was a man named Hor, exceedingly abstinent [Note: [Col. 0350D] This Hor was an Origenist.] (Heraclides, ch. 2). The entire brotherhood of monks testified to his many virtues, but I did not find him alive. They also said this about him: he never lied, swore, cursed, or spoke without necessity.

The blessed Pambo also lived on this mountain. He was the teacher of Dioscorus, who was later ordained bishop, and of Ammonius and John, the brothers of the remarkable Dracontius. Pambo had a great reputation for holiness and virtue, and he despised gold and silver as true reason requires.

The blessed Melania told me that when she first arrived from Rome in Alexandria and heard Isidore recounting Pambo’s virtues—Isidore was also the one who brought her into the desert to visit the holy Fathers—she offered him a treasury of silver weighing three hundred pounds, asking him to accept some of her property and distribute it to the poor.

He was sitting and weaving little baskets from palm leaves. He blessed me, saying: “May the Lord God repay you your reward.” Then he said to his steward Theodore: “Take this and distribute it throughout Libya and among the brothers on the islands, for those monasteries are more in need.” He ordered him to give nothing in Egypt, since that province was more prosperous.

I stood waiting, as though I were to be honored and glorified for what I had offered. Hearing nothing from him, I said: “So that you may know, lord, how much it is: it is three hundred pounds.”

Without even looking at me, he replied: “The one to whom you offered this has no need of weighing it. He who weighs the mountains and the entire mass of the earth (Isa. 40) knows much better the amount of this silver. If you had given it to me, you would rightly tell me how much it was. But since you offered it to God, he who did not despise the widow’s small coins, the poor woman’s offering (Mark 12), will not consign your offering to oblivion.”

Thus the Lord governed and arranged matters: when I entered the mountain, the man of God died a few days later—not from illness, but while sewing a basket. He died without fever at the age of seventy. Finally, as he was piercing and finishing baskets, he called me and said: “Receive this basket from my hands, so that you may remember me. I have nothing else to leave you.”

She herself buried him, wrapping his body in a shroud, and then she left the desert. She kept the basket until her death as a blessing.

At the very hour of his death, with the presbyter Macarius and Ammonius, men renowned for holy discipline, standing beside him, and with other brothers also present, this blessed Pambo is said to have spoken:

“From the time I came to this mountain of solitude, built myself a cell, and remained in it, I have lived by the labor of my hands. I do not remember ever having eaten bread for nothing. Nor do I regret any word I have spoken up to this hour. Thus I am departing as though I were only now beginning to worship God.”

## CHAPTER VI. On holy Benjamin, most patient in dropsy

On this mountain of Nitria there is a certain Benjamin (Heraclides, ch. 2), a holy man who lived to the age of eighty, exceedingly abstinent and devoted to the cultivation of spiritual virtues. He received from the Lord the grace of healings: if he laid hands on anyone or gave him blessed oil, every illness was driven away by him.

This man, who had been considered worthy of such great grace, became dropsical eight months before his death. His body swelled so greatly that you would have thought him another Job.

Blessed Macarius, who was then a presbyter on the mountain of Nitria, took me, Theodore, and Macariolus and said to us: “Come and see a new Job, who, amid such swelling of the body and incurable suffering, continually renders immense thanksgiving to God.”

We went and saw him with such swelling of body that one finger of his hand could not touch another. Looking upon this most cruel affliction, we turned our eyes away. Then blessed Benjamin said to us:

“Pray, my little sons, that my inner man may not become dropsical. This condition neither benefits one who bears it well nor harms one who bears it badly.”

For eight months a broad chair was placed for him, in which he sat continually because of his bodily needs; he could not lie down. Yet while placed in this suffering, he healed others. We have necessarily recounted this affliction so that we may not be disturbed if some exceedingly grave illness should befall righteous men.

After he died, they removed the threshold and the doorposts so that his body could be carried out. So great was the swelling of his body.

Abba Benjamin related [Note: [Col. 0351D] This is absent from Heraclides. Pelagius, little book IV, no. 12.]:

“Once the presbyter from the Cells and I came to an old man living in the desert of Scetis, and offered him a little oil. He said to us: ‘Look, that small vessel which you gave me three years ago remains full to this day.’

“When we heard this, we said: ‘Why, Father, have you not even tasted that oil on feast days?’ He replied: ‘I did not want to partake of it, lest it become a habit for me and I begin to seek foods seasoned with the oil’s pleasantness. Then, because of the opportunity to enjoy a pleasant seasoning, I might be compelled to go down to the city or villages to buy oil, return to the desert, go down again, and return to my cell. Through this opportunity for going down and coming back, my senses and mind might begin to wander, and I might lose the benefit of the more secluded life. The devil is many-formed and weaves various nets to capture human minds.’

“When we heard this, we marveled at the prudence and way of life of the holy elder.”

The same Abba Benjamin also told us [Note: [Col. 0352D] Absent from Heraclides.] that they once went to an old man who kept them for a meal and prepared cooked lentils for them. He added to the seasoning oil made in those regions from radish seeds.

We said to him: “Father, add some better oil, so that we may be able to eat.”

When he heard this, he made the sign of the cross and said to us: “Is there any other oil besides this? I have never heard of it.”

The old man had been brought up in the desert from infancy and had always remained among holy elders. He had never gone out either into cities or into villages.

## CHAPTER VII. On holy Apollonius, who ministered to five thousand monks

A certain man named Apollonius (Heraclides, ch. 3) had been a merchant. Renouncing the affairs of the world and turning to the service of Christ, he lived on the mountain of Nitria. He could neither learn a craft nor devote himself to writing books because of his old age.

Living on the aforementioned mountain for twenty-five years, he devoted himself to purchasing all kinds of provisions from Alexandria with his own money and labor, and he ministered to the sick throughout the brotherhood. From first light until the ninth hour he went through the little monasteries, entering each doorway, lest someone perhaps be lying ill. He carried raisins, pomegranates, and similar things needed by the sick.

He practiced this way of life in his old age. When he died, he left behind a storekeeper like himself and asked him to continue this administration. Such service was necessary for the needs of the five thousand monks living on the mountain, because that place was a desert.

## CHAPTER VIII. On holy Nathanael and his temptations by a demon

There was another among the ancient monks, named Nathanael (Heraclides, ch. 5). I did not find him, for he had departed from the body fifteen years before my arrival; but I found those who had lived with him.

I asked them about the man’s virtue. They showed me his cell in which he had lived, but at that time no one lived there, because it was near a village inhabited by secular people. He had built it at a time when there were fewer servants of God called anchorites—that is, those who withdraw into the more secluded regions of the desert.

They reported this about him, especially: he possessed such great patience in his cell that he was not moved from his purpose. At first, having been deceived by the demon who hastens to deceive everyone, he was overcome by a certain weariness, left his first cell, and built another for himself near a village. When he had completed it, he lived there.

After three months, a demon appeared one night holding a leather strap like an executioner, wearing a garment stitched together like a soldier’s, and making noise with that strap. Blessed Nathanael said to him: “Who are you, that you presume to do such things over my little lodging?”

The demon replied: “I am the one who drove you from that other cell, and I have come to drive you out of this one as well.”

Recognizing that he had been deceived, Nathanael immediately returned to the former cell. He completed thirty-seven years there without crossing the threshold of the cell’s doorway, contending against the demon.

The demon devised so many things and showed them to him in order to force him to leave that it would take too long to recount them. Among these was the following. When he observed a visit by seven holy bishops, whether brought about by God’s promise or by the evil one’s temptation, he almost departed from his purpose.

After the bishops had prayed and were leaving, he did not escort them even a footstep. His attendants, that is, the deacons, said to him: “You have acted arrogantly by not escorting the bishops.”

He replied: “I have died both to the lords bishops and to the whole world. I possess a hidden purpose in my mind, and God knows my heart, why I did not escort them.”

Terrified that this stratagem had failed, nine months before Nathanael’s death the demon disguised himself as a nine-year-old boy driving an ass carrying loaves in baskets. As deep evening approached, he made the ass appear to fall near Nathanael’s cell.

Crying out like a child, he said: “Abba Nathanael, have mercy on me and give me your hand.”

Hearing what sounded like a child’s voice, Nathanael opened the door and, standing inside, said to him: “Who are you, and what do you want me to do for you?”

The demon said: “I am that man’s little boy, and I am carrying bread because it is his brother’s feast, and this offering is needed at dawn on the Sabbath. I beg you, do not despise me, lest I be eaten by wild beasts and lionesses. There are many of them in those places.”

Blessed Nathanael stood there in astonishment. His compassion was stirred, and he was troubled, thinking within himself: “Either I must fall because I have been commanded to do so, or I must fall away from my purpose.”

After this he thought: “It is better for me not to transgress than to destroy the purpose of so many years, to the confusion of Satan.”

After praying, he said to the one speaking to him like a child: “Listen, child. Believe in the God whom I serve, for if help is necessary there, God will send it to you. Neither a lioness nor anyone else will harm you. But if this is a temptation, God will immediately reveal it.”

He closed the door and went inside. The demon, confounded because he had been defeated, dissolved into a whirlwind, like wild asses leaping and fleeing and making noises. This was the triumph of blessed Nathanael, this was his way of life, and this was his end.

## CHAPTER IX. On the life and miraculous deeds of the most holy men Macarius the Egyptian and Macarius of Alexandria

I am reluctant to speak or write about the great, eminent, holy, and most blessed men, lest I incur a reputation for falsehood by recounting things that may seem incredible. But since the Holy Spirit has declared that God destroys all who speak falsehood (Ps. 5), O most faithful servant of God, do not disbelieve one who is not lying.

There were two Macarii (Heraclides, ch. 6): one was Egyptian by birth, while the other sold groats [or: a type of grain]. I shall first tell of the Egyptian, who lived ninety years. He spent sixty years in the desert, entering it as a young man of thirty. He attained such discernment that they called him neapoteponta [possibly νεαρογέροντα, “young elder”] (4), that is, “a young old man,” and for this reason he advanced more quickly.

When he reached the age of forty, he received from God the grace of healings against the spirits of demons and was considered worthy of divine revelations. Two disciples lived with him in the inner desert called Scetis. One served him nearby, because people came to be cured of their illnesses and infirmities; the other withdrew separately into a cell.

After some time had passed, Macarius, foreseeing by the Spirit and seeing with the eye of his heart, said to the one who served him, whose name was John and who later became a presbyter in Macarius’s place:

“Listen to me, brother John, and heed my admonitions. The spirit of greed is tempting you; for this is what I have seen. I know that if you obey me, you will be established in this place, and no scourge will approach your tent (Ps. 90). But if you disobey me, the example of Gehazi will come upon you (2 Kings 5), and you will waste away from that affliction.”

It happened that he did not obey. Fifteen years after the holy Macarius’s death, through defrauding the poor of what belonged to them, he became so elephantine that no unaffected spot could be found on his body where someone could place a finger. This was the prophecy of holy Macarius.

It would be superfluous to recount his food and drink, since even among the more negligent no one in those regions is found to consume food more abundantly or more delicately, both because of the scarcity of what is scarcely available there and because of the example of the many monks living in that place.

It was also said of his other discipline that his mind passed beyond itself without interruption, and that his consciousness clung to God for a far greater portion of time than it dwelt in the habitation of this world. Many miracles are attributed to him, which God performed through him; for the Lord healed through his prayers many who were tormented by demons and suffering from various illnesses.

A certain Egyptian man desired a freeborn married woman. Unable to possess her, he spoke to a sorcerer, saying: “Make her love me, and act in such a way that her husband will cast her out.”

The sorcerer took the matter up and practiced his magic sufficiently, causing her to appear to be a mare. When her husband came in from outside, he was astonished that a mare was lying in his bed. He began to weep and howl, for he spoke to the animal, but it gave no answer.

He therefore entreated the priests of the estate and brought her to them, showing her to them, but they found no cause. For three days she accepted neither hay, as a mare would, nor bread, as a human would; she was deprived of both kinds of food.

Finally, so that God might be glorified and the power of holy Macarius might be revealed, it entered the man’s heart to lead her into the desert. He bound her as though she were a mare and led her into the desert.

When he approached, the brothers were standing near Macarius’s cell, arguing and saying: “Why have you brought this mare here?”

He replied: “So that she may obtain mercy.”

They said to him: “What is wrong with her?”

He answered: “She was my wife, and she has been changed into a mare. Today is the third day that she has tasted nothing.”

They reported this to holy Macarius, who was praying inside. God had revealed the matter to him for this very reason. He replied to the brothers:

“You are the horses, because you have the eyes of horses. She has not been transformed; she merely appears as a mare to the eyes of those who are deceived.”

He blessed oil and anointed her naked body from the crown of her head, praying over her. Immediately he caused her to appear as a woman to everyone. He gave her food and made her eat, then he sent her away with her own husband; she gave thanks to God.

He instructed her, saying: “Never cease from communion.” He added: “This happened to you because for five weeks you did not approach the divine mysteries.”

Another girl was also brought to him [Note: [Col. 0355D] This is absent from Heraclides.]. The obscene parts of her body had rotted away on every side, so that when the flesh had been consumed, the inner and hidden parts of nature were exposed, and an innumerable multitude of worms boiled out from them. No one would approach her because of the horror of the stench.

When her parents had brought her and cast her before his doors, he pitied the virgin’s suffering and said: “Be of good courage, daughter. The Lord has given you this for salvation, not for destruction. Therefore it is more necessary to take care that your health does not bring you any danger.”

After he had persevered in prayer for seven continuous days and blessed oil in the Lord’s name, he anointed her limbs. He restored her so completely to health that the condition of her body was renewed, the full form of a woman appeared in her, and thereafter she could live among human beings without the impediment of her former illness.

Another deed of his continence over a long period is also reported. Beneath the ground he made a passage from his cell for half a stadium and established a cave at the end. Whenever many people were troubling him, he secretly left his cell and went to the cave, and no one found him.

One of his vigorous disciples told us that, going to the cave, Macarius would offer twenty-four prayers to the Lord, and on returning, twenty-four more.

A report arose concerning him that he had raised a dead man and persuaded a heretic to convert, one who did not believe that there would be a resurrection of bodies; and he acquired a reputation in the desert.

For they said that a certain Hieracite had once come to him; this kind of heresy is found in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0355D] This story is absent from Heraclides. It is found word for word in Ruffinus, above, book II, ch. 28.]. Since he disturbed many of the brothers living in the desert by his considerable skill in argument, he even dared to assert the perversity of his faith in Macarius’s presence.

When the elder resisted and contradicted him, Hieracitas evaded his plain words with crafty arguments. But when the holy man saw that the brothers’ faith was in danger, he said:

“What need is there for us to contend with words, to the subversion of those listening? Let us go out to the graves of the brothers who went before us in the Lord; and let all know that the faith of whichever one of us the Lord grants to raise a dead man from the grave is approved by God.”

This proposal pleased all the brothers who were present, and they proceeded to the graves.

Macarius urged Hieracitas to call upon the dead man in the Lord’s name. But he replied: “You proposed this; call him first.”

Macarius prostrated himself in prayer before the Lord. When he had prayed sufficiently, he lifted his eyes upward and said:

“Show, Lord, which of the two of us holds the right faith by raising this dead man.”

After saying this, he called out the name of a brother who had recently died. When the dead man answered him from the tomb, the brothers immediately removed what had been laid above it. They brought him out of the grave, loosened the strips with which he had been bound, and presented him alive.

When Hieracitas saw this, he was struck with astonishment and turned to flee. All the brothers pursued him and drove him beyond the boundaries of that land.

[Col. 0356C] On one occasion a young man afflicted by a demon was brought to him, bound with two ropes by his own mother, who was entirely torn apart with grief. The demon’s attack was of this kind: after he had eaten bread made from three modii and drunk a flask of water, he would belch into the air and discharge the food. For whatever he had devoured or drunk was consumed as though by fire. There is indeed a class of demons called “fiery.” For there are different kinds of demons, just as there are different kinds of human beings—not in substance, but in their wills. This young man, since his food was insufficient for him, even drank his own urine. When his mother was lamenting and entreating holy Macarius, he took the young man and, invoking and supplicating God, after one day and then a second, reduced the affliction. Then he said to the young man’s mother, “How much do you want him to eat?” She replied, “Ten pounds of bread.” [Col. 0356D] He rebuked her because she had said too much. Continuing to pray over him for seven days, he set his allowance at three pounds, so that he might be able to work; and thus, having healed him, he returned him to his mother. Many other things were also reported about him, but they are too lengthy to write down. Yet from these few examples his other deeds may also be recognized. I did not see this man, for he died in the year when I entered the desert.

Once, when someone had come to blessed Macarius wishing to serve Christ in the monastic vocation [Note: [Col. 0356D] Missing in Heraclides.], and was entreating the holy old man to instruct and teach him, to strengthen him from the fountain of saving doctrine [Col. 0357A] which abounded in him through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and to warn him how, with the Lord’s help, he might escape the snares and assaults of the evil one, blessed Macarius replied:

“If you truly desire with all your heart to renounce this world, my son, and cling to the Lord Savior, as the Prophet says in the psalm: ‘My soul clung to you, and your right hand received me’ (Ps. LXII), then the Lord’s right hand is ready to receive those who flee to him. You must renounce this world and cast away all its practices, as the Apostle says when writing to the Colossians: ‘For you have died to this world, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory’ (Col. III).”

Hearing this, the younger man [Col. 0357B] said: “Believe me, most blessed Father, for I have also estranged my mind from this world and from everything in it, so that now I may live in this present life as one who is dead. For I have understood that all the things which appear good in this world are temporal, passing, and corruptible.”

Then the old man said to him: “Listen to me, son, and go to the tombs of the dead. Heap upon them the greatest insults, many abuses, curses, and even stones, so that, provoked, they may become angry with you.”

After hearing this, the younger man immediately went to the monuments of the dead. When, according to the blessed old man’s command, he had inflicted upon them what he thought were many insults, he returned to holy Macarius and told him what he had done. The old man asked him whether those dead men had answered him at all. He replied: [Col. 0357C] “They said absolutely nothing, lord.”

Again he commanded him: “Go tomorrow and praise and glorify them with many laudations.”

The brother again went to the tombs of the dead and began to praise and glorify them with words of honor, saying: “You are great and holy, like apostolic men, and great justice is in you.” After he had addressed many other praises to them, he returned to his cell and said to the old man: “Behold, according to your command, lord Father, I praised and glorified those dead men, and they said absolutely nothing to me.”

Then holy Macarius said to him: “Consider, my son: just as you reproached those dead men with insults and abuse, and they said nothing to you, so you too, if you wish to be saved and to please our Savior in the holy vocation, must imitate the Lord himself, our Lord and Savior, as blessed John the apostle and evangelist says: ‘Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked’ (I John II).

“Therefore, in the Gospel we read that those most faithless Jews, the enemies of our faith, said many insults against our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, at the instigation of the devil, the enemy of the human race: that he was a Samaritan, that he had a demon, and that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. They even dared to call him a deceiver. All these things our pious Lord Jesus Christ himself, creator of heaven, earth, and sea, and of everything in them, patiently endured, [Col. 0358A] so that he might provide us with an example of his patience, gentleness, and humility.

“For if he had wished to display the power of his majesty and avenge the insults, he would suddenly have reduced the whole world to chaos, and neither the human race nor even the world itself would have remained; everything would have perished in an instant. Yet the ineffable goodness of Christ the Lord did not wish to do these things, for he had come into the world not to punish but to save it. He endured everything patiently for this reason: to show us examples of patience and humility. Thus he said to the disciples who followed him: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls’ (Matt. XI).

“Moreover, all the saints from the beginning of the world, both prophets and apostles, afflicted by reproaches, insults, and various torments, always maintained an unshaken virtue of patience and humility, [Col. 0358B] and were never deceived by human praise. Rejecting the empty rumors of the vain glory of this present life, those who desire to please Christ yearn for that one heavenly and eternal glory which comes from God and endures forever; no human tongue can express the splendor of its brightness.

“Considering these examples of patience and humility, therefore, my son, whenever insults are inflicted upon you, guard the virtue of patience and humility with the greatest strength, imitating the Prophet who said: ‘But I was like a deaf man and did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth; I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth’ (Ps. XXXVII). This is indeed sung daily in the synaxis to admonish our understanding.

“Take care also not to delight in vain glory and the praise of men, thereby losing everything you have acquired through labor in good works, and failing to receive from the Lord in eternal life the fruits of your fasting and abstinence and the reward of your vigils and prayers. For he said in the Gospel concerning those who seek human praise: ‘Truly I say to you, they have received their reward’ (Matt. VI). And there are many other passages by which Holy Scripture never ceases to warn us concerning the avoidance of vain glory.

“Take care, therefore, my son, and do not let your spirit blaze with anger at the insults inflicted upon you. Even if your heart is provoked, strictly restrain your spirit from anger in the fear of the Lord, so that you may preserve the virtue of humility and patience. Then you will truly show what you promised when you said that you lived in this world as one dead, if you give no turbulent answer to those who insult you—just as those dead men in the tombs, whom you assailed with many insults and abuses, gave you no answer at all.

“Therefore we must firmly guard the virtue of humility and patience, so that we may be able to attain heavenly rewards and the glory of eternal life, as the Lord says in the Apocalypse: ‘Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown’ (Apoc. III).”

Holy Abbot Macarius often admonished his disciples and taught them, saying [Note: [Col. 0357D] Missing in Heraclides.]: “Always remember that you live before the sight of the almighty Lord [Col. 0359A], who sees the thoughts of all human beings and searches the hearts of each one. Holy Scripture also bears witness to this, and the Apostle teaches it, saying: ‘For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and exposed to his eyes’ (Hebr. IV).

“Therefore, brothers, if the pleasure of the flesh and the desire for fornication assail us, let us hasten to repel and cast out from our heart the most filthy and wicked thought, earnestly invoking the help of our Lord Jesus Christ in prayers and fasts, so that by the power of his might he may rescue and protect us and crush Satan beneath our feet.

“We must also correct ourselves through repentance and abstention from sins, saying to our soul: ‘The bodily pleasure which wrongly delights you lasts only a short time; but the torments and sufferings of soul and body in the eternal fire of Gehenna remain in everlasting punishments.’

“While admonishing our soul in this way, let us also say: ‘If you are ashamed of sinful people like yourself seeing you sin, why should you not much more revere and fear the majesty of the almighty God, who observes all the secrets of hearts, as the Apostle also says: “All things are naked and exposed to his eyes” (Hebr. IV)?’

“If we rebuke ourselves with such thoughts, the fear of the Lord immediately enters our heart, our soul is strengthened in the love of chastity, and we are also urged to carry out all the Lord’s commandments. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ assists us; he has promised those who serve him in holiness and chastity that he will grant heavenly and eternal gifts in the glory and life of the age to come, where they will rejoice forever with the holy angels in the splendor of perpetual light.”

## CHAPTER X  
### The Life and Conduct of Another Macarius, Namely the Alexandrian Presbyter, and of Mark the Monk

I also observed another Macarius, the Alexandrian presbyter (Heraclides, chap. 6), in the place called the Cells. I lived in those Cells for nine years, and he lived three years longer than I did. Some things I saw in his presence, some I heard, and some I learned from others.

This was his practice: if he heard of anything anywhere, he hastened by every means to undertake it. Thus, when he heard from someone that the monks of Tabenna ate no food cooked with fire throughout the whole of Lent, he decided for seven years not to eat anything that had passed through fire, except raw vegetables and, when it was available, soaked legume. He tasted nothing else. When he had completed this practice, he regarded such an observance as nothing.

Again, he heard from someone that another person ate a pound of bread. Breaking bread into small pieces, he put them into a flask and decided to eat only as much as he could bring through the mouth of the flask. As he himself reported [Col. 0360A], “Although I gladly grasped a larger piece of bread, I was not able to remove it because the opening of the flask was too narrow.” He maintained this abstinence for three years, eating four or five ounces and drinking the same amount of water. 992 For a whole year he used only one sextarius of oil.

Again, he adopted the following practice: he decided to overcome sleep and, as he reported, did not go under a roof for twenty days, in order to conquer sleep. Thus by day he was burned by excessive heat, while by night he was constricted by cold. “And,” he said, “unless I had entered under a roof more quickly and fallen asleep, my brain would have become so dried up that I would almost have lost my mind. Therefore,” he said, [Col. 0360B] “the more I conquered myself, the more I yielded to nature, which requires sleep.”

On one occasion he was tempted by the passion of fornication, and condemned himself to sit naked for six months in the Scythian marsh, which is in the desert, where there are mosquitoes like clouds, [5] which even pierce the skin of wild boars. Thus he was entirely pierced by them and developed swellings, so that some thought he had become elephantine. After six months he came to his cell, and he was recognized by his voice as Macarius himself.

On one occasion he desired to enter the burial garden of Jannes and Jambres, as he related to us. That burial garden had been made by the magicians who were formerly powerful before Pharaoh. They constructed the work from squared stones [Col. 0360C], made a tomb for themselves, buried a great quantity of gold, and also planted trees; for the place was moist, and they made a well there. Since he did not know the way, he followed a certain arrangement of the stars, as sailors at sea customarily do when navigating.

Thus he entered the desert, carrying bundles of reeds. At every mile he planted one as a marker, so that he might find the path by which to return. After traveling for nine days, he reached the place. But the demon who always resists Christ’s combatants gathered all the reeds which he had placed as markers from each mile to the garden and tomb and, while he was resting, put them at his head.

[Col. 0360D] When he arose, he found the reeds. This happened, by God’s permission, as a test of him, so that he would not trust in reeds but in the pillar of cloud which went before the children of Israel for forty years in the desert.

He said that he was met by armies of demons coming out of that garden. “They cried out,” he said, “like ravens before my face, saying: ‘What do you want, Macarius? What do you want, monk? Why have you come to our place? You cannot remain here.’ I replied to them: ‘I must enter and see.’

“When he entered the garden, Satan confronted him with a drawn sword, threatening him. To him holy Macarius gave this answer: ‘You come against me with a sword, but I come against you in the name of the Lord Sabaoth, the God of Israel.’”
