Upon entering, [Col. 0361A] he found a bronze bucket hanging there and an iron chain over the well, long since loosened. He also found the fruits of pomegranate trees, with nothing inside them because they had dried up from the excessive heat of the sun, and very many golden abominations of idols.

Then he returned and arrived after twenty days. When the water and bread he was carrying failed, he fell into great distress. As they were running out, a girl appeared to him, standing, as he reported, clothed in the purest linen and holding a water jar dripping with water. He said that she was about one stadium away from him. For three days he continued walking, seeing her standing with the jar, but he could not approach her, as though he were dreaming. Yet he was strengthened by waiting in hope of seeing her.

Afterward a herd of cattle appeared to him, one of which [Col. 0361B] was standing with its calf. There are many cattle in those places, and, as he himself said, milk flowed from its udders for him. Then a voice came from above, saying: “Macarius, approach the cow and suck.”

He placed himself beneath it and, after nursing, recovered his strength. That cow came with him all the way to his cell, nursing him and not accepting her calf.

When he returned to the brothers and told them about the suitability of the place, many were inflamed with enthusiasm to go there with him [Note: [Col. 0361D] Missing in Heraclides.]. [Col. 0361C] But when the holy Fathers perceived that the young men’s spirits had been stirred up to go, they restrained them with sound counsel, saying:

“If this place really was established by Jannes and Jambres, as is said, nothing else should be believed about it except that it may perhaps have been prepared by the work of the devil for our deception. For if it is delightful and abundant, what rest shall we hope for in the age to come if we enjoy delights here?”

Saying these and other things, they restrained the young men’s enthusiasm. Although the place was pleasant with various fruits and abundant in everything necessary, he said that many brothers could not be brought there, lest they be deceived by demons while coming through the desert. For he said that there were many demons whose roarings and cunning the unaccustomed multitude of brothers could not endure.

On one occasion the same holy Macarius was digging a well and, in a nearby thicket of the forest, was bitten by an asp (Heraclides, chap. 6). Seizing the deadly creature by the jaws and tearing it apart with both hands, he said to it: “Why, unless God permits it, did you presume to come?” [Col. 0361D]

He had various little cells: one on Mount Nitria, another in the inner desert of Scetis, and another in the place called the Cells. Some had no windows; he was said to sit in these during Lent. Another was so narrow that, when lying down, he could not stretch out his feet. Another was wider, in which he received those who came to him.

Here, through the grace of Christ, he healed such a great multitude of people afflicted by demons that everyone marveled and glorified the power of our Savior Jesus Christ, who worked mighty deeds through him.

[Col. 0362A] While we were there, a certain virgin from Thessalonica was brought to him. She had suffered from paralysis for many years. He anointed her with holy oil for twenty days and persisted in prayers for her; then he sent her back healthy to her own city. After she reached her home, she sent many offerings to various holy monasteries.

This Macarius had heard that the monks of Tabenna possessed a strict way of life and rule of discipline. Changing his clothing and taking the garments of a peasant, he went up through the desert to the Thebaid for fifteen days. Entering the monastery of the Tabenna monks, he sought the abbot, so that he might be presented to his sight: a holy man named Pachomius, a highly approved servant of Christ, [Col. 0362B] who possessed the grace of prophecy. By God’s will, Macarius’s arrival had been concealed from him.

When he was brought before him, Macarius said: “I entreat you, holy lord Father, receive me into your monastery, so that I may become a monk.”

Pachomius said to him: “You are already advanced in old age 993 and cannot endure abstinence. The brothers are extremely continent, and, unable to bear their labor, you will take offense and return, speaking against them.”

He did not receive him, neither on the first day nor on the second, but continued until the seventh day. When Macarius persevered, remaining even without food, he then said to him: “Receive me, abba, and if I do not fast as the other brothers do, or work as they do, then command me to be thrown out.”

Hearing this, the abbot ordered the brothers to receive him. There is a community of one thousand four hundred men in each monastery [Col. 0362C]. Blessed Father Pachomius was abbot over many monasteries, and the community consisted of many thousands of monks; through the generosity of Christ, there are still many thousands even now.

He therefore entered the monastery. After a short time had passed, Lent arrived, and he saw each of the brothers adding to his abstinence through fasting. Some ate again after two days; others took food after five days; still others kept vigil throughout the whole night, devoting themselves to prayers, and by day performed manual labor.

The holy Macarius stood in a corner, not leaving it at all by day or night until the forty days were completed. Easter also arrived, but even then he did not taste bread or any other cooked dish, except leaves from stalks, and even these he ate only once a week, on Sunday. [Col. 0362D] He did not leave the corner where he had chosen to stand except for bodily necessity, and then he immediately hurried back, shut the door behind him, and spoke absolutely nothing; only his lips moved in silence.

Continually and without ceasing, he meditated in his heart upon the Lord’s sayings and the remembrance of divine Scripture, and he exercised manual labor without interruption, much more than the other brothers.

When the brothers saw this, almost all took offense. They murmured to the superior of the monastery: “Where did you bring this man from, as though he were living without flesh, for our condemnation? Throw him out; understand that the brothers are greatly scandalized by him.” [Col. 0363A]

When the superior of the monastery heard this, he marveled at Macarius’s strict way of life and prayed to the Lord, saying: “Reveal to me, Lord, your sinful servant, what I ought to do.”

It was revealed to him that this was Macarius himself. He led him outside to the oratory, where the altar had been placed, embraced him, kissed him, and said: “Truly you are a blessed man, holy Macarius, and you have remained hidden from us. For a long time we have desired to see your holiness. We give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ, because through spiritual goods, and especially through the virtues of abstinence, you have taught us and our little ones not to think highly of themselves in their way of life. Return, therefore, to your own place. You have edified us greatly, most blessed Father, and pray for us without ceasing.” [Col. 0363B]

On one occasion, for the sake of visitation and edification, I went to him and found a certain presbyter lying before the door of his courtyard, covered with ulcers over his entire body. Even the bones of his head had rotted. He had come so that he might receive healing through Macarius’s prayers.

But holy Macarius would not receive him. I prostrated myself on the ground at his feet and entreated him to receive the man. The blessed man replied to me: “He is unworthy to receive healing. Rather, rebuke him and persuade him not to dare approach the most holy altar of the Lord and offer sacrifice to the Lord, because he offers it while committing fornication; for this reason he is being punished.”

[Col. 0363C] “Persuade him, therefore, to come to his senses and perform worthy repentance, so that he may deserve to receive mercy from the Lord.”

So I went out to the sick man and told him everything. He was terribly shaken, trembled, and swore that until the end of his life he would not presume to approach the Lord’s altar.

After this, Macarius ordered him to enter, received him, and said to him: “Do you believe that God exists, from whom nothing is hidden?”

He replied: “Yes, lord.”

He said to him: “Could you deceive God or remain hidden from him?”

He replied: “No.”

Then he said: “If you recognize the sin of so great a crime and understand God’s punishment, for what reason this great affliction is in your body and why you have been struck, cease from your evil ways, amend yourself from now on, and always confess your sin before the Lord with tears of repentance and the deepest sorrow of heart, so that on the day of judgment you may be able to find some mercy and compassion from the Lord.” [Col. 0363D]

The man gave a solemn undertaking never again to sin, to approach the most holy altar, or to consecrate an offering, but to have the status of a layman. After this, Macarius laid his hand upon him, prayed to the Lord for him, and within a few days he was healed. The hair of his head grew back, and he departed healthy.

During those same days a young man who was being tormented by an unclean spirit was brought to him. He placed one hand upon the young man’s head and the other upon his chest, and prayed over him for so long that the unclean spirit lifted him into the air. The boy swelled up entirely like a wineskin, so that water poured from all his limbs; then, [Col. 0364A] suddenly crying out, he became thin and returned to his normal size. Macarius therefore delivered him healthy to his father, anointed him with holy oil, and commanded that for forty days he neither eat meat nor drink wine. Thus the boy was restored to health.

The same holy man Macarius also related to us, warning us to beware of the demons’ manifold snares. “At one time,” he said, “thoughts of vain glory became exceedingly troublesome to me, suggesting that they should drive me out, by one means or another, from my cell and from my solitary life in the desert. They urged me, for the sake of edification and the healing of people, to go to Rome for the salvation of many souls; for the Lord’s grace was in me against unclean spirits.

“When such thoughts persisted with me for a long time [Col. 0364B] and did not cease even while I was praying, I threw myself face down upon the ground, stretched my feet beyond the threshold of the door of my cell, and cried out, saying: ‘Pull, demons, pull! I am not going anywhere on my own feet; but if you can, drag me away from here. For I call God to witness that I will lie here until evening.’

“Thus I lay there until evening. Afterwards I rose and returned to my customary work for the Lord.”

He also related to us something about a certain brother Mark, a monk of extraordinary abstinence. For holy Macarius was a presbyter. He said:

“I noted the times when holy communion was administered. I never gave communion to Mark the monk; an angel gave it to him from the altar. I saw only the knuckle of the hand of the giver.

[Col. 0364C] “Mark was still a young man, and he had committed the New and Old Testament of Holy Scripture to memory. He was exceedingly gentle and chaste beyond all others.

“When holy Macarius was in extreme old age, I went to him and found the door of his cell closed. Standing at the door, I listened to what he was saying and to whom he was speaking; for I heard him speaking. I thought that someone was with him, to whom he was speaking. He was then a hundred years old—indeed, he had already lost his teeth.

“Since he was alone, he quarreled with himself and, as though speaking to his own body, said: ‘What do you want, you who have aged so badly? Behold, you have now received oil and wine. What else do you want, you decrepit old man?’ Thus he rebuked himself, so that even the devil might be put to shame.”

[Col. 0364D] The man of supreme holiness Paphnutius, his disciple, related to us that one day a lioness, taking her blind cub, brought it to holy Macarius. Striking her head against the door of his courtyard, she opened it; entering while the holy man was seated, she threw the cub at his feet.

He took it, spat into its eyes, and prayed. Immediately its eyes were opened, and it looked about. The lioness nursed it, lifted it up, and departed.

On the following day the lioness brought him a large sheepskin. When the saint saw the skin, he said to the lioness: “Where did you get this, unless you ate someone’s sheep—perhaps even a poor man’s? I do not accept from you what comes from injustice.”

But she bowed her head to the pavement, begged him, and laid the skin at the saint’s feet. [Col. 0365A] He said to her: “I told you that I will not accept it unless you promise me that from now on you will never grieve the poor by devouring their four-footed animals.”

She seemed to consent by nodding her head, as though making a promise. Then he accepted the skin from her.

“And what is astonishing, brothers, if the Lord, creator of all things, who tamed the lions for the prophet Daniel, also made the lioness gentle for Macarius?”

He said that from the time he was baptized he had not spoken an idle word. It had been sixty years since his baptism. He was short in stature and had hair only above his lip and at the tip of his chin. Because of his excessive abstinence, the hairs of his beard grew sparsely.

Once I confessed to him: “What shall I do, abba? Thoughts of acedia trouble me, saying: ‘You are doing nothing; leave this desert.’”

He said to me: “Tell them: ‘For Christ’s sake I sit here and guard these walls.’”

These are a few of the many wondrous deeds I have related about him.

## CHAPTER XI  
### On Blessed Abbot John

The holy Fathers used to say about holy John, who was called Colob [Note: [Col. 0365D] Missing in Heraclides.], that when he returned very tired from the work of the harvest, he presented himself before the holy elders. After praying with them, he immediately went to his cell and for a long time devoted himself in silence to prayers, readings, and meditation on the Holy Scriptures. He also performed manual labor every day and did not allow anyone to come to him.

“For,” he said, “through the demands of the harvest work, the mind’s attention is scattered and suffers distraction, and is therefore bound by various thoughts.”

He also imposed greater abstinence upon himself, saying: “Because of the labor of the harvest I ate bread to satiety every day during those days. Now, since I rest in my cell, I must add abstinence and vigils, so that what was neglected during those days may be compensated for and restored.”

Some of the brothers asked this same blessed John about the reason for abstinence. He replied:

“Because the prophet Daniel said: ‘I did not eat bread according to desire’ (Dan. X).”

He also admonished the brothers, saying: “Consider, beloved, that nothing is stronger among beasts than a lion, yet because of its belly it falls into a snare, and its fierce and great strength is humbled.” [Col. 0365D]

By this example blessed John himself instructed the brothers, saying:

“If an emperor wishes to capture a city belonging to his enemies, he first deprives them of food and drink. Thus, crushed by necessity, they are humbled and subjected to his authority. Similarly, if the passions and vices of our body are weakened by the hunger of fasts and the labor of vigils, then the strength of our enemies—that is, of the demons—is also humbled, the strength which they wickedly habitually exercise against us through the power of our body.”

## CHAPTER XII  
### On Marcianus, the Servant of Christ

[Col. 0366A] We shall also relate a similar example concerning the servant of Christ Marcianus [Note: [Col. 0366D] Missing in Heraclides. Theodoretus, *Philotheus*, chap. 3.].

His sister went with her son to the monastery to visit him after many years. He was unwilling either to receive or to see his sister, but he received her son. They earnestly entreated him and asked him to accept the tunic and cloak they had brought him. But he absolutely refused to accept them, saying:

“From my infancy until this hour my Lord has governed me, and even until the end of my life he will provide me with everything necessary. [Col. 0366D] For it is not fitting to await or receive such things from carnal relatives.”

[Col. 0366B] The nephew prostrated himself at his feet, saying: “We offer these not to you as a relative, but as a servant of God and a monk.”

Blessed Abbot Marcianus replied: “How many monasteries did you pass on your journey to us?”

He answered: “Very many monasteries.”

“And why,” he said, “did you not give these garments to them as servants of God and monks?”

He replied: “Because we gave nothing to anyone.”

Then blessed Marcianus said to him: “Behold, it is clear that you brought these things to me not as to a servant of God and a monk, but as to your relative and kinsman.”

He therefore refused to accept them. He prayed most earnestly for them, entreating the Lord for the salvation of their souls, and dismissed them. He also commanded them never again to come to him.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On a Certain Virgin in Name Alone

[Col. 0366C] I shall not omit to relate also the conduct of those who live contemptibly, for the praise of those who amend their lives and for the admonition of readers.

There was a certain virgin in Alexandria (Heraclides, chap. 2), humble in the form of her clothing but proud in the purpose of her mind. She was exceedingly rich in money, yet never went out, and never at any time gave a coin to a stranger, to virgins, to the church, or to the poor.

Despite the many admonitions of the Fathers, she did not cast away the forest of her riches. She also had a considerable family, among whom she had adopted the daughter of her sister, to whom she promised her possessions night and day. Her mind had been alienated from heavenly desire.

For this is also a form of the devil’s error: under the pretext of love for one’s own family, to labor in avarice. That concern for kindred does not belong to him who teaches fratricide and patricide is evident. Yet if he seems to inspire concern for relatives, he does not do this from the prompting of a right mind, but in order to bind the soul of the one acting unjustly in the snare of avarice, knowing the sentence that “the unjust and the greedy will not inherit the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI).

Anyone may act prudently and reasonably, without despising his own soul, and may provide consolation to his parents, especially if they lack necessities [6] and are in greater need. But when someone neglects his own soul by giving to his descendants, he is subject to the law, because he thinks vainly about his soul. [Col. 0367A]

The holy psalmist David sings of those who are concerned for their soul in fear:

“Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord”—that is, since it is difficult—“or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain” (Ps. XXIII).

But these receive their soul in vain, thinking that it is dissolved together with the body while they neglect the virtues.

Therefore, wishing, so to speak, to tame this virgin, bent toward the revelation of her avarice, the most holy priest Macarius, superintendent of the poor lepers, devised and contrived the following scheme. For he had been a money-changer from his youth—by which they mean one who deals in gems—and he went and said to her:

“Precious stones, emeralds and hyacinths, have come into my possession; whether they are found or stolen I cannot say. They are exceedingly valuable, so splendid that their worth cannot be estimated. The man who owns them is selling them for five hundred solidi. If you would like to take them, you can obtain five hundred solidi from a single stone; the others you can prepare as an ornament for your niece.”

The virgin listened with the greatest attention and was delighted. Falling at his feet, she said: “By your holiness, let no one else purchase them.”

The priest therefore invited her, saying: “Come to my cell and see them.”

She did not agree to this, but, bowing before him, gave him five hundred solidi, saying: “Take them as you wish; I have no further concern.” He received the money and distributed it to the poor.

After some time had passed—for he was a man of great reputation and reverence throughout all [Col. 0367C] Alexandria, a lover of God and exceedingly merciful—for he had reached the age of one hundred years, and we too had lived with him—the virgin mentioned above was reluctant to remind him of the matter.

At last, finding him in the church, she said: “I beg you, lord, what do you command concerning those stones for which we gave five hundred solidi?”

He replied: “From the time you gave me the gold, I handed it over as the price of the gems. If you wish to come and see where they are kept, come and see; they are lying there. If they please you, so much the better; but if not, take back what is yours and go.”

She went very readily to his cell. It was a hospice for the poor, where lepers lay. On the lower floor he had women, [Col. 0367D] and on the upper floor men. Bringing her there, he led her to the doorway and said: “Which do you wish to see first, the hyacinths or the emeralds?”

She said: “Whichever you wish, lord.”

He said: “Look, these are the hyacinths.”

Then he took her down to the lower floor and, showing her the women, said: “Look, these are the emeralds. If they please you, well and good; but if not, take back what is yours.”

Overcome with shame, she went out. As she departed, she fell ill from profound sadness, because she had not acted according to God’s will. Afterward she even gave thanks to the priest. The girl for whom she had been concerned died after her marriage without children.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Life and Conduct of Moses, Once a Robber

[Col. 0368A]

A certain man named Moses (Heraclid., chapter 7), an Ethiopian by birth, was the slave of a local magistrate. Because of his many acts of perversity, thefts, and robberies, his master expelled him. It was said that he had gone so far as murder. I am compelled to recount his evils in order to display the power of his endurance.

It was said, then, that he was the leader of robbers, as is shown by his very deeds in theft and banditry. Finally, bearing a grudge against a certain shepherd, he suddenly wished to attack and kill him at night. He searched for the places where the shepherd kept his sheepfolds, and was told that they lay across the Nile, which was then swollen, and that the crossing was a mile wide.

Holding a sword tightly [Col. 0368B] in his mouth, he placed his tunic over his head and swam across the river. While he was swimming, the shepherd made every effort to hide himself and remain concealed. But Moses, being a robber, killed four rams, tied them together, dragged them across the river, and swam back again. After leaving the river, he skinned them, ate the best parts of the meat, sold the remainder for wine, and drank eighteen cups. Immediately afterward he covered fifty miles on foot during the day and reached the place where his companions were.

Such and so great a man had lived amid such great evils.

At a certain time, hearing the word of God from a devout man [Note: [Col. 0367D] The account is lacking in the Heraclides], and hearing of the future judgment on the day of judgment between the just and sinners, between criminals and saints, as well as of the bitter punishments of Gehenna and eternal fire [Col. 0368C], and of endless torments in the outer darkness prepared for the wicked and sinners; and likewise hearing of eternal glory, eternal honors, and rest in the kingdom of heaven among the holy angels, which God prepared for the saints and the just who serve him, he was pierced in heart and began to weep most bitterly, with groaning and lamentation.

Entering a monastery, he devoted himself to repentance. He tormented himself with many tears, asking the Lord, in his goodness and mercy, for pardon and forgiveness of his sins, and so he remained in the monastery.

At a certain time, robbers entered his cell, not knowing who he was (Heraclid., chapter 7). There were four of them. He bound them together like a bundle [Col. 0368D] of straw (7), placed them on his back, and carried them to the brothers’ church, saying: “Since it is no longer proper for me to harm anyone, decide what you wish to do with these men.”

Then the robbers recognized that he was Moses, formerly the most wicked of robbers. They were pierced in heart and glorified God, who does not reject sinners but receives those who repent so that they may be saved with eternal salvation. Saying this, as I have related, they were pierced in heart and devoted themselves to repentance, renouncing all their evil deeds, lusts, and carnal desires.

The demons attacked this Moses, according to his former habit, introducing into him the lust of fornication [Col. 0369A]. He was tempted with such force, as he himself recounted, that he nearly fell away from his purpose. From then on he abstained more rigorously, increased his vigils, and applied himself more diligently to manual labor, wasting away his body.

Finally, he resolved not to sleep lying down on a mat. Instead, he prayed standing in his cell throughout the night and completed his psalmody. Leaning against the walls, he obtained only a little sleep.

Again he imposed another discipline upon himself. At night he went out, visited the cells of the elders, took the pitchers from which they drew their water, and carried water to them. Their water was far away: some had to go two miles, others even five.

One night [Col. 0369B], unable to endure the fervor of his way of life and faith, the demon struck him in the kidneys from behind as he bent over the well to draw water, and left him there. Overcome by the intensity of the pain, he became speechless and remained as if dead.

The next day someone came to draw water, found him lying there, and reported it to the blessed priest Isidore of Scetis. Isidore sent men, who lifted him, carried him to the church, and there he remained ill for nearly a year, scarcely recovering his strength.

The priest Isidore said to him: “Rest, Moses, and do not presume indiscreetly. Rather, practice both abstinence and vigils and manual labor with discernment.”

Moses replied: “I will not rest, most blessed Father, until, with the Lord’s grace assisting me, the most filthy thoughts [Col. 0369C] and dreams which the wickedest demons send have ceased, as it is written: ‘I will pursue my enemies, overtake them, and not turn back or rest until they perish’ (Psalm XVII).”

When the most blessed Isidore saw that his faith and steadfastness in the Lord were firm, he rose, stretched out his hands in prayer, and said to him: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the gift of his grace, from this day onward the dreams that used to trouble you have ceased.”

Moses therefore glorified and thanked the Lord Savior and returned to his cell. After some time, the priest Isidore asked him about the distress caused by carnal thoughts. He replied: “With Christ the Lord protecting me, and through your prayers, I suffer nothing of the kind.”

God therefore granted him the grace to drive demons from possessed bodies, so that we fear flies no more than he feared those demons.

Such was the conduct of Moses the Ethiopian, who himself was counted among the great Fathers. He died at the age of seventy-five. He left seventy monk-disciples.

## CHAPTER XV. The Life of Evagrius

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Evagrius was an Origenist.]

It is not right to pass over the life of the blessed Evagrius, a deacon truly worthy of God and a man exceedingly learned in divine knowledge (Heracl., chapter 25), but it is necessary to commit it to writing for the benefit of readers and the glory of our Savior Jesus Christ. We must also set it forth at somewhat greater length, showing how, with the help of Christ’s grace, he presented a way of life worthy of God.

He died in the desert at the age of fifty-four. He had been ordained lector by Saint Basil, the bishop. When the most blessed and illustrious bishop Gregory of Nazianzus, renowned for his teaching of Christ, saw that his conduct was blameless, he advanced him to the office of deacon. Thereafter, at the great synod in Constantinople, he was attached to the blessed Nectarius, bishop of that city.

Since he was extremely well instructed in the divine Scriptures, he flourished against every heresy in the great city, possessing also the greatest power of eloquence, so that he was held in great honor and affection by the entire city.

For this reason, the devil’s deceptive vanity, which seeks to obscure good things [Col. 0370B], injected into his heart thoughts of carnal desire and lust for a woman. As he himself later told us, a woman fell in love with him who was the wife of a certain distinguished man among the leading officials of the palace.

Evagrius, however, fearing God and dreading his own conscience, and keeping before his eyes the magnitude of the disgrace—especially the scandal this would give to rejoicing heretics—prayed to the Lord and entreated Christ the Savior that the woman’s furious pursuit of him might be brought to an end. He himself wished to withdraw, but could not, being held fast by the bonds of her attentions.

After he had earnestly entreated the Lord in many prayers to free him from the grave sin that was almost being committed in deed, an angelic visitation came to him in the guise of a prefect’s official (8). The angel seized him, led him to the prefect’s praetorium, and put him in prison, binding his neck and hands with iron chains. But he did not tell him why he was suffering this.

Evagrius himself knew in his conscience why he was enduring these things. He supposed that the husband of the matron had brought an accusation against him. As he became extremely distressed—for he heard the noise and voices of others being tortured before the judge for criminal offenses—and therefore remained greatly terrified and trembling, the angel who had arranged the vision changed his appearance into that of a friend who loved him deeply.

The angel said to him, while he was being held in chains among forty accused men: “Why are you being held here, my lord deacon?”

Evagrius replied: “I tell you the truth: I do not know why I am being held here. I suspect, however, that that distinguished man among the prefects has brought a charge against me before the judge, struck by unreasonable jealousy. I fear that the judge, perhaps corrupted by money, may subject me to torture.”

The other replied: “If you will listen to me as your friend, it is not good for you to remain in this city.”

Evagrius answered: “If God delivers me from this distress and snare, and you see me in Constantinople, know that I justly endure these punishments.”

The angel said to him: “Bring the Gospel and swear to me upon the Gospel that you will leave this city and concern yourself with the salvation of your soul, and I will free you from this danger.”

He therefore brought the Gospel and swore, saying: “I am delayed only for one day, so that I may put my clothes on a ship.”

After giving this oath, he returned from the trance that he had suffered during the night. When he rose, he reflected that although the oath had been given in a trance, he had nevertheless sworn. He put everything he possessed on a ship and came to Jerusalem.

The blessed Melania, formerly a Roman senator’s wife, received him. Her sons and grandsons were leading men in the Senate; she was now a true servant of Christ.

Again the devil hardened his heart as though he were a young man. There he also began to change his clothing, and in the eloquence of his speech he was exalted in vain glory.

But God, who in his great mercy prevents the occasions of our destruction, permitted an excess of fevers to waste away his body, and he was afflicted by a prolonged illness [Col. 0371B] for six months.

The physicians administered various medicines to him, but they accomplished nothing. Then Saint Melania said to him: “My son, I do not approve of this prolonged illness of yours. Tell me, therefore, what is in your heart; for this illness of yours has not come without God’s permission.”

He immediately confessed everything that was in his mind. The servant of God said to him: “Now promise before God that you will keep the promise of the solitary life which you vowed to the Lord. Although I am a sinner, I entreat the Lord to grant you time to live, so that you may fulfill what you have determined for the salvation of your soul.”

He agreed to her saving counsels. Within a few days he was restored to health, and he asked and entreated the servant of God to pray for him. For she had put on the clothing of the monastic vocation [Col. 0371C].

He departed and journeyed to Mount Nitria, which is in Egypt, where he lived for two years. In the third year he entered the desert, where he lived for fourteen years in the place called the Cells.

He ate a pound of bread each day and an Italian measure of oil every three months (9), for he consumed nothing cooked as food and tasted no fruit—certainly a man who had come from great wealth and an abundance of delicacies.

Each day he made one hundred prayers, apart from the night vigils. He wrote in order to obtain food from the work of his hands, for he wrote beautifully in a large hand (10).

Within a few years he deserved to receive from the Lord Christ the light of knowledge, truth, and divine wisdom, together with the grace of discerning spirits. How many books and commentaries on the divine Scriptures he composed is known to everyone, especially to those who, admiring his splendid little works, abandoned error and turned to faith in the Lord Savior.

His teaching was exceedingly admirable and salutary, containing much from the divine Scriptures for the instruction of holy monastic conduct, as well as highly suitable testimonies against vices and the assaults of unclean demons.

At one time the demon of fornication attacked him severely, as he himself told us. Throughout the entire night, in winter, he stood naked under the open sky, so that all his flesh froze.

At another time the spirit of blasphemy attacked him. For forty days and nights he did not enter under a roof [Col. 0372A], so that his body became like that of an irrational rhinoceros (11).

At a certain time three demons came to him in one day, disputing matters of faith. One claimed to be an Arian, another an Eunomian, and the third an Apollinarian. By the grace of divine Wisdom, he refuted them from the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. They were suddenly thrown into confusion, and, making a great uproar, their phantom forms dissolved and disappeared.

He was also frequently beaten by demons; but with divine grace assisting him, he overcame their wickedness.

In the sixteenth year of his way of life, because of the needs of his body and the weakness of his stomach, he was compelled to eat cooked food, although until then he had consumed nothing cooked. He no longer ate bread, but for as long as two years he took vegetables, gruels, and pulses. He died in this condition, receiving the most holy mysteries in the church on the day of the Lord’s Epiphany.

Those who were around him and observed him reported to us that one day before his death he said: “It is now the third year since I have been troubled by carnal desire”—and this after such a long and rigorous life, dry abstinence, labors, sufferings, and unceasing prayers.

While he was living in the monastery, the death of his father was announced to him. He said to the messenger: “Stop blaspheming, for my father is immortal.”

## CHAPTER XVI. The Life of the Priest Cronius and the Long-Suffering of Eulogius

[Col. 0372C]

Cronius, priest of the church at Nitria (Heraclid., chapter 9), told me:

“When I was young and living in a monastery, I suffered from excessive acedia. Fleeing from there, I began to wander through the desert and came to the mountain where Saint Antony lived, that is, between Babylonia and Heraclea, in the vast desert that leads to the Red Sea.

“Coming to a monastery beside the river called Pisper (12), where his disciples Amatus and Macarius were seated—the same men who later buried him—I waited five days to see Saint Antony. They said that he would come to that monastery sometimes after ten days, sometimes after twenty, according as the Lord revealed it to him for the benefit of those arriving at the monastery.

“Very many of us brothers were gathered there, each with different needs. Among them were a certain Eulogius of Alexandria and another man who was a leper; they had both come for the same reason (Pasch., chapter 19, no. 3).

“This Eulogius was a scholar and an educated man. Pierced by divine love, he renounced the crowds of the cities and sold all his possessions, distributing them to the poor, as it is written: ‘He scattered and gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever’ (Psalm CXI); and as the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy’ (Matthew V).

“He therefore kept a few denarii for his own needs, thinking to himself: ‘I cannot work with my own hands, nor can I enter a monastic community.’

“He found a leper lying in the street who had neither hands nor feet, but whose tongue alone remained active. Eulogius stood near him, prayed to the Lord, and made, as it were, a covenant with the Lord, saying:

“‘Lord, in your name I will take this leper into my house, serve him, and give him rest until death, so that through him I too may find your mercy. Grant me, therefore, Christ the Lord, patience for this service.’

“Approaching the leper, he said to him: ‘If you wish, Father, I will receive you into my house and give you rest.’

“He replied: ‘If you are willing to do this, I give thanks.’

“Eulogius then hired a donkey, lifted him onto it, carried him to his house, and carefully cared for him [Col. 0373B].

“For fifteen years he was cared for in this way. He received his needs from Eulogius’s hands and was properly fed.

“After fifteen years, however, the devil laid a trap for him. The leper began to shout against Eulogius and to assail him with many insults and accusations. He said to him:

“‘You have committed many evils, perhaps as a runaway slave from your master. You have stolen other people’s money, and through me you wish to be freed from your sins.’

“And he shouted: ‘Throw me into the street where I used to lie. I want to eat meat.’

“When Eulogius heard this, he offered him meat as food. Again the leper shouted:

“‘I will not agree. Rather, as I said, throw me into the street. I want to see people. Throw me where you found me.’

“If he had possessed hands, he might perhaps have strangled himself; so violently did the demon torment him.

“Therefore Eulogius, greatly troubled, went to the monasteries of the men of God and said to them:

“‘What shall I do, my lords and Fathers? This leper is driving me to despair. I am afraid to throw him out, because I have given my word to God and promised to keep and give him rest until death. If I do not throw him out, but try to keep him here by force, he will make my days most wretched and my nights most bitter.’

“They replied:

“‘While the great and most blessed servant of God, Father Antony, is still alive, board a ship with this leper, go to the monastery where his monks are, and wait there until he comes out of his cave and reaches the monastery. Whatever he tells you, observe it and submit to his decision. Through him God will speak to you.’

“Eulogius therefore put the leper on a ship and boarded it himself. Sailing onward, they came to the monastery of the blessed Antony’s disciples.

“The next day it happened that Father Antony arrived after evening had fallen, as Cronius related. When he came to the monastery, he had this custom: he called Macarius and asked him:

“‘Brother Macarius, have any brothers come here?’

“He replied: ‘Yes, they have come.’

“Again Antony asked: ‘Are they Egyptians or Jerusalemites?’

“For he had given them this sign: ‘When you see those who are more troublesome, say, “They are Egyptians”; but when they are more devout, say, “They are Jerusalemites.”’

“According to his custom he asked: ‘Are the brothers Egyptians or Jerusalemites?’

“Macarius replied: ‘They are mixed.’

“When he said, ‘They are Egyptians,’ the blessed Antony ordered them to be served lentil soup as food. After they had eaten, he prayed for them and dismissed them. But when he said, ‘They are Jerusalemites,’ he sat with them throughout the night, discussing the words of God that concern the salvation of the soul.

“That evening, then, he sat and summoned all the brothers. When they had come, he suddenly called Eulogius three times, although no one had told him his name.

“Eulogius did not answer him, for he supposed that Antony was calling another Eulogius from the monastery. Then Antony said to him:

“‘I am speaking to you, Eulogius, who have come from Alexandria.’

“Eulogius replied: ‘What do you command, lord?’

“Antony asked him: ‘Why have you come here?’

“Eulogius said: ‘Who revealed my name to you and made my reason known?’

“Antony replied: ‘I know why you have come, but declare it before everyone, so that they too may hear.’

“Eulogius said:

“‘I found this leper lying in the street. I lifted him and promised God that I would give him rest, so that I might also be saved and that he might receive rest through my service. But since, after so many years, he wishes to leave me and greatly exasperates me as he hastens to depart, I thought of throwing him out. For that reason I have come to your holiness, so that you might give me counsel about what I should do and pray for me; I am exceedingly troubled and distressed over this matter.’

“Then Antony looked at him with a stern face and said:

“‘You are throwing him out? But the one who made him does not throw him out. You cast him away? But God will raise up someone better than you and will comfort him.’

“Eulogius fell silent and was terrified.

“Then the blessed Antony began to rebuke the leper in harsher words, shouting:

“‘Aged leper, belonging to evil days, unworthy of heaven and earth, will you not cease blaspheming God? Do you not know that it is Christ who serves you? How dare you say such things against Christ? Was it not for Christ that Eulogius made himself your servant and devoted himself to your service?’

“After rebuking him, he left him.

“Afterward, before everyone, Antony told them what was useful for the salvation of their souls, warning Eulogius and the leper not to separate from one another:

“‘Go back to your cell,’ he said. ‘God is visiting you continually. This temptation has come because both of you are near the end, and crowns are being prepared for you. The angel who comes must not find you abandoning the same purpose, lest you lose the reward for so much time spent in good work.’

“When they heard this, they hastened back to their own cell. Forty days later Eulogius died, and three days afterward the leper likewise came to rest.

“After several days, Cronius came down from the Thebaid to the monastery at Alexandria. He found some brothers celebrating the third day of the leper and others the fortieth day of Eulogius. Cronius recognized what had happened and was astonished. Taking the Gospel, he presented it to the brotherhood and swore, telling them how the blessed Antony had foretold everything that happened to Eulogius and the leper [Col. 0375A].”

Cronius also related this to us (Pasch., chapter 19, no. 4; Life of Antony, chapter 38):

“On that night, while the holy Father Antony was teaching us at length from the word of God, he added this:

“‘For a whole year I prayed that the Lord, by his grace, would deem me worthy to have revealed to me the dwelling-place of the just and of sinners. I saw a certain enormous giant reaching up to the clouds, with his hands extended. Beneath him was a pool like the sea, and fire blazed and boiled like a cauldron.

“I saw souls flying about in the form of birds. Those that flew above his hands and head were saved and reached heaven. But those that reached only as far as his hands and were unable to fly higher, he struck with his hands and dashed down; they fell into the boiling pool.

“I also heard a voice saying to me that these were the souls of sinners. Those that flew above the giant were the souls of the righteous, whom the weight of sin does not burden; therefore they can climb to higher places and are saved in the paradise of God.

“The others were the souls of sinners. They were plunged into hell because, while they were in the body, they had not practiced repentance and so had not merited to receive forgiveness of their sins or crimes through the mercy of Christ the Lord. Now they are handed over to the darkness of hell, where there is weeping and the gnashing of teeth because of the excessive severity of the eternal punishments.’”

## CHAPTER XVII. The Life and Endurance of the Blessed Stephen

[Col. 0375C]

A certain Stephen, a Libyan by birth, from the region of Marmarica and Mareotis, lived there for sixty years (Heracl., chapter 12). He possessed the highest self-control and received from the Lord both the grace of discernment and the gift of consolation, so that all the troubled who came to him afflicted by sorrow for whatever reason departed joyful because of his consoling word.

He was also known to the blessed Antony. He lived even into our own times, although I myself did not see him because of the great distance between the places.

Those who had seen him with Saint Ammonius and Eulogius [Heracl., Evagrius] reported to us:

“‘We found him suffering from an illness of this kind in those very places, in his testicles, and with a wound at the summit of his natural parts, which is called cancer or carcinoma [Col. 0375D]. Although a physician was cutting into that wound, he nevertheless worked with his hands, plaited palm leaves, and spoke with us. The rest of his body remained so motionless that it was as though someone else were being cut.’

“When his limbs were cut off, he felt no more than if a hair had been cut from him. Through God’s grace he possessed the strongest endurance.

“When we were saddened and weeping, he said to us:

“‘My little sons, do not be troubled in any way by this matter. Nothing that God permits to happen is evil; it must instead be endured with a good will. Perhaps these limbs were also liable to torments, and it is much better to pay the penalty here than, after this life has ended, to be tortured in eternal fire.’

“In this way he consoled us, strengthened us in faith and patience, and edified us.

“We have related these things so that we may not be disturbed when we see certain saints suffering from the gravest bodily illnesses.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Life and Zeal for Chastity of Saint Innocentius

The blessed priest Innocentius lived on the Mount of Olives (Heracl., chapter 31). I heard many things from those who lived with him for three years.

He was extraordinarily simple. Formerly he had been distinguished at the palace in military service. Nevertheless, at the beginning of Constantine’s reign [Heracl., Constantius], he renounced the world together with his wife.

He had a son named Paul, a domesticus serving in the army, who, at the devil’s instigation, sinned with the daughter of a priest. When his father Innocentius heard this, he prayed to the Lord, saying:

“Lord God, lover of chastity, give him such a spirit of correction that he may no longer find an opportunity to sin in his flesh.”

He considered it better that the young man be tormented by a demon than by lust. And so it happened. To this day he is kept bound in irons on the Mount of Olives, for he is cruelly tormented by an unclean spirit.

If I wished to relate how compassionate this Innocentius was and how great his compassion, I might perhaps incur the suspicion of lying. He frequently stole provisions from the brothers’ supplies and gave them to those in need.

Although he was exceedingly simple, he received from Christ the Lord grace against demons. On one occasion, in our presence, a young man was brought to him who was possessed by an unclean spirit and at the same time suffering from paralysis [Col. 0376C].

When I looked at him, I wished to send away his mother, who had brought him, for I despaired of his being healed. But when the elder saw her standing and weeping over the young man’s indescribable misfortune, he, being exceedingly compassionate, was moved to mercy and wept.

Taking the young man, he entered his oratory, which he had built for himself and in which relics of the blessed John the Baptist were kept. He prayed over him from the third hour until the ninth. By the gift of Christ’s grace, he restored the young man healthy to his mother, and both his paralysis and the demon were driven away by the power of our Savior.

His paralysis had been of such a kind that whenever the boy wished to spit, he spat over his own back; so contorted was he.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Endurance of Eustathius the Lector

[Col. 0376D]

The daughter of a certain priest in Caesarea of Palestine disastrously fell from her resolve of virginity (Heracl., chapter 57). The man who had corrupted her warned her to accuse a lector.

When she conceived and the crime became apparent from the swelling of her womb, her father began to question and investigate her. She immediately accused the lector.

When her father the priest heard this, he reported it to the bishop. The bishop gathered the priests and ordered the lector to be summoned.

Questioned by the bishop, the lector did not confess. How could he say that he had done what he had not done? The bishop, becoming angry, said to him threateningly:

“Will you not confess, wretched man, full of impurity?”

The lector replied [Col. 0377A]:

“I have told the truth: I am not responsible; I am innocent. But if you command that what did not happen be heard, then I say: ‘I did it.’”

When he had said this, the bishop immediately deposed him from the rank of lector.

The lector, however, entreated the bishop and said to him:

“Since I have sinned, command that she be given to me as a wife. For from now on I will no longer be a cleric, nor will she remain a virgin.”

And she was placed under the authority of the lector.

He received her from the bishop and her father, entrusted her to a women’s monastery, and entreated the deaconess who presided over the sisters of the monastery to keep her there until she gave birth.

In a short time the days of childbirth were completed, and the hour of judgment arrived: groaning, pains, anxieties, [Col. 0377B] and the infernal torments of labor. Yet the child did not emerge.

The first day passed, then the second, the third, and the seventh. Because of her excessive pain, the woman was approaching hell. She neither ate nor drank nor slept, but cried out, saying:

“Alas for me, most miserable! I am in the greatest danger, because I falsely accused the lector.”

Those who went away told her father. But the father, fearing that he would be reproached as one who had slandered the lector, kept silent for two more days.

The girl, however, remained in torment, neither giving birth nor dying. Since they could no longer endure her cries, they reported to the bishop:

“She swears under oath, the wretched woman, crying day and night that she falsely accused the lector.”

The bishop then sent a deacon to him and instructed him, saying:

“Pray that the woman who accused you may be delivered.”

But the lector neither answered him nor opened the door. From the day on which he had entered and shut himself in, he had been imploring the mercy of Christ the Lord.

Her father went again to the bishop, and a prayer was offered in the church, but even then she was not delivered.

The bishop rose, went to the lector, knocked on the door, entered, and said to him:

“Eustathius, rise and release what you have bound.”

When the lector knelt together with the bishop, the woman immediately gave birth.

The urgency and persistence of prayer prevailed, exposing the false accusation and convicting the accuser. From this we learn how powerfully persistent prayers can deliver people from dangers, and we recognize before God their power.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0377D]

1. [Note: [Col. 0377] Lacking in Heraclides. The following occur nearly above in other books among the Sayings of the Elders; Rufinus, book III, no. 52; Pelagius, booklet IV, no. 29.]

The blessed abbot Pastor used to explain to the brothers from the writings of the prophets the passage that says:

“For unless Nebuzaradan, the chief cook of King Nebuchadnezzar, had come to Jerusalem, the temple of the Lord would certainly not have been burned.”

He explained this parable spiritually from the following example, saying:

“When the spirit of gluttony— that is, the desire of the stomach—knocks at us, inviting us to various pleasures and to the satiety of the belly, if we obey and fulfill the pleasures and desires of the appetite, then the temple of the Lord is set on fire by the flame of lust, that is, our bodies [Col. 0378A], as the Apostle says:

“‘Do you not know that your bodies are temples of God? If anyone violates the temple of God, the Lord will destroy him’ (1 Corinthians III).”

2. A certain brother came to Abba Pastor and told him that he was suffering a great temptation. The old man said to him: “Go away from this place as far as you can walk in three days and nights, and spend a full year fasting until evening.” The brother replied: “But if I die before the year is over, what will become of me?” Abba Pastor said to him: “I trust in God that, if you are found with such a purpose—or with any kind of repentance—you will be saved.”

3. When Abba Pastor had come to live in the regions of Egypt, it happened that one of the brothers who lived with him had a woman. The old man knew this, but never reproved him. It happened that she gave birth during the night; and the old man learned of it. Calling his junior brother, he said to him: “Take with you a small vessel of Chian wine (13), and give it to the neighbor; for he needs it today.” The brothers did not know his reason. The brother did as the old man had commanded him. That brother was edified and struck with compunction. After a few days he himself dismissed the woman, went to the old man, and repented.

4. A brother asked Abba Pastor: “I suffer harm to my soul because I am with my abba, whose ways I cannot endure. What, then, do you command? Should I remain with him any longer?” Abba Pastor knew that his soul was being harmed by his abba, and he was surprised that the brother asked him whether he should remain with him. He said to him: “If you wish, stay.” The brother went and remained with him.

He came again and said to Abba Pastor: “I am weighing down my soul.” Abba Pastor did not say to him, “Leave him.” He came a third time and said: “Believe me, I will no longer remain with him.” The old man said to him: “Now you are saved; go, and do not remain with him any longer.”

The old man also said to him: “A man who fears suffering harm to his soul has no need to ask about it. But concerning hidden thoughts, one ought to ask, and it belongs to the elders to discern them. Concerning manifest sins, however, there is no need to inquire; one must cut them off immediately.”

The brother then asked him: “How ought I to live in a coenobium?” The old man replied: “He who sits in a coenobium ought to regard everyone as one, justify everyone equally, condemn no one except himself, and guard his mouth and his eyes. Then he will rest without anxiety.”

Abba Isaac said to him when he saw him pouring a little water over his feet: “How is it that some practiced discernment by mortifying their bodies?” Abba Pastor replied: “We have not been taught to be slayers of bodies, but of passions.”

5. The same brother asked Abba Pastor: “If I fall into a small fault, my thought bites me, saying: ‘Why are you sinning?’” Abba Pastor replied: “At whatever hour a man sins and says, ‘I have sinned,’ he is immediately forgiven. I have often said that he has compassion on no one except one who is contrite in heart.”

The brother asked him again, saying: “My thoughts trouble me and do not allow me to attend to my own sins; rather, they compel me to look at the offenses of my brother.”

Abba Pastor told him about Abba Theodore, who sat in his cell weeping for himself while his disciple sat in another cell. The old man’s disciple came to him, found him weeping, and said: “Father, why are you crying?” The old man replied: “My sins.” The disciple said to him: “You have no sins, Father.” The old man replied: “Truly, my son, if I were permitted to weep for my sins, I would not see those of others. Yet it would not even be enough for me to weep for my own sins if three or four others were weeping with me. He who sees himself is a man; but to judge others belongs to God alone.”

“We have abandoned the bright and straight road—that is, that a man should weep for himself and be content with his own sins—and we walk a thorny and dark road, seeing only the offenses of our neighbor and not our own. A monk who repays evil with evil, mocks, and is angry is not a monk.”

6. A brother asked an old man: “Why do the faces of some of the Fathers who labor bloom, while those of others bloom less?” He replied: “All who labor and ask forgiveness for their sins, before the grace that sustains their labor comes to them, are not flourishing but laboring. But those to whom grace draws near after they have first labored blossom through the endurance of Jesus. For a face blooms when the heart rejoices.

“The mind is clear and clean, shining like the sun. When there are no clouds, it shines brightly and clearly; when clouds cover it, it grows dark. So also the soul, as long as passions possess it, is darkened. But when it has been cleansed by the grace of God, it becomes as it is written: ‘Great is his glory in your salvation’ (Psalm 20).”

7. When the brother of the blessed Apollo came to him in the middle of the night, asking him to leave his monastery for a little while to help lift an ox that had fallen into the mud of a marsh, he complained tearfully that he could not pull it out alone. Abba Apollo, whom he earnestly entreated, said to him: “Why did you not ask our younger brother, whom you passed and found nearer than me?”

The other, forgetting that his brother had long ago died and been buried, and judging him, because of excessive abstinence, constant anxiety, and prolonged solitude, to be almost out of his mind, replied: “How could I call him from the grave, since he died fifteen years ago?”

Abba Apollo replied: “Do you not know that I too died to this world twenty years ago? I can no longer offer any assistance from the grave of this cell concerning anything that belongs to the condition of the present life. Christ has seized me so completely from my resolve to renounce the world that he does not permit me to relax even a little in order to pull out your ox, so that he would not grant even the briefest interval to the disciple who followed him for the burial of his father?”

[Col. 0380A]

8. Abba Antony prophesied concerning Abba Ammona, saying: “You will make progress in the fear of God.” He led him out of his cell to a stone and said to him: “Insult this stone and strike it.” He did so. Abba Antony said: “You must complete this measure also.”

When he had become a bishop, they brought him a pregnant virgin and said to him: “This man has done this evil; punish him.” He blessed her womb and ordered six pairs of linen cloths to be given to her, saying: “In case her labor comes upon her and either she or the child dies, she may at least have burial cloths.”

The accusers said to him: “What have you done? Punish him.” The bishop replied: “You see, brothers, that she is near death; what am I to do? The pain and shame she bears are sufficient.” And he dismissed her, not daring to condemn her.

9. A certain old man said to another old man who possessed charity and received both many monks and secular people: “A lamp gives light to many, but it burns its own snout” (Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 2).

10. A certain old man said: “If you hear an evil word about a brother, or that he is doing something wrong, reply by saying: ‘Am I his judge? He is today; I am tomorrow.’ His weak deeds are known to you, and you investigate them; why do you not know his strong and useful deeds? I have already died in my sins; my sins are enough for me.”

11. Again, a certain old man said to a brother: “My son, it is not fitting for a monk to inquire what this or that person is doing, or how someone is drawn away from prayer into slander and empty talk, which will profit nothing. Therefore nothing is better than to remain silent and ask God that, where another falls, you may be kept from falling.”

12. A brother asked an old man: “Abba, my thought rises up against me, saying: ‘I am doing well.’” The old man replied: “He who does not see his sins will never be among the good. In order to see the sins of others, we neglect our own; therefore we are never occupied with what is good.

“Ten thousand thoughts cannot persuade a person who sees his own sins that he is doing well, for he knows what he sees. It is therefore necessary to labor greatly. Negligence and sloth blind us at the end of life.”

13. A certain brother asked the blessed Antony: “What is slander, and what is judging another?” He replied: “Slander is generally understood as every evil word that one would not dare to say in the presence of his brother. To judge is to say of someone: ‘That brother is a merchant, and greedy,’ and so forth. This is judging one’s neighbor. You have judged such acts; this is worse than slander.”

14. A certain brother asked an old man [Note: [Col. 0379] Paschasius, chapter 10, no. 2, names him Elijah; Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 10; Paschasius, chapter 7, no. 1, names him Sisoes; Rufinus, book III, no. 77], saying: “If I have grieved my brother, how shall I ask his forgiveness?” He replied: “From the depth of your heart, reconcile yourself to him with sorrow; and when God sees your purpose, he will satisfy him.”

The brother replied: “I have been injured by my brother, and I want to avenge myself.” The old man pleaded with him: “My son, leave vengeance to God; it is better.” But he said: “I will not desist unless I avenge myself upon him thoroughly.”

The old man said to him: “Since you have once determined this in your heart, let us at least pray.” Rising, the old man began to pray in these words: “God, we no longer need your judgment, nor are you any longer necessary to us to care for us, since we ourselves, as this brother says, both desire and are able to avenge ourselves.”

When that brother heard this, he fell at the old man’s feet and asked forgiveness, promising that he would never again quarrel with the one against whom he had been angry.

15. A certain old man was asked by a brother: “What is humility?” He replied: “If your brother sins against you, forgive him before he is reconciled to you. And in every reproach, do not reproach the person, but yourself, saying: ‘Because of my sins this has happened to me.’

“For if we remember the injuries inflicted upon us by human beings, we remove from ourselves the virtue of remembering God. But if we remember the evils inflicted upon us by demons, we shall be free from wounds.”

He sighed and said: “All the virtues have entered this one cell, and from these labors a person is constituted.” They asked him: “What virtue is this?” He replied: “That a man should reproach himself.”

16. A certain brother went to draw water from the river and, finding a woman washing clothes, sinned with her. After drawing water, he went to his cell. The demons assailed him through his thoughts and troubled him, saying: “Where are you going now? There is no salvation for you any longer. Why are you also destroying the world?”

The brother understood that they wanted to destroy him completely. Rising courageously in confidence, he said to his thoughts: “Where did you enter me from, evil thoughts, and why do you trouble me, wanting to destroy me completely? I have not sinned—and again I say, I have not sinned.”

Entering his cell, he restrained himself just as he had yesterday and the day before. God revealed to an old man living nearby that the brother, though he had fallen, had overthrown the devil in the very fall and had conquered.

The old man came to him and said: “How are you, brother?” He replied: “Well, Abba.” The old man said to him: “Have you not suffered sadness during these days?” The brother replied: “No.”

The old man said: “God has revealed to me that, though you fell, you overthrew the devil and conquered.” Then the brother related to him everything that had happened to him. The old man said to him: “Truly, brother, your discernment has crushed the enemy’s power.”

17. Abba Macarius said: “If you rebuke someone while moved to anger, you satisfy your own passion. You must not destroy yourself in order to save another. Rescue your neighbor from sins without reproach, as far as you are able, for God does not cast away those who turn to him.

“Let no malicious word remain in your heart against him, so that you may be able to say: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’ These are the commands we must fulfill with our brothers. To forgive and to confirm our petition belongs to God.”

18. Some brothers reported concerning Abba Nytera [Pelagius, little book X, no. 36, names him Natyra], who had been a disciple of Abba Silvanus. When he lived in his cell on Mount Sinai, he practiced moderate abstinence according to the needs of the body. But when he was ordained bishop at Faran, he restrained himself excessively through harsher abstinence, and devoted himself more intensely to vigils and more attentively to prayers.

When his disciple saw this, he said to him: “What is this, lord? When we lived in the desert, you did not labor so much in abstinence.”

The blessed man replied: “Consider, brother, that there we had the desert, a solitary life, and poverty. Now, having left the desert, we live among secular people, and many diverse occasions arise for us. Therefore I fear that, at the end of my life, we may offend God on some occasion.

“For if the holy Apostle Paul, who had Christ speaking in him and possessed such great powers of soul that, while still in the body, he ascended even to the third heaven, nevertheless said: ‘I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be found rejected’ (1 Corinthians 9), what ought we humble and sinful people to do?”

19. Once, while Abba Sisoes was sitting in his cell, a brother was near him. Suddenly he sighed, but did not realize that the brother was close to him, for he was in an ecstasy of mind. Then, imposing a penance upon himself, he said: “Forgive me, brother, for I have not yet become a monk; I sighed in your presence.”

[Col. 0381]

## SENTENCES OF THE EGYPTIAN FATHERS, BY AN UNKNOWN GREEK AUTHOR, TRANSLATED BY MARTIN, BISHOP OF DUMIO

[Note: [Col. 0400B] Martin.] He was abbot of Dumio and bishop of Braga. See *Prolegomena* 25.]

[Note: [Col. 0381D] Some of these also occur above in other books.]

(C)

[Col. 0381D] 1002

1. Abba John used to say to his disciples: “The Fathers, eating only bread and salt, became strong in the work of God by constraining themselves; therefore let us also constrain ourselves to bread and salt. For those who serve God must be straitened in these things, because the Lord himself said: ‘Narrow and confined is the way that leads to life’ (Matthew 7).”

2. A brother asked the same old man: “What do the fasts and vigils which we observe accomplish?” He replied: “They make the soul humble. For it is written: ‘See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins’ (Psalm 24). For if the soul labors in these things, God has mercy on it and pities it.”

3. Abba Poemen said: “Do not speak in your heart, or at all assent to their defilement in the soul, with the thought of fornication and with slanders of your neighbor. If you wish to meditate on these things in your heart, you will immediately experience their harm, because it is an incitement to destruction; rather, by prayer and good works bring evil to nothing, repel these things all the more, and you will have rest.”

[Col. 0383B]

4. A brother asked an old man: “What shall I do, Father, against the thoughts of the passions?” He replied: “Pray the Lord that the eyes of your soul may see the help which is from God, who surrounds and preserves a person.”

5. A certain brother going to market asked Abba Poemen: “How shall I sell my work?” The old man said to him: “Do not wish to sell it for more than it is worth; rather, if you are imposed upon, be friendly to the one who forcibly takes more from you, and sell in peace. For I myself, when I once went to market, never wished to gain more from the price of my work while my brother was burdened, having this hope: that my brother’s gain is a work bearing fruit.”

6. A certain brother came to Abba Agathon (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 8), saying: “Father, allow me to live with you.” Receiving him, he saw natron in his hand and said: “Where did you get the natron?” The brother replied: “I found it on the road as I was coming.” The old man said to him: “Did you put it there?” He replied: “No.” The old man said: “Then, if you did not put it there, how did you, coming to live with me, take what you had not put there, when God and his commandments are before our eyes, saying: ‘You shall not covet; you shall not steal’ (Deuteronomy 5)? Or do you not know that one who steals another’s property becomes a demon?” He immediately sent him away, saying: “Take it back to the place from which you took it, and live with me.”

[Col. 0383D]

7. A brother asked Abba Sisoes (Pelagius, little book X, no. 56, under the name Pastor; Paschasius, 36, no. 4): “My parents have left me an inheritance; what shall I do with it?” The old man replied: “What shall I tell you, brother? If I tell you, ‘Give it to the clergy in the church,’ they will feast upon it. If I tell you, ‘Give it to your relatives,’ you will have no reward. Therefore, if you wish to listen to me, give it to the needy, and you will be without anxiety.”

8. Abba Moses said (Pelagius, little book I, no. 14, under the name Pastor): “The renunciation of material things—that is, voluntary poverty—tribulation with patience, and discernment are the instruments of a monk. For it is written: ‘If these three men, Noah, Job, and Daniel, should be there, as I live, says the Lord, they alone shall be saved’ (Ezekiel 14). Noah represents voluntary poverty, Job tribulation and patience, Daniel discernment. Therefore, if the practices of these three holy men are found in any person, the Lord dwells in him with him, receives him, and drives from him every temptation and every tribulation brought by the enemy.”

[Col. 0384A]

9. The holy Fathers related (Pelagius, little book XVII, no. 20):

“Three brothers hired themselves to reap a field. After they had been hired and had begun to reap, one of them fell sick and departed to his cell. The other two brothers said to one another: ‘Our brother is ill; let us encourage ourselves a little and hope in his prayers, for we shall reap his share as well.’

“When they had reaped and received the fixed measure of wheat that was the wage for their hiring, [Note: [Col. 0400B] *Conductelae*. Thus the Toledo manuscript. The manuscript of Saint Florian has *conductilem*. In the later period various words were formed with that inflection. *Conductela* for *conductio* occurs more rarely.] they called that brother too, saying: ‘Come, take the wage of your hiring.’

“But he said: ‘What wage do I have, since I was unable to reap?’ They replied: ‘Through your prayers we completed both your work and ours; therefore receive your wage.’ But he would not receive anything from them. As they pressed him repeatedly and he did not consent, they went to a certain old man for judgment. [Note: [Col. 0400B] *Dijudicari*. Thus the Toledo manuscript; but the Florian manuscript has *dirimari*, ‘to be settled.’]

“The brother who had been sick said: ‘My lord abba, we three went to reap a hired field. But after one day I fell sick and departed to my cell, and now these men compel me to take pay for work which I did not perform.’

“The two brothers answered: ‘Hear, our lord Father: if all three of us had remained, perhaps we should have completed the work only with great labor. Now God helped us through our brother’s prayers, and we completed the whole field; yet he does not wish to take his wage.’

“Hearing this, the old man was greatly astonished. Having summoned his brothers, he said: ‘Come, brothers, and hear today a judgment of justice.’ He set forth every word of each side, 1003 and all were astonished at both: the one refusing to receive anything, the others forcibly urging their brother to accept his wage.

“Then, in the presence of all, he ordered the brother to receive his wage and dispose of it as he wished. But he went away sad and weeping.”

[Col. 0384D]

10. An old man said: “If you live with your neighbor, be like a stone column: if it is insulted, it does not grow angry; if it is honored, it is not exalted” (Paschasius, chapter 42, no. 2).

11. Abba Sisoes said: “Once, when I was with a brother in the market selling little baskets, I saw that anger was approaching me; I left our vessels and fled” (Paschasius, chapter 37, no. 1).

12. Abba John said: “Once, while I was going up the desert road of Scetis and weaving a plait, I heard a camel-driver speaking vain words; and lest I become angry, I left my plait and fled” (Paschasius, chapter 37, no. 2; Pelagius, book IV, no. 20).

13. The same old man, while he was at the cutting of the harvest, heard [Col. 0385A] a brother say angrily to his neighbor: “And do you speak?” He left the field and fled.

14. A brother asked Abba Poemen, saying: “What does the Lord’s saying mean: ‘No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friend’ (John 15)? How can this happen?” The old man replied: “If someone hears an evil word from his neighbor and, though he can return similar words to him, nevertheless struggles in his heart, bearing the burden of sorrow and forcing himself not to answer evil or grieve him in return, such a person lays down his life for his friend” (Rufinus, book III, no. 201; Pelagius, little book XVII, no. 10; Paschasius, chapter 37, no. 3).

15. Likewise Abba Macarius said: “If we remember the evils which we suffer from people, we lose the power of the remembrance of God; but if we recollect the evils which we suffer from demons, we shall be without disturbance” (Pelagius, little book X, no. 34; Paschasius, chapter 37, no. 4).

[Col. 0385B]

16. He also said: “It is a monk’s fault if, when offended or injured by a brother, he does not first meet him in love with a purified heart. For the Shunammite would not have deserved to receive Elisha in her house unless she had had no grievance against anyone. The Shunammite represented the soul, and Elisha the Holy Spirit; a soul which is not pure does not deserve to receive the Spirit of God. Therefore inveterate anger blinds the eyes of the heart and excludes the soul from prayer” (John, little book I, no. 7; Paschasius, chapter 37, no. 4).

17. The brothers asked Abba Poemen about a brother who fasted perfectly six days a week, but was very angry, and why he suffered this. The old man replied: “One who learns to fast for six days but does not conquer anger ought to devote more effort to a small labor.”

18. Abba Poemen had beside him in his cell a monk who had a dispute with another brother living outside their monastery. Abba Poemen said to him: “My neighboring brother, I do not wish you to have any contention with anyone outside our monastery.” But he did not listen. Abba Poemen rose, came to another great old man, and said: “My neighboring brother has a dispute with someone outside our monastery, and we have no rest.” The old man said to him: “Poemen, are you still alive? Go to your cell and put it in your heart that you have been in the grave for a year.”

[Col. 0385D]

19. Once, while Abba Poemen was sitting in his cell, the brothers quarrelled excessively with one another, and the old man said absolutely nothing to them. Abba Paphnutius came in, found them disputing, and said to him: “Why did you leave the brothers and not speak to them so that they would not quarrel?” Poemen replied: “They are brothers; they will be reconciled again.” Paphnutius said: “What is this? You see that, in quarrelling, they have almost come to bloodshed, and you say they will be reconciled again?” Poemen said: “Put it thus in your heart, brother: that I am not here.” Thus Abba Poemen was peaceful and silent in charitable dealings.

[Col. 0386A]

20. Heretics once came to Abba Poemen and began to speak slanderously of the archbishop of Alexandria; but the old man was silent. Calling his disciple, he said: “Set the table, make them eat, and then send them away in peace.”

21. A brother asked Abba Poemen: “How ought one to remain in a cell?” He replied: “To remain in a cell outwardly is to work with one’s hands, meditate on the word of God, be quiet, and eat only bread in solitude. But the hidden progress of one who remains there is always to restrain his self-reproaches. Wherever he goes, he should fulfill the canonical hours of prayer and not neglect private meditation; finally, he should maintain good conduct and withdraw from evil.”

22. A brother asked an old man (Pelagius, little book III, no. 22; Paschasius, chapter 21, no. 4): “My heart is hard and does not fear God. What shall I do that I may be able to fear God?” He replied: “I think that a person who always rebukes himself in his heart attains the fear of God.” The brother said: “What is it to rebuke oneself?” The old man replied: “To rebuke one’s soul in every matter, saying to it that it must stand before God; and again to say: ‘What do I want, to have any malice against another person?’ I think, therefore, that if he remains in these things, the fear of God will come into his soul.”

[Col. 0386B]

23. Abba Macarius said (Paschasius, chapter 38, no. 2): “If contempt becomes praise to a monk, poverty riches, and hunger a feast, he never dies. For it is impossible for one who believes rightly and worships God devoutly to fall into an unclean passion or the deception of demons.”

24. An old man said: “Whether you rise, walk, sit, or do anything else, if God is before your eyes, the enemy will be unable to terrify you in anything. Therefore, if this thought remains in a person, God’s power cleaves to him.”

25. A certain brother said to Abba Peter (Pelagius, little book XI, no. 26): “When I am in my cell, my soul is at peace; but when I go outside, if I hear a brother speaking certain words, I am disturbed.” The old man replied: “Your key opens another’s door.” The brother said: “What does this saying mean?” The old man replied: “Your questioning opens the door of that conversation, so that you hear what you do not wish to hear.” The brother said: “What then shall we do when a brother comes?
