What shall we say to him?” The old man replied: “The teaching of all is mourning. Where there is no mourning, [Col. 0386D] it cannot be kept.”

26. A brother asked Abba Sisoes (Paschasius, chapter 39, no. 1): “After how long ought a person to cut off passions from himself?” The old man replied: “At whatever hour a passion comes, cut it off, because the soul is frail; let it be armed before it is defiled.”

27. A certain brother asked Abba Agathon: “The passions do not depart from me.” The old man replied: “Their vessels are within you; give them the pledges of their requital, and they will flee from you.”

28. A certain brother came to an anchorite. When the latter had received him in charity, as the brother was leaving [Col. 0387A] 1004 he said to him: “Forgive me, abba, for disturbing you from your accustomed way.” The anchorite replied: “My custom, brother, is to refresh one who comes in peace and dismiss one who returns in charity.”

29. A brother asked an old man: “How is it that God promises the soul good things through the holy Scriptures, yet the soul does not wish to remain in them, but inclines toward transient and unclean things?” The old man replied: “Because it has not yet tasted the sweetness of heavenly things, so as to seek God with its whole heart; therefore it returns more quickly to unclean things.”

30. A brother asked an old man: “How does the soul delight in passions?” He replied: “The soul delights in passions, but the Spirit of God restrains it. Therefore we must weep and attend to what is unclean in us, asking God, who is powerful in all things, to cut off from us the evil seeds. Thus Mary, when she bent down into the tomb and wept, he immediately appeared to her; so it is also with the soul, if it loves tears.”

[Col. 0387B]

31. A brother asked an old man: “Tell me, abba, a word of salvation.” He replied: “Go, ask God to grant you mourning and humility, and always attend to your sins.”

32. They said of Abba Poemen that, when he was about to leave his cell to go to the assembly in church, he first sat for about an hour, examining his thoughts within himself, and then entered.

33. A brother asked an old man: “What shall I do about my sins?” He replied: “One who wishes to be freed from sins is freed from them by weeping; and one who wishes to build virtues within himself should build them by weeping. For Scripture itself is weeping. Indeed, our Fathers also said this to their disciples: ‘Weep.’ There is no other way to life but this.”

[Col. 0387C]

34. A brother asked an old man (Pelagius, little book III, no. 13, under the name Pastor): “What shall I do, Father?” He replied: “When Abraham entered the land of promise, he first acquired a tomb for himself, and through the tomb inherited the land.” The brother said: “What is the tomb?” He replied: “It is a place of weeping and mourning.”

35. Abba Moses said (Rufinus, book III, no. 202): “If deeds and prayer do not agree, a person labors in vain; for when someone prays for himself that his sins may be forgiven, let him take care not to commit them again. For when someone has abandoned the will to sin and walks steadfastly in the fear of God, the Lord will immediately receive him with joy” (John, little book IV, no. 4).

36. A brother asked an old man (Rufinus, book III, no. 203): “What should a person do in every temptation that comes upon him and in every thought sent by the enemy?” He replied: “He ought to weep before the goodness of God, that it may come to his aid and help him. For it is written: ‘The Lord is my helper, and I shall take vengeance on my enemies’ (Psalm 117).”

[Col. 0387D]

37. A brother asked an old man: “Suppose a man beats his servant for a fault he has committed. What then should the servant say to his master?” He replied: “If he is not a bad servant, he will say to his master, ‘I have sinned; have mercy on me,’ and say nothing else” (John, little book IV, no. 7, under the name Moses). “But when the servant himself recognizes his sin and confesses that he has sinned, the master forgives him.”

38. A brother asked an old man: “If there is persecution on account of the faith, where should one flee?” He replied: “Wherever you hear that the faithful are orthodox, go there.”

39. A brother asked Abba Poemen: “What shall I do, since thoughts disturb me as I sit in my cell?” (Rufinus, book III, no. 100; Pelagius, little book IX, no. 8; Paschasius, chapter 39, no. 2). He replied: “Despise no one, judge no one, speak evil of no one, and God will give you rest and establish your dwelling without disturbance. Guard your speech; attention to oneself and discernment are the soul’s guides. Therefore, if someone casts himself down before God, does not exalt himself by comparing himself with the great, does not establish his own will, but, sitting in his cell, keeps his rule, he is not disturbed, for these are instruments of the soul. Yet, above all these, preserve this whole virtue: do not establish your own will, and you will have rest.”

[Col. 0388B]

40. A brother asked an old man: “What shall I do, because thoughts trouble me?” He replied: “Go and speak to them: ‘Tell me, what do I seek, or what business do I have with you?’ and you will have rest. Be despised, cast your will behind you, have no anxiety, and the thoughts will flee from you.”

41. A brother asked an old man: “Why is it that sometimes, while I chant psalms, I hasten to reach the end more quickly?” He replied: “How, then, will a person appear to love God unless there is some submission of the demon, and then we compel ourselves by force, being held by love and fear of God?”

[Col. 0388C]

42. He also said: “Flies do not approach boiling pots, but settle upon lukewarm ones. So demons flee a monk kindled by the fire of the divine Spirit, but mock one who is lukewarm” (Rufinus, book III, no. 104; Paschasius, chapter 3, no. 3).

He also said: “If adversaries persecute you, flee the first time, flee the second time; the third time be a sword against them, go out against them, and cut them down.”

43. A certain brother came to Abba Poemen in the days of Lent (Pelagius, little book 13, no. 5), and, after consulting him about his thoughts, said to the old man: “I hesitated to come here during these days; for I said, ‘Perhaps you would be shut in during the days of Lent.’” The old man replied: “We have not learned to shut a wooden door, but rather the door of the tongue.”

[Col. 0388D]

44. Some brothers from Scetis once came to John, a monk sitting in silence and working. When they greeted him, he turned to the other side and began to work. The brothers said to him: “John, who gave you the monastic habit, and why did he not teach you to receive brothers and say to them, ‘Pray,’ or, ‘Sit down’?” John said to them: “A sinful man has no leisure.” To this Abba Theodore said: “You speak truly: a person who is in supplication and repentance, God will not require this observance of him.”

45. A brother asked Abba Poemen: “Father, teach me what I should do.” He replied: “It is written: ‘For I shall declare my iniquity, and I shall be anxious concerning my sin’ (Psalm 50).”

[Col. 0389A]

46. A brother asked an old man (Paschasius, chapter 41, no. 1): “Father, what shall I do?” He replied: “Go, love to force yourself; draw your sword and go out to battle.” The brother said: “The thoughts do not permit me.” The old man replied: “It is written: ‘Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me’ (Psalm 49). Therefore call upon God, and he will deliver you.”

47. Abba Theodore and Abba Or were once putting mud on the roof of a cell (Pelagius, little book III, no. 19), and said to one another: “If God visits us now, what shall we do?” Then both, weeping, left the work unfinished and each withdrew to his own cell.

[Col. 0389B]

48. Abbot Silvanus, while sitting in his cell, fell into ecstasy and remained with his face cast down; after many hours, when he arose, he was weeping (Ruf., bk. III, no. 205; Pelagius, booklet III, no. 25). His disciple, standing nearby, said: “What is wrong, Father?” But he remained silent and wept. When the disciple kept pressing him to tell him why he was weeping, he was compelled to say: “I was carried away to judgment, my son; and I saw many wearing the monastic habit going away into punishments, and many laypeople going into the kingdom.”

49. Abbot Moses came to the well to draw water, and he saw brother Zacharias praying, with the Spirit of God resting upon him (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 17).

[Col. 0389C] 50. It was said of Abbot John that he never allowed an idle thought to rise in his heart, nor did he speak about the affairs of this world (Pelagius, bk. XI, no. 13). Therefore the brothers tested him, saying: “We give thanks to God, Father, for it has rained heavily, and the palm trees, having been watered, are producing shoots, from which the brothers may find leaves to work with.” The old man said to them: “So it is, brothers; and when the Spirit of God descends into the hearts of the saints, they are opened, and they produce fruits in the fear of God.”

51. A brother asked an old man, saying: “What does the Lord’s statement mean: ‘I was in prison, and you came to me’ (Matthew 25)?” He replied: “Although the Lord imputes this deed to those who are near him, nevertheless, since sitting in a cell is a prison, if someone sitting in a cell always has the remembrance of God, it is rightly said to him: ‘I was in prison, and you came to me.’”

52. A brother asked an old man, saying: “What shall I do, since thoughts trouble me?” Abbot Bessarion replied: “Be still, and do not measure yourself against the great; rather, be silent in your heart.”

53. A brother asked Abbot Antony, saying: “What does it mean for a person to consider himself as nothing?” He replied: “To consider oneself like irrational beasts, because they discern nothing, as it is written: ‘But I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you’ (Psalm 72).”

54. Abbot Pambo asked Abbot Antony, saying: “What shall I do while sitting in my cell?” He replied: “Do not trust in the merit of your righteousness, do not think about passing things, and keep both your tongue and your belly under control (Pelagius, booklet I, no. 2).”

55. A brother asked an old man, saying: “Do you think it is good to have a good reputation in the sight of people?” He replied: “These reputations have no virtue. Therefore do not desire to have a reputation with your brother, but flee it instead.”

56. A brother asked an old man, saying: “What is humility?” He replied: “If someone does good to the one who does him harm, that is perfect humility.” The brother said: “But what if someone cannot attain this measure, so as to do this?” He replied: “Let him flee and be still.”

57. A brother asked an old man, saying: “What is the progress of a monk?” The old man replied: “Humility. For to the extent that someone bows down in humility, to that extent he progresses in what is exalted.”

58. A brother asked an old man, saying: “How can the soul receive humility?” He replied: “If it always examines its own evils” (Paschasius, ch. 13, no. 10; Rufinus, bk. III, no. 171).

59. Abbot Poemen said with a groan (Paschasius, ch. 22, no. 2): “All the virtues have entered my cell except one virtue, and by its labor a person stands.” The brothers asked him what this particular virtue was. The old man replied: “That a person should always reproach himself.”

60. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “Come to my cell, if I am worthy to wash your feet.” But he refused. A second and a third time he said this to him, and he did not go. Finally he went to the old man’s cell, and, making a prostration before him [Note: [Col. 0440B] “And making a prostration before him.” A gloss was inserted in the Toledo Manuscript, namely, “throwing himself at his feet,” which is the correct explanation of what in Greek is βάλλειν μετάνοιαν. See the remarks above, on the Life of Saint Basil, ch. 11, no. 54, and the Onomasticon.], he asked him to come to his cell. He rose and came with him. Then he said to the old man: “Why, after being asked so many times beforehand, did you not come?” The old man replied: “When you spoke only with words, you did not satisfy my heart so that I would come; but when I saw in you the monastic work of humility, then I came to you gladly.”

61. The old man said: “What a person has not learned and himself has not practiced—how can he teach it to his neighbor? Therefore always be humble in learning.”

62. The old man said: “The virtue of a monk is to rebuke himself at all times.”

63. The old man said: “A person cannot see his thoughts from outside; but when they rise up within, if he is a warrior, he drives them out.”

64. The old man said: “The work of a monk is to see his thoughts from afar.”

65. The old man said: “A cause that is not foreseen does not allow us to progress toward better things.”

66. The old man said: “Do not measure yourself, but attach yourself to one who lives well.”

67. The old man said: “Whatever cause a person does not cut off from himself, he becomes entangled in it again.”

68. The old man said: “Every labor that comes upon a person is a victory for him.”

69. The old man said: “Every carnal pleasure is an abomination before God.”

70. The old man said: “If a thought concerning carnal necessity comes to you and touches you once, twice, and a third time, do not listen.”

71. The old man said: “If a person does not say in his heart, ‘God and I alone are in this world,’ he has no rest” (Pelagius, booklet XI, no. 5, under the name Allois).

72. The old man said: “To be a stranger is to be silent.”

73. The old man said: “One who presses upon human acquaintance and the belly has rest” [the printed reading is uncertain]. (Paschasius, ch. 32, no. 4).

74. The old man said: “A monk must have a brave heart in every circumstance, and he will be saved.”

75. The old man said: “If you see or hear anything, do not report it to your brother, because such things nourish the battle.”

76. The old man said: “Self-will, ease, and habit in these matters bring a person down.”

[Col. 0391B] 77. The old man said: “Charity, silence, and hidden meditation produce purity.”

78. The old man said: “Whatever is beyond measure belongs to demons.”

79. The old man said: “What need is there to build another person’s house and overthrow one’s own?”

80. The old man said: “For each person, between God and himself, his own will is a bronze wall and an obstacle placed before him. If therefore a person overcomes his own will, he can most truly say: ‘In my God I shall leap over a wall’ (Psalm 17).”

81. The old man said: “Leaving the straight and luminous way, we walk along a thorny and dark one; that is, leaving off mourning for ourselves and our sins, we are always looking upon the negligences of our neighbors.”

82. The old man said: “He is not a monk who slanders another; he is not a monk who returns evil for evil; he is not a monk who is angry; he is not a monk who is greedy, proud, avaricious, boastful, or talkative. Rather, the one who is truly a monk is humble and quiet, full of charity, always having the fear of God in his heart.”

83. The old man said: “See that you do not despise the brother standing before you; for you do not know whether the Spirit of God is in you or in him.”

84. The old man said: “Humility, chastity, and the fear of God are superior to all virtues.”

1006 85. The old man said: “It is the same thing for a monk whether he wishes to bring a legal action against one who has injured him by force as whether he were bringing it against the devil.”

86. The old man said: “From the lesser action to the greater one that a person performs, everything is placed in his vanity, whether in thoughts or in deeds.”

87. The old man said: “Humility is no expense, but it is seasoning in every expense.”

88. The old man said: “To humble oneself and to regard oneself as despised in one’s own eyes is a wall for a monk.”

89. The old man said: “Whoever wishes to build a house procures many necessities so that he may complete it; so too a monk must exercise great care in order to accomplish the works of God.”

[Col. 0392A] 90. The old man said: “Blessed is the one who endures labor with thanksgiving.”

91. The old man said: “There is no virtue stronger than despising no one.”

92. The old man said: “To compel oneself in everything: this is the way of God and the work of a monk.”

93. The old man said: “Whoever compels himself for God’s sake is like a confessor.”

94. The old man said: “A person who has death before his eyes every hour overcomes cowardice.”

95. The old man said: “Be free in speaking, not a slave.”

96. The old man said: “It is impossible for a person to progress in even one virtue without guarding the mouth; for the first virtue is guarding the mouth.”

[Col. 0392B] 97. The old man said: “I fear three things: when the soul is about to leave the body; when I am to come into the presence of God; and when sentence has been passed against me” (Pelagius, booklet III, no. 4, under the name Elias).

98. The old man said: “Wherever you sit, do not look toward those who have their consolation, but toward the needy person who has neither bread nor rest.”

99. The old man said: “If you have a passion and, leaving it aside, pray to the Lord for another matter, you will not be heard. Rather, first ask concerning your struggle; and when, by knocking, you have entered, then ask for something on behalf of others.”

100. The old man said: “There are these three fundamental matters: the fear of God, continual prayer, and doing good to one’s neighbor.”

101. The old man said: “Just as breath comes out of the nostrils, without which one does not live, so a person must always have within himself the fear of God and humility” (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 32, under the name Pastor; Paschasius, ch. 27, no. 2).

102. The old man said: “What is the use of beginning a craft if one does not learn to complete it? Therefore there is nothing that is begun and not completed.”

103. The old man said: “If a person does not satisfy your heart, do not entrust to him the conscience of your heart.”

104. The old man said: “Resolve with yourself never to do evil to anyone, but to keep a pure heart toward every person.”

105. A brother asked an old man, saying: “If I see some negligence among the brothers, do you command me to rebuke them?” He replied: “If they are your elders or your equals, admonish them humbly, without reproach, so that in this very matter you may be found humble.”

106. A brother asked an old man, saying: “Other brothers live with me, and they themselves want me to direct them. How do you command me to act?” He replied: “Do what you command, so that you may offer them not only instructions but also a model” (Paschasius, ch. 43, no. 1, under the name Serapion).

107. It was said of Abbot Macarius the Elder that just as God protects the whole world and bears the sins of human beings, so he was, as it were, a certain earthly god among the brothers, covering their faults and treating what he saw or heard as though he neither saw nor heard it.

108. Abbot Moses asked Abbot Silvanus [Col. 0393A] (Paschasius, ch. 43, no. 2), saying: “Can a person make a beginning every day?” He replied: “If he is a worker, he can make a beginning every day; for he must take a little from all the virtues. Therefore, rising early each day, make one beginning in every virtue and in every commandment of God: with great patience and long-suffering; with fear and love of God; with humility of soul and body; with much endurance; in tribulation and dwelling in the cell; in prayer and supplication, with groaning; with purity of heart and eyes; with guarding the tongue and speech; in renouncing material things and the desires of the flesh; in the struggle of the cross—that is, in crucifixion and poverty of spirit; in spiritual self-control and the contest of battle; in repentance and mourning; in simplicity of soul and silence; in fasting and nightly vigils; in the work of one’s hands, as the Apostle Paul teaches, saying: ‘Working with our own hands’; in hunger and thirst; in cold and nakedness; in labors and tribulations; in necessities, hardships, and persecutions; in pits, caves, and subterranean caverns (2 Corinthians 11). Be a doer of the word, and not merely a hearer; putting the talent to work so that it is doubled; possessing the wedding garment; established upon the firm rock and not upon sand (James 1). Let almsgiving and faith not abandon you, considering every day to be near to death, and, as though already shut in a tomb, caring nothing for this world (Rufinus, bk. III, no. 206). Let abstinence from food, humility, and mourning not depart from you, and [Col. 0393C] let the fear of God remain in you every hour. For it is written: ‘Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived in the womb, and we travailed and brought forth the spirit of salvation’ (Isaiah 26). Examine these things, and whatever other virtue there may be among them, so that you do not measure yourself against the great, but consider yourself lower than every creature—that is, worse than any human being, however sinful. Possess discernment, judging yourself, and do not judge your neighbor; do not look upon the sins of others, but mourn your own sins, and do not concern yourself with anyone’s deeds. Be gentle in spirit and not angry. Think no evil in your heart against anyone, [Col. 0394A] nor harbor enmity in your heart, nor hatred against one who is causelessly hostile to you; do not become angry at his hostility, nor despise him in his need and tribulation, nor return evil for evil, but be peaceful with everyone; for this is the peace of God. Do not trust one who does evil, nor rejoice with one who does evil to his neighbor. Do not slander anyone, because God knows everything and sees each person. Do not believe the slanderer, nor rejoice in his evil speech. Do not hate anyone on account of his sin, because it is written: ‘Do not judge, and you will not be judged’ (Matthew 7); nor despise the sinner, but pray for him, that the Lord may grant him conversion with patience and have mercy on him, for the Lord is able. And if you hear that someone is committing wrongdoing, answer by saying: ‘Am I his judge? I am a sinful person, dead beneath my sins and mourning my own evils; a dead person has no reason to concern himself with another.’ Whoever thinks upon and pursues all these things, 1007 is a worker of all righteousness under the grace and power of our Lord.”

109. These are the seven sayings that Abbot Moses spoke to Abbot Poemen. If anyone, whether in a coenobium, in solitude, or in the world itself, observes them, he will be able to be saved.

1. First of all, as it is written, a person must love God with all his soul and with all his understanding (John, booklet IV, at the beginning, for several numbers).

2. A person must love his neighbor as himself.

3. A person must put himself to death with respect to every evil.

[Col. 0394C] 4. A person must not judge his brother in any matter.

5. A person must not do evil to another.

6. Before leaving the body, a person must cleanse himself from every defilement of flesh and spirit.

7. A person must always have a contrite and humbled heart. The one who can fulfill this is the person who always considers his own sins and not those of his neighbor, with the help of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0399]

ONOMASTICON OF MORE DIFFICULT THINGS AND WORDS THAT OCCUR IN THESE LIVES OF THE FATHERS

[Col. 0399] 1011 Remember, reader, that many matters have been explained in the notes, of which no mention is made here. For the present I touch only upon a few of the rarer items, which were treated briefly above but are now supported by fuller testimony. You will also find some things noted here of which no mention was made in the notes. Yet I do not now present together everything that I have collected concerning each item. Let these things suffice for now to illuminate certain more obscure matters and words.

[Col. 0399C] ABSIDA. The Life of Macarius the Roman, chapter 8: “And behold, before us we found a very large absida, inscribed around its circumference.” Thus the manuscripts consistently read.

Formerly it was disputed whether it should be called absis or absida. Paulinus, in his twelfth letter to Sulpicius Severus: “In which he likewise indicated that an absis had been made. But whether I ought rather to say absidam or absidem, you may decide; I confess that I do not know, because I do not remember having read this form of the word.” Isidore refers to this passage in Book XV of the Etymologies, chapter 8: “But whether we ought to say absidam or absidem, certain learned men consider this form of the word ambiguous. Both forms are used by authorities.”

Absis occurs in Saint Augustine, Letter 225, to Albina: “I was saying this to those whom I could, who had ascended to us into the absis, the more honored and distinguished men.” The Third Council of Carthage, canon 32: “But if the public and notorious crime of any penitent is known to the whole Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the absis.” This is also cited in Book V of the Capitularies, title 53, and in the Decree, cause 16, question 9. Aimoinus, Book IV, chapter 252: “The absis of the church.”

Augustine has absidam in Letter 203, to Maximinus, bishop of the Donatists: “The honor of this world passes away, ambition passes away. At Christ’s future judgment neither stepped absidae, nor veiled chairs, nor crowds of nuns rushing up and singing will be brought forward in defense.” Evodius, Book I, chapter 3, On the Miracles of Blessed Stephen: “When the relics had been placed in the location of the absida upon a veiled chair.” And Book II, chapter 1: “And ascending the steps of the absida by himself, he stood there, visible to all from a distance.” Isidore, Book XV of the Etymologies, chapter 8: “Absida, in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as ‘luminous,’ because, having received light, it shines through the arch.” Walafrid Strabo copies this in On Ecclesiastical Affairs, chapter 6: “Absida is called ‘luminous’ in Greek and Latin, because it admits received light through the arch.”

Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, Book I, chapter 63: “In the wall that was on the side of the oratory, he constructed an absida.” Thus the manuscript commonly reads; elsewhere it reads, “he constructed it in the absida.” The same author, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 96: “He was sitting before the glass absida in which the holy limbs of Albinus are enclosed.” Likewise, in his Book on the Lives of the Fathers, concerning Gregory, bishop of Langres, whose relics Bishop Tetricus wished to transfer: “He laid the foundations before the altar of the basilica, and, having raised it, built an absida with marvelous workmanship and vaulted it.” Thus the manuscript reads.

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, concerning the proceedings undertaken for the divorce of Theutberga, referring to the council: “And the sacred canons command that penitents, at the time when they seek penance, receive from the priest the imposition of hands and the hair shirt upon their heads, as is universally known, before the absida. Every public penitent ought to receive this from his own bishop, in whose diocese he is.” The Annals of the Franks, page 29: “In the absida of the church.” The old glosses: “Absida, the seat of bishops.” That the bishop’s seat was there is made clear by the passage of Augustine cited above, Letter 225, where he says immediately beforehand: “I had returned to our benches, leaving the crowd.”

That absidae were in a more elevated location, and therefore furnished with steps, is shown by the passages of Augustine and Evodius cited above. Leo of Marsica, Book I, chapter 19: “He established the altar in the middle of the absida of the basilica, to which one ascends by eight steps.”

I shall refrain from gathering more passages. I have added these so that the use of absida might become known in some fashion from them. Onuphrius Panvinius, in his explanation of certain ecclesiastical terms, understands by absida what the Italians call the tribune of churches: “Perhaps because it was formerly called a tribunal,” or at any rate because the tribunal was in the absis. Gregory of Tours, Book II of the Miracles, chapter 2: “Finally, after making his prayer, I raise the line of my eyes toward the tribunal, and I see written upon it verses of this kind:

‘This hall contains the twin heroes of Christ,

Julianus in head, Ferreolus in body.’”

When Hesychius explains ἀψίδας as καμάρας, in addition to the circle of a wheel, saying, “Ἀψίδες, the circles of wheels, the circumferences, or vaults,” he understands the thing of which we have been speaking. Thus camera in Gregory of Tours, Book I, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 47: “While the solemn rites of the Mass were being celebrated in honor of those martyrs, one panel fell from the camera.”

Paulinus of Nola, Letter 12: “That basilica, therefore, which has already been dedicated and celebrated in the name of the Lord Christ to our common patron Domnadius, and which was added to his four basilicas, with the relics of the apostles and martyrs consecrated beneath the altars within the trichora of the absis, is venerable not only for the honor of blessed Felix. Its absis, faced with marble on floor and walls, is illuminated by a camera adorned with mosaic.”

From what has been said, four uses of absida emerge: it may signify the curvature of a wheel; an arch upon which an inscription is made; a raised place where the bishop sits; or a chamber in which the relics of the saints are stored. The manuscript Glossary of Camberon expresses nearly the same thing: “Absida is called an exedra, that is, a sanctuary; or a little container, that is, a bier.” Likewise: “Absida is interpreted in Greek as ‘luminous’ in Latin, because, having received light, it shines through the arch.” You can see that this has been taken word for word from Isidore, cited above. Likewise: “Absida, a sphere or hemisphere.”

ABSPES. The Life of Onuphrius, chapter 10: “Many times I was abspes of life”—that is, in Greek, ἀπελπίζων, “despairing.”

[Col. 0402B] ACIES. Leontius, in the Life of Saint John the Almsgiver, chapter 21: “which had been collected by the Moors in their acies.” It might be doubtful whether the Greek had been φάλαγξ, which now means a battle line or multitude of an army, and now a balance. Certainly a steelyard is mentioned here, on which his deeds are said to have been weighed. Hence aginari and acinari, from the shaft of a balance.

Festus: “Agina is the opening into which the shaft of a balance is inserted, that is, the hole in which the balance turns. Hence aginatores are called those who are moved by small profit.” The manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “Aginator, a merchant; so called from agina. For agina is the name of the hole into which the shaft of a balance is inserted and in which the balance turns. Hence aginator is one who is moved by small profit.” Likewise: “Aginare, to explain, to stir, to drive away, derived from agina, which is the shaft of a balance; it is so called because by it the measure of weight is moved.” The Glosses of Isidore: “Agginantes, explaining.” And because g and c interchange their functions, hence in the Glosses of Isidore: “Acinari, to delay, to linger over a small matter.” The manuscript Glossary of Camberon has the same.

In another sense, the Glossary has: “Aginat, στρατεύεται”—“he serves in the army.” “Aginare, στρατεύειν”—“to serve in the army.” For I think that the agentes in rebus are meant, who were a branch of the military. Joseph Scaliger, in his notes on Festus, reads τρακτεύεται and τρακτεύειν, that is, “to conduct business.” Perhaps someone might conjecture that στραγγεύει and στραγγεύεται should be read. For from στράγξ, “a drop,” comes στραγγεύω, “I press out drop by drop,” and metaphorically, “I press” and “compel something to emerge as though through a narrow opening.”

ACUTI. Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 48: “Just as it is impossible for a ship to be built without acuti.” I do not know whether in Greek there was some noun derived from ὀξύς, “sharp,” which gave the translator occasion to render it acuti, “sharp objects.” Nevertheless, I think that by acuti are meant ἥλοι ἢ γόμφοι, “nails or pegs,” both of which are mentioned by Pollux, Book I, chapter 9, section 2, in connection with the joining of ships.

Isidore, Book XIX of the Etymologies, chapter 34: “Clavati, as though calceati, ‘shod,’ because they are fastened with small nails, that is, sharp points, like the nails of a shoe.” So perhaps from acuti, “sharp points,” the harrow, a farming implement, was called in Greek ὀξίνα. Hesychius: “Ὀξίνα, a certain agricultural tool of iron, furnished with pegs, drawn by oxen.” “Oxina, a farming implement consisting of iron pegs, which is pulled by oxen.” Another term, bisacuti, occurs below twice.

[Col. 0403A] ADVIVERE [Note: [Col. 0403] See above, column 208, what Rosweyde and I together noted concerning this verb. (EDITOR.)]. A sound word, often altered into adhuc vivere, “to live still.” Jerome, in the Life of Malchus, no. 3: “while his mother was still alive.” The same author, Book I Against Jovinianus, chapter 28: “Although it is a more certain inheritance, while you are alive, to use your substance well than to leave for uncertain uses what you acquired by your labor.” Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 57: “And especially those who were themselves present when they were still alive.” Gregory of Tours, Book IX: “While he is alive, let him possess it.”

The word is also known to the jurists: law 28, section “Testamento,” Digest, “De liberis et legatis”; law 30, Digest, “De adimendis legatis”; law 30, section “Testamento,” Digest, “De testamentis militum”; Visigothic Law, Book IV, title 2, law 13: “The father, while he lives, shall claim one half for himself, to be left to his sons after his death.” In the same collection, Book V, title 2, law 4: “Likewise, whatever she acquired through this customary use for possession, she shall freely use for her own expenses, without anyone’s disturbance, while she lives.” Likewise, Book XII, title 3, law 13: “They shall swear that they profess with sincere and unblemished heart what their profession contains, and that they will preserve themselves until they live no longer.”

AEGYPTUS. Egypt was formerly divided in various ways, whether one considers its provinces or its dioceses. See Philippus Berterius, Pithanon, Disputation I, chapter 4. Egypt inferior and Egypt superior frequently occur in authors. Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18, contrasts Upper Egypt with Alexandria. Speaking of the two Macarii, he says: “One of them was from Upper Egypt; the other was from the city of the Alexandrians”—Ὧν ὃ μὲν ἐκ τῆς ἄνω Αἰγύπτου ἦν· ὁ δὲ ἐκ τῆς Ἀλεξανδρέιων πόλεως.

The Thebaid and Egypt are generally distinguished from one another. Jerome, in the Life of Paul the First Hermit: “A savage storm devastated many places in Egypt and the Thebaid.” Egypt, when used absolutely, signifies either the whole region of Egypt, or includes the Thebaid as well, or refers to the region around Alexandria, which they call Lower Egypt; just as they call the Thebaid Upper Egypt.

Ptolemy, concerning the Delta and the rivers around the Delta in Lower Egypt: “The region around these rivers is commonly called ‘Lower’”—Καλεῖται δὲ κοινῶς ἡ περὶ τούτους τοὺς ποταμοὺς χώρα κάτω. And concerning the upper region, or Thebaid: “The regions still farther south than the Heptanomis are called the Thebaid and the Upper Lands”—Τὰ δὲ ἔτι μεσημβριώτερα τῶν Ἑπτανομίων καλεῖται Θηβαῒς, καὶ ἄνω τόποι.

The regions and dioceses of Egypt and the Thebaid can be gathered from the subscription of the Council of Nicaea and of other councils.

AETHER, neuter gender. The Life of Onuphrius, chapter 16: “The aether resounding with angelic songs.” Many authors of a later age used aether in this way. Ennodius, Book II, Letter 13: “Not so swiftly does a reed driven by sinews cleave the aether.” The same, Book VI, Letter 38: “I more readily believe that the courses of rivers could be turned in different directions, and that fish, abandoning the nourishment of the streams, could seek the empty aether.” The same author, in the Apologeticus, concerning the Synod: “They saw the aether struck only by arrows directed from them.” Marius Victor of Marseille, Book I:

“But what is it that the world was, that the stars and risings were,

and the aether and the glassy sea.”

Bede, in the Life of Cuthbert, chapter 9:

“Opening to believers the heavens, closed for long ages.”

Fortunatus, Book IX, poem 1:

“May the seasons favor you with the peaceful moderation of the air.”

Aldhelm, On the Eight Principal Vices:

“May I deserve to be led through the aether, with Christ reigning.”

Thus the manuscript reads aethra instead of aethera, where Canisius substituted aethram. The same author, On the Praise of Virginity, in the preface:

“Or the zones of the world that surround the lofty aether.”

The same, chapter 5, on John the Baptist:

“While the Ruler of Olympus speaks, the lofty aether thunders.”

The same, On the Praise of Virginity, chapter 37, on Saint Thecla:

“Although her parents sprinkled her with a shower of words,

just as drops fell from the storm-filled aether.”

The same work, chapter 23, on Saint Babylas:

“Triumphing through conquered death, she seeks the blue aether.”

AFFECTUS, that is, parents, children, and grandchildren, toward whom by nature we ought to have affection and love. Heraclides, chapter 54: “For when they were suffering so greatly from hunger at a certain time that they did not even spare their own relatives.” Apuleius, On Philosophy: “Nor is he distressed when deprived of his dearest relatives.” Marcus the Emperor: “For the present I do not want this published by you, lest it reach Papirius himself or his relatives.” Capitolinus, in Maximinius: “Therefore the soldiers were afraid, whose relatives were in Albano.” The same author, in the Gordians: “He loved his relatives above all, his son and grandson beyond ordinary measure, and his daughter and granddaughter with religious devotion.” The same, in Antoninus the Philosopher: “Antoninus was not greatly moved by Cassius’s revolt, nor did he rage against his relatives.” Vulcatius Gallicanus, in Avidius Cassius: “Yet Antoninus was not seriously angered when the rebellion became known, nor did he rage against his children or relatives.” Paulinus the Elder, to a soldier: “Therefore we must not prefer to God either relatives, homeland, honors, or riches.” Paulinus the Younger, in the Eucharisticus:

“... long since bereft of all loved ones,

my mother-in-law having died first, then my mother and wife.”

AGAPE. Pelagius, booklet XIII, no. 15: “so that they might receive an agape.” Here agape clearly means almsgiving, or some portion given out of charity to a needy person. This word occurs frequently in these books. Pelagius, booklet X, no. 46: “I sow my field and make an agape from it.” The same, booklet XV, no. 31: “Providing him with what was necessary so that he might make an agape for them.” Palladius, chapter 18: “And I am carrying bread, because it is the agape of your familiar brother; and when the Sabbath dawns tomorrow, offerings will be needed.” Heraclides, chapter 5: “Because your brother himself is going to make an agape.” Thus Cassian, Conference XXIV, chapter 12: “He awaits the agape of another’s labor.” He calls agape the assistance of another’s generosity and contrasts it with what someone has acquired by his own labor.

Tertullian, To the Martyrs, chapter 2: “Indeed, the flesh does not lose what is just through the care of the Church and the agape of the brothers.” Paul the Deacon, On the Deeds of the Lombards, Book I, chapter 26:

“He indicates that the agape meal is present, but the livid man stands in the way.”

The word is generally used for the solemn banquet formerly offered in churches or at the memorials of martyrs. See the Council of Gangra, canon 11; the Council of Laodicea, canons 27 and 28.

[Col. 0405A] AGENS IN REBUS. Heraclides, chapter 53: “He disturbed a certain young man who was an agens in rebus, and so forth.” In this passage Palladius, chapter 148, has in Greek μαγιστριανός, “a magistrianus.” He belonged to the Palatine offices. Ambrose, Letter 13, Book II, to his sister Marcellina: “All the Palatine offices, that is, the memorial officials, agentes in rebus, and attendants of various counts.” Nevertheless, in the provinces they also supervised the grain supplies and presided over public transport. They are also called Magistriani. See below.

ALMIRIDENSES. The Life of Epictetus and Astion, chapter 6: “They entered the territory of the Scythians and came to the city of the Almiridenses.” From this it follows that the city of the Almiridenses was in Scythia. But in which author is this city mentioned? I think that the city of the Almiridenses, or Halmiridenses, was named from the lake called Halmyris, which Pliny, Book IV, chapter 12, places in this region: “From the same channel, above Istropolis, a lake is formed, sixty-three miles in circumference, called Halmyris.” The Danube forms this lake, which Pinetus says in his edition of Pliny is commonly called Lac de Notre-Dame de Danubi, that is, “the lake of Our Lady of the Danube.” Perhaps it is the Salmorudes of Antoninus. Nicephorus, Book XII, chapter 29, after saying that Eunomius was transported to Halmyris by order of Theodosius, adds: “Halmyris is a place in European Moesia, situated on the Ister.” Without doubt the city was therefore called that of the Halmyridenses, and should be written accordingly.

From Pliny’s description, it should be located near Peuce, which is in Lower Moesia. Lower Moesia also bears the name Scythia; hence Tomi, the place of Ovid’s exile, is in Lower Moesia, and Ovid himself places it in Scythia. In the Notitia of the Empire you will find many places of Lower Moesia assigned to the Scythian prefecture.

AMMA. Pelagius, booklet XVIII, no. 19: “‘You are foolish women,’ he said, ‘for this Amma is both yours and mine. For that is what they call spiritual women among them.’” Palladius, chapter 42: “For she, being better than both you and me, is an Amma; for thus they call spiritual mothers”—Αὐτὴ γὰρ καὶ ὑμῶν καὶ ἐμοῦ ἀμείνων οὖσα Ἀμμᾶς ἐστιν, οὕτω γὰρ καλοῦσι τὰς πνευματικὰς μητέρας.

Thus in the same Palladius, chapter 37, Amma Piamun; chapter 137, Amma Talida; chapter 138, Amma Taor. The meanings found in Hesychius do not depart from this sense of Amma: “Amma, mother, nurse”—Ἀμμὰ, μήτηρ, τροφός. “Ammas, the nurse of Artemis, and the mother, and Rhea, and Demeter”—Ἀμμὰς, τροφὸς Ἀρτέμιδος, καὶ ἡ μήτηρ, καὶ ἡ Ῥέα, καὶ ἡ Δήμητηρ, that is, Ceres. Therefore, what an abbot was among monks, an Amma was among consecrated virgins.

ANTIQUARIUS. The old Lausiac History of Palladius, chapter 15: “For he wrote beautifully in a bookhand.” The Greek-Latin Lexicon has καλλιγράφος, “a scribe,” that is, an antiquarius. For antiquarii were those who prepared the codices of libraries or repaired manuscripts worn away by age, as the imperial Constitutions teach: Book II, at the beginning of the Theodosian Code, On the Study of the City of Rome, Book XIV. Augustine, On the Words of the Lord, sermon 44: “Just as one who sees letters in a beautifully written codex, but does not know how to read, praises the antiquarius’s hand, admiring the beauty of the characters.” The Latin-Greek Lexicon: “Antiquarius, ἀρχαιόγραφος, καλλιγράφος.” Cassiodorus, Book II of the Tripartite History, chapter 16: “You shall order fifty parchment codices, well made and suitable for use, to be written by skilled antiquarii who perfectly understand their craft.”

APHRODITOS. In the Life of Saint Hilarion, no. 30, Aphroditos refers to Aphrodite, which according to Stephanus is near Athribis and which is Aphroditopolis in Strabo, Book XVIII. It is clear that this passage refers to it from Hilarion’s journey and from the mountain of Saint Antony, toward which he was hastening.

## APOCRISIARIUS

In Moschus, chapter 88, there is mention of Thomas, apocrisiarius of a coenobium; and in chapter 88, of another apocrisiarius of Gennadius, patriarch of Constantinople. From this it may be inferred that apocrisiarii attended to the affairs of churches and coenobia. Isidore’s Glosses: “Apochrysiarius, a minister of the Roman Church.” The Cambridge Manuscript Glossary: “Apocrisiarius, secretary.” Papias the lexicographer: “Apochrysarius, treasurer or envoy.” Justinian, Novel 6: “Through those who conduct the affairs of the most holy churches, whom they call apocrisiarii” (Greek: διὰ τῶν τὰ πράγματα πραττόντων τῶν ἁγιωτάτων ἐκκλησιῶν, οὓς ἀποκρισιαρίους καλοῦσιν). The term occurs frequently in writers of the later period. An apocrisiarius is evidently ὁ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀποκριμάτων, “the one responsible for replies,” from *a responsis*. In George, patriarch of Alexandria, in the *Life of Saint Chrysostom*, the word is ἀποκρισιάριος; Godefridus Tilmannus translates it as “secretary.” On this office, see Hincmar, letter 3, chapter 13.

## AQUA ASPERGI

The *Life of Hilarion*, no. 20: “He ordered an earthen cup to be filled with water, etc.; he sprinkled the horses.” [Col. 0406C] See the passage there.

Sosipater Charisius, *Institutes of Grammar*, book I, under “Defective [Words],” says: “It has been asked whether one should say *ad aequas* or *ad aquas*. Those who say *ad aquas* explain that religious water was customarily brought from the grove of the Camenae for the purpose of purification. But *ad aequas* is better, because formerly herds of horses were led into the Circus, where they were matched in speed by the people.”

Philippus Rubenius, *Electorum*, book II, chapter 18, prefers the reading *ad aquas*, and interprets it accordingly in the passage of Ulpian, *On Those Who Are Branded with Infamy*, book IV: “Neither charioteers nor those who sprinkle water on horses.” He understands this not as ordinary sprinkling or as water used to refresh horses, as Alciatus does, *Parergon*, book VI, chapter 3, but as a particular solemn act associated with religion, indeed with superstition. For it seems to have been customary that, since the Circensian games were sacred and dedicated to the honor of the gods, the horses about to compete were first ritually purified, and water fetched from a particular place was sprinkled over them.

He likewise thinks that Hilarion had this rite in mind and condemned this profane water by means of another water. Thus, perhaps, one should read on an ancient stone, among the offices of the Circus, *Sparsor* rather than *Spartor*, unless, he says, the word derives from *spartum* and refers to the office of whitening the Circus and its turning-posts. For in the Glosses it is written: “*Spartum*, λευκαία ἐν θεάτροις,” that is, “a white substance in theaters.”

## ARCHISTERIUM

The *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 53: “And when the judges, who because of the roughness of the road could not go to the inner archisterium, etc.” The Manuscript Glossary of Stewechius: “*Arcisterium*, monastery.” The Cambridge Manuscript Glossary: “*Archisterium*, monastery.” [Col. 0407A] “*Archisterium*, the principal station; for *sterion* means ‘station,’ and *archos*, ‘chief.’” Likewise: “*Sterion* in Greek, *statio* in Latin.” In the same place: “*Sterium*, the dwelling of a solitary.”

Antony’s inner archisterium was indeed his chief and principal dwelling on the mountain. The word is nevertheless used for any monastery. The *Life of Saint Walburgis*, book III: “And the cemetery adjoining the archisterium.” In the same work: “I was deemed worthy to behold the atrium of this saint’s archisterium.”

Paulus Langus, in the *Chronicle of Zeitz* (volume I of the *German Writers* edited by Pistorius), under the year 1469: “In a certain poem which I had composed in praise of the aforesaid archisterium of Bursfeld.” The same author, p. 886: “Under Trithemius’s obedience I served in the archisterium of Saint James near Würzburg.” Hence *archisterialis*. The *Life of Saint Willibald*: [Col. 0407B] “But now bound by the archisterial yoke, he would never deem it right to depart without the permission of his abbot.”

## ARSINOE

The *Life of Antony*, chapter 14: “Nor will I pass over in silence what happened in the town of the Arsinoites.” Since there are both Arsinoe and the Arsinoite nome in Egypt, this refers to Arsinoe, or the town of the Crocodiles, on the Nile, as is clear here from the surrounding circumstances, since Antony crosses to Arsinoe, on the Nile infested with crocodiles. There is another Arsinoe on the Gulf of Charandra,

## ARTABA

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 3: “He protested that he sold and bought everything by one *campana*, balance, *modius*, and *artaba.” Palladius, chapter 76: “Each received twelve artabas of grain annually, which are approximately forty of what we call *modii*.”

The commentator on Aristophanes, in the *Acharnians*, concerning the *artaba*: “The name *artaba* is Persian and Egyptian” (Greek: Περσικὸν δὲ καὶ Αἰγύπτιον τὸ ὄνομα).

Concerning the Egyptian artaba, Fannius writes:

> There is also, in the lands which the immigrant Nile floods,  
> the artaba, after three modii of which a third of a modius remains.  
> For a triple artaba is filled by ten modii.

Jerome, on Isaiah, chapter 5: “In place of the thirty modii which we have taken for the *corus*, called *homer* in Hebrew, the Septuagint translated six artabas” (Greek: ἀρτάβας ἕξ), “an Egyptian measure which amounts to twenty modii.”

Jerome’s calculation of the artaba agrees exactly with that cited above from Palladius. The same author, on Daniel, chapter 11: “So that Ptolemy Philadelphus received from Egypt each year fourteen thousand and eighty talents of silver, and one million five hundred thousand artabas of grain” [Col. 0407D] “(a measure containing three modii and a third of a modius).”

An unidentified Greek author, in a book on weights and measures: “The Egyptian artaba contains five modii; the Egyptian and Italian modius contains eight *choenices*” (Greek: Αἰγυπτία ἀρτάβη μέτρον ἔχει μοδίους εʹ· ὁ δὲ μόδιος ὁ Αἰγύπτιος καὶ ὁ Ἰταλικὸς ἔχει χοίνικας ηʹ).

Papias: “An artaba is a Syrian measure which makes three modii and a third.”

Concerning the artaba of the Persians and Medes, Hesychius says: “Artaba: a Median measure of grain, an Attic medimnus” (Greek: Ἀρτάβη μέτρον Μηδικὸν σίτου, Ἀττικὸς μέδιμνος).

Herodotus, *Clio*, or book I: “The artaba is a Persian measure, holding more than an Attic medimnus by three Attic choenices” (Greek: Ἡ δὲ ἀρτάβη, μέτρον ἐστὶ Περσικόν, χωρέον μεδίμνου Ἀττικοῦ πλέον χοίνιξι τρισὶ Ἀττικῇσι). “It is a Persian measure, larger than an Attic medimnus by three Attic choenices.”

[Col. 0408A] The artaba, however, was by no means a uniform measure. Eupolemus, quoted by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book IX, chapter 4, explaining Solomon’s letter, says: “The *corus* is six artabas” (Greek: Ὁ δὲ κόρος ἐστὶ ἀρταβῶν ἕξ). Consult our Villalpando, *Apparatus on Ezekiel*, part II, book III, chapter 11.

## ARURAE

Evagrius, translator of the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 2: “He had three hundred arurae, fertile and very good.” The translator retained the Greek word ἄρουραι, for which “palms” has commonly been substituted.

The same word occurs in this same *Life*, chapter 15: “And he immediately understood that, having despised small arurae and walls, or a small portion of gold, he ought not to boast as though he had abandoned great possessions.” For “small arurae,” the Greek has ὀλίγας ἀρούρας, which Haeschelius translated “small fields,” [Col. 0408B] while the Cologne edition has “small treasures.”

The division of land into arurae was peculiar to Egypt. Strabo, book XVII, on the division of Egypt:

> “The country initially had its division into prefectures, which they call nomes: the Thebaid into ten, the Delta into ten, and the intermediate region into sixteen; and, according to some, there were as many such prefectures as there were courts in the labyrinth, though these were fewer than thirty. Again, the nomes had subdivisions without fixed limits; for most were divided into toparchies, and these in turn into further divisions, the smallest portions being the arurae.”

The previous translator rendered *arurae* incorrectly here as “fields.”

Horapollo, book I, chapter 5: “When they depict the coming year, they depict a quarter of an arura. The arura is a measure of land comprising one hundred cubits” (Greek: Ἔτος τὸ ἐπιστάμενον γράφοντες, τέταρτον ἀρούρας γράφουσιν· ἔστι δὲ μέτρον γῆς ἡ ἄρουρα, πήχεων ἑκατόν). 

Herodotus, *Euterpe*, or book II:

> “They alone among the Egyptians, apart from the priests—those called Calasirians, or warriors—had this exceptional privilege: twelve choice arurae were allotted to each, free from taxation. The arura is one hundred Egyptian cubits in every direction. The Egyptian cubit happens to be equal to the Samian.”

The Greek reads: Γέρεα δέ σφι ἦν τάδε ἐξαιρημένα μούνοισι Αἰγυπτίων πάρεξ τῶν ἱρέων· ἄρουραι ἐξαίρετοι δώδεκα ἑκάστῳ ἀτελέες· ἡ δὲ ἄρουρα ἑκατὸν πήχεών ἐστι Αἰγυπτίων πάντη· ὁ δὲ Αἰγύπτιος πῆχυς τυγχάνει ἶσος ἐὼν τῷ Σαμίῳ.

Suidas: “*Arouraia mantis*, ‘the rustic prophetess,’ is used of the sluggish and inactive. It is a locust of very slow movement, green, called *mantis*, that is, ‘prophetess’; some people observe its movements and practice divination. The aroura has fifty feet” (Greek: Ἀρουραία μάντις, ἐπὶ τῶν νωθρῶν καὶ ἀπράκτων. Ἔστι δὲ ἀκρὶς δυσκίνητος, χλωρά, καλουμένη μάντις, ἧς τινες προσέχοντες ταῖς κινήσεσι μαντεύονται. Ὅτι ἡ ἄρουρα πόδας ἔχει νʹ).

Aemilius Portus did not understand the sense here, when he translated the final words as: “The countryside is said to have feet.” He candidly acknowledged this, adding “N.L.” He had read ἔχειν, whereas one should read ἔχει νʹ. Our Antwerp manuscript has this reading. The aroura is half a *plethrum*, and a plethrum contains one hundred feet in every direction, as Suidas likewise says.

The Latin authors also use *arura*, not for a definite portion of land but generally for land or a field. Velius Longus, *On Orthography*: “*Filix*—I believe it was so called because it is less fortunate for the aroura.” Hence *aruraeus*, meaning rustic or rural.

Marcellus Empiricus, *On Medicines*, p. 63: “Small lizards which live in the grain fields, which the Greeks call *aruraeae*.” Hence the proverb, “The rustic prophetess” (Μάντις ἀρουραία), as in the Suidas passage already cited.

## ASPITARE

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 51: “With one [man] thrusting from this side and another from the other.” So the manuscripts read; the printed editions have “standing by.” Isidore’s Glosses: “*Aspita*, a ruin.” The Cambridge Manuscript Glossary likewise has this. It should nevertheless be considered whether *veruina* ought to be read instead of *ruina*. Certainly *spitum* means a spit. The Cambridge Glossary: “*Assium*, a spit,” that is, *spitum*.

## ASSUESCO

That is, “I accustom” or “I habituate.” Jerome, in the preface to the *Life of Malchus*: “They accustom the soldier, arranged along the platforms, to stand firmly with a suspended step and a slipping foot.” So the manuscripts read, whereas the common editions have altered it to “they accustom [him].”

Dionysius Exiguus, *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 23: “But little by little he accustoms [them] to these things, first training [them] with lighter burdens.” So the manuscripts and the old edition read; the Cologne edition substitutes “he accustoms [him].”

Priscian, book VIII, chapter “On Common Verbs”: “*Assuesco*,” although intransitive, is nevertheless found with the meaning “to accustom.” Lucan, book V: “Add that you sufficiently accustom [someone],” that is, “you habituate [someone].”

## BABAE

See VAVAE.

## BAIA

This word occurs in the Greek text of Palladius, as John Meursius cites it in his Greek-Barbarian Glossary, though he did not understand it correctly. Palladius, chapter 61, has: Βαΐα ὀλίγα παρὰ τοῦ πρεσβυτέρου αἰτησάμενος, τοῖς ζώοις ζώνας εἰργάσατο. Gentianus Hervetus correctly translated this: “After asking the presbyter for a few palm branches, he made belts for the animals.” A miracle performed through one of the belts is related immediately afterward.

These were made from palm branches or leaves, which were called βάϊα. Hesychius in his Lexicon: Βάϊς, ῥάβδος φοίνικος καὶ βαΐων, “*Bais*: a palm branch; *baia* [plural], palm branches.”

Jerome, book II *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 9, quoting Chaeremon the Stoic concerning the life of the ancient Egyptian priests, says: “Their bed was woven from palm leaves, which they call *baia*.” Likewise, on Ezekiel, chapter 8, explaining the words, “And behold, they apply a branch to their noses,” he says: “There is no doubt that these are the branches of palm trees, which in Greek are called τὰ βάϊα, so that by this it signifies that they worship idols.”

Meursius was mistaken above in thinking that in this passage of Palladius βάϊα meant any gift generally so called. I see that our Gretzer also noted Meursius’s error, book II *On Benedictions*, chapter 41.

## BAPTISMUS NUDORUM

In former times, both men and women were accustomed to be anointed with the oil of the catechumens and baptized naked. John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 3: “A girl came from Persia to be baptized. She was so beautiful and of such great loveliness that the presbyter could not anoint her naked with the holy oil.” [Col. 0410A]

A dispute nevertheless arose among learned men as to whether those being baptized had been entirely naked or had merely removed their outer garment.

Joseph Vicecomes, in his *Ecclesiastical Observations on the Ancient Rites of Baptism*, book II, chapter 37, and book IV, chapters 10–13, attempts to establish that in former times catechumens were ordinarily anointed and baptized completely naked, wearing no garment or covering of any kind.

Some disagree—among them our John Viringus, in a manuscript treatise on the subject—and believe that the Church was always exceedingly careful to preserve modesty, and that it is not plausible that she would have exposed this sacrament to so obvious a danger of sacrilege.

For my part, after weighing the arguments of both sides, I would say that anyone wishing to exercise sound judgment should assert that in former times both naked and not-naked catechumens were anointed and immersed in baptism.

They were naked with respect to the mystery, by which it was signified that our former life had to be corrected and changed for the better. Those whose outer garment—the garment in which they customarily appeared in public—was removed were considered naked. It was removed entirely, because nothing of the old person could remain.

They were not naked because they retained either an undergarment or some linen loincloth for the sake of decency. Since this was retained, they were not entirely naked but, so to speak, naked; and they could be called naked because someone appearing in public in that condition would be considered to be going naked.

Thus Saul is said to have prophesied naked all day and all night with the prophets in 1 Samuel 19, that is, after laying aside his royal clothing; for the prophets themselves were not naked. Likewise David is said in 2 Samuel 6 to have danced naked before the ark, although at that time he was wearing a linen ephod, as the passage itself states.

Similarly, in John 21 Peter is called naked because he was wearing a shorter garment suited to fishing. Therefore, so that he would not present himself to Christ in that condition of nakedness, he girded himself with his tunic, ἐπενδύτῃ, that is, with a garment thrown over another.

There are also serious authorities—including our own Gaspar Sanctius—who understand Isaiah as naked and barefoot in this same sense in Isaiah 20.

Seneca supports this usage in book V *On Benefits*, chapter 13: “Some things, even if they are not true, have been included under the same term because of their similarity. Thus an unlettered person is not entirely ignorant but has not advanced to higher literature; so one who saw a person badly dressed and in rags says that he saw him naked.”

## BASTERNA

The *Life of Eugenia*, chapter 3: “And so, while the two of you were walking beside the basterna.” It is a kind of vehicle furnished with a softer bedding, commonly used by matrons.

Ammianus, book XIV: “With their heads covered, they run everywhere through the sides of the city in basternae.” Jerome, on Isaiah, chapter 66: “Where the Septuagint placed *umbracula*—which we may interpret as sleeping chambers or basternae—others, using a similar word, translated φορεῖα, which we interpret as vehicles of various kinds.”

Ennodius, epigram 129, has the title: “On the basterna of Bassus’s wife, Viola.”

The Nomical Glossary: “Lecticula, basterna, grabatum”—“a small litter, a basterna, a bed.”

The Cambridge Manuscript Glossary: [Col. 0411A] “Basternae are certain very fierce peoples, not far from Macedonia. Basternae are also called certain traveling vehicles of matrons, covered above and fitted with softer bedding, drawn by two horses.”

Papias: “A basterna is a traveling vehicle, furnished with soft bedding, as though from *vesterna*.”

Isidore’s Glosses: “A covered hand-carried basterna.” I think this means a covered litter carried by hand. Unless one reads *mannualis*, because it was drawn by *manni*, small horses.

Ovid, book II of the *Amores*, elegy 17:

> And the little car, as soon as the swift ponies seize it,  
> herself she shakes the reins through their flowing manes.

The “little cars” seem to be what in a later age were called *basternae*. Since they were drawn by *manni*, perhaps for this reason they were called *mannuale vehiculum*, “a horse-drawn vehicle.” [Col. 0411B] The Cambridge Manuscript Glossary likewise interprets *essedum* as *basterna*.

Jerome, letter 20, to Pammachius, on the death of Paulina: “There, fiery little horses, long-haired boys.” That is, the fiery *manni* were drawing the basterna and running rapidly.

In the same sources occurs: “*Bortanea*, covered hand-carried [vehicle],” for which the Cambridge Manuscript Glossary has “*Bortama*, a hand-carried coffin.” I do not know whether both forms have been corrupted from *basterna*. Our Cerda, chapter 141 of the *Sacred Adversaria*, no. 407, reads: “*Portanea*, a coffin, hand-carried,” meaning something carried by hand.

I would rather understand *tecta* as referring to the basterna because it was closed on every side; indeed, they were usually enclosed with translucent stone. Hence Juvenal, satire 4:

> She who is carried in a closed chamber with broad panes of translucent stone.

The old Glosses explain: “He means a closed litter.”

Ennodius, cited above:

> These covered vehicles, retaining a wandering beauty,  
> are sent by the lady with whatever valuables they possess.  
> For Viola’s golden metal flashes with radiant light,  
> and its owner scatters his rays everywhere.

The beauty and ornament of Viola shone through the translucent stone. Since the litters were enclosed, Jerome calls the basternae “cages” in letter 22 to Eustochium, *On the Protection of a Virgin*: “A procession of half-men precedes the cages of the basternae.” Thus in Isaiah 66 the Septuagint translated σκιάδια, that is, “umbrellas,” which, Jerome says there, “we may interpret as sleeping chambers or basternae.”

Isidore gives this etymology of the word in book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 12: “A basterna is a traveling vehicle, as though from *viae sterna*—‘the road’s bedding’; it is laid with soft bedding and carried by two animals.” Papias seems to have derived his explanation from this, although in his text *vesterna* appears for *viae sterna*.

From the passages of the authors cited above it appears that the basterna was sometimes carried by the hands of slaves and sometimes by animals. For Meursius’s interpretation of the animals in Isidore as slaves is unconvincing.

Among Greek legal writers, *basterna* has another meaning, being used for “curtains” and for “covered structures.” See Cujas, *Observations*, book XIII, chapter 30.

## BELLUAE

Where the translator of the *Life of Antony*, chapter 25, has *belluas*, the Greek text has ὑαίνας, “hyenas.” *Bellua* is sometimes used for a hyena. See what was said above, column 395, note 8, on chapter 6 of Heraclides, who wrote *BELUA*.

Clement, *Recognitions*, book VIII, chapter 7: “Certain other animals would alternately change the male into the female and alter their sex each year, such as hares and hyenas, which they call *belluae*.” The final words, “which they call *belluae*,” were added by Rufinus, the translator of Clement, as an explanatory gloss.

The Glosses: “Ὕαινα, ζῶον”—“a hyena, an animal.”

Elsewhere *bellua* refers to elephants, as in Curtius, book VII; Ammianus, book XXV; and Arnobius, book VII. It also refers to whales and sea monsters, in Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 12, and in the Glossary: “*Bellua*, κῆτος.” Likewise: “κητίς, *pistrix*, a sea monster, concerning an animal.” Also: “*bellua marina*, κῆτος,” “a sea animal, κῆτος.”

## BEMA OR BHMA

The *Life of Saint Basil*, chapter 11: “Into the holy tribunal,” in Greek, εἰς τὸ ἅγιον βῆμα. This certainly denotes a place in ancient churches situated beside the altar. To make this clearer, here is what Genebrardus—or rather Claudius Sanctesius—says about the church of the ancient Greeks in the *Liturgy*, as cited by our Gretzer, volume II *On the Cross*, in the notes to the account περὶ τῆς σταυροπροσκυνήσεως, “concerning the veneration of the Cross.”

The Greek church is divided into five parts.

The first part is called ἅγιον βῆμα, “the holy sanctuary,” which is reached by steps. There are two altars there: the larger in the middle, called θυσιαστήριον, “the sacrificial altar,” “the sacred table,” “the Holy of Holies,” “the place of God’s repose,” “the mercy seat,” “the workshop of the great sacrifice,” “the monument of Christ,” and “the tabernacle of his glory.” The smaller altar, where the priest prepares the sacred offerings, is called πρόθεσις, “presentation,” because the bread to be consecrated is first placed there.

The second part of the church is called ἱερατεῖον, “the choir,” the place assigned to the clergy and singers. It has a screen with two doors, and curtains are hung across both doors.

The third part is the ἄμβων, “the pulpit,” where the Gospels and Epistles are read and addresses are delivered to the people. Hence εὐχὴ ὀπισθάμβωνος, “the prayer behind the ambo” or “behind the pulpit.”

The fourth part is the ναός, “the temple” or “nave of the church,” where the people pray. In it men and women are separated by screens.

The fifth is the baptistery, near the πρόναος, “near the vestibule of the church,” where the penitents remain.

Thus far Claudius Sanctesius. See also what will be said below under the heading “THE GREEK TEMPLE,” from Gentianus Hervetus.

## BENEDICTIO

How highly this was once valued can be seen in the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 39, where he received the blessings of bishops and presbyters with bowed head.

The *Life of Mary of Egypt*, chapter 9: “But he”—Zosimas—“prostrated himself on the ground and asked to receive the blessing according to custom. She too prostrated herself, and both lay upon the ground, each asking the other for a blessing.”

Likewise Gregory of Nyssa, in his discourse on the *Life of Saint Macrina*: “When we had finished both praying and blessing, and they, first bowing their heads to receive the blessing, had departed honorably.”

Bede, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 26: “They hurried forward and rejoiced either to be signed by his hand, with bowed neck, or to be blessed by the mouth of that monk or cleric.”

The *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, under 1 January, describes a crowd of people: some wished to be the first to greet him on his return from exile, while others wished to place their heads beneath his hand as he blessed them.

Palladius, in the *Life of Chrysostom*: “Bow your heads to him in every respect, as to John.” Thus Chrysostom instructs widowed deaconesses to receive the blessing with bowed head, as though from a future bishop.

Children, too, were customarily brought to priests and holy men in order to receive a blessing. Theodoret, in this work, chapter 2, in the account of Julianus Saba, chapter 8, in that of Aphraates, and chapter 9, in that of Peter the Galatian hermit. The *Life of Epiphanius the Bishop*: “A crowd of every age and sex gathered, bringing children.”

The author of the *Opus Imperfectum* on Matthew 19: “This passage instructs all parents to bring their children continually to priests.”

The empress Eudoxia likewise presented Theodosius the Younger, newly born and clothed in purple, to the Fathers, as is related in the *Life of Saint Porphyrius*, 26 February. 1017 When Columbanus was received as a guest at the estate of Vulciacum, “the mother brought her infants to the man of God to receive his blessing.” His *Life*, 21 November. Columba the abbot also blessed the royal infant Domnall. His *Life* by Adamnan, book I.

Even infants still in the womb were offered for the blessing of holy men. Thus the empress Eudoxia offered the child she was carrying in her womb for the blessing of the Fathers, in the *Life of Porphyrius* already cited. Likewise Stephen the Younger, while still in the womb, was offered by his mother for the blessing of Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople.

In this matter Cajetan’s error must be avoided. He believed that through a similar blessing, in accordance with the parents’ vow, an unbaptized child could be saved even while still in the womb. Thus he says in his commentary on the Third Part of Saint Thomas, question 68, article 11:

> “At article eleven, it occurs to me that one should write, and consequently say—subject, however, to correction—that infants endangered in their mothers’ wombs can be saved, just as we said above, in article 2, concerning infants who cannot be baptized. I say that they can be saved through the sacrament of baptism, not actually received but received in the vow of the parents, together with some blessing of the offspring, or its offering to God with invocation of the Trinity.”

For his refutation, see Alphonsus de Castro, *Against Heresies*, book III, under “Baptism,” heresy 9.

For more on the various kinds of blessing, see the index of subjects, and more fully Gretzer’s work published on this matter.

## BEROEA

The *Life of Malchus*, no. 3. [Note: [Col. 0413] See what Rosweyde and we have noted above concerning this name, column 208. EDITOR.] It is a city of Syria, near which lies the desert of Chalcis.

There are two places called Beroea according to Stephanus of Byzantium, one in Macedonia and the other in Syria. The latter is our Beroea, which he says was also called Beroen.

[Col. 0413D] Concerning Macedonian Beroea, see Pliny, book IV, chapter 10. Concerning Syrian Beroea, the same author, book V, chapter 26: “Below the deserts of Palmyra lies the region of Stelendena, and already-mentioned Hierapolis and Beroea, and Chalcis.”

## BIRRUS

The *Life of Pelagia*, chapter 12: “He put on a three-thread tunic and the *birrus* of Saint Nonnus the bishop.”

Heraclides, chapter 51, concerning Athanasius the bishop: “He was clothed only in his own tunic and a *birrus*.” From this it is clear that the *birrus* was a garment of bishops, as is also clear from the *Acts of Saint Cyprian*: “He removed the lacerna-birrus which he had been wearing.”

Baronius, volume II, under the year of Christ 271, in the seventh year of Pope Dionysius and the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, makes the following observations on *birrus*:

[Col. 0414A]

> It is especially important to observe that the text does not simply say *birrus*, but *lacerna birrus*, although Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 14, distinguishes the *birrus* from the *lacerna*, while both were clerical garments. He attacks luxurious clerics in these words: “He assigns these tasks to beloved widows and familiar virgins: let this woman weave him a stiff *birrus*, that one a flowing *lacerna*.”
>
> First, as regards the *lacerna*, if one consults the pagan authors, one will find that it was a short garment used to ward off rain, as is evident from what Cicero says in the Second Philippic and Pliny in book XVIII, chapter 25.
>
> Moreover, Festus Pompeius, under the word *Lacerna*, shows that this type of garment was designed to cover the shoulders and arms. Discussing the *lacerna*, he says that it was shorter than the *capitium*. Varro, in book IV *On the Latin Language*, says that the *capitium* was a woman’s garment covering the breast, so called because it covers and encloses the breast and arms; women who went without it had their breasts and arms exposed.
>
> Gellius, book XIII, chapter 20, testifies that the *lacerna* was worn over the tunic, saying: “When, in my presence, he saw certain pupils of his who were senators dressed on a holiday in tunics and lacernae and wearing Gallic shoes, he said: ‘I would certainly rather have seen you in togas. It is shameful that you are at least belted and wearing cloaks.’”

As for the expression *lacerna birrus* in the *Acts*, the word *birrus* refers to the color. Festus, under *Birrus*, notes that among the ancients *birrus* designated a reddish color. Accordingly, the *lacerna* was red.

Alternatively, one might understand *lacerna birrus* to mean “silken,” since the ancients called silk βῆροι, as Zonaras and Theodore state in their interpretations of canon 12 of the Council of Gangra. See Cujas, on book IV of the Code, *On Silk Garments*, book XI.

Or it may be preferable to understand *lacerna birrus* as meaning the *birrus* itself made in the shape of a *lacerna*. In any case, *birrus* and *birrum* are found in both the masculine and neuter genders.

Whatever the case, the testimony of Saint Augustine establishes that clerics in Africa also customarily wore linen and a *birrus*, while bishops wore a more costly *birrus*. In the sermon by which he regulated the discipline of his clergy, sermon *On Various Matters* 50, he says:

> “No one should give a *birrus*, or a linen tunic, or anything else, except for common use; from the common fund I will take one for myself.”

A little later:

> “Suppose an expensive *birrus* is offered to me; perhaps it suits a bishop, although it does not suit Augustine”—that is, a poor man born of the poor.

Following Saint Augustine’s institution, regular clergy wear a linen tunic and, when they wish, especially on solemn days, also a *birrus* in Italy; in Spain they always wear one.

The same custom also prevailed in the Eastern Church, namely, that bishops wore a *birrus* over their tunic, as may be understood from what Palladius writes in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 51, about Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, saying that he withdrew wearing a tunic and a *birrus*.

Gregory of Tours also mentions Saint Britius, who placed burning coals in his *birrus* to demonstrate his innocence.

[Col. 0415A] Because of the shortness of this garment, Venantius Fortunatus calls the *birrus* itself a little cloak when he describes Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, visiting King Chlothar; of the king he says: “He clings to the little cloak of the holy man.”

As for the fact that the holy Council of Gangra, chapter 12, struck the Eustathian monks with an anathema because they went about wearing cloaks and condemned those who used *birri*, I do not agree with those who interpret *birrus* simply as an expensive garment. It is more likely that the council condemned those who, wrapped in a cloak flowing broadly in length and width, condemned those who wore the shorter garment known as a *birrus*.

Whether this garment was cheap or expensive could, as is certain from Augustine’s statement cited above, have depended on the choice of each person. The more expensive *birri* were those of Arras and Canusium, as Flavius Vopiscus testifies in his life of Carinus.

Since the same *Acts of the Passion of Cyprian* state that he folded up the lacerna-birrus and placed it on his knees, they show that it was very short and that the action required little effort. For they do not say that he did this with his tunic, but that he gave the tunic to the deacons.

From all this it now appears established that the ancient dress of bishops was as follows: after their undergarment they put on a linen garment, over it a loose tunic, and finally a lacerna-birrus covering only the shoulders and arms. In this form of dress we today see the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and those bishops who have been promoted to that dignity from religious orders.

The Roman pontiff wears a *birrus* without a tunic, over linen, but made of silk and red—or sometimes white, according to the season. That the *birrus* was more costly in proportion to rank has already been stated on Augustine’s authority. Thus far Baronius.

1018 In our Palladius the word *birrus* occurs two or three times, as in chapter 83: “They wore cloaks and *birri*.” The Greek has τριβωνοφόροι καὶ βυρροφόροι. Hervetus rendered this in Latin as “those who wore cloaks and caps.”

The Lyon edition had καὶ κιρροφόροι. In his notes, Meursius conjecturally corrects this to σκίρροφοροι. “Perhaps,” says our Fronto, “because the scholiast on Aristophanes explains σκίρρον as ‘the filthy part of cheeses,’ and in Eupolis says, ‘She goes about clothed in filthy garments.’ Thus here they would be called σκίρροφοροι, those dressed in filthy garments.”

But the emendation βυρροφόροι, drawn from the Royal Manuscript, is confirmed by the translator of Heraclides: “All together they ran up, all those whom we see clothed in cloaks and all those whom we see clothed in *birri*.” Moreover, he says that the leading men of that town had assembled; finally, he says that some philosophers gave him a single solid coin. It is therefore clear that not all the people there were poor and abject.

Likewise, chapter 136, concerning Saint Athanasius: “Having taken his *sticharion*, or tunic, and his *birrus*.” Hervetus translated: “Having taken his *sticharion* and a candle.” The Greek reads: λαβὼν ἑαυτοῦ τὸ στιχάριον καὶ τὸ βίρριον. Hervetus may have read κηρόν, “candle.”

More could be added about the *birrus*, but these remarks will suffice for now. As for the *birrus* of regular canons, I think the Cambridge Manuscript Glossary refers to this garment: “*Birrus*: a chasuble, a woolen cloak, a fringed mantle.” Regular canons in Belgium use this garment; even the combination of this garment alone with a linen tunic identifies them as following the institution of Saint Augustine, who clothed his clergy in linen and *birrus*, as is clear from his Sermon 50 *On Various Matters*.

## BISACUTUS

See what was said concerning the *Life of Antony*, chapter 25, and chapter 1 of the *Life of Fronto*.

The *Life of Antony*: “So that he might carry for himself a two-edged hoe together with grain.” I pointed out in my notes that this passage should be punctuated in that way.

Likewise, in the *Life of Fronto*, chapter 1: “And carrying with them into the desert small seeds of vegetables, and small two-edged hoes.”

The Cambridge Manuscript Glossary: “*Bisacuta*: a certain tool that cuts on both sides.”

## BRUCHIUM
