The *Life of Hilarion*, no. 33: “He turned aside to some brothers known to him in the Bruchium, not far from Alexandria.” A little later: “From the Bruchium he entered the Oasis through an impassable desert.”

Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, under the first year of Claudius, before Aurelian: “The Bruchium of Alexandria, which had been under siege for many years, was finally destroyed.”

Ammianus, book XX: “Alexandria lost the greater part of the district called Bruchion, a longstanding residence of distinguished men.”

Epiphanius, in his book *On Weights and Measures*, indicates that the place was notable for the library built by Philadelphus. The Museum was located there. Spartianus, in his *Life of Hadrian*: “At Alexandria, in the Museum, he proposed many questions to the professors.”

Scaliger, in his notes on Eusebius cited above, says without authority that Βρουχεῖον was formerly called before ῥακῶτις. Alexandria itself was called this, according to Stephanus.

Casaubon seeks its etymology in his notes on Spartianus’s *Hadrian*, as though it had once been called Πυρουχεῖον, a word preserved in full by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 32. There Christophorson, the translator, because he had read τοῦ πυροῦ χρείας οὔσης corruptly, translated it “when there was a great shortage of grain.”

In the *Life of Apollonius the Alexandrian Grammarian* it is called Προυχεῖον. It is well known that the letters β and π are interchanged. Thus for the Alexandrians Bruchium would have been what the Prytaneum was for the Athenians, namely πυροῦ ταμιεῖον, “a repository of grain.”

## BRUMOSUM

This is written in various ways: now *brumosum*, now *bromosum*, now *bramosum*. Rufinus, book III, no. 39: “And when the wintry water stank with its odor, he did not permit them to change it for other water.” In the appendix to Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, from the old translator: “For two years I could not endure the stench and *brumum* of my hands, with which I struck, as it were, his face.” Isidore’s Glosses: “*Brumosus*: old, resinous.” Also: “*Brumalia*: resinous rain.” Also: “*Bromosa*: filthy.” Turnebus, book XXVIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 5, cites from the very ancient *Onomasticon* of Peter Daniel: “*Bramosa*: filthy”; he adds that this is a word of the Greek language. Zeno, bishop of Verona, *On Exodus*, sermon 8: “Who does not understand, brothers, that this was not the Passover, but the filthy banquet of a bloodstained robber?” The same, sermon on Psalm XLIX: “If a bodily sacrifice is suitable for bodily gods, then certainly a spiritual sacrifice of God is also necessary: a spiritual one, which is brought forth not from a purse but from the heart, and which is procured not with filthy cattle but with the sweetest conduct.”

## BUCCELLATUM

Bread baked twice, or ξηρὸς ἄρτος, “dry bread,” which was used by hermits and soldiers because it lasts longer. Heraclides, chapter 6: “He put the broken and divided *buccellatum* into small flasks.” Ammianus, book XVII: “From the grain that was to be consumed in the dwellings, he prepared food for long-term use, *buccellatum*, as it is commonly called, and placed it on the shoulders of the willing soldiers.” Book VI of the Theodosian Code, *On the Distribution of Military Rations*: “In time of expedition our soldiers were accustomed to receive *buccellatum* and bread, wine also and vinegar, as well as bacon and mutton.” Spartianus, in *Pescennius Niger*: “He forbade the bakers to follow the expedition, ordering the soldiers and everyone else to be content with *buccellatum*.” Vulcatius, in *Avidius Cassius*: “Besides bacon, *buccellatum*, and vinegar, he forbade the soldier to carry anything on campaign.” Constantine, *On the Themes*: “Βούκελλος τὸ κρικελλοειδὲς ψωμίον καλεῖται”: “*Buccellus* is the name given to a circular piece of bread.” Mauritius, in the *Tactica*: “Χρὴ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ πολέμου, ἐν ταῖς σέλλαις ἐπιφέρεσθαι ἕκαστον στρατιώτην ὕδωρ καὶ Βουκελάτα”: “On a day of battle, each soldier must carry water and *buccellatum* with him on his saddle.”

From this campaign bread, or *buccellatum*, Paulinus and Therasia elegantly named the bread which they sent in place of a blessing, in their letter to Romanianus, letter 36, quoted by Augustine: “So that the service of fraternal kindness might not seem empty, from the *buccellatum* of the Christian campaign, in whose ranks we daily serve for the ration of frugality, we have sent you five loaves together, and likewise to our son Licentius.”

## BUCOLIA

In the *Life of Antony*, chapter 24, the Latin has *pastoralia*, while the Greek has Βουκολία. Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Hilarion*, chapter 36, retained the Greek term: “to those places which are called Bucolia.” Heliodorus: “Βουκολία σύμπας κέκληται πρὸς Αἰγυπτίων ὁ τόπος”: “The entire place is called Bucolia among the Egyptians”—namely, beside the lake mentioned earlier. This place was near Alexandria, beside the sea beneath the cliffs. The *Life of Saint Mark*, after Abdias, by an anonymous author: “Mark came again to Alexandria and found the brothers multiplied in the grace and faith of the Lord, and a church built by them in the place called Buculus, that is, ‘the place of herdsmen,’ beside the sea beneath the cliffs.” Hence the Bucolic soldiers mentioned by Capitolinus in *Marcus Antoninus*: “Throughout Egypt the Bucolic soldiers had committed many serious offenses.”

## BUDA

Pelagius, booklet X, no. 76: “And seeing an Egyptian dressed in soft garments, with a *buda* of papyrus and a skin spread beneath him.” Isidore’s Glosses: “*Buda*: a mat (*storia*).” Should this not be read *storea*? Thus, from the old Spanish form, with the addition or prefix of *hi*, they made *Hispania*. The manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Buda*: bedding straw made from *biblos*, that is, papyrus.” In Isidore’s Glosses I also find: “*Buda*: royal ornaments or camel ornaments.” Likewise: “*Bulla*: royal bedding.” As for what is found in the manuscript Glossary of Camberon, “*Buta, historia*,” I think it should be corrected to “*Buda, storea*.” Donatus, commenting on *Aeneid* II, on the verse “hidden in the sedge,” notes: “Most people say that the sedge is what is commonly called *buda*.” Thus in Papias: “*Buda*: a mat.” Perhaps this last form arose from *Buta*, the historian mentioned by Arnobius in book V: “As Butas writes in his *Causalia*.” Perhaps among the Teutons it means “bed,” from *buda*, because formerly they slept upon mats.

## BULLA AND BULLARE

The *Life of Basil*, chapter 10: “And he sealed that document with lead.” The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 51: “Can you not write, seal, and bring it to me?” And afterward: “He gives him his own sealed note.” The manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Bullae*: wax seals.” Likewise: “*Bullare*: to seal.” So also in later Greek, βούλλα, “a seal,” and βουλλεύειν, “to seal.” See Meursius’s *Greek-Barbarian Glossary*.

## CAMELAUCHIUM

The *Life of Mary, Abraham’s Niece*, chapter 5: “She also placed a long *camelauchium* upon her head, so that her face might be veiled.” And chapter 9: “Also removing the *camelauchium* from her head.” This word is often corrupted in manuscripts and early editions, where it is generally written *calemanchus* or *calamancus*. Hence in Isidore’s Glosses: “*Galeros*, *calamancos*.” Read *camelauchios*. Likewise in Bede, *On the Tabernacle*, book III, chapter 8: “Upon his head he wears a cap in the form of a small *calamacus*, or helmet, which extends over the top of the head.” Read *camelauchii*. In the later period consonants were frequently exchanged with one another or transposed. Thus in manuscripts it is almost always *corcodrillus* for *crocodilus*. But the derivation supports the correctness of καμελαύχιον, or καμαλαύκιον, as found in the *Etymologicum*: “Καυσία εἴρηται μὲν καμελαύκιον, παρὰ τὸ ἐλαύνειν τὸ καῦμα”: “The *causia* is called *camelaucium* because it wards off heat.” In the manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Camelaucus*: the pope’s garment”; and “*Calamaucus*: a cap similar to a tiara.” καμελαύχιον, or καμμελαύκιον, occurs several times in the *Suda*. In Hesychius, under the word “tiara,” one also finds καμελαύχιον, as likewise in the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Acharnians*.

## CAMISIA

Palladius, chapter 149: “When he had dressed her in her own garments—a tunic, a *camisia*, a cloak, and all the clothing of a man.” The Greek there has καμισίοις. The Glosses on the *Basilica*: “Καμίσιον: the tunic worn for labor.” Isidore, book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22: “We call them *camisiae* because we sleep in them, in *camae*, that is, in our beds.” That is, an undershirt or linen garment. The same author, in the same work, chapter 21: “The *poderis* is the priest’s linen tunic, fitted closely to the body and descending to the feet. This is commonly called a *camisia*.”

Regarding Palladius’s passage about the soldier, Jerome is particularly relevant, letter 128: “Soldiers customarily have linen garments, which they call *camisiae*, so fitted to their limbs and clinging to their bodies that they may be unencumbered for running or battle, throwing spears, holding a shield, wielding a sword, and doing whatever necessity may require.” Likewise Bede, *On the Tabernacle*: “For soldiers customarily have linen garments, which they call *camisiae*.”

The same word occurs frequently both for an ordinary *camisia* and for a linen garment especially elaborately decorated. Victor, *On the Vandal Persecution*, book I: “And, shamefully, from the altar cloths they made themselves *camisiae* and undergarments.” Bede in the *Martyrology*: “So that the impious Arians made themselves *camisiae* and undergarments from the very altar cloths.” Pope Boniface, book II of the *History of the English*, in Bede, chapter 10: “Moreover, we have sent you the blessing of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: namely, one *camisia* with gold ornament.” The *Life of Bishop Otto*: “He had *camisiae* provided for them with gold embroidery at the edge of the head opening, and with shoulder and arm seams.”

## CAMPANA

A bell ordinarily hung from herds or flocks of cattle. The *Life of Fronto*, chapter 8: “But he could not hear the sound of the bell because of the resounding noise of the hymns.” Various authors mention this object. Phaedrus, book II:

> And tossing a clear bell from his neck.

Paulinus, *Natale* 6 of Saint Felix:

> …when he saw the cattle’s  
> bare stalls, and no bell-rings sounding;  
> as they were accustomed, shaken from the cattle’s necks,  
> to rattle, or to strike the hollow bronze  
> with their gentle or sluggish tongues.

Endelechius the rhetor, *On the Deaths of Cattle*:

> I had placed beneath the wagons their strong bodies,  
> the bodies of cattle stretched out, with all the care I could;  
> and for them the rattling devices sounded  
> with the harmonious ringing of twin tones.

Sidonius, book II, letter 2: “Resounding through well-grazed pastures among herds bearing bells.”

Fortunatus, book II, *On Saint Medard*:

> One poor man, the more wicked of the two, snatches away the bell,  
> the one accustomed to guard the animals’ stall.

Book VII, title 2, section 11, of the Gothic Law, ancient recension: “If anyone steals a bell from a pack animal or an ox.” Title 4, section 5, of the Burgundian Law: “Whoever removes by theft the bell of a horse or ox.” The same is found in chapter 8, title 11, section 1, of the Bavarian Law.

There are various opinions about why bells were attached to animals. Some think it was done to drive away wild beasts; others, to discover the places in which the animals were grazing in the forests; others, so that they might grow fat more easily, because they believed that cattle were delighted by musical harmony; others, for ornament. From this *Life* it seems possible to infer that it was done so that camels, which carried necessities, might be heard from a distance in the desert by travelers, and so that the travelers could prepare bedding for them. See Jerome Magius, booklet *On Bells*, chapter 8.

See also John Stephen Durandus, book I of *On the Rites of the Church*, chapter 22, where he discusses sacred bells.

## CAMPANA STATERA

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 3: “On one *campana statera*.” Isidore, book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, says that it was so called from Campania, the region of Italy. From him Papias the lexicographer seems to have drawn his entry: “*Campana*: a weighing instrument. It does not, however, have two pans, but is a black [reading perhaps corrupt; read *virga*, ‘bar,’ from Isidore] marked with pounds and ounces. Each weight has its own fixed measure, designated by its proper names. It is called this because it was first discovered in Campania.”

Hence among later writers *campana* and Καμπανός were used absolutely for a steelyard. The Greek-Latin Glosses: “Καμπανός: a steelyard.” The Arabic-Latin Glosses: “*Campana*: a steelyard.” Hence καμπανίζειν, “to weigh,” in Nicetas, *Alexius Angelus*, book III, and in Myrepsus, *On Compounds*, chapter 21; and καμπανιστικόν, “the payment made to the public weighmaster,” in Phrantzes, book III, chapter 24 of his *Chronicle*. Likewise παρακαμπάνισμα, “an unjust weighing,” in Nicetas, book II, *Andronicus*. See Meursius above.

## CANCELLARIUS

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 3: “Sending the stewards, chancellors, and the others to whom the administration of the city had been entrusted.” And chapter 23: “He summons a monk through his chancellor.” It is therefore clear that chancellors were not merely palace officials, as is well known, but also ecclesiastical officials. Hincmar, letter 3, chapter 16: “The *apocrisiarius*, whom our people call the chaplain or guardian of the palace, governed the entire palace clergy under his care and direction. Associated with him was the chief chancellor, who was formerly called the secretary.”

## CANDIDATUS

The *Life of Hilarion*, no. 22: “A *candidatus* of the emperor Constantius.” The *candidati* constituted a definite military corps, generally the shield-bearers and protectors of the emperors. Ammianus, book XXV: “When Julian was amid the dangers of war, the *candidati*, whom terror had scattered, shouted from every side, so as to avoid the mass of the fugitives like the collapse of an ill-constructed roof.” Victor of Tunnuna, in his *Chronicle*: “His nephew Justinian, by name, served in the corps of the *candidati*.” They had two divisions, of senior and junior men. See the Sicilian *Fasti* and Cedrenus.

## CANTHELIUM

John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 107: “He carried a *canthelium* holding four amphorae, and brought water into the monastery.” The Greek is κανθήλια. It was a kind of pack-saddle for carrying water, which asses carry on both sides. For κανθήλια are pack-saddles.

## CARABUS

John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 76: “Behold, I am going up into a *carabus*.” Isidore, book XVIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “A *carabus* is a small boat made from wicker, which, covered with raw hide, provides a kind of vessel.” Papias the lexicographer: “A *carabus* is a little boat that travels on the Po, that is, a lighter. It is made of wicker and hide.” The manuscript Glossary of Camberon.

## CANONARCHOS

That is, the prefect of the canon, who used to strike a piece of wood in order to summon the brothers to the assembly. John Moschus, book XV of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 50: “When I rose one night to strike the signal—for this duty had been assigned to me as *canonarchos*, namely, to awaken the brothers for the assembly.” The Greek is: “Ὅτι ἐν μιᾷ νυκτὶ ἠγέρθην, ἐφ’ ᾧ κροῦσαι τὸ ξύλον (ἤμην γὰρ Κανόναρχος),” that is: “One night I rose in order to strike the wood—for I was *canonarchos*.” The same author, chapter 11: “Καὶ κρούσαντος Κανονάρχου τὸ ξύλον, ἐφ’ ᾧ πάντας τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς συναχθῆναι”: “When the prefect of the canon struck the wood, so that all the brothers might assemble.”

## CARACALLA

A type of garment. Palladius, chapter 117: “A strong woman dressed in a slave’s *caracalla*.” The Greek is παιδαρίου καρακαάλλιον, “a servant-boy’s *caracallion*.” Eucherius, *On Vestments*: “The *ephod* is a priestly garment, called an over-garment or shoulder-piece. It is like a *caracalla*, but without a hood.” The Greek-Latin Glossary: “Καρακκάλλιον: *caracalla*.” Spartianus, in *Caracalla the Emperor*: “He himself received the name Caracalla from the garment which he had given to the people, hanging down to the ankles.” Xiphilinus, in *Caracalla*: “He devised a special kind of garment in the form of a cloak (*paenula*, μανδύης).” Bede, *On the Deeds of the English*, book I, chapter 7: “Then Saint Alban, dressed in the clothing of his guest—for the man was a cleric—and of his master, that is, in the *caracalla* which he wore, presented himself to the soldiers.” Manuscript: “A *carabus* is a certain little boat.”

## CARICAE

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul, the First Hermit*, no. 6: “He was sustained each day by five *caricae*.” Likewise, in the *Life of Saint Hilarion*, no. 5: “Thus, with the juice of herbs and a few *caricae*, he sustained his failing soul after three or four days.” The *caricae* are interpreted as dried figs. Pliny certainly teaches that they belong to the genus of figs, book XIII, chapter 5: “Syria has, besides this, trees peculiar to itself. Among nuts, the pistachio is well known. They are said to be useful against snakebites, both as drink and food. Among figs there are *caricae*, and a smaller variety of the same kind, which they call *cottanae*.”

## CARTICA

Pelagius, book V, booklet X, no. 76: “And seeing an Egyptian dressed in soft garments, with a *buda* of papyrus and a skin spread beneath him, and a small *cartica* pillow beneath his head.” Is *cartica* linen? For what is found in my manuscript of the *Life of Onuphrius* reads: “I worked with the brothers at *charsicaria*”; while in the same matter here, book VI, in John, booklet III, no. 2, it reads: “and my work was the weaving of linen.” Linen is certainly suitable for a pillow. Therefore in the *Life of Onuphrius* one should read either *carticaria*, or in John, *charsica*. In the excerpts from the Greek-Latin Glossary, column 308: “*Carticula*: δεῖπνον,” “a meal.”

## CAUCUS

It is inferred from various passages that this was a kind of drinking vessel. The *Life of Abraham*, chapter 3: “He also had a very small *caucus*, from which he was accustomed to eat or drink.” The manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Caucus*: a wooden vessel for drinking.” Spartianus, in *Pescennius*: “He was so strict that, when he had seen certain soldiers drinking from a silver *caucus* during an expedition, he ordered all silver to be removed from military use, adding that they should use wooden vessels.” Trebellius Pollio, in *Claudius*, from a letter of Valerian: “Likewise, eleven pounds of *cauci*, cups, and *zemae*.” Marcellus Empiricus, *On Medicines*, chapter 25: “An earthworm is dug up and placed in a wooden *caucus*.” Jerome, book II *Against Jovinianus*, on Diogenes: “Once, holding a wooden *caucus* for drinking, he saw a boy drinking from his cupped hand, and is said to have thrown it to the ground, saying: ‘I did not know that nature had a cup.’” In Ennodius, epigram 25, the title is: “On someone’s *caucus* bearing Pasiphae and the Bull.” The same title occurs in epigram 29.

In most passages *cavea*, *cavum*, or *glaucus* has hitherto been printed incorrectly. Papias cites *caucus* as a kind of vessel, apparently from uncorrupted copies. It also occurs in letter 40 among the letters attributed to Boniface: “My devotion has sent to your Reverence a silver *caucus*, gilded inside, and two *repta*.” What *reptum* may be is questioned there by our Serarius and by Gretzer, book II *On Benedict*, chapter 28. The manuscript Glossary of Camberon offers some assistance: “*Renones* are coverings for the shoulders, shaggy with twisted hairs, which are commonly called *repti*, because the length of the hairs seems to creep.” It also occurs in Boniface, letter 77: “We have sent you small gifts, namely, one *reptem ruptilem*.”

## CHAMEUNIAE

That is, lying on the ground; in Greek χαμαιευνίαι or χαμευνίαι. The word is often used by Latin authors. The *Life of Abraham*, chapter 18: “He was never entirely wearied by lying on the ground and by bodily mortification.” The *Life of Mary, Abraham’s Niece*, chapter 9: “Where are the vigils? Where the *chameuniae*?” Papias: “*Cameuniae*: bed mats.” Likewise: “*Cameuniae*: vigils in winter.” He did not grasp the force of the word. Jerome, on Ezekiel XLI: “I think it is clear to the reader that during fasts, lying on the ground, and restraint in food, the things below are always narrower.” The same author, on Amos III: “And he will strike the winter house—those heretics who labor in restraint, fasts, *xerophagies*, and *chaumeuniae*; among them are Tatian and Manichaeus?”

## CHAEREUM

The *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 54: “At the first station of Alexandria, which is called Chaereum.” Perhaps the place was named after an Egyptian city, unless this station itself was the city. Stephanus, *On Cities*: “Χαιρέου, πόλις Αἰγυπτίου, κατ’ ἔλλειψιν τοῦ πόλις· τὸ ἐθνικὸν Χαιρεώτης, ὡς Νικεώτης”: “Chaereum, an Egyptian city,” with the word “city” understood; its ethnic name is *Chaereotes*, like *Nicaeotes*. He also mentions it in *The Island of Argaeus*, according to Procopius, book VI *On Buildings*. Justinian: “Chereaus,” a place in Egypt, which Ortelius thinks is Chercu in Antoninus, near Canopus.

## THE DESERT OF CHALCIS

Jerome’s habitation. The *Life of Malchus*, no. 3: “At last I reached the desert of Chalcis, which lies between Immae and Beroea, farther toward the south.” It is in Syria. Jerome, letter 43, to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius: “For after, Evagrius having sent [them], [things] had been brought to me in that part of the desert which forms a vast boundary between the Syrians and the Saracens…” The same author, letter 41, to Rufinus: “Syria presented itself to me like a most trustworthy harbor to a shipwrecked man.” The same, preface to Abdias: “When I and the dearest Heliodorus were striving to inhabit together the solitude of Syrian Chalcis.”

## CHINOBOSCIUM

*Lives of Pachomius*, chapters 5, 40, and 53. It is more correctly written in Latin *Chenoboscium*, perhaps because geese were pastured there. Nevertheless, Stephanus does not think that it derived its name from this, *On Cities*: “Χηνοβοσκία, πόλις Αἰγύπτου. Ἀλέξανδρος ἐν πρώτῳ Αἰγυπτιακῶν. Ἀντικρὺ δὲ τοῦ Διοπολίτου Χηνοβοσκίον, μηδὲν εἰς τὴν προσηγορίαν ἐμφέρουσα· νομὰς γὰρ χηνῶν οὐκ ἂν ἴδη τις οὔσας”: “Chenoboscia, a city of Egypt. Alexander, in the first book of his *Egyptian History*: ‘Opposite Diopolis is Chenoboscium, which contributes nothing to the explanation of its name; for no one could see that geese were ever pastured there.’”

## CHOREPISCOPUS

Heraclides, chapter 37: “He belonged to the monastery of a certain Timothy of Cappadocia, a *chorepiscopus*.” In Palladius, chapter 106. The manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Chorepiscopi* are called the vicars of bishops, who, established in villages and rural districts because of their concern for the poor, govern the churches entrusted to them, having permission to ordain as far as subdeacons.” For their office, see Baronius, volume III, under the year 357.

## CHYDAEAN WINE

In the appendix to Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, from the old translation, chapter 20, no. 3: “Take with you one small vessel of Chydaean wine.” I think it should be read there as *Chydaei* rather than *Chindii*, as I noted in the annotation. Pliny, book XIII, chapter 4, discussing palms and their dates: “For those among them which we dedicate to the honor of the gods, Judaea, a nation notorious for insulting the divinities, called *Chydaei*.” The same author, book XIV, chapter 16, discussing artificial wines: “First, the wine made from palms, which the Parthians, Indians, and the entire East use: the ripe dates which they call *chydaean* are soaked in a modius of water measured into three congii, and then pressed.”

The meaning of *Chydaei* may perhaps be illuminated by Exodus I:7: “The children of Israel grew, and, as though sprouting, multiplied.” The Septuagint has: “Οἱ δὲ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ ηὐξήθησαν, καὶ ἐπληθύνθησαν, καὶ χυδαῖοι ἐγένοντο”: “But the children of Israel grew, multiplied, and became *chydaioi*.” Arias Montanus translates: “But the children of Israel grew and multiplied, and became abundant.” The Roman edition has: “and they became spread abroad,” translating χυδαῖοι ἐγένοντο. Origen’s interpreter: “and they spread abroad in great multitude.”

Χυδαῖος often means “common,” and, from abundance, “of little value.” Therefore Theodoret, question 1, warns that it should not be understood in this passage as spoken insultingly, as some have interpreted it, but simply as signifying a numerous multitude. For, he says, they grew in such a way that they spread throughout the whole land. Aquila has ἐξήρποσαν, Symmachus ἐξῆρψαν, “they crept forth.” Eustathius, on Homer: “Χυδαῖοι: formerly those who had multiplied were called this; now those who are worthless.”

## CILICIAN AMPHORA

Palladius, chapters 19 and 20: “After he had drunk the water of one Cilician amphora.” Μετὰ τὸ πινεῖν ἀμφορέα Κιλικίσιον ὕδατος. I suspect that it was a very large amphora, for the preceding passage says: “After he had eaten bread of three *modii*, and an amphora,” etc., so that there may be some proportion between three *modii* and one Cilician amphora. The same author, chapter 33: “When, therefore, he had carried many earthen vessels”; the Greek adds “Cilician”: Βαστάσας οὖν ἐκεῖνος κεράμια κιλικίσια. Heraclides, chapter 6: “He compelled him to drink a flaskful from one amphora.” Here one manuscript has “the water of a Cilician flask.”

In Athenaeus, book III, Cilician loaves are large loaves, which Eustathius also mentions in his commentary on Homer. Isidore, book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 6, mentions a Sicilian vessel. *Lagena* and *situla* are Greek names, altered in part so that they might become Latin. For the Greeks say λάγηνος, while we say *lagena*; they say *sicule*, while we say *situla*. Papias the lexicographer: “*Sicula*: a vessel suitable for wine or water, derived from the Greek, namely *sicia*.” And lest you suspect a defect in the spelling here, and think that *situla* should be read, he places *situlam* elsewhere with a different ordering of the letters.

## CINERENTE AND CACCABATE

Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 29: “They treated you well with *cinerente* and *caccabate*.” He is describing himself as sallow and black. In the same work, no. 25, concerning Macarius falsely accused of fornication: “And they hung *caccabatae* pots and the handles of vessels around my neck.” Paulinus, letter 12: “When you see the buildings, which still shine spotless through the grace of your work, darkened by the follies of my ignorance and—as a word worthy of my verses puts it—turned into *caccabata*, you will look upon them amid the confusion caused by many laughing or feeling nauseated.” We have discussed this word more fully elsewhere.

## CLINICUS

The *Life of Fabiola*, chapter 5, and the *Life of Paula*, chapter 4. Here it means a sick person who lies confined to bed and cannot move himself. Pliny, book XXV, chapter 5: “It cures, as we have said, epileptic diseases, vertigo, melancholic, stomachic, spastic, and *clinic* conditions.” Thus Cyprian calls the paralytic in John V a *clinicus*, letter 76: “For I, who know the *clinicus* from the Gospel…”

There were also *clinici*, physicians who sat beside the beds of the sick; Martial alludes to them in book I, epigram 31. For this class of physicians, see our Raderus.

In Cyprian’s time, those who were baptized in bed when near death were also called *clinici*. Cyprian, letter 76: “Moreover, because some call those who have obtained Christ’s grace through saving water and legitimate faith not Christians but *clinici*…”

## COLOBIUM

The *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 14: “The *lebiton* was a linen garment, like a *colobium*.” Rufinus, here, book II, chapter 3: “They used to dress in *colobia*, as though in linen sacks.” The manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Colobium*: a garment resembling a hooded cloak, except that it lacks a hood.” Papias the lexicographer: “*Colobium* is the name of a type of garment because it is long and without sleeves. The ancients used it. But because the nakedness of the arms was blamed, the use of *colobia* was changed into *dalmatics*.”

I think *colobium* was named from κολοβός, “mutilated,” because it was, so to speak, mutilated by the absence of sleeves. Nicetas, *Orthodox Treasury*, book I, chapter 39, discussing the Jewish scribes: “Dressed in dalmatics, which are now called *colobia* and are edged with purple, they displayed their phylacteries—small strips of parchment on which the Law was written. They carried them, decorated with costly bands and embroidered with gold, like teachers of the Jews.”

A sign woven from purple was also placed on the *colobia* of monks. See Dorotheus, *Teaching* 1. One also finds a purple *colobium* in Anastasius, under Eutychianus.

## CONTERNATIO

The *Life of Saint Paula*, no. 11 [Note: Col. 0423. See *Patrologia*, volume XXII, column 887 at the beginning, where, through a typographical error, *consternantem* is printed. Editor.]: “Segor, a heifer *conternans*,” that is, three years old, in Isaiah XV. Papias: “*Conternans*: a heifer entering its third year.” The Vocabulary of Gerard of Scheuren: “*CONTERNANS*, that is in its third year.” See this reading carefully explained in our Gabriel Alvarez’s commentary on Isaiah.

The word is rarer in this meaning. For a long time *consternantem* was read there. Both readings occur in the manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Conternare* or *contrenare* means ‘to tremble.’ Hence the prophet calls Segor a *conternans* heifer: a heifer because it is small; *conternans* because it was often undermined by the trembling of the earth. *Consternans*: repelling or falling. *Consternatio* is called a sudden agitation arising from some fear, from *sternutare*, ‘to sneeze.’ Hence others say that the aforesaid Segor is not *conternans* but *consternans*, as though it were disturbed by sudden fear at the enemy’s arrival.”

This is different from *conternatio* in Hyginus, *On the Establishment of Boundaries*, namely, a comparison of three: “But if they have been permitted to be *conternati* among those who are in agreement, the *conternati* must draw lots to determine which three are to receive the first lot of the century. We shall inscribe the names of each group of three formed by lot.”

## CONTINENCE IN MARRIAGE

This was frequent in the better age. Indeed, examples of perpetual continence are found here in the index: Ammon with his wife; Anastasius and Theognia; Eucharistus and Maria; Magna with her husband; Olympias with Nebridius; and an anonymous man, who was later made a priest, with his wife.

To these add Pelagius, later bishop of Laodicea, with his wife, in Theodoret, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 12; Julian and Basilissa in the *Menaion* of Metaphrastes, January 9; Zacharias the shoemaker with his wife Maria, as found in the Greek *Menaia*, November 17; Cecilia with Valerian, a noble Roman, November 22 in Surius; the two Amantii in Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 33; Conon of Isauria with his wife Maria in the *Menaia*, March; Edward, king of England, with his wife Edith; Henry, emperor Augustus, with his wife Cunegund, as Surius records, March 3; Elzear, count of Ariano, and Delphina, September 27, in Surius, chapter 32; Edelfrida with two kings of England, in Bede, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 23; and Bolesław the Chaste, king of Poland, with Cunegund. See several other similar examples in our Canisius, book II *On the Virgin Mary*, chapter 11.

Antigonus and Eupraxia practiced the chastity of temporary continence after having children; Protocomes with his wife for thirty years; Pinianus with the younger Melania, whom see in the index of the *Lives of the Fathers*. To these may be added Andronicus and Drusiana, in Abdias, book V, in the *Acts of Saint John the Evangelist*; and Andronicus and Athanasia, married anchorites, as recorded in the *Menaia*, October 9, together with the Roman Martyrology, and in Metaphrastes, February 27.

See also several examples of continence in marriage in John Nider, book I of the *Formicarius*, chapter 5, and there the scholiast George Colvenerius.

The following do not seem to belong among these: Macarius the Roman with his fiancée in the *Lives of the Fathers*; Saint Alexius with a girl of royal blood, in Surius, July 17; and Pharaildis with Guido, a most noble man, because mutual consent was lacking.

## COPADIUM

Pelagius, book V, booklet IV, no. 63: “And the archbishop, taking one *copadium*, gave it to the person reclining beside him.” Papias: “*Copadium*: a piece of meat, which the Greeks call *copium*.”

## THE CROWN OF MARTYRS

The language of being crowned and receiving a crown is frequently used of martyrdom. The *Life of Antony*, chapter 23: “Bishop Peter, already crowned with the glory of martyrdom.” The *Life of Malchus*, in the preface: “Through whom the Church of Christ was born and grew to maturity, increased through persecutions, and was crowned with martyrdoms.” The *Life of Paula*, chapter 27: “Your mother has been crowned by a long martyrdom.” The *Life of Pachomius*, in the preface: “Together with Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria, they attained perpetual crowns and immortal rewards.” The Roman Martyrology, January 1: “There, on the Appian Way, the crown of thirty holy soldiers martyred under the emperor Diocletian.” The expression occurs frequently among ecclesiastical writers.

## TO BE CROWNED WITH A WREATH

In former times it was customary for both bridegroom and bride to be encircled with a crown. Palladius, chapter 8, concerning Ammon the bridegroom: “It seemed good to him both to be crowned and to sit in the bridal chamber.” ἔδοξεν καὶ στεφανοῦσθαι. Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 13: “Marriage ceremonies also crown the bridegrooms; and therefore we do not marry pagans, lest they lead us into idolatry, from which marriage among them begins.”

This was indeed observed in the primitive Church, when there was danger of idolatry, since crowns were sacred to some pagan god. Later, once the danger had been removed, this custom also became established among Christians, as you see here. Claudian, *On the Marriage of Honorius*:

> You, Hymenaeus, prepare the festive torches; you, Grace,  
> choose the flowers; you, Concord, bind the twin crowns.

The same author, exhorting Stilicho to marry, says:

> Bind the hair accustomed to shine beneath a helmet  
> with a soft crown.

See more in Carolus Paschalius, *On Crowns*.

## A CROSS WORN AROUND THE NECK

Leontius, in the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*, concerning his disciple Zacharias, chapter 1: “He took from himself the silver cross which he was wearing and gave it to him.” Procopius, or Neanias, a martyr in the time of Diocletian, wore a cross around his neck, as Nicephorus testifies, book VII, chapter 15; the Council of Nicaea, Act 4; and Metaphrastes in Surius, July 8. Likewise Orestes, a Christian soldier, as recorded in the *Life of Saint Eustratius the Martyr and His Companions*, December 13, in the same Surius.

See more examples in our Gretzer, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 78, and book II, chapter 27. Also book II, chapter 34, concerning Encolpius, one of the bishops who wore a small golden cross around his neck.

## CUBA

In the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, no. 61, in the annotation, see that both *cuba* and *guba* may be read. Thus in Theodoret, *Philotheus*, book IX, chapter 13. Macedonius was called *Gubba* because he stood in a deep pit. “That name,” he says, “if transferred from the Syriac language into Greek, means λάκκον, that is, a pit.”

There is another *cuba*, or *cumba*, in Festus: “The Sabines call *cuba* what soldiers call a litter; from this, it seems, *cubiculum* was derived.” In Isidore’s Glosses: “*Cumba*: a wedge, a bank.” The manuscript Glossary of Camberon: “*Cuba*: the extreme part of a ship, so called because it lies upon the waters. *Cumba*, however, is called a litter from lying down.” In the same work: “*Gumba*: a wedge.”

One also finds *cubella* among the latest writers, meaning the small boat in which dough is shaped. Niderus, in the *Formicarius*.

## CURARE

That is, ἐνταφιάζειν: to attend to a funeral—to wash, anoint, season with spices, and perform the other things required before burial. Palladius, chapter 10: “When I had tended to him, wrapped the holy body in linen, and laid it down.” Ὃν ἐνταφιάσασα ἐγὼ, καὶ ὀθόναις τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ἁγίου ἐλίξασα, καὶ ἀποθεμένη.

Hervetus translated this: “When I had buried him, and [wrapped him] in linen,” etc. He evidently believed that ἐνταφιάζειν, “to tend to a funeral,” meant the same as θάπτειν, “to bury.” Yet a body could not be buried before it had been wrapped. The proper order is to tend to the corpse, wash and anoint it, wrap it in linen, and lay it down—that is, bury it. *Curare* is the proper Latin word for this funerary service, just as ἐνταφιάζειν is in Greek.

The passage in Genesis I:2, “And Joseph commanded his servants, the physicians, to season his father with spices,” is rendered in the Septuagint: “Καὶ προσέταξεν Ἰωσὴφ τοῖς παισὶν αὐτοῦ τοῖς ἐνταφιασταῖς, ἐνταφιάσαι τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ”: “And Joseph commanded his servants, his funeral attendants, to perform the funeral rites for his father.” Formerly the Latin had *sepultoribus*, “gravediggers.”

Augustine, in the *Locutions*, under *sepultoribus*: “The Latin language did not find a way to name ἐνταφιασταί. For they do not themselves bury—that is, commit bodies to the earth—which in Greek is not ἐνεταφίασαν but ἔθαψαν. Rather, those called ἐνταφιασταί perform what is done for bodies destined for burial, whether by seasoning, drying, wrapping, or binding them. In this work the care of the Egyptians is especially excellent. Therefore, when the text says that they also buried him, we must understand that they tended to him.”

The same author, in the earlier treatise *On the Resurrection of the Dead*, chapter 12: “The Egyptians carefully tend the corpses of the dead.” Pius, Roman bishop (as is believed), to Justus, bishop of Vienne, letter 2: “Care for the bodies of the holy martyrs as members of God, just as the apostles cared for Stephen.” Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 49: “He ordered water and firewood to be brought at the same time for tending the corpse shortly afterward.” Spartianus, in *Hadrian*: “Having tended the favourites, and buried them.” Unless this must be understood of the depilatory care of catamites, the reading should be “buried them” (*sepelisse*). Eginhard, in the *Life of Charlemagne*: “The body was washed and tended according to customary practice.”

## CURIALIS

Heraclides, chapter 7: “Moses was the servant of some *curialis*.” In Palladius, chapter 22, the Greek has: “He was the servant of some man engaged in civic office.” The old translation of Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 14: “Moses was the servant of a certain *curialis*.” Innocent I, letter 2 to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapter 11: “Frequently some of our brethren endeavor to make clerics of men occupied as *curiales* or with various public functions.”

The *curiales* were those enrolled in the municipal councils. The glosses give: *curialis*, “councilman,” “belonging to the council.”

## CYPHONISMUS

Some wish *cyphonismus* to be described by Saint Jerome in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, no. 2: “He ordered the martyr to be smeared with honey and, under the fiercest sun, with his hands tied behind his back, to be laid on his back—obviously so that he might yield to the stings of the flies.” See Gallonius, *On Tortures*, chapter 1.

## THE PREDICTION OF DEMONS

Saint Antony reasons correctly about this, as is found in chapter 17 of his *Life*. Augustine, however, in volume 3, book 2 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 17, discusses the matter as follows:

“Some of them are permitted to know certain truths about temporal affairs, partly because of the keenness of a subtler sense, partly because they are powerful through more subtle bodies, partly through more cunning experience resulting from so great a length of life, and partly because holy angels, at his command, reveal to them what the angels themselves learn from almighty God, who apportions human merits with the purity of his most hidden justice. Sometimes, moreover, those wicked spirits predict even what they themselves are going to do, as though by divination. Therefore a good Christian must beware of mathematicians and of all who impiously practice divination, especially when they speak the truth, lest they entangle the deceived soul in an agreement of fellowship with demons.”

The same author, volume 3, book 12 of *On Genesis according to the Letter*, chapter 17:

“Furthermore, when they announce that something has already happened far away, which after several days is confirmed to be true, this is not surprising. They can accomplish it not only through a sharpness of vision incomparably greater than ours, even in bodily matters, but also through the marvelous speed of their bodies, which are certainly much subtler. We have also learned that an unclean spirit, having taken possession of a sick man in a house, used to say, when a presbyter had begun to come toward him from twelve thousand [units; the Latin does not specify them], at every point on the route where he was, how near he was, when he would enter, and when he reached the estate, the house, and the room, until he stood before him. Although that sick man did not see all these things with his eyes, nevertheless, unless he saw them in some manner, he would not have announced them so truthfully. He was suffering from fever and said these things as though in delirium.”

The same author investigates this subject splendidly in *On the Divination of Demons*, chapters 4 and 5.

The same author, *City of God*, book 2, chapter 24, concerning the slave of Lucius Pontius who prophesied through a demon:

“He added that the Capitol would burn. After saying this, he immediately left the camp, returned more agitated on the following day, and shouted that the Capitol had burned. In fact, the Capitol really had burned. It was easy for the demon both to foresee this and to report it with extreme speed.”

Likewise, in book 8, chapter 23, he teaches how Hermes Trismegistus could have known that the Egyptian superstitions would be abolished. And in book 9, chapter 22, he distinguishes between the knowledge of demons and that of angels. The angels “know these temporal and mutable things more certainly, because they behold their principal causes in the Word of God, through which the world was made—causes by which some things are approved, others rejected, and all things ordered. Demons, however, do not contemplate in God’s wisdom the eternal causes of times, the causes, so to speak, that govern them; rather, through greater experience of certain signs hidden from us, they foresee many more future events than human beings do, and sometimes they also announce their own plans in advance. In short, these beings are often deceived, whereas the angels never are.”

## THE BLOWING AWAY OF DEMONS

Nothing is more frequent in the acts of the saints than the blowing away, blowing upon, and spitting at demons.

Concerning the blowing away, see the *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 17: “After fortifying his forehead with the sign of the cross, he blew upon him, and he was immediately put to flight.” And chapter 48: “And, blowing upon him, he said…”

Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 9:

“Now, certain women among the most faithful, who possess the fear of God and are not susceptible to deception, whom he had similarly attempted to seduce like the others by ordering them to prophesy, separated themselves from such a madman, blowing upon him and cursing him.”

What is here *blowing upon him* is, in Greek, according to Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, heresy 34, “having blown upon him.”

Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 11:

“With what mouth will a Christian incense-bearer pass through the temples? With what mouth will he spit upon and blow away the smoking altars which he himself has provided for?”

Sulpicius Severus, book 3 of *On the Virtues of Saint Martin*:

“He saw a demon of extraordinary size seated behind Avitianus. Martin blew it away from a distance—using, because necessity required it, a word that is somewhat un-Latin—and Avitianus, thinking that he himself was being blown upon, said: ‘Why, holy man, do you look at me in this way?’ Then Martin said: ‘Not at you, but at him who has settled foully upon your neck.’”

Thus the blowing away of demons appears among the ceremonies of baptism in Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2, and frequently in other ecclesiastical writers. Saint Augustine refers to this when, in tractate 11 on John, he speaks against the Donatists who rebaptized and who blew upon one who had already been rightly baptized, thereby blowing away Christ rather than the demon:

“Against those who blow upon Christ, against those who blaspheme baptism.”

Again:

“When they see Christ, from whom they have been delivered, being blown upon in Christians?”

Desiderius Heraldus did not properly understand this passage in his notes on Minucius Felix.

Concerning blowing upon, Prudentius, in *The Contest of Romanus*, hymn 14, verse 919:

“When he enters and sees them prepared,  
he blows upon them as though he saw demons.”

Palladius, in the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*: “Demons are bound by a single blowing upon believers.”

This blowing away and blowing upon demons often took place together with disputation. The *Life of Antony*, chapter 20:

“But I, repeatedly spitting a great deal into his mouth, armed entirely in the name of Christ, rushed against him.”

Hence spitting and blowing away are sometimes joined together. Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 10:

“With what mouth will a Christian incense-bearer pass through the temples? With what mouth will he spit upon and blow away the smoking altars which he himself has provided for?”

The same author, book 2 *To His Wife*, chapter 5:

“Will you hide when you mark your little bed, when you mark your little body, when you spit out something unclean with your breath?”

Sometimes spitting is used by itself. Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 13: “We spit upon temples no less than upon tombs.” Minucius, in the *Octavius*: “They spit upon the gods.” Prudentius, book 1 *Against Symmachus*:

“Who in the city  
would not spit upon Jupiter’s altar, defiled with filth?”

Hence it is not surprising that in chapter 20 of the *Life of Saint Antony* there is a variant reading, as I noted there, when Evagrius translates it, “I repeatedly spat.” In the Greek it is “I blew upon.”

## DEFENSOR

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 5:

“And when they wished to approach him, they were prevented by fear of the *cancellarii*, the defenders of the church, and those standing beside him.”

And chapter 23:

“The defenders of the church struck him down.”

Canon 2 of the Council of Chalcedon: the Greek term *ekdikos* is in Latin *defensor*. In canon 2, section 23, one finds *ekdikon*, “defender of the Church of Constantinople.” In the Code of Canons of the African Church, canon 117, one finds *ekdikous scholastikous*, “scholastic defenders,” that is, advocates. Just as these were defenders of the church, so others were defenders in the imperial palace. See Codinus, *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*.

## DEHABERE

A rarer and not readily encountered verb. In the appendix to Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, from the old translation, chapter 13, one finds: “Especially if they lack and are poorer.”

Besides Jerome, cited there, Aethicus also uses the word, in *On the Rivers of the Western Ocean*, under the Tiber:

“But the island which it forms within the harbor of the city and the town of Ostia is so green and pleasant that, neither in the summer months nor in the winter ones, it lacks admirable pasture grasses.”

## DEHONESTAMENTUM

The *Life of Antony*, chapter 30: “He gloried greatly in such a disgrace of the body.” This is taken from Gellius, as you will see.

Although the word is uncommon, several authors nevertheless use it. Sallust, book 1 of the *Histories*: “Fusidius, the disgrace of all honors.” Tacitus uses it several times. It also occurs in Justin. Seneca, *On the Constancy of the Wise Man*, chapter 19:

“Let him endure insults, shameful words, disgrace, and all other dishonors as though they were the shouting of enemies.”

Gellius, book 2, chapter 27:

“With that disgrace of the body he was especially delighted.”

Arnobius, book 2: “To be led away to the disgraces of vices.” Trebellius Pollio, in *Claudius*: “Gallus Antipater, the disgrace of slaves and actors.” Ammianus, book 26: “Raised mockingly to this disgrace of all good men.”

The glosses give: *dehonestamentum*, “shame.”

The form *inhonestamentum* is also found. Apuleius, *Apology*: “Lest I admit any stain or dishonor into myself.” Isidore, book 2 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 21, cites C. Gracchus:

“Your boyhood was the dishonor of your adolescence; your adolescence, the disgrace of your old age; your old age, the scandal of the republic.”

Likewise *honestamentum* occurs in Ennodius, book 2, letter 1:

“Nor should he need a teacher whom the corrections and honors of his actions have made conspicuous.”

Apuleius, *Apology*:

“And likewise many philosophers, most honorable in speech, have been handed down to memory, men who adorned the grace of their bodies with the honors of their character.”

## DIPTYCHUM

The *Life of Pelagia*, chapter 7: “Immediately he sent a diptych of tablets through the same boys.”

The Greek word is *diptychon*, δίπτυχον, “diptych,” and was also used by the Latins, though they often corrupted it. The etymological work says:

“*Diptycha*, a neuter noun. It is derived from the masculine *diptyx*, which comes from the verb *ptyssō*, ‘I fold.’ Its future is *ptyxō*, whence *ptyx*, ‘a fold’; and with *dyo*, ‘two,’ comes *diptyx*. *Diptyx* and *diptychos* are declined and transferred into the nominative; and the neuter form is *diptychon*. ‘Making diptycha,’ that is, doubling the fat; but now it says *epiploun*, ‘omentum.’”

The etymological work here alludes to verses of Homer, which will be discussed below.

A *diptych* is therefore understood here as a little book of two folds, or leaves, or pages—as if one said “double tablets.” Thus Ovid, book 1 of the *Amores*, elegy 12:

“Thus I have found you double in accordance with your name,  
yet the number itself was not a favorable omen.”

John Wouwerius, in his notes on book 1, letter 5 of Sidonius, incorrectly refers these verses to paired imperial diplomas.

Martial likewise uses *triplices*, or *triptycha*, for objects consisting of three leaves, in book 7, epigram 52:

“Twelve triptychs twice over, and seven toothpicks.”

And in the same book, epigram 71:

“Nor useless triptychs, and short napkins.”

The same author, book 14, epigram 6:

“Then you will not think my triptychs worthless gifts,  
when your beloved writes that she will come to you.”

Likewise in Martial, book 14, epigram 4, one finds *quintuplices*, or *pentatycha*, consisting of five leaves:

“The fortunate master’s courtyard grows hot from the slaughter of bullocks,  
when high honor is bestowed with fivefold wax.”

There were two uses of diptychs, profane and sacred.

The profane use is mentioned by the ancients, who often sent them as gifts, especially at the presentation of public games. Symmachus, in the supplement to his letters, letter 7, written to his brothers:

“It is a religious and votive practice that ceremonial gifts be offered by candidates for the quaestorship to their most eminent and closest friends. You are rightly counted among that number. Therefore I offer you, in my son’s name, an ivory diptych and a silver basket weighing two pounds; he has staged the quaestorian games.”

The same author, book 2, letter 81, to Flavian:

“Our son Symmachus, having completed the office of candidate, offers you quaestorian gifts and shares our other obligations with equal honor. I therefore ask that you deign to accept, in his name, diptychs and *apophoreta*.”

The same author, book 5, letter 56, to Sallust:

“We have sent you, through your man, a candidate’s diptych and an *apophoretic* gift of two pounds of silver, wishing to show that you have not been absent in spirit from our public presentation.”

The same author, book 9, letter 109:

“You will not, I think, disdain the offering of a diptych and an *apophoretic* gift.”

The diptychs sent as gifts were generally made of ivory; although this epithet is not always added, it seems to be understood. Thus one should take *diptych* absolutely in Symmachus, book 2, letter 81. He adds, as though explaining it:

“I also honored my other friends with ivory writing tablets and silver baskets.”

When such diptychs were sent to the emperor, they were customarily gilded. Symmachus, book 2, letter 81:

“Furthermore, to our lord and emperor, in order to render a diligent though scarcely equal return for his generosity, I sent a diptych surrounded with gold.”

Later it was forbidden for anyone below the rank of consul to give ivory diptychs and golden *sportulae*. Law 1, *On the Expenses of Games*, in the Theodosian Code, establishes this through the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius:

“We also confirm by statute that, except for ordinary consuls, no one else whatsoever shall have the right to give a golden *sportula* or ivory diptychs when public ceremonies are celebrated. The *sportulae* shall consist of silver coin, and the diptychs of another material.”

Hence Claudian, book 3 of *On the Consulship of Stilicho*, sings of the ivory tablets scattered by him among the people:

“Then he gathers the green panthers and the other marvels of the South,  
and the huge teeth of Latona’s offspring,  
which, cut by iron into tablets and glittering with gold,  
inscribed with the consul’s radiant name in chased work,  
pass through nobles and common people. The greatest wonder  
is among the Indians; the elephant, stripped of its teeth,  
wanders ingloriously.”

I do not know why diptychs, or writing tablets, were sent as gifts at the presentation of public games. Ludovicus Carrion, in book 2 of his *Emendations*, chapter 6, cited above, thinks that candidates for the quaestorship customarily offered them because they themselves used them frequently. Yet consuls and others also offered diptychs.

Diptychs appear to have been tablets used by lovers. Thus an old commentator, on the following passage of Juvenal, satire 9:

“And let the gentle, constant, closely packed tablets  
harass him,”

adds: “Let him harass you with flattering letters and diptychs.”

The Camberon Glossary, manuscript:

“*Dipticae* are called tablets on which seducers write their love to their girls.”

Papias the lexicographer:

“*Dipticae* are tablets on which seducers write their love to girls.”

In Ovid too, book 2 of the *Amores*, elegy 15, there are secret tablets used for this purpose.

I believe Carrion is mistaken in thinking that diptychs were generally all made of ivory. It is not plausible that epistolary diptychs—which people commonly sent to one another in place of letters and in which they disclosed their secrets—were made of ivory. They were rather wooden and coated with wax.

Thus Ovid, cursing his beloved’s double tablets, or diptychs, because she had denied him the night, says:

“What should I pray for in anger, unless old age, gnawing with decay,  
should consume you, and the wax become white with filthy neglect?”

From this it is inferred that they were wooden. Again, in book 1, elegy 11, which precedes the poem about his love-tablets, he says:

“I will inscribe it. Naso dedicates these tablets,  
faithful to Venus. Yet recently you were cheap maple.”

Other diptychs were sacred; their use existed in the Catholic Church, where the term had shifted from its common sense to a private one.

These sacred diptychs were therefore double tablets. On one side were inscribed the names of bishops who had piously died; on the other, those of the living.

With respect to the dead, mention is made of these tablets, there called *sacred folds* (ἱεραὶ πτυχαί), in Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, where the mystery of the synaxis, or communion, is discussed:

“And when all have greeted one another, the mystical recitation of the sacred folds is performed.”

Perionius translates it:

“When all have greeted one another, the mystical recitation of the saints takes place.”

Ambrose of Camaldoli:

“And when all have greeted one another, the mystical recitation of the saints takes place.”

Both omitted translating the word *folds*. John Scotus, the old translator of Dionysius, is therefore more accurate:

“And while all greet one another, the mystical proclamation of the sacred books is completed.”

Likewise John Saracenus:

“And when all have kissed one another, the mystical proclamation of the sacred tablets is completed.”

They translated correctly, provided that by books and tablets they understood diptychs.

Again, in the same chapter, in the *Theoria*:

“But the most divine greeting is performed, and the mystical and transcendent proclamation of the hagiographical folds.”

Perionius:

“But the divine greeting, or kiss, is given, and the mystical and heavenly proclamation of the holy souls who are written down.”

Ambrose of Camaldoli:

“Moreover, the most sacred greeting is celebrated, and the names of the saints that have been written down are proclaimed mystically and in a supramundane manner.”

The old translators are clearer. John Scotus:

“But the most divine greeting is performed in a sacred manner, and the mystical and transcendent recitation of the hagiographical books.”

John Saracenus:

“But the most divine kiss is performed in a sacred manner, and the mystical and transcendent proclamation of the hagiographical tablets.”

Again, in the *Theoria* of the same chapter, which contains the contemplation and explanation of this matter:

“But the proclamation of the sacred folds after the peace announces those who have lived piously and have immovably reached the perfection of a virtuous life.”

Perionius translates:

“But the proclamation of the holy souls, which is made after the peace, honors with praise those who have lived piously and holily and have reached the perfection appropriate to a virtuous life.”

Here again Perionius read “souls” (*psychōn*) instead of “folds” (*ptychōn*).

Ambrose of Camaldoli:

“For the proclamation of the sacred names after the peace raises with praise those who lived piously and holily and steadfastly maintained their life to the very end in virtue, never turning away from it.”

John Scotus more clearly:

“But the recitation of the sacred tablets after the peace proclaims those who have been firmly established in holiness and have immovably reached the consummation of a vigorous life.”

John Saracenus:

“But the proclamation of the sacred tablets after the peace proclaims those who have lived holily and have immovably attained the perfection of a life of virtue.”

Just as here we have *sacred folds*, which Maximus and Pachymeres, commentators on Dionysius, interpret as *diptychs*, so there is an explicit mention of *diptychs* in the letter of the Egyptian bishops to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, against Timothy, the usurper of the Alexandrian see. It is found in part 3 of the Council of Chalcedon in the Roman edition:

“He also placed his own name and that of Dioscorus in the venerable diptych—in which are contained the names of bishops who, with pious memory, have departed to heaven and which are reread during the holy mysteries according to the sacred rules—although Dioscorus had been decreed to be under the anathema of God and the universal council; and from it he erased the name of Proterius, of sacred memory and living according to God, who had been canonically appointed archbishop.”

Likewise in the sixth synod, session 13:

“We found that these three men of holy memory—namely Thomas, John, and Constantine—remained in the same status and were commemorated in the sacred diptychs of the most holy churches.”

Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 35:

“This man—Alexander, bishop of Antioch—was the first to insert the name of the great John into the ecclesiastical diptychs.”

The same is found in the *Tripartite History*, book 10, chapter 25, and in George of Alexandria, *Life of Chrysostom*, chapter 71.

Isidore, bishop of Trimithus, in the *Life of John Chrysostom*:

“Inscribe the name of John in the sacred diptychs.”

Pope Innocent, to Arcadius and Eudoxia, in George of Alexandria’s *Life of Chrysostom*:

“But command that John’s name also be inscribed in the sacred diptychs.”

The letter of the emperor Justinian to the fifth general synod, namely the Second Council of Constantinople:

“Just as those who had been unjustly condemned were recalled after death and their names were written in the sacred diptychs. This was also done with John [Chrysostom] and Flavian, bishops of Constantinople of pious memory.”

This is cited in canon *Sane*, section 24, question 1.

In the Sacramentary of Gregory the Great there is a prayer *Over the Diptychs*:

“Remember also, Lord, your servants who have gone before us and have fallen asleep in the sleep of peace.”

And in the liturgy of Saint Mark:

“The deacon reads the diptychs of the departed.”

Cyprian alludes to this custom of reciting the names of the dead at Mass in letter 10 to the clergy and presbyters who had rashly granted peace to the lapsed:

“Their name is offered.”

And in letter 66, to the presbyters, deacons, and people of Furni:

“For he does not deserve to be named in the prayer of the priests at God’s altar who wished to drive priests and ministers away from the altar.”

Just as the names of deceased bishops who were rightly regarded as such were inscribed in the sacred diptychs, so the names of heretics and schismatics were removed from them.

The emperor Justinian, in the *Confession of the Orthodox Faith against the Three Chapters*, or in the edict on the Catholic faith, which is found after the fifth synod:

“Accordingly, the entire body of the church of Mopsuestia, in which he is said to have been bishop, because of the blasphemies by which he was reckoned by the holy Fathers among pagans, Jews, and Sodomites, erased his name from that time onward from the sacred diptychs of the Church.”

The emperor Justinian, in his letter to the fifth synod, found there in session 1, concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia:

“Because of these blasphemies, his name was also erased in earlier times from the sacred diptychs of the Church of which he had been bishop.”

The imperial sacred letter of Constantine Pogonatus to Lord Pope Agatho, prefixed to the sixth general synod, namely the Third Council of Constantinople:

“For both the most holy and blessed patriarch here and Macarius, the most holy patriarch of Theopolis, made a strong demand upon us that Vitalian, the most blessed man, be expelled from the diptychs, asserting that Honorius was commemorated in the diptychs out of regard for the honor of the apostolic see of ancient Rome.”

The ecclesiastical history of Theodorus Lector of Constantinople, cited by Damascenus in his third discourse *On Images*:

“For he advanced to such a degree of audacity that he even removed from the sacred diptychs the names of the blessed shepherds who had been there, and tyrannically destroyed their images by fire.”

Franciscus Zinus of Verona translated this:

“He advanced so far in audacity that he removed the names of the blessed bishops who had been there from the ‘double priests’ and tyrannically burned them.”

He did not properly understand *sacred diptychs*, which he translated as “double priests”; it should be “from the sacred diptychs,” as Jacobus Billius correctly noted in his notes on that discourse.

Likewise, in a passage cited from the same history by Damascenus:

“To anathematize the images of the bishops and erase them from the sacred diptychs.”

Zinus again translated it “to erase the double priests.”

Pope Innocent, in his letter to the emperor Arcadius, in George of Alexandria’s *Life of Chrysostom*, concerning the erasure even of the memory of the deceased Arsacius:

“I judge that not even his name should be inscribed in the sacred diptychs.”

Anastasius, in *Agatho*:

“They removed from the diptychs of the churches the names of the patriarchs, or from the church paintings their figures.”

Victor of Tunnuna, in his *Chronicle*:

“He removes the names of Proterius and Salafatius from the ecclesiastical diptychs, and writes in those of Dioscorus and Aelurus, who killed Proterius.”

Thus far concerning the names of the dead inscribed in the diptychs.

John the Deacon, in book 4, chapter 23 of the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, mentions the living, whose names were customarily inscribed in the diptychs:

“Especially to this day the Eastern sees retain the practice that they write the name of no bishop in their diptychs until they have received his synodical letter; and they count a deceased bishop among the living for as long as his successor takes care to send his letters.”

The Council of Chalcedon, session 11:

“For the blessed Proclus received him, entered into communion with him, issued synodical letters, and placed him in the diptychs.”

Most of the earlier examples, in which it is shown that the names of certain people were erased from the diptychs after their death, sufficiently demonstrate that they had been inscribed in the diptychs while they were alive.

Gregoras, book 5:

“In the sacred hymns they commemorate the pope in the diptychs together with the other four patriarchs.”

Just as the names of living bishops were inserted into the sacred diptychs, so at times the names of living persons were removed from them.

Proclus, archbishop of Constantinople, in a letter to the lord bishop of Antioch on behalf of Athanasius, bishop of Perrha, whose name, while he was still alive, had been erased from the sacred diptychs, is cited in the Council of Chalcedon, session 14:

“And to remove the name of the serving bishop from the sacred tablets.”

The old translator renders it: “And to remove the bishop’s name from the sacred diptychs.”

Pope Vigilius, in the condemnation of Theodore:

“Removing also from the diptychs the priest of the Alexandrian Church, our brother Zoilus, whose name had been communicated to you up to the aforementioned day, you joined to yourselves a certain Apollinaris, a perverse man and adulterer of that Church itself.”

The names of the living that were inscribed in the sacred diptychs were generally those of bishops and patriarchs, as is evident everywhere.

I do not know whether the book of the living, or sacred tablets, which Dionysius the Areopagite mentions in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2, should be referred to these diptychs placed upon the altar. The names of the enlightened and of those who received them were inscribed in these tablets, which Pachymeres thinks were called *the diptychs of the living*:

“Then he places his hand upon the head and commands the presbyters and deacons under him to write in sacred tablets the names both of the person who has approached for baptism and of the sponsor. These, I believe, are the diptychs of the living.”

Chrysostom mentions the living and the dead together in the liturgy:

“The deacon censes the holy table all around and, as he wishes, makes mention of the diptychs, both of the departed and of the living.”

The custom of commending both the living and the dead at Mass has continued in the canon of the Mass, when we first make mention of the living and then of the dead through the two *Mementos*. See Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, the chapter *On the Celebration of Mass*, and Master Florus, who gives the same information about this use of the diptychs.

From what has been said it follows that the diptychs were not so called because they were two books, one of the living and the other of the dead, as Meursius thought in his *Greek-Barbarian Glossary*. One and the same book could contain the names of both groups; and a book solely of the living, or solely of the dead, could likewise be called a diptych. They were therefore called diptychs because that book consisted of two leaves or tablets, as I said above.

Hence, in George of Alexandria, chapter 71 cited above, one reading has *dithyra* instead of *diptycha*, because this book was composed, as it were, of two doors or leaves, or, as Ausonius says, a “two-opening writing tablet.”

In Evagrius, book 6 of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 20, I understand *amphithyron Hunnic* as an *amphithyron*, or diptych, made in Hunnic workmanship—unless one prefers, with others, to understand it as a veil.

I remember seeing such an ivory diptych in the church of Saint Lambert at Liège, on which the names of several saints and certain bishops are inscribed. It appears to have been transferred into an ecclesiastical diptych from a profane consular diptych of the sort consuls customarily sent to their friends at the presentation of public games, as I mentioned above.

Certainly it bears the name of the consul Savinianus or Sabinianus, who was consul in the year of our Lord 505, and it contains various figures relating to profane military service, together with this inscription: “Commander of the household cavalry.” I would have included an image of this diptych here if a corrected inscription had been sent to me. Perhaps on another occasion it will be possible to reproduce it correctly.

That ecclesiastical diptychs were generally made of ivory may also be inferred from Fortunatus, book 10, poem 10:

“May he whose diptych today displays ivory in the temple  
read your names to the patriarchs and prophets.”

That diptychs were formerly made of valuable material, so that they were enclosed in cases, may likewise be inferred from Ekkehard the Younger, a monk of Saint Gall, *On the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall in Alemannia*, chapter 5:

“The chapel just mentioned becomes an oratory, into which are brought crosses, cases for diptychs, and almost the entire treasure of the church, except for the books kept in storage.”

This passage is found in volume 1, part 1 of the *Alemannic Affairs*. The scholiast Goldastus understands *diptychs* there as annual books in which were written the names of those who had bequeathed something to monks and clerics for the benefit of their souls, the cases having been prepared to preserve these books.

I doubt that those common memorial diptychs among monks were ordinarily so adorned that they could be counted among treasures. Rather, I would understand *diptychs* in that passage as diptychs of the saints, or the Gospel book, or similar objects whose diptych covers—that is, the outer boards—were customarily decorated magnificently with gold, silver, and figures, and carried about in procession.

Isaac Casaubon, in his *Annotations on Book 6 of Athenaeus*, chapter 14, traces the origin of the practice of inserting into sacred diptychs the names of holy martyrs, emperors, chief pontiffs, and other men distinguished by faith and merit, and reciting them among the hymns, to Roman paganism. The Romans, he says, decreed that the names of those whom they wished to honor with exceptional distinction should be sung in the Salii’s hymn.

Thus, he says, after Germanicus died this honor was granted to him among others, according to Tacitus, book 2. Marcus Antoninus the philosopher likewise ordered that, after the death of his son Verus, his name be inserted into the Salii’s hymn, as Spartianus testifies. The practice had already been established at Rome, as appears from what Varro, Ovid, Festus, Plutarch, and others write about Mamurius Veturius and Lucia Volumnia.

The ancient Christian Church, he says, also transferred this custom to pious use. On this matter, he adds, he will say much elsewhere, if God prolongs his life—things worthy of knowing and not hackneyed.

How I wish Casaubon had possessed a better judgment, so that he would not derive our sacred practices from the pagans rather than from the Church of the Old Testament, and so that he would not make the Fathers observers of pagan rites more than people knowledgeable about and obedient to the sacred law!

He should have remembered that the great Dionysius, whom he rightly calls and regards as an ancient Father, says:

“Observe that they are also placed in sacred memorials—not as though the divine memory were declared, in a human manner, to exist in that part of memory which receives images, but, as one might say, in a manner worthy of God, signifying the precious and immutable knowledge in God of those who have attained the divine likeness in perfection. For, says the divine Scripture, ‘He knows those who are his’ (2 Timothy 2). And: ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones’ (Psalm 115)—the death of the holy ones being spoken of in place of their perfection in holiness.”

He should have remembered the statement in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 44:

“Let us praise illustrious men and our fathers in their generations.”

There, and in the following chapters, a catalogue of righteous men is set out. Did the ancient Church not look to this rather than to the Salii’s hymns?

Indeed, as our Brouwer notes on Fortunatus, our ancestors seem to have sketched in the diptychs a kind of image of the books of life. For just as some are inscribed in that register who are commended not by an everlasting but by a temporary praise of righteousness, while others are enrolled among the lot of the saints by a firm and immutable decree of the Divinity, so we remember that the names of some entered the diptychs whose simulated virtue for a time had not deserved it, whereas the names of others remained more firmly, because their constancy and unblemished integrity of faith and conduct endured.

The use and purpose of the diptychs in sacred matters was therefore both to preserve the memory of the saints and to establish ecclesiastical peace and communion: they received men worthy of heaven and everlasting remembrance, but rejected and cast out those who were unworthy.

Thus far Brouwer.

On the sacred diptychs, John Baptist Cardona, bishop of Tortosa, once wrote a brief treatise at the request of Cardinal Gabriel Paleotti; Philip Mey printed it, together with some other short works of his, at Tarragona in 1587. [Col. 0438D] John Stephen Duranti also has something on the same subject in *On the Rites of the Church*, chapter 43; there he improperly cites, in the opposite sense, the letters of Pope Innocent and the emperor Arcadius that you have above. Brother Angelus Rocca of Camerino also discusses them in his notes to the *Book of the Sacraments* of Saint Gregory.

Thus far we have considered diptychs as sacred memorial tablets of the dead, which were double, that is, made of two leaves. In this sense Augustine, in volume VI, book XV of *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 4, calls the stone tablets of Moses a diptych: “For in that stone diptych you now understand, no longer with a heart of stone, what was suited to that hard-hearted people.” Likewise, in the letter of Saint Peter, from which he had cited certain passages, he says: “Read that diptych also, and do not be afraid: it is plainly your bridegroom’s.” Again: “By this diptych you repel the adulterer.” [Col. 0439A] Again: “Do not therefore dread the diptych in which those things once written to you, which you would now recognize, were sent.” Again: “This diptych, then, was sent beforehand by the one who, when he came, entrusted these two commandments to you.” Again: “O chaste diptych, in which, under the old figure, that lover and beloved of yours foretold for you the new song on the ten-stringed psaltery.” Again: “O marital diptych, which the adulteress hates for good reason.” Isidore likewise uses the term in book *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 14: “And not outwardly on stone diptychs, but inwardly on the tablets of the heart.”

In this sense some wish Prudentius to have entitled his book, which contains the titles of the histories of the Old and New Testaments, *Diptychon*. With God’s help we shall examine this matter in connection with Prudentius at another time.

[Col. 0439B] There is another diptych in Homer, *Iliad* books α and β, namely, the double membrane or tunic of the omentum, as the *Etymologicum* cited above indicates. I believe that Suidas also has this in view: “Diptycha, having two coverings, so that one part is spread beneath and the other placed over it.” Cujacius, *Observations*, book IV, chapter 27; Carrion, above; and Dionysius Gothofredus, in his notes to book I of the *Code*, title 1, law 7, § 5, *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith*, understand and cite these words as referring to tablet-diptychs. But the text in Suidas is corrupt and mutilated. Those words must be understood of the two tunics of the omentum. A fuller passage occurs in Hesychius:

“Diptycha: having two coverings, or double, so that the omentum is spread beneath one part and placed over the other.”

Of the two tunics of the omentum, see John Gorraeus, *Medical Definitions*, under the word ἐπίπλοον or ἐπίπλουν.

There is also another diptych: that of an oyster, that is, the twofold shell of the oyster in which it encloses itself. Ambrose, book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8, speaking of the crab lying in wait for the oyster, says: “It watches to see whether the oyster, in a remote place sheltered from every wind and facing the rays of the sun, will open that diptych of its own and unlock the fastenings of its shells.”

## DOMNIO

Palladius, chapter 84, says that Serapion the Sindonite at Rome “met a certain Domnion.” Perhaps this is the same man whose memory is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 28 December: “At Rome, Saint Domnion, priest.” Saint Jerome also mentions him in letter 154, to Desiderius: “If you should wish to borrow copies, you can obtain them either from the holy Marcella, who lives on the Aventine, or from Domnion, the Lot of our own time, a most holy man.” Saint Paulinus likewise celebrates him as a most holy man in letter 45, to Alypius: “I found the history of Eusebius with our kinsman, the truly most holy Domnion.” And afterward: “If you have received the actual manuscript of Saint Domnion, you will kindly send us a transcript.” Jerome wrote him letter 51, which contains an apology against Rufinus, who claimed that Jerome had condemned marriage; there Jerome calls Domnion his dearest father. He also wrote to him and to Rogatianus letter 108, which is the preface to the book of Chronicles, and letter 109, which is the preface to Ezra and Nehemiah. Rufinus, book II of the *Invectives*, calls Domnion “an old man of blessed memory.”

## DROMADES or DROMEDES
