The *Life of Hilarion*, section 30: “Having hired dromadary camels.” The *Life of Malchus*, section 10: “And we saw camels which, because of their excessive speed, are called dromedaries.” The manuscript Cambéron Glossary: “Dromedus, dromas, and dromedarius are the same. It is an animal smaller than a camel but swifter and better at running. Hence dromones are also called certain long, swift ships.” The same glossary says: “Dromedarii are also called the drivers of dromadaries.”

Aristotle speaks of the speed of camels in book XI of the *History of Animals*, chapter 50:

“But camels run much faster than Nisaean horses, if they run, because of the greater length of their stride.”

## ECULEUS

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, section 3: “Victorious amid the rack and the metal plates.” Different people have understood and written different things about the *eculeus*, or rack. I shall presently set aside a full treatment of it, since it is mentioned here only in passing; I shall be content to identify several authors who have discussed it. See especially Baronius, in his notes to the Roman Martyrology, 22 January; Antonius Gallonius, book *On the Torments of the Holy Martyrs*, chapter 3; and the posthumous work of Hieronymus Magius, a distinctive little book *On the Rack*.

## ENEUS

A rare word in Latin usage, and I do not remember reading it anywhere except in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Even there it had been corrupted into *aeneus*, or treated as the proper name *Eneus*. The *Life of Abraham*, chapter 5: “And struck with great astonishment, they became, as it were, some sort of speechless men.” Heraclides, *Paradise*, chapter 15: “But returning from the public place like a speechless man.”

Hesychius: Ἐννεὸς, ἔκπληκτος: “Enneus: astonished.” The same: Ἐνεὸς, νωχελὴς, μετέωρος, κωφὸς, βαιὸς, μωρὸς, ὃς οὔτε ἀκούει, οὔτε λαλεῖ: “Eneus: sluggish, suspended in mind, deaf, insignificant, foolish, one who neither hears nor speaks.” The same: Ἐνέοὶ, ἄφωνοι: “Enei: voiceless.” Suidas: Ἐννεὸς, ἄφωνος, κωφὸς, ἐξεστηκὼς, νωδὸς, νωχελὴς, μετέωρος: “Enneus: voiceless, deaf, distraught, toothless, sluggish, suspended in mind.”

## ENNATON

Pelagius, booklet XI, no. 2: “Abbot Theodore spoke of Ennaton.” John Moschus, chapter 184: “We were in the Ninth at Alexandria.” In Greek: Ὄντες ἡμεῖς ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ ἐν τῷ Ἐννάτῳ, “while we were at Alexandria, in the Ennaton.”

Correct the same author accordingly in chapter 145: Ηροεβάλομεν ἐν τῷ ἐννάτῳ Ἀλεξανδρείας, εἰς τὸ κοινόβιον Σαλαμᾶ: “We proceeded to the coenobium called Salama, nine miles from the city.” The printed text has ἐν τὸ ναῷ. See below, **NONUM**.

## EPENDYTES

The *Life of Antony*, chapter 23: “He washed his ependytes.” The *Life of Hilarion*, section 4: “And having a sheepskin ependytes.” In Greek, ἐπένδυμα or ἐπενδύτης denotes every kind of outer garment. Among ascetic writers, *ependytes* is the proper garment of monks. Most think that it was a scapular. Marius Victorinus, in his notes to the *Life of Hilarion*, is mistaken in supposing that ἐπενδύτης was an undergarment, called in Latin an *interula* or *subucula*. It was rather an outer garment, whether a scapular, cloak, or something similar.

## EPIBATAE

The *Life of Epictetus and Astion*, chapter 21: “And when they had disembarked from the ship, they were *epibatae*.” In Clement of Rome’s letter to James, bishop of Jerusalem, placed before the books of the *Recognitions*, Saint Peter speaks as follows:

“The whole condition of the Church resembles that of a great ship which, across the stormy sea, carries men from different places and regions, all hastening toward the one city of the mighty kingdom. Let the Lord of this ship, then, be almighty God himself, and let Jesus Christ be its helmsman. The bishop should fulfill the office of the proreta, the presbyters should occupy the place of sailors, and the deacons that of stewards. Those who catechize should be compared with the ship’s pursers, while the multitude of the whole brotherhood should resemble the *epibatae*.”

[Col. 0441B] *Epibatae*, ἐπιβάται, are so called ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐπιβαίνειν, “from boarding.” They are sailors serving as soldiers, or combatants in naval warfare. Hirtius, book IV of *The Alexandrian War*: “One enemy quadrireme was captured, another sunk, and a third thrown into confusion; then all were stripped of their *epibatae*.” The same author, book V of *The African War*: “And there he filled it with Gaetulian rowers and *epibatae*.” Here the term means the sailors or passengers themselves, that is, ἀντὶ τῶν ὀχουμένων, “in place of those being carried,” as it is sometimes also understood among the Greeks.

## EPITIMIUM

The *Spiritual Meadow* of John Moschus, chapter 78: “So that I may impose on them suitable *epitimia*, or many penalties.” In Greek: Κἀγὼ ταύταις ἁρμόζοντα προσάγω τὰ ἐπιτίμια. In ecclesiastical writers, *epitimium* is used for an ecclesiastical penalty.

The *Menaea*, 15 October, in the martyrdom of an anonymous monk: Καταφρονήσας καὶ τοῦ ἐπιτιμίου ἐπιτιμηθεὶς διὰ τὴν τῆς ὑπακοῆς ἀθέτησιν: “He also despised the penalty of the *epitimium* imposed on him for his refusal of obedience.”

The Eighth Ecumenical Council, published by our Raderus, has the following in act 2 concerning *epitimia*:

“Let the prescribed penalty of the *epitimia* be read to all the fallen who are listening, and so forth. For those who eat meat, let this be the penalty: they shall abstain from meat, cheese, and eggs. Those who otherwise abstain from meat shall abstain from eggs, cheese, and fish on Wednesday and Friday; they shall eat vegetables and legumes with a small amount of oil and wine. Let them kneel fifty times each day, cry out one hundred times, ‘Lord, forgive me,’ and recite Psalms 6, 37, and 50.”

John the Deacon, book II of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, chapter 45: “He was therefore greatly saddened by this, because before he departed this life he did not release him from the *epitimo* [possibly *epitimium*] of excommunication.”

## ERACIESTES

Where the *Life of Hilarion*, section 4, reads, “And having a sheepskin ependytes,” the edition of John Andrew adds, “and an *eraciestes*.” I do not understand the word. Our Peter Lansselius read *eriacestes*, as though it meant wool sewn together with a needle. Perhaps something else will occur to someone. For now it is enough for me to have noted this variant of the reading until something more satisfactory appears.

## EREMI

The word *eremus* occurs in various forms in the *Lives of the Fathers*. I investigated the desert in which Paul the First Hermit lived from the desert, or dwelling place, of Saint Antony; and Antony’s dwelling from Hilarion’s travels. See the Geographical Table.

For the desert of Chalcis, where Saint Jerome and Malchus lived, see **CHALCIS**.

[Col. 0442A] Concerning the desert near Tekoa, Jerome writes in his preface to Amos, addressed to Pammachius:

“He was from the town of Tekoa, which lies six miles south of holy Bethlehem, which gave birth to the Savior of the world. Beyond it there is no village—not even rustic huts or structures resembling ovens, which the Africans call *mapalia*. So great is the vastness of the desert that it stretches as far as the Red Sea and the borders of the Persians, Ethiopians, and Indians. And because the dry and sandy soil produces absolutely no crops, the whole region is filled with shepherds, so that the abundance of livestock may compensate for the sterility of the land.”

For the desert of Oasis, see Baronius, in his notes to the Roman Martyrology, 12 June.

## ESOPHORIUM

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 21: “He removed his *esophorium*.” The word is a compound formed by later Greek writers, ἐσωφόριον or εἰσωφόριον, meaning something worn inwardly—an *interula*. The manuscript Cambéron Glossary: “*Esephorium*: an inner garment, that is, a shirt, which Marcian calls an *interula*.”

## RECEIVING THE EUCHARIST IN THE HAND

In former times it was customary for the Eucharist to be received in the hand, not only by priests but also by laypeople. Palladius, chapter 144, concerning Sylvania: “Behold, I am now sixty years old; apart from the tips of my hands—and this for the sake of Communion—my foot has not touched water, and so forth.”

Tertullian, *On Baptism*, against Quintilla, chapter 20:

“Blessed are those whom the grace of God awaits, when you rise from that most holy bath of the new birth and, opening your first hands before the Mother together with the brethren, ask from the Father, ask from the Lord, gifts, graces, and distributions of spiritual gifts.”

Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 5:

“When you approach the Eucharist, do not come with your palms spread wide or your fingers separated. Rather, place your left hand beneath your right as a kind of throne, since the right hand is to receive the King; and, with your hand hollowed, receive the body of Christ, saying: ‘Amen.’”

The hands were formed in the shape of a cross. The Sixth Synod, canon 102: “When he is about to receive the Eucharist, let him form his hands in the shape of a cross and so approach.”

Thus men received the Eucharist with a hollow, bare hand; women, however, received it only upon a linen cloth. Maximus, against the Monothelites: “Let women present clean linen cloths upon which they may receive the body of Christ with a pure mind and a clean conscience.” Augustine, sermon 252, *On the Seasons*: “Whenever all the men desire to communicate, they wash their hands, and all the women present clean linen cloths upon which they may receive the body of Christ.”

The Council of Auxerre, canon 36: “A woman may not receive the Eucharist with a bare hand.” Hence this linen cloth, or *sindon*, was called the *dominicale*. The same council, canon 42: “Whenever a woman communicates, let each one have her *dominicale*.”

This linen cloth upon which they received the Eucharist seems to have been called *mouzíkion*. The *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 79: Καὶ βαλὼν τὴν ἐν μουζικίῳ ἀπέθετο ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ ἀρμαρίῳ: “Taking it in a very clean linen cloth, he placed it in his own cupboard.”

I do not know whether *mouzíkion* was derived from μοῦσα. The word appears in the *Euchologion* to denote a linen cloth. The *Typicon* of Sabas, chapter 41:

Ἀπογυμνοῦσιν αὐτὴν παντελῶς καὶ πρῶτον μὲν σαίρουσιν αὐτὴν διὰ μούσης καθαρωτάτης.

“They strip it completely and first cleanse it with the purest *mousa*, or linen cloth.”

The same work says:

Κομίζει ὁ σκευοφύλαξ μούσας τε καὶ δισκάρια τὰ κοινῶς λεγόμενα τέστα, ὃ λέγεται λεκάνη, καὶ ἀποσπογγίζεται ἡ ἁγία τράπεζα.

“The keeper of the vessels brings *mousai*, or cloths, and the *diskaria* commonly called *testa*, which is a basin; and the holy table is wiped clean.”

Meursius did not understand this correctly in his *Greek-Barbarian Glossary*, supposing *mousa* to be a tessellated, variously colored pavement. If *mousa* and *mousinion* should perhaps also refer to variegated objects, I shall not strongly object. For it is clear that not only chambers and vaults but also other things were made of mosaic and variegated materials.

This practice continued for several centuries in both the Western [Col. 0443B] and Eastern Church, as is clear from the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 79, where the linen cloth in which they carried the Eucharist home is called in Greek *mousíkion*. Its author lived during the reigns of the emperors Zeno, Anastasius, and Justin. At that time, under Pope Hormisdas, the Council of Zaragoza was held, at which this custom was abolished in the following words:

“If anyone is found not to have consumed the grace of the Eucharist after receiving it in the Church, let him be anathema forever.”

## EVECTION

The *Life of Antony*, chapter 17: “He secretly asked the emperor for an *evectio*.” The word denotes the provision of public transportation. Severus Sulpicius, book II of the *Sacred History*: “Hilary, having been granted the privilege of an *evectio*, is compelled to appear.”

Paulinus, book IV of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*:

“Tell what your swift conveyance, O King,

accomplishes when God delays.”

Symmachus, book I, letter 15: “I received four *evectiones*, extraordinarily convenient for the journeys out and back of my people.” The same author, book VII, letter 48: “It came about through your favor that we obtained the assistance of *evectiones*.” In the same book, letter 95: “If, therefore, you also bring this distinction—that the addition of grain allowances and *evectiones* be increased.” In the same book, letter 105: “Concerning the *evectiones* obtained as assistance for the praetorian office.” The same author, book IX, letter 20: “I appeal to your care so that they may be granted both speed of passage and the additional assistance of *evectiones*.” The word occurs frequently in the books of the jurists. See the *Legal Lexicon* of Barnabas Brissonius.

## EULOGIA

The *Life of Fronto*, chapter 9: “As though he were returning *eulogiai* to the Lord of all things.” Soon afterward: “And he distributed the same *eulogiai* to those in need.” Here *eulogiai* means provisions sent as a blessing. To give or send them to someone after the Masses was a sign of communion and charity. Gregory of Tours, book V of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 14: “After the Masses, he asked that we give him *eulogiai*.”

But the careful diligence of our Gretzer has ensured that I need add nothing further here about *Eulogia*. Consult his book *On the Blessing*.

## EXENIUM

The *Life of Antony*, chapter 27: “While everyone rejoiced at his arrival, Antony, as though bringing *xenia* from the mountain, imparted spiritual nourishment.” Here most manuscripts and the older editions have *exenia*. Is the prefixed *e-* derived from *xenion*?

[Col. 0444A] *Exenium* is otherwise a known word among other writers, though I do not know whether it has the same meaning. The Lombard Laws, book II, title 1, law 6: “If one of his friends, having received an *exenium*, gives something to the woman herself.” The Testament of Saint Remigius: “And the inhabitants of that place, burdened with many *exenia*, earnestly begging that what they owed the king be paid to my church, compelled me to ask for it.” Thus the manuscript reads, rather than the common text, *xeniis*. Balderic, book III of the *History of Jerusalem*: “Having prepared the body with whatever spices they could, they accompanied it with imperial *exenia*.” The old glosses: “*Exenium*: service.” Papias the Vocabularist: “*Exenium*: gift, service.” The manuscript Cambéron Glossary: “*Exenium*: honor, gift.”

Is *xenium* properly a gift or present in the familiar sense, while *exenium* means the service that a subject owes to a superior? Perhaps it is the same as what Anselm, canon of Liège, calls *soniaca* in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège and Utrecht*, chapter 40:

“He ordered that no one should presume to receive from the same place where the body of that saint rests the *soniaca* owed to the bishops of Liège.”

The learned scholiast John Chapeauville, perplexed by *soniaca*, interprets it as a provision owed to the bishops. I think it means a service owed to the bishop, or a fixed annual payment, which the French call *essogne*. See Francis Rageau’s *Index of Royal Rights*.

## FAUNI

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, section 8: “Those whom paganism, deceived by various errors, worships under the names Fauns, Satyrs, and Incubi.” For a substantial collection on the Fauns, see Lilius Gregorius Giraldus, *History of the Gods*, treatise 15, and Natalis Comes, *Mythology*, book V, chapter 9. See also our Conimbricenses, in book II of the *Physics*, chapter 9, question 5, article 3, where they ask whether human beings can be born from a human and an animal form. See also Delrio, *Magic*, volume I, book II, question 27, section 2.

## FRIGORETICI

See **TYPI**.

## FLABELLUM, ῥιπίδιον

Its use in sacred rites, where it was carried by deacons. The *Spiritual Meadow* of John Moschus, chapter 150: “Remove from the altar that deacon standing near me who holds the *flabellum*.” In Greek: Τὸν διάκονον τὸν κατέχοντα τὸ ῥιπίδιον.

Symeon of Thessalonica, *On the Divine Temple*, where he discusses the procession before Mass:

“For this reason the *omophorion* with the cross also goes before, signifying that Jesus and the sign shown from heaven will appear. These are immediately followed by the deacons, who represent the order of angels. This is also signified by the *flabella*, as they are called, which Saint Dionysius calls wings.”

Saint Germanus, in the *Theory of Ecclesiastical Matters*: “The *flabella* represent the type of the cherubim.”

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, letter 7:

“I have sent you a *flabellum*, namely, an instrument suitable for driving away flies. But you should also interpret it as part of our little gift. Consider, then, by what flies the priests sacrificing to the Lord are most grievously troubled, and by what they are frequently hindered in the saving duties of the altar. There are a thousand phantoms of thoughts that rush upon us, a thousand suggestions of the devil, a thousand temptations of human hearts.”

He adds:

“Therefore, when with the *flabellum* sent to you you have driven away the flies descending upon the sacrifices, you must also expel from the mind of the sacrificer, with the fan of catholic faith, the assaults of the temptations that come upon him.”

Jerome also relates the *muscaria* of matrons to this practice and explains them spiritually in letter 20, to Marcella:

“As for the fact that you also provide matrons with small *muscaria*, for fanning away small creatures, it is an elegant signification that luxury must be quickly extinguished, since dying flies destroy the fragrance of the oil.”

This practice was prefigured in the Church by what Abraham did. Hildebert likewise says:

“The patriarch Abraham prefigured the driving away of such swarms of flies when he drove away the birds attacking the sacrifices.”

These *flabella*, or *muscaria*, were made either of thin membranes, peacock feathers, or linen, as is stated in Clement, book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 12.

## FUNUS

Several funeral rites are noted in these *Lives*; I shall explain some of them more fully.

Among the Egyptians, the bodies of nobles and martyrs were wrapped in linen. The *Life of Antony*, chapter 57: “It is the custom of the Egyptians to wrap in linen the bodies of nobles, and especially of blessed martyrs.” Thus also of Christ’s body, John 11: “They bound him in linen cloths with spices.” The *Acts of the Martyr Abibus*, in Metaphrastes, 15 November: “They surrounded him with precious linen and anointed him with perfumes.”

Prudentius, hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*:

“It is customary to spread over them

linen cloths shining with bright whiteness.”

Eusebius, book VII, chapter 17, concerning Asterius’s devotion to the martyr Marinus:

“Having wrapped him very magnificently in the linen appropriate to him, he committed him to a fitting burial.”

In the same book, chapters 10 and 18, he calls those linen coverings *peristolai*. Jerome, letter 49, concerning a woman struck seven times: “The clerics whose duty this was wrapped the bloody corpse in linen.”

Indeed, it was a very ancient custom to wrap corpses in linen. Homer, *Iliad* Ψ, on the funeral of Patroclus:

Ἐν λεχέεσσι δὲ θέντες ἑανῷ λευκῷ κάλυψαν,  
Ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς, καθύπερθε δὲ φάρεϊ λευκῷ.

“Having placed him upon the bier, they covered him with fine linen,

from head to foot; and above him, with a white garment.”

The bodies of some people were also wrapped in gilded garments. The *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 14: “Why do you also wrap your dead in gilded garments?” Although Jerome there censures this vain custom of the world, more splendid adornment was nevertheless not rejected at the funerals of saints. Gregory of Nyssa, concerning his sister Macrina: “It will not now be thought objectionable if we add a more splendid adornment to the dead woman and clothe that pure and undefiled body in brighter garments.”

Eusebius, above:

“Asterius, a man from the number of the Roman senators, placing the body upon his shoulder, carried away the corpse of the martyr Marinus, having covered it with a splendid and costly garment.”

These practices of wrapping corpses in linen or adorning them with more splendid dress were maintained wherever circumstances permitted. Otherwise corpses were wrapped in whatever material was at hand. Thus, in the desert, the body of Paul the First Hermit was wrapped in a cloak. His *Life*, chapter 10: “Bring the cloak that Bishop Athanasius gave you, to wrap my little body.” A cloak was also placed over Macrina’s body, lest more splendid borrowed adornment offend the eyes of some. Gregory of Nyssa, in the *Life of Saint Macrina*.

That corpses were once accompanied and buried with psalms and hymns occurs very frequently in these *Lives of the Fathers*. On this Christian rite, see our Gretzer, *On Christian Burial*, chapter 5. Chrysostom gives the following reason why hymns and psalms were sung at funerals, in homily 4 on the Epistle to the Hebrews:

“Why, then, the hymns? Is it not that we glorify God and give him thanks because he has now crowned the departed person, because he has freed him from labors, because he has driven away his fear and keeps him with himself? Is it not for this that there are hymns? Is it not for this that there is psalmody? All these things belong to those who rejoice.”

Much more could be added here, but our Jacobus Gretzer has already treated the matter in a special book, *On Christian Burial*.

## GABBARA

See what is said about these in the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 57, where Athanasius describes them and Augustine gives the name. The word is known to few. Pliny, book VII, chapter 16: “Our own age, under the deified emperor Claudius, saw the tallest man, brought from Arabia, named Gabbara, nine feet tall and as many inches.” Solinus copies this, chapter 5: “Do not suppose that Gabbara is the proper name of a man. All embalmed corpses were so called.”

Isidore’s glosses: “*Galbares*: embalmed bodies of the dead.” Read *gabbares* or *gabbara*. The same glossary: “*Gabarus*: tasteless, barbarous; hence *gabares*, embalmed corpses.” Papias: “*Gabbari*: enclosed barbarians. Hence *gabbares*: embalmed bodies of the dead.” Here read “tasteless, barbarous.” Thus also in the manuscript Cambéron Glossary: “*Gabator* or *gabitor* is a jocular man.” In German, *gabberen* means “to laugh, to jest.”

## GALILAEI

Thus Christians were once called contemptuously. The *Life of Epictetus and Astion*, chapter 7: “And you stole it from the Galilaeans.” The mother of Astion laments.

Lucian, in the *Philopatris*, speaking of Saint Paul:

“When that Galilaean encountered me—that bald, aquiline-nosed man who traveled through the air as far as the third heaven.”

On this passage, see Baronius, volume I, under the year 68 of Christ.

Julian, *Misopogon*:

“Did the Emisenes love Christ, those who set fire to the tombs of the Galilaeans?”

The same work shortly afterward:

“But now each of you allows his wife to carry everything from within to the Galilaeans.”

The same author, letter 33, to Aetius, bishop and heresiarch:

“As for all the others who had been exiled by the late Constantius because of the madness of the Galilaeans, I have remitted their exile.”

The same author, letter 7, to Artabius:

“I swear by the gods that I do not wish the Galilaeans to be killed, beaten contrary to justice and fairness, or suffer any other harm.”

Theodoret, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 7:

“And first he forbade the children of the Galilaeans—for this is what he called the worshipers of our Savior—to study poetry, rhetoric, or philosophy.”

Chrysostom, in his homily on the holy hieromartyr Babylas, speaking of Julian’s fury:

“He promised that he would tear the nation of the Galilaeans out of the midst of the inhabited world.”

So hateful was the name “Christians” to Julian that he established by edict that no one should call them Christians, but Galilaeans. Chrysostom, in his *Oration against the Gentiles*:

“Calling us Galilaeans instead of Christians in his edicts, and urging the rulers to do the same.”

Gregory Nazianzen, oration 3 against Julian:

“Calling us Galilaeans instead of Christians and legislating that we should be called by that name.”

## GALLICA

The *Life of Malchus*, chapter 4, concerning the Ishmaelites: “Dragging cloaks and broad *calliculae*.” The Audomarus manuscript has *gallicas*. I do not know whether *gallica* should be taken indiscriminately for *caliga*. Tertullian, in his poem to a senator who had become an Egyptian idolater and, from consul, a priest of Isis, seems to distinguish the terms:

“Now you also say that it was not your age

but your religion that made you bald, and that, once the *caliga* was removed,

a *gallica* bound your feet with soft papyrus.”

The passage must be distinguished in this way. Pamelius, who joins *gallica* with *caliga* and thinks that the *a* in *gallica* is shortened here, was mistaken. The meaning is that this senator, having abandoned Roman dress—including the *caligae*, from which Tertullian calls military service *caligata* in book 19 of *On Idolatry*—adopted the Egyptian dress of an Isiac priest, namely, a *gallica* wrapped around the feet in soft papyrus. I therefore think that *gallica* means a *soccus*, since it was soft.

Certainly Apuleius, in the *Milesian Tales*, book 8, attributes yellow shoes to the Galli, devotees of Cybele and Isis: “Their feet were clad in yellow shoes.” Catullus attributes yellow *socci* to the wedding Hymenaeus, because yellow or saffron is the color of love:

“Joyfully come hither,

come hither wearing

a yellow *soccus* on your snow-white foot.”

Bayfius thinks that *gallicae* are what the French call *galoches*.

[Col. 0448A] That they were a kind of footwear may be inferred from Cicero, *Philippic* 2: “As for what you asked, how I had returned: first, in daylight, not at night; then with shoes and a toga, and with neither *gallicae* nor a cloak.” Soon afterward, concerning Antony: “You ran about with *gallicae* and a cloak.” In both places the manuscripts read *gallicis* rather than *caligis*. Gellius, book XIII, chapter 20, relates that Titus Castritius reproached senators who wore cloaks and were shod with *gallicae*. He immediately interprets the latter by *soleati*. The manuscript Cambéron Glossary: “*Gallicula*: footwear of shepherds.” The same appears in Papias.

In Suidas, γάλλιξ is used for a cloak: “*Allica*: a cloak among the Thessalians; ordinary people call this cloak *gallica*.” Certainly in the *Life of Malchus*, *pallium* and *gallica* are joined together.

## GELLO, or GILLO

Rufinus, book III, no. 14: “He would turn over the *gello* containing the water that he had prepared for his drink.” Soon afterward, in the same section, it is called *gellunculus*. In Pelagius, no. 24, the corresponding word is *suriscula*. Cassian, *Institutes*, book IV, chapter 16: “If anyone accidentally breaks a clay *gillo*, which they call a *baucalis*.” Chapter 20: “If they fill the *gillo* with water.”

Isidore’s glosses: “*Gellon*: a *baucalis*.” The Latin-Greek Glossary: “*Gillo*: βαυκάλιον.” Also: “ποδόκοιλον, water vessel, *gello*.” The manuscript Cambéron Glossary: “*Gillo*: a clay vessel, that is, a *baucalis*.” Papias: “*Gelonis*: a *baucalis*, a vessel.” Hence in the Visigothic Laws, book II, title 4, law 4, “superintendents of the *gillonarii*.” The Spanish now call it a *congilon*, the Italians a *boccale*.

Among the *Catalecta* of the ancient poets, book II, there is a poem on the depiction of the months:

“August is thoroughly scorched by the heat of Phaethon,

which the *gillo*, the torch, and the melon refresh when he is weary.”

## GENUFLEXION

This rite of prayer occurs frequently in these *Lives of the Fathers*. I shall now touch on three matters: its antiquity, when kneeling was forbidden, and how frequently some people practiced genuflection.

It is an extremely ancient custom of the Church to kneel in prayer. The Scriptures teach that every knee must bend before the Lord: Psalm 21, Isaiah 45, Romans 14, Philippians 2, and Ephesians 3. Christ too is said to have prayed by falling upon the ground, in Luke 23. Eusebius, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 5, reports that the soldiers, “in the battle formation against the enemy, having placed their knees upon the ground, turned to offer supplications to God, according to the custom familiar to us in prayer.” Jerome, on Isaiah 45: “It is the ecclesiastical custom to bend the knee to Christ. The Jews, displaying the pride of their mind, do not do this at all.”

By bending the knees we obtain more effectively what we ask. Justin, question 115, *To the Orthodox*:

“The bending of the knee in prayers commends those who pray to God more than praying while standing, and it draws divine compassion more powerfully.”

Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chapter 4: “When have even droughts not been driven away by our kneelings and fasts?” The same author, *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 18:

“Why, then, did Moses pray with outstretched hands while sitting only when Jesus was fighting against Amalek? In such an alarming situation, he should surely have commended his prayer more by placing his knees on the ground, beating his breast with his hands, and rolling his face upon the earth.”

Ambrose, book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 9:

“The pliant knee, by which the Lord’s offense is above all appeased, anger soothed, and grace summoned. For this is the gift of the supreme Father toward the Son: that every knee should bend in the name of Jesus.”

Augustine, in *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 5:

“For when we pray, we do with the members of our body what is appropriate for those who make supplication: we fix our knees, stretch out our hands, or even prostrate ourselves on the ground, and perform whatever else we visibly do. Although our invisible will and the intention of our heart are known to God, and he has no need of these signs in order that the human mind may be disclosed to him, a person nevertheless stimulates himself by these actions to pray and groan more humbly and fervently. And somehow, since these bodily movements cannot occur without a movement of the mind preceding them, that inner and invisible movement, which produced them, is again increased by the same visible actions performed outwardly. Thus the affection of the heart, which preceded these actions so that they might occur, grows because they have occurred.”

Jerome, on Ephesians 3:

“When we interpret these things spiritually, we do not immediately abolish, according to the letter, the custom of prayer by which we humbly worship God with the knee bent and, with the knee fixed upon the ground, obtain more effectively what we ask of him. For we read that Paul also prayed in this way on the shore, and that kneeling in prayer was commanded.”

Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, Paschal letter 2, against Origen: “To bend the knee is an indication of an anxious and most humble mind.”

But when the knee is bent, the mind too must be bent—namely, the inward knees; otherwise outward genuflection is of little benefit. Jerome, on Ephesians 3:

“But just as this builds up the simple, so we teach that there is a true genuflection in the mind, because many who bend the bodily knee have in no way bent the knee of their soul; and, conversely, others who pray to God with their bodies upright have bent themselves more deeply in spirit.”

See him discussing in the same place how sinners bend their knees to sin.

And indeed this rite was observed in prayer throughout the whole year, except on Sundays and during the period between Easter and Pentecost. See here, Book IV, chapter 19, from Book II of Cassian’s *Institutes*, chapter 11. Council of Nicaea, canon 20:

“Since there are some who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed similarly in every parish, it has seemed good to the holy synod that prayers be offered to God while standing.”

The same ruling is repeated in the Sixth Council of Carthage, canon 20. It is also found in the canon beginning “Since,” *On Consecration*, distinction 3. Tertullian, *On the Military Crown*, chapter 3:

“On the Lord’s Day we consider it unlawful either to fast or to worship on our knees; we enjoy the same exemption from Easter until Pentecost.”

Hilary, in the prologue to his exposition of the Psalms:

“These Sabbaths of Sabbaths were indeed celebrated by the apostles with such religious observance that during these fifty days no one worshiped with his body prostrate on the ground, nor did he interrupt by fasting the festival of this spiritual blessedness. The same rule was also established externally for the Lord’s Days, which, through the fullness of evangelical preaching, are added beyond the number of the Sabbath.”

Jerome, in the preface to his letter to Paula and Eustochium on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

“He remained at Ephesus until Pentecost: a time of joy and victory, when we do not bend our knees or bow down to the earth, but, rising with the Lord, are lifted up to the heights of heaven.”

The same author, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, chapter 4:

“On the Lord’s Day and throughout Pentecost, neither to worship on one’s knees nor to fast, along with many other practices not written down, has been claimed by reasonable observance for itself.”

Ambrose, Sermon 61, *On Pentecost*, which is also found among the works of Maximus of Turin:

“Your holiness ought to know how we observe this holy day of Pentecost, and why the number of these fifty days is for us a continual and uninterrupted festival: so that throughout this whole period we neither prescribe fasts for observance nor cut down our knees to entreat God; but, as we customarily do on the Lord’s Day, standing upright and keeping festival, we celebrate the Lord’s resurrection.”

Augustine, Letter 119, chapter 15:

“Fifty days are celebrated after the Lord’s resurrection, now symbolizing not labor but rest and joy. For this reason fasts are relaxed and we pray standing, which is a sign of the resurrection. Hence this practice is also observed at the altar on all the Lord’s Days.”

And in chapter 17:

“But whether it is observed everywhere that we pray standing during those days of Pentecost and on all the Lord’s Days, I do not know. Nevertheless, I have stated, as I was able, what the Church follows in this matter, and I think it is clear.”

The reason for this change is given by Justin in the question and answer cited above:

“Our kneeling during the six days is a symbol of our falling through sins. But not bending the knee on the Lord’s Day is a symbol of the resurrection, through which, by the grace of Christ, we have been freed both from sins and from the death that had been inflicted upon us on account of them, etc. During Pentecost we do not bend the knee, because it is equal in dignity to the Lord’s Day, according to the reason stated concerning that day.”

Basil investigates the mystery here still more deeply, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27:

“It is therefore necessary that on this day the Church teach her children to complete their prayers while standing, so that by the continual remembrance of the life that will never end we may not neglect to prepare provisions for that departure. Indeed, the whole period of Pentecost is a reminder of the resurrection that we await in the age to come. For that one first day, multiplied seven times seven, completes the seven weeks of the sacred Pentecost. Beginning from the first day, it ends at the beginning, unfolding fifty times through corresponding days intervening in the middle. Hence by its likeness it represents eternity, as though in a circular movement it began from the same points and ended at the same points. In this period the customs of the Church have trained us to prefer the upright posture of prayer, clearly reminding us and, as it were, transferring our mind from present things to future things. Moreover, whenever we kneel and rise again, we show by the very act that through sin we fell down to the earth, and through the loving-kindness of him who created us we have been summoned back to heaven.”

The same teaching is repeated in Anastasius of Nicaea, *Questions on Sacred Scripture*, question 91. Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, in *Theoria of Ecclesiastical Matters*:

“Not bending the knee on the resurrection-day of the holy Lord’s Day signifies the restoration of our fall, accomplished through Christ’s three-day resurrection. Not bending the knee until Pentecost means that the seven days after holy Easter are multiplied by seven and are completed in the feast of Pentecost: seven times seven makes forty-nine, and with the Lord’s Day added, fifty.”

See also the writers on ecclesiastical offices: Isidore, Book I of *The Offices*, chapter 33; Rabanus, Book II of *On the Institution of the Clergy*, chapter 44; and others; likewise Turrecremata, in the passage of the *Decree* cited above.

The origin of this practice, or change, is referred to apostolic times by Justin, question 115, *To the Orthodox*:

“This custom took its beginning from the times of the apostles, as the blessed Irenaeus, martyr and bishop of Lyons, says in his book *On Easter*.”

As for the fact that Paul is read in Acts 20 as having prayed on his knees during the period between Easter and Pentecost, Baronius, in volume I, under the year of Christ 58, thinks that the custom of not worshiping on one’s knees during that period had not yet become established, but did so shortly afterward. Our Lorinus, in his commentary on that passage, thinks that there is no obstacle to supposing that the practice had already been adopted at that time, though in public and solemn prayers. The prayers poured out on the shore of Tyre do not seem to have been of that kind.

[Col. 0452B] That certain holy men frequently practiced kneeling is evident either from excavated floor slabs or from hardened knees. Concerning a slab hollowed out by kneeling, see John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 185. Concerning the hardened knees of Saint James, Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 2:

“He prayed for the people with his knees bent, to such an extent that his knees were believed to have acquired the hardness of camels.”

The same author, Letter 15 to Marcella, *On the Praises of Asella*:

“Her eyes saw that, through the frequency of prayer, the hardness of camel knees had become calloused upon that holy little body.”

## GRUTARIA

Palladius, *Lausiac History*, from the old translator, chapter 9, concerning Macarius of Alexandria:

“Another was selling *grutaria*.”

Heraclides, chapter 6, simply has: “He was a merchant.” The manuscripts, however, add: “who sold fruit, vegetables, and nuts.” Palladius, in Hervetus’s translation, has: “who sold confections.” The Greek is τραγήματα, “dainties” or “confections.” Perhaps another text had γροῦττα or γρῦτα, from which the old translator of Palladius made *grutaria*. This is supported by the Greek-Barbarous Glosses:

“Ἀναγηστὶς, μάζα, σημηδία, γροῦτα, παννάδα” — “*anagestis*, cake, *semedia*, *gruta*, *pannada*.”

Likewise: “Ἰδέα σημηδίας, ἢ γρούτας” — “a kind of *semedia*, or *gruta*.”

The Latin-Greek Lexicon has: “*Crusta*, γρῦτα”—“crust, *gruta*.” In the Greek-Latin Lexicon one finds: “Γρύτη, *scruta*”—“scraps.” This agrees with what Hesychius says under Γρυμναία: he states that small utensils are called γρύτη; and in the same author: “Γρύται, σκεύη”—“*grytai*, utensils.” Likewise: “Γρυτεύεται, παρασκευάζεται”—“it is prepared.”

## HEBDOMON

See **SEPTIMUM**.

## HEBDOMADARII

See **SEPTIMANARII**.

## HEMIPHORIUM

Palladius, chapter 119, concerning the younger Melania, in Hervetus’s translation:

“She gave all her silk shoulder-coverings to the altars.”

The Greek reads:

“Πάντα αὐτῆς τὰ σηρικὰ ἡμιφόρια καλύμματα τοῖς θυσιαστηρίοις ἐδωρήσατο.”

“She gave all her silk *hemiphoria*, or coverings, to the altars.”

Epiphanius, *Against the Ariomanites*, concerning Arius:

“Ἡμιφόριον ἀεὶ καὶ κολοβιῶνα ἐνδιδυσκόμενος, γλυκὺς ἦν τῇ προσηγορίᾳ.”

“Always wearing a *hemiphorium* and a *colobium*, Arius was pleasant in conversation.”

Hesychius glosses ἡμιφάριον as ἥμισυ ἱματίου, “half of a garment”: *hemipharium*, a half or divided garment. It seems that Hervetus read ὠμοφόρια in Palladius and translated it as “shoulder-coverings.” But since a *hemiphorium* was merely a half-garment, it perhaps covered only the head and a little beyond the shoulders. In that sense it could also be called an ὠμοφόριον, a shoulder-garment.

## HEMITRITAEUS

*Life of Hilarion*, no. 14:

“All were simultaneously seized by the semitertian fever, and the physicians despaired of them.”

This is a semitertian fever. The Greek word ἡμιτριταῖος was adopted by Latin writers. Martial, Book II, epigram 40:

“Tongilius is said to be severely ill with a hemitritaeus.”

The same author, Book IV, epigram 81:

“You declaim while ill; you declaim with a hemitritaeus.”

The same author, Book XII, epigram 92:

“He who was suffering from a severe and burning hemitritaeus.”

Celsus, Book III, chapter 3. Likewise chapter 8:

“But when it is that kind of tertian fever which physicians call hemitritaeus, great care is needed lest it deceive us.”

Latin physicians retained this Greek word, either because it could not conveniently be expressed in Latin or because they preferred to use the Greek term. Quintus Serenus Sammonicus, while suggesting a superstitious remedy against this fever, writes:

“What is more deadly is what in Greek is called *Hemitritaeus*.

“None of our ancestors, I think, could or wished

“To express it in our language, or write upon a tablet

“What is called *Abracadabra*.”

## HIPPOCENTAURUS

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, no. 7:

“He saw a human being joined to a horse, to whom the belief of the poets gave the name Hippocentaur.”

I will not collect here the passages of authors concerning Hippocentaurs. I refer the reader to those who discuss them at length. Among the ancient writers, see especially Phlegon in his *Wonders*. Among the more recent, Jerome Magius, Book I, chapter 20 of his *Miscellanies*; Franciscus Sabinus, Book II, chapter 6 of his *Floridum*; and Covarruvias, Book IV, chapter 2 of his *Various Resolutions*.

## JERUSALEM PILGRIMAGE

Frequent mention of this pilgrimage occurs in the *Lives of the Fathers* from ancient times. Jerome, Letter 17 to Marcella:

“It would take too long now to pass through the individual generations from the Lord’s ascension to the present day and enumerate which bishops, which martyrs, and which men eloquent in ecclesiastical teaching came to Jerusalem, thinking that they possessed less religion and less knowledge, and had not received, so to speak, the finishing touch of virtue, unless they had worshiped Christ in those places from which the Gospel first flashed forth from the cross.”

The same author, preface to Book IV of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*:

“Occupied by the many crowds flowing here from the whole world, and by the concerns of the holy brothers and the monastery, I dictated my commentaries on Jeremiah at intervals, so that what was lacking in leisure might be supplied by diligence.”

## IGNOSCE

Συγχώρησον — “Forgive me.”

This was a very common expression among the hermits and occurs extremely often in these *Lives*. Sozomen noted it, Book VIII, chapter 17:

“Yet the monks, being disturbed and thinking that this certainly ought to be done, while many bishops presided, said the customary expression among them, even when they were being wronged: ‘Forgive me.’”

[Note: Consult the note appended to page 55 of the preceding volume. EDITOR.]

The French say *pardonne-moi*, “forgive me.” It seems that the custom passed into courtly usage when people offered cups to one another, or even received a cup from another’s hand. Pelagius, Book XV, no. 20:

“When Abba Theodore ate with the brothers, they received the cups with reverence and silence, nor did they say, as is customary, ‘Forgive me.’”

## IMMAE

*Life of Malchus*, no. 3:

“At last I reached the desert of Chalcis, which lies between Immae and Beroea, farther toward the south.”

Immae is a city of Syria, near which lies the desert of Chalcis. Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, year 2 of Aurelian:

“Zenobia was defeated at Immae, not far from Antioch.”

Jordanes, *On the Succession of Kingdoms*, under Aurelian:

“Undertaking an expedition against her—that is, against the wife of Odaenathus—Aurelian defeated her at the village of Immae near Antioch.”

## INCARDUUM

The pith of a palm. John, Book I, no. 6:

“There is, however, one *incarduum* in the palm, and it is white.”

I believe the word comes from the Greek ἐγκάρδιον. Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 150, discussing the *elate* palm:

“But the pith of the trunk is also white, and, whether eaten fresh or boiled, it is effective for the same purposes as the *barassus*.”

Dioscorides calls the pith or core of the trunk ἐγκάρδιον, “little heart.” See Janus Antonius Saracenus there, and Dalechamp, on Book XIII, chapter 4 of Pliny, where he discusses the brain, or ἐγκέφαλον, of the palm. Janus Saracenus nevertheless shows that this is distinct from the ἐγκάρδιον. Thus the *anakardion* is said to have received its name as an Indian tree from a fruit resembling a little bird’s heart. See Gorræus.

## INCENTIVUM

*Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 15:

“The incitements of slippery flesh.”

Saint Jerome frequently uses this word. Thus, Letter 4 to Rusticus:

“And trampling upon the incitements of youth—or rather, of puberty.”

Likewise:

“While you trample upon the incitements of youth.”

In the same letter:

“I could not endure the incitements of vices and the heat of nature.”

The same author, Letter 2 to Nepotian:

“The incitements of vices.”

On Isaiah 58:

“The heat of the body overcame me; the incitements of youth prevailed.”

On Ezekiel 16:

“With this linen the loins are girded whenever the rich incitements of lust must be restrained, so that no thick humor remains in them.”

Soon afterward in the same place:

“Which supply the incitements of vices.”

Again:

“The light prick of the senses and the incitements of vices.”

Likewise:

“The incitements of this world.”

The same author, on Ezekiel 33:

“Let him not receive every incitement of his thoughts.”

On Matthew 4:

“To supply the incitements of vices.”

Likewise in the same chapter, 15:

“The devil’s incitement.”

In the commentary on Galatians 6:

“Through each eye of agitation and the incitements of vices.”

The same word is used in the same sense by other authors. Ambrose, Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 4:

“The incitements of hatred.”

In the same author, Psalm 118, and Sermon 15:

“The incitements of sins.”

Cassian, *Conferences*, II, chapter 13:

“The goads of incitements.”

The same author, *Conferences*, VII, chapter 1:

“To be disturbed by natural incitements.”

And chapter 2:

“Behold, the incitements of your flesh have been cut away.”

These two latter passages may be found above, Book IV of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 50. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*:

“The incitement of sin.”

Sidonius, Book VI, Letter 1:

“Nor, inflamed by the incitements of carnal vices, shall we continue to kindle another’s fire upon the Lord’s altar.”

Sometimes the word is taken in another sense. Arnobius, Book VI:

“You exalt yourselves by the incitement of praise.”

Cyprian, *On the Praise of Martyrdom*:

“The reward as an incitement.”

## INCHORIS

John the Subdeacon, Book VI of the *Lives of the Fathers*, Book I, no. 12:

“He had two brothers as neighbors, one a foreigner and one *inchoris*,” from the Greek ἐγχωρής. For χώρα means “region,” hence ἐγχωρής, “one who always remains in his own region,” in opposition to a foreigner.

Saint Ambrose, Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 14, uses *enchorius*:

“There are also other kinds of birds that are *enchoria*, which always remain in the same places; others are migratory, which visit other regions and return when winter is over.”

Thus the Greeks call something ἐπιχώριον when it is characteristic of a particular region or place. Saint Jerome, Letter 140:

“For what we translated as ‘in ivory houses,’ since the Greek has ἀπὸ βαρειῶν ἐλεφαντίνων, some Latins, because of the ambiguity of the word, translated ‘from heavy things.’ But βάρεις is a local word of Palestine, and even today enclosed houses, constructed in the manner of towers and public walls, are called βάρεις.”

## INCUBI

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, no. 8:

“Deceived by various errors, the pagans worship them, calling them Fauns, Satyrs, and Incubi.”

Martin Delrio, our author, discusses Incubi at length in his commentary on Seneca’s *Hercules Furens*, part III, and in his *Magical Investigations*, Book II, question 15.

## JOHN CHRYSOSTOM

John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 128, relates a certain revelation or vision concerning the glory of John Chrysostom above all the teachers of the Church. Baronius severely criticizes this account in volume V, under the year of Christ 407, the sixth year of Pope Innocent, and the thirteenth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius:

“These things are not very secure in credibility, since they are first of all convicted of falsehood by the testimony of John Chrysostom himself (*Chrysostom, Letter 126*), when the account identifies Treius as bishop of Arabissus, rather than Adelphius.”

Moreover, when the author states that John was received as a guest in the house of Adelphius after he had been sent into exile at Cucusus, he is plainly convicted of error. For although Leo and Metaphrastes say the same thing about his lodging at Cucusus, Chrysostom himself, in Letter 13, expressly relates that he was received as a guest by Dioscorus, and not by anyone else, although many had sought that honor. If this account is mingled with such falsehoods, what credibility can the rest possess?

Certainly that envious assertion is also excessive: to place all who have ever been teachers in the Church on a lower level and set Chrysostom above them all, especially since several of them were crowned with martyrdom, among them Hippolytus and Methodius—not to mention the other saints who died without bloodshed, namely Basil, the two Gregories, the Thaumaturge and the Theologian, and the great Athanasius, who should without envy be preferred to all the rest.

And what of that irrational distinction by which all the teachers are said to have been visible to the eyes of the one who saw them, while John alone was invisible because of his outstanding glory—as though Chrysostom alone among the teachers had attained perfect glory? But let these matters now be dismissed; the saints do not need to be glorified by our falsehoods, since they are adorned by their own virtues. Thus far Baronius.

A certain annotator—I do not know whether he was our Fronto—in the Paris Greek-Latin edition of John Moschus thought that the matter could be moderated in this way:

“Nevertheless, we also point out that revelations of this kind sometimes occur not to display the greater glory of a particular saint in every respect, but to indicate some outstanding and distinctive prerogative of a blessed person by which he excelled others. Such was the zeal for justice that burned so intensely in Chrysostom’s heart that, for this reason, he was rightly said in the divine vision to stand beside the throne of God. A vision of this kind was that which was granted to Saint Peter of the Dominican Order. When he saw religious persons of various orders in heaven, he saw none of his own pupils; yet the holy Mother of God, concealing them beneath her mantle through an extraordinary and singular favor, afterward showed them to him.

“Furthermore, the name Treius could easily have slipped into Chrysostom’s letter in place of Adelphius, or Treius Adelphius may have been a person with two names. Finally, why must the word ‘remained’ necessarily refer to lodging? It is plausible that Chrysostom visited the bishop’s house.”

This was the annotator’s defense of a book otherwise possessing excellent authority.

If I may venture an opinion among such great men, I would judge that nothing about the glory of John Chrysostom was divinely indicated here; rather, the response concerned the prerogative of John the Baptist. For divine providence usually either never or rarely gives inquisitive or contentious people a precise answer about the relative prerogative of the saints. Instead, it either gives a general answer, preferring the dignity of none of those about whom the dispute has arisen, or satisfies them in some other way. It appears that John Chrysostom, about whom the question had been raised, was passed over, while the rank and glory of John the Baptist—who is properly the leader of repentance—were introduced incidentally.

For although Adelphius’s request was clear, the response or manifestation was not. The first guide did not satisfy his wish. He had asked to be shown John Chrysostom, but the guide showed him other teachers. Thus he departed sadly without seeing his own John, whose glory he desired to behold. But when the doorkeeper saw him sad and recognized that curiosity was involved, he turned from John Chrysostom to John the Baptist:

“Ἰωάννην τὸν τῆς μετανοίας λέγεις;”

“Do you mean John, the leader of repentance?”

The Greek response follows abruptly, without the questioner interjecting:

“Ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνον ἐν σαρκὶ οὐ δύναται αὐτὸν ἰδεῖν· ἐκεῖ γὰρ περίσταται ὅπου ὁ θρόνος δεσποτικός.”

“A human being living in the flesh cannot see him; for there he stands where the Lord’s throne is.”

This applies to Saint John the Baptist, concerning whom the Truth itself bears witness that no one greater has arisen among those born of women. Christ also restrained the disciples when they asked about precedence in the kingdom of heaven, leaving them uncertain.

Thus Thomas à Kempis rightly advises, Book III of *The Imitation of Christ*, chapter 58:

“Do not inquire or dispute about the merits of the saints—who is holier than another, or who was greater in the kingdom of heaven. Such things displease the saints.”

## IRENARCHA

An *irenarch* is a prince of peace, one who is responsible for peace in the provinces, a peacemaker. Palladius, chapter 116:

“As a certain irenarch was passing by, he recognized the old man.”

Justinian, *Code*, Book X, title 75:

“Irenarchs, who are appointed throughout the individual territories to maintain concord for the protection, tranquility, and peace of the provinces, are to be nominated by the decurions with the judgment of the provincial governors as suitable persons.”

Michael Syngellus, in his encomium of Dionysius the Areopagite, calls Christ an irenarch:

“Ὁ ὄντως ἀρχιποίμην καὶ εἰρηνάρχης Χριστὸς παρὰ πάντων ὁμοφρόνως δοξάζοιτο.”

“May Christ, truly the chief shepherd and irenarch, be glorified by all with one accord.”

## TO SWEAR BY THE EMPEROR’S HEAD

Palladius, chapter 3:

“By the head of the emperor, whom you fear.”

The Greek is:

“Τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βασιλέως σου, ὃν σὺ φοβῇ.”

Potamiaena added “whom you fear,” because it was customary among pagans to swear by the emperor’s head. See Lipsius’s commentary on Tacitus, *Annals*, Book I. Otherwise, swearing by the guardian spirits of the emperors was unlawful. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 32:

“But we also swear—not by the guardian spirits of the Caesars, but by their safety.”

See our Cerdanus’s excellent commentary there.

## LACTORONES

Rufinus, Book III, no. 200:

“And one carried nuts, another *lactorones*.”

When I was writing the notes on this passage, I had not yet encountered that word; it appeared to me only later. Pliny, Book XXIV, chapter 18:

“The wool-bearing plant, given to fasting sheep, produces an abundance of milk. There is likewise a plant commonly known as *lactoris*, full of milk, which, when tasted, induces vomiting. Some say that this is the same plant; others say it resembles the one called *militaris*, because, applied from oil, it heals every wound made by iron within five days.”

## LAMINAE

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, no. 3:

“Victorious amid the torture-horses and *laminae*.”

These require a fuller treatment. In the meantime, consult Gallonius’s book *On Instruments of Torture*, chapter 6.

## SQUARED STONES

Palladius, chapters 19 and 20, concerning the tomb of Jannes and Mambres:

“They built that structure from squared stones.”

The Greek is:

“Ἐκ τετραπέδων λίθων ἔκτισαν τὸ ἔργον ἐκεῖνο.”

Hervetus translated this: “from stones four feet in length,” as though the word were τετραπόδων, or as though the stones were four-footed. Heraclides has: “They built the aforesaid structure with squared stones.” Another old translator has: “They therefore built the structure from square stones.”

Thus Isaiah 9:10: “We shall build with squared stones.” And Lamentations 3:9: “He enclosed my ways with squared stones.” 2 Chronicles 34:2:

“Ἔδωκαν ἀγοράσαι λίθοις τετραπέδοις.”

“They gave [for] purchasing squared stones.”

This is not as Kircher explains it in his Greek index, namely, “stones four feet long.” Squared stones may be four, fourteen, or forty feet long. In Hebrew the expression means “stones of hewing,” or “hewn stones.” Fronto.

## LAPSANUM

*Life of Pachomius*, chapter 8:

“For they were accustomed to eat *lapsana*, that is, wild vegetables and other herbs, without oil.”

In these books wild vegetables frequently occur, called λαψάναι in the Greek text. Pliny, Book XX, chapter 11:

“Among the wild cabbages there is also the *lapsana*, a foot high, with hairy leaves resembling those of the turnip, except that its flower is whiter.”

Pliny also mentions it in Book XIX, chapter 8, where the soldiers reproach their commander that they lived on *lapsana* near Dyrrhachium.

## LEBITON, LEBETON, LEBITONARIUM, LEVITIO

In the *Life of Onuphrius*, chapter 16, the words “Then I tore the tunic in half” are, in Greek, λεβιτονάριον. The translator of Metaphrastes retained the word in Onuphrius as *lebitonarium*, as did many other translators.

*Life of Pachomius*, chapter 14:

“So that they would never wear another *lebiton*.”

An explanation is added:

“A *lebiton* was a linen garment resembling a *colobium*, which the monks use even today throughout the Thebaid and Egypt.”

And in chapter 22:

“Let them put on linen *lebitons* at night.”

In the Greek text of Palladius, chapter 38, this reads:

“ἐν ταῖς νυξὶ λεβετῶνας λινοὺς ἐζωσμένοι.”

“Having girded themselves at night with linen *lebetons*.”

John, Book III, no. 10:

“But afterward that brother threw off the *levitio*.”

Paschasius, chapter 12, no. 8:

“Therefore, clothed in his *lebeton*,”

which was the proper garment of monks. The old Glosses have:

“*Levitonarium*: a linen sleeveless *colobarium*.”

Suidas:

“Λεβητωνάριον, χιτὼν μοναχικὸς ἐκ τριχῶν συντεθειμένος.”

“A monastic garment made of hair.”

## LENTICULA

See **ZIPPULAE**.

## LETHE

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 25:

“And descending into Persia, he was shut up in a prison called Lethe, that is, Oblivion.”

In the later period, there was evidently a prison among the Persians called Lethe, into which no one was thrown except someone destined for capital punishment. Procopius, Book I of *The Persian War*, writes:

“Οἱ δὲ κτεῖναι ἄνδρα βασιλείου αἵματος οὐδ᾽ ὅλως ἔγνωσαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν φρουρίῳ καθεῖρξαι, ὅπερ τῆς Λήθης καλεῖν ἐνενομίκασιν. Ἦν γάρ τις ἐνταῦθα ἐμβληθεὶς τύχῃ, οὐκέτι νόμος σφίσι μνήμην αὐτοῦ εἶναι· ἀλλὰ θάνατος τῷ ὠνομακότι ἡ ζημία ἐστίν· διὸ δὴ καὶ τὴν ἐπωνυμίαν ταύτην πρὸς Περσῶν ἔλαχε.”

“They did not at all consider it lawful to kill a man of royal blood, but to confine him in a fortress which they had decided to call Lethe. For if anyone happened to be thrown into it, their law no longer allowed any memory of him to remain; rather, the penalty for anyone who named him was death. Hence it acquired this designation among the Persians.”

[Note: It was clearly necessary to write ἦν, with a grave accent, and to interpret the whole passage in this way: “For if anyone should be cast into this prison, the law allows no memory of him to remain; rather, it threatens death or a penalty for anyone who mentions his name; hence, and so forth.” Everyone can see how absurd the interpretation admitted by Rosweydus is. EDITOR.]

“Once, however, Armenian history says that Persian power was dissolved by the law concerning the fortress of Lethe, in the following manner.” [The reading is perhaps παραλῦσαι rather than παραλῦσθαι.]

Paul the Deacon, *History*, Book XVII:

“In Persia there is a prison called Lethe, in which the king of the Persians confined many people from different nations, together with the captives of the city of Dara.”

## GOLDEN BUNDLE

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 7:

“He gives me a golden bundle of one hundred coins.”

I scarcely doubt that the Greek had ἀπόδεσμος; certainly this is how it appears in Metaphrastes. Curopalates, *On the Offices of the Imperial Court at Constantinople*, explains what these bundles were when discussing the missiles, or *epicombia*, customarily thrown to the crowd:

“It is as follows. Pieces are cut from cloth, and in each piece they tie three gold coins, an equal number of silver coins, and three obol-coins, and throw them into the crowd. They throw such bundles, or packets, in a number corresponding to however many thousands the emperor has ordered.”

## TO LAY OUT A BOUNDARY  
[According to Vallarsius: **TO LAY OUT A LINE**]

*Life of Hilarion*, no. 25:

“They did not allow him to depart before he had laid out the boundary of the future church.”

This is the reading of the very oldest manuscripts, and it appears to be the correct one. Another reading has “to send a line.” Both expressions are taken from writers on the regulation of boundaries.

Hyginus, *On Establishing Boundaries*:

“And some, lest they lay out established boundaries along the boundaries of neighboring colonies.”

Ovid, Book III of the *Amores*, elegy 7:

“Nor did anyone cleave the earth with a strong plow,

“Nor did the digger mark the ground with any boundary.”

Law of Tiberius Caesar:

“According to the enduring rule, they lay out one line.”

## LOGOTHETA

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 10:

“He adopted the advice of the logotheta and the steward.”

Here the word denotes an ecclesiastical office, which Codinus describes in *On the Offices of the Imperial Court at Constantinople and of the Great Church*:

“Ὁ λογοθέτης, εἰς τὸ λογογραφεῖν, καὶ εἰς τὰς δημοσιακὰς καὶ ἀρχοντικὰς ὑποθέσεις λογογραφεῖν.”

“The logothete is for drafting documents, including documents in public and official matters.”

From the *Life of John the Almsgiver* we learn that he also performed the office of ecclesiastical steward.

## WASHING OF THE HANDS

Water was poured over Antony’s hands. In the preface to his *Life*:

“He spent no little time with him in supplying him with water.”

Thus water was also poured over Elisha’s hands, 2 Kings 3:11. In the Roman Martyrology, June 24, concerning Gallicanus, among his other acts of hospitality:

“They saw him pouring water over their hands.”

Among the ancients, the washing of hands occurred for various reasons. They washed before a meal, washed after a meal, washed when they were about to pray, and washed when they were about to sacrifice. I believe Antony washed before prayer. This was customary among Christians. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39:

“After the washing of the hands and the lighting of the lamps, each person is called forward to sing to God from the sacred Scriptures or from his own understanding, as he is able.”

See our Julius Nigronius’s extensive discussion of this matter in his commentary on our *Rules*.

## ISLAND OF LYCAONIA

*Life of Eugenia*, chapter 28:

“These things took place on the island of Lycaonia before all who were following Eugenia’s contest.”

This island is also mentioned in the *Acts of the Holy Martyrs Eusebius and His Companions*, whose feast is celebrated on December 2. Baronius has the passage, extracted from a manuscript, in volume II of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 259:

“And the bodies were left in the same place, beside the island of Lycaonia.”

Baronius adds in the margin:

“Lycaonia was the name of an island situated between two bridges. It was so called because there was also a temple of Jupiter Lycaon there.”

## MAGISTRIANUS

Palladius, chapter 149:

“A certain handsome young man, a *magistrianus*, pious in mind.”

Ado also uses the word in his *Martyrology*, July 2:

“The feast of the holy Processus and Martinianus, who, being *magistriani*, were chief officials (*melloprincipes*).”

I once annotated the passage as follows: *Magistriani*, or *magisteriani*, are those belonging to the military office of the palace, also called *agentes in rebus*. The Latin-Greek Glosses have:

“*Agens in rebus*, Μαγιστριανός.”

The Glosses of the *Basilicae* identify these same men with the *castrenses*, or *castrensiani*, where Μαγιστριανός is glossed as “ὁ καστρίνσιος.” Justinian’s Code, Book 12, distinguishes *agentes in rebus* from *castrensiani* under a different title. Nevertheless, the *castrensiani* were also subordinate to the *magister officiorum*, as were the *magistriani*, according to title 26.

There are other *magisteriani* in Suidas, also called κανστρίσιοι, from κανστρίον, “basket”; this was an ecclesiastical office. See Meursius, *Greek-Barbarous Glossary*.

In the Glosses of the *Basilicae*, *magistrianus* is also called μανθάτωρ. *Magistriani* occur in the *Acts of Saint Abercius, Bishop of Hierapolis*, October 22, in Metaphrastes, where the emperor Antoninus says:

“We have sent Valerius and Bassianus, *magisteriani* of our divine offices.”

And in Evagrius, Book III, chapter 16:

“Οὐ παρὰ τοὺς Μαγιστριανοὺς ἀπεστάλησαν.”

“They were not sent by the *magistriani*.”

Malchus, in his *Byzantine History*:

“Ἀδεμάντοις δὲ ταῦτα πυθόμενος προπέμπει τῶν ἱππέων τῶν βασιλικῶν τινα, οὓς Μαγιστριανοὺς καλοῦσι.”

“Having learned these things from Adamentus, he sent one of the imperial horsemen, whom they call *magistriani*.”

## MAGNIFICUS

*Life of Simeon Stylites*, chapter 2:

“He went to the monastery of the holy Timothy, a magnificent man.”

Here *magnificent* means one who performs great signs: θαυματουργός, μεγαλοποιός—“a miracle-worker,” or “one who accomplishes great things.”

## MALCHUS

*Life of Malchus*, chapter 1:

“An old man named Malchus, whom we can call ‘King’ in Latin.”

Eunapius, in *Porphyry*:

“Μάλχος δὲ κατὰ τὴν Σύρων [φωνήν?] ὁ Πορφύριος ἐκαλεῖτο τὰ πρῶτα, τοῦτο δὲ δύναται βασιλέα λέγειν.”

“Porphyrius was initially called Malchus according to the speech of the Syrians; this word can mean ‘king.’”

Hence *Naarmalcha*, that is, “royal river.” Ammianus, Book XXIV:

“Another part of the river, called Naarmalcha, which is interpreted as ‘River of Kings,’ passes by Ctesiphon.”

In the same book:

“We came from there to the excavated river called Naarmalcha, which means ‘River of Kings.’”

With a similar formation, in the same author and book, one finds *Braxamalcha*:

“We came to a place called Braxamalcha.”

Likewise *MaiOzamalcha*, in the same book:

“And when he had come to Maiozamalcha, a large city surrounded by strong walls.”

## MANCIPIUM

In the *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 21: “And an animal carrying rye from the *mancipium*, for its own meal.” Here *mancipium* itself means a bakery.

Socrates, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18, concerning the supervisors of breadmaking, says that they “are called μάγκιπες in the Roman language,” that is, *mancipes* in Roman speech.

Paul the Deacon, book XIII of his *Histories*, under Theodosius [Col. 0461A]: “From the beginning there had been built in the city of Rome a house of enormous size in which bread was made. As time passed, the *mancipes* of these establishments turned the public bakeries into robberies, and so forth. Recognizing this, the emperor put the *mancipes* to death by punishments and ordered the bakery itself to be utterly destroyed.”

The *mancipes* are understood in this sense in law I, title *De frumento urbano Constantinopolitano* [On Constantinople’s urban grain supply], book XII; likewise in law II and the final law under the same title in the *Theodosian Code*; and in the single law, title *De pistoribus* [On bakers], book XI. In that law, however, the common reading *mancipiis* is erroneous; Brissonius, in his *Legal Lexicon*, wishes *mancipibus* to be read instead.

Suidas: “Ἀρτοπωλεῖον, τὸ μαγκιπεῖον, ἐν ᾧ οἱ ἄρτοι γίνονται”—“A bakery, or *mancipium*, in which loaves are made.”

## MANSIO

In the *Life of Antony*, chapter 54: “At the first *mansio* of Alexandria, which is called Chaereum.” It is μονή in Greek: a lodging, a fixed and regular place for resting during a journey. Such places were also called ἀλλαγαί and συστήματα, in the manner in which posting stations are arranged today.

Our Fronto says the following about *mansio*, in the Paris edition of Palladius: “Μονή signifies the dwelling and residence of monks.” For this reason Hervetus had translated the passage in Palladius, chapter 28, as: “He passes through eight monasteries.” But, in order to understand how far Paul had traveled, it is more likely that Palladius meant stopping places, which themselves were also called μοναί. Thus Heraclides says: “He went up to eight neighboring stopping places.” In the *Life of Antony*: “At the first stopping place of Alexandria, which is called Chaereum.”

Stopping places, however, are distinguished from *mutationes*, as the very learned Pythaeus rightly warns in his preface to the *Jerusalem Itinerary*. *Mutationes* are stations for changing horses or other animals for the journey; they are found supplied with vehicles and animals, but not with the other necessities required for travelers’ daily life, as *mansiones* are. Hence they are distinguished in books V and XI, title 1, chapter 9, of the *Theodosian Code*. Thus, as may be seen in the *Itinerary of Antoninus* and the *Bordeaux Itinerary*, edited by the same Pythaeus, *mansiones* are distinguished from *mutationes*: from Bordeaux to Arles there are thirty *mutationes* and eleven *mansiones*, while from Sardica to Constantinople there are nineteen *mutationes* and fifteen *mansiones*.

Some also reckon a single *mansio* for a day’s journey without a *diaeta* [a day-stage or lodging], as when Pliny says, in book XII, chapter 14, that the incense-bearing region is eight stopping places distant from the lofty mountain on which the village of the Sabaean Atramitae is situated.

An “arbitrary stopping place” is mentioned in the *Life of Hilarion*, chapter 21 [Col. 0461D]: “With difficulty he obtained from the unwilling man that he should also place his monastery among the stopping places.” Hilarion stayed with some people, while he merely visited others in passing. Earlier in the same work: “And he would arrange on a tablet with whom he ought to stay and whom he ought to visit in passing.”

## MANUUM IMPOSITIO

In the *Life of Abraham*, chapter 5: “Ordained presbyter through the imposition of hands.” From the time of the apostles, the ordination of bishops and presbyters was performed by the laying on of hands, or χειροθεσία.

Saint Paul, 1 Timothy IV and V; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 20, in praise of Basil, concerning Basil’s father returning from the election of the bishop of Caesarea: “He returns firm and strong, carrying his eyes raised aloft, from the laying on of hands and the anointing” [Col. 0462A].

Optatus of Milevis, book I: “These judgments were pronounced against Donatus: that he had confessed to rebaptizing and to laying hands upon fallen bishops, which is contrary to the Church.” This must not be understood to mean that he reconciled bishops to the Church by the laying on of hands—which itself was also a solemn ceremony—but that, after bishops had once been duly created through the laying on of hands, he created them again by a similar ceremony.

## MAPHORIUM, or MAFORTE, or MAVORTE

Palladius, chapter 138: “She did not wish to accept a new garment, a μαφόριον, or a shoe.” The translator of Heraclides, chapter 48, renders this: “She never wished to use a tunic, a *mavorte*, or new footwear.”

Likewise Heraclides, chapter 49: “Whatever silk garments he had in *mavortes*” [Col. 0462B]. Here Hervetus, in Palladius, chapter 119, translates: “all his silk shoulder coverings.” He seems to have found ὠμοφόρια in his Greek text; in the Venetian Greek text it is ἡμιφόρια. See above, under HEMIPHORIUM. I translated ἡμιφόριον as *mavorte*, since I see that Heraclides’ translator rendered it in this way. From this we may also infer that a *mavorte* was a short garment, almost half a small cloak, which explains the name ἡμιφόριον.

Baronius discusses it in volume VIII, under the year 593: “By this word we find a garment of different kinds designated according to the status of different persons. In particular, Cassianus, book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 7, explains that the monastic habit was customarily placed over the shoulders. He says: ‘After this, following both the modesty of dress and the cheapness and economy of its price, they cover neck and shoulders alike with a narrow cloak, which in our language as well as in theirs is called a *maforte*—or *mavorte*’” [Col. 0462C].

Although it bore the same name, this was not the same garment as the one mentioned in the synodal letter of the Council of Poitiers, preserved by Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 16:

“Concerning the cloak, she produced a noble nun, saying that she had given him a silk *maforte*, which she had brought from her parents, as a gift, and that he had cut a portion from it, from which he might make whatever he wished; but from the remainder, insofar as was useful, he had properly made a cloak for the altar’s adornment; and from the piece that remained after the cutting, he had placed purple cloth on his niece’s tunic.”

For it was certainly not a worthless garment if it was made of silk; nor was it short, since an altar cloak had been made from it and a bride had additionally been adorned with it. We therefore think that the *maforte* belonged rather to the type about which Saint Jerome writes to Eustochium in Letter 22, when he says of the excessive luxury of foolish virgins: “And a hyacinth-colored *laena*, fluttering over the shoulders as a *mavorte*.” From this one may understand that it was not a short and narrow little cloak, but a loose garment which, because of its breadth, spread out in the wind, as we also see carved in statues. Nevertheless, the garment was common to both sexes: it was arranged like a cloak for covering the neck and shoulders, and for that reason both garments were equally called *mafortes*. Thus far Baronius.

Cassianus also mentions the *maforte*, book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 13: “Besides the *colobium*, the *maforte*, leggings, the *melotes*, and the *psiathium*” [Col. 0463A].

Isidore, book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25: “The *stola* is a matron’s covering, which, with the head covered, is thrown from the right side over the left shoulder. In Latin it is also called a *ricinium*, but commonly it is called a *mavorte*.” This is expressed by Servius in his commentary on *Aeneid* I: “It is called a *ricinium* because it is thrown back behind the shoulders; commonly it is called a *mavorte*.”

Nonius: “A *ricinium*, which is now called a *mafortium*.”

Suidas: “Κρήδεμνον, κεφαλοδέσμιον, ἢ μαφόριον”—“A *credemnon*, a head binding, or a *maphorium*.”

Phavorinus: “Μαφόριον κεφαλῆς περίβλημα”—“A *maphorium*, a covering of the head.”

The Arabic-Latin glosses: “*Maforium*, a *fascialis*, that is, a narrow cloak used by monks, covering the neck and shoulders alike.” Meursius, in his *Greek-Barbarian Glossary*, reads *fac alis*, which, he says, means φακιάλιον, but he gives no further explanation. Did that glossator call the *maphorium* a *fascialis* because he was referring to the small cords, or bands and arm coverings, which Cassianus discusses in book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 6, and to which he adds the *mafortes* in the following chapter?

George of Alexandria, in the *Life of Chrysostom*, chapter 55: “There are also some of them whose *maphoria* were snatched away from their heads.” That is: “Among them were also women whose veils were torn from their heads.”

The *Passion of Saint Paul*, published under the name of Linus: “Plautilla, lend me the cloth with which you cover your head.” Shortly afterward: “And, tying a bandage over his eyes from Plautilla’s *maphorte*.”

Bede, in his *Martyrology*, September 20: “He also ordered Fausta, stripped naked and flogged without a *maforte*, to be imprisoned and her head pierced.”

Isidore, above, attempts to investigate the etymology of *mavorte*: “They say that it was called *mavorte*, as though *martem*. For it is a sign of marital dignity and power. The head of a woman is her husband; hence it is also placed over the woman’s head” [Col. 0463C]. Papias largely copies this in his *Vocabulary*.

## MARTYRIUM

### The Temple of the Martyrs

Palladius, chapter 67: “We also prayed for him in the *martyrium* and saw him with those who had suffered martyrdom with him.”

The same author, chapter 103: “He entered his *martyrium*, which he himself had built, in which the relics of John the Baptist are placed.”

The same author, chapter 113: “He came on foot as far as Rome, to pray in the *martyrium* of the saints Peter and Paul.”

The same author, chapter 139: “Come, then, and dine with us in the *martyrium*.”

Everywhere the Greek has μαρτύριον, that is, a temple of the martyrs, or an oratory dedicated in honor of the martyrs. Thus, in the Council of Chalcedon, frequent mention is made of the *martyrium* of Saint Euphemia, that is, the temple consecrated in her honor and memory [Col. 0463D].

In the final law, title *De sepulcris violatis* [On violated tombs], of the *Theodosian Code*, we find that the place where a martyr is buried must be called a *martyrium*.

Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 6: “*Martyria* were called churches built in honor of particular martyrs.”

Jerome, in his *Chronicle*: “At Constantinople the *martyrium* of the Apostles is dedicated.”

*Martyrium* was also used in a specific sense for the Church of the Resurrection in Jerusalem. See RESURRECTIO.

## MATTA

Heraclides, chapter 6: “And then she also set fire to the *matta*, on which I was accustomed to stand” [Col. 0464A]. A *matta* is a mat woven from reeds.

Gregory of Tours, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 11: “Having no bed, no preparation of hay or straw, except only that which is customarily made from woven reed stalks, which people commonly call *mattas*.”

Isidore’s glosses: “*Psiathium*, a *matta*.”

An old glossary: “ψίαθος, a mat, a *matta*.”

The ancient commentator on Juvenal, Satire 6: “A mat, like a *matta*, the furnishing of an indecent bed.”

The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 55: “The bedding of the beds should consist sufficiently of a mat and a blanket.” See below, PLUMACIUM.

Peter the Venerable, book III, letter 20: “But if there are marshy places nearby, make the ancient work of the monks, mats, on which you may always sleep or frequently sleep.” The same author, book IV, letter 50: “He himself sat down for him on a monastic mat, which was next to that seat.”

## MEDIMNUS
