Theodoret, book IX of *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 2: “But gathering two *medimni*.” It was called both *medimnus* and *medimnum*. The word is used by Latin as well as Greek authors.

Hesychius: “Μεδιμναῖον, μέτρον μεδίου”—“A *medimnaeum*, a measure of a *modius*.”

“Μέδιμνον, μέτρον ὅμοιον, ἢ χοινίκων τεσσαράκοντα ὀκτώ”—“A *medimnus*, a similar measure, or forty-eight *choenices*.”

The same definition appears in Pollux, book IV, chapter 23, and in Suidas, who adds:

“Μέδιμνος, μέτρον ἐστὶ ξηρὸν, οἷος πυρῶν, ἢ κριθῶν· μέδιμνον οὖν μοδίων ςʹ, ὡς εἶναι μέτρον ξεστῶν οβʹ, ἤτοι λιτρῶν ρηʹ.”

“A *medimnus* is a measure of dry commodities, such as wheat or barley. A *medimnus*, therefore, is six *modii*, seventy-two *sextarii*, or one hundred and eight pounds.”

Cornelius Nepos, in the *Life of Pomponius Atticus* [Col. 0464C]: “He increased this service by another act of generosity, for he gave grain to everyone, so that six *modii* of wheat were distributed to each person. This measure is called a *medimnus* at Athens.”

Faunius:

> Half of this is contained by an urn, as is also the *medimnus*;  
> An amphora holds three *modii*; a *sextarius* draws this up  
> Sixteen times, as the foot is divided into digits.

Cicero, book III *Against Verres*: “But seven thousand *medimni* of wheat were imposed as a penalty, according to the speeches of Nympho.”

The same work: “Nearly a *medimnus* of wheat is sown in a *jugerum* of Leontine land.”

Ausonius, in the *Gryphon of the Number Three*:

> Hence the four-measure vessel of Bromius, and hence the Sicilian *medimni*.  
> Custom explains this by three, and this by two.

## MEMBRANAE PULCHRAE

The *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 134: “He showed me the New Testament, on very beautiful parchment.” The Greek is: “Καὶ ἔδειξέν μοι ἐν σώματι πολὺ καλῷ”—“And he showed me [it] in a very beautiful volume” [Col. 0464D].

Among the Greeks, parchment manuscripts are called σώματα; hence σωμάτια means small pieces of parchment used for writing, while σῶμα means a complete book.

Cicero, in a letter to Atticus: “I shall take care that you have this entire σῶμα.”

Glosses: “σωμάτιον, parchment.”

Longinus, *On the Sublime*, concerning the *Iliad*: “Ἰλιάδος σωμάτιον”—“A parchment copy of the *Iliad*.”

Hesychius: “Ἰλιάς, τοῦ Ὁμήρου σωμάτιον”—“The *Iliad*, a parchment copy of Homer.”

## MENDACIUM OFFICIOSUM

There was formerly considerable disagreement on this subject, many learned men believing that an expedient lie was lawful. Origen held this view in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians and in book VI of the *Stromata*. Jerome mentions that work in Letter 65, to Pammachius and Oceanus, and in his *Apology against Rufinus*, chapter 4, where he cites the words of Origen from book VI of the *Stromata* and those of Plato from book III of the *Republic*, concerning the way in which a lie may sometimes be useful. This passage of Jerome is not noticed by our John de Salas in his treatise *On Laws*, disputation 23, section 9, when he denies that Origen wrote books of the *Stromata*.

Jerome also seems to insinuate this opinion in his commentary on Galatians II and in Letter 89, where he discusses the dispute between Peter and Paul, which he considers to have arisen from dissimulation. Augustine thought that Jerome understood this dissimulation as an expedient lie, in Letters 86 and 97, preserved by Jerome. Baronius, however, volume I, under the year 51, believes that Augustine did not correctly grasp Saint Jerome’s meaning.

The same position appears in Chrysostom, Homilies 32 and 53 on Genesis; Maximus of Tyre, discourse 3; Cassianus, *Conferences* XVII, chapters 10, 15, and following; and book V of the *Institutes*, chapters 37 and 39.

Among more recent writers, Martin de Magistris, a doctor of the Sorbonne, held this view in his treatise *On Fortitude*, question V, *On Martyrdom*. Cajetan refutes him in *Summa theologica* II–II, question 124, article 5, under Doubt 3. Marulus likewise, book IV, chapter 4, admits an expedient lie; indeed, Augustine says in book III of the *Questions on Leviticus*, chapter 68, that it appeared permissible to nearly everyone [Col. 0465A].

Saint Thomas, however, teaches that every lie, even an expedient one, is unlawful, *Summa theologica* II–II, question 10, article 3. So too does Augustine in *On Lying*, *Against Lying*, and Letters 86 and 97, already cited by Jerome. In Part II of the *Decree*, Cause 22, question 2, chapter 14, “Let no one suppose,” a passage is cited from Augustine on Psalm V, stating that no one ought to lie for another person’s temporal life [Col. 0465C].

Alexander III refers to this in book V of Gregory IX’s *Decretals*, title 19, *On Usury*, chapter 4, *Super eo*. When he says that Holy Scripture forbids lying for another person’s life, he seems to understand Augustine’s statement just mentioned. Yet in the same place in the *Decree*, chapter 21, a dissimulation is called useful, according to Jerome’s commentary on Galatians II, and is said to be admissible at the proper time.

Observe that authors strangely confuse and cite Origen in support of this opinion. Jerome, in Letter 65 to Pammachius and Oceanus, cites book VI of Origen’s *Stromata*, where Origen discusses lying; Jerome repeats this in his *Apology against Rufinus*, chapter 4. But in Letter 89, to Augustine, he cites book X of the *Stromata*, which explains Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians.

I think these references can be reconciled by saying that book X of the *Stromata* contains the words of Origen that Jerome cites from book VI of the *Stromata*. But I believe that Jerome calls it the sixth book of the *Stromata* because he adds that tenth book, which deals with the explanation of the Epistle to the Galatians, to five volumes that Origen himself wrote on the Epistle to the Galatians; thus that tenth book, when added to the five, becomes the sixth of the explanatory books on the Epistle to the Galatians.

The words of Jerome’s Letter 89 are:

> “Origen wrote five volumes of his own on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, and completed the tenth book of his *Stromata* with a concise exposition devoted to its interpretation.”

## MENOMENAE

In book I of the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*, chapter 19: “A thousand strings of dried fish, which are called *menomenae*” [Col. 0466A].

Cassianus, book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 22: “Tiny salted fish, which they call *maenominia*, are an exquisite pleasure.”

This is how most of the old books read, although Ciacconus reads μαινίδια here, from Aristotle, which Pliny calls *maenulae* and Gaza *haleculae*. I believe that *maenae*, *maenomenae*, and μαινομένια are small fish of the same kind.

Martial, book XI, epigram 32:

> They proved that they had been *gerres*, or useless *maenae*;  
> The impure odor of the jar confessed it.

The same author, book XI, epigram 32:

> And the tail of a *cybium*, and small *maenae*.

Cicero, book II *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: “They may say that they do not prefer a sturgeon to a *maena*.”

Pliny, book IX, chapter 26: “The white *maenae* change color in winter and become darker in summer.”

He also mentions them in book XXXII, chapters 8–11. Persius, Satire 3:

> And because the *maena* has not yet failed the whale.

Arnobius, book III: “Neptune, lord of sea monsters and *maenae*.”

In Oppian, book I, the fish is called μαινίς.

It is said to derive its name ἀπὸ τῆς μανίας, “from madness,” because it was formerly sacred to Diana—who is also Hecate, the cause of μανία, or madness. See Athenaeus, book VII, and Eustathius on the *Iliad*, book I. Dioscorides also discusses *maenae* in book II, chapter 31, as does Alexander of Tralles in book VIII.

## MENSIUM TABULA

Because the Egyptian months, which differ from the Roman months, are mentioned several times here, I shall give below, from Bede, a comparison between them.

Bede, therefore, volume II, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter IX:

“The Egyptians, who were the first to reckon their months according to the course of the sun—because the moon’s more rapid movement might otherwise produce an error in calculation, whereas the sun’s slower motion could more easily be grasped—began from the autumn season and are said to have divided their months into periods of thirty days. Their first month begins on the following day:

| Egyptian month | Roman equivalent |
|---|---|
| 1. Thoth | IV Kalends of September (29 August) |
| 2. Phaophi | IV Kalends of October (28 September) |
| 3. Athyr | V Kalends of November (28 October) |
| 4. Choiak | V Kalends of December (27 November) |
| 5. Tybi | VI Kalends of January (27 December) |
| 6. Mechir | VII Kalends of February (26 January) |
| 7. Phamenoth | V Kalends of March (25 February) |
| 8. Pharmuthi | VI Kalends of April (27 March) |
| 9. Pachon | VI Kalends of May (26 April) |
| 10. Payni | VII Kalends of June (26 May) |
| 11. Epiphi | VII Kalends of July (25 June) |
| 12. Mesori | VIII Kalends of August (25 July) |

“It begins from this day. Ending on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, they call the remaining five days ἐπαναγόμεναι, or intercalary or added days. In every fourth year they also add a sixth day, which is produced from the quarter-days. Hence their first year after a leap year begins on the third day before the Kalends of September, while the other years begin on the fourth day before those Kalends. Leap years themselves end on the fourth day before the Kalends, and the other years on the fifth day before the same date.”

Thus far Bede. John of Nijmegen, the scholiast, notes that each Egyptian month consists of thirty days, while the last consists of thirty-five, and every fourth year of thirty-six. I append a table arranged according to Bede’s account [Col. 0467A].

[Col. 0469A] 1041. Let us now compare the dates of the two calendars that occur in the *Lives of the Fathers*, and see whether Bede’s comparison between the months is correct.

*Life of Pachomius*, chapter 3: “He gave up his spirit on the fourteenth day of the month Pachon according to the Egyptians, which according to the Romans is around the seventh day before the Ides of May.”

Pachon begins on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, that is, on April 26. Counting from there, the fourteenth day falls correctly on May 9.

*Life of Pachomius*, chapter 29: “On the eleventh day of the month Tybi, that is, the eighth day before the Ides of January, a certain festival is celebrated in Egypt according to custom.”

*Life of Mary of Egypt*, chapter 25: “When the month Parmuthi according to the Egyptians had passed, which according to the Romans is April 9, that is, the fifth day before the Ides of April” [Col. 0469B]. This will be the fourteenth day of Parmuthi, or Pharmuthi, according to the table above.

The *Life of Onuphrius*, by Paphnutius, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 16: “Saint Onuphrius died, therefore, in the month of June, on the eleventh day, that is, the third day before the Ides of that month.”

This does not correspond with the date given by Metaphrastes: “It was the sixteenth day of the month Payni, or Pauni, but the ninth day of the Roman month of June.” If Bede correctly compares the Egyptian months with the Roman, the sixteenth day of Payni will be June 10.

## METANOEAM MITTERE

What the Greeks express by βάλλειν or ποιεῖν μετάνοιαν is generally translated “to send” or “to make a *metanoea*,” or “to perform an act of penance.”

The *Life of Basil*, chapter 11: “And making a *metanoea*, he answered him and said” [Col. 0469C].

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 14: “When both of them were sending a *metanoea*.” This is expressed more accurately in the same work, chapter 35: “And sending genuflections.”

See the comments on both passages. Thus understand the words in John’s work here, book III, no. 2: “Those who, doing penance, said”—that is, those who knelt and bowed their heads before Macarius.

The seventh general council, which is the Second Council of Nicaea, session 4, from a writing of Maximus the Confessor:

“Καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀνέστησαν πάντες μετὰ χαρᾶς καὶ δακρύων, καὶ ἔβαλον μετάνοιαν, καὶ εὐχὴ γέγονε.”

The Vulgate version: “After this, they all rose with joy and tears, they did penance, and a prayer was made.”

Anastasius the Librarian: “And in these things they all rose with joy and tears, and sent a *metanoea*, and a prayer was made” [Col. 0469D].

A scholion is appended in the manuscript codex of John Tilius, bishop of Meaux:

“*Metanoea* is interpreted as penance. In this place, however, it stands for a genuflection. Therefore, when it says ‘they sent penance,’ nothing else is meant than that they placed their knees on the ground. Because it is especially characteristic of penitents to bend their knees, the Greeks often call a genuflection *metanoea*, that is, penance.”

Our Fronto Ducaeus cites this from Tilius’s codex in his notes on the Second Council of Nicaea, after volume III of the Binian edition of the Councils.

The Liturgy of Chrysostom: “Ὁ δὲ ἱερεὺς σὺν τῷ διακόνῳ ποιοῦσι μετανοίας τρεῖς εἰς τὸ ἅγιον θυσιαστήριον”—“But the priest together with the deacon make three inclinations toward the holy altar.”

Erasmus’s translator: “But the priest together with the deacon make three ascents into the holy sanctuary” [Col. 0470A]. This is not correct. Our Fronto is correct: “They make three inclinations toward the holy altar.”

In the Greek *Euchologion*, in many places, the deacon “τῷ ἱερεῖ τρεῖς μετανοίας βάλλει”—“bows before the priest three times in the manner of one doing penance.”

See Baronius, volume VIII, under the year 656, and Billius, scholion 32 on the first oration of John Damascene, *On Images*.

## MILIARISIUM

John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 185: “Yet they had fifty *miliarisia*, which is a type of coin.”

Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*: “Τὸ δὲ ἄργυρον, τοῦτό ἐστιν ὃ οἱ Ῥωμαῖοι μιλιαρίσιον καλοῦσιν, ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται στρατιωτικὸν δόμα.”

“The silver coin is what the Romans call a *miliarisium*, which may be interpreted as a military gift.”

Suidas: “Μιλιαρήσιον, νομίσματος δέκατον”—“A *miliaresium*, a tenth of a coin” [Col. 0470B].

For this type of coin, see our Dionysius Petavius’s careful investigation in his commentary on the work of Epiphanius already mentioned.

## MINO

John, book II, no. 10: “He sends someone pursuing and driving me away from here.”

Heraclides, chapter 5: “Suddenly a little boy, about ten years old, appears, driving an ass carrying bread in a basket.”

Anianus the jurist: “The act by which we customarily drive cattle.”

Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 2: “Take it, so that you may know how you can drive this beast.”

Paul the Deacon: “It means to drive before oneself, that is, to drive.”

The same author: “*Agasones*, those who drive horses, that is, those who drive them forward.”

Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book III: “They drive us two asses away with sticks.”

Hence *comminare* in the same author, book VII of the *Metamorphoses*, and *prominare* in book IX [Col. 0470C].

## MINUTUM

John Moschus, book XV of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 42: “So that for four days he would eat only one offering of twenty *minuta*.”

The Greek text is lacking here. Perhaps the Greek had λεπτά or φολεῶν. Below, chapter 134: “And he received a daily allowance of nine *minuta*.” There the Greek text has πέντε φόλεις. See below, under PHOLES, and our Petavius, in his discussion of Epiphanius, *On Lepta and Minuta*.

## MONTICELLUS

The *Life of Onuphrius*, chapter 11: “Near the summit of that little mountain.” The word is uncommon but was used by agrarian writers.

Innocentius, among the authors on the regulation of boundaries: “And he established a boundary marker on the hillock above the spring.”

The same author: “A small hill descends between valley and valley, and on the side of this hillock is a channel.”

The same author: “A boundary chest established on the hillock.”

Latinus: “There are also hillocks established among the boundaries.”

Vitalis and Arcadius, among the same authors: “He passes across three hillocks and marks a chest near the bathhouse on the third hillock.”

The same Vitalis: “For we also enclosed the hillocks with boundary markers.”

Faustus and Valerius: “We planted hillocks of earth, which we called *botontini*.”

Thus, in Innocentius, one also finds *campicellus*, *collicellus*, and *flumicellus*.

## MURO SEPTI (PRO)

Jerome, in the *Life of Malchus*, chapter 9: “Only the consciousness of chastity served as a wall of protection.”

This is expressed proverbially and derived from Sallust’s *Catiline*: “Audacity is regarded as a wall.”

Cicero, *Against Verres* VIII: “Against all my attacks, the good name of the commander is set up like a certain wall.”

Jerome, on Isaiah XXXVIII: “To shut off indignation from the prayers as though by a kind of wall.”

The same author, on Ezekiel XIII: “When, having turned to God, they surrounded themselves with this as with a wall and a very strong barrier.”

## MUSCUS

The *Life of Pelagia*, chapter 2: “She filled the whole air with the scent of musk.”

The *Life of Marcella*, chapter 3: “To be fragrant with musk-mouse.”

Hence *muscata* in Rufinus, book III, no. 39: “Because of incense and *muscata*.”

Jerome, on Jeremiah XXIII: “Let us consider the heretics: how, once they have despaired of salvation, they give themselves over to gluttony and pleasures; let them eat meat, frequently visit the baths, smell of musk, be smeared with various perfumes, and seek the beauty of their bodies” [Col. 0471B].

The same author, book II *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 7: “The sweetness of scent, various incenses, *amomum*, *cyphi*, *oenanthe*, musk, and the skin of a foreign mouse are appropriate to the dissolute and to lovers—no one but a dissolute person denies this.”

In this passage Volaterranus understands *muscus* as a small mouse, yellow in color, which is extremely fragrant and lives in the forests.

There are various opinions about the origin of musk. Aetius thinks that musk, or *muscus*, which is a type of perfume, is the fluid collected from an abscess of a doe; others, such as Simeon Seth, hold that it comes from an abscess of a unicorn.

Martin of Baumgarten, in his *Pilgrimage*, says that it is a certain animal, somewhat larger but very similar to a cat, which, when provoked to anger by a blow from a rod, emits something fragrant that is sold by weight in gold. Near the navel of this animal an abscess develops; once extracted, it has an extremely pleasant scent and is regarded among the finest human luxuries. The Italians call the animal *zibetto*, the Germans *bifem* [Col. 0471C].

## MYOPARO

The *Life of Hilarion*, no. 41: “When pirates encountered two not-small *myoparones*.”

Paulinus, in his letter to Macarius: “He is said to be the agent of our Christian brother Postumianus, who, on the coast of Bruttium, where the senator’s estate reaches the sea, being greedier than the sea and carrying on piracy on land without a *myoparo*, seized the ship and emptied it.”

This passage should be read in this way, where the common text has “and without my old *paron*” instead of “without a *myoparo*.”

## NATES VERBERARE

The *Life of Marcella*, no. 9: “Let the counterfeit diviner beat the buttocks of fools and, with a twisted staff, shake the teeth of those who bite.”

The same author, book II *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 19: “Every day in the circles of the streets the counterfeit diviner beats the buttocks of fools and, with a twisted staff, shakes the teeth of those who bite.”

The same author, *Apology I against Rufinus*, chapter 4: “Every day in the streets the counterfeit diviner beats the buttocks of fools and, with a twisted staff, shakes the teeth of those who bite.”

This is how the passage should be read in all these places, according to several manuscripts that I consulted. Henry Gravius also handled it in this way. The common printed text has *nares* [noses], which Erasmus and Reatinus attempt to interpret.

But the reading I have defended is clearly supported by Lucian, *The Death of Peregrinus*:

“Εἶτα παίων καὶ παιόμενος νάρθηκι εἰς πυγὰς, καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ νεανικώτερα θαυματοποιῶν.”

“Then he beat and was beaten with a staff around the buttocks, and performed many other more youthful feats in a wondrous and deceptive manner” [Col. 0472A].

## NEAPOLIS

In the title of the *Life of John the Almsgiver*, Leontius is called bishop of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus. He is likewise called this by Metaphrastes, June 1, in the *Life of Simeon the Fool*. The same designation occurs in the First Council of Nicaea, which is the Seventh General Council, and in Damascene’s first and third orations *On Images*.

Which Neapolis is this? Baronius and Possevinus thought that it was Constantia, or Salamis, in Cyprus, as I explained in the text. But this cannot stand. That Neapolis of Cyprus was a different city from Constantia of Cyprus is clear from the same council.

After the words of Leontius in favor of images had been read from his fifth sermon, *Apology for Christians against the Jews*, and concerning images of the saints, Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, adds:

“Οὗτος ὁ ἀναγνωσθεὶς πατὴρ ἐν μιᾷ τῶν πόλεων τῆς Κύπρου ἱεροπρεπῶς διέπρεψε.”

“This Father who has been read out flourished with sacred dignity in one of the cities of Cyprus” [Col. 0472B].

Ortelius, in his *Geographical Thesaurus*, writes that Lusignan thought this city was called by the Greeks Lemisela-Neuve and by the Latins Nemosia or Lemonne.

## NILI ASCENSUS

Palladius, chapter 37: “It happened once in Egypt, when the Nile was rising, that one village attacked another. For they fought over the division of the waters, so violently that killings and ravages followed.”

I believe this refers to what Palladius says in chapter 52, namely that two villages fought over fields, “battling over cultivated lands.” Shortly afterward, pagans and Christians fought “over their own boundaries.”

This may have happened because the overflowing Nile customarily confused the fields and erased the boundaries. Many people were then falling ill.

The same author, chapter 43: “We were traveling by river, for it was the season of the rising, during which many people fall ill; this also happened to me.”

Καιρὸς ἀναβάσεως means “the season of the rising.”

The same author, chapter 22: “At that time, when the river was flooding, it extended for a thousand paces in breadth.”

“Κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον πλημμυρῶντος τοῦ ποταμοῦ, καὶ κρατοῦντος ἐπὶ ἓν σημεῖον τῷ πλάτει”—“At that time, when the river was flooding and measured a mile in breadth.”

I believe the following passage in Palladius, chapter 52, also belongs here, concerning a procession celebrated with a wooden statue for the river water:

“The impious priests led a procession, carrying it around the villages; they raved with the crowd, as though celebrating rites for the river water” [Col. 0472D].

For I suspect that the rising of the Nile is meant here. Accordingly, in Rufinus, book II, chapter 7, *rain waters* should be corrected to *river waters*. In Palladius the Greek has: “ὑπὲρ τοῦ ποταμιαίου ὕδατος”—“for the river water.”

The well-known verse about Egypt is relevant:

> Nor does the dry grass supplicate rainy Jupiter.

## NIXAE SICCAE

Pelagius, book V *On the Lives of the Fathers*, booklet IV, no. 65: “And a certain brother brought dried *nixae* and made a porridge.”

According to Isidore, book XVII, chapter 7, these *nixae* are *coquimella*, a word distorted from the Greek κοκκύμηλον.

“*Coquimella*,” he says, “which the Latins call a plum because of its color, others call a *nixa* because of the abundance of fruit it brings forth. Of this kind, the Damascene plum is better, named from the city of Damascus, from which it was first brought. Only its fruit is considered beneficial to the stomach; the others are said to be harmful. This tree alone drips a sticky and cohesive gum, which physicians and writers use.”

See Pliny, book XIII, chapter 11, concerning *sarcocolla*, where he has *painters* rather than *writers*.

The same author, book XXII, chapter 25: “Wheat bran boiled with rose oil, dried fig, and *myxae* is beneficial as a gargle for the tonsils and throat.”

See also Dioscorides, book I, chapter 175.

The Cambridge manuscript glossary: “A *nixa* is a kind of tree, named from the resemblance of its fruit to something brought forth”—a formulation taken from Isidore.

The scholiast Grialus notes that he found the following addition in the margin of the Roman Codex of Saint Peter, although Chacon said it was written by the same hand:

“This tree the Romans call a plum; the Spaniards, *nixum*; the Vandals, Goths, Suebi, and Galicians, a blue plum” [Col. 0473B].

The Portuguese and Galicians still preserve traces of this word, calling all plums *amevas* or *ameivas*.

In Aurelianus, book IV *On Late Matters*, chapter 8: “For a decoction of *noxarum* and licorice.” I would read *nixarum*.

Some maintain that *myxa* should be read instead of *nixa*. This is confirmed by Paul of Aegina, book VII:

“Μύξα, δένδρου καρπός ἐστι μικρότερος μὲν τῶν κοκκυμήλων, δυνάμει δὲ παραπλήσιος.”

“A *myxa* is the fruit of a tree, smaller than *coccyme la*, but similar in efficacy.”

This supports what we have said about the Galicians, since we frequently see *m* take the place of *n*, or the reverse, in many words.

Thus far Grialus on Isidore.

These *myxae* were also called *myxaria*. Cassianus, *Conference* VIII, chapter 1: “After this he brought in a basket containing roasted chickpeas, which they call *trogalia*. From these we took only five grains each, two *myxaria*, and one fig.”

An old lexicon notes that *myxa* and *myxaria*, among more recent Greek physicians, are smaller than Damascene plums and have a triangular stone inside.

## NOMicus

Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 193: “He therefore summoned the Nomicus, or steward, of the most holy church.” The Greek reads: “He brought the Nomicus of the most holy church.”

There is a varied interpretation of *Nomicus* in the eighth *Pentad* of offices by Curopalates. There, after the chief reader, appears **Ὁ Νομικός** (*ho Nomikos*), whom John Citrius seems to call **νομμοδότης** (*nommodotēs*), as though “distributor of money.” Certainly in this passage *Nomicus* seems to mean “steward,” or one who has charge of accounts and documents. See our Gretzer, on chapter 1 of Codinus’ *On the Offices of Constantinople*.

## NOMINA

John, book II, no. 8: “We went up to reap with him seven *nomina*.” Here nearly all the manuscripts consistently read *nomina*. One might suspect that *septem nomina* arose from the Greek **ἑπτανομία** (*Heptanomia*), a certain region of Egypt, as though the phrase meant “they went to reap in Heptanomia.” But since the Greek text is lacking, this is mere conjecture.

Our Peter Lansselius, learned in many fields, thought that one should read *septem nomia*. “For,” he says, “I believe that the desert of Scythia was divided into various districts, which they called **νόμια** (*nomia*), from **νέμω** (*nemō*), ‘I divide.’” Thus Proclus, in his *Commentary on the Timaeus*, teaches that **νομός** (*nomos*) is so called **ἀπὸ τοῦ νενεμῆσθαι τὴν γῆν**, “from the division of the land.” The Egyptians called **τὰς διαιρέσεις τὰς κατὰ μεγάλα μέρη τῆς Αἰγύπτου**, “the divisions into the great parts of Egypt,” *nomoi*. These *nomoi* were divided into **τοπαρχίαι**, “toparchies,” and these into other **τομαί**, or sections, the smallest of which were **ἄρουραι**, “arouras” or cultivated plots.

Accordingly, in this passage *septem nomia* seems to be understood as seven arouras joined together. Just as the Thebaid and the Delta were divided into ten *nomes*, and the intervening desert was divided into thirty *nomes*, so I believe that Scythia was divided into various *nomes*. One of these, the one under discussion here, was divided into seven *nomia*, that is, arouras or fields—either pasturelands, in which hay was cut, or arable lands, which are meant here.

Perhaps he did not say *Heptanomia*, but *septem nomina*, although the meaning of both expressions is the same, in order to distinguish it from Heptanomos, or Heptanomia, where the hermits of the Oases lived, opposite the desert of Scythia. For Lake Moeris, or Myris, lies between the two regions. So far Lansselius.

## THE NINTH HOUR

The synaxis was customarily completed at that hour. *Life of Macarius the Roman*, chapter 3: “One day, after the synaxis had been completed at the ninth hour.”

The fast was also customarily ended then. *Life of Antony*, chapter 37: “At about the ninth hour, when he had begun to pray before eating.”

Prudentius, hymn 10, *On the Crowns* (*Peristephanon*):

> The priest sees certain people from the crowd  
> Bringing him a cup to be offered.  
> “We are fasting,” he says; “I refuse the drink.  
> The ninth hour has not yet ended the day.  
>   
> I shall never violate the sacred ordinance,  
> Nor shall death itself undo my holy obligation.”

Rufinus, book III, no. 4: “When the ninth hour had arrived, according to custom he completed all his prayers and psalmody according to the rule, and set out bread to eat.”

The same author, book III, no. 55, in the life of Silvanus: “At the ninth hour that brother would look along the road, in case the old man should call him to eat.”

The same is found in Pelagius, book X, no. 69.

John, book III, no. 2: “And around the ninth hour he gave a signal by striking; the younger man came and prepared a small cooked dish of vegetables.”

Augustine, *Rule*, section 2, on the time for eating: “Let them work in the morning until the sixth hour, and from the sixth until the ninth let them give themselves to the books; and after they have refreshed themselves, whether in the garden or wherever they may be, let them work until the hour of lighting the lamps.”

Some extended their fast until evening. Rufinus, book II, chapter 31: “He also ordered him to take food in the evening.” The same is found in Palladius, chapter 28.

Likewise Rufinus, book II, chapter 1: “When this man had asked for food at the usual time, in the evening, after his prayers.” This too is found in Palladius, chapter 46.

Rufinus, book III, no. 23: “They again entered the cell, completed their evening prayers, and worshiped him, saying: ‘If you command us, lord, we shall go and cook the stalk that remains, so that we may taste it, since it is already time for us to take food.’”

Pelagius, book XVI, no. 18: “But he brought that brother only a little bread for late in the day.”

Yet postponing the fast until evening was not approved by all the Fathers; they rather advised taking food at the ninth hour. Cassian, *Conferences*, II, chapter 6, with the abbot Moses speaking:

> Recent food, whether during the evening prayers or the night prayers, does not allow the mind to remain subtle and light. Therefore the ninth hour has been quite suitably and usefully granted as the time for refreshment. When the monk has eaten then, he is found not only light and unburdened during the night vigils, but also thoroughly prepared for the very solemnities of the evening prayers, because the food has already been digested.

## NONNA

*Life of Hilarion*, in the prologue: “The glory and dignity of virgins, Nonna Asella.”

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 10: “I beg you, Nonna.” And in chapter 46: “Nonna Pelagia.”

*Life of Mary of Egypt*, chapter 17: “Take these things, Nonna.”

Pelagius, book VII, no. 10: “Nonna, come with us to the bath.”

This word frequently occurs for a religious mother or lady. Jerome, letter 22 to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*: “Because those who have experienced the domination of husbands prefer the freedom of widowhood, the chaste are called *castae* and *nonnae*.”

The same author, letter 99, to Asella: “They would be called *nonnae* and holy women.” Here *dominae* had intruded in place of *nonnae*.

Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, letter 19: “If he should be found guilty of having had intercourse with a veiled woman, a *nonna* consecrated to the Lord.”

In the same place one finds mention of the adulteries and monasteries of *nonnae*. The synods convened by Boniface, found in book V, titles 2 and 3 of the *Capitularies*, also remember *nonnae*. In the first: “Likewise, veiled *nonnae* shall also be held to the same penance.” In the other: “Likewise monks and *nonnae*.”

*Vision of Flotilda*, page 206: “She saw herself in a certain pleasant place, and she had a black veil over her head. When she asked about it, she heard that she was to become a *nonna*.”

The Camberon Glossary, manuscript: “A consecrated woman, *nunna*, nun, religious woman.”

The *nonnae* also seem to have been called *nonnanae*. This is gathered from book I, title 17 of the *Capitularies*, where the heading is “For Clerics and *Nonnani*.” It then appends a canon of the Council of Laodicea stating that women ought not to enter the altar area.

*Traditions of Fulda*, book II, no. 38, page 509: “The relics which Abbess Einhildis gave and handed over to those *nonnanae*.”

Likewise *nonnanes*. *Capitularies*, book V, title 78: “So that the canons, or monks and *nonnanes*, may have custody worthy of their profession.”

And book VII, title 316: “Likewise, veiled *nonnanes* shall be held to the same penance.”

Hence the French *nonnains*. Vitus Amerbachius vainly derives this word from a Germanic origin in his notes on the *Capitularies*, or Constitutions, of Charlemagne.

Jerome, letter 47, to a mother and daughter living in Gaul, applies the title *nonni* as flattery: “She calls you holy and a *nonnus* in your presence as a form of flattery.””

Arnobius likewise, on Psalm 140: “While we are here, flattering one another, we call one another saints and *nonni*; but when absent, we bite and strike one another so fiercely that we are rightly compared with dogs.”

The same author uses the word in Psalm 105: “Earthly minds are destroyed in this manner: If the man who is called holy and a *nonnus* acts in this way, who or how important am I that I should not act likewise?”

Addition 1 to the *Capitularies* of Emperor Louis, title 54: “Those who are placed in authority shall be called *nonni*.”

These are the very words of the Synod of Aachen, held in 817, which seem to have been modeled on chapter 63 of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “The seniors shall call their juniors brothers; the juniors, however, shall call their seniors *Nonnos*, which signifies fatherly reverence.”

It is also certain that *Nonna* was a proper name. Moschopulus, *On Figures*, page 93: “Nonna, a proper name.”

## NONUM

Pelagius, book VII, no. 7: “They were speaking of Abbot Theodore and Abbot Lucius of Nono of Alexandria.”

Here there was a remarkable variety of readings: some read *de Novo*, others *de Nonno*, and others took it as the name of a place.

An obvious conjecture for someone might be *de Nomo Alexandriae*, “of the Nome of Alexandria,” since Egypt, according to Pliny, book V, chapter 9, was divided into *nomes*, or prefectures. Among these was the Nome of Alexandria. Thus either both men, or certainly Lucius, may have been from the Nome of Alexandria; or the expression may have been used to indicate their homeland, whether as the place where they lived or to distinguish them from others who bore the same name.

Someone might perhaps think of No, in Ezekiel 30 and Nahum 3, which Saint Jerome and the Chaldean interpret as Alexandria in Egypt.

But I consider *de Nono Alexandriae* altogether the most genuine reading: “of the Ninth [district] of Alexandria,” that is, of the ninth climate or region of Alexandria, since Ammianus, book XXII, implies that Alexandria was divided into regions or climates, as Rome once was. He calls the Bruchion, which lay near Alexandria, the largest part of the regions.

Epiphanius, in *On Weights and Measures*, page 536, calls the Bruchion **κλίμα τῆς Ἀλεξάνδρου πόλεως**, “a climate of the city of Alexandria.” This reading is unquestionably the truest. For the Theodore who is here called “of Nono” is called in the same Pelagius, book XI, no. 2, “Theodore of Ennato,” which is the same as “of Nono.”

Likewise, in book XII, no. 9, Lucius is called “in Ennato,” that is, in Nono, namely in the climate of Alexandria.

Thus in the Greek *Menaea*, on 9 October, in the life of the anchorites Andronicus and Athanasia, one finds **ὀκτωκαιδέκατον**, “the eighteenth,” whether a climate, suburb, or coenobium near Alexandria.

See **ENNATUM** and **SEPTIMUM**.

## OBOLUS

Palladius, chapter 10: “He did not even despise two obols.”

Here Palladius calls “two obols” **δύο ὀβολούς**, which in Mark 12:42 are called **λεπτὰ δύο**, “two small coins,” or **κοδράντης**, “a quadrans.” Now an obol is one-fourth of a quadrans. But here *obolus* is used for a very small kind of coin.

In the Septuagint, Exodus 1:30, an **ὀβολός** is called a coin worth one-twentieth of a didrachm, or shekel: **εἴκοσι ὀβολοὶ δίδραχμον**, “twenty obols make a didrachm.”

The Latin Vulgate: “A shekel contains twenty obols.”

—FRONTO

## ORBIS TERRARUM

**Ἡ ὑπ’ οὐρανόν**, “that which is beneath heaven.”

Palladius, chapters 19 and 20: “He was said to spend more time with God than occupied with the affairs of this world or universe.”

The Greek reads: “He was said to spend more time with God than with the affairs beneath heaven.”

Hervetus translated it: “He was said to spend more time either with God or among heavenly matters.”

Fronto read in the Greek: **ἢ τοῖς τῆς ὑπ’ οὐρανόν**, “than with the affairs of that which is beneath heaven.” He says that worldly and secular affairs are called **τὰ πράγματα τῆς ὑπ’ οὐρανόν**, “the affairs of what is beneath heaven.”

Hence the translator of Heraclides: “And to be occupied more with heavenly than earthly affairs.”

Scripture calls the terrestrial world **τὴν ὑπ’ οὐρανόν**, “that which is beneath heaven.” Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, book I: “And when he established the springs of that which is beneath heaven.” The Vulgate has: “and the pivots of the earth.”

Likewise below in Theophilus: **ἐφώτισε τὴν ὑπ’ οὐρανόν**, “he illumines the whole world beneath heaven.”

## ORBUS

One who lacks eyes; in Greek, **ἀπ’ ὀμμάτων**, literally “from” or “out of the eyes.”

Palladius, chapter 4: “Didymus, who was blind.”

The Greek is: **ὁ ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων γενόμενος**, “the one who became deprived of eyes.”

You might render **ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων** as *Abocellus*. The learned writer Peter of Blois uses this word, sermon 18: “Do not pursue retaliations, lest they make you an old *abocellus*.”

And sermon 43: “Withdraw your hand from every gift; do not spare the poor; do not let gifts blind you and make you an old *abocellus*.”

The expression has been formed from **ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων**, as though *Exoculus*, just as **ἀπὸ ὑπάτων** gives *exconsul*, and similarly in other cases.

## TO RECEIVE THOSE WHO ARRIVE WITH A KISS

*Life of Onuphrius*, chapter 8: “He gave me the kiss of peace.”

*Life of Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 8: “And after the holy kiss.”

Ammianus, book XXII, *On the Emperor Julian*: “He brought into Tarsus with him the provincial governor Celsus, received with a kiss, a man known to him from his Attic studies, and invited to take a place in the vehicle.”

The same author, book XXIX: “Maurus, received with a kiss by the general Theodosius, since this contributed to the public interest, and already full of good hope, supplied adequate provisions.”

The same author, book XXII: “Julian received Maximus the philosopher with a kiss and reverence and brought him in with him.”

Thus formerly Christians in church received one another with the holy kiss. See Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*.

## TO KISS THE HANDS

*Life of Hilarion*, no. 14: “The saints kissed his hands.”

It was especially customary to kiss the hands of bishops. Ambrose, *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, chapter 2: “For you see kings’ necks and princes’ necks bent at the knees of priests, and, having kissed their right hands, they believe themselves protected.”

Ivo, part V, chapter 378, quotes this from a letter of Gregory VII to Herimann, bishop of Metz.

Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 1: “Nor does God permit us any longer to be polluted by kissing your unworthy hands.”

*Life of Fulgentius of Ruspe*, chapter 4: “At this the young man, inflamed more and more, humbly kissed the hand that was repelling him,” and so forth. The hand was that of Bishop Faustus.

Sidonius, book VII, letter 2, to the pope Graecus, calls his fingers “sacrosanct fingers”: “things that will be opened by your sacrosanct fingers.”

The same author, book VIII, letter 11, to Lupus:

> Go now to the thresholds of the bishops,  
> And kiss the hand of the holy Gallicinus.

He was the bishop of Bordeaux.

The hands of priests were also kissed. This is found here in the account of Hilarion.

Jerome, letter 99, to Asella, when he was living at Rome and had already been made a priest at Antioch: “Some kissed my hands, while with viperous speech they slandered me.”

## TO KISS THE EYES

*Life of Paul the First Hermit*, no. 12: “Having kissed [Vallarsius: *exosculatis*, ‘having fervently kissed’] his eyes and hands.”

The manuscript *Life of Melania the Younger*, chapter 4, concerning the empress Serena and Melania: “And again embracing and holding her close, she kissed her and her eyes.”

Ennodius, book VII, letter 14, to Archotamia: “So that, together with my lord the presbyter, we may both kiss your hands and eyes.”

I believe that in this way they showed that they regarded themselves as having their eyes dear to one another. In the same way they applied the hands and relics of the saints to their eyes.

*Life of Simeon Stylites*, chapter 17: “I placed his hand upon my eyes, saying: ‘Bless me, I beg you, my lord.’”

And chapter 8, concerning a worm that had fallen from his body: “He ran up, grasped it in faith, and placed it upon his eyes.”

In ancient times, too, people among the pagans kissed the eyes. Arrian, *Discourses*, book II, chapter 20:

> “Has he obtained the tribuneship?” “Look, everyone who meets him rejoices: one kisses his eyes, another his neck, and the slaves his hands.”

Homer, *Odyssey* XVI:

> **Κῦσε δέ μιν κεφαλήν τε καὶ ἄμφω φάεα καλά**  
> “And he kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes.”

## OXYCRATUM

Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 145: “At every other time she was content with *oxycratum* (a vinegar-and-water drink) and dry bread.”

The translator of Heraclides, chapter 42, rendered this: “For the rest of her life she lived content with *posca* and dry bread.”

See below, **POSCA**.

## OXYRYNCHUS SCRIPT

Palladius, chapter 86, concerning Evagrius, the celebrated deacon: “He wrote each year only the price of what he ate; for he wrote elegantly in the rapid script.”

The Greek is: **Εὐφυῶς γὰρ ἔγραφεν τὸν ὀξύρυγχον χαρακτῆρα**, “For he wrote skillfully in the Oxyrynchus script.”

Heraclides, chapter 25, speaking of the same man, retained the Greek word: “He likewise wrote in that hand which the Greeks call Oxyryncha.”

The old translator of Palladius rendered it *libralis* in chapter 15: “For he wrote the libral hand beautifully.”

I do not think that *Oxyryncha* means a rapid hand, as Hervetus translated it; that does not convey such elegance. Rather, it seems to indicate the Roman or rounded script, or the Italian or cursive script. Certainly, if one considers the force of the word *Oxyrynchus*, “sharp-snouted,” it is the Italian script. If someone insists that it may be called rapid because it is written in a running manner, whence it receives the name “cursive,” I shall not strongly dispute the point.

In ancient times there were two kinds of writers: **ταχυγράφοι**, “tachygraphs,” who were also called **ὀξυγράφοι** by Philo, *On the Creation of the Ruler*. They rapidly received and recorded words, either by signs or by individual letters, using abbreviations—**εἰς τάχος**, “for speed”—and hence were called *notarii*, notaries.

Concerning them, see Lipsius, *First Century of Letters to the Belgians*, letter 27, to our Leonard Lessius.

Others were **καλλιγράφοι**, “calligraphers,” who reduced what had been taken down rapidly **εἰς κάλλος**, “for elegance.” Concerning them, see above, under **ANTIQUARIUS**.

Philostratus mentions both kinds in his *Life of Apollonius*, book I: “He drove him out of Antioch with two servants, one writing for speed, the other for elegance.” That is: “one was a notary, the other an *antiquarius*.”

Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 21, concerning Origen: “More than seven notaries attended him as he dictated, taking turns with one another at fixed times; and there were no fewer book-copyists, together with girls trained in elegant writing.”

The same is found in Suidas.

Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 61, under Hippolytus: “Ambrose encouraged Origen to write commentaries on the Scriptures, supplying him with seven or more notaries and their expenses, and an equal number of copyists.”

Since our Evagrius wrote for payment in order to sell books, he seems to have been a **καλλιγράφος**, a calligrapher. Hence copyists were also called booksellers. The commentator on Horace, in the *Art of Poetry*, quoting Suetonius Tranquillus: “Writer, copyist, bookseller.”

It is remarkable that even boys learned those abbreviated signs. Thus Athanasius is said to have been handed over to a notary and grammarian as a boy in Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 197. The same is clear from Prudentius’ hymn 9, *On the Crowns* (*Peristephanon*), concerning Cassian.

## BREAD

Palladius, chapter 2: “So that often even bread fell from his mouth.”

The Greek word here is **ψωμός**, which means “a morsel”; hence Hervetus translated: “so that often a morsel fell from his mouth.”

But Greek authors of a later period used **ψωμός** specifically for bread, and **ψωμή**, or **ψωμί**, as Meursius also notes in his Glossary.

Heraclides: “And bread fell from his lips and mouth.”

Another translator likewise: “So that bread frequently fell from his mouth.”

Thus below, chapter 5: “I take food, bread; **ἐσθίω μου τὸν ψωμόν**, ‘I eat my morsel of bread.’”

—FRONTO

## PAPA

*Life of Malchus*, no. 2: “He came into the possession of Papa Evagrius, my relative.”

In Jerome’s time, bishops too were still called *papae*. On this subject see Francesco Bernardino Ferrario, book III, *On the Form of Ecclesiastical Letters*, chapter 1; and Savaro, on Sidonius, book I, letter 6.

Later, in the time of Gregory VII, after a synod had been held at Rome, it was decreed that the name *papa* should be assigned to the Roman pontiff alone. See Baronius’ note for 10 January in the *Martyrology*.

Our Jacobus Sirmondus makes the following observation on book IV, letter 1 of Ennodius:

> Ennodius seems to have been the first to assert the name *papa* as proper and peculiar to the Roman pontiff alone. For while nearly all the others who lived close to his own time customarily called all bishops *papae*—for example Sidonius, Faustus, and Ruricius—he consistently calls the bishops of the other churches *antistites* or bishops, distinguishing them in this way. He calls only the pontiff of the Roman see *papa*, whether when writing to him, as “to Pope Symmachus” and “to Lord Pope,” or when speaking of him to others, as in book III, letter 10; book VI, letter 33; and elsewhere.

> Cassiodorus used the word with the same distinction after Ennodius. Although he calls Boniface, Agapetus, and John, the pontiffs of the Roman see, *papae*, he calls Eustorgius and Datius of Milan, and other rulers of other cities, nothing but bishops.

> Yet not everyone followed this example. Many writers of different nations, especially those outside Italy, continued to apply the name *papa* to other bishops as well, down to the time of Gregory VII, who, as Cardinal Baronius observed, first decreed in a Roman synod that the name *papa* should belong to one person alone throughout the Christian world.

## PARENS

Heraclides, chapter 50: “The parent of these men, named Pammachius, a proconsular man”—that is, a brother or relative.

Capitolinus, in *Antoninus the Philosopher*: “He showed all his relatives as much respect as he had shown when a private citizen.”

The same author, in *Maximinus the Younger*: “When he was given to a grammarian, one of his relatives presented him with all Homer’s books in purple.”

Lampridius, *Alexander Severus*: “If Alexander found his friends and relatives bad, he punished them.”

Jerome, *Apology II against Rufinus*: “Unless perhaps by *parents* he means relatives and connections in ordinary military and popular speech.”

The word occurs frequently in this sense among writers of the later period, and several times here in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

## PATRICIUS

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 11: “The patrician Nicetas, observing the magnanimity of this man, full of virtues.”

Concerning the dignity and office of the patricians, insofar as is required here, the very learned Nicolaus Alemannus writes in his book *On the Lateran Walls*:

> In former times there were patricians in the Roman state, who lived on equal terms with the rest of the Senate. But by a law of Constantine the Great—if Zosimus is to be trusted—they were made next to the majesty of Caesar and were preferred to senators and praetorian prefects both in rank and in speaking their opinions in the Senate.

> The distinction of this order remained intact until the reign of Justinian, if we believe Procopius, and for a long time afterward. From approximately the time of Justinian, unless perhaps earlier, although that does not presently come to mind, the prefecture of provinces was added to the dignity.

> Those who did not hold a provincial office but were present in the city and Senate were called *praesentales patricii*, as in Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book VIII, letter [unspecified]. Those who held a prefecture were accustomed to be named according to the custom and law of their respective provinces: proconsuls of Africa, exarchs of Italy, strategoi of Sicily, praetors of the East, and so forth.

## PAXIMATES, OR PAXIMATIA, OR PAXAMIDIA

Rufinus, book I, no. 4: “He saw a great smoke rising from the basket where the loaves—that is, the *paximatia*—had been stored.”

Pelagius, book IV, no. 25: “I seized one *paximas*, or twice-baked loaf, and secretly ate it.”

The same passage appears in book IV, chapter 47, in excerpts from Cassian, *Conferences* II, chapter 11: “I would secretly hide one *paximas* in my bosom every day.”

Pelagius, book X, no. 65: “I fast for two days and eat two *paximates*.”

Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 28: “He placed on the table four *paxamidia* of six ounces each.”

Rufinus, book III, no. 31: “He took only one *paximatius* and five olives as food.”

John, book III, no. 2: “He also set the table at the signal of the elder, and placed three *paximates* upon it.”

In the *Cenobitic Rule of the Fathers*, chapter 10—a book which some think is Columbanus’ penitential rule:

> If a brother is disobedient, let him spend two days with one *paximate* and water. If someone says, “I will not do it,” let him spend three days with one *paximatius* and water. If someone does not ask pardon or offers an excuse, let him spend two days with one *paximatius* and water.

Suidas: “A twice-baked bread, which among the Romans is called *paxamas*.”

The same author: “*Paxamas*, the twice-baked bread; the word is Roman.”

By “Romans” here Lipsius, *Roman Military Affairs*, book V, dialogue 11, understands those Greek-speaking Romans in the Byzantine Empire who used this expression.

Nicolaus Rigaltius, in his *Mixed-Barbarian Tactical Glossary*, plausibly thinks that the word was derived from Paxamus, the culinary writer. Suidas says of him: “Paxamus wrote a work on culinary art in alphabetical order, and two books of *Biotica*.”

Various other authors also mention *paximatia*. Leo the Emperor, *Tactics*, chapter 10, section 13: “But also have as provisions twenty or thirty pounds of *paxamadium*, *pistis*, or some other kind of light food.”

The same, chapter 12, section 123:

> On the day of battle, therefore, each soldier must carry at his saddle water in the vessels called flasks, a *paxamadion* in his saddle-bag, and one or two pounds of flour.

The same, chapter 13, section 2:

> When each soldier advances to the battle line, he must have in his saddle-bag one or two pounds of bread, flour, cooked *pistis*, *paxamades*, or meat.

Isidore’s Glosses: “*Paximatium*, bread baked under ashes.”

Liutprand, *On the Embassy*: “They sit alone at the bare table, placing a *paximatium* before themselves.”

Columbanus, *On the Rule of Monks*, chapter 5: “Vegetables, pulses, and flour mixed with water, together with a little *paximate* bread, so that the belly may not be burdened and the mind suffocated.”

Goldastus is wrong when, in the Law of the Alemanni, title 22, section 1, he corrects “two *modia* of bread” to “two *paxamadia*.” This is an excessive emendation, even doing violence to the laws.

Again he is wrong when he claims that *paxamadia* means purple loaves, because they become red from the fire. John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 7, concerning the old man Macno: “He neither drank wine nor ate bread, except purple bread.”

He says that such a bread is reddish in Plautus.

Goldastus is wrong, I say, since the true reading is *furfureum*, “bran bread,” as the first edition has it. Nor would Macno’s abstinence be marked by anything exceptional if he ate *paxamadia*, since that was the food of most monks in Egypt. But to eat bran bread was exceptional in Macno.

Plautus’ *red bread*, in *Casina*, act 2, scene 5, is interpreted by Festus as undercooked, which does not suit *paximatia*, although Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XX, chapter 2, interprets it as “re-cooked.”

Plautus, in *The Menaechmi*, act 5, scene 5, uses “pomegranate-colored” and “purple” bread humorously.

These *paximates* were also called dry loaves. Rufinus, book II, chapter 7, in the *Life of Apollonius*: “They had only a few dry loaves.”

Palladius, chapter 52, in his account of Apollon: “There were several dry loaves and some vegetables stored away.”

Rufinus, book III, no. 19: “He saw nothing in it except a few dry loaves hanging in a basket.”

Pelagius, book X, no. 97: “And he set before them dry bread, water, and salt, saying: ‘Look, for your sake we are having a feast today.’ And he put a little vinegar into these salt dishes.”

John, book III, no. 2: “He gave them an axe and a basket full of dry loaves and salt.” Some books add *dry* there.

Hesychius: “Twice-baked loaves, those baked a second time.”

Their dryness resulted from the second baking; hence they were called **δίπυρος ἄρτος**, “twice-baked bread.” This dryness and rebaking made them last longer. The same is intended in the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 11: “He stored away loaves for six months, as is customary among the Thebans; for they commonly remain unspoiled throughout the year.”

See above, **BUCCELLATUM**.

Since these loaves were dry—and I think also harder—their eaters soaked and moistened them with water. This is frequently said in these *Lives* as “soaking the loaves.”

Palladius, chapter 28: “He placed four *paxamidia* of six ounces each on the table; he moistened one for himself, for they were dry, and three for the other.”

Rufinus, book II, no. 4: “When the sixth hour had arrived, he soaked the bread in water, saying: ‘While this bread is being soaked, I must also wait for the ninth hour.’”

In the same place: “When the sixth hour had arrived, he soaked the bread in water.”

In Pelagius, book IV, no. 58, this is expressed: “He soaked the bread and sat down to eat.”

Likewise Rufinus, book III, no. 19: “He put out water and salt, and added pieces of bread—namely pieces of *paximatius*, or the whole *paximatius*—and they ate together.”

In Pelagius, book XV, no. 66: “He soaked loaves for him and gave him oil and salt.”

## PECCATOR

*Life of Paul the First Hermit*, no. 18: “I beg you, whoever reads this, to remember Jerome the sinner.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in the preface to the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*: “Receive, therefore, this holy work translated by a sinner.”

Thus holy men often used to place *sinner* above or below their writings out of humility.

Lisiardus, bishop of Soissons, in the *Life of Saint Arnulf*, chapter 50, on 15 August, says of Arnulf: “May the body of this sinner Arnulf be returned to the earth.”

Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, in a letter to Grimoald, master of the palace: “To the illustrious Lord Grimoald, mayor of the palace, Desiderius the sinner.”

The same to Medoaldus, bishop of Trier: “To his ever-lord, Medoaldus the pope, Desiderius the sinner.”

And to Codulphus: “To the illustrious Lord Codulphus, Desiderius the sinner.”

See more examples in Francesco Bernardino Ferrario, *On the Form of Ecclesiastical Letters*, book III, chapter 1.

## TO FALL AT THE FEET

Palladius, chapter 15: “To us who touch your feet.”

Here the translator Hervetus departed from the author’s meaning, translating it: “How can it be that these are equal from your feet?” He did not notice that **τῶν ποδῶν σου ἁπτόμεθα**, “we touch your feet,” has the appearance of a plea or supplication.

For in ancient times, when suppliants approached, they threw themselves at people’s knees and feet.

Homer, *Iliad* I: “And he took him by the knees.”

Xenophon, *Cyropaedia* VII: “They kissed both the hands and feet of Cyrus.”

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book VI, *On the Envoys of the Latins*: “They fell at the knees of the entire Senate and placed the insignia of supplication at the feet of Postumius.”

Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 9: “To fall at the feet of presbyters, to kneel before the beloved of God.”

Dionysius, letter to Demophilus: “But you kicked away the man who had fallen at the priest’s knees.”

—FRONTO

## PEDULIS

*Life of a Christian Monk*, prologue 22, section 5: “I found one *pedule*, and in it a large mass of coins.”

Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, in the life of Nicetius, bishop of Lyons: “For when, after cutting his hood, he covered his feet by arranging his *pedules*”—the manuscript reads *pedulibus* instead of *pedulis)—“he was immediately seized by a demon and fell onto the pavement.”

Guigo, fifth prior of the first Carthusian house, in the *Life of Hugh the Carthusian, Bishop of Grenoble*, relates how Hugh, clothing Bishop Odalric of Die in the Carthusian habit, “also ordered that he cut off the *pedules* from his leggings, so that, apart from his feet, he might lie entirely clothed. For he was grieved that some men, to the disgrace of holiness, slept with their shins uncovered.”

The commentator on Juvenal, satire 1: “New *pedules* in breeches. They call them *pedornes*.”

Isidore’s Glosses: “*Pedana*: a new *pedule*, which is sewn onto a boot.”

Benedict’s Glosses: “*Pedulia*, coverings for the feet; some interpret them as *artaria*.”

## PERIODEUTES

A circuit-rider, inspector, or visitor.

Heraclides, chapter 25: “Evagrius, son of a presbyter who had charge of many churches—men whom they call *Periodeutae*.”

Here the office of the *Periodeutes* is clearly expressed, although the name does not occur in Codinus.

In Gennadius, in the *Encyclical*, this order is established: “Bishop, chorepiscopus, *periodeutes*, presbyter, deacon.”

See Meursius, in the *Greek-Barbarian Glossary*.

Those whom we now call rural deans seem to exercise a similar office.

Our Gretzer, in his notes on Codinus, suggests whether this might be the same person who in the *Typicon of Sabas* is called **ἐξυπνιαστής**, “awakener,” whose duty it was during vigils and **ἀγρυπνίαι**, “all-night vigils,” to go around and awaken those who were sleepy.

It does not seem so. The translator of Heraclides clearly explains the matter.

## PHOLES

Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 134: “He received a daily allowance of nine *minuta*.”

The Greek is: “He received five **φόλεις** (*pholes*) daily.”

Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*: “A **φόλης**, which is also called a talent, is double, being composed of two silver coins, which make 208 denarii. A *pholē*, when reckoned in denarii rather than in silver coins, contains two small coins.”

Suidas: “**Φόλλις**, *pholleōs*, an obol; in the plural, **τοὺς φόλλεις**, ‘the *pholleis*.’”

Marcellinus Comes, in his *Chronicle*: “With coins which the Romans call *teruntiani* and the Greeks *follerales*, Anastasius, stamped with his own name, sold a conciliatory exchange to the populace.”

## PHRANGELITAE

Moschus, chapter 49, concerning the lictors who stood by.

The Greek is: “and the *phrangelitae* who stood by.”

They were called this because they carried **φραγγέλια**, that is, “whips.”

The word **φραγγέλιον** is well known from chapter 2 of the Gospel according to Saint John: “And making a whip from cords.”

Hence **φραγγελίτης**, “a lictor.”

George of Alexandria, in the *Life of Chrysostom*: “Having gone up into the episcopal residence, he ordered that its doors be secured and guarded by the servants and *phrangelitae* of the church.”

## PITTACIUM

In the *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 10: “That holy man brought forth a *pittacium* from his honored hand.” And in chapter 51: “Nor could this *pittacium* ever be found in any way by anyone.” The same statement is repeated several times in that chapter. Others write *pyctacium*. Pope Zacharias, in his letter 142 to Boniface, among the *Bonifaciana*: “For they contained the chapters in the *pyctacium* presented by them.” Here our Serarius writes:

“Correctly, *πυκτάκιον* as well as *πιττάκιον* is written. Properly, it is a small piece of cloth, and by analogy a small memorandum written on parchment or paper. The former derives its name from folding; the latter is still used among the Spaniards and Aquitanians, with a slight inflection, as *pedaeo* and *pedas*, and among the French as *une pièce*.”

[Col. 0484D] Hadrianus Junius, in his *Nomenclatura*, thinks that *pittacium* was perhaps distorted from *pettucium*, by which the Dorians designate thinner scraps of leather.

Moschopulus, *On Figures of Speech*:

> *Πεττύκια Δοριὰ λεπτὰ περιτμήματα τῶν δερματίων, ἀφ’ οὗ ἡμεῖς πιττάκια λέγομεν*  
> “*Pettycia* are called in the Doric dialect the thin trimmings of leather; from this we call them *pittacia*.”

Casaubon, in his notes on Lampridius’ *Alexander Severus*, holds that *πιττάκιον* was so called “from *πίττα*.” “For,” he says, “they are short tablets smeared with pitch or maltha, on which inscriptions and other such things were written—things that can be expressed in a few words.”

Later, *pittacium*, or *pettycium*, passed into *petia*, the word used by later ages. Henricus Rebdorffensis, in the *Annals*, under the year 1361: “Likewise, a nail with some piece of the wood of the holy cross. Likewise, a piece of the arm of Saint Anne. Likewise, a piece of the cord with which Christ was bound to the column.” Theodoricus de Appoldia also uses it in the preface preceding the *Life of Saint Dominic*, 5 August.

## PLUMATIUM

Pelagius, little book VII, no. 10: “And he drew a bundle beneath his head, like a *plumatium* made of rushes.” The Greek-Latin glossaries give *πλουμάκιον, πλουμμίον*, *plumacium*. Anastasius, in his account of Sergius: “Inside it he found a *plumatium* overlaid with silk, which is called a *stauracis*.” Godfridus of Viterbo, *Chronicle*, part IX:

> The last king of Assyria, named Sardanapalus,
>
> had made feather cushions, shut up in his hall.

Papias: “*Plumacium*, a cushion, is so called from feathers.” [Col. 0485B] The Camberon Glossary, manuscript: “A cushion, a padded headrest.”

## POEMENIUM

Palladius, chapter 77: “I lived with him for one year in Bethlehem, when he sat beyond the *Poemenium*.”

> *Συνέζησα γὰρ ἐγὼ τούτῳ ἐπὶ ἔτος ἓν ἐν Βηθλεέμ, ὁπηνίκα ἐκαθέζετο ἐπέκεινα τῶν Ποιμενίου.*  
> “For I lived with him for one year in Bethlehem, when he sat beyond the *Poemenium*.”

Meursius notes here: “He understands the monastery of Abba Poemen, whom John Moschus mentions in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 167.” So far, he. But, as I see it, even the most diligent men can fall into error here. Palladius’ Poemen lived several centuries apart from Moschus’ Poemen. The latter was a solitary of Moschus; the other, Palladius’ figure, was an abbot. Indeed, neither of them is meant here. Rather, *Poemenium* here is a place near Bethlehem, so called from the shepherds, where the angels appeared to them—a place not far from Bethlehem, as is clear here and [Col. 0485C] as Jerome testifies in letter 27 to Eustochium:

> “Not far from there, Bethlehem descends toward the Tower of Ader, that is, of the flock, near which Jacob pastured his flocks (Genesis XXXVII), and where the shepherds, keeping watch by night, were deemed worthy to hear: ‘Glory to God in the highest’ (Luke II),” and so forth.

This tower is one thousand paces from Bethlehem, where Helena erected a temple, as Nicephorus testifies, book VIII, chapter 30. Epiphanius the Monk, in his *Itinerary of Jerusalem*: “To the east of Bethlehem a monastery has been founded which is called the Sheepfold, where an angel appeared to the shepherds and said to them: ‘Cease guarding the flocks. Shout aloud in celebration.’” I scarcely doubt that the Greek had *Ποιμένιον*, that is, “sheepfold.”

## POLLUTIO NOCTURNA

Palladius, chapter 22, concerning Moses, formerly a robber, who was tormented by shameful dreams [Col. 0485D] and for that reason abstained from the sacraments, says that after the presbyter Isidore had freed him from them, he told him: “From now on, communicate in the sacraments with a good and confident spirit.” From this it appears that formerly many people, out of religious scruple, abstained from communion when shameful dreams and nocturnal pollution had befallen them during the night. See Cassian, who carefully investigates nocturnal illusion, *Conferences* XXII, chapters 4, 5, and 6. Augustine, apostle of the English, was also uncertain and hesitant on this matter; for this reason he consulted Pope Gregory, as recorded by Gratian, distinction 6, chapter “Testamentum.” Among the Scholastics, consult the foremost of the Scholastics, Saint Thomas Aquinas, part III, question 80, article 7.

## POSCA

Heraclides, chapter 25: “Tasting only vegetables and [Col. 0486A] *posca*, and lentils, for two full years.” Here Hervetus, the newer translator of Palladius, put *ptisana* in place of *posca*. The older translator of Palladius likewise has *ptisanae*. In Greek it is *ὀξύκρατον*. Later, in Heraclides, chapter 42: “For the rest of her life she lived content with *posca* and dry bread.” Here Hervetus, in his Palladius, retained *oxycratum* instead of *posca*, following the Greek. Certainly the old Greek-Latin Lexicon has: “*Ὀξύκρατον*, *posca*.” Pliny too, book XXVII, chapter 4, translates: “The root is boiled in *posca* for toothache.” This passage in Dioscorides, book II, chapter 129, concerns *ononis*, or *anonis*:

> *Ἀφεψηθεῖσα δὲ ἡ ῥίζα ἐν ὀξυκράτῳ, καὶ διακλυζομένη, πόνον ὀδόντων πραΰνει.*  
> “When the root has been boiled in *oxycratum* and used as a mouthwash, it alleviates toothache.”

The same Pliny, book XX, chapter 4, mentions *posca*: “Cultivated radishes, boiled in *posca*, are applied against the bites of snakes.” [Col. 0486B] Likewise, book XXII, chapter 25: “For pains of the liver it is necessary to cook it—that is, barley flour—with *posca*, or with wine.” He repeats the name several times in the same chapter. The same author, book XXX, chapter 7: “The wild pigeon cures colic when boiled in *posca*.” Suetonius, *Vitellius*, chapter XII: “When he had caught someone selling *posca* at Puteoli.” Spartianus, in *Hadrian*: “He also willingly used camp food in public, namely bacon, cheese, and *posca*, following the example of Scipio Aemilianus, Metellus, and his own predecessor Trajan.” Cornelius Celsus, book III: “It may be given mashed, either in hot water or in *posca*.” Alexander of Tralles, book XI:

> *Πάρεχε δὲ αὐτῷ πρὸ ἡμέρας εὐπέπτῳ ὄντι, ἢ εἰς ῥοσάτον, ἢ εἰς φοῦσκαν.*  
> “On the preceding day, give him something easily digested, either in rose wine or in *phusca* [*posca*].”

[Col. 0486C] Most grammarians and more recent lexicographers confuse *posca* with *lora* or *zythum*. Brodaeus refutes them in book IV of the *Miscellanies*, chapter II. The author of the manuscript Camberon Glossary was of the same opinion when he says: “*Pusca*, secondary wine.” But secondary, or second, wine is nothing other than *lora*. The same Glossary explains what secondary wine is:

> “The grape seeds are called the remains of grapes that have been thrown out, and for that reason the penultimate syllable is shortened. Since this noun is derived not from a noun but from a verb: *hic acinus, huius acini*. But *acinum*, in the neuter, is what is used to wash grapes after the wine has been pressed; it is called *acinum*, as though *aquidum*, and is called secondary wine, and is the drink of slaves.”

What *posca*, or *φοῦσκα*, is, Phaemon of Cynosophium explains in chapter 7: “*Phusca*, or *posca*, is vinegar, warm water, and two eggs.” Thus, at any rate, he adapts *posca* as a remedy for a dog that has become overheated. In other cases *posca* is simply a drink made by tempering a mixture of water and vinegar, a beverage used by soldiers and often expressed merely by the name “vinegar.” Plautus, in the *Rope*: “But this king is going to dine on vinegar and salt.” Spartianus, in *Pescennius*: “He ordered that no one drink wine on campaign, but that all be content with vinegar.” Vulcatius, in *Avidius*: “Besides bacon, biscuit, and vinegar.”

Moschopulus seems to have had another *φοῦσκα* in mind:

> *Φύσκη, ἡ κοινῶς φοῦσκα.*  
> “*Physca*, commonly *phusca*.”

Does he mean what Hesychius calls *φύσκη*, “the belly and the large intestine,” or what the *Corona pretiosa* calls *φοῦσκα*, “bladder,” *κίστη*?

## POSTLIMINIUM

The *Life of Malchus*, no. 4: “For I am a hereditary possessor returning after a long *postliminium*.” Jerome frequently uses this word. The same author, letter 12 to Gaudentius: “And after the deaths of my friends and perpetual mourning, I would write, an old man to an infant, after a long *postliminium*.” The same, preface to his commentary on Jonah: “Therefore, after so long a time, as if by a kind of *postliminium*, taking up the beginning of interpretation from Jonah.” The same, in the prologue to Joshua: “And to resume, as if by a kind of *postliminium*, a work that had long been laid aside.” It occurs frequently among the jurists; see Brissonius’ *Lexicon*. Cicero, *For Cornelius Balbus*: “What if a Roman citizen is permitted to be a Gaditanian, whether by exile, by *postliminium*, or by rejection from this citizenship?” [Col. 0487B] Prudentius, in the *Hamartigenia*:

> Then returning by *postliminium*,  
> Faith receives him in her deep bosom.

Lactantius, book IV, chapter 22: “If someone, returning from the dead, had received life again by *postliminium*.”

## PRAEFECTIANI

The old translation of Palladius’ *Lausiac History*, chapter 15, concerning Evagrius: “An angelic visitation came to him in the guise of a *praefectianus*.” Palladius by Hervetus, chapter 25: “An angelic vision appeared to him, presenting the appearance of a prefect’s soldier.” The Greek is:

> *Ἐπέστη αὐτῷ ἀγγελικὴ ὀπτασία ἐν σχήματι στρατιώτου τοῦ ἐπάρχου.*  
> “An angelic apparition came upon him in the form of a soldier of the prefect.”

Novella 124, section 17:

> *Ἐν τάξει τῶν ἐνδοξοτάτων ἐπάρχων ἀναφερόμενοι.*  
> “Being enrolled in the rank of the most illustrious prefects.”

“The officials of the most magnificent and glorious praetorian prefect.” Council of Chalcedon, act 1.

[Col. 0437C]

## PRAEFECTUS

*Ἔπαρχος*, “prefect.” This is different from *praeses*, “governor.” Nevertheless, interpreters often improperly translate *ἔπαρχος* as *praeses*. Palladius, chapter 3: “That he should hand her over to the prefect of Alexandria,” in Greek *ἐπάρχῳ*. Hervetus translated it as “governor,” and generally does so throughout. But in Alexandria and Egypt it was not a governor but a prefect who presided. This work also frequently has *ἀπ’ ἐπάρχου*, “from the prefect,” which here and elsewhere has not been correctly translated. See our Fronto, on Chrysostom.

## PRAEPOSITUS SACRI CUBICULI

Palladius, concerning Lausus, in the preface to the *Lausiac History*: “To Lausus the *praepositus*.” What office he held is explained by Palladius himself in the epilogue of the book, where he calls him *πραιπόσιτον τοῦ εὐσεβεστάτου κοιτῶνος*, “superintendent of the most sacred bedchamber.” This office occurs in *Novellae* 22, sections 3 and 4:

> *ὁ τῶν βασιλικῶν κοιτώνων προεστώς.*  
> “The superintendent of the imperial bedchambers.”

It also occurs in Zosimus. The *Notitia of the East*: “Under the authority of the illustrious man, the superintendent of the sacred bedchamber, the imperial household in Cappadocia.”

## PROASTION

*Προάστειον*, “suburb” or “place outside the city.” The *Life of Basil*, chapter 2: “He found him in the *proastion* with philosophers.” Rufinus, book III, no. 19: “Near the *proastion* that is called ‘at the Seventh.’” In the same context Pelagius, little book XV, no. 66, calls it a suburb.

Paul the Deacon, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 58: “King Liutprand, likewise in his *proastion* at Oloana, erected for Christ, with marvelous workmanship, a dwelling in honor of the martyr Saint Anastasius.” Bonaventure Vulcanius was mistaken in this passage. Because he found *prohastion* in his book, he thought it was the name of an office, derived from *hasta*, as if it referred to someone who carried a spear or royal staff. But he was misled by the custom of later scribes, who aspirated most words.

A letter of the emperor Justinian to Placidius: “With harbors, waters and the courses of waters, woods, and *proastia*.” Germanus, in the *Sanctions*:

> *Κἂν προάστειον ἢ μοναστήριον.*  
> “Whether a suburb or a monastery.”

1049 **PROTOCOMITES**

*Πρωτοκωμίτης*, “the first man or chief of a village.” Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 64, concerning Paphnutius:

> *Καὶ πάλιν φωνή τις γέγονε πρὸς αὐτὸν θεία λέγουσα· Ἔοικας τῷ τῆς πλησίον κώμης πρωτοκωμίτῃ.*  
> “And again a divine voice came to him, saying: ‘You resemble the *protocomites* of the neighboring village.’”

Hervetus translated this: “And again a divine voice came to him: ‘You are like the *protocomites* of the neighboring village.’” Ruffinus correctly translates *πρωτοκωμίτην*, in book II, chapter 16, as “the principal man of the village.”

Another word is *protocomes*, *πρωτοκόμης*, “the first or chief of the counts,” an office that consisted in membership of the imperial court, the army, or the provincial administration. See the Lexicons of the Jurists.

## PSIATRUS, PSIATHIUS, OR PSIATHIUM

This word occurs frequently in the *Lives of the Fathers*. The *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 43: “And so that I would not be idle, I chose to weave *psiathi* with the brothers.” Chapter 47: “He came to the brothers who were working on *psiathi*.” Chapter 52: “They were always working on *psiathia*.” The *Life of Abraham the Hermit*, chapter 3: “And also one *psiathium*, on which he used to sleep.” And chapter 14: “A violent flame began to burn his *psiathium*, on which he had been standing.” The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 20: “How many there are now who, having half a *psiathum* beneath them and half above them, cannot stretch out their feet.” The *Life of Euphrosyne*, [Col. 0488C] chapter 16: “He remained in the same cell, sleeping on the same *psiathium* on which Euphrosyne had slept.” The *Life of Mary, Abraham’s Niece*, chapter 8: “For fifty years of your ascetic life you had lain upon a *psiathium*.”

This word is common in the furnishings of the ancient monks. For the Greeks, *psiathium* is a mat or rush-mat made from reed or papyrus. The Egyptian monks used it as a bed and covering. The Glossary: “A mat, *Ψιάθιον*.” See Cassian, *Institutes*, book IV, chapter 13, and *Conferences* I, chapter 23. Hesychius:

> *Ψιάθια τὰ ἐν τοῖς δικαστηρίοις ἐπὶ τῶν καθέδρων ἐπιστορνύμενα.*  
> “*Psiathia*: those spread over the chairs in the courts.”

The same author:

> *Ψίαθος, ἡ χαμεύνη, καὶ τὸ φυτόν, ἐξ οὗ πλέκεται ψίαθος.*  
> “*Psiathus*: a bed spread on the ground, and the plant from which a *psiathus* is woven.”

See also his entries under *Κάνναι* and *Κάναθρα*.

## PTISANA

Palladius, the old translation of the *Lausiac History*, chapter 15: “Because of weakness of the stomach he was compelled to take cooked food. He no longer touched bread; but taking vegetables, *ptisanae*, and legumes for as long as two years, he died.” In the translator of Heraclides, chapter 25: “Since, because of weakness of his stomach, his body needed him to take cooked food, he never touched bread, but for two full years tasted only vegetables, *posca*, and lentils.”

Palladius, in Hervetus’ translation, chapter 86: “Since, because of the weakness of his body and stomach, the flesh needed him to take something that had passed through fire, he touched bread but did not take it; rather, he took either cooked vegetables, *ptisana*, or legumes for two years.” When this passage is compared with the translation of the earlier witnesses, it seems that one should read: “He never touched bread, but took cooked vegetables, either *ptisana* or legumes, for two years.”

Goldastus is altogether foolish here when, writing to the rule of Saint Columbanus, he reads *pisana* instead of *ptisana*: “*Pisana*,” he says, “is a stew made from these ingredients.” We could dispense with this conjecture, contrary to the agreement of all the interpreters, who either found *πτισσάνην* in the Greek and retained it in the Latin text, or wished to express the same thing by *posca*.

## PTOCHIUM

The *Life of Euphrosyne*, chapter 7: “Behold the *ptochia*, *hierocomia*, *xenodochia*, and monasteries.” Most editions have *tapetia* instead of *ptochia*, which makes no sense. The *ptochia* are frequently mentioned by the ancients. Canon 10 of the Council of Chalcedon, the Fifth Ecumenical Council:

> *Ἤ τοι τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτὴν μαρτυρίων ἢ πτωχείων ἢ ξενοδοχείων.*  
> “Or those martyr-shrines, *ptochia*, or xenodochia that are under it.”

And canon 8:

> *Οἱ κληρικοὶ τῶν πτωχείων, καὶ μοναστηρίων καὶ μαρτυρίων.*  
> “The clergy of the *ptochia*, monasteries, and martyr-shrines.”

The Greek word is also used by Latin authors. The testament of Saint Remigius: “As I shall have arranged concerning the *ptochia*, monasteries, martyr-shrines, deaconries, xenodochia, and all the *matriculae* living under your authority.” The *Capitularies*, book VII, title 2: “Clerics who are placed over *ptochia*, or who are ordained in monasteries or basilicas of martyrs”—words taken from the aforementioned canon 8 of the Council of Chalcedon. More concerning *ptochia* and *ptochotrophia* may be found in the Legal Lexicons.

## RACANA OR RACHANA

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 20: “With mats and *rachanae*.” Hence *rachanellae*, chapter 20: “For four *rachanellae* were sold for one coin.” Ennodius, book IX, letter 17, to Apodemia: “Send me quickly a cloak and *racanae*, of whatever color you wish, red or dark.” Our Jacobus Sirmondus notes there:

“What kind of garment *racanae* were is unclear; they seem to belong among footwear, like *ragae* and *tzangae*. Book III of the Theodosian Code, *On the Dress That Ought to Be Worn within the City*: ‘Within the city of Rome no one may wear either *ragae* or *tzangae.’”
