So far he. I doubt that these *ragae* refer to *racanae*. I would rather think that *racana* is distorted from the Greek *ῥάκη*, meaning a cheap garment, as *racana* is understood here also. For in Ennodius it is joined with *laena*, which is a shabby garment. Claudius Salmasius used a corrupt text of Ennodius when, in his notes on Vopiscus’ *Firmus the Tyrant*, he cited *lanae racanas*.

Hesychius:

> *Ῥάκη, ἀποσκορακίσματα, καὶ ἀποσπάσματα, ἱμάτια.*  
> “Trimmings, torn-off pieces, garments.”

The same author:

> *Ῥάκκος, διεῤῥωγὸς ἱμάτιον.*  
> “A ragged garment.”

Again:

> *Ῥάχη, ἀποραχίσματα καὶ ἀποσπάσματα.*  
> “Torn pieces and fragments.”

Thus they now write *racana*, now *rachana*.

In Nicetas Choniates, book II, *On the Deeds of Alexius Angelus*, there is *ῥακενδύτης*, to which a manuscript Glossary adds *μοναχός*, “monk.” Likewise in the same author’s book *On Events after the Capture of the City*: *ῥακίοις ἐσπειραμένοι*, “wrapped in rags.” And in the same author, book III, *On the Reign of Isaac Angelus*, *ῥακενδύτης* is explained by the Glossator as *ῥασαφορών*, “wearing the *rason*”; concerning this, see under **SCHEMA**.

## RAPHANELAEUM

Pelagius, book V of *The Lives of the Fathers*, little book IV, no. 59: “A little vessel in which there was *raphanelaeum*.” The vulgate editions, with an addition, read: “*Raphanelaeum*, that is, linseed oil.” The Paris edition, omitting the word *raphanelaeum*, substitutes: “oil pressed from flaxseed.”

What *raphanelaeum* is, Pliny describes in book XIX, chapter 5, when discussing the radish: “It is especially celebrated in Egypt for the abundance of its oil, which they make from its seed. They are especially eager to sow it, if permitted, because it yields more profit than grain, is subject to less taxation, and produces no more abundant oil.”

## REGIA

Used absolutely, *regia* signifies the principal door. The *Life of Mary of Egypt*, chapter 5: “The principal door of the monastery was never opened.” Likewise in Ennodius, epigram 17, the inscription is: “Above the principal door of the dining room in the house,” which depicted Mount Helicon with its waters.

Gregory of Tours, book IV, chapter 13: “While they were walking through the church, they approached the principal doors of the sacred building, which had then been opened.” Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Honorius: “He covered the principal doors at the entrance of the larger church, which are called the middle doors, with silver.” Likewise, in his account of Conon: 1050 “Those who had been sent from the army to guard the principal doors of the basilica kept watch over them while they were closed.”

## REGULA

Pachomius received his rule from an angel. His *Life*, chapter 12: “Which rule the Tabennesiotes still observe today.” Therefore John Meursius is mistaken in his Greek-Barbarian Glossary when, under the word *Μοναχός*, he thinks that Saint Benedict was the first to prescribe a rule for monks. Benedict himself acknowledges the earlier rule of Saint Basil in chapter 73 of his own Rule:

> “The conferences of the Fathers, their institutions and way of life, and also the rule of our holy Father Basil—what else are they but instruments of virtue for monks who live and obey well?”

And Pachomius had already received a rule from an angel before this. Therefore, when Hildegard says that Benedict was the first author of rules, understand her to mean in Italy, which he himself first greatly illuminated by his Rule.

## RESCELLA

Pelagius, book V of *The Lives of the Fathers*, little book X, no. 18: “He gave him gold, coins, *rescellae*, and everything he had in his reply.” And no. 76: “My garments were worthy of an inestimable price, and in place of them I use these cheap *rescellae*.” Here *rescellae* seem to mean cheap clothing. Likewise in the same Pelagius, little book XIII, no. 1: “He clothed himself in his *rescellae*, which he had previously owned.”

The manuscript Camberon Glossary: “*Recella*, a diminutive of *recula*, and *recula* from *res*.” Charisius Sosipater, book I of his *Grammar*, derives *recula* from *res*, as *specula* from *spes*. Priscian likewise does so, in his notes on twelve verses of the *Aeneid*, on the words from book III of the *Aeneid*: “After the affairs of Asia.”

Likewise, in the same Camberon Glossary: “*Rescellae*, a kind of garment, that is, skins.” Apuleius, book IV of the *Metamorphoses*: “Why do you give the rich neighbors the poor, ragged little belongings of a wretched old woman?” Therefore [Col. 0491A] from *res* came first *rescula*, and then *rescella*.

Here I may propose my conjecture concerning a passage in Apuleius, book III of the *Metamorphoses*, where he says: “See, finally, how so great a thing is accomplished by such small and worthless means. A little dill, with bay leaves added, is given with spring water as a bath and a drink.” Beroaldus says that the old reading was *Herculis*, and himself restores *Hercules*, so that it is an oath by Hercules, like *mehercules* and *mediusfidius*. Lipsius, book II of his *Letters*, letter 22, says that the great interpreter Beroaldus was asleep. The old reading is *Herculis*. He himself reads: “So great a thing is accomplished by herbs. Dill,” and so forth.

I know, certainly, that many herbs were used in magic, whence in the same author, *Apology* I, we find “little roots, herbs, and shoots,” and in book II of the *Metamorphoses*, “after inhaling shoots, little stones, and things of that sort.” From these it might also seem that *surculis* should be read instead of *herculis*. I would nevertheless prefer to read *reculis*: first, because the ancients were accustomed to write *herculis* as *Hrenus* and *Ludovicus* do in a very old manuscript, from which, by transposition, they made *herculis*; second, because *reculae* include all the things that follow—dill, bay, and spring water—whereas *herbulae* do not fit any of these, if *dill* is taken as seed; third, because *reculae* here correspond to what the same author calls *frivola* in book II; fourth, because the same author uses *reculas* in book IV of the *Metamorphoses*, already cited.

It was also called *reicula*. The *Capitularies*, book VII, title 192: “Those who ask kings for the church’s *reicula* and, driven by dreadful greed, seize the property of the needy.” The *Chronicle of Saint Gall*, *On the Deeds of Charlemagne*: “That the *reiculae* of Saint Gall were collected not from royal gifts but from the small donations of private persons.”

Could these *reiculae* of the churches be the very things that the Greeks called *πτωχικά*? Balsamon, on Apostolic Canon 59:

> *Ὁ ἐπίσκοπος ἤφειλει μετὰ τὴν ἀναγκαίαν αὐτοῦ δαπάνην, καὶ τὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας καὶ τῶν κληρικῶν συνήθη οἰκονομίαν, τὰ περιττεύοντα ἐκ τῶν εἰσόδων τῆς ἐκκλησίας διαδιδόναι πρὸς πένητας· πτωχικὰ γὰρ καλοῦνται.*  
> “After his necessary expenses and the customary administration of the church and clergy, the bishop ought to distribute the surplus from the church’s revenues to the poor. For they are called *ptochika*, that is, ‘the goods of the poor.’”

And Zonaras, on the same canon:

> *Τὰ τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν πράγματα ἡ Γραφὴ πτωχικὰ ὀνομάζει, καὶ δεῖ ταῦτα διαδίδοσθαι τοῖς πτωχοῖς.*  
> “Scripture calls the goods of the churches *ptochika*, and they ought to be distributed to the poor.”

## RESTES PISCIUM

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 19: “A thousand strings of dried fish, which are called *menomenae*.” Thus Martial, book XII, epigram 32:

> “And bald strings of garlic and onions.”

Here he attributes baldness to the strings, to show that they were old and worn, from which garlic and onions were accustomed to hang.

## RICINUS

Palladius, chapter 86: “So that his body was covered with *ricini*, just like the bodies of wild animals.” Hervetus had translated: “was covered with flies.” The Greek is:

> *ὡς καὶ τὸ σῶμα κρότωνας ἐκβρᾶσαι.*  
> “So that his body emitted *krotones*.”

I discussed this at considerable length in my notes on the old *Lausiac History* of Palladius. I now add some material from our Fronto: *Κρότων* is more correctly understood here as *ricinus*, so that it means “the creature found on dogs and cattle.” [Col. 0492A]

Pliny, book XI, chapter 34: “It is an animal that lives with its head always fixed in blood; it is common on cattle, sometimes found on dogs, and on sheep and goats only this one.” Suidas calls it “the lice of dogs,” *κυνεῖοι φθεῖρες*. Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book V, chapter 31:

> *Τὰ δὲ πρόβατα καὶ αἶγες κρότωνας ἔχουσι, τοῖς δὲ κυσὶν οἱ καλούμενοι γίνονται κυνόῤῥαισταί.*  
> “Sheep and goats have *krotones*; on dogs there occurs the creature called *kynorrhaistes*, which takes its name from the same animal.”

Columella, book VI, chapter 2, mentions *rediviorum*; Pliny, book XXII, chapter 18, mentions dog ticks.

*Ἐκβρᾶσαι* literally means “to make boil over” or “to pour out,” as in 2 Maccabees I:12:

> *Αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐξέβραξε τοὺς παραταξαμένους ἐν τῇ ἁγίᾳ πόλει.*  
> “For he himself made those who had drawn up for battle in the holy city boil over.”

## ROSARIUM

The practice of counting prayers offered to God with pebbles is exemplified here in Palladius, chapter 23, concerning Paul, who lived on Mount Pheane: “He had three hundred prayers expressed and prescribed, and had an equal number of pebbles in his bosom, throwing one pebble at each prayer,” *ψῆφος*. Sozomen likewise relates this about him, book VI, chapter 29, and Cassiodorus after him, book VIII, chapter 1.

The acts of the holy woman Saint Clare also reveal that she used prayer pebbles to count her prayers to God. This use of pebbles is not superstitious, any more than the twelve stones that Joshua ordered his soldiers, after crossing the Jordan on dry ground, to carry with them from the riverbed into the camp, namely as a reminder of the benefit granted by God Almighty.

## SABULUM

The *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, no. 14: “He spread sand over his head.” The *Life of Hilarion*, no. 40: “When he had drawn three signs of the cross in the sand.” The manuscript Camberon Glossary: “*Sabulum*, a very light kind of earth.” Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 18: “For beneath it lies sand, and only a grain is held together by mud.” Jerome, on Ezekiel XLVII: “To the mounds of eastern sand.”

To spread sand over one’s head was customary among many peoples in mourning, especially funeral mourning. This *Life* bears witness concerning the Egyptians.

Concerning the Romans, Virgil, book X of the *Aeneid*, about King Latinus, grieving over the fate of his wife and city:

> He goes, his garment torn, Latinus,
>
> stunned by the fate of his wife and the ruin of his city,
>
> disgracing his white hair, drenched in filthy dust.

And in book X, concerning Mezentius, because Aeneas had killed his son Lausus:

> His mind, foreknowing evil, recognized the distant groan:
>
> he disfigures his white hair with filthy dust…

The same in the *Ciris*:

> …terrified by grievous disaster,
>
> he disfigures his unshorn hair with much dust.

Catullus, in the *Argonautica*:

> Defiling his white hair with earth and scattered dust.

Silius Italicus, book XII, concerning the Campanians:

> …now defiling in the dust
>
> their whitening hair.

Ovid, book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, fable 4:

> …Oeneus,
>
> the father, defiles his white hair and aged features
>
> with dust poured upon the ground.

[Col. 0493A] Concerning the Greeks, Homer bears witness in *Iliad* Σ, where Achilles, having heard of Patroclus’ death:

> *Ἀμφοτέρῃσι δὲ χερσὶν ἑλὼν κόνιν αἰθαλόεσσαν,*  
> *Χεῦατο κὰκ κεφαλῆς.*  
>
> “Taking the hot dust in both hands,
>
> he poured it over his head.”

The same in *Iliad* Ω concerning Priam, who, sprinkled with dust, mourns the death of his son Hector.

The Jewish custom in this same matter is abundantly well known from the sacred writings.

## SAITES

Palladius, chapter 22: “After he had drunk eighteen *saites*.” The Greek: “Having drunk eighteen *saites*, according to the Italian measure.”

Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*:

> *Ἀπόῤῥυμα δὲ παρὰ μόνοις Θηβαίοις μετρεῖται. Ἥμισυ γὰρ τοῦ σαΐτου ἐστίν, ὁ δὲ ἀληθινὸς σαΐτης ξέστων ἐστὶν κβʹ.*  
> “The *aporrhyma* is measured only among the Thebans. For it is half a *saites*, while the true *saites* is twenty-two sextarii.”

## SANCTORUM CORPORA INCORRUPTA

The *Life of Hilarion*, no. 46: “And with his whole body intact, as though he were still alive.” John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 121, concerning two monks who died of thirst: “We found both of them intact, and taking them, we buried them at Raythu.”

God has honored the bodies of many saints with this incorruptibility: Saint Ursinus, first bishop of Bourges, in Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 80; Saint Eligius, in Surius, 1 December, by Audoenus, bishop of Rouen; Saint Sigebert, king of the Franks, by Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, in Surius, 1 February, volume VII; Saint Wenceslaus, duke of Bohemia, through John Dubravius, bishop of Olomouc, 28 September, in Surius, volume VII; Saint Stanislaus, bishop and martyr, in Surius, 11 April; Saint Hubert, bishop of Liège, in the same author, 3 November; Saint Othmar, abbot of Saint Gall, by Walafrid, abbot of Reichenau, in Surius, 16 November; Saint Edmund, bishop of Canterbury, in Surius, 16 November; Saint Raynald, archbishop of Ravenna, by Hieronymus Rubeus, 18 August, in Surius, volume VII; Saint Sosius, deacon, by John the Deacon, 5 January, in the same author and volume, 23 September; Saint Honoratus, bishop of Arles, by Hilary, bishop of Arles, in the same author and volume, 15 January; Saint Judocus, by Abbot Florentius, in the same author and volume, 13 December; Saint Hermann, or Joseph, canon of Steinfeld, in the same author and volume, 7 April; Saint Theodore the Studite, by Michael the Studite, 11 November; Saint Ethelberga, virgin, in Bede, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 8, 7 July, in volume VII of Surius; and Saint Ludmilla, martyr, in the *Life of Saint Wenceslaus* cited above.

I will not heap up more examples. Similar examples occur very frequently in the *Lives of the Saints*. See some in John Baptist Signius’ *Reliquary*, chapter 21; in our Gretzer, *Apology 2 and 3 for the Life of Our Saint Ignatius*, book IV, chapter 1, against the Calvinist Misenus; and in Kormannus, *On the Miracles of the Dead*, part III. See also Gretzer, *On Christian Burial*, book I, chapter 4.

## SANCTUARIUM

The *Life of Euphrasia*, chapter 1: “And she offered many offerings in churches and *sanctuaria*.” And chapter 5: “Who also, while she was at leisure there, was in the *sanctuaria*.” I do not know whether here he calls *σεμνεῖα*, that is, monasteries, *sanctuaria*. Elsewhere *sanctuarium* means a definite place in a temple. See **SECRETARIUM**.

Aggenus, commentary on Frontinus, *On the Boundaries of Fields*: “That which was profane, though it had once been sacred and afterward was made available for human use—that is, outside the shrine and outside the sanctuary—is called *profanum*.”

Certain sacred veils or *brandea* were also called *sanctuaria*. Baronius discusses them in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* for 15 January. After quoting the words of Saint Germanus and his fellow apostolic legates to Pope Hormisdas:

> “Therefore, if it seems good to Your Beatitude, order that the *sanctuaria* of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul be generously given to him according to custom; and, if it can be done, it is for you to decide to set down those *sanctuaria* at the second cataract.”

There are letters of Pope Hormisdas to the same legates, written concerning the same matter, and others likewise to Justinian, in which he states that he is sending only *sanctuaria*. By *sanctuarium* we should understand a veil which Saint Gregory, in his letter to the empress Constantina, book III, letter 30, calls a *brandeum*. He says that blood flowed from it when, according to his account, it was cut with scissors by Pope Leo.

Elsewhere the same Gregory calls it a veil that was customarily brought near the holy bodies of martyrs, as in book IV, letter 44, from the Roman synod; and in book XII, decree 4, he also calls that veil a *brandeum*. John the Deacon, in book II, chapter 42 of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, likewise calls it a veil, while recounting a great miracle connected with it. Thus far Baronius.

There were also *sanctuaria* belonging to kings and princes, namely secret and confidential archives. Pliny, book XXIII, chapter 8: “In the archives of Mithridates, the greatest of the conquered kings, Gnaeus Pompey found, in a private memorandum written by Mithridates’ own hand, the composition of an antidote.”

Siculus Flaccus, in *On the Conditions of Lands*: “If anyone objects, one customarily consults the emperor’s archive. For he keeps in the archive the plans of all lands—both those divided and those assigned—as well as the division itself, the records, and the imperial authority. Whatever the plans may be, if doubt arises, one must return to the prince’s archive to establish their authenticity.”

## SARTAGINES IGNITAE

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, no. 3: “Who had previously overcome red-hot frying pans.” This punishment is mentioned in 2 Maccabees VII, which Prudentius expresses as follows, hymn 14:

> She saw before her the funeral instruments
>
> of her own sons, yet the mother was not shaken,
>
> rejoicing whenever the hissing frying pan,
>
> with its oil, had roasted a young man.

For more concerning these matters, see Antonius Gallonius, *On the Torments of the Holy Martyrs*, chapter 7.

## SATYRI

Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, no. 8: “The pagan world, deceived by various errors, worships them, calling them Fauns, Satyrs, and Incubi.” On the Satyrs, consult Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus, *Syntagma 15 of the History of the Gods*; our Martin Delrio, part III of his commentary on Seneca’s *Oedipus*; Natale Conti, book V of the *Mythology*, chapter 8; and our Conimbricenses, in book II of the *Physics*, chapter 9, question 5, article 2.

## SCALPRAE

Jerome, *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, no. 5: “Moreover, throughout the excavated mountain there were not a few dwellings, in which *scalprae*—as well as anvils and hammers, with which money had once been struck—could be seen.” So the most ancient manuscript reads, instead of *scabrae*.

Papias the Vocabulist: “*Scalpere*, to rub, to bore. *Scalprus* is so called because it is suitable for *pituris* [Col. 0495D: as printed; perhaps *picturis*, ‘paintings,’ or *scripturis*, ‘writings’] and holes, as though *scal-phorus*; [Col. 0495B] its diminutive is *scalpellus*. *Scalpra*, an iron tool with which leather is prepared and with which shoemakers’ forms are made. *Scalpellus*, an iron tool with which leather is prepared and with which shoemakers’ forms are made, and with which they correct written pages.”

John of Genoa, in the *Catholicon*: “*Scalprum*, from *scalpo, -is*, is said to be *hoc scalprum, -pri*, and *hic scalprus*, that is, an iron tool with which leather is prepared or scraped; or a knife; or a scribal pen-case. Likewise, *scalprum* or *scalprus* is an iron instrument otherwise called a *celtes*. Hence *hoc scalpellum, -li*, and *hic scalpellus, -li*, a diminutive according to Hugutio. Hence Jeremiah XXXVI: ‘He cut it with a scribe’s knife.’”

The *Vocabulary of Gerard de Scheuren*: “*Scalprum, -pri*, and *scalprus, -pri*: an iron tool with which one scrapes leather, or a sharp little knife of a scribe, or an iron chisel.”

## SCAPULARE

*Life of Antony*, chapter 23: “He washed his *ependytes*, that is, his scapular.” Thus most printed editions; but *scapulare*, the interpretation of the earlier term, has slipped from the margin into the text. Properly, *scapulare* is Greek ἐπωμίς (*epōmis*, “shoulder-garment”).

## SCHEMA

*Life of Euphrosyne*, chapter 7: “And she clothed her in the tunic of the *schema*.” *Life of Euphrasia*, or Euphraxia, chapter 8: “If you love us, remain with us in our *schema*.” Anastasius the Persian, January 22, in the *Menaea*: Καὶ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ μονῇ τοῦ ἁγίου Σάββα τὸ ἱερὸν τῶν μοναχῶν σχῆμα λαμβάνει: “While staying in the monastery of Saint Sabbas, he assumes the sacred habit of the monks.” It occurs very frequently in ascetic writers.

But since there were two monastic *schemata*: one called τὸ μικρὸν σχῆμα, or τοῦ μανδύου, “the small *schema*,” or “the *schema* of the mantle”; and the other called τὸ μέγα or τὸ ἀγγελικόν, “the great” or “angelic *schema*,” it is useful here to append certain details concerning both kinds from the *Euchologion*, omitting the prayers and touching only upon the rites, after first setting out the order for instituting a novice.

### Order for instituting a novice wearing the *rason*

Ἀκολουθία εἰς ἀρχάριον ῥασοφοροῦτα: “Order for instituting a novice wearing the *rason*.”

This is expressed somewhat more fully in the table of contents: Ἀκολουθία γινομένη εἰς τὸ φορέσαι τινὰ ῥάσον μόνον καὶ καμιλαύχιον: “The order observed for one who wears only the *rason* and the *camelauchion*.” Meursius is incorrect in his Greek-Barbarous Lexicon, where under ῥάσα he places the negative particle μὴ before καμιλαύχιον. The novice is therefore instituted as follows:

1. Ὁ ἱερεὺς κουρεύει αὐτὸν σταυροειδῶς: “The priest tonsures the novice in the form of a cross.”

2. Ἐνδύει αὐτὸν χιτῶνα, καὶ καμιλαύχιον: “He clothes him in a tunic and a *camelauchion*.”

From this it is clear that the *rasa* was a tunic. That it was rough and coarse, not soft, is indicated by Nicetas in his *Manuel Comnenus*, book VII:

Τὸ μοναδικὸν σχῆμα ᾔτισε, καὶ οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν ὅθεν εὑρόντες τινὸς μοναχοῦ ῥάσα περιδύουσι μὲν αὐτὸν, καὶ ἀπεκδύουσι τὰ μαλακὰ καὶ ἀρχικὰ ἄμφια.

“He desired the monastic *schema*, and those around him, finding somewhere the *rasa* of a certain monk, clothed him in it and stripped off his soft and imperial garments.”

John Meursius cites it thus in his *Glossary of Greek and Barbarous Terms*, whereas the common edition has:

Καὶ τῆς πνευματικωτέρας ἀμφιάσεως, ἐχούσης τὸ ἀπαράσκευον τριβωνίου μέλανος, οἱ περὶ τὸν βασιλέα ὁθεντοῦν εὐπορήσαντες.

“And those about the emperor, having procured somewhere a more spiritual garment consisting of an unadorned black cloak.”

Thus, where in the same book the garments, namely the monastic garments, are called ἐσθήματα, old manuscript glosses append *rasa*. And in book IV of the same Manuel, where the text has μέλαν ἄμφιον, a manuscript gloss adds *rasa*. Likewise in Nicetas, book II, *On the Empire of Isaac Angelus*, where the text has μέλαν ἄμφιον, a manuscript gloss writes *rasa*. Similarly, in book III, concerning the reign of the same Isaac, *rakendytēs* is explained by a manuscript gloss as ῥασαφορῶν, “wearing a *rasa*.”

We have said enough above about the *camelauchion*.

The garment of the *rasa* mystically signified the robe of sanctification. This is gathered from the prayer found in the *Euchologion*:

Ἔνδυσον αὐτὸν ἁγιασμοῦ στολήν, σωφροσύνῃ περίζωσον τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτοῦ, πάσης αὐτὸν ἐγκρατείας ἀνάδειξον ἀγωνιστήν.

“Clothe him in the robe of sanctification; gird his loins with self-control; show him forth as a champion of every form of temperance.”

### Order of the small *schema*, or of the mantle

Ἀκολουθία τοῦ μικροῦ σχήματος ἤτοι τοῦ μανδύου: “Order for instituting a monk of the small *schema*, or of the mantle.”

1. Τίθησιν ὁ ἱερεὺς ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ τὸ σχηματολόγιον: “The priest places the *schematologion* upon him.”

2. Then, taking a small knife or scissors in his hand, the priest tonsures him in the form of a cross: κουρεύει αὐτὸν ὁ ἱερεύς σταυροειδῶς: “The priest tonsures him in the form of a cross.”

This cutting of the hair signifies the rejection of irrational desires, as is suggested in the prayer recited at the beginning:

Ἵνα τῇ ἀφαιρέσει τῶν ἀναισθήτων τριχῶν, συναποβάληται καὶ τὰς ἀλόγους ἐνθυμήσεις τε καὶ προσάξεις.

“So that, by the removal of senseless hairs, he may also cast away irrational thoughts and practices.”

3. Ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἡμῶν ὁ δεῖνα ἐνδύεται χιτῶνα ἀγαλλιάσεως: “Our brother N. is clothed in a tunic of exultation.”

4. Περιζώννυται τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἀληθείας, εἰς νέκρωσιν σώματος, καὶ ἀνακαίνισιν πνεύματος: “Our brother is girded about the loins with the power of truth, for the mortification of the body and the renewal of the spirit.”

5. Καλύπτεται περικεφαλαίαν ἐλπίδα σωτηρίας: “Our brother is covered with a helmet, as the hope of salvation.”

6. Λαμβάνει τὸ παλίον τὸν ἀρραβῶνα τοῦ μεγάλου καὶ ἀγγελικοῦ σχήματος, εἰς στολὴν ἀφθαρσίας καὶ σεμνότητος: “Our brother takes the mantle, the pledge of the great and angelic habit, as a robe of incorruption and sanctity.”

7. Ὑποδύεται τὰ σανδάλια εἰς ἑτοιμασίαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης: “Our brother puts on sandals in preparation for the Gospel of peace.”

Then they conclude:

Ἔλαβε τὸν ἀρραβῶνα τοῦ μεγάλου καὶ ἀγγελικοῦ σχήματος: “Our brother has received the pledge of the great and angelic habit.”

8. Δίδοται τῷ ἀποκαρέντι κηρός, καὶ τὸ ἅγιον Εὐαγγέλιον, καὶ σταυρός, καὶ γίνεται ὁ ἀσπασμός: “A candle, the holy Gospel, and a cross are given to the one who has been tonsured, and the embrace takes place.”

### Order of the great *schema*

Ἀκολουθία τοῦ μεγάλου σχήματος: “Order of the great and angelic habit.”

1. Ὁ ἱερεὺς κουρεύει αὐτὸν σταυροειδῶς εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Πατρός 1053 etc.: “The priest tonsures him in the form of a cross, in the name of the Father,” etc.

2. Ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἡμῶν ὁ δεῖνα ἐνδύεται χιτῶνα δικαιοσύνης καὶ ἀγαλλιάσεως τοῦ μεγάλου καὶ ἀγγελικοῦ σχήματος etc.: “Our brother N. is clothed in the tunic of righteousness and exultation of the great and angelic habit.”

3. Λαμβάνει τὸ παλίον τοῦ μεγάλου καὶ ἀγγελικοῦ σχήματος, εἰς στολὴν ἀφθαρσίας καὶ σεμνότητος etc.: “He takes the mantle of the great and angelic habit as a robe of incorruption and sanctity.”

4. Ἐνδύεται τὸ κουκούλιον τῆς ἀκακίας, εἰς περικεφαλαίαν ἐλπίδος σωτηρίου: “He is clothed in the cowl of innocence as a helmet of saving hope.”

5. Λαμβάνει τὸν ἀνάλαβον ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Πατρός, καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ, καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, ἀναλαμβάνων τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων, καὶ ἀκολουθῶν τῷ δεσπότῃ Χριστῷ: “He receives the scapular in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, taking up his cross upon his shoulders and following the Lord Christ.”

6. Περιζώννυται τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἀληθείας: “Our brother’s loins are girded with the power of truth.”

7. Ὑποδύεται τὰ σανδάλια εἰς ἑτοιμασίαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης: “He puts on sandals in preparation for the Gospel of peace.”

The conclusion is:

Ἔλαβε τὸ μέγα καὶ ἀγγελικὸν σχῆμα: “He has received the great and angelic habit.”

The rite then recapitulates these matters as though repeating and explaining them, once again in a prayer:

Ἵνα ἐν ἁγιασμῷ πολιτευσάμενος ἄσπιλον διατηρήσῃ, ὅπερ τῇ δυνάμει σου ἐνεδύσατο σχῆμα·  
Τῷ μὲν χιτῶνι τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἀμπεχόμενος·  
Τῇ δὴ ζώνῃ τὴν νέκρωσιν τοῦ σώματος, καὶ τὴν σωφροσύνην ἐν ἑαυτῷ περιφέρων·  
Τῷ δὲ ἀναλάβῳ, τῷ σταυρῷ τε καὶ πίστει κατακοσμούμενος·  
Τῷ δὲ περιβολαίῳ, στολὴν ἀφθαρσίας θωρακιζόμενος·  
Τοῖς δὲ σανδαλίοις, ἵνα ἐπιβῇ τῇ ὁδῷ τῆς εἰρήνης, καὶ τῆς σωτηρίας.

“So that, having ordered his life in sanctification, he may preserve undefiled the habit which, by your power, he has put on:

Clothed in righteousness by the tunic;

Bearing in himself, through the belt, the mortification of the body and temperance;

Adorned by the scapular with the cross and faith;

Armed by the mantle with the robe of incorruption;

And by the sandals, so that he may enter upon the way of peace and salvation.”

After this follow the same rites concerning the cross, candle, and embrace as in the order of the small *schema*.

The habit is apparently called “angelic” because those who wore it were supposed to remember that they ought to live an angelic life. *Euchologion*, p. 102:

Σῇ γὰρ πεποιθὼς συνεργίᾳ τὴν ἀγγελικὴν πολιτείαν ταύτην ἐπεισέρχομαι, φιλάνθρωπε.

“For, trusting in your cooperation, O lover of humankind, I enter upon this angelic manner of life.”

Rufinus, book II, chapter 11, concerning Hor: “He was the father of many monasteries, and by the habit itself appeared to possess angelic dignity.”

Palladius, concerning the same Hor, chapter 9: “Possessing monasteries of a thousand brothers, endowed with an angelic habit.”

Rufinus, book II, chapter 4, concerning Benus: “In every respect a man of an angelic order.”

In Dionysius the Areopagite as well, chapter 6, part II of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, where the mystery of monastic perfection is discussed, there is mention of tonsure with the sign of the cross and invocation of the Trinity, change of clothing, and embrace or salutation:

Τῷ σταυροειδεῖ τύπῳ σφραγισάμενος αὐτὸν ὁ ἱερεύς, ἀποκείρει, τὴν τρισσὴν τῆς θείας μακαριότητος ὑπόστασιν ἐπιβοήσας, καὶ τὴν ἐσθῆτα πᾶσαν ἀπαμφιέσας, ἑτέραν ἀμφιέννυσι, καὶ μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἱερῶν ἀνδρῶν, ὅσοι πάρεισιν, ἀσπασάμενος αὐτὸν κοινωνὸν ἀποτελεῖ τῶν θεαρχικῶν μυστηρίων.

“Having sealed him with the sign of the cross, the priest tonsures him, invoking the three persons of the divine blessedness; stripping him of all his clothing, he clothes him in another garment, and, after saluting him together with the other holy men who are present, makes him a participant in the divine mysteries.”

He then adds the explanation of the mystery:

Ἡ δὲ τοῦ σταυροειδοῦς τύπου σφραγίς, ὡς ἤδη παρ’ ἡμῶν εἴρηται, δηλοῖ τὴν πασῶν ὁμοῦ τῶν σαρκικῶν ὀρέξεων ἀνενεργησίαν.

“But the seal of the cross-shaped sign, as has already been said by us, signifies the mortification of all carnal desires together.”

Ἡ δὲ τῶν τριχῶν ἀπόκαρσις, ἐμφαίνει τὴν καθαράν καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον ζωήν, οὐκ ἐπιπλάστοις σχήμασι τὸ κατὰ νοῦν δυσειδὲς ἐπιθετικῶς καλλωπίζουσαν, ἀλλ’ αὐτὴν ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆς οὐκ ἀνθρωπικοῖς κάλλεσιν, ἀλλ’ ἑνιαίοις καὶ μοναχοῖς τὸ θεοειδέστατον ἀναγομένην.

“Moreover, the cutting of the hair indicates a pure and unadorned life, one that does not artificially beautify the ugliness of the mind by applying counterfeit forms, but that, in itself, rises not through human beauties but through qualities that are unified and monastic toward the closest possible likeness to God.”

Ἡ δὲ τῆς προτέρας ἐσθῆτος ἀποβολή, καὶ τῆς ἑτέρας λῆψις, τὴν ἀπὸ μέσης ἱερᾶς ζωῆς ἐπὶ τὴν τελειοτέραν μετάταξιν ἐμφαίνει· καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῆς ἱερᾶς θεογενεσίας ἡ τῆς ἐσθῆτος ἄμειψις ἐδήλου τὴν ἀποκαθαιρομένης ζωῆς εἰς θεωρητικὴν καὶ φωτιστικὴν ἕξιν ἀναγωγήν.

“The putting off of the former garment and the taking up of the other signifies the transition from a middle stage of sacred life to a more perfect one, just as in the sacred divine birth the changing of the garment signified the elevation of the life being purified into a contemplative and illuminating condition.”

Εἰ δὲ καὶ νῦν ὁ ἱερεὺς τε καὶ πάντες ὅσοι πάρεισιν ἱεροὶ, τὸν τετελεσμένον ἀσπάζονται, τὴν ἱερὰν τῶν θεοειδῶν ἐννόησον κοινωνίαν, ἀγαπητικῶς ἐν εὐφροσύνῃ θείᾳ συνηδομένων ἀλλήλοις.

“And if now both the priest and all the holy men who are present likewise salute the one who has been consecrated, understand this as the sacred fellowship of those who bear the likeness of God, rejoicing together with one another in loving affection and divine gladness.”

The garment in which the monk is clothed was black, as Pachymeres notes, and he explains its significance as follows:

Μοναχικὴ τάξις, ὅτι μοναχῶς καὶ ἑνοειδῶς, καὶ οὐ διχῶς, ἢ τριχῶς, ἢ πολλαχῶς πολιτεύεται. Τοῦτο γὰρ δηλοῖ δὲ τὸ ἀμφιεννύμενον μέλαν. Τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἄλλα τῶν χρωμάτων εἰς ἕτερα μεταπεσοῦνται ῥᾳδίως, καὶ πάντα εἰς τὸ μέλαν· τὸ δὲ μέλαν οὐκ ἔστι μεταβληθῆναι εἰς ἕτερον χρῶμα πώποτε.

“Monastic discipline means that one lives in a solitary and unified manner, not doubly, triply, or in many ways. This is signified by the black garment that is worn. For the other colors readily change into others, and all can be changed into black; but black can never be transformed into another color.”

Let this now suffice concerning the twofold monastic *schema*.

## SCHOLARIUS

John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 25: “As Abbot Gregory, one of the *scholarii*, related to us.” The Greek is ἐκ Σχολαρίων, which Hervetus incorrectly translated as “a scholar” (*scholasticus*). For *scholastici* were advocates engaged in pleading cases, whereas *scholares* were members of the palace guard assigned to protect the emperor. Gregory, therefore, was here “from the *scholares*,” or *exscholaris*, that is, formerly a *scholaris* but now an abbot.

Suidas:

Σχολάριοι, τρισχίλιοι πεντακόσιοι ἐπὶ φυλακῇ τοῦ Πάλλαντος ἦσαν τεταγμένοι, ἀριστίνδην ἐπιλεχθέντες ἐξ Ἀρμενίων, οἷς συντάξεις ἀνέκαθεν πλείους ἢ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασι τὸ δημόσιον ἐχορήγει.

“*Scholarii*: three thousand five hundred had been assigned to guard Pallas, chosen from the Armenian nobility, and from ancient times the state supplied them with greater pay than it supplied to all the others.”

The same author:

Ὑπεράριθμος, οὗτος ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῶν σχολαρίων καλουμένων τρισχιλίων πεντακοσίων ὄντων, ἑτέρους δισχιλίους ἐντέθεικεν Ἰουστινιανός, οὓς οὕτως ἐκάλεσεν.

“‘Supernumerary’: when the number of those called *scholarii* was three thousand five hundred, Justinian added another two thousand to them, whom he called by this name.”

Severus Sulpicius, book I, chapter 1, *On the Life of Saint Martin*: “In his youth he followed a military career and served among the *scholares* under King Constantius and afterward under Caesar Julian.”

## SCHOLASTICUS

Paschasius, book VII, chapter 19, no. 3: “This Eulogius was a *scholasticus*, educated in secular literature.”

Palladius, book VIII, chapter 26: “This Eulogius was a *scholasticus* of the liberal disciplines.”

The old translation of Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, appendix, chapter 16: “This Eulogius was a *scholasticus* and an educated man.”

Jerome, *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 99, concerning Serapion, bishop of Thmuis: “Serapion earned the surname *scholasticus* on account of the elegance of his intellect.”

The Roman Martyrology, February 5: “At whose confession—that of Dorothy—a certain Theophilus, a *scholasticus*, was converted to the faith of Christ.” The same is found in Bede and Usuard.

In a later period, however, *scholasticus* meant “advocate.” Hence in the Acts of Dorothy Theophilus is called sometimes *scholasticus*, sometimes *advocatus*. *Life of Saint Sebastian*, book II: “By the most accomplished *scholasticus*, Tiburtius, a noble and holy man.” He is previously called an advocate: “And I, who was destined to become an advocate for conducting the cases of mortals.”

Council of Sardica, canon 13: “If a *scholasticus* is sought from the forum as bishop.” The Greek interpreter has σχολαστικός ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς, “a *scholasticus* from the marketplace.”

And in book II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Extortions of Advocates*: “Beyond the customary and canonical payments, many things are demanded most disgracefully from the provincials of Africa by officials and *scholastici*. Nor is it unknown to our clemency that *scholastici*, having very often accepted fees beyond measure in the defense of every kind of case, have become accustomed to receive both grain allowances and expenses.”

Likewise, canon 97 in the Code of the African Canons:

Ὥστε δοθῆναι ἄδειαν τοῦ καταστῆσαι ἐκδίκους σχολαστικούς.

“So that permission may be given to appoint *scholastici* as defenders.”

Here advocates are meant. For it adds:

Οἵτινες αὐτὸ τοῦτο τὸ λειτούργημα τοῦ ἐκδικεῖν τὰ πράγματα ἐπιτήδευμα ἔχουσι.

“Those who make the very office of defending cases their profession.”

Therefore Molanus was incorrect, in his note on Usuard’s Martyrology for February 6, to suppose that Theophilus was called *scholasticus* in the Acts of Dorothy as an insult. At that time *scholasticus*, like *advocatus*, was equally current in a favorable sense.

In former times *scholasticus* meant a declaimer, anyone who practiced in fictitious cases. Pliny, book II, letter 3:

“He has passed his sixtieth year and is still merely a *scholasticus*, a class of men among whom there is nothing either simpler, more sincere, or better. For we who are worn down in the forum and in real lawsuits learn a great deal of malice, however unwillingly.”

Understand Jerome in this sense, letter 26 to Pammachius, concerning the death of Paulina: “I think you remember our mutual error, when the entire Athenaeum resounded with the voices of the *scholastici*.”

He himself discusses this training in his letter on Galatians, chapter II: “Several times, when I was a young man at Rome, I declaimed controversies and trained for real contests through fictitious lawsuits.”

*Scholasticus* was also used of an eloquent and learned man, even if he conducted neither fictitious cases, like a declaimer, nor real cases, like an advocate. Prudentius is called such. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25: “Such were composed by Ambrose, Hilary, Bede, the father of the English, and Prudentius, the *scholasticus* of Spain.”

Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 1048: “Franco, the *scholasticus* of Liège, is distinguished both by literary knowledge and by uprightness of character.” He is likewise called this by Aegidius of the Golden Valley in his religious work *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, chapter 1.

Thus Dionysius Exiguus, the Roman abbot and translator of the *Life of Pachomius*, is called *scholasticus* in manuscripts. Thus, I believe, Serapion above was called *scholasticus* by Jerome in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 99; and perhaps Eulogius also, concerning whom we spoke above.

## SECRETUM, OR SECRETARIUM

*Life of John the Merciful*, chapter 2: “He says before everyone to those who were in the honorable *secretum*.” I think this means the part of a church called the *secretarium*. Baronius discusses it as follows in volume VI, under the year 451.

The Council of Chalcedon is said to have been held before the rails of the sacred altar. Liberatus the Deacon, in his *Brief Account*, chapter 42, calls that place the *secretarium*, saying: “When the emperor Marcian came to the *secretarium* with the judges and the sacred senate, he delivered words of address in the council, etc.” On account of this place, he himself borrowed the name and called the individual sessions held there *secretaria*. For it was customary for councils of bishops to be held in the *secretaria* of basilicas. Among many other examples, this is found in the African Church, where the Carthaginian councils were held in *secretaria*, as well as councils of the Roman Church under Martin and of other churches.

But what was the place before the rails that Liberatus calls the *secretarium*? We think it was none other than the place described by Evagrius, book II, chapter 3, when he depicts the church of Saint Euphemia:

“On its northern side there is another building—which he calls the third and innermost part of the temple—which faces the rising sun and is itself constructed in the form of a vault, with columns made with great skill.”

A little later he says:

“Within the vaulted structure, toward the east, there is a sanctuary constructed with great beauty, in which the relics of the most holy martyr were deposited in a large chest,” etc.

Evagrius calls it *sacrarium*, whereas Liberatus calls it *sanctuarium*. That the two terms have the same meaning is shown by canon 21 of the Council of Laodicea in the wording of its first edition:

“Subdeacons must not be permitted to enter the *secretarium*, or *sacrarium*, which the Greeks call the *diaconicon*, or to touch the vessels of the Lord.”

And in another canon of the same council, canon 57 of the first edition:

“Presbyters must not enter the *sacrarium* before the procession of the bishop or sit there.”

It is also called in Greek ἱερατεῖον, that is, *sacrarium*, or βῆμα, because it rises above the other parts of the church.

But how can the *secretarium*, or *sacrarium*, have been before the rails? You must remember—as can also be seen in ancient basilicas—that between the body of the church and the apse, where the bishop’s seat was customarily placed, there was a sanctuary. Its principal altar stood in the middle, enclosed on every side by rails. Eusebius gives a vivid description of its form in book X, chapter 4:

“When this sanctuary had thus been completed and perfected, and certain chambers had been placed in a very high position for the protection and honor of the church, and benches had moreover been arranged in order all around, the whole having been decorated with exceptional beauty and splendor, and finally an altar, as it were the holy of holies, had been placed in the middle of the sanctuary, he enclosed the entire area with wooden rails, so that the common people and the multitude could not enter it.”

Thus the council appears to have been assembled before the altar rails facing the apse, occupying the entire space between the rails and the apse, where the episcopal throne stood. In larger basilicas this space was of considerable breadth and length and was capable of accommodating a large gathering of bishops.

From this, I think, you can understand how far from the truth are those who have held a different opinion concerning the *secretaria*. That they were inside the apse is indicated quite clearly by Paulinus in letter 12 to Severus. He also shows that the sacred vessels for the ministry and the sacred books for reading were kept there.

This too is relevant: Pope Gregory, book II, letter 54, rightly complains against John, bishop of Ravenna, “because during the time of fasting he wore the *pallium* through the squares and streets, although it is not even permitted to use it in the *secretarium*”—namely, the customary place where the bishop sat upon his throne, located in the apse, with the presbyters, but not the deacons. For canon 15 of the Second Council of Arles says: “Deacons may not sit among the presbyters in the *secretarium*.”

Thus far Baronius.

Binius also notes the following, in volume I of the Councils, p. 294:

“The places of the church situated near the apse, which here and by Paulinus in letter 12 are called *secretaria*, are likewise called *pastophoria* by Clement, book II of the *Constitutions*, chapter 62—that is, as Jerome explains in his commentary on Ezekiel 42, two chambers or inner rooms. Paulinus asserts in the passage mentioned above that two *pastophoria* were customarily built in every church and placed on either side of the apse. Their use is made clear by the following two couplets, which were inscribed above by the same author.

On the right of the apse:

> Here is the venerable storehouse where the sacred ministry’s  
> Life-giving splendor is stored and from which it is brought forth.

On the left of the same:

> If anyone possesses a holy desire to meditate upon the law,  
> Here, seated, he may devote himself to the sacred books.”

Thus far Binius.

The *secretarium* was inside a curtain and is also found called the *diaconicum*. Gregory of Nazianzus, oration 20, in praise of Basil the Great, speaking of Valens meeting Basil in the *sacrarium*, says:

ἐὰν εἴσω τοῦ παραπετάσματος ἑαυτὸν ἐποιήσατο.

“When he had placed himself within the curtain.”

There Nicetas interprets παραπέτασμα as διακονικόν. That *diaconicum* means *sacrarium* is clear from canon 21 of the Council of Laodicea, where the Greek has διακονικόν and the old translator has *secretarium*.

In canon 56 of the Council of Laodicea, where the Greek forbids presbyters to sit before the bishop’s entrance ἐν τῷ βήματι, the old translator has *in sacrario*, “in the *sacrarium*.”

The Greek-Latin Code of the African Canons, at the Council of Hippo in the year 393:

Ἐν Ἱππῶνι Ῥεγίῳ εἰς τὸ σήκρητον τῆς ἐκκλησίας πάκης.

“At Hippo Regius, in the *secretarium* of the Basilica of Peace.”

The Council of Carthage, called the Third and, in chronological order among those held after Nicaea, truly the Second: “in the *secretarium* of the restored basilica.” See distinction 23, “It is not permitted,” and the Council of Agde, chapter 166.

Sometimes *secretarium* refers to the session and assembly itself. Hence, among the letters of Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, “with the coming *secretarium*,” and likewise “after the *secretarium* had ended.” The assembly evidently took its name from the place itself.

In Augustine, sermon 2 on Psalm 34, one finds *secretaria mentis*, “the secret chambers of the mind.”

## SEMINA VIRTUTUM

*Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 15: “A nature fitted for this work has been implanted in man.” Thus many of the Fathers write that the seeds of the virtues are innate and implanted in human beings. How they can be called implanted, see Bellarmine, volume IV of the *General Controversies*, *On the Restoration of Grace*, controversy 1, principle, book V, chapter 12, argument 7.

## SEPTIMANARII

*Life of Euphrasia*, or Euphraxia, chapter 22: “Unless I gather wood and complete my week, I will not go up.”

Thus in the Rule of Saint Benedict: “To go out from the week,” which means to complete the week and for the weekly servers to lay down their duties.

Benedict, Rule, chapter 35: “The one who is about to go out from the week shall clean the premises on Saturday.”

Likewise: “Those going out from the week shall say this verse: ‘Blessed are you, Lord.’”

Hildegard, in her explanation of the Rule: “On going out from the week, she cleaned the premises on Saturday, sweeping away dirt and dust with brooms wherever necessary.”

Regino, *Chronicle*, book II: “It happened that, according to custom, the weekly server was assigned to the service of the kitchen.”

Cassian, book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 19: “Each week the brothers take turns performing these duties.”

Likewise: “Each person who undertakes these weeks observes them while serving until the Lord’s Supper on Sunday.”

Cassian discusses these weekly servers, or *hebdomadarii*, in the same book, chapters 20–22. He notes that the custom of serving in the kitchen for successive weeks prevailed in the monasteries of Palestine and Mesopotamia; in the monasteries of Egypt, however, a particular person was assigned to the kitchen for the whole of his life, as long as his strength lasted.

Nevertheless, what we are told about Euphraxia suggests that the other custom was also observed in certain Egyptian monasteries. Thus in the *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 47: “A brother who had been appointed to serve the one who was performing the week passed by.”

And Jerome, in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “In each monastery they have fathers, stewards, weekly servers, and attendants.”

In Saint Benedict as well, Rule 38, a weekly reader is mentioned.

## SEPTIMUM

Rufinus, book III, no. 19: “He lived in a small cell outside the city, near the suburb called *in Septimo*.”

Paul the Deacon, *History*, book XVII: “When everyone had assembled at *Septimium*,” which occurs there several times. Read *Septimum*.

There was a church of Saint John the Baptist there, which explains the continuation: “The tyrant’s proclamation was made in the church of Saint John the Baptist.” The same statement follows shortly afterward in this passage.

There were various districts of the city and suburbs, especially in Constantinople and Alexandria, which were distinguished by definite numbers. Thus in the Greek *Menaea*, April 23, the martyrdom, or church, of Saint George the Trophy-Bearer is said to be ἐν τῷ δευτέρῳ, “in the Second.”

In the same books, on September 18, the feast of the martyrs Charalampus, Pantaleon, and their companions is celebrated ἐν τῷ μαρτυρίῳ αὐτῶν τῷ ὄντι ἐν τῷ δευτέρῳ, “in their martyrion, which is in the Second.”

The Greek-Latin Code of the African Canons, at the Council of Carthage in 404:

Ἐν Καρχηδόνι εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τῆς βασιλικῆς σεκούνδου.

“At Carthage, in the basilica of the Second District.”

Likewise, at the Council of Carthage in 407:

Ἐν Καρχηδόνι εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ δευτέρου κλίματος.

“At Carthage, in the basilica of the Second District.”

Sozomen, book VII, chapter 24:

Λέγεται δὲ τότε τῆς Κωνσταντινουπόλεως ἐκδημῶν πρὸς τῷ Ἑβδόμῳ μηλ` (sic) γενόμενος, προσεύξασθαι τῷ Θεῷ ἐν τῇ ἐνθάδε ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἣν ἐπὶ τιμῇ Ἰωάννου τοῦ Βαπτιστοῦ ἐδείματο.

“It is said that, when he had departed from Constantinople and reached the seventh mile, he prayed to God in the church there which he had built in honor of John the Baptist.”

Christophorsonus translated it this way, reading μηλίῳ for the corrupt word, as did Curterius; Scaliger read μιλίῳ. I think the reading was κλίματι, or κλ., abbreviated. For I do not think that church of Saint John the Baptist was seven miles distant from Constantinople; rather, it was in the seventh *clima*, or district, of the city or its suburbs.

Alternatively, “the seventh mile” must be understood not as a distance in miles but as the palace that was in the Seventh District and was itself also called “the Seventh.” See Jacques Cujas, *Observations*, book XX, chapter 3. Perhaps there were several milestones, or more prominent columns, in Constantinople, and this one was the seventh in that order.

See Peter Gyllius, *Topography of Constantinople*, book IV, chapter 4.

## SEVERIANITAE

*Life of John the Merciful*, chapter 30: “And with the Severianites and the other unclean heretics living around the district.”

I think he means the Acephali heretics, who arose shortly before the time of John the Merciful, in the year 513, under the leadership of Severus, bishop of Antioch. Evagrius discusses him in *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapters 33 and 34.

This Severus lived during the reign of the emperor Anastasius and the pontificate of Hormisdas. See Nicephorus, book XVI, chapter 31, and book XVIII, chapters 2, 7, 9, and 23. They scarcely differ from the Eutychians. See Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 45, and John Maxentius, *Against the Acephali*.

Some call them Monophysites because, with Eutyches, they defended one nature in Christ. Saint Gregory mentions them in book X, letter 55; and in book II, letter 36, he says that the Acephali were condemned by Pope Vigilius.

There are also other Severians, named after Severus, a follower of the Encratites. They arose around the year 170 and are discussed by Eusebius, book IV, chapter 29; Epiphanius, heresy 45; and Augustine, heresy 24.

## SIBINUS

Moschus, in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 123: “And there I found an old man clothed in a *collobium* made of *sibinum*.”

The Greek is Φοροῦντα ἀπὸ σιβίνου κολλόβιον: “Wearing a *collobium made of sibinum*.”

It also occurs earlier, in chapter 120, but the Greek text is absent there. I am still investigating what *sibinum* means in this context.

The well-known Σίβυνοι were a kind of weapon. Justinian, Novel 85: Καὶ τούς τε καλουμένους σιβύνους, ἤτοι μισιβίλια: “And those called *sibynoi*, or *misibylla*.”

Festus says: “The Illyrians call a weapon resembling a hunting spear a *sibina*.”

Ennius: “The Illyrians remain, piercing with swords and *sibinae*.”

## SIGNUM PERCUTERE

Pelagius, booklet XVII, no. 20. Likewise in John, booklet III, no. 2, *percutiens*, “striking.”

*On Consideration*, distinction 2, chapter 50, from the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône: “Many who think they are fasting during Lent, as soon as they hear the signal for the ninth hour, eat.”

Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers* that he composed, in the life of Gregory, bishop of Langres: “When the signal had been sounded, the holy man of God, like the others, rose newly for the divine office.”

The same author, in the life of Nicetius, bishop of Lyon: “When the priest heard this, he rejoiced and ordered the signal to be sounded for the vigils.”

The same, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 23: “The signal for matins.”

Einhard, *Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter*, book III, chapter 15: “The little tower containing the signals of the basilica could have been seen by them.”

The *Capitularies*, book VI, title 168: “That priests should touch the signals at the canonical hours.”

In the *Order of Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury*: “Blessing of the church signal, that is, the bell.”

Leo of Monte Cassino, book III, chapter 42: “The signal by which the death of a brother is customarily announced sounded.”

See Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter “What the Vestments Signify”; Amalarius Fortunatus, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 1; and Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 5.

From *signum* the old Gauls had *seins*, and from this *tocsin*.

These signals were formerly made of wood. The *Book of the Miracles of the Martyr Anastasius*, which is read in the Seventh Council, session 4: “Striking the sacred pieces of wood, they came to meet one another.”

See Baronius, volume I, under the year 58, where he discusses the twofold signal by which the faithful were formerly summoned to church. The signals in monasteries were generally wooden.

## SINGULARIS FERUS

*Life of Pachomius*, chapter 15, from Psalm 77: “The boar from the forest ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast devoured it.”

Here *singularis* is used substantivally, corresponding to the Greek μονιός.

Suidas:

Μονιός, ἄγριος ὗς μεμονωμένος [perhaps νενεμημένος or νεμόμενος].

“*Monios*: a wild boar feeding by itself.”

Hesychius: Ὗς ἄγριος ὁ μὴ τοῖς ἄλλοις συναγελαζόμενος: “A wild boar that does not herd with the others.”

Thus in the fables of Aesop: μονιὸς ἄγριος, “a solitary wild boar.”

Cyril, in his exposition of the prophet Hosea, says that μονιόν means ὄνον, “an ass,” as Hesychius notes—perhaps the animal called ὄναγρος, that is, a wild ass.

## SIPPULAE

See below, *Zippulae*. I do not know whether the following is relevant, from the Latin-Greek Glosses: *Sappulo*, λάμβα. Is the form *Sappula* or *Sippula*? Unless this derives from *sapa*, that is, wine reduced by boiling.

## SOLIDUS

Palladius, chapter 83, concerning Serapion the Sindonite: “He sold himself to actors for twenty *solidi*.”

Here and throughout the Greek Palladius has νόμισμα, which Hervetus always translates as “coin”; but our Fronto prefers *solidus*. Greek writers commonly call gold coins *nomismata*, which the translator of the Latin Vulgate renders *solidi*, as in 1 Chronicles 29:7: καὶ χρυσοῦς μυρίους, “and ten thousand gold pieces,” rendered “ten thousand *solidi*.”

Heraclides, chapter 24, concerning this Serapion: “Because he sold himself to pagan mimes for the price of twenty *solidi*.”

Latin writers call coins *sestertii*, whether silver or bronze; but νόμισμα signifies a gold coin. Horace, *Epistles*, book II, letter 1:

> He brought back the royal *nomisma*, the Philips he had received.

We understand gold and *solidus* to have the same value from various laws of the *Digest* and the Code, and from the fact that Socrates, book IV, chapter 34, says ὀγδοήκοντα χρυσίνους, “eighty gold pieces,” while the translator of Epiphanius in the *Tripartite History*, book VIII, chapter 13, and book XII, chapter 2, renders it “eighty *solidi*.”

Book II of the Code, law 1: “*Solidi* fashioned in honor of the ancient emperors.”

## SOROR

That is, a wife living continently in marriage. In the same way, *frater*, “brother,” is used of a husband living continently.

Palladius, chapter 8, concerning Ammon addressing his wife: “Come here, mistress and sister.”

δεῦρο δὴ κυρία καὶ ἀδελφή: “Come here, mistress and sister.”

*Life of Malchus*, chapter 10: “Loving her as a sister, but not entrusting myself to her as to a sister.”

*Life of Basil*, concerning Anastasius and Theognia: “He calls his wife by name, but in usage calls her ‘sister.’”

Paulinus, letter 26 to Victricius: “The intimate brotherhood of married couples consecrated to God, which nourishes clerics, invites Christ—who rejoices in their works—to visit them through its persistent prayers, no longer at the marital bed but at the brotherly couch.”

Sidonius, book V, letter 16, concerning his Papianilla: “Although you are a good wife, you are also an excellent sister.”

Gregory, book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 11: “A certain presbyter, loving his presbytera as a sister but guarding against her as against an enemy, did not allow her to come near him.”

## SPETLUM

I have retained the Greek word because the term is rare and its meaning uncertain.

John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 184: “Living continually in this manner, when he died he left nothing of his own in the monastery—not a door, not a window, not a *spetlum*, not a candle, not a tablet.”

The Greek is:

Οὐ θύραν, οὐ θυρίδα, οὐ σπέτλον, οὐ κανδήλαν, οὐ πίνακα.

“Not a door, not a small window, not a *spetlum*, not a candle, not a tablet.”

Ambrose of Camaldoli, the translator, omitted σπέτλον. I suspect that σπέκλον is intended, meaning “mirror,” that is, a glass window made of *specular* stone; for θυρίδα can mean a wooden window.

This word occurs elsewhere as well, so it does not appear to be corrupt. Dorotheus, *Teaching* 3:

Ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ λύχνος διὰ σπέτλον, οὕτως ἄρχεται δεικνύναι ἡμῖν ἀμαυρότερον.

“But just as a lamp shines through a mirror, so it begins to show us whatever is dimmer and more obscure.”

The manuscripts of the book here have σπέτλων, from which the editors produced the present σπέκλων.

The *Basilica* has:

Ὥσπερ τὰ ἐμβλήματα τῶν ἀργυρέων σκευῶν, καὶ τὰ σπέτλα τοῦ οἴκου.

“Like the inlaid work of silver vessels and the mirrors of a house.”

The learned Leunclavius thinks that σπέκλα should be read. Perhaps people spoke in that way in that period. One should not rashly depart from the old reading.

Psellus, *On Demons*:

Ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν ἐνόπτρων καὶ τῶν σπέκλων ὁρᾷν ἐστιν.

“As it is possible to see by means of mirrors.”

## STABULUM

**Stable, lodging, inn.** *Life of Abraham’s Niece*, chapter 3: “And she took up residence in a certain stable, having changed her former clothing.” And in chapter 6: “She turned aside into an inn.” Here *stabulum* means an inn. Thus *stabulum* is frequently used by both pagan and Christian authors. Pliny, book VI of the *Letters*, letter 19: “The city and Italy not as a fatherland, but as an inn or stable.” Spartianus, in *Severus*: “Even as he slept in a stable, a serpent encircled his head.” The word is also found among the jurists, for example in *Digest* I, at the end, *On Theft Committed against a Shipmaster*, and in *Digest* IV, *On the Cases in Which a Pledge Is Given*, and in *Digest* CXCVIII, *On the Meaning of Words*. Hence Theophilus translates it as πανδοχεῖον (*inn*) in the penultimate paragraph of the *Institutes*, *On Obligations Arising from Quasi-Delicts*.

Cyprian, letter 67: “Or if, while on the road, some inn should begin to be besieged and held by robbers, so that anyone who entered might be caught by the attack of those lying in wait there, would not travelers, having learned of this danger, seek other, safer inns along the road, where there were trustworthy lodgings and secure shelters for travelers?” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 42: “Thus we live together in this world, not without your forum, not without your market, not without your baths, taverns, workshops, stables, markets, and your other commercial activities.” Hence *stabularius*, the person in charge of an inn. *Life of Abraham’s Niece*, chapter 6: “Smiling, she said to the innkeeper.” Seneca, book I *On Benefits*, chapter 13: “No one considers himself the guest of an innkeeper or tavernkeeper.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39: “A creditor will be required for Salian banquets. The innkeepers will furnish the expenses of the Herculean tithes and sacrificial feasts.” Yet another reading has: “The accountants will calculate the expense.” Apuleius, *Milesian Tales*, 2: “I picked up my little bundle and, having paid the innkeeper the price of our lodging, we set out on the road.”

## STICHARION

This word is written now in Greek as στηχάριον, now as στοιχάριον, and now as στιχάριον; the last form appears to be the more correct. Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 136: “Having received his sticharion and candle.” I noted in my annotations that *birrus* should be read instead of *cereus*. In Greek, Metaphrastes, in the *Life of Athanasius*, has: τὸ στιχάριον καὶ τὸ βίρριν, “the sticharion and the cloak.” The translator of Heraclides, chapter 51, likewise has: “He was clothed only in his tunic and cloak.”

In the Liturgy of Chrysostom: καὶ λαμβάνει στιχάριον, “and he takes the tunic.” The Glossary has: στιχάριον, tunica, “tunic”; this means a white or linen tunic. For when Athanasius, *Apology* 2, writes:

> Καὶ πλάττονται πρώτην κατηγορίαν περὶ στιχαρίων λινῶν ὡς ἐμοῦ Κανόνα τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις ἐπιβάλλοντος.

Peter Nannius translates: “They fabricate as the first accusation that I was imposing upon the Egyptians a tax of ordinary linen garments.” But the translator in this passage did not grasp the force of the word στιχαρίου. Our Fronto most correctly advises, in his notes on the Liturgy of Chrysostom, that it should be translated: “And they fabricate an accusation concerning linen tunics,” and so forth.

The correctness of this interpretation is established by Sozomen, who, recounting the same story, says in book II, chapter 21:

> Πρώτην ὑπομένει γραφὴν ὡς χιτωνίων λινῶν φόρον ἐπιτιθεὶς Αἰγυπτίοις.

“He is first brought to trial on the charge that he had imposed upon the Egyptians a tax on linen tunics.”

In the *Testament of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus*:

> Δοθῆναι βούλομαι στιχάριον αʹ, πάλλια βʹ.

“I wish one tunic and two cloaks to be given.”

The same Fronto notes that Junius translated incorrectly in the *Curopalates, On the Offices of the Imperial Court*: τὸ σύνηθες αὐτῷ στιχάριον, “his customary maniple.” It should have been translated: “his customary tunic.”

## STRINIARI

Pelagius, booklet XVI, no. 14: *ne strinientur*, “lest they be wanton.” In the manuscript *Synonyms of Cicero*, preserved in the Cusan Lexicon: “They will dance, act like stage performers, and be wanton.” The Greek-Latin Glossary has:

> Στρηνιῶ, gerrio, gestio.

“I am wanton; I behave extravagantly; I indulge myself.”

Suidas:

> Στρῆνος, εἰς τὴν παλαιὰν τοῦτο κεῖται. Τὸ «στρῆνός σου ἀνέβη ἐν τοῖς ὦσί μου» τουτέστι . . . «καὶ στρηνιῶ, ἀτακτῶ.»

“*Strenos* occurs in the Old Testament. ‘Your wantonness has risen into my ears,’ that is . . . ‘and I am wanton; I behave disorderly.’”

**STRENUS.** This word is found in the Old Testament: “Your immodesty has risen into my ears,” that is . . . “and I am wanton; I live immodestly.”

Portus supplies the incomplete passage in Suidas as follows:

> τουτέστιν, Ἥ σου ἀταξία, ἡ ὑπερηφανία, ἡ ἀκολασία.

“That is: your disorderliness, arrogance, and intemperance.”

The Old Testament passage cited by Suidas is 2 Kings 19:28. The same word occurs in the New Testament, Revelation 18:3:

> Καὶ οἱ ἔμποροι τῆς γῆς ἐκ τῆς δυνάμεως τοῦ στρήνους αὐτῆς ἐπλούτησαν.

“And the merchants of the earth became rich through the power of her luxuries.”

In the same chapter, verse 7:

> Καὶ ἐστρηνίασε.

“And she lived in luxury.”

Verse 9:

> Οἱ μετ’ αὐτῆς πορνεύσαντες καὶ στρηνιάσαντες.

“Those who committed fornication and lived luxuriously with her.”

Varinus:

> Στρηνιᾷν, ἀτακτεῖν. Καὶ στρηνιῶντες, παρὰ τὸ στερεῖν καὶ ἀποσπᾷν τὰς ἡνίας, ἀπὸ μεταφορᾶς τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων.

“*Striniare* means ‘to behave disorderly.’ And *streniōntes* is derived, metaphorically, from irrational animals, because they lack a bridle and pull away the reins.”

## SUPER PACEM ESSE

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 2: “For he immediately sent for the stewards, and for the man who was called *Super pacem*.” I do not know whether this passage refers to the deacon who recited the εἰρηνικά, the prayers “for peace,” which are preserved in the Greek *Euchologion*. Thus in the *Curopalates, On the Offices of Constantinople*:

> Τοῦ Ἀρχιδιακόνου τὰ εἰρηνικά, ὡς ἔθος, εἰπόντος.

“When the archdeacon had recited the prayers for peace, as was customary.”

For archdeacons were generally the Church’s stewards or administrators, who are mentioned here. Metaphrastes, in the *Life of this saint*, has only: “Having summoned those who administered the affairs of the Church”:

> Μετακαλεσάμενος τοὺς τὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας οἰκονομοῦντας.

I do not think that this passage refers to an *irenarch*, or peacemaker, who maintained peace and order in provinces and cities, about whom we spoke above under **IRENARCHA**. Unless, perhaps, in addition to the secular irenarch there was also an ecclesiastical one.

## SURISCULA

Pelagius, booklet IV, no. 67: “She washed the *suriscula* and filled it with water.” The same author, booklet VIII, no. 4: “Because of the heat they took the *suriscula* and gave it to him to drink from.” Booklet VII, no. 33: “One day, filling his *suriscula* with water.” Booklet XVI, no. 3: “Your *suriscula*, father, is full of poison.” Booklet XVIII, no. 7: “A little boy stood before him, holding bread and a *suriscula* of water.”

I cannot fully determine what this vessel was or why it was called *suriscula*. In excerpts from an old Greek-Latin Glossary, under earthen vessels, one finds: “*Pultorium*, σηρίσκος.” [Perhaps συρίσκος?] Vulcanius reads *pultarium*, σηρίσκος. But who used σηρίσκος in that sense? I find in Hesychius:

> Συρίσκος, ἀγγεῖόν τι πλεκτόν, εἰς ὃ σῦκα ἐμβάλλουσι, τινὲς δὲ ὑρίσκον [read ὑῤῥίσκον].

“*Syriscus* or *suriscus*: a vessel woven from wicker or another material, into which figs are put; some call it *hyrriscus*.”

In the same Hesychius:

> Ὑρισίδα, σπυρίδιον, σπυρίς.

“*Hyrisida*: a little basket, a basket.”

Likewise:

> ὑρισσός, φορμός.

“*Hyrissus*: a basket.”

But these woven, wicker vessels cannot hold water. Some propose σύριχος or συρίσκος, supposedly derived from σῦκων ἄριχος. Since, however, in Hesychius ὑδρίσκη means ὑδρεία, “a water vessel,” we should consider whether *suriscula* arose from *sudriscula* through the loss of *d*. Certainly Greek ὑ is often rendered by Latin *su*, as in ὗς, *sus*, “pig,” and many similar cases. Unless *suriscula* comes from σύρω, “I draw,” because these vessels drew water from wells. Thus in Isaiah 20: ὄστρακον, in which ἀποσυρεῖ ὕδωρ, “a pot by which water is drawn.” See the notes on the Septuagint translators, on chapter 4 of Hosea, from the Roman edition.

## SYNCELLUS, OR SYNGELLUS

*Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 132: “When the patriarch saw him, he said to Menas, his *syncellus*, or assistant.” The word *assessor* did not sufficiently express the force and use of the Greek συγκέλλου; therefore I have placed the Greek word in the Latin text. In the Greek Church the *syncellus* was the patriarch’s immediate subordinate. On this subject see more in our Gretzer’s commentary on Codinus, book III, chapter 14, and in Meursius’s Greek-Barbarian Glossary.

Meursius is mistaken, however, when in the *Martyrology of Notker Balbulus* he takes *congellum* for *syngellum*. *Congellus* is instead the proper name of a holy Irish man, a disciple of Saint Columba, whose feast occurs on June 9. Congellus himself was the teacher of Saint Columbanus. His *Life*, chapter 3: “He went to a monastery called Benchor, in which the blessed Congellus shone forth as a bishop rich in virtues, an outstanding Father of the monks among his own people.”

## TABENNESUS

Palladius, chapter 38: “Tabennensis is the name of a place in the Thebaid.” Our Fronto notes here:

“In the Lyon edition it read ταβέννησίς ἐστι τόπος, and Meursius conjecturally corrected it to ταβέννη τίς ἐστι τόπος, on the ground that *tabenna* meant an island. But the royal manuscript and the Greek manuscript of Nicephorus, belonging to Emperor Ferdinand II, consistently retain ταβεννήσιος, so that it is derived from ταβέννη, just as the district of the Rhône is called Ῥοδανήσιος, and the territory of Lyon Λουγδουνήσιος.”

In the *Life of Pachomius*, Dionysius’s translator has: “It happened that he reached the region of the Tabennesians by boat.” Heraclides likewise translates this passage: “A place in the province of the Thebaid is called Tabennensis.”

## TARICHA

*Life of Antony*, chapter 35: “Everyone asserted that this was the stench of the counterfeit fish and *taricha* placed in the boat.” This is the correct reading, not *caricarum* or *carixarum*, as it has hitherto been printed. *Taricha* were salted or preserved foods; hence ταριχοπῶλαι, “dealers in salted foods,” and ταριχοπωλεῖα, “shops of dealers in salted foods.” See the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Knights*.

## TAUREA

That is, a leather scourge or whip. Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 8: “One night a demon appeared holding a *taurea*, like an executioner.” Hervetus, the recent translator of Palladius, chapter 18, renders this: “Making a noise with a bull’s hide.” Heraclides’ translator is better: “And he seemed to be making a sound with whips.”

Hesychius:

> μαράγνα τῇ ταυρείᾳ. Item μαράγνα, μάστιξ, ῥάβδος, ταυρεία.

“*Maragna*, a *taurea*. Likewise, *maragna*: a whip, rod, *taurea*.”

Athanasius, letter *To Those Leading the Solitary Life*, concerning the Arians who harassed Eutychius, a subdeacon of Alexandria, p. 658:

> Καὶ ποιήσαντες εἰς τὰ νῶτα ταυρείαις ἴσα θανάτῳ κατακοπῆναι.

“First they had him beaten on the back with scourges almost to death.”

Because *taureae* were made from oxhide, Artemidorus—especially with regard to slaves who dream that they are eating beef—conjectures, or rather dreams, that whips threaten them. Book I, chapter 72:

> Δούλοις δὲ βασάνους (σημαίνει) διὰ τὸν ἱμάντα, καὶ τὴν ταυρείαν.

“For slaves it signifies torture, because of the leather strap and the ox-hide whip.”

Eusebius, *Chronicle*, Olympiad 55: “Tarquin the Proud devised fetters, *taureae*, clubs, quarries, prisons, exiles, mines, shackles, and chains.” This appears to have been taken by Jerome from the history of Eutropius.

Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, chapter 5: “Others have walked beneath the ox-hide whips of the hunters upon shoulders most capable of enduring them.” *Life of Pontius the Martyr*, May 14: “Immediately two hunters came out with *taureae* and sinew whips, according to custom.”

Juvenal, Satire 6:

> Why is this curl higher? The ox-hide whip punishes  
> At once the offense and crime of the bent hair.

Old glosses: “*Taureae*: blows, sinews.” The manuscript Camberon Glossary: “*Taureae*: a certain kind of instrument of torture.” The manuscript Claromontes Glossary: “*Taureae*: blows, the genital sinew of a bull.”

Since various objects were made from bullhide, the word sometimes denotes a shield, sometimes a helmet, and sometimes other things as well.

## TEMPLUM

In several *Lives of the Fathers* certain parts of churches are mentioned, such as the sanctuary and tribunal. See what was said above under **BEMA**, or **BHMA**. So that nothing should be lacking for understanding those places, consult what Gentianus Hervetus noted concerning Greek churches in his notes on the Liturgies; he divides a Greek church into three parts. Above, under **BEMA**, you have its division into five parts according to the opinion of others. The substance, however, is the same. See also Meursius’s Greek-Barbarian Glossary, under Πρόθεσις, where he likewise divides Greek churches into three parts.

## TENATTES

*Life of Hilarion*, no. 4: “And wearing a *pelliceum* with an *ependytes*.” At this point Joannes Andreas, the old editor of Saint Jerome’s letters, adds after *ependytes*: “and an *eraciestes*.” In its place three manuscripts used by Ado in his *Martyrology*, October 21, have: “and a *tenattes*.”

I have admitted neither reading into the text, fearing that they might be interpretations of the word *ependytes*. Yet the interpretations themselves are more obscure than the primary word. Above I investigated *eraciestes*; let us now examine *tenattes*. At first sight it seems not to be something distinct from *ependytes*, but rather its interpretation. Should we read *et nactem*, with *te* having crept in from the end of *ependyten*? In Hesychius, νάκος and νάκτα mean “fleece” and “hair.” Some conjecture that *tenattes* derives from the Greek τὴν νάκην, as though meaning “the fleece.” So thinks our Lansselius. But since Jerome wrote in Latin and did not translate from Greek, another explanation must be sought.

I suspect that *tenattem* entered most books in place of *renattem*. *Renattis* was then corrupted and distorted from *reno*. The basis of my suspicion is the very old manuscript of Saint Florian, in which the passage reads: “And wearing a fur *ependytes*—that is, a *renatum*, or cloak.” It evidently explains the fur *ependytes* as a *renatum*, or renewed cloak, made from *renones*, which themselves were also made of fur.

## THEBAIDA

This word frequently occurs in these books in the nominative form in place of *Thebais*. Jerome, *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, no. 2: “A savage storm devastated many churches throughout Egypt and the Thebaid.” The same form is used for *Persida* in place of *Persis*, in the *Life of Saint Sebastian*; and for *Ptolemaida* in place of *Ptolemais*, in Martianus Capella, book VI, chapter “On the Third Gulf.” Likewise, in the same author, *Chalcida* occurs for *Chalcis*, and above we found *absida* for *absis*.

There were, moreover, two Thebaids: one called Lower, the other Upper. Jerome, *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 4: “Where such things were being done in Lower Thebaid.” *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 27: “When he was solemnly visiting the churches of Upper Thebaid.”

## THOLUS

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 26: “For there he had made for them certain long *tholi*.” Palladius, chapter 8: “And he made for himself two *tholi* of cells.” And chapter 43: “Having made for himself three *tholi* at the summit of the mountain, he entered and built himself in. One *tholus* was for bodily needs, another where he worked, and the third where he prayed.”

Here *tholi* means an entire building, not one of its parts. The *Great Etymological Lexicon*:

> Θόλος περιφερὲς οἰκοδόμημα ἀπὸ τοῦ περιθεῖν. Θόλος τόπος τις ἐν τοῖς ἀρχείας κληθείς, διὰ τὸν τρόπον τῆς κατασκευῆς· ἦν γὰρ λιθοειδὴς, καὶ ὀροφὴν εἶχε περιφερῆ οἰκοδομητήν, οὐχὶ ξυλίνην, ὡς τὰ ἄλλα οἰκοδομήματα. Λέγεται θηλυκῶς «ἡ θόλος».

“*Tholos* is a round building, from περιθεῖν, ‘to run around.’ It was also the name of a certain place in archives, because of its method of construction: it was built of stone and had a rounded, constructed roof, not a wooden one like other buildings. The word is feminine: *hē tholos*.”

See also Phavorinus, in his Lexicon.

## THYMIAMA

The practice of burning *thymiama* in honor of the saints was already ancient. John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 57: “Put incense into the censer.” In Greek: βάλλετε θυμίαμα, “put incense in.”

Saint Chrysostom, homily 41, *On Saint Pelagia, Virgin and Martyr of Antioch*, reminds his hearers, on the basis of this practice, that when they return home as though in procession from Pelagia’s tomb, they should converse among themselves about the deeds of the virgin martyr and thus perfume the road as if with spiritual incense:

> Θυμιαμάτων 1059 ἐμπλήσωμεν τὴν λεωφόρον· οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτως σεμνὴ φανεῖται ἡ ὁδός, εἰ διὰ πάσης αὐτῆς θυμιατήριά τις τιθεὶς τῆς εὐωδίας ἀναχρώσεις τὸν ἀέρα, ὡς σεμνὴ φανεῖται νῦν εἰ πάντη ἡ [read πάντες οἱ] σήμερον αὐτὴν ὁδεύοντες τοὺς ἄθλους τῆς μάρτυρος πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς διηγούμενοι, βαδίζοιεν οἴκαδε, θυμιατήριον τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γλῶτταν ἕκαστος ποιῶν.

“We should fill the highway with the vapor of incense. For the road would not appear so venerable if, having placed censers throughout it, one were to fill the air with fragrance as it will now appear venerable if all who travel along it today, recounting among themselves the martyr’s struggles, should walk home, each making his own tongue a censer.”

He then adds a beautiful passage about an orderly and well-composed procession. *Life of Bishop Audoenus*, in Surius, August 24: “Carrying the body on their shoulders with crosses, lamps, and censers,” and so forth.

## TUMULUM COMPONERE

*Lives of Paul*, no. 6: “He prepared the tomb according to custom.” There I said, on Jerome’s authority, that this was the duty of clerics—not of all clerics, but of those called *copiatae*, or laborers, taking the word *cleric* in a broad sense. Certainly some Fathers count the *copiatae* among the clergy.

In Ignatius, *Letter to the Antiochenes*:

> Ἀσπάζομαι ὑποδιακόνους, ἀναγνώστας, ψάλτας, πυλωρούς, τοὺς κοπιῶντας, ἐπορκιστάς, ὁμολογητάς.

“I greet the subdeacons, readers, singers, doorkeepers, laborers, exorcists, and confessors.”

Epiphanius, at the end of the *Panarion*:

> Λοιπὸν δὲ καὶ κοπιαταί, οἱ τὰ σώματα περιστέλλοντες τῶν κοιμωμένων, καὶ θυρωροί.

“Next come the laborers, who wrap and cover the bodies of those who have fallen asleep, and the doorkeepers.”

The Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 2, law 15: “The clerics, or those whom recent usage has established as being called *copiatae*, must be exempt from degrading duties and from the levy, provided that they obtain their meager food and clothing through very small commercial dealings.” For the manner in which the *copiatae* were counted among the clergy, see Bellarmine, volume II, *General Controversies*, book I, *On the Clergy*, chapter 11.

I think that in former times tombs were prepared according to custom—that is, raised into mounds. Hence in Heliodorus, *Ethiopian History*, book I:

> Καὶ χοῦν ὀλίγον ἐπιφορῆσας.

“And having heaped up a little earth.”

They were raised so that they might catch the eye and remind mortals of mortality. Hence *monumenta* is derived from *monere*, “to remind.” Thus Sidonius, lest anyone rashly violate the tomb of Apollinaris, which had once been raised but had sunk through the passage of time, warns the traveler, book III, letter 12, not to “trample upon the piled-up earth.” On the usefulness of looking at monuments, see Chrysostom’s homily *On Faith and the Law*.

## TYPUS TERTIANUS

Rufinus, book II, chapter 1: “He was severely afflicted by a tertian type.” In this passage Melchior Goldastus, in volume I, part II of *Alemannic Affairs*, in his notes on Hepidannus’s *Life of Saint Wiborada*, book I, chapter 27, needlessly substituted *pyretus* for *typus*. He also rashly assumes *pyreticus* instead of *frigoreticus*. Both *typus* and *frigus* are used of a fever.

For *typus*, see what was said on the passage cited from Rufinus. The manuscript Camberon Glossary: “*Typhi* are cold fevers. They are revolutions of attacks and remissions occurring at fixed intervals.” But *typi* should be read. For there is another fever, *typhodes*, τυφώδης, a symptomatic fever belonging to the category of burning fevers, arising from erysipelas of the liver or kidneys. Likewise, a fever arising from erysipelas affecting the lungs is called *krymodes*, κρυμώδης.

The same Goldast, in the *Life of Eugenia*, chapter 12, cites from his manuscript: “Because he was severely afflicted by a quartan type, and had already suffered from it for a year and more.” Here again he restores *pyretus*. But at this point our books had simply *quartana*, with *febris* understood.

The *Life of Saint Winebald, Abbot*, in the *Promptuary of Sacred Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*: “A tertian type afflicted him with the gravest sufferings.” Nicholas Camuzat, the scholiast, thought without cause that *typus* was superfluous and had entered the text accidentally. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 24: “He was shaken by a quartan type.” And chapter 82: “He was afflicted by the heats of a quartan type.” The same author, in the *Life of Gallus*, among the *Lives of the Fathers* composed by him: “When Julian, seized by a quartan type, was suffering severely.” And shortly afterward: “Valentinian was seized by a quartan type.”
