Gregory is likewise evidence for *frigus* and *frigoretici*, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 24: “For how many have suffered from chills, how many have died beforehand as evil pustules thickened with poison?” Here *frigora* means cold fevers.

Hence *frigoretici* in the same Gregory, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 75: “For if any sufferers from cold fevers now celebrate Mass devoutly in his honor and offer an oblation to God for his repose, they are immediately restored to their former health, their tremors being suppressed and their fevers extinguished.”

And in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 59: “For the possessed, sufferers from cold fevers, and other sick persons, often pray at his tomb and depart having received health.” Chapter 64: “At his tomb sufferers from cold fevers and other sick people are frequently healed.” Chapter 101: “For the fevers of those suffering from cold fevers, as well as other afflictions, are extinguished through his merits.”

The same author, in the *Life of Monegundis*, among the *Lives of the Fathers* composed by him: “A sufferer from a cold fever also approached this monument; as soon as he touched the cloth covering it, the fever of his illness was extinguished and he recovered.” And in his *Life of Saint Martius*: “The quivering limbs of those suffering from cold fevers.” The same is found in the *Life of Nicetius, Bishop of Lyon*, in that collection.

In the Greek Palladius, chapter 12—for the Latin version lacks the passage—we read:

> Οὗ τὸ μνῆμα λέγεται θεραπεύειν πάντας τοὺς ῥιγιαζομένους.

“It is said that his monument cures all who suffer from chills.” Heraclides’ translator renders it: “those suffering from various fevers.”

The word τὸ ῥῖγος means a violent chill. Among physicians, ἐπιβολὴ ῥίγους means “an attack of chills”; and in Dioscorides, ῥίγη περιοδικά means “chills recurring in the cycle of fevers,” while ῥιγοῦντες means “those who are shivering.”

## VAVAE

This expression occurs several times in the *Life of John the Almsgiver*. Hesychius:

> Βαβαὶ θαυμαστικὴ φωνή.

“*Babae*: an exclamation of someone expressing wonder.”

Cyril’s Greek-Latin Lexicon: Βαβαί, “Babae.”

## VESPERTINUM LUMEN

Palladius, chapter 38: “And when they came to the evening light.” In Greek: ἐν τῷ λυχνικῷ, “at the lamp-lighting.” Heraclides, chapter 19: “When they came to the evening light.”

In the *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 22, there are twelve daytime hours, twelve evening hours, and twelve nighttime hours. Cassian, book III of the *Institutes*, chapter 3: “Finally, the eleventh, in which the hour of the lamp-lighting is marked.” Theodorus Balsamon, on canon 91 of the Sixth Synod:

> Καὶ καταλήγειν μέχρι τῆς συμπληρώσεως τοῦ λυχνικοῦ ἤτοι τοῦ ἑσπερινοῦ τῆς κυριακῆς.

“And to continue until the completion of the divine office, that is, of Sunday evening prayer.”

**FRONTO**

## VICARIA

Palladius, chapter 123: “Macarius, from the *vicaria*.” Understand this to mean that Macarius had held the office of *vicarius*. In Greek, ἀπὸ βικαρίας means “a former *vicarius*,” one who had held the office of *vicarius*.

Sulpicius Severus, dialogue 3, chapter 1: “With difficulty, however, I obtained his admission of Eucherius, a former *vicarius*, and Celsus, a former consul.” The same author, chapter 18: “Lycontius, a faithful man and former *vicarius*.” Βικαρία occurs in Justinian, *Novels*, 8.

Likewise in Chrysostom, letter 14:

> Οἱ ἀπὸ βικαρίων, οἱ ἀπὸ ἡγεμόνων, σοφισταί, οἱ ἀπὸ τριβούνων.

“Former *vicarii*, former governors, sophists, former tribunes.”

The Anglican commentators did not properly understand this, since they translate “vicarii, governors, tribunes,” whereas they should have translated “former *vicarii*, former governors, former tribunes.” See our Fronto’s notes on that letter. Abraham Ortelius was misled by this passage and thought that *vicaria* in Palladius referred to a particular place.

## VITTA

Palladius, chapter 1: “This holy man, Isidore, wore nothing of linen until the hour of his death, except a *vitta*.” The Greek reads:

> Οὗτος ὁ ἅγιος μέχρι τῆς τελευτῆς οὐκ ὀθόνην ἐφόρησεν ἐκτὸς φακιόλιου.

“This holy man until his death wore no linen cloth except a *phaciolium*.”

The Venetian manuscript explicitly has φακιόλιον. Hervetus seems likewise to have read it in his manuscript when he translated it as *vitta*, “band” or “fillet.” Nor did Heraclides’ old translator find anything else in his text when, in chapter 1 of the *Paradise*, he translated: “He used no linen cloth except that with which he covered his head.”

In Suidas, φακιόλιον is a covering for the head:

> Φάκελλος, τὸ τῆς κεφαλῆς φόρημα, ὃ καὶ φακιόλιον λέγεται.

“*Phacellus* is a head-covering, which is also called *phaciolium*.”

*Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 196:

> Οἱ δὲ τοῖς φακιολίοις ἐῤῥίπιζον.

“But they used their *phaciolia* as fans.”

Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 3, from the history of Nonnosus:

> Τὰ σανδάλια, φησὶ, νυνὶ λεγόμενα, ἀρβύλας ἔλεγον οἱ παλαιοὶ, καὶ τὸ φακιόλιον, φασώλην.

“What are now called sandals, he says, the ancients called *arbylae*; and what is now called *phaciolium*, they formerly called *phasōlē*.”

It does not mean, as the Photian index has it, that “the last two words were formerly used for sandals.”

The royal and Palatine manuscripts of Palladius have ἐκτὸς φακιαλίου. Therefore Fronto and Meursius prefer to translate it “except for a *faciale*,” since this Greek word in a later age may have been formed from the Latin *facialis*. In the Latin-Greek Glossary:

> “Give a *faciale*,” δὸς προσωπίδιον.

Likewise in the *Scholastic Colloquy*:

> Ξύστραν προσόψιον ποδεκμάγιον, λήκυθον.

“A strigil, a *faciale*, a foot-cloth, a flask.”

In the Rule of Saint Caesarius: “Embroidery is never to be made except on the small tablecloths and face-cloths on which the abbess has ordered it to be made.” In the Arabic-Latin Glossary: “*Facitergium* and *manutergium* are so called because they wipe the face or hands.”

Thus he calls *faciale* the linen cloth with which a face streaming with sweat was wiped; such cloths were called *oraria* and *mappulae*.

## VOLUMINA

That is, chambers or vaults. Heraclides, chapter 2, concerning Ammon: “And he made for himself the vaults of two cells.” Palladius, chapter 8: “And he made for himself two *tholi* of cells”:

> Οἰκοδομεῖ ἑαυτῷ δύο θόλους κελλίων.

“Hence *transvolvere*, ‘to make a vault.’ Gregory of Tours, book VIII: “There was a crypt there, displayed in an elegant work vaulted by the ancients.” The same author, in his book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7, in the life of Gregory of Langres: “He lays foundations before the altar, raises an apse with marvelous workmanship, and vaults it.”

The term appears to have been drawn from serpents, which properly form coils by moving forward. Claudian, *Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*:

> Blue Python, struck down by such an Apollo,  
> Enclosed his dying coils among the shattered trees.

Sidonius Apollinaris:

> He would pierce the numerous coils with countless weapons.

See above, **THOLUS**.

## XENIUM

See **EXENIUM**.

## ZABERNA

This seems to mean a cupboard, storage place, or sack. Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, from the old translator, chapter 14: “He bound the robbers together like a *zaberna* of straw.” Heraclides’ translator, chapter 7, has “a sack of straw.” Hervetus, the recent translator of Palladius, does likewise.

My Venetian manuscript excerpts here have ζάβερνον; others have σάκκον, “sack.” But *zaberna* is also used by other authors. Abdias, book IV of the *History of the Apostles*, in the life of James, the brother of John: “Having gathered the magical books, he brought full *zabernae* to the apostle, carried on his own shoulders and those of his disciples.” Again: “Hang stones and lead in the *zabernae* and throw them into the sea.”

The manuscripts there read *zabernis*; the common text has *zabyras* and *zabyris*. Hence Joannes Meursius, in the Greek-Barbarian Lexicon, formed *zabarias*, proposing that *zabarium*, σαβαρεῖον, means a repository for *zabarae*, or breastplates.

But the good reading in Abdias is *zaberna*. Papias the Vocabulist: “*Zaberna*: a chest or small cupboard.” Again: “*Zaberna*: a place where clothes or anything else is stored.” The manuscript Camberon Glossary: “*Zaberna* is a place where clothes are stored, a chest or small cupboard.” *Life of Saint Ulrich*: “Meanwhile he also sought *zabernae* and footwear.”

## ZAETA

In the *Life of Basil*, chapter 5, the expression “in a distinguished dwelling” is, in Greek, ἐν ἐπισήμῳ δίαιτῃ, which another translator of the *Life of Basil* rendered by *zaeta*. Both *diaeta* and *zaeta* were used.

Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 10: “He had withdrawn into a dwelling called the Hermaeum.” Both *diaeta* and *zaeta* frequently occur among authors. See the legal lexicons.

The manuscript Camberon Glossary: “*Zaetae*: houses which have water beneath their floors.” Again: “Winter *zaetae* are houses heated by fire conducted beneath them; summer *zaetae* are houses cooled by water conducted beneath them.” Much the same is found in Papias.

## ZEMA

*Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 20: “How many would wish to dip their bread in the *zema* that my cooks throw away?” Hence ἐπίzema, “a boiling or bubbling over in a pot boiling at the top.”

Saint Jerome, book III on Hosea: “In place of ‘foam,’ the Septuagint translator Theodotion rendered φρύγανον, that is, ‘fuel,’ namely dry herbs prepared for the hearth and fire. Symmachus used ἐπίzema, wishing to indicate the upper waters of a boiling pot, rising into foam and bubbles, which the Greeks call πομφόλυγες.”

## ZIPPULAE, OR SIPPULAE

Pelagius, booklet IV, no. 59: “He made a little cake from flour and *zippulae*.” Rufinus, book III, no. 51, in the same story, has *placentae*, “cakes.” Again, Pelagius, booklet VIII, no. 15: “Give them a few *zippulae*, because they have come from work.” The manuscripts and old editions have this reading. Some had substituted *pultes*, “porridge,” for *zippulae*.

Since the word is written now *zippula*, now *sippula*, we should consider whether it derives from *supare*, *sipare*, or *sipere*. See Festus and Paulus, where *farinula* and *pultes* occur.

Therefore, since the common reading here had *pultes*, this was an interpretation of *sippulae*, which was the true and ancient reading. Palladius, chapter 74: “Pytirion ate a little porridge made from flour.” In Greek: ζωμὸν ἀλεύρου, “a broth or porridge of flour.” I think these were *sippulae*.

# ADDENDA TO CERTAIN OF THE FIRST SEVENTY-FOUR VOLUMES OF THE *PATROLOGIA*, CONTAINING THE AUTHORS OF THE CHURCH OF THE FIRST SIX CENTURIES

## TO VOLUME VIII

### I. HISTORICAL NOTICE ON CONSTANTINE

*(Fabricius, Greek Library, volume VI.)*

### 1

Flavius Valerius Aurelius Claudius Constantine, surnamed the Great, son of Flavius [Note: This is how he is called on coins, as in Tristanus, volume III, p. 395, although others, such as Aurelius Victor, call him Julius Constantius. Besides the other writers who published the coins of the emperors, Constantine’s coins were illustrated by Cangius, in *Byzantine Families*, and by Alexander Wilthelmius, S.J., in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume V, May, p. 22 and following.] Valerius Constantius Chlorus, was born at Naissus, a city of Dacia, in A.D. 274, on February 27.

He succeeded his father in the empire in A.D. 306, on July 25. He first married Minervina, the mother of Crispus; after her death, he married Flavia Maximiana Fausta, the daughter of Herculius, by whom he fathered Constantine, Constantius, Constans, Constantia, and Helena.

After seeing the sign of the cross in the sky, he embraced the Christian religion and gained victory over Maxentius in A.D. 312. From that point onward, after compelling Maximinus to cease persecuting Christians and after also defeating Licinius, he neglected nothing that could adorn and enlarge the Church of Christ and encourage literary studies. [Note: Aurelius Victor, in the *Epitome*, chapter 41, concerning Constantine: “He was highly useful in many affairs: he quieted calumnies by very severe laws, nurtured the liberal arts, especially literary studies; he himself read, wrote, reflected, and heard the embassies and complaints of the provinces.” Compare Eusebius, *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, p. 361, where he speaks of the schools established by Constantine.]

For this reason the Greeks call him ἰσαπόστολος, “equal to the Apostles,” or ὁ ἐν βασιλεῦσι Ἀπόστολος, “the Apostle among emperors,” [Note: See Valesius’s note on Eusebius, book IV, section 60, *Life of Constantine*, and Mich. Le Quien’s note on Damascus, volume I, p. 630.] and solemnly celebrate his memory on May 21.

Theodoret, in his *Religious History*, p. 768, not inelegantly calls him the Christian Zerubbabel, who freed the faithful from captivity and restored their temples to them.

Finally, after accomplishing many distinguished deeds in peace and war, when he was near death he received baptism from Eusebius of Nicomedia at the villa of Achyron, not far from Nicomedia. [Note: The second baptism, which Constantine, covered with leprosy, is said to have received from the Roman bishop Sylvester, is vigorously disputed against Tentzel by the distinguished Schelstraten. They attribute it to fables—not only Protestants, such as, besides the aforementioned Tentzel, Abraham Scultetus in his *Anti-Baronian Dissertation on the Roman Baptism of Constantine*, Neustadt, 1607, quarto, part II of the *Selected Dissertations*—but also many learned men in the Roman Church, such as the Benedictines in their notes on Ambrose, volume II, p. 1209; Tillemont, volume IV of the *History of the Emperors*, p. 634; Papebrochius, *Acts of the Saints*, volume V, May 21, p. 14 and following; and Conrad Janning, in his *Apology for Papebrochius*, prefixed to the *Acts of the Saints*, volume I, June, p. 16 and following.]

A few days later he died on the sacred feast of Pentecost, May 22, A.D. 337, during the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, after reigning thirty years, nine months, and twenty-seven days, and having lived sixty-three years, two months, and twenty-five days.

## II.

Several of his letters survive, preserved by Eusebius and others; they are carefully reviewed by the very learned Cave in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*. If you please, add the following few observations.

The fragment of a letter to Athanasius in support of receiving Arius [Note: Constantine did not thereby approve Arius’s heresy, about which he was not yet sufficiently informed; rather, he hoped in this way to suppress the seed of dissension while it was still in the grass. Compare his conciliatory letter to Alexander and Arius in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, II, 64 ff., and Balthasar Bebel’s *Historico-Theological Exercise*, Strasbourg, 1663, as well as Nicholas Vedelius, *On the Prudence of the Ancient Church*, pp. 202, 267.] is also found in Socrates, Book I, chapter 27, and Sozomen, II, 22.

The earlier edict granting peace to the Christians, which Eusebius reports in Greek, X, 5, was preserved in Latin by Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 48.

The letter to the churches concerning the Council of Nicaea is also read in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 10.

The letter to Arius and the Arians, produced by Gelasius in the *Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, III, 1, appears to Casaubon to be spurious, in his *Casauboniana*, p. 143. This rescript was also published separately, Paris, 1595, octavo.

The letter to the Council of Tyre, which is found in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, IV, 42, and in Theodoret, *History*, Book I, chapter 29, differs from that preserved in Socrates, Book I, chapter 34, Sozomen, II, 28, and likewise in the *Tripartite History*, III, 7, and in Nicephorus, VIII, 50.

The *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, at the end of Eusebius’s books on the *Life of Constantine*, is read in Greek after having been translated from Latin—not by Eusebius, but by another translator, as he himself clearly indicates in Book IV, chapter 32, of the *Life of Constantine*.

Likewise, a brief *Oration to the Council of Nicaea on Peace*, which the same Eusebius presents in III, 12, was translated from Latin into Greek by I know not whom. A longer version, which occurs in Gelasius, II, 7, was also read by Theodoret, as can be gathered from Book I, chapter 7, of his *History*.

[Col. 0523A] Numerous edicts of Constantine are elucidated by Jacobus Gothofredus in his commentary on the *Theodosian Code*; by Franciscus Balduinus, a jurist, in his *Constantine*, Basel, 1556, and Strasbourg, 1612, octavo; and by the writers of annals, who assign each matter to its proper period, especially Tillemont, volume IV of his *History of the Emperors*. Moreover, the edict which Nicolaus Cusanus published under Constantine’s name in Book III, chapter 35, of the *Catholic Concordance*, Cusanus attributes to Honorius and Theodosius; Sirmond published it in a more complete form in his notes on Sidonius, p. 245.

## III.

Constantine’s confession to Silvester, bishop of Rome, which exists in Latin at the end of the *Recognitions* and other writings falsely attributed to Clement of Rome, Cologne, 1569, folio, p. 471, is spurious, just like the *Acts of Silvester*.

[Col. 0523B] The Donation said to have been made by Constantine to that same Silvester is likewise judged fictitious by the most learned men of the Roman Church [Note: The first to demonstrate its falsity in a lengthy and eloquent discourse was Lorenzo Valla. It was also printed separately more than once; together with Ulrich von Hutten’s preface to Ortuinus Gratius’s *Collection of Matters to Be Desired and Avoided*, reprinted at London; and in Simon Schard’s *Syntagma of Treatises on Imperial Jurisdiction*. Elacius, in his *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, and Robert Cocus, in his *Censure of the Ancient Writers*, produced the testimonies of Aeneas Sylvius and several others supporting Valla. To these add Baronius, under A.D. 324, no. 118 ff., and under 1191, no. 52 ff.; Isaac Habert on the *Archieratikon* of the Greek Church, p. 24; Jean Morin, in his French history of the Church liberated by Constantine and of the origin and progress of the secular power of the Roman pontiff, chapter 8; Pierre de Marca, III, 12, *On the Concord of the Sacred and the Imperial Powers*, and VI, 6, § 6; Antonio Pagi, under A.D. 324, no. 16; Tillemont, volume IV of his *History of the Emperors*, p. 226; Pierre Joseph Cantel, *History of Metropolitan Cities*, Part II, dissertation 2, chapter 2, no. 7; and especially Natalis Alexander, fourth century, dissertation 25.

Against these you may readily set Augustine Steuchus, *On the Donation of Constantine*, Lyons, 1545; Jacob Gretser, *On the Munificence of Princes toward the Apostolic See*, Ingolstadt, 1610, quarto, p. 36 ff.; and *Apology for Bellarmine*, chapter 21; as well as Nicolaus Schaten, in *Charlemagne the Roman Catholic*, Book II, chapter 6.

Among Protestants, on the falsity of this donation, see Johann Henelius, in *Uratislavian Leisure*, chapter 22; Gisbertus Voetius, volume II of the *Selected Disputations*, p. 869 ff.; James Ussher, *On the Succession and Condition of the Churches*, p. 60; John Rainolds, *Conference with Hardt*, p. 227 ff.; Franciscus Hotomanus, in *The Blunt Thunderbolt of Sixtus V*, pp. 128, 151 ff.; and most recently the Reverend Johann Andreas Schmid, in *A History of the Fourth Century, Stained by the Fables of Various Persons concerning Constantine the Great*, Helmstedt, 1712, etc.

“An edict,” says Papebrochius, “whether fabricated or corrupted, and therefore unworthy to enlarge the history of Pope Silvester,” in the preface to the *Acts of the Saints*, volume II, April, p. 1.] It is first mentioned by Aeneas of Paris, who wrote around A.D. 854, in his book *Against Ten Objections of the Greeks*, volume VII of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 111. After him came Hincmar of Reims, Peter Damian, Leo IX, Ado, and others.

Very different editions of it are circulated. One is found in the spurious *Acts of Silvester* and was inserted in Latin by Anselm of Lucca in his *Collection of Canons*, Book IV, chapter 32; by Deusdedit, Book IV, chapter 2; by Ivo of Chartres, Part V of the *Decree*, chapter 49; and by Gratian, Part I of the *Decree*, distinction 96, chapter 14—although Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, denies that it is found in the older manuscripts of Gratian, Part I of his *History*, title 8, [Col. 0524A] chapter 2, § 8.

Theodore Balsamon, however, presents a Greek translation of it in his scholia on Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title VIII, in Justellus’s *Canonical Library*, volume II, p. 929 ff. This version of Balsamon, together with another by Matthew Blastares, was also published by Marquard Freher in 1610, quarto, with annotations.

A much longer version was translated from Greek into Latin and dedicated to Pope Julius II by Bartholomaeus Picernus of Monte Arduo. It has prefixed to it the fictitious confession of Constantine mentioned above, and after the Cologne edition of 1515 it appeared several times. It is also found prefixed to Joachim Hildebrand’s dissertation *On the Donation of Constantine the Emperor*, Helmstedt, 1661 and 1703, and inserted in Balthasar Gualter’s *Elenctic Diatribe on the Baptism, Donation, and Embassy of Constantine the Emperor to the Council of Nicaea*, [Col. 0524B] Jena, 1618, duodecimo, p. 67 ff.

John Bodin, *On the Republic*, Book I, chapter 9, p. 221, accuses Augustine Steuchus of having written the Donation of Constantine in Greek in order to disguise the fraud: “But,” he says, “the deception is easily refuted from his own speech and from knowledge of antiquity.”

Another Greek version—“of Constantine by Harmenopulus,” as Nesselius notes, Part II of the *Catalogue of Manuscripts*, p. 27—is found in the Imperial Library and is mentioned by Lambecius, Book V, p. 244. In meaning, however, it is the same as Balsamon’s version, which Lambecius also mentions on p. 237.

Julius Caesar Bulengerus presents this very version, from the King’s codex, in Greek and Latin, Book II, chapter 6, of *On the Roman Empire*, p. 318. Since it is brief, I think it will not be unwelcome or unpleasant to the reader for it to appear here as well.

[Col. 0523]

## THE EDICT OF CONSTANTINE

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0523C] **Edict and divine pronouncement of the great Constantine concerning the Roman pontiff.**

We declare to all governors of the provinces and to the Senate of the Roman Empire that the Roman pontiff, successor of the holy apostles and of my lord Peter, has greater authority throughout the whole world than an emperor can possess; that he is to be revered and honored above the emperor by all [the Greek lacks *and*]; that he is the head of the four ancient sees; and that he is to judge and decree whatever accords with the orthodox faith.

[Col. 0523D] For we grant to my blessed father Silvester and to his successors our palace; the diadem for the head, woven with precious stones and gems; the shoulder-cloth encircling the neck; the purple cloak; the scarlet tunic; all the royal garments; the saddle-cloths spread beneath the royal horses; scepters; the remaining ornaments of imperial authority; and the entire glory of my power.

We order those who have been enrolled in the Roman clergy to be clothed in garments similar (*παραπλησίοις*, “similar,” I read) to those of our Senate, [Note: These are the translator Bulengerus’s emendations.] to ride horses, and to be covered with white garments. Likewise, we order their shoes to be made of white cloth, and that no one be able to prevent any man who has been chosen as a cleric from becoming a senator.

But since my holy father Silvester rejected the golden crown with such humility and moderation, we placed upon his holy head these ornaments signifying the holy Resurrection and the most radiant place [I read *καὶ τὴν ἁγίαν*, “and the holy”].

In the performance of the office of groom, and holding the reins of his horse, we went out from the palace court, out of reverence and fear for my holy lord Peter.

Above all, we considered it useful and pleasing to God to withdraw from the city of Rome and from all the lands and cities of the West, to grant them to the most holy pope, to transfer the strength of the empire to the East, and to take possession of the city of Byzantium, situated in the finest place beneath the sun, and establish the seat of the empire there. For we judged it unjust that the emperor should possess supreme authority in the place where the beginning of the Christian faith had been granted to us from heaven.

Since we have written these things with our own hand and placed them upon the remains of my lord Peter, we swear that we shall observe what we have decreed. We also bind our successors to observe it faithfully and religiously, and we promise this under oath to our father the pope and to his successors.

[Col. 0524C] **Decree of the great Constantine concerning the pope of Rome.**

We decree [Note: The Viennese manuscript adds, “together with all the satraps”: “We decree together with all the satraps and the Senate of our empire.”] to all the satraps and to the Senate of our empire that the bishop of Rome, successor of the holy apostles and of my lord Peter, possesses throughout the inhabited world an authority greater than that of the empire; that he is to be honored and revered by all, far more than the emperor; that he is the head of the four ancient thrones; and that he is to judge and determine whatever accords with the orthodox faith.

For we grant to my blessed father Silvester and to his successors our palace; the diadem upon the head, composed of precious stones and pearls; the shoulder-cloth encircling the neck; the purple cloak; the scarlet tunic; all the royal garments; the trappings of the royal horses; the scepters; the remaining ornaments of the empire; and the entire glory of our authority.

We command those enrolled in the clergy of most holy Rome to be adorned with garments similar to those of our Senate, to ride horses, and to wear white cloths.

We also decree that their footwear be made of white cloth, and that anyone who chooses to become a cleric be in no way prevented from becoming a member of our Senate.

But since my father, the holy Silvester, rejects the golden crown with humility of mind, we placed these things upon his holy head with our own hands, signifying the most radiant place [Col. 0526B] and the holy Resurrection.

Having assumed the office of groom and holding the reins of his horse, we went out from the court of his sacred palace, seized by reverence and fear of my holy lord Peter.

We have judged it wholly useful and pleasing to God to withdraw from the city of Rome and from all the lands and cities of the West, and to grant them to the most holy pope; to transfer the power of the empire toward the regions of the East; to take possession of the city of Byzantium, in the finest location beneath the sun; and to establish the imperial residence there. For we considered it unjust that the emperor on earth should possess authority in the place where the beginning of the religion of the Christians had come to us from heaven.

Having written these things with our own hands and placed them upon the body of my lord Peter, we make sworn pledges that they shall never be violated; and we command those who receive our power to preserve them inviolate, promising this to our father the pope and to his successors.

[Col. 0525]

## LETTER OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE TO THE CHRISTIANS OF THE WHOLE WORLD

(See this letter and what is said about it under Jerome’s spurious letter to Eustochium, *Patrologia*, volume XXX, column 226.)

[Col. 0525]

## II. THE POEM OF C. MAIUS VICTORINUS ON THE MACCABEES

(We have published this poem among the works of Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, volume XLIX of the *Patrologia*, where it may be consulted.)

## TO VOLUME XIII

[Col. 0525]

## I. A POEM ATTRIBUTED TO POPE DAMASUS

This poem is not found in the libraries published before our edition. It was first brought to light by the most diligent bibliographers Miller and Aubenas [Note: *Revue de Bibliographie*, August 1845.] with several observations in our volume XIII. They recovered it from a manuscript of the library of Saint-Germain, where it had lain hidden.

On the initial folio one reads, written in a recent hand: “The author of these verses is believed to be Saint Damasus, supreme pontiff; nevertheless, we are by no means able to affirm the authenticity of the little work.” (C)*

## THE POEM BEGINS

[Col. 0527A]

I do not delay to recall the famous praises of Chrysanthus,  
whom the world rightly celebrates with renowned acclaim.

His father, then, when he was flourishing in the first period of life [Note: For *primo*, which the poet has Latinized. Miller and Aubenas],  
handed him over, by lot, to teachers in the rhetoricians’ school [sic],  
so that, as a boy of natural ability [sic], he might learn the arts of books,  
which worldly wisdom cultivates with foolish understanding.

He is said to have been endowed with an acute mind,  
burning with talent, prudent, and mature in judgment.

Afterward, when as an illustrious reader he had absorbed with his ears  
the sacred volumes written in heavenly language,  
he immediately despised the teachings of the ancient sect,  
and trampled underfoot the empty folly of the old laws.

Having quickly acquired the rudiments of faith,  
he washed away the disgrace of sin in baptismal water.

[Col. 0527B] Soon he publicly and willingly preached Christ to the pagans,  
scorning the dreadful torments of their proud threats.

Then his father, violating the laws of nature,  
thrust the young man into the dark shadows of a confined prison,  
greatly fearing the decrees of the wicked treasury;  
and, trembling, he also dreaded the bitter capital punishment.

But when the young man’s mind willingly endured the torments,  
his father soon contrived another scene [sic].  
He brought forward the slippery pleasures of worldly displays,  
offering silken coverings in purple hangings—  
silk which the dying silkworm produces with festive effort—  
and clothed the noble youth in costly, gleaming garments.

Then, at his father’s command, girls, adorned with various garments and beautiful of face, brought abundant banquets,  
delicacies, and the luxuries of the kitchen,

[Col. 0527C] so that by such spectacles the bold soldier might be softened—  
the iron weapons with which [Note: For *queis*, that is, *quibus*. Miller and Aubenas.] they frequently strike [Note: Read *cedunt*, “yield,” for *caedunt*. Miller and Aubenas.] the hearts of men [Note: For *virorum*, “of men”; but there is a prosodic error. Miller and Aubenas].

Yet the young soldier, armed with Christ’s shield,  
despised the slippery kisses of maidenly lips,  
and did not allow the darts of debauchery to pierce his breast;  
but from afar he shook off the arrows hurled by deceit.

Not otherwise than the poet sang in a nuptial song:

“But Christ’s sweet lips soothe the lips;  
then honeyed lips grow dark upon rose-red lips.”

At last the mature maiden came to the contest,  
Daria, a Vestal, blushing with a beautiful face,  
whom a golden crescent accompanied with pale-blue gems.

She strives to bind the young man in the bond of a gift [sic],  
so as to bend his mind toward the marriage of the bridal chamber.

She was adorned with brooches and relied upon eloquent speech;

[Col. 0527D] finally, the eloquent teachers were astonished  
at the girl’s intelligence, supported by the utterance of books (*biblorum*);  
for she had a firm grasp of Scripture and was swift in reading.

But the outcome of the dark fortune turned out otherwise.

While the pious man set contrary fate against fate,  
Daria, who had long guarded the rites of Vesta,  
believed in the Most High, who governs the scepters of heaven;  
the maiden was converted to Chrysanthus by his eloquent words.

Then together they pretend that fate has joined them in marriage,  
and both live in harmony with chaste conduct,  
so that they might wholly avoid the foul stain in their hearts

[Col. 0528A] and drive the black blemish of the flesh from their hearts.

After this she is dipped in the consecrated waters of baptism,  
so that she might strip from her mind the old garments  
and take a new robe from the liquid stream.

Then the maiden rejected the teachings of the ancient books  
and followed the doctrines of Christ in the squared books of Scripture.

Who could count the great crowds of the people  
whom their examples led to believe in Christ?

For this reason he is handed over to be tortured with harsh punishments,  
and is guarded by seventy men [sic], in a dense military force,  
in the temple of Hercules, lest perhaps he offer incense.

Then the savage soldier began to torment the one who refused,  
the athlete of the Lord, relying on heavenly strength;  
he oppressed him with wet and raw cords of sinew,  
intending to expose him to the burning heat of the blazing sun.

But more quickly than a moment, the ropes are loosened from his arms,  
as almighty God releases the wicked bonds.

Behold, again the stakes close around him in fetters,  
and they bound his legs, swollen with rigid pieces of wood.

Immediately the Ruler of Olympus splits the stocks,  
although the foolish had fastened him there with blinded minds.

Then the cruel executioner ordered urine (*lotia*) to be scattered,  
wetting the sacred limbs with foul-smelling filth.

That liquid, they say, drove away the black phantom,  
while necromancy hoped concerning the Lord’s servant (*vernam Domini fretum*; sense uncertain);  
but the stench blazed with the sweet fragrance of ambrosia.

Next the torturers order a heifer-hide (*bucula*), “de globo rebyrsa” [sic],  
and the limbs to be bound with raw hide,  
for the martyr, who was to endure the blazing sun in its brightness.

But the burning Titan restrained his fiery thunderbolts,  
so that, they say, no fire touched the innocent limbs.

Then they shut the holy man in alternating prisons;  
they fasten his arms with tight chains,  
and bind his neck together with his paired legs.

Behold, suddenly the pious Judge frees his knotted limbs  
and immediately breaks the tightened bonds of iron.

Moreover, when the unfortunate soldier was striking the holy man  
with a knotted rod, rejoicing in red blood,

[Col. 0528C] strange to relate, the blessed martyr felt no harshness  
from the blows of the rods.

Indeed, the rods softened like feathers for the holy man,  
just as green papyrus bends gently in the stream.

Claudius, a distinguished man, was pierced with remorse and willingly believed;  
he converted the seventy men through the clear teaching  
and had those who were immersed cleansed in the waters of baptism.

[Col. 0528D] Therefore the fortunate soldier Ada led those stained  
with the purple of red blood to the heavenly Olympus.

Then a blessed cave enclosed them, buried there together,  
to see the bright rewards of everlasting life.

While these rightly survey the vaulted height of heaven,  
Daria and Chrysanthus endure harsh torments.

But that tireless man, bound by the weight of iron,  
is thrust into dark prison, destined to bear the blackness of confinement,  
where foul excrement flowed through putrid crypts;  
but the stench yields to nectar, as darkness yields to light.

Meanwhile Daria is handed over to criminal prostitutes,  
entering the brothel without committing any crime.

[Col. 0529A] But a roaring lion is sent from its narrow enclosure  
to guard the maiden’s virgin limbs.

If anyone wished to violate her sacred chastity,  
handling her honorable body with obscene gestures,  
he would touch the chest just as the infamous Uzzah once did;  
immediately the shameless man would die, confounded in face,  
and, torn by the teeth of the raging lion,  
would suffer the avenging punishment of a beast’s death.

[Col. 0530A] At last, under the decree of Augustus who ruled Rome,  
they received red crowns through death,  
and together they rest, buried in a cavern at Sabulo—  
those whom cruel punishment had tormented together in life.

We believe that, gathered into blessed ranks by right,  
when the earth of its own accord opens from the bosom of the tomb,  
and the human race rises from the dark graves,  
he will raise them to rest when he loosens the world’s reins.

[Col. 0529]

# HISTORICAL DISSERTATION ON DAMASUS AND LAURENTIUS, OR DAMASUS AND LAURENTIUS CLAIMED AND VINDICATED AS HISPANIARDS

By Fr. Pérez Bayer, priest of Valencia, Rome, 1756.

## DEDICATORY LETTER

To the most illustrious and distinguished gentleman, Don Juan Francisco Gaona Portocarrero, etc., Count of Valleparadiso, knight of the Order of Calatrava, counselor in the Council of the Indies to Ferdinand VI, Catholic king of the Spains, and chief administrator of the royal revenue, etc., etc.

Franciscus Perezius Bayerius wishes happiness.

That I have wished to dedicate to you, most illustrious count, whatever this labor of ours may be, may appear less an act of duty than an excuse. For since an account must in due time be rendered to you of the tasks which the most merciful king, and true father of our Spain, Ferdinand VI, prescribed for me to undertake on my Italian journey—and indeed of the whole arrangement of our business and leisure—there may perhaps be some who, when they see me turning aside to these studies, will think that this work proceeded from a guilty conscience seeking to forestall judgment, rather than from a dutiful client’s desire to deserve the favor of an excellent Maecenas.

Indeed, because I had foreseen from the beginning more than once the vanity and importunity of such judgments, I came close to abandoning the plan of writing and, from fear of private criticism, deserting the public cause of our countrymen. But why should I not rather, spurning these petty objections and trivialities, promise myself a few months’ leave from the excellent prince who loves the honor of his fatherland, especially with you as my patron—not to spend them in lazy idleness, but, if possible, to restore to Spain the ancient and ancestral glory which I knew certain Italian writers of great name were about to take from her?

Or how, if I hoped that I might in some way raise the declining and almost prostrate cause of the Spaniards, could I have neglected to come to its aid? Would I not then be said to have betrayed my homeland?

You yourself, most illustrious count, will acknowledge that the Spanish position concerning Damasus and Laurentius—which for so many past centuries had made them compatriots of the Spaniards—now stands at such a point and in such danger, when you see that since 1741, the year in which the new opinion assigning both men to the citizens of Rome was first publicly advanced, so many outstanding men, publishing books in rivalry with one another, have conspired to overthrow the old view. They no longer argue on both sides as though the matter were doubtful or merely probable; rather, they assert that the case has been decided in favor of the Romans and that the whole matter has been demonstrated.

Whether Spaniards should thereafter hope for anything better is not merely something we cannot foresee; we cannot even conjecture it. For although I see that our arguments and conjectures in support of claiming Damasus and Laurentius for Spain are approved in no ordinary degree not only by those to whom this little work was publicly entrusted for examination, but also by men of the highest distinction to whom I had previously given it privately to read, the more I have come to know their humanity, the more I fear that something may be attributed by them to goodwill rather than judgment.

Yet because I know them to be upright and incorruptible—so that no one could suspect, without doing them grave injustice, that they had delivered a judgment contrary to their convictions—I am not without a clear hope that our arguments, strengthened by their support, may at last withstand the attack of our opponents until the cohort of Spanish writers, whom we hope will come to our aid, can take up the fight from a more favorable position and contend with the enemy in the decisive battle over the whole matter.

Certainly, if I alone undertook to engage so many vigorous men, I would deserve to be considered more confident than that wrestler in Plautus. But if, surrounded by the strongest ranks of others who appear to stand with the Spaniards, I were to refuse the contest, I would be heard as both unjust to them and, deservedly, the most cowardly of all mortals.

Another reason also compelled me to write, most illustrious count. Not long ago I completed a *Collection of the Monuments of the Spanish Name Surviving in the City*, in which the portraits, epitaphs, and family coats of arms of about three hundred distinguished men of our nation are displayed, as accurately and elegantly as possible, on an equal number of large sheets. My purpose was that, opposite each person’s sepulchral inscription, his homeland, lineage, and rank, as well as the noteworthy deeds he had performed, should be briefly indicated.

It was therefore necessary either to demonstrate that Damasus and Laurentius—whom we had assigned the first place of all in that collection—were Spaniards, or, what would have been most disgraceful, to remove them from their position and dismiss them entirely stripped of their rank.

Now, since I had at hand arguments with which I hoped not implausibly to meet the objections of my adversaries, what stain of disgrace would I have brought upon myself, not only among Spaniards but also among foreigners, if I had preferred sluggish and dishonorable leisure to so noble a labor?

I have said these things, most illustrious count, with this purpose and on that occasion: if anyone should perhaps think that whatever this offering of ours may be was consecrated to your name merely as a pretext for an excuse rather than as an act of duty. For your innate and ancestral kindness, and especially your constant zeal in protecting and enhancing the affairs of your country, make me think quite otherwise.

Although I have not yet been granted the opportunity of addressing you face to face, I am nevertheless not unaware of how warmly you embrace letters and those who cultivate them, and how deeply fixed in your mind is the resolve to enlarge the liberal arts and disciplines among our countrymen.

That this particular virtue among your eminent praises is celebrated not only here in Rome, the queen of cities, but everywhere among the nations, is most gratifying to me. Yet it was far more gratifying and pleasant that I was once permitted to see and admire in person a living and utterly faithful image of these qualities.

Two years ago, when I was staying in Venice and was engaged in some trifling research in the famous library of Saint Mark, chance brought before me the most illustrious Marquis Annavetius, your worthy son and the second hope of a most illustrious house. With excellent judgment you had sent him away from his father’s embrace at an early age so that, in the vast book of the world, he might learn the customs of men and the character of cities.

That same fortunate day on which rumor had spread there that our most prudent king had summoned you to the highest administration of the royal revenue gave me the opportunity to pay my respects to him. He received me so kindly and generously that, for as long as we were together in Venice, I enjoyed his most delightful company and conversation.

In that most distinguished young man I was able to admire manly prudence joined immediately to remarkable ease of manners. When he then applied himself to examining more closely certain learned notes which I had collected during my Italian journey, together with the extensive journals of that journey, I experienced his incredible courtesy and his singular devotion to letters.

Thus, when I looked upon a young man endowed beyond his years with so many outstanding qualities, it seemed to me that not only his father’s virtue and spirit, but—if I may speak as the jurists do—the very inheritance of his living father, stood before my eyes.

Since this is so, most illustrious count, I do not think I need greatly fear that you will not receive with a tranquil countenance this modest offering, which seeks the light under your auspices.

If I learn that these efforts—which patriotic love compelled me to make while engaged in another task—are approved by you, a man of the highest integrity and devoted above all to Spanish glory, I shall understand that I have been most honorably rewarded by this alone.

But what if, through the authority and favor which you possess with our Augustus, you were to persuade His Majesty to cast his eyes upon these reflections of ours, without being deterred by their modesty?

Since I am not permitted seriously even to hope for this, it remains for me to pray, with vows for your safety, that all things fortunate and prosperous may be granted to you by the supreme giver of blessings.

Rome, on the eve of Saint Laurentius the Martyr, 1756.

## EPIGRAM

**On the book concerning Saint Damasus and Laurentius, assigned to Spain, written by Franciscus Perezius, a most learned man, by A. A. G. Augustinidus.**

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following poem are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0531A]

Franciscus restores to Hesperia her ancient honors,  
so that Rome can no longer say that they are hers.

Overcome in a thousand ways, Rome is compelled to confess  
that she stole a twin radiance from the Spaniards.

Yet she rejoices openly, crowned with a double wreath,  
when she is seen to be the mother of so great an offspring.

If Damasus, dying, and Laurentius, dying,  
left their bones enclosed in sacred marble to the Romans,

she does not envy them at all; she is sufficiently renowned by this name,  
if Hesperia alone is the homeland of the saints.

This glory has come to the Spaniards, but greater glory will come,  
when a prince at home so greatly promotes the Muses.

[Col. 0532A]

Franciscus has again given Hesperia her honors,  
so that Rome may no longer hold them as her own.

Though convicted in many ways, she knows and acknowledges  
that she took two saints away from the Spaniards.

But, possessing the two crowns, she rejoices,  
as a queen, mother of a blessed offspring.

For if Laurentius or Damasus left  
their ever-undying bodies to the Romans,

she does not begrudge it. For the Iberians it is enough  
if Hesperia alone is the homeland of the saints.

This glory has now come, and greater glory is to come,  
since the king cares greatly for the Muses and his own renown.

## A VOW OF THE AUTHOR TO THE DIVINE FATHERS LAURENTIUS AND DAMASUS

[Col. 0531]

O light of the Western lands and of the regions of the East,  
a twin torch shining before the Iberians;

illustrious pair, gracious Damasus and you, Laurentius,  
whom the long consensus of the centuries,

not only while barbarism still prevailed,  
but even after Attic speech had been brought into Latium,

assigned—no one among the ancients forbidding it—  
to the Spaniards as their homeland and citizens;

because, when you were nearing old age,  
torn from your domestic hearths,

stripped of your homeland and made new Romans,  
the Trojan race, in a city rejoicing,

Janus, the Rostra, the Forum, the Fathers, the Senate,  
and finally the supreme pontiff greeted you.

There is no reason for us to grieve,  
or, begrudgingly, to make the noisy forums of Spain resound

against the city, mistress of the world.  
She knows, surely, how much will be added to her own adornment

if she obtains a union of the two for herself,  
as a precious stone added to her own necklace.

And so, as happens amid uncertainty on both sides,  
in the blind whirlwind of controversies,

while several cities reclaim Laurentius and Damasus  
and each boasts of both as its own,

one city assigns one of them to itself by a special right,  
without troubling over the ancient and earlier common homeland.

[Col. 0532B]

What then? Shall our Spain remain silent in the face of this, unmoved,  
and make no reply?

And will you, Laurentius and Damasus,  
whom the Hesperians have until now twice called their own—  
both as Spaniards and as stars—  
at last permit yourselves to depart with hands lowered?

Let those who have no sense of honor  
and no concern for piety do so,  
those harsh souls.

The Hesperian land kindly instills in her own people spirits too gentle  
either to endure this fate in silence  
or to endure it unavenged.

Hence our patriotic love, Laurentius,  
and the equal ardor for Damasus,  
add sharper spurs to us,

so that, unprepared, we may enter the danger  
and attempt great things though we are weak.

There will be, I think, men who,  
while we gird on the weapons of a skirmish,

will be glad to fight in the battle line,  
better prepared for combat.

Here we implore your loyalty, Iberians;  
we likewise implore your aid, blessed Laurentius,

and yours, Damasus, author of our labor.  
Kindly stand by us,

and never abandon our Hesperia,  
which cherishes you both in her motherly bosom

and receives you as her children—  
even if Rome should henceforth deem you worthy

of the more blessed honor of citizenship.  
Do not abandon her native borders.

## FIRST PART OF THE DISSERTATION

### ON THE HOMELAND OF DAMASUS

[Col. 0533]

## CHAPTER ONE

**The occasion of the writing. The state of the present controversy. The grounds on which the Spaniards claim Damasus as one of their own.**

[Col. 0533A]

Since, with new matters continually succeeding one another, I had been detained in the city longer than I had initially planned, and since it would have been inglorious and almost shameful—especially for a man whom they said was not averse to such studies, or at least took great pleasure in them—to return home empty-handed from so rich a field of both kinds of antiquity, I immediately resolved to set aside a little plot of ground to cultivate in my spare hours, one whose produce would nevertheless chiefly consist in matters relating to our own Spain.

While considering how I might accomplish this, I recalled that not long before Francisco Emmanuel Mena, a Madrid bookseller, had begun preparing a new edition of the distinguished Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca Hispanica*, greatly enriched by the addition of numerous authors and works not previously published. Since he wished it to answer the wishes of everyone, he had sent letters of invitation to learned men throughout Spain, asking each to contribute, according to his ability, something toward completing so considerable an undertaking. As soon as this thought entered my mind, I decided that no further deliberation was needed about carrying out my plan.

For I hoped that literary treasures are never entirely exhausted, and that even after the libraries of the city had been thoroughly searched by that most discerning and diligent author, and after so abundant a harvest had been gathered, some gleaning would remain for us that was not unworthy of notice. Nor did the outcome deceive me. [Col. 0533C] As soon as I was granted the opportunity to visit the Vatican, the foremost of all libraries, I began to examine its manuscript catalogues with the utmost diligence. Whatever in them seemed, whether by the name of an author or by the subject of a work, capable in any way of enriching the national library, I rapidly transferred, as time allowed and without any selection, to my notebooks, intending later, at home and at leisure, to compare it with the works published by Nicolás Antonio.

In about three months I had completed my examination of the Palatine and Urbino collections, as well as the collection that had once belonged to Christina, Queen of the Swedes—the three most distinguished additions to the Vatican Library. Not a day passed on which comparison of the manuscripts with the printed works did not enrich me with the discovery of some new author or work.

I had reached the principal library itself when the death of Cardinal Angelo Maria Quirini, [Col. 0533D] librarian of the Holy Roman Church, occurred—a death to be mourned by everyone, but by no one more grievously than by me. During my journey I had met this man at Brescia, a person distinguished for his piety and born for the advancement of letters. Because the illustrious Balthasar Oltrochi, prefect of the Ambrosian Library at Milan, had mentioned something to him about our studies, he not only received me with the greatest kindness and repeatedly invited me to private conversation, but—what is no small sign of affection—did not allow me to depart without a gift.

Often, when we prolonged the night with varied conversation, the very old man would ask about the nature of our studies and our journey: whether letters were lying neglected among the Spaniards or were held in esteem. He would then speak at length of the talents of our countrymen, which, as he said, were by no means ordinary, and, without failing to praise any of those whom he had once known at Rome or whose writings he had read—especially the dean of Alón [Note: [Col. 0533D] This is the distinguished Emmanuel Martin, whose name and published monuments of talent and learning are too illustrious to be hidden anywhere.], the Marquis of Mondéjar [Note: [Col. 0533D] Namely, Gaspar Ibáñez de Segovia, whose works, after many that had appeared during his lifetime, have recently been published: the distinguished Father Juan María of the Society of Jesus’s *Notes on Spanish History*, in folio; and the *Chronological Work*, in folio, edited by the most illustrious literary society of the city of Valencia, in the years 1744 and 1746.], and indeed even the living—he would inspire in me amazement at the intensity of that great man’s devotion to letters and learned men, as well as at the remarkable memory he retained at such an advanced age.

The fact that I pursued this matter somewhat more fully than my purpose required was due both to my longing for so dear a man and to the bitter recollection of what followed his death. For only a few days had passed when I received the most grievous news: first that I should interrupt my undertaken work for a while, and soon afterward that I should abandon entirely all hope of finishing it. It would be painful to reopen the causes of the wound, were it not that, under the eminent and truly πολυμαθέστατος—“most learned”—Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Domenico Passionei, who alone, in the judgment of the most eminent and prudent pontiff Benedict XIV, was approved and considered suitable to succeed Quirini in the lofty office of apostolic librarian, a clear hope now shines upon us that the interrupted work may at last be completed under his auspices.

[Col. 0534C] From then on, as I devised new projects and, so as not to remain idle in the meantime, visited the city’s sacred churches during the afternoon, I encountered everywhere sepulchral inscriptions of illustrious men of Spanish name who, while pursuing public or private business in the city, had been overtaken by death and entrusted the remains of their bodies to the altars of their patron saints until the day of their transformation. As I diligently occupied myself, according to my custom, with copying their epitaphs and sketching, however imperfectly, their family coats of arms, my handbook gradually grew into the bulk of a proper volume, although I had scarcely surveyed a third of the city’s sacred buildings.

This was the first reason why I began to investigate the monuments of Spaniards in the City somewhat more carefully than before, and seriously to consider collecting into one work everything that still survived. I hoped that the received history of Spain through the centuries might derive some assistance from this, if a succession of illustrious men of our nation were placed before the eyes of scholars to be surveyed at a single glance. In order that this might be done with greater benefit, I further resolved to append a brief sepulchral notice concerning those whom I knew to have excelled in piety and learning and to have performed public offices with distinction—especially those whose memory I knew to have been buried together with their ashes—giving a few details about their homeland, studies, and principal achievements, and indicating the sources from which fuller knowledge of them might be obtained.

This was the whole plan of our undertaking. But when we began to pursue it more closely, we again found ourselves at a standstill. Since we judged that the supreme pontiff Damasus, distinguished above all others by the glory of his learning and dignity, and by the archetypal monuments bearing his name that still survive at Rome, was especially worthy to lead the procession of Spaniards in our work, the authority of certain recent writers intervened. Preferring slippery conjectures to the testimony of the ancients, they decided that Damasus should be counted among Roman citizens, contrary to what had hitherto been believed—and, if heaven please, that Laurence too, the deacon and unconquered martyr, should be counted a Roman.

At first I complained of the injustice of our times, which had allowed the authority of such a tribunal of hypercritics to become so great. Then an extraordinary weariness and satiety with the undertaking overcame me, so that, had I not already advanced to the point from which shame and the law of the work forbade retreat, I should not have hesitated for a moment to abandon it altogether. For I was insufficiently prepared to overcome these difficulties, had no assistance from the books at hand, and was not at leisure—as would have been necessary—to calm the disturbances stirred up by others or, whenever I wished, to raise new ones myself.

Only one course remained: to evade the attack of my opponents by some stratagem and blunt their weapons as best I could, thereby opening a kind of path toward my subject until one of my countrymen, better equipped and in a more favorable position, could take up the battle and engage the enemy in the decisive contest.

From this arose the material of my discussion and the subject of this work. While I was trying to pursue it somewhat more fully in the vernacular for the benefit of Spaniards, this little book slipped from my hands, contrary to anything I had intended.

When it was meanwhile handed to several friends whose judgment carries great weight with me, and when it did not appear so shapeless to them, they came to me with urgent requests that I should as soon as possible present it to the Latin world and make it public. At first I refused, pleading lack of time; but this was merely a pretext. In reality I was avoiding a contentious and wholly polemical subject, in which one cannot exercise one’s intellect freely, and in which, whenever one detects the errors of others or defends one’s own rights with somewhat greater energy, people attribute the result to malice and party spirit.

They, on the contrary, appealed to their own trustworthiness, to our common friendship, and finally to the glory of the Spanish name, which they knew I placed above everything else. They did not cease their entreaties until I had pledged my word to undertake it. Accordingly, with God’s favor—and may the outcome be auspicious—I now begin to discharge that pledge.

The first of all who attributed the holy pontiff Damasus to the Romans, although he had been regarded by the general agreement of many centuries as a Spaniard, and who judged that the testimony of recent and ancient writers and the authority of the most ancient manuscripts should be subordinated to conjectures alone, and conjectures not particularly firm, was Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0535D] Tillemont, *Mémoires pour servir à l’Histoire*, vol. VIII, pp. 386 and 773, in the Venetian edition of 1732.].

Knowing that Damasus had begun the novitiate of sacred service at Rome as a boy and had ultimately attained the highest ecclesiastical office through all the grades, from the lectorate onward; and knowing further that his father, Antonius, had first been an *exceptor* and afterward a lector, deacon, and priest [Col. 0536B] in the basilica dedicated to Saint Laurence—the church once called “at the Theatre of Pompey,” but now commonly known as “in Damaso” after its founder, or rather its restorer—as an ancient epigram of Damasus himself teaches [Note: [Col. 0535D] Damasus, epigram 35, in Merenda, p. 241:

[Col. 0536D]

“Here his father had advanced as exceptor, lector, deacon, and priest

…”], Tillemont thought that the father as well as the son must have spent his boyhood at Rome, since both had attained there the rank of lector, which according to the discipline of the age was assigned to boys. Nor did he regard it as probable that Damasus’s father had moved from Spain to Rome with wife and children; at least, he found no clear account of how this could have happened.

The distinguished Antonius Maria Merenda agrees with Tillemont. I hear that he was most recently promoted to a canonry of the same basilica of Saint Laurence in Damaso. In the year just past, 1754, he prepared a new collection of the works of that same holy pontiff, and it was this work that occasioned the present treatise for us—who had long thought that Tillemont’s earlier opinion had found little favor among learned men and had fallen out of use.

Merenda therefore adds new conjectures of his own to Tillemont’s, but only conjectures, to which, according to the opinion of the jurists [Note: [Col. 0536D] See *Digest* 45.1.137 §2, *de Verborum Obligationibus*.], there is no place in a matter that is not doubtful. He exaggerates the difficulty of the very long journey from Spain, the impediments presented by children who were almost infants and scarcely capable of enduring it; and he adds that Damasus’s father, a complete stranger and wholly unknown at Rome, immediately upon his arrival had enrolled himself among the clergy and had at once been honored in the basilica of Saint Laurence, first with the title of notary and then with that of lector. Both circumstances, he thinks, are insufficiently consistent with, indeed foreign to, the discipline of those times. [Note: [Col. 0536D] Antonius Maria Merenda, *Works and Deeds of Saint Damasus*, ch. 1, no. 1.]

According to that discipline, he says, a man first had to be baptized and then, after an interval, tested to determine whether he was worthy to be enrolled in the sacred service. At least nine years, or seven at the minimum, had to be spent in exercising the offices of the lesser orders and observing the intervals before receiving them, so that, after the requisite testing, he might be advanced to the higher grades of the Church. A little later he continues: “Were father and son, then, placed in the lower orders at one and the same time and in the same church? Let others judge.”

Gregorius Jacobus Terribilinus [Col. 0537A] the Roman offers nothing better, [Note: [Col. 0537D] Abbot Terribilinus, in the appendix to his *Work on Saint Damasus*, p. 1.] a man celebrated for his friendly regard for our countrymen, among whom he had once lived. Like the two earlier writers, he makes Damasus a Roman; and, as though reheating the same cabbage were not enough, he serves us Tillemont’s predictions for a third time.

He says that he had noticed one thing himself, lest he appear to have come entirely empty-handed: among the ancient writers who discuss Damasus, cited by Martius Milesius Sarazanius [Note: [Col. 0537D] Martius Milesius Sarazanius, *Work on Blessed Damasus*, Rome, 1638.] and Father Constantius, there is not a single one who calls him a Spaniard before the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, which they think was compiled under Felix IV—namely, around the year of Christ 530—or before Anastasius the Librarian, from whom that Felician catalogue is believed to have been copied.

He asserts that neither of these writers possesses great authority, and that the Spaniards who have written about Damasus have offered no sound argument in his favor concerning his homeland. He further says that they disagree about the place in which the most holy pontiff was born.

Thus far Terribilinus. Yet after robbing our Spain of Damasus—that is, after driving a sword hilt-deep into the very vitals of the Spaniards—he attempts to soothe them with empty consolation, repeatedly calling the nation illustrious.

Now, to state my own judgment concerning Tillemont’s conjectures: although I do not deny that they possess some significance and weight, nor that the question of when Damasus’s father moved to Rome with his wife and children—or rather, whether he moved without them, or perhaps long after Damasus—has not hitherto been sufficiently clarified, I nevertheless do not think that critics should value those conjectures so highly that they can in any way be preferred or opposed to the testimony of ancient writers and manuscripts. Rather, they should be assigned the same status as hearsay witnesses, whose role in history is represented by those conjectures, when set against eyewitnesses.

At least there would be some, however slight, support on which they could rely. Their strength would then be reinforced with something like triple bronze, and we would not be fighting, as now, in a most unequal battle and one scarcely honorable to the victors. But, except for Terribilinus, who shamelessly asserts it without warrant and, as they say, speaks without legal authority, no one—not one of the ancient writers, nor even one of the recent writers since the restoration of criticism—has ever thought of undermining the testimony of the Felician catalogue of pontiffs or of Anastasius, in both of which Damasus is expressly made a Spaniard.

Could Baronius, Panvinio, Ciacconius, Fleury, Pagius, and the other more distinguished critics who dealt with our Damasus have been unaware—not only that he had served at Rome from boyhood in the lectorate and the other ecclesiastical grades, but also that his father Antonius had held, in the basilica of Laurence, the office of lector among the orders customarily assigned to boys? Certainly not.

But because they saw that the difficulty arising from this—namely, the question of when Damasus’s father could have moved from Spain to Rome with wife and children—was supported by no testimony, ancient or recent, they did not assign it as much weight as Tillemont did. Nor did they sink so far into confidence as to judge that the uncertain testimony of conjectures should be entrusted with the certain authority of writers and manuscripts.

I admit that the word “confidence” slipped from me unwisely; yet I would not wish it to be taken maliciously by my opponents or to injure them in any way. But if we examine the matter with minds free of prejudice, I simply do not see how they can escape that reproach among learned men. For what much more distinguished critics could long ago have advanced, guided by those same conjectures, they were prevented from doing by their reverence for the ancients. These men, supported by no newly discovered manuscript and by no argument or additional conjecture, do not hesitate to assert it, and regard this as their chief accomplishment.

At least Merenda should be forgiven while he continues to oppose the common and most widely accepted opinion concerning the homeland of Saint Laurence, although we think that he too suffered something human in this matter. He should not be accused of doing so without grounds, since he supports his position with more than one recently discovered ancient manuscript and with a multiplicity of arguments, apparently sufficiently firm. But to draw new and entirely different conclusions from what has hitherto been established, without introducing any new proposition or assumption—that is a feat of extraordinary, indeed extreme, subtlety.

Before, therefore, I disclose my own opinion concerning the Roman journey of Damasus’s father and explain how it could have occurred—namely, in a manner that does no violence to the trustworthiness of history and observes the ecclesiastical laws exactly, and, as I believe, most probably— I thought it appropriate to set out the testimony of the ancients on which the opinion of those Spaniards who claim Damasus as one of their countrymen rests.

Domestic historians have neglected this portion of Spanish history, since each prefers to serve his private interests rather than the public good and strives to make Damasus a fellow citizen—that is, a countryman—and have left it entrusted to the testimony of only Anastasius the Librarian, as though either the authority of so great a man would safely place it beyond the attacks of the hypercritics, or we were still living in the Pythagorean age.

The distinguished Nicolás Antonio was more cautious in this matter [Note: [Col. 0537D] Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book II, ch. 6.] and, as though he had perceived from a distance where the matter would eventually lead, fortified the path to our discussion somewhat more securely. Thus, after convicting the Magdeburg Centuriators of falsehood, since they had rashly and shamelessly asserted that Platina had somewhere made Damasus a Roman [Note: [Col. 0538D] Platina explicitly makes our Damasus a Spaniard, beginning his life with these words: “Damasus, by birth a Spaniard, and son of Antonius.” Venetian edition, 1730, p. 66.], he proceeds to reclaim the most holy pontiff for our Spain.

For this purpose he produces the ancient Acts of Damasus from a manuscript in the archives of the basilica of Saint Peter, brought forward by Martius Milesius Sarazanius at the beginning of his edition of Damasus’s works [Note: [Col. 0539D] Rome, 1638, from p. 40 onward.]. In these Acts Damasus is first expressly called the compatriot of Saint Laurence, deacon and martyr, and then a Spaniard. Finally, when a question arose whether certain miracles should be attributed to Damasus or rather to the martyr Laurence, the writer of the Acts asserts that those whom one homeland brought forth and one Church likewise advanced should not be separated in the miracles.

Merenda had partly noticed this. Directing his discussion to the words last cited by us, he says [Note: [Col. 0539D] Ch. 1, no. 1.]:

“I do not deny that in the Life of Saint Damasus, published by Sarazanius from a manuscript of the Vatican basilica, Saint Damasus himself is said, like the holy martyr Laurence, to have been of Spanish stock, and that the writer therefore says that they were born of one homeland and advanced by one Church, etc.”

At first, I think, Merenda attempted to transfer the phrase *una genitos patria*—“born of one homeland”—from the place of birth to the place of origin, in whatever way he could. When he noticed that this did not proceed according to his wishes, he stumbled and, lacking confidence in himself, declared that the homeland of Laurence was a matter hitherto unexplored, and that it could strongly be doubted whether Laurence himself had been born at Rome. For in the ancient Sacramentary published by the distinguished Joseph Blanchinus, whom he considered to be its author, Laurence is plainly called *ROMANUS NASCENDO CIVIS*—“a Roman citizen by birth.”

Thus far Merenda has presented only doubts as certainties in response to the objections we raised against him, I think because, when he wrote this at the beginning of his work [Note: [Col. 0539D] Ch. 1, no. 1.], he had not yet read Blanchinus’s later annotations on the book of prayers of the ancient Gothic-Hispanic rite, of which we shall speak later; nor had he investigated this author’s opinion concerning the homeland of Saint Laurence [Note: [Col. 0539D] The book was published from an old manuscript of the very extensive chapter archive of the Church of Verona by the distinguished Joseph Blanchinus, priest of the Roman Oratory, in the prolegomena to the liturgical works of the venerable Cardinal Joseph Maria Thomasius, Rome, 1741; he also enlarged it with extensive annotations. In the second of these, namely annotation 106, p. 292, he discusses at length the homeland of Saint Laurence, unambiguously making him a Roman and declaring the case for the Romans decided.].

But once his work was already in progress, when he again began discussing the homeland of Laurence—not in its proper place, to be sure [Note: [Col. 0539D] §3, concerning the works of Damasus, which, in my judgment, have nothing in common with the homeland of the most holy deacon. See Merenda there, p. 146.]—he says that the most valiant deacon must be counted altogether among Roman citizens, and that all doubt on the matter was removed once Blanchinus had published the Veronese Sacramentary. Merenda’s answer therefore ultimately comes down to this: Laurence was no less Roman by homeland than Damasus, and in that sense the two are joined by the writer of the Acts and called compatriots of one another.

However much these statements may meanwhile seem capable of weakening the force of the authority cited by Merenda, they cannot at all be reconciled with what immediately precedes them in the Acts. I cannot sufficiently express my astonishment that, although Merenda brought against himself the final words of the Acts—in which Damasus and Laurence are said to have been born of one homeland—he should remain completely silent about what is read shortly before in those same Acts, where Damasus is expressly called a Spaniard. I shall relate the matter in order.

The writer of the Acts had described Damasus’s principal deeds and, on that occasion, introduced a mention of Laurence. He then called him the compatriot of Damasus [Note: [Col. 0540D] “For at a certain time, when blessed Damasus was laboring to restore ruined churches, he asked the emperor Valentinian the Younger to give him a certain garden in which he might build a church of his compatriot, blessed Laurence the martyr.” (*Acts of Damasus* from the manuscript of the archives of the canons of Saint Peter, in Sarazanius, p. 47.)].

Soon afterward, near the end of the Acts, perhaps by a more recent hand—or at least in a somewhat different style—the author appears to begin again, adding: “Now blessed Damasus was Spanish by nation” [Note: [Col. 0540D] In the same Acts, in Sarazanius, p. 60.].

Finally, and last of all, he says that Laurence and Damasus were born of one homeland [Note: [Col. 0540D] “Some attribute these miracles to blessed Laurence the martyr, others to blessed Damasus the confessor; nevertheless, we do not divide them in the miracles whom one homeland brought forth and one Church advanced.” (*In the same Acts*, in Sarazanius, p. 62.)].

These are plainly three different clauses, yet Merenda seems to have noticed only the third. At least, he directs against himself only that one, while entirely ignoring the two earlier ones, which certainly possess greater force. In the Acts, however, Damasus and Laurence are not merely said to have been born of one homeland; the former is expressly called a Spaniard. If Merenda has straightforwardly called both of them Romans, does he think that the words of the Acts have thereby been satisfied in some way? We shall leave this matter aside for now, since it must be reconsidered when we discuss the homeland of Laurence, and shall present to our readers the testimony of the ancients in support of our position.

First of all is the catalogue of the supreme pontiffs compiled under Felix IV, around the year 530 of Christ. Although its author was anonymous, we shall show below that he was in charge of the apostolic archives, or at least used them in composing the succession of the Roman pontiffs and the deeds performed by them, and borrowed from that treasury genuine and wholly uncorrupted records.

According to the edition of the Fathers Henschenius and Papebrochius, inserted in the prolegomena to volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum* for April, this catalogue says of Damasus:

“Damasus, Spanish by nation, son of Antonius, sat seventeen years, two months, and eleven days.”

Since, as we recently said, Terribilinus judged the authority of this manuscript not to be highly valued, we shall soon take care to support and reinforce it by many other arguments and by the testimony of ancient writers.

Second, we present the most ancient catalogue of pontiffs, which once belonged to the library of Count Palatine Rhenanus and was transferred from there to the principal library, the Vatican—as its former prefect Schelstratius, who had earlier published it, left on record [Col. 0541A] [Note: [Col. 0541D] Volume I of *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, in the appendix to the *Chronological Work*, no. 22, p. 611. Roman edition, 1692. — Senior Blanchinus, volume II of Anastasius, from p. 14 onward.]—and which bears the title: “Names of the Bishops of the City of Rome.”

In that manuscript, which, as I write this in the year of Our Lord 1755, is approximately nine hundred and thirty years old in its ordered sequence, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place, the following is said of Damasus:

“Damasus, Spanish by nation, son of Antonius, sat eighteen years, three months, and eleven days.”

Third, we shall set forth another very ancient manuscript entitled *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, from the Blessed Apostle Peter to Saint Paul I*. Joseph Blanchinus, nephew of Francis through his brother—whom we shall therefore call “the Younger” in the course of this work—was the first to publish it from the archives of the extensive chapter of the Church of Verona, and inserted it in the prolegomena to the fourth volume of Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0541D] From p. 1 onward.].

Concerning Damasus, it agrees completely with the preceding manuscripts:

“Damasus,” it says, “Spanish by nation, son of Antonius, sat eighteen years, three months, and eleven days.”

The authority of this manuscript is demonstrated by Blanchinus the Younger himself, certainly a worthy judge, who more than once calls it outstanding and did not hesitate to place it alongside the celebrated Veronese Sacramentary—that is, a manuscript a full thousand years old. Indeed, although in the prolegomena he ranks that Sacramentary second, as they say, the first place there is assigned to the manuscript of which we are speaking.

It remains for us to set forth the testimony of Anastasius the Librarian from the book of the pontifical deeds, which is otherwise entitled *The Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, or *The Pontifical Book*. Something must first be said about its author.

Marcus Velserus, an Augustan triumvir, was the first, after Peter Crabbe, to publish this work, and attributed the whole of it to Anastasius the monk, commonly called the Librarian, though he offered no suitable guarantor for the claim [Note: [Col. 0541D] Marcus Velserus, preface to the *Pontifical Book* published at Mainz in 1602, in Schelstratius, *Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. 7, no. 1.].

Panvinio first adopted Velserus’s opinion [Note: [Col. 0541D] In the notes to Platina, under Nicholas I, in Schelstratius, ibid.], followed soon afterward by Cardinal Bellarmine [Note: [Col. 0541D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Damasus, in Schelstratius, [Col. 0542D] ibid.] and others.
