Baronius, however [Note: [Col. 0542D] Under the year 867, no. 139.], after subjecting the book to the most exact scrutiny, discovered that Anastasius could in no way be called its author, but only the compiler of the pontifical deeds down to Adrian II. Finally, Schelstratius [Note: [Col. 0542D] *Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. 7, no. 2, and Holstenius there.], Holstenius, and others demonstrated with decisive arguments that only the Life of Nicholas I can be attributed to Anastasius as its certain author; the lives of the remaining pontiffs must not be regarded as the work of one particular writer or one particular age [Col. 0541D].

In the first part of this *Pontifical Book*, which scholars believe was composed at the beginning of the eighth century [Note: [Col. 0542D] See Senior Blanchinus, preface to volume I of Anastasius, nos. 6–7.], and which contains the lives of the Roman pontiffs down to Constantine, one finds—whether one examines the Vatican manuscripts or the surviving copies in the libraries of Christina, Queen of the Swedes; the monastery of Monte Cassino; Saint Mark’s in Venice; the Laurentian Library; and the other celebrated libraries throughout Italy—a completely consistent account of Damasus, expressed in precisely these words:

“Damasus, Spanish by nation, son of Antonius.”

I could certainly produce other testimonies of writers on the same subject, but I think we should spare the reader’s time and detain him instead with a more agreeable novelty. There is, however, one matter that occurred to me while reading the Life of Damasus, formerly written by a certain priest named Benedict and prefixed by Sarazanius to his work from an ancient manuscript of Abbot Constantine Cajetanus; I cannot pass over it in silence.

That pious writer, turning to Damasus near the end of his Life, implores the aid of the holy pontiff first for all the faithful people, and especially for those who celebrate his nativity devoutly and from the heart. These are his words:

“Holy Damasus, therefore, come to the aid of and have mercy on all the people, if anyone devoutly, earnestly, and with the whole affection of his heart celebrates your nativity.”

He then asks for the protection of Damasus over the Roman people in these terms:

“Holy Damasus, be their intercessor, helper, and defender—the Roman people, among whom you deserved to possess the honor of the pontificate.”

Let the prudent reader judge, I ask, whether the writer of Damasus’s Life would have remained silent about his homeland if it had truly been Rome, when, in recalling the supreme dignity he had obtained there, he prays to Damasus with such confidence that he not abandon those among whom he had deserved to possess the honor of the pontificate.

Or why, if Damasus had been born at Rome, did he not invoke their common homeland more insistently and ask that his aid be rendered to the Romans—not as a free gift, but as though it were owed by right—to his fellow citizens? Finally, why did that writer not insert the homeland of Damasus into his prayer at the appropriate and useful point, addressing the holy pontiff in these words: “Holy Damasus, be the defender of the Roman people, among whom you were both born and deserved to possess the honor of the pontificate”?

I have no information immediately available concerning the antiquity of this manuscript, nor did Sarazanius indicate it to us. But the fact that the writer of the Acts, although he stated his own name and dignity or rank, did not likewise disclose his nation or family, is for me a not inconsiderable conjectural indication of antiquity, wonderfully confirmed by the plain and unadorned style of his speech.

If it is permissible to conjecture about such matters, I suspect that the passage, “Come to the aid of and have mercy … if anyone devoutly and earnestly celebrates your nativity,” was borrowed from Prudentius, who had long before composed something similar concerning Vincent, deacon and martyr [Note: [Col. 0543D] In the hymn of Saint Vincent the Martyr, stanza 115. Similar expressions may also be found among the Latins. Terence, *Hecyra*, prologue:

“If I have never greedily set a price upon my art …

Allow me to obtain my request.”

Likewise in the prologue to the *Heautontimorumenos*, and elsewhere. Indeed, also among the Greeks, Homer, *Iliad* I, line 39:

“ … if ever I roofed a graceful temple for you,

or if ever I burned rich thigh-bones for you …

May the Danaans pay the price.”

And frequently elsewhere.]

Here are his words:

“Have mercy on our prayers,

that Christ, appeased, may incline

his gracious ear,

and not reckon all our sins against us.

If with mouth and heart

we duly venerate the solemn day,

if amid the joy of your footsteps

we lie prostrate.”

## CHAPTER II. The authority of the Felician catalogue of pontiffs and of Anastasius, accepted not only by Catholics but also by the heterodox themselves.

Here we are dealing with Terribilinus, who, speaking of the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs compiled under Felix IV—the one we said is commonly called the Second and shall henceforth designate by that name—and of the book of pontifical deeds compiled by Anastasius, does not hesitate to assert that the authority of both writers should not be highly esteemed.

I would not dare confidently to assert whether Merenda himself agrees with Terribilinus on this point. Yet he seems to incline toward Terribilinus’s opinion because he has neglected the authority both of Anastasius and of the Second Catalogue, each of which stands directly against his own position, as though he had nothing to fear from that quarter.

First, then, it will be worthwhile to indicate of what parts the book of Anastasius’s *Pontifical Book* consists, and who its authors are; above all, from what sources they drew the lives of the pontiffs and appended the succession of events performed by them.

For the whole work of Anastasius may, for the sake of fuller understanding, be divided chiefly into three sections. The first presents the succession of the Roman pontiffs from Saint [Col. 0543C] Peter to Liberius. As far as their names, homelands, and years of pontificate are concerned, it is taken wholly from an ancient and exceedingly old catalogue of the Roman prelates.

This catalogue is called by some the Bucherian Catalogue, because Aegidius Bucherius was the first to publish it [Note: [Col. 0544D] In the commentary on Victor’s *Paschal Canon*, Antwerp, 1634, p. 269.]; by others, the Catalogue under Liberius; or simply the First Catalogue.

Its author has not yet been sufficiently determined. Some attribute it to Damasus, remarkable as he was [Note: [Col. 0544D] Panvinio, commentary on book II of Sarazanius’s *Fasti*, in the note to Damasus’s epigram IX, in Merenda, p. 249.]; others think that Pope Anterus also labored to compile it [Note: [Col. 0544D] Henschenius, volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum* for April, in the prolegomena preceding the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs.]. From what Schelstratius presents [Note: [Col. 0544D] *Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. 2, no. 10.], however, I consider it more probable that its author was anonymous and lived under Liberius—that is, when the fourth century from the birth of Christ was first beginning to decline.

[Col. 0543D] The second section of Anastasius’s *Pontifical Book* presents the succession of Roman prelates from Liberius to Felix IV. This succession was transcribed almost word for word from another catalogue of pontiffs. Because it was first compiled under Felix IV, namely toward the end of the first thirty-year period of the sixth century, it is called the Felician Catalogue; because it is a century and a half more recent than the earlier one, it is commonly called the second catalogue. Like the earlier catalogue, it was compiled by an anonymous writer.

Finally, the last section of Anastasius’s book presents the deeds and achievements of the more recent pontiffs, from Felix IV to Nicholas I. We have long maintained, following Holstenius, Scheelstratius, and Senior Blanchinus, that only the life of Nicholas is genuinely Anastasius’s own work. The lives of the pontiffs who occupied the see between Felix and Nicholas for three centuries and more plainly cannot be the work of one writer or one period; the mere variety of their styles, already observed by Holstenius [Note: In Scheelstratius, *Dissertation on the Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 7, no. 7], would sufficiently demonstrate this, even if all other evidence were lacking. Accordingly, ecclesiastical historians rightly judge that the individual lives—at most two or three at a time—were written by different authors and appended to the *Pontifical Book* at different periods, in chronological sequence.

We therefore do not intend to defend the reliability and authority either of that earlier, Liberian section or of this later, third part of Anastasius’s work; in neither case, as the saying goes, is our own cause at stake. But since Damasus is repeatedly and explicitly called a Spaniard in both the second and the Felician Catalogue, and since we have previously brought forward their authority and words in support of our position, we therefore undertake to defend the reliability of both writers against Terribilinus and whoever else may be their opponents.

Nor need we labor greatly over this matter, since Holstenius, Scheelstratius, and Senior Blanchinus—men certainly of the highest distinction—have adorned both of these fields. We shall therefore set out their testimonies in order. Holstenius first devoted himself to the task of collating the ancient manuscripts of the *Pontifical Book* in order to recover the author’s true and genuine text, and he accomplished this to a considerable extent. Soon afterward Scheelstratius, having subjected the second catalogue of pontiffs and Anastasius’s book to the most exact scrutiny, and having diligently traced the streams back to their sources, gave the following judgment concerning the Felician Catalogue and its author:

“Regarding the author’s name,” says Scheelstratius [Note: *Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 5, no. 12], “I have no definite information, since the catalogue was written in the sixth century, when no one among the ancients is remembered to have collected the deeds of the Roman pontiffs. Yet, so far as can be inferred from the deeds themselves, the author flourished at Rome and perhaps presided over the apostolic archive. That the author wrote at Rome is indicated by his extensive knowledge of the city and of the Roman territory. He knew all the cemeteries, even those situated at the greatest distance from the city; all the tombs of the martyrs, even those located in crypts and caverns; all the churches and districts of the city; all the relics and titular churches; all the roads and the distances between them; and, finally, everything else with complete familiarity.

“That he may have been prefect of the apostolic archive seems to follow from what he says about Leo the Great: ‘He composed many letters setting forth the true Catholic faith, which are preserved today in the archive of the Roman Church’; and from the Acts of Hormisdas, whose little book is kept in that same archive. For how could the author have cited the Roman archive had he not seen it and perhaps presided over it? Indeed, what he repeatedly asserts concerning the decrees of the individual pontiffs, their deeds, and the ordinations of bishops, priests, and deacons clearly indicates that he drew everything from the archive’s registers.”

[Col. 0545B] Nor was Senior Blanchinus satisfied with this. After undertaking a truly arduous investigation, he went further [Note: Preface to volume I of Anastasius, no. 17]: what records of the Roman pontiffs were still preserved in the city when the Felician Catalogue of which we are speaking was first written; what reliefs depicting their deeds, and what commentaries by ancient writers on the same subject, remained, from which the succession of pontifical lives could be carried without interruption along the thread of history from Peter to Felix IV; what deeds of the most ancient pontiffs had then been engraved in the ancient churches and cemeteries on stone tablets, which they called *platonias* because of their shape [Note: That is, because of their breadth; for πλατύς means “broad.” In Spanish, we would call them *valdosas* (“tiles”). Cassiodorus also calls columns *platonias* (*Letters* III.9). See Henri Estienne under that word]; what epitaphs existed on their tombs, in which, as is customary, their native places, principal deeds, decrees, and ecclesiastical ordinances had most probably been recorded [Col. 0545C]; and, finally, what monuments of the ecclesiastical history of earlier centuries still survived—original documents, moreover, and so publicly displayed that they would have been encountered everywhere by even a minimally attentive writer.

Anyone who wishes to consider with slightly greater attention the traces of ecclesiastical antiquity that still remain to us after the passage of twelve centuries will easily infer how abundant the harvest of such materials must have been in those ancient times. We must likewise recognize, by an argument drawn from both sacred and profane matters, that the ancient pontiffs, in order to preserve and enhance the dignity of the supreme priesthood, were no less concerned to record in writing or on tablets the sacred rites of the Christians, the ordinances of the Church, its acts and functions proper to the supreme office, and other monuments of this kind in the records of the Roman prelates, than the pagan priests of that age were concerned to preserve the worship of their deities and their own dignity against the injuries of time.

The extraordinary diligence of those priests in this respect is sufficiently demonstrated by the innumerable epigrams still surviving in Gruter, Reinesius, Muratori, and other collectors of ancient inscriptions. These inscriptions vividly or symbolically preserve the offices of the *flamen Dialis*, the Arval Brothers, and the priests of Isis, Serapis, Mithras, and other ancient superstitions, together with the worship and principal rites of their gods. Thus, whoever the writer of the second catalogue may have been, he could easily have joined together an uninterrupted succession of pontifical deeds from the archetypal monuments that survived into his own age; indeed, unless he deliberately turned his eyes away from the tablets displayed everywhere in Rome, he could not have deviated from the truth even by a finger’s breadth. This concludes what may be said generally about the authority of the second catalogue of pontiffs.

As for Anastasius, setting aside what William the Librarian, Trithemius, Platina, Baronius, and other authors wrote in his praise—on which subject Senior Blanchinus should be consulted [Note: *Prolegomena* to volume I of Anastasius the Librarian, after the preface]—we shall likewise present Scheelstratius as our authority [Note: *Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 9, from no. 1]. He first demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently that the author of the *Pontifical Book* attributed to Anastasius, in writing the lives and deeds of the Roman prelates from the apostle Peter to Zacharias—including our Damasus—had at hand the second catalogue of pontiffs, whose authority we have just discussed, and used it throughout in constructing their succession. Consequently, the same credibility must necessarily be accorded Anastasius in this respect as to the Felician Catalogue of pontiffs.

After this same writer had delivered his judgment concerning the later part of the *Pontifical Book*, containing the lives from Zacharias to Nicholas I, and had highly commended its reliability, since it was drawn from ancient ecclesiastical monuments and apostolic archives by contemporary writers, he proceeds to express his opinion about the earlier section of the same *Pontifical Book* [Col. 0546C], in which our Damasus appears. He says:

“Although the earlier part of the *Pontifical Book* was not written by contemporary authors, it was nevertheless COMPOSED IN LIKE MANNER FROM THE ANCIENT MONUMENTS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH. It may therefore rightly be cited for distinguishing the rites of the Roman Church and for learning its discipline and doctrines, since knowledge of all these matters may be extracted from it. If we inquire about the rites of sacrifice that began from the earliest times; about the ordinations of bishops and the lower clergy, and their offices; about the relics of the martyrs, the invocation of the saints, the psalms and prayers customarily recited by the Church; about the various methods of electing the pontiff; or about six hundred other aspects of ecclesiastical discipline and doctrine, we shall certainly find in this *Pontifical Book* material sufficient to satisfy everyone. From it we may easily infer in what ways the government of the Church was constituted during the span of the first eight centuries. Indeed,” he concludes, “I scarcely know whether any other work can be found in the whole of antiquity from which so many things can be learned as from the *Pontifical Book*.”

That Senior Blanchinus also held the *Pontifical Book* in no lesser esteem is shown by his most illuminating testimony in the preface to volume I of Anastasius [Note: Specifically from no. 31]. We also know that he observed that the surviving records in Rome and its suburbs of pontifical ordinations, basilica dedications, and other ecclesiastical functions of this kind correspond remarkably with Anastasius’s account, since he carefully compared them with him. This confirms Anastasius’s unimpaired reliability even in other matters for which corroborating evidence is unavailable. He also knew that many more remains of ecclesiastical antiquity survived in the city during this author’s lifetime than survive today. Thus, even if all else were lacking, the historical succession of the Church’s earlier centuries could to some extent have been continued, or at least greatly supplemented and assisted, from those materials alone; and the author of the *Pontifical Book* certainly made use of such monuments.

I would not wish to wrong the distinguished Giovanni Ciampini, who shortly before Scheelstratius had expressly written an examination of the *Pontifical Book*, printed at Rome in 1688 [Note: Senior Blanchinus—in the preface to volume I of Anastasius—implies that Scheelstratius published his work *Ecclesiastical Antiquities* four years after Giovanni Ciampini, namely in 1692. This is true if he is referring to the Roman edition of that work, enlarged by many dissertations and appendices; nevertheless, the same work, though much more abridged, had previously been printed at Antwerp in 1678, in what is called quarto format], by silently passing over his judgment on this matter. Ciampini had examined the collations of ancient manuscripts made by Holstenius and, after again subjecting every consideration to scrutiny, expressed the following assessment of the *Pontifical Book* [Note: *Examination of the Pontifical Book*, section 11, p. 107]:

“Nevertheless, although we believe that the codex of the Roman pontiffs was written by several authors, we nevertheless judge that it deserves the greatest and highest confidence, as though it had been excerpted from the autograph and genuine writings—especially because, on account of its antiquity, it is held in exceptional veneration and contains a continuous history which the Church has received through the agreement of so many centuries, since it was committed to writing by authors who were either contemporaries of the pontiffs whose deeds they recorded or lived shortly afterward.”

This was Ciampini’s judgment.

[Col. 0547C] Nor were there lacking among the heterodox themselves more clear-sighted men who praised the *Pontifical Book* with no ordinary commendation, as we shall state in its proper place. For the present, however, we take no account of Pearson [Note: Dissertation I on the succession of the Roman pontiffs, chapter 12, no. 8, in Scheelstratius, *Dissertation on the Catalogues*, chapter 8, no. 4], Molinaeus [Note: In Ciampini, *Examination of the Pontifical Book*, immediately afterward], Hospinian [Note: *On the Origin of Temples*, book II, chapter 14, §7, in Ciampini, immediately afterward], Dodwell [Note: *Dissertation on the Small Number of Martyrs*, in Ruinart, preface to the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 67], and any other men of this sort, whose livers, swollen with difficult bile against ecclesiastical rites, spew the venom of their bitterness upon Anastasius and the author of the *Pontifical Book*. They call this writer suspect, wholly ignorant of the affairs and condition of the primitive Church, and one who patched his book together from ancient but apocryphal writings; and they assail both men with savage abuse.

Scheelstratius refutes all of these men except Ciampini [Note: Section 12, p. 108], using the very arguments we have just reported. Against Pearson, however, who had called the author of the *Pontifical Book* an uncertain sixth-century writer, he adds a witty concluding observation [Note: *Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 9, no. 9, at the end]. Since Pearson had made a human error in assigning the date of this book’s author—for the author lived not in the sixth century, as Pearson claimed, but at the end of the seventh and perhaps the beginning of the eighth—Scheelstratius rightly reproves him for calling the author of the *Pontifical Book* wholly ignorant of the condition of the primitive Church, when Pearson himself was evidently ignorant of the period in which the author of the *Pontifical Book* flourished.

“Since, then,” Scheelstratius continues, “Pearson admits that the author of the *Pontifical Book* wrote as early as the SEVENTH century” [a typographical error for “sixth”], “he ought also to have acknowledged that this author was better informed about the Roman Church, its discipline, rites, and faith than those born in more recent times.”

I know that even among Catholic writers there have been some who wished to detract substantially from the authority of the *Pontifical Book* and Anastasius. Ciampini mentions two [Note: *Examination of the Pontifical Book*, section 12, p. 108], whom I nevertheless pass over, knowingly and willingly, out of respect [Col. 0548B]. One of them says that Anastasius distorted the lives of the pontiffs and filled them with errors; the other asserts that the same author employed the foulest flattery toward Pope Nicholas I. But anyone who wishes to consider without partisan bias what Ciampini there adduces in Anastasius’s defense will easily infer that both men judged Anastasius with an unjustly hostile spirit.

I myself will not deny that many things are found in Anastasius which either he, as human beings do, failed to notice sufficiently at the outset, or which antiquarians distorted through the frequency of copying. Nevertheless, I do not think these matters should be valued as highly as the authors mentioned above contend. Nor, if Anastasius allowed himself somewhat more freedom in praising Nicholas I—whom he was bound to honor not only by the common duty owed to supreme dignity but also by the particular right and obligation of clientage—should he therefore be judged to have imposed disgraceful flattery upon him. Such excess is customary among writers, especially in dedicatory letters. But we shall discuss these matters elsewhere.

Meanwhile, to return from this digression to the road, I shall never be persuaded to believe that Terribilinus, even if Merenda supported his side, agreed either with those earlier heterodox writers whom we have just refuted or with these later Catholic writers. I would nevertheless wish ecclesiastical men in particular to be more cautious, since it would have been safest for them to avoid not only the rocks but also the danger of being dashed against them.

For this is not, as the saying goes, a dispute about goat’s wool; nor are we asking how many winters the boy Laertes wandered, or about other ornaments of poetic fables. Nearly the whole of pontifical history is at issue, and anyone who wishes to detract from the authority of the second catalogue and Anastasius will decide the matter at the same time. Both books concern the deeds of the Roman pontiffs and their acts, ordinations, and decrees; the authority of the supreme priesthood; sacred relics and prayers; the invocation of the saints; and the antiquity and origin of sacred rites, especially liturgical rites—both of which innovators strive so vigorously to undermine—as well as the entire body of ecclesiastical affairs. Thus one may rightly say that nearly the whole law of the Church’s discipline depends upon these two works, or at least that the principal hinge of the history of the Roman prelates of earlier times turns upon them.

Nor should it be thought merely the work of human planning or industry that Christ preserved both of these monuments of ecclesiastical antiquity, while almost all other things suffered shipwreck, so that they might be brought forth from darkness especially in these stormy times for the benefit of His Bride. Nor is it insignificant that He gave certain heretics—whose judgment was certainly sound in this matter—the disposition to regard the authority of the *Pontifical Book* as firm and valid.

David Blondel, writing against Francisco Turrianus [Note: In Scheelstratius, *Dissertation on the Ancient Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 9, no. 9], calls the author of the *Pontifical Book* “perhaps not a bad writer.” The emphasis of this statement is explained by Blondel’s following words [Note: Ibid., in the same author]:

“For in that book the ancient records of the Roman Church are contained, and nothing is more incorrupt than that written work.”

Salmasius, likewise a heterodox writer, is not far removed from this judgment. Scheelstratius reports [Note: Ibid., in the same author] that Salmasius somewhere says that the author of the *Pontifical Book* wrote as though by the rays of the sun.

These, then, are the general observations to be made about the second catalogue and Anastasius’s *Pontifical Book*.

# CHAPTER III

## The text of the Felician Catalogue of Pontiffs and of Anastasius, in which both call Damasus a Spaniard, is wholly uncorrupted

[Col. 0549C]

Thus far we have demonstrated that the authority of the second catalogue of pontiffs and of Anastasius should and does generally stand. But since neither of these writers is thereby entirely free from every blemish—for that is the exclusive privilege and particular prerogative of divine Scripture—we have therefore decided to examine individually the reliability and integrity of both manuscripts. Our concern is specifically the passage in which both writers most explicitly call Damasus a Spaniard, for that is the center and goal of our entire dispute.

Horace, that great critic and appraiser of writers, used to say that it was permissible [Note: In the *Art of Poetry*, line 360], especially in a long work, for sleep occasionally to creep upon one. And although we must admit that this happened to the writer of the second catalogue and also to Anastasius, and not very rarely, I do not think anyone will therefore judge that these two writers—whose industry is otherwise so useful—should be denied at least the ordinary indulgence granted in other desperate cases.

But if their learning could nevertheless be subjected today to the most exact sifting, and if someone knew how to distinguish its solid grains from the unfortunate darnel and perhaps from the tares sown over it—I mean glosses, the errors of antiquarians, sigla, abbreviations of letters, numerical signs, and other matters of that kind—then the reliability of the second catalogue of pontiffs and of Anastasius would perhaps be regarded as more consistent and even, and one would not see anything in either writer that might disgust delicate stomachs afflicted with feminine languor.

Critics principally identify the following as the sources from which the most frequent defects of manuscripts, especially historical manuscripts, have reached us: the depravity of the heterodox, who often corrupted and defiled ancient writings in order to diminish Catholic doctrine by slander; at times, the ambition of Catholics themselves, whom the evil desire to serve private opinions or interests more than was proper compelled to falsify texts; also, the excessive and wholly undiscriminating simplicity of the credulous. These men, thinking that the faith of peoples could be strengthened by a false or badly attached scrap of history, often obscured the native brilliance of historical truth with old-womanish fables.

There are also marginal glosses, which the negligence or incompetence of antiquarians admitted into the text; scribal abbreviations insufficiently understood by those same antiquarians; variation in readings; and, finally, the frequent use of sigla and numerical signs, especially in chronological matters. When even the smallest of these is placed in the wrong position, it introduces irreconcilable errors. I think the matter will become clearer through examples.

The perversity of the Luciferians and other detractors of Liberius is commonly believed to have corrupted the genuine acts of this pontiff, and to have interpolated certain passages in order to defame his reputation by slander. Clear traces of this crime, originating in those earliest times, still survive for us today in Anastasius [Col. 0550C]. For the life of Liberius, as it circulates in the commonly published manuscripts of Anastasius, displays a certain inconsistency and an inexplicable variety of style, so that it can immediately be recognized as not being the work of one author.

Nor was our Damasus more fortunate in this respect. Learned men strongly suspect that the hands of Ursicinus—or, if you prefer, Ursinus—his rival and the followers of that rival did great harm to the genuine history and acts of Damasus, as we shall explain in its proper place. This is what may be said concerning the first cause originating with heretics.

The dispute of the Alexandrian and Antiochene Churches with the Roman Church over primacy—since each of those Churches claimed to be apostolic no less than Rome—is commonly believed to have provided the occasion for attaching to the life of this pontiff certain material from an apocryphal letter in the name of Pope Clement, addressed to James, the brother of the Lord. In particular, it is said to have supplied the account of Clement’s appointment to the dignity of the apostolic office by the blessed apostle Peter, in precisely the same manner in which Peter himself had received from Christ the Lord the charge of governing the Church—a story which we also read in Anastasius.

Those who asserted the special dignity of the Roman Church above the other Churches thought that this special appointment of Clement by the blessed Peter would serve as evidence of the special excellence of the Roman see above all others and of its primacy over the universal Church—as though, even at that time, there had been no other indisputable monuments by which the primary dignity of the Roman see could likewise be upheld and demonstrated. Here is another cause of the corruption of manuscripts, and one that originated with Catholics.

But what shall we say about Anastasius’s passage in the life of Pope Pius I, where a certain Hermes is said to have composed a book during his pontificate, “in which is contained the command that the angel of the Lord gave him when he came to him in the dress of a shepherd, ordering him that holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday” [Note: See Anastasius, under Pius, volume I, p. 14; these words are transcribed there literally]?

Senior Blanchinus suspects that this was rashly borrowed by the compiler of the catalogue from the apocryphal book of Clement’s *Constitutions* to fill a gap in the very ancient Liberian catalogue of pontiffs, or from some acts of Saint Pudentiana, the virgin [Note: Volume II of Anastasius, under Pius I, p. 117; also p. 22]. There may be some who believe that the entire sentence was added during the pontificate of this pope because of the dispute between the Asians and the Roman bishops over Easter, which soon afterward broke out again under Pope Victor. They may think it was inserted to demonstrate that the solemn observance of Easter on Sunday derived not only from the tradition of the apostles but also from divine institution.

However the matter may stand, it is certain that the story of the angel appearing in the dress of a shepherd is another of the scraps we have just mentioned, rashly sewn into the history by some simpler person under the guise of piety. It is therefore a third, and by no means uncommon, cause of the corruption of manuscripts.

A fourth example is supplied by a sentence in Anastasius’s life of Damasus:

“Damasus was alive during the time of Julian” [Note: Anastasius, under Damasus].

Although, as Blanchinus likewise reports [Note: Volume III of Anastasius, under Damasus, p. 33], some suspect that this sentence descended from the corrupted acts of Liberius, I am more inclined to believe that it was first written in the margin of the manuscript by an unskilled glossator concerning chronological matters and then, as usually happens, entered the text after being introduced by an antiquarian. What almost compels me to believe this is the fact that, if you tear those words out of the text by the roots, not only does the meaning remain intact, but the sequence of the narrative no longer appears interrupted, as it formerly did.

Whatever the truth may be, it is evident that the sentence contains an utterly false statement. Julian had already died while Liberius was alive, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July in the year 363—three full years before Damasus’s pontificate. Blanchinus himself clearly demonstrated that Damasus’s pontificate began only on the Kalends of October in the year 366, during the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus [Note: In the second prologue to volume II of Anastasius, p. 68, column 1].

As for chronology—that is, the specification of the period during which each pontiff held the see—the manuscripts and earlier catalogues differ astonishingly both among themselves and from Anastasius. This is due in large part to arithmetical signs being placed backward or otherwise out of position, or to one of them being inappropriately added or omitted. In this matter, such small details, if neglected, create major difficulties in working out the chronology.

We need not go far for an example. Anastasius assigns Damasus eighteen years, two months, and ten days of pontificate; the second catalogue, however, says that he held the see for only seventeen years, though it gives him three months. The discrepancy is thought to have arisen from the negligence of an antiquarian who, after removing the numerical sign I from the column of years, restored it immediately afterward while counting the months of Damasus’s pontificate, most improperly treating it as though it belonged to the months rather than to the years.

The errors arising from sigla and abbreviations of letters are, I believe, so abundant that there is no need to confirm them with examples. I also have no doubt that Anastasius, and perhaps the writer of the second catalogue, omitted certain things in each of these categories. Yet these are faults which I am willing to forgive. For when many things in a work shine, those who possess a horse, a father, and property do not immediately take offense at a few stains either inflicted by injustice or insufficiently guarded against by human nature. On the contrary, they judge that an author should be treated more gently and that his industry should be supported with the greatest fairness whenever it happens to labor.

Indeed, I believe that Anastasius and the writer of the second catalogue deserve not merely indulgence in this respect but, further, that their reliability should be strongly commended precisely on account of the blemishes visible in both works. For since we have already said that Anastasius was a compiler, not the author, of the *Pontifical Book*—and that the writer of the second catalogue must, in my judgment, likewise be regarded in that capacity and under that name—the one preferred to leave whatever he had found in the Liberian catalogue, however doubtful or insufficiently known to him, as it stood. The other preferred to retain what he had long before seen written by the authors of the earlier Liberian and Felician catalogues and in the lives of the more recent pontiffs, whatever their reliability might be, rather than by changing or adding anything to make the entire succession of pontifical deeds in some sense his own and thereby assume responsibility for defending its truth.

Now, to see what relevance all this has, we must first ask Terribilinus whether it was in the interest of Ursicinus and his followers that Damasus should have been a Spaniard rather than a Roman or someone born elsewhere, so that they might falsely present him as a Spaniard and disgracefully corrupt or interpolate the second catalogue of pontiffs and Anastasius when they spoke of Damasus’s true birthplace; or whether, if Ursicinus had shown Damasus to be a Spaniard, he would have brought against him some disgraceful name or harsher charge, so as to win favor for himself and kindle hatred against Damasus among the Roman clergy and people.

At that time, neither the hope nor the fear connected with common birthplace, the patronage of powerful men, or party interests had yet advanced so far that anything in this respect would have prevented Damasus from being judged worthy of so great an office and hailed as Roman pontiff by common suffrage.

Nor do we read that at that time, or anywhere else, the Churches of Spain brought a legal dispute against the preeminence or prerogative of the Roman see, to which it could have made any difference, in deciding the matter on behalf of the Spaniards, whether Damasus had been born among them or elsewhere. Thus there is no basis for suspicion on this ground that the ancient manuscripts of the second catalogue and Anastasius were corrupted.

Moreover, it is plainly evident that nothing slipped from the margin into the text of these writers, and that no little narrative of doubtful reliability was introduced or rashly attached at this point. The entire matter is settled in precisely three words: “Damasus, a Spaniard by nationality.” Every avenue has thereby been closed so completely that no one can fail to see that not even a single letter could be superfluous or missing for the completion of our argument.

Furthermore, this is not a matter of numerical signs or chronology; nor does it concern sigla or abbreviations of letters, so that one might readily infer from the frequency of errors in such matters that the writer of the second catalogue and Anastasius made an error when speaking of Damasus’s birthplace, or that antiquarians did so while copying their ancient manuscripts.

Finally—and this should be regarded almost as miraculous—despite the immense number of copies of the second catalogue and Anastasius preserved in libraries throughout Italy, France, Germany, and Belgium, copies that Holstenius [Note: In Blanchinus, preface to volume I of Anastasius] and, after him, Senior Blanchinus [Note: Volume II of Anastasius, in the prolegomena, from p. 85 onward] collated with astonishing labor, especially since in other passages of these writers there is an almost infinite variety of readings, we have so far found not even one copy which, when speaking of Damasus’s birthplace, does not agree remarkably with all the others.

[Col. 0553C] Since this is so, I cannot sufficiently wonder why Terribilinus attempts with such effort to cast doubt upon the reliability of the second catalogue and Anastasius. At the very least, I should like to know by what trick he thinks this Danaë, surrounded on every side by so many guards, could have been deceived and corrupted, so that he asserts that Damasus’s birthplace cannot safely be entrusted to or believed on the authority and testimony of either of these writers.

But let us grant Terribilinus—without evidence—that there was some room for suspicion against Anastasius and the writer of the second catalogue. Would that make the catalogue of Veronese pontiffs published by Junior Blanchinus [Note: In the prolegomena to volume IV of Anastasius, p. 1], or the Palatine-Vatican manuscript, which, as we shall see, is older than Anastasius, both of which we have cited in our support, also deficient in reliability and authority? Or, with two further and suitable witnesses supporting Damasus’s Spanish origin, should that origin still be regarded as insufficiently established?

Conversely, when the glory of the Spaniards is at issue, many examples readily occur to us in which we know that foreign nations have gratuitously enhanced it, either by falsely proclaiming deeds magnificently performed by Spaniards or by attributing to them distinguished men renowned for piety, learning, or military excellence. If Terribilinus had noticed this single point, it ought to have made him more cautious, so that he would not sharpen his pen against Anastasius and the writer of the second catalogue.

At the very least, Merenda’s friendly observation against Tillemont should have secured this caution from him. Merenda had discussed a certain Arsenius whom Damasus sent as tutor to the boy Arcadius, who had already been proclaimed Augustus. Baronius, who had first read this in Metaphrastes, calls Arsenius a deacon of the Roman Church. Tillemont, in accordance with his character, objected and refused to acknowledge Arsenius as a deacon unless another and suitable witness to Metaphrastes were produced.

Merenda, however, intervening, addressed Tillemont in these words:

“But for what benefit could that writer [Metaphrastes] have fabricated this dignity for Arsenius? Why would he have written this, unless he relied upon some older and entirely undisputed testimony?”

I would certainly wrong the writer of the second catalogue and Anastasius if I were to compare either of them with Metaphrastes. The proverbial “Greek faith” is well known.

In the meantime, Terribilinus may consider how he will escape Merenda, who shares his opinion, if Merenda continues to ask him: “For what benefit would the author of the second catalogue and Anastasius have invented Damasus’s birthplace at their own discretion?”

# CHAPTER IV

## The opponents’ foundations are weak. The journey of Damasus’s Roman parents from Spain is straightforward and entirely plausible

What Terribilinus brings forward against us, so far as I can see, is of little importance. I therefore think it should be touched upon very lightly and almost passed over altogether. The whole of his argument ultimately comes down to this: that no ancient writer who dealt with Damasus called him a Spaniard before the second catalogue of pontiffs under Felix IV or Anastasius; that the authority of these two writers should not be highly valued; that recent Spaniards rely upon no solid foundation when they claim Damasus as their countryman; that they also disagree about the place of his birth and vigorously dispute among themselves; and therefore that Damasus was not a Spaniard.

First of all, however, the catalogue of pontiffs from the Palatine-Vatican Codex, which we cited in our favor in second place under the heading “Names of the Bishops of the City of Rome,” most clearly demonstrates that the catalogue is in part false; for its author, who likewise calls Damasus a Spaniard, lived a full forty years before Anastasius. Let us calculate the matter carefully. When Scheelstratius first published the catalogue in question [Col. 0554D], namely in the year 1691—for he could not have done so much later, since he is said to have died at the beginning of the following year [Note: [Col. 0553D] In the manuscript catalogue of the Casanatense Library, where Scheelstratius’s works are listed, the following note appears beside the author’s name: “He died on 6 April 1692.”]—that Codex, as he himself attests [Note: [Col. 0554D] *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, vol. I, in the appendix to the chronological work, no. 22, p. 611.], was 865 years old. It follows that in the year of Christ 1755, the year in which we are now writing, the Codex would be 929 years old. Now, if we subtract this total from the current year, 1755, there remain 826 years; that many years, therefore, had elapsed from the Nativity of Christ when the catalogue [Col. 0555A] in question was first written. But Anastasius compiled his *Pontifical Book* after Nicholas I had died—the life and deeds of whom, as we said earlier, he subsequently wrote—that is, after the year 867. Consequently, the author of the catalogue must necessarily have been a full forty years older than Anastasius.

As for the second catalogue of pontiffs, I shall agree with Terribilinus on this one point: no author survives who, before that catalogue, called Damasus a Spaniard—or at least I have hitherto been unaware of any such author. Yet if we recall what has been said elsewhere about the surviving Roman records from the beginning of the sixth century, at which time that catalogue is known to have been written, and about the writings and deeds of the pontiffs and the other ecclesiastical monuments existing everywhere at that time, I consider it no less true that the author of the second catalogue spoke about Damasus’s homeland only on the basis of some document—indeed, an archetypal document that guided him, although it is not easy now to point to that document with one’s finger. At the very least, surely, would this not be fairer and more reasonable than to suppose that the author of the second catalogue fabricated Damasus’s homeland out of his own brain, just as Jupiter fabricated Minerva?

Indeed, even if everything else were lacking, should not the antiquity of the second catalogue alone be considered sufficient to establish its own credibility? After the passage of twelve centuries, does it really need an outside guarantor to defend its authority? Or why should we not judge the testimony of the second catalogue concerning Damasus’s homeland to have come from a contemporary author? Certainly its writer, even if he himself had not known Damasus while he was alive, could very easily have known many who had associated with him [Col. 0555C]—people who, while the holy pontiff was still alive, had been able frequently to see him, speak with him, and honor him publicly and privately—and could have learned from them, as commonly happens in conversation, what concerned Damasus’s homeland and deeds.

Here again we must calculate. From the death of Damasus, which occurred in the year of Christ 384, to the pontificate of Felix IV, at which time the second catalogue was written, no more than 142 years elapsed; but if the death of that pontiff—which chronologists place in October of the year 530 of salvation—is to be taken as the relevant point, only 146 years intervened. This interval could easily be filled by two generations, even without supposing exceptionally long-lived men: to the first we may assign the time up to puberty, during which he could have seen Damasus frequently, received from others what was commonly said about him, and retained it in the faithful memory characteristic of boys; while the second, not yet eighty years old, could have composed the catalogue in question [Col. 0555D].

[Note: [Col. 0555D] Plato, Simonides, Stesichorus, and many others [in Turlius, *On Old Age*] produced excellent works when they were older than eighty, nor did old age make them fall silent in their studies. But why should we resort to ancient pagan examples, when our own most holy lord, Pope Benedict XIV, is today present in the sight of all? Indeed, he himself is a light set above the Church’s candlestick, shining upon all who are in the house—not merely by the radiance of supreme majesty on earth, but also by the rays of his most brilliant writings, even at that age. [Col. 0556D]]

In my judgment, these considerations are so straightforward that anyone who dared to compare them with, much less prefer to them, the conjectures of Tillemont or of our opponents [Col. 0556A] would necessarily prove himself an unjust evaluator of facts.

“But nevertheless,” says Terribilinus, “none of the ancient writers before the second catalogue called Damasus a Spaniard.” As though that had any bearing on the matter. None of them expressly appended a biography of Damasus. Jerome, certainly, is wholly occupied with reviewing his writings. Optatus, Rufinus, Marcellinus, Symmachus, and others dealt chiefly with his deeds, and did so in connection with the pontificate of Liberius, during which everyone knows that our Damasus played the leading role after Liberius against the Arians. We also know that ancient writers, especially ecclesiastical writers, were extremely sparing of words when it came to the homelands of the saints; we shall return to this matter below. Therefore, it was of no concern to the discussion they undertook whether Damasus had been a Colchian or an Assyrian, raised at Thebes or at Argos. But let me ask: did any ancient writer for that reason call Damasus a Roman? “Now,” he will say, “this was not the place for such a statement.” Yet I shall reply that neither was it the place for them to assign him to the Spaniards; consequently, the silence of the ancients on this point is plainly ἀμφίβολον—ambiguous—and can be pressed no more against us than against our opponents.

Nor do I consider Terribilinus sufficiently free from partisanship—if I may say so without offense—to be able to pronounce judgment on the arguments of our writers in favor of Damasus’s homeland. I appeal to fairer judges. But let their arguments be, as Terribilinus has wished, somewhat weaker than the matter requires: when the question concerns evidence a thousand and a half years old, must the right itself therefore immediately be considered to have failed because proof is lacking? Terribilinus will offer stronger arguments on his behalf, no doubt. But we have already said that, apart from the nation’s innate neglect of domestic matters, Spanish writers served private interests in this matter rather than the public cause. Thus, while each of them, by using the term more narrowly, made Damasus his own countryman, they were not collectively as concerned as they ought to have been with the substance of the matter—that is, with asserting generally that he was from Spain—because they considered that proposition to be beyond dispute.

Their private disagreement, however, concerning the city in which Damasus drew his birth, which Terribilinus finally presses against us, cannot either injure their public cause or in any way help Terribilinus. Some think that the city was Madrid, others Guimarães or Idanha, and still others Tarragona. Terribilinus could also add the western Gades [Note: [Col. 0556D] See Joseph Maria Suarezius, a Gaul and formerly bishop of Vaison, in Nicolaus Antonius, *Old Spanish Library*, book II, chapter 6.] and Saguntum, famous for its fidelity [Note: [Col. 0556D] Bernardinus Carvaialius, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in an oration delivered to Pope Alexander VI on 23 November 1492. Hence also Gaspar Scholanus, in his *History of Valencia*, cited by the same Nicolaus Antonius in the immediately preceding passage.], twelve miles from our Valencia, now called Monviedro by the inhabitants. Yet, I repeat, the Spaniards’ private disagreement on this matter can neither harm their public cause nor help Terribilinus in any way. Shall we therefore conclude, because seven once-celebrated cities disputed Homer’s homeland with such passionate feeling, that Homer must be assigned to the Greeks, or that the whole of Greece should be sued over the matter? This is my answer to Terribilinus’s objections.

At least in appearance, the conjectures of Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0557D] “It is claimed that Saint Damasus was a Spaniard, the son of a man named Antonius, although there can scarcely be any doubt that he was born at Rome, and that his father appears to have lived there from his earliest years; for Baronius reports an inscription in which it is said that his father had been a clerk, lector, deacon, and priest in the church of Saint Lawrence at Rome” (Tillemont, *Memoirs for the Service of Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VIII, Venetian edition, p. 386. “There is even little likelihood that Saint Damasus’s father came from Spain to Rome, and brought his children with him, as this History [speaking of the Acts of Saint Irene, which the Bollandist Fathers present on 21 February] seems to say: since he had served at Rome as a clerk and lector, which suggests that he had lived there from childhood” (the same, ibid., in the notes, p. 773).] which Merenda brings forward against us [Note: [Col. 0557D] Merenda, at the beginning of the *Minor Works of Saint Damasus*.] are certainly stronger. Since not only Damasus but also his father Antonius had served as a lector in the city, and the latter had attained the priesthood in the basilica dedicated to Saint Lawrence, now called San Lorenzo in Damaso, by passing through all the ecclesiastical grades—as Damasus himself tells us—and since the office of lector, according to the discipline of those times, was entrusted to boys, Tillemont infers from this that Damasus’s father, like Damasus himself, had spent his childhood in Rome.

He continues: it is scarcely credible, or at least scarcely probable, that Damasus’s father first went to Spain, took a wife there, had children in that region, and then returned to Rome with this family burden, only to be immediately enrolled in the ecclesiastical order in the office of notary and, within a short interval, to be honored with the ranks of lector, levite, and priest.

Merenda does not stop there. After calculating the length of time, the difficulties of the journeys, the ecclesiastical discipline of that age, and finally various other considerations, he declares that the whole matter is filled with immense difficulties and obscure turns. Thus Damasus, he says [Note: [Col. 0557D] At the beginning of the *Minor Works of Saint Damasus*, no. 1.], when he exercised the office of lector, was at least thirteen years old. Yet he must have come to Rome with his father and mother as an infant of four or five years. Let us grant that he was fit at that age to endure so long a journey; but could his father Antonius, a completely new and unknown man, have enrolled himself in the Church as soon as he came to Rome and been appointed lector of its basilica [Col. 0557C]? That would certainly have been contrary to the discipline of those times. First he had to be baptized, and then, after some interval of time, it had to be determined whether he was worthy to be enrolled among the clergy. Finally, he had to spend either nine years, or at least seven, exercising the offices of the minor orders; when that time had elapsed, if he had proved himself suitable, he could be elevated to the higher grades.

Now, Merenda continues, if to this nine- or seven-year period—which Antonius must have spent exercising the minor orders—you add another five or six years, which must have elapsed between the birth of his son and the Roman journey, and before the father was enrolled among the clergy, you will already arrive at the age at which Damasus was when he heard the *Acts of the Holy Martyrs*—Peter and Marcellinus, that is [Col. 0557D]—and wrote them down for preservation in memory. Yet at that time he already appears to have been a lector. Were father and son, then, placed in the lower orders at almost the same time and in the same church? Let others judge. Thus far Merenda.

Since this argument contains many points, each of which must shortly be examined carefully and individually, I believe I shall do something worthwhile if, at the outset, I place before the eyes of readers the ecclesiastical discipline of that age—that is, the discipline prevailing at the time when Damasus’s father Antonius must be thought to have come to Rome, as we shall soon explain. We must consider at what age ecclesiastical readers were appointed to that office; how much time those placed in the minor orders needed to spend in each grade before being advanced to the higher grades; whether those who devoted themselves to the Church’s clerical service were enrolled in some order immediately after baptism or only after an interval; and, finally, whether a fixed period of probation had been established for those to be promoted. Through these considerations, I believe, the entire force of the argument will be dissolved, and the replies we intend to make will also become clearer.

First of all, it must be established that at the beginning of the fourth century of salvation—or at least after the peace restored to the Church by Constantine, which is precisely the time at which Damasus’s father Antonius must have come to Rome, as we shall shortly say—the ecclesiastical grade of lector was very frequently entrusted to boys. This may properly be gathered from the Second [Note: [Col. 0558D] Second Roman Council, under Sylvester, act 2, chapter 11, vol. I of Labbé, p. 1586.] and Third [Note: [Col. 0558D] Third Roman Council, under the same Sylvester, under the heading “On Appointing Persons to the Orders.”] Roman Councils held under Sylvester in the year 324 and the following year. Although critics do not entirely endorse the authority of the former [Note: [Col. 0558D] Pagius, under the year 324, nos. 17–18, in Labbé, vol. I, col. 1576.], the testimonies of others, together with the arguments presented by Thomassinus [Note: [Col. 0558D] *On the Old and New Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 35, nos. 2, 5, and 7.], demonstrate sufficiently and more than sufficiently that, insofar as our purpose is concerned, it transmitted a valid and accepted doctrine of the Church’s practice [Col. 0558C].

Tillemont and Merenda had deeply absorbed this doctrine. It may therefore be inferred that neither of them had any scruple whatever concerning the age at which Damasus’s father could first have been enrolled among the clergy, since both consistently assert that he exercised the office of lector from childhood [Note: [Col. 0558D] Tillemont, in the passage cited above and in the notes, p. 773: “Damasus’s father had served at Rome in the capacity of clerk and lector, which seems to indicate that he had lived there from childhood” (Merenda, chapter 1, no. 1, there). “For Damasus’s father was first a clerk, then a lector, in the basilica of Saint Lawrence; these are the first grades for boys. Thus Damasus’s father seems to have begun his apprenticeship in that basilica from his earliest years.”]. We shall now determine whether this is indeed so.

For the moment, we should briefly examine the argument by which Merenda proceeds to prove from the ecclesiastical discipline of that age that the office of lector was customarily assigned to boys. “That boys were customarily appointed to the grade of lector,” he says [Note: [Col. 0558D] In the immediately preceding passage.], “is evident both from the letters of Siricius and Innocent and from various examples cited by Thomassinus and Bonarotius.” But the letters of Siricius and Innocent are at least a solid century later than the period about which the question must concern us, namely, the time when Damasus’s father was a boy. Let us bring the matter to a calculation. Damasus is said to have been born in the year of Christ 304; therefore his father’s childhood, during which our opponents wish him to have obtained the grade of lector, must have begun in the year 285 or not long afterward—that is, a full century before Siricius. What, then, shall we say about Innocent, who is known to have been elevated to the pontificate only at the beginning of the fifth century? Nor are the examples of Thomassinus [Note: [Col. 0559C] Thomassinus cites examples of twelve boys who, while they were lectors, confessed Christ at Carthage during the Vandal persecution. He also cites Epiphanius of Ticinum, John of Chalon-sur-Saône, Chrysostom, Euthymius, and others, whose examples are much later. As for Felix of Nola, whom Paulinus says served God as a lector in his earliest years, neither is it sufficiently established which Felix among his namesakes he was, nor is the age at which he flourished sufficiently known; on this, see Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs*, Verona edition, p. 216. Paulinus may also have referred “the earliest years” not to Felix’s childhood but to his entire youthful age; for the phrase “from childhood he began to serve God” belongs to the preceding period. See Paulinus, in the same Ruinart, p. 218.] and Bonarotius [Note: [Col. 0559D] The example of the boy lector Messius Romulus, the sole example cited by Bonarotius, is shown to be later both by the style of the epigram and perhaps by the monogram of Christ added beside it. Yet this author should be consulted (*Observations on the Florentine Glass Fragment*, 1716 edition, p. 115).] any less recent than those of Siricius and Innocent, and therefore they cannot easily be applied to the time when Damasus’s father was a boy. But let us return from this digression to the road [Note: [Col. 0559D] See below the first of the notes appended to this dissertation under the stated title. Editor.].

[Col. 0559B] It is not known whether, before the time of Sylvester, any fixed age had been prescribed in one of the councils or ecclesiastical canons at which the office of lector was to be entrusted to persons. Whatever the case may have been, it is clear that more mature men could also obtain that grade, and that this had been possible from the very beginnings of the Church. Certainly, in the canons called apostolic, those who had come to the Church from pagan life and had been baptized are not forbidden to be admitted to the clergy [Note: “A person who comes from pagan life—that is, to the Church—and has been baptized, or who comes from an immoral way of life, should not immediately become a bishop” (*Apostolic Canon* 79, vol. I of Labbé’s Collection, Venetian edition, 1718, p. 42).], as is expressly stated in canon 79 of those canons.

I know, of course, that the authority of certain persons [Note: In the work of the learned Cardinal Aguirre (vol. I, *Councils*, dissertation 3, excursus 2, 3, and 4).]—and even a decree of Pope Gelasius [Note: “On Apocryphal Scriptures,” in the Roman Council held in the year 494.]—stands in the way of our assenting safely to these canons. Nevertheless, the canon we have cited, since it had already long before been cited by Origen against Celsus [Note: Origen, *Against Celsus*, book III, cited by Severinus Binius (in the note on Apostolic Canon 79, vol. I of the Labbé Collection, col. 62).], should by no means be judged to suffer from the defect of falsehood [Col. 0559C]. The same conclusion is most clearly drawn from canon 2 of the Second Council of Nicaea—a council held at precisely the time when, as we shall say below, Damasus’s father came to Rome [Col. 0560A] [Note: “Since many things have been done either out of necessity or because of otherwise pressing circumstances contrary to ecclesiastical canon—for example, that men who had recently come to the faith from pagan life and had been catechumens, that is, initiates, for only a short time should immediately be brought to the spiritual washing and, as soon as they had been baptized, be advanced to the episcopate or presbyterate—it has seemed right that nothing of this sort should henceforth occur” (Council of Nicaea, canon 2, vol. II of Labbé’s Collection, col. 49).]. For if it is said there that mature men could be baptized and, only after time had passed, reach the episcopate if they proved themselves worthy, it follows that they could certainly also obtain the preceding lower grades, and therefore the office of lector.

In particular, the passage of the Council of Sardica concerning the office of lector is more precise and most clearly relevant to our case [Note: “Bishop Hosius said … that if someone from the marketplace, whether rich or a scholar, is judged worthy to become a bishop, he should not be appointed until he has performed the ministry of lector, deacon, and presbyter” (Council of Sardica, canon 10, vol. II of Labbé’s Collection, col. 300).]. But since it is known to have been held a full twenty years after the period under investigation, namely in the year 347, we deliberately pass over its testimony and rely with greater justification on the decretal letters of Siricius [Note: To Himerius of Tarragona, no. 10.], Innocent [Note: To Felix of Nocera, nos. 4–5.], and Zosimus [Note: To Hesychius of Salona, no. 3.], in which this same doctrine concerning the office of lector is expressly transmitted.

There is, however, one point that we do not think should be omitted. Cyprian, speaking of the confessors of Christ Celerinus and Aurelius, implies [Note: Book II, letter 5; book III, letter 22, in Thomassinus, part I, book II, chapter 30, no. 6 and following. See also no. 12.] that the African Church was accustomed to elevate to the grade of lector those who had already attained the glory of confessors—that is, those who had entered upon the apprenticeship of martyrdom. It is extremely probable that these men were of full rather than tender age.

Indeed, since, besides the excellence of the lectorate among the minor orders at that time [Note: On the excellence of the lectorate among the minor orders, see Thomassinus, part I, book II, chapter 30, nos. 11 and 13.], many duties were imposed upon lectors that required mature age and manly steadfastness—for beyond reading the Scriptures, which was their proper function, they were very frequently entrusted with the custody of the sacred books, as may be gathered from various passages in the Acts of the Martyrs [Note: In the Acts of Saint Felix, the African bishop, we read: “He ordered the presbyter Aper to be brought before him, and Gyrus and Vitalis, lectors. The curator Magnilianus said to them: ‘Do you have the divine books?’ Aper said: ‘We do.’” (In Ruinart, *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, Verona edition, 1731, p. 313.) Likewise, in the Acts of Saturninus, Dativus, and others, the tyrant Anulinus questioned the younger Saturninus, a lector: “Tell me whether you have any Scriptures” (Ruinart, p. 338). In the proconsular Acts of the African persecution under Munatius Felix: “The curator Felix said to Marcuclius and Silvanus: ‘Why have you brought only one book? Produce the Scriptures you have.’ Marcuclius and Catulinus said: ‘We have no more, because we are subdeacons; but the lectors have the books’” (Baronius, under the year 303, Lucerne edition, 1738, p. 341). Likewise, in the Acts of the Council of Cirta under Secundus of Tigisis: “Felix said to Bishop Paul: ‘Produce the Scriptures of the Law.’ Bishop Paul said: ‘The lectors have the Scriptures’” (Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Donatist*, book III, chapter 29). There are similar passages elsewhere in other authors.]—it is scarcely credible that, at least toward the end of the third and the beginning of the fourth century of salvation [Col. 0560C], when the fury of the persecutors raged most cruelly against the sacred books, boys were appointed to the grade of lector.

[Col. 0561A] For this reason, when I observed that so many dangers threatened lectors because of their custody of the sacred books, so that this order could rightly be regarded as a kind of battle line of martyrdom [Note: See Thomassinus, part I, book II, chapter 30, at the beginning.], and when I further observed that the doctrine of boy lectors rested on no ancient law or established example—for Celerinus and Aurelius are irrelevant here [Note: Aurelius and Celerinus received the lectorate as the reward for their confession because of their youthful steadfastness under torture.]—but was very frequently contradicted [Note: Gyrus and Vitalis in the Acts of Saint Felix; Saturninus, called “the Younger” because of his father of the same name, in the Acts of Saints Saturninus and Dativus; and finally Pollio in the Acts of Saint Pollio, etc. (in Ruinart, p. 359), as well as other lectors, were not boys, as may be gathered from their replies and from the proconsular Acts of the African persecution.], while, on the other hand, I discovered that the authorities and examples cited in favor of boy lectors by the authors mentioned above belonged to the times of Theodosius, Arcadius, Honorius, and later periods, when the Church enjoyed the peace and leisure it desired, I therefore judged, from a comparison of all these matters with one another—and especially from the transformation of circumstances under Constantine the Great—that it could reasonably be inferred that only then, after peace had been restored to the Church, was access to the lectorate first opened to boys; that the seeds of this new arrangement were sown by Sylvester in the Roman Councils [Note: Specifically, the Second Council (act 2, chapter 11) and the Third, under the heading “On Appointing Persons to the Orders.”], later cultivated by the letters of Siricius [Note: Letter to Himerius of Tarragona.] and Innocent [Note: Letter to Felix of Nocera.], and spread very widely throughout the Church.

Since under Constantine no fear of persecution threatened, lectors no longer needed the same steadfastness that had formerly been required; and, in any case, childhood was considered altogether more suitable both for preserving the innocence of those who were to be enrolled in the Church and for learning ecclesiastical rites. I submit this doctrine—or rather conjecture—concerning the age of lectors to the examination of those more skilled in ecclesiastical discipline [Note: See below the second of the notes appended to this dissertation under the stated title. Editor.], since I scarcely know whether it has previously been presented or noticed by anyone else [Note: Perhaps this doctrine occurred to the distinguished Ludovico Muratori, who, in his notes on Paulinus of Nola’s passage concerning Saint Felix the Martyr, “As a lector he served in his earliest years” (*Notes*, no. 238, Verona edition, 1736, col. 933), writes as follows: “Formerly, even in Cyprian’s time, as may be seen in his letters 33, 34, and several others, the office of lector was entrusted only to men of mature age distinguished by merit and learning … Later, however, minors and very young children were admitted to it.”].

[Col. 0561C] As for the intervals between the minor orders—that is, the periods during which those established in the minor orders were supposed to await the higher grades while exercising their respective offices—we have not found that any definite intervals were established for those who were enrolled in the Church at a more advanced age. Certainly, the Council of Sardica, if we are permitted to use its testimony through Merenda [Note: Canon 10, in Labbé, vol. II, col. 666.], prescribes a considerable length of time for each grade, but does not define exactly how long it was to be. The Second [Note: Act 2, chapter 11, in Labbé, vol. I, col. 1585.] and Third Roman Councils [Note: Under the heading “On Appointing Persons to the Orders,” in Labbé, vol. II, col. 417.], under Sylvester, which we have just cited, the reliability of whose testimony is doubtful, must be understood as establishing intervals only for those who had entered the Church’s service as boys, for in both cases a longer span of years is decreed than mature men could have been expected to await.

As we have seen, Merenda says that those established in the minor orders—and therefore Damasus’s father—had to wait nine years, or at least seven, before they could be advanced to the higher grades according to the discipline of those times [Note: “Finally, he had to spend either nine years or at least seven exercising the offices of the minor orders; when that time had elapsed, if anyone had proved himself suitable, he could be elevated to the higher grades” (Merenda, at the beginning of the *Minor Works of Saint Damasus*, no. 1).]. Yet we can neither refute this nor affirm it as certain until suitable evidence is brought forward. Certainly, the later letters of Siricius, Innocent, and Zosimus, to which Merenda leads us in confirmation of this doctrine [Col. 0562B], have, as we have just said, nothing in common with the discipline of the period about which the question ought to concern us.

Even if we were to grant Merenda, without proof, that a seven-year interval between the minor orders had been prescribed by the Church in the time of Damasus’s father, our path would not thereby become more difficult, as we shall explain in its proper place. Meanwhile, it is permissible to suppose that bishops had been granted considerable authority in this matter, so that, for just reasons, they could advance to the higher grades anyone whom they judged suitable for the Church’s ministries without waiting for the full seven years to elapse. It would also seem that such indulgence concerning the time was particularly granted to those who had entered the sacred service at a somewhat more advanced age; equity and natural reason appeared to recommend this. For it was not equally possible for them, as for boys, to wait for a longer interval before proceeding to the remaining grades [Note: See Thomassinus, *Old and New Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 36, nos. 5 and 6.].

We have several well-attested examples of this kind of dispensation: Gallus and Julian, both descended from the imperial family of Constantine the Great; Nectarius of Constantinople; Ambrose; Epiphanius of Ticinum; Martin of Tours; Gaudentius of Brescia; and others. Yet these examples are somewhat later than we would wish. It is nevertheless credible that, from the earliest centuries of the Church, bishops already possessed the right to grant an exemption from the seven-year period in question—or at least to mitigate that interval—for those who entered at an advanced age [Col. 0563A]. Certainly, in Apostolic Canon 79, which we cited earlier, after establishing the general rule that no one who came from pagan life or from an immoral way of life should immediately become a bishop, an exception is added at once: unless this occurred by divine grace. From this it is permissible to infer that bishops were granted some authority in the matter. Let others judge.

Thus far we have seen that even men of advanced age could be enrolled among the clergy and consequently obtain the grade of lector. We are speaking of those who had not previously served in the military or held public office, and who were not curials, penitents, bigamists, or otherwise barred by the canons. It remains to inquire whether such men were enrolled in some grade of the sacred service immediately after baptism, or rather only after an interval serving as a kind of probation.

Merenda [Note: At the beginning of the *Minor Works of Saint Damasus*, no. 1.], after raising the difficulty that Damasus’s father, a completely new and unknown man, could have enrolled himself in the Church as soon as he came to Rome and immediately been made notary and lector of the basilica of Saint Lawrence, explains the grounds of that difficulty by saying that such a procedure was contrary to the discipline of those times: first he had to be baptized, and then, after some interval, it had to be determined whether he was worthy to be enrolled among the clergy.

To persuade us of this, he appeals for the third time to the letters of Siricius, Innocent, and Zosimus [Note: Here Merenda cites and adduces, in confirmation of this doctrine, Siricius’s letter to Himerius, no. 14; Innocent’s letter to Felix of Nocera, chapter 5; and Zosimus’s letter to Hesychius of Salona, chapter 5.]. But our dispute with him here is no longer about an anachronism, but about the truth of his statement, since Siricius and Zosimus, in the very passages cited by Merenda, and perhaps Innocent also, plainly proceed in an entirely different direction. We present Siricius’s words [Note: Letter to Himerius of Tarragona, under the headings “On Those to Be Admitted to the Clergy” and “On Those Who Turn to the Sacred Service at an Advanced Age,” chapters 9 and 10. The number 14 of this letter, cited by Merenda, concerns penitents, not those to be promoted, in the Venetian edition of Labbé’s councils, 1728, which we have used.]:

“Therefore, whoever has devoted himself to the service of the Church from infancy must be baptized before the years of puberty and must be associated with the ministry of the lectors.” Then, in the following chapter, he continues:

“But whoever, already advanced in age, hastens from the lay state to the sacred service, prompted by a way of life directed toward a better purpose, WILL NOT OBTAIN THE FRUIT OF HIS DESIRE OTHERWISE THAN BY BEING ASSOCIATED, AT THE VERY TIME WHEN HE IS BAPTIZED, IMMEDIATELY WITH THE NUMBER OF THE LECTORS OR EXORCISTS; provided that it is established that he has had or has only one wife—which wording must be noted—and that he took her as a virgin.” These are Siricius’s words in the aforesaid letter.

Zosimus, in the letter he wrote to Hesychius of Salona, does not differ greatly from this [Note: No. 3, vol. III, col. 400. The number 5 cited by Merenda does not exist there; the letter ends with number 3.]:

“Moreover,” he says, “the following periods must be observed in each grade. If someone has devoted himself to ecclesiastical ministries from infancy, he shall remain among the lectors under continuous discipline until the twentieth year of his age. But if someone comes when older and advanced in years, PROVIDED THAT AFTER BAPTISM HE DESIRES IMMEDIATELY TO BE ENLISTED IN THE DIVINE SERVICE, he shall be retained among the lectors or exorcists for five years … with this law observed, that neither a bigamist nor the husband of a widow may be admitted to these grades.”

Here I observe first that Siricius and Zosimus say absolutely nothing concerning those who devoted themselves to the Church from childhood about the interval between baptism and clerical enrollment which Merenda wanted to establish and attributed to these pontiffs. But when they proceed to those who desire to be enrolled among the clergy after reaching adulthood, Siricius expressly decrees that they are to be associated, at the very time of their baptism, immediately with the number of lectors or exorcists; while Zosimus says that anyone who comes to the clergy at an advanced age and desires immediately after baptism to be enlisted in the sacred service is to be retained among the lectors or exorcists for five years. Consequently, from Zosimus’s words it is entirely permissible for those who devote themselves to the sacred service at an advanced age, if they wish, to be initiated immediately after baptism into the grades of lector or exorcist [Note: Whether someone could be enrolled in the Church without an office or order during the first five centuries, see Thomassinus, part I, book II, chapter 34, from no. 2 onward, who entirely denies that this was possible. Yet see the same author, part I, book II, chapter 67, no. 2.].
