Anyone who compares this with Merenda’s doctrine will find that the two are not merely different or poorly compatible, but plainly contradictory.

One avenue of refuge remains for him: Innocent, who writes the following in his letter to Felix of Nuceria, under the heading “On Those Who Can Become Clerics from the Laity.” [Note: [Col. 0564D] Chapter 4, volume III of Labbe’s Collection, col. 21.] “Laymen, however, who were baptized while having wives, and who so conducted themselves that their reputation in no respect wavered, whether they have been attached to the clergy or have remained in monasteries FROM THE TIME THEY WERE BAPTIZED . . . are not forbidden to assume the lot of the clergy.” From this it seems to follow that laymen who have had, or have, wives may lawfully be admitted to the clergy only if, after the passage of time since their baptism, they have shown themselves upright and continent.

Yet since the decretal letters of Siricius and Zosimus cited above by us speak most explicitly even of laymen who, as they say, actually have wives—for we have deliberately placed the words of both pontiffs side by side—and since Siricius orders that they be enrolled in the clergy immediately after baptism, whereas Zosimus leaves this to their own choice and discretion, [Note: [Col. 0564D] Siricius, in the place cited: “At the time when he is baptized, let him immediately be associated with the number of readers or exorcists, provided that it is established that he has had or has one wife, and that he took her as a virgin.” Zosimus likewise: “After baptism, let him immediately desire to be enrolled in the divine army . . . with this provision observed, that neither a twice-married man, nor a penitent, nor the husband of a widow may be admitted to these grades.” Here it should be noted that the husband of a woman who was married as a virgin is not rejected.] and since, moreover, we know from the ecclesiastical laws that only bigamists—or husbands of women previously married—and likewise husbands of non-virgins were prohibited from the ministry of the altar, but not those who married virgins; and since these latter, even while the sacramental bond remained, could nevertheless—as the canons say, with the marriage chamber set aside—be admitted immediately to the clergy, as is made perfectly clear by innumerable decrees of the councils of that age, [Note: [Col. 0565D] See our distinguished countryman Ferdinand Mendoza, *On the Confirmation of the Council of Elvira*, canon 33, and especially the ancient Vatican manuscript of the Council of Nicaea, reported by the same Mendoza in Alfonso Pisano, *Book III, On the Acts of That Council* (ibid., col. 1234, letter D): “The Fathers of the Council of Nicaea had therefore decreed concerning the fact that clerics of sacred order—whether bishops, or subdeacons, or anyone from the sacred catalogue—ought not to SLEEP WITH THE WIVES WHOM THEY HAD MARRIED WHILE STILL LAYMEN,” etc.] the words of Innocent on which Merenda relies ought therefore to be understood as containing advice concerning a more excellent good, not as imposing any necessity of an interval after baptism; and in this way the teaching of that pontiff can be reconciled with Siricius and Zosimus. Let us make the matter clearer.

Felix had consulted Innocent about matters so well established that, at the beginning of the letter, the pontiff says that he was astonished that a prudent man had wished to consult him about things that were certain and clearly known to all, and that he was answering him not as though he were ignorant, but as though he were occupied with, or had forgotten, other matters. Among other things, Felix had asked categorically about laymen: Could they be admitted to the clergy? Then he also asked about those who had been baptized while having wives. Felix immediately reveals himself as a haughty man of severe disposition, and not very inclined to receive laymen—especially married laymen—into the clergy. To the first question the pontiff replied that it had not been established concerning all laymen that they could not be enrolled in the clergy, adding, not without irritation: “For clerics cannot be born; they must be made.” To the second he replied that those who had been baptized while having wives could also be received into the clergy—especially, for this is clearly the pontiff’s meaning, if, from the time they were baptized, they conducted themselves so that their reputation in no respect wavered—as though he were saying that they were not to be prohibited, particularly if they were such men. It is obvious that this contains advice rather than a requirement.

It may also be said simply that Felix’s consultation concerned certain married men who, some time after being baptized, had first turned their minds toward the Church; consequently, that rescript—not a decree or general law—should be understood as applying to the matter. Whichever way the case may stand, this much is certain: even if the times of Siricius, Innocent, and Zosimus had coincided with the age of Damasus’s father, there would have been no need for him, nor any reason anywhere, to prove through an interval after baptism whether he was worthy; yet this is what Merenda, as I believe, was falsely persuaded of. But enough on this subject.

We must now pass from ecclesiastical discipline to historical matters, indeed to conjectures, or εἰς τὰ πειθανὰ—that is, to what is plausible. First of all, let us establish that Laurence, the most unconquered deacon and martyr—whose homeland will be discussed fully in the second part of this work—suffered under the emperor Valerian, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, that is, in the year of Christ 258, [Note: [Col. 0565D] In Bollandus, under 10 August, § 4, no. 36, and Blanchinus the Elder, *Life of Sixtus II*, volume II, p. 225.] although the Acts and Martyrologies generally place his death during the persecution of Decius, an opinion which I see is preferred by some. [Note: [Col. 0565D] In Baronius, *Notes on the Martyrology*, under 10 August.] Whichever of these two opinions is more correct—and for the present it makes no difference to our argument—it is absolutely certain that, if Damasus’s parents themselves could not have known Laurence well because of their age, his grandparents on either side could at least have done so, associated with him, and indeed enjoyed his intimate friendship, if a shared homeland or some chance had brought them together somewhere.

I should certainly like to be permitted, with Blanchinus, Merenda, Victorius, Acamus, and any others who assert that Laurence was Roman by birth, to claim the holy deacon for our Spain for a time, while from this shared homeland I infer how great and how intense our countrymen’s devotion to him then was, and what piety the peoples showed toward the illustrious martyr while his blood was still warm. But when I perceive that this concession would be difficult to obtain from those very authors, I set aside this conjecture for the moment, considering instead the religious devotion inherent in the Spanish people, their steadfastness hardened against every extreme danger, and the abundance of martyrs and confessors of Christ that already existed in that region. Certainly, that the memory of the most holy deacon was preserved nowhere more faithfully or more brilliantly than in our Spain is demonstrated by the elegant hymn of Prudentius, which still survives and was composed not long after those times; consequently, so much authority has been attributed to it that, amid the frequent loss of authentic Acts of Laurence, it alone now supplies their place and function for us. [Note: [Col. 0566D] Theodoric Ruinart, *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, beginning at p. 162, Verona edition, 1731. From this Blanchinus the Younger, annotation 105 on the *Book of the Most Ancient Orations of the Gothic Rite*, p. 283, has the following: “Since the Acts as they are commonly circulated have been corrupted, it seemed appropriate to seek elsewhere an account of Laurence’s passion. From the many brief works of the holy Fathers and ancient writers that were composed in praise of, and concerning the passion of, that blessed martyr, we selected Hymn 2 of Aurelius Prudentius’s book *περὶ Στεφάνων*, or *On Crowns*, because there the entire sequence of events is set forth clearly and distinctly.”]

In this widespread fame of Laurence’s name throughout Spain, it would not be improbable that the parents of our Damasus, moved by pious devotion to the most holy deacon, perhaps even bound by a religious vow, or for some other reason that is not easy to conjecture, dedicated to his service a son who was still a minor—let us suppose twelve years old—and naturally very ready for works of piety, so that, serving at Rome at the altar near Laurence’s sacred relics and being enrolled in the clergy, he might begin and complete his ecclesiastical career. There was by then no fear of persecution under Constantine; three years earlier the Church had obtained peace and had assumed a new appearance; everything, finally, was safe and tranquil.

Moreover, Spain was subject to the Romans, and proconsuls, emperors, legions, and military garrisons were sent there daily; after being recalled, so that the soldiers would not grow soft through idleness, they returned to Rome once their terms of service had been completed. Some, having completed their public offices, returned to their native homes, apart from those whom the love of wealth drove toward that most prosperous region. Amid such a great stream of travelers moving back and forth, it is therefore credible that among their friends, and perhaps even their relatives, Damasus’s parents could have found someone to whom they might safely and honorably entrust the transportation of the boy to Rome and his placement in the basilica of Laurence.

This seems to me all the more plausible because Prudentius himself, whom we have just praised, abundantly teaches us that, not long before those times, and perhaps during Damasus’s own lifetime, the children of distinguished men throughout Spain were customarily offered as a votive gift to the illustrious martyr of Christ. After the sacred poet had most elegantly described Laurence’s passion, wishing to show how much glory it had brought to Christians and disgrace to the pagans, he says that the temples of the gods had been utterly deserted; then priests, Vestal Virgins, augurs, and everything in the city that was most deeply sunk in superstition did not disdain to visit and kiss the thresholds of the holy martyrs and of Laurence himself. Nor, he says, were parents more sparing of their own blood, so as not to dedicate and consecrate their children to the service of the most holy martyr. We present Prudentius’s passage. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Hymn 2, *On Blessed Laurence*, stanza 131.]

“We see illustrious houses,

Noble in either sex,

Offering as votive gifts

Their dearest children.”

From the word “we see,” and from the fact that it is otherwise established that the hymn of which we are speaking was composed in Spain, why should we not suspect that this passage was applied by its author to Damasus—whom he may perhaps have known, from the recent memory of the Fathers, to have been dedicated to Laurence from childhood?

Thus, once Damasus had been placed in the basilica of Laurence, he could very easily have been enrolled there, immediately after baptism, in the college of readers—unless, because of the dangers of travel, he had previously been baptized in his homeland, as was permitted by the canons. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Council of Elvira, canon 38, “Those traveling overseas,” etc., and other sources.] There he could have displayed that remarkable example of piety and learning which, as Eginhard testifies, already seemed to be raising him to a great height of distinction. [Note: [Col. 0567D] *Acts of the Saints Peter and Marcellinus*, 2 June, volume I of that month, in Bollandus, pp. 170, 173; cited in Merenda, *Brief Work on the Deeds of Saint Damasus*, chapter 1, no. 1.] There, too, he could most conveniently have received from the mouth of Dorotheus the persecutor the Acts of the holy martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, in order to transmit them to posterity, and finally could have carried out and accomplished the other things that seemed insufficiently probable to Merenda.

As time advanced, and as the young man’s wisdom increasingly appeared venerable, while the fame of his holiness and learning spread far and wide, anyone can easily conjecture how quickly it would have reached our Spain, to the anxious and expectant parents who were longing for news of their son. That news could have led them either to consider returning to Rome once more in order to visit their son, or, if such a plan had already occurred to them earlier, to hasten and complete it. Thus, so far as we have been able to determine from Damasus’s age, the chronology, and finally the other conjectures, the journey of Damasus’s parents and sister from Spain to Rome should certainly be placed around the year of Christ 325, when Damasus was more mature and at least twenty years old.

Whether Damasus’s parents had already formed the plan of remaining in the City and transferring their fortunes there, or whether they intended merely to visit their son for a time and then return home at the proper moment, is not easy to determine. I would rather believe that at first they had no such thought at all, but, concerned only with their son—as parental love naturally is—had put everything else second. Once, however, they had attained their wish and had discovered, by experience, that Damasus’s reputation was surpassed by his exceptional qualities, especially when the appointed time for their return began to approach, their longing for the son from whom they were reluctant to part first supplied a reason, or at least an occasion, for postponing the journey as long as possible, and soon for forming the plan of remaining in the City.

Whether, then, the couple had already conceived this plan in Spain, or whether the piety of their son had finally drawn it from them, it is likewise plausible that, once the decision to remain in the City had been made, a new proposal arose in Antonius’s mind concerning entering the clerical service. After he had disclosed it to his wife and the two of them had undertaken a mutual commitment to preserve chastity—for this was absolutely required by the discipline of the Latin Church—Antonius prepared for himself in this way an entrance into the Church. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Council of Elvira, canon 33; and, in confirmation of that council, our distinguished countryman Ferdinand Mendoza, volume I of Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, Venice, col. 1231; Thomasin, part I, book XI, chapter 61.] Damasus, moreover, worked eagerly toward this end, as toward the most welcome of all things that could happen to him, until he fulfilled his parents’ wishes; and through his efforts it was finally arranged that Antonius—who, like Damasus, could have been baptized in Spain—would soon be honored with the rank of reader, while in the meantime being entrusted with the office of notary.

Lest this seem difficult or insufficiently probable to anyone, one must consider first Damasus’s authority and reputation, then the industry and integrity of his father Antonius, and finally the condition and needs of the Church in those times. In Damasus’s case the matter is clear. For when, by the year of Christ 325—the time at which we believe these events finally occurred—he was in the very flower of youth, and had accumulated a reputation for piety and learning beyond his years, turning everyone’s attention and interest toward himself, it is credible that the clergy and people of Rome would not have resisted a request made on behalf of his father, but would rather have gladly exerted all their influence in support of his hope.

Much, moreover, must be believed to have existed in Antonius, who, as we suppose, was then scarcely fifty years old—qualities that foretold that he would be an industrious and trustworthy minister and that his service would be extremely useful to the Church. It is not right to regard him as a rustic or some man of the common people, or as anything other than notably pious and upright, since so deep a desire had taken root in him to send his son from the farthest West to Rome for religious purposes. Such things rarely touch ordinary souls. Prudentius likewise records that distinguished families were accustomed to dedicate their children to Laurence as a votive offering. But if the brave are born from the brave, and doves do not beget the eagle, as the profane poet once sang, [Note: [Col. 0569D] Horace, *Odes*, book IV, ode 4, stanza 8.] I do not think Antonius’s praise was least of all that he had received a son so distinguished and so great as Damasus already was at that age. Finally, although the Church at that time enjoyed peaceful tranquility and leisure, it had not yet covered over the scars of the recent wounds inflicted under Maximian and Licinius; thus it was most prudent for it to fortify and prepare itself in advance, with the support of men such as Antonius, against the storm of war, should it ever arise.

Once Damasus’s father had been established in the office of notary, it should not be judged especially difficult for him later to become a reader and complete the remainder of his ecclesiastical career. The man’s integrity and industry, observed in the office of notary, could by themselves, even if everything else were lacking, have provided him with a perfectly suitable path to the rank of reader and the other orders, without the expected intervals of time. Nor, however, shall we strongly resist if Merenda insists that the strictness of the ecclesiastical laws asserted above was observed in his case exactly, and that the full seven years had to be awaited by one placed among the minor orders. Even so, Antonius, scarcely sixty years old and therefore still in the fullness of his age, could easily have been advanced to the presbyterate.

Thus far we have woven together a series of probabilities; yet, if I see correctly, there is nothing in it that should trouble a reader free from partisan bias. Nor would I say that these are merely probabilities: historical truth itself should be thought to lend them at least some strength, indeed even to have supplied their cause. It is therefore worth examining the matter from a somewhat earlier point. Merenda and Tillemont, along with us, have acknowledged that Damasus’s father proceeded from the office of notary to the order of reader; and Damasus himself gives the clearest testimony to this in the epigram *On the Temple of Saint Laurence*, where, speaking of his father Antonius and enumerating his ranks, he says: [Note: [Col. 0569D] In Merenda, p. 241.]

“By this path my father had grown to be

Notary, reader, deacon, priest,

And so forth.”

Nor should we believe that Damasus placed the rank of reader after the office of notary merely to serve the meter. Rather, he did so in order to set forth for us the order in which the events occurred; otherwise it would have been very easy for him, while preserving the rules of poetry, to begin in this way:

“By this path my father, reader, notary, deacon, priest.”

Now this progression from the office of notary to that of reader—although not very common—wonderfully confirms that Antonius entered the clergy not as a boy but at a more advanced age. For those who, once peace had been restored to the Church, were enrolled in the divine service from childhood were brought into the college of readers immediately after baptism, before reaching puberty; only later did they attain the office of notary, provided that they had shown themselves energetic and industrious in that service. Ennodius gives us a notable example in the case of Epiphanius of Pavia. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Ennodius, *Life of Epiphanius of Pavia*, Paris edition, 1611, p. 360.] After saying that Epiphanius had undertaken his military apprenticeship in the heavenly service under Crispinus and had performed the office of reader, he continues:

“Having soon mastered the abbreviations used in writing and the various signs that represented a multitude of words, he distinguished himself when dedicated to the number of the notaries.”

This should not be regarded as unique to Epiphanius. Rather, it was an established custom of the Church that notaries, or exceptors, were very often selected from the college of readers, as Menardus shows by numerous examples. [Note: [Col. 0569D] In his notes on the *Gregorian Sacramentary*, note 300, where he says: “Notaries here are the bishop’s scribes, who for the most part were taken from the college of readers.” He then adds examples from Photius’s *Bibliotheca* (no. 256), from the constitution of Saint Metrophanes, and elsewhere. Merenda does not disagree; in his annotation on Damasus’s poem XXV, p. 241, he says: “You see also that from the order of reader a rank was established leading to the office of notary.”]

Nor do we deny for that reason that the office of notary was very frequently entrusted to boys from the fourth century onward. Apart from the passage concerning Epiphanius that we have just cited, Ausonius makes this perfectly clear when he says: [Note: [Col. 0570D] Epigram 137.]

“Boy, swift servant of signs,

Skilled in writing, hasten here.”

We assert only this: among those who were enrolled in the ecclesiastical service from childhood, there was never a progression from the office of notary to that of reader. Consequently, whoever is known to have begun his service to the Church with the office of notary certainly entered the Church at a mature age, after renouncing worldly display. Indeed, I believe that no one at all will be found in ecclesiastical history who, having been enrolled in the Church from childhood, first obtained the rank of notary and then that of reader—as Antonius, Damasus’s father, did.

For this reason I judged that the journey of Damasus, his parents, and his sister Irene from Spain to Rome could have taken place without violating the credibility of history, while observing the ecclesiastical laws to the letter—indeed, in all likelihood it could have happened in precisely this way. At least, I have so far noticed no obstacle that would require great effort to avoid. As for the question Merenda raises among us—whether father and son, placed in the lower orders, could have served or ministered at approximately the same time and in the same church—that is not a matter of such importance. Even if we join the father’s office of notary with the son’s readership in time and place, nothing prevents it. For the office of notary is [Note: [Col. 0570D] At that time there were also keepers of sacred objects, interpreters, defenders, attendants who cared for the bodies of the dead, stewards, and other officials of the Church without any ordination. On this see Thomasin, part I, book II, chapter 31, nos. 2 and 5.] not a rank or ecclesiastical order; nor is it an office assigned to the Church as such, but rather to a district or region of the city, which we commonly call a parish. [Note: [Col. 0571C] Merenda, annotation on the epigram “By this path my father,” etc., 35, p. 241: “Although, therefore,” he says, “our Damasus’s father may have been attached to the title of Saint Laurence, nothing prevents him from having been a notary and exceptor for the seventh ecclesiastical region, to which that basilica belonged.”] It was therefore permissible to combine Damasus’s readership with Antonius’s office of notary without thereby violating the ecclesiastical ordinances.

If Merenda continues to ask about father and son serving together in the same basilica, for example as readers, or established in some other of the minor orders, we shall admit that the matter is not so straightforward. Yet since we have declared that Damasus’s father was not enrolled in the sacred service from childhood, Merenda—whether he was Roman or Spanish—must run against the same obstacle as we do. For how could a father who entered the Church long after his son, yet was ordained a priest long before him, become gradually closer to his son and then minister in the same rank as he, if we wish both to have been attached to the same basilica? [Note: [Col. 0571D] It is established by Damasus’s testimony that Antonius ministered in the basilica of Saint Laurence at the Theatre of Pompey. The same is not established of Damasus, since from the earliest centuries there were several churches in Rome dedicated to Laurence. The most famous and oldest of all was in the Field of Veranus, where his sacred remains are still preserved; another is one of the seven sacred churches of the City, commonly called San Lorenzo fuori delle Mura. But what if we say that Damasus was attached to this church because of Laurence’s relics?] Or shall we rather say that father and son were both deacons in the same church and at exactly the same time? Both alternatives are difficult; yet I plainly do not see how either Merenda— even if we freely grant him that Damasus was Roman—or we, if we hold him to have been Spanish, can avoid one or the other and remove this obstacle while preserving the strictness of ecclesiastical discipline. It remains, therefore, for him to take refuge with us in whatever degree of leniency the ecclesiastical laws may have allowed in this matter, as required by the circumstances of place and time and by the needs of the Church.

Nor do the Acts of blessed Irene, Damasus’s own sister, brought forward by the Bollandist Fathers, [Note: [Col. 0571D] Under 21 February, volume III, p. 245, Venetian edition.] create a small difficulty for us by making Irene likewise one of the Roman virgins—provided that the Acts are genuine—for Merenda asserts that no one will deny this when they are compared with the epitaph composed by Damasus for her. [Note: [Col. 0571D] § 2, *On the Poems of Damasus*, p. 144. “But if any credence can be given to those Acts”—namely, those of Irene—“no one will deny that Irene must be counted among the Roman virgins.”]

I do not deny that, if we date Irene’s death from this source to the twelfth year of Damasus’s pontificate, that is, to the year of Christ 378, as the Acts state, and if from the epitaph we infer that she had only just passed her twentieth year, then our entire account of Irene’s homeland and of her journey from Spain to Rome collapses. For if both conclusions follow, she must have been born only in the year 358 or thereafter. How, then, could she have come to Rome in 325, or have died in 378 while not yet twenty, when by that time she would have been almost sixty? But we shall discuss this elsewhere.

Meanwhile, our opponents are no less troubled by reconciling the statement of the Acts with that of the epitaph concerning Irene’s age. If they wish the testimony of both to be true, at what time could Irene have been born—that is, in the year 358—when her parents, unless they had already died, as I consider more probable, would at least have been of an age at which they could scarcely have devoted themselves to bearing and raising children? But let us grant the point. Would not the commitment to chastity have stood in their way, since according to the practice of the Latin Church it was necessary for the father to be enrolled in the clergy? Or how could Damasus have preceded his own sister by a full fifty-four years, as follows from the two accounts together? I have deliberately added “his own sister,” as Irene is called by Damasus, [Note: [Col. 0571D]

“You, own sister, now bear witness to our love.”  
(Damasus, in Irene’s epitaph.)]

lest anyone think that they were merely blood relatives, as canonists like to say, and not uterine siblings, and suppose that the knot of the difficulty is thereby loosened. Finally, if Damasus’s father had taken another wife after the death of his first, how could he have entered the clergy or ever been ordained a priest as a bigamist? [Note: [Col. 0572C] I would not wish this passage to be understood by some as referring to the bigamy of unbelievers, or to two successive marriages contracted by Damasus’s father before and after baptism. Although, as I think, the question concerning this subject had already arisen in Damasus’s time, and there were those who believed that multiple marriages contracted while still an unbeliever produced no irregularity—Jerome held this opinion in his letter to Oceanus—Siricius nevertheless settled the dispute, establishing the same rule concerning all marriages (Letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapters 10 and 11), and afterward Innocent I stated it even more clearly (Letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 6, in Labbe, volume III of the *Collection of Councils*, Venetian edition, col. 9).]

Merenda, and before him Tillemont, had these matters fully in view. Since they recognized that one or the other of those statements necessarily had to be false, they pronounced against the Acts. The former asserted that the credibility of those Acts was exceedingly slight in either direction; [Note: [Col. 0572D] Merenda, *On the Poems of Damasus*, § 11, no. 13, p. 144. “But, to speak frankly, the authority of those Acts”—namely, Irene’s—“is altogether exceedingly slight, whichever way one takes it.”] the latter, to the extent that such statements go, classified them among old women’s tales. [Note: [Col. 0572D] Tillemont, volume VIII, p. 773, in the notes: “Thus this document”—he means the Acts of Irene—“can still be placed among those that render the faith of the Spaniards in historical matters highly suspect.”]

If meanwhile we choose to follow them, we have an easy answer. But since, if one removes the disagreement between the Acts and the epitaph—which they have prejudged—there is nothing in the Acts that is not internally consistent and that does not harmonize very well with the other materials resting on historical credibility, and since our distinguished countryman Thomas de Herrera, the Augustinian, whose testimony concerning a matter of fact it would be impious to reject, testifies that he drew them from a very ancient Spanish Martyrology, [Note: [Col. 0573D] In the Bollandist Fathers, under 21 February, volume III, p. 244, on Saint Irene.] it was necessary to try every other course before condemning the truth of the Acts as a whole. For my part, however, I do not undertake to defend their cause in any way, at least not in the form in which our Tamayus published them. [Note: [Col. 0573D] In the same Bollandists, ibid.] Indeed, from the ingenuity of this otherwise most learned author, and from the inappropriateness of the subject matter, I strongly suspect that Damasus’s homeland and lineage were interpolated at the beginning of the Acts. Let others judge this matter.

One point seems to me beyond dispute: if we once admit that Irene’s epitaph was added at the end of the Acts by no one other than the author of the Acts, then he understood the fifth verse, which indicates Irene’s age, in a meaning very different from that commonly assigned to it. Merenda and Tillemont seem to have felt no difficulty, in accordance with what I believe to have been the accepted custom for indicating age in epitaphs, [Note: [Col. 0573D] In the passage cited immediately above.] in referring the phrase “she had not yet completed twice ten winters,” as it appears in the verse in question, to the year in which Irene ceased to live. I confess that the same thought occurred to me when I first read the verse. But when I found the meaning sufficiently ambiguous in itself, and, if taken in that sense, plainly opposed in several places to the Acts that had just preceded it, I readily allowed myself to be persuaded that the author of the Acts referred that sentence not to the year of Irene’s death, but to the year in which she dedicated herself to Christ through her vow of virginity—as though Damasus wished to tell us that Irene had been consecrated as a virgin to God in the very flower of youth.

Certainly, since the passage has been corrupted through the fault of antiquarians and its meaning is highly intricate, I do not at all see why it should be understood of Irene’s death rather than of the vow made by her. On the contrary, many considerations lead us to think that the author of the Acts used it in the latter sense. For if he was referring to Irene’s premature death, why would he have immediately appended an epitaph that so clearly contradicted the truth of the Acts? Moreover, since the Acts present Irene as persevering in her resolve to remain a virgin and advancing day by day, even when Damasus was elected pontiff, how could the author have believed that she died before reaching twenty in the twelfth year of Damasus’s pontificate, unless he simultaneously believed that she had taken the vow of virginity before the age of eight, and that at that age her brother Damasus had dedicated to her a little book on the same subject? Finally, another verse of the epigram, in which Damasus admits that he grieved at his sister’s death because he had lost the companionship of his life, sufficiently indicates that Irene died only at an age when, both parents having already died, Damasus had no other comfort in her companionship—something more plausibly occurring when both of them were advancing into old age.

Nevertheless, we leave the matter to the judgment of our readers, as the epigram is presented at the end of the Acts. [Note: [Col. 0573D] In the Bollandist Fathers, 21 February, volume III, p. 245.]

“In this tomb the limbs now consecrated to God rest.

Here is Damasus’s sister; if you seek her name, Irene.

She had vowed herself to Christ while life remained,

So that holy modesty might itself attest the merit of the virgin.

SHE HAD NOT YET COMPLETED TWICE TEN WINTERS OF AGE,

Though her age had already been surpassed by her outstanding character.

The purpose of her mind, the venerable piety of the maiden,

Had borne magnificent fruits in better years.

You, [perhaps: “This”] own sister, now bear witness to our love,

When, as she fled the world, she had given me an honorable pledge.

When the better royal realm of heaven seized her for itself,

I DID NOT FEAR death, because she was entering heaven free.

But I GRIEVED, I CONFESS, TO LOSE THE COMPANIONSHIP OF MY LIFE.

Now, as God comes, remember me, O virgin,

And, through the Lord, may your torch provide light for me.”

[Col. 0574C] If it is permissible to divine Damasus’s intention, I would think that every pair of verses in this epigram completes a separate period. The sense of the first period would be: “Here rests Irene, Damasus’s sister.” The second, in the two verses that follow, would be: “This virgin had vowed herself to Christ forever, and holy modesty confirmed the sanctity of her purpose.” The third, contained in the fifth and sixth verses, would be: “She had scarcely reached her twentieth year, and in her excellent character had surpassed her age.” The fourth, in the seventh and eighth verses, would be: “The virgin’s purpose and piety produced magnificent fruits in her youthful years”; for I think the words should be understood in this sense, with *melioribus annis* referring to her better or more mature years. This, moreover, strongly confirms that Irene did not die at twenty, but made her vow of virginity at that age. The remaining verses are not so very obscure.

One matter—which I do not know whether Merenda noticed—may create some difficulty for us concerning Damasus’s father’s journey from Spain to Rome and his being enrolled immediately as a new man in the clergy: namely, canon 24 of the Council of Elvira, which prescribes that those who have been baptized abroad, because their life is entirely unknown, are not to be promoted to the clergy in foreign provinces. [Note: [Col. 0574D] In Labbe, volume I of the *Collection of Councils*, col. 995.] Gratian reports that the same provision was made not long afterward by Pope Sylvester at the Roman council. [Note: [Col. 0574D] Chapter “Nullus,” Distinction 98, in the work of the distinguished Ferdinand Mendoza, *On the Confirmation of the Council of Elvira*, canon 21.] We likewise know that it was repeated by the Fourth Council of Carthage in canon 24. [Note: [Col. 0574D] In the same Ferdinand Mendoza, *On the Confirmation of the Council of Elvira*, chapter 50.] Indeed, because of the frequent frauds of the Manichaeans, the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* says that Anastasius I established that no foreigner from overseas was to be admitted to the clergy under any circumstances unless he produced the signatures of five bishops. [Note: [Col. 0574D] Under Anastasius I, and in this pontiff’s letter to all the bishops of Germany and Burgundy, chapter 2.]

Yet since the purpose of all these enactments was to prevent anyone whose life and conduct had not been investigated, in accordance with Paul’s dictum, from being enrolled in the clergy, Damasus’s father could readily have established the uprightness of his former life either by letters of recommendation from bishops or by the testimony of trustworthy persons; or, finally, once he had been appointed to the office of *exceptor*, he could have offered such a proof of his faith, integrity, and diligence as would have served him in place of the most complete examination. Damasus’s piety, moreover— which everyone would rightly have believed to have been imbibed from his parents—could subsequently have contributed greatly to the completion of the undertaking. Nor do we anywhere read that the name “foreigner” was then attached to Spaniards as an odious designation on account of the Manichaeans; nor was there, at that time, anything to be feared from the regions of Spain, since Arian depravity had not yet invaded it, nor had Priscillian disseminated the errors of the Gnostics, as will be clear to anyone who weighs the matter carefully.

I scarcely know whether anything in this series of conjectures, which we have appended as plausible, conflicts with ecclesiastical law or historical truth. We nevertheless present it to fair-minded readers, examined as best we could when it was first offered to us amid other occupations. For on a journey we had no leisure to investigate it further, nor were books at hand—especially during the nocturnal hours, when the lovers of the Muses desire longer encounters with them. Whoever discovers that we have somewhere mistaken uncertain matters for certain, or seized upon incongruous things as resembling the truth, and wishes in good faith to warn us of them, will render us bound to him by the greatest and everlasting gratitude.

# Appendix on the Monuments of Damasus Still Surviving at Rome

[Col. 0575]

At the outset we had no intention of treating this subject, since it was hardly demanded by the plan of our work; and for that reason we had thought that the inscriptions of Damasus now extant in the city should be deferred to our collection of the monuments of the Spanish name surviving at Rome—a collection which our hands are now laboriously bringing to completion and which will shortly be finished. But since that Collection, which will consist of three volumes of the larger format, as it is called, is not being prepared by us for publication among the general public, but rather so that, deposited in the royal library at Madrid, it may rescue from destruction the surviving remains of the Spaniards at Rome—remains which have hitherto endured so many adversities and which are finally threatened with complete extinction—and may place them before our countrymen at home for leisurely and unified contemplation, we have judged it fitting to consecrate the original poems of Damasus, inserted into our work, to posterity on pages that shall never die.

Of the forty or so epigrams of Damasus collected by Sarazanius, to which Merenda also added several from Gruterus and the Palatine Codex, only four now remain to us, together with a fragment of another. We have transcribed them from the originals as accurately as possible. Here they are.

## 1. In the Basilica of Saint Sebastian at the Catacombs, on the Appian Way, two miles from the City

Marble: three feet and one-sixth in width; seven and a half feet in length.

**Eutychius the martyr**

The glory of Christ showed that Eutychius was able to overcome  
the tyrant’s cruel commands  
and likewise the executioners’ thousand ways of doing harm.

After the filth of the prison, a new punishment follows through his limbs:  
they prepare fragments of pots,  
so that sleep may not approach him.  
Twelve days passed; food was denied.  
The holy man is sent into the abyss;  
the holy blood washes all the wounds  
which death’s dreaded power had inflicted.

In the sleep-bringing night nightmares disturbed the mind.  
The darkness revealed what limbs of the innocent man it held.  
He is sought, found, and honored;  
he cherishes all and provides all.

Damasus expressed his merit.  
Honor the tomb.

## 2. In the Church of Saint Agnes, commonly called Santa Agnese fuori delle Mura, on the Nomentan Way, two miles from the City

Marble: three feet and five-twelfths in width; ten and a half feet in length.

*[Note: We have distinguished the letters supplied by us in italic type. — Editor.]*

**Fame reports that the holy parents long ago related how Agnes**

when the trumpet had sounded mournful songs,  
suddenly left her nurse’s lap;  
how, of her own accord, she trampled the threats  
and rage of the tyrant,  
when he wished to burn her noble body with flames.

With small strength she overcame immeasurable fear  
and, naked, let her loosened hair fall over her limbs,  
lest a face doomed to perish should see the Lord’s temple.

O venerable one, holy glory of gracious modesty,  
I pray, illustrious martyr, that you may favor Damasus’s prayers.

## 3. At the Crypts of the Vatican Basilica, opposite the Altar of the Blessed Pregnant Virgin Mary

Marble: eleven feet and one-sixth in length; three feet and one-third in width.

Waters encircled the hill with gentle flow,  
and drenched the bodies of many  
with ashes and bones.

Damasus did not endure that those buried  
under the common law should, after rest,  
pay sorrowful penalties a second time.

At once he undertook the great labor  
of overcoming the immense mound;  
he cast down the summit of the hill,  
carefully searched its innermost depths,  
and dried all the earth that the moisture had saturated.

He found a spring which provides gifts of salvation.  
Mercurius, the faithful deacon,  
took care of this.

## 4. In the Church of the Four Crowned Saints

A fragment, whose rear portion has recently been supplied. In the wall.

At the far end a tomb lay hidden  
beneath the mound of the hill.  
Damasus points it out, which preserves the limbs of the pious.

A better palace of heaven holds you, Protus;  
proved by purple blood, you follow him, Hyacinthus.

Brothers in spirit, both great:  
here the former victor deserved the palm,  
the latter the crown.

## 5. In the pavement of the Church of Saints Martin and Sylvester, the title of Equitius, at San Martino ai Monti, near the middle

Marble: seven feet and one-sixth in length; two feet and one-sixth in width.

What shall I say, or keep silent?  
Grief itself forbids me to be silent.  
This tomb contains tears.  
Learn, parent, that Projecta, who had first been joined to a husband,  
was beautiful in her adornment,  
content with modesty alone.

Alas, beloved all too dearly  
by her wretched mother’s love,  
learn what befell her.

After the first bonds of the marriage chamber,  
snatched from the eyes of her father Florus [reading uncertain],  
she departed, desiring to ascend  
to the heavenly light.

Damasus offers consolations to all who weep.

She lived sixteen years, ten months, twenty-five days.

She was buried on the third day before the Kalends of January,  
in the consulship of Flavius Merobaudes and Flavius Saturninus.

[Col. 0577A]

There is nothing—not even among the errors—about which a reader need hesitate. Rather, let him wonder with us that Merenda, although he professes to have collated the epigram of Agnes, which we have given second, once and again with the original and to have corrected it [Note: Merenda, *On the Poems of Damasus*, § 2, no. 13, p. 143. “I have,” he says, “collated and corrected the poem on Saint Agnes with the original.” Likewise, in his notes, p. 237, concerning the same epigram: “Immediately afterward there is read” (in the Vatican Codex) “a poem of Saint Damasus in almost the same words in which it still exists carved on the stone in the same basilica, where I collated it a second time.”], nevertheless left many things still to be corrected by the labors of others—and not of a kind that can easily be blamed on the printer.

To show that we are not making this assertion without evidence, we have chosen to set before the reader two passages for comparison with our copy [Note: In verse 7 Merenda has:

> *Nudaque perfusos crines et membra*  
> “And your hair and limbs drenched and uncovered.”

But the epigram has, as we have seen:

> *Nudaque profusum crinem per membra*  
> “And your loosened hair over your limbs uncovered.”

Likewise, in the final verse Merenda has:

> “... favor me, I pray, illustrious virgin,”

whereas the epigram reads:

> “illustrious martyr.”]

But this is not of great importance. We think the reader should more appropriately be informed that the beginnings of the first three verses of that epigram, as well as the latter part of the poem concerning the saints Protus and Hyacinthus, were supplied by a recent hand, since they were missing from the original [Note: The distinguished Giovanni Marangoni, by whom the epigram of Agnes is said to have first been discovered in 1728, restored the beginnings of the verses somewhat differently. In the first he has *FAMA PRAEFERT* (“Fame reports”), which neither orthography nor meter permits; in the second, however, he has *AGNEM* instead of *AGNEN*, as the original has. The remainder is exact. See the *Acts of Saint Victorinus*, illustrated by the same author, in the Appendix *On the Original Inscription of Saint Damasus*, Rome, 1740, p. 138.]

Here someone might reasonably raise the question whether, since it is certain that Pope Vigilius, a century and a half after Damasus’s death, restored in the City the tombs of martyrs destroyed by the Goths—as we learn from an old epigram of Vigilius himself—the monuments we have presented derive from those earlier originals erected by Damasus, or from those later ones restored by Vigilius.

## On Saints Vitalis, Martial, and Alexander

When the Goths had pitched their doomed camps beneath the City,  
they first waged an impious war against the saints.  
With sacrilegious hearts they overturned  
all the tombs once rightly consecrated  
to the pious martyrs.

When God revealed them, Pope Damasus  
warned that they should rightly be honored  
by means of an inscription affixed to the stone.

But the holy inscription perished when the marble was broken;  
nevertheless, it was not possible for these men  
to remain hidden a second time.

For afterward Pope Vigilius, grieving over this,  
once the enemies had been expelled,  
renewed the entire work.

[Note: Quoted by Merenda, § 2, *On the Poems of Damasus*, p. 135.]

But since those five inscriptions appear to have been carved in marble at precisely the same period, and perhaps by the hand of the same craftsman—as is sufficiently shown not only by the forms of the letters but also by the ribbons and ornamentation attached to them, which are remarkably alike, and by the wholly identical character of the writing—and since, moreover, in the epigram which we have placed last, the age and day of Projecta’s burial, as well as the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus—which, according to Merenda’s calculation [Note: Chapter 22, p. 119.], falls in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Damasus—are marked with the greatest precision, I would believe that it was carved in marble in the time of Damasus rather than of Vigilius. Consequently, I think that this and the other monuments we have cited are originals surviving from the earlier monuments written and erected by Damasus.

For it is not credible that, in the time of Vigilius, the minute details of the months and days during which Projecta had lived would have been calculated so exactly that they could be recorded with such precision in her epitaph. Moreover, it is clear from the epigram of Vigilius quoted above that he restored only the tombs of martyrs; and I do not know whether Projecta, whose epitaph this is, should be numbered among them. Finally, so far as I can see, the style of the inscription does not reject the age of Damasus. On these matters, however, let the judgment rest with the readers.

Blanchinus Senior, from the ancient inscriptions once collected by Fulvius Ursinus, presents us with another inscription bearing the name of Damasus. He asserts that it contains an account of the consecration of the basilica of Saint Lawrence *in Damaso*, performed by that same holy pontiff, and that it may perhaps be the most ancient genuine document of this ecclesiastical rite.

He says that it was first rescued from destruction through the generosity of Alexander, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Cardinal Farnese; and that afterward, by order of the Most Serene Francesco, Duke of Parma and Piacenza, it was placed in a more distinguished location, together with other objects, in his palace at the Campo de’ Fiori in the year 1718. Blanchinus testifies that he saw it frequently.

But we, who had long cherished the intention of reproducing it from the original, were not so fortunate, even after a thorough search of the innermost parts of the household had been undertaken with the diligence of ourselves and our friends [Note: In this matter we were greatly assisted by the distinguished citizen and our friend Don Joachim Ibáñez Carolo, secretary in the Roman embassy to Charles, the Infante of Spain and King of the Two Sicilies. Through his efforts the hidden recesses and most secluded rooms of the extensive palace were opened to us.], and after we had examined one by one the surviving remains of Fulvius’s Collection of ancient descriptions, which are kept there in chests [Note: Joseph Vasi, the custodian of the Farnese furnishings—called the *Guarda Robbam*—very courteously showed them to us. He is shortly to publish the remarkable monuments of the Old and New City, contained in ten volumes of the larger format.].

We think that the inscription is concealed by its smallness, for Blanchinus states that its marble slab is only half a palm thick. Since nothing more is possible, we therefore present it as that author published it in second place [Note: Blanchinus first published this stone in the preface to volume I of Anastasius the Librarian, no. 35; afterward he reprinted it, with some alterations, in volume III of the same work, section 54, under “Damasus,” p. 34. We borrowed the earlier example from that passage.]

Blanchinus interpreted the initial letters occurring beneath the beginning of the epigram in this way: “Title in the name of Christ,” and so forth. The later abbreviations of the same inscription he interpreted as: “Dedicated in the ninth region, in the month of September, by Saint Paul and Saint Peter.” Merenda, however, who also gives the inscription [Note: § 3, *On the Works of Damasus*, p. 145.], proceeds by another route and explains it as follows: “renewed, restored, dedicated to the holy martyr.” This interpretation seems to me clearer and more appropriate. Let others judge the matter.

As for what Merenda tells us shortly before—that Damasus deserves indulgence, even if at times he seems to violate the laws of meter [Note: At the end of § 2, *On the Poems of Damasus*, p. 144.]—I would not want readers to understand this as though the errors with which the epigrams of Damasus are everywhere crowded should be attributed to the author. The incompetence of copyists and the multiplication of exemplars had already disfigured them; afterward the carelessness of printers inflicted so many wounds upon them that in some places it is scarcely possible to reach Damasus’s meaning by conjecture, while in others it is not easy even to guess it. Such is their obscurity.

Nor is it surprising if Damasus, being more intent on nurturing—or, while composing his verses, on serving—the devotion of the faithful than on the reckoning of syllables, sometimes took little care with the rules of meter. Given the general failing of the age in which he flourished, it is more credible that he knowingly neglected such details than that he was ignorant of them.

Certainly Prudentius, almost a contemporary of Damasus—whom no one has yet denied the praise of an outstanding poet—pays no heed to meter when, as he himself says, he inserts the name of Saturninus into a Sapphic line, despite meter’s resistance, adding [Note: In the hymn on the Seventeen Martyrs of Zaragoza, stanza 41.]:

> The love of golden names  
> makes light of the laws of verse...

This was sometimes permitted not only to poets of a later age but also to those ancient writers whom we commonly call poets of the Golden Age, although in this respect they deserve neither praise nor, still less, admiration. Nor do I know whether Damasus may not have stumbled more than once on the same point.

At any rate, among the verses which we have brought from the originals, I think that—if one excepts the second verse of the epigram of Agnes, which we said was mutilated at the beginning and recently supplied—there is now nothing that Scioppius could justly criticize.

Moreover, we know from the testimony of Jerome, who knew him very well, that Damasus possessed an elegant talent for composing verses [Note: *On Illustrious Men*: “Damasus possessed an elegant talent in composing verses.”]. In the *Acts*, too, he is described as possessing a more polished knowledge of both languages [Note: *Acts of Damasus*, published by Martin Sarazanius from a manuscript Codex of the archive of the canons of Saint Peter, p. 42: “Furthermore, when Liberius was being led into exile, he left Damasus in the City as his vicar, a man of ELEGANT KNOWLEDGE IN BOTH LANGUAGES...”], that is, of Attic and Roman eloquence, just as Horace speaks of Maecenas [Note: Horace, book III, ode 8, to Maecenas, stanza 2:

> Learned in the speech of either tongue.]

It is therefore plausible that the most holy pontiff cultivated the more agreeable, though still sacred, Muses with no ordinary skill.

But these observations may seem somewhat general. In my judgment, the decisive evidence that the errors under discussion must be laid at the door of copyists and typesetters is this: in the fourth epigram concerning the saints Protus and Hyacinthus, which we have cited, the first part—which we called the original—contains absolutely nothing deserving criticism; whereas in the latter part, which has recently been supplied and consists of no more than six half-lines, the laws of meter are violated twice, as becomes clear to anyone who examines its first and fourth verses carefully by finger and ear [Note: They read as follows:

> ... lay hidden beneath the mound of the hill  
> ... you follow, O proven Hyacinthus.

As to the former, I scarcely know whether the physicians’ hand of the poets can help it. The latter can in some fashion be defended—not by the common refuge of grammarians in their *hepthemimeral* caesura, which is irrelevant here, but by reference to Greek usage, in which a short syllable at the end of a word, when closed by a consonant, is very frequently lengthened when the following vowel is marked with rough breathing.

Among the Aeolians, that breathing—which corresponds to the Latin H—assumes the nature of a consonant because of its roughness; and our Baeticians do not differ greatly from them in this respect, aspirating that letter more strongly. Damasus could therefore, if the half-line in question belongs to him, lengthen the final syllable of the otherwise short word *sequeris* because of the aspiration that follows in the word *Hyacinthus*.

Examples of this are extremely common in Homer, as in *Odyssey* XIII, 343:

> Χωόμενος, ὅτι οἱ υἱὸν φίλον ἐξαλάωσας  
> “Angered because you blinded his dear son,”

and elsewhere:

> Οἰόμενος Ἑλένην  
> “Thinking of Helen,”

and so forth. Virgil too, because of the same word *Hyacinthus*, lengthens the preceding short syllable in *Eclogue* VI, 53:

> *Ille latus niveum molli fultus Hyacintho*  
> “He, reclining against soft Hyacinthus, his snowy side.”

The syllable *tus* was not lengthened by the poet on account of the caesura, as the common run of grammarians thinks. But these are childish matters.]*

If the originals, so to speak, or uncorrupted copies of the remaining epigrams of Damasus survived for us, a more consistent and uniform judgment of the holy pontiff’s poetry might perhaps be formed.

For this reason, while writing these pages, I was repeatedly struck by the thought of gathering into one collection the verses of Damasus, which have been sought out from every quarter, and, if possible, restoring them to their former polish and integrity. But the labor seemed difficult for anyone undertaking it, and the burden not easily manageable, especially without the support of ancient Codices, from the collation of which the author’s genuine wording must be entirely recovered.

Meanwhile, lest I appear to have accomplished nothing, I have decided to offer a specimen of our attempt in the epigram *On the Titles of Christ the Savior*, which Sarazanius places eleventh [Note: Sarazanius, p. 83.] and Merenda sixth [Note: Merenda, p. 224.].

In it, since the first verse limps, the former writer thought that a syllable was missing [Note: *Notes on the Poems of Damasus* XI, p. 168.]. But it seems to me to have been shortened by a complete pyrrhic foot and to be restorable in this way: if, after its first word *spes* (“hope”) and before the following word *vita* (“life”), we insert a third word, *via* (“way”), the verse should most plausibly be read not, as formerly, “Hope, life, salvation,” but “Hope, way, life, salvation.”

Thus we assign to Christ another name entirely appropriate to him—indeed, one bestowed upon him by himself—which had previously had no mention in the epigram; and the verse now flows with perfect rhythm according to the laws of meter and the ear.

I believe that Damasus alluded here to John’s statement concerning Christ [Note: John 14:6.]: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” But the copyist, ignorant perhaps both of metrical principles and of the Latin language, suspecting from the graphic similarity of the words *via* and *vita* that one of them had accidentally been repeated in the older exemplar, removed the other and, thinking that he had restored the verse, miserably disfigured it.

I have decided to set out the entire epigram as I believe it ought to be read:

> Hope, WAY, life, salvation, reason, wisdom, light,  
> Judge, gate, giant, king, gem, prophet, priest,  
> Messiah, Sabaoth, rabbi, bridegroom, mediator,  
> Rod, column, hand, rock, son, and EMMANUEL,  
> Vineyard, shepherd, sheep, peace, root, vine, olive,  
> Foas [term uncertain], wall, lamb, calf, lion, propitiator,  
> Word, man, net, stone, house, all things, CHRIST JESUS.

But let no one henceforth object to us that the phraseology of Damasus in his epigrams is thin and his manner of expression clumsy—we do not conceal the fact. The reader should finally be reminded of the style of the holy Fathers, which is called ecclesiastical: just as the ancient masters of the Attic and Roman languages were concerned to elevate their speech, so the ecclesiastical Fathers labored to lower theirs, adapting it to the understanding of ordinary people through the clear simplicity of their style. They were not pursuing the praise of eloquence but the usefulness of the faithful [Note: Whoever wishes to learn many things—and golden ones—about the style of the holy Fathers, which is called ecclesiastical, should read the longer encomium of Du Fresne Du Cange in the preface to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, nos. 58–60.].

Jerome himself bears abundant witness to this in his *Life of Paul the Hermit*, in a letter to Paul of Concordia [Note: Jerome, *Letter to Paul of Concordia*, near the end: “Meanwhile we send you yourself to yourself—that is, the elder Paul to the elder Paul—in whom, for the sake of the simpler people, we have labored greatly to lower our style.”]. It is therefore not surprising if Damasus, who flourished in the same century as Jerome, made it his principal concern in his epigrams that their meaning should immediately seize the uneducated people and even those who were only slightly attentive.

Certainly, whoever recognizes the poem addressed to Christ the Savior as a genuine offspring of Damasus—and Merenda openly declares himself among those who do so [Note: § 2, *On the Poems of Damasus*, p. 136.]—will, I think, be far from grudging Damasus the praise of an outstanding poet.

Thus far concerning Damasus and his monuments still surviving in the City. Merenda’s response now to that passage in his *Acts* in which the holy pontiff is called the **COMPATRIOT** of the most blessed Lawrence—an expression which we formerly interpreted [Note: Chapter 1, p. 9.] as though the writer of the *Acts* had understood and declared by that word that both men were Roman—leads us elsewhere. It summons us to become more concerned with asserting and vindicating for our Spaniards the unconquered deacon and martyr Lawrence, and to undertake voluntarily a new and exceedingly difficult task.

# Second Part of the Dissertation: On the Homeland of Lawrence

[Col. 0583]

## Chapter One. Introduction: The Former and Present State of the Controversy

At last the ingenious appetite of our age, and its lavishness and discipline in dining, have carried refinement so far, and have brought such disgust to the palate, that anything Apicius has not seasoned in a highly sophisticated manner now tastes foolish and stale. It is not enough to have said “pelorides” or “oysters” unless you add “Lucrine”; nor will the wolf-fish receive its proper honor today unless it has come from the Tiber and been thrown in among the bridges—an extravagance which Horace once reproached the Romans for treating as a fault [Note: Book II, *Satires* 2, lines 31 and following.].

It matters also whether such things are available everywhere or whether they are foreign and brought from far away. These stimulants of pleasure must be procured at the highest and most distinctly royal, rather than ordinary, expense. But if anyone does not immediately distinguish them, he is called rustic and said to have a plebeian stomach.

Meanwhile, however, we see health, strengthened by these supports, gradually rushing toward decline; and, in place of the enduring and vigorous strength of age, we see wasting and a new troop of fevers settling upon the earth.

Nor is the assembly of learned men more sparing of expense or labor when it prepares literary banquets for itself—especially those by which the taste is raised and stimulated when it lies sick and exhausted from the abundance of ordinary writers. Nothing has been left unattempted by the critics of our age. Everywhere one sees them searching most deeply into the chests of scholars, libraries, the old archives of sacred buildings, and the innermost sanctuaries; surveying seas and lands with excessive labor and expense; carrying everything from one place to another and mixing one thing with another.

We do not disdain cockroaches, moths, or other enemies of that kind, against whom we fight as new Andabatae (blindfolded gladiators); nor does anyone who possesses some monument of venerable Antiquity—even if it is worm-eaten and half torn apart—believe himself safe in the most hidden recesses and corners against the penetration of the ingenuity of our age.

Yet we know that, despite the addition of so many ancient Codices, literary scholarship has not been greatly increased, nor in proportion to the labor and expense; while devotion may perhaps have grown colder, so that one might wholly fear that, in the face of the excessive wisdom of the hypercritics of our age, that ancient simplicity—simple and vulnerable to the frauds of earlier times—might at last prove more desirable.

“But you commend,” you say, “the skill of our age and its honorable greed for the resources of learning and intellect.” We do not deny this, provided that you set a limit to that zeal; for vices lie close beside virtue. Because hands are diligently employed and minds nobly exercised on both sides, would you therefore call the audacity of bad men courage, or call the generosity of giving away what belongs to others liberality? These things are different.

Nor do I doubt that in these times the harvest of learning and books is far greater than it once was. Yet when it is thrown into the literary granaries—that is, the libraries—to be cleansed, we discover that not only sterile oats but also wretched darnel has grown up together with the wheat, while the desire of most writers to exalt their own works, and their premature love of praise, very often drives them off course.

We nevertheless had to offer these preliminary remarks against the hypercritics of our age [Col. 0584C] and their intemperance. If, with bleary eyes in a doubtful light, they happen to glimpse something, they advertise it as established—as though they had seen through it completely—thereby drawing the people, deceived by the lure of novelty, to themselves and seeking to win the reputation of the learned.

From the sequence of what we shall discuss below, we hope it will be evident that these remarks have not been made inappropriately or merely to beat the air, but are entirely relevant to our discussion. Nevertheless, we intend to harm or ridicule no one [Note: Although the term “hypercritics”—which we have deliberately used up to this point—sufficiently shows that these remarks were not made with the intention of applying them in any way to our opponents, men distinguished in learning and scholarship, we nevertheless wish to warn the readers again, and more openly, and we expressly call them to witness. Indeed, we acknowledge that the distinguished Blanchinus, who, as we shall soon say, was the first to publish a new opinion about Lawrence’s homeland, did not depart from the ancient and common view on the basis of some slight foundation, but relied upon an old and apparently most explicit authority, although, as we think, it should be referred to something other than Lawrence’s homeland. There will be an opportunity to discuss this below.]

Let us now explain the ancient and recent state of our controversy.

A certain Manlius, formerly a Calvinist—I do not know who—held that Lawrence, the unconquered deacon and martyr, was Roman by birth. Gretserus attacked him, intending to demonstrate the falsity of the Manlian thesis by the testimonies of the heterodox themselves—Hospinianus, Fabricius, and other members of the same sect [Note: Jacob Gretserus, S.J., *On the Feasts of Christians*, book II, chapter 9, fol. 348; in the Bollandists, 10 August, § 10, “On the Homeland of Saint Lawrence,” no. 101.]. Yet the Bollandist Fathers did not consider his arguments sufficiently strong to establish the matter; we have reported this judgment from them [Note: Father Jean Pinius, in the passage cited immediately above.].

But when those same Fathers had subsequently subjected to the most exact examination the force of the arguments on which Manlius relied in assigning Lawrence to the Romans—arguments elsewhere examined by the distinguished Francisco Carrillo of Córdoba [Note: In the work entitled *Historical Contest for the Homeland of Saint Lawrence*, Córdoba, 1673.]—they considered them so unworthy of consideration that they did not even think they should be proposed.

“As for the City of Rome,” they say [Note: Father Pinius, 10 August, § 11, “On the Place in Spain in Which Lawrence Lived,” no. 110], “as though Lawrence had drawn his birth from it, the opinion that asserts this appears to be so devoid of every appearance of probability that it deserves not even to be proposed, much less refuted.”

The compilers of the saints’ biographies valued no more highly the arguments on which the Roman birth of Lawrence was based. This was in the year of salvation 1733, when the distinguished John Pinius finally succeeded in arranging the Life and Acts of the most holy martyr.

But Fortune—which, as the poets say, celebrates or obscures human affairs according to its pleasure—seemed in this controversy too to be playing an extraordinary game. Barely two years had passed when, after the discovery at Verona of a Mass Sacramentary Codex from approximately that period, some learned men—men of the highest distinction, certainly, but, as I think, insufficiently acquainted with the character of liturgical Codices or with the purpose of the Church in arranging them—supposed that the homeland of Lawrence was expressly contained in it. So complete a change followed that anyone who now contends that the unconquered martyr was born anywhere other than in the City must be judged to have undertaken the defense of a difficult and wholly desperate cause.

I shall explain the matter in the order in which it occurred.

As the year of salvation 1735 was drawing to a close, the distinguished Joseph Blanchinus, a priest of the Roman Congregation of the Oratory and formerly a canon of Verona, was devoting himself entirely to completing the Vatican edition of Anastasius the Librarian—a work which his illustrious uncle Francis had left unfinished when death overtook him—and to enriching it with new additions.

In the prolegomena to the fourth volume of that work, pp. 12–57, he inserted a Sacramentary discovered by him not long before in the library of the distinguished chapter of the Church of Verona: that is, a very ancient Codex of Masses. If we may speak freely, he gave it the name “Leonian” somewhat more hastily than he ought to have done, simply entitling it as follows [ibid.]:

> **An Old Codex of the Sacraments of the Roman Church, Composed by Saint Leo, Pope I**

In this Codex, near the beginning of the month of August, where several Masses for the birthday of Saint Lawrence the Martyr are recorded, the twelfth in order has the following declaration, or preface [p. 38, column 1]:

> “Although, Lord, as you cause it to spread, the glory of your saints is renowned throughout the whole world, yet Rome rejoices in a singular way above the others in the solemnity of the blessed Lawrence, whose citizen by birth is a sacred minister and an offering dedicated to your name, belonging particularly to you.”

As soon as Blanchinus first greeted this passage from the threshold, he allowed himself easily to be deceived by the appearance of the words, immediately believed that Lawrence was Roman by birth, and judged that the ancient and widely accepted opinion favorable to the Spaniards should be erased from the minds of scholars.

The reason he did not at that time entrust a matter so far untested to the stage of the learned was that other and more serious concerns, into which he had voluntarily thrown himself, stood in the way. Scarcely had the Sacramentary been published, and the previously unheard-of name “Leonian,” together with the title prefixed to the Codex—by which it was said to have been composed **by Saint Leo**—become known to those more skilled in liturgical matters and ecclesiastical libraries, when Blanchinus was accused by them of violating criticism, indeed even summoned on a charge of injury, as though he had falsely attributed the Sacramentary to the most holy pontiff.

He therefore devoted himself entirely to clearing himself. After various and repeated examinations of the Sacramentary, and frequent consultations back and forth with learned men throughout Italy—whose replies plainly threatened his position [Note: The following distinguished men were consulted on this matter: Cajetan Maria Merati, a Theatine cleric regular and consultant on sacred rites; Eusebius Amort, canon regular of the Holy Savior; Polinganus; Ludovico Antonio Muratori; and the Reverend Father Joseph Augustine Orsi, master of the Apostolic Sacred Palace while we are writing this. All of them, whether in published studies or in private letters to Blanchinus, nevertheless with unanimous agreement judged that the Sacramentary should be denied to Saint Leo, as we are informed by Count Acamus (*Apologetic Dissertation on the Antiquity and Author of the Leonian Sacramentary*, part II, § 12 and following).]—he did not consider it opportune, while matters were still unsettled, to bring into the open the deeply absorbed opinion that Lawrence was Roman by birth.

But when, as time passed, he noticed that the rivalries of the parties had gradually cooled—as usually happens—and that some people were now calling the Codex Leonian, and even liturgists were using that name for it, in order to distinguish it from the Gelasian and Gregorian books, he finally judged that the time had come to publish to the general public the new opinion about the homeland of the most holy martyr which he had drawn from the Sacramentary.

Thus, when in 1741 he prepared the Collection of the Liturgical Works of the venerable Joseph Maria Thomasius, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, he published among its prolegomena, pp. 1–136, an ancient Codex of prayers belonging to the Gothic-Hispanic rite, recently recovered by him from the library of the Church of Verona and illustrated with notes. He maintained that it had once belonged to the Church of Tarragona, in the province of that name in Nearer Spain [Note: Annotation 22, p. 157, at the end and the following page.].

In that Codex, however, when discussing the prayers that formerly used to be sung or recited on the feast day of Saint Lawrence, in the Mass and Office of the saint himself—prayers corresponding among Blanchini’s annotations to the one numbered 106 [Note: p. 292, in the prolegomena]—he entered at length into a discussion of the birthplace of the unconquered martyr. With such force of conviction and confidence does he claim him for the Romans that one may rightly marvel at it in a learned man.

Thus, having dismissed the Spanish case and entirely ignored the arguments commonly advanced in its favor [Col. 0587A], as though he had nothing whatever to fear from that quarter, he proceeds confidently through a field thick with hazards, over fires concealed beneath treacherous ashes. First, from the Gothic-Hispanic prayer book that he himself published; then from another old Vatican manuscript, in which Lawrence is called *CIVIS ROMANUS*; next from Prudentius’s hymn, which he composed with consummate elegance concerning Lawrence’s passion and triumph; and finally from those words of the Veronese Sacramentary that we recently transcribed, he believed that the whole business of the controversy had been settled. He therefore delivers his judgment in these words [Note: p. 293, near the beginning]:

> If I said nothing else concerning the citizenship of Saint Lawrence, the case would be settled. For how could the testimony of so great a pontiff be weakened? [Col. 0587B]

(By “so great a pontiff” he means Saint Leo the Great; we shall discuss the matter below.)

Blanchinus, moreover, intoxicated by this false image of triumph, having summoned the Senate and Roman people—or rather, a gathering of the Fathers of the sacred apostolic college—asks what honor, according to ancestral custom, should be decreed to him who alone, after a long exile lasting many centuries, has restored to his fatherland and reclaimed for it the most illustrious Roman citizen, driven into exile by the unjust prejudices of historians [Note: “Shall I never restore him? ‘I, I am here!’ And since by decree of the S.P.Q.R. I am a Roman citizen, I say, claim, recall, and affirm that Lawrence was a Roman, to the everlasting glory and praise of that same Roman people.” And a little farther on: “From this, therefore, most limpid fountain”—he means the Veronese Sacramentary—“I shall draw purer waters and shall assuredly bring it about that all acknowledge that Lawrence is not to be excluded (sic: *segrepandum*) from the number of citizens, since he is a Roman citizen; but, on the contrary, that he is to be reclaimed amid the acclamation of the whole City and of the sacred apostolic college” (Blanchinus, Annotation 106, p. 292).]. Thus, although otherwise a modest and prudent man, he cannot restrain himself from overflowing like a torrent under the pressure of his excessive joy, and by this further argument reveals to us the happiness that he had long held back and suppressed in his heart.

Now, protected by this aegis, several other arguments of a conjectural [Col. 0587C] kind—arguments that until then had not even been permitted to whisper—take great courage, raise themselves up, and dare openly to cry out against the opinion favorable to the Spaniards. Nor are the spirits of the writers under Blanchinus’s leadership more downcast, nor is their fortune different.

Count Giacomo Acami, whom—as we shall show elsewhere [Note: In the dissertation *On the Author of the Veronese Sacramentary*, which we shall have prepared for publication when the time is ripe.]—there is the strongest suspicion of having written, not without Blanchinus’s prompting, a dissertation on the antiquity and author of the Veronese Sacramentary [Note: It appeared at Rome in 1748 in Italian, under the title *On the Antiquity, Author, and Merits of the Veronese Sacramentary Published by the Most Reverend Father Giuseppe Bianchini*.], thrusts the question of Lawrence’s birthplace upon his readers at the very point where he is completing that dissertation, under the heading “On the Supreme Authority of the Roman Church and Other Matters Pertaining to It” [Note: Part III, under this heading: “The Supreme Authority of the Roman Church, and Other Matters Pertaining to It,” § XII.]. On the basis of the words of the Sacramentary in question, which he himself quotes there, he declares that Lawrence was from Rome and that the matter is entirely beyond dispute.

When I read that dissertation, and found that, as its conclusion approached, it maintained a profound silence about Lawrence’s birthplace, I could not sufficiently marvel at what was happening—if indeed the matter was to end in that way. For Acami then bursts in unexpectedly (what, after all, has the supreme authority of the Roman Church to do with Lawrence’s birthplace?) and in the final words of the dissertation presents the reader, who was expecting nothing of the kind, with the testimony of the Veronese Sacramentary and a new opinion concerning Lawrence’s birthplace.

Acami, I suppose, was distressed that Lawrence should depart from the dissertation without being mentioned, and that the opportunity offered him to promote a new thesis should slip uselessly from his hands. But when, perhaps through an inadvertent interruption, the thread of his composition had been cut, the ingenious man preferred to attach to his work a patch sewn on somehow rather than conceal it through a silence that would plainly have harmed his cause.
