Nor, as I think, did it more properly belong to Merenda’s subject to insert Lawrence’s birthplace into his work while discussing the writings and deeds of Damasus [Note: Merenda’s work appeared at Rome in 1754 under the title *The Opuscula and Deeds of Saint Damasus, Pope*. Folio.], except by way of an occasion provided by the ancient Acts of the holy pontiff [Note: These are the Acts published from a manuscript Codex of the Basilica of Saint Peter by M. Milesius Sarazanius; we have often referred to them elsewhere.], in which Damasus is said to have been born in the same country as Lawrence. Yet, in the very place that properly called for a discussion of this question, he dared to pronounce nothing [Note: “For it may be strongly doubted whether Lawrence himself was born at Rome” (Merenda, *Opuscula and Deeds of Blessed Damasus*, ch. 1, p. 2).]; he merely asserts that it may be doubted whether Lawrence himself was born at Rome.

Later in the work, however, under the heading “On the Buildings of Damasus”—a substantially different subject—he pursues Lawrence’s birthplace at somewhat greater length [Col. 0588C], and does not hesitate to claim that the case for the Romans has been argued and demonstrated by the clear testimony of Saint Leo the Great [Note: “The illustrious man Joseph Blanchinus has demonstrated that this most powerful martyr [LAWRENCE] must be numbered among the Roman citizens, contrary to what had hitherto been believed, by the clear testimony of Leo the Great” (Merenda, *Opuscula and Deeds of Damasus*, § 3, “On the Works of Damasus,” p. 146, col. 1).]. He even adds a conjecture of his own, from which, if God so wills, it follows clearly [Note: “From this”—he means the conjecture drawn from Prudentius’s hymn—“it clearly follows that Lawrence is in no way to be separated from those illustrious sons of the City of Rome, Cossus, Camillus, and Caesar” (Merenda, at the place just cited).] that Lawrence should be listed among Roman citizens no less than Scipio or Laelius. Since we have indicated the cause of this *ἀναρμοστία*—this irrelevance—elsewhere, when discussing Damasus [Note: Namely, in the first part of this work, ch. 1.], we have decided to pass it over here.

Furthermore, the most distinguished Roman knight, Francesco Vittorio—as I learned after completing this work through an accidental conversation with him at Blanchinus’s house—having published during that period a philological dissertation [Note: It appeared at Rome in 1751, from the press of the Palearini brothers.], in which several monuments of sacred antiquity concerning our Lawrence are illuminatingly discussed, found an opportunity to speak of the posthumous glory of the most holy martyr on earth and of the sacred buildings in the City dedicated to his name. He therefore did not think that his earthly birthplace should be passed over in silence.

As though it were not enough to claim outright that Lawrence belonged to Rome and to declare that this must be regarded as certain [Note: “This much must be held certain concerning him [Lawrence]: Rome itself was his birthplace” (Vittorio, *Philological Dissertation*, p. 91).], he then censures the supporters of the contrary—and most widely accepted—opinion, and especially the Spaniards, because they had unjustly called Lawrence one of their countrymen.

“For what reason,” he says [Note: A little farther on, in the same work and on the same page.], “I ask, would persuade us that a foreigner, HISPANIC BY NATION, as some wrongly believe, and likewise a young man, immediately upon arriving in the City, should have been chosen from among many to serve the most holy pontiff” (he means Sixtus), “and should have been appointed and proclaimed deacon of the Roman Church? Would such an office be entrusted to a complete stranger? Would a man who knew no one in the City be appointed overseer of the poor and guardian of the Church’s treasury?”

Vittorio proceeds to defend his new opinion concerning Lawrence’s birthplace by the very arguments that Blanchinus had previously advanced. To these he adds, from the praises of our Spain that he claims are scattered throughout other hymns of Prudentius [Note: “For Prudentius, himself a Spaniard, recorded nothing concerning Lawrence’s Spanish origin, although, when speaking of others who derived their birth from that region … he mentions them explicitly, and the praises of the Spains are contained in several of his hymns concerning the deeds of the saints …” (Vittorio, at the place just cited).], and from Prudentius’s profound silence about Spain in the hymn dedicated to the martyr Lawrence, what he considers a further powerful conjecture.

Since these arguments are numerous and varied, but in my judgment too slight to deserve systematic treatment, I have decided to refute them briefly in passing and to ask Vittorio as a friend how he knows that Lawrence, immediately upon arriving in the City, was made deacon of the Roman Church by Sixtus, and appointed a complete stranger, entirely unknown, as overseer of the poor and guardian of the ecclesiastical treasury. Or why would Sixtus not rather have chosen for those offices a man whom he had long known, even before his pontificate, and had tested by repeated experience?

As for the foreign origin that Vittorio adds, he ought to have remembered that Sixtus too was a foreigner and was born in the middle of Greece. As for his censure of the supporters of the common and most widely accepted opinion, I have preferred to protect the reputation of both of us by silence rather than avenge the insult that, as we believe, he inflicted on so many learned men.

There is, however, one point concerning the praises of Spain in Prudentius’s hymns that I do not know how Vittorio overlooked, since Prudentius scarcely mentions the Spaniards at all. Certainly no praise of Spain, not even the slightest, is to be found in the entire book *Περὶ στεφάνων* (*On Crowns*) [Note: In the hymn concerning the saints Hemeterius and Chelidonius there is indeed a mention of *TERRA IBERA* (“Iberian land”); but this refers to Calahorra, watered by the river Ebro and preserving the sacred remains of those martyrs, not to Spain, as is clear from what follows:

> This happy IBERIAN LAND is mighty throughout the world by its crown.

> This PLACE seemed worthy in God’s sight to preserve their bones.

And a little farther on:

> When he consecrated the limbs of the martyrs in OUR CITY,

> which now protects the COLONISTS WHOM THE EBRO WATERS.

Prudentius also mentions *HESPERIA* in the hymn concerning Saint Cyprian; but it is clear from the word itself, without the addition of the epithet *ULTIMAE* or *EXTREMAE*, and from the sense of the passage, that Italy is meant. For he says:

> … he cherishes the Gauls, he imbues the Britons.
>
> He presides over HESPERIA; he sows Christ among the FARTHEST IBERIANS.

But if Vittorio wishes the praises of Spain to be contained in these last words, then by the same token he will have to say that Prudentius praised Gaul and Britain as well in his hymns. Finally, in the hymn concerning the saints Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius, Prudentius mentions the Spaniards in these words:

> God looks kindly upon the SPANIARDS.

I consider this praise, however, more general than Vittorio intended. In the remaining hymns there is profound silence concerning Spain and the Spaniards.] Yet enough of this.

More closely—and, as befits a historian, more cautiously—does the most reverend Father Joseph Augustine Orsi, at the time of writing this, Master of the Apostolic Sacred Palace, proceed in this matter. When I first heard that he opposed the Spanish opinion, I was somewhat shaken and collected myself, reconsidering afresh the arguments on which that opinion rests, and especially our conjectures, while reflecting deeply within myself on the gravity and learning of that outstanding man.

He does indeed seem inclined toward the new opinion favorable to the Romans. Indeed, he explicitly calls Lawrence a ROMAN CITIZEN, and in support of this brings forward the testimony of the Veronese Sacramentary that we have just quoted [Note: The learned M. Orsi, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. III, book VIII, § 114, p. 440, Roman edition of 1750, octavo: “He attributes [he says] especially to Prudentius the whole conversion of Rome to the prayers, merits, and glorious martyrdom of this illustrious citizen of hers” (he means Lawrence and cites the testimony of the Veronese Sacramentary), “of whom she rightly glories no less than Jerusalem does in Stephen.]. But since the words of that testimony, although at first sight they seem to proclaim Lawrence’s birthplace, do not entirely quiet the mind and are capable of multiple interpretations—we shall discuss this matter fully below—we do not yet know with sufficient certainty in what sense the learned author called Lawrence a Roman citizen.

If, however, in the course of his most complete work, so gratifying to our Spanish compatriots [Note: The Reverend Father Orsi is also heard among us when speaking Spanish; for his *Ecclesiastical History*, translated into Spanish, has already appeared in large part from the elegant presses of Madrid.], he should openly declare himself an advocate of the new opinion, it will not be so shameful for us to be defeated by so great a man as it will be honorable to have contended with him on behalf of our country.

Such, then, was the state of the controversy concerning Lawrence’s birthplace, and such the position occupied by the opinion favorable to the Spaniards, in the year 1755, when we write this. Whether other recent writers have subscribed to the new opinion assigning Lawrence to the Romans, we do not know. At least, apart from those already mentioned, we have so far been unable to find anyone; we shall therefore examine Blanchinus’s arguments and conjectures, and those of the others, individually, in their proper place and time.

Meanwhile, when we observed that one of them had argued the case for the Romans, another had demonstrated it and declared it indisputable, and still others were freely making various assertions, it more than once occurred to us to wonder whether, just as we see happen in military affairs, military stratagems might also be at work in these literary controversies—stratagems devised to break the spirit of the enemy—and whether Blanchinus might have wished to test the Spaniards with a *στρατήγημα* (“stratagem”) and try the fortunes of war.

At least, the example of so great a man, if it should be established that he seized upon uncertain matters as though they were certain, will remind us that the more strongly someone is inclined toward a cause, the more open he is to deception; and that no one is so prudent that he does not become imprudent when one attacks him while he is willing to be attacked.

Now let us turn to the arguments that favor the Spanish opinion.

## CHAPTER II  
### The Ancient Arguments of the Spaniards Confirmed. Merenda Refuted in Passing

I am not so confident as to hope that I alone can bring to a halt a matter disputed with such intense feeling—especially now that the adversaries have renewed the battle by adding fresh forces, namely recently unearthed Codices—or that I can place the Spanish side and its rights in a position of security.

I know that, until monuments concerning this question become as clear to us as the rays of the sun customarily are when the sky is clear, the dispute will remain, as the ancient comic poet once said, “before the judge.” I therefore reverence the most holy martyr, praying that in these our times he may graciously reveal such things for the protection and advancement of the worship properly owed to him among us, and that he may not abandon his own people—that is, the Spaniards, among whom he himself has hitherto wished to be counted by right and title—undeserving and anxious about losing the same honor. May so great an offspring of our Spain no longer be begrudged by foreign nations.

If I achieve only this—that by the arguments and replies soon to be brought forward against the objections of Blanchinus and his supporters I make the minds of the wise more favorably disposed toward the Spanish opinion, even though those arguments do not meanwhile add a decisive vote—I shall consider myself to have received a sufficiently ample reward for the scale of the labor undertaken.

For in this way that opinion will not lose the greater degree of probability that it possessed above the others, the degree assigned to it by the Bollandist Fathers after examining all the monuments discovered down to the year 1733 [Note: See under 10 August, § 10, no. 106; § 11, no. 3; and elsewhere.]. Nor will the ancient Spanish possession concerning Lawrence’s birthplace—strengthened by the decree of the learned, by the testimony of ancient Codices, and by the long consensus of the centuries—appear to have been in the least disturbed by the new efforts of Blanchinus and his followers.

Setting aside, therefore, in the interests of brevity, the testimonies drawn from the ancient Breviaries of the Churches of Toledo, Apt, Córdoba, and other churches throughout Spain, in which Lawrence is explicitly called a Spaniard, as well as the countless judgments of historians that we could produce—for we know very well that our critics would consider them of little value unless one credited them with a thousand years of antiquity—we cannot for that reason pass over in silence the testimony of a recent but illustrious Roman writer, who, as it is otherwise known, was by no means hostile to the Spaniards: namely, Maffeo Barberini, who soon afterward presided over the Catholic Church with supreme authority under the name of Urban VIII.

In the hymns that he composed as a singer of the sacred lyre, in the manner of Pindar, he addresses our Spain in one place with this elegant personification [Note: In the ode concerning Saint Lawrence, antistrophe 1.]:

> I shall sing of you, radiant with sacred light,  
> as the parent of Lawrence.

And shortly afterward [Note: Epode 1.]:

> Why do you heap up your anger, barbarous king?
>
> The HISPANIC YOUTH has learned fearlessly to despise  
> the savage commands of kings.

These passages, however, are offered merely for appearance’s sake, so that this new work of ours may not lack its own embellishment. In earnest, I wish to press upon our adversaries the testimony that I formerly produced from the Acts of Damasus. In those Acts the most holy pontiff is called Lawrence’s *COMPATRIOTA* (“fellow countryman”), and this occurs in the body of the Acts, which is their most ancient part.

We present their words [Note: In M. Milesius Sarazanius, p. 47.]:

> When blessed Damasus was working to restore the ruined churches, he asked the Emperor Valentinian the Younger for a certain garden situated below the walls of the City, so that he might build there a church of his FELLOW COUNTRYMAN, THE BLESSED MARTYR LAWRENCE.

(It is permissible to suspect that the word “Younger” was either added altogether or substituted for “Elder”; for just as the former was zealously favorable to the Catholics, so the latter was an ardent supporter of the Arian heresy [Note: There are nevertheless some who think that one should not despair of his eternal salvation, although he was killed while still a catechumen; Ambrose is among them.].)

At the end of the Acts [Note: Sarazanius, *Acts of Damasus*, p. 62.], when a question arose concerning miracles divinely performed in the Basilica of Saint Lawrence by the Theater of Pompey, where the remains of Damasus rest—namely, whether they should be attributed to Damasus or to Lawrence—their author adds:

> In miracles, however, we do not divide those WHOM ONE COUNTRY BROUGHT FORTH and one church advanced.

These statements should now be judged more probable, and more directly relevant to our case, than they were formerly, when we were discussing Damasus. For if the things we reported in the first part of this work concerning the birthplace of the holy pontiff are true, it will follow plainly from the passage in which the two are joined together that Lawrence too must be numbered among the Spaniards.

Thus either neither of them, or both of them, must be Spaniards, so that we may repeatedly employ that Persian maxim: “Either both or neither.”

As for the genuineness and antiquity of the Acts, Baronius has scarcely left us any room for doubt. “The Acts of Damasus,” he says [Note: Baronius, under the year 384, no. 19; and in the Bollandists, 10 August, § 10, no. 102.], “which were formerly accustomed to be read in the Church, exist among us in two very ancient Codices, namely in the fifth and tenth volumes of the *Lives of the Saints*. The same material is presented by the Vatican Codex and another belonging to Saint Mary Major, which we have seen; at the end of these the following words are read.” At that point he recounts the miracles of Damasus that Peter, a deacon of the Apostolic See, in a sermon delivered concerning the holy pontiff, records as having occurred in the same place—by which he means the Basilica of Lawrence.

Baronius himself explains why a question had arisen concerning the author of the miracles, and why some wished to attribute them to Lawrence rather than to Damasus—a circumstance that strongly supports the antiquity of the Acts.

“There still survived,” he says [Note: Baronius, under the year 384, no. 19.], “certain adherents of Ursicinus who, envying Damasus—even after his death—such glory, namely the glory of the miracles, declared that those miracles had been performed not through the merits of Damasus but through the intercession of blessed Lawrence.”

Now, since the doubt or controversy concerning the author of the miracles arose not long after Damasus’s death, we may infer that at that time the faction of Ursicinus and his followers had not yet died down. Thus Peter the Deacon—or whoever ultimately was the writer of that portion of the Acts—was free to borrow the matters concerning Damasus from the most ancient and uncorrupted monuments that lay before him.

The earlier portion of the Acts, in which, as we said above, Damasus is called Lawrence’s *COMPATRIOT*, must also be believed to derive from those same sources. Indeed, if nothing else could be brought forward in support of its antiquity, the single Life of Damasus written by the presbyter Benedict—which we cited from Sarazanius near the beginning of the first part of this work [Note: Ch. 1, pp. 12–13.]—amply demonstrates it.

Whether one considers the simplicity of its style, the author’s name and rank—though not his family profession—or finally the meaning of *Exiguus*, the surname by which he chose, in accordance with ancient usage, to be called, it is nevertheless sufficiently ancient in itself. It is a compendium, almost a brief version, of the Acts of Damasus under discussion here, as becomes immediately clear to anyone who compares the two.

Lest the word *COMPATRIOTA* cause anyone scruple, as though it were of more recent origin, we point out that it was already in use in the time of Nicholas I [Note: Nicholas I, in a letter to Egilo, Archbishop of Sens, vol. IX of Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, Venetian edition, col. 1525: “Moreover, when we sent letters to you and your FELLOW COUNTRYMEN and fellow priests.” Gregory [Book VIII, letter 37, to Innocentius, prefect of Africa]: “But if you desire to be nourished by a delightful food, read the works of blessed Augustine, your FELLOW COUNTRYMAN”—a passage that escaped the painstaking attention of Du Cange.] and even from the time of Gregory the Great.

As for Peter the Deacon, the author of the sermon on blessed Damasus, the Bollandist Fathers, after listing several men bearing that name who flourished from the sixth to the twelfth century [Note: Under 10 August, § 10, no. 104.], found none of them who had written about Damasus, and are therefore entirely uncertain which of them composed the sermon on the holy pontiff under discussion.

Baronius, however, Joseph Maria Suarez, and others [Note: In Nicholas Antonius, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book II, ch. 6, under Damasus, no. 180.] think that it should be attributed to a certain Peter the Deacon of Cassino, who flourished in the ninth century and is regarded as the author of the Life of Saint Athanasius, bishop of Naples. The earlier writer of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* discusses him under the years 850, 861, and 872.

Whichever of the two he may have been, Baronius’s testimony establishes that the Acts of Damasus, into which a compilation from his sermon was stitched near the end, were much older than that sermon.

Merenda, as we said elsewhere while discussing Damasus, thinks that he has not merely escaped the difficulty but has confined us in new straits by a new and convenient form of reply. Thus, after attempting several other futile expedients, he asserts that Lawrence, no less than Damasus, must unquestionably be numbered among the Roman citizens, on the authority of the Veronese Sacramentary. In that sense, he says, the writer of the Acts of Damasus could most truthfully have called them *COMPATRIOTS*, and Peter the Deacon, in the appendix to those Acts, could have called them *BORN OF ONE COUNTRY*.

Unless I am greatly mistaken, however, these arguments are far better suited to evading the difficulty—that is, to cutting the knot—than to untying it. To make the matter somewhat clearer, Damasus must be separated from Lawrence, and the question of Damasus’s birthplace must again be examined individually. For the moment, however, we shall place before the eyes of our readers what Peter the Deacon and the writer of the Acts thought about it, and what the common and generally accepted popular opinion concerning the question was in their time.

First of all, we must ask Merenda whether, during the lifetime of Peter the Deacon—whoever he ultimately was—or of the writer of the Acts in question, that is, from the sixth to the twelfth century, any doubt had already arisen concerning Damasus’s birthplace, or whether it had ever occurred to anyone anywhere to assign Damasus to the Romans [Col. 0594C] and to wage a dispute with the Spaniards over the matter.

Absolutely not, I say. In those more unlearned and simpler centuries, hypercritics had not yet arrogated to themselves as much authority as they have in our time: they did not permit the authority of ancient Codices to be abandoned, or opinions received and fixed in the minds of peoples to be uprooted or in any way weakened, merely on the basis of conjectures, however closely those conjectures might approach the truth.

And what are we to say of ecclesiastical books, which the people of that age revered as treasures of sacred antiquity and the most trustworthy guardians of the ancient and uncorrupted history of the pontiffs and the Church—just as they revered the Codices of both Covenants as sacred? Does Merenda think that if anyone at that time had dared to contradict the accepted ecclesiastical Codices and to diminish their reliability and authority—which, nevertheless, Terribilinus was permitted to do in our own age—he would have escaped unpunished under the canonical sanctions?

Moreover, how could that Peter, the deacon of the Apostolic See, or the writer of the Acts of Damasus—both of whom, by virtue of their rank and their undertaking of ecclesiastical writing, we must believe to have been no strangers to such matters—have ignored the clearest testimony in favor of the Spaniards concerning the birthplace of the most holy pontiff in Felicianus’s catalogue of the popes, when it is highly probable that, in the copies of that catalogue still surviving today, the Codex was already readily accessible at that time?

Are we also to suppose that the testimony of the *Pontifical Book*, written from the beginning of the eighth century; of the Palatine-Vatican Codex, which we have said was composed around the year 826; and finally of Anastasius, a contemporary of Peter the Deacon—as we conjecture—whose testimony explicitly calls Damasus a Spaniard, was entirely unknown to both writers? (I leave aside any ancient writings on the same subject that existed at that time but have not survived to our own age or still lie hidden in libraries.)

Or, if on the contrary they had examined all these sources, how could they have dared not merely to believe Damasus to be a Roman as a private opinion, but to propagate that belief publicly from the pulpit before a large gathering and even in published books—or, what amounts to the same thing, to proscribe and denounce as false the catalogue of the popes, Anastasius, and the other ancient Codices that asserted the contrary?

Furthermore, if no writer known to us, whether earlier or contemporary, ever conceived of making Damasus a Roman, how can we believe that these authors wrote or uttered the word *COMPATRIOT* and the phrase *BORN OF ONE COUNTRY* in that sense—as though both understood the holy pontiff to be a Roman by that statement, just as they understood Lawrence?

Moreover, the Acts under discussion were written at Rome, and their author plainly appears to address Romans in them. This is evident from the simple designation of places in the City where several events involving Damasus are recorded—designations that no one but a Roman or someone residing in the City could have understood [Col. 0595C].

We have deliberately placed certain passages from the Acts alongside them [Note: “And Liberius lived outside the City, at the third milestone, in the cemetery called Novella, on the Salarian Way” (*Acts of Damasus*, in Sarazanius, p. 42). The Ostrian Cemetery was not far from the Novella Cemetery (ibid., p. 45). “And on the third day Damasus came to the church of Saint Peter and purified that place which is on the right as one enters the Basilica of Saint Peter” (ibid., p. 46). “Damasus, meeting them, conducted the venerable relics [of Saints Julian and Caesarius] as far as the palace and reverently deposited them within the imperial chamber” (ibid., p. 50).].

Baronius also asserts, as we said elsewhere, that these Acts were formerly accustomed to be read in the Church. I interpret this as referring to the Roman Church; otherwise he would have specified a particular church.

Furthermore, that Peter, the deacon of the Apostolic See, was certainly a Roman, or at least a resident of the City, is clear from his rank and dignity. The place from which he delivered his sermon on Damasus was the pulpit of the Basilica of Lawrence, namely the center of the City. It must therefore have been a Roman assembly composed of every order.

How, then, could that Peter the Deacon and the writer of the Acts—being Romans and addressing Romans—if they likewise believed Lawrence and Damasus to be Romans, have called or asserted that they were *COMPATRIOTS* and *BORN OF ONE COUNTRY* in the very center of the City, without being greeted by the uproarious laughter of the assembled people and readers?

Or, if both writers believed Damasus to be a Roman, why would either of them call him the *COMPATRIOT* of Lawrence alone, rather than the *COMPATRIOT* of all Romans, or at least of those present at the assembly?

I do not think that Merenda sufficiently considered these points before replying to the words of the Acts.

The designation “citizen,” which, when we indicate a common fatherland, inferior Latin replaced with *CONCIVES* and *COMPATRIOTAS*, is, for those living outside their fatherland, a very common token of affection for their shared parent. But among those dwelling in their own fatherland, if someone wished to address his fellow citizens in that way, it would be unusual and plainly comical.

Let us imagine that in Suetonius, or in another Roman writer discussing Caesar, we read that Brutus had asked Caesar for the gardens that he owned in the Transtiberine region [Note: “Across the Tiber, far away, lies the place near Caesar’s gardens” (Horace, *Satires*, book I, satire 9, line 18).] so that he might build a villa there for Cassius, his *COMPATRIOT*—which is precisely what the account concludes Damasus asked from Valentinian.

Would we not think that such a statement had come from a mime or an actor rather than from a historian, since the event took place in the very center of the City and among Romans?

Why, then, would the writer of the Acts or that Peter the Deacon, when both were Romans and believed Damasus likewise to be a Roman, absurdly call him Lawrence’s *COMPATRIOT* in the center of the City and before a large Roman assembly?

Whoever attempts to reconcile these things achieves no more than one who, while physically present at Rome, searches for himself outside Rome. Let us, however, return from this digression to the road.

Saint Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, who composed the Martyrology published under his name in the ninth century, speaking of the martyr Lawrence, presents him as being asked by a tyrant who and what he was, and as replying in these words [Note: Saint Ado, in his Martyrology, under 10 August.]:

> As regards my descent, I am a SPANIARD; I was educated and brought up at ROME, and have been a Christian from the cradle.

If the adversaries once grant this passage credibility, it is obvious that the entire matter is settled. I have deliberately added that qualification because I know that Blanchinus relegates Ado’s Acts of Lawrence, together with those commonly circulated—namely, those of Surius [Note: They are found in his work, vol. IV, under 10 August.], those of Saint Maximinus of Trier [Note: His copy is praised by the Bollandist Fathers (10 August, § 12, no. 119).], and those of the Vatican Codex [Note: They are reproduced in full in Blanchinus’s prolegomena to the liturgical works of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius (Annotation 106, p. 293).], as well as those falsely attributed by someone to Donatus of Servitanus [Note: Fr. Bonaventure Ausina—or whoever hides under that name—in the booklet *On the Life and Passion of Saint Lawrence*, Salamanca, 1636. See the learned Augustine Salesius, my fellow citizen, in his letter to the most learned Gregorio Mayans, near the end of the work *Censure of the Fabulous Histories*, Valencia, 1742.]—as weak and entirely untrustworthy, to his “kinsmen and gentiles,” as they say.

But, with all due respect to him, “pigs have one smell, puppies another.”

[Col. 0597A] I readily acknowledge that the Acts of Lawrence whose opening is prefaced by an account of the deeds of the saints Abdon and Sennen, brought from Persia, the deaths of Decius and Valerian, and other matters scarcely consistent with historical truth, are rightly relegated by critics to the realm of fable, as Baronius long ago taught us [Note: [Col. 0597D] In his note on the Martyrology, 10 August.]. We likewise recognize that the Acts in which Decius’s expedition against the Persians is recorded suffer from the same defect of corruption or interpolation; for since that expedition can be made to agree or conform neither with the chronology nor with the other matters resting upon reliable historical testimony, the eminent Cardinal Norisius detected and demonstrated it to be suspect and wholly imaginary [Note: [Col. 0597D] Dissertation III, On the Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians, chapter 20, cols. 363–366, vol. II, Verona edition.]. Senior Pagius [Note: [Col. 0597D] In the Bollandists, 10 August, § 12, no. 124.], Dominicus Georgius [Note: [Col. 0597D] In the notes on Ado’s Martyrology, 10 August.], and other more recent critics followed him. Nor should those Acts of Lawrence be held in greater esteem which contain, under a common title, the passion of the saints Sixtus and Hippolytus, published a few years ago by Blanchini from an Old Vatican Codex IX—as he himself states—in order to confirm his opinion concerning Lawrence’s Roman nationality [Note: [Col. 0597D] Annotation 106 on the Gothic Orationary, in the Prolegomena to the work of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius, p. 293.]. For in them one finds not only that fictitious expedition of Decius against the Persians but also—as though this were not enough to weaken their credibility—the deeds of the saints Abdon and Sennen and the death of the emperors Decius and Valerian. We have said that these constitute the threefold mark of falsity in the Acts of Lawrence, so that from this very point we may judge the force and effectiveness of the argument Blanchini presses against us from that Codex [Note: [Col. 0597D] Antonius Maria Lupi, S.J., in his excellent work entitled *The Epitaph of the Martyr Severa*, p. 7, lists other Acts of Saint Lawrence, which critics consider wholly untrustworthy because of the intrusive history concerning a certain Tryphonia, concubine of Caesar Decius.].

This common taint of the Acts of Lawrence could very easily spread and infect whatever genuine material remained concerning the same subject, eventually making room for the prevailing prejudice against the corrupted Acts of the most holy martyr [Col. 0597C], so that thereafter no one would dare safely entrust himself to their testimony or adduce them as evidence on his own behalf in a doubtful matter. Perhaps for the same reason—and because Ado’s work is not entirely free of points at which one may hesitate—the distinguished Theodoricus Ruinart preferred the passion of Lawrence, most elegantly described by our Prudentius, together with the scattered testimonies of the ancient Fathers, to the published Acts of the most holy martyr and even to Ado’s Acts, and inserted the former into his excellent work; he consequently pronounced the common shipwreck of the Acts of Lawrence [Note: [Col. 0598D] *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, beginning at p. 180.]. Yet, if I may differ slightly from so great a man, Ado ought not to have been judged by the same standard as the other writers of the Acts of Lawrence [Col. 0597D] [Note: [Col. 0598D] It should be noted that Ruinart admitted into his work only those Acts which he understood to be entirely free from doubt. Thus he says in his Preface, p. XII: “If, however, anyone should judge some of the Acts which I perhaps rejected to be genuine, I shall not object, provided that he can prove this by sound arguments. Otherwise, let each person abound in his own opinion.”].

[Col. 0598A] The Bollandist Fathers were certainly fairer toward Ado, although Ruinart’s judgment could not have been unknown to them. Accordingly, after rejecting and proscribing as apocryphal or corrupted the Acts of Lawrence commonly circulated under the names of Surius, the Treviran copy, and others, they nevertheless rightly judged that Ado’s honor should remain intact and that he should not be relegated to the ranks of ordinary writers of Acts. We present their words [Note: [Col. 0598D] 10 August, § 12, no. 121.]:

“Ado inserted the Acts of Saint Lawrence—or, if you prefer, a summary of them—from a longer narrative which, as we suspect, had been placed before him and from which they were extracted. In them are related matters that concern Saint Lawrence more closely, without those digressions which have been ineptly mixed into the copy found in Surius and likewise into the Treviran copy.”

Moreover, in Ado we read nothing about the deeds of the saints Abdon [Col. 0598B] and Sennen, nor about Decius’s expedition against the Persians, nor about his sudden death and that of Valerian—those three marks of falsity in the Acts of Lawrence which we mentioned a little earlier. Consequently, on this ground there is no room for suspecting that they are defective. It is evident, furthermore, that the substance of the remaining narrative agrees remarkably with two other Codices cited by the Bollandist Fathers [Note: [Col. 0598D] They are designated P. Ms. 10 and P. Ms. 21 and are reported by the Bollandists in the passage cited immediately above, no. 119.] and even with Prudentius’s hymn; hence it would not be surprising if, among the other materials used by Ado in attaching this narrative to the series of Acts under discussion, our Prudentius too had served as a source placed before him.

One matter may cause us some hesitation: Ado explicitly states that Lawrence suffered under Decius, whereas otherwise it is certain that he obtained the crown of martyrdom only in the year 258, under the emperor Valerian, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, when Cornelius Saecularis was prefect of the City [Col. 0598C], a full six years having elapsed since Decius’s death. Yet that writer ought not to be blamed, since he may have read this long ago in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0598D] “Decius, after killing Philip father and son out of hatred for them, began a persecution against the Christians, in which Lawrence the deacon suffered martyrdom at Rome.” Eusebius, *Chronicle*, later book, under Decius.], from which this error spread very widely among later writers, as Baronius teaches us [Note: [Col. 0598D] In his note on the Martyrology, 10 August, letter B.]. Nor was that passage of Eusebius merely an occasion for writers to err indiscriminately before it was tested against the rules of chronology. Even after it had become clear from the testimonies of Pontius the deacon, Cyprian, and others, as well as from the chronology itself, that Decius had died much earlier and that Lawrence had suffered under Valerian, authors nevertheless devised various explanations to defend Eusebius’s statement, such was the authority of that writer. Thus some invented that Lawrence suffered under Valerian as prefect of the City, but under Decius as emperor; others claimed, contrary to the testimony of ancient writers, coins, [Col. 0598D] and inscriptions, that Gallienus, the son who ruled as Caesar with his father, had borne the praenomen Decius [Col. 0599A], although, as Baronius reports in the same place, Eusebius’s passage appears to have been corrupt or interpolated [Note: [Col. 0599C] Gallienus’s praenomina were Publius Licinius. On Greek coins Egnatius and Valerianus are also sometimes read. Numismatic writers should be consulted, in Patarol, on Gallienus.].

Indeed, those words—“in which Lawrence suffered martyrdom at Rome”—are not found in the Petavian or Bongarsian Codices of Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0599C] On this matter see Joseph Scaliger, *Observations on the Chronicle of Eusebius*, Amsterdam edition, 1658, p. 235, col. 2.]. Indeed, since nearly the same words are read almost verbatim in the same Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 39), except that Fabian’s name is substituted for Lawrence’s, we may suspect that the period was transferred from the *History* into the *Chronicle*. We present Eusebius’s passage from the *History*:

“Decius succeeds Philip. Because of his hatred toward Philip, he launches a persecution against the Churches. During it, when Fabian had completed his martyrdom at Rome, Cornelius succeeds to the episcopate.”

Similar, indeed almost identical, are the statements that follow in both places concerning Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem.

In the midst, then, of so great and so widespread a plague of error, it is not at all surprising that Ado, a ninth-century writer—at whose time chronological studies were entirely neglected—should, carried along by the common prejudice of others, have asserted, without investigating the chronology, that Lawrence suffered under Decius. This is even less surprising because his purpose was to report the deeds and passions of the martyrs truthfully rather than to bring chronological calculations into conformity with chronology. Indeed, I have more than once suspected that our own Prudentius too, swept along by the storm of common prejudice [Col. 0599B], inclined to the view that Lawrence suffered under Valerian not as emperor but as prefect of the City. The frequent mention of the prefect in his hymn gives rise to this conjecture [Note: [Col. 0599D]

“The prefect of the royal City busies himself with the hunger for money.” (Stanza XII.)

“Then the prefect swells,

joyful with delight . . .” (Stanza XXXIII.)

“The prefect trembles, stunned.” (Stanza XLVI and frequently elsewhere.)].

It is possible, however, that Prudentius never named him because of the meter. I leave the matter open for consideration.

If anyone nevertheless wishes to defend Ado’s testimony, where he asserts that Lawrence suffered under Decius, and reconcile it with the other authors, we may indeed say that Adso used *under Decius* (*sub Decio*) in the sense of *during the persecution of Decius*; for the persecution under Valerian which we are discussing retained the name of Decius. In this sense Adso could most truthfully have said that Lawrence suffered under Decius. Although Augustine, [Col. 0599C] Severus Sulpicius, Orosius, and others [Note: [Col. 0599D] In Baronius’s note on the Martyrology, letter B.] distinguish the persecutions of Decius and Valerian, and invariably call the former the seventh and the latter the eighth—a view which I do not deny to be the more widely accepted—there are nevertheless ancient Fathers who maintain that the two were one persecution, though a two-headed hydra. Besides the various examples from Martyrologies and Acts of Martyrs [Col. 0600A], in which that persecution is designated indiscriminately by the name of either emperor, this is demonstrated by the testimony of Optatus [Note: [Col. 0599D] “That war,” he says, “is called a persecution, which was carried out under the two beasts among those four whom Daniel saw rising from the sea. This was the persecution under Decius and Valerian.” Optatus of Milevis, book III.], who asserts that Daniel saw both under the single figure of a lion, and by the explicit authority of Jerome [Note: [Col. 0600C] At the beginning of the *Life of Paul the Hermit*: “Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, at the time when Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage were condemned to a glorious death,” and so forth. Likewise in his *On Illustrious Men*, under Methodius: “Under Decius and Valerian he was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece.”].

Some think that this happened because Decius appointed Valerian as his colleague in the empire [Note: [Col. 0600D] Zonaras, in Baronius’s note on the Martyrology, letter B.]. Baronius says that this was approved by none of the ancients; on the contrary, we know that Valerian was first hailed emperor by the Rhaetian army. The truth of the matter must therefore be sought from Baronius himself, whose words we shall give as concisely as possible [Note: [Col. 0600D] Baronius, in the same place.]:

“When Decius,” he says, “had granted Valerian extensive authority by decree of the Senate, as Trebellius Pollio writes—not merely the censorship according to ancestral custom, but also an authority increased by the power voluntarily to enact laws—it resulted that the measures promulgated against the Christians, just like other edicts, were inscribed with the names of Decius and Valerian. Thus the persecution announced under this common title at the beginning continued into Valerian’s time, especially since he had no need to write new laws against the Christians, seeing that those previously promulgated by Decius were still in force” [Col. 0600B] [Note: [Col. 0600D] See Senior Blanchini, who in volume II of Anastasius, under Sixtus, section XXV, p. 225, in his historical notes, offers several other conjectures to show that the persecution of Decius and Valerian was not without reason regarded by the ancients as one and the same.].

From this, the distinguished father of the *Annals* thinks, it follows that the persecution of Decius and Valerian is often called by their common name and sometimes by the name of only one emperor, though indiscriminately—especially by that of Decius, who perhaps first proclaimed it, although he had long since been taken from the living. He adds, by way of a most illuminating confirmation, the example of the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian: even after its authors had been removed, it retained their name under Galerius Maximianus Armentarius, who carried it out with extreme severity. This is shown by various Acts of Martyrs and by the unmistakable testimony of Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0600D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 2. That persecution began in the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, A.D. 302, or the following year, since the authorities differ on the point. After it had afflicted the Church for ten continuous years, as Eusebius himself testifies in the same book, chapter 16, Diocletian and his colleague Maximian Herculius carried it out only during the first two years; during the following eight years it was carried out by Galerius Maximianus Armentarius. Even in his time the persecution retained the name of the earlier emperors and is consistently called in the Acts and Martyrologies the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian Herculius.].

From this shared use of the names of Decius and Valerian, let me add this in passing, a strong suspicion has arisen in my mind that the fictitious expedition of Decius which we discussed earlier may have arisen from the genuine expedition of Valerian against Sapor, king of the Persians, with only the name of the author changed. But these matters are insufficiently established.

To return to the subject: it seems to me beyond dispute that Ado’s Acts possess a much greater—or rather, a different—degree of credibility than those which we cited from Surius, the Treviran copy, and the Vatican Codex published by Blanchini. Indeed, without doing Ado an injustice, his Acts cannot at all be compared with the others commonly circulated or indiscriminately relegated to the category of corrupted texts. Baronius too, while warning us to beware of the Acts whose opening includes the deeds of the saints Abdon and Sennen, immediately adds [Note: [Col. 0601D] In his note on the Martyrology, letter A.]:

“We say this for the purpose of enabling the prudent reader to separate those Acts from the genuine Acts of Saint Lawrence.”

That eminent man would have given this warning in vain if no Acts of Lawrence that had not been corrupted then existed, or if he had believed the credibility and authority of all of them equally defective and weak. Why, then, should he not have considered Ado’s Acts more genuine than the others and directed his discussion toward them, since he found in them none of the threefold mark of falsity mentioned above and since their narrative sequence is otherwise simpler and more self-consistent?

Although this is so, we do not wish such authority to be attributed to Adso’s Acts that we can safely assent to everything in them, nor do we wish their testimony to be compared with the Acts of holy martyrs known to have been written by eyewitnesses or contemporary authors. Nevertheless, we do not despair that more judicious critics, on the authority of Ado alone—even if other evidence were lacking—might become somewhat more inclined toward the opinion favorable to the Spaniards. Those others, however, whose great pleasure consists in bringing novelties before the public, should be restrained, lest they dare hereafter to assert that Ado, when discussing Lawrence’s homeland—on which matter no one before Blanchini had ever brought a suit against him, and which is wonderfully supported by the very long and nearly fifteen-hundred-year consensus of authors—did not speak with the degree of reliability appropriate to a historian.

The Bollandist Fathers understood this very well. Besides the constant tradition of the Spaniards, Ado’s single testimony inclined them more strongly toward the widely accepted opinion concerning Lawrence’s homeland:

“Although we do not readily possess,” they say [Note: [Col. 0601D] 10 August, § 10, no. 106, toward the end.], “the most ancient testimonies we would wish to have in support of the Spanish tradition and possession, nevertheless, so far as we are concerned, nothing shall prevent the devout Spanish nation from claiming Saint Lawrence as its own, invoking him as its own, and continuing to venerate him with steadfast devotion—especially since, as early as the ninth century, we find him regarded as a Spaniard in Ado’s Martyrology on this day, where the martyr is introduced as speaking thus:

‘AS TO MY ORIGIN, I AM A SPANIARD, EDUCATED AND BROUGHT UP AT ROME.’

And shortly afterward, in the notes on Ado’s Martyrology [Note: [Col. 0601D] On the same day, under the heading “Other Acts,” letter Q. Venetian edition, p. 520.], after the words ‘AS TO MY ORIGIN,’ and so forth, they say:

‘It is chiefly on the basis of these words that we have granted Saint Lawrence to the Spaniards.’

Elsewhere, speaking of that deacon Peter whom we said had been discussed in connection with Damasus, they say [Note: [Col. 0601D] 10 August, § 10, no. 104.]:

‘Although it is not known to us with certainty whether one of the deacons named Peter wrote those Acts of Saint Damasus which Baronius cited above, nevertheless, since that eminent man affirmed that they exist in two very ancient Codices, this provides some additional and not unwelcome support for the opinion of the Spaniards, who claim Saint Lawrence as one of their countrymen.’” [Col. 0602B]

## CHAPTER III. New Efforts on Behalf of the Spanish Opinion

The arguments advanced on behalf of the Spaniards thus far—if one excepts Merenda’s refutation—were first set forth by the Bollandist Fathers. Nor do I, when I find that in the matter of elucidating Lawrence’s homeland nothing had been left unattempted by the greatest men, who had labored mightily on both sides, nevertheless find everything exhausted; I ought rather to hope that this work of ours, undertaken after the earlier efforts on the same subject, may prove more effective. Yet, in addition to the human inclination to penetrate into every hidden matter, my mind was strongly stimulated by this: when our native writers had neglected Lawrence’s homeland, I observed that the opponents had attempted everything in order to add weight and authority to a new opinion. Whether, then, as they say, I have made a worthwhile effort after casting the die, will be decided and judged by the readers.

First of all, we must know that at the beginning of the seventh century, at least from the year 633, when it is established that the Fourth Council of Toledo was held under Sisenand, king of the Visigoths [Note: [Col. 0601D] We may suspect that this communion in sacred liturgy between the Spaniards and the Gallo-Goths already descended from the Third Council of Toledo, held under Reccared in the year 589, as seems to be indicated in its second canon.], the rite of celebrating Masses, and consequently the Missal or Sacramentary Codex used by the churches of Spain—apart from one or another distinctive feast or rite—was entirely the same as that used in sacred liturgy by the Church of Gothic Gaul, or Narbonensis, and by that part of Aquitaine which at that time obeyed the Spanish kings. This has been recognized by more expert liturgists on the authority of that same council [Col. 0602D] [Note: [Col. 0601D] Fourth Council of Toledo under Sisenand, A.D. 633; especially canon 13, where it says: “Let Spain and Gaul likewise celebrate”—that is, Narbonensis, which obeyed Sisenand.], including Cardinal Bona [Note: [Col. 0602D] Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 12, no. 6; Cardinal Thomasius, Preface to volume VI of *The Gothic Missal*, in Muratori, *Ancient Roman Liturgy*, volume II, p. 513; Mabillon, Preface to the *Gallican Sacramentary*, no. 4.], to whom Blanchini too does not dissent [Note: [Col. 0602D] Annotation XVI on the most ancient Orationary of the Gothic Rite, p. CLIV.].

We must also know that the properly so-called Gothic Missal—that is, the one used at that time by the churches of Spain—was, no less than the Gothic-Narbonensian and Gothic-Aquitanian Missals, very different from the books of Masses then in use among the Romans. This difference concerned not merely the calendars and the sequence of feasts, for it would hardly be surprising if these were celebrated differently in different places, but also the syntax and arrangement of the book. This will become immediately clear to anyone who compares Thomasius’s Gothic-Gallican Missal with the Gelasian Missal published by the same venerable cardinal, and also with the three Gregorian Codices of Pamelius, Rocca, and Menard [Note: [Col. 0603D] The Gelasian and Gregorian Missals are extant in Muratori’s dissertation on ancient Roman liturgy, published at Venice in 1748.].

Third, it must be known that the Gothic-Gallican or Narbonensian Missal was uniform with the Missal of the other Gauls—Belgian, Celtic, and Frankish—as regards the structure of both and the rites and parts of the celebration of Mass. It was nevertheless dissimilar with respect to the collections, calendars, and *Contestationes*, and especially with respect to the sequence of feasts, which were celebrated differently in each region. The first part of this thesis has Cardinal Bona [Note: [Col. 0603D] In Cardinal Thomasius’s preface to the Frankish and Gallican Missals, volume II of Muratori’s dissertation on ancient Roman liturgy, p. 514.], Thomasius [Note: [Col. 0603D] Cardinal Thomasius in that preface.], Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0603D] Preface to the Boviensis Gallican Sacramentary, no. 2; Muratori’s dissertation, volume II, p. 770.], and Blanchini himself [Note: [Col. 0603D] Annotation XVI on the most ancient Orationary of the Gothic Rite, p. CLIV.] as its authorities. The second is demonstrated by a comparison of the Missals with one another. Each Missal presents the solemnities more celebrated in the region or province to which it belongs; and, where the title is absent from the Codices, liturgists infer to which church the Missal once belonged.

Nor should anyone be disturbed by Cardinal Thomasius’s statement [Note: [Col. 0603D] In the same preface, toward the end of the section on the Frankish Missal.]:

“The very order of the Mass was the same throughout Gaul, whether in Narbonensian and Aquitanian Gaul, which once obeyed the Visigoths, or in Celtic and Belgian Gaul, where the Franks established the beginnings of their kingdom in Gaul.”

This must be understood as referring to the structure of the Missal and to the parts of the Mass and the sequence of prayers recited in it, not to the similarity or uniformity of the collections or Contestationes, much less of the Feasts and the calendar—and this according to the mind of the venerable cardinal himself. For a little farther below [Note: [Col. 0604D] In the passage cited immediately above.], when speaking of the Frankish Missal—which Morinus [Note: [Col. 0604D] In Cardinal Thomasius, in the same place.] wished to assign to the Church of Poitiers—he says:

“I add only this: this Frankish Missal clearly demonstrates that the ancient rite of Gaul in the Mass was in many respects unlike the Roman, but similar, IF WE CONSIDER THE SEQUENCE OF THE PRAYERS (these words should be noted), to the Gothic and Gallican Missals published here.”

Mabillon agrees [Note: [Col. 0604D] Preface to the Boviensis Gallican Sacramentary, no. 7, in Muratori, volume II, dissertation on ancient liturgy, p. 771.]. He says that the Boviensis Sacramentary of the province of the Sequani, for this reason, does not agree in all respects with the Gothic-Gallican Missal:

“For although before the reign of Charlemagne there was a uniform rite of celebrating Mass in the churches of Gaul, and the same parts, nevertheless the collections, readings, and contestationes were not everywhere the same . . . It is therefore not surprising if the province of Narbonensis, which at that time obeyed the rule of the Goths, did not agree in all respects with the other Gallican provinces.”

Now, because it greatly supports our purpose, I shall readily explain the origin of this twofold difference between the two Missals. The difference of rule could have caused the dissimilarity of the prayers; for it prevented the Fathers of the province of Narbonensis—although we know that they came to Toledo for councils—from joining the other bishops of Gaul in a single national synod. It is also clear that each diocese had feasts proper to itself. Each province displayed and celebrated in its calendars the solemnities of its saints—apart from those of Christ, the most blessed Virgin, and the Apostles, which were common to all churches—whose deeds performed in those churches, and whose assumption of the episcopate, preaching, or passion, were commemorated; especially those whose sacred remains rested in those places and whose Acts of martyrdom were preserved there.

If the matter were not already clear, we could readily demonstrate it with numerous examples drawn from the ancient liturgies of the churches. Concerning the relics and Acts of the martyrs, we cite the distinguished Ruinart abundantly [Note: [Col. 0604D] Preface to the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, no. 18.], and we even have Blanchini agreeing with us in part [Note: [Col. 0604D] Annotation XII on the most ancient Orationary of the Gothic Rite, toward the end, p. CXLIX.]. Speaking of the sacred relics of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen, which our distinguished fellow-countryman Paulus Orosius brought from Africa to Spain at the beginning of the fifth century [Col. 0604C] [Note: [Col. 0604D] The distinguished fellow-countryman Nicholas Antonius seems somewhat doubtful whether the sacred relics of the most blessed protomartyr ever reached the Church of Braga, to which they had been sent; see *Old Spanish Library*, book III, chapter 2, no. 43, p. 187.], this author thinks that the following was the reason why, from that time onward, an office for the most holy protomartyr was celebrated in Spain. He might also have added that this was why Stephen’s feast was celebrated among the Spaniards with a more solemn rite than the feasts of the other distinguished local martyrs. But perhaps more on this elsewhere.

Now, to come closer to our objective, we must determine whether at the beginning of the seventh century, or not long before that time, relics of the most holy levite Lawrence existed somewhere among the Spaniards. The Bollandist Fathers, who treated this subject expressly, enumerated the cities throughout Germany, Belgium, Gaul, and the East that possessed these sacred pledges [Note: [Col. 0604D] 10 August, §§ 3 and 7, no. 65.], but they maintain a profound silence about our Spain. Consequently, Spain was not permitted to be so blessed until the time of King Philip II and the construction and dedication by him of the distinguished Escorial monastery to the most holy levite [Col. 0604D].

For the centuries following Lawrence’s death we produce Prudentius as an authoritative witness. After describing the glorious martyr’s passion with the greatest elegance, he piously envies the Romans the privilege of the tomb, because they could venerate his sacred bones in their presence. These are Prudentius’s words [Note: [Col. 0605B] Stanza 133, verse 529.]:

“O thrice, four times, and seven times blessed

is the inhabitant of the City

who celebrates you, Lawrence, and the resting place

of your bones close at hand.”

And a few lines later:

“But we who lack these blessings,

and cannot see before our eyes

the traces of his blood,

gaze from afar upon heaven.”

As for the Acts of Lawrence, those same Fathers rightly question [Note: [Col. 0605B] 10 August, § 12, no. 125.] whether any original and genuine Acts existed at Rome or elsewhere in the fifth century. From this alone we may already infer that they did not reach the farthest West at a very early date [Col. 0605B]. We know in addition that, if our opponents grant that Lawrence ever left our Spain, he never returned there—whatever someone may tell stories about journeys undertaken by him and Pope Sixtus is wholly devoid of any appearance of truth [Col. 0606A]. We also know that he was brought up and educated at Rome from childhood, that there he attained the rank of levite and the dignity of archdeacon, and that he suffered and was buried in the City. Thus, if we except his homeland, even the Spaniards themselves do not deny that Lawrence was Roman in every other respect [Note: [Col. 0605B] See below the third note appended to this dissertation under the name “Addenda.” EDITOR.].

Nevertheless, in that Gothic-Gallican Missal which we mentioned earlier, and which we may reasonably call Spanish, or at least related to Spain [Note: [Col. 0605B] I know that the very learned Father Alexander Lesleus does not approve the view that the Gothic Missal under discussion belonged to any of the Gothic-Gallican churches, but rather to Gaul subject to the Frankish empire. He bases this on the practice of the three-day Rogation observances before the Ascension and on the non-continuous observance of Lent throughout the forty days; he asserts that neither practice existed among the Spaniards. Yet it is otherwise known that the same ecclesiastical rites were used in Spain and in Narbonensian Gaul from the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo. Nevertheless, the opinion of Cardinals Bona and Thomasius, as well as of Mabillon, Lebrun, Blanchini [Annotation VI, p. CXLI], and other liturgists, seems to us far more probable. All of them unhesitatingly assigned that Codex to Narbonensian Gaul and regarded it as belonging to that church—not merely on the basis of the more recent title prefixed to the Gothic Missal, as Lesleus claims, but on the basis of various prayers transferred from the Gothic Missal into this Codex; also on the basis of its agreement with the Gallican synods, which Thomasius draws from canons 13 and 30 of the Council of Agde, held under Alaric, king of the Goths, in the year 506; and on the basis of other arguments and conjectures that may be consulted in those authors. Indeed, apart from the feast-days of our Lawrence, and of Sixtus and Hippolytus, which are expressly found in the Codex under discussion, although none of them is found in the Luxovian, Frankish, or Boviensis Codices, nor in the Old Gallican Codex belonging to Celtic, Belgian, and Frankish Gaul, there is one feast of Eulalia of Mérida celebrated in the same Gothic Missal, while the Gallo-Frankish Codices are entirely silent about her—even though we know from the testimony of Venantius Fortunatus and Gregory of Tours that Eulalia was also famous among the Gauls. This almost proves beyond doubt that the material came from the proper Missal of the Goths and passed into the churches of Narbonensian Gaul. As for the three-day Rogations objected to by Lesleus, that ancient custom of Gaul, deeply rooted in the minds of the peoples, might have been retained by the Gallo-Gothic churches even after the Fourth Council of Toledo. What if we should suspect that, although first instituted in Gaul, they were also observed in some places among the Spaniards? Rabanus certainly states that a three-day fast before the Ascension was customary among the churches of the West (*On the Instruction of Clergy*, book II, chapter 40). Saint Isidore also mentions the three-day fast (*On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 40); but Walafrid Strabo is an authoritative witness that among the Spaniards this was observed after the Ascension, indeed after Pentecost (*On Ecclesiastical Matters*, canon 28). As for the non-continuous observance of Lent throughout the forty days, it is entirely uncertain whether this prevailed in the church to which the Codex in question belonged. Indeed, I think that the fast in that church, as in the churches of Spain, consisted of no more than thirty-six fasting days; otherwise, in that Codex the fast would necessarily have had to begin on the Wednesday before the First Sunday of Lent, which for this reason is called the “Beginning of the Fast” in the Gregorian Sacramentary (Muratori, volume II, in *Roman Liturgy*, col. 300), and by Amalarius (*On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 7), Alcuin (under the heading “On the Beginning of the Fast”), and others; nor would the Lenten period end after six weeks. The statement in that Codex concerning “the forty days of fasting completed continuously by Christ the Lord, and observed by the faithful for the same number of days, though in portions because of their weakness” need not trouble anyone. It is not necessary to understand that number of forty days as referring to an equal number of fasting days on which an evening meal was taken; rather, because of the roundness of the number, it may properly be understood of the whole period of fasting—that is, the Lenten season—even though this consisted of forty-two days. The days are said to be observed in portions, perhaps because the fast was not continuous, as Christ’s fast had been, but was released and interrupted four or five times on Sundays. Isidore also indicates this (*On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 36), saying: “For when the Sundays are subtracted from Lent, on which the fasts are relaxed, we come together to the church on these thirty-six days, as though they were the tithes of the whole year,” and so forth. Finally, the communion of rites between the churches of Spain and Gothic Gaul was not so extensive, even after the Fourth Council of Toledo, that they did not still differ in some respects. This may be gathered from canons 2 and 3 of the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, held under Egica in 694, and likewise from Egica’s *Exhortation to the Fathers of that Council*. Indeed, it is clear from canon 3 of the Eleventh Council of Toledo, held under Wamba around the year 675, and from other decrees of the councils of Spain, that even among the churches of Spain there was some diversity in the rites of the Mass and of the ecclesiastical Office, not long after the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo.], although neither the famous levite and martyr Vincent, nor Felix, who died as a martyr at Gerunda, on the slope of the Pyrenees and indeed at the very entrance to Gothic Gaul, nor Cucufas, who suffered not far from Barcelona, nor Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius, who suffered at Tarragona, nor, finally, any other of the more illustrious Spanish martyrs—with the exception of Eulalia of Mérida—has an office, a Mass, or even a mention in the feasts of their births; in that Missal, I say, our Lawrence is not only celebrated in a particular Mass for his own feast, which would not be so surprising, but is also given so prominent an encomium in the feasts of Saint Sixtus, the pope who preceded him in the struggle by three days, and of Saint Hippolytus, who completed his martyrdom three days after Lawrence, that it seems as though the feast of the most holy levite, rather than that of either martyr, or indeed Lawrence’s own feast, were being celebrated in both cases. Conversely, in the Mass proper to Lawrence, there is not a word about Sixtus and no mention at all of Hippolytus. We shall present Lawrence’s entire Mass; but, to spare the readers weariness, we shall give only the *immolationes* of the Masses of Sixtus and Hippolytus.

# MASS FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT LAWRENCE THE MARTYR

[Note: [Col. 0607D] *Gothic-Gallican Missal*, first edited by Em. Thomas and inserted by Cl. Muratori into his dissertation *On the Ancient Roman Liturgy*, vol. II, col. 627.]

God, savior and ruler of your faithful, almighty and everlasting God, graciously attend to the prayers of today’s solemnity, and kindly look upon the joys conceived by the Church over the glorious passion of your martyr, **BLESSED LAWRENCE** (thus printed) [Col. 0607B]. May the faith of all be increased by the rise of so great a virtue, and may the hearts of those rejoicing be set aflame by the sufferings of the martyrs, so that by your mercy we may be aided by the merit of him whose example fills us with exultation. Through our Lord.

The Collect follows.

God, creator and ruler of the world, who consecrated this day through the martyrdom of this, your **LEVITE LAWRENCE** (thus printed), mercifully hear your suppliants, and grant that all who venerate the merits of his martyrdom may, through his intercessions, be freed from the everlasting fires of Gehenna. Through the Lord.

Collect after the names.

Grant us, Lord, your manifold grace in the celebration of **BLESSED LAWRENCE** the martyr, so that the Christian people may learn from the contest of so great a struggle both to strengthen steadfast endurance and to rejoice in a devout victory.

Collect for peace.

May the just prayer of Saint **LAWRENCE**, Lord, we ask, protect us; and may that which our conscience does not presume to request be granted to us through the prayer of him who pleased you. Through our Lord, your Son.

## Sacrificial Prayer of the Mass

It is truly worthy and just, almighty and everlasting God, to offer you sacrifices of praise for so great a martyr, **LAWRENCE**: you who today received a living sacrifice through the ministry of this, your **BLESSED LEVITE LAWRENCE**, in the flower of his chaste body. We heard his voice, in the hymnlike modulation of the Psalm [perhaps: *modulati*, “having sung melodiously”], singing and saying: “You have tested my heart, O God, and visited the night” (thus printed), that is, amid the darkness of the world: “You tested me with fire, and no iniquity was found in me.”

O glorious strength of the contest! O unshaken constancy of the one confessing! Living limbs, placed upon the gridiron, hiss; and amid raging coals, panting [perhaps: *anhelantia*, “panting things”], they present their burning as an odor, after the manner of incense (*thymiamatis*), to the divine nostrils. For the martyr himself says with Paul: “We are the good odor of Christ.” He was not thinking how, once placed upon the earth, he might escape the danger of suffering, but how he might be crowned among the martyrs in heaven. Through Christ our Lord. Through whom.

# ON THE FEAST OF SAINT SIXTUS, POPE AND MARTYR

## Sacrificial Prayer of the Mass

[Note: [Col. 0607D] In Muratori, *Dissertation on the Roman Liturgy*, col. 626.]

It is truly worthy and just, right and salutary, to sing continual praises to you, holy Lord, almighty Father, everlasting God. Through Christ our Lord. By his coming he permitted those who believe in him to pass into the heavenly kingdom, because those who offer themselves as witnesses of your truth kill the enemy when they are killed. Among them is the holy and venerable martyr **SIXTUS**, whose solemnity is celebrated today. When he had received the insignia of the apostolic see and saw himself to be first among the priests, he embraced the opportunity of a saving passion, and not only stripped off the worldly stains of corruption but also became an example to the others. For immediately his own distinguished minister, the venerable Lawrence, likewise imitating his victory, received the palm of victory—the adornment for which he was bound to undergo punishment—so that he might deserve to attain eternal glory (thus printed). Through Christ.

# ON THE FEAST OF SAINT HIPPOLYTUS THE MARTYR

## Sacrificial Prayer of the Mass

[Note: [Col. 0608D] In Muratori, *The Ancient Roman Liturgy*, vol. II, col. 628.]

It is truly worthy and just, almighty and everlasting God, that you suddenly made blessed **HIPPOLYTUS**, still occupied in the tyrant’s service, the companion of **LAWRENCE** (thus printed). Set ablaze with spiritual fervor, while he truthfully confessed your only-begotten Son, our Lord, before the authorities, he was subjected to punishments, bound in chains, pierced with *cardis* [perhaps: *carduis*, “thistles”], and torn apart by the ferocity of horses; and, having attained the palm of martyrdom, he was crowned with perpetual life together with the victor and teacher **LAWRENCE**. Through Christ our Lord.

From this highly distinctive panegyric of our Lawrence in the feasts of the saints Sixtus and Hippolytus, anyone will immediately infer that a far greater regard was held for that most holy levite than for these martyrs in the Gothic-Gallican Missal, and consequently among the Fathers of the Council of Toledo. But to make this somewhat clearer, I thought it useful to compare the Gothic-Gallican Codex with those Sacramentaries which are known to have been arranged for the use of the Roman Church by the supreme pontiffs Gelasius and Gregory the Great, and also with that Codex of Masses which Blanchinus recently published under the title of the Leonian Codex.

In these three Roman Codices, then, since, if his homeland is set aside, Lawrence would in every respect have been Roman, and since it would have been of interest to Romans more than to anyone else to celebrate with a special panegyric the most holy martyr whose solemnity—as it stands in the Blanchinian Codex—Rome rejoiced in more particularly than in the others, I have so far been able to find no mention of him, except in the Masses proper to Saint Lawrence on his feast, in the feasts of Sixtus or Hippolytus, or in those of any other martyrs—not even a single word about the most holy levite. Thus the panegyric of Lawrence which we have reported from the Gothic-Gallican Codex must be regarded as peculiar to Gothic Gaul and, as we think, to our Spain, and as having been assigned by both provinces for a reason.

There is indeed in the Blanchinian Codex—lest I seem deliberately to conceal anything—a tacit mention of Lawrence in the first and second *contestations* of the Masses of Saint Sixtus, where it is said [Note: [Col. 0608D] Anastasius, vol. IV, p. XXXVI, col. 1, on the feast of Saint Sixtus] that he encouraged the sons of his teaching to earn the same glory of martyrdom, and so forth: that it was divinely granted to Sixtus not only to win the triumph of his own passion but also to benefit his ministers subject to him, and that the glorious palm of the teacher was followed by a victory of the disciple no less glorious. Although it is clear that our Lawrence is not obscurely indicated by these words, nowhere outside the Mass proper to the most holy martyr is his name or panegyric expressed, as it is found in the Gothic-Gallican Missal—even though that Codex contains seven Masses for Saint Sixtus and thirty collects and prayers. I pass over the fact that Lawrence’s name is repeated three times in the same Sacramentary, though without a panegyric, in Masses for the dead for the soul of a certain bishop [Note: [Col. 0609D] *Veronese Sacramentary*, vol. IV of Anastasius, among the Prolegomena, p. L, col. 2, nos. 4 and 5. See below, the fourth of the notes appended to this dissertation under the title “Addenda.” EDITOR.], for our opponents themselves, together with us—and among them Acamus—have acknowledged that this happened by chance [Note: [Col. 0609D] Acamus thinks (*Dissertation on the Antiquity of the Veronese Sacramentary*, part I, § XII) that the Masses containing these collects were celebrated on the day of the deposition of Pope Sixtus III for his repose; and that Lawrence is mentioned in them because that pontiff ceased to live on the day after Lawrence, namely 11 August, in the year 440.]

Now, passing from the Romans to the Missal Codices of Belgian, Celtic, and Frankish Gaul, we shall find no mention whatsoever of our Lawrence in them, as though the most holy levite had never lived anywhere in the world and the Churches or inhabitants of these regions had never heard of him. Whether this can be affirmed universally of all the Codices of the Gallic regions, I have not sufficiently determined. Certainly, in those which I have so far been able to see, not a word is read either about Saint Lawrence or about Sixtus or Hippolytus.

They are the following:

1. The Luxovian Lectionary, written in Merovingian script, edited by Mabillon in his *Gallican Liturgy* [Note: [Col. 0609D] *Gallican Liturgy*, book II, pp. 106–173], which the same author says once belonged to the province of Maxima Sequanorum, that is, the Besançon region.

2. The Sacramentary of Saint Columbanus, which Mabillon likewise brought from the Bobbio library into his *Gallican Liturgy* [Note: [Col. 0610D] This Codex is found in Muratori, *The Ancient Roman Liturgy*, vol. II, from col. 775 onward], and which he judged to belong to the same Besançon province.

3. The so-called Frankish Missal, first edited by the venerable Cardinal Thomas and reprinted by Muratori in his *Dissertation on the Roman Liturgy* [Note: [Col. 0610D] Vol. II, from col. 662 onward], which Thomas, following Morinus, thinks once belonged to the Church of Poitiers, as he states in the preface to the same work.

Finally, the old Gallican Missal [Note: [Col. 0610D] Edited by Muratori, vol. II, *Dissertation on the Roman Liturgy*, from col. 697 onward] of the same venerable cardinal, prepared for the use of the Church of Auxerre—as we may infer from Saint Germanus, bishop of that city, who is the only saint mentioned in the Codex. In all of these I have been unable to find a word about Saint Lawrence.

From these facts, unless I am greatly mistaken, it becomes clear that Blanchinus’s thesis [Note: [Col. 0610D] Annotation CV on the *Most Ancient Prayers of the Gothic Rite*, p. CCLXXXII.]—that “all martyrologies and the most ancient calendars . . . and likewise the Sacramentaries unanimously commemorate the glorious passion of Lawrence throughout the entire Church,” no differently from the related statement of the distinguished Domenico Georgi in his notes on Ado’s *Martyrology* [Note: [Col. 0610D] Under 10 August, Roman edition, p. 392], where he writes: “In the most ancient liturgical books everywhere among Western peoples, the solemn celebrations of Mass are everywhere marked for the feast of blessed Lawrence”—would be weak and plainly false as a universal assertion, unless it is supported by the qualification that must be applied to the Gallican Codices of Masses which we have just listed.

I know, certainly, that similar things are read in Maximus of Turin [Note: [Col. 0610D] *Homily II on Saint Lawrence*, toward the end], namely: “The triumph of blessed Lawrence is celebrated throughout the whole world with harmonious devotion.” But those words are much more general, and, since they concern the greater part of the Churches, they ought to be interpreted more generously, as we would say in the schools, “according to the genera of the individual cases.”

From the silence of the Gallican Codices regarding our levite—as a passing observation—and also from the fact that in the Orationary of the Church of Tarragona, first published by Blanchinus, no mention whatsoever of Saint Sixtus is found, and finally because I see no other reason why in our Spain, especially in the Missal of which we are speaking, the feasts of Saints Sixtus and Hippolytus should be celebrated with a special office, it has more than once occurred to me that a place was made for them in the Gothic-Gallican Codex because of Lawrence. The former was his teacher, the latter his disciple, and both were in a certain sense companions in passion; and it was perhaps thought inappropriate that those whose single contest could be seen—and whose passions were very frequently read in the same Acts [Note: [Col. 0610D] The passions of Saints Sixtus, Lawrence, and Hippolytus are found in those same Acts, as elsewhere, so also in the Vatican Codex, whose wording Blanchinus finally brings against us. We shall return to this below]—should be separated in the worship of a single Church’s liturgy. Indeed, in whatever Codices or calendars the feast of Lawrence happens to be passed over in silence, you will look in vain there for the solemnities of Saints Sixtus and Hippolytus.

Now, to see finally what all this amounts to, I should very much like Blanchinus to tell me:

1.
