If he assigns Lawrence to Rome, so that the most holy levite ought no longer to belong to the Spaniards any more than to the Gauls, why—while the Sacramentaries of Gaul remain entirely silent about him—do the Spanish Codices contain such a distinctive panegyric of Lawrence, not only on his own feast but also on those of Sixtus and Hippolytus?

2. If, with his homeland excepted, Lawrence has nothing in common with the Spaniards—whether one considers his rank, dignity, and accomplishments, or the place of his passion and relics—why does the Gothic-Gallican Codex, so sparing in national feasts, in which no place at all is assigned to Vincent the levite, Felix of Gerona, Fructuosus, or other illustrious Spanish martyrs, contain so prominent and vivid a mention of our Lawrence, and not in only one place?

3. Let us grant what we freely concede to Blanchinus: let us grant, I say, that apart from a common homeland there was some hidden reason why Lawrence should be mentioned in the Gothic-Gallican Codex under discussion. Can it be believed that this reason was of such weight that, because of it, the feast of Lawrence—born, educated, and raised outside Spain, as Blanchinus thinks, and having no portion of his relics there—would be celebrated in that Codex more prominently and solemnly than either the feast of the celebrated martyr Eulalia of Mérida, whose homeland, residence, passion, and place of relics were Spanish in every respect [Note: [Col. 0611C] We have consistently said that Eulalia, whose feast is celebrated in the Gothic-Gallican Missal, was Eulalia of Mérida, although the distinguished Lesleus suspects that she was from Barcelona. Since the latter suffered not far from Gaul, whereas the former suffered in the most remote part of Spain, this author thinks it credible that the Eulalia of Barcelona was once more famous among the Gauls than the Eulalia of Mérida; indeed, he thinks that the sacrificial prayer of the Mass under discussion, in which the virgin is said to have voluntarily offered herself to the governor, suits her better than it does the Eulalia of Mérida. Yet the authority of Venantius Fortunatus and Gregory of Tours, cited by Cardinal Thomas (*Preface to the Gothic Missal*), sufficiently shows that this Eulalia too was once famous in Gaul. Nor do I think that Lesleus can be helped by the conjecture drawn from the sacrificial prayer of her Mass, since it is most probable that the Acts of both Eulalias have been confused to a considerable extent. For my part, from the place assigned in that Codex to the Mass under discussion, I think it plainly follows that this was Eulalia of Mérida, whose feast is celebrated on the fourth day before the Ides of December. For there, after the Mass of Saint Andrew the Apostle on the day before the Kalends of December and before the Mass of the Conversion of Saint Paul on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, the feast of Eulalia is observed; whereas otherwise it would necessarily have had to be placed around the middle of February, when the feast of Eulalia of Barcelona falls. See below the fourth of the notes appended to this dissertation under the title “Addenda.” EDITOR.], or even than Lawrence himself in the Gelasian, Gregorian, and other Codices prepared for the use of the Roman Church?

These arguments will seem to Blanchinus to have been pursued at excessive length, and perhaps, given his intelligence and learning, he has at hand some concealed explanation of this peculiarity which, to tell the truth, has so far not occurred to me. But lest he take refuge in the worship of Lawrence, widely spread throughout the world, as though from that fact the distinctive worship of the most holy levite in the Churches of Gothic Gaul necessarily arose, let him once again be reminded of the silence of the Churches throughout Belgian, Celtic, and Frankish Gaul.

Let him also remember that Augustine, just as Maximus did concerning Lawrence, once said of the illustrious levite and martyr Vincent [Note: [Col. 0611D] Sermon 276, the third on Saint Vincent the Levite, no. 4, edition of the Maurist Fathers, Paris, vol. V, col. 1113]: “In his time there was no region, no province, wherever the Roman empire or the Christian name extended, that did not celebrate Vincent’s feast.” Yet Blanchinus would have sought this in vain in the Gallic Codices we have cited, and even in the Gothic-Gallican Missal.

Finally, although the common worship of Lawrence throughout the world might have supplied a reason for inserting his feast among the solemnities of the other martyrs in the Gothic-Gallican Codex, it could not nevertheless have supplied a reason for granting that distinguished and special panegyric to him on his own feast and on those of Saints Sixtus and Hippolytus. But enough of this.

At this point the reader may rightly desire—and plainly wonder—that, amid such a wealth of liturgical Codices, we have so far cited none that properly belongs to the Churches of Spain, since that ancient Isidorian rite of our Gothic ancestors, commonly called Mozarabic, has always been held—and still is held—in such high esteem by students of liturgy.

For my part, although I knew that some people had disparaged the Mozarabic Missal published by the incomparable Cardinal Ximénez, on the grounds that its compiler had transferred into that Codex from ancient Missals whatever he pleased, I nevertheless retained the desire to examine carefully a copy of that Missal which I had heard was preserved in the excellent library of the Corsini family and in the Vallicellian library, in case some light might thereby be shed upon these conjectures of ours.

At that time, fortunately, the distinguished Alexander Lesleus, S.J., published the Mozarabic Codex of Ximénez itself, augmented with a preface and notes [Note: [Col. 0611D] The work appeared at Rome in October 1755 under the title *The Mixed Missal According to the Rule of Blessed Isidore, Called Mozarabic*]. In it, uncommon learning—not gathered from the streets—seems to compete with the highest expertise in liturgical matters.

In that Missal, which bears more directly upon our subject, I observed that the feast of Lawrence is celebrated with a Mass proper and distinctive to it, not only on his own feast day, the fourth day before the Ides of August, but also on the octave of that day, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, and with the most solemn rite of the six *cappae*; whereas the feasts of Sixtus and Hippolytus are celebrated only on their respective feast days, each has nothing proper to itself, and everything is taken from the common of several martyrs, while the rite is far inferior to that of Lawrence [Note: [Col. 0612C] Pages 357–361: Lawrence’s feast is observed with a Mass proper to it on his feast day. Page XC, col. 2: the rite of six *cappae* is indicated in the calendar. Page 365 contains the octave of Lawrence, for which everything is ordered to be said as on the feast day. Likewise, the calendar mentions Lawrence’s octave. By contrast, concerning Sixtus, p. 356, col. 3, the following words alone are read: “Pope Sixtus: Felicissimus and Agapitus. Let everything be said from the common of several martyrs.” The same words are repeated at the feast of Saint Hippolytus, p. 361, col. 1.].

From this alone one may already infer how much greater was the regard paid among the Spaniards to the most holy levite than to the feasts of Sixtus and Hippolytus [Note: [Col. 0612C] I am not unaware that the distinguished Lesleus, in his notes (p. 585, col. 2), thinks, because of what I take to be the frequent mention of Sixtus in the Mozarabic Mass of Lawrence, that this Mass is not proper to Lawrence but common also to Sixtus. The practice of joining these martyrs, and even Hippolytus, once prevailed among the Greeks, as is clear from the Menologion of Basil. But I do not know how the distinguished author can maintain this, since a day proper to Sixtus, just as to Hippolytus, is assigned in that Missal, as we said above. Moreover, if anyone pays even brief attention to that Mass, although Sixtus is frequently mentioned in it—namely, in the second prayer, in the prayer after the names, in the *Illation*, and in the Benediction—he will nevertheless discover that it belongs more to Lawrence, indeed exclusively to him. First, the Office or Introit, as we would call it, which is “Glory and great splendor,” etc., is taken in that Mass from the common of one martyr, p. 421, whereas otherwise it should be “I will give my saints,” from the common of several martyrs, p. 426. Second, the two readings, one from Ecclesiasticus, “He who loves gold,” etc., and the other from the Apostle, “He who sows sparingly,” etc., as well as the Gospel, “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves,” etc., wonderfully suit Lawrence. Finally, the remaining prayers and petitions in the same Mass are proper to Lawrence and have nothing in common with Sixtus. They are as follows: First prayer: “Lord Jesus,” etc.; *Lauda*: “Blessed is the man,” etc.; *Sacrificium*: “I am the Lord,” etc.; Mass: “For works of mercy,” etc.; *Ad pacem*: “God, who [is] of the most blessed Levite,” etc.; after the Sanctus: “Hosanna in the highest,” etc.; after *post pridie*: “Mindful,” etc.; at the Lord’s Prayer: “God, who [is] in the true holocaust,” etc.; and after Communion: “Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. The mention of Sixtus in that Mass could have been made because of a certain fellowship in martyrdom with Lawrence. For the *Illation* also contains a double and striking panegyric of Hippolytus, yet for that reason we cannot call Lawrence’s Mass common to Hippolytus; nor did Lesleus intend this.].

It was also our wish to examine carefully any ancient liturgical Codices belonging to the Churches of Spain or Narbonese Gaul which we might find in the Vatican Library, and to bring forward from them whatever seemed capable of contributing to our purpose. Why we have not done so has been explained elsewhere.

We have carried out the one remaining task: namely, we wrote earnestly to the very distinguished and most learned expert in both law and antiquity, Don Juan Antonio de las Infantas, the doctorial canon—as they call it—of that holy Church, urging him, for the sake of this work, to examine the Mozarabic Codices of the sacred liturgy which we knew to be preserved in the extensive library of the holy and primatial Church of Toledo, and which we had several times been able to handle when we were staying at Toledo by order of the Catholic and invincible Ferdinand VI, king of Spain. If, with that assistance—which we by no means despair of—our efforts should happen to be advanced, as soon as we obtain a reply from that most courteous man and lover of his country’s honor, we shall immediately arrange for it to be inserted into our study or added separately [Note: [Col. 0613D] It was most unfortunate for this study—although otherwise it had been greatly desired by the common wishes of the Spaniards—that, at the time when our letters reached Spain, the distinguished man was absent from Toledo, serving in the extensive office of ecclesiastical vicar-general at the royal court in Madrid. At that same time, or not long afterward, when the eminent and most reverend prince Louis, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of Córdoba, had been summoned from the deanery of Toledo to the sacred College of Cardinals and to the supreme government of that same Church of Toledo, amid the greatest applause of all Spain, he alone, by the judgment of the most just and prudent king of Spain, was approved as the man who should succeed the most eminent cardinal archbishop in the deanery of Toledo, the most honorable priestly office in all Spain.]

# CHAPTER IV. PRUDENTIUS SUPPORTS THE COMMON OPINION. Several Arguments for the Spaniards Drawn from His Hymn on Lawrence

Thus far we have striven, as far as our powers allowed, to establish Lawrence as belonging to our Spain. Now, to show that the most holy levite was not born at Rome according to the mind of Prudentius—the very author whom our opponents insist stands on their side—we are perhaps undertaking a hazardous and difficult task.

At the outset, however, it must be noted that the sacred poem’s author had an entirely different intention and purpose from expressing the homeland of the most holy levite in it. Nor would such a treatment be judged sufficiently appropriate or timely for either the hymn simply entitled *The Passion of Lawrence* or the title of the book *περὶ Στεφάνων*, that is, *On Crowns*, namely, of the martyrs.

If anyone still has doubts about this matter, we present Prudentius himself, who most plainly reveals his intention and the aim of the hymn in these words [Note: [Col. 0614D] Hymn on Saint Lawrence, stanza IX, line 33]:

> By what words, with how many praises,  
> Shall I celebrate the order of his death?  
> With what song shall I worthily unfold  
> The course of his passion?

And again [Note: [Col. 0614D] Stanza CXXXVIII, line 548]:

> Thus, holy Lawrence, we seek  
> To tell your passion.

Accordingly, if anything is found in that poem from which some light may be shed upon Lawrence’s homeland, or from which it may finally be divined through more penetrating inquiry, it should be regarded as something said with minimal effort by the author, as though a word more significant than he intended had perhaps slipped out while he was thinking of nothing of the kind.

The Bollandist Fathers, after examining the hymn with the greatest care, observed that their attempt to extract from it even a spark capable of illuminating Lawrence’s homeland had failed completely; they therefore warned others that anyone who tried the same thing thereafter would be undertaking work of no value [Note: [Col. 0614D] Under 10 August, § IV, at the very beginning].

On the other hand, the authority of that hymn seemed so pliable in both directions to others that a learned doctor—my fellow citizen and formerly a competitor for the chair of sacred languages at the University of Valencia [Note: [Col. 0614D] This was Doctor Augustine Salesius, a priest and historian of the city of Valencia, famous for his published works (a catalogue of which may be found in Vicente Ximénez, *Bibliotheca Valentina*, vol. II, under the year 1747, p. 304)—in a letter to our learned Mayans dated 19 July 1741, in the appendix to his work *Censorship of the Fabulous Histories*] tried to prove from these words [Note: [Col. 0614D] Stanza CXLIII, line 569]:

> As though you were always present [Note: [Col. 0613] Arevalus conjectures that *tu* should be read for *ceu*, and observes that Terence used *adsies* for *adsis*. EDITOR.],  
> And embracing your urban pupils  
> In your nourishing bosom,  
> You fostered them with paternal love.

And from what follows:

> Among these, O glory of Christ,  
> Hear the rustic poet—

He tried to prove that, since Prudentius was from Zaragoza—which may perhaps be true—Lawrence should not be separated from that city as his homeland. For he maintains that Prudentius asks Lawrence to embrace with paternal love his urban pupils—that is, the people of Zaragoza, as he understands it—and Prudentius himself among them.

Amid such a diversity of preconceived opinions, when I saw Blanchinus and Merenda, after examining the hymn with meticulous care, raising flimsy and plainly perishable conjectures drawn from it to the heavens and selling them as geometrical demonstrations, I did not wish these writers to deprive me of the freedom granted to me, or to begrudge me any small gains I might be able to make.

Accordingly, after proceeding through the poem section by section and observing the author’s purpose with the greatest care, I readily arrived at the view [Col. 0615A] that Prudentius did not even think that Lawrence was Roman by birth. This follows from the arguments below.

## 1

In that hymn our poet introduces Lawrence, after he had rejected the tyrant’s commands, inwardly touched by grief and earnestly beseeching Christ to uproot pagan superstition from the city, with these words [Note: [Col. 0615C] Stanza CIII, line 409]:

> When he had said this in jest,  
> He then looked up to heaven  
> And, groaning, entreated,  
> Pitying the city of Romulus.

Why, however, did he not rather say:

> Pitying his native city,

using the final word *patriam* adjectivally? In this sense Virgil too spoke somewhere of his native land [Note: [Col. 0615C]:

> I could not, dear friend,  
> See you, nor, departing, lay you  
> In your native land.  
> (*Aeneid* VI.508)],

and Horace of ancestral ashes [Note: [Col. 0615C]:

> May he urinate upon his ancestral ashes, etc.  
> (*The Art of Poetry*, line 471)],

as did others among the ancients.

Prudentius could certainly have done this according to the laws of meter and Latin usage; and, in my judgment, *patriae* would otherwise have been a more precise and meaningful addition, much more suitable for expressing the piety of the most holy martyr toward the city, in connection with the words *groaning* and *pitying*, which immediately precede it.

## 2

The most holy levite then continues, and amid the flames prays that the Roman people may embrace the Christian religion, saying [Note: [Col. 0615C] Stanza CIV, line 433]:

> Grant, O Christ, that for your Romans  
> The city may be Christian.

Here the poet may seem not to have attributed the Romans to Christ appropriately. For Rome had not yet bowed its neck beneath Christ’s yoke in Lawrence’s time, when this prayer was made.

Why, then, if Lawrence had been born in the city, would the poet not more accurately have said:

> Grant, O Christ, that for my Romans—

especially since neither meter nor the character of the Latin language would have prevented him?

Indeed, shortly before, when he was speaking of the poor among whom the most holy levite had distributed the treasures of the Church, he did not hesitate to call them “his own,” in relation to Lawrence. For he addresses the prefect in these words [Note: [Col. 0615C] Stanza LIX, line 233]:

> Any one of your rich men,  
> Who shine in clothing and appearance,  
> I would judge more feeble  
> Than any one of **my poor**.

Why, then, would Lawrence not likewise call the Romans “his own,” since earlier he had not been ashamed to call the poor his own?

## 3

That devout writer begrudges the Romans the privilege of being able to look upon the sacred relics of the most blessed martyr while they were still present and to kiss the threshold of his tomb. He says that this was not granted to him or to the other Spaniards, separated from Rome by the distance of two Alps [Note: [Col. 0615C] Stanza CXXXIII and following]:

> O thrice, he says, and four times, and seven times  
> Blessed is the inhabitant of the city  
> Who celebrates you, Lawrence, and the seat  
> Of your bones close at hand!  
>   
> The Iberian Basque separates us,  
> Removed by **two Alps**,  
>   
> Beyond the ridges of the Cottian Alps,  
> Beyond the snowy Pyrenees.

[Col. 0616C] It should also be noted that by the name of the Alps our poet calls the Pyrenees, which separate Gaul from Spain, so that no one may think that he meant the Julian, Pennine, or Cottian Alps here. For the Julian and Cottian Alps could not be called “two” by Prudentius, since they separate the Italians from the Spaniards not twice but only once. They are continuous mountain ranges whose passes receive different names according to the variety of the regions. Yet it is not improper to call the highest mountains “Alps.”

There are those who think that *Alps* derives from *albus* or *alpus*, and *alpus* from ἄλφος (*alphos*), which is λευκός (*leukos*), that is, “white,” as Hesychius holds; they say that the name was given from the whiteness of the snows. A more plausible etymology, however, is that the word descends rather from the Hebrew *eleph*, which simply means “a thousand” and sometimes “an ox.” From it comes *aluph*, that is, “leader” or “teacher,” and figuratively whatever is greatest, chiefest, highest, or primary.

Hence the Greek ἐλέφας (*elephas*), which in Latin is also *elephas* and *elephantus*, is named from its size; likewise the Hebrew *eleph*, “ox,” because this is the largest of European animals. Moreover, *aleph*, *eliph*, and *olaph* are the first letters of the Hebrew, Arabic, and Syriac alphabets; the Greek equivalent is *alpha*. In this sense Codrus is called by Martial (*Book V, epigram 27*) “the *alpha* of the cloak-wearers,” that is, the first of beggars.

Glosses: *Alpes*, ὄρη ὑψηλά (*orē hypsēla*), that is, “lofty mountains.” Isidore says (*Etymologies* XIV.8): “In the language of the Gauls, high mountains are called *Alps*.” See Vossius under *Albus*.

Among the Greeks, moreover, the notion of a mountain is general, as if one were to say “conspicuous” or “spectacular,” or a very elevated place from which the surrounding region can be viewed over a great distance. For ὄρος (*oros*), “mountain,” perhaps derives from ὁράω (*horaō*), “I see,” although the aspiration of the two words differs.

Ἰδή or εἰδή (*Idē* or *eidē*), by which name mountains were also once called among the Greeks—as is shown by two mountains, both extremely high, one in the Troad and the other on the island of Crete, bearing that name—is entirely derived from εἴδω (*eidō*), “I see.” Hence εἰδής (*eidēs*), “conspicuous,” and εἰδέα or ἰδέα (*eidea* or *idea*), “appearance” or “form.”

There will be those who wish mountains to be called from οἰδέω (*oideō*), “I swell,” for they are swellings of the earth. Traces of both these Greek notions of “mountain” are plainly found in the ancient chorography of our Spain. For in our country there were two very lofty mountains, called by the ancients Orospeda and Idubeda. The first parts of these names—*oros* and *idu*—are undoubtedly Greek and signify “mountain,” that is, something conspicuous and remarkable; Bochart somewhere interpreted the latter part, *peda*, as “silver-bearing.”

Orospeda is today called *la sierra de Segura*, whereas Idubeda is called by our people in their vernacular *Montes de Oca*, following the opinion of Father Mariana. Yet the very learned countryman of ours, Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, should also be consulted: he discussed the location of these mountains excellently with Fernando Pintianus in book III, letter 48 to J. Quignonius.

Here it should be observed that Prudentius does not begrudge those born at Rome because they shared a homeland with Lawrence, but those—even if they were foreigners—who nevertheless lived in the City, not far from the sacred relics of the most holy levite: inhabitants, that is, not citizens. For the former, as he himself sings, could cast themselves down and water the most blessed martyr’s tomb with tears, a privilege not granted to those who lived outside the City.

## 4

Our poet then asks the most holy levite, rejoicing that he may be present among the people of Quirinus—that is, that he may deal kindly with the Romans—calling them Lawrence’s pupils, in these words [Note: [Col. 0616D] Stanza CXLIII, line 569]:

> As though you were always present,  
> And embracing your urban pupils  
> In your nourishing bosom,  
> You fostered them with paternal love.

In this passage too, if Lawrence had been born at Rome, Prudentius could—and indeed ought to—have called them not merely “pupils” but plainly Lawrence’s Roman citizens, according to Latin usage, especially since the laws of the poem do not reject that word.

Why, then, did he not say:

> And your **urban citizens**?

If Prudentius had wished to refer either to the original derivation of the word—since we know that *cives* were so called from *coire* (“to come together”)—or to the right of Roman citizenship, or finally to Laurentius’s permanent residence in the City, he could certainly have called Laurentius a Roman citizen in the true sense. But since he knew that this word very frequently designated a common homeland, the Spanish author deliberately abstained from it, lest he produce an ambiguous statement; or lest, if someone used the word in that latter sense, he should exclude Laurentius from his fellow Spaniards. For that reason he preferred to call the Romans the most holy Levite’s *alumni* (“nurselings”) rather than his citizens.

These matters, however, are conjectural. What is certain is that the word *alumnus*—whether one considers its etymology or analogy, or rather its usage in the Latin language—properly signifies someone who is sustained by another’s bodily nourishment and is related to *nutritus* (“one who is nourished”). By analogy, however, it is transferred to the mind; in this sense we read among the ancients of *alumni* of discipline and piety. So far as I know, it has never been used to mean “citizen” or “fellow-countryman”; indeed, without violating its proper meaning, it could never have been used in that way.

Nevertheless, we must determine the force of this word in Prudentius from authors of Middle Latin, especially from the ecclesiastical Fathers of the same period. Leo the Great, who flourished not long after Prudentius, speaking of the holy apostles, says [Note: Sermon II on the Nativity of the Holy Apostles]:

> But if the Apostle Peter, as we must believe, extends this care of his piety everywhere to the people of God, how much more does he deign to offer his aid to his **alumni**—the Romans—among whom he rests on the sacred bed of his dormition in the same flesh in which he presided?

Let our opponents consider, I ask, in what sense the Romans are called the alumni of the Apostle Peter by Saint Leo, who likewise was born at Rome. To my mind, by that word he seems to mean sons of discipline and teaching, or those entrusted to his patronage; perhaps also inhabitants of the City, nourished at the breast of their common mother—people whom one might properly call in Greek τοὺς συντροφίμους (“those brought up together”); but they do not seem to be understood more strictly as citizens or fellow-countrymen. Nor does Prudentius use the word in an entirely different sense when somewhere he calls the executioners and lictors the alumni of the prison, saying [Note: In the hymn on Saint Vincent the Martyr, stanza XXXV, line 137]:

> But you, **alumni of the prison**,  
> A matching, unconquered pair for me,  
> Restrain your right hands for a little,  
> So that exhausted strength may draw breath.

As though he were saying: “you whom the prison feeds.” Indeed, in this same hymn on Laurentius, the poor are called *alumni of the light* in a very elegant metaphor. I interpret this literally as “those who graze upon the light”; allegorically, however, I think Prudentius meant those who, because they do good works, love the light—unless perhaps by that expression he wished to designate the alumni of Christ, who is the unfailing light.

The cause of our pursuing these matters somewhat more idly than was appropriate was our distinguished countryman, to whom Spain owes a very great debt, Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis. In his note on this passage of Prudentius, he interprets *alumnos* as “citizens” [Note: In the note on this passage of Prudentius. In Nicolaus Heinsius’s Cologne edition of Prudentius, 1750, p. 227]. A more recent commentator on the same poet [Note: P. Chamillart, *Commentary on Prudentius*, on this passage: “Since you are always present to the Romans; since you cherish your fellow-countrymen in a mother’s lap and pursue them with a father’s love: among these, O martyr of Christ, hear the poet—not a good one.”], while replacing that word with *populares* (“fellow-countrymen”), seems to have followed Nebrissensis. Yet I think both men were greatly mistaken, unless they are willing to use both words in an exceedingly broad and wholly improper sense—ἀκύρως, that is, “incorrectly.” But let us return to the proper subject.

### 5.

Our poet proceeds further. After Laurentius’s passion and the victory of the cross achieved through him, he contemplates the glory of the most holy Levite as though carried outside himself, saying [Note: Stanza CXXXVIII, line 549]:

> Thus, holy Laurentius, we seek  
> Your passion. For you have a double hall:  
> Here, that of the body; there, in the ineffable heaven of the mind,  
> Enrolled as a citizen of the City,  
> In the citadel of the eternal senate  
> You bear the civic crown.  
> I seem to see the man  
> Flashing with brilliant gems,  
> Whom heavenly Rome  
> Has chosen as her perpetual consul.

I have no doubt that Prudentius is here speaking of Laurentius’s heavenly municipal citizenship. Perhaps he was also referring to Paul’s statement [Note: Philippians 3:19, or 3:20]: “Our *conversatio* is in heaven,” for which the old translator—without any disagreement from the Greek text [Note: Ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει (Philippians 3). For τὸ πολίτευμα means just as much “government” or “administration of a state or city,” from πολιτεύω or πολιτεύομαι, meaning “I rule, administer, govern a state,” and so forth. For this reason our eminent countryman Benedictus Arias Montanus rendered it “our administration.” The Vulgate translator, however, preferred *conversatio*, which is certainly a highly suitable word and does not exclude municipal citizenship. The sense of the passage is this: “We live as though dwelling in heaven, and our actions are directed toward the place where the reward of the righteous will finally be, which we hope also to share.” Thus we possess the right of citizenship—that is, municipal citizenship—in heaven. Erasmus also seems to have had this in mind when he interpreted the passage: “We conduct ourselves as citizens of heaven.” This interpretation is wonderfully supported by another ancient interpretation, which we shall discuss below, and also by the Greek phrase πολιτεύματος μετέχειν in Plutarch, which is most suitably rendered “to share in the right of citizenship,” that is, “to be a citizen.” See Henri Estienne under Πολίτευμα.]—rendered it *municipatus* (“municipal citizenship”) [Note: “But you are a stranger in this world, a citizen of heavenly Jerusalem. Our municipal citizenship is in heaven,” says Paul (Philippians 3). Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 13, in C. Dominic Georgius, *Testimonies concerning Ado*]. In my opinion, however, the poet’s purpose in this passage was to say that the most holy Levite, already a citizen of earthly Rome, had, after his glorious contest and triumph, been enrolled among the citizens of heavenly Rome and honored with the perpetual consulship of that blessed City—as though he were saying that Laurentius’s passion transferred him from temporal to eternal municipal citizenship.

So that we may not seem to have said this merely by conjecture, we must first consider the proper force of the word *allectus*, which indicates a transition from one order into another, as does the corresponding Greek word προσκατειλεγμένος. Above all, however, we must consider the *apodosis* of the preceding stanza:

> For you have a double hall, O Laurentius:  
> Here, of the body; there, in the heaven of the mind.

Unless I am greatly mistaken, these words most clearly contain a double homeland for our Laurentius and a twofold municipal right. They are almost literally borrowed by Prudentius from Cicero, who, speaking of Marcus Porcius Cato, born at Tusculum, says [Note: Book II of *On the Laws*, near the beginning]:

> I certainly believe that he and all municipal citizens have two homelands: one belonging to nature, the other to citizenship.

If we compare this statement with Prudentius’s words, “Enrolled as a citizen of the City,” and with “For you have a double hall,” we shall find that they wonderfully correspond—in fact, that they are identical. Prudentius did not say “a double homeland,” because the meter rejected the latter word in that particular position, and he substituted *hall* for it. If this interpretation is correct—as certainly it is plausible—we have Laurentius, in Prudentius’s view, a municipal citizen and therefore not a Roman by homeland.

I have thought it appropriate to add, although out of order, another conjecture drawn from the subject matter of the book *On Crowns* (*περὶ Στεφάνων*). Since the principal part of that book is claimed by Spanish martyrs—or, if we temporarily set aside Laurentius, who is the subject of the dispute—Hemeterius and Chelidonius, Vincent the Levite, the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, Eulalia of Mérida, Fructuosus of Tarragona, and even Cyprian, whom Prudentius, although an African, calls a Spaniard in love and speech [Note: In the hymn on Saint Cyprian, line 111]:

> He is a martyr belonging to his homeland,  
> But ours in love and speech—

it is clear from their hymns throughout that they were composed by the author in their homeland. Conversely, Prudentius himself testifies that the remaining poems in that book, concerning martyrs who were not Spanish, were composed outside his homeland and on particular occasions: those concerning the Apostles Peter and Paul at Rome, and likewise that concerning Hippolytus; that concerning Cassian at Forum Cornelii, after he happened to hear the history of his passion from the church custodian.

The matter is uncertain regarding the hymns of Agnes and Quirinus, the two who remain. The celebration of the former’s feast in Rome, however, and the fact that the remains of the latter martyr were, as I believe [Note: See Baronius in his notes on the *Martyrology*, June 4, letter B], transferred to Rome from Siscia—now a settlement in Croatia—during Prudentius’s time [Note: At that time called Sisseg by the natives, at the confluence of the Colapis and the Savus. Baudrand] provide grounds for conjecturing that they were composed at Rome.

Since, therefore, Prudentius most clearly testifies that the one poem containing Laurentius’s passion was written in Spain, more clearly than any of the other poems in that book, as the passages recently cited from it demonstrate, why should we not infer from this also that Laurentius, like the other martyrs whose passions that author celebrated in their homeland, was born in central Spain?

If our opponents were to present these considerations to us, drawn from Prudentius’s hymn or elsewhere in support of their position, I would frankly admit that I would attach little importance to them individually. Yet, since they all seem to be directed toward the same conclusion as though by prior agreement, I would not entirely despise them collectively. It is extremely rare for a six-stringed instrument to be tuned by chance to the laws of harmony. Nevertheless, whatever their ultimate value, we submit them to fair-minded readers for judgment and for comparison with the conjectures that our opponents draw from the same hymn. We do not despair, however, that from what has so far been brought forward it may henceforth be less possible to reproach the Spaniards with being abandoned by their own Prudentius in this controversy.

## CHAPTER V

### The arguments of the opponents are examined in order, especially Blanchinus’s argument drawn from an Orationary Codex of the most ancient Gothic rite

Blanchinus first of all presses upon us a little book of prayers belonging to the most ancient Gothic rite, which he himself recovered from the archives of the Church of Verona and included among the prolegomena to the liturgical works of the venerable Cardinal Giuseppe Maria Tomasi in the Roman edition of 1741 [Note: Pages 1–136]. He maintains that this little book once belonged to the Church of Tarragona, the namesake of the province in Nearer Spain, and says that it wonderfully contradicts the generally accepted opinion concerning Laurentius’s homeland. We reproduce Blanchinus’s words [Note: Annotation CVI, p. 292]:

> “But this little book wonderfully contradicts the common opinion of the Spaniards. For it celebrates the feast day of Saint Laurentius—a great and solemn day, and more glorious than the others after those of the Apostles—at Matins with only three prayers and a *completoria*, although the same little book adorns the offices of other saints who are genuinely Spanish with numerous prayers, as may be seen in the general index that we prefixed with the greatest care and diligence to the same little book of the Church of Tarragona [Note: Although it makes no difference to us whether this little book belonged to Tarragona or to another of the Churches of Spain, we nevertheless thought it necessary to warn the reader that the matter is not so thoroughly established. The passages by which Blanchinus thinks it can be established and demonstrated that it belonged to the Church of Tarragona (Annotation XXII, pp. 167 ff.) are somewhat obscure. Moreover, in the prayers concerning Saint Vincent the Martyr, whose homeland we believe was Zaragoza (pp. 60, at the end, and 61), there is considerable reason to doubt whether this Codex once belonged to the Church of Zaragoza. For in the prayer beginning “Almighty Father,” we read: “Grant, Lord, being appeased, that through diligent intercession he [Vincent], who was chosen from those same members to fight for you, may apply power to weakness, glory to humility,” and so forth. A little farther below, in the prayer beginning “Almighty God, who [didst make] the martyr,” there seems to be a reference to that celebrated stole of Vincent sprinkled with blood and held in the highest honor among the people of Zaragoza, concerning which Prudentius, Eugenius the Younger of Toledo, and others speak. The words are these: “Grant, Lord, that through diligent intercession he [Vincent] may restore the garments of baptism, badly torn, whom, as he fought for you, you clothed with a stole of honor sprinkled with the blood of martyrdom.” We, however, make no determination on this point.], to it. This alone is an argument of the greatest weight.”

Let us nevertheless be permitted, through Blanchinus, to weigh this matter in the proper balance. In the prayer Codex under discussion, Laurentius’s feast consists of only three prayers, but *completoriae* and blessings for Vespers and Matins are also added; Blanchinus, as we think, omitted the former by accident [Note: Page 130 and following]. There are seven collections altogether, and no more. By contrast, the feasts of the saints Vincent the Levite, Valentinus the Martyr, Leocadia of Toledo, Eulalia of Mérida, Fructuosus, and others who are genuinely Spanish, as Blanchinus says, have twenty prayers each in that Codex, and sometimes more. Thus far Blanchinus has had a favorable wind and, as they say, full sails. But let him, I ask, take care lest he be forced to come to a halt in mid-course.

The same little book of which we are speaking [Note: Pages 5 and following; Blanchinus, in the index of the Offices of the Orationary, p. 122, and Annotation II, pp. 137 ff.] provides only four collections or prayers for the feast of Saints Acisclus and his companions. These should more properly be assigned to the Sunday of Advent, into which period their anniversary falls, than to the solemnity of the martyrs. Moreover, for the feast of Saints Justus and Pastor the little book supplies only one proper prayer with a blessing; it directs that three, or at most four, other common prayers be taken from the Mass of the Holy Children—that is, the Innocents [Note: Page 130, and Blanchinus’s index, p. 129]. Thus even together they do not reach the number seven. Yet Blanchinus himself will acknowledge with us that the former martyrs must be counted among those of Córdoba, and the latter German brothers among those of Complutum. But these are minor matters.

Felix of Gerunda the Martyr has, in the prayer book mentioned above, thirteen proper prayers in addition to a blessing. Four further prayers, likewise with a blessing, must be added to these, since they are shared with the holy Maccabees; thus the combined total is nineteen [Note: Pages 127 and following]. Nevertheless, Cucufas of Barcelona, who was not only Felix’s fellow citizen and companion on his journey but was commonly believed to have been his own brother, and whom the little book itself calls a famous martyr [Note: Page 127], Prudentius calls renowned [Note: In the hymn on the Holy Martyrs of Zaragoza, stanza IX], and the Bollandist Fathers call most celebrated on the basis of ancient Martyrologies [Note: July 25, § I, no. 1], is honored in that little book, remarkably, with only one *completoria* and one blessing [Note: Page 127].

Add to this that Barcelona was already a distinguished city, famous for commerce, and therefore very populous, and was also neighboring Tarragona, to whose Church Blanchinus assigns the little book. By contrast, we know from Prudentius’s testimony that Gerunda was small [Note: In the hymn on the Holy Martyrs of Zaragoza, stanza VIII] and at least a three-day journey from Tarragona. The cult of this martyr, therefore, ought to have been greater than that of Felix, or at least equal to it. We may perhaps indicate the reason for this difference elsewhere. In the meantime, from the unequal number of prayers in that Codex, let Blanchinus infer that the former Felix was a Spaniard, but not Cucufas—for that conclusion follows from his reasoning regarding both.

But what if Laurentius had been entirely omitted from the prayer book? Blanchinus would have declared the whole matter settled and would have pronounced the Spanish opinion finished. Yet by the same argument—so that we may derive from this point also a demonstration of its weakness—he can now likewise establish that neither Eulalia of Barcelona [Note: Blanchinus may perhaps not approve the view that there were once two Eulalias among the Spaniards, but only one, namely the Eulalia of Mérida. In fact, in his annotations on the Gothic Orationary (IX, p. 146), he seems not obscurely inclined toward that opinion, on the basis of the Orationary’s silence concerning Eulalia of Barcelona. Prudentius appears to support him, since, passing over the illustrious maiden of Barcelona, he celebrates the former Eulalia of Mérida in an outstanding poem and reveals the distinctiveness of her feast day somewhere—in the hymn on Saint Hippolytus. Yet the opinion is much more widespread and more probable among those who think that, because of the similarity of their names and the affinity of their Acts, the two Eulalias were confused by some people and made into one from two; we know that the same thing happened with Hippolytuses, Cyprians, and other martyrs bearing the same name. Ruinartius also seems not to dissent from this view (*Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, Verona edition, p. 396), although he himself makes no determination. Indeed, in addition to the authorities of the Mozarabic Missal and Breviary, of Eulogius, and of other ancient authors, which are commonly cited in favor of Eulalia of Barcelona, there is the ancient Toledan Calendar formerly published by Francisco de Pisa and included by Father Joannes Pinius in the *Hispanic Liturgy*. He considers it (chapter 9, § 6, no. 445) to have been written in the fifth or early sixth century, while the distinguished Cennius (in Blanchinus’s *Gothic Orationary*, p. 134) believes it was written at the end of the seventh. It wonderfully confirms the latter opinion—that there were two Eulalias—for it reads: “On the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr, of Barcelona.” Furthermore, the Acts of Leocadia of Toledo, recently recovered from the Franciscan monastery of that city and reported by the distinguished Henrique Flórez in volume VI of *Sacred Spain*, p. 315, make a most explicit mention of both Eulalias. We swear most solemnly that we have stated these things—notwithstanding that we are bound by every form of duty both to our most extensive Church of Barcelona, in whose bosom the sacred ashes of Eulalia are most reverently venerated, and to the noble city of Spain that kindly received us into her embrace—more from our sincere conviction than from any desire to gratify either of them, or one of them. The distinguished Lesleus should also be consulted (notes on the *Mozarabic Missal*, p. 566), who vigorously contends for two Eulalias; his work, however, first appeared after this dissertation had been completed.], nor Vincent and his companions of Ávila, nor Servandus and Germanus of Cádiz, nor finally the most celebrated martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius of Calahorra, whose victories Prudentius celebrated in a special hymn [Note: “In honor of the Holy Martyrs of Calahorra, Hemeterius and Chelidonius.” It is first among all the hymns in Weitz’s edition, Hanover, 1612], should be assigned to the Spaniards, since we see that no mention of any of these martyrs occurs in the prayer Codex under discussion and that their anniversaries are entirely omitted [Note: See the sixth of the notes appended to this dissertation under the title “Addenda.” Editor].

Nor should this be regarded as peculiar only to that little prayer book; it is common to nearly all ancient liturgical Codices and Martyrologies that some martyrs who otherwise ought not to be passed over are occasionally omitted. The matter will become clearer through examples. The Gothic-Gallican Missal of Tomasi—which, as we said earlier, contains not only a special feast of Laurentius but also an encomium of the most holy martyr on the feasts of Saints Sixtus and Hippolytus—has not a word either about Felix and Cucufas, or about Fructuosus and his companions, or about Vincent the Levite and other illustrious Spanish martyrs, nor does it contain any commemoration of them, as we have indicated elsewhere. If anyone wished to deprive our Spain of that distinguished company of martyrs on the basis of the Codex’s silence, how far would he stray from the path of truth—even by Blanchinus’s own judgment!

Furthermore, the Isidorian Missal, commonly called the Mozarabic [Note: I had previously read this in Ruinartius, whose words are almost these (Preface to the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, no. 18). Later, having obtained a copy of that Missal—namely, the edition published by the distinguished Lesleus—I verified the matter by inspection. In the Calendar of his Missal, in the month of July (p. 90), one does indeed read: “The eighth day before the Kalends of August: Christopher, etc.; Cucufas and his fellow martyrs.” But in the body of the Missal itself there is not the slightest mention of Cucufas, as may be seen in the Mass of Saint Christopher on July 25], does not mention Zoilus or Zoellus of Córdoba, as Prudentius calls him [Note: In the hymn on the Holy Martyrs of Zaragoza]; nor Cucufas of Barcelona, nor Encratis of Zaragoza; indeed, it does not even mention the eighteen martyrs of that same city, whose praises Prudentius celebrated in a special hymn [Note: This is the seventh in Weitz’s edition].

Finally, the Calendar of the Church of Carthage sometimes passes over Africans, even martyrs of that same city. It does not include Rutilius, who, according to Tertullian, after repeatedly avoiding his persecutors, was finally arrested and completed his martyrdom in the fire [Note: “Rutilius, a most holy martyr, although he had so often fled persecution from place to place and had already, as he thought, bought off the danger with money . . . was unexpectedly seized and brought before the governor, broken by tortures—I believe as punishment for his flight—and then handed over to the flames; thus he surrendered to the mercy of God the passion he had avoided.” Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter 5]. Nor does it include Mavilus, who, according to the same Tertullian in his work *To Scapula*, was condemned to the beasts at Hadrumetum under Severus—Ferrarius calls the place Toulba or Mahammeta [Note: “At Hadrumetum.” And likewise Baudrand], while Baudrand calls it Hammameth, not far from Carthage [Note: “We also hope for you [Scapula, governor of the province of Africa] that the only warning you received was that, after you had condemned Mavilus of Hadrumetum to the beasts, this affliction immediately followed, and now, for the same reason, there is an appeal for blood.”” Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chapter 3, no. 3]. Nor, finally, does it include Bassus, Fortunio, and the other Carthaginian martyrs praised in Cyprian’s letters, as the distinguished Ruinartius testifies [Note: In the preface to the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, no. 18]. What, then? Shall we affirm, on the basis of the silence of both these Codices, that neither those earlier men were Spaniards nor these later men Africans?

I think it will be useful to cite the testimony of the distinguished author in confirmation of this doctrine; from it we shall at the same time understand why some martyrs were occasionally omitted even in their own Churches. “But why,” says Ruinartius, speaking of the silence concerning martyrs in ancient Calendars [Note: In the same place, but somewhat farther below], “should we resort to such ancient examples, when anyone can easily observe the same thing in modern Calendars? In these, not only the martyrs and patrons of foreign Churches, but also those of neighboring and provincial Churches, are for the most part not celebrated; indeed, sometimes the martyrs or bishops of one Church are venerated in another Church, while they have no cult in their own. I think this happened because their sacred relics had been transferred elsewhere, or at least because their Acts were not available.”

The distinguished Muratorius strongly confirms this doctrine. He had found it surprising that the feast of Saint Eugenia, virgin and martyr—whose passion at Rome was celebrated on the very feast day of the Lord’s Nativity in the ancient Hieronymian Martyrology, in Usuard, and elsewhere—was entered in the Gallican-Bobbian Sacramentary, which, as we have said, belonged to the province of Besançon and therefore to the Gallic Franks, on the vigil of that same Nativity. He suspects that the reason was that the relics of this holy martyr had been brought to one of the Gallican Churches [Note: Dissertation on the ancient Roman liturgy, volume II, column 766, in the preface to the Gallican-Bobbian Sacramentary first edited by Mabillon].

From this doctrine too, by an argument from the greater to the lesser, as they say in the schools, I think it could have happened that somewhere the cult of a martyr who was a citizen was inferior to that of someone whose Acts or relics were present in some Church or diocese, even though the latter had acquired his homeland elsewhere. We have a ready example in Stephen. Although he was a foreigner, his feast is nevertheless celebrated in that little book with a longer series of prayers because his relics had been brought to Spain, as we said earlier, than the feasts either of Acisclus or of Justus and Pastor, who were undoubtedly native martyrs; indeed, longer than those of Justa and Rufina of Seville, whose anniversary in that little book has no more than fifteen collections [Note: *Orationary*, pp. 125–127], whereas twenty or more are assigned there to the feast of Stephen [Note: The same work, pp. 39–43].

Since, therefore, as we previously demonstrated from the Bollandist Fathers and from Prudentius’s own testimony, during the centuries immediately following Laurentius’s death—and indeed in later centuries as well—our Spain had acquired none of the most holy martyr’s relics, and since no Acts of his passion were present in that region, it could very readily have happened for this reason that Laurentius’s feast was celebrated in the Church to which the little book under discussion belonged with a smaller number of prayers than that of some Spanish or foreign martyr whose sacred remains were venerated in that Church or elsewhere in Spain. Just as no one could properly infer from the greater number of prayers given to Stephen in that little book that the most holy protomartyr should be assigned to the Spaniards, so neither should Laurentius be taken away from them on the basis of the smaller number.

I also think that from the same doctrine one may derive the remarkable inequality between Felix of Gerunda and Cucufas of Barcelona with respect to the number of prayers. The relics of the former martyr remained continuously from his death down to our own times at Gerunda, the city in which he suffered. Prudentius says [Note: In the hymn on the Holy Martyrs of Zaragoza]:

> Small Gerunda will display the glory of Felix,  
> Rich in his sacred limbs.

As for the relics of Cucufas, although I have no doubt that in Prudentius’s time they existed at Barcelona or nearby—namely, at the fortress of Octavianus, where the famous monastery of Saint Cucufas was later built, now called by the natives Sant Cugat del Vallès, by Charlemagne or, as others maintain, by Louis the Pious—the Mozarabic hymn of that martyr explicitly confirms the matter, despite Tillemont’s objection [Note: Tillemont indeed contends (in the Bollandist Fathers, July 25, § 11, no. 15) that the hymn concerns Cucufas’s tomb without his body, that is, περὶ τοῦ κενοταφίου (“the empty tomb”). Yet this is demonstrably false from stanzas II, III, and IV, especially X, in which Cucufas of Barcelona is called a **citizen**—obviously because his sacred relics were preserved there]. The Bollandist Fathers reproduce the hymn [Note: July 25, § 1, no. 7]. It is nevertheless beyond dispute that his relics were transferred to Gaul in the eighth century and rested in the Vosges forest at Fulrad’s Cell in the year of salvation 777. This is clear from the testament of Saint Fulrad, which Mabillon published [Note: In *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century III, part II, p. 341; in the Bollandist Fathers, July 25, § 3, no. 21]. Ado does not disagree, although he asserts that Cucufas’s body was transferred directly to Paris—a statement that is not equally accurate. He says [Note: In the *Martyrology*, July 25]:

> Cucufas was brought eight miles from Barcelona and completed his martyrdom after being struck with the sword. His body was buried reverently by Christians; afterward it was transferred and buried not far from the city of Paris, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.

Since the seat of Saint Felix’s relics at Gerunda was fixed and undisturbed, the ancient cult of this martyr could very easily be preserved by the constant devotion of the people. But the cult of Cucufas could gradually decline, especially after his sacred body had been transferred to Gaul. I regarded this as the cause of the remarkable inequality in the number of prayers that we discussed earlier.

“But,” you say, “this would mean that the prayer book under discussion was written only after Cucufas’s body had been transferred to Gaul, and therefore that it is not more than a thousand years old, as Blanchinus maintained [Note: Volume I of the collected works of the venerable Cardinal Tomasi, preface to the reader], nor does it belong to the seventh century or precede the Moorish devastation of Spain, as the distinguished Cayetanus Cennius asserted [Note: Volume I of *On the Antiquities of the Spanish Church*, p. 28, in Blanchinus’s notes on the Orationary, p. 133], but must have been written at the earliest toward the end of the eighth century.”

“What then?” I reply. I know that both these writers possess very great authority, and I earnestly wish that it may increase daily. But if I may philosophize freely, I consider that, in comparison with that authority and with the conjectures offered for determining the age of the Codex, the single disparity between Felix and Cucufas in the number of prayers is far stronger. The age of the Codex must among other things be measured from that disparity—or these writers must produce some more immediate explanation for so great an inequality.

Judgment concerning the age of Codices is also fleeting and slippery. After the more cautious palaeographers recognized that they had been miserably deceived and exposed, they declared that everything in this matter was deceptive and full of traps, and that absolutely nothing could be found on which one might safely plant one’s foot. Nor, after Blanchinus had exhibited as carefully as possible a specimen of the script of that little book [Note: Volume I of the liturgical works of the venerable Cardinal Tomasi, among the prolegomena, p. 131], do I think that any reason or conjecture can be found for assigning it more readily to the seventh century than to the eighth—especially since very few Codices of the former century survive written in the non-square script, or in a script approaching what is called the square style. We know, moreover, that the cursive writing in which the little book is composed began to be used frequently only in the three centuries that followed and then became extremely common.

And for my part, if I may freely state my judgment on this matter, had I ever encountered a manuscript in a similar script, the character of the late eighth century, and perhaps of the early ninth, would immediately have struck my eye. But if Blanchinus and Cennius should argue that the antiquity of the manuscript must be inferred not from its script—which may be more recent—but from its diction and subject matter, I will so far agree with them: the manuscript contains passages that savor of the most remote antiquity. Among these is the following, concerning the complete defeat of the superstition of idols, in one of the Orations on Saints Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius:

> “Grant that we may always love you in truth, and also faithfully adore you, so that, once every superstition of idols has been defeated, we may follow, by imitating, the footsteps of your martyrs, pleasing to you.”

[Note: Among the Orations on Saints Fructuosus and his companions, p. 56. I think this should be referred to the period when traces of paganism still remained in Spain.]

[Col. 0627A] Yet even from these considerations no sufficiently strong argument for the age of the manuscript can be drawn, since ancient Orations are generally retained even in more recent liturgical books. Moreover, although Cennius found this very Oration in the Mozarabic Breviary, as Blanchinus testifies—

[Note: In the margin opposite that Oration, p. 56, one reads: “Mozarabic Breviary, fol. 352, col. 1.”]

—he nevertheless judged that Breviary to belong to the tenth century.

[Note: Vol. I of *Antiquities of the Hispanic Church*, p. 28ff., nos. 8 and 10, cited by Blanchinus, *Orationary*, p. 133ff.]

Besides, in most places the manuscript’s inflated style displays at least the Carolingian period and extreme barbarism.

[Note: Among other passages, we selected the Oration of Saint Hippolytus found in the *Orationary*, p. 131:

> “Light of angels and of men, splendor of days and of times, brightness of souls and of bodies, Christ the Lord God: on account of the reverence due to your martyr Hippolytus, receive the offering of flame-crowned radiance, sprinkling it with the light-bearing descent of the Holy Spirit; make it pleasing by your commands and render it fruitful for us, so that by visible brightness it may restrain the dark gloom of night-wandering, and by invisible gift consume the rough errors of sins.”]

Such was the condition into which our Spain was brought by the Moorish devastation, as we learn from the testimony of Alvarus of Córdoba, who flourished not long after that century.

[Note: In the *Luminous Catalogue* of our Flórez, vol. XI of *Sacred Spain*, p. 274:

> “They do not know their own law,” he says, “and the Latins do not attend to their own language, so that throughout the entire Christian community scarcely one man in a thousand can rationally compose a greeting-letter to his brother.”]

Indeed, if God wills, we can observe in that manuscript unmistakable traces even of the Moorish devastation of Spain itself.

[Note: In the Oration on Saint Stephen, p. 41, at the beginning:

> “So that, overcoming both external and internal wars by the fortification of Christian faith, we may deserve to be led to the eternal crown.”

A little farther below, concerning the same Stephen, p. 41:

> “That by whose power the multitude of unbelievers was defeated, by his intercession may the hope of believers, once strengthened, be made firm.”

These passages are certainly ambiguous.

Likewise, among the Orations on Saint Vincent the Martyr, p. 60:

> “Lord God, who grant salvation to kings and deliver your martyr Vincent from the sword of the wicked … deliver us from the hand of foreign sons, so that our life may not lie open to enemies lying in wait; nor may their savage insolence rejoice in the falls of our ruin, but, girded with the sword of your word, may we here also overcome adversity without fear,” etc.

And again, concerning the same saint, ibid.:

> “God, who made your most blessed martyr Vincent a bronze wall for your people, so that by the power of your name he might wondrously overcome those fighting against him.”

Finally, on the same page, at the end and the beginning of the following page:

> “Almighty God, who granted to the most blessed Vincent that through you he might become … from soldier, commander; from servant, friend … grant in your mercy that, through diligent intercession … he may apply discipline to military service and freedom to servitude,” etc.

There may be other examples.]

But let us resume the interrupted discussion.

## CHAPTER VI. Other arguments drawn from Prudentius’s Laurentian hymn against the Spanish position are examined.

[Col. 0627B]

Blanchinus’s second argument against the accepted opinion concerning the homeland of Laurence is established from the silence of our Prudentius. As we recently saw, that earlier writer had magnified his conjecture drawn from the Tarragonese little book of Orations; he immediately adds:

[Note: Annotation CVI, p. 292.]

> “To this, however, a second argument borrowed from Prudentius is added. For he is silent about the native soil of the great Laurence. But if the most holy Levite had been born in Spain, the Spanish poet would not have been silent. It was not his custom to do so in the hymns that he composed about national saints.”

Here Blanchinus seems to pause and collect himself somewhat; then, almost in irritation, he continues:

> “But what am I saying? He is not silent. He raises Rome to the heavens. He calls Rome his parent. His testimonies are indeed obscure, but they will now be made clearer by us.”

Thus far Blanchinus.

For my part, I would not wish to prejudge the readers’ judgment on this argument, nor to contend with Blanchinus by means of abuse. Yet since I must deal at length with him and with matters of no importance, if the reader should detect anything said by us that is somewhat too harsh or severe, I ask him to regard it as a reply rather than an attack; and whatever waste of leisure is necessarily incurred in reading these matters—or whatever further tedium must be endured—let him charge not to me, as though I had voluntarily pursued trivialities, but to the man who compelled me to write.

Blanchinus’s argument therefore consists of four theses, which we must examine in order:

1. That Prudentius is silent about Laurence’s homeland.
2. That he would by no means have passed over it in silence if Laurence had been born in Spain.
3. That it was not Prudentius’s custom, in the hymns he composed about national saints, to leave their homelands unmentioned.
4. That nevertheless, if one pays attention, Prudentius did not altogether conceal that the most holy Levite had been born in the City, since he raises Rome to the heavens and calls Rome his parent.

As for the first thesis, I do not deny that in the hymn under discussion not even a word escaped Prudentius from which we could remotely conjecture or suspect that Laurence was born in Spain. Yet if Blanchinus wishes to consider, with somewhat greater attention than before, the author’s purpose both in that hymn and throughout the entire book *περὶ Στεφάνων*—“On Crowns”—he will not be able to deny with us that the subject of Laurence’s homeland had no bearing whatsoever on Prudentius’s purpose in either work, not even incidentally, since there is no mention of our Spain anywhere in that poem.

On the contrary, since Prudentius directly addresses Rome in the poem itself, and is wholly occupied with recounting its religion, triumphs, empire, and sacred relics of the martyrs—especially those of our Laurence—let the fair-minded reader consider how appropriately Prudentius could have inserted Laurence’s homeland into his poem, if the renowned Levite had been born at Rome, and could thereby have gained a new argument for praising the City. Or at least let him consider how likely it would have been for a word to escape Prudentius, while careless or occupied with another thought, from which more discerning readers could scent out that Laurence had been born at Rome.

If to this we add the conjectures formerly drawn by us from the same hymn, by which we excluded Laurence from the Romans, it will follow that Prudentius’s silence about Spain was compatible with his purpose and harmless to the Spaniards; whereas, if Laurence had been born at Rome, his silence about Rome would have been in some sense inconvenient, or at least of no advantage to the Romans. To use the terminology of the schools, we might say that, so far as Spain is concerned, Prudentius passed over Laurence’s homeland negatively; but so far as the City is concerned, he passed it over exclusively.

Blanchinus’s second thesis is this: Prudentius would by no means have passed over Laurence’s homeland in silence if the most holy Levite had been born in Spain. Since, however, he gives the reason for this in the following thesis, we shall demonstrate the falsity of both at the same time below.

Meanwhile, lest we rashly claim that he knew more than he ought to know, Blanchinus should be asked whether he consulted Aegeria—or the Sibylline leaves—on this matter. But if he was permitted to assert, because he knew Prudentius’s practice of not keeping silent about such things, that Prudentius would not have passed over Laurence’s homeland, even though it will presently be shown that Prudentius had no such practice of declaring the homelands of saints, why may we not in turn affirm that the homeland of Laurence, no less than that of the other martyrs, ought to have been omitted by Prudentius in this hymn, unless he wished to contradict himself?

In the third thesis Blanchinus asserts that it was not Prudentius’s custom, in the hymns he composed about national saints, to remain silent about their homelands. “Is that really so?” I ask. Yet Vincent was a Spaniard, a most celebrated Levite and martyr, and, as is believed, born in the same city of Zaragoza as Prudentius; he was likewise raised, educated, and suffered among Spaniards—in short, Spanish in every respect.

Nevertheless, in the hymn that Prudentius composed with the greatest elegance about his passion, and which is scarcely shorter than the hymn on Laurence—

[Note: It is the second in order in Weitzius’s edition. It consists of 144 strophes, whereas the hymn on Laurence, which is numbered third in that edition, contains 146 strophes in all.]

—I find the homeland of the invincible martyr entirely unmentioned. There is neither a word nor a particle from which it can be extracted or even suspected. Let Blanchinus, I ask, compare this with what he wrote in his second thesis: namely, that if Laurence had been born in Spain, Prudentius would by no means have passed over his homeland in that hymn.

Perhaps, however, Blanchinus will regard this as an exceptional feature of the hymn on Vincent, and therefore as insufficient to challenge in any way the otherwise established custom of Prudentius in his other hymns, namely, to announce the homelands of the saints. I would not object if the matter stood thus.

But what if Prudentius never declared anywhere the homeland of any of the Spanish martyrs whose hymns are contained in the book *περὶ Στεφάνων*, and did not even call a single one of them a Spaniard in general terms? This will certainly seem paradoxical to Blanchinus. Nevertheless, we undertake to defend and demonstrate it at our own risk—a conclusion that even the single title of his book, *On the Crowns, or Passions, of the Martyrs*, clearly suggests.

The entire series of hymns in his book, as John Weitzius presents it, must therefore be traversed by us in order.

[Col. 0630A]

The first of all is addressed to the holy martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius, whom Prudentius calls Calagurritans at the outset.

[Note: Hymn I, in honor of the holy martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius of Calagurris.]

Twice in the hymn he praises the Iberian land—

[Note: Strophe II, verse 4.]

—and the settlers whom the Ebro waters—

[Note: Strophe XXXIX, verse 117.]

—that is, Calagurris and the people of Calagurris. Still more explicitly he does so in the hymn concerning the holy martyrs of Zaragoza, where, speaking of those same Hemeterius and Chelidonius, he says:

[Note: Hymn VII, on the holy martyrs of Zaragoza, strophe VIII, verse 21.]

> “Our Calagurris will bear both of them,
>
> whom we venerate.”

As I conjecture, Blanchinus thought that in these passages Prudentius was designating the homeland of both martyrs. Yet Prudentius, who was thinking of no such thing, had in view the place of their passion, and especially of their burial. This is clear from the preceding distich, and much more clearly from the martyrs’ own hymn. At its beginning, speaking of Calagurris, Prudentius says:

[Note: Strophe II, verse 5.]

> “This place seemed worthy to God for holding the bones.”

At the end, however:

[Note: Strophe XXXIX, verse 116.]

> “When it consecrated the bodies of the martyrs to our city.”

Nor could Prudentius, who lived not very long after the age of these martyrs, have been unaware that they were believed to have descended from Marcellus the Centurion at León, a city separated from Calagurris by only a few days’ journey.

The second hymn of his book contains the passion of Saint Vincent the Levite; in it, as we have just said, his homeland is entirely passed over in silence. The third is about Laurence. From it Blanchinus and Merenda wished to draw that Rome was the homeland of the most holy martyr—that is, they wished to draw water from a stone.

[Col. 0630C] We, on the contrary, recently declared that it contains nothing by which our Spain is designated, or from which one could infer that Laurence was born there. The fourth contains the passion of Saint Hippolytus; the fifth, that of Saint Cyprian; and the sixth, those of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Since these do not concern Spanish martyrs, we deliberately pass them over.

Blanchinus thought that the seventh hymn of his book, entitled *Praises of the Eighteen Holy Martyrs of Zaragoza*—

[Note: Hymn VII, in praise of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza. Weitzius, p. 103.]

—was so entirely on his side that it stood by itself. Yet, if I see correctly, he was wonderfully deceived by the appearance of the words. I shall explain the matter as briefly as I can.

In this hymn Prudentius exalts his Zaragoza because it is strongly fortified against the vicissitudes of life by the sacred protection of the eighteen martyrs whose ashes it preserves; and because, on the day of final vengeance, it will offer Christ the King of martyrs, as a votive gift, many more sacred remains than other cities.

He then proceeds to enumerate the neighboring places in which the sacred treasures of relics are stored, and says: Córdoba will offer Acisclus and Zoilus; Tarragona, Fructuosus and his companions; Gerona, Felix; Barcelona, Cucufas; Calagurris, Hemeterius and Chelidonius; Narbonne, Sergius Paulus; Mérida, Eulalia; and finally Complutum, Justus and Pastor.

[Col. 0631A] “Each of these cities,” he adds, “will offer one, two, or three bodies of martyrs. Perhaps one will strive to appease the anger of the eternal Judge with the fivefold sacrifice of saints. But you, Zaragoza, more illustrious in this respect than the others, will alone display the relics of eighteen martyrs—so many as scarcely Carthage, scarcely Rome herself, the mother of the world, could offer—and you will spring forth joyfully to meet Christ.”

Such is the substance of the hymn.

When Blanchinus, as I suppose, viewed this from a distance, thinking that the hymn contained the temporal homelands of the martyrs because the names of Spanish cities were expressly given and attached to them, he did not hesitate to assert that it was not Prudentius’s custom to pass over in silence the homelands of truly Spanish martyrs in the hymns he composed about them.

Yet both Prudentius’s mind elsewhere and especially in the hymn under discussion were very different. He was looking not to the homelands of the martyrs but to the places of their passions, and above all to the places where their sacred ashes were preserved. The very subject of the poem, which we explained earlier, makes this evident. For Prudentius does not say that the cities will offer the empty names of their native martyrs, but their sacred bones.

[Note: Strophe IV, verse 15ff.]

Nor does he praise Zaragoza because it is the homeland of the eighteen martyrs—a matter to which we shall return below—but because their sacred bodies had been buried there.

[Col. 0631C] Here are several passages from the hymn. At the beginning:

[Note: Strophe I, verses 1–2.]

> “Twice nine of our people preserve
>
> the ashes of the martyrs in one tomb.”

At the end:

[Note: Strophe XLIII, verse 173ff.]

> “Then the angel will gather eight
>
> and ten saints before the Father and the Son,
>
> possessing the governance of one city
>
> by right of the tomb.”

And similarly elsewhere throughout.

I can already see Blanchinus wavering; but let us proceed, making the matter clearer by the examples just given. In that hymn Felix is assigned by Prudentius to Gerona, and Cucufas to Barcelona. Yet it is well known that neither of these cities was the homeland of either martyr—or of either one of them individually. Rather, it is established that they were born in the African city of Scillium, which I conjecture, from its location and the similarity of the name, is called Mezilla by the natives in their vernacular today.

[Note: Perhaps this was the city that gave its name to the celebrated Speratus and his companions, who are called the martyrs of Scillium. Yet when, with the help of Cellarius (*Notitia Orbis Antiqui*), Baudrand and Ferrari in their lexicons, Nicholas Antonius (*Historical Censure*, book VI, chapter 2, no. 42), and others cited by them, I tried to determine the modern name of that city, I became much more uncertain than I had previously been. The disagreement and variety of opinion among these authors are so great.

The learned Lesleus (*Notes on the Mozarabic Missal*, p. 603) considers it probable that Scilla was a town of the Proconsular Province, called by others Scillita, distinguished by an episcopal see; this also appears to be the opinion of Nicholas Antonius in the passage just cited. But since it is clear from the Acts of Saint Cucufas supplied by the Bollandist Fathers—25 July, after section 5—that Cucufas emigrated with Felix from his homeland to the coastal city of Caesarea, now commonly thought to be Algiers, for the sake of study, I suspected that Scillium was closer to Caesarea than to Carthage, to which, as the more celebrated city, it would otherwise seem likely that these most holy martyrs were sent for study; and thus that the city belonged not to the Proconsular Province but to Caesarian Mauretania.

Moreover, when I found on recent geographical maps, not far from modern Algiers, a town called Mezilla, I was led by the similarity of the name to conjecture that this was the ancient Scillium, the homeland of Felix and Cucufas. For if the initial consonant, which is certainly servile, together with its vowel, is removed from that name, Zilla remains.]

Calagurris is likewise listed as offering the relics of Hemeterius and Chelidonius to Christ; yet we recently said, on the basis of the common and most widely accepted opinion, that they were born at León. In that poem Prudentius assigns Paulus and the aforementioned Sergius to Narbonne in Gaul because the sacred bones of the martyr rest there to this day. Yet he is believed to have been born in the City and to have held distinguished offices both at home and in the provinces, as well as the proconsulate; certainly he was not a native of Narbonne.

Nor do we know whether Zoilus and Acisclus belong to Córdoba by right of birth, although Prudentius assigns them to that city because of the place of their martyrdom and burial.

[Note: It is a constant tradition of the authors, derived from ancient Breviaries, legendary collections, and Acts, that Zoilus and Acisclus were once inhabitants of Córdoba. Our learned Flórez discusses this in vol. X, pp. 289 and 307. We have no certain information about their homeland, and that author has reported nothing definite.]

Indeed, I believe that the eighteen martyrs themselves, whose special hymn is under discussion, were assigned by Prudentius to Zaragoza by no other right than that of burial. Certainly he does not claim that any of them lived at Zaragoza while they were alive, saying:

[Note: Strophe XXIX.]

> “Since none of the martyrs, while life remained,
>
> happened to inhabit our lands.”

But if Blanchinus should gratuitously assert that these same martyrs were born at Zaragoza, we have an oracular pronouncement as stubborn as a ram: Prudentius is equally silent about their homeland and about that of the other martyrs.

Since this is so, it will now be clear that in the hymn under discussion Prudentius by no means had in view the temporal homelands of the martyrs, but only the places where their sacred relics were then honored.

“But,” Blanchinus nevertheless says, “the hymn also mentions Eulalia, whose ashes Mérida is said to bring joyfully to Christ; likewise Justus and Pastor of Complutum; and Fructuosus and his companions of Tarragona. Yet we know that these martyrs drew their birth from the very cities to which they are assigned. Therefore it cannot be said that Prudentius was always silent about the homelands of the martyrs in that hymn.”

What then? These martyrs happened to be summoned to the palm of martyrdom in the very city that had earlier given them to the world, and there they were laid in a tomb by Christians. Therefore, when Prudentius enumerated in that hymn the seats of their passions and relics, he could not separate the homelands of these martyrs from those places. Since the place of their burial and birth was one and the same, he could not designate the former—the place where they had suffered—without also indicating the latter.

Yet nowhere did that author deliberately enumerate their homelands, nor did he even think about them, as the subject of the hymn makes clear.

Another passage of the poem itself, sufficiently clear in its own right, will demonstrate this. Although Prudentius elsewhere believed Vincent the Levite to have been born and raised at Zaragoza—

[Note: This is clear to me from the twenty-sixth and following strophes.

Prudentius is joined in this opinion by Eugenius the Younger, bishop of Toledo, in his epigram on the Basilica of Saint Vincent the Martyr at Zaragoza, in the middle of which one reads:

> “Sacred passion raised your name to heaven.
>
> May your sacred passion preserve your people.”
