Our learned citizen and friend Dominicus Lopezius Barrera, director of the archives of the Spanish embassy in Rome, had previously pointed out this passage to us from Sirmondus when he read these reflections in our *Adversaria*. It is also found in Lesleus, *Notes on the Mozarabic Missal*, p. 551, col. 1.]

—nevertheless, because Vincent had suffered and been buried outside his homeland, namely at Valencia in Edetania, Prudentius does not dare to include him among those martyrs whom he calls, with full right, Zaragozans. Rather, setting aside the temporal homeland of the most holy Levite, he assigns him to the group added to the Zaragozans in the hymn as an appendix and outside the regular order.

Thus, after listing the names of the eighteen holy martyrs, he establishes, so to speak, a second class: those who cannot be assigned to Zaragoza by as equal a right as the former group. Among these he counts Encratis, who, as Prudentius himself says, survived her own death; likewise the two confessors of Christ, Gaius and Crementius, whom he relates to have stood unbroken against the roar of robbers after lightly tasting the flavor of martyrdom; and finally Vincent.

Although Vincent had suffered and been buried outside his homeland, a portion of his sacred blood was nevertheless preserved at Zaragoza.

[Note: Whether it was the tunic or stole of the most blessed Levite, or rather a little linen cloth—that is, his sweat-cloth sprinkled with the same blood—is disputed among the authors. See Lesleus, *Annotations on the Mozarabic Missal*, p. 561.

Eugenius of Toledo’s epigram appears expressly to speak of the linen cloth, for he says:

> “Here lies that blood which you give as a pledge for the body,
>
> your blood, flowing from the dripping nostril;
>
> here lies that blood.”]

Prudentius says that the Zaragoza community valued it no less than if it possessed the remaining relics of the sacred body. Here are Prudentius’s words:

[Note: Strophe XXIIff., verse 89.]

> “Did you not, Vincent, though destined to die
>
> a martyr in foreign lands, mark upon these lands
>
> with a fine sprinkling of blood the likeness”—[Note: I think *specimen* should be restored, although all the manuscripts read *speciem*, as can be seen in the variant readings of Prudentius in Weitzius. The sense does not reject this, and grammatical reasoning seems to require it; for what follows is: “This they honor”—that is, the *specimen*. Certainly, near the end of the same hymn, speaking of Encratis, he says:

> “The girl alive after the token of punishment.”]—“of your approaching death?

> “This the citizens honor, as though the earth itself
>
> enclosed the very limbs and, embracing them,
>
> preserved in a father’s tomb
>
> the bones of the blessed martyr.”

For the same reason, to return to our subject, in the ninth hymn of his book, addressed to Saint Eulalia of Mérida—we deliberately passed over the eighth, which contains the passion of Saint Agnes—Prudentius says that because the renowned virgin and martyr had suffered in her homeland of Mérida and had been buried there, and because that city still preserved Eulalia’s sacred relics in Prudentius’s time, she had been brought forth there into the light of day. This is mentioned incidentally, and perhaps merely to fill a gap in the strophe. Here are the words of the hymn:

[Note: Hymn IX, in honor of the blessed martyr Eulalia.]

> “Noble by birth, Eulalia,
>
> nobler still in the character of her death,
>
> adorns her sacred Mérida,
>
> from whose breast she was born,
>
> and cherishes it in love with her bones.”

[Col. 0633D]

Here it should be noted that the clause “from whose breast she was born,” appended to the period, is plainly an *ἐπισύναψις*—a syntactical attachment. Therefore, if you remove it entirely, nothing is taken away from the author’s meaning or purpose in that strophe, just as nothing is lost if a parenthesis is removed from a sentence.

The sense is this: Eulalia protects her Mérida by the love of its citizen, and the city is adorned with her sacred bones. Prudentius repeats this twice near the end of the same hymn, saying:

[Note: Strophe XXXVIII, verse 186.]

> “Now Mérida is the place of the tomb.”

And a little farther below:

[Note: Strophe XXXIX, verses 191, 194ff.]

> “Here, where the venerable earth
>
> preserves in its gleaming marble
>
> the sacred relics and ashes in its bosom.”

Thus Prudentius seems to have had in view the place of burial, not the homeland of Eulalia.

[Col. 0634B]

The tenth hymn of his book remains for us to examine, containing the passion of Fructuosus and his companions of Tarragona. The remaining four do not concern Spaniards or do not treat of saints. In this hymn, although much is clearly said about the tortures and remarkable steadfastness of these martyrs, about their sacred ashes, and about the place of their burial, I have so far been unable to find anything that could be referred to their homeland. Nor is Tarragona praised except in connection with the martyrdom and sacred relics of Fructuosus, which the people of Tarragona preserved in Prudentius’s time.

From this I am entirely convinced that Prudentius deliberately designates the homeland of none of the Spanish martyrs whose hymns are contained in the book *περὶ Στεφάνων*; and that Blanchinus’s third thesis is extremely weak and false in every respect.

Finally, we undertake to refute the fourth thesis, in which the same author asserts that in the hymn under discussion Prudentius is not silent about Laurence’s homeland, and that he sufficiently implies that it was Rome, provided that Spaniards are willing to pay attention, since he raises the City to the heavens and calls it his parent.

But we shall show that Blanchinus suffered here as well from a somewhat human error. For the moment, however, I would very much like to know from him how he came to think that the praises of the City collected by Prudentius contained anything about Laurence’s homeland. In my judgment these are different matters—indeed, very far removed from one another.

Prudentius praises Rome, as we said earlier, for its religion, triumphs, empire, and sacred relics of the martyrs. But what, I ask, does this have in common with the homeland of our Laurence? Or why would Prudentius not praise the City for all the other reasons for which it deserved praise, especially when he addressed it as though it were present before him from the farthest reaches of the West?

“But,” says Blanchinus, “he does not merely praise it; he also calls it his parent.”

“Whose parent?” I ask. Laurence’s? Certainly not. Rather—and this comes to the same thing—the parent of shrines. Is Blanchinus speaking seriously, or does he deliberately wish to make sport of us? Here is the outline of the hymn.

At the beginning Prudentius addresses Rome, which he calls the former parent of shrines, though now dedicated to Christ; and he congratulates it that nothing is now lacking from its glory, since it has conquered and overthrown not only the mortal race of men but also the immortal gods—the sole remaining obstacle—and Jupiter himself.

[Col. 0635B] We have retained the pagan expression for the sake of emphasis in the Christian argument.

He then proceeds to describe the prophecy of Sixtus concerning Laurence’s death, the dignity of the most holy Levite, the greed of the governor, and finally the events preceding his passion, until, as Prudentius says—

[Note: Strophe LXXXII, verse 348.]

—“with his body half-burned,” the martyr is represented as speaking from the rack and, praying to Christ amid the flames, asks that he who commanded all nations to obey the Roman Empire may make those same nations, once the monsters of superstition have been driven from them, unite in one faith.

Since we have already wasted so much leisure uselessly on other matters, permit me now, I say, to compare Laurence’s prayer as it appears in the hymn with the prayer that the most holy Levite offered to Christ, the King of martyrs, amid the turmoil of the flames. How much loftier, more effective, and more penetrating was the style of that primitive and, so to speak, archetypal prayer than that of this later example, elegant though it is! Compared with the prayer of Laurence, how childish is Prudentius’s eloquence, how crude his speech, how inarticulate his rhetoric!

What groans would the most holy Levite have uttered, what sighs amid the flames, and, when his eyes were already swimming in death, what vision of the light he was about to receive from above would he have fixed upon heaven! Attic and Roman eloquence would plainly have yielded, even if they had combined their strength to sketch the fiery eloquence of the invincible martyr.

But let us return to our subject.

The poet then proceeds to recount how much faith and strength were added to the Christians by Laurence’s triumph, and how much shame and disgrace accrued to the pagans, saying that their shrines were gradually deserted while the churches were attended more and more each day.

He piously envies the Romans because they possess Laurence’s sacred relics and can venerate them as present—something not granted to him, separated from the City by such distances. He adds that such efficacy resides in Laurence’s merits that no one departs from his tomb sad or empty-handed; and finally he prays that he may be graciously heard among those devoted to his worship.

This is the whole substance and sequence of Prudentius’s Laurentian hymn. Others with sharper eyes may perhaps find something in it relevant to Blanchinus’s purpose; but although I have read the hymn more than a hundred times, I have not managed to find a single word relating to that subject.

Thus far concerning Blanchinus’s objections.

But another scruple of Merenda’s does not yet allow us to depart, although he himself considers it a very powerful argument. Since Prudentius writes that the only thing lacking from Roman glory was that, after conquering the world, it should also defeat filthy Jupiter—

[Note: Strophe IV, verse 13ff.]

> “Not by the turbulent forces
>
> of Cossus, Camillus, or Caesar,
>
> but by the battle not without blood
>
> of the martyr Laurence”—

the aforementioned author thinks that it follows, and follows clearly, that Laurence should by no means be separated from those famous commanders whom Prudentius names in that strophe and who are known to have been born at Rome.

Yet Merenda had no need to torment and torture himself so miserably in extracting this meaning from Prudentius’s hymn, since one everywhere encounters Leo’s statement concerning Laurence in the same sense: as Jerusalem was glorified by Stephen, so Rome would become illustrious through Laurence.

[Note: Sermon on the feast of Saint Laurence.]

Yet I scarcely know whether anyone, ancient or modern, has hitherto used this statement to establish a Roman homeland for Laurence. Why not? Obviously because they knew that Leo was not speaking there about Laurence’s homeland; the parallelism between the cities was not established by the birthplaces of the two martyrs but by their contest and triumphs. In the same way Prudentius compares the wars of the ancient commanders with the victories of our Laurence, and declares the latter more illustrious than the former to the degree that heavenly beings surpass mortals, and the supreme God himself surpasses Jupiter.

These triumphs, these laurels of the martyrs, were what the ancient Fathers of the Church celebrated, without concerning themselves meanwhile with the temporal homelands of those martyrs, since they knew that such homelands contributed nothing to virtue. Apart from Prudentius, Tertullian, Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and others are exceedingly weighty witnesses to this; there is no leisure to set out their passages here.

I therefore think that Merenda’s scruple can easily be removed. For in the hymn under discussion Prudentius compares not the births of Laurence with the births of Cossus, Camillus, or Caesar, but their triumphs with his triumph. Anyone who considers the words and the meaning of the sentence with a mind free from prejudice will acknowledge with us that this was entirely the poet’s purpose.

If, however, Merenda wishes to extend the comparison to their homelands as well, we think he must be driven by Prudentius’s own hymn either to assert that Peter and Paul were Romans by birth, or conversely to make Nero a Galilean or a native of Tarsus. Let us see on what grounds.

In that hymn Prudentius introduces our Levite, who attacks Jupiter fiercely and commands him in these very words to go into perpetual exile from the City:

[Note: Strophe LXXVII, verse 469ff.]

> “Depart, adulterous Jupiter,
>
> forgetful of your sister’s defilement;
>
> leave Rome free,
>
> and flee the people who now belong to Christ.
>
> “Paul drives you out from here;
>
> the blood of Peter thrusts you forth;
>
> what you yourself once armed—
>
> the deed of Nero—works against you.”

The meaning of the latter strophe is this: “Depart, impure Jupiter. Peter and Paul are not merely your perpetual haters and enemies; Nero himself, who once worshiped you with exceptional devotion and into whom you inspired the monstrous plan of murdering them, drives you far away and expels you from the City. Now all are united in the purpose of your exile.”

Now, if from Laurence’s contest with the ancient Cossus, Camillus, and Caesar—obviously intended to glorify the City through their triumphs—Merenda may infer that Laurence, like those commanders, was Roman by birth, then, since Nero also conspires with the blessed apostles to drive Jupiter from the City, we may likewise make either the apostles Roman by birth or Nero a Galilean or a native of Tarsus.

But these are mere absurdities.

## CHAPTER VII. The Principal Argument of Blanchini, Drawn from the Veronese Sacramentary, Is Refuted

Thus far Blanchini has brought only his skirmishers and spearmen into the line, supposing, as I imagine, that the whole affair could be settled by a light engagement and that there would be no need for him to join battle in earnest. Now, however, having noticed that the fight must be renewed with somewhat greater force, he summons his cuirassed triarii and cataphracts—that is, a vigorous force for serious warfare—which he throws against us in the densest possible formation. Yet, since the outcomes of wars are varied, he does not abandon the auxiliary cohort, which may come opportunely to the aid of the hard-pressed soldier. We therefore need a great effort [Col. 0637C], if indeed so great an assault must be sustained.

In the argument preceding this one, Blanchini had promised to illuminate for us Prudentius’s testimony concerning the homeland of Lawrence, which he does not deny to be somewhat obscure. He then proceeds to enumerate the cities that contend over Homer’s birthplace, and suggests that the dispute concerning Lawrence is similar, since each party claims the invincible martyr for itself and vindicates him as its own. At this point, somewhat stirred, he says:

> “Shall I never reply? I—I am here. And since by decree of the Roman Senate and People I am a Roman citizen, I SAY, VINDICATE, CLAIM, AND CONFIRM THAT LAWRENCE WAS A ROMAN, to the everlasting glory and praise of that same Roman People.” [Note: [Col. 0637D] Blanchini, Annotation CVI in *The Most Ancient Orationary of the Gothic Rite*, p. 292.]

Nor, he continues, do I indulge in conjectures alone; I also produce a most authoritative witness, namely the Leonian Sacramentary.

This work, he goes on, which I made publicly available in Volume IV of Anastasius the Librarian, was admired by the entire republic of letters, and rapidly attained the distinction of being foremost in the glory of antiquity. For the Church of Paris, which was capable of judging the author’s genius, “MOST FIRMLY ASSIGNED IT TO THE GREAT LEO” in the preface to the new Missal published in 1739, in these words.

Blanchini quotes the words of the Missal, which appear to have proceeded more from its editors than from the Church of Paris; and, what is decisive, they do not establish that either those earlier authorities or this later one attributed the Sacramentary in question to Saint Leo. They say only [Note: [Col. 0637D] “From that distinguished monument”—namely, the Veronese Sacramentary—“we have borrowed many prayers breathing an exceptional piety and reflecting the style and teaching of the great Leo, to whom, as their most certain author, they are attributed.” These words belong to the editors of the Missal, not to the Church of Paris; Acamus himself admits this on pp. 124, 265, and elsewhere. Preface of the new Missal published at Paris in 1739, in Blanchini, Annotation CVI, *Gothic Orationary*, p. 292.] many prayers breathing an exceptional piety and reflecting the style of the holy pontiff, “TO WHOM THEY ARE ATTRIBUTED AS THEIR MOST CERTAIN AUTHOR.” We present the substance of the passage, since it would be too long to transcribe it in full.

“From this perfectly clear fountain,” Blanchini adds, “I shall therefore draw purer waters, and shall surely prove that LAWRENCE, SINCE HE IS A ROMAN CITIZEN, MUST NOT BE SEPARATED FROM THE NUMBER OF CITIZENS; BUT, ON THE CONTRARY, THAT ALL MUST ACKNOWLEDGE THAT HE OUGHT TO BE CLAIMED AGAIN, WITH THE ACCLAMATION OF THE WHOLE CITY AND OF THE SACRED [Col. 0638B] APOSTOLIC COLLEGE.” He continues:

> “Behold, I recite the preface of Mass XII for the feast of Saint Lawrence, which is found on page XXXVIII of the Leonian Sacramentary:
>
> “It is truly right. Although, Lord, through you the glory of your saints is renowned throughout the whole world, nevertheless ROME REJOICES MORE PARTICULARLY THAN OTHER CITIES IN THE SOLEMNITY OF BLESSED LAWRENCE, WHO IS BY BIRTH HER CITIZEN, HER SACRED MINISTER, AND HER PARTICULAR OFFICE DEDICATED TO YOUR NAME.”

“If I were to say nothing else about Lawrence’s citizenship,” he concludes, “the case would be settled. FOR HOW CAN THE TESTIMONY OF SO GREAT A PONTIFF BE WEAKENED?” Behold the sum of Blanchini’s strength.

Before we join battle, it would certainly be useful to say a few words about the author of the Veronese Sacramentary, whose testimony Blanchini presses upon us so vigorously [Col. 0638C], so that readers may weigh the force of his authority on a proper scale. When I first sketched this work, so much concerning that subject came to mind that, after completing my treatments of Damasus and Lawrence, I planned an additional, separate work specifically on the author of the Veronese Sacramentary. I was also able to bring it to the desired conclusion.

In that work—and here I am pleased merely to indicate its substance, since it will be published separately in due course—I not only traced at length the history and vicissitudes of the Sacramentary, an otherwise distinguished work that underwent truly immense changes almost from its infancy; but, if I may say so without ill omen, I also showed and demonstrated fully that Saint Leo was not the author of that Sacramentary [Col. 0638D], nor its author and compiler at the same time—as Blanchini’s new associate, in order to come to the aid of his hard-pressed colleague, has playfully invented the term *δευτερόπρωτον*, “second-first” [Note: [Col. 0638D] Count Acamus, *Dissertation on the Antiquity, Author, and Merits of the Veronese Sacramentary*, Part II, § II, pp. 58, 165, 227, and passim.]. Indeed, Leo never even saw the Sacramentary, since the archetypal codex first appeared long after Leo’s lifetime.

Nevertheless, we do not want readers to place their confidence in these statements of ours without investigation. For the moment, let them remain attached to the title *Leonian*, which the Sacramentary bears [Col. 0639A], remembering that “to believe without rashness is the sinews and limbs of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0639D] A saying of Epicharmus, quoted by Cicero, *On the Petition for the Consulship*, no. 10.].

But lest I appear too scrupulous to Blanchini in the meantime, I shall not hesitate, if our Spanish compatriots permit it, to attribute the Sacramentary, as broadly as it stands, gratuitously to Saint Leo. Nor, moreover, do I fear that the passage placed before us may contain some defect of the sort that commonly creeps into ancient codices through the long succession of their owners and their differing abilities: whether, that is, something in it has been erased or rubbed out; whether some gloss, which ordinary people call a marginal annotation, has been introduced into the text; or whether there is anything else that might in any way render the reliability of the reading suspect.

If Blanchini had detected any such defect in that passage, I believe that, given his integrity, he would not have concealed it; even if the codex had ceased altogether to exist, he would have disclosed it frankly and faithfully, as befits a religious man [Col. 0639B].

As for the antiquity of the codex, although the specimen of its script published by Blanchini among the *Prolegomena* to Anastasius does not entirely remove every doubt, I nevertheless think that it may conveniently be assigned to the eighth century or the beginning of the following century [Note: [Col. 0639D] Volume IV of Anastasius, p. 21.]. It would nonetheless be helpful if Blanchini would also tell us about the quality of the parchment—whether it was polished or prepared—and especially about its shape, whether square or oblong. For in a doubtful matter such as the dating of codices generally is, these aids confirm an opinion concerning their antiquity; indeed, more expert paleographers often draw strong conjectures from them [Col. 0639C].

I might reasonably suspect one thing: whether the passage under discussion was corrupted through the carelessness of a copyist; and especially whether the two words “a citizen by birth” slipped into the text from a gloss in an older codex, or were interpolated in some other way. Acamus has preceded us in a similar suspicion, although it was very much in his interest to preserve the codex in question whole and uncorrupted.

For when he was pressed somewhere by one of Blanchini’s opponents to retract their common opinion concerning the author of that codex, and was challenged to do so on the basis of the codex’s own words, he did not hesitate to declare that the passage brought against him had been corrupted or damaged by the carelessness of a copyist. I shall explain the matter in order.

When the Veronese Sacramentary was first published, the republic of liturgical scholars admired not so much the codex itself—as Blanchini falsely persuaded himself—as the previously unheard-of name *Leonian* that had been assigned to it. Its principal students, men of the highest distinction, aroused by the novelty of the title, unanimously charged Blanchini with a prejudged attribution, each rejecting the Sacramentary’s assignment to Saint Leo the Great on his own grounds.

Among them, the learned Meratus [Note: [Col. 0639D] In the observations and additions to Bartolomeo Gavanti’s *Thesaurus of Sacred Rites*, vol. I, part I, p. 8; cited in Acamus, *Dissertation on the Veronese Sacramentary*, Part II, p. 126.] appears to argue from the mention of Pope Simplicius that he found in the Sacramentary. Since Simplicius was somewhat later than Leo, he seems to conclude that the codex was written not in Leo’s time but in that of Simplicius, and therefore cannot be attributed to Leo.

Acamus readily answers this argument—which everyone can see is highly effective—by proposing either that the mention of Simplicius was added to the codex after Simplicius’s death, as happens in books assigned for the use of churches, or that through the carelessness of a copyist the name of Saint Simplicius was inserted where the name of Saint Silvester ought to have been written [Note: [Col. 0640D] Acamus, Part II, p. 126: “Or it could be answered that through the negligence of the person who copied the Sacramentary, the name of Saint Simplicius was substituted for that of Saint Silvester.” He says the same on the following page.].

Nor does the learned Muratorius disagree. Speaking somewhere of this same mention of Simplicius, he says [Note: [Col. 0640D] Dissertation on the Ancient Roman Liturgy, vol. I, chap. 3, col. 26.]:

> “We have already seen above that prayers were offered to God in this Sacramentary for the soul of Simplicius the bishop. It is permissible to suspect that this passage was corrupted by a copyist.”

And shortly afterward:

> “We may conjecture that three prayers in honor of Saint Silvester had been placed in the codex . . . But when the copyist was writing this collection, he carelessly passed by a leap from one to another.”

If, then, both of these writers, and especially Acamus—whenever the words of the Sacramentary seem to proceed poorly from his own opinion and that of Blanchini—may safely assert that the passage in question is damaged or corrupted, precisely where it pricks them, why should the same indulgence not be granted to us? Why should we not likewise be permitted to suspect that in the *Contestatio* brought against us, the words “a citizen by birth,” if we wish to understand them as containing Lawrence’s homeland, were added, superimposed, or interpolated in some other way? “The itch reaches its extreme limit.” [*O cupet extremum scabies*: a proverbial expression, literally “the itch desires the ultimate point.”]

Moreover, there are conjectures that plainly assist us in strengthening this suspicion and that could tire not only a fair and impartial reader but Fabius himself [Col. 0640C], so abundant and varied is their number. Lest anyone think that this has been said more splendidly than truthfully in order to occupy the minds of readers, it will be worthwhile to present the principal ones.

We said earlier that the Fathers and writers of the Church, when dealing with the temporal homelands of martyrs, were exceedingly sparing of words, while, on the contrary, they were most diligent in describing the martyrs’ sufferings and identifying the places where those sufferings took place. That statement, however, was somewhat general. We now add that even in the Acts of the martyrs—where their homelands might in some sense seem to have their proper place, since everything else concerning their sufferings is described in minute detail—their birthplaces are narrated only very rarely [Col. 0640D].

What shall we say of the Martyrologies, in which the place of martyrdom is recorded almost constantly, but the place of birth only exceptionally? The same may be observed in the sermons or homilies that the ancient Fathers preached to the people concerning the martyrs, and even in the Lives of the saints themselves.

I pass over Prudentius, about whom enough and more than enough has been said. I pass over the other ancient writers, with the single exception of Jerome, who, in his treatise *On Illustrious Men*, after briefly appending the writings and lives of those who had flourished in learning from apostolic times down to his own age [Col. 0641A], disclosed the birthplace of none of those who died as martyrs—apart from Justin and Phileas, whose homelands he explicitly identifies, and Cyprian, whom he generally calls an African.

We add the reason, lest anyone suppose that the ancients did this gratuitously: the Acts, homilies, Martyrologies, and Lives of the saints were written not to glorify cities or flatter the ears, but to form the minds of the faithful in piety. For that purpose, nothing concerning the martyrs’ race or ancestors was useful, whereas their outstanding deeds and sufferings were exceedingly valuable.

With the same purpose, and not without divine providence, the Church established from the earliest centuries that from the Acts of the martyrs a very brief remembrance of their passion should pass into the books of the sacred liturgy; and that in their proper Masses the torments of the martyrs should be recounted concisely, as Hilduin says [Note: [Col. 0641D] In the Letter to Louis the Pious prefixed to the *Areopagitica*, in Th. Ruinart, Preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, § 1, no. 5.].

Ruinart confirms this clearly from the most ancient liturgies, saying [Note: [Col. 0641D] *Preface to the Acts of the Martyrs*, somewhat below.]:

> “Moreover, the principal deeds of the martyrs were inserted even into the prayers of the Mass, as can be proved from the most ancient liturgies—the Gallican, the Mozarabic, and even the Gregorian. For in them the *contestationes* of the Mass, which are now commonly called prefaces, are nothing other than an exposition of the splendid deeds of the martyrs in whose honor the Mass is celebrated.”

It is also useful to cite a passage from Gregory of Tours [Note: [Col. 0641D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, Book II, chap. 14, Paris edition of 1699, col. 1046.]:

> “It happened on the day of the solemnity of blessed Martin, while we were saying Mass and, as we duly celebrated the sacred solemnities, were recounting in the *contestatio* the miracles of the holy lord, that suddenly the paralyzed girl began to cry out,” and so forth.

From these points, I think it becomes clear that, in accordance with what we have continually observed in the Acts, homilies, and histories of the martyrs by the ancient Fathers of the Church—namely, that their authors paid little attention to the martyrs’ temporal homelands—so also in the Sacramentaries and the martyrs’ proper Masses, in a remarkable harmony between the Fathers and the sacred liturgy, their torments and principal deeds, as Gregory and Hilduin stated, were recounted, but not their homelands.

This was even less likely to occur here than in the Acts, Martyrologies, and homilies, since the authors of all those works had a broader field for composition and expression than did the compilers of the liturgy. In the liturgy, only a very brief and concise remembrance of the martyrs’ passion could be given [Col. 0641D].

Since it is established that the ancient ecclesiastical Sacramentaries—the Gelasian, the Gregorian, and the very Leonian one under discussion—are nothing other than Mass books that the earlier pontiffs, from whom they took their names, used for the sacred liturgy and made available for the use of the Roman Church, the following conclusion seems entirely justified.

Whenever a passage in these Sacramentaries—or the same judgment may be applied to the other liturgical books, especially those prepared for the use of the Roman Church—is found to contain the temporal homeland or lineage of a martyr, a rare occurrence indeed, that passage ought rightly to be regarded as suspect, since it accords poorly with the spirit of the Church.

I therefore think that Blanchini should be made somewhat uneasy if he insists that the words “a citizen by birth” contain Lawrence’s homeland, and that he should ask what credibility is ultimately to be assigned to them. These considerations are minor, however, unless he also observes that the Church’s practice of omitting the martyrs’ homelands from liturgical books has been confirmed by continuous usage.

Let him read, if he please, the Gelasian, the three Gregorian Sacramentaries, the Bobbio Sacramentary, and whatever other Sacramentaries of the ancient rite exist. I deliberately omit the Leonian, which is in dispute and must eventually be examined separately in its proper place [Col. 0642B]. Let him also read the Missals, Legendary books, Orationaries, and other liturgical codices published by Pamelius, Mabillon, Cardinal Thomasius, and Muratorius. Finally, let him reread the *Orationary of the Most Ancient Gothic Rite*, which he himself published with notes.

If, throughout these works, extensive as they are, or in any one of them, he encounters a word by which the homeland of one of the saints contained in them is even remotely indicated, I promise him in good faith, with every trick of argument excluded, that I shall regard the *Contestatio* of the Veronese Sacramentary under discussion—and therefore those words “a citizen by birth”—as a genuine, authentic, and uncorrupted product of Saint Leo.

Yet lest I seem to sin against the public interest by imposing so much tedium upon a man already burdened with more serious matters [Col. 0642C], I can assure Blanchini in all solemnity—or even swear it in explicit terms, if necessary—that I have carefully examined the Sacramentaries commonly circulated: namely, Cardinal Thomasius’s Gelasian Sacramentary; the three Gregorian Sacramentaries of Jacopo Pamelius, Angelo Rocca, and Hugo Menard; Mabillon’s Gallican Sacramentary, often called the Bobbio Sacramentary; another attributed to Grimoald; as well as the anonymous Sacramentary attributed to Alcuin and published by Pamelius.

I have also examined the following Missals: the Gothic-Gallican, the Frankish, and the Old Gallican, or Auxerre, Missal; the most ancient Luxovian Legendary; the Ambrosian and Gelasian Prefationaries; the ancient Roman Orders of Hittorp, Martène, and Muratorius; and finally the *Orationary of the Most Ancient Gothic-Hispanic Rite*, published by Blanchini among the prolegomena to Cardinal Thomasius’s works and supplied with notes.

Yet in all these works I have so far found no passage in which the homeland of the saints is stated, or from which it might even be conjectured or secretly inferred, apart from those apocryphal words of the Gothic-Gallican Missal in which the homeland, lineage, and journeys of Pope Clement and the martyr are described [Note: [Col. 0641D] In Leslie’s Mozarabic Missal—which, as we stated earlier, was only published after this entire work had been completed—there is indeed, in the Masses of the martyrs Vincent, Fructuosus, and Eulalia of Barcelona, some mention of their homeland.

In the case of Vincent, the statement is entirely general, from which nothing more can be inferred than that the most holy deacon was a Spaniard—though whether a martyr or a citizen, nothing further can be determined.

The statement concerning Fructuosus and his companions is more precise, since in the admonition or preparatory address of their Mass we read [p. 310, col. 1]:

> “Let us praise, by prayer, the ineffable majesty of almighty God, who has granted us, through the most blessed passion of the saints of Tarragona—Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius—great protectors of the Church and of their homeland.”

A little farther on:

> “And although that region which received them—the heavenly homeland, namely—is a source of delight to them, let this other homeland, which gave them birth, not be forgotten.”

But since it is established that these martyrs flew from Tarragona, the city in which they suffered, to their heavenly homeland, the passage must not be understood of temporal birth but of eternal generation through martyrdom. The text immediately continues:

> “Let that homeland”—the heavenly one, clearly—“have in its fellowship those whom it crowned; let this one”—Tarragona—“have in its protection those whom it sent forth.”

The final verb, like the earlier phrase “through the most blessed passion,” deserves careful attention. The text does not say “those whom it bore,” nor “through birth,” but “those whom it sent forth”—to the stars, that is, through the most blessed passion.

The clearest testimony of all concerning the homeland of Saint Eulalia of Barcelona is found in her own Mass [p. 308, col. 2]. For we read:

> “We undertake to celebrate the feast of blessed Eulalia the virgin, in which that same martyr, a citizen and inhabitant of Barcelona, adorned the native soil that she preferred in the distinction of her merits also with the honor of her tomb,” and so forth.

We acknowledge that these words plainly designate the illustrious martyr’s temporal homeland. But this is a special feature of Eulalia of Barcelona, and must be thought to have been done for a reason.

For since we know that, because of the similarity of their names and the relationship of their Acts, Eulalia of Barcelona and Eulalia of Mérida were once confused, made into a single person, and that person taken to be Eulalia of Mérida—the point being demonstrated not only by the hymn of Prudentius but also by the famous cult of Eulalia of Mérida among the ancients, with Bede as the sole exception—while, on the contrary, calendars and Martyrologies commonly pass over Eulalia of Barcelona, the following consequently occurred.

First, the deeds of this Eulalia were attributed to the Eulalia of Mérida, which I believe happened in the case of Prudentius; and, conversely, Eulalia of Barcelona was occasionally venerated in December in place of Eulalia of Mérida [Calendar of Corbie, in Martène, vol. III of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, col. 1604]. Then, as the fame of Eulalia of Mérida grew day by day, the cult of Eulalia of Barcelona gradually declined, and the very name and homeland of the most holy virgin slowly faded from the minds of the Spaniards.

The compilers of the Hispanic liturgy therefore introduced this designation into the Mass of Eulalia of Barcelona in order to revive her cult among their people and remove all doubt among the Spaniards concerning her; and, by eliminating the occasion for confusing the two Eulalias thereafter, they prefixed to the Mass of Eulalia of Barcelona—about whom alone there could be doubt—a title naming her temporal homeland, contrary to the otherwise customary practice both in that liturgy and in others.

Nor would it otherwise be surprising, even if we were to say that this was done gratuitously, if the compilers of the Missal of a private church had occasionally departed from the practice received in other liturgies, especially concerning local martyrs—that is, martyrs sharing the homeland of the church itself—since the desire to magnify that homeland urges everyone on.

It should also be noted that in this Missal the mention of the homelands of Vincent, Fructuosus, and Eulalia occurs immediately at the beginning of the Masses, in the preparatory admonition, and not in the Prayers or *Contestationes*, or, so to speak, in the body of the Mass.

It is established that this admonition did not properly belong to the Mass itself. It was nothing more than an address by the priest to the people, announcing the solemnity for which they had assembled so that they might take part in it piously and devoutly. It took place before the deacon ordered silence; only after that did the Mass begin with the priest’s greeting to the people.

But the testimony from the Veronese Sacramentary cited by Blanchini, in which he thinks that Lawrence’s temporal homeland is contained, is taken from the middle of the *Contestatio* itself. In that passage, the torments and passion of the most holy deacon ought to have been recounted on the authority of Gregory and Hilduin and in accordance with the mind of the Church, rather than his homeland.] On this matter, more elsewhere.

The ancient Sacramentaries mentioned earlier, especially those prepared for the use of the Roman Church, do not differ so greatly in structure from modern ones that, if the Lessons and Gospels distributed throughout the annual cycle are removed from the latter—for in former times these were kept separately in Legendary and Gospel codices—no considerable analogy between the two will remain. At the very least, Blanchini will not deny that the spirit formerly and now prevailing in the Church, and continuing perpetually in the composition of liturgical books, has been the same: namely, that the piety of the faithful should be nourished by the examples of martyrs and saints, and that their minds should be made more ready for martyrdom, should the occasion arise, or for patiently enduring the hardships of human life.

I scarcely know, however, whether the modern Missal anywhere makes mention of the homeland of a martyr, even incidentally. At least, no example on that subject or anything similar comes readily to my mind [Col. 0643B].

Now, as we formerly promised, and as the matter itself in some way demands, we must examine whether the Leonian Sacramentary, apart from the *Contestatio* concerning Saint Lawrence that Blanchini brings against us, contains anything else relating to the temporal homelands of martyrs.

Throughout the whole codex, as far as it extends—which is why the most reverend master of the Apostolic Sacred Palace, Orsius, argued that it was not Leonian but entirely Gelasian [Note: [Col. 0644D] The most reverend Father Orsius, master of the Apostolic Sacred Palace, in a manuscript letter to the learned Joseph Blanchini concerning the author of the Veronese Sacramentary, mentioned by Acamus, Part II, § 13, p. 132 and following.]—and amid the great forest of Masses and prayers with which it abounds, only one example besides that *Contestatio* of Lawrence occurs to us: the Mass of Saint Clement, pope and martyr. We have thought it necessary to set down its words [Note: [Col. 0644D] Volume IV of Anastasius, *Prolegomena*, p. LII.]:

> “It is truly right. As we celebrate the anniversary of your martyr Saint Clement, who left behind both kindred and homeland, and, passing across lands and seas after the fragrance of your name, denying himself, followed you in the footsteps of your apostles, you, Lord, in accordance with the promise of your Son, repaid him with a hundredfold reward both in the present age and in the age to come. For, once the most blessed Peter had entrusted him to instruction, you restored to him in a foreign region the parents whom he had lost in his native land. Then, by appointing him in due succession as his master's successor, you established him as ruler of the city of Rome, whose dignity he had despised for your sake.”

These are the only two examples. Since we know that this could not have occurred in a work of such considerable size except by the most deliberate design—indeed, it would have to be regarded as a miracle—we must defend the earlier *Contestatio* of Saint Lawrence solely by its own authority, whose weakness we know, since no other liturgical codex agrees with it.

The later *Contestatio* concerning Saint Clement, on the other hand, has on its side a witness of a thousand years of antiquity: the Gothic-Gallican Missal of Cardinal Thomasius, in which the homeland, kindred, and rank of the most holy martyr are stated in the *Contestatio* of his proper Mass in precisely the same words as in the Leonian Sacramentary [Col. 0645A].

It is impossible to determine here, and not easy to guess, which of the two codices borrowed this passage from the other, especially since the codices are not at hand. We may, moreover, reasonably suspect from the evidence published by Cardinals Bona [Note: [Col. 0645D] *On Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chap. 12, no. 6.] and Thomasius [Note: [Col. 0645D] Volume II, col. 513, in Muratorius’s Dissertation on the Ancient Roman Liturgy.] that the Gothic-Gallican Missal may perhaps be no less ancient than the Veronese Sacramentary.

Meanwhile, however, this much is clear: the *Contestatio* concerning Clement’s homeland and kindred is full of old-womanish tales, since it has been taken almost word for word from the fabricated *Itinerary of the Apostle Peter*, entitled the *Recognitions*, which Pope Gelasius listed among the apocrypha at the First Roman Council [Note: [Col. 0645D] First Roman Council under Gelasius, in the year 494, in the decree on apocryphal writings: “Likewise, the *Itinerary in the name of the Apostle Peter*, which is called *of Saint Clement*, in eight books”—elsewhere nine or ten—“is apocryphal.”].

For that very reason it was rightly banished from the other liturgical books, a point that Blanchini himself will not deny. Let the fair-minded reader infer from this that, since the *Contestatio* of Lawrence appears to present the homeland of the most holy deacon no less than the *Contestatio* of Clement just cited, and since it can summon no other liturgical codex among so many to its aid, its credibility must ultimately be very slight.

From one aspect of this inconvenient argument, then, we have seen how suspect the *Contestatio* is of falsification or interpolation, if Blanchini wishes to maintain that Lawrence’s homeland is contained in the *Contestatio* of his Mass that is brought against us.

Now, if we turn our attention for a moment to the phrase “a citizen by birth,” we shall find that it accords neither with the character of the Latin language nor with the age or style of Leo the Great, to whom Blanchini nevertheless insists that it must wholly be attributed.

First, as regards the expression itself, I suppose there is no reader who does not know that it is poor Latin to say that someone is *nascendo* a citizen, freeborn, or a freedman. Ancient authors—and even the authors of what is called medieval Latin—would say *natura*, “by nature,” or, if they wished to speak somewhat less elevatedly, *naturaliter*, “naturally.”

In this sense Cicero calls the Carthaginians “naturally deceitful” [Note: [Col. 0645D] *On the Agrarian Law*.] and victory “naturally proud” [Note: [Col. 0645D] *For Marcus Marcellus*, IX.]. Horace speaks of a poem “laudable by nature” [Note: [Col. 0645D] *Art of Poetry*, line 408.] and of Romans “sublime by nature” [Note: [Col. 0645D] *Letters*, Book II, 1, line 165.], as do many other authors in similar expressions.

I certainly know that the ancient jurists use impeccable Latin when they say *solvendo*, “capable of paying,” *fidejubendo*, “by giving surety,” and *satis dando*, “by providing sufficient security.” We also read that a person becomes the nearest heir *agnascendo*, “by being added to the family,” and that a will is broken by this event [Note: [Col. 0645D] Cicero, *On the Orator*, I, 241.]. Virgil too says somewhere that fortune must be overcome *ferendo* [Col. 0645D], “by enduring” [Note: [Col. 0645D] *Aeneid* V, 710.].

These expressions are nevertheless different. In the first group, the words *idoneus* or *par*, “fit” or “equal,” are understood, so that the expression is equivalent to saying, for example, “a beam equal to bearing a burden,” “a maiden mature for a husband,” and similar phrases belonging to genuine Latin. Or, if the gerund is used by itself, it must be thought to derive from some ancient and obsolete formula of the jurists [Col. 0646A].

As for the age of the phrase “to be a citizen by birth,” “to be freeborn,” or anything similar, I have so far been unable to find any example among medieval writers from which we could derive it. The learned Ducange produces a single example from the laws of the Lombards, in which we read [Note: [Col. 0646D] Under the letter N, “To be by birth,” from the *Laws of the Lombards*, Book II, title 21, § 9.]:

> “And he who strikes and has accepted the *wadia* must name only the nearest oath-bound kinsmen who are by birth.”

Although these words appear to be written in Latin, as God is my witness, I understand them no better than Plautus’s *Poenulus*. I think they cannot be assigned earlier than the seventh century, and perhaps not earlier than the eighth [Col. 0646B].

But what need is there of examples? The words themselves—“to be a citizen by birth”—sound heavy and rustic, indeed barbarous, and immediately reveal themselves to anyone who is not entirely a stranger to Latium as having been drawn from the dregs of the lowest Latin.

If anyone still insists that the phrase under discussion accords with the style of Saint Leo or proceeded from his mouth, he must necessarily be doing an injury to that most eloquent pontiff.

I know that even in Leo’s style there are features for which the more censorious grammarians of our own age have found fault—men whose hearts, and even the joints of their fingertips, taste of Cicero. Nor shall I deny that some things in his works may appear insufficiently vigorous in expression; that his diction is sometimes tinkling; or that he perhaps pursues the balance of clauses—*τῶν ἰσοκώλων*, “equal-limbed” or “parallel-membered” clauses—with excessive anxiety.

But even if these points are certain, which we do not determine here, they concern the substance and structure of his discourse rather than the propriety of his words. In the weaving of words themselves, however, apart from one or two blemishes, we know that the most holy teacher was remarkably careful.

Nevertheless, without pausing over the harsh sound of the phrase “a citizen by birth,” or over the inconvenience of the argument, I intend by another route to show that those two words—if, with Blanchini, we wish to assign them to Leo’s age—are uncertain, inelegant, and poorly connected with what surrounds them.

Indeed, on their account I intend to show that the entire *Contestatio* of Lawrence’s Mass under discussion was corrupted and excluded from the liturgical books, although it may otherwise have had Saint Leo as its author [Note: [Col. 0646D] The same or a related statement is found in Saint Leo’s Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Apostles, in these words:

> “But today’s festival”—that is, of Peter and Paul—“besides the reverence that it has deserved throughout the whole world, must be honored with the special and particular rejoicing of our city, so that where the death of the chief apostles was glorified, there on the day of their martyrdom the primacy of joy may be found.”

Muratorius also suggests that this *Contestatio*, up to the words “a citizen by birth,” bears the stamp of Leonine phrasing (*Dissertation on the Ancient Liturgy*, chap. 3, col. 18.)].

For the matter to become more fully clear, it should be known that after the storm of persecutions had subsided and peace had been restored to the Church through Constantine, the seeds of piety—scattered in the minds of the faithful and long shut up—immediately began to sprout and grow from day to day, God giving the increase.

Hence new prayers gradually arose in the Church, new formulas for imploring divine assistance, and finally a new crop of liturgical prayers, among which, as commonly happens, a certain amount of harmful tares also grew. For although these prayers were very often arranged by learned men appointed for that purpose, some nevertheless had authors who were more devoted to piety than to learning. Consequently, many things—superfluous, uncertain, and poorly connected with what preceded and followed—crept into the liturgical codices, through the fault sometimes of the authors and sometimes of the copyists [Col. 0647A].

[Col. 0647B] This evil, which as time went on had penetrated deeply into the interior of the liturgy, began to be remedied by ecclesiastical laws as early as the fourth century, or at the beginning of the fifth. Thus the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, “lest anything should perhaps be composed contrary to the faith through ignorance or insufficient care,” as they themselves put it, enacted the following law: that no prayers, orations, Prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands should be said in the church except those which had been considered by wiser men or approved in synod [Note: [Col. 0647D] Canon 12, vol. III of Labbe’s Collection of Councils, Venetian edition, col. 383. It is nevertheless uncertain whether this canon should be assigned to the First or the Second Council of Milevis; for these two councils have been joined into one through the carelessness of copyists or compilers. See Labbe, in the same place, and in the First Council of Milevis, in the same volume III, col. 83.]. This provision had itself already been made in the code of canons of the African Church [Note: [Col. 0647D] In Labbe, vol. III of the Collection of Councils, col. 1336, at the beginning.], and in one of the Councils of Carthage, according to the testimony of Walafrid Strabo [Note: [Col. 0647D] Book on Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 22, Roman edition of 1591, p. 346, col. 2. “Therefore,” he says, “we believe that it was decreed by the Councils of Carthage and Milevis that prayers and orations should not be said unless they had been approved in Council.”]. Pope Gelasius, too, at the end of the fifth century, devoted himself to the same undertaking, as the Sacramentary inscribed with his name bears witness; this is confirmed both by Strabo and by Anastasius. The former says that Gelasius arranged prayers composed both by himself and by others [Note: [Col. 0647D] In the passage cited immediately above.]; the latter, however, relates that he composed “the Prefaces of the Sacraments in cautious language” [Note: [Col. 0648D] In the Life of Gelasius.]—that is, with discrimination and critically, in resistance to the blows of detractors. Horace used the word in this sense in another passage [Note: [Col. 0648D] Art, verse 266:

“. . . and, safe below,

Cautious of hoping for pardon.”].

We have a substantial witness in John the Deacon concerning Saint Gregory the Great, who applied himself to the same task no less diligently than Gelasius or those earlier Fathers. In his Life of Gregory he says [Note: [Col. 0648D] Life of Gregory the Great, book II, chapter 17.]:

“He also compressed the Gelasian Book on the solemn rites of the Mass into a single volume, removing much, altering a little, and adding some things for the exposition of the Gospel readings.”

Walafrid indicates what Gregory removed from the liturgical books in the passage cited above, saying [Note: [Col. 0648D] Book on Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 22, p. 346, col. 2.]:

“And because many things, whose authors were so uncertain, appeared uncertain and did not possess integrity of meaning, Gregory took care to gather together whatever was reasonable and, excluding those things which seemed either excessive or inelegant, composed the book called the Sacramentary, as is most clearly shown by its title.”

Since, therefore, it is entirely beyond doubt that Gelasius and Gregory chiefly arranged and restored to better form those liturgical books which the Roman Church used—and that they could have been no others than those written in the times of the earlier pontiffs—a conclusion that agrees remarkably with the judgment of Blanchini [Note: [Col. 0648D] In the title prefixed to the same work, vol. IV of Anastasius, p. 12.], Muratori [Note: [Col. 0648D] Dissertation on the Ancient Roman Liturgy, vol. I, chapters 3, cols. 18 and 23.], and others [Note: [Col. 0648D] Eusebius Amort, in Acamus, Part II, § 14, p. 149; and Acamus himself, Part I, § 13, p. 41.]—and since, as we have learned from Walafrid, Gelasius and Gregory removed from the more ancient Sacramentaries of the Roman Church things that were uncertain, inelegant, and badly connected with the others; and since the words *nasciendo civis*—“a citizen by birth”—are no longer found in the Gelasian Codex of Cardinal Thomasius, nor in the three Gregorian codices of Pamel, Rocca, and Menard, nor is the Contestation of the Laurentian Mass, with which we are concerned, found there either: it consequently seems altogether likely that Gelasius and Gregory detected in that Contestation something uncertain, inelegant, or badly connected with the other elements resting on historical testimony—whether, with Blanchini, we assign it to the age of Leo—and for this reason removed it from the liturgical books. But what could that have been, I ask, except the words *nasciendo civis*? For the remainder of the Contestation contains nothing incongruous and, moreover, breathes the style and doctrine of Leo the Great, as we said earlier.

[Col. 0648C] Now, if Blanchini should think that our trifles amount to something, he will finally suppose that all this is directed toward asserting that those words *nasciendo civis*, as spurious and inserted into the text, possess no force or credibility whatsoever. He will make this the substance of our reply; indeed, with the foresight and acuity for which he is distinguished, he would extract from our very reply the following most forceful argument against us: the person who added the words *NASCENDO CIVIS* to the Codex and corrupted or interpolated the passage under discussion must at least have been uncertain about Laurence’s birthplace; and, what follows closely from this, as early as the eighth century or the beginning of the ninth, when the Verona Sacramentary is said to have been written, there must already have been dispute on both sides concerning Laurence’s birthplace.

[Col. 0648D] Whether what we have adduced is sufficient to discredit those words altogether will be for readers to decide and judge. Our intention is very far from being to oppose Blanchini’s efforts by this route. [Col. 0649A] But suppose that the Spaniards had placed their only hope in that reply. Even then, we believe that something could be answered. For if that Codex had been deliberately corrupted by an antiquarian, then certainly he must be thought to have been uncertain about Laurence’s birthplace and, with the purpose of settling a dispute that already existed at that time, to have inserted the words *nasciendo civis* into the text.

But why should we not instead suppose that this happened through the carelessness or drowsiness of the antiquarian, as formerly occurred in the mention of Simplicius? Why should we not attribute it to ignorance of the Latin language, which at the time when the Codex is said to have been written was remarkable, almost astonishing? A copyist, unable to grasp the sense of the sentence, could very easily have passed heedlessly from one sentence to another before completing the first, and thus made one sentence out of two—though a hybrid one—which Muratori suspected had happened in the mention of Simplicius. He could have omitted a word, comma, colon, or something else that stood in the autograph, the restoration of which would have produced a very different sense of the Contestation.

The two words *nasciendo civis*, or at least the former, *nasciendo*, could likewise have been added in the margin of an older Codex by a glossator who did not refer it to Laurence’s temporal birthplace, and then admitted in good faith into the text by the antiquarian; so that the authentic wording of the Contestation with which we are concerned would have been this: “Rome rejoices more particularly, whose sacred minister,” or, “whose citizen, a sacred minister,” and so forth. Why should we not suspect that this happened, since, if both words—or even the first word alone, *nasciendo*—are completely torn away from the text, not only does the sentence and its meaning remain intact (which is no small aid in distinguishing these glosses), but the twofold stumbling block of barbarism and inappropriateness is also avoided?

Finally, lest we weary our readers, the similarity of the words *CVIVS* and *CIVIS*—if, disregarding the sound produced by their pronunciation, we attend only to their written form—could have provided the words under discussion with a place in that Contestation. To make this similarity clearer, it should be understood that at the beginning the Romans always represented the letter V, whether consonantal or vocalic, by two strokes open at the top, joined below, and ending in a point resting on the base of the stroke, in this form: V. They nowhere knew that crescent-shaped or arched form consisting of a single curved line, whose lower curve rests upon a base, in this form: U [Note: [Col. 0649D] Perhaps there is a unique ancient inscription from Tibur, in the possession of the illustrious eques Paulus Colonna, in which the consonantal letter U approaches that Gothic arched form, with an obtuse support also added on the left. Since it has recently been excavated and, as we believe, remains unpublished, we reproduce it from the original as we have copied it:

VICTORI

HERCVLI

SACRVM].

Rather, that form descended from the Gothic character [Note: [Col. 0650D] Mabillon, *On Diplomatics* I, 11, 4, p. 47, in Heineccius, *Foundations of Style*, Part I, chapter 1, § 6, note 1. Cellarius, *On Latin Orthography*, under the vowel V.], and a later age also used it in the middle of a word, with a support added on the left, in this form: U [Note: [Col. 0650D] Heineccius, *Foundations of Style*, Part I, chapter 1, § 6, note 3.]. It is also clear from ancient coins and inscriptions that the Romans did not know the dot by which, according to modern usage, we see the letter I marked, especially in smaller writing; nor was this used anywhere before the year 1000 of the Christian era, as even the specimen of the character of the Leonine Sacramentary edited by Blanchini can show those who regard such minutiae as unworthy of attention.

[Col. 0650A] From this, however, I think the analogy between the words *CVIVS* and *CIVIS* becomes somewhat clearer if we consider the writing of the eighth century. According to that writing, in the Codex from which the Leonine Sacramentary was copied, the words must have been written in precisely this way—or not very differently—*CUIUS CIUIS*. We could prove this by numerous examples from Codices of that period, were the matter not obvious. Now the copyist, whom we suppose to have been ignorant of Latin, when he encountered one of these words, thinking that both *CVIVS* and *CIVIS* could be read there, yet uncertain which reading was preferable, made two words out of the single one: he placed one in the text and the other in the margin of the Codex opposite it, with the intention that the reader should prefer whichever seemed more suitable to the meaning of a sentence that the copyist himself did not understand, rejecting the other. Once this had happened, the marginal word could very easily slip into the text, and *CVIVS CIVIS* could be joined together; finally, the word *NASCENDO* could have been added to remove the ambiguity of the latter word.

I therefore think it entirely possible that those words *nasciendo civis*, which have caused us so much confusion, crept into the genuine text of Saint Leo, without any culpability on anyone’s part, solely through the ignorance or carelessness of antiquarians. This could also be confirmed by countless examples of corrupted Codices, were it not preferable to be brief. Whether Blanchini wants that Contestation to be considered corrupted or intact matters little to us, since we have already said that we shall obstruct his efforts by another route. It matters greatly, however, to Saint Leo that we remove from him the stain of barbarism; and it matters still more that the most prudent pontiff not be said to have inserted into the liturgical books something so inappropriate and so utterly alien to the spirit of the Church.

But why all this, Blanchini will object, if we do not wish to derive any support from it for our reply? Precisely so that, from the doctrine already laid down, we may be permitted to draw from it two theses—or rather, as we believe, liturgical principles—one of which must wholly govern the interpretation of the Contestation in question. [Col. 0650D] They are as follows:

**First.**

It was always foreign to the Church’s purpose to insert the temporal homelands of the saints into liturgical books. Therefore, if anything of this kind is found anywhere in ancient Sacramentaries, especially those prepared for the use of the Roman Church, it should be regarded as inconsistent with the spirit of the Church and as bearing the mark of falsity or of the strongest suspicion.

[Col. 0651A] **Second.**

If, anywhere in the ancient Sacramentaries of the Church, especially those of the Roman Church, or in other liturgical books, a passage or word occurs that is ambiguous or equivocal between referring to the homelands of the saints and signifying something else, then, according to the mind of the Church, it should by no means be referred to the temporal homelands of the saints.

With these points established, in order to draw somewhat nearer to our reply, we must inquire whether the passage which Blanchini objects to us from the Verona Sacramentary, although at first sight it appears immediately to proclaim Laurence’s birthplace, can conveniently receive another interpretation; and what the most holy pontiff intended by the words *CVIVS NASCENDO CIVIS*—since, for the sake of accommodating Blanchini’s practice, we shall meanwhile attribute them to Saint Leo. I think the matter will be made clearer by examples from antiquity and the testimony of the ecclesiastical Fathers than by argument and reasoning.

When Roman soldiers at Jerusalem had rescued Paul from the hands of the Jews, and the tribune had ordered them to take him to the camp and scourge him in order to discover the cause of the Jewish uproar, the Apostle, just as he was about to be flogged, addressed the centurion standing beside him in these words: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman man, and one who has not been condemned?” (Acts 22:25). Paul asks why he is being treated wickedly and unjustly: namely, because punishment was preceding condemnation, contrary to the common law of nations; and because a Roman citizen was being ordered to be scourged in violation of the Porcian [Note: [Col. 0651D] “But, by the immortal gods,” says Sallust in the *Catiline*, “why did you not add to the motion, Decimus Silanus, that punishment should first be inflicted upon them [that is, Lentulus and the other conspirators] by scourging? Was it because the Porcian law forbids it?”] and Sempronian laws [Note: [Col. 0651D] Gaius Sempronius Gracchus enacted two laws; one provided that if anyone in office killed a Roman citizen without trial, he should be punished by judgment of the people. Plutarch, *Life of Gracchus*.].

When the centurion heard this, he reported the matter to the tribune, saying: [Col. 0651C] “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen” (Acts 22:26). The tribune was disturbed by this and, now somewhat anxious about Paul, approached him to learn from his own mouth whether the matter was as reported: “Tell me,” he said, “are you a Roman?” (Acts 22:27 ff.). Paul replied: “Yes.” The tribune continued: “I acquired this citizenship at great cost.” Paul answered: “But I was born one”—that is, born a Roman citizen. If the character of the Latin language had permitted it, or if the Book of Acts had only been written in the eighth century, or translated into Latin at that time, it is credible that the author or translator would have rendered the words “But I was also born [a citizen]” in the Latin of that age as “But I am a citizen by birth,” especially since the Greek text does not reject that rendering [Note: [Col. 0651D] *Ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ γεγέννημαι*, Acts 22:28.]. In that case we would have the same meaning expressed both in Acts and in the Leonine Sacramentary, indeed expressed in both places by exactly the same words.

Meanwhile, we must carefully consider the passage of the Acts as it stands. First, Paul says in it that he is a Roman man; then he is called a Roman citizen by the centurion. Again, in replying to the tribune, Paul simply calls himself a Roman; and when the tribune questions him once more and asserts that he had acquired Roman citizenship by a kind of privileged right, Paul immediately adds that he had not become a Roman citizen but had been born one. At first sight these statements seem so clearly to proclaim Paul’s birthplace that, unless he himself had elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0652D] At the beginning of the same chapter, 22:3, and chapter 22:39.] said that he was born at Tarsus in Cilicia [Note: [Col. 0652D] I know that Jerome says Paul was born at Gischala, a town of Judea in the tribe of Benjamin; when it was captured by the Jews, he says, Paul migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia. See the holy Doctor in *On Illustrious Men*.] and had unquestionably been a citizen of that city, I do not doubt that, even in Blanchini’s judgment, Paul would be considered to have been born in Rome just as Scipio or Laelius was.

To make this somewhat clearer, we must construct the following hypothesis. Imagine that the sacred Codex of Acts had perished, or remained hidden because it had not yet been discovered; and that nothing else had survived from ancient records by which we could certainly recognize Paul’s homeland. Imagine further that, just as the Spaniards now dispute with one another concerning Laurence’s birthplace, a dispute with the people of Tarsus concerning Paul’s birthplace still remained undecided. Suppose, moreover, that Blanchini, while vigorously defending the Roman side, had discovered in some ancient archive a Codex of extraordinary antiquity and authority, into which the biblical cento that we have just quoted from the Acts of the Apostles had been incidentally stitched, although the subject matter of that Codex was entirely different.

You would see Blanchini exulting and triumphing, immediately declaring the case proved for the Romans, and demanding for himself, according to ancestral custom, an oaken crown because he had restored to the City Paul, a most illustrious citizen. On the other hand, the wretched man defending the cause of the Tarsians would cry out in vain, appealing to the authority of the wise and protesting that the passage from Acts should be understood not of Paul’s birthplace but of the right of Roman citizenship—or municipal citizenship—which Tarsus enjoyed, according to the testimony of Dion, Pliny, and Paul himself [Note: [Col. 0652D] Acts 21:39: “I,” Paul says, “am indeed a Jewish man from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city,” and so forth.]. Blanchini would press the opposing argument: that Paul is not merely called a Roman citizen in that passage—for that would not be particularly significant—but is most explicitly declared to have been born one. Now “born” can properly be said only of birthplace; all other uses of that word are transferred and metaphorical. It is useless to resort to an improper meaning where the proper meaning is available. He would then raise the Codex’s thousand-year antiquity and authority to the heavens; gather two or three negative or conjectural arguments from here and there; and bring the principal point, armed with these, into battle. With such a painted and deceptive display of words he would finally prevent the advocate of the Tarsian cause from uttering even a syllable. But whoever carelessly lent an ear to Blanchini’s arguments—how much ridicule would he owe the more discerning once the truth was exposed!

[Col. 0653A] These observations are intended to remind Blanchini how cautiously one ought to place faith in such patchwork centos, however brilliant and precious they may be in themselves, when they migrate into the works of others, especially works on a different subject. What if, in addition, their meaning is plainly flexible and ambiguous, and capable of multiple interpretations—as is certainly the Contestation of the Verona Sacramentary in the passage under discussion? Let Blanchini now go off with his Codex and extol its antiquity, credibility, and every other virtue as much as he can. I do not think that, even if we freely granted that it was a pure Leonine work, he would ever consider it comparable with the volume of the Acts of the Apostles. Nor is the Sacramentary a clearer witness for Laurence’s birthplace than the passage from Acts which we have just examined is for Paul’s.

[Col. 0653B] Now, if we wish to answer Blanchini, I think nothing prevents us from asserting freely that in the Verona Sacramentary, just as in Acts, Laurence is called a Roman citizen in the same sense as Paul. Whether we say that Laurence was born at Huesca, or rather at our Corduba or Valencia in Edetania—an inquiry that we leave aside because we despair of bringing it to a successful conclusion—we can defend him as a Roman citizen no less than Paul, because Paul drew his birth from Tarsus. For the three cities we have mentioned—we deliberately do not add Zaragoza—were Roman colonies or municipalities [Note: [Col. 0653C] Concerning Corduba, see Pliny, book III, where he lists that city among the colonies of Baetica. See also the eighth Dialogue of the illustrious Antonio Agustín, and Vaillant, *Imperial Coins*, vol. I, p. 53, under Augustus.

Pliny, in Antonio Agustín’s seventh Dialogue, calls Huesca “of Roman citizens” in one place; the distinguished author interprets this expression as “municipality.” On coins one frequently finds V. V. OSCA, that is, “victorious city”; sometimes VRB. VICT. See Vaillant, under Augustus, vol. I, *Colonies and Municipalities*, p. 55.

Finally, Pliny lists Valencia among the colonies of Hither Spain, book III, chapter 3. See Antonio Agustín, Dialogue V, and Vaillant, under Julius Caesar.]. Moreover, we know that in those times Corduba was famous for its glory and power [Note: [Col. 0653D] Strabo, book III: *Πλεῖστον δ᾽ ἣ Κόρδυβα εὔξηται Μαρκέλλου κτίσμα καὶ δόξη καὶ δυνάμει.* That is: “Corduba, the foundation of Marcellus, grew most greatly in glory and power.”], Huesca had been a great city since the time of Sertorius and the mother of learning in Spain [Note: [Col. 0653D] Plutarch, *Life of Sertorius*: *Τοὺς γὰρ εὐγενεστάτους ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν συναγαγῶν εἰς Ὄσκαν πόλιν μεγάλην διδασκάλους ἐπιστήσας Ἑλληνικῶν τε καὶ Κωμαϊκῶν μαθημάτων.* The eminent Vaillant, although otherwise highly skilled in Greek, translated this passage, I do not know whether sufficiently accurately, as follows (vol. I, *Colonies and Municipalities*, p. 55, under Augustus): “For, having gathered the noblest of the nations into Huesca, a large city, he appointed teachers of Greek and Latin letters over them.” I would render it this way: “Gathering the noblest men of those peoples into Huesca, a great city, he appointed teachers of Greek and Roman disciplines over them.” Thus *τὸ εὐγενεστάτους* should refer not to the city but to the Spanish youths whom Sertorius gathered into it.], and Valencia, after being destroyed by Gnaeus Pompey [Note: [Col. 0654D] See Sallust, *Histories* III, and Vaillant, under Julius Caesar, vol. I, *Coins: Colonies and Municipalities*.], was soon restored and made a colony by Caesar, from whom it is said to have taken its name for that reason. All three were also honored with the privilege of striking coinage, as numerous coins published by Vaillant and others demonstrate.

But Blanchini would then rise up and say that there was not sufficient reason for Rome to rejoice more particularly in Laurence’s solemnity if we did not make the most holy deacon a Roman citizen in a more specific sense, as Paul was. For at the time when Laurence could have been brought into the world, Roman citizenship—I mean *πολιτεία*—was so widespread that it was considered more a disgrace and dishonor not to be a citizen than a source of praise to be one. I shall settle the matter briefly. We know that during the time of the Republic and immediately after Caesar seized power, the right of citizenship was held in the highest honor among the Romans and was communicated to foreign peoples only very sparingly [Note: [Col. 0654D] See Suetonius, *Life of Julius Caesar*. He nevertheless granted citizenship to the people of Gades and other Spanish cities during his second consulship, as Dio Cassius records, books XLI and XLIII.]. We also read that Augustus was so jealous of Roman citizenship that he declared he would more readily allow money to be taken from the treasury than the honor of Roman citizenship to be made common [Note: [Col. 0654D] These are Suetonius’s words in the *Life of Augustus*.]. Nor is it evident that Galba [Note: [Col. 0654D] “He rarely granted Roman citizenship.” Suetonius, *Life of Galba*.] and those who held the imperial power down to Trajan were much more generous. Trajan, however, and after him Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and others, gradually diminished the value of that right by frequent grants of Roman citizenship, until Antoninus Caracalla issued a most avaricious law under the appearance of generosity [Note: [Col. 0654D] For the occasion of the enactment of that law, see the law cited by Heineccius, from whom we have taken this material, *Illustrated Roman Legal Antiquities*, Appendix to Book I, § XIX.], by which all who were in the Roman world were made citizens [Note: [Col. 0654D] The law is found in *Digest* 1.5.17, *On the Status of Persons*.]. That supreme right of Roman citizens was thereby degraded and treated as worthless. Since that law was promulgated sometime between the year 211 and the year 218, during which Caracalla ruled, while we know that Laurence, flourishing in the vigor of youth, suffered martyrdom in the year 258, under the consuls Tuscus and Bassus, it seems clear that the most holy deacon must have been born only after Caracalla’s constitution had been issued and Roman citizenship made common. At that time, therefore, there was no longer any reason for Rome to rejoice more particularly in Laurence’s citizenship.

If no other reason for the particular joy were indicated in that Contestation, I would certainly acknowledge the force of this argument. Yet the Contestation itself also contains the sacred ministry of Laurence and his passion—for I think the later words, “the offering dedicated to your name,” should be understood in this way—from which Rome would additionally derive a twofold reason for particular joy. Let us hear Leo speaking of the holy Apostles: “There ought to be the primacy of joy where their glorious departure took place” [Note: [Col. 0654D] Sermon 1, *On the Feast of the Holy Apostles*.]. Likewise Maximus of Turin, speaking of our most holy deacon: “Hence it is,” he says, “that joyful Rome marvels at Laurence’s unconquerable faith” [Note: [Col. 0654D] Homily 11, *On Saint Laurence*.]. Finally, Augustine and the ancient Fathers of the Church drew from the triumphant death of the martyrs their chief source of spiritual joy and subject of praise.

But if we examine the matter somewhat more carefully, we shall find that even after the time of Caracalla a considerable measure of honor still remained in Roman citizenship itself. Since it is established that Caracalla’s law was enacted only for those born free, not for those of freedman status [Note: [Col. 0655C] Justinian, *Novels* 78, chapter 5, in Heineccius, Appendix to Book I of *Illustrated Roman Legal Antiquities*, § XX.], we may certainly refer the right of citizenship attributed to Laurence in the Contestation to his free birth—that is, to his nobility—over which, among other things, Rome would rejoice in his solemnity. Anyone who wishes to consider the rights and immunities of Roman citizens in Cicero [Note: [Col. 0655C] *Against Verres* V, 54, and elsewhere in the same work.] and in more recent writers who have treated this subject [Note: [Col. 0655C] Carlo Sigonio, *On the Ancient Right of Roman Citizens*; Cardinal Noris, *On the Syro-Macedonian Era* IV, p. 428; in Heineccius, *Appendix to Roman Antiquities*, book I, p. 428; and others.] will certainly find it by no means absurd if here we use “citizenship” to mean free birth.

Indeed, although the condition of the Italians was far inferior to that of citizens, we nevertheless know that the former right was commonly used to mean immunity from taxes [Note: [Col. 0655D] See the title *Digest*, *On Censuses*. Robert Estienne, *Treasury of the Latin Language*, under the word *Jus Italicum*.]. Since the patricians and equestrians—whom we call nobles—possess this privilege in our Spain, excluding the common people, they are still called *hidalgos*, that is, *Italici*, in the vernacular [Note: [Col. 0655D] Apart from the affinity of meaning, which is certainly considerable between these words, their notable structural analogy also makes us more confident in this etymology.
