Thus *Galgo*, the word by which Spaniards mean a greyhound, descends from the Latin *Gallicus*—scilicet *canis*, “dog”—just as *algo*, meaning exactly the same as *aliquid*, comes from that word. Likewise from *caballico*, that is, “a horseman” or “one who rides”—a word that occurs more than once in the laws of the Lombards, and also in those of the Visigoths and in the *Usatges* of Barcelona—comes the Spanish word *cabalgo*, of the same meaning, which we often write *cavalgo* according to usage rather than origin. This derivation had already occurred to our distinguished countryman Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda in his *Letter to the Prince of Spain*, book III, letter 34.]; and *hidalguía*, which we would call *Italicitas* in Latin, means nobility.

Yet in the time of our Laurence the name “Roman citizen,” whatever precisely it contained, was held in great honor and esteem; nor were the ecclesiastical Fathers ignorant of this. A passage from the Mozarabic hymn concerning Saint Julian, the martyr of Antioch, which Baronius attributes to Isidore [Col. 0655C] [Note: [Col. 0656C] In the notes to the *Martyrology*, 9 January, letter A. The hymn is cited by Blanchini in Annotation XX of the *Ancient Orational of the Gothic Rite*, p. 161.], proves the point most fully. It reads as follows:

“Here Julian, of illustrious lineage by birth,

A citizen of the toga-clad city, instructed in every

Discipline of the arts, etc.”

Here Julian is plainly called a Roman citizen as a mark of honor; for I scarcely know whether the epithet “toga-clad” can properly belong to any city other than Rome [Note: [Col. 0656C] I know that Antonio Agustín also called our Tarragona *Togata*. Thus, he says, the two T’s which some of its coins bear may be interpreted as *Togata Tarraco* (Dialogue VII, at the beginning). Yet he himself does not seem satisfied with this interpretation, and in the same place asserts that *Tyrrhenica* perhaps ought to be read instead of *Togata*. Certainly Isidore could not have been referring in that hymn to Tarragona, as though Julian had been a citizen of it, since Julian never even saw that city.]. Since it is credible that this martyr was born at Antioch—a fact that the Ambrosian Breviary published by order of Saint Charles Borromeo plainly indicates [Note: [Col. 0656D] *Ambrosian Breviary*, published by order of Saint Charles Borromeo and revised in the year 1625, 21 June, lesson III at Matins, in the Bollandists, 9 January, § V, no. 21.]—and since we know that he also suffered in that same city [Note: [Col. 0656D] *Roman Martyrology*, shorter recension, 9 January.], and was not a resident of Rome, it remains that the hymn’s passage must be understood of the right of Roman citizenship; and that Julian is called a citizen by Isidore in this respect, because he was born in a city endowed with the right of citizenship, such as Antioch in Syria was [Note: [Col. 0656D] See Vaillant, vol. I, *Imperial Coins: Colonies and Municipalities*, under Claudius.]. Since Julian suffered under Diocletian and Maximian—that is, at the very end of the third century of the Christian era—it follows that even at that time, or at least when the hymn was composed by Isidore, the name “Roman citizen” was still held in no ordinary esteem. This concludes the first interpretation of the words *NASCENDO CIVIS*.

Another interpretation remains. If we wish to admit those two words as genuinely Leonine, I consider it more consistent with the opinions of the holy Fathers and with the spirit of the Church [Col. 0656B]. The Latin meaning of the word *nascor* is well known. Cicero, Sallust, Livy, and the other dictators of that language, however, used it continually to mean “to be brought into the world” or “to emerge.” By contrast, beginning already in the fourth century, the ecclesiastical Fathers, in the Acts of the martyrs and in their homilies, but especially in the sacred Liturgy, consistently understood it to mean what in Latin is expressed by *mori*, “to die,” and interpreted it in that sense. For since they believed that on the day when martyrs completed their contest they were born into heaven—that is, into their eternal homeland—they transferred, out of faith and piety rather than according to the usage of the Latin language, the proper meaning of this verb into one that is not merely different but plainly contrary. Hence the birthdays and birth-days of the martyrs, which secular writers would call their days of death in Latin; and clear traces of this usage remain even in the modern Mass books.

We would utterly overwhelm the reader with examples in confirmation of this doctrine, so many occur among the ancient Fathers of both the Latin and Greek Churches [Note: [Col. 0656D] Saint Polycarp’s *γένεθλιον ἡμέραν*, which we would translate literally into Latin as *natalitium diem*, “a birthday,” Rufinus renders “the day of his passion,” as cited by Ducange under the word *Natalis*.]. Nor were only those who were said to be born with the addition “into heaven” described simply as being born; in later centuries too, all who happened to die for Christ or in his embrace were so described. On this subject we set opposite it the elegant testimony of Pope Nicholas I [Col. 0657A] [Note: [Col. 0657C] “It should not seem new to anyone if one who has departed this life is called ‘born.’ For just as, according to ordinary usage, someone is said to be born when, proceeding from his mother’s womb, he comes forth into this light, so also anyone who passes from the darkness of this life to the light of the living may rightly be called born.” Pope Nicholas I, in his response to the questions of the Bulgarians, in Labbe, *Collection of Councils*, Venetian edition, vol. IX, col. 1537.]. When we see the word *nascor* accompanied by “into heaven,” not only among the ancient Fathers but also in modern Martyrologies and even in the offices and Masses of the saints, this was done for the sake of antithesis, so that the temporal birth of the martyrs might be more clearly compared with their eternal birth. Thus the martyrs of Nicomedia are said to have deserved to be born in heaven on the day on which Christ was born on earth [Note: [Col. 0657D] The words of the Martyrology, 25 December.]. Likewise Paula of Rome is remembered in her Office as having been born into heaven where Christ deigned to be born into the world [Note: [Col. 0657D] 26 January, Paula’s proper day in the Office of the Saints of Spain.].

The usage of the words *natale* and *natalitium* in the ecclesiastical authors in the sense under discussion became so established that if anyone wished to express a genuine birthday, as the man of Venusia put it [Note: [Col. 0657D] Book IV, ode 11, to Phyllis, verse 18.], or actual births, as it is read on a coin of Constantine [Note: [Col. 0657D] On its reverse it reads: *PLURES NATALES FELICITER*, “Many birthdays, happily.” This coin was admirably elucidated by the distinguished Spanish scholar whom I particularly esteem, Alexander Xavier Panel, a Jesuit priest, from the treasury of the Catholic King, of which he has charge; he published a commentary on the subject a few years ago, which we do not now have at hand.], he would necessarily have to add *genuinus*, “genuine,” or something similar, lest he should appear, contrary to his intention, to be speaking of death rather than birth. There is a clear testimony to this in the Sacramentary of Gelasius; accordingly, we present the Mass inscribed [Note: [Col. 0657D] Muratori, *Ancient Roman Liturgy*, vol. II, col. 724.]:

**ON THE GENUINE BIRTHDAY**

**Secret Prayer**
Attend, Lord, to our supplications, and graciously and kindly accept this offering of Your servant N., which he offers to You for the day of his genuine birthday, on which day You commanded him to be born from his mother’s womb into this world. Through the Lord, etc. And in the Post-Communion:

You who have deigned to bring Your servant, with a year having elapsed, to this day of his genuine birthday, etc.

[Note: “N.” That is, someone whom we conceive in our mind and designate, while withholding his proper name. In modern Missals and other books of ecclesiastical Offices, N. is used for him. Italians say *il tale*; Greeks, τοῦ δεῖνος or δείνατος, that is, “of a certain person”; Spaniards say *Fulano*, perhaps from the Hebrew *polah* or *pala*, which, among other things, signifies “hidden.” Hence also *peloni*: hidden, unnamed, concealed. Ruth 4:1: *xebah pon peloni*, that is, “Sit—or remain—here, Peloni,” for which the Greek text has κάθισον ὧδε κρύφιε, “Sit here, O hidden one.” The Hebrews likewise begin their contractual formulas in this way: *ani Peloni bar Peloni*, that is, “I am N., son of N.” In Spanish: *lo Fulano, hijo de Fulano*; and if the person is female, *pelanitha*, in Spanish with nearly the same words, *Fulanita*.]

[Col. 0657C] Since this is so, and since elsewhere, according to the rule we established, whenever a doubt arises in liturgical books—such as the Leonine Sacramentary—about a word or statement that may ambiguously signify the native place of martyrs or something else, we ought, in accordance with the mind and spirit of the Church, to prefer the interpretation concerning the martyrs’ native place: why should we not, when we are compelled—though not without some suspicion—to recognize the words NASCENDO CIVIS as genuinely Leonine, interpret them as referring rather to Laurence’s death, through which, by being born into heaven, he became a Roman citizen, than to the temporal homeland of the most holy deacon?

[Col. 0658A] In precisely this sense we know that ecclesiastical authors, disregarding the martyrs’ earthly birthplace, assigned them to those cities in which they endured their final sufferings for Christ. Thus Prudentius, certainly on no other ground, assigns the martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius to Calahorra, Paul to Narbonne, Felix to Girona, Cucufas to Barcelona, and others to other cities. Just as the martyrs’ birthday—the day on which they were born into this world—was disregarded by the ecclesiastical Fathers in comparison with the day of their triumph, and only the latter was celebrated annually by pious gatherings and the vows of the faithful, so, with their temporal homeland passed over, those ancient Fathers recognized as the martyrs’ true homeland only that place in which they had been born into heaven through their passion.

Speaking specifically of Cucufas, the Isidorian hymn reported by Blanchini [Note: Annals, no. CII, in the ancient Gothic Orationary, p. 276.] openly calls this martyr a CITIZEN OF BARCELONA. Its author had just said that the blood of the most holy martyr had established a seat at Barcelona and had transferred his dwelling and household gods there from Africa, in these words:

> From this point the blood of blessed Cucufas  
> became heir to our region;

and he continues [Note: Stanza X, lines 37 ff.]:

> Now favor, O martyr, the prayers of your clients;  
> instruct your citizens and protect the people, etc.

That is, imbue your citizens of Barcelona with the teachings of the faith—those whom inferior Latin would have called “fellow citizens.” For in the same sense our Prudentius, speaking of the garment or scarf of the deacon Vincent, stained with the blood of the most holy martyr and preserved at Zaragoza in his own time, says [Note: Stanza XXI, line 93.]:

> This the citizens revere as though their own soil  
> enclosed the very limbs, and, embracing them,  
> preserved within a father’s tomb  
> the bones of the blessed martyr;

as though he were saying: “Through this pledge, Vincent, your citizens of Zaragoza rejoice and triumph no less than if they possessed in full the sacred remains of your body; and as though Zaragoza, your mother, had received you dead into her bosom, to be placed in the tomb of your ancestors.”

Yet we shall adduce a clearer testimony of Damasus, and one especially decisive for the matter under discussion. It comes from an epigram that was once read at Rome in the basilica of Saint Sebastian at the Catacombs, where the bodies of the holy apostles had rested, as Baronius [Note: Under the year 384, among the poems of Damasus; and in Sarazanius’s notes, p. 188.], Sarazanius [Note: In the notes to Damasus’s poems, Epigram XXX, from Bede, Anastasius, Ado, and the old Roman Breviary.] and Merenda [Note: On the Poems of Damasus, no. 3, p. 137, col. 1.], who also calls it clear and extremely ancient, have left recorded. In this epigram Peter and Paul are most explicitly called ROMAN CITIZENS by Damasus. We reproduce it in full, so that the reader may at the same time understand the occasion on which it was composed [Note: It is given by Sarazanius among Damasus’s poems, p. 91, and by Merenda, p. 226.]:

> Here you must recognize that the holy ones once dwelt,  
> whoever you are who seek the names of Peter and Paul together.  
> We willingly confess that the East sent them as disciples.  
> Because of the merit of their blood, and because they pursued Christ  
> through the stars into the heavenly realms and the kingdom of the righteous,  
> Rome rather deserved to defend her own citizens.  
> Damasus reports these praises of yours to the new stars.  
>   
> [Note: I think *referat* should be restored.]

These words are so perfectly clear that no further doubt can remain: because the chief apostles gained together at Rome the glory of combat and the palm of triumph, Damasus called them Roman citizens.

Although, concerning Paul—whom we have already said from the Book of Acts was born at Tarsus and possessed municipal citizenship—someone might still suspect that Damasus had in that epigram referred to the right of citizenship rather than to the place of martyrdom, this can scarcely be maintained of Peter. Peter is known to have been born at Bethsaida, a small village of Galilee with no connection whatever to that legal status, and to have come from humble parents. If the place of his passion is excluded, I scarcely know whether anything else remains with respect to which Damasus could have called him a ROMAN CITIZEN.

The condition of the two apostles, then—whether we consider their origin or their homeland—was different. Thus neither did they receive the same place, nor did the same fate of punishment befall them [Note: Fleury, Ecclesiastical History, book I, century 1, under the year 66.]. Yet their courage and triumph were equal; and the supreme triumph they achieved at Rome acquired for both of them that highest right of Roman citizenship, so that from then on both were equally made and regarded as Roman citizens.

Perhaps Ambrose had this in mind in the hymn beginning “The passion of the apostles,” where, speaking of Saints Peter and Paul, he says [Note: In Blanchini, Annotation XCIX to the Orationary, p. 270.]:

> The blood of triumphant death  
> joined equal men.

Bede says [Note: In Cardinal Tommasi’s Hymnary.]:

> The hour of departure  
> joined them as they sought heaven’s gate.

Paulinus also says this, as do others whose passages it would take too long to transcribe.

[Col. 0660A] Nor do I doubt that, if the ancient Acts of the martyrs and the treatises that writers of the ancient Churches, both Greek and Latin, composed concerning their passions were carefully examined, more than one passage would be found in which martyrs are counted among the citizens of the city or town where they won the palm [Note: The Mozarabic Missal edited by Lesleus agrees. In its Mass for Saint Vincent the martyr (p. 292, col. 2) we read: “Through your intercession, Vincent, may he gladden both inhabitant and stranger, and render equal aid of protection, *pro cineribus mundo civibus pro sepulcro* [‘for ashes to the world, for citizens in exchange for a tomb’].” That is, the “citizens” are the citizens of Valencia, since the most holy deacon was buried in that city. Moreover, in the Mass for Saints Servandus and Germanus (p. 395, col. 1): “O God, who locate the body [*corpore*, thus printed] of Your martyrs in divided regions, undivided in the recompense of one glory, and grant Servandus to the site of Cádiz, and assign Germanus to the citizens of Mérida.” This refers to the body of Saint Germanus, which was transferred to Mérida; concerning this, see Lesleus himself in the notes, p. 597, col. 1. There may be other examples.]; indeed, even where they eventually remained for a long time and rested in peace, as we shall say in its proper place concerning Paula the Roman.

We think that the examples already given will satisfy readers, so that they may conclude that the words *born a citizen* can most appropriately be interpreted as referring to the Roman citizenship acquired by our Laurence through the palm of martyrdom, rather than through temporal birth, and that this interpretation accords with the usage of the ancient Fathers and even of the Church herself.

There is, however, one point at which Blanchini may perhaps hesitate. [Col. 0660B] If we wish to refer the words NASCENDO CIVIS to Laurence’s death, for what purpose, then, do we say that the clause “the offering dedicated to Your name is proper” was needlessly repeated by the author of the contestation, since it contains the same or a closely related meaning? But the principle of division, or distribution (*τοῦ μερισμοῦ*), must be taken into account.

If, adhering to the first interpretation, we understand the words *born a citizen* as referring to the right of citizenship, nothing prevents us from referring the following words—“the offering dedicated to Your name is proper”—to Laurence’s passion. But if, as in the second interpretation, we understand those words as referring to the place of martyrdom, then we shall refer the immediately following clause, in which Laurence is said to be an offering dedicated to God, to the divine worship to which he was specially devoted in the Levitical rank, or to his vow of virginity, or to something similar, so that we do not claim that the same meaning is inculcated twice in the same place.

Lest anyone think that we have invented this latter interpretation of the second clause without basis, it seems to me that Blanchini and Muratori themselves had long embraced it. For when the Leonine Sacramentary read, “The sacred minister, and the offering dedicated to Your name, is proper,” both rejected the conjunction *et* and restored *dedicatum* in place of *et dicatum* [Note: Blanchini, vol. IV of Anastasius, p. 38: “In place of *et dicatum*, read *dedicatum*.” Muratori printed in the text itself: “The sacred minister, dedicated to Your name,” etc. Vol. I of *Ancient Roman Liturgy*, col. 398.]. Thus, from the two-part statement that previously existed, they made a single, though still two-membered, sentence, whose second part contains nothing except an explanation of the first—as though they were saying: “The sacred minister—that is, the offering dedicated to Your name—is proper.”

But even here we cannot, with Blanchini and Merenda, stop; rather, they endeavor by another argument to oppose the Spanish opinion. If, they say, the Spaniards concede that the Veronese Codex, in which Laurence’s contestation is found, was written as early as the eighth century—even if, for the moment, we freely grant them that this Sacramentary was not composed by Saint Leo—we have at least an older testimony on our side than those on which the Spanish authors rely, and therefore a much stronger argument.

Indeed, if, setting aside for the moment the dispute concerning the antiquity of the Veronese Sacramentary [Note: Learned men—Meratus, Amortius, Muratori, Cennius, Orsius, and others—have long treated this question. Their view seems to amount to the opinion that the Sacramentary was already composed in the fifth century. Nevertheless, perhaps several portions of it were added in later centuries, as we indicate elsewhere; this is in addition to the general tendency of liturgical codices to admit new additions, as we see happening repeatedly in other books of the same kind.], we accept as true what we said near the beginning of this chapter concerning the age of the Codex recovered by Blanchini, we are certainly compelled to acknowledge that this Codex is at least a full century older than Ado, from whose Martyrology we drew the more precise testimony in support of our view.

But even if we assert that Blanchini’s Codex was written in the eighth century, its testimony concerning Laurence’s citizenship or homeland must necessarily be at least five centuries later than the matter about which it gives evidence. I therefore do not see how that greater antiquity of one century over Ado—assuming all other things to be equal—could help to establish the reliability of the Codex, any more than if someone, in asserting a fact belonging to the year 1200, considered the testimony of the seventeenth century, which had just elapsed, more authoritative than that of the eighteenth century in which we live.

Moreover, there are reasons for thinking that Blanchini’s Codex, and even the Contestation of Laurence’s Mass as it is presented to us from that Codex, are not older than the eighth century: the specimen of its script exhibited by Blanchini and the wording of the latter passage provide grounds for this conjecture.

I deliberately added: “assuming all other things to be equal.” But what if a later Codex is preferable to an older one, or the testimony of the latter is clearer and less corrupt than that of the former? We know that Ado was a distinguished ninth-century author, commended by numerous testimonies [Note: See the learned Dominicus Georgius in the preface to his new edition of Ado, Rome, 1745, no. 10.], whereas whoever the writer of the Veronese Codex may have been—although the Codex is older—or rather, whoever compiled it by collecting indiscriminately and without order whatever liturgical prayers he encountered into a single Codex [Note: Muratori, Dissertation on the Ancient Roman Liturgy, ch. 3, cols. 21 and 29.], remains unknown.

Furthermore, the passage in the Veronese Codex is ambiguous not only with respect to Laurence’s homeland, citizenship, passion, and residence, but is also highly suspect of corruption or interpolation, as we have seen. Ado’s text, by contrast, is uncorrupted and precise, and must be interpreted as referring entirely to the homeland of the most holy deacon.

Again, every ancient writer, and every writer from Ado’s time onward, followed Ado’s opinion; whereas, apart from the Calvinist Manlius, no one followed the Veronese Codex. Finally, Ado’s testimony is supported by the reliability of ancient codices and by numerous inferences from liturgical books and the Fathers of the Church. The authority of the Veronese Codex is isolated, for the passage in the Vatican Codex that Blanchini offers as its sole confirmation proves nothing, as we shall say below.

I pass over the weak reliability of the Veronese Codex in the passage that gives the homeland of Pope Clement the martyr. Thus, if Blanchini maintains that the Contestation of Laurence’s Mass also concerns the same matter, it is credible that this Contestation too is unreliable.

Indeed, if we examine the matter somewhat more carefully, it will not be sufficiently certain whether the privilege of antiquity belongs to our foundations or rather to those of our opponents. For, as we said earlier, Baronius affirms that he saw two very ancient Codices once customarily read in the Church, in which Damasus was called Laurence’s fellow countryman; and elsewhere that holy pontiff is most explicitly called a Spaniard by the author of the catalogue of Roman bishops written under Felix—that is, at the beginning of the sixth century.

Why should we not suspect that those two Codices, or one of them, were older than the eighth century? Or why should we not believe that, in the single homeland of Damasus given by the Felician catalogue of pontiffs, Laurence’s homeland is also included—especially since our opponents themselves acknowledge that he was Damasus’s fellow countryman? [Note: Merenda, *Works and Deeds of Damasus*, at the beginning, p. 2.] But perhaps enough of this.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Opponents’ Final Efforts Are Suppressed

[Col. 0662C]

I would not wish to appear, as the idle poets commonly do in Cicero’s expression [Note: *On Old Age*, no. 2], more negligent in the final act. Yet the objections that Blanchini makes against us here are not important, and have already been partly refuted elsewhere; besides, some concession must be made to readers, whose patience we may perhaps have abused thus far. Therefore, just as we dealt at length with the removal of the earlier arguments when the matter required it, so in the single argument that remains we shall be sparing of words.

Blanchini consequently objects to us, as his final point, the Vatican Codex, which he says was written in the ninth century and which, among other things, contains the Acts of Saints Sixtus, Laurence, and Hippolytus. In these Acts our deacon is most explicitly called a Roman citizen. Sixtus is introduced in the Acts, as his own passion approaches, calling Laurence and entrusting to him the distribution of the Church’s resources to the poor, in these words [Note: Blanchini, Annotation CVI to the Orationary, p. 283.]:

> And when he had discussed these and similar matters in his holy discourse, Sixtus called Laurence, his archdeacon, a ROMAN CITIZEN, worthy of God and a man devoted to God—conspicuous both in habit and in holiness—and handed over to him all the resources of the Church, etc.

As for the antiquity of the Codex, Blanchini adds [Note: In the passage cited immediately above.], there is no reason for doubt: the book is preserved in the foremost library of the City, under number 612.

Now these statements will appear all the more probable than those we examined in the preceding chapter because nothing prevents the words “Roman citizen” from containing a reference to Laurence’s homeland. Since these words derive not from some liturgical book but from the Acts of the martyrs, into which the martyrs’ homelands could freely be inserted, the writer of the material in question could, on the basis of information learned elsewhere, have attached Laurence’s birthplace to his narrative without incurring any criticism.

[Col. 0663B] But we have already indicated elsewhere how highly these Acts should be valued [Note: Above, ch. 2, p. 78.]. Blanchini himself does not deny that they are extremely corrupt [Note: Annotation CVI, p. 293.]. We add, however, the three signs of falsehood that we mentioned earlier: the fictitious history of Saints Abdon and Sennen, who are said in the Acts to have been brought from Persia by Decius; the fictitious expedition of that emperor into the East; and finally the ridiculous and utterly insane story that Decius and Valerian suddenly perished at the same moment, each of them separately sufficient to cast the greatest suspicion of falsehood upon the Acts, but all of them together having flowed into them as though into a cesspool.

We omit the passions of Saints Sixtus, Laurence, and Hippolytus under Decius, a circumstance that has caused so many difficulties for Ado’s Acts, as well as the other passages full of pitfalls and evasions, in addition to the inconsistent variety of style. All these things seem from every direction to conspire to diminish the credibility of the Acts.

Moreover, when anyone sees the name “Roman citizen” inserted so awkwardly into the Acts between Laurence’s ecclesiastical rank and his eulogy, who would not immediately detect a grafted shoot, barely joined to the trunk? But why, I ask, did the compiler of the Acts call Laurence only a Roman citizen, using a plainly ambiguous phrase capable of several meanings, rather than writing “born at Rome,” “Roman by homeland,” or something of the sort that would have settled the entire dispute in a single word? He could have done so at no greater expense than when, shortly before, he had called Sixtus born and educated at Athens [Note: At the beginning of the Acts, in Blanchini, Annotation CVI, p. 293.].

Yet on what authority did he do that? Heavens above! We had learned from Anastasius and others that Sixtus was Greek, and even from the most ancient catalogues of the popes, first published by Schelstratius [Note: Vol. I, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, in the appendix to the *Chronological Work*, no. 22, p. 611.] and the elder Blanchini [Note: Vol. I of Anastasius, p. 24; likewise vol. II, p. 14, and the same volume, p. 222, under Sixtus.]—although there is someone who wishes him to have been Roman [Note: Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs from the Veronese Church’s Codex, which the younger Blanchini included in the Prolegomena to vol. IV of Anastasius, p. 4, col. 1.].

Nevertheless, I remember reading nowhere except in these Acts that Sixtus was born at Attic Athens. Therefore, provided that truth is safeguarded, I think the author of the Acts deserves from the Athenians the *gospel*—τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, “good news”—as his reward. There is indeed a reading in the two Codices, Mazzarinian and Thuanean: “Greek, from Athens” [Note: In the elder Blanchini, vol. II of Anastasius, p. 26, among Fabretti’s variants.]; but scholars consider the latter word highly suspect, indeed spurious, and Blanchini will not deny this.

I would not, however, have these remarks considered a preliminary attempt to evade the need for an answer. Therefore, if we wish the words of the Acts that Blanchini brings against us to be sincere and genuine, we can conveniently interpret them as referring to the right of citizenship, or to free birth, but especially to Laurence’s residence at Rome.

Since Laurence had been raised and educated at Rome from childhood and had been advanced to a distinguished ecclesiastical rank, and since he had established his home there without intending to return to his former homeland, he could acquire Rome as his legal homeland, just as Marcus Cato did in Cicero, and in that sense be called a Roman citizen—especially since, by that time, the ancient distinction between municipal citizens and residents had almost died out.

Indeed, Paula the Roman is said by Jerome to have become a CITIZEN OF THE SAVIOR—that is, a citizen of Bethlehem—not by any other right than that of residence, because she left her own land and established a permanent home at Bethlehem [Note: In the concluding part of Jerome’s *Epitaph of Paula to Eustochium*.].

To understand the words of the Acts as referring to Laurence’s homeland is prevented by Ado’s authority, which we have cited elsewhere in support of our view. For since Laurence is explicitly called a Spaniard in Ado’s Martyrology, unless we turn the words of the Acts—which are far more general than Ado’s—to some other meaning, we necessarily make one of these writers a liar.

What excellent praise would an ecclesiastical interpreter deserve if, whenever the testimonies of the ancients were not precisely contradictory but merely different—especially when the dispute concerned not a legal right but a fact and its truth, as here—he preferred to set them against one another and call one of the authors false, rather than, by gently bending the words of one, reconcile the opinions of both in a friendly manner!

But if Blanchini insists that the passage of the Acts in question must be referred entirely to Laurence’s homeland, and therefore maintains that the testimonies of the two writers are not merely different but conflicting and wholly contradictory, Ado will not shrink from the contest with the writer of the Acts. Even if we grant Blanchini that the latter lived as early as the ninth century, he will still not be older than Ado; and we know that he is anonymous and entirely obscure, and guilty of numerous falsehoods.

By contrast, there is nothing in Ado that conflicts with the credibility of history, at least nothing that cannot be supported by some argument, as we have shown elsewhere.

But if Blanchini persists, I shall freely concede to the writer of the Acts not merely equal authority but much greater authority than Ado possesses. I ask only that the words of the two be compared with one another.

The Acts call Laurence a Roman citizen; Ado asserts that he was Spanish by origin, but educated and raised at Rome. Although the former phrase may perhaps refer to his origin, its meaning is nevertheless narrowed by the latter, and it is made perfectly clear that the sentence must be understood as concerning his homeland. Thus the passage in the Acts is far more general than Ado’s.

Now, according to the canon of the best interpretation, when two testimonies—whether of Sacred Scripture or of the ancient Fathers—appear to conflict, the more general must be accommodated to the less general, not the reverse. The jurists express this in the familiar maxim: “The specific derogates from the general” [Note: Law 80, *Digest*, On the General Principles of Law.].

And now let us bring the work to an end.

## CONCLUSION

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665B] I think that the arguments brought forward in support of the common and most widely accepted opinion concerning Laurence’s homeland are sufficient to enable the Spaniards, for the present, to meet the arguments of Blanchini and his opponents, until some more industrious member of their nation claims this neglected subject for himself and adorns it more thoroughly than we have done. As we noted at the beginning, that was our purpose.

Perhaps the old opinion of the Spaniards—that Laurence belonged to them—will easily retain, among domestic and foreign writers alike, a greater degree of probability and dignity than the competing views; and their tradition, received from their ancestors, confirmed by ancient monuments, and carried down to the present through an unbroken and continuous thread, may acquire new strength.

Indeed, the Spaniards may hope that the ancient possession—older even than human memory, or nearly fifteen centuries old—by which they have held Laurence’s birthplace among themselves, and from which their opponents boast that they have been dispossessed, may be protected by what is called the interdict of retention: namely, that they have possessed, and still possess, Laurence neither by force, secretly, nor precariously; and that a literary praetor may assist them in retaining him and forbid violence against that possession.

But if, contrary to our intention, and certainly against our hope, these efforts of ours should in no way succeed in helping the public cause of the Spaniards—as I think I said in the earlier work in which we dealt with Damasus—we prefer that our own inadequacy should be blamed rather than that either or both of these opinions should lose even the smallest degree of probability among learned men.

We shall certainly never regret the labor we undertook. Apart from our first duty toward God, we could never have devoted ourselves to a greater task, nor placed our efforts more honorably than in serving our homeland.

Meanwhile, if Blanchini wishes, with the Apostle, to be a debtor even to the foolish, let him kindly endure my friendly warning: after the loss of our Spain, let him not continue to seek new praises for the City, but rather direct his commendable labors and vigils elsewhere.

For if he takes Laurence’s birthplace away from the Spaniards, he will think that he has deprived a people most tenacious of the religion, piety, and glory of their ancestors of a very great honor. If, on the contrary, Blanchini assigns the most holy deacon to the City, he will add no more to the Roman cause than if he poured a bucket of water into the sea.

Rome has, moreover, far more than our Spain that it can rightly claim in Laurence: she received him as a child into her bosom, raised him as her own, advanced him while living through ecclesiastical honors, and, when he died, placed him in a most honorable tomb and has honored his sacred ashes with exceptional devotion down to the present day.

Let Rome, then, rejoice, exult, and triumph in her foster son and martyr. Our Spain does not begrudge, and never will begrudge, the mistress of the world and mother of our common religion her true and unfeigned praises; nor does she fear that the City will in turn begrudge Laurence’s birth to Spain, the most dutiful of all her daughters.

Especially since Rome has given birth to so many martyrs—not only for Christ but also for the world—that on this account as well she has deserved to be called blessed, eternal, and the chief of cities.

Since Rome therefore possesses so many dishes with which she can prepare a richly furnished banquet for guests flocking from the whole world, without diminishing anyone else’s share, let Blanchini, I beg him, spare the little sheep that our Spain has hitherto nourished as her own among her children, feeding it from her bread, giving it drink from her cup, and letting it sleep in its mother’s lap—unless he wishes to hear the angry Lord, or the prophet, pronounce:

> “As the Lord lives, the man who has done this is a son of death” (2 Samuel 12:5).

When, at the conclusion of the dispute, Blanchini asks pardon from the Spaniards because, in reclaiming so great a martyr as Laurence, he fought out of love of truth and with sincere charity [Note: Annotation CVI to the Orationary, p. 294, at the end], it remains for us to hope that, if in avenging what we believe to have been the injury he inflicted upon the Spaniards we have exceeded the bounds of a just and civil defense, or have appeared somewhat sharper to readers than was expedient, they will kindly forgive us for it.

To the outstanding man Blanchini—also our friend, and otherwise most deserving of the Spaniards—we apply Horace’s words [Note: *Art of Poetry*]:

> We know; and this pardon we ask and grant in turn.

## ADDITIONS AND EXPLANATIONS

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667A] After a substantial portion of this work had been released from the printers’ hands, I came upon passages in several distinguished writers by which I think the teaching presented above could be confirmed or explained. I have therefore decided to indicate them briefly here, giving also the number of the page to which each passage corresponds, so that the reader may easily compare the two.

First, when I was discussing the age required for admission to the rank of lector in the earlier centuries of the Church (col. 559, note c), I judged that the example of a certain boy lector named Messius, cited by Bonarotius (*Observations on a Fragment of Glass*, col. 626), was later than the age of the emperor Constantine. I based this both on the rather crude style of the epigram and also on the chi-rho monogram of Christ added beside it.

This was not because I was entirely unaware that the monogram had been used among Christians even before Constantine, and perhaps among the pagans themselves, but because at that time Christians did not employ it very frequently—indeed, only rarely. The small number of examples makes this clear [Col. 0667B] (see the most learned Mamachi, *Christian Origins and Antiquities*, vol. III, pp. 54 ff.), whereas in the fourth century and thereafter it was found everywhere, not only on tombs but also on lamps, rings, spears, shields, and other monuments of Christians generally.

When, at the time this sheet was being hurried through the press, I noticed a certain lingering scruple in our most learned and singular friend on this point, I decided for the time being to make a corresponding substitution in the copies still awaiting publication [the precise reading is uncertain in the supplied OCR], and to warn readers here about the matter, lest they accuse us of inconsistency or frivolity.

Secondly, our conjecture that, when dealing with the same subject (Col. 562), we had suspected that boys gained access to the rank of lector only after the peace restored to the Church by Constantine, seems to be contradicted by the man of admirable learning and erudition, Alexius Symmachus Mazochius, canon of the Neapolitan Church. In his remarks on the Greek Acts of Saints Theodulus and Agathopus, published by the Bollandist Fathers at the end of volume I for April, speaking of the martyr Theodulus, who is known to have suffered under Maximian, he asserts that Theodulus, having scarcely entered puberty, was a lector (*Commentary on the Ancient Marble Calendar of the Church of Naples*, p. 152, col. 2), adding:

“This is useful to have observed, lest anyone should think that at that time a more advanced age than now was necessary for the lectorate.”

Yet I cannot agree with that most distinguished scholar on this point. The passage of the Acts on which he relies does not, in my judgment, establish that Theodulus was already at the very threshold of puberty when he became a lector, but rather that he was carried off to martyrdom as a young man, or at most as an adolescent. For although the Acts say that he was of an age at which the first down had not long before begun to blossom around his cheeks, I think this was done for the sake of contrast, so that Theodulus’s youthful and flowering age might be set more vividly against the old age and gray hair of Agathopus. For a few lines later the Acts read:

> Καὶ τοιοῦτος μὲν ὁ Θεόδουλος, ὁ δὲ το τοῦν [Perhaps τούτῳ, that is, “to this man”] συμπνέων Ἀγαθόπους, ἀνὴρ πρεσβὐτης, ἤδη τῇ πολιᾷ τὴν κεφαλὴν ἔντιμος· Ἀμφότεροι καθαροὶ etc.

That is:

> “Such, then, was Theodulus; but Agathopus, who joined him in this [martyrdom], was already an old man, venerable for the grayness of his head. Both were pure,” etc.

Now this comparison of Theodulus with Agathopus stands perfectly well even if we call the former a young man, and sufficiently indicates that the word referring to the down on Theodulus’s cheeks should not be taken so narrowly as though, at the time when he suffered martyrdom as a lector, he had scarcely entered puberty. The sense is: “Theodulus had not yet entirely shed his down,” that is, he had not yet worked off the youthful heat of his age.

Let this suffice concerning the first part of that period. As for the latter part, in which the same distinguished scholar thinks that the writer of the Acts alluded to “the body of our humiliation” (Philippians III, 21), I find myself more inclined to admire his extraordinarily refined ingenuity than to embrace his interpretation on this point. For why should the writer of the Acts not rather have had in mind other passages of Scripture, in which we are commanded to become little children if we wish to enter the kingdom of heaven?

Although the word ταπεινοφροσύνη properly signifies abasement of mind, or humility, here, unless we twist it elsewhere by metaphor or improper usage, we must make the sentence incongruous—even absurd. For what, I ask, does this mean: “Theodulus was a man who had newly grown down upon his cheeks, but was otherwise still a child with respect to the humility of an incorrupt body, or the abasement of the mind”? Or by what right is abasement of mind attributed to the body?

For this reason I would believe that, in the passage under discussion, τὸ ταπεινοφροσύνης means integrity, or virginal modesty—that is, chastity or reserve. In this sense Cicero understood the latter word (*On Divination* I), and it can be used without impropriety. The meaning of the sentence would then be:

> “Theodulus, in the flower of youth, was indeed ardently moving along the slippery path of his age; but he was still a child in respect of the integrity of his uncorrupted body, or of the virginal modesty and chastity of his countenance.”

Finally, it should be noted that ἀνὴρ, both of Theodulus and of Agathopus, carries no special emphasis, but in both cases is simply redundant according to ordinary idiom.

But perhaps I have prolonged this discussion somewhat further than was necessary.

Thirdly (Col. 605 ff., note c), where we said that the *Gothic-Gallican Missal*, first published by the venerable and distinguished Thomasio, belonged not to that part of Gaul which obeyed the Frankish kings, as the distinguished Lesleus maintains, but to one of the Churches subject to the Gothic rule of Narbonensian Gaul, there is further evidence that can be brought in confirmation of this view.

That author, as we have seen, thinks that, from the practice of the three-day Rogations before the Ascension—which he knew to have prevailed in the Church to which the *Gothic-Gallican Missal* belonged, but not in the Churches of Spain—and from the communion of ecclesiastical rites prescribed and ordered to be observed between the Churches of Spain and Narbonensian Gaul at the Fourth Council of Toledo, it follows that the three-day Rogations were not observed in Narbonensian Gaul, and consequently that the Missal in question did not belong to that part of Gaul.

We, on the contrary, said there that this ancient practice of the three-day Rogations, fixed in the minds of the peoples of Gaul, could have been retained by the Gallo-Narbonensian Churches even after the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo—that is, after the Hispanic rites had been incorporated. The strongest evidence for this is as follows.

First, from the testimony of Gregory of Tours, quoted by Amalarius Fortunatus (*On Ecclesiastical Offices* I, chapter 37), we know that the three-day Rogations, instituted by Saint Mamertus of Vienne toward the end of the fifth century against earthquakes and the madness of wolves, were in Gregory’s time—that is, shortly before the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo—in use among all the Churches, namely, the Churches of Gaul, as Amalarius interprets the passage in the same place.

Walafrid Strabo likewise asserts (*On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 28) that in his own time—that is, around the middle of the ninth century—the same Rogations were customarily celebrated in all the Churches of Gaul, and even of Germany. Anastasius further teaches us in the Life of Leo III that Leo, who held the pontificate at the beginning of the ninth century and the end of the eighth, introduced the same Rogations into the city and Church of Rome.

I say nothing here of Rabanus Maurus, whose testimony on this matter we cited earlier; nor of the commonly known Albinus, or Alcuin, who asserts (*Book on Various Ecclesiastical Offices*, rubric “On the Days of the Rogations”) that in his own time the same custom was most devoutly observed among the Gauls on account of various calamities.

From these testimonies it seems to me wholly established that the three-day Rogations before the Ascension were customary not only throughout Gaul but were also extended elsewhere, specifically to avert public calamities and appease the anger of the divine Majesty.

Now, since not long after the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo—or rather, at the very end of the seventh century—Narbonensian Gaul was afflicted by so many calamities that, according to the testimony of Flavius Egica, king of the Goths (*Exhortation to the Fathers of the Seventeenth Council of Toledo*, in Labbe, vol. VIII, col. 83), it was described as deserted and utterly desolate both through the invasion of a foreign people and through the destruction caused by the bubonic plague; and since, for this reason, the king urged the Council Fathers not to impose anything more severe upon the Jews living in that region, who could believe that those Rogations, which had formerly prevailed in Gothic Gaul, and which the neighboring city of Vienne had experienced for two centuries as a most effective remedy against public evils, were suspended by those same Gallo-Narbonensians in so grave a crisis?

Let this suffice concerning the three-day Rogations.

As for the non-continuous observance throughout the entire forty fasting days of Lent, which the same distinguished author asserts prevailed in the Church that used the *Gothic Missal*, I think that we have said more than enough in the same place (Col. 606, in the note) to enable readers to understand that in that Church the Lenten fast consisted of no more than thirty-six fasting days, interrupted five times by the five Sundays that occurred within the period. We know that this same practice was observed in the Churches of Spain.

There are, nevertheless, many further arguments that could be brought forward in confirmation of our position, if brevity of expression did not have to be observed. But since the same distinguished author maintains that those who used the *Gothic Missal* fasted for precisely forty days, though interrupted at intervals, and that they therefore observed not Quadragesima but Quinquagesima, and perhaps Sexagesima or Septuagesima, and for this reason asserts that the Missal was customary not in Gothic Gaul but in that part of Gaul subject to the Frankish empire, it follows from both claims that, in the part of Gaul subject to the Frankish empire, not Quadragesima but Quinquagesima—and perhaps Sexagesima, or even Septuagesima—was observed in full.

I do not know how that conclusion can be maintained by the distinguished scholar, since in the Gallican Sacramentary of Bobbio of Saint Columbanus, and in the Lectionary of Luxeuil edited by Mabillon (*Museum Italicum* I, and *Gallican Liturgy*)—both of which, as we said earlier, belonged to the province of Vesontio, that is, to the Gallo-Franks—there is no mention at all of Quinquagesima, Sexagesima, or Septuagesima, but only of one Quadragesima, whose observance is completed in six weeks.

Indeed, the Gallo-Frankish Fathers themselves, in the First and Fourth Councils of Orléans, having rejected the observance of Quinquagesima and Sexagesima, order that only one Quadragesima be celebrated equally by all the Churches of that region of Gaul.

We set out the words of both councils. The earlier council, canon 24 (Appendix to Labbe, vol. V, col. 547), says:

> “It has been decreed by all the priests that before the solemnity of Easter not Quinquagesima but Quadragesima shall be observed.”

The later council, canon 2 (in the same author, vol. V, col. 1364), says:

> “We also decree that this be observed: Quadragesima shall be kept equally by all the Churches; and no priest shall presume to prescribe Quinquagesima or Sexagesima before Easter.”

We deliberately omit the *Frankish Missal* and the *Old Gallican*, or *Auxerre*, Missal, which belonged to the Gallo-Franks, since in the latter only very few seasonal Masses occur, while in the former none occurs at all.

Fourthly (Col. 609, letter a), I said that Lawrence was mentioned three times in the Leonine Sacramentary, apart from the Mass on Lawrence’s feast day—and that is true. But I should also have added that, among the Masses for the month of April, under number 20 (vol. IV of Anastasius, p. 14, col. 1), I found a further mention of Lawrence.

Since, however, that passage concerns a Common of Martyrs, and since the remaining prayers for that month, with very few exceptions, are common prayers in which the proper names of the martyrs are omitted, it is credible that the name of Lawrence slipped into the text of that Sacramentary in place of *illius*, or of the modern N, as Muratori observed (*On the Ancient Roman Liturgy* I, col. 293). It is also possible that the compiler of the codex transferred the complete prayer of Lawrence from his proper Masses and placed it here; we know that the same carelessness occurred elsewhere. Indeed, among the very Masses of Lawrence, his vigil was more than once placed after the feast itself (see *Leonine Sacramentary*, vol. IV of Anastasius, p. 37, col. 2, nos. 9–12).

Whatever the case may be, this mention of Lawrence, since it occurs without an encomium, cannot affect our argument.

Fifthly (Col. 611, note a), where we said, against the distinguished Lesleus, that Eulalia, who is mentioned in the *Gothic-Gallican Missal*, was not Eulalia of Barcelona but Eulalia of Mérida, and where the Acts of the two Eulalias had been confused, it is worth bringing forward Lesleus’s own testimony. Having observed in the *Mozarabic Missal* (p. 31) that the following passage was also said of Eulalia of Mérida—

> “She goes to the tribunal of the bloodthirsty governor, and, without being asked, she leaps”—

he says (in the note, p. 482):

> “These words do not refer to Eulalia of Mérida but to Eulalia of Barcelona.”

Moreover, the same distinguished author states (in the note, p. 481) that Eulalia of Mérida was the most famous Eulalia among all the peoples of the Western Church. It therefore would be no wonder if among the Gallo-Goths, and even among more distant peoples, her feast day were celebrated with a special Mass.

Sixthly (Col. 622, note b), among the saints whom the Blanchini Codex of the *Orationary* does not mention, although they are genuinely Spanish, Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis, martyrs of Córdoba, must also be listed. Their feast is celebrated in the *Mozarabic Missal* on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, and their proper Mass is found in Lesleus’s edition, p. 387.

Prudentius perhaps also understood these same martyrs when, after listing Acisclus and Zoellus of Córdoba (*Hymn on the Eighteen Martyrs of Zaragoza*), he adds three further crowns to that same city, saying:

> Córdoba shall give Acisclus and Zoellus,  
> and three crowns besides.

Finally, what had escaped us in its proper place—namely, Col. 535, where we discussed the antiquity of the Life of Damasus written by the priest Benedict—seemed worth adding. I remember having read in Mabillon (*Museum Italicum* I, p. 129) that in the Oratory of Saint Sebastian in Rome, commonly called San Bastianello, on the slope of the Palatine Hill above the Arch of Titus Augustus, an ancient painting was found in the oldest apse of the Church, behind the principal altar. In its lower part, in Mabillon’s time, the following could be read:

> I, BENEDICT, PRIEST AND MONK, HAD THIS PAINTED.

The most learned scholar suspects that this Benedict was the same man who wrote the Life of Damasus in question (ibid., p. 130).

We, however, who had long been deeply interested in investigating, if possible, the age of that Benedict, examined the painting with the greatest care, but could scarcely make out the fading traces of the inscription. If the Benedict whose name was read there was indeed the author of the Life of Damasus, I would have no hesitation in assigning him to the eighth, or perhaps even the seventh, century. For if one considers the painting—whether its general character, or the images it displays of Christ and of the saints Sebastian, the unnamed martyr, Lawrence, and Stephen standing beside him, and especially the images of certain figures who appear to shine with royal dignity, as well as their adornment and dress—it seems to exhibit no lesser antiquity.

But more perceptive scholars will judge this matter.

There may perhaps be other points on which the reader would desire fuller illumination, but they are too minor to require us to linger over them any longer.

# TO VOLUME XX

[Col. 0671]

## Poems Attributed to Sulpicius Severus (C)*

When the highly honored gentlemen Miller and Aubenas were once weighing the twentieth volume of our *Patrology* on the scales of a kindly and impartial examination, in a review entitled *Revue bibliographique*, they happened upon some panegyric verses on Saint Martin. They thought, not without reason, that these could be attributed to Sulpicius Severus, since they had not previously been published, and they were the first to bring them to light from a parchment codex of the Royal Library of Saint Victor, no. 480, containing 123 folios.

That codex contains:

1. The *Life of Saint Martin of Tours*, by Sulpicius Severus;
2. three letters of the same author, one to Eusebius, another to Aurelius, and a third to Bassula;
3. three dialogues on Saint Martin;
4. finally, the verses mentioned above, which occur on folio 53 verso and are here transcribed by us as a supplement.

We have already filled a similar lacuna in volume XIII with the previously unpublished verses of Saint Damasus, gladly and readily responding to the honored admonitions of the most learned Miller and Aubenas, mentioned above.

*Editor.*

### On the doorway of the first cell

[Col. 0671A]

We have come indeed to this place; here, alas, the sound is heard no longer.

We have come indeed to this place, and the arms of the cross are silent.

You were truly the Lord’s warrior—[Note: The Sangermanensis manuscript has “now sleeps in that very place,” which is better.] sleep, O pious one!

The warrior sleeps, a man to be longed for.

Yet let us enter, and with tears and prayers let us pray

to the Lord of the saints and the God of Martin,

and let us prostrate ourselves upon the place which the saint watered with his tears;

[Note: The Sangermanensis manuscript reads *auscilio*.] His spirit will be our help.

The warrior sleeps; but do protect us, O Christ,

you who do not sleep, [Note: Read “protect,” from the Sangermanensis manuscript.] protect Israel.

### Likewise in another cell

Here dwelt one who kissed the footsteps of the Lord;

here dwelt a man who bore the arms of the cross;

here dwelt a holy and pure priest;

here dwelt one upright in body and heart;

here dwelt one whose shield was holy faith,

and whose splendid and shining boss was the word of the cross.

Here dwelt the blessed hermit beneath a cave;

here dwelt the man whom Paradise possesses.

### Likewise in the inner cell

Holy God, have mercy on the place you have always loved;

love it, increase it, protect it, always love it.

For when our shepherd’s appointed time was complete,

you carried him away to bright, holy, and blessed places.

Protect us too, O holy one, beneath the shelter of your wings;

preserve us, love us, always love us.

We humbly ask that in your kindness you grant and bestow

that the saints and he alike may help us.

### Likewise there, above the place of his bed

[Col. 0671C]

What weapons of the warrior, here, did we often see,

when he was absent, yet was present as a man:

black coals and ashes, everything dreadful,

dust and mists, all things exceedingly filthy.

Beneath his head, a hair shirt, a stone, and a high heap of ashes—

here was, as you might see, a bed for his wasted limbs.

For a little seat was his rest during the silent night,

and by day this same seat served him instead of a bench or chair.

### The basilica begins. First inscription on the tower, on the eastern side

As you enter the temple, turn your face toward the heights;

lofty faith looks up toward the exalted entrances.

[Col. 0672A] Be humble in understanding, but pursue the hope that calls you; II

Martin opens the doors which you are to venerate.

This is a secure tower, set against the trembling proud,

rising high to exclude them and shelter gentle hearts.

Yet higher is that tower which carried Martin

to the citadel of heaven by starry paths.

From there he calls the peoples, he who as a forerunner entered and sanctified

the starry path to Christ’s blessings.

### Another inscription

As you are about to enter the hall, reverencing the lights of Christ,

drive worldly cares from your whole heart,

and empty your mind of profane desires.

Whoever prays rightly returns having obtained what he sought.

Whoever, with a tranquil mind, comes to seek the temple of God,

entering to ask forgiveness for long-standing sins,

must not waver in mind or falter in faith.

You obtain what you seek if you ask with a pure heart;

believe—as he himself says—and you will likewise be saved.

### Likewise at the entrance, on the western side, above the door: a painted history of the widow

Let everyone who comes to offer vows to the highest God

learn to confess Christ in the language of the Gospel.

Though trembling in heart, suppliant, kneeling low, and with bowed face,

if works cease, faith is empty indeed.

Under this law both rich and poor are held alike;

the one whose mind lacks understanding has proved his work by his intention,

and no one is excused by a narrow or inadequate means.

Glory depends upon affection, not upon price.

Whoever gives whatever he can [Note: Another manuscript reads “what is required.”] gives the most;

though he may have given little, he desires to give the greatest things.

Among heaps of wealth and the gifts of the powerful,

we know that the faith of the poor widow was preferred,

when, buying the kingdom of heaven with two coins,

the just Father raised her sublime to the stars.

She deserved praise from the mouth of God the Judge,

not because she gave much, but because she kept nothing for herself.

### Likewise, verses above the door on the Loire side

When the Lord commanded his disciples, sailing on the sea while the winds blew and the waves rose, the Lord walked upon the sea with his feet, stretched out his hand to holy Peter as he was sinking, and rescued him from danger. The most holy Church of Christ, mother of all the Churches, which the apostles founded, in which the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles in the form of tongues of fire, contains the throne of the apostle James and the column at which Christ was scourged.

Whoever, bent down upon the ground, has pressed your face into the dust,

and has struck your moist eyes against the earth,

raise your eyes and take in the miracles with trembling sight,

and entrust your cause to the excellent patron.

No page can contain such powers;

although cement and stones record these things in inscriptions,

a work of earth does not enclose what the royal heaven

receives, and what the stars inscribe with their red gems.

If you seek Martin’s help, rising again beyond the stars,

touch the pole of heaven, having sought out the company in the ether.

There seek the patron joined to the Lord,

following always the footsteps of the eternal King.

[Col. 0673B] If you doubt, behold the miracles placed before your eyes:

see how the true Savior honors the merit of his servant.

You approach as a witness among the others, amid so many thousands,

while carefully observing the things to be narrated and recounting what you have seen,

everything that the page has recorded in the holy books.

As God restores, you see by what number they rejoice:

the blind, the lame, the destitute, the mad, the anxious, the sick,

the weak, the oppressed, the captive, the sorrowful, the needy.

Every healing rejoices in apostolic signs.

Whoever comes here weeping returns joyful; all clouds disperse.

What affliction troubles, medicine makes clear.

Seek his protection; you do not knock at these doors in vain.

Such lavish mercy extends throughout the whole world.

### Likewise above the place of the apse, on the altar

[Col. 0673C] How fearful is this place! Truly, it is the temple of God and the gate of heaven.

### Likewise around the tomb, on one side

Here lies Martin, bishop of holy memory, whose soul is in the hand of God; yet here he is wholly present, manifest in every grace of his virtues.

### On the other side

He fought the good fight, completed the course, kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for him the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just Judge, will give him on that day.

### Above

In merits a confessor, in the cross a martyr, in deeds an apostle,

Martin here surpasses the heavens in his tomb.

May he be mindful and, cleansing the sins of our wretched life,

hide our crimes by his own merits.

### In the apse

[Col. 0674A]

Martin’s body, venerable as a gift to the earth,

in which honor lives after the passage of life.

Here a structure had first enclosed it in the ordinary manner,

a structure not equal to its confessor.

Nor did it cease to burden the citizens with shame;

the man’s glory was great, but the glory of the place was small.

But the bishop, counted sixth from that very man,

lifted the long-standing reproach forever,

removing the inner shrine of the small chapel

and raising spacious roofs within the outer building.

And both grew together, the powerful patron granting it,

in the spaces of the building, though its founder was undeserving,

which is able to rival the temple of Solomon,

the seventh wondrous work in the world.

[Col. 0674B] For if that temple shone with gems, gold, and silver,

this one surpasses all metals through faith.

Away, gnawing envy, and let those who came before be excused.

Let talkative posterity neither alter nor add anything,

and when Christ comes to raise all peoples,

may these eternal roofs endure forever.

### Here begins the deposition of Saint Martin

On the third day before the Ides of November he rested in the peace of the Lord, at midnight.

### Here begins the inscription in memory of holy Remigius

This house preserves five blessed crowns,

whose titles and names, if you read them, you will know

to be written in heaven, where they remain and will always remain.

[Col. 0674C] Here the holy John the Baptist rejoices, born from the womb.

Here are Felix and Victor, and the gracious Gervasius;

and sacred Protasius, witnesses here throughout the ages,

who adorned the true faith through cross, blood, and death.

The five joined fingers, all together, from the body of Christ,

form a lofty palm through great struggle,

which they adorn with flowers perpetual and worthy of God.

### Title of the book of the life of Saint Martin, bishop

If you possess holy faith and a mind devoted to Christ,

here, diligent reader, you can learn of the enduring mass of the sacred bishop Martin’s merits:

origin, military service, birth, deeds, parents,

teaching, character, praises, battles, triumphs,

punishments [Note: Perhaps *supplicium*, singular, “punishment.”], homeland, dangers, sayings, labors,

[Col. 0674D] rewards, virtues, age, and sacred praises.

# TO VOLUME LI

## The Chronicle of Idatius, Bishop, Illustrated with Corrections, Notes, and Dissertations by Joannes Matthaeus Garzon, Spaniard, Theologian of the Society of Jesus and Former Chancellor of the Academy of Gandia

Published from the autograph codex of the Royal Library of Brussels by P. F. X. de Ram, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Canon Law, Fellow of the Royal Historical Commission of Belgium.

(The numbers printed in heavier type in the text correspond to the pages of the edition reviewed here.)

[Col. 0675]

## Editor’s Notice

The matters concerning the life and writings of Idatius have been treated fully and more than sufficiently in the preliminary dissertation [Note: See p. 9 ff.]. A few points concerning his *Chronicle*, which Garzon illustrated better than anyone, should nevertheless be prefaced here.

This *Chronicle*, regarded by the Spaniards as one of the principal monuments of their history, runs from the year 379 of the Christian era to the year 469 [Note: Sigebert of Gembloux, under the year 490, says: “Idatius brought his *Chronicle* down to this point.” Vossius rightly observes that Sigebert was mistaken because he had encountered a codex in which several years had been added to Idatius’s text by another hand. See also Nicolás Antonio of Seville, *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*. Madrid, 1788, folio, vol. I, p. 259.]. It therefore covers nearly ninety years, from Theodosius to Leo.

The author himself divided it into two parts in such a way that he frankly acknowledged the first to have been taken from other sources, while he asserted that the second, from the year 427 to the end, had been written by himself as an immediate eyewitness [Note: Compare the preface to Idatius, p. 50.].

Christian Frederick Roesler states [Note: *Chronicles of the Middle Ages, More General in Subject, More Celebrated in Authority, More Common in Use, Expounding the Events of the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Centuries after Eusebius and Jerome*. Tübingen, 1798, octavo, p. 90.] that the writers whom Idatius appears to have followed in the first part of the *Chronicle* were Sulpicius and Orosius, common sources for those times and writers and also especially familiar to the Spaniards.

From the third year of Valentinian—that is, from the year 427 of the Christian era—Idatius himself begins to be a source from which many afterward watered their own certainly rather arid fields. Among these none did so more extensively than Isidore, both of Seville and of Pacensis.

That Idatius deserves to be counted among the best fifth-century writers as an eyewitness and truthful historian is testified by Papirius Massonus [Note: *History of the Calamities of Gaul*, p. 97.]. He held a position from which he could observe and judge many matters more accurately. He served not only as bishop for many years but was also employed on embassies and public duties [Note: Compare below, pp. 16 and 74.]. Involved in the events themselves, he learned them through personal experience and committed them to writing.

In writing he generally uses a brief style, one that is barbarous and difficult. This, however, cannot prevent Idatius’s *Chronicle* from being held in the highest esteem. For, as Sirmond says [Note: In the preface to Idatius’s *Chronicle*], not only were the accounts of the affairs of the Goths, Suevi, and other peoples in Spain and Gaul during those times, which are found in Isidore and other writers, composed in almost no other words than those of the *Chronicle*, but many additional matters, both sacred and civil, are taught here—matters which, since all the others who survive leave them untouched, we too would be compelled to ignore if Idatius had not revealed them.

Perhaps no better-known or more celebrated *Chronicle* survives whose manuscript copies are so rare. Floresius testifies [Note: *Sacred Spain*, vol. IV, p. 321.] that even in Spain they are scarcely found, and that almost nothing useful for correcting the text can be obtained from comparing them. The remarkable authority enjoyed by Prosper’s *Chronicle* seems scarcely to have allowed Idatius to be copied more frequently outside Spain.

Nevertheless, several editions exist, both of fragments and of the complete Idatian *Chronicle* [Note: Roesler, cited work, p. 92, and Bahr, *The Christian Poets and Historians of Rome*. Karlsruhe, 1856, octavo.].

Certain excerpts from this *Chronicle*, collected by a Gallic compiler who was a contemporary of Charlemagne, were first published by Heinrich Canisius [Note: *Ancient Readings*, vol. II. Ingolstadt, 1602. Compare the same work, Amsterdam edition, 1725, vol. II, part I, p. 165.]. Joseph Scaliger retained that abridgment in the first edition of his *Eusebian Chronicle* [Note: *Thesaurus temporum*. Geneva, 1609, folio.]. It is also found in volume IV of Andrea Schott’s *Illustrated Spain*, published by his brother Francisco [Note: *Illustrated Spain, or Various Writers on the Affairs and Cities of Spain, Portugal, Ethiopia, and India*. Frankfurt, 1603–1608, four folio volumes.].

After those three publications of the *Chronicle*, which had been badly abridged, the complete *Chronicle* finally appeared under the care of Ludovicus of Saint Lawrence of Córdoba at Rome in 1618, taken, as he says, from a Parisian codex.

Soon afterward a new edition appeared in Paris from the press of Sebastian Cramoisy, in 1619, octavo, through the work of the most learned Jacques Sirmond. He admits that the same manuscript codex from which the Roman editor had worked was not Parisian but genuinely Messine—that is, written at Metz—and that he possessed it as an ancient archetype.

Labbe mentions this manuscript codex [Note: *Bibliography of Manuscript Books*, p. 2.]. Papirius Massonus had another in his possession, copied seven hundred years earlier [Note: *History of the Calamities of Gaul*, p. 98.].

[Col. 0677] The Roman edition was reprinted in the same year or the following year in which it appeared by Prudentius Sandovalius, a Benedictine and bishop of Pamplona.

The Sirmondian edition was repeatedly reprinted, especially first by Sirmond himself [Note: In 1629. Compare Sirmond’s works, Venice, 1729, vol. II, p. 228.], then by André Duchesne [Note: *Writers of the History of France*. Paris, 1636.], by Alexander Morus [Note: Scaliger, *Thesaurus temporum*, new edition, Amsterdam, 1658, folio, p. 17.], by the editors of the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum* [Note: Lyons, 1677, vol. VII, p. 1231, and Galland’s *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. X, p. 323.] and of the *Councils of Spain* [Note: *Maxima Collectio Conciliorum Hispaniae*, vol. II, p. 168.], by Bouquet [Note: *Collection of the Historians of Gaul and France*, vol. I, p. 612.], by Flores [Note: *Sacred Spain*, vol. IV, pp. 239–415.], by Roncalli [Note: *Ancient Latin Writers of Chronicles, Corrected from Manuscript Codices*. Padua, 1787, quarto, part 2.], and by Roesler [Note: Cited work, pp. 84 and 131.].

Through the carelessness of copyists, Idatian chronology was corrupted in many places. Moreover, all the editions derived from a single exemplar and manuscript codex; therefore Idatius’s text could not yet be fully corrected through comparison of manuscript codices [Note: Compare Roncalli, from the preface to the cited work, p. 24.].

No one was more diligent in illustrating Idatius than Flores, who wrote prolegomena and notes in the Spanish language [Note: *Idatius Illustrated with Notes, Corrections, and a More Exact Arrangement than in the Earlier Editions. Two Unpublished Chronicles Added: the Idatian Fasti and Tables of Olympiads, Consulates, and the Years from the Foundation of Rome, Reduced to the Years of Christ. All with New Observations*. Cited work, vol. IV.].

Pagius frequently and extensively used Idatius in his *Criticism of Baronius*, and Petavius likewise used him in his *Doctrine of the Times*. The former often assisted the *Chronicle* through interpretation, correction, and notes. But Pagius, like the other editors of the *Chronicle*, very often went astray, so that Matthaeus Aimerichius rightly observed that Garzon had corrected Pagius in many places and recorded sixty or more errors of Pagius, especially concerning Spanish affairs, in the ninety years of Idatius’s *Chronicle* [Note: *Specimen of Ancient Roman Literature, Lost or Still Hidden*. Ferrara, 178[?], quarto, part I, p. 14.].

Aimerichius ranks our Garzon among the leading chronologists of his age, and gave the following testimony about him and the work that we are printing:

> “The *Chronicle* discovered by Sirmond was illustrated with corrections, notes, and dissertations by my former colleague and friend, the Spaniard Joan Matthaeus Garzon, a most learned chronologist. This posthumous work, which by order of the distinguished J. Santander, recently deceased royal librarian, is preserved in the Royal Library at Madrid, would already have been printed together with our *Natural and Economic History of Catalonia*, with me overseeing the correction of both editions, if Fortune, stubborn in playing an insolent game, had not disrupted the entire undertaking by suddenly raising a storm.”

[Note: For its printing, Peter Navarro, provincial superior of the Society of Jesus in the province of Aragon, had granted permission on 30 September 1763. The royal censors had likewise granted permission.]

For at that time, when that new edition of the Idatian *Chronicle* was to be printed, the Society of Jesus was suppressed in Spain, and its members were punished with an unjust exile.

Joannes Santander bequeathed Garzon’s manuscript codex in his will to Carlos de la Serna Santander, custodian of the Public Library of Brussels. When that distinguished man’s library was offered for sale in Brussels in 1816, Charles Van Hulthem purchased Garzon’s codex on 19 March. It is now preserved in the Royal Library of Brussels under no. 17971 of the manuscript codices.

From this autograph codex I have copied the illustrated *Chronicle of Idatius* that is now being brought to light. Everyone who wishes to compare this newest edition of Idatius with the earlier ones will understand how much labor and study Garzon devoted to preparing this work.

Louvain, 16 May 1845.

P. F. X. DE RAM

[Col. 0677]

## To the Reader

[Col. 0677B] I. Here you have, dear reader, the newly printed *Chronicle of Idatius, Bishop of Aquae Flaviae*, illustrated with almost continuous scholia and shorter notes at the foot of each page, fuller notes appended at the end of the work, and occasional corrections.

After the latest editions of Bouquet and Florius, you will say? Yes indeed—and, I think, not without reason or some expenditure of effort. For the very learned Bouquet offers us not Idatius’ Chronicle, but rather a kind of index or commentary on events that occurred in the time of Idatius, since he removed all the chronological notices by which Idatius arranged his work in annals and substituted others according to his own opinion. The most learned Florius, on the other hand, preserved all the chronological markers found in the printed books; nevertheless, he tore the Abrahamic and Olympian years away from the places where they had been inserted and often added his own years to those assigned by the author to the emperors, in order to restore him to the right path, since he believed that Idatius had strayed from true chronology. Yet readers of Idatius will owe much to both men, because under their guidance they will be able to overcome the stumbling-blocks of the ancient editions; Idatius himself, however, will not owe them so much. For while they profess to extend a helping hand to him, if I may put it so, Bouquet gave him a carriage, as though he were lame in both feet, while Florius supplied him with a staff, as though he limped with only one foot—thereby declaring that his sickness was incurable.

## II

But as I carefully examined this Chronicle and its structure, it appeared to me quite otherwise. For its chronology is not so disordered that, if only we are willing to direct our eyes to its words and our minds to the sequence of the whole work, we cannot find the author proceeding almost always along a straight path. Nor does he need those aids, as though he were unable to walk on his own feet. Rather, whenever the ignorance or carelessness of copyists has caused him to be led away from the even course upon which he proceeds, he himself shows his reader that violence has been done to him and, in a manner, begs that he be rescued from the injury and blemish inflicted upon him.

To make this clear by one or two examples, take, reader, the Chronicle edited by Sirmond. There, between the paragraph beginning “Asturius the man” (under the twenty-sixth year of Theodosius and Placidius Valentinian) [Col. 0678C] and the paragraph beginning “In the second year of the reign of the emperor Marcian,” you will find the chronological numbers altered. What, then? Has Idatius—by now nearly sixty years old, a bishop in rank, and hitherto such a careful writer—suddenly become so careless that he records the death of Theodosius and Placidia one year later than it actually occurred? But let us grant it. Suppose that Idatius did not know that Theodosius and Placidia died in the common era 450, which was the twenty-sixth year of Theodosius and Valentinian, and which in Sirmond’s edition is assigned to the same paragraph, “Asturius.” Could he have failed to know of the Attilian war and that grim battle fought in the Catalaunian Fields in the twenty-seventh year of the same Valentinian, in the common era 451—an event made known throughout the languages and writings of all nations? But if, in the paragraph “The mother of the emperor Valentinian,” Idatius attached the twenty-eighth year of that emperor, he must be said to have placed that battle in the common era 452.

Yet we have no need of conjectures, since in the paragraph “In Gallaecia,” which in Sirmond’s edition follows the twenty-eighth year of Valentinian, Idatius says that the fourth of April fell on a Tuesday.
