But this occurred in the year 450 of the Dionysian era, the twenty-sixth year of Valentinian’s reign, which was marked by solar cycle 11 and dominical letter A. Idatius therefore assigned to the paragraph “In Gallaecia” and to the preceding entries under that twenty-sixth year [Col. 0679B]; and the copyists dealt very badly with him when they placed the two years, 27 and 28 of Valentinian, before that paragraph, although Idatius had plainly placed them after it. More on this in the notes.

## III

A little later, at the paragraph “Of the Romans, XLIII,” Idatius added the following mark, 1, by which he intended to designate Avitus’ first year. The copyists, however, understood the same mark not as the sign of Avitus’ first year alone, but also as an indication of a new Olympian and Abrahamic year. It was as though Idatius himself had not already warned, under the seventeenth year of Theodosius the Great, that the sequence of the Olympiads must not be disturbed or anticipated because of the addition of the fifth year of an emperor’s reign, whenever in one and the same civil or Julian year both the first year of a ruler beginning his reign and the last year of a ruler departing from it were designated. The same must also be understood of the Abrahamic years.

Idatius makes his intention concerning the meaning of that mark exceedingly clear in the same place, since he introduces no change there in the years of Marcian, but retains the very year that he had previously assigned in the paragraph “In the fourth year of the reign.” Likewise, immediately afterward he writes:

> “Gaiseric … enters Rome before Avitus became Augustus,” etc.,

by which words he plainly indicates that he is continuing the narrative of that same year in which Valentinian was killed and Maximus and Avitus were proclaimed. In order to present their successions in one continuous sequence, he reports Gaiseric’s invasion of the city—which occurred between the death of Maximus and the proclamation of Avitus—after that proclamation, expressly warning us of the point: he was also indicating that the invasion belonged to the preceding year and that he was narrating it outside its proper place and time, if by the paragraph “I, Of the Romans, XLIII” he were beginning a new civil year, namely 456.

## IV

A similar error introduced into the Chronicle by the copyists is detected much more clearly in the paragraph “Theodoric in adversity.” A little earlier Idatius had introduced Theodoric, after the death of Rechiarius—who is said to have been killed in the month of December—as he was preparing to plunder the city of Emerita. Meanwhile, when the new year had arrived, he recorded him under the heading “Avitus, third year.” After briefly mentioning the deaths of Avitus and Marcian and the accession of Leo and Majorian to imperial power, he again resumed the narrative of Theodoric’s actions. This is followed by the paragraph “Theodoric in adversity,” to which he attached the mark 1, designating the beginning of the reigns of Leo and Majorian.

But the copyists, reading these passages with excessive carelessness and thinking that a new year was beginning, increased the number of civil years there. Thus they make Theodoric linger at Emerita for nearly sixteen months, although the sequence of Idatius’ narrative clearly demonstrates that he remained in that city scarcely four months.

## V

These are the blemishes, together with some others—but certainly not many—by which Idatius was disfigured by the copyists. It is almost a miracle that so consistent a writer has been preserved in a single manuscript—for no other has yet been found. Since the distinguished men who devoted their efforts to illustrating this Chronicle were able to detect these few blemishes, I do not know why they preferred to introduce their own chronology into it rather than restore the chronology of Idatius.

“But,” they will say, “who would dare to do this against the authority of the manuscript?” Rather, who would not dare, if the author’s intention is certain? Should greater trust be placed in the pens of copyists than in the words of the authors themselves? What kind of scruple is it, I ask, to spare a copyist by refusing assistance to a most worthy author who begs for it and, as though by an applied hand, points out the wound inflicted upon him, so that you may wish to heal it?

I, for my part, have resolved to do the opposite. In this edition I shall correct the passages cited above and several others, restoring the genuine reading of Idatius and removing the reading introduced by the carelessness, ignorance, or audacity of the copyists. Where no manuscript is available, I shall emend on the basis of conjecture and historical probability; such cases will be very few. More often I shall emend from the context of this Chronicle itself; elsewhere from the Fasti of Idatius, from Isidore, from the excerpts printed in volume IV of *Hispania illustrata*, or finally from the *Short Chronicle* and the other chronicle attributed to Severus, which Florius brought to light in volume IV of *Hispania sacra*.

## VI

As I pursue one by one the considerations by which I have judged these emendations capable of being established with the greatest probability, I may perhaps seem to someone excessively, and more diffusely than is reasonable, prolix. But let him note, I ask, that the observations in which the numerical marks are discussed, and the place in which each was inscribed by the author, are essential to the whole matter. For whenever this remains doubtful and contested, Idatius’ work may be called some sort of historical commentary, but it cannot be called a Chronicle.

This, then, was the reason why, whenever a question arose concerning the chronological numbers, I brought forward every argument that seemed to me capable of restoring some genuine light to the true reading. Nor was I reluctant to devote time and effort generously to this purpose. These and other longer annotations, concerning history and the glory of Spain, I have relegated to the end of the Chronicle. Had I inserted them beneath the text of the Chronicle wherever they occur, I would have torn that text apart too much and imposed delays of this kind upon readers who wished to run through Idatius in a rapid reading.

## VII

So that the reader may lose nothing from the ancient editions, if anything has been removed or transposed in this one, I reproduce all of it in the scholia, without omitting even a single letter, and at the same time indicate what has been added, deleted, or changed, and where.

I shall discuss below the eras with which Idatius marked his Chronicle, when I treat his writings in the following dissertation. I have added the Christian era to the others that he himself uses because, being in common use among everyone, it will be more convenient and easier both for me and for the reader. Also, for the sake of brevity, whenever I use this era, and likewise whenever I cite passages from other writers, I often employ Arabic numerals, as they are commonly called. For I write 450 more quickly than “the twenty-sixth year of Theodosius and Valentinian III” 8, and likewise 389 more quickly than CCCLXXXIX.

## VIII

Finally, if you find here anything that Bouquet had previously occupied, know that I have never seen him, nor is it possible for me to see him in the little nest in which I now live. What I said above about him I learned from Father Florius. Nor do I know whether I shall omit anything, even if I obtain his work before I bring this one to light. I gathered this material from the public forest, and it owes nothing to Bouquet.

# Preliminary Dissertation on the Life and Writings of Idatius

## § I. The Homeland of Idatius

### 1

Idatius, as he himself testifies concerning himself, was born in the city of Lemica in the province of Gallaecia. We cannot determine whether Idatius wrote *Lemica* or *Limica*. Between the Gallaecian rivers Durius and Minius there is another river, called *Limia* by Pliny (*Book IV, chapter 20*) and Mela (*Book III, chapter 1*), *Limius* by Ptolemy (*Table II of Europe*), and finally *Limaea* by Strabo (*Book III*). All these writers use the third vowel, *i*, not the second, *e*. Moreover, among the ten cities listed in the inscription that can still be seen at Aquae Flaviae—commonly called Chaves—on the bridge over the river Tamega, and which Gruter and others reproduce, the Limici are counted in seventh place.

The date at which that inscription was set up is revealed by the inscription itself. Here is its beginning:

> IMP. CAES. VESP. AUG. PON. MAX. TRIB. POT. X IMP. XX P. P. COS. IX IMP. VESP. CAES. AUG. FIL. PON. TRIB. POT. VIII IMP. XII. COS. VII.

“Imperator Caesar Vespasian Augustus, chief pontiff, in the tenth year of tribunician power, acclaimed emperor twenty times, father of his country, consul nine times; Imperator Vespasian Caesar Augustus, son, chief pontiff, in the eighth year of tribunician power, acclaimed emperor twelve times, consul seven times.”

These are precisely the words presented to his readers by Panvinius (*Book II, On the Fasti*, year 832 from the foundation of the City), except that in his text Titus’ seventh consulship is inscribed 10, whereas here it is sixth. Nevertheless, the Fasti of Idatius agree with this reading, as do the Greek text and the Cuspinianus manuscript, which, according to Panvinius himself, assign Titus’ seventh consulship to the following year of the City, 833.

### 2

But this is not relevant to our present purpose. I have mentioned all these matters solely to make it clear that, at least before the time of Idatius, the adjective *Limicus*, derived from *Limia* with the third vowel, was more probably pronounced and written in common usage than *Lemicus*, with the second vowel. Even today that river is called the Lima, and the neighboring region is called Limia.

Therefore, the fact that *Lemica* is now read in Idatius may have arisen from a copyist’s error. What if this was also the source from which many writers made Idatius a bishop of Lamecum? Further, if *Limica* were read in Idatius, Sigebert would have called him the bishop of Limica, not of Lemica. Other writers, finding *Forum Limicorum* in Ptolemy and *Limici* on the Aquae Flaviae inscription, would either have called the bishop *Limicensis*, along with Sigebert, or at least would not have invented an episcopate of Lamecum, which they attribute to Idatius through the same error by which Sigebert called him *Lemicensis*. That error, however, took hold of many minds and sank deeply into them, not without some appearance of truth. For the bishopric of Lamacum still exists on the coast near old Gallaecia, close to the river Durius. But Lemica appears nowhere, neither among the ancient geographers nor in ecclesiastical monuments.

In any event, it was the opinion of Nicolás Antonio that the city of Lemica or Limica, where Idatius says he was born, stood at the place where there is now the village commonly called Puente de Lima. Certainly, the *Itinerary of Antoninus* places Limia nineteen miles from Bracara toward Tude, and, if we trust Zurita, it refers to a river, not a town. But there is nothing to prevent us from saying that both a city and a river called Limia existed there, just as on the opposite coast of Spain Sucro was both a river and a town, according to Pliny (*Book III, chapter 3*), who likewise mentions the town and river Aerninium in neighboring Lusitania (*Book IV, chapter 19*).

## § II. The Birth of Idatius, His Pilgrimage to Palestine, and His Return from There to Spain

### 3

In what year Idatius was born is also uncertain; but if conjecture is permitted, I shall cautiously place his birth around the year 393. A very learned man, who deserved great credit for his work on Idatius, believed that Idatius was born around the year 390 and returned to his family in the year 400 after completing his pilgrimage to Palestine.

But concerning Idatius’ return from the East, that great man was deceived in the ordinary course of human error, as the *Acts of Saint Porphyry, Bishop of Gaza*, preserved by Surius and Bollandus under 26 February, clearly demonstrate. For there, in chapter 8, we read that John, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, arrived at Majuma from Constantinople in the year 401, on the fifteenth day after Easter, and departed from there for Caesarea three days later—obviously healthy and vigorous, since he had entrusted himself in midwinter to the sea and to a sufficiently difficult voyage.

Since Easter that year was celebrated by the Greeks on 14 April, John was still alive on 2 May of the same year. But when Idatius was traveling through Palestine, Eulogius governed the Church of Caesarea after John’s death. Read Idatius himself under the twelfth year of Honorius, A.D. 406, and again under the thirteenth year of that same Honorius, the common era 407. There he testifies that, when he was still an infant and orphan, he saw this same Eulogius already bishop of Caesarea. Nor, if I say that Idatius remembered John of Jerusalem, Eulogius of Caesarea, and the others under the year 407 because it was in that very year that he saw them in Palestine, do I fear that anyone will accuse me of error.

### 4

The same distinguished man further believed that, when Idatius wrote under the eleventh year of Theodosius and Placidius Valentinian, the common era 435:

> “At that time Saint John, Jerome, and the others whom we mentioned above died …”

Idatius was speaking of those whom he had praised in the year 406. Since Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, had been mentioned among them, he believed that Idatius did not know when Epiphanius had died, because Idatius had returned to Spain from his Syrian pilgrimage before 12 May in the year 401, on which date some say that Epiphanius died.

But first, it is much more probable that under the year 435 Idatius was speaking of those whom he had remembered in the year 407, among whom Epiphanius does not appear. Furthermore, it could not have happened that Idatius saw Eulogius as bishop in the Church of Caesarea and that he himself departed from Palestine before Epiphanius’ death—if Epiphanius died in 401—unless John, Eulogius’ predecessor, ceased to live immediately after his journey from Constantinople; Eulogius was immediately appointed in John’s place; Idatius had already sailed to Palestine; and he departed from that province without any delay. No one can persuade himself that all these events occurred within one incomplete month, without records or witnesses.

### 5

But even if Epiphanius died in 402 or 403, as Baronius (*Annals, 402, no. 25*), Pagius (*Annals, 402, no. 7*), Papebrochius (*Life, no. 42*), and Valesius (*Notes on Socrates, Book VI, chapter 14*) debate, it does not therefore follow that Idatius was unaware of his death because he had returned from the East to Spain before it happened.

For it could have happened that, although the name of Epiphanius had been famous in Syria, and especially in Palestine, while he was alive, Idatius heard nothing of his death during the whole time he was there, because he arrived in Palestine in the third or fourth year after Epiphanius’ death—that is, in 406 or 407—when all discussion of Epiphanius had fallen silent.

Since, according to our opinion, Idatius was then in his thirteenth year, he could truly have called himself an infant and orphan. Jerome often says that he withdrew into the desert as an adolescent, and in one place even as almost a boy, although everyone agrees that he was then a young man or even a mature man. Cornelius Nepos likewise calls Marcus Brutus an adolescent in the *Life of Atticus*, chapter 8, after the time when Caesar had been killed by Brutus and his associates in the senate; and in chapter 2 he calls Atticus himself an adolescent when he was already in his twenty-third year. Thus such expressions will often mislead us if they are reduced to the conventional limits commonly assigned to infancy, boyhood, and adolescence.

When Idatius brought his Chronicle to an end, he was not unjustified in writing in the prologue that he was passing through the final course of his life; for he was then almost eighty years old, as we shall see below.

## § III. Idatius Devotes Himself to God, Becomes a Bishop, and the Rest of His Life until His Death

### 6

Having returned from Syria before the year 412, in which Theophilus of Alexandria died—for when Idatius departed from there, he left Theophilus alive, as is shown by what he writes under the eleventh year of Placidius Valentinian—he devoted himself to God as a cleric, monk, or religious, having previously professed such a way of life, in the year 417 or 418 of the common era.

This, and nothing else, is signified by the words that appear in the *Short Chronicle*—as its editor Florius chose to call it—after the marriage of Constantius and Placidia, and before the death of Wallia:

> “The conversion of Idatius the sinner to the Lord.”

Salvian, a writer of that period, uses the same expression in *Book IV of On the Government of God*:

> “If one of the nobles,” he says, “has begun to be converted to God.”

Immediately explaining what he means by “conversion,” he adds:

> “If anyone has tried to become better”;  
> “if some person of higher rank has attached himself to religion.”

Ausonius speaks similarly of Paulinus (*Letter 25*):

> “You have changed your ways, dearest Paulinus.”

Idatius himself likewise writes below, under the thirtieth year of Honorius:

> “Paulinus, most noble and most eloquent, made still nobler long ago by his conversion to God.”

Anyone wishing to learn more about this matter should consult the same Paulinus (*Letter 39, To a Soldier*) and Sidonius (*Book IV, Letter 24*).

### 7

Then, in the third year of Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian, the common era 427, he was appointed bishop of Aquae Flaviae. Philip Labbe, the distinguished Jesuit writer, was the first to notice this when he published the complete Fasti of Idatius; most recently, the very learned Florius has confirmed it with many arguments.

That the city was worthy of a bishopric is demonstrated by an inscription in Gruter (*p. 23, no. 10*), in which it is honored with the title of colony. As I indicated above, Sigebert made Idatius bishop of Lemica, and several made him bishop of Lamecum; worst of all, Paschasius Quesnellus made him bishop of Lucus. Adding further errors to these, Quesnellus asserts that Idatius was a metropolitan, and says that Idatius himself indicates this when, in the prologue to the Chronicle, he writes that he was appointed “to the highest office of bishop.”

But Lucus Augusti was not honored with metropolitan status until many years later. Moreover, the highest office of the episcopate designates not only metropolitans but also any bishop, if the matter concerns the power of ordination, as theologians and interpreters of ecclesiastical law express it.

An ancient writer [Note: *Life of Saint Castrensis*, chapter 1, in Bollandus, 1 February] says that the African bishops Castrensis, Romus, Priscus, and Tammarus, although not metropolitans, were endowed with the honor of the highest priesthood. Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, speaking of himself in a sermon on the day of his ordination and concerning his episcopate, says:

> “I have received the office of the highest priesthood.”

But if we are speaking of jurisdictional power, even metropolitans do not enjoy the highest priestly office, since they have patriarchs, primates, and the supreme pontiff above them.

These points had to be noted because we are dealing with an implacable enemy of the Church and of its supreme head.

### 8

Idatius lived in the episcopate for at least forty-two years, since he continued his Chronicle to the year 469. Indeed, we read in it certain things that could not have been written by Idatius before the year 472, as I shall show below (no. 34). Nevertheless, he must have died before the year 474 if he died under the emperor Leo Augustus, as Saint Isidore relates (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9); Isidore deserves more credence in this than Sigebert, who asserts that Idatius lived as far as the year 490. Leo, however, ended his life in January of the year 474. Therefore, it can scarcely be doubted that Idatius lived for nearly eighty years.

### 9

From the time when he became bishop, he was exercised by the greatest labors and immense sufferings in the school of Christian endurance. For continual savage wars, together with the fires, plunder, captivity, and slaughter that accompanied them, devastated unhappy Gallaecia.

These, however, were injuries to bodies and possessions. The anguish of his soul tormented the holy bishop much more sharply, when he saw his flock dragged and scattered here and there and, as wolves attacked—that is, the heretics, the Priscillianists and Arians—torn apart with the utmost savagery.

Meanwhile he was dear and venerable to rulers and peoples alike. Thus, when he undertook an embassy on behalf of his fellow Gallaecians to Aetius, Aetius, overcome by his prayers, soon induced the Suevic king Hermeric to enter into peace with the Gallaecians. Idatius, however, without mentioning his own name, asserts that this peace was obtained through episcopal intervention.

The reader will understand this and much else better from the Chronicle itself. Nevertheless, I cannot pass over in silence the words of Saint Leo the Great, which strongly commend our Idatius. For when that most vigilant pontiff was discussing the convocation of a general council from all the provinces of Spain in order to confront the fury of the Priscillianists, he wrote the following, among other things, to Turibius of Astorga:

> “But if anything—which God forbid—should prevent a general council from being held, let the priests of Gallaecia at least meet together in one place. When they have assembled, our brothers Idatius and Ceponius will attend to the matter, together with your united urgency, so that a remedy may more quickly be brought to such great wounds, even through a provincial assembly” (*Letter 93, end*).

Saint Leo seems to have named Idatius and Ceponius in particular on the recommendation of Turibius. Turibius himself also wrote to them concerning the sect of the Priscillianists; you will find his letters in Morales (*Book XI, chapter 26*).

## § IV. The Writings of Idatius

### 10

Two writings are attributed to Idatius: namely, the Chronicle and the Consular Fasti. The Chronicle is accepted as his by the consensus of all periods and learned men; but ancient writers are entirely silent about the Fasti, while later writers either doubt their authenticity or even deny it without hesitation. I shall soon demonstrate, in section 11, that these Fasti are a genuine work of Idatius, by arguments which, if I am not mistaken, are irresistible.

The *Short Chronicle*, published a few years ago, is a patchwork cut out of the complete Chronicle by an unskilled hand and badly stitched together. The *Book Against Priscillian*, which Trithemius reports as having been written by our Idatius, belongs to another Idatius—or rather to Itarius—who, according to Saint Isidore (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 15), lived many years before our Idatius, bishop of Aquae Flaviae.

After writing these things, a dissertation on the history of the Priscillianists by the learned Francis Girvesius came into my hands. There he shows that he believes our Idatius to be no different from the author whose work against Varimadus of Ansa appears in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* (volume V). But since our Idatius did not leave Gallaecia until extreme old age, in the year 471 or 472, as is clear from the Chronicle, and died one or two years later, it follows that Idatius could not possibly have written the words found at the beginning of that work against Varimadus:

> “Long ago, established in the city of Naples in Campania, …”

## § V. The Eras Inscribed in the Chronicle, Beginning with the Spanish Era

### 11

To begin with the Chronicle, there is no reason for me to exaggerate its usefulness, which the distinguished Sirmond and Florius have commended. Concerning the chronological marks with which Idatius distinguished this work, I shall say openly and frankly that nowhere in the Chronicle did he use the era of Spain.

Why? Idatius undertook to continue the Chronicle from Eusebius and Jerome, who had marked it with the years of the Olympiads, of Abraham, and of the rulers. Would he therefore have added a new era, unknown to foreign peoples, without saying anything about it or warning his readers? Would he have remained entirely silent throughout the Chronicle concerning the addition of this new era?

Moreover, Idatius undertook to continue this Chronicle in such a way that he joined its three parts into a single volume, as though it were one work and the labor of a single author, and published it in that combined form. Labbe testifies to this, asserting that in the manuscript of the Jesuit college in Paris he found the Chronicle of Eusebius, together with the additions of Jerome and Idatius, in one continuous volume.

But the strongest authority is Idatius himself: first, in the prologue, where he writes:

> “Since, as the preceding reading shows, the account of the years has flowed down to the course of our own time”—

for by the words “the preceding reading,” Idatius indicated the Chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome that had been placed before him in the same volume.

Second, in the Chronicle under the thirteenth year of Honorius, where we read:

> “After the Arians mentioned above, who were bishops of Jerusalem before John, …”

Ask, reader, from the beginning of Idatius’ continuation where he mentioned these Arian bishops. You will find them nowhere. You will find them, however, in Jerome’s additions, under the first year of the 283rd Olympiad.

Who, then, does not see that Idatius could not have spoken in this way unless he had joined his own book to Jerome’s Chronicle as a kind of appendix in a single volume? But if he joined them, is it credible that he distinguished his continuation from the rest of the body by the mark of a new era, without first warning the reader?

### 12

“But,” you will say, “we find the Spanish era once and again, not merely in the margin of the book but within Idatius’ own words.” I know this well; but even so I cannot persuade myself with certainty that the two instances of that era inserted into the Chronicle—one under the fifteenth year of Honorius and the other under the sixth year of Leo—come from Idatius’ hand.

In both places, the era may first have been assigned to the book by one copyist and then transcribed by another into the body of Idatius’ work. Furthermore, in the manuscript Fasti, under the consuls Augustus II and Paulus—read Tullus—there appears the following, according to the testimony of the most learned Labbe:

> “Under these consuls, the first era. The course of the moon was discovered.”

But the anonymous Cuspinianus, under the consulship of Lucius Antonius and Iauricus, into which the first year of the Spanish era perhaps fell, reads *luna prima* (“the first moon”) instead of *aera prima* (“the first era”).

This variation demonstrates how much liberty copyists allowed themselves when transcribing ancient monuments: one wrote *aera prima*, the other *luna prima*. The former, when copying Idatius, assigned the first era to the year before Christ 33, which Idatius did not do.

Therefore, just as in the Fasti the blemish *aera prima* was distorted by a copyist, I believe the same thing happened in the two passages of the Chronicle that are brought against us. Finally, the distribution of the eras that we observe in the Chronicle, and especially in the Fasti, seems highly suspicious to me because it is excessively exact, as I shall explain below.

### 13

For my part, I would not merely willingly, but most gladly, join hands with those who believe that Idatius distinguished his Chronicle by the chronological mark of the Spanish era, especially because it is sufficiently certain that this era was in some public use around the sixth year of Leo, the common era 462, when the Chronicle displays the era 500.

For in Ambrosius Morales, a careful man of exceptional integrity (*Book XI, chapter 31*), we read the following inscription, approved by everyone:

> **ALEXANDRIA, A MOST ILLUSTRIOUS WOMAN, LIVED ABOUT TWENTY-FIVE YEARS. SHE DEPARTED IN PEACE ON THE TENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JANUARY, ERA DII. PROBUS, HER SON, LIVED TWO YEARS AND ONE MONTH.**

Nevertheless, the arguments set out above, together with the example of Saint Isidore and John of Biclaro—who never use this epoch of the Spanish era in their Chronicles arranged by the years of rulers, except perhaps once at the end of Isidore—compel me to disagree with those men.

This is especially true of the era-numbers appended to the individual years of the Chronicle. As for the two other instances mentioned above and rejected below the text of the Chronicle, there is no reason for us to oppose so persistently the possibility that Idatius himself inscribed them in those places.

## § VI. The Era of Abraham

### 14

The remaining chronological markers—namely, the years of Abraham, the emperors, and the Olympiads—certainly come from Idatius. That the writers of Latin, Jerome and Idatius, began the years of Abraham in January is indicated by the fact that, from the beginning of the Chronicle, the marks of those years are continuously written alongside the years of the rulers, unlike the Olympiads. It can scarcely be doubted that the years of the rulers flow from beginning to end together with the Julian years.

But if anyone is uncertain about this, let him read the Chronicle almost at its threshold, under the fourth and fifth years of Theodosius the Great. He will find that Idatius records the peace between the Romans and the Goths under the fourth year, while in the Fasti Idatius himself says that it was completed on the fifth day before the Nones of October; Pagius agrees with him (*Critique, year 481, no. 2*).

From that day to the seventeenth—or, granting Pagius this point so that we do not dispute over nothing, the fourteenth—day before the Kalends of the following February, under which he assigns the inauguration of Arcadius, the Fasti pass over to the fifth year. Therefore, I think no one can deny that Idatius began the Abrahamic and imperial years in January.

The same can also be observed under the fourth year of Majorian and Leo. There Idatius proceeds from February to November, ten consecutive months, under the mark of one and the same year. If he took October as the beginning of the years, as Pagius constantly insists, he would have designated a new year when he reached the paragraph “Idatius, who above,” or even earlier. But this will recur more often in the notes.

### 15

Now let us speak of Jerome. Under the twentieth year of Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, he writes:

> “Julian, the brother of Gallus, is proclaimed Caesar at Milan on the eighth day before the Ides of November.”

Immediately assigning the twenty-first year of that same Constantius, he says:

> “The remains of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople.”

Idatius testifies in the Fasti that this occurred on the Kalends of June. No one places this translation later except Theodorus Lector (*Book II of the Collection*), who nevertheless assigns it to the twenty-fourth day 22 of the same month of June.

Jerome, therefore, proceeding from November to the following June, began a new year. In what month, then, except January? Certainly he did not wait for autumn.

It is also perfectly clear that Eusebius, in the Latin Chronicle, began the years of rulers in January. For under the seventh year of Constantine the Great he attaches the death of Diocletian. Whether correctly or incorrectly—which Pagius debates (*Critique, year 316, no. 3*)—is irrelevant at present: he does attach it there. Idatius records in the Fasti that this death occurred on the third day before the Nones of December.

Then, when Eusebius is about to relate the proclamation of the three Caesars—Crispus, Licinius, and Constantine—which, according to Idatius, took place on the immediately following Kalends of March, he assigns the eighth year of that same Constantine the Great. Between December and March we count only two months, January and February. I do not think that Eusebius tied the beginning of Constantine’s eighth year to February.

Many further points could confirm this; but I think the foregoing will suffice for Petavius, who writes concerning Eusebius that it is merely probable and plausible (*Ration.* II, I, 10) that he began the years in autumn, like the Syrians.

### 16

Nevertheless, I must deal with the very learned Pagius at some length, because he asserts this more frequently and emphatically, and not only of Eusebius but also of Jerome and Idatius in his *Critique*. From this opinion of his he prescribes a method which he calls certain and easy for determining the reckoning of the Eusebian, Hieronymian, and Idatian years—not only for recognizing the errors of Eusebius, Jerome, and Idatius, but also those of all who cite them incorrectly (*Dissertation on the Greco-Roman Periods*, no. 79).

Thus, imbued with this opinion, and judging that he had to describe a large part of Idatius in his *Critique*—because the eminent Baronius had not seen Idatius and therefore had not included him in his *Annals*—he frequently corrects, censures, and interprets him unfavorably. Since I must often refute him, I have now decided to take up again, at greater length, this question concerning the beginning of the Idatian years and to settle it by clear arguments, so that no one may later think that I oppose this most learned man out of a desire to contradict him, rather than from the dutiful wish to defend Idatius.

17. Since in the Chronicon, as we have it from Jerome, we see the years of Abraham entered opposite the years of the emperors, without being placed even a finger’s breadth earlier or later, who would allow himself to be persuaded by Pagius that the Latin Eusebius (not to mention the Greek autograph), Jerome, and Idatius began Abraham’s years in October, but those of the emperors in January, as has been demonstrated [Col. 0688D]? This is especially implausible since it is clear that they marked the Olympiadic years—which they assigned a different beginning from that of the emperors—in another place either earlier or later.

Moreover, Idatius is so opposed to multiplying the beginnings of years within the epochs he uses that, whenever emperors assume power after January and after the year already current in the Chronicon, he either does not add a new indication of the accession, or, if he does add one, suppresses it at the first opportunity; for when the following January comes around, even if the first year of the reign has not been completed, he designates the second. Examples of both practices may be found in Placidius Valentinian, Avitus, Majorian, and Leo.

This was surely a prudent policy, by which he wished to prevent new obscurities from being cast over chronology, a subject already sufficiently complicated in itself, through which the reader might be led into error. I shall not go far afield, nor depart from the path I ought to follow, when I show that this interpretation of the Eusebian, Hieronymian, and Idatian years as beginning in October or autumn (apart from the fact that it is false) would become the cause of six hundred errors, not merely for beginners but even for chronologists who are not unlearned.

18. Furthermore, the same most learned Pagius, when discussing this matter, spoke in a way that displays some appearance of error and contradiction. For, after adducing the testimony of Eusebius, who writes as follows (Dissert. de period. Graeco-romana, no. 78): “All the years of Abraham up to the Nativity of Christ amount to 2,015 years, including, of course, in this number the first year of Christ,” he adds: “It is certain that in Julian year 43 Eusebius began the first year of the Incarnation.” And lest anyone interpret this to mean that Eusebius attached Christ’s birth to that year of Abraham which began in the autumn of Julian year 43, he immediately adds: “Eusebius derives the beginning of the Incarnation from Julian year 43.”

The beginning of the Incarnation—taking “Incarnation” as equivalent to “Nativity”—means, in our present way of speaking, the first day on which Christ was born, or a day very near to it; everyone will admit this, just as everyone knows that Julian years begin from the Kalends of January. Since, therefore, Eusebius, following the Greeks, attached Christ’s Nativity to 6 January of the same Abrahamic year 2015, could Pagius, without an appearance of error and contradiction, write that Eusebius derived the beginning of the Incarnation from Julian year 43? [Col. 0689C]

For that 6 January to which Eusebius assigned Christ’s Nativity was likewise the sixth day of Julian year 44, since that year began on the first day of that same January. Thus, even if Eusebius had begun the year to which he attached the Incarnation in October of Julian year 43, it could not on that account be said that he assigned Christ’s Nativity to one of the three preceding months of that same year—October, November, or December—or to the consulship of Lentulus and Messalla, since that consulship and those three months had already ended by 6 January of the following year. In the same way, Eusebius cannot be charged with assigning Christ’s Nativity to Julian year 43, since that year, no less than those three months of the consulship of Lentulus and Messalla, had entirely elapsed by that sixth day.

[Col. 0689D] 19. I certainly do not see why Pagius, who in the apparatus to the Annales, no. 146, under the heading “Julian year 43,” expressly admits that Eusebius believed Christ was born on 6 January of the following year—which he himself, in the same place, no. 153, counts as Julian year 43, should, in the Critica (on year 14, no. 6), correct Petavius for writing that Eusebius assigned Christ’s Nativity to that same Julian year 44.

Could Eusebius, merely because Pagius believes that the years with which Eusebius marked his Chronicon began in autumn, tear the Julian years—which he never uses—from their own boundaries and thereby make it impossible for year 44 to have begun on the Kalends of that January whose sixth day he associated with Christ’s Nativity?

Petavius had observed (Ration. part II, book I, chapter 10), before Pagius, that it was probable that the Eusebian years began in autumn. Nevertheless, because the greater part of the Eusebian years coincides with the following Julian years, he recommends that, in ordinary usage, Abrahamic year 2015, for example, be compared with Julian year 44, with which it overlaps for nine months, rather than with year 43, with which the aforementioned Abrahamic year 2015 shares only three months.

Petavius was entirely right in this. For what confusion and disorder, I ask, would it introduce into chronology if, while connecting the first year of Christ with Abrahamic year 2015 from 6 January, one separated it from Julian year 44, which had begun six days earlier? Or if, while asserting that Christ was born in the thirteenth consulship of Augustus, one denied that he was born in that same Julian year 44 and criticized those who affirm this? Did that consulship and Julian year 44 not begin on the same day?

But I pity human weakness when I see that Pagius himself elsewhere proves precisely what he here censures in Petavius and teaches that Petavius’s rule should be followed (Prologue to the dissertation on the Hypotheses, no. 15). For, discussing the second year of the reign of Gaius Caligula, he writes:

“The second year of Caligula’s reign is rather Christ’s year 38 than 39, since Christ’s year 38 corresponds to nine months of that second year of the reign, whereas year 39 corresponds to only three, and those incomplete.”

20. Pagius then increases the obscurity by saying: “In the Dionysian era the first year of Christ begins on the Kalends of January of Julian year 46. For Julian year 43 is three years distant from 46; and whoever assigns Christ’s Nativity to Julian year 44 is considered to place it three years earlier than one who assigns it to year 46” (Dissert. de period. Graeco-romana, no. 79).

Since Pagius had said that Eusebius attached Christ’s Nativity to Julian year 43, but Dionysius to year 46, no one could hear him without convincing himself that the Eusebian Nativity of Christ preceded the Dionysian by three years. Indeed, these words of Pagius misled a very learned man, who believed what I have just stated and explained it as follows:

“Eusebius attached the first year of Christ to Julian year 43, and Dionysius to year 46, as Pagius says in the dissertation on the Graeco-Roman period, nos. 78 and 79. Consequently, whoever wishes to derive Christ’s years from Abraham’s years, according to the way we count them, must differ by three units, etc.”

The distinguished man was deceived when reading Pagius and derived from him the conclusion that the Eusebian Nativity of Christ preceded the Dionysian by three years. Nor did the error stop there. The blemish was subsequently carried into the new edition of the Chronicon which that same learned man had prepared. For he did not notice that Jerome could not have brought his Chronicon to an end in Abrahamic year 2395, but ended it in year 2394. See below, no. 26 and following.

What is more astonishing is that Pagius, who led Florius into this error, did not himself fall into it. For he shows that he believed Idatius’s Chronicon began in Abrahamic year 2395, since he assigns year 2400 to the sixth year after its beginning.

21. “But,” you will say, “in that same place Pagius expressly taught the opposite; for he stated in so many words: ‘It is established that Eusebius begins the years of the Incarnation three years before the Dionysian era.’”

I hear you. Yet, distracted by the difference between the Eusebian and Julian years, he so obscures his own writing that he appears to speak contradictorily, and the reader I just mentioned—neither unlearned nor careless, and one who disagreed with Pagius about the beginning of the Idatian years, which he believed flowed from January rather than October—fell into error because of him.

Therefore, to avoid these difficulties, Jerome—for Pagius himself wrote elsewhere most truthfully, “The multiplication of periods is burdensome to memory and mind” (ibid.)—although he found the Abrahamic years in Eusebius’s Chronicon reckoned from autumn (a question that need not be investigated here), began those years, and the imperial years as well, from January together with the Julian and Roman civil years, for which he was producing that Chronicon in Latin and to which the Syrian method of reckoning years was unknown. He did this so that the minds of his readers would not be overwhelmed by a triple period: one of Abraham, another of the Olympiad, and a third of the emperors, each of which began its years in a different month.

Moreover, Jerome himself expressly acknowledged in the preface how much freedom he had allowed himself in translating Eusebius’s Chronicon, when he said that he had performed partly the office of translator and partly that of author. I consider it so certain that Idatius imitated Jerome that I do not think he had even read the Greek Chronicon as it had been issued by Eusebius.

§ VII. On the Olympiadic Years

22. These years must be treated differently from the Abrahamic and imperial years. It must be asserted without hesitation that Eusebius, Jerome, and Idatius attached the beginning of the Olympiads to the summer season, and left this attested by the placement and marking of the Olympiads themselves.

Accordingly, the latest edition of Idatius was wrong to set the Olympiadic years on an equal footing with the Abrahamic and imperial years, as though the former, like the latter, were to be counted from January. In the Chronicon the years of these epochs should certainly not have been connected in that way; rather, the Olympiadic years ought to begin and end approximately six months later than the beginnings and endings of the others.

Idatius teaches us this most clearly when, in the Sirmondian edition—which was transcribed from the one surviving manuscript—he entered Olympiad 290 not opposite Theodosius’s second year, but below it, approximately midway between the second and third years, at the section “Alexandria.” [Col. 0691D] He preserves this arrangement throughout the rest of the Chronicon whenever it has not been corrupted by the carelessness of copyists.

In this he followed Eusebius and Jerome, who preceded him in the same practice. Eusebius entered Olympiads 268 and 272 between Diocletian’s seventh and eighth years and between Constantine’s first and second years, equally distant from the intervals on either side. Jerome likewise entered Olympiads 218 and 289 between Constantine’s twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth years and between Valens’s eleventh and twelfth years.

There are many such examples scattered throughout the Chronicon printed at Venice in 1483 and Basel in 1529. I have chosen to cite only those that leave no room for quibbling.

23. The reader should not be surprised that I have said that, in Eusebius and Idatius, the Abrahamic years began from January, whereas the Olympiadic years did not. Apart from the fact that the examples cited above establish this, a year beginning in autumn, of the kind Pagius proposes, was, as has been said, in use among the Syrians alone and known only to them. But an Olympiadic year beginning in summer and ending in the summer of the following year was well known to all peoples throughout the Roman Empire and was reckoned by everyone according to one and the same method.

Therefore, the danger of error would be equal for readers if an Olympiadic year were inserted into the Chronicon running parallel with a Julian year, as it would be if an Abrahamic year were introduced alongside the Syrian civil year. But these points ought to be clear to everyone. I nevertheless did not wish to pass over them in silence [Col. 0692B] on account of Pagius and Florius: the former teaches that the Olympiadic years in our Chronicon must be counted from October, the latter from January, although Idatius most certainly began them from the month of July.

§ VIII. In Which Abrahamic Year Did Idatius Begin the Chronicon?

24. Since what has been said thus far about the beginning of the Olympiadic year, and about its use among both Greeks and Latins, is known to everyone, I shall cite only Censorinus’s testimony—not to confirm an uncertain matter, but to proceed from it to an investigation of the first and last year of the Idatian continuation.

Censorinus says:

“This year, of which the consulship of Ulpius and Pontianus is, as it were, the index and title, is the 1,014th from the first Olympiad, counted only from the summer days on which the Olympic contest is celebrated. From the founding of Rome, it is the 991st, and indeed from the Parilia, from which the years of the City are reckoned. Of those years which bear the name Julian, it is the 283rd, but counted from the Kalends of January.”

This is Censorinus. From it it is plainly established that Jerome and Idatius must have assigned the beginning of the Olympiadic years to the days of summer, lest they introduce into the Chronicon a new and unusual method of reckoning them.

From this I also think it can be demonstrated that Jerome withdrew his hand from the Chronicon in Abrahamic year 2394, in the third year of Olympiad 289, while the sixth month of that Olympiad was coming to an end, and in Christ’s year 380 according to Eusebius. Therefore Idatius, who applied his pen to the same Chronicon in the following year in order to continue it, ought at the entrance to his work to have entered Abrahamic year 2395, likewise the third year of the aforementioned Olympiad, and, if he used this epoch according to Eusebius’s view, Christ’s year 381.

25. Accordingly, almost everyone nowadays considers the year designated by Censorinus with so many chronological markers to be the same as the year 238 of the common era. From that year to the end of Jerome’s Chronicon, 140 years are counted, since it ended in the consulship of Valens VI and Valentinian the Younger II, which opened the year 378 of the Dionysian era.

Yet Jerome must have counted 380 years in this year—that is, two more years than Dionysius—by as many as the beginning of the Eusebian era of Christ precedes the Dionysian. Whoever, therefore, has trusted the ancient copies of Jerome’s Chronicon in which the year at which Jerome ends is designated as Christ’s year 381 is seriously mistaken.

For, since the epochs in question contain the same number of days, with neither one containing more years than another nor fewer within the same span of time, if the common era counts 378 years from its first year to the sixth consulship of Valens, the Eusebian era must necessarily count the same number, not more. If you find 381 years in Jerome’s Chronicon, know that this could not have occurred without the interpolation of one additional year.

Again, if Jerome asserts that 351 years elapsed from Tiberius’s fifteenth year and Christ’s thirtieth to the fourteenth year and death of Valens (Preface to the Chronicon, Basel edition, 1529), then either in this total he includes Tiberius’s fifteenth year and Christ’s thirtieth, or that passage too has been corrupted through the negligence of copyists. Idatius certainly counts only 350 years, as I shall immediately demonstrate.

The argument just derived from so many chronological markers and fixed positions proves that the total of 381 years from the Eusebian Nativity of Christ to Valens’s death and sixth consulship is manifestly false, and likewise that the final total of 351 years from Tiberius’s fifteenth year and Christ’s thirtieth to Valens’s death is false—unless Tiberius’s fifteenth year and Christ’s thirtieth are included in that same total.

26. Once it has been demonstrated that Jerome ended the Chronicon in Eusebian year 380 of Christ’s Nativity, there is no reason why the learned Florius should deny that he completed it in Abrahamic year 2394.

Censorinus supplies a new argument for establishing this very point when he says that the consulship of Ulpius and Pontianus fell in Julian year 283. If from this you subtract the 43 years that had elapsed before the Eusebian Nativity of Christ, you obtain 240. Add to this the 140 years that you will extract from the Fasti, from that consulship to the sixth consulship of Valens, and the total is 380 years. Finally, if you add the 2,014 Abrahamic years that Eusebius had counted before the Nativity of Christ, the total becomes 2,394 years.

Jerome therefore completed the Chronicon in this Abrahamic year, and left it to Idatius for continuation in the following year, 2395.

27. What misled Florius into believing that Jerome had carried the Chronicon through Abrahamic year 2395 were both the printed books, which display this number at the end of the Hieronymian continuation, and Pagius, whose words, because of the man’s great authority, he accepted without examination.

Pagius expressly pronounces the following concerning the Abrahamic years:

“The epoch from Abraham’s birth, which Eusebius, Jerome, and Idatius use in their Chronica, begins in year 3477 of the Graeco-Roman period, and indeed on the first day of October” (Dissert. de period. Graeco-romana, no. 78).

Therefore, if Pagius had disregarded the three months of that year—October, November, and December—and attached the first year of Abraham to the following year, namely year 3478 of the Graeco-Roman period, as Petavius advised that it should be attached, and as Florius actually attaches it, then an even number of the Graeco-Roman period would never correspond to an even number of the Abrahamic epoch, nor an odd number to an odd number.

But if Jerome had entered Abrahamic year 2395 for the fourteenth year of Valens, in which he ended the Chronicon, then, since Pagius assigns Graeco-Roman period year 5871 to that same fourteenth year of Valens, an even number of the period corresponds to an even number of the Abrahamic epoch, and an odd number to an odd number, as is self-evident.

It remains, therefore, that Jerome ended his Chronicon in Abrahamic year 2394, not 2395. It has already been observed above, no. 20, that Pagius himself both recognized and approved this conclusion.

28. Let us now demonstrate the matter from Eusebius’s own Chronicon. Eusebius attaches Abrahamic year 2020 to Augustus’s forty-seventh year, which was the fourth year of the common era. Therefore every tenth Abrahamic year must thereafter fall in the fourth year after each successive decade of the common era.

Thus Abrahamic year 2030 falls in Dionysian year 14; Abrahamic year 2040 in Dionysian year 24; and finally Abrahamic year 2400 in common-era year 384.

Idatius indeed distributes all the decades from this same Abrahamic year 2400—which was the first of the decades he encountered—to 2460 according to the stated order. Nor is this order disturbed in the Chronicon until the remaining numerical notations at the end of the book were corrupted.

The Sirmondian edition preserves this order, which should in no way have been reversed, as has now been done by transferring the decades of Abrahamic years to the third year after each decade of the Dionysian era. Pagius himself praises this order as the only correct one in the Chronicon and attached the first decade to the sixth year of Theodosius the Great, which for Florius is common-era year 384.

Therefore, if Dionysian year 384 corresponds to Abrahamic year 2400, the Dionysian year 379 in which Idatius began the Chronicon can correspond to no other year than Abrahamic year 2395.

29. Accordingly, no one should thereafter be misled by the rule that Pagius prescribes for extracting Dionysian-era years from Abrahamic years (Dissert. de period. Graeco-romana, no. 79). He says that 2,017 years are to be subtracted from the Abrahamic years, and that the remainder after this subtraction will show the Dionysian year.

But in which month will it show that year? In October, naturally, and therefore after nine months of that year have already elapsed. For example, subtract 2,017 from Abrahamic year 2018; 1 remains. Thus the first Dionysian year is obtained, but not as beginning at that moment: rather, its tenth month is then in progress.

This follows Pagius’s opinion, according to which the Idatian years begin in October. But anyone who counts them from the following January, as Florius does, and uses this rule to derive Dionysian year 1, will be completely deceived.

For Abrahamic year 2018, having begun in October, does not reach the first Dionysian year until its tenth month, since this is Pagius’s meaning. The same Abrahamic year, if begun in the following January, will coincide with that Dionysian year in none of its parts.

Therefore, whoever begins the Eusebian, Hieronymian, and Idatian years in January must subtract 2,016, not 2,017, from their Abrahamic years in order to obtain the Dionysian years. Similarly, to obtain Eusebian Christ’s first year, one must subtract 2,014, not 2,015.

§ IX. On the Olympiadic Year in Which Idatius Began the Chronicon

30. I shall now establish briefly what I asserted about the Olympiadic year in which Jerome ended and from which Idatius began the Chronicon.

As for Idatius, he speaks for himself. For a year and a half after beginning the Chronicon, he prefixed Olympiad 290, as is clear from the Sirmondian edition. Thus there can be no doubt that Idatius began his continuation approximately in the seventh month of the third year of Olympiad 289.

It follows that Jerome completed his Chronicon in the sixth month of that same Olympiadic year. Jerome himself also clearly testifies to this when he says that 1,155 Olympiadic years had elapsed from the first Olympiad to the sixth consulship of Valens [Note: [Col. 0695] Pontacus testifies that this is found in many manuscripts]—not complete years, however, since only six months of the final year had elapsed when he placed the closing statement in the Chronicon.

This was nevertheless sufficient for him to count 1,155 years from the first Olympiad to that year of Valens, the final year of the Chronicon. The same number results if one counts 288 complete Olympiads, multiplied by four, and then adds three years of Olympiad 289.

From Jerome’s testimony, but especially from Idatius, we may conclude with sufficient certainty that, after the lifetimes of both men, that blemish attached itself to Jerome’s Chronicon which now, or rather from the time of Marcellinus Comes—if what he relates in the preface to his own Chronicon is true—has disfigured it: namely, the placing at its end of world-year 5579, or Abrahamic year 2395 and Olympiadic year 1156, each of these epochs having been increased by one year.

The same error entered Socrates, who records Valens’s death in the 289th Olympiad. But whatever may have been the occasion and date when this defect overtook Jerome’s Chronicon, I think no one can deny that either Idatius did not encounter it or, if he did encounter it, corrected it, as I believe is abundantly clear from what has been said.

31. To demonstrate this again more clearly, I shall not hesitate to repeat the argument derived from comparing the Olympiadic years with the Abrahamic years.

Since Eusebius began the Olympiad in Abrahamic year 1240, under which he placed the first Olympiad, it necessarily follows that Olympiadic year 1155—which was the third year of Olympiad 289—was assigned to Abrahamic year 2394, and that the fourth year of that same Olympiad, the first to appear in Idatius, was assigned to Abrahamic year 2395.

In Eusebian chronology it can never happen that an even Olympiadic year begins with an even Abrahamic number, or an odd one with an odd one. Because the recent editor of Idatius failed to notice this, he attached the fourth year of Olympiad 289—which is Olympiadic year 1156 from the beginning of the Eusebian Olympiads—to Abrahamic year 2396.

Therefore, at the entrance to Idatius’s Chronicon, the chronological notations must be arranged so that under “Theodosius, by nationality” there appears Theodosius’s first year and Abrahamic year 2395, and under “Among the Romans,” Olympiad 289, year 4. This will be entirely evident to anyone wishing to calculate these chronological systems.

32. But if Censorinus attaches Olympiadic year 1,014 to common-era year 238, beginning from the summer days of that same Dionysian year, then after the 140 years that elapsed from 238 to 378, where Jerome’s Chronicon ends, he ought to count only 1,154 Olympiadic years.

Yet in Jerome and Idatius that same summer completed year 1154 from the first Olympiad and began year 1155. Jerome and Idatius therefore precede Censorinus by one year in their calculation of the Olympiads.

So it is indeed. For Eusebius, whom Jerome and Idatius followed, took the beginning of the Olympiad one year earlier than Censorinus and the other writers generally did. He joined its beginning not with Abrahamic year 1241, as Petavius says (Ration. part II, book I, chapter 10), but, as is apparent from the Chronicon itself, with year 1240, which corresponds to Julian-period year 3937.

Censorinus and almost all the others, however, attach the beginning of the Olympiad to the following year. Pagius and Florius have already discussed this difference between the Eusebian and common Olympiads. Petavius too noticed it, and it had occurred to him earlier; but, as he says in the same place, he did not wish to examine the matter too minutely or linger longer over its complications.

Finally, it must not be passed over in silence that anyone who believes Jerome completed the Chronicon in Abrahamic year 2395 will not correctly assign Olympiadic year 1155 to its end, but must count 1156, since that is the number counted from Abrahamic year 1240—the year to which Eusebius attaches the beginning of the Olympiad—to the same Abrahamic year 2395.

The Eusebian Olympiads would consequently precede the ordinary Olympiads not by one year only but by two. For in the sixth consulship of Valens, in which Jerome’s Chronicon ends, the ordinary reckoning counted Olympiadic year 1154.

This reasoning strongly reinforces everything said above about the year in which Jerome ended and Idatius began the Chronicon.

§ X. In Which Abrahamic and Olympiadic Year Did Idatius End the Chronicon?

33. Idatius’s history comprises 91 years. He withdrew his hand from the Chronicon in Abrahamic year 2485, in the second year of Olympiad 312, in Christ’s year 471 according to Eusebius and 469 according to Dionysius, in the thirteenth year of the emperor Leo Augustus and the third of Anthemius.

It must, however, be carefully observed that from Leo’s eighth year onward everything in the Chronicon is disturbed—or rather, undifferentiated. For Leo’s eighth year itself has been removed from its proper place, and all the remaining years up to the thirteenth, in which the Chronicon ends, had already been omitted in the time of Isidore, as may be inferred from Isidore himself (De viris illustribus, chapter 10). Consequently, one cannot know what belongs to one year or another.

Something similar occurred in the Fasti. After Olybrius’s consulship is recorded, the three following years—namely 465, 466, and 467—are omitted. After the consulship of Anthemius Augustus, which Idatius, as usual, entered under the year 468, the consulship of the following year, 469, is also omitted.

The reason is that, during these four years, no consul had been appointed from the West. Idatius, situated in the farthest part of Gallaecia and surrounded by wars raging in every direction, was completely ignorant of which consuls had been proclaimed in the East.

Indeed, he seems to have heard nothing about Olybrius’s consulship until several years later. For in the Fasti it is entered in these words: “The lord Olybrius.” From this it may be inferred that the consulship was not recorded there before the year 472, since Olybrius had not previously been proclaimed Augustus, so that he could be called “lord.”

Because of this omission of the imperial epoch, certain errors were transmitted to Isidore and others. We have been left the task of finding a place in the Chronicon for Leo’s ninth, tenth, and eleventh years and of restoring the eighth year to its proper position.

But since the consulship of Anthemius in the Fasti—which gave its name to Dionysian year 468—and also the third year of Anthemius’s reign in the Chronicon—which falls in year 469—are recorded, it is certainly deduced from this, and especially from Olympiad 312, which was still entered a year and a half before the end of the Chronicon, that the history contained in it comprises 91 years, namely from 379 to 469, since the Chronicon encompasses both.

34. These matters must be established in this way whenever the numerical notations do not extend beyond that year. Nevertheless, since the deposition of Aspar and the killing of his son are mentioned at the end of the Chronicon—events that occurred in the year 471—there is nothing reckless in what the most learned Labbe wrote: that this Chronicon runs from the year 379 of the Christian era to the year 471 of that same era (Preface to the Idatian Fasti, vol. I of the Nova Bibliotheca).

Yet there can scarcely be any doubt that the material concerning Aspar and his son was added in the margin, after Idatius had completed the Chronicon, either by Idatius himself or by someone else, and that copyists subsequently incorporated it into the body of the work.

As for Isidore, when he says, “Idatius follows the history from the first year of Theodosius Augustus to the eighth year of the reign of Leo” (in the work cited above), we must regard it as certain that he found no other year designated beyond Leo’s eighth—not of Leo himself, nor of Anthemius.

For, after writing these words about Idatius, when transcribing words from Idatius’s own Chronicon (History of the Goths), he says: “In the eighth year of the reign of Leo, Euric succeeds to the kingdom with the same crime as his brother.”

These words now appear in the Chronicon under the first year of Anthemius, which was Leo’s eleventh year.

The following words, which he likewise transcribes from the same Idatius (History of the Suevi), “Olysipona too is occupied by him—the city having been handed over by its own citizen Lusidius, who was in charge of it,” now stand near the end of the Chronicon, under the third year of Anthemius.

From all this two conclusions seem certainly possible:

1. Isidore saw in the Chronicon everything that is now contained in it, at least up to the words “Olysipona too,” etc., which belong to Anthemius’s third year, Leo’s thirteenth, and common-era year 469.

2. In the copy used by Isidore, only Leo’s eighth year was designated, while no year of Anthemius was entered at all. Otherwise, if he had read that the Chronicon extended to Anthemius’s third year and that Euric was reigning in Anthemius’s first year, he would certainly not have written that Idatius followed the history only to the eighth year and that Euric invaded the kingdom in that same eighth year.

But did a copyist fail to enter the chronological notations for those years in the copy used by Isidore? Or, as I said above concerning the consulships, did Idatius, after the death of Severus Augustus, being uncertain whether Leo was still alive in the East, omit them, after which either Idatius himself or someone else added the years of Anthemius? Who can know?

In the meantime, however, we seem to have greater freedom to arrange the chronological notations in the final five years of the Chronicon, since it is not certain that they came from Idatius. I shall not use this freedom, except in arranging Leo’s eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh years, leaving entirely untouched the notations that refer to the years of Anthemius.

§ XI. On the Fasti, and on Their Being the Work of Idatius

35. The other work of Idatius, as I believe, is the consular Fasti, which are attached to the Chronicon in a Parisian manuscript.

When the learned Sirmond published them, he prefaced them as follows: “We have called these the Idatian Fasti, not so much because they are appended to Idatius’s Chronicon in the same manuscript, as because …” I shall give the remainder below.

But the fact that these Fasti are appended to Idatius’s Chronicon, although they bear no author’s name, does not seem to me as slight an argument as it appeared to Sirmond; rather, it seems an important one. The reason is that the entire volume, in the form in which it is still said to exist in that manuscript, came from Idatius’s workshop. Consequently, the author’s name was not appended to the Fasti because it had already been placed at the beginning of the preceding Chronicon.

36. That these Fasti were joined to the manuscript by their author himself is certainly indicated by what they contain under the consulship of Verus III and Quadratus, namely: “In the Chronicon you read that …” The copyist truncated the remainder.

The name of the author of the cited Chronicon would necessarily have had to be identified by the writer of the Fasti, unless that same Chronicon had been placed before the Fasti and the name of its author explicitly given there.

But Eusebius’s name and his Chronicon were indeed inscribed there. In that work, under the seventh year of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, which corresponds to that consulship, we read: “When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom.”

I have no doubt that the author of the Fasti had this passage before his eyes. Idatius, moreover, follows the practice of referring to Eusebius without explicitly naming him. In the prologue to the Chronicon, under the words “In the preceding work,” and likewise in the Chronicon itself, under the words “After the Arians mentioned above,” he identifies the Eusebian Chronicon as augmented by Jerome.

For this reason I do not rashly judge that both the Fasti and the Chronicon were the work of the same author, and that all of them were gathered together by the same person into a single volume along with the Chronica of Eusebius and Jerome.

37. “But,” you will say, “in the same Fasti we read above that the martyrdom of Polycarp and Pionius was recorded under the consulship, as the text says, of Antoninus V and Aurelius Caesar.”

That is true; but this is one blemish among the many that have disfigured these Fasti.

The great Baronius writes the following about Polycarp in his notes on the Martyrology for 26 January:

“He suffered martyrdom, as Eusebius writes, in the seventh year of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Verus, when Lucius Aurelius was consul for the third time with Quadratus.”

Thus the martyrdom was first recorded correctly, since Idatius himself entered it under those consuls. Later, some half-blind copyist advanced it by six years. Finally, another copyist, when writing under the consulship of Verus and Quadratus the words “In the Chronicon, under these consuls, you read that …,” omitted the names of Polycarp and Pionius, which he had copied six years earlier from the corrupted manuscript.

The death of Cicero was likewise entered twice in the same Fasti through a similar error, though with a different defect: in the first place it was recorded correctly, in the second incorrectly. Such blemishes are common in ancient manuscripts, and a reader who has had experience of them will not be surprised.

I wish to point out here that the name of Pionius was added by Jerome, for it is not found in the Greek Chronicon of Eusebius; and Pionius suffered martyrdom many years after Polycarp, under Decius (see Bollandists, 1 February).

Idatius therefore transcribed this material into the Fasti from Jerome’s Latin Chronicon without consulting the Greek.

43 38. But the strongest argument for the author of these Fasti is supplied by their ending, which, as I noted above (§ 33), is strikingly similar to the conclusion of the Chronicon. For when the final five years are reached, the author is found in both works to have suffered from an equal—or rather identical—ignorance of events outside Spain. The Fasti lack the consuls who would distinguish the years within them; the Chronicon has been stripped of its chronology. Anyone can observe something similar almost at the very threshold of both works: in both, the inauguration of Honorius, who ruled in the West, is passed over in silence for the year 393. Yet it is incredible that this sort of [Col. 0699C] ignorance or forgetfulness should have occurred to two different writers, both Latin, neither of whom forgot to record, under the year 383, the inauguration of Arcadius, who was always in the East. Moreover, if an error is found in the Chronicon—not a copyist’s error but the author’s—we encounter the same error in the Fasti. Thus the earthquakes by which Palestine was shaken in the year 419 are said in both the Chronicon and the Fasti to have occurred under John, bishop of Jerusalem, although he had died two or three years earlier. See note 30. Who, then, after this, will deny that the Fasti and the Chronicon have the same author—namely, Idatius?

But I continue. Sirmond, in assigning these Fasti to Idatius, was moved, as he himself admits, by the following consideration:

> The affinity and kinship of subject matter and wording in both works (in the Fasti themselves and [Col. 0699D] in the Chronicon), the equal care devoted to epochs and periods of time, and finally the identical character and genius of the entire composition sufficiently show that both works had the same author, although the title bears no author’s name.

Sirmond wrote this in the preface to the Chronicon and the Fasti. Yet some deny the affinity of style, and deny that the character and genius of both writings are the same; they assert that the Chronicon was written more purely and accurately than the Fasti. But, above all, there is no reason for anyone to praise Idatius’s Latinity excessively, since it sufficiently betrays its own age. Moreover, Idatius may perhaps have composed the Fasti for private use. When someone writes privately for himself, no one is unaware that he ordinarily uses words and expressions [Col. 0700A] common in everyday speech. This could have been the reason why Saint Isidore did not see these Fasti: Idatius, when issuing the Chronicon publicly, kept the Fasti at home among his papers. Later, either through the importunity of friends or after his death, and because they were joined to the Chronicon in the same volume, they may have been published; indeed, a copy containing both works may have circulated as widely as the Chronicon.

39. The greater quantity of historical material that these Fasti provide from Constantine to Arcadius, whereas in the remainder of the work they record scarcely more than the bare names of the consuls, far from indicating a different author from Idatius, seems to me, on the contrary, to prove most powerfully [Col. 0700B] that no one but Idatius could have written such a work. Who besides Idatius would have written these Fasti and narrated so much about events before the year 400, while omitting what occurred in the fifth century—that is, in his own time? Idatius can rightly be inferred to have written them for himself and private use, because in the Chronicon he had already related, from Arcadius and Honorius to the year 469, when the Fasti end, whatever he judged worthy of being handed down to posterity. In the Chronicon, however, he had said nothing about events before the reign of the great Theodosius, and very little about the period from Theodosius to his sons. Perhaps, too, he composed the Fasti because of his interest in chronology, which is more reliably derived from the succession of consuls; and for that reason, in this work his concern with the consulships of his own time took precedence over historical narrative.

[Col. 0700C] 45 40. But let us now see what those who reject the Fasti as Idatius’s, on the grounds of their style, criticize in them. They object, namely, to: *ad Fossatum*, *Romania*, and *levatus est imperator* (“he was raised as emperor”). They further add that the author of the Fasti was not very careful in recording eclipses, whereas Idatius was extremely diligent in the Chronicon.

But, to begin with Fossatum: when the author of the Fasti writes, under the sixth consulship of Valens, “Valens Augustus set out from the city to Fossatum,” what is it that displeases learned men? Is it the word *Fossatum*, or the construction? But how could the construction be objectionable, since it is, so to speak, thoroughly Latin? Is the objection, then, to the word *Fossatum*? Yet in the age of the historian Pliny it possessed Latin legal standing, as the various readings of the manuscript codices appended to the work itself indicate.

[Note: [Col. 0699] *Ad oram*, chapter 21 of book XVIII, in the Lyon edition of 1561.]

If this testimony is nevertheless unsatisfactory because it is uncertain, Gothofredus supplies other evidence older than Idatius [Col. 0700D] in his commentary on book 1 of *On the Border Troops* in the Theodosian Code. The word *Fossatum* occurs in that law, which was enacted in the year 409—sixty years, that is, before Idatius completed the Chronicon.

41. Next, the name *Romania* was commonly used in the time of Orosius. He himself attests this when he says (*Book* VII, chapter 43): “And, to speak in the ordinary manner, it would be Gothia, whereas it had been Romania.” Possidius, too, who was somewhat earlier than Idatius, uses the same word (*Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 30). Finally, although the expression “he was raised up” does not occur in any author who wrote before Idatius—at least, I have not read it there—the anonymous Cuspinianus frequently uses it. As for the period in which this author wrote, [Col. 0701A] Panvinius, a man of great diligence and learning, determines it as follows (*Book* III of the *Fasti*): “This uncertain author undoubtedly lived around this period, namely, approximately 455 of the common era.”

But Idatius was then alive and lived at least fifteen years longer. Therefore there is no reason to regard that manner of speaking as unworthy of Idatius’s age and pen. Moreover, those who deny that these Fasti belong to Idatius because, as they claim, the style and character of this composition seem to them more recent and more decadent encounter another difficulty: they could find and offer no reason why its author should have remembered no consulships beyond Idatius’s lifetime and should have transmitted almost nothing about the events of the fifth century. If he had lived with Count Marcellinus, or with Cassiodorus, or with Marius of Avenches, [Col. 0701B] could he not have extracted from their works—or from wherever they themselves obtained them—many other pairs of consuls and much information about the events of the following years?

42. As for the eclipses, since Idatius had appended these Fasti to the Chronicon, in which he had described them sufficiently accurately, he judged it superfluous to insert them again in the Fasti. Indeed, when he began to transcribe into the Fasti, together with the fifth consulship of Arcadius and Honorius—which fell in that year—the solar eclipse that he had first expressed under the eighth year [Col. 0702A] of Honorius in these words, “A solar eclipse occurred on the third day before the Ides of November, on the second day of the week,” he stopped his pen after passing through the opening words, “A solar eclipse occurred on the third day before the Ides of November,” omitting the two remaining words, “on the second day of the week.” I think he did this for no other reason than that, having decided to pass over such matters in the Fasti, he began to copy that eclipse from the Chronicon in forgetfulness of his purpose; then, before he had finished copying it all, he remembered his purpose and omitted the latter two words.

43. Finally, to conclude, the same judgment should be formed concerning the notes of the Spanish era inserted throughout the Fasti as concerning the few notes appended to the Chronicon. Indeed, I have even less doubt that these were introduced into the Fasti after Idatius’s lifetime. First, [Col. 0702B] from era 10 onward, the remaining 47 [eras] proceed continuously and corruptly, something that does not usually occur in ancient manuscripts. Second, the first era found within the body of the Fasti does not agree with the others; it would agree if all of them had been recorded in the book by Idatius. But if they were not all recorded by Idatius, then neither was any one of them.

[Col. 0701]

# CHRONICON OF IDATIUS, BISHOP. (C)

## PREFACE

48. Idatius, servant of our Lord Jesus Christ, sends greeting in our Lord Jesus Christ and in truth to all the faithful.

The labors of men approved in every respect—men whom the profession of divine worship, especially in Catholic faith and perfect conduct, teaches to be witnesses of the truth—are adorned by the distinction of their words and commended by the honor of their merits, so that they possess extraordinary firmness in every work. But Idatius, born in the province of Gallaecia, in the city of Lemica,
