[Note: [Col. 0701C] I discussed the name and location of this city above, in the preliminary dissertation, § 2.]

having been created, more by divine favor than by his own merit, chief bishop of the highest office,

[Note: [Col. 0701C] He means the episcopate, concerning which see the same dissertation, § 7, and the dissertation on Priscillian.]

being as remote in region as he was at life’s end, very little trained in secular learning and much less instructed by the salutary volume of sacred reading, followed, according to the capacity of his own understanding or expression, the example of the holy and most learned Fathers in his earlier work.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] Namely, the Chronicon of Eusebius expanded by Jerome, which Idatius had joined in the same volume with its continuation.]

[Note: [Col. 0701C] The sentence is excessively extended and suspended, and is never completed below.]

The first of these was Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, who wrote ecclesiastical histories in books of his own composition and, beginning with Ninus among the Assyrians and the holy patriarch Abraham among the Hebrews, together with the years of the other kings contemporary with them, brought the history of Greek chronography down to the twentieth year of Constantine Augustus, who was then reigning.

After him came his successor, the accomplished chronicler Jerome—also called Eusebius—interpreter of this work from Greek into Latin. Beginning with the twentieth year of the aforementioned emperor, he extended the history down to the fourteenth year of Valens Augustus:

[Note: [Col. 0701C] Other editions read *esto ut*, omitting *qui*; everyone can see that this passage requires this or some similar correction.]

who, let it be said, while he was in the holy places where he stayed in Jerusalem, may perhaps have appended very much from the year of the aforementioned Valens to the time during which he remained in the present life, since, as long as he had strength, he never ceased from a different kind of literary work. I am certain that I saw him, still a very young child, at some point during my own pilgrimage in the regions mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] See the Chronicon under the year 407.]

If, after some years, he added anything to the work which he had appended, while he remained blessed—as he was—in the body, there is certain and complete knowledge of this among those to whom the whole or the greater part of his written work has come down. But since it is clear that in one of his writings he stated:

> Since barbarians are now raging on Roman soil, everything is in a state of mixture and confusion,

we infer from this indication of his words that he added nothing concerning the succession of times to the volume of years that follows here on its own.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] These words appear to have been taken from the end of Jerome’s preface to the Chronicon, although I think I have read similar statements elsewhere in Jerome.]

[Note: [Col. 0702C] The Eusebian-Jeronymian Chronicon, which contains history down to the fourteenth year of Valens and which, as the higher reading now, again, and shortly afterward, in the passage above, testifies for a third time, was placed by him before his own Chronicon in the same volume. If this was in some way released by Idatius for public circulation, it would have reached our own times. I have no doubt that at the end of Jerome’s continuation one would find Abraham’s year 2394, and beneath it the third year of the 289th Olympiad recorded; for the chronological notes that follow in Idatius’s Chronicon require these from the Jeronymian text.]

[Col. 0703]

50. Nevertheless, because the account of the years had flowed down to the course of our own time, as the preceding reading shows, when the care of the parchment of this history had come to an inexperienced man, it prompted the mind of the unskilled man to cast himself upon the traces of his predecessors in matters known to him, even if with unequal progress. Having undertaken these matters with the faithful attention of his heart, partly from the study of written sources, partly from the trustworthy report of certain persons, and partly from knowledge which the already lamentable period of his own life had revealed, we have added what follows. You who read the content of these events and times will distinguish them as follows.

From the first year of Theodosius Augustus to the third year of Valentinian Augustus, son of Placidia, the material was written by us either from the style of written sources or from the reports of informants. Thereafter, having been undeservedly drawn into the office of the episcopate, and not unaware of all the calamities of a pitiable age and of the Roman Empire shut up in straits, we have set down boundaries destined to collapse. And, more grievously still, within Gallaecia at the very end of the whole world: the deformed condition of the ecclesiastical order, the destruction of honorable liberty through indiscriminate appointments, the near-extinction of religion almost everywhere in the discipline of God, amid the mingled disturbance of wicked nations, the *dominantem* of raging peoples [the printed sentence remains grammatically incomplete].

[Note: [Col. 0704A] I would read *dominationem*, or, more attractively, *imminentem*.]

These matters have now indeed been inserted, but we have left them [variant: *we leave them*] for posterity to complete in the times in which they encounter them.

# CHRONICON OF IDATIUS, BISHOP.

[Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]

He is called Augustus by Gratian [Note: Theodosius was proclaimed Augustus at Sirmium on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. Thus Idatius himself in the Fasti and Marcellinus in the Chronicle. Theodosius was then thirty-three years old, as may be inferred from Victor and as Paul the Deacon expressly reports.].

But in the West only an excerpt from it seems to have been known, a period of one hundred or ninety-five years, by Cyril, Theophilus’s nephew. Leo mentions it in letter 64.].

53. Theodosius, calling his son Arcadius (5) Augustus [Note: Arcadius was declared Augustus on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, as our Idatius reports in the Fasti. Pagius disputes this, but wrongly. See note 5.], makes him his partner in the empire.

But the anonymous author anticipates the year and assigns it to the preceding one.]

The most learned Florus left this seventh year of Theodosius blank. The Sirmondian edition places under it “victory” and also the section beginning “Priscillianus, declining…” They must be separated, and one assigned to year 7, the other to year 8, as you see done here. See note 7.]

Priscillianus, declining into the heresy of the Gnostics, is ordained bishop at Ávila by bishops whom he had gathered to himself in the same depravity. After being heard by several councils of bishops [Note: This makes clear that not merely one Council of Zaragoza but also several other councils were convened in Spain against Priscillian before he was put to death in 386.], he proceeds to Italy and to Rome [Note: Damasus died in 384; this journey cannot have been postponed beyond that year.], where he was not even admitted to the sight of the holy bishops Damasus and Ambrose. 54. He returns to Gaul with those who had gone with him. There likewise he was judged a heretic by Saint Martin the bishop and by other bishops [Note: At the Council of Bordeaux, in 385.]. He appeals to the emperor, because in Gaul at that time the tyrant Maximus [Note: After Gratian was killed on the eighth day before the Kalends of September in the year 383, Maximus, as Marcellinus and the anonymous author of the Cuspinian manuscript report, seized the empire. Prosper and Cassiodorus incorrectly assign this to the following year.] held imperial power.

The people of the Greuthungi [Note: The Greuthungi were a portion of the Ostrogoths. I shall give some information about them and about this war in note 8.] are defeated by Theodosius (8).

In the wrong order, the commonly circulated books first present the section on Arcadius under Theodosius’s year 8, and then the section on Priscillianus under year 9. But they must be arranged as I present them here; I shall demonstrate this in note 7, paragraphs 3 and 4.]

Priscillianus, expelled from the episcopate because of the aforesaid heresy, and with him Latronianus (9) [Note: Jerome calls him Matronianus, On Illustrious Men, no. 130. Prosper and Severus, however, call him Latronianus, as does Idatius. On the companions of Priscillian who were put to death, see note 9.], together with several followers, are executed at Trier under the tyrant Maximus [Note: The sentence was pronounced by Evodius and the praetorian prefect.].

See above, note 3.]

Arcadius’s quinquennalia are celebrated [Note: On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, as Idatius says in the Fasti; Pagius corrects him without justification.].

Siricius is recorded as the thirty-sixth bishop of the Roman Church [Note: Since Idatius, Prosper, and Marcellinus count Siricius as the thirty-sixth pontiff, they follow Eusebius, who began counting from Linus and, confusing Cletus with Anacletus and Marcellus with Marcellinus, while also omitting Felix because he considered him an intruder, makes Siricius thirty-sixth instead of the fortieth. Siricius became pontiff in 385, not in 387, the year in which Idatius mentions him. Florus thinks that Idatius refers not to the date of his accession but to the period during which he was regarded as bishop, when he mentions him in the Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs.].

Idatius repeats in the Fasti, under the consuls of this year, the same account of the place and time of Maximus’s death. Socrates, book V, chapter 14, assigns the day of his death to the sixth day before the Kalends of August. The anonymous author of the Cuspinian manuscript gives the fifth day before the Kalends of September. See further, note 10.]

At the same time, or in that very year, in Gaul, the son of Maximus, named Victor, was killed by the count Arbogast.

Idatius gives more information about this distinguished man in the Fasti under this same year. If you wish, read it in note 11.]

He, endowed with remarkable achievements and penetrating as far as Egypt, overthrew the images of the nations.

Idatius himself reports in the Fasti that Theodosius entered Rome on the Ides of June. The anonymous author of the Cuspinian manuscript agrees. Idatius adds that Theodosius gave a largess to the Romans, from which we understand that he also celebrated a triumph at that time.]

Idatius has the same account in the Fasti. Cassiodorus, however, writes in his Chronicle: “Valentinianus, wearied of life, hanged himself with a noose at Vienne.” This was indeed circulated by his murderers as a gross slander. Orosius, book VII, chapter 35, explains the matter exactly. The blessed Jerome gives a briefer but more significant account in letter 3: “Valentinianus was killed, and his lifeless body was dishonored by hanging.” He was killed on the Ides of May, the day before Pentecost, as others have already observed from Epiphanius.]

56. And Eugenius becomes tyrant (12) [Note: In this same year Eugenius seized tyrannical power. See note 12.].

Here Idatius forgot to note that in this year Honorius was taken by his father into partnership in the empire. See note 13.]

[lacuna]

Eugenius is killed. This occurred in the consulship of Arcadius III and Honorius II, that is, in this year. Thus Claudian says in the fourth consulship of Honorius, verse 637; Idatius himself says so in the Fasti, as do Marcellinus and the anonymous author of the Cuspinian manuscript, who gives the day as 6 September. Prosper and Cassiodorus incorrectly assign the victory over Eugenius to the following year.]

Theodosius not only did not complete the eighteenth year of his reign, but did not even reach it: he was proclaimed Augustus on 19 January 379 and died this year on the fifteenth of the same month, according to the anonymous author of the Cuspinian manuscript, or on the seventeenth, according to Socrates, book VI, chapter 1. Idatius nevertheless assigns to him all the civil or Julian years touched by his reign.]

And this year, which is Theodosius’s seventeenth, is the first of Arcadius and Honorius at the beginning of their reign [Note: It is called “first” because, while their father was alive, the sons, although partners in the empire, received no share in its administration, and their age scarcely permitted it. In the celebration of quinquennalia, decennalia, and so forth, however, their original inauguration was taken into account.].

This is indicated so that the addition may not disturb the five-year Olympiad; here it is inserted only on account of the reigns [Note: The remaining books read: “Inserted here only on account of the reign of the princes.” See note 14.] of the emperors (14).

Idatius again declares that he begins the years of Arcadius and Honorius’ empire from this point.]

They reign for thirty years (15) [Note: I explain how these years are to be understood in note 15.].

In the first edition Sirmond enclosed these words in parentheses; in the Venetian edition they are printed in a different type. Did he judge them to have been inserted into the Chronicle? In any event, Anastasius became the forty-first Roman pontiff at the end of the year 398, not in 397.]

In the Sirmondian edition, the section “In the province of Carthage” is placed under this year, while year 6 is left blank. The reverse should have been done. See note 16, paragraph 1.]

[lacuna]

Since it is clear from the council itself that Symphosius was already an old man, this Symphosius is certainly different from the Symphosius of whom the Chronicle speaks under the year 435; likewise, this Dictinius is different from the one mentioned under the year 460.]

Dictinius and the other bishops of the province of Gallaecia [Note: It is therefore evident that Idatius was right to write that in 386 the heresy of Priscillian spread into Gallaecia after Priscillian’s death. Severus had earlier stated generally, book II of his History, at the end: “After Priscillian was killed, the heresy that had broken out through his influence was not suppressed; rather, it was strengthened and spread more widely.”], followers of Priscillian, condemn by signing the same profession of faith the most blasphemous heresy of that man together with its advocate.

58. Certain matters concerning the discipline of the Church are also established [Note: Even now twenty canons composed at this council are extant. I shall discuss it further in the dissertation on the Priscillianists; there I shall defend the authenticity of these canons against Quesnel.], with Bishop Ortigius participating in the same council. He had been ordained at Celenes [Note: The meaning is that Ortigius sat in the council as the legitimate bishop of Caelenae, at Aquae Caelenae, called Caelenae by Antoninus and now Ourense.], but, when the Priscillianists acted against him, he was driven out by factions on behalf of the Catholic faith and lived in exile.

These words are wrongly assigned to year 9 in the commonly circulated books. See note 16, paragraph 2.]

Theodosius, son of Arcadius, is born (16).

In the Fasti Idatius passes over the weekday in silence; perhaps he did not express it here either. Moreover, whenever the Chronicle mentions an eclipse, it frequently gives the day of the month or the week incorrectly. This eclipse occurred on the third day of the week, not the second; in the year 418, on the sixth day, not the fifth. In 447, the eclipse of the sun occurred on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, whereas the Chronicle gives the ninth. The most learned Florus corrected all these points in notes 5, 7, and 13 on Idatius. Finally, Petavius, Chronological Rationals, part II, book IV, chapter 13, says that for the fifth day before the Kalends of October—which the Chronicle gives when narrating the lunar eclipse of 451—one should read the sixth day before the Kalends.]

Innocent is proclaimed the forty-second in the order of Roman pontiffs, at the beginning of the year of the common era 402.]

Here the commonly circulated books give the birth of Theodosius, which I assigned to year 7. See note 16, page 2.]

[lacuna]

59. He suffers the most hostile Eudoxia, wife of Arcadius [Note: Just as Justina persecuted Ambrose, so Idatius believed that Eudoxia persecuted Chrysostom on account of the faith; this may likewise have been widely believed in the West. But Eudoxia was not an Arian; she was Catholic.], as an Arian.

Epiphanius [Note: Epiphanius was no longer among the living in this year, for he had died earlier.] and Theophilus of Alexandria, mentioned above [Note: He spoke of Theophilus in the year 380 and now refers back to him.], are counted among the distinguished bishops.

He means the Arian bishops whom Jerome mentions under the eleventh year of the sons of Constantine the Great. He calls them “the aforesaid” because, in the same volume, Idatius joined his Chronicle to Jerome’s Eusebian Chronicle, as was observed in the Preliminary Dissertation, no. 11; Isidore confirms this in On Illustrious Men, chapter 9, when he implies that Idatius’s history was appended to Jerome’s Chronicle.]

The Arian bishops who had been at Jerusalem before John (17) [Note: He could not have known this with certainty, since no Arian besides those whom Jerome lists held that episcopate. See note 17.] were certainly unknown to Idatius, who writes this. He saw this holy man together with the saints Eulogius, Theophilus, and Jerome [Note: Idatius seems now to remember all these men because in this year he saw them while, as a small child, he was traveling through Palestine.], both as an infant and as an orphan.

In this year Arcadius died on the first day before the Kalends of May, leaving his son Theodosius as successor.]

[lacuna]

60. They entered Spain [Note: I regard what follows to the end of the section as suspect. Idatius generally omits such notes, except when he is dealing with solar or lunar eclipses; then he usually gives the day and weekday. See note 18.] in Spanish Era 457. Some report the day as the fourth day before the Kalends, others as the third day before the Ides of October; it was the third day of the week, in the consulship of Honorius VIII and Theodosius, son of Arcadius, III.

The distinguished Florus assigns Honorius’s sixteenth year here. Sirmond, following a manuscript, instead places that year under the section “While the barbarians rage.” I thought it best to adopt a position between the two, and it is more likely that Idatius did so as well. See note 19, paragraph 1, concerning the year of the city’s destruction.]

Alaric, king of the Goths, entered Rome. While slaughter was being carried on inside and outside the city, all who fled to the thresholds of the saints were granted immunity (20) [Note: Idatius wrote this most truthfully; for not merely one church but several served as places of asylum for the Romans. See note 20, concerning the restraint of the Goths during that invasion of the city.].

Placidia was captured in the year 409. See note 10, paragraph 5.]

I have moved back here, from the section “While the barbarians rage,” this note belonging to Honorius’s sixteenth year. See note 21, concerning Alaric’s death and Ataulf’s succession.]

Alaric dies, and Ataulf succeeds him in the kingdom.

Here Sirmond, following a manuscript, expressed Honorius’s sixteenth year, which I have attached above to the words “Alaric dies,” guided by the authority of Isidore, who assigns the beginning of Ataulf’s reign to 410, in which year Alaric must likewise have died; this is the common opinion of all.]

While barbarians raged throughout Spain and the evil of pestilence nevertheless continued, a tyrannical tax collector seized the wealth and property stored in the cities [p. 61], while the soldier exhausted their very bodies.

Olympiodorus gives a more detailed account, saying: “A woman, the mother of four children, devoured them all, pretending in each case that she wished to feed and save the others, until, after everything had been consumed, she was stoned to death by the populace.” In this same year the Romans, afflicted by famine and plague, nevertheless attended the circus, where that ominous cry was heard: “Set a price on human flesh.” Thus Zosimus.]

The beasts, accustomed to the corpses of those killed by the sword, famine, and pestilence, slaughtered the strongest among the human beings and, fed on their flesh, spread everywhere to destroy the human race. And thus, with the four scourges—sword, famine, pestilence, and beasts—raging everywhere throughout the whole world, the announcements foretold by the Lord through his prophets are fulfilled.

Orosius mentions this allotment of the provinces among the barbarians, book VII, chapter 40, writing: “After carrying on great and bloody raids for some time, and after the severe devastation of lands and people—which now causes even them remorse—by lot they took possession and, having divided it, remain settled to the present day.”]

They divide among themselves the regions of the provinces for habitation.

62. The Vandals occupy Gallaecia [Note: The Vandals obeyed King Gunderic, son of Godigisel, or Godagisclus, or Gudegisclus—for the authors vary his name—under whom the Vandals attempted to cross the Rhine. But after Godigisel was killed by the Franks, as Gregory of Tours relates from Frigeridus, book II, chapter 9, Gunderic became the first Vandal king in Spain, as Isidore correctly records in his history. Procopius must therefore be corrected, since in book I of The Vandalic War he says that Godigisel came to Spain.], and the Suevi [Note: The Suevi had Hermeric as their king, who is frequently mentioned by Idatius from this point onward.] occupy the region situated at the western extremity of the Ocean; the Alans draw lots for the provinces of Lusitania and Carthaginensis [Note: Atax was king of the Alans; Idatius mentions him below, under the year 418.]; and the Vandals called Silingi [Note: Since Idatius calls Fredibalus king of the Vandals under the year 416, I understand the Siling Vandals here, for Gunderic ruled the others.] receive Baetica as their allotment.

The Spaniards remaining in the cities and fortified places [Note: The peoples who had invaded Spain did not know how to blockade places fortified either by nature or by human art, or to capture them by bringing up siege engines. Therefore the Spaniards fled to those places.] submit themselves to servitude [Note: I shall discuss this servitude in note 22.] under the barbarians ruling the provinces (22).

Concerning this same Constantinus, our Idatius says in the Fasti, under the consuls of this year: “The head of the tyrant Constantinus was brought in on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.” He therefore seized tyrannical power in 408.]

After three years of usurped rule, he is killed within Gaul by Constantius, the general of Honorius [Note: Prosper says that he was defeated and captured at Arles—Orosius adds that he was killed—by the generals of Honorius, Constantius and Ulfilas. Sozomen and Olympiodorus also mention him.].

The commonly circulated books read auctorum (“of the authors”), but it is plainly established that actorum (“of the proceedings”) must be read. Augustine often disputed with the Donatists, and the proceedings of these conferences, recorded by notaries, were subsequently made public. Idatius here appeals to their reliability.]

Marcellinus, in his Chronicle, mentions the usurpation and death of Jovinus and Sebastianus under the preceding year. See note 23 concerning them.]

They were killed at Narbonne (23) [Note: Prosper and Cassiodorus correctly assign the arrival of the Goths in Gaul to the preceding year; this does not conflict with Idatius, because when Ataulf entered Gaul he did not proceed to Narbonne in a continuous march. How could he have done so when he was leading with him a population of children, old men, and women, for whom he had to provide food and often clear a path by force of arms? Olympiodorus indeed left it recorded that Ataulf besieged Massilia during the journey and was driven back from there by Boniface?].

Orosius, book VII, chapter 42, describes the tyranny of Heraclianus, his invasion of Italy, and his punishment, and adds that he prepared the expedition with a fleet of 3,700 ships.]

The Short Chronicle gives the number killed at Utriculum not as 50,000 but as 20,000, which may perhaps be more accurate.]

Moving his army from Africa against Honorius, he was defeated in battle at Utriculum in Italy and fled back to Africa, with 50,000 armed men killed at the aforesaid place [Note: The new year marked here by Idatius is clear evidence that he begins the years from January.].

He himself was killed at Carthage, in the shrine of Memoria, after Honorius sent assassins against him.

I shall quote some details about this marriage from Olympiodorus in note 24.]

In this event the prophecy of Daniel is thought to have been fulfilled [Note: Daniel, chapter XI, prophesies concerning the king of Egypt, Ptolemy Philadelphus, who gave his daughter Berenice in marriage to Antiochus, surnamed Theos, king of Syria. Laodice, Antiochus’s former wife, grieving that she had been rejected, brought death upon Antiochus himself, Berenice, and the son of both, and made Callinicus, her own son by the same Antiochus, king. Jerome, Appian, and Justin give a fuller account.], which says that the daughter of the king of the South will be joined to the king of the North, yet no offspring of hers will survive [Note: Just as no surviving son born of Berenice obtained the kingdom of Syria, so the son born to Placidia and Ataulf, named Theodosius, did not succeed his parents in the kingdom. He died shortly after his birth and was buried in a silver coffin in a church near Barcelona, amid the immense grief of both parents.].

Above, under the years 406 and 407.]

With the bishop presiding, Saint Stephen, first and chief martyr after Christ the Lord, is revealed (25) [Note: Marcellinus has the same account in his Chronicle. Idatius, however, adds several details in the Fasti, which you may see in note 25, where the birthplace of Paul Orosius is investigated by conjecture.].

Above, under the years 406 and 407.]

He was preeminent in all things, even highly skilled in the elements, a Hebrew learned in the law of the Lord, continually occupied in day-and-night meditation on what is written in that law, and he left behind countless works of scholarship. Finally, he crushed the sect of the Pelagians [Note: Jerome first attacked Pelagius in his letter to Ctesiphon, which forms a book of considerable length; he then composed three books of dialogues against him. Both works are still extant.] together with its author beneath the adamantine hammer of truth.

65. Against these and other heretics his most authoritative writings remain extant.

When Ataulf, leaving Narbonne in the preceding year, came to Barcelona, where, in this year—which was the common era 416—while making for Spain, he was murdered by a certain Goth [Note: Olympiodorus calls the murderer Bobbius; Jordanes calls him Vernulfus. See the same note.] amid familiar conversation [Note: Olympiodorus says that he was killed in a stable.].

Vallia succeeded him [Note: Orosius, book VII, chapter 43, Jordanes in Getica, no. 45, Isidore, and others make Sigeric Ataulf’s successor. Idatius and Prosper pass over Sigeric in silence because, as Olympiodorus reports, he was killed after ruling for seven days.] in the kingdom. Together with the patrician Constantius, after peace was soon made (27) [Note: Pagius’s opinion concerning the date of this peace is refuted in note 27. There I indicate to whom law 14 of the Theodosian Code, “On Invalidating Acts Performed under Tyrants,” applies.], he opposed the Alans and the Siling Vandals, who were settled in Lusitania and Baetica.

I did not know this when writing these words. From this passage we understand that Idatius wished to append to his Chronicle a series of Alexandrian bishops, as Jerome and Eusebius had done. But he seems to have omitted not only these but also the bishops of Jerusalem and Antioch, because he could not have known their successions.]

Olympiodorus assigns this marriage to the beginning of the following year. See note 28.]

The Sirmondian edition encloses these words within lines. Did they seem spurious to Sirmond? Certainly the Short Chronicle omits them and substitutes the following: “Idatius’s conversion from sin to the Lord.” Isidore likewise omits the passage about Fredibalus. Sigonius, however, book XI of On the Western Empire, attributes it to Jordanes in his Annals, but I have found it nowhere in Jordanes.]

Fredibalus, king of the Vandal people [Note: He means the Siling Vandals, for Gunderic ruled the others.], having been cleverly captured without any battle, is sent to the Emperor Honorius [Note: Constantius sent him; Constantius was the one by whom Fredibalus was captured.].

Read “the sixth day of the week,” as was noted above under the year 402.]

Zosimus presides from the beginning of 417 as the forty-second among the Roman pontiffs.]

A knot occurs here which must necessarily be cut, since it cannot be untied in any way. Therefore the section beginning “While the bishop was in office…” must be transferred; you will find it after the two following sections, “The Vandals and Alans.” These notes, numbered XXV, must also be transferred with it. See note 29.]

While the bishop mentioned above was in office, and so forth (29).

The Short Chronicle omits the word “all.”]

They were destroyed.

Of the four barbarian kings whom I distinguished above under the year 411, with Atax now dead and Fredibalus dead in 416, only two remained: Hermeric of the Suevi and Gunderic of the Vandals.]

After the name of the kingdom had been abolished [Note: Other editions read: “After the name of the kingdom of King Gunderic had been abolished,” and so forth. I have erased the preposition de, which entered against the rules of grammar.], the few survivors, with their king Atax removed, submitted themselves to the protection of Gunderic, king of the Vandals, who had settled in Gallaecia.

67. While the bishop mentioned above was in office [Note: Above, under the year 415, Idatius mentions John; we learn from his Fasti that the same man is designated here. But John had died two or three years earlier. See note 30.], the holy places in Jerusalem were shaken by a very severe earthquake (30).

And other events [Note: Marcellinus mentions them in his Chronicle under the consuls of this year.] concerning the same bishop.

He means the war with the Vandals and Alans, mentioned earlier.]

They were recalled to Gaul by Constantius and received settlements in Aquitania [Note: Read Aquitania from the Short Chronicle, or secunda Aquitania from Isidore. Its capital was Bordeaux, and together with certain other cities of the neighboring provinces, as Prosper says, it was given by Honorius to the Goths in this year. From the neighboring provinces of Novempopulana and first Narbonensis, in which Toulouse lay, a portion was certainly assigned to Vallia.] extending from Toulouse to the Ocean.

Isidore, in his History of the Goths, assigns Vallia’s death to Spanish Era 457. See note 31.]

Theodoric (32) succeeds him in the kingdom [Note: The man whom Idatius calls Theodoric is called Teuderic, Theuderedus, Theudores, Theudoridus, Theodoricus, and Theudo by other writers. The Spaniards commonly call him Theodoredo. Concerning his lineage, see note 32.].

Other editions, with the exception of the Florentine, place Honorius’s twenty-fifth year here; but it has been shown above that it ought to be assigned to the section “While the bishop was in office,” and at the same time restored to its proper place, without fear that anyone might reproach the correction or deny that it reflects Idatius’s intention.]

68. When strife arose between Gunderic, king of the Vandals, and Hermeric, king of the Suevi, the Suevi were besieged by the Vandals in the mountains of Nervasius [Note: Ptolemy mentions the Tori Narbassi in the second map of Europe, a city which Ortelius places on the river Douro. Hence in the time of Idatius a mountain called Nervasius or Narbassus stood there; in antiquity it was called Herminius, not far from the modern city of Ciudad Rodrigo. Morales and Mariana hold a different view and think that the Nervasian Mountains mentioned here by Idatius are those now called the Arvas, between León and Oviedo.].

Valentinian, son of Constantius and Placidia, is born (33) [Note: Valentinian was certainly born this year, since Honoria was born earlier. See note 33.].

Asterius, or Asturicus—for Idatius and other writers call him by both names—was a man distinguished by the office of count, by command of both military branches, and finally by the consulship and the patriciate. More will be said about him under the year 449.]

[The Vandals], with Asterius as count of the Spains and with Maurocello as deputy [Note: From this passage we learn that at this time the Spains were administered through the deputy of the praetorian prefect of Gaul.], after some of them had been killed at Braga during their departure, left Gallaecia and crossed into Baetica.

At the end of the year 418, Boniface was elected the forty-fourth bishop of the Roman Church. These words, as also those read above concerning Anastasius under the year 397 and below concerning Leo under 441, appear to have been added by Idatius.]

The bishop Boniface presides.

Constantius’s inauguration is assigned to this year by Prosper and Cassiodorus; they deserve greater confidence than the Eastern Theophanes, who postpones it to the following year.]

He makes him his partner in the kingdom [Note: The printed books give Honorius’s twenty-seventh year here, contrary to Idatius’s clearest words, which force us to remove the notes belonging to that year from this place. See note 34.].

The Emperor Constantius dies at Ravenna in his third consulship (34).

I left this year blank because other editions place under it material that belongs to the preceding year, as explained above.]

In this same year Cassiodorus mentions this war. Prosper also mentions it, adding here and under the consuls Theodosius XL and Valentinian in the year 425 several further details about Castinus.]

When he had reduced them to such poverty by the force of the siege that they were already preparing to surrender, he rashly engaged them in open battle [Note: You will learn from Prosper and Salvian why this expedition turned out badly in note 35.], deceived by the treachery of his auxiliaries [Note: Prosper says nothing of this treachery, nor does Salvian. Castinus, growing proud and trusting in himself, rashly engaged and lost his army; for 20,000 of his men were killed, if we believe Prosper of Pithaeus.]. Defeated at Tarragona [Note: It is evident from this and other passages of Idatius that the Romans at that time retained Hispania Citerior, except for the province of Gallaecia.], he fled.

Prosper shows that Boniface, departing from Castinus, first reached Italy and then Africa. See note 35, paragraph 2.]

He invades Africa (35).

[Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]

[II.] CCCCXL.

Concerning the death of Honorius, our Idatius says in the Fasti, under the consuls Asclepiodotus and Maximianus: “In these consulships Honorius Augustus died at Ravenna.” Prosper, Marcellinus, and Cassiodorus likewise assign the death of Honorius to this year, which was the year 423 of the Dionysian era. Socrates, book VII, chapter 22, gives the day of his death as 15 August; Olympiodorus gives the 27th, which may perhaps be more accurate, even though Theophanes agrees with Socrates. Olympiodorus and others report that he died of dropsy. It is evident that he could not have celebrated his thirtieth anniversary after the year 423, since he died in that year. Why, then, did Idatius, who was not unaware of this, assign both his death and his tricennalia to the year 424? I shall explain my conjecture in note 36.]

[Note: From the Kalends of May in the year 408; for his father Arcadius died on that day.] In the eastern regions, after his father's death, he held sole rule of the empire after the death of his uncle Honorius [Note: He held sole rule because he alone was the legitimate prince; John, however, was a tyrant.], being twenty-six years old [Note: The copyist changed XXIV, which Idatius certainly wrote, into XXVI, placing the sign for one, I, after the sign for five, V, through an easy slip, when he should have placed it before it. See note 37.] (37).

John, formerly chief of the notaries, seized tyrannical power either at the end of 423, as Prosper says, or at the beginning of 424, as Idatius and Marcellinus record. Castinus and Aetius were his accomplices in the rebellion, according to Prosper.]

71. Theodosius makes Valentinian, the son of his aunt Placidia [Note: Olympiodorus reports that he was proclaimed Caesar at Thessalonica. See note 38.], Caesar at Constantinople and sends him against John (38).

Socrates, book VII, chapter 23, and Olympiodorus and Philostorgius give a detailed account of this expedition, which you may read if you wish. Its principal commanders were Ardaburius, Aspar, Candidianus, and Helion. See note 39.]

Felix is appointed patrician [Note: Prosper writes that Felix was made patrician during the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, that is, in 429.] from the position of master of the soldiers.

He is called Augustus (40).

Marcellinus says in his Chronicle that this occurred at Ravenna, but he is mistaken. See note 40.]

From this passage of Idatius, and especially from Isidore’s History of the Vandals, where he writes that the same islands were plundered by the Siling Vandals around the year 411, it is shown that Prosper’s statement concerning the Vandals under the consulship of Hierius and Ardaburius is not wholly true—namely, that until their crossing into Africa, which occurred in 429, they did not know how to use ships.]

72. Then, after Carthage in Spain [Note: This city suffered a greater disaster than Hispalis. This is demonstrated by what is reported about Hispalis under the year 428. Nor do I doubt that Carthage was then utterly destroyed.] and Hispalis had been overthrown and the Spains plundered, they invade Mauretania [Note: They invade it for plunder, not to remain there; that happened only four years later.].

The bishop Coelestinus presides. Coelestinus was created the forty-fifth pontiff in the year 422, in September.]

Thus, three years earlier, when these same Vandals attacked Hispalis, they neither completely devastated it nor retained it for themselves. It therefore remained under the Romans, under whom it had been, as Carthage had also been before that time.]

When he himself, in his arrogance, had stretched out his hands against the church of that city [Note: Saint Isidore, in his History of the Vandals, says that this church was dedicated to the martyr Vincent.], he was immediately seized by a demon through the judgment of God and died [Note: According to Isidore, in the passage cited above, Gunderic reigned for nineteen years, which cannot be counted from the arrival of the barbarians in…]
the Spains, in the year 409; but he seems to reckon from the division of the provinces made by them in 411. Yet, when he discusses Hermeric, king of the Sueves, he takes the beginning of his reign from the year 409.]

Gaiseric was his brother [Note: In Victor of Vita, Gaiseric is called *Geisericus*; nearly all the other writers call him *Gensericus*. He was the son of Godigisel and the brother of Gunderic, but by a mother of unequal status, as Procopius observes in Book I of his *History of the Vandals*, chapter 3; and, if we are to believe Sidonius, she was a slave woman. For, speaking of him in the *Panegyric on Anthemius*, line 358, he says:]

He loudly proclaims an uncertain father, although a slave woman is his certain parent [lacuna] succeeds to the kingdom. According to the report of some, having become an apostate, he is said to have passed from the Catholic faith into the treachery of Arianism.

After the multitude of the Vandals whom Gaiseric was taking with him had been counted—those found, says Victor at the beginning of Book I, numbered eighty thousand: old men, young men, little children, slaves, and masters—and after seventy-three of their families had been left behind in the month of May, he crossed from the Spains to Mauritania and Africa (41).

[Note: Gaiseric began his African kingdom in this year, in which, as Hydatius relates, he invaded Africa. See Note 41.]

Before he crossed, having been warned that Hermigarius the Sueve was plundering the neighboring provinces along his route, he turned back with a small number of his men and caught up with the plunderer in Lusitania. Not far from Emerita—which he had scorned to the injury of the holy martyr Eulalia—after many of those whom he had with him had been slain by Gaiseric, Hermigarius, having caught, as he thought, in the Eurus a more rapid aid to flight, was hurled by the divine arm into the river Ana and perished. With him thus destroyed, Gaiseric soon sailed away toward the place where he had begun.

[Note: It was noted above, under the year 411, that this Hermeric was king of the Sueves; and he ruled alone and together with his son Rechita until the year 441, as Hydatius frequently repeats. Therefore Hermigarius, mentioned shortly before, must have been some Suevic commander or prefect. Florius makes Hermigarius king and falsely asserts that Hermeric succeeded him, vol. XIII, p. 82.]

While they were plundering the central regions of Gallaecia, the populace, who held the safer forts [Note: Hydatius often mentions that the Spaniards, upon the Barbarians’ arrival, fled to cities and forts, where they defended their freedom against the enemy’s attacks; this was explained in Note 22.], having inflicted partly slaughter and partly captivity upon their men, compelled them to restore the peace which they had broken by returning the families who were being held.

[Note: Prosper does not accurately record this war as having occurred six years earlier. Isidore adds several details about it. See Note 42.]

Having captured Anaolfus, one of their nobles (74).

Sidonius mentions this war in the panegyric of Avitus, saying in verse 233:

> For after the Juthungi and Noric wars had been subdued ...

Victor of Vindelicia. . . . . See Sirmond on the same passage. Meanwhile, do not be surprised that, after the Gothic war had ended at the beginning of this year, another war with the Juthungi was conducted in the summer and thereafter.]

and Nori[?]. Felix, who was called the patrician, is killed in a military mutiny at Ravenna [Note: That this Felix was a wicked man is shown by what Prosper relates about Patroclus, bishop of Arles, and Titus, a Roman deacon, who were killed at his command. See note 43.]. The author of this Chronicle.]

An embassy is undertaken to Aetius, the general who was conducting a campaign in Gaul (44) [Note: From the following entry it appears that this campaign was undertaken against the Franks, whom Aetius drove back beyond the Rhine. Prosper discusses it prematurely. See note 44.]. Vetto [Note: What deceptions Vetto contrived, since Hydatius is silent, we cannot determine.], who had come deceitfully from the Goths into Gallaecia, returns to the Goths without accomplishing anything.

Censorius, a comes of the Roman party, is sent as ambassador to the Suebi, with Hydatius, mentioned above, returning with him. Censorius was not employed on only one embassy to the Suebi. Hydatius mentions him in the years 433, 437, and 448.]

Boniface was in many respects an outstanding man and, according to Olympiodorus, exceptionally loyal toward Placidia. If you want more about him, see note 45.] After Aetius had been driven out, Boniface succeeded him; but a few months later, having engaged Aetius in battle, he died from the wound he had received. His son-in-law Sebastianus was appointed in his place, but Aetius defeated him after he had left the palace and drove him out [Note: Sebastianus was expelled from the palace by Aetius not in this year but in the second year afterward, as Hydatius relates there. But since he had just been speaking of Boniface his father-in-law, Hydatius now added this account of Sebastianus so that what both men suffered through Aetius’ jealousy might be displayed together before the eyes of his readers.].

Since Censorius and Hermeric could not agree about peace, Censorius departed, while the bishops of the province exerted their influence; peace was finally established, with the Gallaecians handing over certain hostages to Hermeric. But in order that it might be confirmed in the name of the Romans, Hermeric sent Bishop Symphosius to the imperial court; but in vain. Hope of peace there was completely broken off. This is how I understand the two sections of Hydatius. Do I not understand it? For *arreptis* read *abruptis*. And know that this Symphosius is different from the one mentioned in the year 400, in the account of the Council of Toledo.]

In the diocese of Agrestius, although he was not the metropolitan, a foreign bishop could not perform this act without his consent. Therefore Quesnellus wrongly infers from this passage of Hydatius that Lugo was at that time a metropolitan see.] Pastor [Note: Is this Pastor the man of whom Gennadius speaks, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 76? The subject of the book and the date itself also suit him, a Spanish bishop.], and Syagrius are ordained bishops.

[Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [II.] 450.

Hydatius has already mentioned above that Sebastianus was expelled by Aetius. He repeats the same matter now because, in fact, Sebastianus fled to the East this year. Read the account from Prosper in note 46.] He sails to the palace of the East (46).

Xistus, or Sixtus, was proclaimed Roman pontiff in May of the year 432.] Bishop Xistus is in office.

Juvenal was indeed presiding over the Church of Jerusalem in this year, and Hydatius reports this correctly; but he had obtained that episcopate long before. He was discussed in note 30.]

From the report of Germanus, a presbyter of the Arabian region, and of other Greeks who subsequently came to Gallaecia, we learned that he had been summoned to Constantinople with other bishops of the province of Palestine and of the East, and that, in the presence of the emperor Theodosius, he had taken part in the council of bishops convened [Note: This council was held at Ephesus in the year 431. Therefore either Germanus and the other Greeks did not indicate to Hydatius the time at which it was convened, or Hydatius, when writing this, had forgotten it. Juvenal joined it during the octave of Pentecost, and there energetically defended the interests of his Church, perhaps more than was proper.], to destroy the heresy of the Ebionites [Note: Cassianus also calls Nestorius a heretic Ebionite, *On the Incarnation*, book I. Yet Ebion alone was not the teacher of his heresy: he also had Paul of Samosata and the two Theodores, of Mopsuestia and of Tarsus.], which Nestorius, bishop of that same city [Note: Constantinople.], was reviving by the perverse ingenuity of a most foolish sect.

See note 30 concerning the year of John’s death.] The report of the informants did not state whether Jerome [Note: Concerning Jerome, Prosper writes under the year 420: “Jerome the presbyter,” he says, “dies in the ninety-first year of his age, on the day before the Kalends of October.” There is no disagreement about the year of Jerome’s death, but there is some about his age. See Pagius, year 420, no. 21.] and the others whom we mentioned above [Note: Besides John and Jerome, Hydatius previously praised two others: Eulogius of Caesarea and Theophilus of Alexandria, under the year 407. Theophilus died on the Ides of October in the year 412, according to Socrates, book VII, chapter 7. Eulogius is known to have held first place at the Synod of Diospolis, which was held after 20 December 415. I have not yet been able to discover how long Eulogius lived after that.] had died, or who had succeeded John before Juvenal—although it is known that a certain elder did so shortly afterward (47) [Note: The elder who succeeded John in the Church of Jerusalem was Praylius. Hydatius did not know his name, but expressly testifies that he died shortly afterward. Hence Papebrochius’ opinion that Praylius died before the year 421, against Cardinal Noris and Pagius, is confirmed. See note 47.].

Prosper and Cassiodorus assign this rebellion to the consulship of the year 435; but perhaps it began in that year and ended in this one.] They are defeated by the Romans under the leadership of Aetius.

Thus Cyril and Nestorius held the episcopate at the same time for three years and nearly three months, from the beginning of April 428 to the end of July 431: the former at Alexandria, the latter at Constantinople. But this was already the sixth year since Nestorius had been expelled from the Church of Constantinople.] A letter of Cyril himself to the same man, both destroying the heresy and setting forth the rule of faith, demonstrates this.

These writings, together with others [Note: See note 48 concerning these writings of Cyril.], are produced (48).

Concerning the liberation of the city of Narbonne under the consulship of the year 436, in which, as Hydatius records, its siege began, Prosper writes: “The Goths disrupt the terms of peace and occupy many towns near their own settlements, being especially hostile to the town of Narbonne, which, after suffering for a long time from siege and famine, was freed from both dangers by the comes Litorius.”] Under the command and military leadership of Aetius [Note: It was not under the command of Aetius but of Litorius, as Prosper says, that Narbonne was liberated—a fact Hydatius did not fail to know. The passage must therefore be punctuated so that “under the command of Aetius” is joined with what follows, not with what precedes.], twenty thousand Burgundians are killed (49).

The Goths had not withdrawn from the siege of Narbonne because they had withdrawn from the war. Therefore, while they were fighting Aetius, eight thousand of them were killed.] Eight thousand Goths are killed under the command of Aetius.

Between the Suebi and the Gallaecians peace was never stable; at times there were brief truces. Censorius and Fretimundus, who had come the previous year as ambassadors from the Romans to the Suebi, seem to have arranged this sort of peace between the two sides.] They bring it to an end.

Isidore, in his *History of the Suebi*, has the same account and adds that Hermeric, previously afflicted by illness, made peace with the Gallaecians—the peace of which Hydatius has just spoken. He also notes that Andevotus was a general of the Roman army. From this it seems that at that time the Romans possessed under their authority, besides the towns and fortresses in Gallaecia that were held by the natives in their name, the remaining provinces of Spain as well—unless the Suebi had already torn away some portion of Lusitania.]

Singilio is now called the Genil by the Spaniards.] At the river of Baetica he defeated him in open battle, taking possession of his great riches in gold and silver.

Marcellinus wrongly assigns the destruction of Carthage to the tenth day before the Kalends of October; for Prosper gives the same day as Hydatius and asserts that the city was captured by treachery. Hydatius records its destruction in the year 439, not 438 as Pagius says. See note 50.] On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, King Gaiseric invades all Africa.

He means the Huns whom Litorius was leading with him as auxiliaries, as Prosper makes clear under this year.] He himself, wounded, is captured [Note: This is explained more fully from Prosper and Salvianus. See note 51.] and killed a few days later (51).

I demonstrate in note 52 that the Romans sought and obtained this peace, contrary to Prosper’s account.] Peace is established between the Romans and the Goths (52).

Gaiseric, impiously exalted, expels the bishop and clergy of Carthage from the city [Note: Victor of Vita vividly depicts Gaiseric’s cruelty toward the Catholics throughout book I of *The Vandal Persecution*. The bishop was Quodvultdeus; that he was expelled from his Church in this year is conclusively demonstrated by this passage of Hydatius.]. And, in accordance with the prophecy of Daniel [Note: He understands the “abomination of desolation” foretold by Daniel in chapter 11:31, which we read that Antiochus brought into the Temple at Jerusalem in book II of *2 Maccabees*, chapter 6.], having changed the ministers, he hands over the holy Catholic churches to the Arians.

It is evident that Rechila was energetic and warlike: he deprived the Romans of several provinces, namely Lusitania, Baetica, and Carthaginensis. See below, under the year 441. Isidore asserts that he retained Emerita, which he had seized, for himself thereafter.] He enters.

From the time Gaiseric captured Carthage, he immediately harassed all the coastal provinces of both empires with raids. See note 53.]

Those who had been condemned by the Catholic bishops of Maximinus [Note: This is, I think, the Maximinus with whom Augustine of Hippo held that disputation which is included among Augustine’s works. See note 54.], the Arian general in Sicily, are driven, at his instigation, against the Catholics, so that he might compel them by any means whatever to embrace Arian impiety. Some withdrew; others, persevering in the Catholic faith, completed their martyrdom.

Hydatius speaks of this embassy above, under the year 437. After undertaking it, Censorius remained in Spain.] While residing at Myrtilis [Note: This is a town of Lusitania on the farther bank of the river Ana, now called Mértola with little alteration of its name.], he surrenders himself to Rechila, who has besieged him, in exchange for peace.

Isidore relates the same events in his *History of the Suebi* and notes that Hermeric reigned for thirty-two years. Since he died in this year—for Hydatius, who was living among the Suebi, testifies to this, and Isidore habitually copies him—his reign must have begun in the year 409 and ended in 441. Therefore, at the beginning of the Suebi history, the era should have been recorded as 447, and at Hermeric’s death as era 479, not the other dates, as Floresius had already observed, volume VI of *Sacred Spain*, p. 526.] He retains the same provinces in the year 446.] He brings the provinces under his own authority.

Since Leo’s pontificate is again recorded below under the year 447, these words were certainly written by someone other than Hydatius and appended to the Chronicle; for that Hydatius knew nothing of Leo’s election in the current year 445 is shown especially by the words found there: “through the bishop then presiding at Rome,” and so forth. Certainly, if he had known the pontiff’s name, he would not have spoken in that way but would have said, “through Leo,” and so on.] Epiphanius is ordained in his place by fraud, not by right.

The *Short Chronicle* says of this Sabinus under era 495: “After twenty years, having been expelled from Gaul, where he had contended, he returned to his own Church.” Therefore, if he was expelled this year, he could not have returned before era 499.]

Asturius [Note: He calls him Astericus in the year 420, but now calls him Asturius; likewise in the years 443 and 449.], general of both armies, is sent to Spain and massacres a multitude of Bagaudae in Tarraconensis (55) [Note: See note 55 concerning the faction of the Bagaudae.].

Marcellinus mentions this comet under the consulship of Eudoxius and Dioscorus. From this passage we learn again that Hydatius reckons the years not from October to October but from January to January. For the December of Abraham’s year 2458, to which Hydatius attaches this comet under the year 441, could not coincide with the December of the common era 442, when these men were consuls, unless his year began in January.] It appeared for several months and presaged the subsequent plague, which spread through almost the whole world.

At this time Flavianus did not yet preside over the Church of Constantinople; after Nestorius was expelled from it in the year 451, he was not his immediate successor. For after Nestorius, Maximianus ruled that Church for three years, then Patroclus for thirteen years. Finally Flavianus held that episcopate in the year 447.]

You will find these matters concerning our fellow countryman Merobaudes confirmed in note 56.] In the short period of his power he breaks the insolence of the Aracellitani [Note: Pliny, book III, chapter 3, mentions the Arocelitani, whom he assigns to the conventus of Caesaraugusta and declares to have been tributaries. Whether Pliny’s Arocelitani, Florus’ Arracillum, Orosius’ Aracillum, and the place called Aracoelim by Antoninus are entirely the same as those whom Hydatius here calls Aracellitani is uncertain. But it is very likely that all refer to the same town, which still exists and is commonly called Araciel, as Zurita believes.], the Bagaudae. Soon, as the jealousy of certain men pressed him, he is summoned to the city of Rome by an imperial order.

[Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [II.] 460.

Ten years earlier Hydatius related Sebastianus’ flight to the palace of the East. Prosper reports that he crossed from there into Africa in the year 440, whereas Hydatius says that he came from the East to Aquitaine in this year and migrated from Spain to Africa in the following year. See note 57.] He enters as an enemy (57).

Hydatius and Turibius composed these acts after being prompted by Leo’s example. Did they send them to Antonius of Emerita as metropolitan? See note 58.] They were sent to Bishop Antonius of Emerita, who had heard them.

Hydatius mentions that Turonius was attached to the episcopate by a division, supposedly made at the Council of Lugo, held in era 607; this division counts Turonius among the parishes of the bishopric of Tui. In the year 1171 the count of Urgell, ruling in Limia and Turonius, confirmed the privilege which Floresius reproduces in volume XVI of *Sacred Spain*. His name was Armengaudus, and he died in the year 1184, as Zurita and Mariana relate.] Suddenly transported to the shore of Gallaecia, they seize the families of many people.

Sebastianus, driven out of Barcelona, migrates to the Vandals [Note: Sidonius calls Sebastianus headlong, *Carmen* IX, 277, because, following varied and sudden plans, he seemed unable to remain long in the same state of mind.].

This was Leo the Great.] Accounts [Note: Prosper reveals the reason why Leo sent these acts to the provinces in the previous year, saying: “From the confessions of the Manichaeans captured in the city, it became known who their teachers were, who among them were bishops or presbyters, and in what provinces or cities they lived.” Once the Manichaeans had been detected, therefore, they were denounced to the provinces, so that the provinces might beware of them.] concerning the Manichaeans are sent throughout the provinces.

Vitus was sent by Valentinian to free Spain from the Suebi yoke, but instead ravaged it himself.] When he was harassing the Carthaginienses and the Baetici, and the Suebi were arriving there with their king, the Goths who had come to assist him in plundering were defeated in an engagement; terrified by miserable fear, he fled. The Suebi then laid waste to those provinces with extensive devastation.

Bishop Leo presides over the Roman Church from July of the year 440, in the forty-eighth succession.] His writings against the Priscillianists are brought to the bishops of Spain through Pervincus, the deacon of Bishop Turibius. Among them, a lengthy disputation concerning the observance of the Catholic faith and the blasphemies of the heresies is sent to Bishop Turibius (59) [Note: Hydatius touches here on many matters that cannot be explained in a brief scholium. See note 59.], and some of the Gallaecians approve it by a deceitful judgment.

Under the year 402 I warned that one should read “the tenth day before the Kalends of January,” not “the ninth day before the Kalends,” because the eclipse in fact occurred that year on 23 December, which fell on the Tuesday designated by Hydatius, whereas 24 December was Wednesday. Pagius and Calvisius must likewise be corrected. Concerning these matters, see note 60.] which was Tuesday.

The Suebi were pagans. Rechiarius was the first of their kings to profess the Catholic faith. But after his death, seduced by a certain Galatian named Atacius, they fell into Arian impiety in the year 466, as Hydatius relates there. Finally, under King Theodemir, around the year 560, they renounced it and became Catholics through the preaching of Saint Martin of Dumio. Thus Isidore in his *History of the Suebi.*] He succeeds to the kingdom, with certain rivals from his own nation secretly opposing him. Once he had obtained the kingdom, however, he immediately invaded the farther regions for plunder.

Was this Pascentius fleeing from Rome while Leo was there, and from Asturica while Turibius and Hydatius were investigating the Manichaeans there?] Antonius the bishop captures a Manichaean who had fled from Asturica, examines him, and also causes the man to be expelled from the province of Lusitania [Note: Observe here the right and ancient custom of bishops to act against heretics.].

At Hispalis Censorius is slaughtered.

The *Short Chronicle* calls him Agiulfus. In the *Gothic History*, no. 74, Jordanes writes that Athiulfus was born from the stock of the Varni and was far removed from the nobility of Gothic blood. He seems at this time to have attached himself to the Suebi. Since Censorius was among them, having surrendered himself to their king at Myrtilis, he could have been slaughtered by Ajulfus—whether justly or unjustly, let the reader decide.]

The name of this daughter of Theodoric is nowhere, so far as I know, reported, nor is the year in which she married Rechiarius.] At the beginning of his reign, he ravages the Vascones in the month of February.

Basil may perhaps have risen from the rebellious leader of the Bagaudae; his bold action would have consisted in descending from forests and the rugged, precipitous ridges of the mountains into open and level places, and bringing war upon towns and provinces. But these are conjectures.]

As evidence of his outstanding daring, having assembled the Bagaudae at Tyriassone, he kills the federated troops [Note: Should Hydatius understand *foederati* as soldiers who were so called, or more simply as the people assembled in the church? Let the reader decide. The former seems more probable, for Hydatius does not expressly say that this slaughter took place in a church, nor does he seem likely to call the populace and citizens “federates.” Tyriasson is called Turiaso by some and Turiasso by others; but on coins the form Turiaso is consistently found. It is now commonly called Tarazona.]. There also Leo, the bishop of that same Church, dies wounded by the same men who were present there with Basil.

[Note: Here too, as above, when Hydatius mentions the consulship of Constantius, a chronological notation was anticipated by the copyist. In both places, after the name of the consulship was read—as though a new year were beginning—a new number was written, although in both cases it should have been recorded one line later. I think no one will doubt that Hydatius himself wrote the text otherwise; for that reason I did not hesitate to correct both passages.]

Asturius, an illustrious man (61) [Note: I said something about Asturius under the year 420. See note 61.], is elevated to the honor of the consulship.

The year 26, which the copyist inserted prematurely under the section concerning Asturius, was certainly recorded by Hydatius here or in the following section concerning Gaul. See note 63, no. 2.] Sebastianus (62) [Note: See note 62 concerning Sebastianus.], having become an exile, fled to the power of Gaiseric, to his own ruin, as the outcome later demonstrated. A short time after he had arrived, Gaiseric ordered him to be killed.

Saint Leo sent these writings from Gaul to Spain. From this Quesnellus foolishly seized an opportunity to exalt the Gallic bishops and disparage the Spanish bishops. See note 63, no. 1.] Letters of Bishop Flavianus sent to Bishop Leo [Note: There are two letters, found after the eighth among the Leonine letters in the old editions.] are brought from Gaul [Note: I have enclosed this in parentheses so that it might not be joined with what follows; for it certainly belongs with the preceding words, which should be connected as follows: “From Gaul letters are brought, sent by Bishop Flavianus to Bishop Leo, concerning Eutyches, etc.” For Cyril’s writings attacked Nestorius, not Eutyches. I discussed these writings of Cyril in note 48.] together with the writings of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to Nestorius of Constantinople, concerning Eutyches, the Ebionite heretic [Note: I have absolutely no idea why Eutyches is called an Ebionite. For Eutyches was so far from the heresy of Ebion, which taught that Christ was merely human, that he inclined toward the opposite error of Apollinaris, who denied the human element in Christ—although Flavianus, speaking of him, says: “He confirmed the impiety of Nestorius and girded himself to fight on Nestorius’ behalf.” These words may have led Hydatius into error, since Nestorius was an Ebionite. But Avitus of Vienne, writing after Hydatius, also applied the errors of Nestorius to Eutyches in letter 2.], and the replies of Bishop Leo to that same man [Note: Leo replied to Flavianus in the celebrated letter beginning *Having read your beloved letter*, concerning the faith of the Incarnation. Cardinal Noris unjustly attributes this letter to Prosper rather than to Leo. See note 63, nos. 3 and 4.], which, together with the acts and writings of other bishops [Note: Flavianus mentions these acts in letter 1, formerly numbered 2, and Leo in letter formerly numbered 16.], are circulated throughout the Churches.

I have unhesitatingly erased the note 27 inserted at this point against the manifest intention of Hydatius, as I demonstrated in the preface and shall shortly demonstrate again.]

The emperor Theodosius dies at Constantinople in the forty-eighth year of his age (64) [Note: Theodosius died after completing the forty-ninth year of his life. See note 64.].

XLII passes into XLIII, with XLII omitted. This is of little importance, but it should nevertheless be noted.]

Immediately [Note: The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle records the beginning of Marcian’s reign under the consuls of this year in the following words: “Marcian was ordered by the army to reign at Hebdomon in the month of August, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, on Thursday.” Yet he is mistaken either about the month or about the day of the week; for in this year 25 August fell not on Thursday but on Friday.] at Constantinople, Marcian is made emperor by the soldiers and the army, with Theodosius’ sister, Queen Pulcheria, also pressing the matter [Note: He calls Pulcheria “queen” in accordance with the custom of that age. For daughters and sisters of the Augusti were commonly so called. Cyril of Alexandria sent two books to Pulcheria and her sisters, entitled *On the Faith to the Queens*. Moreover, if I remember correctly, Claudian somewhere honors Serena, daughter of Theodosius the Great’s brother Honorius, with the title of queen. Pulcheria, for her part, was proclaimed Augusta by her brother Theodosius in the year 414, as Marcellinus and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle relate.], and, having taken her in marriage [Note: Pulcheria had given a pledge concerning her virginity, which she had vowed to God, that it would not be violated.], he rules in the regions of the East.

In other editions it reads as follows: “In the twenty-eighth year of the emperor Valentinian, his mother Placidia dies at Rome.” I deleted the chronological notation and the three preceding words. See note 65, no. 1.] Placidia dies at Rome (65).

These details plainly show that Hydatius appended the same event under the Dionysian year 450 and Valentinian’s twenty-sixth year; for in that year 4 April fell on Tuesday, since the solar cycle was XI and the dominical letter A.]

After sunset, from the northern quarter the sky becomes red like fire or blood, with brighter lines intermingled through the fiery redness and distorted into the appearance of gleaming spears [Note: Antiquity believed that signs and portents of this kind announced something by divine will; nor does the author of *2 Maccabees*, chapter 5, compel us to believe that this interpretation was always false. Even now there is nothing to prevent us from saying that God wished through these signs to give warning of that dreadful and deadly war of Attila, as Hydatius and, with him, Isidore suggest. But if anyone wishes to recognize no portent here and instead has recourse to what is called the northern aurora, let him enjoy his own judgment.]. The display of the sign lasts from nightfall until approximately the third hour, and is soon made fully known by a great outcome [Note: He means the battle against Attila.].

Hydatius inserted these notes, XXVII. I, at this point; the copyists improperly dragged them backward to the section concerning Placidia. See note 66.] The nation of the Huns (66), having broken the peace, ravages the provinces of Gaul. Many cities are breached [Note: Much concerning this war against Attila is found in Paul the Deacon, book XV, and in Jordanes, no. 60. In addition, in the longer Acts of Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, on 29 July, you will find considerable material concerning the provinces devastated by Attila and the cities plundered or even destroyed. Hadrian Valesius collected nearly all these and many other matters in volume I of *The History of France*, book IV.].

In the Catalaunian fields (67) [Note: Gregory of Tours calls these fields the Mauriac plain. They had both names, according to Jordanes, no. 6. See note 67 concerning their location.], not far from the city which they had breached, Metz, they engage in open battle with the general Aetius and King Theodoric, who were allied in peace (68) [Note: Hydatius counts only the Goths as allies of Aetius in this battle. Sidonius explicitly says that the Franks were also with Attila. Therefore Pagius and other Gallic writers tell improbable stories when they claim that Merovech, king of the Franks, joined Aetius with his men, and that they had a large or even principal share in the victory won over Attila. See note 68.]. They are defeated, slain by divine aid. Nightfall interrupted the battle. King Theodoric fell there and died [Note: I shall discuss Theodoric’s death, kingdom, and sons in note 69.], and about 300,000 men are counted as having been killed in that battle (69).

This date must be corrected, as I explained under the year 402, and I warned on the authority of Petavius that VI Kalends should be restored in place of V Kalends. This eclipse of the sun now supplies us with a further argument by which to demonstrate the copyists’ negligence. For it is incredible that Hydatius, who recorded the years of eclipses with such precision, would have placed this one under Valentinian’s twenty-eighth year, that is, the year of Christ 452. Therefore he recorded it under Valentinian’s twenty-seventh year, the year of Christ 451.] On the eastern side the moon is darkened.

On the days of the following Easter [Note: I fear that Hydatius may have written “of the preceding Easter”; for if this belonged to the following year, why would he have appended it to the present year? I shall say something about Euphronius in note 67.], certain phenomena seen in the sky over the regions of Gaul are clearly demonstrated by a letter concerning them written by Euphronius, bishop of Autun, to the comes Agrippinus.

A comet begins to appear on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July; on the third day before the Kalends, it is seen at dawn in the East and immediately after sunset in the western quarter; on the Kalends of August it appears in the western quarter.

Theodoricus, Jordanes says, left four sons at home—Frederic, Turic (read Euric), Rotemer, and Himmerit—and took with him only Thorismund and Theodoricus as companions in the struggle; that is, he brought them with him to war against Attila. From this we learn that Thorismund succeeded his father by precedence of age, though by election. The kingdom was conferred upon him amid the shouts and rejoicing of the soldiers; for at that very moment, as Jordanes relates, no. 6, while the Goths were still paying the last rites to Theodoric, with the clash of weapons they were conferring royal majesty upon Thurismund. Observe here that the man whom Hydatius calls Thorismo is called Thorismod by Prosper, Thorismund by Jordanes, and Thurismund by Isidore.]

He ascends the throne.

Hydatius never designates the years of rulers by anything other than numerical signs. Therefore he does not seem to have recorded Marcian’s first year with words of this kind; otherwise, in so clear a matter, that first year could not have escaped the copyists’ eyes—as it plainly did, since we do not find it designated in the Chronicle. These words, therefore, are interpolated and ought to have been removed here and in the following years, with the numerical signs restored. I restored the signs, but retained the words as well, so as not to remove anything from the old editions.] That is, in the second year of the reign of the emperor Marcian.

The Huns, who were ravaging Italy and had also broken into certain cities, are struck by heavenly blows, partly through famine and partly through some disease. Auxiliaries sent by the emperor Marcian under the command of Aetius also attack and slaughter them. Likewise, in their own settlements, they are subdued both by heavenly afflictions and by the army of Marcian; [Note: It is evident from this that in this year the war with the Huns was conducted both in Pannonia and in Italy under the auspices of Marcian.] and thus, having been subdued and having made peace with the Romans, they return to their own settlements.

Their king Attila soon returned there [Note: Attila, the savage enemy of the human race, was conquered and killed not so much by the weapons of soldiers as by heavenly power, as Hydatius indicates. See note 70.] and died (70).

Mansuetus, comes of the Spaniards insofar as they were subject to the Romans, and Fronto [Note: Hydatius mentions this Fronto again under the year 456. He was an Arvernian and is praised by Sidonius, book IV, letter 21.], likewise a comes, are sent as ambassadors for peace and obtain the conditions imposed.

Tyro Prosper writes under the consuls of the following year: “Among the Goths settled within Gaul, dissension arose among the sons of King Theodoric, of whom Thorismund, the eldest, had succeeded his father. Since the king was undertaking measures opposed both to Roman peace and to Gothic tranquility, he was killed by his brothers because he persisted irrevocably in harmful designs. Gregory, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 7, relates that Thorismund subdued the Alans in war.] He is slaughtered by his brothers Theodoricus and Frederic (71) [Note: I shall discuss the year of Thorismund’s death in note 71.], and Theodoric succeeds him in the kingdom.

Opposite the third year of Marcian, the printed books give Abraham’s year 2470; namely, because the number of the rulers’ years was increased above the section concerning the emperor Theodosius, it followed that the calculation reached that year of Abraham earlier than it should have.] That is, in the third year of the reign of the emperor Marcian.

Queen Pulcheria dies in the month of July (72) [Note: Marcellinus and the Alexandrian Chronicle also testify that the blessed Pulcheria died this year, during the consulship of Vincomalus and Opilio. Cardinal Noris and Pagius wrongly disagree with Hydatius concerning the month. See note 72.].

Through Frederic, the brother of King Theodoric, the Bagaudae of Tarraconensis are slaughtered by Roman authority [Note: Because Frederic conducted this war under the auspices of the Roman Empire, not in the Gothic name, he is said to have killed the Bagaudae by Roman authority.]

[Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [II.] 470.

Here I shall show in note 73 that the signs XXX. IV, designating Valentinian’s thirtieth year and Marcian’s fourth, have fallen out, and I did not hesitate to restore them here, although they are omitted in the other editions.]

The general Aetius (73), a patrician, having been deceitfully summoned alone into the palace, is killed by the hand of the emperor Valentinian himself [Note: Procopius, book I of *The Vandal War*, relates that Valentinian, deceived by the eunuchs—Prosper names only Heraclius under the consuls of this year, and Marcellinus mentions the same man under the following consulship—believed that Aetius was plotting against him. He accuses Maximus of being the author of this deception; Hydatius hints at the same thing below, and Marcellinus expressly asserts it. Moreover, Sidonius, *Carmen* V, 203, disclosed that Aetius and his wife, whom he says was descended from Gothic and royal blood, desired the empire for their son Gaudentius. Prosper also records in its proper place that Aetius favored the tyranny of John. Finally, at this very time he was pressing insistently for another of Valentinian’s daughters to marry his son. Yet who could deny that Aetius was a man renowned in war and peace?]. Along with him, several distinguished men who had been admitted individually through his sword-bearer are slaughtered.

The printed books read: XXXI. In the fourth year of the reign of the emperor Marcian. I deleted these words and added the note V, because it is clear from what has been said that Hydatius assigned Marcian’s fifth year here.]
