By two barbarians, companions of Aetius [Note: Marcellinus calls these barbarians Optila and Transtila; Jordanes’ *On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths* differs little from him.], Valentinian, emperor at Rome, is killed in the Campus [Note: In the Campus Martius, as Marcellinus explicitly says under the consuls of this year.], while the army surrounds him, in the thirty-sixth year of his age [Note: Cuspinianus, uncertain, says that Maximus was elevated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, while Marianus Scotus reports that Valentinian was killed one day earlier, that is, on 16 March. Valentinian therefore lived thirty-six years, eight months, and fifteen days; he was in the thirtieth year of his reign from the tenth day before the Kalends of November of the preceding year. Cardinal Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 13, records these matters less accurately than was fitting for a chronologist. Hydatius, however, made two years—year I and year XXXI—from fewer than five complete months of the reign, as he also did in the case of Avitus.] and the thirty-first year of his reign.

Immediately afterward, Maximus, one of the former consuls, is proclaimed Augustus at Rome.

When he had become emperor, he took Valentinian’s widow as his wife and gave Valentinian’s daughter in marriage to his own son by a former wife, Palladius, whom he had made Caesar (74) [Note: Which daughter? Placidia or Eudocia? No one explains. See Note 74.] He was racked by anxiety over the great disturbances that he feared; and because he had directed criminal schemes, carried out in pursuit of the throne, against those killed by Valentinian and against Valentinian’s own death [the transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain], he wished to abandon the empire [Note: Sidonius expresses the same view. In Book II, chapter 13, he says of Maximus: “He was suffering beneath the crown a kind of dizziness from boundless power. Nor could he bear to be master, since he had not borne being under a master.”] and Rome [p. 95], scarcely four months of his reign having been completed, he was killed in the very city amid a popular tumult and a military revolt (75) [Note: The same Sidonius writes the following about the death of Maximus in Poem VII, line 441:

Meanwhile, the Vandal, with stealthy, unsuspected arms,

captures you (Rome), and the Burgundian, by treacherous leadership,

wrests from you your trembling wrath to slay the ruler.

Here he suggests that Maximus perished under the guidance or by the hand of some Burgundian. Others relate the matter differently. Note 75.

Avitus was, of course, an Arvernian.

He was first proclaimed emperor by the Gallic army and by the leading men at Toulouse, and thereafter at Arles.

[Note: Sidonius, *Carmen* VII, relates that Theodoric the Visigoth, while Avitus was at Toulouse in the king’s palace, was the author of his assumption of power. He says that Avitus accepted it reluctantly, so that, through that king’s influence and assistance, he might come to the aid of the state. But it was fitting that a son-in-law should conceal his father-in-law’s ambition and keep silent about all that Avitus did in order to be proclaimed Augustus by the Gallic army, with the consent of the Goths. He was elevated, as the Cuspinian Anonymous puts it, on 10 July.]

Concerning this proclamation of Avitus, Sidonius says in *Carmen* VII, 574:

> A crash fills the halls  
>   
> of Ugernum, where, by chance, a pious throng—the senate—  
>   
> had brought its force, its vows, and prayers. The place, the hour, and the day
It is said to have been prosperous under imperial rule. Ugernum, however, was a fortress belonging to the people of Arles. For this reason Idatius says that Avitus was proclaimed Augustus at Arles.], he was called Augustus and proceeded to Rome, where he was received [Note: That Avitus was received by the Romans, as Idatius relates, is confirmed by the panegyric delivered to him at Rome by Sidonius.]. This note I designates not the beginning of a new year but the beginning of Avitus’s reign. Note 76.] as the forty-third [Note: He is now counted as the forty-third emperor.] emperor of the Romans, while Marcianus [Note: The printed books incorrectly give the fourth year instead of the fifth.] was already holding sole rule in the fifth year of his reign.

Through Avitus, who had been both proclaimed and received as emperor by the Romans, envoys were sent to Marcianus on behalf of the unity of the empire. Thus also relate Marcellinus in his *Chronicle*, Jordanes in his book *On the Succession of Events and Times*, Paul the Deacon in book 15, and others.], before Avitus became Augustus [Note: These words clearly indicate that Idatius is still relating the events of the year 455 and of Marcianus’s fifth year, with which he joined the first year of Avitus, just as above he joined the first year of Arcadius and Honorius with the seventeenth of Theodosius. But this has been discussed in the note mentioned above, note 76.], entered Rome, and after plundering the wealth [Note: On this sack of the city Prosper writes: “After fourteen days, Rome was emptied of all its wealth by a secure and unrestricted search, and many thousands of captives, selected according to the age or skill of each, were carried away to Carthage with the queen and her daughters.” Prosper’s account was copied by the author of the *Miscellany*, book 15. The queen was Eudoxia; her daughters were Eudocia and Placidia.] of the Romans, he returned to Carthage, taking with him Valentinian’s widow, his two daughters, and Aetius’s son Gaudentius by name.

Isidore, in his *History of the Sueves*, records that Rechila restored these provinces to the Romans. Rechila, however, died in the year 448.], they plundered. Marcianus and Avitus exercised imperial authority in concord.

At the beginning of the new civil year, which was the year 456 of the common era, Idatius designated the sixth year of Marcianus and the second of Avitus—for it is his custom, whenever the opportunity first presents itself, to join the years of two emperors together. Indeed, in this very place the *Short Chronicle* retains Marcianus’s sixth year. See note 77.] Through the emperor Avitus (77), Count Fronto was sent as envoy to the Sueves. Likewise, King Theudoricus sent envoys to them, because he was loyal to the Roman Empire, so that, since they were bound together with both him and the Roman Empire by a single treaty of peace, they might keep the promises of their sworn alliance [Note: These words clearly show that Avitus diligently sought the friendship not only of Marcianus but also of other rulers, with the assistance of Theodoricus.].

When the envoys of both parties had been sent back and every principle of law had been violated, the Sueves invaded the province of Tarraconensis, which was subject to the Roman Empire [Note: From this it is evident that Idatius began relating the events of the year of the common era 456, and therefore of Marcianus’s sixth year, at the section “Through the emperor Avitus.” The events that he relates down to the section “Soon the Spains” demonstrate the same thing even more clearly. For so many and such great events could not have been completed between 10 July of the year 455, when Avitus became emperor, and the end of that year. It is therefore remarkable that his second year, which ran in its entirety together with Marcianus’s sixth, could have been transferred by scribes so much later to the section “Rechiarius.”], and having carried out a plundering raid there, they led a large number of captives into Gallaecia.

Of the Heruli, a brief notice. Note 78.] Some four hundred armed men, who had arrived in seven ships on the coast of Lucus, were overwhelmed by the sudden attack of an assembled multitude; only two of their number were killed, and the rest escaped. As they returned to their own settlements, they most savagely plundered the coastal regions of Cantabria [Note: Ancient writers spoke of the Cantabri, Varduli, and Vascones, but not of Cantabria, Vardulia, or Vasconia; these names belong to a later age. Pliny, book 3, chapter 3, says: “Toward the Ocean the remaining peoples extend, and among those already mentioned are the Varduli and Cantabri.”] and Vardulia [Note: The city and harbor of the Varduli was Flaviobriga. The same is stated by Pliny, book 4, chapter 2. Many believe that Flaviobriga was the city now called Bilbao by the Spaniards.].

Again, after Avitus had been proclaimed emperor, envoys of the Goths came to the Sueves to reprimand them for their invasion of the province of Tarraconensis. But this protest accomplished nothing; indeed, the Sueves invaded the same province a second time. From this it is clearer than daylight that, unless Idatius was completely blind, he could not have compressed this double Gothic embassy and the Sueves’ invasion into the year 455 after Avitus’s proclamation.], and after devastating the area there, they carried a great number of captives into Gallaecia.

The order of events at this time was as follows. At the end of the year 455, after concord had been established between Marcianus and Avitus, the latter sent his envoy Fronto, together with envoys of Theudoricus, to the Sueves at the beginning of the year 456. But the Sueves, paying no regard to the pledge they had given, invaded the province of Tarraconensis. When Theudoricus heard of this, he sent a second embassy to Rechiarius. Yet it achieved nothing, and the Sueves again invaded Tarraconensis. Meanwhile the year 456 was turning toward autumn when Theudoricus came into the Spains against Rechiarius, as Idatius relates here.]

The Gothic king Theudoricus entered the Spains with his immense army [Note: Isidore says the same in his *History of the Goths*, assigning it to the fifth year of Theodoricus’s reign. He joined his first year with Marcianus’s second. It is therefore clear that Idatius recorded these events under Marcianus’s sixth year, and consequently under the year 456. Jordanes, in the *Getica*, section 74, relates that the Burgundian kings Gundiac and Hilperic came into the Spains with Theodoricus.] and with the permission and authorization of the emperor Avitus [Note: Isidore, in the passage cited, says: “Theodoricus entered Spain with a vast multitude of troops and with the permission of the emperor Avitus in the fifth year of his reign.” It is therefore clear that Theodoricus, with equal right, wrested the kingdom of the Spains from the Sueves and acquired it for himself.]. King Rechiarius, meeting him with a multitude of Sueves, was defeated after battle was joined at the twelfth milestone from the city of Asturica, at a river called the Urbicus, on 5 October [Note: Today it is commonly called the Órbigo, and it faces Asturica from the east. An ancient anonymous annotator of the *Chronicle of Victor of Tunis* records that this battle occurred in the field of Paramus, beside the river Orbicus. From this we infer two things: first, that the river was called both Orbicus and Urbicus, through the frequent exchange of *u* and *o*; second, that Ptolemy’s Septimanca Paramica lay in this region, sufficiently far from the city now called Miranda de Duero.]—a Wednesday [Another reading: Friday]. The ranks of his men were cut down, some were captured, and many were put to flight; he himself, wounded, scarcely escaped and fled to the remotest regions of Gallaecia.

This day was 28 October, a Sunday, while the fifth day of the same month, mentioned shortly before, fell on a Wednesday in the year 456. There can therefore be no doubt that Idatius is now continuing the events of this year, and that the headings above, the sixth year of Marcianus and the second of Avitus, are correctly assigned.], although without bloodshed, the plundering of that city nevertheless became mournful and tearful. A great captivity of Roman captives was carried out [Note: That is, of the Gallaecians who were under Roman rule or protection.]; the basilicas of the saints were broken open, the altars removed and smashed; the virgins of God were indeed carried away, but their chastity was preserved [Note: Salvianus praises the chastity of the Goths magnificently in book 6 of *On Providence*.]. The clergy were stripped even to the point of nakedness; people of both sexes, together with children, were dragged from the holy places of refuge; the sacred place was filled with the horror of beasts of burden, sheep, and camels; and it recalled, in part, the examples written concerning Jerusalem under heavenly wrath [Note: Daniel 9:24; Matthew 24:15.].

Only through the extreme ignorance or negligence of scribes could the second year of Avitus have been transferred to this point. See note 79.] Rechiarius (79), fleeing to a place called Portucale [Note: In Idatius’s time there was only one fortress of this name on the bank of the Douro, near its mouth. If there had been two, he would certainly have distinguished them, so that we might know which one Rechiarius reached. In a later period a new fortress was built, also called Portucale, from the nearby village of Cale. This later fortress, elevated to an episcopal see, was subject to the bishop of Coimbra, as is clear from the division of the episcopal sees attributed to the Council of Lucus. It therefore appears that, for those ascending the Douro from the sea, the new fortress lay on the left, where the city of Porto now stands, while the old fortress lay on the right; Rechiarius arrived here because at that time it was the only one.], was brought as a captive to King Theudoricus. After he had been placed in custody, the remaining Sueves who had survived the earlier battle surrendered themselves; nevertheless some were killed, and the kingdom of the Sueves was destroyed and ended [Note: Isidore, in his *History of the Goths*, reads the passage this way: “For the greater part, the kingdom of the Sueves was destroyed and brought to an end”; but in his *History of the Sueves*: “It was almost destroyed and brought to an end.” Were the words “for the greater part” lost from Idatius, or the word “almost”? Certainly throughout the rest of the *Chronicle* we read of Suevian kings and a Suevian kingdom.].

The sacred envoy—so called because he had been sent by the emperor—came to Gallaecia, announcing to him what has been stated above: that a multitude of Vandals had been defeated in Corsica, and that Avitus had succeeded from Italy to the Gauls at Arles (80) [Note: It is especially important here to observe the order followed by Idatius in relating the events of this year. From it one can understand that the events proceeded in the continuity and sequence in which Idatius narrates them. From this, in turn, we shall be able to establish something more certain concerning the time when Avitus was removed from the imperial office. See note 80.].

He reports that ships from the East, arriving at Hispalis, announced that an army had been defeated on Marcianus’s behalf [Note: The scribes altered this passage so ineptly that it has no meaning. I therefore think it should be read, from the second fragment of *Hispania Illustrata*, as follows: “He reports that ships from the East arriving at Hispalis announced that an army had been defeated on behalf of Marcianus”—namely, the army of Gaiseric, which had landed in Corsica. See note 81.] (81).

The *Chronicle* edited by Sirmond expresses this passage as follows: “Avitus in his third year, after he had been made emperor by the Gauls,” and so forth. But Henri Valois, who had seen Sirmond’s manuscript, testifies in his notes on Evagrius, book 2, chapter 7, that it read there: “In the third year of Avitus, in the seventh month after he had been made emperor by the Gauls,” and so forth. The learned Florius offers this reading in his edition. But that the authentic reading is the one we give will be demonstrated in note 82.] Avitus, after he had been made emperor by the Gauls and the Goths, lost the empire [Note: He was stripped of the purple by Ricimer, as stated in note 80. Did Ricimer seek a senatorial decree for Avitus’s deposition? I very much doubt it.], deprived of the promised aid of the Goths [Note: Gregory of Tours and Victor of Tunis, who lived many years later, report that Avitus was appointed bishop of Placentia after abdicating the empire. Contemporary writers, however, do not mention his episcopate; indeed, when Idatius relates Avitus’s arrival in the Gauls and the embassy sent by him to Theodoricus, he seems to me certainly to deny that he held such an episcopate. See note 83, section 5.], and lost his life as well.

Marcianus held the empire from 24 or 25 August of the year 450 until the beginning of February of the year 457. Thus Marcellinus correctly says that he reigned six years and six months, except that he exceeded this by a few days; Idatius, following his customary method, counts otherwise, as has often been stated.], and Marcianus died.

As the forty-fourth emperor of the Romans, Majorianus in Italy, and Leo at Constantinople, were called Augusti [Note: Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, and others testify that both obtained the empire in this year. According to the anonymous author of the Cuspinian manuscript, Majorianus was elevated on the Kalends of April; Leo on 7 February, according to the Alexandrian Chronicle.].

This note I merely designates the epoch of Leo and Majorianus; the chronology, however, is governed by the note entered above under the third year of Avitus. See note 83.] Theodoricus (83), terrified by the unfavorable news he received, departed from Emerita shortly after Easter, which fell on 2 [Note: The printed books read “5 Kalends.” I corrected this to “2 Kalends,” not merely because Easter was celebrated on 31 March in this year—for an error could have arisen from forgetfulness—but because it is more likely that a scribe changed this note’s 2 into 5. Moreover, the printed books read *Paschae quod*; I corrected it according to the rules of grammar to *Paschatis, quo*, the form Idatius uses below in the section “Frantanes.”] Kalends of April, and, returning to the Gauls, sent part of the force of various nations that he had with him [Note: I noted above from Jordanes that the Burgundians came into the Spains with Theodoricus.] with their commanders toward the plains [Note: He says “toward the plains,” either because the Sueves possessed only open and level places, or rather because Theodoricus sent his soldiers toward the region that we now call Tierra de Campos. The Palentine plains are praised by Orosius, book 7, chapter 40; yet there *Palentinis* should be read, with Livy, or *Palantinis*, with Strabo, instead of *Palatinis*.] of Gallaecia.

They, equipped with deceit and perjury, as they had been ordered, entered Asturica, which the king’s plunderers had already entered under the pretext of Roman authorization [Note: As has been stated elsewhere, the Gallaecians who in the year 409, when the barbarians invaded the province, withdrew to safer places were still counted under the Roman name. Idatius indicated this shortly before when he affirmed that a great captivity of Romans had taken place at Bracara. This explains why Asturica, Palentia, and other towns admitted within their walls the Goths who professed to be waging war on behalf of the Roman Empire and by the emperor’s authorization.], pretending that the expedition against the Sueves who remained had been assigned to them, and entered under the appearance of peace, following their customary practice of treachery.

Without delay, a multitude of every kind found there was slaughtered; the holy churches were broken open, their altars plundered and demolished, and all sacred ornament and use were removed. Two bishops found there, together with all the clergy, were led into captivity; a pitiable captivity was inflicted on the weaker people of both sexes, while the remaining and deserted houses of the city were set on fire. The places of the fields were laid waste (84) [Note: Theodoricus raged against the Gallaecians because of Avitus’s deposition from the empire, since they supported the Roman party. See note 84.], and the city of Palentia perished by the Goths’ destruction in the same way as Asturica.

One fortress of Coviacum [Note: In the year of the Christian era 1050, a council was held in the fortress of Coyacum, which is none other than the one mentioned here by Idatius. It lies in the territory of Oviedo and is now commonly called Valencia de Don Juan.]—thirty miles from Asturica—, exhausted by a long struggle, both resisted the enemy and prevailed over them with God’s aid. After very many of the enemy had been killed, the survivors returned to the Gauls.

It is apparent from what Idatius, an eyewitness, writes that Ajulfus was neither appointed over the Sueves by Theodoricus nor killed by his command, as Jordanes relates in the *Getica*, section 74. For Ajulfus deserted the Goths before Theodoricus departed from the province; here he is said to have died, not to have been killed. Idatius does not conceal that he aspired to the kingship; nevertheless, he could have sought the kingship without offending Theodoricus, who had granted the Sueves the power to choose a king for themselves.] in the month of July.

That is, the Gallaecians who enjoyed freedom and were not subject to the barbarians.]. From among them, some proclaimed Frantanus king, others Maldra [Note: Idatius recorded Maldra’s election in the preceding year; but somewhat later, after disagreement arose among the Sueves, some established another king for themselves, namely Frantanus. Isidore clearly explains the matter in his *History of the Sueves*, where he writes: “The Sueves made Maldra, son of Massilia, their king. Soon, divided into two parties, some proclaimed Frantanus king, others Maldra.”].

Following their customary treachery, part of the Sueves who followed Maldra plundered Lusitania. After a massacre of Romans had taken place there and booty had been gathered, the city of Ulyxipona was entered under the appearance of peace.

Here, from the following section, I have moved back the second year of Majorianus and Leo. Note 85.] Frantanus (85) died between Easter and Pentecost.

At Maldra’s command, the Sueves, reverting to their customary treachery, plundered the region adjoining the river Douro. On 5 [Note: Petavius and Ricciolus, as we have noted elsewhere, show that “5 Kalends of June,” not “5 Ides,” must be written.] Ides of June, a Wednesday, from the fourth hour to the sixth, the sun appeared diminished in the light of its disk to the appearance of a fifth- or sixth-day moon.

The published books give the second year of Majorianus here through scribal error; for, as has been demonstrated in note 85, Idatius assigned this note above to the section “Frantanus.”] A Gothic army, sent to the Spains in July by King Theodoricus under its commander Cyrila, arrived [Note: We understand from this again that Idatius began relating the events of the year 458 at the preceding section, reporting there what happened in May and here what happened in July of the same year.] in Baetica.

Envoys of the Goths and Vandals alike came to the Sueves and returned [Note: The outcome itself showed where these embassies were headed and what the Goths, Vandals, and Sueves were planning. For all of them, by common agreement, turned their arms against the Romans, whom they had observed could easily be defeated while they were engaged in private hatreds and disputes among themselves. Theodoricus’s hatred of the Sueves had by then died out, since Avitus—the cause for which he had undertaken the war against them—had been killed or had died, and Rechiarius had been killed, although Theodoricus privately hated him as a relative because of the matters related by Jordanes in the *Getica*, section 73.].

Theodoricus sent part of his army to Baetica with his commander Suniericus. Cyrila was recalled to the Gauls. Nevertheless, some Sueves plundered parts of Lusitania with Maldra, while others, with Remismundus [Note: In Saint Isidore’s *History of the Sueves* we find the forms *Recchimundus* and *Remismundus*. But since the name Recchimundus is never found either in all copies of that history or in Idatius, I think that there was only one king of the Sueves at this time, and that his name was Remismundus. Moreover, in some editions of Isidore’s *History of the Goths*, Remismundus is called Maldra’s son; in the Labbean edition these words are absent, and Idatius makes Maldra and Remismundus kings of different factions. I therefore consider it more likely that Remismundus was not Maldra’s son.], plundered Gallaecia.

The same enemy invaded this fortress (86) [Note: I think that this fortress was in the possession of the Gallaecians at that time. Note 86.] I now first read among the Goths of counts and masters of soldiers. Were Nepotianus and Suniericus really such men? Or did Idatius transfer Roman titles to them? Certainly I have no doubt that Suniericus was a Goth. Although the name Nepotianus is not Gothic, Idatius testifies below that he served under Theodoricus. Yet he could have joined the Goths after Avitus’s death, as Suniericus also did; and the former retained among the Goths the dignity of master of soldiers, the latter that of count, which they had acquired among the Romans. The Ostrogoth Theodoricus shortly afterward introduced such ranks of honor into his Italian kingdom; among the Visigoths we do not find them until much later.] They came to the Gallaecians, sent by the master of soldiers [107] and by the count Suniericus, announcing that the emperor Majorianus and King Theodoricus had established the firmest guarantees of peace between themselves, after the Goths had been defeated in a certain battle [Note: Idatius does not say where this war, in which the Goths were defeated by the Romans, took place. From Sidonius it can be inferred that the two sides fought in Gaul. Note 87.] (87).

From the time when Maldra is known to have reigned, it is clear that Idatius referred these events to Abraham’s year 2476, which coincides with the year 460 of the common era. Note 88.] He was slaughtered and deservedly perished in such a death.

The Vandals, stirred up by traitors, seized ships from the shore—not from the harbor—of Carthage. Idatius says that the ships were seized from the shore of Carthage. Yet the shore extends farther, namely along the maritime coast of the entire province. I therefore think that what Marius of Avenches writes more specifically is true, when he says that these events occurred near Ilici. On that coast there is a promontory of which I find no mention in the ancient geographers; now, however, our people call it Cabo de Santa Pola. It provides two anchorages, one toward the east, where Alona lies, and the other toward the west, where there is a fortress and village commonly called Lugar Nuevo; both are sufficiently safe and convenient for ships.] 108. Majorianus, thus thwarted in the expedition he had undertaken, returned to Italy.

In the Venetian edition of 1728, it is noted that the manuscript contains the following: “He plunders the Sueves living near Lucus,” and so forth. I think this is Idatius’s authentic reading. It appears in the preface to volume 2 of Sirmond’s works.]; but when the informers Dictinius, Spinio, and Ascanio spread it and scattered the poison of their own treachery to cause terror [Note: It appears that Dictinius, Spinio, and Ascanio were treacherous men who betrayed at one time the Sueves and at another the Gallaecians—handing the former over to the Goths and the latter to the Sueves.], the report [Note: I regard this word as doubtful. In Sandoval’s edition of Idatius there is a lacuna at this point.] returned to his own people.

Soon afterward, at the instigation of the same informers mentioned above, Frumarius, with the band of Sueves under his command, seized Bishop Idatius on 26 July in the church at Aquae Flaviae [Note: The fact that Idatius was found by Frumarius in the church at Aquae Flaviae and returned there after three months sufficiently proves that he was bishop of that church.], and overthrew the same district with great destruction.

The region and the coastal areas of the Lucensian district were laid waste. Are the Auregenses whom Idatius calls here the same people who are called Aobrigenses on the inscription at Aquae Flaviae? Certainly the name is not very different. And if the city of the Auregenses is the same as the place now commonly called Orense, it unquestionably belonged to the Lucensian district and could and should, because of its proximity, have helped in the construction of the bridge at Aquae Flaviae. John of Biclarum also mentions the Aregensian mountains in the seventh year of Leovigild.

Suniericus captured the city of Scalabis [Note: Scalabis is now known as a city of Lusitania under the name Santarém. For Ptolemy it was a colony; for Pliny, a municipality of Roman citizens.], which opposed him.

Does this not show with complete clarity that Idatius now begins the year with January, not October, since he passes from August to November under the same chronological heading with which he designated Majorianus’s fourth year?], by the merciful grace of God, contrary to the wishes and arrangements of the aforementioned informers [Note: He means Dictinius, Spinio, and Ascanio, who, as appears, were especially hostile to Idatius.], returned to Flaviae [Note: Morales and Mariana changed *Flaviae* to *Iria Flavia*, misled by Roderic of Toledo, who, while relating these events, wrote *Flavia* instead of *Aquae Flaviae*. Isidore likewise named not Aquae Flaviae but the city of Flavia. Morales and Mariana had not seen Idatius.].

That is, of the Suevian people.]. Gaiseric had indeed disrupted Majorianus’s expedition to Africa by destroying his fleet on the Carthaginian shore; nevertheless, he had begun to fear the brave and energetic emperor and therefore requested peace from him.].

The printed books place two notes here, V and I, signifying the fifth year of Leo and the first of Severus. But Idatius’s unvarying practice is never to record the year of a ruler before first announcing his accession. The circumstances themselves demand this: a reader cannot know whose epoch a new number indicates if the new ruler has not yet appeared in the *Chronicle*. Moreover, Idatius assigned to every earlier ruler the year in which that ruler died, even when the death occurred at the beginning of the year. Therefore he attached here only the single note V, signifying the fifth year of Leo and Majorianus, who died as the year was passing.] Majorianus, returning from Gaul to Rome and arranging what was necessary for the Roman Empire or Roman name, was ambushed and killed by Ricimer, inflamed by jealousy and supported by the counsel of envious men [Note: The frequently cited anonymous author, under the consuls of this year, says: “Majorianus was deposed by the patrician Ricimer at Dertona on 2 August and was killed beside the river Ira on 7 August.” Cassiodorus assigns both the same year; Marcellinus gives both the same year and the place of death, but neither specifies the day.], in the fifth year of Leo’s reign.

Concerning Severus, the same anonymous author says: “He was elevated as emperor on 19 November.” Marcellinus and Cassiodorus assign the accession of Severus to this same year, while Marius of Avenches says that it took place at Ravenna. But Idatius relates events occurring in their own time, whereas Marius does not do so here.], Suniericus returned to Gaul. Nepotianus, by order of Theodoricus, received Arborius as his successor.

From this passage it is clear that Idatius’s chronology was disturbed by the scribes. See note 89, where you will find further evidence.]. It was undoubtedly written by Idatius as follows: “Antioch, the chief city of Syria, disobeying the salutary warnings . . . was swallowed up, together with some inhabitants who, obeying those warnings and fearing the Lord,” and so forth. See note 90, section 1.] Antioch, the chief city of Syria, disobedient to salutary warnings [Note: See the same note 90, section 2, for the warnings that Saint Simeon Stylites gave the Antiochians at this time.], was swallowed up when the earth split open [Note: The same note, section 3, discusses the year in which this earthquake occurred.], while only some of the inhabitants of the city, who followed those warnings in obedience to the fear of the Lord, were saved from destruction; even the tops of the towers alone remained above the earth.

Together with the empress Eudoxia, her daughter Placidia was sent back to Constantinople, and indeed in this year, contrary to what Pagius incorrectly denies. See note 91.]. Her daughters were married: one, Eudocia, to Gento [Note: Some say that Eudocia, the other daughter of Eudoxia, married Huneric; others, that she married Thrasamund. Note 92.], the son of Gaiseric; the other to Olybrius, a senator of the city of Rome, by right of marriage.

I shall discuss Aegidius and Agrippinus in note 93.] A Gaul, both a count and a citizen, hostile to the distinguished Count Aegidius, handed Narbonne over to Theodoricus so that he might obtain the support of the Goths.

I have inserted these notes here with certainty, although the other printed books omit them. For, as I demonstrated above, the first year of Severus had to be entered at the section “Suniericus returns.” Since, therefore, the third year of the same Severus was added at the section “Nepotianus departs,” which follows much later, the second year of Severus can nowhere be more appropriately recorded than here—especially since Marius of Avenches testifies that this battle of Aegidius with Fredericus occurred under the consuls Basilius and Vivianus, who held the consulship in this year. If someone wishes to assign these notes to the preceding section, “Agrippinus,” I shall not strongly object, provided that he agrees with me that they must be assigned to one of these two sections. Indeed, Agrippinus could have handed Narbonne over to the Goths in this same year, 463.] Against Count Aegidius, commander of both armies, a man whom reputation commends as pleasing to God through good works [Note: Others also bear witness to Aegidius’s integrity. I therefore regard as false what someone reports, with Pagius’s approval: that Agrippinus accused him before the emperor of treason by means of a slanderous charge. See what was said in note 93.], in the province of Armorica [Note: As Marius of Avenches writes, under the consuls of this year the battle was fought between the Loire and the Ligericinus. Since the Ligericinus, or Ligerulus, rises only one short league from Orléans and has a course of equal or slightly greater length, according to Masson, *On the Rivers of Gaul*, p. 57, we say that the battle was fought two or three miles from that city. On this war, see note 94.], Fredericus (94), the brother of King Theodoricus, rose against him and was killed together with those with whom he had been defeated [Note: I have written the name *Fredericus* consistently, because above, in the years 452 and 453, the form *Fredericus* is found, not *Fridericus*, as appears now in the printed books. He was the king’s brother, not the king, as Marius of Avenches falsely relates. Pope Hilary calls Fredericus “our magnificent son” and indicates in his letter to Leontius of Arles that he had received letters from him.].

The sense is this: Cyrila, sent by Theodoricus as envoy to Remismundus, king of the Sueves, set out from Toulouse with Palegorius, a noble man of Gallaecia who had gone from Gallaecia to Theodoricus [for this seems to be the correct reading, not *had been*], and encountered envoys who were being sent by Remismundus to Theodoricus at the same time. After completing their embassy quickly and returning from Toulouse to Gallaecia, these envoys met Cyrila in the city of Lucus, as he likewise was proceeding to Toulouse after completing his embassy, and received him there. Unless this passage is interpreted in this way, it can scarcely, if at all, be understood.] With Palegorius, a noble man of Gallaecia who had gone to the aforesaid king, Cyrila, as envoy, came to Gallaecia and met the envoys who were going to the same king, Remismundus. When they had quickly returned, they received Cyrila, who was returning, in the city of Lucus. Soon after his departure from Gallaecia, the Sueves, false and treacherous as always in their promises, plundered the various regions of unhappy Gallaecia in their customary manner.

This Regismundus must have been a Goth, since he obeyed the Gothic king Theodoricus. He must certainly be distinguished from Remismundus, king of the Sueves.] Cyrila and some Goths who had come earlier were sent back, while Cyrila remained in Gallaecia. When Remismundus soon returned to the king, undisciplined disorder prevailed between the Gallaecians and the Sueves.

Hilary was proclaimed Roman pontiff as the forty-eighth pope.

Bishop Hilary presides. [Hilary was proclaimed Roman pontiff at the end of the year 461.]

The eighth year of Leo should have been recorded here; but because the scribe had omitted to enter the seventh year above, at the section “Against Aegidius,” he transferred it here, and the printed books offer it to their readers in this place. See note 95.] Of Abraham [Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they are to be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [II.] 480:

Isidore assigns the death of Frumarius to the year 502 of the Spanish era. There is therefore no doubt that Idatius recorded here, and Isidore found recorded, the year of that ruler’s reign which corresponded to this Spanish year and to the year 464 of the common era.], Remismundus, having recalled all the Sueves into his own dominion by royal right, restored the peace that had lapsed.

These words clearly show that Aegidius administered the province, or that part of Gaul which he ruled, by his own authority and not under the authority of the emperor Severus. Nor is it surprising that, since he was an outstanding and courageous man, he refused to submit to the monstrous tyranny of Ricimer, who trampled on distinguished men as well.] Envoys crossed the Ocean to the Vandals and returned to their own people by the same route in September.

Thus it happened that in Leo’s eighth year, the year 464 of the common era, 20 July fell on a Monday, while the Sunday letter was E. On that same day, Petavius recorded in the *Rationarium Temporum*, part 2, book 4, chapter 13, and in book 8 of *The Doctrine of Time*, p. 848, that the sun was eclipsed; there he assigns the same date, 20 July, not 22 July, as Pagius incorrectly reports under the year 464. We must therefore regard it as certain that Idatius assigned these events to Abraham’s year 2480 and to Leo’s eighth year.], in the appearance of a fifth-day moon, the sun was observed diminished in its light from the third hour to the sixth.

Mariana and others report that the wife sent to Remismundus was this daughter of Theodoricus. It is certainly plausible; but since Idatius and Isidore are silent, I do not venture to assert it.] the wife whom he had.

I have presented some information about Marcellinus from Priscus in note 94; I shall discuss him again in note 104. He was a Dalmatian by nationality and, as Marcellinus says in his *Chronicle*, a patrician of the West and a pagan; his power increased so greatly that he became a source of great fear to both empires. Procopius indicates in book 1 of *The Vandal War* that he sought revolutionary changes. Sidonius speaks more plainly in book 1, letter 11, when he says: “When a conspiracy was being prepared by Marcellinus to seize the diadem.” But I strongly fear that he suffered this accusation from Ricimer, who, according to Priscus, hated the man most bitterly.] They were slaughtered and driven from Sicily.

These notes, signifying Leo’s ninth year and Severus’s fourth, are absent from the printed books. Note 96.] Aegidius died (97) [Note: The *Chronicle of Verdun* says that Childeric, son of Merovech, after expelling Aegidius, commander of the Romans, from the kingdom and killing him, invaded the kingdom in the year 466 from the Incarnation of the Lord. But Gregory of Tours, book 2, chapter 18, Rorico, book 1 of *The Deeds of the Franks*, and Aimo say that he died, not that he was killed. This is certainly necessary for the rumor about poison mentioned by Idatius to have arisen; for if he had fallen in battle, what uncertainty could there have been about the manner of his death? I shall examine the remaining matters reported by that *Chronicle* in note 97. When Idatius says that Aegidius protected the regions in the Roman name, do not understand this as meaning that he then obeyed the Roman emperor; that is not the case. Idatius speaks this way because Aegidius boasted that he stood for the empire, although he refused to submit to rulers whom he regarded as illegitimate.], some say by ambush, others that he was deceived by poison. After his death, the Goths immediately invaded the regions that he had protected in the Roman name.

The Sueves deceitfully entered Conimbriga, plundered the noble household of Cantabrius, and carried away the mother and her sons as captives.

Sulpicius Severus and Fortunatus, in the *Life of Saint Martin*, mention a certain Arborius, a man of praetorian rank, who may have been this Arborius’s father, or rather grandfather; for I think that both were Aquitanians.] was summoned.

These words of Idatius clearly indicate that he wrote this after Severus’s fourth year; otherwise he would simply have said, “Severus died,” or, “The envoys report that Severus died.” That is how he should have spoken if Severus’s death had occurred in the year that was then running. Therefore…

Nowhere can we more suitably assign Leo’s tenth year—if we wish to continue the chronology that Idatius abandoned after Leo’s eighth year—than at this point after Severus’s death, which certainly occurred in the preceding year. See Note 98. Moreover, since I demonstrated in Note 96 that what Idatius writes in the preceding section concerning the legates in that same year belongs to Leo’s ninth year and Severus’s fourth, if a new year is now to be designated, it is unquestionably not Leo’s ninth but his tenth.]

On their return, the Suevian legates report that Severus had died in the fourth year of his own reign (98). Those mentioned above are referred back to Conimbriga.

Does he call Ajax a Galatian in the Greek manner, intending to indicate that he was a Gaul? Or did he rather say “Galatian,” that is, Greek, just as Ennodius, in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius of Ticinum*, calls the emperor Anthemius a Galatian? Certainly, if Ajax had originated in Gallaecia, Idatius would have called him a Gallaecian, not a Galatian. Therefore Orosius is wrong to make him a Gallaecian. All the Spanish historians mention him, because through him the Suevian nation was first infected with the poison of the Arian heresy, whereas previously it had remained free and pure of this stain, even among the Vandals.]

He became an apostate and an elder [Note: He did not wish to call him a presbyter.] among the Suevi; with the aid of his king, he emerged as an enemy of the Catholic faith and of the divine Trinity [Note: In the manuscript these words are transmitted as follows: “To the Gallican settlement of the Goths this pestiferous [poison] …” But since the same passage is read in the *History of the Suevi* by Saint Isidore, the learned emendation made by the eminent scholar should be retained in Sirmond’s first edition.]. From the Gallican settlement of the Goths this pestiferous venom of the hostile man arrived.

Since these events belong to the year 467, according to the chronographers Cuspinian, Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, and the common testimony of all writers, Leo’s eleventh year, which coincides with it, ought to be written here.]

From Constantinople, Anthemius, the brother [Note: I have no doubt that *filius Procopii*—“son of Procopius”—should be read instead of *frater Procopii*—“brother of Procopius.” See Note 99.] of Procopius (99), was sent by Leo Augustus to Italy, under divine providence, together with Marcellinus and other distinguished companions, and with a very large and well-equipped army.

Cassiodorus says: “At the third milestone from the city, in a place called Brontotas.” It is not easy to decide whether Cassiodorus or Idatius should rather be believed.]

At the third milestone from Rome he is proclaimed emperor in the month of August (in the eighth year of Leo’s reign [Note: These words in Idatius are wholly interpolated: “In the eighth year of Leo’s reign.” They passed from Idatius into Isidore, as I shall soon explain. The error arose because Idatius designated only Leo’s eighth year in the *Chronicle*, as has often been observed elsewhere. The copyist added these words to aid the reader’s memory, in case he had forgotten that Idatius was still narrating events belonging to Leo’s sixth year; for he himself assumed this, since he found no other year designated in the *Chronicle* after that eighth year.], under the consuls of that year [Note: Cuspinian is uncertain about the consuls of this year: “Anthemius,” he says, “was raised to the imperial office at Rome on the day before the Ides of April.” As you see, his account of the place agrees neither with Cassiodorus nor with Idatius. He also differs from Idatius concerning the month.]).]

The printed books present here, through a manifold error, Leo’s ninth year together with Anthemius’s first; but only Anthemius’s first year, which he himself began during Leo’s eleventh year and the common era 467, ought to be assigned here, as you see done in this edition. See Note 100.]

An expedition against Africa and the Vandals was organized (101) [Note: Preparations for the expedition to Africa began in this year; it was not completed, however, until the following year. See Note 101.]. It was recalled because of a change of *metabolorum* [Note: Isidore says in his *Glossary* that *metabulum* means a favorable voyage; in this sense, or in some related sense—namely, as a suitable time for sailing—Idatius uses *metabulum*, although the word otherwise means in Latin “change” or “conversion.”] and the inopportune timing of the voyage.

The killing of Theudoric occurred in Leo’s eleventh year, Anthemius’s first, and the common era 467; for Idatius places it immediately after Anthemius’s proclamation, which certainly took place in that year. Therefore Theudoric reigned fourteen years—indeed, full and completed years—and even reached his fifteenth year. Isidore counts differently. See Note 102.]

Clearly, just as Theudoric entered upon the kingship through the killing of his brother Thorismund, so Euric also usurped the kingship by inflicting death upon his brother Theudoric.]

He, advanced by office and by crime, sent legates to the king of the Suevi. When these were immediately sent back by Remismund, legates of that same king [Note: It is uncertain to whom “that same king” refers: Euric or rather Remismund. When Idatius says of the same king that he sent legates to the emperor, to the Vandals, and to the Goths, he seems to be speaking of Remismund; for the Gothic king would not send legates to himself. Yet Idatius shortly afterward reports that the Goth sent legates to the Vandals, and Isidore, describing Idatius, says that Euric, as soon as he had obtained the kingship, sent legates to the emperor Leo. I therefore judge that Isidore read in Idatius only the following: “Some legates of that same king [Euric] were sent to the emperor, others to the Vandals,” and that the two words “to the Goths” were added after Isidore’s time and inserted into Idatius.] were sent, some to the emperor, others to the Vandals, and others to the Goths.

And here is what I said earlier: the Gothic king Euric had sent his legates to the Vandals, and therefore the words “of that same king” are to be understood of him.]

Those who had been sent, terrified by the report of the aforementioned expedition, returned quickly [Note: From this we learn: first, that the expedition to Africa began to be prepared in the year 467, and that it was publicly reported that a fleet would be sent against the Vandals in that same year, as has already been observed above; second, that not only the Vandals but also the Goths and Suevi were struck with fear and kept in suspense while they awaited the outcome of so great a preparation for war.].

Likewise the Suevi, who, after the legates had departed, had been scattered in the customary manner through various places for plunder, were recalled. But a few months later the king of the Suevi himself crossed into Lusitania.

In the commonly circulated books, Leo’s twelfth year is also missing. I added it, and likewise the thirteenth year, which had also been omitted—not because they were needed for the continuation of the chronology, as the tenth and eleventh certainly were when there was an interregnum in the West, but because Leo retained the empire during these and several subsequent years, and Idatius had begun recording it from the beginning.]

Conimbriga, deceived in time of peace [Note: Conimbriga, Scalabis, Olisipo, and likewise the cities and towns of the Lucenses, Auregensians, and Aunonenses in Lusitania and Gallaecia, were plundered by the Goths and Suevi through hostile invasion during this period. This demonstrates that many towns still remained under the jurisdiction and authority of the provincials.], is plundered. Houses are destroyed, together with part of the walls; the inhabitants are captured and dispersed, and the region and the city are laid waste.

Although Isidore copies a large part of this section in his *History of the Goths*, he entirely omits the portent of the two suns, which Idatius seems to narrate in the opening lines. Nor can we supply from elsewhere the other missing material, except for this one word—or another similar one—which both the event itself and the grammar show to have been written in the *Chronicle*.]

They report [120] that several portents were seen in Gaul in the sight of [lacuna] [Note: Livy, Book XXVIII, chapter 11, relates that bloody ears of grain were seen at Antium and two suns at Alba in the year 544 from the founding of the City. Plutarch also records a similar prodigy in his *Life of Marcellus*.]: a sun similar to it appeared continually, and another was seen [lacuna] at sunset; and that, when the Goths of his council had assembled one day [Note: Rodrigo of Toledo, Book II, chapter 10, and Morales, Book XI, chapter 34, say that these events occurred at Arles; but neither Idatius nor Isidore reports this. The same Isidore misled these most learned men: he relates the events after mentioning that Arles and Massilia had been captured by Euric, although that happened long after this year. Yet Isidore’s own words clearly show that he does not wish to specify in which year of Euric’s reign this portent occurred, since he writes indiscriminately: “One day he [Euric],” followed by the other details that I shall give immediately.], the weapons which they held in their hands—some on the iron or blade side green, some rose-colored, some saffron-colored, and some black—had for a time [Note: The common editions read: “For some time did not have their appearance changed.” I deleted the word *non*, “not,” which was evidently inserted into Idatius. It was also falsely attributed to Isidore in Labbe’s edition of the *History of the Goths*; in other copies the passage reads: “One day he [Euric], with the Goths gathered in an assembly, saw that the weapons which they held in their hands—some on the iron or blade side green, some rose-colored, some saffron-colored, and some black—had for a time their natural appearance of iron changed.” I therefore restored *mutatam* in Idatius, since previously *mutata* had been read.] their natural iron appearance changed; and in the middle of the city of Toulouse, on those same days, blood burst forth from the earth and flowed throughout the entire course of the day.

This note, XIII, is absent from the common editions.]

A considerable number of Goths pursuing the returning Suevian legates [Note: These Suevian legates appear to have been sent to the Goths; the Goths are said to have pursued them as they came from Aquitania.] makes for Emerita.

“Euric,” says Saint Isidore in his *History of the Goths*, “advanced by office and by crime, immediately sends legates to the emperor Leo. Without delay he ravages the regions of Lusitania with great force.” Here you have Euric’s embassy to the emperor Leo, which I said above was mentioned by Isidore. But what he adds—“Without delay he ravages the regions of Lusitania,” and so forth—occurred two years later, namely in this year. For after usurping the kingship Euric remained quiet and did not dare to begin a war until he had learned of the disastrous outcome of the Romans’ expedition against the Vandals. See Note 103.]

Serving them in Lusitania (103), they return, reporting in his presence [Note: They were therefore at the emperor’s court in the year 468, when these events occurred.] that an exceedingly large army [Note: For the immense number of soldiers and ships and for the entire expedition, see Baronius and Pagi under this year.] with three generals [Note: Besides Basiliscus and Heraclius, whom Procopius mentions, I find no third general unless he was Marcellinus. Yet Idatius seems to indicate that he was someone other than Marcellinus.] selected against the Vandals had departed from the emperor Leo; that Marcellinus (104) had been dispatched [Note: Marcellinus was killed in Africa itself by the Romans whom he had come to assist, if we trust the *Count Marcellinus*. The Anonymous Cuspinianus and Cassiodorus say that he was killed in Sicily. See Note 104.] with a large force, likewise joined to him by the emperor Anthemius; that Ricimer (105), the son-in-law of the emperor Anthemius and made patrician [Note: Ricimer did not become Anthemius’s son-in-law and patrician in this year, but two years earlier, namely in 467. See Note 105.]; and that Aspar (106) [Note: The material concerning Aspar was certainly added to the *Chronicle* after it had been completed, either by Idatius or by someone else. Everything else appears to be Idatius’s. See Note 106.] had been degraded to private life, his son killed, because they were discovered to be advising the Vandals against the Roman Empire.

I do not know how Pagi, under the year 457, no. 3, could have forgotten to confirm his opinion concerning the years of Hilary’s pontificate by this explicit testimony of Idatius, a contemporary author—especially since he knew of no other person of such great age whose name was known and whose age was comparable to Idatius’s, while his opinion had so many opponents. Yet in reality that opinion is correct, if we believe Idatius.]

XLV [Note: According to Pagi, Simplicius, mentioned in the cited passage, was ordained on 25 February, the sixth day after Hilary’s death, in the year 468. He was the forty-ninth Roman pontiff.]

Simplicius is ordained bishop of the Roman Church.

I have not yet been able to discover where the Aunonenses were situated. I think they were within, or near, the district of Lucus.]

They make peace with the king of the Suevi, who invades and plunders certain places both in Lusitania and in the district of the Astures.

We have often seen that the Hispani who defended their liberty in Lusitania and Gallaecia were attacked by the Goths and Suevi.]

From this it is inferred that Lusidius admitted the Suevi within the walls of Olisipo, so that they might defend that city against the Goths, who were then more hostile to the Romans than the Suevi. For this reason he does not hesitate to go with the Suevi to the emperor.]

Lusidius is sent [to the emperor].

Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 494, tells the story differently. He says that fish were caught in the river Minho bearing an inscription of the Spanish era that referred to that year, and therefore the era would have been 532. But Idatius does not say that the fish displayed the fixed year of any era; rather, they bore the number of days making up each solar year. Therefore either the portent reported by Sigebert is a different one, or, if it is one and the same, these words were added to Idatius after the *Chronicle* had been completed, in its twenty-fifth year. Otherwise the matter is related here differently from the writing from which Sigebert took it. The *Chronicle* does not reveal what the Hebrew letters or the Greek letters signified. Nor can I understand what those letters were meant to indicate at equal intervals of months.]

Something seems to have fallen out here, leaving the sentence suspended and gaping. Perhaps it was what the Hebrew and Greek letters signified, or the Hebrew and Greek words themselves.]

Marked with Latin numerical signs of the eras, thus containing the yearly cycle of 365 days [Note: Idatius joins together only three things here—or, if someone added these words to the *Chronicle*, the era, the number, and the year. Unless these are distinguished to some extent, he must necessarily have expressed himself badly. I therefore think that by “the numerals of the eras” he means numerical signs, such as the Latin signs I, V, and X, and such as those we call figures: 1, 5, and 10—], at equal intervals of months.

Not far from the aforementioned municipality, a kind of herb, in the form of a very green lentil-shaped grain and full of bitterness, flowed down from the sky [124]. It is tedious to recount the many other portents.

[Col. 0749]

127 NOTES ON HYDATIUS.

Note I, p. 51.

[Col. 0749B]

Cauca, which is Caucia in Livy, is counted among the cities of the Vaccaei by Pliny, book III, chapter 3, and by Ptolemy, on the second map of Europe. The similarity of the name and the site itself suggest that it was situated where Coca now stands; for, if we trust the Itinerary of Antoninus, it is encountered at the twenty-ninth milestone by travelers going from Segovia toward Palentia. That it was attached to Gallaecia is testified, as you see, by Hydatius and, on the basis of Hydatius, by Orosius, book V, chapter 7. Claudian agrees in his poem *On the Praises of Serena*, the daughter of Honorius’ brother Theodosius, where, beginning at verse 70, he depicts her native land exulting with joy at her birth, saying:

> At your birth, they say, the Tagus, swelling  
> through rich fields and overflowing with wealth,  
> rejoiced; Gallaecia smiled with flowers,  
> and the beautiful Duria, with its rose-colored banks,  
> everywhere changed the fleece of the fold  
> into purple.  
>   
> The Cantabrian Ocean, along the neighboring shore,  
> spewed out its gems . . .

These lines imply that Serena was born in Gallaecia, specifically at Cauca, where the family of Theodosius had settled. Otherwise, if she had been born at Italica, Claudian would have inserted the Baetis, Baetica, and the Tartessian sea into his poem, not Gallaecia, the Durius, and the Cantabrian Ocean. I say the Durius; for if anyone interprets *formosus Duria ripis*—“the beautiful Duria with its banks”—as referring to the Turia, the river of the Edetani, let him believe those who wish; he will never persuade me. For how could a poet who was neither careless nor unlearned, after depicting Gallaecia as “smiling with flowers,” suddenly leap to the banks of the Turia, omitting the Durius, the river of that very province, and disregarding every consideration of poetic propriety? Claudian called the Durius *Duria*, just as it had earlier been called *Dorias* by Strabo. Nor does the authority of Mela move me, in whose work *Duria* is read, since there he is speaking of the Turia; this is a scribal error, which Hermolaus, Pincianus, Schottus, and, besides them, Petrus Joannes Oliverius and also Petrus Joannes Hunnesius—both Valencians by birth and outstanding in learning—corrected long ago. I know that Claudian more than once traces the origin of Honorius to the Ulpian family, which was from Italica. Aurelius Victor likewise asserts that Theodosius himself descended from the emperor Trajan. Granted; but that does not mean that he must have been born at Italica.

Note II, p. 52.

Theophilus was made bishop of Alexandria in the year 385 as the twenty-third bishop, not the twenty-first, as Hydatius says. In counting the bishops of that Church, Hydatius followed the order of Eusebius, beginning the catalogue of the Alexandrian bishops not with Saint Mark but with Anianus, the successor of Mark, just as he began the Roman catalogue with Linus and the Antiochene with Evodius, rather than with Saint Peter. Moreover, after Peter—whom Jerome had named last—Hydatius omitted Timothy, who was appointed Peter’s successor before Theophilus, around the year 380. Thus, counting Saint Mark and this Timothy among the Alexandrian patriarchs, the Antwerp Jesuits correctly number Theophilus as the twenty-third bishop in the chronology prefixed to their fifth volume of the *Acts of the Saints* for the month of June.

Note III, p. 52.

At the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius, who gave their names to the year 381 of the common era, Idatius writes the following about Athanaric in the *Fasti*: “Athanaric, king of the Goths, entered Constantinople on the third day before the Ides of January; in the same month, Athanaric himself died on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.” Marcellinus designates the same year and month in his *Chronicle*; he omits the day. Moreover, this most splendid triumph over a formidable enemy was a divinely assigned reward to the most religious emperor Theodosius for the destruction of Arianism in the preceding year [129]. Saint Ambrose interprets it in this way in the prologue to Book I *On the Holy Spirit*. But it is preferable to hear Marcellinus, who, under the consulship of Gratian V and Theodosius, relates the following:

> “Theodosius the Great, after triumphing over the Scythian peoples, immediately expelled the Arians from the orthodox church, which they had held for forty years, and restored it to our Catholic orthodox people as emperor in the month of December.”

He means the church of the city of Constantinople, to which, in the preceding year, that famous edict on the Catholic faith, Book II of the *Theodosian Code*, had been sent by Theodosius. Speaking of Constantinople and Athanaric in the passage cited, Ambrose says:

> “After it [Constantinople] had driven out the exiles from the faith, it saw the very enemy whom the kingdom had always been accustomed to fear surrendered; it received him as a suppliant, overwhelmed him as he was dying, and possesses him once buried.”

Although, to be sure, Theodosius had not yet entered Constantinople after assuming the imperial office, and although the heretics possessed enormous power there, he nevertheless, with equal boldness, fearing none of this, declared war on heresy immediately after receiving baptism at Thessalonica. The outcome was so fortunate that, while he himself fought for the faith and religion, God subjected all the enemies of his empire to him and, as time went on, placed the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius beneath his feet. But before these events, as Ambrose says, he received Athanaric as a surrendered suppliant.

## Note IV, p. 52

Orosius, Book VII, chapter 34, writes the following about the peace concluded between the Romans and the Goths in the fourth year of Theodosius, A.D. 382:

> “All the Gothic peoples, after the death of their king, seeing the courage and kindness of Theodosius, surrendered themselves to the Roman Empire.”

Paul the Deacon, Book XI, and Marcellinus, in his *Chronicle*, copy Orosius. Saint Isidore, in his *History of the Goths*, says:

> “After their own king had died, the Goths . . . having entered into a treaty, surrendered themselves to the Roman Empire.”

Synesius too, in his *Oration to Arcadius*, speaking of Theodosius and this peace, says:

> “He raised the Goths, together with their wives, as they fell suppliant at his feet; he enrolled them as allies in war, granted them citizenship, shared all honors with them, and assigned them a portion of Roman land.”

Furthermore, there is no ancient writer who, when speaking of this peace, accuses the Goths of bad faith. Indeed, the divine Ambrose—no one at that time knew better what had happened—says of these matters in Letter 22:

> “Did not the Lord perform similar miracles in Macedonia through the prayers of Saint Acholius—indeed, almost greater ones? For the Goths were disturbed and terrified not by empty fear or needless suspicion, but by a raging plague and burning pestilence. Finally, they fled then in order to escape; afterward, they came out and asked for peace in order to live.”

In this passage Ambrose touches upon events extending over several years. First, he alludes to the war concerning which Idatius says in the *Chronicle*, under the year 371:

> “Many battles were fought between the Romans and the Goths.”

In the *Fasti* he likewise reports that the victories of both Augusti were announced in that same year. As we have seen, Ambrose attributes these victories not so much to the weapons of the soldiers as to the prayers of Saint Acholius, bishop of the Thessalonians; through his prayers plague and pestilence struck and drove away the Goths. Then Ambrose recalls the peace now under discussion, which belongs to the year 382. He certainly would not have proclaimed it obtained through the merits of Acholius or granted by divine providence if the Goths had requested and secured it in bad faith. Therefore, I believe that I have correctly replaced *pro infida*, which the printed books contain, with *in foedera*; but, if one prefers, one may read, following Isidore and Jordanes, *inito foedere*.

Idatius again writes about this peace between the Romans and the Goths in the *Fasti*, under the consulship of Syagrius and Antonius:

> “The entire Gothic people, together with their king, surrendered itself to Roman territory on the fifth day before the Nones of October.”

He now gives the day, which he had omitted in the *Chronicle*. From this it appears that Marcellinus should be corrected, where we read:

> “In the same year the entire Gothic people, after the death of Athanaric, their king, surrendered itself to the Roman Empire. In the month of October Damasus, etc.”

For it should be read:

> “surrendered itself to the Roman Empire in the month of October. Damasus, etc.”

Thus *in the month of October* refers to the surrender of the Goths, not to the death of Damasus, which occurred two months later.

When Idatius says, “together with their king,” I understand him to mean Fritigern; for at that time peace was negotiated with the Goths who were under him—namely, with those against whom Theodosius waged war in the years 379 and 380, after that fatal battle in which Valens and his army perished.

Moreover, since the Goths who had followed Athanaric’s party were left without a king when he was removed, they resolved to submit to Theodosius, having gladly heard that their king had been received with the greatest humanity and treated with the greatest distinction. Thus it came about that the entire nation of the Visigoths, one of its kings still living and the other dead, sought and received peace from Theodosius. There is therefore no reason to correct Idatius and change his words, “together with their king”—that is, Fritigern—into “together with his kingdom,” as Pagius attempted in his *Critica*, under the year A.D. 381, no. 2.

## Note V, p. 53

Idatius says in the *Fasti* that Arcadius was taken by his father into partnership in the empire on the sixteenth day of January. But Pagius, in his *Dissertation on Hypatus*, under the consuls of the year 383, asserts that the day of this inauguration was the nineteenth of the same month. He cites Marcellinus in the *Chronicle*, Paul the Deacon, and the Alexandrian *Chronicle* as witnesses. But Marcellinus and Paul the Deacon do not give the day. The Alexandrian *Chronicle* frequently errs in such matters. There is therefore no reason to believe it rather than Idatius, especially if, as Pagius testifies in the same passage, Socrates agrees with Idatius. Nevertheless, the copy of Socrates that I use gives the nineteenth as the day.

What the same Pagius adds in his *Critica*, under the year 383, no. 12—that this day, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, was chosen for Arcadius’s inauguration because on the same day his father Theodosius had been proclaimed emperor—is of no importance. Honorius, too, was proclaimed Augustus by the same father, Theodosius, and the younger Theodosius by Arcadius, on a day different from that of their respective fathers. Furthermore, Idatius, in the *Fasti* under the year 383, confirming what he had written in the *Chronicle* about the day of Arcadius’s inauguration, says that his quinquennalia were celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. Pagius again attacks this in his *Critica*, saying that in that year Idatius persists in error. Yet to assign both the beginning of the reign and the quinquennalia to the same day is an indication not of error but of consistent truth.

## Note VI, p. 53

Regarding the embassy of the Persians to Theodosius, Orosius, Book VIII, chapter 37, says:

> “The Persians voluntarily sent ambassadors to Theodosius at Constantinople and humbly requested peace; and a treaty was then concluded, through which the whole East has enjoyed the utmost tranquility down to the present.”

For the purpose of concluding this treaty with the Persians, Stilicho was sent as ambassador by Theodosius, as Claudian teaches us in his first panegyric in Stilicho’s praise, verse 51, where he says:

> “You were scarcely of mature age when you were sent as the author of peace  
> with Assyria. To strike a treaty with so great a people  
> was entrusted to a young man, etc.”

## Note VII, pp. 53–54

1. That Theodosius triumphed over the Greuthungi in the eighth year of his reign, A.D. 386 according to the Dionysian era, Claudian does not allow us to doubt. In his poem on the fourth consulship of Honorius, verse 654, addressing Honorius himself, he says:

> “The world owes this to you:  
> the Danube drove the fate of the Goths  
> and the defeated tyrant through bloody waves, while you were consul.”

For he refers these words to the first consulship of Honorius, which he held in that year. This was not unknown to Idatius, since in the *Fasti*, under that same consulship, he writes:

> “Under these consuls the nation of the Greuthungi was defeated and conquered and brought captive into Roman territory by our emperors Theodosius and Arcadius. Then, having entered with victory and triumph, they came into Constantinople on the fourth day before the Ides of October.”

Therefore Florius, with excellent reason and on the authority of Idatius, transferred the triumph over the Greuthungi from the seventh year of Theodosius, to which it is assigned in the Sirmondian edition, to the eighth year.

2. Under the same seventh year of Theodosius, Sirmond entered in the *Chronicle* the section entitled “Priscillianus declining,” in which Idatius relates matters concerning Priscillian that certainly took place before the eighth year of Theodosius, A.D. 386, as has been noted individually in the scholia. Consequently, this section, “Priscillianus declining,” ought to have remained under the seventh year of Theodosius, where Sirmond exhibited it from the manuscript. It does not follow that it belongs to the eighth year merely because the section on the Greuthungi belongs there and is described immediately before it.

This defect entered the *Chronicle* through the carelessness of a copyist, who passed from the section “The Persian envoys” to “The Greuthungi,” omitting “Priscillianus declining.” When he ought to have corrected his error by deleting “The Greuthungi” there and transferring it to its proper place—namely, to the eighth year—he disregarded this correction. It was enough for him to place “Priscillianus declining” before “The Greuthungi,” assigning both to the seventh year of Theodosius, although the former ought to be assigned to the seventh year and the latter to the eighth. This, I believe, is clear from Idatius and from the points already stated.

3. When Idatius joined “Priscillianus because of” to “The Greuthungi” under the same eighth year of Theodosius, the copyist who had placed “Priscillianus declining” there was compelled to move “Priscillianus because of” elsewhere, lest he himself join both by place and by year those whom Idatius had separated in both respects. Hence, after “Priscillianus declining,” which he had placed under the seventh year of Theodosius, he added the eighth year and Arcadius’s quinquennalia. After this, under the ninth year, he wrote “Priscillianus because of,” and through these interpolations completely overturned the chronology of three years.

As I attempted to restore it, Idatius himself provided me a torch: in the *Fasti* he assigns the victory over the Greuthungi to the eighth year, as stated above, and Arcadius’s quinquennalia to the ninth year of the common era, A.D. 387. For under the consuls of that year he writes:

> “Arcadius Augustus celebrated his quinquennalia, together with Theodosius Augustus, his father, with public performances and games, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.”

Therefore the material must be ordered as follows: under the seventh year, “Priscillianus declining”; under the eighth, “The Greuthungi” and “Priscillianus because of”; under the ninth, “Arcadius’s quinquennalia.” All of this is drawn from the *Chronicle* and *Fasti* of Idatius. Who could reproach us for using his help to heal the wounds inflicted upon the text itself by the copyists?

One might ask only whether “Priscillianus because of” was assigned by Idatius to the eighth year of Theodosius. But, apart from the fact that what I said above is extremely probable—namely, that the section was expelled by a copyist from its proper place when he inserted “Priscillianus declining”—the events narrated in it certainly occurred in that eighth year of Theodosius.

4. Thus Priscillian, as Prosper reports in his *Chronicle* under the consuls Arcadius and Bauto, who gave their names to the year 385, realizing that he was to be condemned at the synod of Bordeaux, appealed to the emperor Maximus. In the *Chronicle* published by Sirmond, Idatius likewise assigns this event to the same year 385, saying that Priscillian, judged a heretic in Gaul by Saint Martin and other bishops, appealed to Caesar.

Since, therefore, the principal punishment of Priscillian must have taken place after the Council of Bordeaux and before Maximus invaded Italy, we are compelled to assign his death to the eighth year of Theodosius, A.D. 386 according to the Dionysian era. This is especially so because the events which Severus describes in Book II of his *History* as having occurred between the synod and Priscillian’s death could in no way have taken place before the end of the year 385; and the events which he narrates in that same *History* and in Book II of the *Dialogues* as having occurred after Priscillian’s death and Maximus’s arrival in Italy require, at the very least, a full year.

Yet Maximus brought war into Italy as autumn approached in the year 387, or even earlier. It follows that Priscillian and his companions were put to death in the year 386, the eighth year of Theodosius.

## Note VIII, p. 54

[Col. 0754D]

1. Jordanes and Ammianus Marcellinus count the Greuthungi among the Ostrogoths. For Jordanes, in the *Getica*, no. 46, calls Ermanaric king of the Ostrogoths; Marcellinus likewise calls him, in Book XXXI, king of the Greuthungi. Claudian everywhere calls the same people *Gothuni*. Therefore the Greuthungi of Idatius, the Greuthungi of Ammianus, and the Gothuni of Claudian are entirely the same people, whatever Salmasius may assert to the contrary in his notes on Trebellius, p. 329. Whether, however, this name has been corrupted in Claudian is another question.

2. Theodosius first waged war against the Greuthungi through the general Promotus, and afterward in person. Zosimus, Book IV, gives a full account of the former campaign, as does Claudian, though less fully, in his poem on the fourth consulship of Honorius. From the latter, take the following, verse 623:

> “A Goth dared to cross the Danube;  
> they broke the forest into skiffs; three thousand rushed  
> down the river in full-grown alders,  
> bristling with monstrous wedges.”

[Col. 0755A]

Their leader was Odothaeus. “An age still beginning and its first year crushed the efforts of so great a fleet . . .” By “the first year,” Claudian means the first consulship of Honorius, in which these events occurred, as I observed above.

Idatius testifies in the *Fasti* that the Greuthungi were not merely conquered but also taken captive and transported into Roman territory, where some were assigned to cultivate the fields and others were enrolled in military service. Claudian records both facts in Book II against Eutropius, saying:

> “The Phrygian field is cultivated by Ostrogoths and by Gothuni mingled with them.”

Here is the first point. He adds:

> “A legion long ago made the Goth a Roman.”

Pacatus says the same in his panegyric to Theodosius:

> “Shall I say that the Goths received into service supplied soldiers for the camps and cultivators for the lands?”

Here is the second. Although he may appear to distinguish the Gothuni from the Ostrogoths, in reality the Gothuni, or Greuthungi, were no more distinct from the Goths than the Silingi were from the Vandals or the Gallaeci from the Spaniards.

## Note IX, p. 54

Together with Priscillian, as Severus and Jerome attest, Felicissimus, Julian, Asarinus, Aurelius, Armenus, Latronianus, and Eucrocia, the wife of the rhetor Delphidius, were condemned to death. Concerning their daughter Procula, Severus says:

> “It was commonly reported that she had become pregnant through Priscillian’s violation and had caused herself to miscarry by means of herbs.”

Ausonius signifies both the punishment of Delphidius’s wife and the disgrace of his daughter when, in *Epigram* V of the *Professors of Bordeaux*, he says of Delphidius—Gislenius noted this long ago:

> “Who was taken away in the middle of his life:  
> wounded by the error of his daughter who did not stray,  
> and by the punishment of his wife.””

Other followers of Priscillian, subjected to milder punishments, were sent into exile. But the heresy was not extinguished; rather, as Idatius says, it subsequently increased and invaded Galicia.

## Note X, p. 55

I scarcely understand why so many call Maximus a Briton, when, in the judgment of many, it was his end rather than his cause that made him a tyrant. For when Claudian sings of him, in the poem on the fourth consulship of Honorius:

> “This savage man Britain produced,”

he does not mean his homeland, but the province where he seized power. Zosimus expressly says that he was a Spaniard, in Book IV. Depranius, in the presence of Theodosius himself, indicates him as a household servant of the Theodosian house, as though he had been born within it. Who would not believe witnesses who were contemporaries and almost eyewitnesses? Pagius offers further discussion in his *Critica*, under the year 383, no. 4.
