Severus praises Maximus repeatedly and at length, and in Dialogue II, no. 7, commends the piety and religion of his wife in many ways. Orosius, Book VII, chapter 34, calls Maximus a vigorous and upright man, worthy of the title Augustus. Indeed, Theodosius himself, addressing Valentinian—according to Suidas, under the word *Valentinianus*—says of Maximus:

> “He rightly worships Christ, who did not unjustly expel you; and your perverse faith”—for Valentinian had adhered to the Arians—“gave Maximus this opportunity.”

Finally, even the most holy Pope Leo commends Maximus’s religion in his letter to Thuribius. I omit Rufinus, Book II, chapter 16, where he indicates that the causes of Maximus’s tyranny and rebellion against Valentinian were the latter’s impiety and heresy.

## Note XI, p. 55

1. Concerning Cynegius, Idatius writes in the *Fasti*, under the consulship of Theodosius II and Cynegius:

> “Cynegius, prefect of the East, died at Constantinople during his consulship. He restored to their former condition all the provinces that had been ruined by the corruption of a long period; he advanced as far as Egypt and overthrew the idols of the nations. Hence his body was escorted with great mourning by the entire populace of the city to the Apostles, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April. A year later his wife Achantia transferred him overland to Spain.”

Do you see, reader, how our Cynegius, made illustrious by the offices he held, was made still more illustrious by his zeal for the Catholic faith and justice? I say “our” Cynegius; for why would his wife Achantia transport him from Constantinople to Spain over an almost immeasurably long journey, unless it were to bury him in the monument of his ancestors?

The same thing happened at nearly the same time to Arborius, who died in the same city of Constantinople and was transferred to his homeland, whether that homeland was Toulouse or Bordeaux. Ausonius, the son of Arborius’s sister, records this in the passage cited above, *Epigram* XVII:

> “But the piety of the ruling Augustus restored you  
> to your homeland, the dwelling and monuments of your ancestors.”

2. Cynegius, therefore, was a Spaniard. But because of the persistent silence of the ancient writers, or through other circumstances, it has happened that neither his homeland nor that of several other Spaniards whom Theodosius must have had with him is recorded anywhere in writing.

Claudian certainly testifies in the panegyric on the fourth consulship of Honorius that Spanish nobility attended Honorius’s side, when he says in verse 582:

> “The Tagus surrounded you with illustrious offspring,  
> Gaul with learned citizens,  
> and Rome with her entire senate.”

Why should not even more Spaniards have followed Theodosius the father than followed his son?

But to return to Cynegius: that Idatius did not praise him beyond his deserts is testified by Zosimus, Book IV, a witness by no means suspect, since he is frequently hostile even to Christian men and emperors. The great Theodosius too, addressing Cynegius in Book XV *On Accusers* of the *Theodosian Code*, says:

> “By the justice and equity for which you are known, etc.”

If you want more, read Gothofredus in the *Prosopography* of the *Theodosian Code*, under the name *Cynegius*, where he discusses accurately Cynegius’s offices, his membership in the *comitiva sacrarum largitionum*, his prefecture of the praetorium in the East for several years, and his consulship.

3. As for the place where Cynegius died, do not let Zosimus mislead you when he says that he died on the road. That is true; but for Cynegius to travel from Egypt to Theodosius, by whom he had been summoned, in Illyricum, he had to pass through Constantinople, and there, as Idatius says, death overtook him.

Law XVI on heretics in the *Theodosian Code*, since it is addressed to Cynegius, prefect of the praetorium, on the sixth day of August of that year, might also lead a reader to believe that Cynegius was still alive on that day. But the inscription is misleading, as Law III, on those who dispute religion, in the same Code proves; from it we learn that Tatian held that prefecture on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July of the same year. Therefore Cynegius died around March 19, on which day, according to Idatius, he was carried to the Apostles.

4. In the acts of Saint Porphyry, in Surius and Bollandus, under February 26, notable mention is made of another Cynegius, whom Augustus Arcadius and his wife Eudoxia, in the year 401, charged with demolishing the temple of Marna at Gaza. The name of Cynegius, his ardent religious zeal, and the extraordinary favor he enjoyed at court indicate that he was the son or relative of the earlier Cynegius. Thus the illustrious family of the Cynegii may seem to have been born for storming and leveling to the ground the strongholds of idolatry.

Yet this Cynegius may perhaps be the same to whom the divine Ambrose sent Letter 72. The piety and outstanding character of that young man, together with the time when the letter was written, suggested this thought to me. In any event, this Cynegius’s father was named Paternus. Ambrose dissuades him from joining this son in marriage with his granddaughter, who was born of his daughter and therefore of this Cynegius’s sister.

The devout young man abhorred this marriage. Wishing to avoid it without violating his filial devotion toward his father, he appealed to Ambrose to dissuade his father from it. The most holy bishop did so in Letter 47 to Paternus, a letter most worthy of reading. Ambrose also mentions a law given by Theodosius that forbade, under the severest penalty, marriages between paternal cousins and between first cousins. If you wish, read the eminent Baronius under the year 390, at the end.

Finally, in Ennodius, after Letter 7 of Book IV and elsewhere, there is an epitaph for Cynegia, the wife of Faustus, a very distinguished man who held the highest honors. She may have been the granddaughter of one of these Cynegii.

## Note XII, p. 56

Prosper, Marcellinus, and the anonymous author of Cuspinian’s work incorrectly assign the beginning of Eugenius’s tyranny to the year 391; the latter gives its day as the eleventh day before the Kalends of September. Marcellinus and the Anonymous do not relate the matter in a way that is intrinsically incredible, for they assign Valentinian’s death, which was followed by the tyranny of Eugenius, to the same year 391.

But Prosper, who says that Valentinian was killed in the year 392—as indeed he was—is contradicting himself and writes mutually inconsistent accounts. Petavius, failing to notice this, likewise assigns the beginning of Eugenius’s seizure of power to the year 391, following Prosper.

## Note XIII, p. 56

I do not know how it could have happened that Idatius failed, under the year 393, to mention Honorius’s being taken by his father Theodosius into partnership in the imperial office. Socrates, Book V, chapter 24, reports that under the consulship of Theodosius III and Abundantius, who gave their names to the year 393, Honorius was proclaimed Augustus on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

But since Socrates writes that Theodosius departed for Gaul against Eugenius not long afterward, while Laws XXXI on public works and XXIV on heretics in the *Theodosian Code* teach us that at the beginning of July of the following year Theodosius had not yet left Constantinople, who does not see that Socrates is inconsistent with himself? For how could it be true that Theodosius moved from Constantinople toward Gaul shortly after Honorius had been taken into partnership in the empire, if he had still not departed from Constantinople a year and a half later?

Moreover, Prosper and Marcellinus speak in such a way that they seem to assert that the sun was eclipsed on the same day on which Honorius was proclaimed his father’s imperial colleague. Yet according to the rules of astronomy, this solar eclipse could not have occurred on January 9 in the year 393.

The distinguished astronomer Petavius therefore judges more correctly, in Part II, Book IV, chapter 2 of his *Rationarium Temporum*, that Honorius was taken by his father into partnership in the empire on November 20, the day on which the sun suffered an eclipse in the year 393. That date lies ten months and more from July of the following year, 394, when Theodosius set out from the East against Eugenius, whereas January 9, the date given by Socrates, is separated from it by only five months.

Ptolemy Silvius, in his *Calendar*, assigns Honorius’s birthday to February 18—by “birthday” I mean the birthday of his accession to the purple, which is the matter now under discussion. If one must depart from Petavius’s opinion, I would agree with Silvius rather than with Socrates, because Silvius lived in the West, or even in Rome itself, where this birthday of Honorius was solemnly celebrated every year in Silvius’s own time.

The Anonymous of Cuspinian disagrees with all the others, assigning the eclipse to the sixth day before the Kalends of November and Honorius’s inauguration to the tenth day before the Kalends of February.

## Note XIV, p. 56

When some sleepy copyist had first written the passage in this form:

> “In this place only, beyond the reigns, only the inserted reigns of the emperors,”

carelessly repeating the word *tantum* (“only”), another later copyist attempted to cleanse the blemish. He retained the adverb *tantum* in the first position, but in the second combined it with the preceding word *regna* (“reigns”), making from the two words *regna* and *tantum* the single word *regnantum*. This has been retained in the printed books down to the present, as I noted in the scholion.

Nevertheless, an unmistakable indication of the ancient reading was left to us: that reading placed the adverb *tantum* only once, and indeed in the final position, modifying, so to speak, the words *propter regna* (“on account of the reigns”). Nor was it ever Idatius’s intention that in this one passage we should count five years of imperial rule under a single Olympiad, for we shall see the same thing several times below.

Whenever this occurs, under one civil year you will find two emperors: one whose reign is ending and another whose imperial rule is beginning. Yet because neither year is complete, both are marked by a single civil year.

What Idatius observed about the Olympiad must likewise be understood of the decades of the Abrahamic years, lest the addition of the eleventh year of a reign disturb the reckoning. Bouquetius and Pagius, failing to notice this, count eleven years from Abrahamic year 2410 to Abrahamic year 2420. Consequently, Pagius, under the year 405, no. 14, incorrectly assigns Abrahamic year 2416 to the fifth year of Honorius, as I shall show under the year 400.

Bouquetius, in Florius, no. 116, also errs when he says that the seventeenth year of Theodosius corresponds in Idatius’s *Chronicle* to Abrahamic year 2410. Apart from the fact that this Abrahamic year comes closer in the *Chronicle* to the sixteenth year of Theodosius, all the remaining years down to 2460 necessarily require that Abrahamic year 2410 be assigned to the sixteenth year of Theodosius. If you wish, you will find more on these matters in the preliminary dissertation, nos. 25 and 26.

## Note XV, p. 57

When Idatius, speaking of Arcadius and Honorius, says that they reigned for thirty years from the death of their father, he intended to signify not that both of them reached thirty years of reign, but that one of them—namely Honorius—reached the thirtieth year of his reign. Nor is it true that Honorius ruled for a full thirty years. Arcadius died in the fourteenth year of his reign, in the fourth month—specifically, on the Kalends of May in the year 408 of the common era. Honorius, however, did not complete even twenty-nine years.

But when Idatius assigns to his reign the period extending from the death of Theodosius the father to the accession of Valentinian III in the year 425, or rather to the beginning of that year, where, after performing his calculations, he prefixed the first year of the younger Theodosius, he arrived at a total of thirty years. Hence we gather that Idatius assigned the year 424 of the common era to Honorius. This is also clearly confirmed by the designation of the chronological notes themselves.

## Note XVI, p. 58

1. In the Sirmondian edition, this Council of Toledo is assigned to the fifth year of Arcadius and Honorius, but to the year 399 of the Christian era. The distinguished Florius was the first to place it under the sixth year; and although this correction is supported by no other testimony from Idatius, it nevertheless seemed to me that it must be firmly retained.

The reason is first that the heading of the council itself gives the consulship of Stilicho, which can scarcely, or perhaps cannot at all, be anyone other than the Stilicho who was consul in the year 400. The second reason is that it was easy for a copyist to anticipate the section “In the province of Carthage” by one stroke of the pen, especially since that space was blank.

Nevertheless, the most learned Pagius judges that the ancient reading should be retained, because he believes that Idatius assigned this council to Abrahamic year 2416, which, he says under the year 405, no. 14, began on the Kalends of September in the year 399 of the Christian era.

But first, if Abrahamic year 2416 began on the Kalends of September in the year 399, it must have ended on the preceding day of those same Kalends in the year 400. Yet the council was convened on these Kalends of the year 400, if it was convened under Stilicho’s first consulship. Therefore it was not celebrated within Abrahamic year 2416, but on the first day of year 2417—a conclusion Pagius would reject.

Furthermore, according to Idatius, the fifth year of Arcadius and Honorius could fall neither in Dionysian year 400, when Stilicho was first proclaimed consul, nor in Abrahamic year 2416, since their first year as Augusti is linked by Idatius to Abrahamic year 2410, which coincides with Dionysian year 395.

Therefore, anyone who maintains that this Council of Toledo was celebrated in the year 400 of the common era and in Abrahamic year 2416 cannot avoid placing it in the sixth year of Arcadius and Honorius. I would be greatly astonished that Pagius failed to notice this, unless he himself had not elsewhere warned that the multiplication of chronological periods is burdensome to memory and understanding. I have no doubt that this error of his arose from the different method of reckoning Idatian and common years that Pagius follows.

2. I moved the birthday of the younger Theodosius, which in other editions of this *Chronicle* is assigned to the ninth year of Arcadius and Honorius, back to the seventh year of the present reckoning. I have no doubt that Idatius assigned it to that year and that it was transferred through the error of copyists to the ninth year of the common era, 403.

For in the *Chronicle* published by the most learned Florius under the name of Severus Sulpicius, under the seventh year—Florius corrected this to the eighth, but without justification—the manuscript reads:

> “The younger Theodosius was made Augustus.”

It is generally agreed that nearly everything written in that *Chronicle* from Theodosius the Great to Anthemius was drawn from Idatius. I therefore have no hesitation in believing that Idatius wrote in the *Chronicle* as follows:

> “VII. Theodosius, son of Arcadius, is born and is made Augustus.”

Indeed, in the *Life of Saint Porphyry, Bishop of Gaza* (February 26), it is written:

> “When Theodosius had first been born, he was proclaimed emperor.”

We may at least interpret this as referring to the acclamation and assumption of the purple. But if someone wishes to interpret Idatius’s words as referring to a formal inauguration, assigning it, with Marcellinus and the Alexandrian *Chronicle*, to the fourth day before the Ides of January in the eighth year of Arcadius and Honorius, I would say that Idatius distinguished the matters as follows:

> “VII. Theodosius, son of Arcadius, is born.  
> VIII. Theodosius is made Augustus.  
> A solar eclipse occurred on the third day before the Ides of November.”

Moreover, after the words “the younger Theodosius” in Severus, something is plainly missing. The passage cannot be better restored than by reading:

> “The younger Theodosius was born and was made Augustus.”

This is also suggested by what follows in the same passage, for he immediately adds:

> “The sun suffered an eclipse,”

and that eclipse certainly occurred in the eighth year.

All these considerations clearly demonstrate that Idatius assigned the birthday of Theodosius to the seventh year of Arcadius and Honorius and that, through the carelessness of copyists, it slipped into their ninth year.

3. Furthermore, under the thirtieth year of Honorius, A.D. 424, Idatius says of this same Theodosius:

> “After the death of his paternal uncle Honorius, he held sole rule of the empire when he was twenty-six years old.”

This must be false if Theodosius was born in the year 403. But if, instead of *XXVI* (“twenty-six”), one reads *XXIV* (“twenty-four”), with the numeral I placed before the numeral V—where, in my opinion, a copyist carelessly placed it afterward—everything coheres, and Idatius will not have written contradictory statements.

For if Theodosius was twenty-four years old when Idatius entered him into his *Chronicle* under the year 425, he must have been born in the year 401; and if he was born in that year, then when the year 426 was reached he was certainly twenty-four years old.

Theodosius was born on the fourth day before the Ides of April, according to Socrates, Book VI, chapter 6, and Marcellinus, both in the *Chronicle* published before Sirmond and in the Bruges manuscript possessed by Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius. In the Sirmondian edition, however, the third day before the Ides is read.

Bollandus concludes from the acts of Saint Porphyry, bishop of Gaza, that he was born on March 23. But the events narrated in those acts do not necessarily require that date. Perhaps he was born on March 29 of the same month, and through a copyist’s error the fourth day before the Kalends was written in Socrates and Marcellinus as the fourth day before the Ides of April.

## Note XVII, p. 59

Since, after Cyril—of whom Jerome, in his *On Illustrious Men*, no. 122, left it on record that, having often been expelled from the Jerusalem church and restored, he ultimately held an undisturbed episcopate for eight years under the emperor Theodosius—John was appointed as his successor around the year 387, no Arian bishop had occupied the church of Jerusalem before John, except for the one whom Jerome had mentioned in his *Chronicle*.

Indeed, since Cyril’s orthodoxy and holiness are abundantly established—for he has been entered in the calendars of the saints (see the acts of the Jesuits of Antwerp, under March 28)—there was never during that period a legitimate Arian bishop of Jerusalem. Cyril succeeded the Catholic Maximus, and John succeeded Cyril immediately after Cyril’s death.

Therefore, those whom Jerome counts in the eleventh year as two Arian bishops, on account of Constantine’s sons, must be called intruders and pseudo-bishops, both because they were heretics and because, while the legitimate bishop Cyril was still alive, they occupied that church.

## Note XVIII, p. 60

Concerning the entry of the barbarians into Spain, under the consulship of Honorius VIII and Theodosius III, Idatius wrote only this in the *Fasti*:

> “Under these consuls the barbarians entered Spain.”

Nothing more is added. I have acknowledged in the scholion that the rest of what the *Chronicle* contains on this subject seems suspect to me.

Since the entry of the barbarians into Spain occurred under the observation of Idatius, who would believe that he wrote the following?

> “Some report the fourth day before the Kalends, others the third day before the Ides of October,”

especially since September 28 and October 13 cannot fall on Tuesday in one and the same year, while Idatius places that entry on a Tuesday. Therefore one of those dates is an interpolation. Why not also everything else beginning with the word “entered”?

But if anyone wishes to retain the common reading, let him correct the date “the third day before the Ides of October” from the *Short Chronicle*, reading “the fourth day before the Ides,” or reject it altogether, following the *Excerpts from Hispania Illustrata*, where only the first date, the fourth day before the Kalends, is given.

Since the entry of the barbarians into Spain cannot be removed from this year—for Idatius confirms it in the *Fasti*, with Isidore, Prosper, and Cassiodorus themselves agreeing—it is better either to change the date “the third day before the Ides,” which fell on Wednesday, for this year had solar cycle 26 and Sunday letter C, into “the fourth day before the Ides,” which fell on Tuesday, as did the fourth day before the Kalends, or to retain the latter date and reject the former entirely.

## Note XIX, p. 60
1. When Sirmond, on the authority of a manuscript codex, had assigned the sixteenth year of Honorius—which was the common era 410—after his account in the *Chronicle* of the city’s invasion and Alaric’s death, to the section “While they were raging,” the learned Florius moved those entries and added the section “Alaric, king of the Goths,” so that the invasion of the City and Alaric’s death would be read under that year of Honorius. I, however, just as I readily agree with Idatius that he did not attach Alaric’s death to the year 409 and that he added those entries to the section “Alaric dies,” whose beginning is the same as that of the other section, “Alaric, king,” so likewise believe that what he wrote about Placidia’s captivity and the devastation of the City was entered under the fifteenth year of Honorius, the common era 409. For although the testimony of almost all writers establishes that Rome was captured and plundered by Alaric in the sixteenth year of Honorius, nevertheless, since it is equally established that Alaric made more than one invasion of the City, Idatius could reasonably have attached everything he narrates from the section “The Alans and Vandals” through at least “Alaric dies” to the fifteenth year of Honorius, A.D. 409, because most of those events occurred in that year. Many were killed within and outside the City; the citizens were grievously afflicted; Alaric entered Rome and took Placidia away as a kind of hostage, after peace had been concluded with the senate and was to be confirmed by Honorius. Since Idatius was therefore recounting these events in the year 409, he added the City’s disaster because it was connected with them. However that may be, since the Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book I, chapter 2, and Ivo of Chartres, in a manuscript *Chronicle* preserved by Schelestratus, volume I, dissertation 2, page 229, report that the destruction of the City occurred in 409—a view which Pagius has most recently undertaken to assert at length—I did not think that the sixteenth year of Honorius should be transferred in Idatius to the section “Alaric, king,” lest I seem to wish to deprive him of this patron of his opinion.

2. In any event, I too most firmly agree that the devastation inflicted upon Rome did not occur before the year 410. For all historians teach this, except the Bede and Ivo just mentioned; yet we may doubt whether, in their calculation, they follow the same reckoning as the others. Moreover, this is demonstrated by the magnitude of the events that took place between Stilicho’s death and that final invasion of the City. Alaric did not march against the City immediately after Stilicho was killed; he marched somewhat later, after Eucherius, Stilicho’s son, had also been put to death. Then, when Alaric approached the City and surrounded it with a siege, a double embassy was sent by the senate to Honorius, who was then at Ravenna, to negotiate peace with the Goth. After this Alaric himself also approached Ravenna with his army. There long negotiations concerning the terms of peace took place between him and Honorius through intermediaries. Furthermore, Attalus was clothed in and stripped of the purple once and again, whatever Pagius may protest, at the year 410, no. 10, against the clear words of Orosius and Olympiodorus by maintaining that Attalus assumed tyranny for the second time in 414. Finally, at that time Attalus himself organized an expedition to Africa; and because it failed—having been undertaken with Roman troops alone, the Goths having been excluded—Alaric deprived Attalus of imperial power. All these events require a longer period than one year. Therefore, since Stilicho was killed on 23 August and the City was also devastated by the Goths on 24 August, all historians assign Stilicho’s death to August of the year 408 and the final invasion of the City to August of the year 410.

[Col. 0761A] 3. But it is better to hear Zosimus, who, as Photius reports in his *Bibliotheca*, says:

> “When Alaric was besieging Rome for the second time, and the citizens had been reduced to want, he raised the siege and gave them an emperor, Attalus, whom he afterward again deprived of imperial power; then he sent him to Honorius Augustus, who was at that time residing at Ravenna, to conclude a treaty with him. But Assarus”—the others consistently call him Sarus—“himself also a Goth, impeded Alaric’s affairs.”

And Photius adds: “Zosimus brings his sixth book of histories to an end at this point.”

Pagius acknowledged this very point at the year 410, no. 5, when he says:

> “He”—Zosimus—“then speaks of the battle fought between Alaric and the commander Sarus; after partially relating that battle, his work comes to an end, the rest having been lost through the injury of time.”

From this it is perfectly clear that Rome was besieged three times by the Goths, as Sozomen explicitly relates, book IX, chapters 6, 8, and 9. Zosimus expressly mentions the repeated siege and relates that Alaric raised it, then considered and seriously negotiated peace with Honorius, but that Sarus placed an obstacle in the way of its conclusion. Pagius himself acknowledges that we read no more in the history of Zosimus as we now possess it, at the year 410, no. 5. Yet after he had brought his history to an end, and Sarus had provoked Alaric by his insult, that invasion followed in which Rome was captured and devastated. It is therefore wholly incredible that this third and final capture of the City occurred before the year 410.

4. Tertullus’s consulship also, in my judgment, demonstrates this most clearly; and I am astonished that the learned Pagius, at the year 410, no. 8, inferred from that consulship that Rome was devastated by Alaric in 409. Would Tertullus have dared to assume the name of consul after Attalus’s abdication, after the plundering of the City, and after the Goths had departed from it? Pagius, citing Zosimus, says:

> “On the day after Attalus was called emperor, he entered the senate and designated Tertullus consul—something that was certainly done in 409—and Rome was then plundered by Alaric.”

In the first place, I still do not understand what this designation of Tertullus has to do with the matter. On the contrary, the consulship, which Tertullus held in the year 410 for several months and only within the walls of the City, shows that at the beginning of that year it had not yet been plundered and abandoned by the Goths. Therefore, as that year 410 approached, while affairs were especially disordered and the Goths occupied everything around the City, Tertullus was permitted to act within it as a counterfeit consul, until, after Rome’s disaster and the Goths’ departure in August of that same year 410, even that shadow of a consulship vanished. Hence Orosius calls Tertullus a shadowy consul, book VII, chapter 42; Prosper and Marcellinus, in their *Chronicles*, not only pass over his consulship but expressly note that the only consul in that year was Varanes of the eastern provinces. Idatius likewise asserts Tertullus’s consulship in such a way that he seems closer to denying it than affirming it.

Furthermore, where did Pagius read that Rome was captured and plundered by the Goths immediately after Attalus had been called emperor and Tertullus designated consul? Zosimus was so far from writing this that he expressly reports the opposite, saying:

> “When Alaric was besieging Rome for the second time, and the citizens had been reduced to want, he raised the siege,”

and so forth, as quoted above.

What is more, so many and such great events took place between that time and the destruction of the City that scarcely could a full and uninterrupted year suffice for them; I believe I have already demonstrated this abundantly. The reason Pagius wrote so much about the year of the City’s plundering that was contrary to the truth was that he undertook his work persuaded that Rome had been besieged by the Goths only twice. Thus he interpreted what occurred in the third capture—and what the ancient writers relate about that event—as belonging to the second capture, which preceded the third by one year. Therefore, when Idatius had begun to speak of the City’s calamities in the preceding year, when it was besieged once and again, he mentioned the final disaster in that same year, before the end of the scene, so to speak.

5. At that point he also mentions that Placidia had been captured by Alaric in the City; and in fact she was carried away by the Goths from there in the year 409. For Zosimus, who, as has just been said, brought his history to an end before the third invasion of the City, writes the following about Placidia in book VI:

> “Placidia, the emperor’s sister, remained with Alaric, fulfilling in a certain way the role of a hostage, yet enjoying every honor and royal treatment.”

From this several points stated above are confirmed, and Alaric’s courtesy and magnanimity are displayed: he treated the royal maiden splendidly and, to speak with Plautus, in kingly fashion.

## Note XX, p. 60

1. Idatius deliberately wrote that, during the City’s destruction, the Goths granted mercy to those who fled to the thresholds of the saints. For in that devastation it was not only the basilicas of the Apostles but also, as Saint Augustine testifies, *The City of God*, book I, chapter 1, the places of the Martyrs that received those who fled to them, their own and others alike. Thus the Goths judged that what they might lawfully have done to the Romans by the right of war was unlawful for them. In the same work, book II, chapter 2, Augustine says that Alaric even ordered all his soldiers to refrain, as far as they could, from bloodshed, though they were eager for booty. Orosius reports the same, book VII, chapter 39. The greatest part—or rather almost all—of the houses and buildings of the City was also spared. Orosius, speaking of this disaster in chapter 40, says:

> “Although the memory of this event is still recent, nevertheless, if anyone should see the multitude of the Roman people and hear its voice, he will think that nothing happened—as they themselves also admit—unless some ruins still remaining from the fire should prove it.”

This is how the Goths acted toward the Romans. Olympiodorus confirms it, reporting that in the fourth year after the invasion, when Albinus was prefect of the City, Rome had returned to its former condition. Whoever compares these facts with the impious and cruel deeds that the Romans themselves at that time committed against both God and human beings will certainly find that they suffered treatment far milder than what they had inflicted.

2. For, apart from the enormous vices with which they were then afflicted, and which Saint Augustine, Orosius, Salvianus, Sozomen, and others reproach them for, how much more savagely did they ravage almost the whole remainder of the world? To say nothing of the illustrious cities of Carthage, Corinth, Syracuse, Tarentum, and Numantia, which surpassed all these in renown for valor, and of countless others, one Sempronius Gracchus devastated three hundred towns within the boundaries of Spain with sword and fire. Polybius attests this in his fragments. Orosius, book IV, chapter 20, says that 350 towns were destroyed by this Gracchus. But read 305, for the manuscripts vary, and this number comes closer to Polybius.

And what of Julius Caesar in Gaul? In addition to his civil victories, he himself admitted that 1,192,000 men had been killed by him in battle. These are the words of Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chapter 25. That Julius, this sacrificer to his insane ambition, slaughtered just as many victims in a single Gallic war.

But there is no need to search among more ancient examples. At this very time Heraclianus, the count of Africa, raged against his fellow Romans more savagely than the Goths did; those Romans who emerged from the shipwreck of the City found the shores of Africa more cruel, as Jerome writes in letter 8. Finally, the Goths then gave many examples not of barbarous or savage, but of excellent character, as Jerome, Augustine, Orosius, Sozomen, and others relate.

I know that, less than two centuries ago, a great man wrote that, after the City had been occupied by the Goths, Titus the Deacon, while distributing money to the poor, was killed by Arian Goths at the command of a barbarian tribune. I do not know what injury the Goths had done to this very distinguished man; but everyone knows how undeservedly he often maligns the Goths and their descendants. Saint Prosper, however, the sole witness to Saint Titus’s death, gives a very different account under the consulship of Theodosius XII and Valentinian II, as learned men in Gaul observed long ago. You will find Prosper’s words copied below, in note 43.

## Note XXI, p. 60

Alaric, as Isidore relates in his *History of the Goths*, died shortly after the City’s disaster, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, the sixteenth year of Honorius, the common era 410. Since Isidore copied Idatius, I did not rashly believe that Alaric’s death had been assigned to the fifteenth year of Honorius through a scribal error, as we see in the printed books, but rather that it should be attached to the sixteenth year of that same Honorius, and that this note should be detached from “While they were raging” and placed before “Alaric dies.” Thus, on the third day—not the sixth, as Marcellinus incorrectly reports in his *Chronicle*—Alaric voluntarily departed with his people, traversed Campania and Lucania, and finally, having been seized by illness in Bruttium near Consentia, died.

After he had been carried away amid immense mourning and a magnificent funeral, the Visigoths entrusted the kingdom to his kinsman Ataulf—certainly a relation, since he was Alaric’s wife’s brother—a man distinguished in appearance and intellect. So Jordanes relates in his *Getica*, nos. 54 and 55, where you may read other details if you wish.

On what day Alaric died, or on what day Ataulf became king, cannot be determined with certainty, since none of the historians committed these matters to writing. But it may be inferred that neither event occurred before November of the year 410, because Rome was captured on 24 August, as Paul the Deacon and Theophanes testify. After three days—that is, on the 27th or 28th of that same month—Alaric abandoned it; then, invading Campania, he traversed the rest of Italy as far as the Strait of Sicily, a journey requiring at least two or three months.

## Note XXII, p. 62

1. When Idatius says that the Spaniards who had withdrawn into forts and cities submitted themselves to the slavery of the barbarians, do not understand his words in such a way as to suppose that they lost their freedom. In these places, since they could not be conquered by the barbarians, peace was finally established between the two sides, and the Spaniards in a certain sense acquired greater freedom than before, since they were compelled to serve neither the barbarians nor the Romans. The fortification of the places protected them from the barbarians, while the barbarians themselves protected them from the Romans and from the Romans’ unrestrained domination at that time.

Moreover, the Spaniards still wished to be counted among the Romans because of the majesty of the empire to which they had long been subject, and so that, should fortune permit, they might be assisted by the Romans. The Gallaeci in particular experienced this repeatedly, as Idatius records in several places. I also think that they received magistrates from the emperor whenever such officials were sent to them from the City. But I would believe that they were rarely sent to Gallaecia, where, from the year 400 onward, the Suevi, spread across the plains, blocked all the roads for travelers from Rome to Gallaecia.

Therefore, during this period I believe that in every city and town the people elected a magistrate who administered the state, and that the peoples preserved their freedom. Indeed, Isidore clearly attests this in his *History of the Suevi*, where he says:

> “The Gallaeci”—so you should read; they do not read *Galliciae*, as Grotius does, nor *Galliae*, as Labbe does—“enjoyed their own kingdom in part of the province.”

Nevertheless, Idatius says that the Spaniards submitted themselves to the barbarians because they allowed them to settle in the province and possess its richer and more fertile fields. Often not satisfied with these, the barbarians continually ravaged the remaining fields as well, which under the terms of peace had been ceded to the former owners of the places; they also continually threatened the cities and forts. It is therefore of this slavery that Idatius speaks: the condition that exposed the Gallaeci to the frequent and almost daily attacks of the Suevi.

2. Yet however burdensome this slavery was to the Spaniards, Orosius and Salvianus testify that during these times they and the Gauls endured something far more grievous from the Romans while they were subject to them. Orosius, speaking of this matter in book VII, chapter 41, says:

> “After this”—that is, after the great and bloody barbarian invasions of Spain, which he had mentioned earlier—“the barbarians immediately abhorred their swords and turned to plows; and they cherish the Romans who remained”—he means the Spaniards, who had been part of the Roman Empire—“as associates and friends only. Thus some Romans are now found who would rather endure poor freedom among barbarians than tributary slavery among Romans.”

Salvianus says something similar in book VI of *On the Government of God*, speaking of the Gauls who voluntarily turned to the Goths:

> “They migrate to the barbarians, and do not regret having migrated; for they prefer to live free under the appearance of captivity than to be captives under the appearance of freedom.”

## Note XXIII, p. 63

[Col. 0764A]

In the *Fasti*, under Lucius, the consul who gave his name to the year 413, our Idatius says: “Jovinus and Sebastianus were killed, and Heraclianus was abolished”—that is, eliminated. Prosper agrees. Marcellinus, however, assigns Jovinus’s and Sebastianus’s deaths to the preceding year. The authority of Idatius and Prosper is preferable.

Of these same tyrants Orosius says, book VII, chapter 42:

> “Jovinus, a most noble man of Gaul, fell as soon as he rose to tyranny; his brother Sebastianus chose only this, to die as a tyrant, for immediately after he had been elevated he was killed.”

Olympiodorus reports that Jovinus seized tyranny at Mundiacum—read *Mogunciacum*—a city of Germany, through the efforts of Goar the Alan and Guntarius, prefect of the Burgundians; the latter is called Gundicarius by others. He further adds that Jovinus was displeased that Ataulf was approaching him, and that Ataulf likewise became angry with Jovinus because, against his will, Jovinus had declared his brother Sebastianus emperor. Thus, hostile to both, Ataulf cut off Sebastianus’s head but sent Jovinus alive to Honorius.

This is what Olympiodorus says, clearly indicating that Jovinus was killed in Italy, where Honorius was. Prosper and Marcellinus, however, agree with Idatius in saying that both brothers were killed in Gaul.

## Note XXIV, p. 64

1. Olympiodorus reports the following concerning the marriage of Ataulf and Placidia, as preserved by Photius:

> “Through the initiative and planning of Candidianus, the marriage with Placidia was arranged for Ataulf. The wedding day was fixed in the month of January, in Narbonne, a city of Gaul, in the house of a certain prominent man of that city named Ingenius. Placidia sat in the more honorable place, in a Roman-style atrium adorned in royal fashion; Ataulf sat beside her, clothed in wool and in every other Roman garment. Among the other wedding gifts, Ataulf”—but “by Ataulf” must be read; for it was not Ataulf who was given these gifts by Placidia, but Placidia who was given them by Ataulf—“was also presented with fifty handsome boys dressed in silk garments, each carrying in both hands two enormous dishes, one filled with gold and the other with precious stones, or rather with objects of inestimable value, which the Goths had plundered from the sack of the City of Rome. Then epithalamian verses were sung, with Attalus leading, followed by Rusticius and Phoebadius. The wedding ended amid immense sport and joy among both the barbarians and the Romans who were with them.”

2. It follows plainly from this that the author of the *Miscellany* did not know either the time or the place of this marriage when he says, in book XIII, that it was celebrated at Forum Cornelii before Ataulf had departed from Italy.

It is also clear from the month of January assigned by Olympiodorus to the wedding that the learned Pagius was seriously mistaken when he embraced the firmly held opinion that the Idatian years began in October. For if that were so, the vintage of the common era 413 and the marriage of Ataulf and Placidia, celebrated in the following January, would certainly have been assigned by Idatius in the *Chronicle* to the same year—namely, Abraham’s year 2430, in whose first month the vintage and in whose third month the marriage would have occurred.

But Idatius did not proceed in this way. Instead, he assigned the vintages, at whose time the Goths entered Narbonne, to the nineteenth year of Honorius, and the marriage to the twentieth year. It is therefore evident that Idatius extended the nineteenth year of Honorius and of Abraham 2429 through the end of December, which followed immediately after those vintages; when that year had ended there, he began a new year in the following January, namely, the twentieth year of Honorius and Abraham 2430, on the first day of the Christian year 414. The placement of the chronological entries in the *Chronicle* demonstrates this most clearly.

3. Finally, Philostorgius, otherwise a most mendacious writer, reports that Ataulf married Placidia while his first wife was still alive. No one else has reported this, nor, I think, will anyone believe it.

## Note XXV, p. 64

1. In the *Fasti*, under the consulship of Honorius X and Theodosius VI—that is, in the year 415 of the common era—after relating that the discovery of the sacred relics of Saint Stephen occurred on Friday, 3 December, our Idatius adds:

> “There survive from these events a letter of the priest Saint Lucian and of the priest Saint Avitus of Bracara, who were then residing in Jerusalem. Lucian, to whom the revelation was made, wrote the history of this discovery in Greek; Avitus rendered it into Latin.”

It is found in volume X of the works of Saint Augustine, page 630 in my edition.

2. Someone may perhaps think that this Avitus was the same man to whom Jerome sent letter LIX, in which the errors of Origen are discussed. There was, moreover, a substantial reason at that time why the Spaniards should consult Jerome about Origen. Orosius explains it in the *Commonitorium* included in volume VI of Saint Augustine’s works.

The chronology also fits very well. That letter dates from about the year 413, as is clear from its opening, where Jerome says that ten years earlier he had written to Pammachius on the same subject. Those letters to Pammachius, however, were written about the year 404; in them we read that 151 years were then being counted from Origen’s death. Origen died in the year 253; from all this, therefore, the year 414 follows. If, however, the years were not all complete, we may correctly assign the letter to Pammachius to the year 403 and the letter to Avitus to the year 413; but if they were complete, one was written in 404 and the other in 413.

3. I know that the learned Pagius assigns the letter to Pammachius to the year 399, relying on Jerome’s own testimony, in which Jerome indicates that twenty years before sending those letters to Pammachius he had been in Constantinople with Gregory of Nazianzus. But Pagius, and the great Baronius as well, was deceived when they believed that Jerome met Gregory at Constantinople in the year 379.

For after the synod of Antioch, held in October of that same year 379, Gregory departed from Syria for Constantinople, and Jerome afterward joined him there. Nothing, however, is more likely than that Jerome did not undertake this journey until news had reached the East that the churches of Constantinople had been taken from the Arians and restored to the Catholics by an edict of Theodosius the Great. That edict was promulgated or enacted at Thessalonica on 27 February of the year 380 and is found in book II, *On the Catholic Faith*, of the Theodosian Code. It could scarcely have been possible, therefore, for Jerome to have arrived at Constantinople before the end of that same year 380.

He also remained in that city during the following year, 381, while the general council was being held. Baronius himself testifies to this under that year, and it may also be inferred from Jerome’s own work, *On Illustrious Men*, in the section on Gregory of Nyssa.

Since it follows correctly from all this that the twentieth year from Jerome’s residence in the city of Constantinople could not have been completed before the year 402, while Jerome himself says that it had been completed when he writes, “A book published twenty years ago is in men’s hands”—his words in the aforementioned letter to Pammachius, no. 65—it is much more probable that the twenty years, and even more, which he himself counts from his residence in Constantinople to the letter he wrote to Pammachius, and ten years from that letter to the letters written to Avitus, should be reckoned backward from the year 412 or, preferably, 413, rather than from the year 379. This is especially so because this calculation agrees perfectly with the earlier one I derived above from the chronological data concerning Origen.

4. If this Avitus was also the man who brought Origen’s books back to his homeland from his pilgrimage to Jerusalem, he could have sailed again to Palestine after the year 409, either from longing for the holy places, from weariness with his homeland, which he saw being torn apart by the barbarians, or in order to consult Jerome, since he had already made that pilgrimage once before when he returned carrying Origen’s books.

If this is so, Orosius must certainly be called a native of Bracara, since in the *Commonitorium* he himself calls that Avitus his fellow citizen. From Avitus’s name—which was already common in that region of Spain, as is clear from ancient inscriptions in Gruter, page 31, no. 8; page 93, no. 2; page 252, no. 5, and in Barveirus, *Itinerarium*, page 49—from the pilgrimage to Palestine, which the Gallaeci frequently undertook in those times, and finally from the errors of Priscillian, which had become prevalent nowhere more than in Gallaecia, and which Orosius set before Augustine together with the Origenist errors in the same *Commonitorium*, I think it may be believed, not altogether rashly, that Avitus, who transported Origen’s books to Spain, was a native of Bracara or at least of Gallaecia.

I do not, however, assert that this is certain. I have merely wished to set forth this suspicion of mine, out of a desire to illuminate our history.

## Note XXVI, p. 65

1. As was noted in the scholium, Ataulf left Narbonne in the preceding year and occupied Barcelona in Spain, where he was killed in the following year, which was the common era 416. Morales therefore, book XI, chapter 12, wrongly postponed the entry of the Goths into Spain and the beginning of their kingdom there to this same year 416.

Majansius strayed even farther when he wrote in the preface to the works on the chronology of the Marquis of Mondéjar, no. 80:

> “The kingdom of Spain began in the year 420 … when the Goths divided the provinces of Spain among themselves in the manner described by Idatius, bishop of Lamego, in his *Chronicle*, and by Saint Isidore, who copied him in his *History of the Vandals*, era 459.”

This is incorrect. For according to Idatius, the Gothic kingdom in Spain by no means began in the common era 420, but in 415. The division of the provinces by the barbarians took place, according to the same Idatius, in the year 411, when the Goths had not yet left Italy or crossed the Alps in order to come to Spain. Therefore it was not the Goths, but the Vandals, Alans, Silingi, and Suevi who divided the provinces among themselves.

Isidore assigns this same division of the provinces to era 449, not 459, as Majansius says. He made all these claims in order to infer from them that the 985th year of the Gothic kingdom fell in the Dionysian year 1407. In order to establish this, he had to attach the beginning of the Gothic kingdom to the common era 423.

Nor was the learned Pagius more accurate in moving Ataulf’s death back to the year 415—read there, no. 23—on the authority of the Alexandrian *Chronicle*, in which the following appears under the consulship of Honorius X and Theodosius VI:

> “In the month Goripiaeus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, Friday, news was brought of the murder of the barbarian Ataulf in the upper regions.”

From this Pagius infers that Ataulf died on 24 September of the year 415, the year in which that consulship occurred, and that Idatius began the year from the Kalends of October.

But if Pagius has now reminded us of this beginning of the year in order to persuade us that Idatius agrees with the author of the Alexandrian *Chronicle* about the year of Ataulf’s death, he is mistaken. On that day, 24 September, Abraham’s year 2332, to which Idatius assigns Ataulf’s death, had not yet begun; according to Pagius, it began eight days later, namely on the Kalends of the following October.

Therefore it must be stated without hesitation that Ataulf was killed in the common era 416, to which Abraham’s year 2332 and Honorius’s year 22 correspond in full in Idatius’s *Chronicle*. This is especially clear because Saint Isidore, in his *History of the Goths*, assigns six years to Ataulf’s reign; yet he would not even have reigned five years had he been killed on 24 September of the year 415.

For, from November of the year 410—before which, as I showed in note 21, Ataulf could not have received the kingdom—to 24 September of the year 415, fewer than five complete years are counted. Therefore, unless Pagius wishes to contradict Isidore and Idatius, whose testimony is far more authoritative, especially in matters concerning Spain, than that of the Alexandrian *Chronicle*, he must assign Ataulf’s death to the year 416.

It is also clear from this that the argument drawn from Ataulf’s death contributes nothing toward determining the beginning of the Idatian years. Saint Isidore, who begins the years of the Spanish era in January, assigns Ataulf’s death to era 454 and to the twenty-second year of Honorius—that is, to the common era 416—since he assigns Sigeric’s reign to that year. Since Olympiodorus establishes that Sigeric reigned only seven days, it is necessary that the death of the deceased Ataulf in September and Sigeric’s reign fell within the same Julian year, the common era 416, as Isidore reports.

Thus the author of the Alexandrian *Chronicle* may perhaps not be wrong about the day and month of Ataulf’s murder; his only error would lie in identifying the year, when, instead of Honorius and Palladius, who held the consulship in 416, he wrote Honorius and Theodosius and placed Ataulf’s death under them.

Finally, when Jordanes says of Ataulf in his *Getica*, no. 55, “He died in the third year after he had subdued Gaul and Spain,” he speaks so ambiguously that, if one wishes, one could infer from him that Ataulf died in the year 418 or 419.

2. Olympiodorus gives the following account of Ataulf’s murderer, the place of his death, and its cause:

> “Ataulf was killed while, as was his custom, he was inspecting his horses in the stable, by a certain Goth of his household named Dobbius, who had seized this opportunity to avenge an old hatred. For his former master, the king of the Gothic faction, had been put to death by Ataulf. Afterward Ataulf had received Dobbius and admitted him into his own household; but Dobbius, in revenge for his former master, violently struck down this second man with his own hand.”

This is what Olympiodorus says. Jordanes, however, in *Getica*, no. 55, gives the following account of the same death of Ataulf:

> “He died pierced by the sword of Vernulf, whose stature he was accustomed to ridicule.”

In these accounts by Olympiodorus and Jordanes, the name of Ataulf’s murderer differs. The remaining details differ neither from one another nor greatly from those of Idatius, except that Olympiodorus gives a fuller account. Since he describes several other matters about Ataulf so distinctly and individually, he appears to have been with Ataulf himself at Narbonne and Barcelona.

## Note XXVII, p. 65

Pagius, at the year 415, no. 25, thinks that from book XIV of the Theodosian Code, *On Invalidating Acts Done under Tyrants*, it may be inferred that peace was agreed upon between Vallia and Honorius before the Kalends of March of the year 416.

But since Vallia was not proclaimed king of the Goths before this year, but only while the year was already passing, as is abundantly clear from what has been said above, it is necessary that this peace was concluded long after the Kalends of March of that same year.

Moreover, in my judgment that law does not concern people who had followed one of the tyrants, but those who, surrendering themselves to plunder and brigandage amid the disorder of affairs, revived in Gaul at the beginning of this century the faction of the Bacaudae, which had been almost extinguished since the time of Diocletian. It lasted not only there but also in Spain for a hundred years and more.

To draw these men back from forests and inaccessible places into houses and towns, Honorius entices them with the more favorable words of that same law: “If, through flight or through the gathering of unfortunate peoples, etc.” Furthermore, since laws XI and XII, *On the Indulgence of Crimes*, in the same Code, were issued when war was raging throughout Italy, why could the aforementioned law, *On Invalidating Acts Done under Tyrants*, not have been issued before peace was made with the Goths?

It is therefore more certain that this treaty was struck at the end rather than the beginning of the year 416. Nor could it have been concluded immediately after Vallia’s election. Indeed, after the election had been heard of at Ravenna:

> “Emplutius Magistrianus was sent by Honorius to Vallia, prefect of the Goths, to establish the terms of peace and receive Placidia. He received her without difficulty, and after six hundred thousand measures of grain had been sent, Placidia was handed over to Emplutius and returned to her brother Honorius.”

Olympiodorus left this account in writing, and these events could not have been completed in a short time. Therefore, if Ataulf was killed toward the end of the year 416 and Vallia received the kingdom after him—for the moment there is no reason to count Sigeric—this peace was concluded at the end of that same year. Marcellinus assigns these events to the year 414.

## Note XXVIII, p. 65

Olympiodorus gives the following account of the marriage of Constantius and Placidia:

> “The emperor Honorius gave Placidia, although unwilling, into the hand of Constantius on the very day on which he entered upon the consulship.”

He entered the consulship on 31 December 416—the second day before the Kalends of January of 417—for Olympiodorus is speaking of this matter.

Our Idatius, Prosper, and Cassiodorus mention this marriage under the year 416 because Placidia was then betrothed to Constantius by Honorius, although she was not handed over until the first day of the following year.

## Note XXIX, p. 66

1. In the transcription of the section “During Bishop Durante’s episcopate,” the scribes introduced a double error. They both removed him from his own place and deprived him of the twenty-five chronological entries that Idatius had certainly assigned to this section, transferring them to “Among Gunderic’s deeds,” where the Sirmondian edition now presents them. Florius corrected this latter error and restored the aforementioned entries to their proper place.

He did this very well, and on the authority of Idatius himself in the *Fasti*, where he assigns those earthquakes in Palestine to the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta, which fell in the common era 419 and the twenty-fifth year of Honorius. There he writes:

> “Saint John, bishop of Jerusalem, who sends the letter mentioned above throughout the churches of the world, concerning signs and terrors divinely brought about.”

And so that no one may doubt that the Idatius who speaks here is the same man who wrote the *Chronicle*, please note that in both works the author asserts, with the same error, that these events occurred under Bishop John. This is certainly an argument that both works derive from the same source, as was observed in the preliminary dissertation, no. 37. Marcellinus too records those earthquakes in Palestine in his *Chronicle* under the same consuls.

2. Through the correction of the very learned Florius, the aforementioned section “During the episcopate of Durante” was restored to its proper year, namely the twenty-fifth year of Honorius, but not to its proper place. For it unquestionably ought to have been positioned after the sections “The Silingian Vandals and the Alans,” where Idatius recounts the wars waged by Vallia in the year 418. For he was not killed in that year, as Orosius testifies. Bringing his *Histories* to an end in that same year, he writes in the final chapter of Book VII:

> Now we learn from frequent and reliable reports that wars among the peoples are being waged daily in the Spanish provinces, and that slaughter is being inflicted by both sides. They say especially that Vallia, king of the Goths, is intent upon bringing about peace.

Pagius, however, contradicts this at the year 417, no. 23, where he asserts, with a double error, that Orosius completed his work in Spain. First, Orosius himself declares that he brought his work to an end in the 5618th year of the world according to Eusebius—for it is clear from Book I, chapter 1, that he followed Eusebius’s chronology—which coincides with the year 418 of the common era, as will be evident to anyone who performs the calculation. For in Eusebius’s chronology, year 1 of the common era corresponds to the year 5201 of the world. Consequently, the year 418 of the common era must coincide with the year 5618 of the world.

Nor can an odd number of years in the common era—for example, 417—ever correspond to an even number of years according to the chronology of the world, Abraham, or Eusebius, since the Christian epoch began from an odd number belonging to those epochs. Therefore, in Prosper’s *Chronicle*, where the year 5618 of the world is connected with the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta, who gave their names to the year 419 of the Christian era, a mistake has entered: the year 5619 of the world certainly ought to have been recorded there. Indeed, this kind of error has disfigured the whole of that *Chronicle*, beginning with the year 5580 of the world inscribed at its opening, when 5579 ought to have been recorded, as has already been demonstrated elsewhere.

3. Furthermore, the words just quoted from Orosius himself clearly show that, when he wrote them, he was somewhere other than Spain. For he says: “Now we learn daily that wars are being waged in the Spanish provinces … through frequent and reliable reports.” Could Orosius have written this while he was residing in Spain? Where, then, was he at that time? In Africa. He himself makes this perfectly clear in Book V, chapter 2.

Both facts may also be inferred with sufficient certainty from the letter of Severus, bishop of Minorca, preserved by Baronius under the year 418. Speaking of Orosius, Severus writes:

> A presbyter of outstanding holiness, coming from Jerusalem, stayed at Magona for a short time. After he was unable to cross over to Spain, as he had wished, he decided to return again to Africa.

Severus says that this happened at the beginning of February, after the second consulship of Honorius and Constantius, who were consuls in the year 417. Severus says that Orosius came from Jerusalem because Orosius had begun his journey to Spain from there and had obtained the relics of the sacred remains of the blessed Stephen; in honor of those relics God had performed the great miracles that Severus recounts in his letter.

Nevertheless, before he reached Magona, Orosius had gone to Africa, as is evident from the letter of Aurelius of Carthage and the other bishops of the proconsular province to Innocent, bishop of Rome, written from the synod held on 23 August of the year 416. It is almost certain that Orosius remained in Africa until the beginning of the year 418. But when he departed from there and landed on one of the smaller Balearic islands, and learned that everything in Spain was being harassed by the barbarians, he decided to return to Africa. There, having been received as a guest by Augustine, as I believe, and at Augustine’s request, he either composed the whole of his *Histories* in that year 418, from beginning to end, or finally completed the work he had begun earlier, whether in 416 or 417.

## Note XXX, p. 67

Idatius states both in the *Fasti* and in the *Chronicle* that those portents which occurred at Jerusalem in the year 419 of Christ were recorded in writing by John, bishop of that city. But it is absolutely certain from the second letter of Pope Zosimus to Aurelius and the other bishops of Africa that, after John’s death, Praylius obtained the Jerusalem episcopate in 415 or at the beginning of the following year. Moreover, after Praylius too had died, Juvenal was governing that Church in the year 418, as I shall show in Note 47.

Therefore, either the name of the bishop was not given in that written account of the signs and portents seen at Jerusalem, and Idatius supposed that it was John; or, in the copy that he possessed, “John” had been substituted for “Juvenal.” In any event, the *Fasti* should certainly be corrected as follows: “In the consulship of these men, Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, [wrote] …” And in the *Chronicle* the four words “During the episcopate of the aforementioned [bishop]” ought to be deleted.

Nevertheless, we are not at liberty to change anything, since it appears that it was written in this way by Idatius himself: the name of John is found in both works, and Idatius himself has left it on record that, under the year 435, he could not know in what year John had died. Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* and the blessed Augustine, in volume IV of the Benedictine edition, sermon 19, recount what those portents and prodigies were that occurred at Jerusalem at that time. Phereponus, who mocks every form of piety, ridicules them all and most piously reproaches Sirmondus for having, in his notes to that sermon of Augustine, suppressed the earlier words of Marcellinus out of shame.

## Note XXXI, p. 67

Since Saint Isidore, in his *History of the Goths*, copies out Idatius in its entirety and assigns Vallia’s death to the Spanish era 457, who could doubt that Idatius recorded this death under the twenty-fifth year of Honorius—a year likewise displayed in the editions of Isidore by Labbe and Grotius—and that he did not move these twenty-fifth-year chronological notes into the section “Under Gunderic,” after narrating Vallia’s death?

Thus Vallia died in the year 419 of the common era, and, in my opinion, not before autumn. For since, according to Isidore, he held the kingdom for three years, and entered upon it at the end of the year 416, as is clear from what was said above in Note 27, it follows that he died after September of the year 419.

Jordanes, through a grave error, counts Vallia among the living in the year in which the Vandals crossed into Africa. Most later writers followed him, extending Vallia’s life and reign as far as the year 429. Nor does Jordanes more correctly assign to that same year the shipwreck that Orosius records as having been suffered by the Goths in the Strait of Hercules in the year 417, when he brought his *History* to an end in the following year.

I do not, however, think that Jordanes was equally mistaken when he writes that Vallia died at Toulouse. Vallia left a daughter who, married to a man of the royal stock of the Suevi, gave birth to a son, Rechimer. Sidonius teaches us this especially in his panegyric of Anthemius, verse 360, where he writes:

> They call Ricimer  
> To two kingdoms, since his father was a Suevian,  
> But on his mother’s side he was a Goth. At the same time he recalls  
> That Vallia, his grandfather, laid low in the Tartessian lands  
> The Vandal troops and the Alans joined in battle,  
> And covered the setting Pillars of Hercules with corpses.

Here Sidonius alludes to the war that Vallia waged against the Vandals and Alans in the years 417 and 418, of which he says, “Gaiseric remembers”; for it is Gaiseric whom he is speaking about there.

## Note XXXII, p. 67

Apollinaris Sidonius indicates that Theodorus, king of the Goths who succeeded Vallia, was Alaric’s son—or rather his son-in-law—in *Carmen* VII, verse 501, where he presents Theodoric, son of this Theodorus, speaking as follows:

> I call to witness, Rome, your venerable divine power:  
> I preserve peace with you, or desire to erase  
> What my grandfather did wrong; the one thing that darkens him  
> Is that he captured you, Rome …

Here Theodoric, son of Theodorus, calls Alaric his grandfather; for Alaric is the man who stormed and captured Rome. Therefore Theodorus must either have been Alaric’s son or his son-in-law. The beginning of his reign must, according to what was said above, be assigned to the closing part of the year 419.

## Note XXXIII, p. 68

Olympiodorus, who writes that Placidia was given to Constantius on the Kalends of January in the year 417, records that Honoria was born from this marriage before Valentinian. Valentinian therefore cannot have been born before the year 419.

Marcellinus, in the *Chronicle* published by Panvinius and again in the Heidelberg edition of 1588, gives the day and place of Valentinian’s birth, saying that he was born at Ravenna on the sixth day before the Nones of July. Under the same day, the calendar of Ptolemy Silvius, in the Antwerp *Acts of the Saints*, volume VI, June, has the following: “The true birthday of the lord Valentinian.” Prosper likewise assigns him the same day in his *Chronicle*. Therefore Marcellinus must be corrected in the Sirmondian edition, which gives the fifth day before the Nones.

## Note XXXIV, p. 69

1. When the copyist was writing the words of the *Chronicle*, “The emperor Constantius dies at Ravenna in his third consulship,” he understood “consulship” as a mark of the new year—namely, the twenty-seventh year of Honorius—and appended that note to the same words, as though he were copying a consular chronicle.

But Idatius plainly contradicts this when he says that Constantius died in his third consulship, which in the *Fasti* of Idatius himself corresponds to the twenty-sixth year of Honorius, the year 420 of the common era. The copyist made a similar error below, under the year 449, as I shall show.

Accordingly, Idatius, who lived in the year 420 under the rule of Constantius—a prince extremely well known and celebrated throughout Spain, under whose authority Idatius himself was living not as a boy or adolescent but almost as a mature man—assigned Constantius’s death to that same year in the explicit words: “He dies in his third consulship.” Those words cannot easily be corrupted, whereas chronological notes are very frequently falsified by copyists, who record them earlier or later than the authors had written them.

Panvinius, in Book I *On the Roman Princes*, agrees with Idatius, whom he had not seen; so too does the eminent Baronius, who, under the year 419, in the section on Constantius, says: “We know that he died in the following year.” Prosper and Cassiodorus say that Constantius died in the year 421. Finally, Theophanes states that he assumed the reign on 8 February of the year 421 and died on the second day of September of that same year.

Theophanes therefore disagrees with all the ancient Western writers: with Prosper and Cassiodorus concerning the beginning, and with Idatius concerning both the beginning and the end of Constantius’s imperial rule. Yet it is possible that, when Theophanes says that Constantius assumed the empire on the sixth day before the Ides of February in the year 421, he was reporting the true day of his inauguration, although what he says about the year is wholly false.

2. Meanwhile, the learned Pagius, under the year 420, no. 2, preferred to place his trust in Theophanes—who lived in the East almost four hundred years later and who was conspicuously mistaken in recounting Constantius’s death—rather than in Idatius, a contemporary writer who committed to posterity events occurring almost before his eyes and who marked Constantius’s death with a distinctive chronological formula, saying: “He dies in his third consulship.”

Pagius thinks that Theophanes is supported, besides Prosper and Cassiodorus—although we have seen above that they support Theophanes no more than Idatius does—by the laws that he cites from the *Theodosian Code*, following Siguonius and Gothofredus.

First, however, it must be observed that during the whole period of Constantius’s reign—if he died on 2 September of the year 420—not a single law was issued in which Constantius’s name could in any way have appeared, even if he had ruled from February to September of that year. For in the laws issued by Theodosius, his name was certainly not expressed, since Theodosius had refused to admit Constantius into partnership in the reign.

Honorius, however, issued two laws that year: one, Book V, title VI, “On Legitimate Inheritances,” on the fifth day before the Kalends of October; and the other, now divided into two laws although originally one, as is clear from the appendix to the *Theodosian Code*, no. 10, in Sirmondus, volume I, p. 409. Gothofredus notes that the latter was subscribed at Anianus on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. Both laws, therefore, were issued after Constantius’s death, if he died on 2 September of the year 420.

3. Furthermore, among the seven laws issued in the year 421, the second, “On Repudiations,” is recorded in Anianus and other manuscript copies of the Code as dated on the seventh day before the Ides of November, as Gothofredus attests. By that time, according to Theophanes, Constantius was dead.

The other four—namely, the single law “On the Five-Year Prescription,” the twenty-third “On Prescriptive Rights,” and the thirty-ninth and thirtieth “On Petitions and Final Judgments”—were originally one law, but are now divided into four. The first, second, and last of these—two in the *Theodosian Code* and the last in the *Justinian Code*—do not contain Constantius’s name.

The sixth, which is law XLV “On Bishops,” does not mention Constantius.

The seventh, the single law beginning “If a definite claim is sought from a signed document,” retains Constantius’s name. But this is not enough to establish that Constantius was still alive at that time, since the inscriptions of laws so often mislead us that they impose Gratian’s name upon us more than sixty times even after his death. Indeed, law XXXI “On Petitions and Final Judgments” of the *Theodosian Code*, issued in the year 422, bears Constantius’s name at its head, although no one doubts that by then Constantius had ceased to live.

Therefore, unless firmer evidence is available from elsewhere, no certain conclusion can be drawn from such inscriptions about the year in which Constantius died or the manner of his death. His death was not violent, as Theophanes reports in the same place—whose reliability in what he relates about Constantius must consequently be reduced—but resulted from pleurisy. Olympiodorus, a writer of that period, testifies to this, saying:

> In the seventh month of his reign—just as he had indicated in a dream: “The sixth has departed; the seventh is beginning”—he was extinguished by pleurisy.

Nor would Idatius have written “he dies” if Constantius had perished by violent slaughter.

4. Cardinal Baronius under the year 420, the learned Joannes Garnerius in Dissertation 3 *On the Imperial Constitutions against the Pelagians*, and others cite a letter of Constantius to Volusianus, prefect of the City. Garnerius and several other highly learned men think that this letter was written in the year 421.

Accordingly, in the passage cited, after correctly asserting above that Idatius is almost everywhere corrupt and then claiming, contrary to the truth, that Idatius supposed Constantius to have assumed the empire as early as the year 419, Garnerius insists that the beginning of Constantius’s reign must be assigned to the year 419 on the basis of the aforesaid letter.

But he is wrong, both because the letter lacks a date and consular designation, and because its title in Garnerius—“Letter of Constantius the emperor, father of Valentinian III Augustus” (which differs in no respect relevant to our matter from that found in Salmasius’s *Eucharisticus*)—shows that the codex containing the letter was written long after Constantius’s death.

It could therefore have happened—and I have no doubt that it did—that a copyist added the title “emperor” in the superscription of the letter, even though it had been written before Constantius assumed the empire. For it is established that Constantius had issued letters of this kind to various magistrates and bishops before his elevation to the empire.

5. Baronius, under the year 419, gives an example of such a letter addressed to Symmachus, a man of clarissimus rank. A little earlier, under the same year, he transcribes two letters of Honorius. In the first, addressed to Aurelius of Carthage, Honorius says:

> And although the written instructions of my lord and brother, the Augustus, would have sufficed …

In the second, addressed to Augustine and others, he says:

> But although the sacred authority of my lord and brother, the emperor, summoning the synod of Italy, has been issued and must not be neglected …

These letters are Honorius’s, not Placidia’s, as the eminent Norisius supposes in Book I, chapter 16 of his *History of Pelagianism*. This is clear both from the testimony of the manuscripts possessed by the eminent Baronius and from the words themselves.

Let the reader weigh them carefully: he will find that Placidia would not have spoken of the authority of the emperor Honorius in such humble and submissive terms, especially since she speaks of herself in this way: “We judge that the writings of Our Serenity should also be joined to them.” Nor is it credible that Placidia wrote not merely to Aurelius but also to seven other bishops.

Finally, in the appendix to the *Theodosian Code*, in Sirmondus, volume I, p. 417, Honorius writes to Constantius:

> You, Constantius, dearest parent, will make this known to all the ordinary judges.

This letter is dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh consulship of Honorius and the third of Constantius. But there is scarcely any doubt that “Constantius II” must be read, so that the letter may be assigned to the year 417, in which Constantius was consul with Honorius for the second time. For if the letter belonged to the year 420, in which Constantius held his third consulship with Theodosius, the copyist would have changed Theodosius IX into Honorius XI. It is far more credible, however, that “Constantius III” was written in place of “Constantius II.”

6. From all this we may draw several conclusions:

1. Before he had been admitted into partnership in the empire, Constantius had been honored by Honorius with the title of Augustus. I believe that this happened to no other man before his solemn inauguration—that is, before his assumption of imperial power and kingship—or at least I do not recall another example.

2. After Constantius married Placidia, he exercised a certain authority under which even the highest magistrates—the prefects of the praetorian guard and of the City—were subject to him. We may not improperly call this a vicariate of the empire or a proconsular authority.

3. By virtue of this authority, in which he was pre-eminent, Constantius could have issued the aforementioned letter to Volusianus even before he assumed the empire.

Unless it is otherwise established that the letter was written in the year 421, Garnerius has accomplished nothing. Yet, as observed above, this cannot be deduced either from the attribution, since the letter lacks a date, or from the title “emperor” assigned there to Constantius.

It remains, therefore, to determine the time of its composition from the person to whom the letter was sent. Volusianus assumed the prefecture of the City in the year 1170 from the foundation of Rome, as Rutilius Namatianus testifies in Book I of his *Itinerary*, where he asserts that Volusianus succeeded him immediately in that prefecture.

Rutilius, however, administered it in the year 1179 from the foundation of Rome, as he himself testifies in this couplet:

> Although sixteen tens and a thousand have been completed,  
> And, in addition, your ninth year is now passing.

Panvinius connects this year of the City with the Christian year 417. Therefore, if Volusianus held the prefecture of the City in the following year, he certainly held it in the year 418.

You may object that, in Panvinius’s chronology, the year which for him corresponds to the year 417 of Christ according to Dionysius’s calculation is 416, because Panvinius counts the Christian epoch from the consulship of Caesar and Paulus. Consequently, you may conclude that Cardinal Norisius correctly wrote in his *Adventoria to Macedus*: “Rufius Volusianus held the prefecture of the City in the year 417 of the Christian epoch.”
