It is neither necessary nor useful to examine what opinion Namatianus followed concerning the foundation of the City, or whether the second verse should read “your ninth year is passing,” meaning that the year he designates was still in progress, or “your ninth year was,” as the Panvinian edition reads, which signifies a year already completed.

It is enough to establish, on Namatianus’s authority, that Volusianus held the prefecture of the City immediately after him. For since law IV “On the Dress That Must Be Worn” of the *Theodosian Code* shows that Probianus was administering that prefecture on 12 December of the year 416, Volusianus’s prefecture cannot have fallen anywhere but in the year 418, since Namatianus stood between him and Probianus.

Thus the most learned cardinal was deceived, and Volusianus’s prefecture must be assigned to the year 418 of the common era. Since, therefore, beginning on 30 April of that same year, constitutions and edicts against Pelagius and Coelestius began to be promulgated by the emperor Honorius Augustus and the prefect of the praetorian guard, and since Volusianus, prefect of the City, was excessively negligent in enforcing the emperor’s sanctions against the enemies of the faith, Constantius judged that he should be admonished by a severe correction. He did so by sending him the letter under discussion.

7. From these considerations it clearly follows that the only basis for saying that this kind of letter was written in the year 421 is the fact that the title attributes the name “emperor” to Constantius.

On the other hand, the following considerations recommend assigning it to the year 418:

1. The prefecture of Volusianus, which we have just shown belonged to that year. There is no other evidence, so far as I know, that he held it in the year 421.

2. The fact that the letter is not marked with the names of the other Augusti, at least not that of Honorius, whereas in Honorius’s letter to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, concerning these same men, Pelagius and Coelestius, the name of Theodosius is explicitly included.

3. The same conclusion is suggested by Volusianus’s edict, in which we read:

> Until now, friendly hiding places for defendants have withdrawn Coelestius, the disturber of the divine faith and public peace, from the courts. Now laws and edicts will pursue him even in his absence, etc.

Volusianus would have issued this edict in the year after the sentence against Coelestius had been pronounced.

4. If Volusianus had issued his edict in the year 421, would he have said that edicts had already been issued—or rather, had long ago been hurled—against this disturber of the divine faith and public peace?

8. In my judgment, the matter occurred as follows. From October of the year 417 to May of the following year, 418, after a great many serious ecclesiastical letters had passed back and forth between the apostolic see—as Augustine reports in Book II, chapter 3, *To Boniface*—and the African bishops, Pope Zosimus finally decided, although he had until then treated Coelestius more leniently, to summon him again for examination and to judge his case more severely.

Accordingly, when Coelestius’s presence was demanded—as Augustine adds in the same place—so that either the man’s craftiness or his correction might become clear through definite and lucid answers, and so that no ambiguity might remain for anyone, he withdrew and refused to submit to the examination.

This is Augustine’s account. Marius Mercator relates the same events in his *Commonitorium*, expressly noting that Coelestius not only failed to appear at the fuller hearing summoned by Zosimus but also fled from the city of Rome.

While these things were occurring, the date of 30 April 418 arrived. On that day Honorius Augustus issued a constitution against Pelagius and Coelestius, ordering that they be expelled from the city along with their other followers. The emperor’s constitution was followed by an edict of the prefect of the praetorian guard, ordering that Pelagius and Coelestius, removed from the venerable City, should be punished by confiscation of their property.

Pelagius was then absent from Rome. Nevertheless, because he was regarded as the teacher of the error and the founder of the sacrilegious sect, the imperial constitutions and prefectural edicts also took action against him; and, so that he might not be permitted to approach the City in the future, they ordered him expelled from it as though he were present.

But Volusianus’s edict concerns Coelestius alone. From this we may reasonably infer that it was issued in the year 418, some time after the emperor’s constitution had been promulgated, because it was uncertain whether Coelestius had left the City, and Constantius either suspected—or had certainly learned—that he was hiding in Rome.

Garnerius, in his dissertation *On the Authors and Defenders of the Pelagian Heresy*, chapter 5, writes in explicit terms:

> Coelestius either did not in fact flee from the City when he withdrew from the judgment, but hid among powerful people, especially women; or, after the storm had died down, he returned safely to the City, with the prefect of the City conniving at it.

Therefore, if Coelestius did not leave the City out of fear of Honorius’s constitution promulgated against him, or if he fled only temporarily and slipped back into it as soon as the opportunity arose, who can deny that, before the year 419—that is, in the year 418—one might have desired the prefect of the City to take care to keep him away from it amid so great a plague?

9. Anyone who carefully considers what has been said thus far will acknowledge how closely it accords with the truth and how much more plausibly it can be assigned to the year 418 than to 421. If the name “emperor” had not been added to Constantius in the letter, I think no one would ever have assigned it to the year 421.

But who does not see that the title “emperor” could have been added by a copyist so that we might know who the author of the letter was, just as, for the same reason, the words “father of Valentinian Augustus in his third consulship” were added at its head?

Furthermore, when Photius discusses the writings of the emperors against the Pelagians, in *Bibliotheca* 53, he calls Theodosius and Honorius emperors, but does not do the same for Constantius. Thus the letter provides a highly doubtful, not to say futile, argument for believing that Constantius lived until the year 421.

We can form a much more effective argument from the consulship that Constantius held in the year 420, so that we may confidently assert that he rose to the summit of imperial power in that same year. We know that this happened more than once elsewhere, and Spartianus testifies concerning another man that, because he had been designated for the empire, he was designated consul for a second time.

Accordingly, when Honorius decided to name Constantius Augustus in the year 420, he designated him consul for that same year, so that he would enter upon the Kalends of January as both consul and emperor. But Theodosius resisted, refusing to admit Constantius into partnership in the kingdom; and as messengers went back and forth, the matter was prolonged until the sixth day before the Ides of February. Then, when all hope of obtaining Theodosius’s consent had been abandoned, Constantius was made Augustus without him, in that year 420.

Hence arose Constantius’s anger against the East, which Theodosius governed; hence the expedition planned against him.

There is an inscription in Gruter, p. 449, no. 7, in which we read that Honorius, Theodosius, and Constantius, the Augusti, ordered a statue to be erected to Petronius Maximus, prefect of the City.

The most learned men think that Maximus held the prefecture of the City in the year 420 and assert that law VI “On Legitimate Inheritances,” issued on the fifth day before the Kalends of October of that same year 420, was addressed to him. Although it is inscribed “To Maximus, prefect of the praetorian guard,” it is established that in that year 420 Palladius, not Maximus, was prefect of the praetorian guard. Therefore they correct the subscription and read “To Maximus, prefect of the City.”

From all this we conclude that, if Constantius was proclaimed Augustus in February, as Theophanes says, he was proclaimed in no other February than that of the year 420, and that he died in the same year after six months of imperial rule.

## Note XXXV, p. 69

1. Salvianus, in Book VII *On the Government of God*, discussing the battle that Castinus fought against the Vandals, says:

> When our side advanced against the Vandals settled in Spain, carrying such confidence born of presumption for conquering them as it had recently carried against the Goths—he alludes to the battle at Toulouse, which Idatius records under the year 439—they collapsed with equal arrogance and equal outcome.”

This was the first cause of the misfortune of that battle: contempt for the enemy and confidence in their own strength.

Prosper notes the second cause under the consuls of this year, 422:

> Castinus, by an inept and injurious command, turned Boniface, a man distinguished in the arts of war, away from participation in his expedition. For Boniface, judging it dangerous and unworthy to follow a man whom he had found to be quarrelsome and arrogant, quickly hurried to the harbor of the City and from there to Africa.

Thus, while Castinus alienated Boniface from himself, he was overcome and defeated by the enemy. Another Prosper states, under the entry “Theodosius XX, 8” [reading uncertain], that nearly twenty thousand Romans were killed by the Vandals.

2. Idatius passed over in silence the fact that Boniface was at that time in Spain and hastened from there to Italy. Yet together with Prosper he testifies that Boniface proceeded from Italy to Africa. He eventually returned to Africa, from which he had come to Spain at Honorius’s command to wage war under Castinus.

I infer this from a letter of the blessed Augustine, formerly numbered 70. Augustine further reports that, at this time, after his wife’s death, Boniface took a second wife outside Africa, and that she was an Arian. But that she was a relative of King Gaiseric, as Baronius says, is not suggested by Augustine. He gives the woman’s name, which was Pelagia.

## Note XXXVI, p. 70

Since it is perfectly clear from the *Fasti* of our Idatius—whatever Pagius may object—that he did not fail to know that Honorius died before the year 424 and therefore did not reach the thirtieth year of his reign, why does Idatius assign him thirty years of rule and record his death and tricennalia under the year 424?

Unless I am greatly mistaken, Idatius noticed that the epoch of the emperors was a measure of other chronological systems, namely the Abrahamic and Olympiad systems. Since he was accustomed to express these not every year, as with the imperial chronology, but every tenth year in the Abrahamic system and every fourth year in the Olympiad system, he thought that he ought not to interrupt the imperial years in his *Chronicle*. Otherwise, in the absence of such yearly markers, the reckoning of the Abrahamic years, Olympiad years, and the whole chronology would be disrupted.

Indeed, it was disrupted below from the eighth year of Leo onward, after Idatius ceased to arrange his narrative and no longer divided it by noting each year at the beginning of an emperor’s reign.

To prevent this, Idatius assigned the periods of interregnum to the rulers who had preceded them. I shall demonstrate this below in the case of Avitus.

Thus Idatius, assigning to Honorius the period of interregnum between him and Valentinian III, extended his reign to thirty years. When he reached the end, he announced Honorius’s tricennalia and death, so that no one would find it absurd that he presented Honorius as celebrating his tricennalia before the thirtieth year of his reign and continuing to exercise the empire even after his death.

## Note XXXVII, p. 70

Theodosius, son of Arcadius, was unquestionably in his twenty-fourth year of age in the year 425 of the Christian era, to which Idatius attaches the first year of his reign in the *Chronicle*. In this passage Idatius designated this year, not the twenty-sixth. Reread what was said in Note 16.

In both places, therefore—here and under the year 401—Idatius was corrupted by copyists. Consequently, Pagius had no reason, under the year 428, as I observed in the preceding note, to accuse Idatius of being insufficiently careful or ignorant of Roman history on the basis of the copyists’ error in transcribing the years of Theodosius and of the death of Honorius, which Idatius recorded under the thirtieth year of Honorius, that is, the common year 424.

Pagius himself will have to be corrected with greater justification below. For under the year 448, no. 13, forgetting himself, he imposes upon Idatius the claim that Theodosius’s regnal years began in October of the year 423, although the years that he assigns to Honorius as well—and for assigning them Pagius criticizes him under the year 428—clearly show that Idatius attached Theodosius’s first year to the year 425 of the common era.

## Note XXXVIII, p. 71

Olympiodorus writes that Valentinian received the title not of Caesar but of *Nobilissimus* at Constantinople; Olympiodorus himself and Philostorgius report that he was made Caesar at Thessalonica.

Valentinian had already been honored with the title *Nobilissimus*, and Placidia with that of Augusta. Nevertheless, Theodosius appears to have wished to confer these honors upon both of them because he had refused to admit Constantius into partnership in the government, as a result of which these earlier distinctions had first passed to his wife Placidia and his son Valentinian.

Law XIV *De Muril. et Gynaec.* (“On the purple-dye and imperial-weaving workers”) of the *Theodosian Code*, issued on 16 October of the year 424, calls Valentinian Caesar. But a law in the same Code, XXXIII “On the Grain Supply and Taxes,” issued six days earlier, bears only the name of Theodosius.

From this it may reasonably be inferred that Valentinian was proclaimed Caesar on one of those six days extending from 10 to 16 October of the same year 424.

## Note XXXIX, p. 71

Philostorgius, in Book XII, asserts that the tyrant John was killed at Aquileia. Pagius, under the year 42, no. 4, insists that this must not be doubted because Idatius, who says that John was executed at Ravenna, was, in Pagius’s view, poorly informed about events outside Spain.

Yet in the same passage Philostorgius shows that he was not even well informed about events occurring in Greece, when he writes that, after Honorius’s death, Placidia and Valentinian fled from Italy to Byzantium.

But Augusta Placidia, expelled by her brother Honorius, departed for the East with her daughter Honoria—for read *Honoria*, not *Honorio*, since the feminine meaning is intended, contrary to the implausible explanation that Norisius gives somewhere—and with her son Valentinian. Prosper recounts this under the consulship of Mariniano and Asclepiodotus; Cassiodorus and the author of the *Miscella* report the same, and Olympiodorus gives the fullest account of all.

We must therefore place greater trust in Idatius than in Philostorgius. I shall believe that John was put to death at Ravenna, unless a better authority than Philostorgius testifies that he was killed at Aquileia.

## Note XL, p. 71

Marcellinus writes in his *Chronicle*, under the consuls of the year 425, that the younger Valentinian was made emperor at Ravenna. Idatius says that he was proclaimed Augustus at Rome; Olympiodorus had preceded him in this, when, at the end of his *History*, he wrote:

> After the tyrant John had been killed, Helion, master of the offices and patrician, entered Rome. When everyone had gathered there, he clothed Valentinian, already seven years old, in the imperial robe.

Valentinian had entered his seventh year on the second day of July of that year. Therefore, do not understand that he was then seven years old as though he had already completed his seventh year.

That Valentinian had not yet been proclaimed Augustus on 8 October of this year 425 is shown by law XLVII “On Bishops of Churches and Clergy” of the *Theodosian Code*, in which he is called Caesar on that date. Nevertheless, fifteen days later, on 23 October, he was inaugurated as Augustus.

Ptolemy Silvius, in the calendar cited above, writes: “The tenth day before the Kalends of November: the birthday of Valentinian’s purple,” and so forth.

On the same day that Valentinian put on the imperial robe at Rome, he was proclaimed Augustus at Constantinople by decree of Theodosius, as may be inferred from Prosper’s *Chronicle* and from Socrates, Book VII, chapter 25. For Socrates’ words must be understood in this sense.

## Note XLI, p. 73
The Vandal kingdom in Africa had its beginning in May of the year 429 [the supplied text reads “329”; the accompanying discussion of 428 and the following year suggests this correction], as noted above in the scholium. But Cuperus—and, as cited by him, the *Life of Saint Victor of Vita*, XXIII—together with Chiffletius and Ruinart, attach the Vandals’ incursion into Africa, on Prosper’s testimony in his *Chronicle*, which Cassiodorus customarily follows, to the year 427. [p. 178] Yet no one will doubt that in this matter the [Col. 0776D] authority of Idatius is preferable, since he was then living among the Vandals and had already been made bishop three years earlier. Besides, Prosper’s *Chronicle* is thickly strewn with frequent chronological errors. Indeed, Cuperus himself, in the *Chronotaxis of the Deeds of the Divine Augustine*, under 28 August and the year 428, says:

> This occurred either in that year or the following, when the Vandals entered Africa.

2. Nor did the method of reckoning the years employed by Idatius escape the notice of those great men, as Pagius conjectures under the year 428, no. 3—although, because this most learned man repeatedly insists upon the point, I must also repeatedly refute him. For in the chronology of Idatius, the month of May in Abrahamic year 2445 is precisely the same month of May in Dionysian year 429, whether that Abrahamic year is reckoned from October of the common era 428 or from January of the following year, 429. Therefore, whoever assigns the Vandals’ crossing into Africa either to Dionysian year 427 or to 428 has not been deceived because he failed to notice the method Idatius uses in reckoning the years, but because he forgot Idatius’s testimony or held it in contempt. [Col. 0777A]

3. Moreover, this also led those most learned men to persuade themselves that Victor of Vita began writing his books on the Vandal persecution in the year 487. Yet, according to what Idatius writes, the sixtieth year of the Vandal kingdom in Africa—the year in which Victor told us that he was writing—fell in the year 489, since no more than fifty-eight years are counted from 429 to 487. The sixtieth year, therefore, in which Victor was writing, was Dionysian year 489.

4. Besides, although Gaiseric began his African kingdom in the year 429, historians customarily reckon it from the capture of Carthage, that is, from the year 439; Victor himself does so as well. For at the end of book I he writes that Gaiseric reigned thirty-seven years and three months—an Anonymous of Augsburg, edited by Canisius, adds six days—which he reckons from the capture of Carthage, not from his entry into Africa. Since he seized Carthage on 19 October [fourteen days before the Kalends of November] in the year 439, [p. 179] as Idatius assigns it to that year, if you add thirty-seven years and three months to this number, you will conclude that Gaiseric died in the year 477, on 19 January [fourteen days before the Kalends of February], or six days later, according to the Anonymous of Augsburg. [Col. 0777B]

5. Victor of Tunnuna must therefore be corrected, for he says that Gaiseric died during the consulship of Olybrius and Rusticus, who gave their names to the year 464 of the common era and the fortieth year of the African kingdom. The holy Isidore followed this Victor, and consequently all the dates of Gaiseric and his successors are corrupted in Isidore. But Florius has already undertaken to discuss these matters in his *History of the Vandals by Isidore himself*.

## Note XLII, p. 74

1. Under the consulship of Theodosius XI and Valentinian—who held that office in the year 425—Prosper says:

> Arles, a noble town of Gaul, was attacked with great force by the Goths; but when Aetius approached, they withdrew without escaping punishment.

The fact itself, as well as the wording of both authors and of Isidore, whom I shall immediately cite, shows that Prosper and Idatius are describing one and the same war in the year 430. Yet Prosper records it five years earlier than Idatius. Pagius adheres to Prosper and mocks the other Prosper, the Prosper of Pithou, who comes closer to the opinion of Idatius, saying that during this period his *Chronicle* is greatly corrupted with respect to the years of the emperors.

But this objection could more truly have been made against Prosper of Aquitaine, who during these years describes this Gothic war, the Vandals’ crossing into Africa, and, in addition, the Frankish war in a severely disordered sequence. As for the matter at hand, it is surprising that the most learned Pagius did not notice that in the year 425 Aetius was first occupied with supporting the tyranny of John and then with leading the Huns into Pannonia; he therefore could not have been waging war against the Goths. Prosper consequently places this war five years too early. [Col. 0777C]

It was ended by a treaty made between the Romans and the Goths and by the delivery of hostages from Gaul to King Theodorus. Among them was Theodore, a relative of Avitus, whom Sidonius mentions in *Carmen* VII, line 218:

> Your Gaul was ordered to give  
> hostages as pledges of peace to the Gothic king; among them  
> you come, Theodore, noble hostage, whom you seek,  
> Avitus, out of devotion to your kinsman, in the fur-clad prince’s court,  
> trusting in the pledge of good faith.

Yet I would not readily believe that in the year 425 Avitus, then still a young man—since he became emperor thirty years later—had such authority among the Goths. For this reason I again agree with Idatius rather than Prosper. [p. 180; Col. 0777D]

2. Concerning this same war Isidore says in his *History of the Goths*:

> Theodoric, not content with the kingdom of Aquitaine, rejects the treaty of Roman peace and occupies many Roman municipalities adjoining his settlements. He attacks Arles, the most distinguished town of Gaul, with great force; but when the valor of Aetius, commander of the Roman army, threatened him, he withdrew from the siege without escaping punishment.

Immediately afterward he adds:

> Therefore, when Aetius had been removed from military command by order of the emperor Valentinian …

Yet Aetius was removed from the Gallic army in the year 432, after he had brought about Boniface’s death. It follows clearly from the sequence of Isidore’s narrative that this Gothic war could not have preceded Aetius’s removal from Gaul by seven years—the interval by which it would have had to precede it if it had occurred in 425, the year to which Prosper assigns it. [Col. 0778A]

3. Idatius does not specify what other towns Theodoric attacked, nor does Isidore. But in order to penetrate as far as Arles, he must necessarily have conquered several places along the way.

## Note XLIII, p. 74

Prosper assigns Felix’s death to the year 430, writing under the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III:

> When Aetius had perceived that Felix, together with his wife Padusia and the deacon Grumatius, was plotting against him, he killed him.

Prosper himself had elsewhere reported that this same Felix was a wicked man. Under the year 426, during the consulship of Theodosius XII and Valentinian II, he says: [Col. 0778B; p. 181]

> Patroclus, bishop of Arles, was killed by a certain barbarian tribune, after being torn apart by many wounds. This crime was attributed to the secret order of Felix, master of the soldiers. At his instigation Titus the deacon, a holy man who distributed money to the poor at Rome, was also believed to have been killed.

You see, reader, with what just cause God, the avenger of outrages and crimes, punished Felix through the agency of Aetius! But also observe what Prosper reports concerning Titus’s death. He testifies that the same Felix was believed to have been the author of that impious murder; Pagius holds that Felix was not a Goth but a Roman or a Gaul, under the year 428, no. 1. Prosper certainly testifies that a barbarian tribune killed Patroclus. But he says nothing at all about Titus’s killer. Nevertheless, concerning this murder of Titus, matters are reported—and indeed in a place where they were least appropriate—which I touched upon above in Note 20.

## Note XLIV, p. 74

1. The expedition which Idatius says Aetius undertook in Gaul against the Franks in the year 431, Prosper assigns to the year 427. Then, under the consulship of Felix and Taurus, he says:

> After killing many Franks, Aetius recovered that part of Gaul near the Rhine which they had occupied.

In this disagreement it is better for us to agree with Idatius than with Prosper, since Idatius was then with Aetius in Gaul and did not leave him until this war had ended in the year 432, when he returned to his homeland. Idatius’s clearest words appear in his *Chronicle* under the years 431 and 432. [Col. 0778C]

Besides, Prosper himself records this expedition of Aetius in the second year after the Vandals’ crossing into Africa. The Vandals crossed into Africa in the year 429. How, then, could that Frankish war have been completed in the year 428? But, as I noted above—and anyone may observe it—the chronology in Prosper is seriously corrupted during these years.

The Franks whom Aetius then defeated were driven back to their native Neckar (*Nicer*). Hence, in the year 450 or 451, they invaded Gaul with Attila, as Sidonius testifies in *Carmen* VII, line 325. I therefore do not know what induced Aegidius Voechtius, reported by Papebrochius in Appendix 2 to the *Exegesis on the Bishops of Tongeren*, volume IV of the *May Saints*, no. 105, to assert—against the authority of Prosper and Sidonius, writers of the same age and Gauls themselves—that all the Franks had crossed over from the year 406 or 407 into Taxandria and neighboring Tongeren, to their kinsmen the Salian Franks, and had thereafter not lived beyond the Rhine. [Col. 0778D; p. 182]

Nor do others do better when, although Prosper expressly testifies that this war was fought near the Rhine, they refer it to the passage in which Sidonius, *Carmen* V, line 212, sings of Aetius and Majorian fighting against the Frank Chlodio, saying:

> Shortly afterward  
> you fought together, where the Frank Chlodio had overrun  
> the open lands of the Atrebates. What have the Atrebates to do with the Rhine?

2. Moreover, these verses concerning the war with Chlodio do not refer to the year 427 or 431, nor even to 437, as Valesius more tolerably erred, but point to approximately the year 447. For, as Sirmondus says in commenting on this passage of Sidonius: [Col. 0779A]

> How could Majorian have been present in the war and fought so fiercely in the year 428, when thirty years later, during his consulship in the year 458, he was still a young man, as is clear from Sidonius himself in the same work, line 524?

The authority of the Chronicle of Verdun, which is not altogether to be despised, also supports this view. Under the year 446 it says:

> In the land of the Franks kings began to reign, and the first of them to reign was Chlodio.

Nevertheless, Frankish writers, on the basis of the aforementioned passage of Prosper, proclaim that Chlodio reigned in the year 428 and, on the basis of Prosper of Pithou, that Pharamund reigned among the Franks on both sides of the Rhine in the year 418 or earlier.

Although Pagius, under the year 418, no. 81, concerning Pharamund, and under the year 428 concerning Chlodio, speaks in such a way—especially concerning Pharamund—that it is sufficiently clear that he wished to express not his own opinion but the commonly held opinion of his countrymen concerning the beginning of Frankish rule in Gaul. But perhaps I shall say more about these matters elsewhere.

3. Two errors of Pagius in his *Critica* under the year 428, no. 9, must now be corrected. [Col. 0779B; p. 183]

The first is that he says Sirmondus brought forward nothing to support his opinion concerning the date of Chlodio’s war. The evident argument drawn from Majorian’s age, which I have just produced in Sirmondus’s own words, counts for nothing with Pagius.

Sirmondus therefore distinguishes that war of the year 427, as Prosper holds—or, more correctly, of the year 431, as Idatius observes—from the war of Chlodio. He denies that the latter was waged during this period and assigns it to after the year 445. He believes that Sidonius is speaking of this Chlodian war, as are Gregory of Tours, Sigebert, and with them the *Annals of the Franks*, and he assigns it to the same period.

Nor is there any reason for Pagius to object to Sirmondus that Sidonius proclaims the Franks defeated, whereas Sigebert and the *Annals* proclaim them victorious. For when have the Franks ever been victorious in the histories written by their own people? When do they not celebrate triumphs?

4. Pagius’s second error is that he says Idatius here does not mean that the Franks were defeated in that Abrahamic year—2448, the year of Christ 432—but only that they made peace with Aetius. He adds shortly afterward:

> Here Idatius is speaking of the former dignity recovered from Aetius, although we shall see that this did not occur until several years later.

Thus writes Pagius, whom Idatius most clearly refutes when he says under the year 431:

> Idatius the bishop undertook an embassy to the commander Aetius, who was conducting an expedition in Gaul.

Immediately, under the year 432, he adds:

> After the Franks had been defeated by Aetius in battle and received into peace, Count Censorius was sent as envoy to the Sueves, while the aforesaid Idatius returned with him.

What expedition, then, was Aetius conducting in Gaul in the year 431 except the one that ended in the following year, when the Franks were defeated by him and received into peace?

But I am weary of dwelling on these matters any longer. I shall mention only two points at the end. First, Idatius was an eyewitness to these events; therefore there is no danger, nor even suspicion, that he reported them out of their proper place and time. Second, during those years Idatius says not a word about former dignity being recovered from Aetius.

## Note XLV, p. 75 [p. 184]

[Col. 0779D]

Take the following brief extracts concerning Boniface, in place of a commentary, on several passages of Idatius, drawn from Augustine, Prosper, Olympiodorus, and others.

Boniface, a Thracian by birth and distinguished in the arts of war and peace, was mistreated by Castinus after the Spanish war against the Vandals. In the year 432 [as printed; the chronology here appears corrupt] he went to the court of Honorius Augustus and from there crossed into Africa. After the death of Honorius, while then tribune of the soldiers, he defended this province against the tyranny of John and preserved it for Placidia and her son Valentinian.

Thereafter Placidia, having found Boniface everywhere utterly faithful to her, appointed him to that province with the rank of *comes domesticorum* and as governor of Africa. Aetius bore this very badly. Accordingly, in order to make Boniface suspect to Placidia, he began to accuse him before her, repeatedly claiming that Boniface was aspiring to kingship and would not obey if recalled from Africa.

At the same time he wrote to Boniface that Placidia was plotting against him, and that this would be the sign: Boniface would suddenly be summoned to the palace without any stated reason. By these devices Aetius deceived both Placidia and Boniface. Placidia ordered Boniface to come to her from Africa, but Boniface refused to come. He was therefore condemned for treason. When war was publicly declared against him, he summoned the Vandals from Spain to aid him. [Col. 0780A]

Later, however, when Aetius’s stratagems had been exposed and the suspicions that had alienated Placidia from Boniface and Boniface from Placidia had been removed, Boniface did everything possible to drive the Vandals out of Africa, although all his efforts were in vain. At Placidia’s command, in rivalry with Aetius and, as Prosper says under the year 432, with the whole world, Boniface came from Africa to Italy, to Rome, in a remarkable peace and reconciliation [or “agreement”?], having received the dignity of master of the soldiers.

Aetius, consequently driven on by sharper goads of envy, attacked Boniface, who was armed with the shorter weapon, with a longer one of his own, and wounded him. Three months later Boniface died of his wound, advising his very wealthy wife to marry no one except Aetius.

Observe here that Aetius was at that time without a wife; otherwise Boniface’s advice to his wife concerning marriage with Aetius would have been intrusive and improper. If she did marry Aetius, and if she was the mother of Gaudentius of whom Sidonius speaks in *Carmen* V, line 205, she was certainly of Gothic rather than Vandal origin. [Col. 0780B; p. 185]

Although the name Pelagia—which Marcellinus reports as the name of Boniface’s wife—has a neutral sound, Boniface could have found an Arian wife outside the Gothic and Vandal peoples as well.

It is clear from Priscus and Cassiodorus that Aetius had another son named Carpilio, who was older than Gaudentius. For Sidonius calls Gaudentius “little Gaudentius” by his mother at the time when Carpilio had already undertaken an embassy to Attila.

Therefore, if Carpilio was not yet dead when the imperial power was being sought for Gaudentius, his younger brother, what reason could there have been except that the wife of Aetius who speaks in Sidonius was Gaudentius’s mother and Carpilio’s stepmother?

Stiltingus collected further material about Boniface in his preliminary commentary on the *Life of Saint Augustine*, § 52. [Col. 0780C]

## Note XLVI, p. 76

Concerning Aetius after he had killed Boniface, Prosper records the following under the consulship of Aetius himself and Valerius, that is, in the year 430:

> When Aetius, having laid down his office, was living on his estate, and when an enemy of his attempted to overpower him there by a sudden attack, he fled to Rome and from there to Dalmatia, then to Pannonia, and reached the Huns. Through their friendship and assistance he obtained peace with the emperors and the right to exercise his interrupted authority.

In the copy of Prosper that I use, the word written where I print *and the right* is *Aetius*. But the marginal notes were written on the basis of manuscripts, and among them are many excellent corrections and annotations which I suspect derive from the scholarly work of the great Antonio Agustín. One of these is the correction that, by deleting the word *Aetius*, restores the reading *and the right*. [Col. 0780D]

From Prosper’s words as transmitted, therefore, everyone can see that Aetius, fearing the anger of the emperors after killing Boniface, left the palace. Sebastian, who succeeded Boniface, remained there for as long as Aetius was absent. But when Aetius returned to the court in the year 433 and was proclaimed Patrician, he soon expelled Sebastian from the court and forced him to sail to the East. [p. 186]

Accordingly, what Prosper relates concerning Aetius’s withdrawal to his estate and his flight to Dalmatia and Pannonia belongs for the most part to the year 433.

## Note XLVII, p. 77

1. I briefly explained in Note 30 that Praylius succeeded John in the Jerusalem episcopate in the year 416 or at the beginning of 417, died before the year 419, and was succeeded by Juvenal. Accordingly, the most learned Papebrochius, whom I follow, assigns Praylius’s death to the year 418 in his *Chronological History of the Bishops of Jerusalem*.

The distinguished Pagius, however, in his *Critica* under the year 429, no. 27, asserts that Praylius died in the year 425. Neither of them produces any ancient writer who clearly and precisely supports his opinion. [Col. 0781A]

Indeed, Pagius must subtract nine years or more from the twenty years of episcopacy which he admits Nicephorus and Theophanes assign to Praylius; even then his calculation does not stand. Similarly, Papebrochius says that in Cyril, the author of the *Life of Saint Euthymius*, under 20 January, where Juvenal is said to have succeeded Praylius in the forty-sixth year of his episcopate, one should read “fortieth” for “forty-sixth,” since he believes that his chronology requires this.

Both Pagius and Papebrochius, then, while attempting to prove their respective opinions, either refute or correct the writings of the ancients because each sees that they contradict his own view. Papebrochius’s correction of Cyril, however, is not so outrageous as to be self-evidently impossible, whereas Pagius’s alteration of Nicephorus and Theophanes is extreme, since he uses it to draw them over to his own opinion. Yet, to speak truthfully, these writers deserve a much harsher correction, because they deviate very far from the truth.

Moreover, returning to Papebrochius, it would have been very easy for the author of the *Life of Euthymius* to count Juvenal’s episcopate from John’s death, omitting Praylius through forgetfulness. Since Idatius affirms that Praylius held the episcopate only briefly—that is, for a short time—Papebrochius could have made his opinion appear to readers, if not certain, at least highly probable on the basis of Idatius’s testimony. [Col. 0781B; p. 187]

A ten-year episcopate, however, such as Pagius assigns to Praylius, cannot be called brief. If Praylius’s episcopate was brief, as Idatius reports, he died in the second year after John’s death, that is, in 418; and Juvenal was elected in the same year after him.

2. Cardinal Norisius indicates that he believes Praylius did not die before the year 421. In his *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 4, he writes that in that year—421, which is reckoned as the first year of Theodotus’s occupation of the see of Antioch—it happened that Pelagius was expelled from the holy places of Jerusalem.

Here this most learned man asserts two things: first, that Theodotus was elected in the year 421; second, that Pelagius was expelled from Jerusalem after Theodotus’s election.

But Eusebius of Cremona—or, as the great Baronius conjectures under the year 417, no. 15, if he was not from Cremona, at any rate the man whom Jerome mentions in a letter now counted among Augustine’s letters—writing to Cyril of Alexandria, says the following, as reported by Baronius in the same place:

> How is it now that, when Innocent of blessed memory condemned Pelagius and Coelestius together with their leaders, and all the Easterners rejected them, the Church of Alexandria has received them into communion, though it alone and first among its provincial churches ought to have rejected such men?

If “now,” that is, when Innocent—who died at the beginning of the year 417—condemned Pelagius, the Eastern Syrians and Palestinians rejected him, is Norisius not assigning his expulsion far too late when he places it four or five years afterward? Moreover, Jerome appears to have spoken of Pelagius’s expulsion from the holy places under the name of Catilina in Letter 55 to Riparius. Yet Jerome died before the year 421. [Col. 0781C]

Perhaps Jerome spoke even more clearly elsewhere about Pelagius’s expulsion from the sacred places, but the writing in which he related this has perished. Many works of the holy doctor have been lost through the injuries of time.

3. Praylius therefore expelled Pelagius from Jerusalem after the Synod of Antioch, which could not have been convened later than the year 417. When Pelagius escaped condemnation from the Synod of Diospolis at the end of 415, the orthodox, who ardently desired his condemnation, immediately brought the case before the patriarch of Antioch, to whom the bishops of Palestine were subject.

But at that critical moment it unfortunately happened that Alexander, bishop of Antioch, died, and the case was postponed until the election of Theodotus in the year 417. Garnerius, in Dissertation 2 on the synods held in the Pelagian case, believes that Theodotus succeeded Alexander in the year 411, but without justification.

Marius Mercator, in chapter 3 of the *Commonitorium*, after relating that Pelagius deceived the fathers of Diospolis, immediately records what was done concerning him at Antioch, saying:

> Later, when he was clearly exposed—his accusers pressing the matter—by a subsequent synod over which Theodotus of blessed memory, bishop of Antioch, presided, he was also expelled from the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem.

Therefore, if “later,” and if “with the accusers pressing the matter”—namely, the same men who had accused him at the Synod of Diospolis—he was condemned by Theodotus, who could believe, with Norisius, that this occurred in the fifth year after that synod, or with Pagius, who under the year 424, no. 8, thinks it occurred in the eighth year—that it happened so many years after Zosimus’s celebrated decree had passed through the whole world? [Col. 0782A; p. 188]

Indeed, I do not think that either Norisius or Pagius would have believed this unless these most learned men had adopted the opinion that Theodotus occupied the see of Antioch long after the year 417.

4. The facts, however, are entirely otherwise. Theodotus became bishop of Antioch in that year, 417, as the most learned Jesuit Boschius clearly demonstrates in the *History of the Patriarchs of Antioch* prefixed to volume IV of the *July Saints*. His opinion is strongly confirmed by the testimony of Mercator just cited and by the words of Eusebius quoted above.

Since Eusebius mentions only the rescript of Innocent and makes no reference to any later decree—such as that of Zosimus—he provides us with an especially strong basis for believing that the letter was sent to Cyril in the same year, 417.

But why delay? The same eminent Norisius and Pagius—the latter under that year, no. 9—admit this very point: namely, that Eusebius’s letter was written at the beginning of the pontificate of Zosimus, who, according to Pagius in the same place, no. 12, was consecrated on 18 March of that year, 417. [Col. 0782B]

Since, therefore, Pelagius was expelled from the sacred places of Jerusalem by the authority of the Synod of Antioch, at which Theodotus and Praylius sat—and Mercator also seems to testify that Praylius was present—for immediately after the words of Theodotus cited above he adds:

> This is attested by the writings sent by that same holy Theodotus to the most reverend bishop of the city of Rome, and by those of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem of holy memory,

does it not clearly follow from all this:

1. that the Synod of Antioch was held in the year 417, not after 421;

2. that Theodotus had already become bishop of Antioch at that time, as Boschius maintains against Norisius and Pagius;

3. that even if Pelagius was expelled from Jerusalem by Praylius after Theodotus’s election, and Praylius died either at the end of 418 or at the beginning of the following year, he could nevertheless have expelled him—and in fact did expel him—in the year 417, not after 421, as Norisius and Pagius contend when they suppose that Praylius had not yet died in that year?

5. “But,” you will object, “it is established that Praylius was more favorably disposed toward Pelagius at the beginning of his episcopate and then wrote on his behalf to Pope Innocent. How, therefore, could he so quickly—indeed, in the very first year of his episcopate—reject Pelagius and expel him from Palestine?” [Col. 0782C]

By similar reasoning, who could assert that Zosimus’s *Tractoria* was issued after the year 418, because until 21 March of that same year Zosimus tried to excuse Pelagius and Coelestius, sharply rebuking their accusers?

Praylius certainly wrote a letter on behalf of Pelagius to Innocent, and it was delivered during the interval between the first and second letters of Zosimus—who had succeeded Innocent—to the African bishops. This is inferred from the fact that Zosimus made no mention of Praylius’s letter in his first letter to the Africans, although he would certainly have done so if he had already received it; but in the second, dated 22 September of the year 417, he mentions that he had received it.

Meanwhile, as Praylius’s letter was being delivered to Innocent, his decree condemning Pelagius was brought to the East. Theodotus, aroused by this decree and by the pressure of Pelagius’s accusers, immediately convened a synod. In the presence of Praylius, Pelagius was condemned there and, as Eusebius said above, rejected by all the Easterners. [Col. 0782D; p. 189]

At that time, moreover, an embassy had appropriately been sent to Rome by the Eastern bishops. Pope Boniface, in his letters to certain bishops of Macedonia, volume IV of the Council Collection of Labbe, column 1708, says:

> A short time ago—that is, under my predecessor Innocent of blessed memory—the bishops of the Eastern Churches, grieving that they had been separated from the communion of blessed Peter, requested peace through envoys, if your Charity remembers.

The Easterners—Constantinopolitans and Egyptians—had separated themselves from communion with the Roman see because they refused to insert the name of Saint John Chrysostom in the diptychs, which Innocent was pressing them to do.

Innocent himself testifies that Alexander, Theodotus’s predecessor, was the author of the Eastern embassy. In his letter to Bishop Maximianus, volume II of the Councils, column 1266, he writes:

> Our brother and fellow bishop Alexander of the Church of Antioch both carried out and approved an embassy worthy of its purpose, namely, the matter of reconciling the Easterners with the Roman Church. [Col. 0783A]

Therefore, when Alexander’s envoys returned from Italy to Antioch at the end of 416, or rather at the beginning of 417, it is entirely credible that the newly issued decree against Pelagius was appended to the other rescripts delivered by Innocent himself. After Theodotus had received these letters of Innocent—for Alexander had meanwhile died—and wishing thereby to commend himself more fully to the Roman pontiff, he immediately convened a synod, condemned Pelagius, and decreed that he should be rejected by the East.

6. But now Norisius, in book I of his *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 11, contends that Innocent issued no decree against Pelagius. First, he says, because Saint Augustine nowhere mentions such a decree; and second, because Pope Zosimus did not cite it against Coelestius, although he required him to assent to the letters of the Apostolic See that had proceeded from his predecessor of holy memory, as Augustine reports in book II, chapter 3, *On Original Sin*.

Pagius, as usual, followed Norisius wholeheartedly under the year 416, nos. 15 and 16.

But first, even if Saint Augustine had made no mention of that decree of Innocent, this would not be sufficient reason for denying that it had ever existed. Gennadius expressly records it. Norisius at times assigns Gennadius’s testimony such weight—as we shall see below in Note 63, section 3, where the discussion will concern Leo’s letter to Flavian on the mystery of the Incarnation—that this point cannot be dismissed. [Col. 0783B; p. 190]

The *Liber Pontificalis* also testifies to it, as the Eusebius cited above indicates clearly enough. For why, when he says that the Pelagians were rejected by the Easterners, does he expressly note that this occurred when Innocent of blessed memory condemned Pelagius and Coelestius together with their leaders?

7. Next, I deny that Augustine failed to remember Innocent’s decree or that Zosimus did not cite it against Coelestius. Is Augustine to be understood as referring to one or more letters rather than to a decree merely because he uses the word “letters” rather than “decree”?

He may have avoided the word “decree” either deliberately or by chance. Does not Possidius, speaking of Innocent and Zosimus in chapter 18 of the *Life of Augustine*, say:

> Those bishops of so great a see, at different times condemning the same men—the Pelagians—by letters sent both to the African Churches of the West and to the Churches of the East, decreed that they should be anathematized and avoided by all Catholics. And this judgment concerning them, pronounced by the Catholic Church of God, was such that …

Possidius calls the constitutions issued against Pelagius by both Zosimus and Innocent “letters,” and he testifies that they were sent not only by Zosimus but also by Innocent to the Churches of the East.

Augustine himself, in Letter 190, formerly 157, to Optatus, speaking in the same way of the constitutions of Innocent and Zosimus, says:

> Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned throughout the entire Christian world by two venerable bishops, Innocent, pope of the Apostolic See, and Zosimus, pope. Concerning them there are examples of recent letters, or those which proceeded universally to all bishops from that renowned see …

There is no doubt that Zosimus issued a decree against the Pelagians.

Finally, the eminent Baronius, Garnerius, and others agreed with Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, who, according to Pagius’s reading, says of Innocent:

> He wrote a decree issued to the Churches of the West and the East against Pelagius. After him, his successor, Pope Zosimus, promulgated it more widely.

8. And indeed, if Innocent is to be believed to have sent, and to have sent in writing, his decisions against Pelagius, the diocese of the East was the place to which they must have been sent. There Innocent had learned in good time how many and how serious things Pelagius had perpetrated: on the one hand, deceiving bishops personally in synods; on the other, savagely harassing Jerome and the holy virgins Eustochium and the younger Paula through members of his faction. This is clear from Innocent’s letter, formerly numbered 95 among Augustine’s letters and now 193, and from another letter that he wrote to John, bishop of Jerusalem, which may be found in Baronius under the year 416. [Col. 0784A]

But we have already argued too long about the name, especially since the dispute can be settled in a single sentence. We may say that Augustine did not know of Innocent’s decree against Pelagius because it had been sent to the East, just as he did not know of the synod held in that same East, in the same case and the same year, by Theodotus. Saint Augustine nowhere mentions that synod.

If, then, no one will rashly accuse Mercator of falsehood because he says that the synod was held and that Pelagius was condemned in it, why should Gennadius, the *Liber Pontificalis*, or even the Eusebius cited above be accused of falsehood because Augustine does not mention Innocent’s decree under the explicit name “decree”?

Whenever I read these and many similar passages in the *History of the Pelagians* and the same author’s *Defenses of Augustine*, I customarily repeat the following, changing only one word:

> The king’s honor loves judgment.

Nevertheless, whether Innocent issued a decree against the Pelagians and sent it to all the Churches, or whether he arranged for a copy of the letters written to the Africans to be transmitted to Palestine and the East, the testimony of Eusebius and Mercator establishes with complete certainty that the Easterners rejected Pelagius because they had learned that Innocent, though not yet Zosimus, had condemned him. [Col. 0784B; p. 193]

Since this occurred in the year 417, or at the latest at the beginning of 418, while Praylius occupied the see of Jerusalem, John, who had preceded him in that episcopate, could not have still held it in the year 419, when the earthquakes recorded by Idatius occurred. Moreover, Praylius having died after a brief life, Juvenal was then occupying the Jerusalem see.

## Note XLVIII, p. 78

I. The eighth of the letters of Saint Cyril of Alexandria, which begins, “Certain people speak nonsense,” was addressed to Nestorius. Saint Leo says of it in Letter 33 to the emperor Theodosius:

> By that letter Cyril wished to correct and heal Nestorius, refuting his perverse teachings and explaining more clearly the faith defined at Nicaea; the archives of the Apostolic See received the letter sent by him. [Col. 0784D]

Saint Flavian also mentions this letter of Cyril in the first and second letters that he sent to Saint Leo. These letters are found in the early editions of Leo after Letter 8.

In the first, therefore, Flavian testifies that all the fathers of the Synod of Ephesus agreed with that letter of Cyril. In the second, he adduces certain words which, since they are taken from that same letter of Cyril, clearly demonstrate that in his first letter Flavian was speaking of this letter and not of another letter of Cyril. They also show that Leo, in his letters to Theodosius, and Idatius in his *Chronicle*, were speaking of the same letter when they mention a single letter of Cyril sent to Nestorius, destroying his heresy and setting forth the rule of faith.

2. Therefore Quesnellus is wrong to maintain that Flavian indicated, besides this letter of Cyril, *Certain People Talk Nonsense*, which in volume 1 of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 12, has a different beginning, namely, “I understand that certain people,” and also the letter concerning peace to the Orientals, which begins, “Let the heavens rejoice,” 194. For when Idatius testifies that another document was sent with this letter, we may—and more reasonably should—interpret him as referring to another writing of Cyril, which Leo identifies in the passage cited, saying: “Let him also review the acts of the Council of Ephesus, in which testimonies of Catholic priests concerning the Incarnation, inserted and cited by Cyril of holy memory against the impiety of Nestorius, are found.” Although nothing compels us to say that the other material which Idatius says was brought forward belonged to Cyril.

3. Moreover, against the poison of the Nestorian heresy, which had also infected these regions of the West, these writings supplied a most effective antidote. For, to pass over the monk Leporius of Marseille, whom we read in Sirmond’s *Opuscula*, vol. I [the printed text reads “opuscui.”; probably an abbreviation or typographical corruption of *opuscula*], confessing in his booklet of correction—written, as Tillemont believes, in the year 427:

> We used to say that it was not God himself who was born from holy Mary, but a perfect man who was born with God;

Vitalis and Constantius wrote from Spain to Capreolus, bishop of Carthage in Africa:

> There are certain people here who say that one ought not to say that God was born; for this too is their faith—or rather, their heresy—that a mere man was born from the Virgin Mary, and afterward God dwelt in him.

That the letter of Capreolus was written to these devout men, Vitalis and Constantius, after the Council of Ephesus is shown by the letters which they wrote to him; these may be read in volume I of Sirmond’s *Works*, page 215. Since they cannot have been written after Carthage was occupied by Gaiseric on 19 November 429—for from that time everything in that most troubled city was in confusion—I think that Vitalis and Constantius sent those letters to Capreolus in one of the years between 432 and 439. And if we say that they were written before the documents mentioned by Idatius in that year, 436, had been brought to Spain, we shall perhaps not depart from the truth.

### Note XLIX, p. 78

Idatius records once and again that the Burgundians rebelled against the Romans in the years 436 and 437, and testifies that twenty thousand of them were slain in this last war. The following lines of Sidonius, *Carmen* VII, verse 324, must be understood as referring to this:

> … the Belgian whom the savage Burgundian  
> Had crushed, he set free, joined with you.

That is, Aetius, joined with Avitus. Sidonius further adds:

> There the Herulian is defeated by speed,  
> The Hun by spears, and the Frank by swimming;  
> The Sarmatian by the shield, the Salius on foot, and so forth.

Here he indicates that both Frankish peoples—the Atthuarii, who lived by the Nicer, and the Salii, who lived by the river Sala or Isala—joined the Burgundians. In any event, the sole commander and instigator of the war was Gundiac, king of the Burgundians; the remaining peoples followed the Burgundian king’s leadership and fortune. Yet Marianus Scotus, born six centuries later, writes under the consuls of this year:

> Clodius added to the kingdom of the Franks the Batavians, Tungrians, Menapians, Tervani, Morini, Ambiani, Cameracenses, Tornacenses, Atrebates, Bellovacenses, and whatever lies between these regions, and beyond the Seine and the Loire.

To compare this with the account of Sidonius is to refute it. Sirmond reports that the Goths came to the aid of the Burgundians at this point in Sidonius, and that eight thousand of the former and twenty thousand of the Burgundians were killed at the same time and place. But the learned man is mistaken: the Goths perished in a different year from the Burgundians, as is clear from Idatius, and they seem also to have fought in a different place—namely, in the province of Narbonensis—while the Burgundians were fighting in Belgica.

### Note L, p. 79

When Idatius was about to narrate the events of the year 439, he did nothing wrong by placing first the destruction of Carthage, that most celebrated city, even before the events that had occurred earlier in that same year. Pagius, however, wants him to have been mistaken—or rather, makes him mistaken—by imagining that the year 2455 of Abraham, to which Idatius assigns the destruction of Carthage on 19 October, must be reckoned from 1 October of the Dionysian year 438. If that were so, Idatius would certainly have assigned the destruction of Carthage to that same year, 438. But let Pagius reckon the years of this *Chronicle* from January, and the destruction will fall in the year 439. Since there can be no doubt that Idatius referred it to that year, let Pagius at last acknowledge his own error and cease so often insisting that the Idatian years must be reckoned from October.

### Note LI, p. 79

Concerning the war at Toulouse, which Idatius records under the year 439, Prosper writes under the consuls of that same year:

> Litorius, who, with the assistance of the Huns, held the second command under the patrician Aetius, while he sought to surpass Aetius’s glory and trusted in the responses of diviners and the signs of demons, rashly engaged the Goths in battle. He was therefore deservedly defeated, captured, and killed, since, swollen with vanity and stained by sacrilegious impiety, he had undertaken the battle.

Salvian, in book VII *On the Government of God*, compares this commander of the Catholic emperor with Theodoric, the Arian king of the Goths, and philosophizes piously and wisely as follows:

> When the Goths were afraid, we presumed to place our hope in the Huns, while they placed theirs in God. They asked for peace; we refused it. They sent bishops; we drove them away. They even honored God in foreign priests—for the Goths were sending Catholic bishops to the Romans as envoys and intermediaries of peace—while we despised him in our own. As were the deeds of the two sides, so was the outcome of events. Thus Litorius, the commander of our side, entered as a captive the same enemy city, Toulouse, which he had presumed he would enter as a victor on that very day. The chains that he had prepared for others he himself endured. He who had displayed the greatest arrogance of a brave man suffered the death of a coward, consumed over a long period by prolonged wasting away in the prison of the barbarians.  
> The enemy king himself, as events revealed and proved, lay prostrate in sackcloth and poured out prayers until the day of battle. Before the war he lay in prayer; he rose from prayer to go to war. Before he took up the battle with his hands, he fought with supplication. Therefore he advanced confidently to battle, because by prayer he had already earned victory.

I have transcribed these passages from Salvian in abridged form, because they are eminently worthy of reading and display the outstanding character of Theodoric, our Gothic king. Meanwhile, observe that Idatius asserts that Litorius was killed a few days after his capture, whereas Salvian says that he was consumed over a long period by prolonged wasting away in the prison of the barbarians. Salvian was closer to these events both in place and in time, for he was writing in Gaul during those days or shortly afterward.

### Note LII, p. 79

Sidonius attributes the credit for the peace concluded between the Romans and the Goths in the same year, 439, to Avitus, *Carmen* VII, verse 299, where he depicts in these verses the alarm of Aetius and all Gaul after Theodoric had defeated Litorius:

> Gaul … was pale with fear at the Gothic rage.  
> Neither by prayer, nor by payment, nor by soldiers  
> Could Aetius accomplish anything, broken as he was;  
> With Litorius captured, the losses of the lands  
> Lay exposed. Theodoric had resolved to extend  
> His own boundaries to the Rhône; nor was it necessary  
> To fight, but to withdraw before the Goths.  
> After no protection remained anywhere,  
> And nothing was left to your commanders, Rome,  
> You mark the treaty, Avitus, and so forth.

These lines of Sidonius may be regarded as brilliantly written if Prosper is believed, for, speaking of this same peace, he says:

> Peace was made with the Goths, after they had sought it more humbly than ever before, following the grievous experience of an indecisive battle.

But we cannot doubt that this passage of Prosper is corrupt, both because of Salvian’s testimony, which confirms Sidonius, and especially because Paul the Deacon, who plainly appears to copy Prosper, reports in book XIV:

> Peace was made with the Goths, after the Romans had sought it more humbly than ever before, following the destruction caused by this grievous war.

Therefore the word “Romans,” which fell out of Prosper’s text through the negligence of copyists, must be restored.

### Note LIII, p. 80

Concerning Gaiseric’s incursions, by which he was accustomed to ravage year after year the coastal regions of both empires, Victor of Vita writes at the end of book I:

> As for what he did in Spain, Italy, Dalmatia, Calabria, Apulia, Sicily, Sardinia, Bruttium, Lucania, Epirus, and Greece, those who themselves suffered these things will more fittingly recount them there amid their miserable lamentation.

Hence, in Cassiodorus, *Variae* I.4:

> A savage and sudden enemy is mentioned, from whom that senator’s grandfather liberated Sicily and the Bruttians. Perhaps this is happening now.

From this Sicilian expedition Prosper relates, under the consuls of this year, that Gaiseric was recalled through fear of Sebastian, who had crossed from Spain into Africa; he adds that Gaiseric finally killed Sebastian. See Note 57.

### Note LIV, p. 81

In volume IV of the works of the divine Augustine, in the edition of the Louvain theologians, there is a disputation between Augustine himself and Maximinus, an Arian bishop who, according to Possidius in *The Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 17, had come into Africa with the Goths. At the beginning of the disputation Maximinus himself says that he had been sent from Carthage to Hippo by the king’s count. But read “by Count Sigisvultus,” as Sirmond advised that the passage should be read; I do not know why the Benedictines removed his observation from one of Sirmond’s notes on sermon 140 of the divine Augustine.

Sigisvultus, therefore, a Goth by nationality, conducted the war in Africa on behalf of Valentinian against Boniface. When he withdrew from Africa, I believe that his countryman Maximinus withdrew with him. At any rate, no one will deny that after Gaiseric had defeated Aspar and Boniface, and after Boniface’s return to court in the year 432, which Idatius records, Marcellinus departed from Africa. Thus, when Gaiseric invaded Sicily in this year, 441, the Arian bishop could meet him and court the favor of the Arian king. Idatius said that Maximinus had been condemned by the bishops because Saint Augustine, besides the disputation mentioned above—which is now the first of the works we possess by Augustine against Maximinus—also refuted him with great force in two further books, II and III.

### Note LV, p. 81

“Bacauda” is not the name of a people but of a faction devoted to brigandage. It became so powerful in Gaul in the time of Diocletian that Maximian had to be sent against the Bacaudae; he did not so much destroy them as restrain them. After the barbarian invasions of Spain and Gaul, however, they grew together into a monstrous force and occupied all the passes of the Pyrenees, from the Mediterranean to the Ocean. From one direction the Aracillitani, and from another the Tarraconenses, burst forth as Bacaudae and ravaged towns, cities, and entire provinces. They are also mentioned in several places in the *Chronicle*. If you wish, read at the end of this work the short dissertation on the Bacaudae [Note: [Col. 0787D] It was stated in the preface that this dissertation was not actually composed by the author.].

### Note LVI, p. 82

Sirmond believes that Merobaudes, whom Idatius praises highly under the year 443, was the same poet whom Apollinaris Sidonius celebrates in *Carmen* IX, verse 293:

> Nor should that third man now be read here,  
> Who, once leaving his ancestral Baetis,  
> Went to Ravenna, thirsty for its waters.  
> For him the applauding Quirites,  
> And a prince beloved for his popularity,  
> Erected a shining statue in the Trojan Forum.

Idatius says nothing of Merobaudes’ homeland, while Sidonius gives his name; nevertheless, the other details that each separately expresses are sufficient for us to believe that both are speaking of the same man. The poems of Merobaudes have either perished or remained hidden until now, except for one epigram on Christ, which begins:

> True offspring of God, older than all the ages,  
> Now begotten—you who always were—and discoverer of light.  
> Before all things, and parent also of your mother, whom  
> The coeternal Father sent from the stars and commanded  
> The seed of the Word, poured forth, to dwell in  
> The Virgin’s womb, enter the paths of bodily members,  
> And remain in a small abode.

You will find the rest in the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*. Was this Merobaudes the son or grandson of another Merobaudes, who held the consulship once and again in the years 377 and 388, or did he have no relationship to him? We cannot determine either possibility without an author or any witness. The rarity and unusualness of the name, however, suggest that it was retained within a single family. For the man whom Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXX, and Prosper mention under the consuls Clearchus and Richomer as king of the Gauls and master of soldiers was called not Merobaudes, as it appears in those authors, but Mallobaudes. That Merobaudes, a former consul, perished under Maximus the Tyrant, as Latinus Pacatus relates in his *Panegyric addressed to Theodosius*.

### Note LVII, p. 83

Idatius says that in the year 434 Sebastian fled from Ravenna to the palace in the East. He affirms that in this year, 444, he came as a refugee from the East to Aquitania, and records in the following year, 445, his crossing over to the Vandals in Africa. Prosper, however, under the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the fifth time and Anatolius—that is, in the year 440—indicates that Sebastian sailed to Africa.

I believe that Idatius knew Sebastian’s affairs better than Prosper did. If anyone judges that Idatius’s testimony must be accepted, he should posit two crossings by Sebastian into Africa: the first in 440, after which he returned to the East and remained there for several years, then came to Theodore in Aquitania and afterward occupied Barcelona; from there, in 445, he hastened again to Africa, as Idatius testifies. But, to tell the truth, since Idatius quite frequently records events prematurely and sometimes anticipates them by an entire quinquennium, it will not be surprising if he has here likewise anticipated by the same number of years Sebastian’s crossing to the Vandals. I determine nothing, however, but leave the matter to the judgment of the reader.

### Note LVIII, p. 83

Prosper likewise, under the consuls of the year 443, praises the diligence of Pope Leo, who brought the Manichaeans hiding in the city out of their hiding places and exposed them to the eyes of the entire Church. He adds:

> Many priests of the Eastern regions imitated the zeal of the apostolic ruler.

Turibius, bishop of Astorga, also imitated him. Taking our Idatius as his associate in his labor and vigilance, he discovered the Manichaeans hiding in Astorga and summoned them to appear. I think that the episcopal proceedings conducted against these heretics were sent by Turibius and Idatius to Antonius, bishop of Mérida, just as what Bishop Adiginus of Córdoba reported concerning Priscillian to Idatius, bishop of that same church of Mérida, around the year 480, was sent to him—as Severus has left on record near the end of book II of his *History*. This was not because Córdoba or Astorga was subject to the metropolitan see of Mérida—for that was never the case, either then or afterward—but either because of the dignity of that city or because of the renown of the bishops Antonius and Idatius. The same thing often happened among our fellow Spaniards: outside their own province, the bishops of the most celebrated cities—Cyprian and Capreolus of Carthage, Ambrose and Simplicianus of Milan—were consulted about more serious matters. All this is established by Cyprian’s letter 68, by the letter of Capreolus cited above in Note 48, and by the acts of the First Council of Toledo.

### Note LIX, p. 84

1. Turibius, bishop of Astorga, in order to confront the Priscillianists spreading throughout Spain, first wrote, I believe, a *Commonitorium* for the Orthodox. He then composed a booklet in which he summarized, in sixteen chapters, the opinions of Priscillian that had been condemned. Sixteen, I say: for Saint Leo calls the last one number 16, and declares that number 17 was expressed not in this booklet on the errors of Priscillian but in a personal letter from Turibius sent to him.

Turibius sent these writings to Pope Leo at Rome, as we learn from Leo’s letter 93, now numbered 15. Besides this letter to Turibius, Leo at the same time sent letters to all the bishops of Spain, as these words of his make clear:

> We have sent letters, he says, to our brothers and fellow bishops in Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Galicia.

The First Council of Braga adds the Baetici; there was no reason why Leo should have passed them over. Leo continues:

> And we have summoned them to a council of a general synod.

Since the eyewitness Idatius explicitly affirms that all these things were sent by Leo through Pervincus, the deacon of Turibius himself, I do not know what those writings were which Leo, according to the testimony of the same Council of Braga, sent through Turibius, the notary of his see, to the synod of Galicia. This is especially puzzling because Leo adds there:

> But if anything—which God forbid—should prevent a general council from being held, at least let the priests of Galicia assemble together. When they have gathered, our brothers Idatius and Ceponius will preside over them, together with your united diligence, so that, by a provincial assembly at least, a remedy may more quickly be brought to such great wounds.

After this, therefore, Leo had no need to write anything else to the synod of Galicia. Nor, if he did write anything, does it seem possible that Idatius, a bishop of that province and a major participant in the subsequent synod, would have made no mention anywhere of this document of Leo.

2. Nor is it permissible to suspect that a defect entered the Council of Braga and that the collector added the words “the notary of his see.” Innocent III repeats them in book II, letter 133, where he says:

> It is stated in the First Council of Braga that Theoribius, a notary sent by Pope Leo to the synod of Galicia—which Innocent likewise says had by then disappeared—was sent there.

Nevertheless, I consider the following very probable: that this Turibius, of whom the Council of Braga speaks, was no different from Turibius of Astorga, whom the council—or rather its collector—called a “notary” in a sufficiently improper sense, and one not customary in the fifth century. Florius likewise considers them identical in volume VI of *Hispania Sacra*, dissertation I, at number 200, where he refutes Pagius and Quesnellus, who distinguish Turibius, Leo’s notary, from Turibius, bishop of Astorga.

But whether one was distinct from the other or not, Turibius, Leo’s notary, must not be confused with that Turibius, or Theoribius, to whom Montanus, bishop of Toledo, wrote a letter eighty years later. It was published after the Second Council of Toledo, and a note added in the margin there says that it was written to Turibius of Astorga. How could that have been possible after eighty years? Another letter of the same Montanus to the Palentines is also found there, in which the writings of our Turibius are warmly commended.

### Note LX, p. 85

1. Pagius once again makes Idatius err, attributing to him an eclipse which he assigns to December of the Abrahamic year 2463 and links with the common era 446. This follows if Idatius began the years with which he marked his *Chronicle* from October; for Abraham’s year 2453, begun in October of the common era 446, contains a December belonging to that same Dionysian year. But it would have been fairer for Pagius not to believe that Idatius had fallen into errors so frequently and so disgracefully, but rather to convince himself that Idatius counted the years from January. On that reckoning there would be no reason and no basis for charging this ancient and accurate writer with so many errors.

Idatius therefore assigns that eclipse to December of the Dionysian year 441, with which Abraham’s year 2453 coincides from its first to its last day. The day, however, is incorrectly designated in the *Chronicle*: for the Tuesday on which the eclipse is said to have occurred was the tenth day, not the ninth day before the Kalends of January. But this was noted above in a scholion.

2. Pagius goes on and, under the same year 447, number 13, reveals his own error and that of Calvisius, when they assert that Idatius begins the years of the reign of Theodosius with the year 423 of the common era. The sequence of years observed in the *Chronicle* demonstrates this most clearly. The same is shown by the thirty years which Idatius assigns to Honorius from the death of his father Theodosius and arranges in order beginning with the year 395 of the common era, in which he began the reign of Honorius. If twenty-nine years are added to this first year in order to complete thirty, one reaches the year 424 of the same era. Therefore the following year, to which Idatius attached the beginning of the reign of the younger Theodosius and Placidius Valentinian, was the common-era year 425, their twenty-third year, and the common-era year 447.

Moreover, since it is evident from the *Chronicle* itself that in the designated year 50 of Theodosius Idatius placed the beginning of Valentinian’s empire, and thereafter continued to designate the years of both reigns with the same chronological notation, who cannot see that he began those years with Dionysius’s era 442, since Valentinian Augustus was proclaimed at the end of that year? Furthermore, since Idatius joined Honorius’s thirtieth year with Abraham’s year 2440, as his *Chronicle* demonstrates, it necessarily follows that he linked the first year of Theodosius and Valentinian with Abraham’s year 2441. Their twenty-third year, therefore, could not fail to coincide with Abraham’s year 2463 and the common-era year 447, on 23 December of which the eclipse occurred.

Idatius therefore did not err when he assigned this eclipse to the twenty-third year of Theodosius and to Abraham’s year 2463. Rather, Calvisius and Pagius are mistaken: the former falsely says that Idatius began counting the years of Theodosius’s reign a year and a half too early, while the latter falsely asserts that the years of Abraham must be reckoned from October.

### Note LXI, p. 86

1. That Asterius, Protogenes’ colleague in the consulship in the year 449, was highly esteemed by the Spaniards, and that our people were likewise dear to him, is shown by his long residence in Spain and by his daughter’s marriage to the Spaniard Merobaudes. His piety is praised by the poems of Sedulius, the Christian and religious poet, which Asterius himself collected and published.

For Sirmond attributes to this Asterius our present Asterius the task of publishing Sedulius’s poems, in his note on letter 24 of book I of Ennodius. There he produced an epigram of Asterius from the Reims Manuscript, preceded by this note:

> Sedulius left this work scattered among his papers. It was collected, arranged, and published with every refinement by Turcius Rufius Asterius, a man of illustrious rank, ordinary consul, and patrician.

There follows Asterius’s epigram to that same Macedonius to whom Sedulius sent his work by letter. Receive it here as transcribed from the emendation of Gaspar Barth:

> Take, holy man, the words of the truthful poet,  
> Composed without the blemish of fabrication—  
> A blemish from which kindly faith is free, by which is the grace of holy Christ,  
> Through which righteous Sedulius speaks such things.  
> And command that your Asterius always be remembered,  
> Through whose aid and care these were given to the people,  
> Whom, although the highest Fasti celebrate through the ages,  
> It is still a greater honor if he flourishes on your lips.

2. Cardinal Noris, in the sixth dissertation of his *Pisan Cenotaphs*, seems to have wished to make this opinion of Sirmond contemptible to his readers, when he says that Usserius and Pearson held it in such contempt that they did not even wish to pause to mention it—as though it were not customary for most non-Catholics to wish to appear to think nothing of men of this profession, such as the great Sirmond was.

But when Noris was dealing with a man of outstanding integrity, learning, and modesty, a priest who was held in the highest esteem by the leading men of the Church and even by the most Christian kings of France, he certainly ought not to have fought with such weapons.

Sirmond’s argument for attributing to this Asterius the collection and arrangement of Sedulius’s work was drawn from Gennadius.
