From complete copies, Sirmond says, he learned that Sedulius died during the reigns of Theodosius the Younger, to whom he dedicated his work, and Valentinian. A poem also survives in which Sedulius addresses Theodosius the Younger and writes, among other things:

> May you reread these things, preserve them for a long time,  
> And hand them on to the younger Arcadius; may he give these  
> To his own descendants. May your imperial offspring  
> Always receive them and teach them to their own.

Nor does the name Arcadius inserted into the poem compel us to believe that these verses were addressed to Theodosius the Great. This younger Arcadius is the son of Theodosius the Younger, not one who had already been born to him, or who ever happened to be born, but one whom the poet, flattering Theodosius, foretells will be born. Likewise, the poet prophesies offspring and sons for Arcadius himself when he adds, “May he give these to his own descendants.”

He calls him “the younger Arcadius” because, according to the custom of that age, the first male offspring of Theodosius was to be named after his grandfather, who was Arcadius. To distinguish this second Arcadius, he had to be called “the younger,” just as Theodosius himself was called “the younger” to distinguish him from his grandfather, Theodosius the Great.

Nor should we suppose that the passage refers to Arcadius, the father of Theodosius the Younger. The chronology argues against it, and still less can we interpret it as referring to Arcadia, the sister of that same Theodosius. Besides the fact that Arcadius, not Arcadia, is read in the poem itself, why would the poet have named Arcadia rather than Pulcheria or Maria?

3. Sirmond’s second argument for assigning to Asterius, Protogenes’ colleague in the consulship, the preparation of Sedulius’s work was drawn from the epigram of Asterius quoted above, addressed to that abbot Macedonius to whom Sedulius himself had decided to send his work and to whom the letter preceding the poem in the Reims Manuscript is addressed.

Since Sedulius, according to Gennadius, died before the year 450—for Theodosius died in that year, and Gennadius says that Sedulius died during Theodosius’s reign—to say nothing of Cardinal Noris’s conjecture, according to which in the poem mentioned above one should read “Arcadia, who died,” referring to Arcadia’s death recorded by Marcellinus in the *Chronicle* under the year 444, so that Sedulius would have completed his work before that year—it is exceedingly improbable that Macedonius belonged among the living nearly fifty years after Sedulius’s death.

Yet this was necessary if that epigram had been sent to Macedonius by Asterius, the man who held the consulship with Praesidius in 494 and whom Pearson, Usser, Noris, and Pagius assert collected and published Sedulius’s work. Besides, poems neglected and scattered among papers and loose sheets for so many years would more easily have perished than the Sibylline oracles written on leaves.

Finally, no one has yet proved that all the names expressed in the note of the Reims Manuscript are incompatible with our Asterius. On the contrary, Sirmond judged that they were not foreign to him. He wrote learnedly on the names of the Middle Ages, and there is no reason why we should not prefer his judgment on this matter to the conjectures of others.

4. But suppose that this Asterius of ours was called Flavius Asterius, and not Turcius Rufius Asterius. What follows? I would say that scribes attached the name Turcius Rufius to him. Did they not do this more easily than they could have attached to Sedulius the letter to Macedonius and the poem to Theodosius—something which those who despise or reject Sirmond’s opinion say was done in order to support their own view?

They assign the poem to Proba Falconia because it was at some point prefixed to this poetess’s *Cento*, as though it could not have been transferred from Sedulius’s work into Falconia’s *Cento*, just as it is said to have been transferred from Falconia’s poem into Sedulius’s work.

Moreover, if some clever person thought that Sedulius’s poem to Theodosius referred to Arcadius as already born, that alone was sufficient reason for him to attribute the poem to Falconia, since he knew that she lived in the time of Theodosius the Great, who had a son named Arcadius.

As for why they wish the letter to Macedonius to be attributed to Asterius, I do not know. Unless it is because, as stated, if it is attributed to Sedulius, and he died before the year 450, no one will ever believe that the poem which Asterius, the arranger and editor of Sedulius’s work, wrote to that same Macedonius was written by the man who held the consulship in 494.

Certainly we frequently find both writings—the letter to Macedonius, I mean, and the poem to Theodosius—under Sedulius’s name and prefixed to his work. See the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, published at Lyon in 1677, volume VI. In the same work, volume V, you will find Falconia’s *Cento* without the poem to Theodosius.

### Note LXII, p. 86

“Gaiseric,” says Victor of Vita in book I, “feared Sebastian, that renowned man of war, just as he had need of his counsels.” Wishing to destroy him, he sought an opportunity for his death in religion; that is, he attempted to draw him into Arianism. But when Sebastian repelled Gaiseric’s suggestion with a sharp and most splendid response, Gaiseric fell silent at the time. Nevertheless, Victor adds, he later killed the warlike man by another kind of stratagem.

Victor did not reveal what that stratagem was. But if religion alone had made Sebastian guilty in the eyes of the impious king, then, whatever other pretext he used to kill him, his name, says the eminent Baronius under the year 446, remains inscribed on the tablet of heaven and in the book of life with an indelible mark.

### Note LXIII, p. 87

1. Whoever reads Leo’s letter to Ravennius, bishop of Arles, which is numbered 110 in the old editions, will certainly understand that Idatius is speaking here of those writings which the most holy pontiff ordered Ravennius to circulate, so that by the care of his vigilance he might make them known to all the brethren—not merely to the Spaniards but also to the Gauls.

The responsibility for transmitting these writings to the Spaniards was entrusted to Ravennius because, as the geographical arrangement of the provinces required, they were accustomed to be sent to Spain through Gaul, as is clear from Leo’s letter 52 to the same Ravennius.

I therefore cannot sufficiently marvel at the frivolity of Paschasius Quesnellus, who took occasion from this to utter the following in his notes on Leo’s letter 15, number 9:

> Since the Church of Spain was at that time living in great ignorance, with many of its bishops either infected by error or insufficiently instructed in the Church’s doctrine, it was highly appropriate that the synods of Spain should receive reinforcement from the faith and learning of the Gallican bishops.

Thus Quesnellus, with no more honorable purpose than to seek an exceedingly vain glory for his fellow Gauls, dishonors the bishops of Spain.

But this is more tolerable than what follows, and what follows is more serious. Since no doctrinal principles or writings were sent into Spain by the bishops of Gaul except those which Saint Leo sent to Ravennius, there was no way in which the synods of Spain could receive reinforcement from the faith and learning of the Gallican bishops—unless Quesnellus should say that the writings of Saint Cyril, approved by and incorporated into the general Council of Ephesus, and the dogmatic letter of the supreme pontiff Leo received new strength from Ravennius and his colleagues, because they carried those same writings with them into Spain to be incorporated into the synods of that province.

2. But the letters of Ravennius and the forty-three other bishops of Gaul assembled with him in synod show how far they were from this vanity. In them they thank Leo for the great gift sent to them, declaring that Gaul and the entire world had been illuminated by the rays of his letter.

Let us hear them:

> Your Beatitude’s letter has been brought to us—the letter which you sent to the East in defense of the Catholic faith … Who could consider himself capable of offering sufficiently worthy thanks to your apostolate for so great a gift, which has adorned not only Gaul but the whole world as if with certain jewels?

And again:

> Whoever does not neglect the mysteries of redemption has inscribed the writings of your apostolate on the tablets of his heart as the symbol of faith.

Do you hear this, Quesnellus? The writings of the Apostolic See on a dogmatic matter, such as the bull *Unigenitus*, are to be inscribed on the tablets of our hearts as the symbol of faith. But if, conversely, you obstinately wish to appear to magnify the grace of the Redeemer in magnificent words, you in fact neglect, despise, and trample underfoot the mysteries of redemption by your deeds.

But let us return to the matter begun. From the words of the bishops of Gaul which have been quoted, even if nothing else were available, Quesnellus could have seen with perfect clarity—if his eyes had not been closed—that those writings were sent by Leo into Gaul not so that the Gallican bishops might give them new light and strength before they were carried into Spain, but because the route to Spain, to which they were sent just as they were sent to the other provinces of the world, lay through Gaul.

3. Quesnellus appears to have wished to diminish the force and authority of Leo’s letter by obscure and ambiguous expressions. But Norisius, while still living a private life among his own confrères, tried far too openly and boldly to transfer to Prosper the praise of having dictated that same letter, thereby taking it away from Leo. But it is preferable to hear Norisius himself, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 13, where he made no more of this letter of Leo than of that lengthy dissertation on the monks of Lévennes [Latin: Levinenses], Agaunum, and Jura, or of six hundred other matters. Thus Norisius, having produced Gennadius’s testimony, where he says of Prosper:

> “The letters also of Pope Leo against Eutyches concerning the true Incarnation of Christ, sent to various persons, are believed to have been dictated by him [Prosper],”

adds the following from Baronius, in the notes to the *Roman Martyrology*, 25 June [Col. 0793B]:

> “Ado of Vienne and others relate that Prosper was secretary for the letters of Saint Leo the Pope, and that the most famous letter of Saint Leo to Flavian concerning the Incarnation of the Word is said to have been written by him. This is testified not only by Gennadius, Honorius, and others, but also by Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*.”

From this the eminent Norisius concludes—and exclaims:

> “Amid such extensive agreement among the ancients, there scarcely remains any legitimate room for Bellarmine to doubt this matter.”

4. But, first of all, since Norisius could not have been unaware—and certainly ought not to have been unaware—that Baronius held the same opinion as Bellarmine concerning the author of this letter, 211 with what justification did he set them before his readers as though they disagreed with one another? Moreover, Baronius writes the following about the letter in his *Annals*, under the year 449:

> “For the rest, I would say that it belongs to Saint Leo alone; for I certainly recognize in the letter the same diction that appears in the sermons of that same Saint Leo.”

Bellarmine, however, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Prosper, says:

> “If any letter belongs to Saint Leo, that one certainly does, whether one considers Leo’s style or his doctrine.”

Here, then, are two men of outstanding sanctity and wisdom. If we are to believe Norisius, they could scarcely have had any legitimate grounds for doubting that the letter was Prosper’s; yet they unhesitatingly assign it to Leo.

5. Furthermore, the agreement of Ado, Marcellinus, and Honorius with Gennadius is not so much an agreement among ancient authorities as an agreement among antiquarians copying the writings of others. For, as Norisius himself admits in the following chapter, 14, Marcellinus speaks in the very words of Gennadius, while Honorius transcribes everything word for word from Gennadius. Ado’s words, too, are these:

> “From him [Prosper] the letters against Eutyches concerning the true incarnation of Christ are believed to have been dictated.”

These are plainly the same words that I cited above from Gennadius. Thus one Gennadius produces that entire multitude of “ancient” authorities, from whose agreement Bellarmine scarcely has any room left to assign that divine letter to Saint Leo with justification.

Conversely, certain modern critics think that they may derive a right for themselves from any obscure and isolated twig, so that, contrary to the unanimous testimony of all antiquity—of the Gallican bishops, as we saw above—and contrary to the testimony of the heavenly signs reported by the eminent Baronius in the cited passage, they may proclaim Prosper the author of that celebrated letter. Prosper was indeed a highly learned man and a pious one, and deserved exceedingly well of God’s grace in his opposition to the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians; but he was nevertheless a layman and otherwise obscure. Consequently, everyone can see that Saint Leo could not have begged from such a man, without disgrace to himself and to the entire episcopal order, the written work in which everything that had to be held by faith concerning the economy of the most sacred mystery was set before the whole world and before a general council of more than six hundred bishops.

But happy are you, Gennadius, 212 who, with the credulity of a Gaul—forgive me for speaking with Valerius Martial, since Gennadius himself says, “they are believed to have been dictated”—deprived the wisest and greatest pontiff of the work by assigning it to Prosper! For if you had touched anyone whom Norisius loves, you would undoubtedly have been well received by him, just as that poor Prosper Pithoeanus was well received, because under the twenty-third year of Honorius he mentioned the heresy of the Predestinarians. See below, note 68, II. 6.

6. Leo’s letter to Ravennius was written on the third day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and Avienus—that is, in the year of the Christian era 450. Hence we cannot doubt that the writings which Leo there instructs Ravennius to make known to the brethren had not reached Spain before that year. Since Idatius was not unaware of this—for he belonged to the number of those to whom those same writings were sent—he could not have mentioned their reception before Valentinian’s twenty-sixth year, which coincides with the common year 450.

Accordingly, Idatius ought not to have assigned the numeral XXVI, signifying Valentinian’s twenty-sixth year of imperial rule, after the section “On Gaul,” and certainly did not assign it there; otherwise he would have attached the transportation of those writings to Spain to Valentinian’s twenty-fifth year, the common era 449—namely, one year earlier than the year in which they were sent by Leo. Therefore Idatius assigned Valentinian’s thirty-sixth year to the section “Sebastianus.” From there the copyist transferred these numerals to the section “Asturius,” when he saw there the name of the consul, which appeared to him to be an indication of a new year. He was led by the same sort of error to transfer the year of Honorius 28 to the section “Constantius,” as we noted above.

### Note LXIV, p. 88

I have deleted the year 27 of Valentinian, entered under the section “The Emperor Theodosius Dies,” without any hesitation that this numeral was inserted there not by Idatius but by copyists. From this, not merely one but several errors entered the *Chronicle*, which I shall soon list one by one.

The death of Theodosius, therefore, could not have been assigned to Valentinian’s year 27, which falls in the year 451 of the common era. Theodosius did not reach that year, since he died in 450—on 28 July, if we believe Theodore the Reader, book III of the *Collectanea*. Theodosius lived forty-nine years and approximately three months. Therefore, in Idatius, XLIX must be read instead of XLVIII. For this number is preserved by *Fragment 1 of Illustrated Spain*, while in the *Short Chronicle* the year is given as 44. This is strong evidence that the genuine ancient reading was XLIX, from which the XLIV of the *Short Chronicle* arose through the alteration of X into V.

It follows clearly from this that the sequence of chronological numerals in Idatius was not disturbed during these years because Valentinian’s year 26 had been written before the section “The Emperor Theodosius Dies,” but because the numeral 27 of that same Valentinian was added to the same section, whereas it should have been transferred to the section “The Race of the Huns,” where Idatius entered it, as I shall soon show.

### Note LXV, p. 89

1. Tyro Prosper recorded the death of the empress Placidia under the consulship of Valentinian for the seventh time and Avienus, who were consuls in the year 450 of the common era. The other Prosper gives the day of her death as the fifth day before the Kalends of December; this date is also given by the funerary inscription visible at Ravenna in the church of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus, which can be found in the eminent Baronius under the year 419, no. 167.

Pseudo-Severus, who describes the events of this period from Idatius, attaches the deaths of Theodosius and Placidia to the same year. There can therefore be no reasonable doubt that Idatius subjected both deaths to the same chronological numeral—namely, XXVI, which is assigned under the section “Sebastianus,” and designates the common year 450, with which, as has been said, Valentinian’s twenty-sixth year coincides.

Accordingly, in the other editions of Idatius’s *Chronicle*, where one reads:

> “In the twenty-eighth year of the emperor Valentinian, his mother Placidia dies at Rome,”

this passage suffers from three defects:

1. It bears the chronological numeral XXVIII, although Idatius carried the previously mentioned numeral XXVI from the section “Sebastianus” through to the section “The Race of the Huns”;

2. One numeral, XXVIII, has been formed from two numerals, one XXVII and the other I;

3. The words “mother of the emperor Valentinian,” which are not Idatius’s, have been inserted into this passage.

[Col. 0795A] 2. From the year 451 of the Dionysian era, when Valentinian’s year 27 was being counted, Idatius therefore inserted into his *Chronicle* the regnal years of both emperors, of the West and of the East: those of the West because Idatius himself lived under that emperor; those of the East, I suppose, because the rulers there customarily reigned legitimately and for a longer period.

When, therefore, he came to narrate the events that took place in that year 451—which he does under the section “The Race of the Huns”—he placed there the numerals XXVII. I., signifying Valentinian’s twenty-seventh year and Marcian’s first year.

But when several people read and copied these numerals, one person—I do not know who—struck by the novelty of the matter and understanding neither what it meant nor what it was, since the years of Honorius and Arcadius, and again those of Theodosius and Valentinian, had flowed equally from the beginning and Idatius had marked the years of each pair with one simple and undifferentiated numeral, combined these two numbers, XXVII and I, into a single XXVIII.

Then, when he reread what had been written earlier and found Valentinian’s year 27 nowhere, he assigned it to the section “The Emperor Theodosius Dies,” thereby throwing the entire chronology of Idatius into confusion.

3. Another copyist, rereading the numerals XXVII. I. and grasping their meaning, distinguished them for clarity in this form: XXVII V. I. M. These should have been interpreted as:

> “In Valentinian’s twenty-seventh year, and in Marcian’s first year.”

But someone was found who interpreted the later numerals V. I. M. as:

> “Mother of the emperor Valentinian.”

From this interpretation, together with the first error by which the two epochs of the two rulers—namely XXVII and I—were fused into the single XXVIII, arose the reading found in all books:

> “XXVIII. Mother of the emperor Valentinian, Placidia, dies at Rome.”

Thus Idatius’s chronology was utterly disturbed.

For the person who saw that this interpretation could not remain attached to the section “The Race of the Huns”—for what sense would these words make: “XXVIII, mother of the emperor Valentinian. The race of the Huns”?—separated the chronological numeral and the three preceding words, namely “XXVIII. Mother of the emperor Valentinian,” from the section “The Race of the Huns,” and joined them to the words “Placidia dies at Rome,” which had appeared somewhat earlier. He thereby formed this sentence:

> “XXVIII. The mother of the emperor Valentinian, Placidia, dies at Rome.”

Because this yielded a tolerable meaning, readers lost the opportunity to observe the corruption that was displacing the *Chronicle*. Now that it has been exposed, I trust, reader, that you will judge the reading which I present here to be genuine and to have come from the pen of Idatius.

For although what I have just said concerning the method and cause by which the chronology of Idatius was overturned during these years is mere conjecture, nevertheless, apart from the fact that the conjecture is highly probable—especially when compared with what I shall say under Marcian’s seventh year, note 82, no. 1, where I shall expose another corruption of the *Chronicle* precisely similar to this one—the corrections I have introduced have been taken either from Idatius himself or from those who copied him.

### Note LXVI, p. 87

1. The arguments given above prove that the numerals XXVII. I. belong under the section “The Race of the Huns,” and that they designate Valentinian’s twenty-seventh year and Marcian’s first year. No one will deny this concerning Valentinian’s year 27. But concerning Marcian, I fear that someone may argue that his year should be attached to Valentinian’s year 26, the common era 450.

For many writers reckon Marcian’s reign from that year. Historians do so because Marcian was actually proclaimed emperor in August of the year 450. Yet the writers of chronicles and consular fasti, when they record the accession of a ruler in the year in which it occurred, assign the first year of his reign to the following consulship.

Moreover, Marcellinus and Cassiodorus attach Marcian’s first year to the consulship of Marcian himself and Adelphius, which falls in the year 451. In Panvinius, it is made perfectly clear that Marcian’s years begin from that point, not only by the designation of the consulship but also by the numeral I placed in the margin.

And indeed it is evident that Idatius equated Marcian’s first year with Valentinian’s year 27, beginning with January of the Dionysian year 451, from the order he follows in designating the other years of that same Marcian.

Idatius could certainly have attached the beginning of Marcian’s reign and its first year to the year 450, already in progress, and then attached Marcian’s second year, beginning in 451, to Valentinian’s year 27. For we shall see below that he followed this practice in the case of Avitus and others. Why he did not do the same in the case of Marcian, we cannot determine.

2. It is useful here to observe that the diversity among writers in numbering Marcian’s years has caused differing and contradictory statements to be recorded concerning the year and the consuls under whom the Fourth Synod was held.

Since the second year of Marcian and the consulship which he held with Adelphius in 451 were entered in the synod’s records, the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, focusing on the second year of Marcian designated by the synod, and then looking at the consular fasti and seeing in them Marcian’s second year fully aligned with the common year 452—or, what amounts to the same thing, with the year in which Sporatius and Herculanus were consuls—wrote the following about that synod:

> “In Marcian’s second year, in the consulship of Sporatius and Herculanus, the Fourth Synod of Chalcedon was held.”

But the synod counts Marcian’s second year not from the first day of January in the Dionysian year 452, but from 24 or 25 August of the year 451, when Marcian had completed the first year from the beginning of his reign.

Since, therefore, Marcian and Adelphius were consuls in the year 451, and the Fourth Synod was convened in October of that same year, the synod itself correctly says that it was held under Marcian and Adelphius. The *Alexandrian Chronicle*, however, incorrectly assigns it to the consulship of Sporatius and Herculanus.

Panvinius’s account of the same synod in his *Chronicle* is affected by a lesser, though different, error. Looking at the consuls who are assigned to it, he says that the synod was held in Marcian’s first year, under the consulship of Marcian and Adelphius. Thus he gives the same consuls as the council, but a different year of Marcian’s reign. In writing this way, however, Panvinius does not depart from the epoch for Marcian’s reign that he himself established.

3. Meanwhile, examples from the Alexandrian, Onuphrian, and other chronicles show that not only Idatius but several other writers were accustomed to attach Marcian’s first year to the consulship of Marcian and Adelphius—that is, to the year 451—and his second year to the consulship of Sporatius and Herculanus, the common era 452.

Finally, in Isidore’s *History of the Goths*, Marcian’s first year and that of Turismund—whom Idatius calls Thorismus—is attached to the Spanish era 490, that is, to the year 452 of the common era.

But since the same Isidore, in his *Chronicle*, attaches Marcian’s first year to the year of the world 5649, which according to Isidore himself corresponds to Spanish year 489 and Christian year 451, the two statements cannot both be true, nor can both have come from the same Isidore.

Moreover, at the end of his *Chronicle*, Isidore equates the year of the world 5845 with Spanish era 654. If, therefore, you wish to count backward from the year of the world 5649—the year to which, as has been said, Isidore attaches Marcian’s first year—you must subtract 165 years. Subtracting those same years from era 654 leaves 489, not 490.

Hence the passage in that *History of the Goths* must be corrected where Marcian’s first year and Turismund’s is assigned to era 490; era 489 must be restored.

### Note LXVII, p. 89

It is the common opinion of scholars that the Catalaunian Plains, where the Romans and Goths fought Attila in battle, received their name from Catalaunum, a city of Gallic Champagne on the Matrona, commonly called Châlons.

But what if they were so called from Cabillona, a town of the Aedui? Certainly, there is evidence that this Cabillona, situated on the Arar, was once also called Catalaunum, just as the earlier Catalaunum on the Matrona is still commonly called Châlons.

Furthermore, Eumenius, in his panegyric to Constantine Augustus, where he had set himself the single task of recounting what the Aedui had done and suffered for the Romans, mentions a certain Catalaunian defeat. Yet a defeat at Catalaunum on the Matrona did not suit his purpose at all, whereas one at Cabillonum on the Arar suited it very well.

In addition, we see with our own eyes the plain surrounding that Cabillona of the Aedui, and Eumenius himself mentions it in the same place.

Finally, Roderic of Toledo relates in book II, chapter 8, that Euphronius, bishop of Augustodunum—the chief city of the Aedui—buried countless thousands who had been killed in that battle.

Although Roderic lived much later, he appears to have had a far more ancient author as his witness for this matter. For Pseudo-Severus, published by the learned Florius, writes under Marcian’s first year:

> “Countless corpses [of those killed in the Catalaunian battle]—Euphronius, bishop of Augustodunum, is buried.”

Here there can be no doubt that the text should read:

> “The bishop of Augustodunum buried them.”

I do not conceal, however, that the following is also added in this passage of Severus:

> “Aetius fights against Attila at Tricasses, in the place called Mauriacus.”

But Tricasses is farther from Cabillona on the Arar than from Catalaunum on the Matrona. Euphronius, guided and accompanied by charity, could have hastened there, even if he had been far from the site at the time of the battle; for so great a number of dead could not have been buried in less than several days.

### Note LXVIII, p. 90

1. In the passages cited in the scholia, Jordanes, Gregory of Tours, and the author of the *Miscella* report that not only the Goths but also the Franks were with Aetius against Attila. Jordanes, the oldest of them all, wrote a full century after these events.

Yet the writers of that age, Idatius and Prosper, are completely silent about the Franks. They expressly state that only the Goths joined the Romans in fighting against Attila. You have Idatius’s words above. Prosper, under the consulship of Marcian and Adelphius, says:

> “It was quickly agreed by our people and the Goths that the fury of the arrogant enemies should be resisted with united forces.”

The author of the *Life of Saint Genevieve* (3 January) is likewise silent concerning the Franks and joins only the Goths to Aetius. He is thought to have written near the year 500, and we should believe that he would not have diminished or concealed anything concerning the glory and praise of the Franks, since by that time they were already ruling at Paris.

Most important of all, Sidonius, who reveals in book VIII, chapter 15, that he had begun to write the history of this war, is so far from joining the Franks with the Romans that he explicitly testifies that they stood against the Romans on Attila’s side, *Carmen* VII, verse 325. He says:

> “With the Hun,
>
> whom the wooded Nicer bathes with his stream,
>
> the Frank bursts forth.”

Therefore, when the most authoritative men—Prosper, Idatius, and Sidonius—are silent or even contradict the claim, these men who committed to posterity events occurring in their own time and before their own eyes, who would not be astonished that the exceptionally discerning Pagius wrote the following under the year 451, no. 22?

> “From a comparison of Gregory of Tours and Priscus, several matters otherwise shrouded in great obscurity are brought into clear light. It is evident:
>
> 1. that Clodion, king of the Franks, who had died four years earlier, left two sons;
>
> 2. that after his death a dispute arose between them concerning the succession to the kingdom;
>
> 3. that one of them fought for the Romans in the war against Attila;
>
> 4. that this man was Meroveus.”

2. But Gregory of Tours, especially in book II, chapter 7, writes nothing more than that the Franks adhered to Aetius.

If Pagius interprets this either of the entire nation or of so large a multitude of it as to constitute a kingdom and have a king over it, rather than thinking of these Franks as he thinks of the Sarmatians, Riparioli, Ibriones, and other peoples whom Jordanes also adds as allies to Aetius, then his interpretation is so refuted by the silence of Idatius and Prosper and by Sidonius’s explicit testimony that one must admit that the matters he reports have not been brought into clear light but still lie hidden in dense darkness.

This is especially true because the same Saint Gregory, in the following chapter, 9, while searching among the insignificant branches of popular tradition—for he explicitly identifies the ancient authors from whom he drew his material—reports:

> “Some assert that from the stock of this Clogio, or Clojo, or Clodion, there was a certain king Meroveus, whose son was Childeric.”

Are these the words of a man who himself acknowledged and wished to transmit to posterity that the Franks under Meroveus, the son of Clodion, had served in the Roman cause?

3. But let us also hear Priscus, whom Pagius himself, in the same place, no. 20, cites. He says:

> “The reason that provoked Attila to make war upon the Franks was the death of their kings and the dispute among their sons concerning the kingdom. Attila supported the elder, while Aetius protected the younger. We saw him at Rome while he was carrying out an embassy, before his beard had begun to blossom, with blond hair and locks so thick and abundant that they fell over his shoulders.”

Pagius therefore interprets the deceased king—although Priscus does not state his name—as Clodion, as though that were perfectly certain. He asserts by conjecture that the son, whose name Priscus likewise omits, was Meroveus. For Gregory does not testify that Meroveus was the son of Clodion, but that people said he was descended from his stock.

If you object that Meroveus could not have been beardless after the death of his father Clojo—which Pagius elsewhere assigns to the year 447—since his son Childeric is accused by Gregory of Tours, chapter 12, of excessive licentiousness eleven years after this, namely in 458, Pagius replies that Priscus did not see Meroveus at Rome in the year 448—or, as the sequence of events narrated by Priscus seems to require, in 448 or later—but in the year 432, when he had been sent as an envoy by his father Clodion to Aetius or to Augustus.

Yet, apart from the fact that Aetius was occupied at that time with more urgent matters—namely, destroying Boniface, whom he could scarcely bear after Placidia had summoned him to the palace and whom he finally eliminated in that same year, forcing Aetius himself to flee to Pannonia—Priscus not only does not support this view but openly destroys it.

For after mentioning the father’s death and the son’s embassy, when he was about to explain what the Frank had come to ask of the emperor and by whom he had been sent to Rome, he adds:

> “Aetius had also adopted him as a son and, having adorned him with many gifts, had sent him to the emperor so that he might establish friendship and alliance with him.”

Could Priscus have expressed more clearly that the Frank whom he himself saw carrying out an embassy at Rome had been instructed by Aetius and adorned with gifts, and had been sent there by Aetius not to secure friendship and alliance with Valentinian for his father, but for himself?

Could Aetius have done this in the aforementioned year 432, when, fleeing Valentinian’s anger, he withdrew into Pannonia?

Therefore, although Pagius claims, while explaining these tangled matters, to have brought them into clear light, he could not have shown more effectively that the greater part of what the Frankish annals boast about that king is wholly uncertain and obscure—things illuminated by no other light than that borrowed from conjectures of this sort.

4. Yet all the writers of Frankish history agree that Meroveus reigned after Clodion. Let it be so. But where in the world did he reign?

For if we believe Pagius, Meroveus’s elder brother held both banks of the Rhine. The time when Meroveus began his reign is also obscure.

After their father died around 448, as Pagius reports under the year 432, no. 19, dissension arose between the brothers. After Meroveus was forced to yield to his brother, he fled to Aetius, with whom he must have remained for a considerable time; he could not have earned Aetius’s friendship and adoption in a single day.

After this, he had to travel to Rome to plead with the emperor that he should be restored to his father’s kingdom by Roman arms and by imperial command. All this requires a considerable amount of time.

Yet nowhere do we read that Meroveus then obtained the kingdom, or that the Romans helped him obtain it. Indeed, anyone who considers the profound silence of the writers of that time, the immense movements of Attila, and the alarm of the Romans will certainly understand that the Romans undertook no war on behalf of Pagius’s Meroveus before the year 453, nor could they have done so.

5. It may therefore be quite consistent with the truth to say that Meroveus, the father of Childeric, was either the son, relative, or son-in-law of Clodion, and that he entered Gaul from trans-Rhenane Francia after the war with Attila, or even after the death of Aetius. To this period should perhaps be referred what is read in Sidonius, *Carmen* VII, verse 372:

> “The Frank was laying low the first German
>
> and the second Belgian.”

Furthermore, Henschenius, in the *Exegesis on the Bishops of Tongeren* prefixed to volume IV of the May publication, no. 2, indicates that he thinks the city of the Tungri, after it had been devastated by Attila, was occupied by the Franks.

Let us therefore say that around the year 453 Meroveus established his seat in Gaul near the Rhine and laid the first foundations of the Frankish kingdom. This is also suggested by the fact that the first dynasty of Frankish kings in Gaul took its name from Meroveus and was called Merovingian.

But the kingdom of Clodion—without speaking of Pharamund—ruling in the territory of the Tungri, is highly doubtful, or rather false. Nearly all the manuscripts of Gregory of Tours’s *History* read not “of the Tungri” but “of the Thuringians,” and the latter are often mentioned in the same *History*.

Moreover, while historians speak of the Tungri, who were cruelly afflicted by the Huns in this war, they mention neither a king nor a kingdom nor a Frankish people connected with them.

I pay no attention to the fragment taken from Sigebert, a ninth-century writer, and sewn onto the *Acts of Saint Lupus*, in which Meroveus is mentioned.

It is therefore certain that Clodion invaded Gaul at some time; it is no less uncertain whether he remained there. The Gauls themselves are not unaware of this; indeed, they are so far from being unaware of it that Adrian Valesius often attacks Saint Gregory of Tours, the father of Frankish history, with great irritation, because he says nothing of Pharamund and speaks very scantily of Clodion and Meroveus.

It is as though Gregory could have read everything that later writers of Frankish history, drawing on Prosper Pithoeanus’s most foolish interpolations, relate about these kings—and not only about these kings, but also about Priam and the Trojan origin of the Franks—or as though, if he were now to return to life and read those accounts, he would approve them in any way.

Valesius nevertheless deserves praise for candidly admitting in his *Notice of Gaul* that Pharamund possessed no territory in Gaul, while Clodion and Meroveus held most of their territory beyond the Rhine and only a small amount in Gaul.

6. I call Prosper’s *Chronicle* interpolated because Henschenius demonstrates this from the evidence of two very ancient manuscripts in the passage cited above, chapter 10. Concerning one of them, written in the year 623, or at least copied from another manuscript of such great antiquity, he says:

> “In this most ancient *Chronicle of Prosper*, or at least in a copy of a manuscript of such antiquity, there is absolutely no mention of Priam, Pharamund, Clodius, or Meroveus.”

Pagius nevertheless denies that it was interpolated. Under the year 418, no. 31, he maintains that all these matters were omitted from Henschenius’s copies but inserted into no others.

But on what grounds does Pagius prove this? Did he possess a manuscript written before the year 623, or some other manuscript faithfully copied from one of such antiquity as the one Henschenius had and cited?

In any event, it makes no difference whether these stories about Priam, Pharamund, and Clojo were invented by copyists or by the author himself. Are they not rightly called inventions when the writers of that period never mention those figures, even when the opportunity arose and the subject itself demanded it?

Indeed, Pagius himself admits that they were not mentioned there, saying:

> “Only Pseudo-Prosper, in the imperial chronicle, mentions the beginning of the Frankish monarchy.”

Nor do I suppose that this learned man was unaware of the judgment which Cardinal Norisius passed upon that writer in book II, chapter 15 of his *History of Pelagianism*, where he wrote:

> “I am accustomed to marvel that learned men have placed such confident trust in Prosper Tyro, when the man appears throughout his chronology not as a novice but as a child, entirely inexperienced in history and ignorant of everything he committed to writing.”

He then lists several of the man’s shameful errors and concludes:

> “I would rather clean the Augean stable than recite the errors of this novice from the index.”

How filthy, then, must we believe this Prosper to be, who deserved such a judgment from a man whose own words are:

> “We wish harsh expressions to be kept far away, and always to speak with the greatest gentleness.”

*History of the Fifth Synod*, chapter 22.

To search in such filth for the beginnings of the most illustrious and glorious kingdom of the Franks is therefore vain and disgraceful.

### Note LXIX, p. 90

Saint Isidore, in his *History of the Goths*, indicates once and again that the Romans and Goths fought against Attila, and relates that Theodoric was killed in the first engagement and magnificently avenged by his son Thurismund in the second battle.

Jordanes, no. 66, says that Theodoric was thrown from his horse while urging his Goths into battle and died after being trampled by them. He adds:

> “Others say that he was killed by the weapon of Andagis, from the side of the Ostrogoths, who were then following Attila’s rule.”

He further says that the great king died after beginning the thirty-third year of his reign.

Isidore must be understood in this way when he assigns thirty-three years of rule to him, unless you prefer to say that Isidore assigned Theodoric thirty-three years because he recorded his death one year after it occurred, namely in 452.

In reality, Theodoric scarcely reached the thirty-third year of his reign. He began to reign around the autumn of 419, as was said in note 31, and died at approximately the same time in the year 451.

Under this ruler the Gothic kingdom increased greatly. Initially confined within narrow boundaries, it was extended by him as far as the Loire and the Rhône. He left six surviving sons, whose names I have copied from Jordanes in the scholion.

He also left one daughter, whom he joined in marriage to Rechiarius the Suevian in the year 419. As for the other daughter, whom Jordanes says was married in Africa to Hunneric, son of Gaiseric, and whom her father-in-law discovered plotting to kill him and sent back to her father Theodoric with her nose cut off, the matter is not sufficiently established, and these accounts resemble fables.

### Note LXX, p. 92

Prosper, under the consulship of Sporatius and Herculanus, relates that Attila was driven beyond the Danube by the miraculous virtue of Saint Leo. After that, he never again returned to these regions of the West.

Therefore Jordanes should not be followed when he asserts that Attila again advanced against the Visigoths and was driven back by Thurismund in almost the same manner as before, on the Catalaunian Plains.

Attila died after this year. Idatius, with deliberate brevity, wrote:

> “Soon afterward he died.”

Prosper and Cassiodorus assign his death to the year 453, while Marcellinus assigns it to the following year.

Jordanes relates much about Attila in the *Getica*. In no. 82, however, he gives a remarkable account of the manner of his death and of his funeral, which may be read there.

Among other things, he testifies that Attila’s death was divinely foretold to Marcian, an excellent and especially religious ruler, saying:

> “A remarkable thing also occurred: when the emperor of the East, Marcian, was troubled by concern over so savage an enemy, a divine presence appeared to him in a dream and showed him, on that same night—namely, the night on which Attila perished—that Attila’s bow had been broken.”

### Note LXXI, p. 92

Although Prosper assigns the death of Thurismund to the year 453, and Isidore appears to agree with him when he records the beginning of Thurismund’s reign under Spanish era 490 and says that he reigned only one year, nevertheless Isidore also says in the same passage that Thurismund was raised to the kingship in Marcian’s first year, which was the common era 451, as has been shown above.

If Thurismund was killed after one year, it necessarily follows that his death fell in the year 452.

In reality, Isidore must be judged to agree with Idatius, in accordance with what was said about that passage of Isidore in note 66, no. 3. We therefore assign the killing of Thurismund to the year 452, in agreement with both of them.

Jordanes, in the *Getica*, no. 72, says that Thurismund reigned for three years, but he should not be followed. Roderic of Toledo, book II, chapter 8, may appear to reconcile this disagreement when he writes:

> “Thorismund reigned for one year, and for two years together with his father, which are counted as part of his father’s reign.”

But it is false that Thurismund reigned together with his father.

Jordanes notes that Thurismund was killed when his blood was drawn from a vein.

### Note LXXII, p. 93
Pagius, under the year 453, no. 5, did not hesitate to assert that the eminent Noris had demonstrated from the Alexandrian Chronicle that Saint Pulcheria died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February]. Nevertheless, the most learned Joannes Stillingus, in his Life of that same Saint Pulcheria, under 10 September, demonstrates more clearly that Noris misunderstood the words of the Alexandrian Chronicle. Therefore Stillingus himself, together with Tillemontius and Cangius, agrees with Idatius—and rightly so.

For that Chronicle, narrating in a continuous account both the discovery of the head of Saint John the Baptist and Pulcheria’s death, refers not Pulcheria’s death but the discovery of Saint John’s head to that twelfth day before the Kalends of March, as becomes clear from the Greek words of the same Chronicle, if they are rendered exactly and faithfully. See them in the previously cited place in the Antwerp *Acta Sanctorum*.

Marcellinus likewise records both events in his *Chronicle*, and his words are these:

> “This venerable head [of John the Baptist] is known to have been discovered under Uranius, bishop of the aforementioned city [Emesa], by the presbyter Marcellus mentioned above, in the consulship of Vincomalus and Opilio, in the month of February, on the twenty-fourth day, in the middle week of the Paschal fasts, while the emperors Valentinian and Marcian were reigning. Pulcheria Augusta, wife of the emperor Marcian, completed the atrium of blessed Lawrence with incomparable workmanship and brought her life to a blessed end.”

Thus Marcellinus records the day on which Saint John’s head was discovered, while saying nothing about the day of Saint Pulcheria’s death. The Alexandrian Chronicle does the same. Since everyone else is silent, whereas Idatius explicitly testifies that Pulcheria died in July, it is fair to agree with him.

Marcellinus assigns the discovery of Saint John’s head to 24 February, whereas the Alexandrian Chronicle assigns it to the 18th. So it is; yet I do not dare determine which of the two ought to be believed. Saint Leo very frequently proclaims the praises of this empress and remarkable virgin, born of a Spanish father, grandfather, and ancestors, and of her who was the most holy and the greatest figure that age produced, even in those qualities that rise above the weaker sex; the Council of Chalcedon [227] and innumerable others proclaim them as well. You will find more about her in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*.

## Note LXXIII, p. 93

1. That, at the margin of § “Aetius the commander,” the scribes omitted the numerals XXX and IV—which signify Valentinian’s thirtieth year and Marcian’s fourth year, and which Idatius had inserted there—is proved by two arguments of the greatest force in this matter.

The first is this: immediately afterward Idatius says that Valentinian was killed in the thirtieth year of his reign. But he must have been killed in the thirtieth year if no new numeral was entered at § “In the third year of his reign.” For it has already been demonstrated at ample length above that Idatius assigned Valentinian’s twenty-ninth year to § “In the third year of Valentinian’s reign.”

The second argument is this: when Idatius is discussing the years in which Marcian reigned, he says below: “In the eastern regions, Marcian died in the seventh year of his reign.” I therefore ask you, reader, to look for the four remaining years between § “In the third year of his reign” and Marcian’s death. You will find them nowhere. For the numeral I attached to § “The forty-third year of the Romans” does not increase the number of Marcian’s years, as I shall show there; indeed, even the Sirmondian *Chronicle*, however corrupt, demonstrates this by itself. For there it notes that Marcian’s fourth year was still in progress, although it had attached this same fourth year of Marcian to the preceding note, namely Valentinian’s XXXI.

Thus, from § “In the third year” to Marcian’s death, only three years of his reign are counted in the printed books. Therefore the fourth year was cut away from § “Aetius the commander,” or from one of the two entries preceding it. For my part, I have placed the numerals XXX and IV at § “Aetius the commander,” because Aetius’ death certainly belongs to Marcian’s fourth year and Valentinian’s thirtieth. It is uncertain, however, whether the events that Idatius recounts there concerning Frideric’s war against the Bacaudae and the earthquake in Gallaecia belong to that year.

Finally, after Aetius was killed, Valentinian sent his envoys to all the provinces, including the Suevi, to announce this death, as Idatius testifies. Since he was then among the Suevi, is it credible that he did not know the date of that death and connected it with the third year of Marcian, that is, with the year 453 of the common era? We can reason similarly concerning Valentinian’s death, which we see connected in the commonly circulated editions of this Chronicle with Marcian’s fourth year, namely the year 454 of the common era. Could anyone believe that Idatius wrote this?

2. But I wish here to disclose to the reader the occasion for the deletion of those numerals XXX and IV opposite § “Aetius the commander.” Unless I am greatly mistaken, the matter is as follows.

Valentinian’s thirtieth year and Marcian’s fourth year are expressed by precisely the same signs as Valentinian’s thirty-first year and Marcian’s fifth year—namely XXX. IV—so that they are distinguished only by a single point placed here or there. If one places the point before the I, writing XXX. IV, one indicates Valentinian’s thirtieth year and Marcian’s fourth. But if one attaches the point after the I, writing XXXI. V, one denotes Valentinian’s thirty-first year and Marcian’s fifth.

This tiny matter, whether omitted in the manuscript or overlooked by the scribe, inflicted the damage upon Idatius of which we are speaking. From it arose the belief of some unknown person that one and the same number was signified by both sets of signs, and that the signs had been written twice in the Chronicle by mistake. Influenced by this error, he removed them from the first place—namely from § “Aetius the commander”—but preserved them in the second place, at § “Through two barbarians,” where it was subsequently necessary for Marcian’s fourth year to be read, since his third year had just previously been recorded. In this way, finally, Marcian’s fifth and sixth years vanished from the manuscript copies of the Chronicle.

## Note LXXIV, p. 94

If what Nicephorus, book XV, chapter 2, and others relate is true—namely, that Placidia, Valentinian’s daughter, had been betrothed to Olybrius before Rome was captured by Gaiseric—then Eudocia, her sister, must have been given by Maximus to his son Palladius.

Unless someone prefers to suppose either that Maximus took Placidia away from Olybrius, or that Olybrius, after Maximus and his son Palladius had been killed, betrothed Placidia to himself during those three days that elapsed between Maximus’ death and Gaiseric’s entry into the City, as Victor of Tunnuna testifies. Both alternatives, however, are sufficiently incredible.

But since Evagrius, book II, chapter 7, and also Priscus, contrary to what other writers frequently relate, state that Eudocia was older than Placidia, it may seem most probable that Valentinian—who had no male offspring and who knew that both he and his father Constantius had risen to the imperial throne through his mother Placidia—delayed the marriage of his elder daughter Eudocia, lest, while he himself was still vigorous and in the prime of life, he should take a successor to himself from among his sons-in-law; and that for the same reason Maximus wished to unite Eudocia rather than Placidia with his son Palladius.

## Note LXXV, p. 95

[Col. 0802D]

The writers disagree about the killers of Flavius Anicius Petronius Maximus, who seized the empire after Valentinian Placidius had been killed. Prosper, Cassiodorus, Jornandes, and Theophanes relate the matter with remarkable diversity: Prosper says that Maximus was torn to pieces by servants of the empress Eudoxia; Cassiodorus, that he was killed by soldiers; Jornandes, that he was slain by a Roman soldier named Ursus; and Theophanes, that he was killed by his own men.

Prosper then briefly but clearly touches upon the matters relating to the deaths of Valentinian and Maximus. Maximus was killed, according to the Cuspinian Anonymous, on the day before the Ides of June. Marcellinus, in his *Chronicle*, says that he was killed in the third month of his tyranny; the *Chronicle* attributed to Severus says, in the seventieth day of his reign. Sidonius differs in no respect from Severus, assigning Maximus’ reign a little more than two months in book II, letter 13.

But Idatius, in his customary manner, also assigns to Maximus the period of interregnum that lasted until 10 July, when Avitus was made emperor. If one counts backward from 10 July to 17 March, when Maximus usurped the empire, one finds four months less seven days. Therefore Idatius spoke with complete accuracy when he said that Maximus had scarcely completed four months of his reign.

Nor was the eminent Baronius less correct when he asserted that the interregnum from Maximus’ murder to Avitus’ proclamation lasted twenty-eight days [230]; Pagius therefore wrongly corrected him under the year 455, no. 10.

## Note LXXVI, p. 95

Idatius gained nothing by having stated the following concerning the first year of Arcadius and Honorius: “So that the addition of five years of Olympiads may not cause confusion, since they have been inserted only on account of the reigns of emperors.” I say, he gained nothing; rather, he confused the scribes, who, on Avitus’ accession to the empire, counted five years of an Olympiad because his first year ought to have been recorded without increasing the civil years, just as the first year of Arcadius and Honorius did not increase them.

Indeed, Idatius loudly proclaims that he follows the events of this same year from § “Through two barbarians” to § “(at least) the Suevi [and] the Carthaginian regions.” First, he signifies this most clearly when he says: “In that same year, Avitus”; then when he says: “Marcian, already in the fifth year of his reign,” retaining the same year of Marcian that he had designated above.

Something similar also occurs in other editions, in which by mistake not the fifth but the fourth year is read. It makes no difference whether one reads “fourth” or “fifth,” provided that the same year is retained in both places. But if the numeral I attached to § “The forty-third year of the Romans,” which signifies Avitus’ first year, indicated a new civil year, it ought to have increased the number of Marcian’s years and would have joined his sixth year to Avitus’ first, his seventh to Avitus’ second, and his eighth to Avitus’ third. It does not do this; rather, in clear and explicit words it assigns him only seven years of imperial rule.

Finally, Idatius below relates Gaiseric’s entry and invasion of the City, which he says occurred before Avitus became Augustus. What follows, then? One would have to be exceedingly foolish to refer to the year after Avitus’ accession something that Idatius himself says occurred before his inauguration.

Whatever was done during that year 455, including Avitus’ renunciation—which occurred after the devastation of the City—he mentioned before it, so that he might announce in a single continuous account the successor of Maximus, whose murder had both been perpetrated before Gaiseric’s invasion and had been narrated in the Chronicle. Idatius therefore assigned the first year of Avitus to § “The forty-third year of the Romans,” just as he had assigned the first year of Arcadius and Honorius to § “The fortieth year of the Romans” above, and as he will assign below the first year of Majorian and Leo to § “The forty-fourth year of the Romans,” without thereby introducing any alteration into the civil years.

Accordingly, Idatius continues to count Marcian’s fifth year, the year 455 of the common era, even here at § “The forty-third year of the Romans,” and will continue to do so until he reaches § “Through Augustus Avitus,” where Avitus’ second year, Marcian’s sixth, Abraham’s 2472nd, and Christ’s 456th year must be counted.

## Note LXXVII, p. 97

[Col. 0803D]

Sirmondus had formerly noticed that the chronological numerals had fallen out at § “Through Augustus Avitus.” When he brought Idatius to light, he added to the margin of this Chronicle the words “Marcian’s fifth year,” which the learned Florius omitted from his edition. And rightly so, for those words are Sirmondus’ own, not Idatius’.

Sirmondus correctly observed the place where the new numeral had to be supplied, but not the numeral itself. For it was not Marcian’s fifth year but his sixth that had to be written there.

Both points can be seen in the *Short Chronicle*. Immediately after the words “Marcian and Avitus exercise the imperial power in concord,” it adds: “In the sixth year of Marcian,” except that the manuscript read *annis* (“years”), which the distinguished Florius correctly emended.

That Isidore likewise read this way is shown by what he writes both in his *History of the Goths*, where he says that Theodoric entered Spain in the fifth year of his reign and shortly before had said of the same Theodoric that he began to reign in Marcian’s second year, and in his *Chronicle*, where he says explicitly: “In the sixth year of this emperor [Marcian], Theodoric, king of the Goths, entered Spain with a great army.”

Thus the scribes most negligently omitted Marcian’s sixth year everywhere and displaced Avitus’ second year—which Idatius most certainly joined to Marcian’s sixth—to § “Rechiarius,” as far as possible from its proper place.

## Note LXXVIII, p. 97

[232]

Concerning the Heruli, Jornandes, in *Getica*, no. 43, describes them from Ablavius as situated near the Maeotian Sea and distinguished for infantry service. Mamertinus, in the panegyric addressed to Maximian Augustus, says:

> “When the Heruli, first among the barbarians in strength but last in location, had burst into these provinces [Gaul], …”

He then says that they were defeated and destroyed there. From this we understand that, once expelled from the borders of Gaul, they either settled near the river Amasius or Amisius, beside the German Ocean, or, having already possessed those places, returned to them. That they were neighbors of the Batavians is also apparent from the fact that Heruli are often mentioned as mixed among Roman soldiers and Batavians.

From those regions, therefore, practicing piracy like their neighbors the Saxons, they harassed the coasts of Belgium, Gaul, and Spain with continual raids for many years. Sidonius, concerning the Heruli, book VIII, letter 9, says:

> Here the Herulian with gray cheeks wanders,  
> Dwelling in the deepest recesses of Ocean,  
> Almost the same color as the seaweed-covered deep.

The same Sidonius speaks of the maritime raids of the Saxons, which were altogether similar to those of the Heruli, in the same book, letter 6.

## Note LXXIX, p. 100

There is no need for words here. Examine for yourself, reader, the order of the writing and of the events in the Chronicle. You will clearly infer that the scribes wrongly assigned Avitus’ second year to § “Rechiarius,” although it ought to have been recorded at § “Through Augustus Avitus.” Even if it belonged to § “Rechiarius,” it ought not to have been separated from Marcian’s sixth year; both should have been entered together in the same place.

Thus we learn, from Idatius himself, that everything that follows, up to § “Avitus afterward,” belongs to the year that followed Valentinian’s murder—that is, to the year 456 of the common era [233].

Nor can Pagius’ opinion do anything to excuse the scribes’ error: he holds that Idatius began counting the years from October. For Idatius had already properly left October at § “Soon afterward, to the Spaniards,” as is most clearly evident from the Chronicle itself. Indeed, there is scarcely another place in the entire Chronicle from which Pagius’ opinion can be more plainly shown to be false.

## Note LXXX, p. 101

1. After Idatius had related what happened on 28 October of Avitus’ second year and Marcian’s sixth, the year 456 of the common era, he adds that the tribune Hesychius arrived in Gallaecia as an envoy from Avitus and announced that Avitus had proceeded from Italy to Gaul and had succeeded at Arelate.

He then records the death of Rechiarius, whom he says was killed in December. From this we may reasonably infer that Hesychius reached Gallaecia in November of the same year.

Anyone who reads Idatius attentively will scarcely be able to doubt that he narrates the events of that year in the very order in which they occurred. The fact itself suggests, and Idatius hints below, that Hesychius had come to Theodoric to request the auxiliary forces that Theodoric had promised Avitus, when he writes of Avitus: “Deprived of the promised aid of the Goths, he lacks both assistance and life.”

We must suppose that Avitus, as soon as he realized that he had been stripped of the empire, requested help and assistance from Theodoric. If, therefore, Hesychius met Theodoric in Gallaecia in November, it follows that Avitus was deposed from the empire by Ricimer in October; for Hesychius would not have needed a longer time to travel from Italy to Gallaecia.

We have, moreover, the clearest testimony of the Cuspinian Anonymous, who states that Avitus was thrown down from the imperial throne on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November. His words, under the consulship of Varanes and John, are:

> “The emperor Avitus was captured at Placentia by Ricimer, master of the soldiers, and his patrician, Messianus, was killed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November.”

Thus it is read in that Chronicle which Joannes Baptista Solerius—or rather Conrad Janingus—of the Society of Jesus copied at Vienna in Austria in 1683 [234] and later had printed in volume V of the June *Acta Sanctorum*.

It is more reasonable to believe and fully trust this edition, prepared by a man highly experienced in such matters who had himself newly transcribed the Cuspinian manuscript, than the old edition of Panvinius, in which, in place of the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June is read.

This is especially so because the following words occur immediately beforehand in Panvinius’ edition: “Remiscus was killed in the palace at Classis on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.” They are immediately followed by: “The emperor Avitus was captured,” and so forth. If this latter event belonged to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, the author of that Chronicle would certainly have mentioned it before Remiscus’ death.

2. The pseudo-Severus differs scarcely at all from the Anonymous, since he says that Avitus reigned one year and three months—that is, only seven days fewer than the period counted by the Anonymous. Perhaps he omitted those days, being content to designate the year and months in round numbers.

The Roman inscription cited by Athingus in *Roma subterranea* and by Sirmondus in the sixth book of Sidonius also supports this view. It reads:

> DEP. THIMOTHEA. IN. PACE. D. KAL. NOV. CONS. D. N. AVITI.

“Timothea was buried in peace on the day of the Kalends of November, in the consulship of our lord Avitus.”

If Avitus had been stripped of the purple so long before—namely, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June—the emperor would certainly not have been called ‘Lord’ within the City by a Roman citizen.”

Therefore, in that inscription dated to the same day, which Sirmondus and Aringhus likewise cite:

> LOCUS. GERONTI. PRESB. DEPOSITUS. XIV KAL. JUL. CONS. EPARCHI. AVITI.

“The burial-place of Gerontius, presbyter, buried on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Eparchus Avitus.”

the Avitus mentioned is some consul suffectus, not Avitus Augustus. For the latter was named not Eparchus but Flavius Maecilius Avitus, as is clear from a coin cited by Mediobarbus and as Morales had long ago observed in book VI, chapter 28, together with the great Augustine.

3. Avitus therefore held the empire from 10 July of the year 455 until 17 October of the following year; consequently, he reigned one year, three months, and seven days.

Evagrius must therefore be corrected, since in book II, chapter 7, he assigns him only eight months; Pagius, who in the *Critica*, under the year 456, no. 6, followed the corrupt reading of the Cuspinian Anonymous and assigns him ten months and seven days; and Valesius, who in his notes on Evagrius says that Avitus reigned only seven or eight months.

4. The place, time, and manner of his death are very uncertain. The fact that Idatius inserts his death under the year 457 is not sufficient to prove that he did not die before that year.

For Idatius entered Honorius’ death under the year 424, although Honorius died before that year, namely in 423. Idatius was not unaware of this, as he himself indicated in his *Fasti*. But because he assigned to Honorius the period of interregnum that then occurred—excluding John from the number of emperors, just as Idatius excludes him—he remained silent about Honorius’ death in the Chronicle until the year 424.

Idatius may have done the same in the case of Avitus, assigning to him the period of interregnum that preceded Majorian’s proclamation. From Idatius, therefore, we cannot determine with certainty whether Avitus departed this life at the end of 456 or at the beginning of 457.

Idatius repeatedly indicates that some time elapsed between Avitus’ abdication and his death. He states here that Avitus proceeded from Italy to Gaul, to Arelate, after being stripped of the empire; afterward he gradually records this deprivation and Avitus’ death, saying:

> “After Avitus had been made emperor by the Gauls and the Goths, he lacked the empire; deprived of the promised aid of the Goths, he lacked both power and life.”

He expressed the same point even more clearly above, when he says that Hesychius reported that Avitus had proceeded from Italy to Gaul.

From this it may reasonably be inferred that Avitus, having been deposed from the empire at Placentia on 17 October, as the Anonymous relates, fled from that city to Gaul at the first opportunity and sent the tribune Hesychius to Theodoric in Spain to request assistance.

Hesychius met Theodoric in Gallaecia, where Idatius was living, at the end of November or the beginning of December in the year 456. After obtaining no assistance from Theodoric, he returned to Avitus as the year 457 was approaching.

Then Avitus, either from despair of his affairs, from fear of death—which Ricimer was seeking for him—or from both causes, fell ill and died, as the account of Turonensis indicates, whose words I shall now give.

5. The place and manner of his death are described, in any event, by the Gregory of Tours mentioned above, book II of the *History*, chapter 11, where he writes:

> “Avitus, expelled by the senators at the city of Placentia, was ordained bishop. But when he learned that the still-angry senate wished to deprive him of life, he set out for the basilica of Saint Julian, martyr of Auvergne, with many gifts. Having completed the course of his life on the journey, he died; he was carried to the village of Brioude and buried at the feet of the aforementioned martyr.”

This is Gregory’s account.

What he relates about Avitus’ appointment to the episcopate of Placentia—which Victor of Tunnuna had also previously recorded—may perhaps be true; certainly it is not inconsistent with the practices of that age. Nevertheless, I think it more likely that when Ricimer wished to compel Avitus to accept the bishopric of that city, Avitus fled to Gaul before being ordained and there thought more about recovering the empire than about undertaking the episcopate.

6. Since mention has been made of the illustrious martyr Julian of Brioude, it is worth noting in passing what the same Gregory of Tours relates in book II of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 4: namely, that a Spanish woman was the first of all people to dedicate a church or shrine to this holy martyr.

When she was passing through Brioude and hurrying toward Trevirus, where her husband was just about to be condemned to death by the tyrant Maximus, she heard of Julian’s miracles and promised to build him a little chapel if her husband were rescued from so great a danger. Having therefore obtained the fulfillment of her vow, she completed the promise she had made with immense gifts.

## Note LXXXI, p. 101

[Col. 0806C]

Theodorus Lector, book I of the *Collection*, testifies in these words that after Gaiseric’s invasion of the City and the removal from there to Africa of the empress Eudoxia and her daughters, Marcian decided to wage war against Gaiseric:

> “When Marcian learned what the Africans were doing against the Roman state and the empresses, moved by the majesty of the empire, he prepared himself for war.”

From this one may reasonably doubt whether what Procopius, book I of *The Vandalic War*, and others following him write is true—namely, that Marcian had once been captured in Africa by Gaiseric and had pledged his faith to him, promising never to trouble the Vandals.

But to return to our subject: the expedition against the Africans of which Theodorus speaks could have occurred at no other time than this, and it could have been no other kind than a naval expedition.

I therefore interpret Idatius, when he says, “Ships from the East arriving at Hispalis announce that the army has been defeated on Marcian’s behalf,” as meaning that the ships he calls “Eastern” belonged to a fleet sent by Marcian toward the Pillars of Hercules and Hispalis, which, reinforced by troops from Avitus, was to invade Africa.

For it is established by the testimony of Priscus that both emperors liberated Eudoxia and her daughters. Therefore this fleet, having arrived at Hispalis, announced once again the slaughter of the Vandal army in Corsica by Ricimer, which Avitus had previously reported to Theodoric through Hesychius.

Idatius said “on Marcian’s behalf” because those Eastern ships had come from Marcian’s side. This reading and interpretation seem sufficiently appropriate and, moreover, necessary; for the reading offered by the commonly circulated books is meaningless and refers to nothing.

## Note LXXXII, p. 102

1. Just as, under Marcian’s first year, the scribes corrupted the numerals that Idatius had written there—first through the interpolation “XXVII V. I. M.” and then through the gloss “Valentinian the emperor’s mother”—so also, under Marcian’s final year, they interpolated the numerals III, VII, by which Idatius intended to signify Avitus’ third year and Marcian’s seventh.

First, someone wrote “III A. VII M.”; afterward another interpreted them as “In Avitus’ third year, in the seventh month”—a monstrous reading that has confused everyone who has read it up to the present.

That earlier corruption, “Valentinian the emperor’s mother,” was indeed difficult to recognize after the signs “V. I. M.” had been transferred from § “The race of the Huns” to § “Placidia dies,” because it produced a meaning that was not entirely absurd. Therefore, so far as I know, no one ever questioned that reading, however strange it was.

But Sirmondus regarded our present reading—which changed “VII M.” into “the seventh month,” or “seven months”—as so suspect, or even false, that in his edition he deleted the two words “the seventh month.”

Henricus Valesius, who informed us of Sirmondus’ correction, as was stated in the scholion, offers no better reading. He says:

> “Sirmondus omitted the two words ‘the seventh month’ in his edition; he would have acted more wisely if he had deleted the two words ‘in the third year.’”

Florius, note 14 on Idatius, no. 6, agrees with Valesius, except that he suggests that Idatius may have written “the tenth” instead of “the seventh month.”

2. These three most distinguished men all wish to remove something from Idatius’ text. But Sirmondus rejects what, in my opinion, Idatius never wrote and could not have written in that place. For from that point he begins the account of the events that occurred in the year 457; when that year arrived, nearly eighteen months, not seven or ten, had elapsed since Avitus’ inauguration.

Valesius and Florius, however, would remove something that Idatius most certainly did write.

The outstanding critic Pagius, in *Dissertation on the Hypati*, chapter 14, while discussing the consuls of the year 456, asserts that both readings can stand together. Yet he did not even attempt to reconcile them, either there or in the *Critica*, where he revisits this passage of Idatius.

Indeed, in no. 7, under the same year 456, he concludes:

> “Therefore those words about which the question is concerned—namely, these two, ‘in the third year’—appear to have been inserted into Idatius.”

3. Yet, with due respect for such great men, I shall say that the sign III, which signifies Avitus’ third imperial year, must not be erased from the Chronicle. It was written by Idatius’ hand beyond any doubt.

Idatius consistently follows this practice throughout the Chronicle: after recording the first year of each emperor, he assigns to him thereafter as many years as he actually reached while ruling, even if he did not complete the final year, or scarcely even began it.

He did this in the case of Theodosius the Great, to whom he assigned the year 395, although Theodosius died on the seventeenth day of that year. He likewise counted the years of Valentinian and Marcian.

Whatever may be the case with the passage now under discussion, he immediately assigns Marcian seven years of reign in explicit words, saying:

> “In the eastern regions, Marcian dies in the seventh year of his reign.”

From what has been said it is clear that Idatius connects this seventh year of Marcian with the year 457 of the common era. Yet Marcian scarcely lived through the first month of it, since his successor Leo was elected on 7 February of that same year, according to the Alexandrian Chronicle.

4. Moreover, whenever a period of interregnum occurred, Idatius assigns it to the emperor who immediately preceded it.

We have an example in Honorius, who died in 423, although Idatius extends his empire to the year 425, in which he inserts first Theodosius the Younger and then Valentinian into the Chronicle.

Therefore, following his usual practice, when Avitus’ principate and the interregnum that followed it covered three civil years—namely 455, 456, and 457—Idatius assigned three imperial years to Avitus, which he designated by the sign III; he added the other sign, VII, indicating Marcian’s seventh year.

As stated above, some ignorant person interpolated these signs, and from this arose the reading “In Avitus’ third year, in the seventh month.”

Nor would the assignment of three imperial years to Avitus have introduced any confusion into the Chronicle if readers and scribes had remembered the rule that Idatius set forth under the seventeenth year of Theodosius the Great. From that rule they would have understood that Avitus’ first year was the same as Marcian’s fifth, and Majorian’s first the same as Avitus’ third. Therefore the civil years were not to be increased either where Avitus’ first year or where Majorian’s first year was written.

In this way Idatius’ chronology is wholly consistent, and it is clear to everyone that he made no mistake, even though he assigned three imperial years to Avitus. They must be counted in the same way that Idatius himself counts the seventeen years of Theodosius the Great and the thirty-one years of Placidus Valentinian.

## Note LXXXIII, p. 102

Whoever believes that Idatius began a new civil year at § “Theodoricus,” that person has not merely forgotten the rule that Idatius prescribed under the first year of Arcadius and Honorius, but must also have kept his eyes entirely shut.

For it is as evident that Idatius continues at § “Theodoricus” the narrative he had begun at § “Theodoricus at Emerita” as it could possibly be. Anyone who reads these passages even inattentively cannot fail to perceive this plainly.

The events themselves rule out a delay of sixteen months, which would necessarily have elapsed between Theodoric’s contemplated plundering of Emerita and his departure from that city if a new common year were counted at § “Theodoricus.”

Moreover, Saint Isidore, narrating these same events in his *History of the Goths*, says:

> “When Theodoric was preparing to plunder the city of Emerita, he was terrified by the power of Saint Eulalia the martyr and immediately departed with his entire army and returned to Gaul.”

Isidore would have said that Theodoric immediately departed from Emerita if, when copying this passage from Idatius, he had believed that the sign I attached to § “Theodoricus” indicated not only a new reign but also a new year? But below, under the year 460, I shall show that Isidore did not count a new civil year in this place.

Therefore Idatius, beginning a new year at § “III. VII. Avitus afterward,” connects to it the imperial epoch of Leo and Majorian, which began after January. He recorded at § “Theodoricus at variance” the sign I, which consequently signifies a new reign, not a new civil year.

## Note LXXXIV, p. 104

When Theodoric learned through the tribune Hesychius that Avitus had been driven from the empire, whether seized by anger or by a sudden desire to add to his kingdom whatever Roman jurisdiction remained in Gallaecia and the other provinces of Spain—for Idatius and Sidonius repeatedly testify that until then he had been loyal to the empire—he allowed, or even ordered, his own Goths to perpetrate the actions that Idatius recounts under the year 457.
