Those actions were atrocious and savage, and far too alien to the character of Theodoric that Sidonius describes in book I, letter 2.

Nevertheless, he afterward granted the entire province to the ancient possessors of Gallaecia, no less unworthy than the Suevi, and, in keeping with his innate generosity, allowed the Suevi to choose a king from their own people.

Jornandes relates the matter more fully in *Getica*, no. 74:

> “When the Suevi witnessed the death of their ruler, King Rechiarius, they sent the priests of the region as suppliants to Theodoric. Receiving them with pontifical reverence, he not only granted the Suevi impunity but, moved by compassion, allowed them to appoint as their prince someone from their own people.”

These priests were Catholic bishops, for at that time there were no others in Gallaecia. Theodoric nevertheless showed them reverence, and on their account dealt with the Suevi more leniently than the law of war would have permitted.

I have observed this respect of the Goths toward bishops, often attested by other writers, and above, in note 51, I cited Salvian’s words on this same matter.

## Note LXXXV, p. 105

Florius scrupled to restore the second year of Majorian and Leo to its proper place at § “The Gothic army,” which follows after § “Frantanes,” even though he knew perfectly well that it belonged there.

Nothing more is needed for anyone to recognize that this is what Idatius wrote than to read Idatius himself. Above, at § “Theodoricus at variance,” he mentions one Easter, and at this § “Frantanes” he mentions another—another, I say, as no one will deny if he carefully considers the sequence of Idatius’ narrative.

Therefore the first Easter belongs to the year 457 of the common era and to Majorian’s first year; the second belongs to the year 458 and to Majorian’s second year. It is plainly evident that Idatius designated this second year at § “Frantanes.”

## Note LXXXVI, p. 106

I believe that Portucale was under Roman— that is, Gallaecian—control, the inhabitants having remained exempt from the yoke of the Suevi, when Rechiarius, driven there by the violence of a storm, arrived, as Jornandes relates.

Theodoric left that fortress to these people, together with whatever jurisdiction had belonged to them before the war undertaken against Rechiarius. This can be gathered clearly from Idatius’ own narrative.

That there was then only one fortress called Portucale is noted under the year 456, in the scholion at letter P.

Later another fortress of the same name was founded. It soon developed into a distinguished city and gave its name to Portugal, from the time when our Catholic kings, moving southward from Gallaecia against the Saracens, subjected that city to themselves and called Portucale both the suburban region extending from it and whatever territory they subsequently occupied continuously along that coast.

It is therefore clear that some people are wrong to write *Portugallia* with a double l.

## Note LXXXVII, p. 107

1. Idatius mentions the firmest peace concluded between Majorian and Theodoric under the year 459. Sidonius praises Peter, who was Majorian’s secretary of correspondence, in the fifth poem, verse 571, and says:

> Yet recently, most gracious Caesar,  
> After receiving a hostage,  
> You drove from the walls of our city  
> The enemy thrust into its wretched vitals.  
> And because, amid affairs exhausted,  
> You came as the one hope,  
> First succor our ruins;  
> And, as you pass by your Lugdunum,  
> Look upon it, victor.  
> Your labors have been immense;  
> The broken city asks you for repose.  
> To the one to whom you grant peace, restore courage.

This enemy, who compelled Lugdunum to mourn so miserably, and with whom peace has now been arranged after hostages were given, was not a foreign soldier, if we believe the most learned Sirmond, but a garrison soldier imposed upon the people of Lugdunum to keep them in their allegiance. Sigonius, however, in *On the Western Empire*, book XIV, on the Goths who had occupied Lugdunum, interprets this passage of Sidonius in that sense. I too entirely agree with him. For whoever reads Idatius attentively will be unable not to understand that Theodoric, as soon as he learned through Hesychius the tribune that Avitus had been deposed, turned against the Romans the war he had undertaken against the Sueves. In Baetica he conducted it through legates, but in Gallaecia in person. Idatius himself relates that Theodoric hastened to leave Spain after Easter of the year [Col. 0809D] 457.

2. Moreover, it is highly probable that the Gauls who had been responsible for Avitus’s assumption of the imperial power bore his deposition with resentment, and that Sidonius, Avitus’s son-in-law, together with others, especially the Avernians, negotiated with Theodoric so that he might declare war against Ricimer and the emperor Majorian whom Ricimer had created, and avenge the injury inflicted upon Avitus, whom the Gauls and Goths had jointly made emperor. Sidonius plainly uses there the terms not “garrison” but “enemy,” and not “rebellion” but “war”; and in his preface he admits that he had taken part in it, saying:

> As for you, Flaccus, who followed the battle-lines of Brutus and Cassius,  
> the author of the poem was also the author of your pardon;  
> so you, victorious, ordered me, lately falling beneath  
> a different Mars, to remain calm in spirit.

Sirmond himself, in his note on book VII, letter 13, of the same Sidonius, had observed that at this time the Goths attacked Arles and were struck down and put to flight by Aegidius the count, through God’s aid and the prayers of Saint Martin, according to Paulinus. [Col. 0810A] I shall give the poems of Paulinus in note 93; they will shed new light on these matters. Finally, in this war, which was fought toward the end of the year 459, the Goths, after suffering defeat, eventually made peace with Majorian. Suniericus and Nepotianus arranged for this to be announced to the Gallaecians, as Idatius relates under the same year, 459. Majorian was then present in Gaul and, at Arles on 17 May, issued Novels concerning adultery.

## Note LXXXVIII, p. 107

Since Isidore, in his *History of the Sueves*, reports in almost exactly the same words as Idatius the accession of Maldra to the kingship and his departure from life, and assigns his death to Hispanic Era 498, it can be gathered with sufficient certainty that the numbers of the Chronicle had not yet been corrupted in this section in Isidore’s time. [244] Wherever Idatius recorded Maldra’s death, those numbers yielded the year 460 of the common era, to which the Hispanic Era corresponds.

Furthermore, since Isidore says that Maldra was murdered by his own people in the third year of his reign—disregarding the few days by which he reigned beyond it—it is entirely clear that, from the section “The Sueve” where the beginning of his reign is recorded to the section “Maldras” at the end, he found only three Julian years entered by Idatius. Yet he would have found not merely three but four if the corresponding civil-year number were increased at the section “Theodoric”; for the numerical signs are multiplied five times from one place to another. Therefore the sign I printed opposite the section “Theodoric” designates the first year of Majorian and Leo, not a civil year.

## Note LXXXIX, p. 111

Petavius writes concerning this lunar eclipse in *Rationarium temporum*, part II, book IV, chapter 13:

> At the beginning of this year 462, on the sixth day of the week—that is, shortly after midnight on the second day of March—the moon was obscured to the extent of three-quarters.

It therefore cannot be doubted that the lunar eclipse which Idatius now records was assigned by him to that year of Abraham and Leo which corresponds to the year 462 of the Dionysian Era; this is also clearly demonstrated by the Hispanic Era 500 entered there. And although that date was not written by Idatius himself, it was certainly entered by the ancient writer who, in this place in Idatius, numbered that year of Christ.

The other *Short Chronicle* mentions one of these prodigies, saying:

> In the district of Braga the portent of two newborn children was seen; that is, two infants joined together, their flesh solidified into one another.

Thus we learn from the fragments of *Hispania Illustrata*, although there *albescente* is read instead of *infantes*.

## Note XC, p. 111

1. I supplied a correction in the scholium for the twofold corruption affecting the section “Antioch.” First, I stated that the reading should be *Antioch of Greater Syria*, not *Antioch the Greater of Isauria*, as the printed books have it; for in Isauria there is neither a greater nor a lesser Antioch. The phrase “of Greater Syria,” however, occurs on a Tarraconensian inscription in Gruter, p. 1091. Nor is it surprising that a copyist changed *maioris Syriae* into *maior Isauriae*: from the first word *maioris* he carried the final two letters *is* over to the following *Syriae*, producing the form *Issyriae*, which was later changed into *Isauriae*.

Second, where the printed books have *eum*, I noted that *ea* should be read, so that it refers to the salutary admonitions mentioned above. Otherwise neither the sense nor the grammar is coherent.

2. Baronius, who describes this disaster at Antioch from Evagrius, asserts under the year 458, no. 27, that the Antiochenes suffered it because of the heresies they supported. But in the *Life of Saint Simeon Stylites* (5 January, in Bollandus), the Antiochenes are said at that time to have been especially reproved by that most holy man for luxury, intemperance, and other vices of that kind. It is not only the crime of heresy, but also countless other offenses, that provoke heavenly wrath and bring God’s vengeance upon human beings.

3. As for the time when the earthquake at Antioch occurred, it must be admitted that Idatius sometimes had insufficient knowledge of affairs in the East, especially matters not connected with public affairs; we have already seen this above, and Idatius himself occasionally acknowledged it. Another example now presents itself in this earthquake, for it is more certain that it occurred in the year 458 than in 462, to which Idatius assigns it.

Idatius could, however, have been misled by Eastern writers. One of them wrote—and others may have written it before Evagrius—that this earthquake occurred 347 years after another earthquake which took place in the time of Trajan. That earlier earthquake is assigned by Eusebius to Abraham’s year 2130. If, therefore, you add 348 years to that figure—namely, the 347 years which, according to Evagrius, had already elapsed, together with the additional year then in progress when this later earthquake occurred—you will arrive at Abraham’s year 2478. It was precisely this year that Idatius was reckoning when he mentioned the earthquake.

If you wish, read the most learned Pagius, under the year 458, no. 6, where he detects and refutes more than one error of Evagrius on this subject. [246]

## Note XCI, p. 111

1. Pagius, under the year 457, no. 14, citing the testimony of Theophanes, asserts that the empress Eudoxia arrived from Africa in the East with her daughter Placidia in that same year, 457. But I am more inclined to agree with Idatius, who assigns Eudoxia’s departure from Africa to the year 462, than with Theophanes. My first reason is that in the *Life of Saint Daniel the Stylite*, 11 December, in Surius, no. 22, we read of the same empress:

> When fame was proclaiming the holy man everywhere, the empress Eudoxia came to him—he who was living upon the column—she who had recently been rescued from Africa, and so forth.

But it is established that Daniel ascended the column after the death of Simeon, who died on Good Friday, or, as Pagius more plausibly maintains, on the Kalends of September in the year 440. How, then, could fame have proclaimed Daniel everywhere before the year 462? And if this could not in fact have happened, nor Eudoxia have come to Daniel before that year, how can she be called “recently rescued from Africa,” if she had come from Africa to the East five years earlier, namely in 457, as Pagius holds?

2. Furthermore, Eudocia, the mother of this Eudoxia, died on 20 October in the year 460. This is stated in the *Life of Saint Euthymius*, according to Pagius under that year, no. 7, although in Bollandus (20 January) the date of Eudocia’s death is not given. It is unbelievable that Eudoxia, immediately upon arriving in the East, would not have gone to her mother if the latter were still alive. It is equally unbelievable that, if she did hasten to her mother, all the writers should have been completely silent about the meeting—especially Cyril, who, in writing the *Life of Euthymius*, did not omit mentioning that Eudocia was heartbroken when she heard of the murder of Valentinian’s son-in-law and of the captivity of her daughter and granddaughters.

Moreover, Theophanes, under the year 464 according to the Alexandrian reckoning, did not fail to report that the granddaughter Eudocia, immediately after returning from Africa, hastened to Jerusalem to venerate her grandmother’s remains. [247] For this reason, what Idatius relates seems to me more credible. He was a contemporary author, closer to Africa, and had lived with Gaiseric in Gallaecia, where he could also have seen Gaiseric’s envoys in the year 458 and could have learned with certainty from them what had occurred among the Vandals in the preceding year—especially concerning Eudoxia and her daughters, whose fate was then awaited with great concern throughout both East and West.

3. Pagius also improperly draws Priscus into support of his opinion, as though Priscus in any way indicated that Gaiseric sent Eudoxia and her daughter Placidia to the East in the year 457. Apart from the fact that Priscus’s narratives are distinguished by no chronological markers by which it can be established with certainty what he assigns to each individual year, his account of Eudoxia and her daughter being restored to freedom begins as follows:

> When Genseric had decided no longer to abide by the treaties made with Majorian, and so forth.

He then adds:

> An embassy was sent to Genseric by Ricimer, urging him not to violate the treaties.

After this he narrates Eudoxia’s and Placidia’s liberation. It follows plainly from these statements that Priscus placed their return from Africa only after peace had been concluded between Gaiseric and Majorian, and indeed after the Vandal had grown weary of that peace and, following Majorian’s murder, Severus was reigning. Consequently, according to Priscus, it can scarcely have happened that Eudoxia and Placidia were sent by Gaiseric to the East before the year 462.

## Note XCII, p. 111

There is no uniformity among the writers concerning which son of Gaiseric received in marriage Eudocia, the daughter of Eudoxia and Valentinian. Idatius names Gento; Paul the Deacon and Gottfried of Viterbo name Trasamund; Priscus, Procopius, Victor of Tunnuna, Evagrius, Saint Isidore, Theophanes, Zonaras, and others assert that Hunneric married Eudoxia.

There is no reason to discuss Trasamund, since Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book V, letter 43, and book IX, letter 1, establish that Amalafrida, the sister of Theodoric, king of Italy, had him as her husband. Of those who maintain that Eudocia was married to Hunneric, if we except Priscus—who nevertheless makes a shameful error by changing the name Eudocia into Honoria—the others wrote more than a hundred years after these events and simply repeated what one had committed to writing after another.

Moreover, Procopius, the most authoritative among these writers, seems to have been ignorant of many facts concerning Gaiseric’s sons and grandsons. He reports that Theodoric, Hunneric’s brother, died while Gaiseric was still alive and left no offspring; yet Victor, an eyewitness, makes it certain that this is entirely false.

At that time Idatius was more than sixty years old, when Eudocia was taken to Africa, and he lived for at least another fifteen years. Furthermore, since he had seen Gaiseric crossing from Gallaecia to Africa after Idatius had already become a bishop, I have little doubt that he knew virtually all the affairs of Gaiseric. Therefore, even if so many other writers relate matters differently from him, his testimony should not for that reason be disregarded.

Victor of Vitensis alone, who was present at the events of that time, could have freed us from these doubts and hesitations. Yet throughout his entire history he never once mentions Eudocia’s name. Although in book III he states that Hunneric had a son named Hilderic, he nowhere reveals from which wife he was born.

2. Apart from the authority of Idatius, the following considerations also prevent me from immediately agreeing that Eudocia was Hunneric’s wife. First, Victor’s silence itself: although he mentions her sister Placidia, he would not seem to have remained silent about Eudocia if she had been Hunneric’s wife and Hilderic’s mother. Second, nowhere is it recorded that Hunneric ever complained about Eudocia’s flight to the East.

Indeed, at the request of her sister Placidia he permitted a bishop to be ordained in the Carthaginian Church, which had been without a bishop for twenty-four years. He also preserved for Placidia the estates she possessed in Africa and allowed them to be administered by Alexander, her agent, whom the emperor Zeno had made *comes rerum privatarum*. These actions plainly show that Hunneric was not hostile in spirit toward Placidia, Eudocia, or the relatives with whom she had taken refuge. [249]

But if, through Eudocia’s flight, he had been deprived not only of his wife but also of his children, no one will believe that he would have borne so great a bereavement with equanimity. Theophanes testifies that Eudocia took her children with her and, when dying, entrusted them to the bishop of Jerusalem, in these words:

> Eudocia, having used Curcus—whose service and aid she had employed as though he were entirely faithful to her—when she fled from her husband Hunneric, and Curcus, together with the children, having been entrusted to the archbishop of Jerusalem, breathed forth her soul in peace.

To understand the words “with the children” as referring not to Curcus’s children but to Eudocia’s own, among whom Hilderic may have been included, is supported by what Procopius writes in book I of *The Vandalic War*. He says:

> Hilderic was joined to Justinian by the closest bond of friendship and hospitality, although Justinian had not yet obtained the imperial power, but was already managing it at his discretion.

3. Thus we may reasonably interpret and accept the account of Hilderic as having been brought by Eudocia with her from Africa to the East, where, after his mother’s death, he remained for a long time with his maternal aunt Placidia and his cousin Anicia Juliana, the wife of Arcobindus. The contrary account—that Hilderic was Hunneric’s son—is scarcely intelligible. For Hilderic was in Carthage when, several years after Eudocia’s flight, his father Hunneric ordered the Catholic bishops to proclaim:

> Swear whether, after the death of our lord the king, you desire his son Hilderic to be king, or whether none of you will send letters to the regions across the sea.

This is Victor’s statement in the passage cited above.

From this a new argument in favor of Idatius’s account may be drawn—not a particularly powerful one, but not wholly insignificant. To whom would the Catholic bishops write across the sea to ask help in their distress, when, the Western Empire having been abolished, barbarians held Spain, Gaul, and Italy? From the East, however, Hunneric had no need to fear that war would be waged against the son whom he and Eudocia had in common, since her relatives at Constantinople were extremely powerful and influential. Yet what Hunneric fears and dreads is precisely this: Hilderic, whom Eudocia had borne, was the son not of Hunneric but of Gento. After Gento’s death, Hilderic fled with his mother Eudocia to the East, and this placed Hunneric in fear that the East might take up arms against him on behalf of Hilderic.

For this reason he presses the bishops to promise under oath that they will not conspire with those overseas against this Hilderic of theirs.

4. Accordingly, when Victor of Vitensis begins his account of Hunneric’s cruelty after he had obtained the kingship, he writes among other things in book II:

> He began to persecute cruelly his brother Theodoric and Theodoric’s sons, as well as the sons of his brother Gento. He would have spared none of them, unless death had taken from him the fulfillment of his desire.

Again, concerning Gento’s son:

> He sent Gento’s elder son, named Godagis, into cruel exile, together with his wife and the assistance of a little servant or maidservant.

From these statements and from the other matters explained above, if conjecture is permissible in a matter so obscure, I draw four conclusions:

1. When Hunneric assumed the kingship, Gento had already died. For if he had still been alive, who could doubt that Hunneric would have persecuted the father as well as the sons?

2. Gento had married twice. By his first wife he had Godagis, who married in the year 477, and perhaps other sons; by his second wife, Eudocia, whom he received as wife in the year 462, according to Idatius, he begot Hilderic—and indeed not Hilderic alone.

3. Sixteen years after her marriage to Gento, around the year 478, Eudocia, fearing for herself and her sons because of Hunneric’s hostility toward all his kinsmen, which she saw him displaying so savagely, fled from Carthage to the East.

4. This was the reason Hunneric made no complaint about Eudocia’s flight: she was not his wife, and he did not love the sons of his brother Gento; on the contrary, he sought to drive them away, as is shown in the case of Godagis.

Nevertheless, I have no doubt that Hunneric was deeply displeased that Eudocia had taken refuge with her sons among her relatives. He could not fail to see that this exposed both himself and his son Hilderic to some danger of war. To avert that danger, he seems to have shown favor to Zeno and Placidia in the matters reported by Victor.

Finally, it is clear that Eudocia could not have escaped from Africa while her husband Gento and her father-in-law Gaiseric were alive. I therefore think that, after the deaths of both men, when she was not watched as closely as before, she was able to flee. But these are conjectures, which readers are free either to accept or reject. Let them at least not dogmatically assert that Idatius was caught in manifest falsehood when he relates that Eudocia was married to Gento.

## Note XCIII, p. 111

1. Agrippinus the count, whom Idatius relates under the year 462 to have handed Narbonne over to the Goths because of the hostility between himself and Aegidius the count and master of the soldiers, is said to have been falsely accused of treason by that same Aegidius in the *Life of Saint Lupicinus*, which the Antwerp *Acts of the Saints* present under 21 March. From it, omitting much, take the following brief extract:

> The once illustrious man Agrippinus had been brought into disrepute before the emperor by the count Aegidius, then master of the soldiers, through a cunning and malicious stratagem, on the grounds that, while shining with Roman honors, he was plainly favoring the barbarians and was secretly attempting, by covert seizure, to remove the provinces from public authority. Therefore the emperor ordered Agrippinus to be summoned to Rome, subjected without investigation or hearing to a capital sentence, and meanwhile thrown into prison. Agrippinus escaped from there to the basilica of Saint Peter by a remarkable miracle. Soon afterward he was brought before the emperor; when the suspicion had been removed, he returned to Gaul. He visited Saint Lupicinus, by whose prayers he had been rescued from such danger, and publicly gave him thanks for so great a benefit.

These events, whatever their truth may be, cannot be assigned to the year 462. Nor can Agrippinus be said to have been accused of treason by Aegidius before the emperor after Agrippinus had handed Narbonne over to the Goths. For, as the rhetorician Priscus testifies—his words will be given in the following note—Aegidius, hostile to the Romans after Majorian’s murder, withdrew himself from their authority and from that of the emperor Severus. [Col. 0814B] Having established a kind of dominion for himself in central Gaul, he was accustomed, on his own authority and under his own auspices, to wage wars and arrange all affairs.

Idatius expressly recorded this for the years 463 and 464. Therefore, if Aegidius made an accusation against Agrippinus before any emperor, that emperor was Majorian, certainly not Severus.

2. Agrippinus therefore betrayed Narbonne to the Goths two or three years after he had been accused of treason before the emperor. Even if everything else were lacking, this alone is sufficient to make us suspicious of the account cited above from the *Life of Saint Lupicinus*. For once Agrippinus is plainly held guilty of treason, who can believe that he was accused before the emperor by Aegidius through a cunning and malicious stratagem, when Idatius says that reputation commended Aegidius as a man pleasing to God through good works, and when not only Idatius but also Paulinus—who was writing the *Life of Saint Martin* at the same time—celebrates him with the highest praise, singing of him in book VI:

> A man illustrious in virtue, but still more distinguished  
> by gracious character, and great in faith, by which he shines more brightly:  
> a hostile siege, with a great army, had surrounded Aegidius,  
> with weapons set before him, enclosing the walls.

These praises of Aegidius are clear. Paulinus then proceeds to recount what was done during the siege, and, briefly indicating its end, says:

> But by the Lord’s protection thousands are overthrown and put to flight,  
> and the army that has gone out through the wide-open gates  
> restores its solid strength under the secure prince.

After the enemy had been routed and driven away, Paulinus says, the soldiers who had defended the city, concerned for the safety of Majorian—for “the secure prince” must be understood of Majorian—go out to meet him. Finding him safe and secure, they rejoice with great enthusiasm and joy.

From this it is easily understood that the war had been extremely dangerous. I have shown in note 77 that it was fought with the Goths. After this Paulinus returns to Aegidius and shows what the people thought of him, portraying everyone as fearful, sorrowful, and deeply anxious and concerned for his safety. [Col. 0814D] But it is better to hear Paulinus himself, whose words are:

> Meanwhile the neighboring region, trembling with fearful grief,  
> grew pale at the peril of so great a leader, Aegidius;  
> the anxious concern of the terrified peoples hung in suspense,  
> while each person thought himself destined to endure a similar storm,  
> and in one man tottered whatever stood upon one man.

Finally, what he had earlier attributed to God’s power and aid—the city’s liberation from its enemies—he now ascribes to the prayers of Saint Martin, saying:

> The city was freed from the siege while Martin prayed,  
> and God granted him both the people and their leader.

The city beneath whose walls the Goths were struck down in so remarkable a miracle, he says, was one that:

> subdued the rushing Rhône with a gentle bridge  
> and joined its twin banks by a connected passage.

[Col. 0815A] These words clearly identify the city of Arles, as the most learned Sirmond long ago observed in his note on book VII, letter 13, of Apollinaris Sidonius.

The historical accuracy with which Paulinus sang these events confirms what Sidonius himself wrote poetically in *Carmen* V, line 555, where he says of our Aegidius, then master of the soldiers:

> Worthy that Sulla should yield to him alone in battle,  
> Fabius in genius, Metellus in piety,  
> Appius in eloquence, Fulvius in strength, Camillus in skill.

Therefore Pagius had no reason to diminish the glory of this man or to detract from Idatius’s testimony concerning him because of the authority of the author of the *Life of Saint Lupicinus*. Apart from the fact that it is unknown who that author was and precisely when he wrote, so that he cannot be compared with contemporaries of great and certain authority—Idatius, Paulinus, and Sidonius—the little work itself is not accepted by everyone. Indeed, some have regarded it as spurious or at least interpolated. Read Papebroch, volume II of the May volume, p. 805 of the Venetian edition.

## Note XCIV, p. 112

[Col. 0815B]

After Majorian’s death, a fierce war broke out between the Romans serving under Aegidius and the Goths. Narbonne was occupied by the Goths, Agrippinus having handed it over to them, and Frederic the Goth was killed in battle by Aegidius’s forces.

Priscus mentions this war. From his *Excerpts of Embassies*, take the following words relevant to the history of this period:

> Among the Western Romans, Marcellinus’s increasing power was causing fear, lest, strengthened by such forces, he should make war upon them. For at that time their affairs were utterly disturbed in various ways: on one side the Vandals were threatening them; on the other, Aegidius, a man born in Gaul, who had accompanied Majorian in his wars, possessed great forces around him and was hostile because of the murder of the emperor Majorian. But the dispute that had arisen between him and the Goths in Gaul had diverted him from making war upon Italy. He was waging a vigorous war against them for the neighboring territory, and at the same time he performed brave deeds in battle.

From this we learn:

1. Aegidius was a Gaul by origin.

2. Having been deeply angered by the death of Majorian, an excellent ruler, Aegidius was therefore vehemently hostile to the Romans and retained under his authority, so far as can be inferred from the monuments of that period, the Gallic armies and provinces—Lugdunensis, Senonia, Belgica Secunda, and part of some neighboring provinces.

The Frankish annals, moreover, derived from Gregory of Tours, frequently call him king and affirm that the Franks, having rejected and expelled their gentile king Childeric, submitted themselves to Aegidius. Calmet unjustly attempted to cast doubt upon this in his *Chronicle*.

3. Priscus teaches us that Aegidius fought a war with the Goths, and a prolonged one at that. If this is compared with what Idatius relates, nothing can appear more probable than that Agrippinus, driven by envy, handed Narbonne over to the Goths, incited them against Aegidius, and provoked them to declare war upon him.

These facts in turn render highly suspect the story of Agrippinus’s miraculous rescue by Saint Lupicinus, discussed above. Meanwhile, reader, observe how wretchedly the Western Empire was being torn apart on every side, while the emperors bore only the shadowy appearance of authority and Ricimer drew everything into his own hands. Thus in Gaul alone Aegidius, Agrippinus, and Arvandus were stirred up, each by different methods, to obtain some share of dominion.

## Note XCV, p. 113

I showed in the scholium that the sign VIII should be placed before the following words of the Chronicle: “Nepotianus departs from life,” as the sign of Leo’s eighth year. But I have been unable to understand by what reasoning Cardinal Norisius retained there the sign of Leo’s seventh year—especially since the evidence he himself derives from Idatius so clearly exposes a copyist’s error that nothing more decisive could be produced in confirmation of the correction I have now adopted.

Here are the words of that most eminent man, from *Historia Pelagiana*, book II, chapter 3:

> Idatius illustrates the period of Aegidius and Agrippinus with several chronological signs. He states that the year in which Agrippinus betrayed Narbonne to the Goths was Leo’s sixth year, Hispanic Era 500, in which year, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, the moon was eclipsed after sunset on the sixth day of the week.

Thus, Norisius admits, Idatius assigned Leo’s sixth year to the year 462 of the common era. He then adds:

> Marius of Avenches writes: “In the consulship of Basiliscus and Vivianus a battle was fought between Aegidius and the Goths,” and so forth. It was the year 463 and therefore Leo’s seventh year.

The same most learned man continues:

> Idatius, a writer of that period, states that Aegidius died in the following year, namely 464, and demonstrates the same year by notable chronological signs: it was Leo’s seventh year, when, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, the sun was eclipsed from the third hour to the sixth hour.

Indeed, in the year 464, Leo’s seventh year, on 20 July, and so forth.

Did Idatius demonstrate the year 464 by that chronological sign because it was Leo’s seventh year? If, in Hispanic Era 500—that is, in the year 462—on the sixth day before the Nones of March, he reckoned Leo’s sixth year, then after two years and nearly five months had elapsed from the lunar eclipse that occurred on the sixth day before the Nones of March in that year 462 to 21 July of the year 464, when that solar eclipse occurred, Idatius, unless he was completely blind, ought to have reckoned Leo’s eighth year.

“But,” you will say, “the Chronicle that Norisius had before his eyes displayed the seventh year in that place.” So it did. Yet who would not be astonished that so great a chronologist and critic failed to notice that the seventh year of Leo had been written there by a copyist, not by Idatius, in place of the eighth year?

We can see that such a thing was possible. Let us therefore acknowledge the copyist’s error and, with Idatius himself as our guide, restore Leo’s eighth year at the section “Nepotianus departs.”

## Note XCVI, p. 115

In the preliminary dissertation, no. 30, I stated from Isidore’s words that, from Leo’s eighth year to the end of the Chronicle, the signs had been omitted which would have arranged and divided into annals the events of at least five years through which Idatius continued his reckoning. Consequently, the task was left to us of assigning, in their proper places, the signs of Leo’s ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth years.

[Col. 0816C] Since the three years of Anthemius—his first, second, and third—coincided with Leo’s eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth years, and since these years of Anthemius had already been marked in the Chronicle, whether by Idatius himself or by someone else, we shall compare Leo’s twelfth and thirteenth years in full with Anthemius’s second and third, and shall place the eleventh shortly before Anthemius’s first. For Idatius’s own narrative establishes that, while the year 467 was already passing—a year that was Leo’s eleventh—Anthemius began the first year of his reign.

Accordingly, once the sign of Leo’s eighth year, which had been displaced, has been restored to its proper place, Leo’s ninth year and Severus’s fourth year, which corresponded to the year 465 of the common era, will nowhere be more suitably entered than at the section “Aegidius dies.” For it is perfectly clear that the embassies Idatius mentions under the sections “The Legates: Remismundus” and “The Legates” belong to different years. Since the first embassies, under “The Legates: Remismundus,” refer to Leo’s eighth year, Severus’s third year, and the common year 464, there can be no doubt that Idatius assigned the later embassies to Leo’s ninth year, Severus’s fourth year, and the common year 465.

If you ask why I have placed these signs under “Aegidius dies” rather than under either of the following two sections, I frankly admit that the argument just given proves only that the section “The Legates” should be written under these signs. Nevertheless, since the *Verdun Chronicle* assigns Aegidius’s death to the year 466 from the Incarnation, it seemed more probable to me that he died after the year 464 of Christ.

Therefore, at “Aegidius dies,” where Idatius narrates his death, I have placed the signs IX and IV, signifying Leo’s ninth year and Severus’s fourth year, because that year was the year 465 of the common era. [257]

## Note XCVII, p. 115

1. We have already seen what the *Verdun Chronicle* relates concerning the year of Aegidius’s death. It then adds that he was killed by Childeric, the son of Merovech, who invaded his kingdom.

Idatius, by contrast, expressly states that after Aegidius’s death the Goths invaded that part of Gaul which he had defended, without making any mention of the Franks:

> At the same time, when Severus died, an interregnum followed, together with immense disorder in public affairs. These circumstances emboldened Arvandus, prefect of the Gauls, to lay waste to the province miserably and to plot some hostile action against the commonwealth. As witnesses to this crime, the provincials produced letters dictated by Arvandus and sent to the king of the Goths. In them he advised that no treaty should be made with the Greek emperor—whether he meant Leo or Anthemius is uncertain—urged that the Britons settled beyond the Loire should be attacked, and maintained that Gaul ought to be divided with the Burgundians according to the law of nations.

This is Sidonius, book I, letter 7, describing the trial by which Arvandus was condemned for treason in the second year afterward. Since we see that Arvandus makes no mention of the Franks—neither among those against whom the Goths ought to fight nor among those with whom they ought to divide Gaul—we shall reasonably conclude that the power of the Franks in Gaul was then either nonexistent or exceedingly weak, and that Childeric could neither have fought Aegidius nor killed him in battle.

2. In a matter sufficiently obscure, and one clearly and distinctly transmitted by none of the writers of that age, I may therefore express in words what I regard as more probable.

Aegidius died in the year 465. After his death, those among the Franks who favored Childeric—a very small group, which Sidonius for that reason never mentions during these years—arranged for him to be recalled from Thuringia. Thus Childeric returned to Gaul around the year 466, eight years after he had been rejected by his own Franks and Aegidius had been called king in his place by those same Franks, as Gregory of Tours testifies in book II, chapter 12. In the following years he waged war against Syagrius, the son of Aegidius, and against others.

Certainly no one can extract anything more about his wars from the cited passage of Gregory of Tours. For when Gregory says that, while Aegidius and Childeric were reigning, Basina left her husband and came to Childeric, it is not necessary to understand this as meaning that Childeric was reigning in central Gaul. We may instead understand it of Childeric conducting war on the Rhine and at Trier, when, as Rorico relates in book I, he occupied Cologne. The author of the *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 8, also mentions that war and further notes that Aegidius died at that time.

But that Childeric had not yet firmly established his kingdom or put down roots in central Gaul is shown by what Sidonius recorded in book VIII, chapter 3, concerning Euric, king of the Goths, who much later granted peace to the Franks at the Vahalis.

3. I stated that Arvandus’s trial took place in the year 467—at the end of that year, to be precise—because it is almost certainly clear from the same letter 7 of book I of Sidonius, cited above, that the trial took place while Sidonius had not yet obtained the prefecture of the City. Otherwise Arvandus would not have reproached him for being unworthy of a prefect’s father, as Sidonius says he did there; rather, he would have accused him of being unworthy of the prefecture. Sidonius administered that office in the year 468.

I also stated that Childeric returned to Gaul in the year 466. Pagius asserts under the year 464, no. 6, that he returned in that year. But this contradicts Gregory of Tours in the passage cited, where he says that Childeric was summoned from Thuringia when Aegidius had been reigning for eight years.

Since Aegidius began to rise to prominence under the emperor Majorian and could not have reigned among the Franks before the year 458—as Gregory of Tours says— it follows that the eighth year of Aegidius’s reign began in the year of Christ 465 and ended in the year 466.

## Note XCVIII, p. 116
Concerning the death of the Emperor Severus, Count Marcellinus, under the consulship of Hermenericus and Basiliscus, who gave their names to the Dionysian year 455, says: “Severus, who seized the leadership of the West, died at Rome.” The Anonymous writer cited by Sirmond in the second poem of Sidonius, verse 317, says: “Severus ruled at Rome for four years and died there while living devoutly.” Finally, the Cuspinian Anonymous, under the same year, says: “The Emperor Severus died at Rome, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.” Yet among the Novels there is a constitution of Severus [Col. 0818A] said to have been issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, under the same consuls. Thus you have the year, day, and place of Severus’s death. As for the poison added by Cassiodorus, I do not believe it, since the three writers just cited, together with Hydatius, indicate that he died a natural death.

Note XCIX, p. 117.

Anthemius Augustus’s father was Procopius, whom Sidonius praises superbly in Poem II, beginning at verse 68, saying:

> You shine through your father Procopius, whose ancient lineage  
> brought forth an Augustus from his forefathers; to call him by a worthy name  
> is beyond the power of speech.

Read the remainder in Sidonius and in Sirmond’s notes on that passage, if you wish. Hydatius therefore rightly commends Anthemius as the son of such a distinguished father. But who could persuade himself that he intended to commend him on account of a brother, whom Procopius is nowhere even said to have had as a namesake?

Note C, p. 117.

If Hydatius himself appended this note I to the section “Expedition to Africa”—the note that he habitually entered everywhere after announcing the accession of a new emperor—it must certainly not be understood as indicating a new civil year, but rather the first year of Anthemius’s reign; otherwise Hydatius would have assigned his inauguration to a year different from that in which he came to Italy. Yet we cannot believe this of so great a man, who seems to have written down day by day the events taking place at this time (for he died shortly afterward). Therefore that note I, appended to the section “Expedition to Africa,” adds nothing to the Olympiadic or Abrahamic years, just as a similar note entered at the beginning of the reigns of Honorius, Avitus, and Majorian produced no increase in the civil years of the Chronicle.

Thus, in contrast with the section “Concerning Constantinople,” where he began his account of the events that took place in the year 467, Hydatius assigns the eleventh year of Leo; then, after announcing Anthemius’s inauguration, which was celebrated in the same year [Col. 0818C], in April or August, he assigns his first year to the section “Expedition to Africa,” without wishing to multiply the chronological years by adding an Olympiad of five years. For both the inauguration of Anthemius and everything else recorded in the Chronicle down to the section “Conimbriga at Peace” belong to the same year 467, as is made perfectly clear by the following Olympiad 312 in the section “Envoys concerning the Gothic War.”

Note CI, p. 117.

Unless a double expedition to Africa was undertaken, both naval—one in the year 467 and the other in 468—which I do not believe, Hydatius mentioned it there prematurely. For it is most certainly established from Marcellinus’s Chronicle and from Sidonius, whose words I shall soon quote, that the fleet prepared during this period through the combined forces of both Empires against the Vandals did not set out for Africa until the year 468, under the prefect Basiliscus.

Nevertheless, since preparations and fitting-out began in 467, and it was commonly announced in every direction that the fleet would extend its voyage to Africa in that same year—although this did not happen, either because of the obstinacy of contrary winds or, as I think more likely, because not everything had been arranged and prepared in time—Hydatius, or whoever entered the chronological figures in this final part of the Chronicle, attached the expedition to the first year of Anthemius, Dionysian year 467.

As for what the recent writer of Ecclesiastical History, Book XXXV, no. 12, relates—that Ricimer equipped this fleet in 466, while the interregnum following Severus’s death continued in the West—I consider it to have been stated without any ancient witness. The expedition to Africa, therefore, was carried out in the year 468 with a huge force of soldiers and ships. Sidonius, in the panegyric delivered for Anthemius in that same year, on the Kalends of January, says of this expedition at verse 540:

> Yet, O prince, what fleet and weapons  
> are now being mustered for you; how great things you undertake, how in so short a time  
> [Col. 0819A]

These words clearly demonstrate that, from the time he came to the West in the preceding year, Anthemius had directed all his concerns toward preparing the war against the Vandals. That it was to be undertaken in the same year was feared by Gaiseric in Africa and believed throughout Europe, as the Chronicle indicates in the section “The Goths, who [went] against the Vandals.”

Note CII, p. 118.

1. Isidore, in his History of the Goths, assigns the death of Theodoric and Euric’s accession to the eighth year of Leo. But since he connects these events there with the Spanish Era 504, he is plainly writing contradictory things; for Era 504 coincides with Leo’s tenth year and with the year of Christ 466. We have Isidore himself as a witness to this in his Chronicle, where he connects the beginning of Leo’s reign with the year of the world 5670, to which Era 495 is linked. But from that Era to 504, if you count both terminal years in the total, you will find not merely eight years but exactly ten.

Moreover, in the History of the Goths itself, Isidore had shortly before written that Theodoric reigned for thirteen years and had linked the beginning of his reign to Era 471. These statements certainly cannot both be true if Theodoric was killed in Leo’s eighth year. For if you add XIII to CCCCXCI, you obtain DIV. This Era refers to Dionysian year 466 and to Leo’s tenth year, as stated above.

When Isidore says that Euric succeeded Theodoric in Leo’s eighth year, either a copyist corrupted the text, or Isidore himself happened upon a copy of Hydatius that was either defective or lacked chronological notes. Hence everything that he took from the point where he found the note for Leo’s seventh year through the end of the Chronicle was assigned by him to Leo’s eighth year.

2. In any case, Isidore will not agree with Hydatius even if he assigns Theodoric’s death and Euric’s accession to Leo’s tenth year and Spanish Era 504. For Hydatius connects both events with the year in which Anthemius Augustus was proclaimed, as is evident from the Chronicle itself. Anthemius, however, entered upon the Empire in Leo’s eleventh year, the year of Christ 467, Spanish Era 505.

Marius of Avenches agrees with Hydatius. Although he is a source of little value for Welser, he has Hydatius as a corroborating witness—a contemporary writer and almost an eyewitness of these events—and the testimony of both is therefore not without considerable weight. Accordingly, since Thorismund was killed in 452 and Theodoric reigned from that same year until 467, it must be said that he held the kingdom for fourteen years and more, not merely thirteen, as almost everyone counts; and that Euric seized the kingdom in that same year, 467.

The exceptionally diligent Morales clearly perceived these facts concerning the end of Theodoric’s reign and the beginning of Euric’s, and assigned them to this year. But both he and Mariana, since they had never seen an unabridged Hydatius, began Theodoric’s reign with Isidore’s year 454. Later writers followed them, and from this arose the error of those who allot only twelve years of reign to Theodoric. Finally, Sidonius composed an extensive eulogy of Theodoric in Book I, Letter 2, where he praises superbly his virtues, worthy of any great king.

263 Note CIII, p. 121.

1. Isidore lists Euric’s wars in the following order in his History of the Goths [Col. 0819D]:

> He ravages the regions of Lusitania with a great assault. Then, having sent an army, he captures Pamplona and Caesaraugusta. He also brings Upper Spain under his power. He overthrows by an invasion of his army the nobility of the province of Tarraconensis, which had resisted him. Returning to Gaul, he gained the city of Arles and Massilia by war and added both to his kingdom. One day, after the Goths had assembled for a conference, etc., as I have presented in the scholium.

In fact, since Euric was eager to dominate the whole of Spain that obeyed the Romans, after learning that the Romans had been defeated by Gaiseric in Africa in 468, he moved his arms into Spain in the following year, 469. He began the war from Lusitania, into whose territory the Goths had set foot from the year 456 and where, as I suppose, they had established a military garrison. He first sent a force of his men against Emerita, as Hydatius relates.

There, when the Goths learned that Olisipo—for this city’s name must be written thus, since it is consistently engraved in this form on stones, not *Ulissipo*, whatever Ortelius may say, misled by Clusius—had been handed over by Lusidius to the Suebi, whom they did not wish to extend their rule beyond Gallaecia, they attacked those Suebi and the Lusitanians subject to them, stormed their cities, and plundered them.

Soon, turning their arms southward and southeastward, they subjected almost the whole of Spain to themselves, nearly obliterated the Roman name and overthrew Roman rule there. But more on this later.

The Gallic war followed this Spanish war; in it Euric added Arles and Massilia to his kingdom around the year 473, after the Emperors Anthemius and Olybrius had died. Thus we learn from Jordanes, who writes in his *Getica*, no. 75:

> Euric, king of the Visigoths, seeing the frequent changes of Roman emperors, attempted to occupy Gaul by his own right.

And in no. 76:

> Euric occupied Arverna, a city of Gaul, after the Emperor Anthemius had already died.

He occupied it, to be sure, not by force, but because the Emperor Nepos ceded it to him. Sidonius has more on these matters, as does Sirmond in his notes on his first letter, Book III.

2. Leaving aside the other matters relevant to our subject [Col. 0820B] 264, two points are certain:

First, Hydatius brought his Chronicle to an end in the year 469, since he mentions no war of Euric’s except the one he waged in Lusitania, which, in accordance with what was said in the scholium, cannot be postponed beyond that year.

Second, that portent concerning the Goths’ weapons being changed into various colors occurred in the year 468, to which Hydatius attaches it, and therefore several years before Euric carried arms across the Rhône and occupied Arles.

Note CIV, p. 121.

The Cuspinian Anonymous, under the year 468, says: “Marcellinus was killed in Sicily in the month of August.” Cassiodorus agrees with the Anonymous writer concerning the year and place of the murder. Count Marcellinus, in his Chronicle, has the following under the same year:

> Marcellinus, patrician of the West and also a pagan, while bringing aid and assistance to the Romans fighting against the Vandals near Carthage, was treacherously stabbed by those for whom he had openly come to fight.

Here he indicates that Marcellinus was killed not in Sicily but in Africa. Yet it is preferable to believe the contemporary anonymous writer and Cassiodorus rather than Marcellinus. Damascius, in Photius, *Bibliotheca*, Codex 262, p. 370, relates that Gaiseric, on hearing of Marcellinus’s murder, said: “The Romans have cut off the right hand with the left.”

Note CV, p. 121.

The Emperor Anthemius, according to Ennodius in his *Life of Epiphanius, Bishop of Ticinum*, said:

> Which of the emperors of old ever did this: that, among the gifts which it was necessary to give to the fur-clad Geta [Ricimer] for the sake of public peace, a daughter should be included?

Anthemius therefore unwillingly gave his daughter in marriage to Ricimer. But the marriage took place at the end of the year 467, not in 469, when Hydatius mentions it, as is clearly inferred from Sidonius, Book I, Letter 5, and Poem II, verse 543.

The matter of the patriciate also raises a doubt. The frequently cited Anonymous writer, under the consulship of Constantine and Rufus—that is, in the year 457 of the Dionysian Era—writes:

> Under these consuls [Col. 0820D] Ricimer, master of the soldiers, was made patrician on the day before the Kalends of March.

Therefore Ricimer had been honored with the dignity of patrician before Anthemius. Although this is true, Ricimer could have sought new documents confirming his patriciate for two reasons. He had received the earlier documents during the interregnum, when affairs were in extreme disorder, or had prepared them for himself; and afterward, because of the disgraceful accusations he brought against Majorian and Severus, he might have appeared to have forfeited that honor.

Moreover, since a patrician was chosen as the father of the emperor according to Book I, title XII, of the *Institutes*, Ricimer thought it more reverent that the title of his patriciate should be conferred by Anthemius himself. For the man whom the emperor himself had chosen as his patrician was regarded as his particular patrician. This is indicated by the Cuspinian Anonymous, who, under the consulship of John and Varane, calls Messianus “the patrician of Avitus.”

Note CVI, p. 122.

1. Marcellinus, in his Chronicle, under the consulship of Leo IV [Col. 0821A] and Probianus, in the year of the common era 471, records the following concerning Aspar and his sons:

> Aspar, first among the patricians, together with his sons Ardabur and Patriciolus—the former once a patrician, the latter a Caesar and called the son-in-law of the Emperor Leo—an Arian with his Arian offspring, was wounded by the swords of eunuchs in the palace and died.

Marcellinus relates this about Aspar and his sons briefly, but more clearly and even more accurately than Hydatius, or whoever enlarged Hydatius’s Chronicle with this addition. Candidus, however, in Photius, *Bibliotheca*, Codex LXXIX, writes that Patriciolus the Caesar escaped alive despite the wound.

Cassiodorus assigns the same event to the same year as Marcellinus, and it must have occurred toward the end of that year, since Theophanes refers it to the Alexandrian year of the Incarnation 464, which began on the Kalends of September in Dionysian year 471.

2. Hydatius, therefore, could scarcely, if at all, have learned in Gallaecia of the fate of Aspar and his sons before the year 472. Consequently, if he himself wrote this passage concerning Aspar, it follows that he did not live beyond that year. But if these words were not written by Hydatius and were appended to the Chronicle by someone else, to which year, and to whose pen, shall we assign the other material that follows?

My own judgment is that Hydatius wrote everything, and that all of it belongs to the year 469 except what is related here concerning Aspar and his son [Col. 0821B] 266. For Hydatius did not receive this information from the envoys whom he had mentioned shortly before; rather, it was reported several years after their return and added to the Chronicle.

Otherwise, if the envoys reported to Hydatius what happened in the year 471, why did they announce nothing about the outcome of the expedition to Africa, but only the military preparations and the fleet sent against the Vandals? Who could believe that Hydatius knew the end of that war and passed over it in silence?

Furthermore, it is even less credible that the envoys remained with the emperor from the year 467, when Anthemius gave his daughter in marriage to Ricimer, until the end of 471, when punishment was inflicted on Aspar and his sons. Thus, after it had been announced that the fleet had set sail toward Africa, the envoys left Rome and reached Gallaecia either at the end of 468 or at the beginning of 469. There they reported the matters that Hydatius inserted into the Chronicle, expressing from the beginning of the section “The Envoys Who Went to the Emperor” up to the point at which Patricius was made.

The remainder, through the end of the same section, was, as I think, first written in the margin either by Hydatius or by someone else, and afterward transferred into the interior of the Chronicle by some copyist, together with the material that Hydatius had certainly written there—not because everything belonged to the year 469, but because, as he himself says, it was then reported by the envoys. It was transferred in the same manner as the rest.

I have interpreted these matters on the authority of Marcellinus, Cassiodorus, and Theophanes. If anyone nevertheless prefers to trust the Alexandrian Chronicle, he will say that Hydatius could quite well have heard in 469 what he relates about Aspar and his son, since that Chronicle, under the consulship of John and Pusaeus, says that the event occurred in 467.

3. Theophanes confirms that the addition concerning Aspar and his sons—namely, that action was taken against them because they were found to favor the Vandals—was made for this reason. He says:

> Aspar and Ardaburius, followers of Arius, promised that they would hand over the Empire to Basiliscus, the commander and prefect of that African expedition, provided that he would betray the fleet and the entire army to Gaiseric, who likewise followed Arian opinions. For this reason, they say, Basiliscus was inclined to betray the army.

[Col. 0821]

TWO DISSERTATIONS ON TWO PASSAGES OF THE CHRONICLE THAT REQUIRE ANNOTATION.

FIRST DISSERTATION [Note: [Col. 0821D] In the Garzoni Codex this dissertation is entitled the second, and the following one, concerning the beginning of the Spanish Era, is called the third; for the preceding dissertation on the life and writings of Hydatius is numbered first. The author had combined the second and third into a single dissertation, but because of the difference in subject they were made into two. Other dissertations, on the Priscillianists, the Goths, and so forth, are lacking, since the author was prevented by death from completing them.] ON THE SEVENTH JUBILEE FROM THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0821C] 269 1. In the margin of Hydatius’s Chronicle, under the fourth year of Theodosius the Great, which coincides with the Dionysian year 382, the following is written:

> 420. The seventh jubilee from the time when the Lord ascended.

If these words had been written by Hydatius, he would certainly have agreed both with Dionysius concerning the year of Christ’s death and with most of the writers of this period concerning the beginning of the Spanish Era, which is expressed by that number 420. For, according to Dionysius, from Christ’s death or Ascension—if he suffered at the beginning of his thirty-third year of life—to the fourth year of Theodosius, 350 years, or seven times fifty, are counted, by which one arrives at the seventh jubilee. In that same year the Spanish Era must be reckoned as 420, if, as is commonly believed, it began in the year 38 before the Dionysian Nativity of Christ.

But I judge quite differently and have always believed that these words were inserted into the Chronicle after Hydatius’s time [Col. 0821D]. The arguments that led me to this opinion I have decided to examine in this dissertation. First I shall discuss the jubilee and then the Spanish Era.

That Hydatius marked neither his Chronicle [Col. 0822C] nor his Fasti with this Era, unless I am greatly mistaken, I demonstrated sufficiently in the preceding dissertation, no. 9. But now I shall speak chiefly about its beginning—a matter whose obscurity cannot be overstated, and concerning which the deductions drawn from the statements of ancient writers are mutually contradictory. Guided by their authority, later writers persuaded themselves that its beginning should be assigned to the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus, to Julian year 4676, and to the year of the world 5163 according to Eusebius—that is, to the year 38 before the Dionysian Nativity of Christ.

In any case, whatever I say is not intended to discourage the customary computation of the Era, for a thoughtful and modest man may not dissent from the common opinion of writers without certain and evident arguments. Indeed, even if it were now established with certainty that the Era began either before or after the year 38 before the birth of Christ the Lord, nothing at all should be changed in the use of this epoch. The method of reckoning it that is now observed ought to be retained, since for a thousand years and more, wherever it has been used—whether in histories, councils, or other documents—it has preceded the common era by precisely thirty-eight years. Thus, unless everything is rewritten, the error cannot be corrected, if an error was admitted in such a calculation.

What I intend to demonstrate in this dissertation concerning the beginning of the Spanish Era is therefore only this: that the matter is wholly uncertain, and that neither from this passage of Hydatius nor from any monuments of antiquity has it so far been clearly established that its beginning must be assigned to the year 38 before the common era. If I can convince my readers of this, it may perhaps result in learned men of so erudite an age excavating from the ruins of antiquity some evidence by which the common opinion concerning the origin of our Era may be established more securely and firmly.

§ I. That the words “the seventh jubilee,” etc., were attached to the Chronicle is proved by the silence of the ancient writers concerning such a jubilee.

[Col. 0823B]

2. The jubilee was first instituted among the Hebrews (Leviticus 25). As Saint Gregory Nazianzen says (*Oration* 44), they honor the number seven in accordance with the prescription of the Mosaic Law. This honor among them extends not only to days but also to years, and not only to weeks but also to weeks of weeks, in days as well as in years. Indeed, weeks of days produce Pentecost, while weeks of years produce the year of jubilee.

I have never read that this kind of jubilee, counted every fiftieth year from the Ascension of Christ the Lord into heaven, was ever solemnly established or celebrated by any special rite in the Church [Col. 0823C]. Isidore of Seville (*Etymologies*, Book V, chapter 31) indicates plainly enough that it was not in use. After mentioning the jubilee celebrated among the Hebrews every fiftieth year, he says: “We too celebrate this number in the days of Pentecost after the Lord’s resurrection”; but he is entirely silent concerning a jubilee of every fiftieth year from Christ’s Ascension, or of every hundredth year.

3. Furthermore, if such a jubilee had been instituted in the Church before the time of Hydatius, there would not now be so many disputes and so many opinions about the year of the world in which Christ the Lord died. For by this public and solemn institution it would have been established for everyone that Christ suffered under the consulship of Persicus and Vitellius, from whose consulship to the fourth year of Theodosius seven jubilees, or 350 years, are counted.

Nor would so many ancient writers whom I shall list below have said that Christ suffered under the two Gemini, among them Hydatius himself. I am not unaware that Venerable Bede (*The Reckoning of Time*, chapter 65) handed down to posterity the following report: that brothers who were in Rome in the year 750 according to Dionysius, on the Nativity of the Lord, saw written on the candles of Saint Martha and copied the words as follows:

> From the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ there are 668 years.

But Bede expressly testifies that this practice occurred long after the age of Hydatius, after the method of counting years from the Incarnation had been introduced by Dionysius. Consequently, it not only does not undermine our argument but strongly confirms it.

For if, from the time when the custom was introduced of announcing to the people each year which year according to Dionysius’s reckoning was then running from Christ’s death, nothing was ever disturbed in this epoch, and no one doubted whether the year to be counted then and there from Christ’s death was one year or another, then, if the custom of celebrating a jubilee every fiftieth or hundredth year from the Lord’s Ascension had prevailed from the earliest times of the Church, there would now be no disagreement among writers concerning which year should be counted today from that same Ascension.

And if in some Churches, even before the fifth century, and in Alexandria much earlier, from the time of Saint Mark—if Papebrochius’s conjecture is correct (*Chronological Essay*, p. 33, no. 11)—the people were told each year on which day Easter was to be celebrated, nevertheless the year then running from Christ’s death was not announced [Col. 0824B], as is clear from the formula by which the deacon proclaimed Easter in the Church of Milan. He said:

> Let your charity know, dearest brothers, that, with the mercy of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ granting it, we shall celebrate Easter with joy on such-and-such a day.

From this one may reasonably infer that this note concerning the seventh jubilee from the Lord’s Ascension was added to Hydatius’s Chronicle after the times of Boniface VIII and Clement VI, when, after the model of the Hebrew jubilee, a Christian jubilee was decreed to be celebrated at fixed intervals—first every hundredth year, and afterward every fiftieth year.

Unless one prefers to suppose that the note was inserted into the Chronicle after Boniface, but before Clement had reduced the jubilee to every fiftieth year. Concerning the jubilee, the quite curious book entitled *Image of the First Century of the Society of Jesus*, no less excellent than it is reviled by its opponents, records several matters in its prologue, Dissertation V.

§ II. That the same words were attached to the Chronicle is shown by Hydatius’s own Fasti.

4. Under the consulship of Augustus for the thirteenth time and Silvanus, Hydatius records the following in his Fasti:

> Under these consuls Christ was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

Silvanus was consul with Augustus two years before the Dionysian Era. Therefore, whether Hydatius followed the common opinion among writers of his age concerning the year of Christ’s death—which I scarcely doubt, as I shall say shortly—or whether, with Eusebius, whom he had before his eyes, he thought that Christ suffered in the fourth month after completing the thirty-second year of his life [Col. 0824D], it is necessary to arrive at the seventh jubilee year—or, which is the same thing, at the year 350 from his Ascension—before the fourth year of Theodosius.

For since the year of Christ’s death is the first year of the first jubilee, just as the day of his Resurrection is the first day of Pentecost, the year 350 from the Lord’s Ascension, and the seventh jubilee from it, would coincide with the consulship of Gratian for the fifth time and Theodosius, who gave their names to the common-era year 380 and to the second year of Theodosius the Great, as will become clear from counting the consuls.

5. But it is far more probable that Hydatius believed Christ died under the consulship of the two Gemini, Rubellius and Fuscus, for he explicitly records this himself in his Fasti under that consulship, saying:

> Under these consuls [Col. 0825A] Christ the Lord suffered.

Even if someone denies that these words were written by Hydatius and contends that they were inserted into his Fasti by another hand, he cannot deny that this was the opinion of almost all antiquity from the time of Tertullian onward, especially among those who wrote during Hydatius’s lifetime.

This is taught by the continuation of the Chronicle of Tiro Prosper, in Labbe’s edition, and the writers themselves plainly bear witness to it: Sulpicius Severus (*History*, Book II), Saint Augustine (*City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 54), Victor of Aquitaine (*Paschal Canon*), and the two Cuspinian Anonymous writers, one of whom was edited by the distinguished Janingus (*Acta Sanctorum*, June, vol. VI), and the other by the distinguished Schelstrat (*Appendix to the Chronological Work*).

I think Quintus Julius Hilarion and Prosper of Pithou held the same opinion. The former (*On the Weeks of Daniel*) left the following written:

> From the Passion of the Lord to the consulship of Caesar—read “Caesarius”—and Atticus, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, 369 years have passed.

The consulship of Caesarius and Atticus fell in the year 397 of the common era. If from this you subtract the nineteen years within 369 that are in excess of seven jubilees—that is, in excess of the 350 years from the Lord’s Ascension—the remainder will be 350. Therefore, according to Hilarion, the seventh jubilee from Christ’s death must be counted in that year.

Furthermore, Prosper counts 360 years from Christ’s Passion to the third consulship of Valentinian the Younger. Since that consulship coincided with the common-era year 387, if you subtract from these figures the ten years that must be removed from 360 in order to obtain 350, or seven jubilees, you return to the year 377, in which the seventh jubilee fell.

Thus, according to the calculations of Hilarion [Col. 0826A] and Prosper, who wrote somewhat earlier than Hydatius, the seventh jubilee from the Lord’s Ascension preceded the fourth year of Theodosius’s reign by four or five years, so that the first jubilee must be counted from the consulship of the two Gemini—or, according to Prosper, if no error has entered his Chronicle, from the year one year earlier.

Who, then, would sensibly affirm that Hydatius departed from the opinion of so many and such eminent men of his age, or that Hydatius himself, who wrote the consular Fasti, did not know how many years had elapsed from the consulship of the two Gemini to the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius and the fourth year of Theodosius the Great?

6. If Hydatius followed their opinion, as can scarcely be doubted, then according to him the seventh jubilee ended in May of the year 379. Since Theodosius had been proclaimed emperor on January 19 of that same year, the first year of his reign shared nearly four months with this jubilee.

From this someone might think that, when Hydatius entered those words in his Chronicle—“the seventh jubilee from the time when the Lord ascended”—he assigned them to that same year 379 in order, by this note, as though by an omen of future happiness, to mark the beginning of Theodosius’s reign. Since no other mention of such a jubilee occurs anywhere, and only Hydatius remembers it, someone might suspect that he did this in praise of Theodosius, who was then entering upon the Empire. Whoever finds this pleasing may enjoy his own judgment, as far as I am concerned.

But I think that Hydatius assigned those words neither to Theodosius’s first year nor to his fourth, and that they were attached to his Chronicle by copyists.

SECOND DISSERTATION. ON THE BEGINNING OF THE SPANISH ERA.

[Col. 0825]

§ I. How freely copyists indulged themselves in creating or revising chronological notes while transcribing ancient records. A passage of Augustine corrected.

[Col. 0825C]

1. Since the Spanish Era was never in use among foreign peoples and was never employed outside Spain by anyone for the purpose of constructing chronology, who would not be astonished at the audacity of the copyists who more than once assigned this epoch to the letters of Saint Leo the Great? They also prefixed it to most of the councils, namely the First Council of Nicaea, the Council of Sardica, the First Council of Constantinople, the Council of Chalcedon, the Fourth and Fifth Councils of Carthage, and six hundred others.

But if those who considered themselves entitled to do this in recording synods held outside Spain allowed themselves such freedom, what did they not permit themselves when transcribing Spanish councils? Therefore the argument advanced by Florius is utterly weak (*Sacred Spain*, vol. II, part II, final chapter), when, against Majansius and on the basis of the councils cited there—the Councils of Tarragona, Gerunda, and Ilerda—he attempts to demonstrate that the Spanish Era was in use in the province of Tarraconensis before the tenth century.

For the Era is expressed only in the titles of these councils, where it was not written by notaries at the time of the councils but was entered later by copyists, just as was certainly done in the ecumenical and African synods listed above. Yet we possess no codex of the councils whose having been written before the tenth century is established.

In the Third Council of Zaragoza, however, the Era may perhaps have been entered at the time when the council was held, namely in the year 691 of the common era. For the words found there—

> In the name of the Lord, here begin the acts of the synod in the city of Zaragoza, on the Kalends of November, Era 729, in the fourth year of the orthodox and most serene lord King Egica—

are not wholly unlike something written by the notary of that council.

Nevertheless, Florius had no reason to argue against Majansius with evidence that was not entirely certain or even with false evidence, since he could have drawn a most effective argument from the constitution of the Fiscal Court of Barcelona (*In the Collection of Loaysa*, p. 250), where the following is written:

> In this agreement, we who have agreed below have subscribed with our own hands. This agreement was made on the day before the Nones of November, Era 630, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord—

namely Reccared.

Concerning this Era there can be no doubt that it was used by the person who prepared that document at Barcelona. Since it was drawn up in the year 592 of the common era [Col. 0826D], it is clear that the Era was in use in the province of Tarraconensis long before the tenth century.

But let us leave these matters to the most learned Florius and Majansius [Col. 0827A]; we shall now return to the Eras recorded in the councils of Spain.

2. This, then, is my judgment concerning them. All those found in the inscriptions of most synods—such as these: the Council of Elvira, Era 362; the Council of Zaragoza, Era 418; the constitution of the council of bishops at Toledo in the time of Arcadius and Honorius, Era 438; the Council of Tarragona, Era 554; the Council of Gerunda, Era 555; and the Council of Ilerda, Era 583—are later insertions. They were entered by antiquarians or collectors of the councils themselves, not by the notaries who recorded the decrees of the Fathers and were responsible for marking them with the day and year.

Those who formerly collected or transcribed these councils, although they found no Era recorded in them, added one themselves, just as Loaysa later added it to certain synods in which the Era was missing in his day. He candidly admits this in the chronology of the councils that he prefixed to his collection.

That events occurred as I have stated is plainly demonstrated by the codices from which the councils were printed by the typographers. Sometimes all of them omit the Era; at other times each prefers an Era different from the others.

The Emilian Codex, also called the Sevillian Codex, the oldest of all, has no Era recorded in any of those councils held before the sixth century. The distinguished and most illustrious Peres testified to this in the chronology of the councils of Spain, which you will find in Loaysa’s collection and elsewhere.

Yet is it credible that the notaries forgot to record the day and year on which the synods were held? Even now, in some of these councils, there remain indications of the notaries’ diligence in this matter [Col. 0827C] 279. For in the First Council of Toledo the consulship of Stilicho is expressed; in the Council of Tarragona, the consulship of Peter and the sixth year of Theodoric; and in the Council of Gerunda, the consulship of Agapitus and the seventh year of Theodoric.

In many other cases, however, copyists cut these details out for the sake of brevity and indicated the time at which the councils were convened in a single phrase, writing: “The Council of Zaragoza, Era 418”; “The Council of Elvira, Era 362.”

But whether, when they substituted an Era for the consulship and the year of the emperor, they did so without error, or whether, on the contrary, they falsely rendered the year indicated by those notes through the Era they supplied, we cannot know at all. This could only have been determined from those same notes, but once the copyists erased them from the books, no path to discovering the truth was left to us.

### 3.

Nevertheless, the variant readings of the manuscripts, and also certain examples, do not allow us to doubt that copyists often twisted the numerical signs and the method of calculation that they found in the books they were copying according to their own judgment and understanding. One especially clear example occurs in Augustine (*City of God* XVIII.54), where, concerning the year of Christ’s death, of which we were just speaking, we read:

> “Christ died under the consulship of the two Gemini, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April”;  

and a little later:

> “The Holy Spirit was sent on the Ides of May.” [Col. 0828A]

Accordingly, when the consuls are counted, 365 years are found to have elapsed by the same Ides during the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus. This flatly contradicts Augustine’s meaning and words. For since he states in the same passage that the Lord’s death occurred under the consulship of the two Gemini—those who gave their names to the year 29 of the common era—one cannot count from that year to the consulship of Honorius IV and Eutychianus fewer than 369 years, since they held the consulship in the year 398 of the common era.

Who, then, would fail to recognize and condemn the audacity of the copyists who, in this passage of Augustine, and perhaps often elsewhere as well, dared to reshape whatever total of years had been reckoned from Christ’s birth or death, contrary to the meaning and words of the authors they were copying, according to the calculations of the Dionysian era? [Col. 0828B]

Yet even by corrupting this passage of Augustine they did not achieve their purpose. For from the year of Christ’s death—if one says that the Lord died after completing thirty-three years of life—to that consulship of Honorius, according to Dionysius, only 364 years had elapsed, not 365.
