Coquaeus, concerning the first of the Augustinian words quoted above, “The Lord Christ died under the consulship of the two Gemini,” did not hesitate to assert (*Augustine*, in the same place):

> “Augustine, perhaps without examining the consular Fasti . . . placed Christ’s Passion under the consulship of the two Gemini.”

This cannot be said, with due respect to Augustine, of at least the final words, since the holy teacher expressly said: “When the consuls are counted, the years are found.” How many? Certainly not 365, as the copyist dared to invent while attempting to twist Augustine’s chronology toward the Dionysian system, but 369—the number Augustine counted from the consulship of the Gemini to the fourth consulship of Honorius and committed to writing. [Col. 0828C]

From all this, at any rate, it is clear what we may fear from copyists when they compare our era with the Christian era—whether Dionysian, Eusebian, or any other—and add thirty-eight years to the latter in order to derive the former.

## § II. At what time, and on what occasion, public use of the era began in Spain

### 4.

Of all the monuments that bear the Spanish era, the oldest and most worthy of belief is the one that I described in the preliminary dissertation from Morales (*Book XI, chapter 31*); it is also found in Gruter, [Note: [Col. 0827D] p. 1049. See above, p. 20.] where the reader will find it. Since the era 503 is inscribed upon it, anyone who wishes to maintain that it was in public and common use among the Spaniards before the fifth century will certainly obtain no one’s assent unless he excavates older monuments and produces witnesses who may prudently be believed.

I say “in public and common use.” For there can be no doubt that it was used many years earlier by the *rationalis*, that is, in the office of the fiscal administrator, and by the imperial procurator throughout Spain, from the very beginning of the era. Otherwise, how could the era 503 have been recorded on that stone, if it had not originated and been used by some people for that many years previously? [Col. 0829A]

### 5.

Before the beginning of the era, however, the Romans who ruled the Spaniards were accustomed in public documents to designate the year in which they were drawn up by the consuls. At some point it was even established by law [Note: [Col. 0829D] Law I, *De constitutionibus principum*, in the Theodosian Code, issued to the Lusitanians; this also applies to the *Acts of the Church*, as is clear from Augustine, vol. IX of the Benedictine edition, in the *Brief Account of the Collation* of day 3, no. 27, and canon 89 of the Council of Milevis, held in 401.] that no document lacking the consul’s name should have any legal force.

Accordingly, that calculation of the era was retained in the fiscal office, among the quaestorian scribes, and in the mouths of the common people, who were compelled each year to pay the census tax assessed by the era. It did not pass into other public documents until, as the Roman Empire declined and the Goths and Suevi occupied a large part of Spain, it was no longer even possible in those regions to know who was holding the consulship at Rome. [Col. 0829B]

From that time, therefore, compelled and instructed by necessity, the Spaniards began to designate times and years by eras. At first, as usually happens, one or two followed this practice; soon it spread throughout the entire nation and into every kind of document—charters, stones, and all the rest.

Subsequently, notaries also became accustomed, especially in more solemn acts, to express the years of emperors and, during the reign of Theodoric, the consuls of the king of Italy. Examples of imperial years occur everywhere. You will find the consulship of Peter in the Council of Tarragona and the consulship of Agapitus in that of Gerunda, mentioned above, inscribed there. For when Theodoric designated consuls in the West—not only for Italy but also for Spain, which he administered on behalf of his grandson Amalaric—he ordered it to be made known who had been appointed consul by him each year. In my opinion, Theodoric was pleased that, just as formerly, so also then, the name of the consul whom he created should be inserted into official acts. [Col. 0829C]

### 6.

I therefore conclude that the era’s epoch, when it was introduced into public monuments, must be dated from approximately the time when Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, first with the consent of the emperor Avitus and then from a desire to enlarge his own kingdom, attacked Spain with a great army and occupied Gallaecia, Lusitania, and part of Baetica. From Hydatius, Isidore, and others, it is established that this occurred in the year 456.

From that time onward, everything in Spain appears to have been thrown into confusion and Roman affairs to have plunged headlong downward. Thus in Gallaecia, when Hydatius was writing the consular Fasti, he was unable to know who the consuls were after the year 464. [Col. 0829D]

According to the common opinion about the beginning of the era, that inscription at Alexandria which bears the era 503 belongs to the following year. After this, public use of the era became widespread, and funerary inscriptions frequently display it. Morales (*Book XI, chapter 41*) reports two belonging to the beginning of the sixth century; Gruter reports one of them (*p.* 1054), and many others of later date occur everywhere.

The First Council of Braga is dated to the era 598, and there can be no doubt about its inscription, since its character and wording inspire complete confidence. It reads:

> “The Synod of Braga, our Lord Jesus Christ reigning, the era 598 being current, in the third year of King Ariamir, on the Kalends of May.” [Col. 0830A]

By contrast, there can scarcely be doubt that the era 438 was added by copyists to the First Council of Toledo. Although the synod’s text contains the words “the era as above,” those words belong to the compiler who interpolated the acts of that council many years after it was held. This is established most clearly by the fact that in the same passage he mentions another council that Pope Leo ordered to be assembled from all parts of Spain in the year 447, or era 485. This is gathered from Leo’s letter (*formerly Epistle 93*) and from the Chronicle of Hydatius. [Note: [Col. 0830D] A.D. 447. See above.]

In the Second Council of Toledo, although an era is expressed at the end of the heading after Amalaric’s fifth year has been recorded, it too could have been added by a copyist. The fact that it was added is suggested by the three councils that follow it up to the First Council of Braga, which possess an era only in titles added by the editors of the collection of councils. [Col. 0830B] For this reason, the era 565 of the Second Council of Toledo has always seemed to me doubtful, indeed spurious.

Setting these matters aside, then, let us say on the basis of the more reliable monuments and arguments brought forward above that public use of the era was introduced toward the end of the fifth century and gradually spread throughout Spain.

### 7.

As for the time when the audacity of copyists attached this era to written manuscripts that originally lacked it, it is remarkable what Loaisa—a great ornament of Spain—relates, as he says, from Hincmar of Rheims. [Note: [Col. 0830D] In the notes to the Council of Elvira, section “What the Era Is.”] He brings forward Hincmar in a book on councils which he says he possessed in manuscript, claiming that our era is found there in the First Council of Constantinople and in the universal Council of Ephesus. [Col. 0830C]

But Hincmar of Rheims died in 882. The calculation of the era would therefore have had to be introduced into the monuments of peoples outside Spain almost nine hundred years earlier. I do not deny that this could have happened; but the passage produced by Loaisa proves nothing. That book cannot be by Hincmar of Rheims, since it mentions “Lord Herman,” that is, Herman the Lame, who lived approximately two centuries after Hincmar.

### 8.

These statements about the beginning and development of public use of the era seem to me closer to the truth, and I cannot agree with Florio and Majansius in everything. These highly learned men dispute the beginning of the era’s introduction into common use. Florius (*Hispania sacra*, vol. II, part I, chapter 7) indiscriminately asserts that this reckoning was introduced before the Goths, whereas Majansius says that it was introduced by the Goths. [Col. 0830D]

But one ought to distinguish two uses of the era: one public and employed everywhere, the other private, used not everywhere but only by those who collected taxes and tributes.

As for public use, I deny Florius’s assertion that it was ever employed before Spain was invaded by the Visigoth Theodoric in 456, since no indication of this exists anywhere. For the epitaph of a certain Udella, which the distinguished scholar cites (*Hispania sacra*, vol. II, part I, chapter 7, p. 123), and any other similar examples, were already shown by many learned men before me to belong in their proper place. [Col. 0831A]

It is incredible that, amid so abundant a harvest of inscriptions, which are scattered throughout books and were dedicated in Spain not only by Roman magistrates but also by municipal communities, cities, and private natives, the era should never be found before Theodoric and the year 465, if public use of it had prevailed among our people for four or more centuries before Theodoric—especially since in those same epitaphs and inscriptions the consulships were sometimes recorded even among the Spaniards, and among foreign peoples very frequently, including on funerary stones.

### 9.

Florius calls this argument weak. He contends that from the absence of monuments bearing the era before the fifth century one cannot properly infer that it was not used before that time—as though, in order to deny the existence of something, it were not enough to find no evidence of it.

Yet nothing is more frequent in Florius himself than this kind of argument. He repeatedly rejects the opinions of writers dealing with ancient matters on the ground that they lack testimony from authors of the same period. Therefore the author of the *Chronicle of Burgos*, evidently a careful writer, very correctly recorded the following 545 years ago:

> “From the time when the Goths entered Spain, the custom prevailed of reckoning times by eras.”

From that time, then, this custom became established among the Spaniards, necessity compelling them, as stated above, to take it from the speech of the common people and from the fiscal office—not, as Majansius wishes, introduced by the Goths, to whom it seems to have been neither customary nor even known while they remained in Aquitaine and beyond the Pyrenees. [Col. 0831C]

## § III. The first year, or beginning, of the era

### 10.

Before Dionysius Exiguus devised the calculation of the Christian era, we find nowhere that the beginning of the Spanish era was linked to any of the earlier epochs, whether the Olympiads, the founding of Rome, or any other.

Since, however, it is an ancient and widespread opinion among our people that it began thirty-eight years before Christ, we shall derive the beginning of the era from whatever year each writer holds to be the year of Christ’s birth, and from whatever year he likewise believes the era began. Since opinions about the year of Christ’s birth differ, opinions about the beginning of the era will likewise differ.

Therefore, in order to treat this question more clearly and efficiently, it will be worthwhile to take the chronology of some distinguished writer as an example and, according to the variation of opinions, establish different years for Christ’s birth and for the era in relation to it.

The careful and ancient author Isidore of Pax, at the end of his Chronicle (no. 80), wrote:

> “In the forty-second year of Octavian, Christ was born, according to the *Ecclesiastical History* of the lord Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, in Book I, at age 6, and now according to the Chronicle of the lord Isidore . . . all the Scriptures proclaim it.”

From this testimony, and from Orosius, Hydatius, and John of Biclaro, we can certainly conclude that our Spanish chronologists followed Eusebius of Caesarea and his method of reckoning the years of the world above all. Accordingly, nothing could now be done better or more securely than to measure the various opinions of writers about the beginning of the era against Eusebius’s calculations and compare them with his chronology.

I shall therefore show in order which of our writers assigns the beginning both of the era and of Christ’s birth to which year of the Eusebian Chronicle. I shall also add the corresponding consulships and the years of the Julian period and of Augustus, so that by means of these certain chronological markers it may be clear to readers in which year each of the five opinions that I find in the writings of the ancient Spaniards—apart from the common opinion—either does or ought to place the beginning of the era.

I shall begin with the opinion that departs least from the common and now accepted epoch of the era: the one that begins with Eusebius’s world-year 5163, Julian period 4676, year 6 of Augustus, in the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus.

The years of Augustus, however, are counted from the Kalends of January of the year in which Gaius Livius Pansa and Aulus Hirtius were designated consuls. The Eusebio-Hieronymian Chronicle designates this year—and indeed begins it on the first day of January—by assigning the first year of Augustus to world-year 5158.

I have no doubt that our chronologists followed Eusebius, except for the author of the *Chronicle of Burgos*.

### 11.

The first opinion therefore assigns Christ’s birth to Eusebian world-year 5200, one year before the Dionysian era. That era places Christ’s birth in world-year 5201, Julian period 4714, year 44 of Augustus, in the consulship of Caesar and Paulus. [Col. 0832C]

The learned Majansius, in the preface to the chronological works of the most distinguished marquis of Mondéjar, no. 53, makes Julian of Toledo the author or proponent of this first opinion. In Julian’s work *On the Six Ages of the World*, we do indeed occasionally find Christ’s birth assigned to world-year 5200. But since elsewhere in the same work it is assigned once to year 4525 and once even to year 5325, we cannot determine anything certain about Julian’s meaning from these passages, which have plainly been corrupted by copyists—especially since other, more genuine passages that I shall present below show that he held a very different opinion.

Whoever has held, or now holds, this first opinion must place the beginning of the era thirty-eight years earlier, in world-year 5162, Julian period 4675, year 5 of Augustus, in the consulship of Censorinus and Sabinus.

### 12.

The second opinion may be attributed to the earliest fathers of Spanish history: Hydatius, John of Biclaro, and in some places also Saint Isidore.

Hydatius, in the preface to his Chronicle, where it would have been especially appropriate, does not mention the era. Hence the era-notes attributed to that Chronicle and to Hydatius’s Fasti have always seemed to me, as I have said elsewhere, suspect and of very doubtful reliability.

Nevertheless, let us suppose that Hydatius says nothing at all about the era. In his Fasti he assigns Christ’s birth to the consulship of Augustus XIII and Silvanus, that is, to Eusebian world-year 5199, Julian period 4712, year 42 of Augustus. If, in order to derive our era and its birth-year, we subtract thirty-eight years, we arrive at the consulship of Calvinus and Pollio and at Eusebian world-year 5161, Julian period 4676, year 4 of Augustus. [Col. 0833A]

Similarly, John of Biclaro never uses the era. But since at the end of his Chronicle he counts the same 2,015 years as Eusebius from Abraham to Christ—concluding with this the very year of Christ’s birth, as Orosius formerly did and others later did—he assigns the beginning both of Christ’s era and of the Spanish era to the same year as Hydatius.

Finally, Isidore expressly assigns Christ’s birth in his Chronicle to the forty-second year of Augustus, together with Hydatius, John of Biclaro, and others. Nevertheless—and this must not be concealed but carefully observed in view of what we shall say below—he connects the first year of Augustus with world-year 5156. [Col. 0833B]

When Majansius happened to read this passage of Isidore, he made a gross error, writing in the preface to the chronological works of the marquis of Mondéjar that Isidore assigned Christ’s birth to world-year 5155.

If in Isidore’s calculation one seeks Christ’s birth by the years of the world—as he counts them at the end of the fifth age—one arrives at year 5197. If, however, one calculates by the years of Augustus expressed by Isidore in the same place, but counted from world-year 5158 with Eusebius rather than from world-year 5156 with Isidore, one arrives at year 5199, never at year 5155, which Majansius says Isidore affirmed.

Luke of Tuy and the author of the *Albeldensian Chronicle* adopted the same opinion as these chronologists. The latter writes of Christ’s birth:

> “The whole period from Adam to Christ amounts to 5,199 years.”

The author of the *Compostellan Annals* likewise writes:

> “In the forty-second year of Augustus’s reign, under the first era, [after] thirty-eight, Jesus was born in Bethlehem.”

The word “after” had dropped out, and the sense of the words had consequently been lost. It is now perfectly clear and expresses the writer’s meaning: he wishes Christ to have been born in era 39, which is the first era after 38. At least, this is the genuine meaning of the passage. [Col. 0833C]

### 13.

The author of the *Chronicle of Burgos*, mentioned above, after criticizing the errors and defects of other writers and explaining his own care in arranging the chronology, links the beginning of the era to the fourth year of Augustus and says:

> “Because the diligence of writers often errs in numbers, contradiction arises for readers in the succession of years. Those who wish to reconcile them encounter difficulty, because some manuscripts assign more years to emperors or kings and others fewer. I calculated the times of emperors and kings from various copies, from the beginning of the first era, by the years during which they ruled, and I adopted the eras, so that in the chronological reckoning of the emperors the calculation begins from the beginning of the fourth year of Octavian Augustus, from which the era is said to have begun, etc.”

It should be read in this way, not “from the beginning of whose,” as it is ineptly read elsewhere.

The author of that Chronicle left this passage in writing. Since he brings his work to an end in year 212, he appears to have flourished at that time. But one must observe that he reckons the years of Augustus from the death of Julius Caesar. Accordingly, his fourth year of Augustus is the third year of Augustus according to others—those who begin from the Kalends of January of Julian year 5—and coincides with the consulship of Antony and Isauricus.

Hence he links the beginning of the era sometimes to the third year of Augustus, according to the opinion of others, and sometimes to the fourth, according to his own; or rather, he counts the third year exclusively and the fourth inclusively, as is commonly said. [Col. 0834A]

This writer therefore compared, as he himself testifies, several copies of ancient manuscripts, which were either archetypes or at least more carefully corrected than those that, several centuries later, served the needs of typographical editions.

After reviewing all these materials, he discovered that the Spanish era was three years older than the common opinion holds, and he referred its beginning to the first day of January of Julian year 5, Eusebian world-year 5160, Julian period 4673, in which L. Antonius and Isauricus held the consulship. [Col. 0834B]

Saint Julian, bishop of Toledo, appears to have adhered to this third opinion when he writes in Book I of *On the Proof of the Sixth Age*:

> “Caesar Octavian reigns for fifty-six years. In his forty-first year, according to the testimony of Tertullian and Jerome, Christ the Son of God is born of the Virgin Mary.”

For it is highly probable that Julian counted the years of Augustus with Eusebius from world-year 5158.

### 14.

The fourth opinion about the beginning of the era is derived from what Saint Isidore of Seville relates in his Chronicle. There, while reporting that Christ was born in the forty-second year of Augustus, he assigns the first year of Augustus to world-year 5156, as noted above.

It follows that Christ’s birth must be placed in world-year 5197. [Col. 0834C] If we subtract thirty-eight years from this in order to return to the beginning of the era, only 5159 remains. According to this passage of Isidore, therefore, the era began in this world-year, or in Julian period 4672, during the consulship of M. Lepidus II and L. Munatius Plancus.

That this was not the opinion of Isidore of Seville alone—if indeed it was his opinion, rather than the result of corruption in his Chronicle—is indicated by another Isidore, called Isidore of Pax, in his Chronicle, no. 79, where we read:

> “When the fifth year of Julius Caesar has been completed, there are 5,154 years of the world. When the forty-two years of Octavian are added, there are, from Adam to the Nativity of Christ, 5,196 years. After subtracting the four years which, as we stated above, certain people subtract from world-year 5200, and adding to the 5,196 years mentioned above the 754 years of the Lord’s Incarnation, which are correctly reckoned in era 792, there are found to be 5,950 years, with four omitted and diminished.”

“*Oblitis*” must be read, according to Mariana’s manuscript, not “*obitis*”; it derives from *oblino*, not from *obeo*. The distinguished Florius labors greatly to disentangle these words of Isidore; see him in volume VIII of *Hispania sacra*, where he offers Mariana’s reading.

For the present, it is enough that from Isidore’s words we can clearly conclude that some people assigned Christ’s birth to world-year 5197. For when Isidore says:

> “If the 754 years of the Lord’s Incarnation, which are correctly reckoned in era 792, are added to the 5,196 years mentioned above, there are found to be 5,950 years,”

this cannot be true unless Christ’s first year is connected with world-year 5197 and the beginning of the era with year 5159, placing it four years before the common reckoning of the Christian and Spanish eras. [Col. 0834D]

Thus far I have set forth four opinions, all opposed to the beginning of the era as commonly and popularly received. The fifth, on which we shall dwell longer, must now be explained.

## § IV. Examination of the passage of Saint Julian, archbishop of Toledo, in which he compares era 724 with the second year of King Ervig

### 15.

The most holy and most learned Julian, bishop of Toledo, handed down the following statement about the era: [Note: [Col. 0835D] Book III of *On the Proof of the Sixth Age*, in the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, 1610, vol. IV, col. 251, and in several other editions that I have seen.]

> “The era was devised thirty-eight years before Christ was born.”

Among those who have given testimony about this beginning of the era, Julian is pre-eminent both in authority and in antiquity. To confirm what he had taught in words by an example, he added:

> “Now it is proclaimed that the era is 724. Therefore, after thirty-eight have been subtracted—from the time when the era was devised until the Nativity of Christ—986 remain.”

The manifest typographical error must be corrected, and 686 restored, as it is read shortly afterward once the error has been removed. [Col. 0835B]

Let us now undertake the calculation, after first listening to Julian himself. He says that he wrote these things when the most serene Ervig, as prince, appeared to be in the first year of his reign. Julian completed these books and presented them to Ervig when the anniversary of his inauguration as king recurred, on the day falling on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

For Julian admits that he composed this work at the request of Ervig, already king. The work is so carefully and elaborately constructed that it could not have been completed in a short time. Moreover, at the beginning of Ervig’s reign Julian was burdened with many concerns: the king’s inauguration, the holding of the Twelfth Council of Toledo, and others. [Col. 0835C]

Accordingly, on or about the day when Ervig had completed one year of his rule, Julian completed these books. At that same time he wrote what we read at the end of his work:

> “Now it is proclaimed that the era is 724.”

Therefore, in that October in which Ervig’s first year ended and his second year began, Julian reckoned 686 as the year of Christ and 724 as the year of the Spanish era.

But in other monuments and Chronicles of our Spain, this same year of Ervig is Christ’s year 681 and era 719. Julian therefore places both Christ’s birth and the beginning of the era five years earlier than the common opinion holds.

Thus, if according to the chronology commonly received Christ’s first year falls in the consulship of Caesar and Paulus, and the first year of the Spanish era in the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus, then in Julian’s calculation the first year of the Spanish era falls in the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa, Eusebian world-year 5158, Julian period 4671, and the first year of Augustus. [Col. 0835D]

### 16.

Since this is almost exactly what many highly learned men formerly undertook to demonstrate—namely, that Dionysius recorded Christ’s birth five years later than it actually occurred—it may seem astonishing that, in Scheelstrat’s very large work on this subject, the testimony of so great a scholar is not cited in confirmation of this opinion.

I know that the excellent marquis of Mondéjar (*On the Spanish Era*, dissertation 3, section 14) thought Julian’s passage should be read as follows:

> “When the most serene Ervig, as prince, appears to be in the fourth year of his reign.” [Col. 0836A]

First, all who believe that the era precedes Christ’s birth by only thirty-eight years will reject this correction and contend that “5,” not “4,” should be read. They will say that the marquis inserted the 4 in order to confirm his own opinion that the era exceeds Christ’s birth by thirty-nine years.

In the second place, all the books refute both parties, since nowhere do they read either 4 or 5. Finally, an unqualified year—first, second, third, and so forth—is used in ordinary speech by all reputable authors, as by Plautus, who says (*Menaechmi*, scene 3, act 1): “I bought her in that year.” When it is expressed absolutely in this way, it signifies one year or the first year.

There is therefore no reason to make any correction in Julian, unless someone wishes to drag him, despite his resistance, toward his own meaning and interpretation.

Nor does the fact that we saw above that he assigned Christ’s birth to the forty-first year of Augustus matter, since we cannot know from what point he began counting the years of Augustus. It is plausible that, like Isidore of Seville, he connected the first year of Augustus with world-year 5156 and assigned the forty-first year—the year in which he says Christ was born—to world-year 5196, Julian period 4709, during the consulship of Augustus XII and Sulla.

If this is so, we shall say that in both places he held this fifth opinion, and nowhere the third. [Col. 0836B]

## § V. The Spanish era may appear to have originated in the triumvirate of Lepidus, Antony, and Octavian

### 17.

If the opinion of Saint Julian mentioned above is correct, the Spanish era must have begun in the very year in which M. Lepidus, M. Antonius, and Octavian Caesar claimed the triumvirate for themselves. This will not be difficult to believe for those who, having embraced the opinion that the era received its name from *aes*, know that from that very time Antony and Octavian began to collect money and demand taxes with the greatest eagerness.

Appian of Alexandria and Dio Cassius abundantly testify to this, and Suetonius does not deny it. Dio says (*Book XXXVII*):

> “Some taxes, previously abolished, were restored; others were newly established.”

Although Dio relates this after mentioning the consulship entered upon by Lepidus and Plancus in the year 712 of the City—that is, world-year 5159—it is scarcely doubtful that the triumvirs did not make the preceding year exempt from tribute as well.

Moreover, Appian (*Book IV*) preserved the formula of the triumviral edicts. It bore the names of the triumvirs in this order:

> “M. Lepidus, M. Antonius, Octavian Caesar,”

and so forth. Although, speaking of Lepidus, Appian adds that Antony and Caesar decided that he should govern Spain on behalf of them both, edicts were nevertheless promulgated in Spain, as in the other provinces, under that formula.

Thus the money that was first imposed upon the Spaniards in Caesar’s name—although not in his name alone—and subsequently, after the abolition of the triumvirate, for many years in the name of Caesar alone, could very appropriately have given the Spanish era both its name and its beginning from Caesar.

It may therefore have received its beginning from Caesar and his associates, but its name from Caesar alone, because of the long duration of his rule and because the other emperors afterward retained the name of Caesar for themselves. [Col. 0836D]

### 18.

“But if the triumvirate was established in the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December,” you will say, “tribute could not possibly have been demanded from Spain until the following year.”

That is certainly true. Nevertheless, in the year 712 of the City, before the battle of Philippi, two years’ taxes could have been demanded from the Spaniards: one pertaining to that very year 712 and the other to the preceding year 711, in which Hirtius and Pansa were consuls.

It is no less clever than amusing that, when the triumvir Antony demanded a double tribute from the Asians in that same year 712 of the City, Hybraeus objected:

> “If you can, Antony, demand tribute twice in the same year, you should also make it possible for us to have summer twice and autumn twice.”  
> (Plutarch, *Life of Antony*)

Eusebius, in his Chronicle, reports that in the year after Cicero’s death—Cicero having been killed during the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa—Curtius Talassus was burned alive with four cohorts on the island of Aradus because he was exacting taxes too harshly. This must be understood as referring to the same exaction that Hybraeus said Antony had imposed, whether Antony had already arrived in Asia or was still staying in Greece. [Col. 0837B]

Since, then, the triumvirs, preparing for war against Brutus and Cassius, needed an immense quantity of gold and silver, it is not entirely unlike the truth that, just as after the war they did with the Asians, so before it they imposed upon the Spaniards a double tribute—that is, the taxes for two years—in the year 712 of the City, and that the first and second years of the Spanish *aes* were recorded accordingly; then in the third year, 713 from the founding of the City, and thereafter the fourth, fifth, sixth, and so on, each successive year.

### 19.

We cannot determine whether these payments or taxes were ordered in the name of Lepidus, Antony, or Caesar, or—in my view the more attractive possibility—in the formal formula reported by Appian.

But if the Spaniards believed from the beginning that they were paying Caesar, and if the name of the era was consequently derived from Caesar and its beginning likewise traced to him, I should believe that this happened because Antony was so often far away and Lepidus assented to Caesar in everything, so that Caesar’s name and authority prevailed.

Xiphilinus testifies that this was the case during the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa, saying (*Book XLVI*):

> “All power was in Caesar’s hands.”

The following verses, which I have read somewhere, are also to be understood of the triumvirs and bear on the same matter:

> “This burden does not approve the two partners,  
> yet one is praised by the two.  
> Either he is Maximus,  
> or the two are nothing.”

Accordingly, if in the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa, in the year 711 of the City, the first year of Augustus, Julian period 4671, world-year 5198—or, as stated, in the following year, 712 from the founding of the City—a new tax was imposed upon the Spaniards and collected from them, while the triumvirs were raking in money everywhere with insatiable greed, I do not know why the Spanish era should not trace its origin and beginning to that very year. [Col. 0837D]

### 20.

I cannot sufficiently wonder that certain men, certainly great scholars, report that they believe they can establish from Dio’s authority (*Book XLVIII*) that the beginning of the Spanish era fell in the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus.

Dio does indeed relate that immediately after the battle of Philippi Antony surrendered Spain to Caesar, taking it from Lepidus, and that two years later—that is, in the year 714 of the City—it came under Caesar’s power. He then says that in the year 715 from the founding of the City the senate ordered everything that the triumvirs had done from the beginning of their magistracy to be ratified.

Finally, he mentions new taxes which the triumvirs had already established. But how the Spanish era can be derived from these facts as having begun in the year 716 from the founding of the City, in the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus, I plainly do not see.

For that decree of the senate is no more relevant to the matter than the triumvirs regarded the senate as relevant; Dio himself says of them (*Book XLVI*):

> “They did everything according to their own will, even though they had referred none of these matters either to the senate or to the people.”

What, then? Even if Lepidus, Antony, and Octavian did not impose new taxes upon all the provinces under their control immediately upon entering the triumvirate, is it credible that Caesar, possessing Spain—so rich in gold—with full right and dominion from the year 714 of the City, would have wished to leave it exempt from tribute for one or two years, until 716, while wars were raging everywhere and the soldiers were not only demanding their pay but also threateningly pressing for the lavish gifts that had been promised to them? [Col. 0838B]

Nor does Dio, which is the point most relevant here, mention any tax instituted in the year 716 of the City. He does, however, mention taxes that had already been instituted.

21. But if I said that it was highly uncertain whether, as the most learned men have thought, the beginning of the Spanish Era can be assigned to the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus on the authority of Dio, no one should therefore suppose that I am claiming the matters I have presented as more certain. Indeed, whatever may be deduced from Roman history concerning this matter [Col. 0838C] must be nothing certain, but merely conjectures, since there is profound silence there about our Era. But if the Era is called after the tribute imposed upon the Spaniards, and if we say that its beginning must be referred to the first establishment of that tribute or tax, anyone who reads Appian, Dio, and Plutarch may perhaps judge that what I have presented and argued is more probable.

I wish here to add that I am not now beginning any dispute with those who think that our Era precedes the Nativity of Christ by no more than thirty-eight years. For I myself have no doubt that this is true: such is the belief of the whole nation. Why should I obstinately and uselessly resist it? Nevertheless, the arguments set out above make us doubt which Nativity of Christ is meant, and which of those five opinions, drawn from our earlier writers, is the one whose Nativity the Spanish Era precedes by thirty-eight years: is it the Dionysian year, or any other of them? Each of those opinions still has its own most learned defenders. Accordingly, everything I have said thus far about the beginning of our Era is directed toward showing that the thirty-eight years by which it is said to exceed the Nativity of Christ are not established by arguments so certain that they must necessarily be counted upward from year 1 of the Dionysian Era, as though it were a sacrilege to question or investigate the matter.

§ VI. The beginning of the Era will remain uncertain until more decisive evidence appears. Nevertheless, the common and customary method of reckoning it must be retained.

22. Saint Julian, more than eleven hundred years ago, wrote what I quoted above: “The Era was established thirty-eight years before Christ was born.” Sixty years after Julian, the same was reported by Isidore of Pax, who said: “In Era 792, the year 754 of the Incarnation of the Lord is accurately reckoned.” From these statements we clearly infer two things:

1. Ancient Spanish writers, when acting as chronologers, use the word “Incarnation” in the same sense as “Nativity of Christ”; that is, they take both expressions to mean Christ’s Nativity. I shall demonstrate this immediately from Isidore, who uses the word “Incarnation.”

2. The belief of all antiquity was that the Spanish Era began thirty-eight years before the Nativity of Christ.

I add that Isidore measures this excess of the Spanish Era over the Christian Era according to the Christian Era as devised by Dionysius Exiguus. For he says [Col. 0839B] in the *Chronicle*, no. 79:

“Thus, from the beginning of the world up to the beginning of Era 792, in the tenth year of the reign of Constantine [Copronymus] . . . there are reckoned 5,954 years.”

This year of the world—for the other Eras which Isidore gathers there need not be discussed—designates the Dionysian year 754. In order to descend from Era 792, which Isidore says runs concurrently with that same year, one must subtract neither more nor fewer than thirty-eight years. Isidore, therefore, more than a thousand years ago explicitly and plainly held and embraced the common opinion of his age concerning the beginning of our Era: that it began precisely thirty-eight years before the Dionysian Era, which is reckoned from the Nativity of Christ, not from the Incarnation. For Isidore could not count the world-year 5,954 as year 754 of the Christian Era unless, with Dionysius, he began that Era with world-year 5,201, as anyone can discover from the calculations that follow.

23. These statements are indeed true. But since, shortly before, Isidore—following another opinion, without refuting it—attached the same Era and the same year of Christ to world-year 5,950, as was noted above, no. 20, we learn from this that the writers of his time did not all hold one uniform opinion on the subject. Indeed, Isidore is not even consistent with himself when he joins Era 792 and Christ’s year 754 to world-year [Col. 0840A] 5,954. For, as we saw above, no. 12, he places the Nativity of Christ, with Eusebius, Isidore, and all writers—for so he speaks—in the forty-second year of Augustus, which coincides with world-year 5,199. Yet from that world-year to 5,954 there are 756 years, not 754. And if the Spanish Era arose thirty-eight years before Christ, 794 must be counted, not 792. Isidore, therefore, contradicts himself and writes mutually inconsistent things.

Furthermore, it is extremely remarkable and difficult to understand how those who believed that our Era preceded the Nativity of Christ by precisely thirty-eight years—neither more nor fewer—and who assigned it respectively to the thirty-ninth, fortieth, forty-first, forty-second, or forty-third year of Augustus, could almost all make that same Era thirty-eight years earlier than only one Dionysian Nativity of Christ, namely the one connected with none of those Augustan years except the forty-fourth.

To place this inconsistency before the eyes of the reader, I present here two tables of Augustan years. The first gives the six years from 1 to 6 in which, according to six different opinions, the Spanish Era began; the second gives the six years from 39 to 44 in which, according to those same opinions, the Nativity of Christ occurred, preserving the order of antiquity. In each table, the first line represents the opinion that assigns the beginning of the respective Era to the earliest year: the Spanish Era to Augustan year 1, and the Christian Era to Augustan year 39. The second represents the opinion that assigns the Spanish Era to Augustan year 2 and the Christian Era to Augustan year 40, and so forth.

I shall add the Augustan consular years, together with the corresponding years of the world and of the Julian Period, so that the variety and contradiction of these opinions may be more easily and clearly recognized from the figures. If any beginner in history is surprised to learn that there have been so many opinions concerning the year of Christ’s Nativity, let him consult the very learned Lamy, who lists them and the supporters of each one (*Apparatus Chronologicus ad concordiam*, part I, chapter 7, § 4).

**Table of the Spanish Era**

[Col. 0839]

I. Augustan year 1. Consuls Hirtius and Pansa. World-year 5158; Julian Period 4671; Era 1.  
II. Augustan year 2. Consuls Lepidus II and Plancus. World-year 5159; Julian Period 4672; Era 2.  
III. Augustan year 3. Consuls Antonius and Isauricus. World-year 5160; Julian Period 4673; Era 3.  
IV. Augustan year 4. Consuls Calvinus and Pollio. World-year 5161; Julian Period 4674; Era 4.  
V. Augustan year 5. Consuls Censorinus and Sabinus. World-year 5162; Julian Period 4675; Era 5.  
VI. Augustan year 6. Consuls Pulcher and Flaccus. World-year 5163; Julian Period 4676; Era 6.

**Table of the Christian Era**

XXXIX. Augustan year 39. Consuls Augustus XII and Sulla. World-year 5196; Julian Period 4709; Era 1.  
XL. Augustan year 40. Consuls Sabinus and Rufus. World-year 5197; Julian Period 4710; Era 2.  
XLI. Augustan year 41. Consuls Lentulus and Messalla. World-year 5198; Julian Period 4711; Era 3.  
XLII. Augustan year 42. Consuls Augustus XIII and Silvanus. World-year 5199; Julian Period 4712; Era 4.  
XLIII. Augustan year 43. Consuls Lentulus and Piso. World-year 5200; Julian Period 4713; Era 5.  
XLIV. Augustan year 44. Consuls Caesar and Paulus. World-year 5201; Julian Period 4714; Era 6.

[Col. 0839D] After examining these tables, the reader cannot fail to understand in which of the six opinions mentioned above one either actually assigns, or at least ought to assign, the Spanish Era.

24. Whoever believes that Christ was born in Augustan year 39—that is, in Eusebian world-year 5196—must attach the first year of the Spanish Era [Col. 0840D] to Augustan year 1 and world-year 5158.

Whoever connects Christ’s Nativity with Augustan year 40 must attach the Spanish Era and its beginning to Augustan year 2 and world-year 5159, and so on for the others. We are speaking of those who believe that the Spanish Era began thirty-eight years before the Christian Era, and conversely. Such people can never, unless they wish to contradict themselves, place the beginning of the Spanish Era in the last year of the first table if they assign Christ’s Nativity to one of the first five years of the second table. Nor, if they assert that the Spanish Era began in one of the first five years of the first table, can they assign Christ’s Nativity to the last year of the second table.

Yet we see that what we say cannot happen has in fact happened. How it happened, however, we do not know. We conjecture, with great probability, that it arose from the paschal cycle of Dionysius after that cycle had been introduced into the churches. Everyone knows that all the ancient monuments transmitted to us were either written or copied by clerics and monks. No one acquainted with the ancient Alexandrian and Roman custom of announcing Easter will deny that, as soon as Dionysius’s cycle had been completed, it was sent by the Roman pontiff to all the churches of the West.

Thus, when those ecclesiastics used that cycle to show Christ’s Nativity as falling in the last year of the second table, they accepted Dionysius’s authority without hesitation, not realizing that he followed a different chronology from that which they themselves—or those whose works they copied—had hitherto used. Hence, by sometimes retaining the reckoning of themselves or of the authors whom they copied, and sometimes abandoning it in order to adhere to the Dionysian reckoning, they entangled all chronology in their books in inextricable knots and made it uncertain in which year each person had assigned the Spanish Era and in which year the Christian Era [Col. 0841C].

25. Nevertheless, since it cannot be doubted that, if the Spaniards continually used the reckoning of the Era in their fiscal register or at least in the office of the procurator of the imperial treasury, they could not have been mistaken in designating it any more than we can now be mistaken in assigning the current Era by counting its year as 1758, then—if it were demonstrated by certain and irresistible arguments that our writers had always reckoned the Era received uninterruptedly from their ancestors in such a way that exactly thirty-eight years, neither more nor fewer, intervened between it and the common Era of Dionysius Exiguus—it would certainly be proved that the beginning of our Era fell in the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus, in Augustan year 6, Julian Period 4676, and world-year [Col. 0841D] 5163.

For example, the following is read on the stone from Toledo cited by the distinguished Florius (*Hispania sacra*, vol. II, p. 23, and elsewhere):

> IN THE NAME OF THE LORD, THE CHURCH OF SAINT MARY WAS CONSECRATED ON A CATHOLIC DAY, ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE IDES OF APRIL, HAPPILY, IN THE FIRST YEAR OF THE REIGN OF OUR LORD, THE MOST GLORIOUS KING FLAVIUS RECCAREDUS, ERA 625.

This inscription would settle the matter, provided that two things could be established: first, that the Era had been recorded without error, because this epoch had remained in use among the Spaniards from its origin up to that year; and second, that the letters DCXXY signify Era 625, not 630. For if these points are certain, the other indications yield the year 587 of the common Era, in which the first day before the Ides—or the Ides—of April was a catholic day, that is, a day to be observed by the whole people, and was also the first day of the week. If thirty-eight years are added to 587, the result is Spanish Era 625.

26. Nevertheless, the testimony of Saint Julian quoted above, and the very form of the final letter Y, raise doubts in my mind and make me fear that, because of the difficulty of the Gothic letters, or because the lower part of that Y has been worn away on the left, writers took it for a V, whereas in reality it may be an X. This is especially to be feared if the person who first copied the inscription—and I think the same of those who still read it—was influenced by the prejudice of the common opinion, so that he derived Spanish Era 625 from it.

Nor can we derive any argument from the Sunday date recorded there that would resolve this doubt, since both Julian’s Era 630—according to the authority mentioned by him—and the Era 625 of others coincided with the year of Christ 587. Moreover, in the year of Christ 592, with which, according to the common opinion, Spanish Era 630 is joined, the Ides of April also fell on a Sunday.

But if that letter Y is not V but X, this stone will express precisely the epoch of Saint Julian, namely Era 630, and it will be confirmed by this new argument that our Era began a full five years earlier than is now commonly believed. It is therefore of the greatest importance that the genuine reading of this inscription be established publicly and unmistakably.

27. But even that is not sufficient to make the reckoning of the Era certain and indisputable. For after it has been demonstrated that either DCXXV or DCXXX was written on the Toledo stone, it is additionally necessary to establish that the person who engraved those letters knew the origin of this epoch exactly, so that neither more nor fewer years had elapsed since the Era began than the number he recorded.

I would not dare to affirm this confidently, nor perhaps would anyone else, since in the monuments preserved among us the Era is not mentioned until after the five-hundredth year from its beginning. Yet we see that Dionysius Exiguus, when he devised the common Christian Era in the sixth century, was a full five years away from the truth, according to the present opinion of most highly learned men.

Therefore, if someone says that something similar must be feared in the method of reckoning our Era, there is no reason to be angry with him or condemn him for rashness. For if Dionysius—before whom stood the infallible testimony of Saint Luke, who, recounting events that occurred in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, says, “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age” (Luke 3)—was grossly mistaken, if we believe the most learned chronologers, could not the person who in the sixth century wrote that inscription of the Spanish Era on the Toledo stone have been similarly mistaken?

He could certainly have erred, and all the more easily than Dionysius, since, as appears, indications concerning the beginning of our Era have always been rarer than those concerning the year of the Incarnation of Christ the Lord. For in discovering the latter, Dionysius could use not only ecclesiastical writers but also the consular lists and the entire history of the Romans, in addition to the fifteenth year of Tiberius assigned there by Saint Luke.

28. To bring this lengthy discussion to an end, everything said thus far plainly teaches us, I think, that it is not sufficiently certain that the epoch of the Spanish Era descends from the consulship of Pulcher and Flaccus, from Augustan year 6, world-year 5163, and Julian Period 4676. The point must therefore be confirmed by clearer arguments. Since this can be derived only from ancient inscriptions [307] and monuments, scholars and learned men interested in Spanish antiquities will surely understand how important it is that any such materials still hidden in darkness be brought into the public and common light.

29. In the meantime, because I began to write this out of love for the truth, and because I long considered whether the widely accepted opinion about the beginning of the Era could be maintained despite the arguments brought against it above, I shall not conceal from my reader that those arguments might plausibly be answered by saying that the writers previously praised, and their most ancient predecessors, reckoned the Era from the year before the consulship of Caesar and Paulus—that is, what amounts to the same thing, thirty-eight years before the Dionysian Nativity of Christ—having received this calculation from popular usage and from the fiscal register.

As I observed in no. 22, this reckoning cannot therefore be uncertain, even if later writers, when designating Christ’s Nativity by the Augustan years, appear to place it three, four, or more years earlier. For whatever Augustan or world-year they assigned to the Nativity of the Lord, they believed that Dionysius also assigned it to that same year. This is clear in the case of Isidore of Pax, whom we saw above, no. 16, most emphatically attach Christ’s Nativity to Augustan year 42. Yet, when he adds together the years from the beginning of the world to Era 792—in which, he says, 754 years of the Lord’s Incarnation are accurately reckoned—he produces a total of 5,954 years.

If, therefore, Isidore counted Christ’s year 754 in this world-year, he could not fail to attach the beginning of the Christian Era to Eusebian world-year 5201, the very year to which Dionysius Exiguus attached it. Yet Augustan year 44 was connected with Eusebian world-year 5201. Thus Isidore verbally joined Christ’s Nativity to Augustan year 42, but in reality joined it to year 44 [308] and held the common opinion concerning the beginning of our Era. Let the reader reread what was written in no. 28.

If anyone finds this response persuasive, let him consider whether the other testimonies cited above can be trusted. I myself do not think that the authority of Saint Julian, cited in no. 21, can be dissolved by such an interpretation; the words of the Chronicle of Burgos, which I quoted in no. 19, also seem to reject it.

Nor should I pass over in silence the fact that the distinguished and highly learned Joannes Vergara, a canon of Toledo, when two hundred years ago he attempted to derive the beginning of our Era from histories, chronologers, and consular lists, connected it with the consulship of Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus and Gaius Asinius Pollio. Although, in accordance with the common opinion, he affirmed that Christ’s Nativity preceded the Era by thirty-eight years, he placed it, both verbally and in reality, in Augustan year 42.

30. Finally, if someone should happen to believe that he has certainly discovered that the Era began in a year other than the one commonly supposed, he should not therefore think that he may use its reckoning differently from the way everyone now employs it. After learned men began disputing the beginning of the Christian Era, and some believed that they had demonstrated that Dionysius began it three, others four, others five, or still more years later than he should have done, they nevertheless did not think that they were entitled to cite it in any way other than according to common usage. Someone aptly said while discussing this matter: “Keep knowledge for yourself; leave custom and ancient usage to the common people.”

Furthermore, when you read the histories, chronicles, and other monuments of our writers, take the Era according to the common reckoning. For it was used almost everywhere by the writers themselves or by the scribes according to that reckoning.

# For Volume LII: Saint Severinus, Bishop and Abbot

[Col. 0843]

## Historical Notice on Severinus

(*Fabricius, Library of the Middle and Later Ages*)

[Col. 0843D] Severinus, a bishop of uncertain date and see, is conjectured by the Reverend Pez to have been Colomensis ("of Colom"). His small work, entitled *Doctrine*, or—as the monastic codex of Saint Hilary in Austria has it—*Doctrine of Wisdom*, was first published by Pithaeus at Paris, then in the Parisian supplement to the *Library of the Fathers*, in the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*, in volume II of Sirmond’s works, in Pez’s latest *Treasury of Anecdotes*, volume IV, part II, page 1, and finally in our Fabricius, near the end of book VI of this work, page 227.

A homily beginning, “Christ in human actions,” which is to be read among the works of Saint Peter Chrysologus as sermon 50, is attributed to Saint Severinus the bishop in an old manuscript homiliary of the library of the canons of the principal church of Lucca. The manuscripts do not agree in assigning that homily to Saint Peter [Col. 0845A] Chrysologus: some bear the name of Saint Jerome, others that of Saint John Chrysostom. Whether it should in fact be taken away from the bishop of Ravenna and assigned to another is uncertain. If it is said to be Severinus’s, we shall likewise remain uncertain whether the Severinus meant is the one whose *Doctrine of Wisdom* has often employed the printing presses.

[Col. 0845]

## Doctrine of Saint Severinus the Bishop (C)

[Col. 0845A]

I. Love God.  
II. Learn wisdom.  
III. Do everything with measure.  
IV. What you hate and do not wish done to yourself, do not do to others.  
V. Always hope in the Lord.  
VI. Await the future time.  
VII. Be subject to necessity.  
VIII. Follow justice.  
IX. Do not use oaths.  
X. Teach what is useful.  
XI. Hate injustice.  
XII. Honor wise men; flee fools.  
XIII. Do not be ashamed to learn what is good.  
XIV. Govern your tongue.  
XV. Be magnanimous.  
XVI. Never lie.  
XVII. Keep faith.  
XVIII. Bear witness to the truth.  
XIX. Do not covet what belongs to others.  
XX. Do not be a lover of money; seek as much as is sufficient for your needs, and when you have it, give to the one who asks.

[Col. 0845C]

XXI. Attend to your own affairs, but do not meddle in those of others.  
XXII. Hate talkativeness, for silence is good and verbosity is bad.  
XXIII. Be a lover of good counsel.  
XXIV. Despise no one.  
XXV. Revere the older person; honor the younger, if he is wise, as an old man.  
XXVI. Praise the truth, and strive to learn what benefits the soul.  
XXVII. Think well of your friends.  
XXVIII. Do not exasperate your enemies; for it is more useful to make them friends than to have them as enemies.  
XXIX. Speak with just men.  
XXX. Raise your children well.

[Col. 0845D]

XXXI. Associate with the simple.  
XXXII. When showing mercy, do not become sorrowful or hesitant.  
XXXIII. Give from the heart whatever you are going to give, because you do not know the future.  
XXXIV. Let mercy, truth, and charity not be lacking in you; these good things will cover a multitude of sins.  
XXXV. Speak no reproach to anyone.  
XXXVI. Be even-tempered, gentle, and self-controlled.  
XXXVII. Flee anger, for it is the mother of sin.  
XXXVIII. Practice justice in judgment.  
XXXIX. Love servants.  
XL. Speak evil of no one.  
XLI. Give true testimony at the appropriate time.

[Col. 0846A]

XLII. Hate quarrels.  
XLIII. Reconcile those who are disputing.  
XLIV. Patiently endure the evils that come upon you.  
XLV. Judge justly, for remember that you are human.  
XLVI. Do not be anxious about certain matters; a wise person is not quickly disturbed.

[Col. 0846B]

XLVII. Quarrel with no one.  
XLVIII. Let your tongue speak what is of good repute.  
XLIX. Pursue silence, because it is without repentance; tumult is followed by repentance.  
L. Dissolve enmities.  
LI. Do not be unbelieving, and strive to do good without becoming more boastful.  
LII. Flee empty glory.  
LIII. Be gentle toward your own people and useful to strangers.  
LIV. Conquer the desires of your soul.  
LV. Do not quickly make friends; but do not quickly reject those whom you have made friends.  
LVI. Do not concern yourself with sinners, for it will profit you nothing.

[Col. 0846C]

LVII. Do not give wisdom to beasts; afterward they will persecute you.  
LVIII. Reveal the sacraments of God only to the worthy.  
LIX. Do not choose imprudent men as leaders, lest you become a leader of demons.  
LX. Do nothing against the law of God.  
LXI. Distinguish between good and evil, and let the difference between the just and the unjust be clear to you. The works of injustice are these: hatred, fornication, theft, robbery, sorcery, lying, false testimony, greed, slander, deceit, pride, wickedness, recklessness, dishonesty, boasting, contention, hypocrisy, evil-speaking, love of money, ungodliness, and everything that alienates one from the teaching of God. The works of justice are these:

[Col. 0846D]

Always to give thanks to God; to love the worshipers of God; to harm no one or cause anyone grief; to live chastely; to be merciful; to love one’s neighbor as oneself; to feed the hungry; to give drink to the thirsty; to clothe the naked; to be hospitable and humane; and to give generously to those in need.

LXII. Do not be bitter toward those who are in sorrow.  
LXIII. Do everything that belongs to justice.  
LXIV. Use human laws as a human being, and the law of God as belonging to God.  
LXV. Do not envy the good, for you are not immortal.  
LXVI. Be like a burning lamp, and you will be called an angel of God.  
LXVII. Do not approach prayer with a bad conscience, for you will be condemned by your own conscience. Confession of sin is the beginning of salvation.

[Col. 0847A]

LXVIII. Always be submissive to God, and act so that you may be regarded as blameless.  
LXIX. Permit no one to speak evil, lest you be regarded as a supporter of injustice.  
LXX. Do not condemn the absent; receive the present justly.  
LXXI. Do not condemn on the basis of accusations, lest you too be condemned, for such things displease God; and judge as you wish to be seen acting.  
LXXII. Do not accept a woman as a witness.  
LXXIII. Forgive every sin except murder and adultery.  
LXXIV. Do not consent to one who commits an injury, lest you be punished as an accomplice of injustice; but let the person whom you have rejected be to you as one ignorant.

[Col. 0847B]

LXXV. Nourish servants as sons; for before the Lord they are equal, since he does not show partiality.  
LXXVI. Do nothing beyond measure, and do not associate with the proud, lest you be regarded as a friend of injustice.  
LXXVII. Always seek the faces of elders, so that you may be instructed by their words, for the minds of the wise are full of the fruits of life.

[Col. 0848A]

LXXVIII. Regard the leader of your life as God, for he has been sent to you by God so that you may be saved; and make him a participant in all your possessions. For the one who makes you a fellow participant in divine things ought to be a participant in human things.  
LXXIX. Do not reproach the poor, lest you too become reproachable; for God’s judgment is over all, and he judges justly.  
LXXX. Show mercy secretly, and do not disgrace yourself. If you act so that you may be seen publicly by others and praised by men, it will profit you nothing.

[Col. 0848B]

LXXXI. Worship the Lord secretly, and do not choose a conspicuous place; for God is everywhere, and wherever he is invoked, he is present. Give him thanks every day, waking and sleeping, so that you may have him favorable to you and he may fulfill your desires. When you pray, do not speak at excessive length, lest you seem like a fool; for God knows your petitions before you ask, and is not ignorant of what you are thinking.

# Appendix to the Fifth Century

[Col. 0847]

## Muratori’s Dissertation on Liturgical Matters

### Preface

[Col. 0847C] Sacred liturgy presents an extensive field of ecclesiastical learning to the studious, since it treats of the rites employed in the public worship of God, in administering the divine sacraments, and in the other observances of the Catholic religion.

From the time when Charles Augustus the Great and his son Louis the Pious stirred both the Gauls and the Germans to restore the kingdom of fallen learning, learned men began devoting themselves to the adornment of this subject: Amalarius, Florus the Master, Agobard, Rabanus Maurus, and Walafrid Strabo. In subsequent centuries there were Berno, abbot of Reichenau; the *Micrologus*; and the writer published under the name of Alcuin.

Later, William Durand and John Beleth also handed down many works on the divine offices. Then, in the sixteenth century, James Pamelius, Gregory Cassander, John Stephen Duranti, Claude de Saintes, and others who gave the liturgies of the Eastern Churches to the Latin world exercised themselves in this field.

The patrimony of ecclesiastical liturgy was enlarged with far greater success in the following seventeenth century. To pass over others, Joseph Vicecomes, John Baptist Casalius, Bartholomew Gavanti, James Goar, Gabriel Albaspinaeus, Leo Allatius, John Morin, and Hugh Menard wrote more accurately about the sacred rites.

But above all we acknowledge ourselves indebted on this subject to three writers: Cardinal John Bona, who treated liturgical matters with such learning and judgment; the venerable Cardinal Joseph Maria Tomasi, who brought so many excellent monuments on this subject out of darkness and published them; and John Mabillon, a man of immortal name, who extended the strength of his learning to this subject also in more than one work.

Stimulated by these Catholic studies, Joseph Bingham among the Anglicans, after undertaking during the early years of the present century to cultivate the origins or ecclesiastical antiquities in many books, also began to illustrate sacred liturgy, serving his sect according to his ability, but not always the truth.

At almost the same time, the distinguished Eusebius Renaudot of Paris produced an excellent work, namely a collection of the Eastern liturgies, which he also enlarged with learned notes.

Father Don Edmund Martene, a Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint Maur, likewise served the same liturgy wonderfully well by publishing four volumes on the ancient rites of the Church.

In addition, Father Pierre Le Brun, a priest of the Paris Oratory, gave us four further volumes of an extremely useful *Explanation of the Mass*, together with a compendium of all liturgies and several liturgical dissertations deserving exceptional praise.

In Italy, Father Joseph Blanchini, a priest of the Roman Oratory, conferred a notable benefit upon the Christian commonwealth by discovering and publishing the Leonine Sacramentary, and also by bringing to light and illustrating an ancient prayer book of the Gothic-Hispanic rite.

Moreover, Father Don Gaetano Maria Merati, a cleric regular, enlarged Gavanti’s *Treasury of Sacred Rites*.

The most holy pontiff now reigning, Benedict XIV, also, out of his love for the same liturgy—several parts of which he has already adorned in books he has published—did not neglect the liturgical academy among the other academies he established in Rome, and has rejoiced that he has already reaped fruit from it.

For Domenico Giorgi has illustrated the Pontifical Mass with multifaceted learning. Father Joseph Pinius of the Society of Jesus also devoted much study to elucidating the Mozarabic and other Spanish liturgies. Peter Morettus, a canon of Saint Mary across the Tiber, in explaining the rite of conferring the presbyterate, covered many liturgical matters. Other learned men are considering other subjects, and we have good hope that the harvest will continue.

Someone might nevertheless object that this material now appears exhausted, and that, since the field has been occupied by so many distinguished writers, only refuse or goods of little value have been left to their successors.

I confess that I had already been seized by this very thought when the recently mentioned Father Blanchini, called away from liturgical studies because the most highly praised supreme pontiff had imposed upon him the task of preparing the ecclesiastical annals of Odoricus Raynaldus, sent me the most ancient copies of the Gregorian Sacramentary that he had already obtained, so that through me the Catholic Church might receive this gift with some return.

“For who,” I said to myself, “could persuade himself that he could provide this Sacramentary with commentaries and embellishments, when the Benedictine monk Hugh Menard has performed this task so successfully?”

I therefore set myself one objective: to present to readers together the three Roman Sacramentaries—namely, the Leonine, which has so far reached the hands of only a few and is plainly worthy of better fortune; then the Gelasian, whose copies had already become extremely rare; and finally the Gregorian, transcribed from the oldest manuscript codex of its kind, whose age I have found to exceed nine hundred years.

In these three Sacramentaries the whole of the ancient Roman liturgy is contained, and I thought that many would find it agreeable to have it presented together.

But I reflected with myself: among all those who devote themselves to sacred learning, how many, I asked, will think that any benefit can be extracted from this work?

“They have our Missals,” they will say. “Whatever appears in the ancient, indeed even in the most ancient, books—whether prayers or rites—is also found in ours; indeed, ours contain more than those do. Why, then, does this man wish to rummage through obsolete codices consumed by decay, only to offer us something we have possessed for so long?”

My present task, then, is not with true scholars and most learned men, who know well how highly such Sacramentaries must be valued both in themselves and because of their antiquity, and how much weight antiquity itself carries in ecclesiastical controversies. It is with those who, although they have gold mines before their eyes, do not recognize their value or do not know how to extract the gold.

I therefore think that only these people need to be warned that no more serious or celebrated controversy is raging between us and the non-Catholics than the one concerning the Eucharist and the sacrifice of the Mass. The authority of liturgical codices contributes wonderfully to settling this controversy, provided that we can produce codices older than the rotten fable about Paschasius Radbertus, whom the heterodox have foolishly imagined, in their fantasy, to have corrupted the ancient Catholic doctrine.

I have therefore undertaken to demonstrate, chiefly by means of the most ancient Roman liturgy, that this doctrine has always been a stable and never-changing truth in the Church of God. I have added the agreement of all the other ancient liturgies of the Christian world, as well as that of the holy Fathers, so that one may see the same Eucharistic dogma maintained most consistently in the Churches of every age and every place, and that the innovators departed from it by a great sacrilege.

I entered this contest with all the greater confidence because, as will be shown below, the heterodox continue to oppose us with the same weapons that distinguished champions of the Catholic communion have so often wielded, as though their strength remained undiminished and were sufficient to keep the flock of their fellow-countrymen in the faith.

If any of them should ever read these few pages and deal honestly with himself concerning a matter of such importance, perhaps I shall not have gathered these materials in vain. If not, I at least hope to achieve this: that any one of our own people who is less experienced in such controversies, when brought to read these pages, may find them a consolation, recognizing both that the faith he received from childhood is confirmed by the agreement of all antiquity and that those who have rashly deprived the ineffable mystery of the Eucharist and the sacrifice of the Mass of their proper dignity, and still do not cease to insult its truth, are entirely undeserving of excuse.

Finally, so that the reader may have the older Sacramentaries of the Western Churches before his eyes, I wished to append the Gothic Missal, the Frankish Missal, and the ancient Gallican Missal, published by Cardinal Thomasius; likewise another Gallican Missal, together with two of the most ancient ritual books of the Roman Church, published by Mabillon. I shall say something about the latter in its proper place.

# ON THE ORIGIN OF THE SACRED LITURGY

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0851A]

As several learned men have already observed, the Greek word *liturgy* signified among the pagans a public service, so that a *λειτουργός* was one who performed some public office, and to perform it was *λειτουργεῖν*. The same word was also transferred to those engaged in sacred things. We have Saint Luke as our witness (Acts 13:2), when he writes of the prophets and teachers of the Church: *Λειτουργούντων δὲ αὐτῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ*—“While they were ministering to the Lord.” To distinguish this liturgy from others, it was therefore called sacred.

In its particular sense, liturgy is the manner of worshiping the true God through outward and legitimate rites, both to testify to his honor and to convey his benefits to human beings. Taken in a stricter sense, it refers only to those rites by which sacrifice is performed, and to whatever belongs to the office of sacrificing, such as, among the children of the Catholic Church, the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass. This sacred office is designated by other terms among both Greeks and Latins; nor does it include priests alone, but extends also to the other ministers of the Church who perform sacred functions.

The Jewish people, too, had their liturgy when they offered bloody or peace offerings to God. For this reason the Apostle said of the priests of that people: “And every priest indeed stands daily ministering, and often offering the same sacrifices” (Hebrews 10:11). In Greek, *λειτουργῶν* occurs for “ministering.” Their sacrifices, as the Apostle himself testifies, were “a shadow of things to come” (Colossians 2:17), concerning which Saint Augustine has much to say.

Chrysostom, however, writes:

> “Whether a sheep was sacrificed,” he says, “it was an image of the Savior; whether an ox, it was an image of the Lord; whether a calf, or a heifer, or any other of the things that were offered, whether a dove or a turtledove—all referred to the Savior” (Chrysostom, Homily 166, vol. V).

When, through the coming of the Son of God, the old law was reformed for the better, and bloody sacrifices ceased, as had already been foretold by the prophets, more perfect sacraments and new rites took their place, with most of the ceremonies of the ancient people abolished. That is, a new liturgy of the Christian commonwealth took its place, or a discipline in sacred matters, whose kinds must be reckoned as two.

The first consists of rites prescribed by the Savior himself or by his Apostles for the Church as it was coming into being, concerning which the divine books or apostolic tradition, transmitted through the Fathers of the primitive Church down to us, assure us. The second includes those rites which the universal Church, or particular Churches, introduced from time to time into sacred worship, according as their pastors judged them more suitable to the majesty of the mysteries, [Col. 0851D] or more effective for nourishing and increasing the devotion of the people.

[Col. 0852A]

It is of this sacred liturgy that we are now speaking, encompassing the rites of the Mass and of the other sacraments. There can be no doubt that some form of liturgical practice existed while the Apostles themselves were still living, consisting of various prayers used in the celebration of the awesome sacrifice of the altar. According to Saint Luke, “they continued steadfastly in the breaking of bread and in prayers” (Acts 2:42). The Apostle, moreover, wishes that “supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings” be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high position (1 Timothy 2:1).

But when were these things performed? In the ineffable sacrifice of the Christian people, as Saint Justin Martyr recorded. At that time the faithful gathered “for common prayers and supplications, both for themselves and for the one who had been enlightened, and for all others everywhere throughout the world, with attentive minds” (Justin Martyr, *Apology* II).

Tertullian reports the same practice:

> “Accordingly,” he says, “we sacrifice for the welfare of the emperor, but to our God, who is also his” (Tertullian, *To Scapula*).

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem described this custom as observed by the Church around the year of Christ 347, saying:

> “Over that propitiatory offering”—that is, the propitiatory sacrifice which those who impiously and rashly abolished the Mass have dared to deny—“we beseech God for the common peace of the Churches, for the proper ordering of the world, for kings, for armies, and for allies, etc.” (Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* XXIII, no. 8).

[Col. 0852C]

Therefore Saint Augustine, considering what had been done in the Church of God from ancient times, interprets the supplications, or prayers, recently mentioned by the Apostle as “those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before that which is upon the Lord’s table begins to be blessed.” He says that the prayers also signify “those which we utter when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution; and nearly the whole Church concludes this entire petition with the Lord’s Prayer” (Augustine, Letter 159, formerly 59, to Paulinus).

Here you have, outlined in a few words, the sacred canon of the Mass as it is still used among Catholics. We therefore recognize that even in the earliest centuries of the Church there existed a certain order of prayers and supplications, which priest and faithful people used in the divine mysteries.

Saint Cyprian also mentions the Preface still in use, namely when we say, “Lift up your hearts,” and the people respond, “We have them with the Lord” (Cyprian, *On Prayer*). Tertullian likewise indicated that certain rites of baptism were observed in his time; both he and Cyprian also alluded to a prayer used in administering the sacrament of Confirmation, not to mention other matters.

[Col. 0853A]

The most learned Father Pierre Le Brun, a priest of the Paris Oratory, maintains that “before the fifth century of the Church none of the liturgies, whether Greek or Latin, had been committed to writing” (Le Brun, vol. II, *Liturgical Dissertation*), but that all prayers and rites handed down by memory had been transmitted to later generations solely through oral tradition.

For my part, I confess that I have not yet been able to incline toward this opinion. His arguments do not seem to me to possess sufficient force to establish the matter. He cites Epiphanius, who writes of the Apostles:

> “They were themselves the authors and founders of the mysteries, together with James, the brother of the Lord, etc.” (Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* LXXIX).

[Col. 0853B]

Epiphanius does not say that what the Apostles did and said in celebrating the divine mysteries was also committed to writing. Thus Father Le Brun argues—but entirely without foundation—for he neither proves that Saint Epiphanius denies that the liturgy established by them was transmitted in writing, nor is it likely that whatever is arranged for instructing successors would not also be committed to writing.

When Justin Martyr lists the rites of the unbloody sacrifice, he says:

> “The presider, as far as he is able, offers prayers and thanksgivings; and the people joyfully acclaim, saying: Amen” (Justin Martyr, *Apology* II).

Since the priest prayed at length, and as far as he was able, Le Brun concludes from this that the prayers of the assembly were by no means fixed and constant. But no such force can be extracted from the words of the Greek text, *ὅσα δύναμις αὐτῷ*, for they can signify what we say in Italian: “The priest, for his part,” or “according to what belongs to him,” offers the prayers and thanksgivings.

We may reasonably infer that these prayers were not extemporaneous but had already long been established. If the Apostles were, as we have seen, the founders of the mysteries, then the supplications and thanksgivings must also have been handed down by them and observed by their disciples.

Le Brun next presents Tertullian to us:

> “Let us ask whether an unwritten tradition ought not also to be received” (Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 27).

He also cites Saint Basil, who writes:

> “We receive some things from teaching committed to writing, while other things, handed down to us in mystery, we have received from the tradition of the Apostles, etc.” (Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27).

[Col. 0853D]

Then he adds:

> “Who among the saints has left us in writing the words of the invocation by which the Eucharistic bread and the cup of blessing are consecrated?”
