From these passages Le Brun thought he could establish that the formulas of the sacraments had not yet been committed to writing in the age of Tertullian and Basil.

It has always been a common doctrine of the Catholic Church that we received one part of Christian teaching from the Apostles through the written Gospels and Epistles, while another part was commended to the disciples and their successors without writing, by living voice alone.

> “For,” Basil says, “we are not content with those things which the Apostle or the Gospel mentions; rather, we say other things both before and after the consecration, as possessing great importance for the mystery, which we have received from unwritten tradition.”

[Col. 0854A]

The part of the liturgy that descended from the Apostles—whom Basil calls “the saints”—was not left by them in writing. But it does not at all follow from this that no one later committed to writing what the Apostles had handed down without writing. Even if this teaching was subsequently put into writing, it was still called an unwritten tradition, because it was not actually read in the books of the Apostles. The Church firmly believed that it had received it from them through the tradition of its forebears, who had previously been hearers of the Apostles.

Nor does what Le Brun adds later carry any greater weight: namely, that when, during the persecution of Diocletian, the Christians’ sacred books were handed over to the flames, no liturgy is mentioned as having suffered this punishment. For, as Eusebius records, Christians were ordered to surrender the sacred Scriptures, *ἱερὰς Γραφάς*—“the holy Scriptures” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, 2)—not the other books of religion or of the holy Fathers.

Optatus of Milevis likewise writes that “the instruments of the divine law, the divine instruments, the most sacred Scriptures” were surrendered by some (Optatus, Book I), but he does not say that every volume belonging to the Christian people was surrendered. If, however, you suppose that other Christian books also perished at that time—which Cardinal Baronius thought happened to the Acts of the Martyrs—why should the same not have happened to the sacred liturgies?

[Col. 0854C]

Father Le Brun therefore offers nothing that can persuade us that no liturgy, or at least no canon of the Mass, had been committed to writing before the fifth century of Christ. On the contrary, Saint Justin himself describes its more important part; indeed, he does not hesitate to produce the very words of the Lord by which the consecration is performed.

He also adds:

> *Ἔπειτα ἀνιστάμεθα κοινῇ ἅπαντες, καὶ εὐχὰς πέμπομεν*—that is: “Then we all rise together, and we offer prayers” (Justin Martyr, *Apology* II).

If the prayers and supplications of the sacrifice had not already been established, how could the people have continued in harmony while reciting them? But if they had been established, they must also have been handed down in writing.

The same must be said of bishops and presbyters performing sacred functions. To preserve harmony in celebrating the divine mysteries, they needed to have some booklet of prayers before their eyes. It was not permitted to everyone to compose or alter them at will; nor did it seem suitable or safe to rely solely on memory for prayers and rites of such importance.

The highly praised Saint Basil, speaking of baptism, asks:

> “The threefold immersion of a person—where did we derive it? And the other things that are done in baptism, such as renouncing Satan and his angels—from what Scripture do we have them? Is it not from this teaching, not publicly disclosed and secret, which our Fathers preserved in quiet and undisturbed silence?” (Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*).

Basil’s thought always comes back to this: the rites we now have were transmitted to us from the Apostles without writing, not that it was forbidden to hand them down in writing for the use of the sacred mystery.

Basil himself has no hesitation in inserting these same matters into his writings, just as Tertullian does, who wrote:

> “Finally, to begin with baptism: when we are about to enter the water, and also somewhat earlier in the Church, under the hand of the bishop, we testify that we renounce the devil, his pomp, and his angels. Then we are immersed three times, making a more extensive response than the Lord prescribed in the Gospel” (Tertullian, Book I, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3).

[Col. 0855A]

In former times there were also certain rites and sacred doctrines which the Church customarily concealed from those not yet initiated, especially the mystery of the Eucharist. But ministers of sacred things were never forbidden to transmit these to the faithful or to commit them to writing.

Saint Basil himself may serve as an example. That he composed some liturgy was acknowledged not only by the ancient Greeks but also by Gregory of Nazianzus himself in his oration in praise of Basil (Oration XX). Nazianzus calls it *Εὐχῶν διατάξεις*—“An Order of Prayers”—and it was unquestionably written long before the end of the fourth century.

[Col. 0855B]

Nor can it be denied that Saint Cyril of Jerusalem incorporated into his *Catecheses*, around the year of Christ 347, a substantial portion of the liturgy observed in baptism and in the sacred assembly.

At nearly the same time in Gaul, Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, according to Jerome, “composed a Book of Hymns and another of Mysteries” (Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*). We also possess extensive documents concerning the liturgy in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, published under the false name of Clement, although their origin belongs at least to the fourth century.

What more need be said? Certain chapters concerning the grace of God are attributed to Celestine I, Roman pontiff, and certainly originated in the fifth century of Christ; they are found in collections of councils.

[Col. 0855C]

That author proclaims such great antiquity for the sacred liturgy—if, as I think, he is speaking of the canon—that he traces it back to the Apostles themselves. He says:

> “Let us also consider the sacramental mysteries of the supplications, which, handed down by the Apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the whole world and in every Catholic Church, so that the law of praying establishes the law of believing.”

Then, from those same prayers, he lists several, saying:

> “The bishops of the holy peoples pray that faith may be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may come to their senses through receiving the Catholic faith,” etc.

If prayers of this kind were celebrated uniformly throughout the whole world and in every Catholic Church, and indeed from the age of the Apostles, who could ever believe that they could have been celebrated without writing, and that every bishop and presbyter had retained in memory alone such an extensive series and arrangement of prayers?

[Col. 0855D]

In the fifth century of Christ, as we learn from Gregory of Tours (*History* II, 22), Apollinaris Sidonius, the celebrated bishop of Clermont, “after the little book by which he had been accustomed to perform the sacred solemnities had been wickedly taken from him, nevertheless completed the entire work of the festival from beginning to end, fully prepared, so that he was admired by everyone.”

It was evidently regarded as a marvelous thing that a bishop, without a book and relying solely on memory, had performed the divine mysteries.

Finally, hear what the Fathers of the Third Council of Carthage report. It was held in the year of Christ 397:

> “The first fruits, or honey and milk, which on one most solemn day are customarily offered for the mystery of infants, although they are offered on the altar, nevertheless have their own proper blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood” (Canon 24).

[Col. 0856A]

Who does not see that these blessings had long since been transmitted in writing? They clearly had to be taken from a book, not from memory.

It may also seem astonishing that Father Le Brun should maintain that for four or five centuries of the Church “the Apostles’ Creed” was written down by no one, but had been entrusted solely to memory.

In this connection he presses the following words of Saint Jerome against the errors of John of Jerusalem:

> “In the Creed of our faith and hope, which is said to have been handed down by the Apostles not on paper and in ink, but on the tablets of the heart, after the confession of the Trinity and the unity of the Church, the entire sacrament of Christian doctrine is concluded with the resurrection of the flesh” (Jerome, *Against the Error of John of Jerusalem*, chapter 7).

[Col. 0856B]

He also introduces Saint Augustine, who writes:

> “Say the Creed daily among yourselves. No one writes it down so that it may be read; rather, it is written down for repetition, lest forgetfulness erase what diligence has handed down. Let your memory be your book” (Augustine, *On the Creed for the Catechumens*).

Le Brun uses these passages to show that down to the time of Jerome and Augustine the Apostles’ Creed had been committed by no one to papyrus or parchment, but had been entrusted solely to the memory of the faithful.

The most learned man plainly seems to have forgotten that the Apostles’ Creed was committed to writing by Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, whose *Catecheses* Jerome himself mentions (*On Illustrious Men*).

It is also well known that, before Augustine’s time, Rufinus of Aquileia had explained the same Creed in a commentary, and that it can still be read written out in the Acts of the First Council of Nicaea and of the First Council of Constantinople. It did not cease to be the Creed previously used in the Church on account of certain additions.

What, then, was the meaning of Jerome and Augustine? Nothing other than this: the Creed published under the name of the Apostles was of such great importance that every member of the faithful was to be ordered to commit it to memory and recite it frequently, retaining it written in the mind rather than on paper. This distinguished Christians from the Jews, who carried the law written on tablets of stone and on paper phylacteries, whereas the Christian law was to be inscribed upon the heart.

[Col. 0856D]

Jerome uses the words of the Apostle:

> “You are manifestly an epistle of Christ, prepared by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshy hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3).

Because the Corinthians properly retained the teachings of the Christian law impressed upon their hearts, Paul calls them the epistle of Christ. But those teachings were also read in books.

Indeed, Augustine himself, in the passage recently mentioned, teaches us that the Creed itself had been committed to writing—not so that it might be recited by reading, since each member of the faithful ought to embrace it in memory and recite it from memory, but so that it might, if necessary, be recalled from a written text. This is what he means when he says, “but for repetition”—that is, “for reading again”—“lest forgetfulness erase what diligence has handed down.”

[Col. 0857A]

Saint Leo I, pope, had written a letter to the bishops of Gaul. Here is what they wrote back to him:

> “Your Apostolic writings, just as each person who does not neglect the mysteries of redemption inscribes the Creed of the faith upon the tablets of the heart, he has commended to a tenacious memory, so that he might be more prepared to confound the errors of heretics” (Augustine, *On the Creed for the Catechumens*).

The letter of Leo the Great was certainly written, yet those bishops simultaneously committed it to memory.

See also the Gelasian Sacramentary, edited by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius. There the Creed of the faith is written in Greek, and nevertheless the catechumens are instructed:

> “Therefore learn the Creed with attentive minds; and what we hand down to you, as we have received it, inscribe not upon some material that can perish, but upon the pages of your heart.”

The same is read in the Gallican Missal published by the same Thomasius. Who could infer from this that the Creed had neither been written nor ought to be written?

## CHAPTER II  
### On the Liturgy of the Roman Church

[Col. 0857B]

If you ask what the liturgy of the Roman Church was in the ineffable sacrifice during the first four centuries of the Church, you ask in vain. For what Saint Gregory I, pope, wrote—namely, that “it was the custom of the Apostles to consecrate the sacrificial offering solely by the Lord’s Prayer” (Book VII, Letter 64)—does not compel our agreement, since he asserted it without written documents or witnesses.

This is especially so because the more ancient Fathers of the Church thought otherwise. We saw in the preceding chapter what Saint Basil handed down on this matter.

Now hear what Pope Innocent I wrote concerning the Roman Church itself in the year of Christ 416, that is, so many years before Gregory the Great:

> “If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed Apostles,” he says, “there would be no diversity or variation in those very orders and consecrations” (Letter to Decentius of Gubbio).

He adds below:

> “For who is unaware, or fails to notice, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, the chief of the Apostles, and is preserved down to the present, ought to be observed by all?” etc.

For this to happen, who does not see that writing was necessary?

Finally, he says:

> “There is no doubt that your beloved self has often come to the City, met with us in the church, and learned what custom he observes both in consecrating the mysteries and in carrying out the other secret rites,” etc.

[Col. 0857D]

Innocent, then, believed that the liturgy of the Mass that was in use at that time had descended from the Apostles. Nevertheless, this should not easily be accepted in so broad a sense. It was the custom of those times to refer to the Apostles whatever in sacred matters bore the marks of antiquity, even when its origin was not known; yet some of these things are found to have been instituted after the age of the Apostles.

One thing must be established for certain: whatever belongs to the substance of the sacraments, in which the necessary aids of souls or the chief power of the ineffable sacrifice resides, has always been observed throughout the universal Church from the age of the Apostles down to our own times.

There has never been any disagreement in these matters between Latins and Greeks, or between them and the other faithful of the East—and even now there is none, although many of them have been, or appear to have been, separated from communion with the Roman Church.

There has always been an offering, always a consecration and communion; it has always been believed that the sacred gifts are truly changed into the precious body and blood of the Lord.

Thus the entire variety and dissimilarity, not only between Easterners and Westerners but also among the Churches of the West themselves, lay in the variety of prayers, the diversity of words, and discretionary ceremonies. The Latins used one set of rites and the Greeks another in celebrating the sacraments, while the essence of those sacraments remained untouched. This can be observed especially in the administration of baptism and in the sacrament and sacrifice of the Eucharist.

[Col. 0858B]

Moreover, it is extremely well known that this very variety of rites and prayers once prevailed among the Churches of the West themselves. The Spanish and Gothic liturgy differed from the Roman; the Gallican liturgy differed from both; and the Ambrosian Church had another.

Indeed, every Church and every bishop was permitted to construct his own liturgy with new prayers, and to expand or abridge them. The Greeks attribute the rites of their Masses to Saints Basil and Chrysostom; the Church of Milan attributes the order of its prayers to Saint Ambrose. We have seen that Saint Hilary composed a Book of Mysteries in Gaul. We likewise know, on the testimony of Gennadius, that a Sacramentary and a Hymnary were written by Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, around the year of Christ 412.

In Spain also, various highly learned pastors or presbyters composed and adorned the sacred rites, each according to his own prudence and devotion.

Nor should you think that this was disapproved; rather, you will find it approved by Saint Gregory the Great, Roman pontiff, in a letter sent to Augustine, bishop of Canterbury.

Augustine’s question was:

> “Since the faith is one, why are the customs of the Churches so diverse, and why is one custom of Masses observed in the Roman Church, while another is maintained in the Churches of Gaul?”

Saint Gregory responds to him in these words:

> “Your fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church in which it remembers having been nourished. But it pleases me that, whether in the Roman Church, or in the Gallican, or in any Church, you have found something that can please almighty God more, you should carefully select it and pour into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith, as a special instruction what you have been able to gather from many Churches. For things are not to be loved by us on account of places, but places on account of things. Therefore select from each of the Churches whatever is pious, religious, and right; and, having gathered these things as into a bundle, establish them as a custom among the minds of the English.”

You may gather the same from Saint Augustine of Hippo (Augustine, Letter 64 to Januarius, formerly 118), and from Saint Ambrose—or from the very ancient author of the work *On the Sacraments*.

What is more, even the Roman Church itself was not free from this kind of variety. For, as we shall note below, Pope Leo the Great appears to have restored the sacred liturgy.

[Col. 0859A]

Certainly Pope Gelasius I gave it a new order; then Gregory the Great once more brought it back to the form that has subsequently always been observed, apart from not a few additions of festivals and prayers introduced by the devotion of later ages.

But as regards the canon, in which the awesome mystery of the sacrifice is principally celebrated, no innovation was ever made in it. If some words of slight importance were added by certain Roman pontiffs, this was recorded in their Lives by Anastasius the compiler.

Pope Vigilius offers an illustrious testimony on this matter in a letter written in the year of Christ 538:

> “We declare that the order of prayers in the celebration of the Masses has at no time, on no feast, been divided; rather, we always consecrate the gifts offered to God according to the same form. Whenever the feast of Easter, or of the Lord’s Ascension, or of Pentecost, or of the Epiphany, or of the saints of God is to be celebrated, we append the individual sections appropriate to those days, in which we make remembrance of the holy solemnity or of those whose birth into glory we celebrate; but we continue the rest according to the customary order. Therefore we also send below the text of the canonical prayer, which, by God’s favor, we have received from apostolic tradition” (Pope Vigilius, Letter to Eutherius, or Profuturus).

[Col. 0859B]

The “canonical prayer” mentioned here and said to proceed from apostolic tradition refers to the one canon of the Mass, which was the same in all Masses and was not subject to alteration.

Other rites in the Mass also always remained stable, such as the readings from the Old Testament, the Epistles of the Apostles, and the Gospel, as well as other elements about which liturgical writers have handed down much information.

The difference that we now see between the Mass of the Roman Church and that of the Greeks is not insignificant. It seems to have existed even in the earliest centuries of the Christian faith. For the Romans did not receive their sacred rites from the Greeks, but from the chief Apostles.

Nevertheless, in essentials Rome and the other Churches of the Christian world always continued in agreement. It may be, however, that before Popes Gelasius and Gregory the Great the daily liturgy of the Roman Mass was more extensive than that used in our times.

In the Greek Mass, before the Preface, prayers are said for the Church, for kings, for catechumens, and so forth. Other prayers are also added after the consecration, for the clergy and others.

The Latin author of *On the Sacraments*, if he was not Ambrose, was certainly a very ancient Italian. He says:

> “Praises are offered to God; prayer is requested for the people, for kings, and for the rest” (Author of *On the Sacraments* IV, 4, among the works of Ambrose).

Now in the Roman liturgy the pope, the bishop, and kings are commended to God briefly, and in the Secret prayer. In former times, perhaps, prayers were made for them in distinct prayers at every solemn Mass, as now occurs in the Mass of Good Friday. Some who rely on mere conjecture consider this Mass the most ancient of all, although it is celebrated with the pre-sanctified elements.

[Col. 0860A]

Certainly in ancient centuries many Prefaces were in use. Saint Gregory the Great reduced them to the few now used. Entire psalms were also formerly employed, or sung, in the Mass; this is clear from more than one passage of Saint Augustine and from the homilies of Saint Peter Chrysologus. In our times, however, only a verse from them is sung or recited.

As for why the liturgy was shortened by Pope Gregory, it is permissible to suppose that this was done for the greater convenience of the faithful, so that everyone might be able to participate in the divine mysteries. Formerly many people were occupied with caring for children, guarding fields and animals, serving their masters, and other obligations that I shall omit. As one may reasonably suppose, the length of the liturgy deterred these people from sacred worship.

It therefore seemed better to shorten it, especially after the command to hear Mass every Sunday and on the other solemn feasts had gained force.

[Col. 0860B]

Since it is not now possible to display the liturgy of the earlier centuries of Rome, let us at least bring forth its more ancient monuments and specimens.

A few years ago, the distinguished Father Joseph Blanchini, a priest of the Roman Oratory, published a work after adding a fourth volume to the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs collected by Anastasius and illustrated by his distinguished uncle, Francis. It bore the following title:

> *An Ancient Sacramentary of the Roman Church, Composed by Saint Leo the Pope, Now Published for the First Time from a Manuscript Book Written a Thousand Years Ago, Which Exists in the Library of the Very Distinguished Chapter of Verona.*

It is truly an outstanding and precious monument of venerable antiquity, without equal in this field, since it presents the most ancient liturgy ever used by the Roman Church.

The only regrettable point is that the work has not reached us complete, since much has fallen away, especially the prayers for numerous Sundays, which constitute a principal part of the patrimony of divine worship.

In addition, in the year of Christ 1680, Joseph Maria Thomasius, a cleric regular and later a venerable cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, a man distinguished no less for piety than for learning and highly deserving of sacred letters, published three books of the Sacramentaries of the Roman Church from the distinguished Codex of Christina, Queen of Sweden.

He maintains, and indeed on weighty grounds, that the Missal restored by Pope Gelasius I around the year of Christ 494 is contained there, although he admits that certain items were added in the following century.

[Col. 0860D]

Finally, we have the Gregorian Sacramentary, arranged, that is, by the distinguished pontiff of the Roman Church, Gregory the Great, around the year of Christ 598. Several very ancient copies of it survive in writing.

The oldest of all, as I believe, was supplied to me from a Vatican Codex by the highly praised Father Joseph Blanchini, a man born, according to his ability, to advance the study of sacred letters.

I therefore resolved to present these three Sacramentaries belonging to the Roman Church together, so that readers might have before one view whatever remains of the Roman liturgy from remote antiquity.

Before doing so, however, it is useful to say something about each of these Sacramentaries and to make clear the esteem in which they ought to be held.

## CHAPTER III  
### On the Leonine Sacramentary, to which the name of Saint Leo the Great was prefixed by conjecture

[Col. 0861A]

It was first published, as I recently noted, by Father Blanchini, and below the Sacramentary that he himself conjectured had been composed “by Saint Leo I, pope” will be reprinted. Blanchini subsequently investigated what the judgment of more learned men might be on this matter, and, out of his affection for me, sent me their letters. The distinguished Father Joseph Augustine Ursius, of the Order of Preachers and secretary of the Congregation of the Index, replied that the Sacramentary published by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius did not seem to him to be a work of Gelasius, and that, if the one published by Blanchini is certainly older than the other, it ought rather to be attributed to Gelasius. Since Saint Gregory the Great condensed the Gelasian liturgy, “removing much” (so Ursius argues), and reduced it to a better order, these words do not at all agree with the Thomassian Codex, which is found to be smaller in bulk than the Gregorian. By contrast, such characteristics fit the Blanchinian Codex, which, had it reached us intact, would far surpass the Gregorian in bulk; moreover, what proceeds without order in the Gelasian received its order from Saint Gregory.

But what Ursius presses most strongly to settle this question is that the following prayer occurs on page 51 of the Blanchinian edition in the Leonian Codex:

> We humbly beseech your majesty, O Lord, that the soul of your servant Simplicius, the bishop, stripped of all that it contracted in human life, may be counted among the company of the holy shepherds.

Simplicius ruled the Roman Church after Saint Leo and died in the year of Christ 483. Therefore this Collection could by no means have belonged to Leo the Great. Again, since this prayer must have been composed after the death of Simplicius, the Codex seems to belong to the period of Gelasius, for Gelasius was proclaimed Roman pontiff in the year of Christ 492.

The distinguished Eusebius Amort, regular canon of the collegiate church of the Holy Cross at Polling in Upper Bavaria and professor of sacred theology, also joined the debate over this controversy. Here is his judgment:

> This Sacramentary is not the work of any one pontiff, but is the Sacramentary of the Roman pontiffs, received into use in the earliest times, though enlarged and interpolated by various pontiffs down to the time of Pope Gelasius. In this Sacramentary the hands of Sixtus III, Leo I, and Felix III can be recognized in particular.

He pursues all these matters learnedly and shows, with keen judgment, that they accord with his opinion. Certainly both views deserve praise, and I shall proceed between them—though with hesitant steps—for since this matter can rest only on conjectures, no entirely unshakable judgment should be expected either from them or from me.

First, then, it seems wholly probable that prayers and supplications which had been used in the Roman Church during the first five centuries of the Christian religion, and which could be recovered, were brought into this liturgical treasury. Such is the abundance and variety of them. Additions were repeatedly made to the prayers of the first, second, and third centuries, as seemed to the most holy pontiffs more suitable for increasing reverence for the sacraments and the devotion of the Christian people. In the fourth and fifth centuries, however, a greater number of prayers was probably added, as one may conjecture.

If this conjecture has force, we now understand how highly this Sacramentary should be valued, since it contains the profession of Christian piety and the supplications used in those earliest periods of the Church. Among such prayers, gradually added to the sacred mysteries, it is easy to recognize those that owe their origin to the third, fourth, or fifth century. For whenever new heresies arose and were condemned in orthodox councils, the most learned and pious pontiffs also took care that the Church’s genuine doctrine should be set forth in sermons and sacred prayers and more frequently impressed upon the ears and minds of the Catholic people.

Hence, as circumstances changed, numerous prayers and prefaces arose in which the heresies of Manes, Sabellius, Paul of Samosata, Arius, Apollinaris, Macedonius, Pelagius, Nestorius, and Eutyches were refuted. In the Blanchinian Sacramentary, documents of this truth are scattered throughout. But who the authors of these individual additions were, no one now can indicate, much less determine. Certainly no one would dare deny that whatever appears in the aforementioned Sacramentary should be attributed to the Roman pontiffs, for we recognize most clearly that this Codex was used in the Roman Church.

On the feast of the holy martyrs Paul and John, at Mass 5, we read:

> You have granted us not only to crown the circuit of this City with the sufferings of the martyrs, but also to bury the victorious members of John and Paul within the very heart of the city.

And on the feast of Saint Lawrence, at Mass 5:

> Although the glory of your saints is renowned throughout the whole world, Rome nevertheless rejoices above all others in the solemnity of blessed Lawrence.

Many things also demonstrate with the utmost clarity that the Roman pontiffs themselves used this Sacramentary. On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, number 20, the Preface contains these words:

> You made this see the governing seat of the whole Church, and, to show that what it had preached was to be observed everywhere, you placed in it both the chief of apostolic dignity and the teacher of the nations.

On the birthday of bishops, number 5:

> Although you never cease, through the generosity of your gifts, to enrich your Church, spread throughout the whole world, you nevertheless regard the see of your blessed apostle Peter with all the greater favor, the more exalted you wished it to be. Grant that I, your servant, may fittingly perform the duty required by the arrangements of your providence, etc.

These words have the character of the teaching of Saint Leo I. I pass over other examples of the same kind.

We also learn that this Collection was composed for the use of the Roman Church from the cemeteries and other holy places of the Eternal City, where feasts and stations were once celebrated. There, on the day before the Kalends of October, “the birthday of the basilica of the Angel on the Salarian Way” is recorded.

Elsewhere:

> The birthday of Saint Stephen in the cemetery of Callistus; and of Felicissimus and Agapitus in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way.

And on the sixth day before the Ides of July, the following are recorded concerning the sons of Saint Felicity:

> The birthday of the holy Felix and Philip in the cemetery of Priscilla; of Vitalis, Martial, and Alexander in the cemetery of the Jordanians; of Silanus in the cemetery of Maximus on the Salarian Way; and of Januarius in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way.

These entries breathe an astonishing antiquity.

Second, when we ask who was the author or compiler of this Sacramentary, Father Blanchini, recently mentioned, to whom we owe this treasure, immediately presents himself, asserting that it seems it should bear the name of Saint Leo I. His opinion is indeed supported by not a few conjectures, and by very weighty ones.

Although we have learned from John the Deacon that Sacramentaries for the use of the Roman Church were prepared only by the holy pontiffs Gelasius and Gregory I (John the Deacon, *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*), nevertheless the Roman pontiffs undoubtedly had their own liturgy even before Gelasius. Saint Leo the Great, who deserved well of religion in so many other matters and possessed singular eloquence, could easily have contributed his assistance to adorning and enlarging it.

Indeed, the ancient author of the book entitled *The Jewel of the Soul* writes:

> Leo the pope established that it should be said, “Pray for me, a sinner.” He also composed the Prefaces. (Author of *Gemma animae*, ch. 49.)

Then he adds:

> Pope Leo added to the Canon: “The holy sacrifice, the unblemished victim.” (Same, ch. 90.)

This too is read in the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* by Anastasius the Librarian. Below he says:

> “Let us bless the Lord” is taken from the Psalter; “Thanks be to God,” from the Apostle. But Pope Leo established that these should be said.

Quesnellius further observes:

> Whoever reads the Pontifical and Roman Missal with somewhat greater attention will easily perceive that many passages inserted there bear entirely the flavor of Leo’s phrasing and diction. I therefore have no doubt that a large part of what is recited either in the ecclesiastical offices, especially those of the ancient solemnities—Easter and Pentecost, for example—or elsewhere, was composed or restored by the most holy pontiff Leo I. Among these I believe the Prefaces that precede the Canon of the Mass should be counted, as well as two others contained in the Roman Pontifical, one at the consecration of a bishop and the other at the ordination of a priest. (Quesnellius, vol. I, edition of the works of St Leo, on Sermon 96.)

Nor was the opinion of Cardinal Thomasius different when he wrote:

> Do not, I beg you, attribute the whole of it to Gelasius, but partly to Leo the Great and to his Roman predecessors. Not without reason: I had begun comparing Leonine phrases and sentences with this Codex, and I found here not merely Leo’s style but his very words being recited. Thus, having become more certain, I do not hesitate to assert this with somewhat greater confidence. (Cardinal Thomasius, preface to the *Sacra Gelasiana*.)

It would be easy to confirm what the eminent Thomasius writes with many examples, for the eloquence of Saint Leo and his elegant style strike the eye both in his sermons and letters and in the Blanchinian Sacramentary. I shall offer only one or two examples.

In his first sermon on the Pentecost fast, the holy pontiff says:

> These teachers, then, began the training of Christian warfare with holy fasts, so that, when they were about to fight against spiritual wickedness, they might take up the weapons of abstinence.

In the Sacramentary, at the fast of the fourth month, the following is repeated:

> Grant us, O Lord, to begin the defenses of Christian warfare with holy fasts, so that, as we prepare to fight against spiritual wickedness, we may be fortified with the aids of self-restraint.

Later in the same sermon Saint Leo adds:

> Therefore, after the holy days of joy which we spent in honor of the Lord rising from the dead and afterward ascending into heaven, and after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, the practice has been established, both salutary and necessary, that if negligent freedom and disordered license have perhaps presumed upon anything amid the very joys of the festivities, the discipline of religious abstinence should chastise it. This should also be carried out with greater diligence so that what was bestowed upon us by the Church on this day may remain within us.

But in the Sacramentary, at the fast of the fifth month, the Preface presents the same ideas in almost exactly the same words:

> It is truly right. For after those days of joy which we spent in honor of the Lord rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, and after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, these holy fasts have necessarily been provided for us, so that what has been divinely bestowed may remain in those who live with a pure way of life.

Thus, in Sermon 76, we read:

> The solemn fast, salutarily instituted for the healing of souls and bodies, must be celebrated by us with devoted observance.

The same words occur in the Sacramentary at the fast of the fourth month:

> Be present, O Lord, to our supplications, so that we may celebrate with devoted service this solemn fast, which has been salutarily instituted for the healing of souls and bodies.

Someone might indeed argue that prayers and Prefaces of this kind were extracted from Saint Leo’s sermons by one of the pontiffs who followed him—for example, by Saint Gelasius, the author of the revised Sacramentary. But it is more reasonable to believe that they should be attributed to Leo the Great himself, who in both places—in his sermons as well as in composing sacred prayers—used phrases and ideas familiar to him.

Nor is the foundation of this opinion shaken by the fact that the name of Pope Simplicius appears here. One may conjecture that, when a scribe was copying the Leonine work, he carelessly substituted the name of Simplicius for that of Silvester. Moreover, many things contained in this Sacramentary seem entirely to correspond to the circumstances of the times in which Saint Leo occupied the apostolic see.

Scholars know that during that pontificate Attila’s savage invasion of Italy took place. His enormous army ultimately threatened destruction to the terrified City. Then, in the year of Christ 455, the same City was captured and plundered by Genseric, king of the Vandals. In both events the hand of the merciful God shone over the Romans: first, because he restrained Attila, that most savage devastator of cities, so that he would not advance victoriously against Rome; and then because he removed Genseric so quickly from the captured, though not ravaged, City.

The Sacramentary appears to portray such utterly wretched times. At the fast of the fourth month, number 11, we read:

> O God, who, by the power of your Son and the Holy Spirit, destroyed the treachery of the ancient devastator, and gave us victory over captivity, grant, we beseech you, that those who plot to attack us may be crushed by the right hand of your power.

In July, number 28:

> With thanksgiving we bring gifts to your name, O Lord, because, having been freed from hostile enemies, you grant us to receive the paschal sacrament with tranquil mind.

In the Preface:

> So drive away our vices as you destroy the deadly enemies of our bodies, and do not allow us to endure inward captivity, from which outwardly you have delivered us.

Above, we also find:

> We acknowledge that it belongs to the punishment deserved for our sins that what was acquired through the labor of your servants should be snatched away before our eyes by alien hands, and that what you grant to be produced through the toil of your servants should be suffered to be consumed by enemies, etc.

> We humbly beseech you, by unceasing mercy, to protect us from every assault of mortality.

There are other passages that I pass over, indicating that the Roman people were then subject to severe oppression—something that certainly occurred in the time of Leo the Great. Hear what the holy pontiff himself says:

> Who restored this City to safety? Who rescued it from captivity? Who defended it from slaughter? The Circus games, or the care of the saints? Certainly, by their prayers the sentence of divine judgment was bent, so that we, who deserved wrath, might be preserved for pardon.

Below he adds:

> Return to the Lord, recognizing the wonders that he has deigned to work in us; and attributing our deliverance not, as the impious suppose, to the influence of the stars, but to the ineffable mercy of almighty God, who deigned to calm the hearts of the raging barbarians. (St Leo, Sermon 81, on the octave of the Apostles.)

You may therefore understand that Blanchini had just grounds for attributing the Sacramentary he published to Saint Leo.

Third, these considerations nevertheless cannot provide us with anything certain, and whoever weighs the remaining evidence must admit that the matter is still doubtful. If I may advance what I suspect, it seems more probable to me that this Collection was compiled by someone after the time of Saint Leo. He gathered into a single Codex whatever prayers and Prefaces he found to have been composed by Saint Leo himself and by his Roman predecessors, and did so without that careful selection and refined order which the importance of the matter required.

Permit me to add another conjecture. This same Collection could have been made by Pope Gelasius or under Gelasius, toward the end of the fifth century after Christ. Yet it seems more probable that the work was undertaken under Felix III, who immediately preceded Gelasius. Here is what led me to this opinion.

In July, number 18, the following appears in the Preface:

> You teach us constantly to release the offenses of those who oppose us and to overlook their faults, so that under the appearance of grace we may avoid the malice in which those who wish to harm us strive to persevere. For you wish us to remain, O Lord, like doves and to become wise in the manner of serpents—not, certainly, so that we may harm anyone, but so that we may carefully avoid the deceit of others. You command us to be gentle toward all, while at the same time ordering us to rebuke the restless. For it is one thing to pass over an insult; it is another to be watchful lest we be caught through heedless kindness. Your clemency also releases our errors under this condition: that you forbid us to err again, lest we undergo worse things. Nor should anyone judge that his offense has not been forgiven, or suppose that he has been harmed if the opportunity to harm is instead taken away from him, since by this very act a great benefit is conferred upon such persons: they learn to cease being wicked because they are unable to sin.

Anyone who considers these words carefully draws two conclusions from them quite plainly. First, this Preface was composed by some Roman pontiff who had suffered a powerful enemy, or powerful enemies—calumniators or conspirators—and still feared them. It may refer to the schism raised against Pope Damasus by Ursicinus in the year of Christ 367. It should, however, be referred rather to the schism of Eulalius against Pope Boniface I in the year 419, or to the accusations brought by the former consul Bassus against Pope Sixtus III in the year 433. The *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* and other records attest to these events, although Pagi objects and calls the matter into question.

Nor does this seem to concern the schism of Symmachus and Laurentius, which occurred in the following century. The second conclusion is that these words do not at all agree with the life, character, and deeds of Pope Leo I, toward whom the Roman clergy and people showed perpetual love and obedience. Nor can he reasonably be imagined as the author of such a Preface, since no domestic enemy ever rose against so great a man or plotted against him.

Indeed, the same Preface seems to have been inserted inadvertently into this Collection. It may have been useful to some Roman pontiff in a private dispute with his rivals, but it should not subsequently have found a place in a Sacramentary formed for the use of the later Church.

Other Prefaces not unlike it follow the same one:

> O God, who have willed prudent and sincere concord to dwell in the hearts of your people, grant us to maintain the measure of legitimate love, so that those who depart from the purity of just peace may nevertheless find nothing in us which they can rightly tear apart.

In the same place, at Mass 8:

> Restrain, O Lord, we beseech you, the mouth of those who speak wickedly, and confound those who plot to accuse us.

In the Preface:

> You deign to instruct your servants so that the foolish tearing-apart of the proud may not so much harass us as move us to pity for those who tear us apart.

At Mass 3, the following deserves notice:

> It benefits nothing those who do not perceive their own disgraces and blemishes; and because they do not see themselves, they suppose that they are not seen by others. For when the Apostle cries, “Look at what is according to appearance,” how can those who, as it is written, deceive hearts through their flattering words, and who, as the Gospel says, seek Christ in an inner chamber, trust that they can conceal themselves? They openly and plainly reveal what they accomplish both in words and in deeds. Nor does it support or protect them that, in order to maintain their claim to strength, they run through the divine books; for through these very books they rather both profess and condemn their wicked ways, not knowing that they have been handed over to a debased mind, so that they do what is unfitting, etc.

You find more serious passages at Mass 20 in July, where the Preface reads:

> You instruct us in every respect through heavenly disciplines how we should distinguish false brothers from your faithful ones, etc. For these are puffed up with carnal conceit; these are the ones who, setting their minds on earthly things, despise the words of those who pray to you because, being animal and carnal, they do not grasp in their foolish minds the things that belong to the Spirit of God. These are the ones who, rejected with regard to the faith, although they do not know what they are saying or what they are affirming, have often attempted to overturn it. These are deceitful workers who enter in order to investigate the freedom that the Church has in Christ, so that they may reduce it with themselves to shameful slavery. These are the ones who enter houses and take captive little women burdened with sins, devouring not only the possessions of widows but also those of married women. These people neither seek to appear righteous nor are they, even outwardly, whitened or washed; instead, openly trampling upon shame, they even boast of their depraved way of life. Gathering filth at home and abroad, they are not so much filled with the bones of the dead as themselves dead, etc. These not only deter those who come to your grace by their own foulness, but, while set among the brethren for whom Christ died, they also set before them the stumbling block of their perversity. You command us to beware of such people, etc.

These passages are rather long, but they must not be concealed. Indeed, the more frequently I consider them, the less able I am to persuade myself that they were introduced into the sacred liturgy by any Roman pontiff, much less by one of the more prudent pontiffs. Such things may be tolerated and praised in sermons and letters. But so harsh a censure directed against private individuals sits badly within the divine mysteries and can scarcely be reconciled with their majesty, gentleness, and moderation.

If Prefaces of this kind were composed by a private individual or by some pontiff for a particular emergency, they were certainly not worthy of being preserved in the public and common liturgy. A certain very learned man, in a letter sent to Father Blanchini, interprets these passages as referring to the Manichaeans detected under Saint Leo. He could have added that they might also refer to those under Saint Gelasius. Nevertheless, everyone must plainly acknowledge that these Prefaces do not concern the heretics whom Saint Leo attacks with the keenest eloquence (Sermons 33 and 41; Letter 8 to the bishops of Italy), but rather brothers whose corrupted morals are depicted with unmistakable vividness. From the words quoted, one may also easily infer that at least some members of the clergy were included in their company. And if some of these passages slipped into the Gelasian Sacramentary, no excess of this kind is nevertheless to be detected there.

Now hear why it has seemed to me that this liturgy was compiled during the time of Felix III rather than under his successor Gelasius. We have already seen above that prayers were offered in this Sacramentary for the soul of Simplicius the bishop. It is permissible to suspect that this passage has been corrupted by a scribe. For why is the death of Pope Simplicius joined with the feast of Saint Silvester, when, according to the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* collected by Anastasius, Simplicius was buried on the sixth day before the Nones of March? Why are two prayers there presented in honor of “Saint Silvester,” while a third, which by custom should also have referred to him, speaks of Bishop Simplicius?

We may conjecture that three prayers in honor of Saint Silvester had been placed in the Codex, followed by another Mass for the deposition of Pope Simplicius. While copying this Collection, the scribe may carelessly have passed by a leap from one to the other. Nevertheless, this very mention of Pope Simplicius seems capable of indicating the date of the Collection.

In the Roman Church the custom still persists that an annual funeral is held for the pontiff who most recently died. If Gelasius had composed such a liturgy, why would he have inserted the name of Simplicius rather than that of his predecessor, Pope Felix III? This note seems to indicate the true period, especially because it agrees with the observations made above.

We have already seen how many storms the Roman City endured while Saint Leo I was seated on the pontifical throne, and it has therefore been shown that many things contained here fit his age. But those plunderings, the greater dangers that threatened, and the liberation that followed can also appropriately be referred to the pontificate of Felix III.

For at that time a savage war raged among the barbarians—that is, between Odoacer the king and Theodoric, the Gothic leader and later king—and the dominion over Rome and all Italy was contested. It could not have happened otherwise than that the Roman countryside suffered the gravest hardships and that great alarm shook the City, which divine mercy nevertheless delivered.

In July, at Mass 12, this prayer occurs:

> Assist our times, O Lord, so that your right hand may protect us everywhere, and so that both the integrity of religion and the security of the Roman name may be restored and endure.

Odoacer brought a mob of pagans into Italy, and Theodoric brought the Goths, an Arian people. Because of them, under Pope Felix III, danger was feared both for religion and for the City. Under Pope Gelasius, however, everything at Rome was peaceful, so that these passages seem more properly to be referred to the time of Felix III.

You should also note that, as custom required, prayers were offered to God in this Sacramentary for those ruling at Rome. Thus, in July, at Mass 25:

> Protect, we beseech you, O Lord, the rulers of the Roman name.

At Mass 34:

> Assist the Roman princes.

In August, at Mass 43:

> Defend the rulers of the Roman name.

The same expressions occur in the Gelasian Sacramentary. Why is the name of the emperors or Augusti nowhere used? Apparently because first Odoacer and then Theodoric ruled the City, each content with the title of king, and neither daring to assume the name of emperor or Augustus. Indeed, both revered the Greek Augusti, as did the Roman people, as the supreme lords of the City.

For this reason, at that time the Roman liturgy, praying both for barbarian kings and for emperors, was accustomed to call them in its prayers “the rulers of the Roman name” or “the Roman princes”—a title suitable to both kinds of ruler.

Finally, we should recall what appears in this Sacramentary at Mass 4 in September, on the birthday of bishops. There the Preface reads:

> It is more fitting and appropriate that we celebrate the beginning assumed by the episcopal office on these days, when the devoted observance of the whole Church also comes together, and when the birthday of the very person to whom the priestly ministry has been assigned is celebrated as a sacrament. As, by living more strictly and more chastely, we are transferred into the members of the supreme pontiff and advance in them, we hope that, having attained this temporal honor, it may rather become eternal.

The following prayer comes next:

> Grant, O Lord, we beseech you, that we may rejoice in the increase of our advancement and in the fitting observance of the paschal sacrament.

You find similar words in the following Mass.

From these passages it is evident that, at the time of the fast of Lent—which in the Gelasian and Gregorian liturgies is known by the name of “observance” and “observation”—there coincided a birthday, that is, the anniversary of the ordination or consecration of that Roman bishop or priest—for bishops were then also designated by this name—who should be regarded as the compiler of this Sacramentary, or under whom it was composed.

How I wish this could be applied to Saint Leo the Great! But if we follow Cardinal Baronius, Leo I was ordained supreme pontiff after Easter in the year 440, that is, on the tenth of May; if we follow Papebrochius, on the eighth of September; and if we follow Pagi, on the twenty-second of the same September. Thus you see that Leo is excluded by these calculations.

On the other hand, those who consider Gelasius the author of this Sacramentary find the Codex itself in agreement with them, since he was ordained pontiff on the Kalends of March in the year of Christ 492. That was therefore the second Sunday of Lent, since in that year Easter fell on the fifth of April, not on the seventh of April, as is read through the negligence of the printers in Pagi’s *Baronian Criticism*.

But if this Sacramentary is thought rather to belong to the time of Pope Felix III, his consecration does not conflict with the theory. For according to Anastasius, Pagi, and other writers—Cardinal Baronius differing from them by only two days—the same Felix III was consecrated Roman pontiff in the year of Christ 483, on the sixth of March. Since Easter was celebrated that year on the tenth of April, his birthday must also have fallen on the second Sunday of Lent.

It remains, then, if these conjectures are to be trusted, that this Sacramentary should apparently be referred to the time of Saint Felix III. But who would ever presume to determine whether its author was that pontiff himself or someone else? Someone may have joined together what he judged should be selected from various Sacramentaries then in circulation and burdened the old Roman work with new materials.

Certainly the order and careful selection of material do not appear here in such a form as to persuade us without hesitation that its construction must be attributed to the prudence of some Roman pontiff. Exact chronological connection and the distribution of the feasts are lacking. In September you find a Mass for Saint Peter the Apostle and also a Mass for Saint Lawrence. In September there is an invitation to the people for the fast of the tenth month. Masses for vigils are sometimes confused with Masses for feasts. At times Prefaces are placed without the prayers that precede or follow them.

In July various Masses for the fast and daily prayers are heaped together, followed by a few morning and evening prayers. Daily prayers with their appropriate contents follow, as do other Masses for the fast. Here there is a great accumulation and confusion of Masses and prayers, with no indication of the days on which they were to be used.

In a word, the compiler seems to have written down whatever came before him, without taking the care that was necessary to arrange and order it. Yet you should not charge him with the absence here of any mention of Lent, Easter, or the Sundays recurring throughout the year; for this Sacramentary did not reach us complete, but is mutilated at the beginning and the end. Nevertheless, we find scattered throughout it quite a few prayers for those very Sundays, which must be considered among the most ancient in the liturgy.

In the meantime, whatever one may decide about the author of the Sacramentary itself, it must be repeated that in it we possess a precious and outstanding storehouse of sacred antiquity and of the Roman liturgy. No other liturgical Codex of the Western or Eastern Church survives that approaches such antiquity.

Among the Latin and Greek liturgies known to us—those bearing the names of Saints James, Basil, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Gelasius, and other Fathers—show us any one into which some additions from a later age have not gradually crept. But here, besides the millennial origin of the Veronese Codex, established by Father Blanchini, a competent judge of such matters, you encounter nothing inconsistent with the conditions and learning of the fifth century. Indeed, there are passages that plainly reveal its extraordinary antiquity.

At Pentecost, when those baptized were coming up from the font, the following blessing is read:

> Bless, O Lord, these creatures of yours: the water of the font, honey, and milk. Give your servants to drink from this font of living water, everlasting, which is the Spirit of truth; and nourish them with this milk and honey, as [you did] our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob . . . [deign] to bring them into the promised land, a land flowing with milk and honey. Join your servants, O Lord, to the Holy Spirit, just as this honey and milk are joined, whereby the union in Christ of heavenly and earthly substance is signified, etc.

These, I say, are traces of the more remote centuries after Christ. In the earliest centuries of the Church, it was customary to offer infants emerging from the sacred washing a taste of milk and honey, as sacred symbols signifying their entrance into the lot of the children of God, as into the promised land flowing with milk and honey.

We saw above that this custom, and indeed this prayer, was mentioned in the Council of Carthage, held in the year of Christ 397. Saint Jerome, writing at approximately the same time, said:

> Many other practices observed in the Churches through tradition have claimed for themselves the authority of written law, such as immersing the head three times in the font and then, after emerging, tasting the mixture of milk and honey. (Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*.)

We also have a witness to this rite from the second century after Christ in Tertullian, who, while appealing to tradition, speaks about baptism:

> We are immersed three times, he says, answering something more than the Lord determined in the Gospel. Then, having been received, we taste beforehand the mixture of milk and honey. (Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 3.)

In *Against Marcion* (Book I), he mentions “the association of honey and milk, by which the Creator nurses his little ones.”

Someone may find it strange that the aforementioned Jerome elsewhere writes that not the harmony of milk and honey but “of wine and milk” was offered to those newly baptized. He says:

> This custom and type is preserved to this day in the Churches of the West, so that wine and milk are given to those reborn in Christ. (Jerome, commentary on Isaiah, ch. 55.)

Someone might suspect that a scribe wrote *wine* in place of *honey*. But one should note that Clement of Alexandria, after acknowledging the mixture of milk and honey in baptism, adds:

> Milk is also mixed with wine, etc. (Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, book I, ch. 6.)

Although this passage does not clearly refer to baptism.

In any case, this rite still continues in the Ethiopian Churches, where milk and honey are given to those who have been baptized. We may conjecture, however, that this rite ceased in the Western Churches after the fifth century of Christ, on the basis of the silence of the ancients. For no trace of it survives in the Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries, nor in the most ancient Roman Orders published by Mabillon,
This prayer does indeed occur in the most ancient Roman Order of the divine offices, which Melchior Hittorp published in 1568, but on the sacred day of the Lord’s Resurrection [Col. 0871C], and without any mention whatsoever of the rite of offering milk and honey to the newly baptized. There too are found the blessing of the lamb at Easter, the blessing of other meats, and then the blessing of milk and honey.

I do not wish, however, to conceal that the distinguished Father Martène judged that in the West this rite of presenting milk and honey to neophytes continued until the ninth century (Martène, vol. I, ch. 1, art. 15, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*). For the deacon John, in a letter to Senarius published by Mabillon, introduces an inquirer asking: “Why are milk and honey put into the most holy chalice and offered with the sacrifices on Easter Saturday?” (*Museum Italicum*, vol. I).

Observe carefully what the custom was in the time of that deacon John. Milk and honey were not blessed separately, as in the Leonine Sacramentary [Col. 0871D], but were offered mixed together with wine. Deacon John replies:

> “This kind of sacrament is offered to the baptized, so that they may understand that not others but they themselves, who become participants in the body and blood of the Lord, will receive the promised land. As they begin their journey toward it, they are nourished like little children with milk and honey.”

Here, however, I cannot agree with the very learned men Mabillon and Martène when they attribute this letter to that deacon John who, in the ninth century, acquired considerable renown from his *Life of Gregory the Great* and other books. Was there only one deacon John in the Roman Church? They would have understood that the author of this letter was much older than the other John if they had paid closer attention to what he writes about confirmation conferred by priests [Col. 0872A]. His words are as follows:

> “Nor should this disturb your mind: that necessity sometimes assumes a certain power for itself—for example, as is now said to happen in Africa, that priests prepare the holy chrism. This would rightly be troubling if pontifical authority had not granted this permission.”

In the ninth century, the Christian religion had been entirely cut off in Africa, with the rule and superstition of the Arab people spread everywhere there. What you read here therefore warns us that this deacon John must at least be assigned to the end of the fifth century, when Huneric, the Arian king of Africa, stirred up persecution against the Catholics. It began in the year 485 and then grew more violent. At that time, after the Catholic bishops had been driven into exile, priests were permitted, out of necessity, to confer the chrism [Col. 0872B]. It is also possible that that deacon John flourished before those events.

Here we may repeat what is found in the Council of Carthage of the year 397:

> “In the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord, nothing more is to be offered than what the Lord himself delivered: namely, bread and wine mixed with water. The firstfruits, however—that is, honey and milk—which on the most solemn day are customarily offered in the mystery of infants, namely baptism, although they are offered on the altar, nevertheless have their own proper blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the body and blood” (Third Council of Carthage, canon 24).

Since deacon John did not disapprove of the mixing of milk and honey with the blood of the Lord—a practice disapproved by the Fathers of Carthage—there arises a suspicion that he himself flourished in the fourth century of the Christian era [Col. 0872C]. Yet this contributes to our subject, since in the Leonine or Blanchinian Sacramentary the blessing of milk and honey is distinguished from the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord. From this we may rightly infer its exceedingly remote antiquity. An argument of no less strength is also supplied by the small number of feasts; we shall discuss this matter in the following chapter.

Nor should what is found here concerning confessors be passed over in silence. In April, at the ninth Mass, this preface occurs:

> You are wondrous in strength not only among your martyrs but also among your confessors; for although the martyrs are renowned for their suffering, since they endured bitter punishments under manifest torments, these others too, afflicted and tortured by a resolve to practice hidden self-discipline [Col. 0872D], have followed in their footsteps through the practices of spiritual observance.

In the following preface there is this further passage:

> While even now you glorify your confessors with so great a solemnity, you teach at the same time both that no holy purpose before you is without reward and that, apart from more arduous struggles, you also invite the weak to the gift of your recompense.

The distinguished palms of your confessors and martyrs are also mentioned in the thirty-eighth Mass.

It is possible that this mention of confessors may seem to detract somewhat from the antiquity of this Sacramentary. For learned men know that in the earliest centuries of the Church there was a distinction between martyrs and confessors. Those who gave their blood, and thereby their lives, for Christ were called martyrs; those who endured exile, prisons, or torments [Col. 0873A] in confessing the Christian profession were given the name confessors. As time proceeded, however, the name confessor was transferred also to those who surpassed others in a most devout manner of life and in virtue.

But this does not conflict with the antiquity of this Sacramentary. For in the fifth century of the Christian era, when we have said that it was compiled, the term *confessor* had already been extended to men distinguished by holiness of every kind. Feasts of such confessors were instituted later than those of martyrs; nevertheless, in the fifth century itself their celebrations also began to become established.

Most famous under this title was Saint Martin, bishop of Tours. Concerning him, Apollinaris Sidonius wrote in the year 482:

> “Perpetuus, bishop and successor worthy of so great a predecessor, renovated the basilica of the holy pontiff and confessor Martin, making it much more spacious than the former building, which until then had been sufficiently capacious” (Apollinaris Sidonius, book IV, letter 16).

And below:

> “Which was not equal to its own confessor.”

Indeed, observe that this Sacramentary contains no feast of confessors, except that of Saint Sylvester. Yet it is highly plausible that he did not lack the merits of the ancient confessors, since he lived under pagan emperors before Constantine the Great gained possession of Rome. It may also be questioned whether he had already been added to the roll of the saints, since prayers seem here to have been used at his burial, and the title “saint” was at that time also given to living bishops.

What is more, the commemoration of Saint Sylvester [Col. 0873C] is placed here in November, and no feast of his is presented on the day before the Kalends of January, although one finds such a feast in the Gregorian Sacramentary. This too provides some indication of remarkable antiquity.

In April, at the twentieth Mass, you may read these words:

> “Whose Church is now composed in such a way of true and false confessors that the changeability of human frailty must nevertheless always be guarded against, and the conversion of no one may be despaired of.”

I do not think these words concern confessors of the second kind, that is, devout men. For who would call false confessors those to whom the name *confessor* did not at all belong? They should rather be interpreted of confessors of the first kind, who before the pagans pretended that they had confessed the name of Christ.

Unless one prefers to understand this as referring to the African persecution stirred up under Pope Felix III, as we hinted above, this preface must be assigned to the third century of the Christian era [Col. 0873D]. For we know that in the age of Saint Cyprian there were confessors unworthy of that name, as is clear from his writings (*On the Unity of the Church*, ch. 18; Letter 57).

To confirm more fully the antiquity of the Leonine Sacramentary, it is also useful to observe that it employs not the Vulgate that we use, but the old Italian version of Holy Scripture.

In June one finds:

> “Unless a grain of wheat (*tritici*) falling into the earth …” (John 12:24).

The Vulgate has:

> “Unless a grain of grain (*frumenti*) …”

In July the following is found here:

> “Separate yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly” (2 Thessalonians 3:6).

The Vulgate has:

> “That you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly” [Col. 0874A].

In September one reads here:

> “Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work” (1 Timothy 3:1).

But the Vulgate has:

> “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work.”

In December we have here:

> “Behold, a Virgin has conceived in the womb, etc., whose power is upon his shoulders” (Isaiah 7:14; 9:6).

The Vulgate has:

> “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive, etc., whose power is upon his shoulder.”

It therefore appears that when this liturgy was compiled, the use of the Vulgate had not yet been established in the Roman Church.

What remains is that from this outstanding Sacramentary we can gather a rich harvest of ecclesiastical learning. Here there is an abundance of statements refuting the Arian, Pelagian, Nestorian, and Eutychian heresies. Here are the primacy of the apostolic see and the unimpaired doctrine of that same Church, which God also established as teacher of the other churches. Here it is said that the holy apostles Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom on the same day, though not in the same year—a view also held by Saint Jerome, Prudentius, and others. On this matter, however, see Pagius (*Criticism of Baronius*, under the year 258).

No learned person is unaware of what the British scholar Dodwell wrote concerning the small number of martyrs (*Dissertation 11*). Should greater trust be placed in him, or in the writers of the ancient centuries? To say nothing of others, Paulinus of Nola, bishop, wrote in the year 406, in the thirteenth *Natalicium*, which I have rescued from obscurity:

> Here are Peter, here Paul, the leaders, here all the martyrs,
>
> Whom the circuit of the great City holds together in countless numbers. [Col. 0874C]

Saint Leo, in his sermon on the feast of the apostles (Sermon 8), records:

> “Thousands of blessed martyrs, emulating the triumphs of the apostles, surrounded our City with purple-clad peoples shining far and wide.”

You have similar passages in this Sacramentary. In April, at the seventh Mass, its preface reads:

> “For it is the work of your hand and your mercy that to an innumerable multitude of your saints it has been granted not only to believe in your Son, our Lord, but also to suffer for him.”

And below, at the twenty-eighth Mass:

> “Grant us, Lord, we ask, to escape together all sins and all dangers of body and mind, whom you surround with the devout confession of innumerable martyrs.”

Many other matters also occur there: the intercession of the saints; vigils before their feasts; suffrages for the dead; the nuptial blessing; the ordinations of the clergy; and other such doctrines and rites of the Catholic Church transmitted to us from the venerable antiquity of earlier centuries.

You will also observe that so many prayers now used in the sacred liturgy have descended to us from the religious devotion and sacred eloquence of those times. The Ascension of the Lord is mentioned both here and in the Gelasian and most ancient Gregorian Sacramentaries, as you will see below. Elegant Latin required *Ascensionem* and *Ascensum*. *Ascensa* was in use among the Christian people, and the word still survives among the Venetian people, the people of Modena, and other peoples of Italy.

Since you find here so many Masses and prayers for martyrs, as we now call them, “of the common,” you should know that this was done so that Masses might be available for individual martyrs and other saints whose sacred bodies were buried within the City—or rather, in the suburban cemeteries—or in whose honor temples had been dedicated to God.

Saint Gregory the Great writes as follows to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria:

> “We possess in a single book the names of nearly all the martyrs, with their sufferings distinguished according to each day”—by these words he means a martyrology—“and on each day we celebrate the solemn rites of Mass in their honor” (Gregory the Great, book VII, letter 29, indiction 1).

At that time, I think, a common Mass of the martyrs would have been celebrated. But what is meant by saying that Mass was performed daily in honor of those same martyrs perhaps requires some explanation. For it cannot be believed that a Mass of martyrs was celebrated during Lent or on Sundays [Col. 0875B–0876A]. Nevertheless, in those cemeteries or sacred buildings where their bodies lay, it must be supposed that it was formerly customary to celebrate Mass in their honor when the annual commemoration of those martyrs came around.

Finally, the reader should be advised that although we have no certain information about the author of this precious and most ancient of all Sacramentaries, it may nevertheless retain the name of Saint Leo the Great, under which Father Blanchini has published it. This is so both because it contains more material originating from that most holy pontiff than anyone might suppose and also so that it may henceforth be distinguished from the Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries.

The antiquity of the Veronese Codex from which the Sacramentary itself was copied will be confirmed by a specimen of its script, engraved on copper in the following table through the care of the same Father Blanchini [Col. 0876B].

[Col. 0877]

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the Feasts Occurring in the Leonine and Other Sacramentaries of the Roman Church

[Col. 0877A]

If the Leonine Sacramentary had come down to us complete, perhaps a greater light would have been shed for determining its age. Let us nevertheless test whether the few portions that escaped the injuries of time may assist us in this inquiry.

For my part, when I consider the feast days mentioned in it, I think that a strong indication of great antiquity can be drawn from them. No solemnity of a confessor is seen there except that of Saint Sylvester, pope; yet below you will see his name added to the calendars of the blessed as early as the fourth century of the Christian era. Perhaps, too, the Mass found there was celebrated not for his feast but only for his annual burial commemoration [Col. 0878A].

There is no mention there of the Finding or Exaltation of the Holy Cross, nor of the Assumption or Nativity of the Mother of God. But what it is especially useful to remember is that the catalog of feasts described here is exceedingly similar to the oldest of all calendars, which Aegidius Bucherius of the Society of Jesus once published. It is rightly believed to have been written around the middle of the fourth century, both because no Roman pontiff later than that period is mentioned among its feasts and because in that Codex the catalog of Roman pontiffs ends with Liberius, without any mention of him.

Since this calendar is brief and rare, no one will object to its being transferred here and viewed alongside the Leonine calendar, so that the similarity between them may more easily be detected.
