## THE LEONINE CALENDAR

[Col. 0878B]

(The earlier months have been lost.)

- 14 April: Saint Tiburtius. The Paschal season.
- 23 April: George the martyr. The dedication of the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. The Ascension of the Lord. The day before Pentecost. At Pentecost, for those ascending from the font. Pentecost Sunday. The fast of the fourth month.
- 24 June: The feast of Saint John the Baptist.
- 26 June: The feast of Saints John and Paul.
- 29 June: The feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.
- 10 July: The feast of the holy martyr Felix.
- 10 July: Philip in the cemetery of Priscilla; Vitalis, Martial, and Alexander in the cemetery of the Jordanians; Silanus in the cemetery of Maximus on the Salarian Way; and Januarius in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way.
- 3 August: The feast of Saint Stephen in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.
- 6 August: The feast of Saint Sixtus in the cemetery of Callistus; and of Felicissimus and Agapitus in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way.
- 10 August: The feast of Saint Laurence.
- 13 August: The feast of Saints Hippolytus and Pontianus.
- 30 August: The feast of Saints Adauctus and Felix.
- 14 September: The feast of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian.
- 16 September: The feast of Saint Euphemia.
- The fast of the seventh month.
- 30 September: The feast of the basilica of the Angel on the Salarian Way. The burial of Saint Sylvester.
- 9 or 8 November: The feast of the Four Crowned Martyrs.
- 22 November: The feast of Saint Cecilia.
- 23 November: The feast of Saints Clement and Felicity.
- 24 November: The feast of Saints Chrysogonus and Gregory.
- 30 November: The feast of Saint Andrew the apostle.
- 25 December: The Nativity of the Lord, and of the martyrs Pastor, Basileus, Jovianus, Victorinus, Eugenia, Felicity, and Anastasia.
- 27 December: The feast of Saint John the Evangelist.
- 28 December: The feast of the Innocents.

[Col. 0879B]

Now compare the two calendars: the Bucherian, which learned men judge to have been written around the year 355 of the Christian era, and the Leonine, which from conjecture we think was written around the year 488. They agree in many matters and differ in others. Some feasts are recorded in the former that are not found in the latter. Conversely, other feasts are presented in the Leonine calendar of which the Bucherian contains no mention.

For our purposes, nothing occurs in the Leonine calendar that conflicts with the opinion concerning its age. “The day before the Kalends of October” is marked as “the feast of the Basilica of the Angel on the Salarian Way.” This solemnity might arouse a suspicion of lesser antiquity, for, according to Anastasius, “in the time of Pope Gelasius I the church of Saint Michael on Mount Gargano was discovered”—that is, around the year 495 of the Christian era—and from that time other basilicas appear to have been erected in honor of Saint Michael.

But apart from the fact that those words are not found in three manuscripts of Anastasius, it certainly cannot be inferred from them that no basilica in Rome had been built much earlier in honor of the holy Angel. According to Anastasius himself, the Roman pontiff Symmachus, around the year 499, “enlarged the basilica of the archangel Michael, built steps, and brought in water.” Do you see that this basilica had previously been built and was merely enlarged by Symmachus?

Therefore take care not to interpret Adon, when he records that after the apparition of the archangel at Gargano, “not long afterward” Pope Boniface—who can be none other than Boniface II—built in Rome “the church of Saint Michael at the summit of the Circus,” as though that had been the first sacred building in the City to bear the title of Saint Michael [Col. 0880B–C]. Before Boniface II, as we have shown, at least one basilica of that angel was already venerated by the Romans.

The basilica mentioned in the Leonine Sacramentary was situated on the Salarian Way, and its “feast,” that is, its annual dedication day, was honored. We also find the custom of annually renewing the dedication of churches attested by Saint Leo the Great.

Moreover, observe that the feast of that dedication is recorded on the day before the Kalends of October, whereas for many centuries the solemnity of Saint Michael has been celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of October. That dedication therefore did not concern the basilica at Gargano, but rather a Roman basilica built on the Salarian Way.

The feast day of Saint Stephen in the Leonine Sacramentary must also be considered. There he is commemorated only on 5 August: “the feast of Saint Stephen in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.” In the fourth Mass he is called “his birthday.” But in the ninth Mass the annual dedication of some basilica built in honor of the holy protomartyr seems to be marked, for the preface reads:

> “Rejoicing in this festival, on which blessed Stephen the martyr marked the basilica dedicated to your name with his own honor.”

In the fifth century of the Christian era there was more than one basilica of Saint Stephen in the City and outside it, as is recorded in the Lives of the Roman pontiffs Saints Leo I and Simplicius preserved by Anastasius [Col. 0881A].

At first glance I had persuaded myself that, at the time when this Sacramentary was committed to writing, the feast of the protomartyr Stephen had not yet been celebrated after the Nativity of the Lord, namely on 26 December, since there is no mention of him on that day. But, looking at the seventh Mass, I found these words in the preface:

> “And therefore the Nativity of your Son is rightly followed, above all others, by the festival of his passion: the first martyr encounters his everlasting glory.”

Thus the feast of the holy protomartyr was already in use on 26 December as well, although the compiler’s negligence has left no mention of him on that day.

On the other hand, in both the Gelasian and the most ancient Gregorian Sacramentary that we shall publish below, you will find no feast of Saint Stephen on 5 August. Nor is there any trace of it in the Vienna and Modena Codices. You should therefore understand that the feast of the Finding of Saint Stephen does not possess the antiquity attributed to it by some.

In the most ancient times, as is clear from the Leonine calendar, the dedication of some basilica was celebrated on 5 August. Later, when this feast had fallen out of use and the devotion of subsequent pontiffs toward the holy protomartyr sought renewal, the feast was given the title of the Finding of his relics.

In the Bucherian Calendar, on 14 November, there is the feast of the martyrs “Clement, Sempronianus, Claudius, and Nicostratus at the Palace.” In the Leonine calendar there is only “the feast of the Four Crowned Martyrs.” I suspect that instead of *in Comitatum*, which admits no tolerable sense in the Bucherian calendar, *Quatuor Coronatorum* was written, and that Bucherius, because the characters were corrupt, read *in Comitatum* [Col. 0881C]. Perhaps the date there was also 9 November, or 8 November, since on that day the feast of the Four Crowned Martyrs recurs in the most ancient martyrologies.

Their names are given in the Bucherian calendar: “Clement, Sempronianus, Claudius, and Nicostratus.” Among the martyrologists there is no slight disagreement, indeed considerable confusion. The ancients related that in the age of Pope Miltiades the names of these martyrs had been lost, and that consequently the name “Four Crowned Martyrs” came into use.

The Bucherian Calendar exposes this as a fable, since it expressly gives their names, apparently as they were conjectured under Pope Liberius. In Cardinal Baronius’s Roman Martyrology, these names are later said to have been revealed, namely “Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus.” Usuard and others had previously held the same view. But this very Roman Martyrology calls for correction, since foreign names were substituted after the true names of the Four Crowned Martyrs had been abandoned [Col. 0881D].

You have already learned from the Bucherian Calendar what names the Four Crowned Martyrs bore. Perhaps the name Clement should be replaced by Castor, for this is how it is written in the most ancient Martyrologies. In the Gelasian Sacramentary, on 8 November, the feast is recorded as that of “the Four Crowned Martyrs: Costianus, Claudius, Castor, and Simpronianus.” The names Claudius and Sempronianus are correct; Costianus may have been substituted for Nicostratus.

The ancient Gregorian Codices present on this day “Claudius, Nicostratus, Simphronianus, Castorius,” and “Simplicius.” But this Simplicius was unwillingly brought into the ranks of the Four Crowned Martyrs. The Martyrology published under Jerome’s name has only “Claudius, Castor, Nicostratus.” Sempronianus, or Symphorianus, has dropped out.

The same names are repeated in the most ancient Gregorian Codex of Modena. But on the margin some pedant, writing in another hand, inserted another Mass under the false title of the Four Crowned Martyrs, namely “Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus,” and “Victorinus.”

Nor should Father Sollerius of the Society of Jesus be left unmentioned. In his commentary on Usuard’s Martyrology (*Acta Sanctorum*, Bollandists, vol. VII, July), he sought the names of the Four Crowned Martyrs in the Bucherian Calendar on 7 August, where the feast of “Secundus, Carpophorus, Victorinus,” and “Severianus, at Albano and on the Ostian Way” is recorded [Col. 0882A]. But they should have been sought on 9 or 8 November.

He adds: “But what do ‘at Albano’ and ‘on the Ostian Way’ mean?” These words indicate that some of the sacred bodies were preserved in the town of Albano, unless one prefers to understand “on the road leading to Albano,” while the remainder were on the Ostian Way.

You should also observe that just as after the Sacramentary was restored or organized by Saint Gregory I the list of feasts was not fixed in the Roman Church, nor among those who imitated it, so before Saint Gregory there were various customs in this matter.

In the Gregorian calendar, 18 January contains “the feast of Saint Prisca”; 22 January, “the feast of Saint Vincent”; and 23 April, “the feast of Saint Gregory,” to omit other feasts. Yet nothing concerning these is found in the Gelasian calendar. Conversely, the Gelasian Codex presents feasts for which there was no place in the Gregorian.

The Bucherian Calendar, the most ancient of all, has on 2 August the feast of “Saint Stephen, pope, at Callistus,” which you also find in the most ancient Gregorian Missals. Yet in the Leonine and Gelasian calendars there is no trace of this feast.

The Catholic Church now celebrates the feast days of the apostles, commemorating them individually or in pairs. But in the ninth century, when the oldest Gregorian Codices were written, there were only five feasts of the apostles. For the feast of the apostles Philip and James was celebrated on 1 May; that of Saint Peter on 29 June; that of Saint Paul on the following day; that of Saint Andrew on 30 November; and that of Saint John the Evangelist on 27 December [Col. 0882D].

From the Gelasian calendar we learn that “the feast of all the apostles” was formerly celebrated within the octave of the apostles Peter and Paul. See there, in book II, chapter 35, the Mass “for the feast of all the apostles.”

The antiquity of this feast and Mass is confirmed by the Leonine Sacramentary, in which, at the twenty-first Mass, during the octave of those chief apostles, the following prayer is read:

> “Almighty and everlasting God, who have granted us to venerate the merits of all the apostles in a single celebration, we ask that, as intercessors are multiplied, you may bestow the abundant and swift favor of your mercy.”

From this source the prayer once used by the Church on the feast of All Saints was taken.

I may also observe that the Roman Calendar published for the public by the celebrated Benedictine monks Martène and Durand is not of such great antiquity. In it the feast of “Saint James the apostle” appears on 25 July; on 25 August, “Saint Bartholomew the apostle”; and on 21 September, “Saint Matthew the apostle.”

But in the ninth century of the Christian era such celebrations had not yet been established in the Roman Church, as is clear from the most ancient Codices of the Gregorian Sacramentary: the Vatican, Ottobonian, Vienna, and Modena [Col. 0883B]. Consequently, those Codices used by Pamelius and Menard must be judged inferior to them in antiquity; for in them the feasts of the three apostles just mentioned are found.

Nor will you find in the ancient Gregorian Codices, in the month of January, the solemn day of “Saint Vincent the martyr,” which nevertheless appears in the Martenian Calendar. That calendar also records on 23 July “the feast of Saint Apollinaris, martyr of Ravenna.” But such a feast is nowhere found in the most ancient Gregorian Sacramentaries. You now understand that considerably less antiquity must be assigned to that calendar than those most learned monks believed.

Although from the Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries, which we shall publish below, the reader can determine for himself how many feasts were gradually introduced into the Roman Missal and Breviary down to our own times, I have nevertheless thought it useful to append their calendars as well, so that the feasts of the several periods may be viewed together at a single glance.

# The Ancient Gregorian Calendar

[Col. 0884B]

## January

On the Kalends, the Octave of the Lord. On the eighth day before the Ides, the Epiphany. On the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, Saint Felix in Pincis. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, Saint Marcellus, pope. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, Saint Prisca. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, Saints Fabian and Sebastian. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, Saint Agnes. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, Saint Vincent. On the fifth day before the Kalends of February, Saint Agnes for the second time.

## February

[Col. 0884C]

On the fourth day before the Nones, the Ypapante, or Purification of Saint Mary. On the Nones, Saint Agatha. Septuagesima. Sexagesima. Quinquagesima. Quadragesima. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, Saint Valentine.

## March

On the fourth day before the Ides, Saint Gregory the Pope. On the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the Annunciation of Saint Mary. Easter.

## April

On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, Saints Tiburtius and Valerian. On the ninth day before the Kalends of May, Saint George. On the fourth day before the Kalends of May, Saint Vitalis.

## May

On the Kalends, the Apostles Philip and James. On the fifth day before the Nones, Saints Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus. On the day before the Nones, the feast of Saint John before the Latin Gate. On the sixth day before the Ides, Saints Gordian and Epimachus. The Ascension of the Lord. On the fourth day before the Ides, Saint Pancras. Pentecost. On the third day before the Ides, the feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs. On the eighth day before the Kalends of June, Saint Urban, pope.

## June

[Col. 0886A]

On the Kalends, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Nicomedes. On the fourth day before the Nones, Saints Marcellinus and Peter. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, Saints Mark and Marcellian. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, Saints Protasius and Gervasius. On the eighth day before the Kalends of July, the feast of Saint John the Baptist. On the sixth day before the Kalends of July, Saints John and Paul. On the fourth day before the Kalends of July, Saint Leo, pope. On the third day before the Kalends of July, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul the Apostles. On the day before the Kalends of July, the feast of Saint Paul.

## July

On the sixth day before the Nones, Saints Processus and Martinian. On the sixth day before the Ides, the feast of the Seven Brothers. On the fourth day before the Kalends of August, Saints Felix, Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrice. On the third day before the Kalends of August, Saints Abdon and Sennen.

## August

[Col. 0886B]

On the Kalends, Saint Peter in Chains. On the fourth day before the Nones, Saint Stephen, bishop. On the Nones, Saints Sixtus, bishop, Felicissimus, and Agapitus. On the sixth day before the Ides, Saint Cyriacus. On the fourth day before the Ides, the feast of Saint Lawrence. On the third day before the Ides, Saint Tiburtius. On the Ides, Saint Hippolytus. On the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, Saint Eusebius, priest. On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, the Assumption of Saint Mary. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, Saint Agapitus. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, Saint Timothy. On the fifth day before the Kalends of September, Saint Hermes. On the fourth day before the Kalends of September, Saint Sabina. On the third day before the Kalends of September, Saints Felix and Adauctus.

## September

[Col. 0886C]

On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, Saints Cornelius and Cyprian. Also, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, the feast of Saint Nicomedes. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, the feast of Saints Euphemia, Lucia, and Geminianus. On the fifth day before the Kalends of October, Saints Cosmas and Damian. On the third day before the Kalends of October, the dedication of the basilica of the holy angel Michael.

## October

On the Nones, the feast of Saint Mark, pope. On the day before the Ides, the feast of Saint Callistus, pope.

## November

[Col. 0886D]

On the Kalends, Saint Caesarius. On the sixth day before the Ides, the Four Crowned Saints. On the fifth day before the Ides, the feast of Saint Theodore. On the third day before the Ides, the feast of Saint Menas. Also, Saint Martin, bishop. On the tenth day before the Kalends of December, Saint Cecilia. On the ninth day before the Kalends of December, Saint Clement. Also, Saint Felicitas. On the eighth day before the Kalends of December, Saint Chrysogonus. On the Ides, Saint Lucia. On the eighth day before the Kalends of January, the Nativity of the Lord. On the seventh day before the Kalends of January, the feast of Saint Stephen. On the sixth day before the Kalends of January, Saint John the Evangelist. On the fifth day before the Kalends of January, the Holy Innocents. On the day before the Kalends of January, Saint Sylvester, pope.

# Chapter V. On the Gelasian Sacramentary

[Col. 0887A]

As regards the Sacramentaries of the Roman Church, the ancient records have nothing else to report except that Pope Gelasius I composed, around the year of Christ 495, “prefaces and prayers of the sacraments in carefully composed language,” as is clear from his Life by Anastasius the Librarian. In an older catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, however, which the distinguished Father Joseph Blanchinius, priest of the Roman Oratory, made publicly available, the following is reported concerning Gelasius: “He also composed hymns in the manner of blessed Ambrose. He also composed prefaces of the sacraments in carefully composed language” (Blanchin., in the prolegomena to vol. IV of Anastasius). Nothing is said there about prayers.

There was undoubtedly a Sacramentary belonging to the Roman Church before the time of Saint Gelasius; and therefore Gelasius should be thought to have merely restored it, arranged it in a better order, and enlarged it with other prefaces. Saint Gregory the Great, then, as John the Deacon testifies, around the year of Christ 591, “having removed much from the Gelasian Book concerning the solemn rites of the Mass, altered a little, and added some things for the exposition of the Gospel readings, compressed it into the volume of a single book” (John the Deacon, *Life of Gregory the Great*).

Those words—“for the exposition of the Gospel readings”—are obscure, unless we are to understand that an Evangelistary too was restored by the holy pontiff, of which nothing is found among the ancient writers. Cardinal Bona and Mabillon observed that Gelasian books of the Sacraments still survived in the ninth century. Certainly, in the year of Christ 831, at the monastery of Centula, as is established from its Chronicle preserved by D’Achery, there were kept “fourteen Gelasian Missals and three Gregorian ones” (D’Achery, *Chronicle of the Monastery of Centula*, *Spicilegium*).

In the year 1680, Joseph Maria Thomasius, a Cleric Regular and later an eminent and venerable cardinal of the holy Roman Church—a man distinguished no less for piety than for learning, and one who rendered outstanding service to sacred letters—published three books of the Sacraments of the Roman Church from the distinguished manuscript Codex of Christina, Queen of Sweden, which had been brought from Gaul into Italy. Being a most modest man, he advanced only conjectures that seemed to suggest that this was the Gelasian Sacramentary, although he himself also acknowledged and admitted that certain feast days had been added to it in subsequent centuries.

Before Thomasius, the celebrated men John Morinus and Cardinal Bona had adopted the same opinion. They were not unfamiliar with the same manuscript Codex of the Queen of Sweden, and believed that it ought to be attributed to Gelasius as its author. Their opinion, indeed, seems wholly deserving of adherence. For it is certain that the Sacramentary presented there was constructed for the Roman Church and formerly used there, since its title reads, “Book of the Sacraments of the Roman Church,” and since Masses are recorded there for saints whose feasts were celebrated in that Church.

Whether, then, it is the Gelasian or the Gregorian Sacramentary—for no others were in use in the Roman Church after the end of the fifth century—it is not Gregorian; therefore it must be Gelasian. The same truth is confirmed by what is transmitted in Book Three, Mass 58 and the following Masses, for wartime, where God is asked to protect the dominion of the Roman kings subject to him; to crush the enemies of the Roman name by the power of his majesty; to be present with the princes of the Roman kingdom; to defend the rulers of the Roman Empire; to crush the ferocity of barbarian peoples; and where God, “the protector of all kingdoms, and especially of the Roman Empire,” is asked to grant his servants, our kings, triumph, and so forth. God, “in whose hand are the hearts of kings,” is asked to place the governance of our princes, his servants, under his wisdom, and so forth.

In the time of Saint Gelasius, prayers were offered to God for the Greek emperors, because they retained supreme rule in the City, but at the same time prayers were offered for the Gothic kings who ruled that same City. There is a Mass there for the Kalends of January entitled “To Be Kept from Idols.” Read the learned notes of Cardinal Baronius on this day in the *Roman Martyrology*, and you will understand how much the Roman pontiffs and the other bishops labored in the fourth and fifth centuries of Christ to remove pagan superstitions from that day. These matters belong to the time of Saint Gelasius.

Likewise, in Book One, Mass 85, we read: “Blessing over those who return from the Arian to the Catholic unity.” These things agree with the age of Gelasius, as you see. For the Arian heresy had not yet been extinguished, and while Gelasius himself was alive the Goths, who ruled Italy, professed it.

Cardinal Thomasius long ago observed that the Codex from which this Sacramentary was taken had been written in Gaul, and had there been intended for the use of some Church. In Gaul and Spain, however, before the year 800, the addition of *Filioque* had been made to the Constantinopolitan Creed concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son; and thus the Creed was sung in the sacred rites. Pope Leo III nevertheless by no means approved this in the year 809, as the Acts published by Cardinal Baronius under that year show. Since this addition is not found in the Creed of this Sacramentary, it is rightly inferred that the Codex had been written before that time.

Moreover, according to Anastasius, Pope Gregory II, around the year 720, “instituted that during Lent, on Thursday, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place in the Churches, where this had not been done.” Since no Mass is assigned in this Sacramentary to the Thursdays of Lent, its antiquity may also be estimated from this fact. It is further significant that no feast days are assigned here to the holy pontiffs Sylvester, Leo the Great, or Gregory the Great.

You will find the remaining arguments used by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius in his preface to establish its antiquity. Yet additions were made to the Sacramentary itself after Gelasius. We do not deny this at all. But it does not prevent Saint Gelasius from being called its author, just as no one deprives the Gregorian liturgy of its author because other prayers, feasts, and rites were introduced into it after Saint Gregory.

Certainly, the following occur here: on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, a Mass for the feast of Saint Juliana; on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, a Mass for the feast of Saint Magnus; on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, a Mass for the feast of Saint Rufus; and on the Kalends of September, a Mass for the feast of Saint Priscus. These feasts belonged not to the Roman Churches but to the Gallican Churches. There is also a Mass there for the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, a feast which, as learned men know, was instituted after the time of Saint Gelasius. The beginning of the Lenten fast is likewise assigned to the Wednesday of Quinquagesima, which cannot be reconciled with the age of Gelasius.

These facts, I say, do show that the Codex was written long after the age of Gelasius; but they do not at all prevent the Sacramentary itself from being called Gelasian and rightly attributed to that pontiff. Since under Charles the Great, king of the Franks, before the year 800, the Gallican liturgy was abolished, the Gregorian liturgy prevailed, and the Gelasian ceased in those places where it had previously been used, we are led to recognize that the Codex itself was written before that time.

At the end of the preceding century, however, James Basnage, Samuel’s cousin, a member of the Calvinist party, rose up against the Gelasian liturgy—or rather against the Codex published by the venerable Thomasius. Speaking of the ancient liturgies (J. Basn., *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, book XVI, chapter 10), he maintained that this Missal had been written only in the tenth century.

Anyone who reads his words will encounter remarkable confidence in that man. Before examining his opinion, however, it is useful to report what Christoph Matthäus Pfaff, professor at Tübingen, wrote in 1718 in a short work on liturgies concerning the Gelasian liturgy. Here are his words:

“James Basnage shows that it is much later than Gelasius and belongs to the tenth century. Since no one among the Roman Catholics has hitherto overthrown his arguments, and since Basnage has not answered the reasons which Thomasius brought forward in support of his opinion, we would leave the matter undecided here, were there not for us a principal reason—one not mentioned by Basnage—on account of which we judge that this liturgy should be attributed to Gelasius.”

What is this reason?

“Here it is,” Pfaff continues: “Gregory the Great says that he added the Lord’s Prayer to the Canon of the Mass, although it had not previously existed in it. Therefore it ought not to be found in the Gelasian Codex; yet it is found in the one published by Thomasius” (Gregory the Great, Book VII, Letter 64).

But if Pfaff had examined Saint Gregory’s words more carefully (Gregory the Great, Letter 12, Book IX, Benedictine edition, formerly Letter 64), and had consulted Cardinal Bona or the notes of the Benedictines, he would not, I think, have uttered such an ill-considered opinion.

Saint Augustine said that “almost the whole Church concludes the Canon with the Lord’s Prayer” (Augustine, Letter 149, formerly 59, to Paulinus). Saint Cyprian, Jerome, Optatus of Milevis, Cyril of Jerusalem, Ambrose—or whoever was the author of *On the Sacraments*—and others confirm the same thing. Could it have happened that the Roman Church alone once omitted so important a prayer in the sacred rites? Away with such a thought! It certainly did not omit it, nor did Gregory the Great first introduce it into the liturgy. He merely established that it should be recited after the consecration, condemning for that reason certain people who recited it either before the consecration itself or after Communion, or who substituted another prayer for it.

There was murmuring against the pontiff in Sicily “because he had established that the Lord’s Prayer should be said immediately after the Canon.” He replied to them by writing to John, bishop of Syracuse:

“We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer, because it was the custom of the Apostles that by that prayer alone they should consecrate the sacrificial offering.”

And below:

“Among the Greeks the Lord’s Prayer is said by all the people, but among us by the priest alone.”

There was therefore already at Rome a custom of reciting the Lord’s Prayer “immediately after the Canon.” The holy pontiff ordered that this custom be maintained, and merely disapproved those who recited it out of its proper place or had introduced a new prayer into the sacred rite in its stead. I consider this sufficient response to Pfaff’s criticism.

James Basnage must now be heard. To show that the Missal published by Cardinal Thomasius belongs to the tenth century, he uses the following arguments:

“A candle,” he says, “is blessed in this Missal with many ceremonies. Some people borrowed this custom from the pagans, who lit torches during their festivals. Tertullian and the Fathers of the Council of Elvira condemned it. Saint Jerome, however, judged that what was customary in the East ought to be tolerated. Gregory I the Great, a lover of ceremonies, introduced it into the West in the seventh century. But the people by no means embraced this rite; for a few years after Gregory’s death they formally opposed it. It is disputed whether the Gauls or the Galicians resisted it. Thus a great number of years was needed to introduce it together with all the ceremonies which usually follow one another.”

Basnage forgot to instruct the reader that this was evidence by which he was to learn that the Missal published by Thomasius belonged to the tenth century; but without such instruction he persuaded himself that the conclusion would follow by itself. As for the origin of candles in the sacred rites, see below, chapter 20.

When he drags the rite of the Paschal candle into later centuries, he seems plainly to have wished to mock his readers. As he himself knew, among Catholics a candle is lit, and a preface is sung over it to display its mysteries. All the ceremonies whose establishment, if we listen to him, required so many years are contained in this. He likewise knew that in the Gothic liturgy published by Thomasius and in the Gallican Sacramentary made public by Mabillon the blessing of the candle is found, and that these liturgies precede the year 800; nevertheless he dares to drag this custom into a much later period.

He mocks the reader still more clearly when he says that the custom was introduced from the East into the West by Saint Gregory, without producing any witness, thinking that everyone would agree with him simply because he asserted it. I shall therefore provide the passage on which he relied in making this pronouncement.

Gregory the Great writes to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, who was suffering from ill health:

“You must also refrain from vigils, and the prayers which are accustomed to be said over the candle in the city of Ravenna (by the bishop), or the expositions of the Gospel which are given by priests (that is, bishops) around the Paschal solemnity, should be delivered by someone else. And let Your Charity by no means impose labor upon itself contrary to its strength” (Gregory the Great, Book XI, Letter 33, formerly 28, Indiction 4).

Is this the introduction of the rite of the candle into the West? It was already in use there in the time of Saint Gregory. From this you can already understand that it could have appeared in the earlier liturgy of Saint Gelasius.

Basnage adds: “The people showed themselves opposed to the same rite a few years later.” He produces no witness for this either. I shall provide one: canon 9 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in the year 633, where these words occur:

“In certain Churches the lamp and candle are not celebrated among the privileges of Easter, and they ask why they are blessed by us. For the sake of the glorious mystery of that night we solemnly bless these things. And because this observance is commended in the Churches throughout many lands and regions of Spain, it is fitting that, for the sake of the unity of peace, it be preserved in the Gallican Churches.”

In certain Codices, *Gallicanis Ecclesiis* is read instead as *Galicianis Ecclesiis*. I think this was done by the ignorant, who did not know that part of Gaul—namely Septimania, or the province of Narbonne, now Languedoc—was once subject to the Goths.

What, then, are we to say of Basnage? He saw that the rite of the Paschal candle was observed only a few years after the death of Gregory the Great “throughout many lands and the regions of Spain,” and nevertheless boldly writes that the peoples abhorred it and resisted it, when the Fathers of the Council of Toledo say only that it was “not celebrated in certain Churches” of the Gothic kingdom.

Moreover, the matter is settled not by the letter to Praesidius, which circulates under the name of Saint Jerome, but by two blessings of the Paschal candle published by Sirmond, whose author was Ennodius of Ticinum, who flourished in the time of Saint Gelasius.

In the Gothic Missal and in the Gallican Sacramentary, the blessing of the Paschal candle is attributed to Saint Augustine, namely:

“Let the angelic host of heaven now rejoice.”

This attribution is not easily believed, although it is entirely consistent with probability, since the same holy doctor says that he composed two verses “in praise of the candle” (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XV, chapter 22).

Yet do you want further evidence, so that you may touch with your own hand how weak an argument Basnage used when he undertook to diminish the antiquity of the Gelasian Codex on account of the Paschal candle?

But he presses the matter again, saying:

“In this liturgy, on Good Friday, we read: ‘Look favorably and graciously upon the Roman, or Frankish, empire.’ Everyone knows that this empire began in the year 800 through Charlemagne, and therefore the Codex must necessarily be referred to the period following his coronation.”

Even if we granted that it could be inferred from this that the Codex had been written after the year 800, would it therefore follow, as Basnage dreamed, that it belonged to the tenth century?

But why delay? We are compelled to miss good faith in this critic, who saw the preceding prayer and concealed it, although it explains the following one. For there it says:

“Let us pray also for our most Christian emperor, or king, that God may make all barbarian nations subject to him.”

In Rome, prayers had been offered to God for the emperor from ancient times; and certainly the Roman Empire continued among the Greeks until the year 800. But in Gaul, at the time when the Codex was written, prayers were still being offered for “our king.” Indeed, if the Codex had been written after the empire had been transferred to the Frankish kings, it would have said only: “Look favorably and graciously upon the Roman empire”; for at that time the designation “empire” also embraced France.

Therefore this notation not only does no harm, but openly confirms the antiquity of the Gelasian liturgy, before the year 800.

Basnage continues, pointing out that this Sacramentary mentions “the feasts of the Assumption and Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary,” which, he says, were instituted only in the tenth century.

As for the feast of the Assumption of the Mother of God, this critic argues pointlessly because certain people in the ninth century called the assumption of the Virgin’s body into heaven into question. That does not remove the fact that the feast of the Burial, or Dormition, of Saint Mary had previously been celebrated.

Nor is the question here whether such a feast was instituted in the time of Gelasius—which no one indeed claims—but whether its institution took place before the year 800 and whether it was added to the Gelasian Sacramentary, as happened with other feasts added to it, and as likewise happened in the case of the Gregorian Sacramentary. For Saint Gregory himself does not appear to have introduced the feasts of the Nativity and Assumption of the Mother of God into his Sacramentary.

In any case, there can be no doubt that the solemnity of the Assumption is extremely ancient and preceded the year 800. Pope Sergius I, as Anastasius the Librarian reports, around the year 690 ordered that a litany be held “on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity, and the Dormition of the holy Mother of God.”

That the feast of the Dormition was celebrated in Gaul in the year 590—that is, while Gregory the Great was pope at Rome—is testified by Gregory of Tours:

“Its sacred festival,” he says, “is celebrated in the middle of the eleventh month” (Gregory of Tours, Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 9),

that is, on 18 January. It occurs on that same day in the Gothic Missal published by the venerable Thomasius, in the Gallican liturgy apud Mabillon, and in the Hieronymian Martyrology of Florentinius, to omit other witnesses.

In the Roman Church, however, the same feast was celebrated on 15 August. According to Nicephorus, the Emperor Maurice, in the time of Gregory the Great, “ordered that the Dormition of the most holy Mother of God be celebrated throughout the whole world on the fifteenth day of the month of August” (Nicephorus, Book XVII, chapter 18).

For this reason, in the very ancient Martyrology of Bede published by the Bollandists, under the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, we read: “The Dormition of Saint Mary” (Bollandists, *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II, March).

Likewise, the very ancient Calendar of the Roman Church preserved by Fronto has under that day: “The solemn rites concerning the Repose of Mary.” The same appears in the aforementioned Hieronymian Martyrology; and in the Roman Calendar, which Father Martène published as a notable monument of antiquity, there occurs under that day: “The Assumption of Saint Mary” (Martène, *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. V).

After the Gregorian liturgy had been received in Gaul under Charlemagne, the celebration of this feast on 15 August also prevailed in those Churches, as Mabillon observed.

Thus you can understand how unjustly Basnage opposed the feast of the Marian Assumption to the antiquity of the Gelasian Codex. Indeed, we can also infer its antiquity from the responses of Pope Nicholas I to the inquiries of the Bulgarians. In the year 866, among the fasts “which holy Roman antiquity received and the Church maintains,” that pontiff mentions “the fast before the solemnity of the Assumption of the holy Mother of God.”

The feast of the Assumption was therefore commended by antiquity in those times. Since no vigil—that is, no fast before the same feast—is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, this too shows that the Sacramentary had been composed more than a century before the time of Pope Nicholas I.

There is no need to add anything concerning the Nativity of Saint Mary, since above we have already seen that her feast was in use at Rome under Pope Sergius I in the year 690, and nearly all the ancient martyrologies mention it in September. The celebration of such feasts in the Churches and their observance by command among the people are two different things, a distinction Basnage entirely failed to make; and it was only concerning the latter that the question was at some point disputed.

Finally, he launches his last missile, saying:

“The style of this Sacramentary differs from that which Gelasius used in his surviving letters. Nor does it seem likely that he forced himself to imitate the style of Leo I, so very different from his own.”

The learned reader scarcely needs my warning to recognize how futile this argument is. Gelasius did not construct the Sacramentary anew or from the beginning; rather, he arranged what had already been in use in the Roman Church for earlier centuries and enlarged it with certain prefaces, as we have seen above. Perhaps he also added some prayers of his own, and it is certain that the Gelasian contains so many prayers and prefaces whose author is not Gelasius but Saint Leo.

We may also suppose that many prayers instituted in the earliest centuries of the Church were preserved there. Therefore anyone who wishes to measure the origin of this Sacramentary by Gelasius’s style deserves ridicule.

Nevertheless, after all the empty arguments Basnage used in order to take it away from Gelasius and drag the Codex into the tenth century, he awards himself the victory. He admits that in liturgies preceding the time of Paschasius Radbertus the “transubstantiation” of the Eucharist is found; but at the same time he maintains that, after the books published by Paschasius around the year 831, those additions were made to the liturgies themselves “through changes which cannot be called into question, after we have shown that they could not have occurred except in the tenth century.”

Whether this glorious soldier has shown what he boasts of having shown, we have thus far shown. But it is especially regrettable that learned men should be so preoccupied and carried away by love of contention and schism that they do not seek the truth with the sincerity that is required, but feed themselves and the people on mere imaginings in a matter of such importance and rest so calmly in them.

For, as the most learned Catholic writers long ago demonstrated, it is an utterly absurd imagination, born in the brain of the Calvinist Claude, that Paschasius corrupted the Church’s doctrine concerning the Eucharist and first introduced the real conversion of the offerings into the body and blood of the Lord, as we shall show below.

And what was the doctrine of the Gallican and British Churches concerning the Eucharist in the years shortly before Paschasius Radbertus? Alcuin, also called Albinus, a man of the highest standing among all the theologians of his time, can teach us this. He writes to Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia:

“Please do not forget the name of your friend Albinus in your holy prayers; but store it in some treasury of your memory and bring it forth at the fitting time, when you consecrate bread and wine into the substance of the body and blood of Christ” (Alcuin Albinus, chapter 113, to Paulinus).

The most foolish imagination of all is the second one: namely, that Paschasius’s books had such power that all the Churches of the West, without anyone opening his mouth or objecting, and without anyone commanding it, embraced transubstantiation against the earlier faith and peacefully introduced that doctrine into the liturgies and other books.

As I have said, this is a mere imagination and wholly ridiculous. For they produce no witness who noticed and acknowledged this supposed change in so great a matter.

But what matters most is that Catholics have long since made it clear that all the Churches, both of the West and of the East, before and after the time of Paschasius, have always proceeded unanimously in affirming the doctrine which the Catholic Church still professes.

I add nothing further here, since I have resolved below to attack such imaginings of the heterodox, when we still see them obstinately advertised and offered with such confidence to unwary readers.

In the meantime, we conclude that nothing has so far been produced that would persuade us to attribute to Saint Gelasius the Sacramentary published under his name. At the same time, we have shown that the Codex from which it was copied had been written before the year 800.

Here, however, I think it should incidentally be observed that, in all likelihood, through the carelessness of a copyist, the commemoration of the dead—which is used by the Roman Church after the consecration—fell out of this Sacramentary, namely:

“Remember also, Lord, your servants and handmaids who have gone before us,” and so forth.

For scarcely any liturgy, whether of the Western or Eastern Churches, can you show me in which this pious rite is lacking. Nor should you entertain any doubt whether, in the age of Saint Gelasius, the commemoration of the faithful departed was in use in the sacred rites and prayers were offered to God for them.

Already in the third and fourth centuries of Christ, not to mention the fifth, we have the Fathers as witnesses to this doctrine and rite. I shall mention none of them in a matter so well known and familiar. But in this very Sacramentary several Masses for the dead are also found, which attest the antiquity of this doctrine in the Church.

Nor should the Masses, prayers for certain private needs, or some blessings arouse in you any suspicion of lesser antiquity. The devotion of the earlier centuries of the Christian faith knew and employed these as well.

I shall give an example. In Book III, chapter 83, there is a prayer for one who first cuts his beard, where these words occur:

“Graciously attend upon this servant of yours, rejoicing in the youthful beauty of his age and cutting off the flower of his youth at its first beginning.”

Write *juvenilis* (“youthful”) rather than *juvenilia*.

This custom was once a festive practice among the pagans. Christians retained it and consecrated it to their own use. Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, when as a young man he was growing his first beard around the year 373, seems to have cut it off before the tomb of Saint Felix. For, addressing Saint Felix, he says (On the thirteenth feast-day, verse 324, *Anecdotes*, edition of Muratori):

> Then also the first offerings of my beard . . . [perhaps: “placing them”]  
> I cut them before your throne, as though you yourself were taking them.

The antiquity of the Gelasian Codex will be confirmed still more clearly by the appearance of its script, which I acknowledge as having been communicated by Father Blanchinius.

# Chapter VI. On the Gregorian Sacramentary

We know that the Gelasian Sacramentary was abridged by Saint Gregory the Great and reduced to that order which thereafter was observed in the Roman Church and in the other Churches that imitated it down to our own days, although many additions—minor ones—were made from time to time, without anything substantive being removed.

Gregory’s work.

We have John the Deacon (*Life of Saint Gregory the Great*), Pope Adrian I (in his letter to Charlemagne), and other very ancient writers and Missals as witnesses to this work. The only question that remains is whether any Codex survives that presents the pure and genuine text of the Gregorian Sacramentary.

I answer without hesitation that none has so far been found; indeed, all hope of finding one seems to have been removed. Since not only the Roman Church but also the other Churches introduced new feast days into the ancient liturgy, it could scarcely happen that a Codex of such antiquity would reach us in which no addition appeared.

Thus my sole wish was to present to the reader whatever Gregorian text I could find that surpassed the others in antiquity.

In the year of Christ 1571, James Pamelius was the first to publish a Gregorian Sacramentary from a very ancient Codex (vol. II of the *Liturgies*). Anyone who compares it with the text that I am about to publish will immediately observe that it yields to the latter in antiquity; for many additions are found in it which are entirely absent from the edition I shall publish below.

A second was later published by Angelus Rocca, sacristan of the apostolic palace.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] Angelus Rocca, in the edition of the works of Saint Gregory produced at Rome under Clement VIII.]

It too is less ancient than the Pamelian text. Finally, Hugh Menardus printed a third, copied from the manuscript Codex of Saint Eligius and provided with notes (*Gregorian Sacramentary*).

[Note: [Col. 0896D] A new edition of the works of Saint Gregory I, prepared by the Benedictines of Saint-Maur.]

The distinguished Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur subsequently gave it to us again.

Two things must be considered there: namely, the text of the Gregorian Sacramentary and Menardus’s notes. As for the notes, they are highly commendable and worthy of being handled by everyone, because of the wide-ranging learning in liturgical matters in which that most learned man excelled.

With regard to the Gregorian text published by him, this is what the highly praised Benedictines thought of it in their preface to the same Sacramentary:

“Indeed,” they say, “after weighing everything in a more equitable balance, we judged that no other text should be preferred to it, whether on account of its antiquity or its integrity, having read the preface which the most learned man placed before his edition.”

The venerable Cardinal Thomasius, however, as I read in the account preserved in his Life, thought otherwise. He would have preferred the Benedictines to place before Menardus’s Gregorian Sacramentary the one published by Pamelius in their edition of the works of Saint Gregory the Great, since he judged it more conformable and more similar to the original text of the holy pontiff than the other, published by Menardus.

They were prevented from doing this, however, because they had decided to incorporate Menardus’s highly useful notes into their edition, and those notes would not have corresponded at all to a text different from Menardus’s.

Moreover, no one who weighs both texts in a more careful balance will be able to doubt that Pamelius’s text is to be preferred to Menard’s, as Thomasius judged and the distinguished Father Mabillon subsequently confirmed. For there are far too many things in Menard’s Gregorian Sacramentary that in no way acknowledge Saint Gregory as their author and that depart from the ancient customs of the Roman Church, so that the codex of Saint Eligius—though it was not Saint Eligius himself who used it, but formerly the monks of Saint Eligius, and Menard later used it for his edition—does not possess the antiquity and integrity that the Benedictine monks believed it did.

The first things to strike the eye are those innumerable prefaces, if I may call them so, which are appended to nearly every individual feast day, to all the Sundays of the entire year, to the vigils themselves, and to Masses for private needs. Yet ancient monuments deter us from believing that so great a supply of prefaces proceeded from and was approved by Saint Gregory. All the Churches of the Christian world did indeed proceed in agreement with a certain preface, or preparation, for the canon, which they concluded with the seraphic hymn; and this common preface is mentioned by Saints Cyprian, Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom, Augustine, and other Fathers. But gradually a custom prevailed in the West whereby something particular, pertaining to each individual festival, was added to this preface.

We have evidence for the antiquity of this custom from the Second Council of Milevis, held in the year of Christ 416 in the presence of Saint Augustine. There we read:

> “It was also resolved that the prayers, or orations, or Masses that have been approved in the council, and likewise the prefaces, etc., should be celebrated by all. Let no others whatsoever be said in the Church except those which have been discussed or approved by the more prudent men in synod, lest something should perhaps have been composed contrary to the faith, either through ignorance or through insufficient care” (Second Council of Milevis, canon 12).

Behold what emulation there formerly was among pious Latin Christians—even in the fifth century of the Church itself—in composing new prayers, prefaces, and Masses. There was an equal zeal in the Roman Church itself. See the Leonine Sacramentary, into which, it seems, everything that existed in Rome by way of prefaces had flowed at the time when that work was compiled. See also the Gelasian Sacramentary, where there is no small abundance of prefaces; and indeed, as we have already learned from Anastasius, Saint Gelasius composed “prefaces of the Sacraments.”

Since the Roman Church continued to use the same Gelasian Sacramentary until Gregory the Great, there is consequently room for reasonable doubt whether the letter of Pope Pelagius II to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, which is found in collections of councils and in the ecclesiastical Annals of Cardinal Baronius under the year of Christ 590—that is, one hundred years after Gelasius’s death—should be attributed to him. Those bishops requested “the order of prefaces that the holy Roman Church had hitherto maintained.” The pontiff replied:

> “On rereading the sacred Roman Order and the sacred enactments of our predecessors, we find that these nine prefaces are to be received into the sacred catalogue, which longstanding tradition has hitherto preserved in the Roman Church: one for the Paschal season in white vestments; another for the Ascension of the Lord; a third for Pentecost; a fourth for the Nativity of the Lord; a fifth for the Epiphany (that is, the Manifestation); a sixth for the Apostles; a seventh for the Holy Trinity; an eighth for the Cross; and a ninth, to be said only for fasting and Lent. These prefaces the holy Roman Church holds and preserves. We command you to hold them.”

Labbe suspected this letter to be an adulterine fabrication of Isidore Mercator. Cardinal Bona, however, formed the suspicion “that it may perhaps belong to some other, later pontiff and have been mistakenly attributed to Pelagius.” He then gives the reason for his suspicion, saying:

> “For if, in Pelagius’s time, the Roman Church used only those prefaces, as having long before been received and approved in it, how did Gregory, his immediate successor and the most tenacious guardian of sacred rites, compose other new ones? For it is evident that in the ancient books of the Sacraments bearing the title of the Roman Church more prefaces are found, and scarcely any Mass exists to which its own particular preface has not been assigned.”

Pagius subscribed to Cardinal Bona’s opinion with even greater emphasis (Baronius’s *Critica*, under the year 590), using the same arguments. I too believe that the letter of Pope Pelagius II is spurious, or rather should be attributed to some other later Roman pontiff—but not for the reasons they adduce. Bona and Pagius were deceived by Menard’s edition and persuaded themselves that so many prefaces in Menard’s edition of the Gregorian Sacramentary had proceeded from Gregory the Great himself. Yet this conflicts with the truth, since it will soon become clear that only those few prefaces which we now use were received and approved by Saint Gregory.

The reason, therefore, why the letter just mentioned must be judged spurious is that, in reality, before Pelagius II and before the year 590, the Roman Church used a considerable number of prefaces, as is clear from the Leonine and Gelasian Sacramentaries and from Anastasius, who wrote that “prefaces of the Sacraments” had been prepared by Saint Gelasius. Those words do not indicate merely nine—and those very brief—prefaces, but many, such as we find in the Gelasian liturgy. Thus Pelagius II would have written falsely. The author of that letter, however—perhaps Isidore Mercator—when composing spurious letters at the beginning of the ninth century, or under Charlemagne, could rightly assert that the Roman Church had for a long time used only nine prefaces. For in fact, from the time of Gregory the Great, it used only eight, or nine, or ten in its sacred rites, as the most ancient codices attest.

[Col. 0898D] But how did such a great abundance of prefaces enter the Sacramentary edited by Menard? The eleventh-century writer known as the Micrologus states that Alcuin Albinus, toward the end of the eighth century, composed or collected various prefaces, which nevertheless did not have Saint Gregory as their author:

> “The same Albinus accomplished a work in the holy Church that was not to be despised. For he is said to have collected the Gregorian prayers in the books of the Sacraments, adding a few others, which, however, he indicated should be marked with an obelus so that they might be distinguished from the Gregorian prayers. Then he collected other prayers, or prefaces, which, although not Gregorian, were nevertheless suitable for ecclesiastical celebration, as the prologue bears witness—the prologue that he placed in the middle of the same book, after the Gregorian prayers” (*Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 9).

Those who excelled in piety in the Gallican and German Churches introduced such proper prefaces into the Gregorian liturgy in order to procure greater veneration on certain days. In the *Chronicle of Centula*, preserved by D’Achery, it is recorded:

> “The Gregorian and Gelasian Missal was arranged by Albinus in modern times” (D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, book III, chapter 3).

Compare the Gelasian Sacramentary with the one edited by Menard. You will find that not a few of the Gelasian prefaces migrated into the Gregorian liturgy—for example, at the night vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, on the sixth feria in the Easter Octave, and on the second and fourth Sundays after the Octave of Easter, to omit other examples. The remaining prefaces, which are not Gelasian, were collected elsewhere by Alcuin Albinus.

It was customary, when copying the Gregorian Sacramentary, to append such non-Gregorian prefaces separately, as compositions not to be attributed to that holy pontiff, although they could be used devotionally according to the needs of the feasts. It is uncertain whether the codex of Saint Eligius, which Hugo Menard used, had these prefaces inserted into each Mass, or whether they had been relegated to the end of the codex.

In the Imperial Library of Vienna there is a remarkable monument of antiquity, namely the celebrated Gregorian Sacramentary which Peter Lambecius (*Imperial Library*, volume II, chapter 5) judged to be the very book sent by Pope Adrian I to Charlemagne, king of the Franks and Lombards, as appears from letter 82 of the *Carolingian Codex*.

Since I was uncertain whether such a codex should be judged to be of so great an antiquity, I wrote about it to my most learned friend, Dominicus Bricherius Columbus, asking him to examine it or to seek the judgment of Monsieur Forlasia, the chief librarian. He replied that in the prayer for the sixth feria of Good Friday he read: “Let us pray also for our most Christian emperor”; but that above it, in another hand, had been written **REGE** (“king”). The Gregorian Sacramentary could not and did not have anything other than “for our emperor,” for Saint Gregory wrote it in that form in his own time. At what time, however, the word “king” was written in that codex is uncertain.

There too is found, on Sunday, a Mass of the Holy Trinity; on the second feria, one of Wisdom; on the third feria, one asking for the gift of the Holy Spirit; and so forth. But such Masses, as the ancient liturgical writers have warned us, acknowledge the aforementioned Alcuin Albinus as their author. Thus we learn that the codex may perhaps have been written before the end of the eighth century; yet it cannot have been the one sent by Pope Adrian I to Charlemagne.

Moreover, before the same Viennese Sacramentary, written in the original hand, there occur prefaces of Masses from the first Sunday of Lent up to the sixth feria of Good Friday. Then follow a Mass for the patrons of the Church, the blessing of candles on the day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a Mass of Saint Christopher, and a calendar. Finally there follows this title, formed in alternating letters of gold, silver, vermilion, and ink:

> In the name of the Lord. Here begins the Book of Sacraments for the cycle of the year, set forth by Saint Gregory, Roman pope, edited from the authentic book of the library of the chapter, and written according to the manner in which the Roman Mass is celebrated.

Do you see how the prefaces are distinguished from the Gregorian Sacramentary? The reason is certainly that they do not have that illustrious pontiff as their author.

That this codex belonged to the celebrated monastery of Reichenau, situated in the diocese of Constance, may be inferred from the calendar, in which the anniversary of the death—and sometimes of the ordination—of those abbots is noted; in addition, the death-days of kings and of other persons who had deserved well of that monastery are marked in various scripts. The last of the kings is King Henry, evidently the first of that name in Germany; among the abbots is Folewinus, who was elected in the year of Christ 809.

In that codex several Masses, prayers, and blessings are found which are absent from Menard’s codex; and, conversely, other items appear in Menard’s codex that the Viennese codex lacks.

There are also other very ancient codices of the same Gregorian liturgy in Italy. I asked the distinguished John Dominic Berroli, canon of the illustrious patriarchal Church of Aquileia, whether that Church preserved any such codex. He replied that it possessed a most elegant codex whose age appeared to belong to the ninth or tenth century. Its title is:

> In the name of Christ, here begins the Book of Sacraments for the cycle of the year, edited by Saint Gregory, Roman pope, describing how the Roman Mass is celebrated. First, the Introit, etc.

The same Sacramentary also exists in the library of the distinguished chapter of the Canons of Verona, with the customary title:

> Here begins the Book of Sacraments for the cycle of the year, set forth by Saint Gregory, Roman pope, edited from the authentic book of the library of the Chamber, written according to the manner in which the Roman Mass is celebrated.

I consulted Bartholomeus Campagnola, archpriest of Saint Cecilia and highly knowledgeable about Veronese affairs. He wrote back to me that in the blessing of the candle on Holy Saturday he read the following:

> “That we, your servants, together with our pope and our most glorious king Otto, and also with our venerable bishop WUOLFKANG, may enjoy the peaceful continuity of the times,” etc.

On the authority of this Missal, the distinguished Marquis Scipio Maffei included Vuolfkangus in his catalogue of the bishops of Verona, as is clear from the latest Venetian edition of *Italia Sacra*. But the aforementioned Campagnola thought that this Sacramentary had formerly belonged to the Church of Regensburg under Otto III, king of Germany but not yet emperor, at the time when Vuolfkangus was bishop of Regensburg, from the year of Christ 974 until 994. He believed that the codex had been brought to Verona by Bishop Obertus, who occupied the Veronese see from 992 to 1008 and was exceedingly dear and close to Otto III, out of devotion to that holy prelate.

If this is true, Vuolfkangus must be removed from the catalogue of the bishops of Verona.

In the same Sacramentary, besides the customary prefaces of the Roman Church, no others occur. Among the canons of Modena there also survives a very ancient copy of the Gregorian Sacramentary, though mutilated, since many leaves have been lost from the Nativity of Saint Fabian, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, up to the Wednesday within the Octave of Pentecost.

The title of the codex is:

> In the name of the Lord, here begins the Book of Sacraments for the cycle of the year, set forth by Saint Gregory, Roman pope, edited from the authentic book of the library of the Roman Church. Here begins the Mass of the Roman Church. Throughout all ages of ages.

The codex appears to have been written in the ninth century of Christ; its date must at least be placed in the tenth century. This is demonstrated both by the form of the script and by certain marginal annotations written in another hand.

Among other things, the following is read there:

> “On the third day before the Kalends of July, which was the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, Gotefredus of Bologna died; and his wife Emerada also died from this world on the Kalends of July. He was the father and she the mother of Lord Warinus, bishop of Modena, in the first indiction” (that is, in the year of Christ 1003 or 1018, when the same Warinus was bishop).

Here is another marginal annotation:

> “From this hour onward I, John the archpriest, promise you, Bishop Warinus, that during the days of my life I will not commit adultery with another man’s wife, nor fornication with an illicit prostitute. And if I do so, I declare myself liable to punishment.”

Take also this third annotation:

> “I, Naira the priest, promise before God and all the saints, and to you, Bishop Guarinus, that I will not commit carnal intercourse. And if I do, I shall lose both my honor and the benefice of the Church.”

There too, only those prefaces are read in the text which remain in use in the sacred rites. If any others have been added, they were written in the margin by another hand.

The diligence and ancient affection toward me of the distinguished Father Joseph Blanchini, whose published books have made him famous and to whom the continuation of the ecclesiastical Annals has been entrusted in the Roman Oratory, supplied me with examples of the Gregorian Sacramentary that are far more ancient. He sent me, I say, two codices, which on account of their venerable antiquity deserve to be preferred above the other Gregorian codices.

One of them formerly belonged in Gaul to Paul Petau, senator of Paris; then it came into the possession of Christina, the illustrious queen of the Swedes; finally it was brought to Rome and placed in the Othobonian Library, where it now rests. Its rare antiquity is confirmed by the form of its script, a specimen of which Father Blanchini wished to have transferred to a copper plate, and which I too wish to display here for all to see.

The antiquity of this codex may also be inferred from the necrology that was repeatedly added to the same Sacramentary, in various hands and at different times. It is certain that the codex had already been written before names of the dead, the sick, and other living persons were added, as chance dictated, in a confused manner in the margins or on blank pages, for whom prayers were offered in the dread sacrifice. To report them all would serve no useful purpose. I shall mention only the principal names.

### Names of the Canons of Paris

[Col. 0901] [Col. 0901C] Bishop Ercanradus, Ercanfredus, Ragoboldus, Falcaldus, Hadericus, Gabilo, Remigius, Fulcricus Alo, [Col. 0901] Amalingus, Amalgarius, Vuacco, Aganus, again Aganus, Ercanfredus, again Ercanfredus, Eltbertus, Martinus, [Col. 0902C] Ambrico, Atroldus, Everladus, Jonas, Melismus, Berthaus, Ainricus, Gislefredus, Johannes, [Col. 0902] Bernardus, Magenardus, Gillardus, Vulfuinus, Drogo, Vuinebaldus, Rotgamus, etc.

What I observed elsewhere concerning Italy (Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 41), you may now observe concerning the Gauls. Namely, the men are recorded under a single name, since at that time the use of surnames did not yet exist. This custom could not fail sometimes to cause confusion. Here you have three Ercanfreduses and two Aganuses. What, I ask, distinguishes one from another?

### These Names Occur on Other Pages

[Col. 0903] [Col. 0903A] Charles, emperor; Louis, emperor; Pepin, king; Constantius, bishop; Hewardus, deacon; Sirmundus, priest; Alfredus, deacon; [Col. 0903] Drogo; Elisardus, bishop; Hodolricus, dean; Fulcherius, dean; Frotmundus, dean; Otramnus, deacon; [Col. 0904A] John, subdeacon; Giroldus; Fulbertus; Waldrit, deacon; Otulfo, deacon; Adelenda, woman; [Col. 0904] Flaremburgis, woman; Godevertus, layman; Ingelrannus; Anstasius; Heribertus; Anstasius, etc.

I omit the remaining multitude of persons recorded here. Their names generally appear written in different forms of script and were therefore added after the Sacramentary had been written.

The two Ercanraduses, or Erchenraduses, who were bishops of Paris, seem to be numbered among them. Mabillon published a very ancient catalogue of the bishops of Paris (*On Diplomatics*, book IV, p. 625), in which two Erchanraduses are listed. The elder, omitted by the Sammarthani in the first edition of *Gallia Christiana*, flourished in the year of Christ 775. The younger took part in the Council of Thionville around the year 835 and is believed to have died around 853. Therefore the Othobonian codex seems to have been written at least before that year.

In the same codex there is a Roman Litany, written in a somewhat less ancient script and adapted for the use of the Church of Paris. I shall not hesitate to present it to the reader. It prays for the lord emperor and the Frankish army. Therefore this Litany was in use before the year of Christ 887.
