[Col. 0903D] The Vatican Library, richer than all the others—that is, filled with manuscript codices—preserves another codex of the Gregorian Sacramentary, written at least at the beginning of the ninth century of Christ. The aforementioned indefatigable hunter of ecclesiastical learning, Father Blanchini, had procured a copy of it and eventually entrusted it to me for my use, together with a specimen of the script of the same codex engraved on a copper plate.

It bears, like others, the following title:

> Here begins the Book of Sacraments for the cycle of the year, set forth by Saint Gregory, Roman pope, edited from the authentic book of the library of the Chamber, written.

In other codices, as you saw above, there appears—against the principles of Priscian—*liber expositum, editum, scriptum* (“the book set forth, edited, written”), with the wrong grammatical gender. If any codex expresses the title differently, a much later correction must be suspected.

This observation leads me to believe that the individual copies of the Gregorian Sacramentary were not all formerly taken directly from the authentic book of the library of the papal Chamber. One copy transcribed from it and transferred to some Church of Gaul, Germany, or Italy was sufficient for many other Churches to derive new copies from it. This happened especially in the ninth and tenth centuries, when collegiate bodies of canons were established in nearly every city and competed to arrange their rites according to the model of the mother of all Churches, namely the apostolic Roman Church. If each copy had been derived directly from the Roman codex, it would scarcely have been possible for the same grammatical error to appear in so many copies.

Nevertheless, in the Othobonian codex of which we recently spoke, the title is expressed as follows, written in large letters and vermilion:

> In the name of the Lord. Here begins the Book of Sacraments for the cycle of the year, edited by Saint Gregory, Roman pope. How the Roman Mass is celebrated, etc.

It must be repeated here that neither codex—the Vatican, namely, nor the Othobonian—presents a completely pure Sacramentary, exactly as it proceeded from Saint Gregory’s hands. Certain additions of feasts were subsequently made to both. It is enough to mention the feast day of Saint Gregory himself, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, and the Mass of Saint Mary among the Martyrs, on the third day before the Ides of May, which is said to have been instituted by Pope Boniface IV around the year of Christ 610.

Nevertheless, the two codices just mentioned—the Vatican and the Othobonian—retain their claim to the highest antiquity, so that both should be judged to date either from the end of the eighth century, that is, before the year 800, or from the earliest years of the ninth century.

Pope Leo III began his pontificate in the year 795 and died in 816. Hear what Anastasius the Librarian records about this pontiff in his Life:

> “Protected by God, that illustrious pontiff established that litanies should be celebrated on the three days before the Lord’s Ascension: namely, on the second feria, when the pontiff went out with all the clergy and the entire people, with hymns and spiritual songs, from the Church of the Mother of God to the Praesepe, etc.; on the third feria, when they went out from the Church of Saint Sabina the Martyr, etc.; and on the fourth feria, when they went out from the Church of Jerusalem,” etc.

Here you have the time at which the lesser litanies, or Rogation rites, which had been instituted in Gaul several centuries earlier, were introduced into the Roman Church. They are indeed mentioned in Menard’s Sacramentary, but there is no mention of them in the Vatican or Othobonian codices. It may therefore now be firmly concluded that these two codices were written either toward the end of the eighth century or at the beginning of the ninth.

Moreover, in the Sacramentaries of Pamelius and Menard there are Masses for the Nativity of Saint Mark the Evangelist, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, and for the Nativity of Saint James the Apostle, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August; these are not found at all in the Vatican and Othobonian codices.

Again, in Menard you find Masses for the Nativity of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, for Saint Augustine the Bishop, for the vigil of Saint Luke the Evangelist, for the Nativity of Saints Simon and Jude, and for Saint Thomas the Apostle. None of these Masses is found in either of our two codices. This sufficiently proves that the Sacramentaries of Pamelius and Menard yield to both those codices in antiquity.

This becomes still clearer from the feast of All Saints, which, according to the testimony of Ado and Usuard, Pope Gregory IV instituted under the rule of Louis the Pious, around the year of Christ 830. Since the Mass for that day is read both in Pamelius’s and in Menard’s codex, but no Mass occurs in the Vatican or Othobonian codex, a legitimate inference—and indeed a decisive conclusion—arises that the latter possess greater antiquity.

The Viennese Imperial Codex presents Masses agreeing with both our codices; and since no word concerning the Rogation rites occurs there, you may likewise determine its age from this fact.

I now return to the many prefaces with which you see the Gregorian liturgy burdened in Menard’s edition. I repeat that their insertion into the text of the Masses gave occasion for the error that Saint Gregory himself was their author, just as Cardinal Bona and Antonius Pagius, placing excessive confidence in Menard, believed.

Yet it is certain that no other prefaces occur in the Gregorian text than those still in use in the Roman Church, as is demonstrated by the very ancient Viennese, Vatican, Othobonian, and Modenese codices—except for the Mass of Saint Anastasia at the Nativity of the Lord, to which a proper preface was formerly assigned.

There were also formerly particular prefaces for the vigil and the Nativity of Saint Andrew, but these are different from Menard’s. Most codices, however, contain at the end collected prefaces and blessings that priests and bishops used according to their discretion.

Finally, the most ancient compiler—whom Pamelius believed to have been Grimoldus the abbot, while Menard thought him to have been Rodradus the priest, but whom, on the authority of the Micrologus, we shall more reasonably judge to have been Alcuin Albinus—warns us in the prologue, which I too shall present before the blessing of the candle from the Othobonian codex, that he found these materials “inserted in other little books of the Sacraments,” but that they are presented separately from the Gregorian text so that everyone may recognize “which things are by blessed Gregory and which have been published by other Fathers.”

Then, below, he adds the following about the prefaces themselves:

> “As for the prefaces that we have placed at the end of the codex, we beg that they be received and sung with charity by those who approve of them. But from those who understand them yet are not pleased by them, and likewise from those who want them but do not understand them, we ask that they neither be taken up nor sung.”

These things sufficiently show that the author of such peculiar prefaces was by no means Saint Gregory, and that no one devoted to the Gregorian liturgy was compelled to use them; rather, at that time everyone was free either to use them or not to use them. Most of them also proceed in agreement with those published by Menardus.

Moreover, I ask you to note that several prefaces in the Othobonian Codex differ from those of Menardus: for the feast of Saint Agnes (*Agnae* or *Agnetis*); on Holy Saturday; at Easter; on the Annunciation of Saint Mary; on the Ascension of the Lord; and on the fourth Sunday after Pentecost, to pass over others. Again, the Othobonian Codex contains more prefaces, while the Vatican Codex contains only a few. These facts compel us to recognize that such prefaces—and especially because of their variety—were drawn not from the Gregorian Sacramentary but from other sources.

You will also observe, rejected at the end of the Gregorian liturgy, the episcopal blessings which we nevertheless find improperly inserted by Menardus into the Gregorian text. In the pontifical Mass bishops formerly blessed the people with these before the words, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you”; for we must acknowledge that such a custom was extremely ancient. There was consequently a special book which they called the *Benedictional*. Nor should these blessings be judged to be the work of Gregory the Great, since in the ancient Roman Ordines published by Mabillon there is no mention of them, and none are found in the Gregorian Codex of the Mutinensian Sacramentary, written in the ninth or tenth century. They do exist at the end of the Vatican and Othobonian Codices, but there are more in one than in the other, and they sometimes differ from the Codex of Menardus. If the Sacramentary of the Roman chamber, from which the old exemplars were taken, had contained all of them, there would be no difference among the ancient Codices.

For this reason Mabillon rightly judged that these blessings ought not to have been inserted into the Gregorian Sacramentary; indeed, he conjectured that they had been disapproved by Pope Zacharias for use in the office of the Gallican Church (Mabillon, *Commentary on the Roman Ordo*, chapter 8, p. 52). We may also conjecture that the Roman pontiffs never used them from the Gelasian and Leonian Sacramentaries, in which there is no trace of them.

I am compelled to wonder at this: almost all the Masses for the recurring Sundays throughout the year, both in the Vatican and Othobonian Codices and in those published by Pamelius, are relegated to another book, as though they did not proceed from Saint Gregory the Great. Indeed, in the most ancient Mutinensian Sacramentary, after the Mass for the ordination of a pontiff, the following is written:

> THE SACRAMENTARY EDITED BY SAINT GREGORY THE POPE IS COMPLETED.

Then follows:

> The Masses for Sundays begin.

In the Othobonian and Pamelian books, however, a prologue or note by Alcuin is inserted, as though indicating that the Sunday Masses do not belong to Saint Gregory. Yet can it be that this holy pontiff omitted Masses which were more than any others concerned with divine worship and the Sacrament? What are we to say here?

If we consult the very ancient Vatican Codex, which I shall use for this edition, no note or prologue is inserted there distinguishing the Sunday prayers from the Gregorian text. On the contrary, in the prologue or preface of Alcuin placed before these Masses, we read:

> “But since there are also certain other things which the holy Church necessarily uses, and since that same Father”—that is, Saint Gregory—“seeing that they had already been published by others, omitted them, we therefore considered it worthwhile to pluck them, as blooming flowers of the meadows,” etc.

And in fact the Sunday prayers, the most elegant and devout of all, do not acknowledge Saint Gregory as their author. See the earlier Sacramentaries, namely the Leonian and Gelasian, in which most of them are found. If Gregory omitted them from his own book—which nevertheless cannot easily be granted—it was for no other reason than that they were already in the hands of all those Churches which used the Roman liturgy.

What I am now compelled to complain about is indeed the Gregorian Sacramentary; but we do not possess a complete view of the daily Mass as it existed in the age of that same holy pontiff. In saying this, I am not concerned with the text of the readings, Gospels, and antiphons, of which there is no mention there. Formerly there were various Codices for the use of the solemn Mass, or Mass celebrated with song.

Thus, an Antiphonary containing the psalms and antiphons to be sung at Mass on the various days was available to the clergy singing in the choir. A Lectionary, containing readings drawn from the Old Testament or from the canonical Epistles, was available to the subdeacon. An Evangelistary, presenting the various portions of the Gospels to be sung on each day, was given to the deacon. Sometimes one Codex contained the readings both of the Epistles and of the Gospels.

The clergy also had a book called the *Comes* (also styled *liber Comitis*, “book of the Comes”), an unquestionably ancient book, so much so that some, wrongly, attributed it to Saint Jerome. It indicated the readings to be used on each day in the sacred rites. I say that it indicated them, for it was nevertheless necessary to have a Codex from which the readings themselves, in their full form, could be taken.

We now have all these things joined together in our Missals. But no one, so far as I know, has yet brought forth a Missal written before the year 1000 of the Christian era in which this entire sacred apparatus is assembled, ordered, and distributed in sequence. Consequently, it is scarcely possible to understand how private Masses could then have been celebrated without a deacon, subdeacon, and choir without inconvenience, since the complete Mass had to be obtained from different Codices: the prayers from the Sacramentary, and the antiphons, readings, and Gospels from other books.

It must surely have been a great inconvenience to carry four, or at least three, Codices to the altar and to proceed from one to another in order to join together what belonged to the particular order of the Mass being celebrated. Whether this could have been done otherwise, and whether such inconvenience could have been avoided, others may judge. But, as I said, I am not dwelling on these matters.

I maintain only this: the ancient Sacramentaries composed by Saint Gregory do not contain everything that had to be recited in each Mass according to the unaltered Rite. For they generally contain no rubrics and nothing concerning the greetings addressed to the people—that is, “The Lord be with you,” or “Peace be with you,” with the people responding, “And with your spirit.” This greeting recurs more than once in the sacred liturgy to renew attention, and is attested from late antiquity.

The complete canon of the Mass proceeds as far as “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord,” etc.; after this has been recited, nothing else is added in the Gregorian book except, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.” The response is: “And with your spirit.” Nor do you find more in the Gelasian Sacramentary; indeed, there is no mention there of the *Agnus Dei*.

Furthermore, the Gregorian book contains no words concerning the breaking of the consecrated bread, transformed into the body of Christ; nor concerning the placing of a particle into the chalice; nor is that important formula reported which the priest was to recite, namely: “May this commixture and consecration of the body,” etc.

This breaking is believed to have come down from apostolic tradition, and the Eastern faithful of Christ have also used it from ancient centuries to signify the Lord’s Passion. We cannot doubt, however, that the Roman Church used the words mentioned above at the breaking, since in the First Roman Ordo—frequently mentioned by Amalarius, and judged by Mabillon to be considerably earlier than the ninth century of the Christian era—the same formula is prescribed, namely: “May the commixture be made,” or, “May this commixture,” etc.

Nor are these the only things lacking in the Gregorian Sacramentary. Also absent are the remaining elements concerning the giving of peace, which formerly was confirmed by the holy kiss. You will likewise see omitted the things that precede and follow the Communion of the priest and the faithful people, although it is well established that the priest, when offering the heavenly bread to the people, used the words, “The body of the Lord,” etc., and that those receiving Communion responded, “Amen.”

The formula “Go, the Mass is ended” is also extremely ancient, as is some form of blessing at the end of Mass—not only in the ancient Ordines of the Roman Church, but also as mentioned by Rabanus Maurus (*On the Instruction of Clergy*, Book I, chapter 33) and by Amalarius (*Eclogues* and *On the Offices of the Church*, Book III, chapter 36). Yet you will look in vain for any mention of these in that same Sacramentary.

As we may reasonably suppose, what is now lacking in the ancient books, both in prayers and in rites, was formerly supplied by bishops and priests. Either they retained in memory whatever had not been committed to writing for the completion of the sacrifice and Communion, or rather—as we see done even now—they had these things written on a tablet placed upon the altar, which they consulted when necessary. Not everyone can rely on memory, nor is that safe in matters of such importance.

Let this suffice concerning the Gregorian Sacramentary. You will see what the form of the letters is in the Vatican Codex from which these materials were reproduced in the following specimen, which Father Blanchinus sent to me.

# CHAPTER VII. Where formerly the variety of those using the Roman liturgy lay

After the sacred Council of Trent and the many efforts of the Roman pontiffs, the liturgy pertaining to the Mass of all the Catholic Churches in the West achieved a stable unity. The Ambrosian Church must be excepted, since it still uses its own ancient rites.

Its difference from the Roman rite in the unbloody sacrifice chiefly concerns the prayers, or collects; other readings from the sacred Epistles and Gospels; and the use of several prefaces. As for the canon, however, the Ambrosians themselves proceed in almost everything in agreement with the Roman Church.

Likewise, in a corner of the city of Toledo, a place is preserved for the ancient Mozarabic liturgy. That certain groups of monks still use a particular, though minor, rite at Mass is of no importance.

In ancient centuries, although the Roman liturgy of the Mass was observed by most of the Churches of Italy, Gaul, Germany, Britain, and other provinces, considerable variety could nevertheless be found in their Missals. As we have already observed, this did not affect the substance of the mystery or the essential and principal rites of the Mass. It consisted in additions to the prayers, sequences, and especially the feasts, and consequently the Masses, with which each bishop was permitted to enrich his Missal. But it was always forbidden to alter the sacred words of the canon.

The readings from the prophets or the canonical Epistles, together with sections of the Gospels to be recited at each Mass, were indicated by the book called the *Comes*, because it was always available to the ministers of the church. The antiquity of this book was especially venerable, since, as Mabillon observed, it is mentioned as early as the fifth century of the Christian era. Yet it has come down to us through Pamelius and Baluzius burdened with so many new saints and Masses that perhaps more new wares have been added to it than ancient ones.

The venerable Cardinal Thomasius gave us this book from a very ancient Codex.

Anyone wishing to recognize the diversity of the ancient Missals, increased in accordance with the variety of the Churches, should consult the distinguished Father Martene, who assembled the ordinary, or customary, course of the Mass from many Gallican Missals and Rituals (Martene, vol. I, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*). Anyone consulting the surviving ancient manuscript Missals of the Italian Churches could show a similar variety.

In 1736 the learned Joannes de Joanne, canon of the Church of Palermo, illustrated the various rites of the Sicilian liturgy (*On the Sicilian Divine Office*). Let me also disclose the rites by which the Church of Mutina formerly celebrated the dread sacrifice.

As I mentioned above, that Church possessed—and still possesses—a Gregorian Sacramentary written in the ninth or at least the tenth century. In ancient Sacramentaries of this kind, however, rubrics are generally lacking, that is, all the rites to be used for the sacred assembly. Such rites began to be added to Missal books after the year 1000.

Two parchment books of this kind, written six hundred years ago, are preserved in the archive of the chapter of the canons of Mutina. I believe that one of them belonged to the knights, or brothers, of the Templars, for the following names were written beside various days of the Calendar in a more recent and varied hand:

> “On the fifth day before the Ides of July died Hugh de Payns, the first master. On the second day before the Ides of July died the venerable Philip, king of France”—that is, Philip II, in the year 1223. “On the seventh day before the Ides of September died Brother G. Carnoc., the thirteenth master. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October died Brother Bernard of Tremelay, the third master. On the sixth day before the Nones of October died Brother Arnold of Torroja, the eighth master.”

I pass over the names of the others. I have supposed that these were the grand masters of the Order of the Templars.

The other Codex, however, deserves greater attention, because it presents a more careful description of the rubrics of the Mass then in use. Here, therefore, is what I thought should be excerpted from it.

> “The rites of the daily Mass, copied from a Codex of the Church of Mutina written six hundred years ago.

# [Col. 0911]

The Order begins: how a bishop or priest ought to prepare himself for Mass. First, let him sing by himself and with those standing around him the following psalms with the litanies and the antiphon: “Sanctify us, O Lord.” Psalm: “How lovely.” Psalm: “You have blessed.” Psalm: “Incline.” Psalm: “I believed,” with the Our Father and these prayers:

> “Arise, O Lord; help.”  
> Response: “And deliver.”  
> “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us.”  
> Response: “As we have hoped.”  
> “You will revive us, O God.”  
> Response: “And your people will rejoice.”  
> “Show us, O Lord, your mercy.”  
> Response: “And your salvation.”  
> “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord.”  
> Response: “And from those belonging to others.”  
> “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord.”  
> Response: “For no one living will be justified.”  
> “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.”  
> Response: “And let your saints rejoice.”

Then let him remove his ordinary tunic, saying:

> “Strip me, O Lord, of the old man with his deeds, and clothe me with the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.”

For washing the hands:

> “Wash, O Lord, my hands and my heart, so that I may be found worthy to become a temple of the Holy Spirit.”

For the ephod (*ephot*):

> “Grant, O Lord, the helmet of salvation upon my head, to overthrow and conquer all the deceits of the devil.”

For the alb:

> “Clothe me, O Lord, with the garment of salvation, and always surround me with the tunic of joy, chastity, and self-control.”

For the cincture:

> “Gird, O Lord, my loins, and cut away all the vices of my heart and body, together with the guardianship of my mind.”

For the stole:

> “Surround my neck, O Lord, with the stole of righteousness, and purify my mind from every corruption.”

For the chasuble:

> “Clothe me, O Lord, with the breastplate of faith and the helmet of salvation, and fill my heart with perfect charity.”

For the maniple:

> “Give, O Lord, to my hands the maniple, to wipe away the filth from my heart and body, so that without pollution I may be able to praise and bless your name forever and ever. Amen.”

And when he has been prepared, let him say:

> “Make me, I beseech you, almighty God, so clothed in righteousness that I may deserve to rejoice in the exultation of your saints; so that, cleansed from all the filth of sins, I may obtain fellowship with the priests who please you, and that your mercy may strip me of all vices, though the guilt of my own conscience weighs me down. Through the Lord.”

Another prayer:

> “I beseech you, most high God of Sabaoth, holy Father, deign to gird me with the tunic of chastity, surround my loins with the belt of your love, and burn the kidneys of my heart with the fire of your charity, so that I may be able to intercede for my sins, merit pardon for the people standing by, and offer peaceful sacrifices for each person. Do not allow me, though approaching boldly, to perish; rather, deign to wash me, adorn me, and receive me gently.”

After this has been said, the entrance to the altar is made, beginning as follows:

> Antiphon: “I will enter.” “Judge me, O God.”

When he has arrived before the altar, with his face humbly inclined:

> “Place, O Lord, a guard over my mouth.”  
> Response: “And a door of enclosure [*circumstantiae*].”

And let him make the confession according to custom. After the confession has been completed, let him say:

> “O God, I have declared my life to you.”  
> Response: “You have placed my tears.”  
> “I have made my sin known to you.”  
> Response: “And into righteousness.”  
> “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord.”  
> Response: “And you forgave.”

> “For this every saint will pray to you.”  
> Response: “At an opportune time.”

> “O Lord, hear my prayer.”  
> Response: “And my cry.”

> “Take away from us, we beseech you, O Lord, through the intercession of these and all your saints, all iniquities, so that with pure minds we may deserve to enter the Holy of Holies. Through.”

When he has straightened up, let him place incense in the censer, saying:

> “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, may this incense be blessed and become acceptable as an odor of sweetness.”

Then let him take some of it and kiss the Gospel, as the Roman [rite] commands. Next, proceeding a little nearer to the altar and inclined, let him say this prayer:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world, be merciful to me, a sinner, lying in sin in every way; for you alone, Lord our God, are immortal and without sin. Forgive me, wretched as I am, for presuming to approach your holy altar and invoke you; for I have sinned before you from my infancy until now, before your angels and all your saints. But through their intercession grant me divine clemency and pardon for my offenses, and teach me to do your will all the days of my life. You who live and reign.”

Then let him straighten up and kiss the altar, and say this prayer:

> “Almighty Lord God, who are a great and wondrous Lord, who have given us entrance into the Holy of Holies through the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, your only-begotten Son, we beseech and implore your kindness. Therefore we are in fear and trembling, wishing to stand before your holy and glorious altar. Send upon us the gift of your Holy Spirit, and renew our souls and bodies, so that with a pure heart we may offer you a sacrifice for the remission of our sins and of all your peoples, who have been redeemed by the grace and mercy of your Christ. You who live with him.”

Then let him say “Glory to God in the highest,” if the time permits; and when it has been fully completed, let him say this prayer:

> “Before the sight of your divine Majesty, O God, I stand guilty, presuming to invoke your holy name. Have mercy, O Lord, on me, a sinful man. Forgive the unworthy priest through whose hands this offering appears to be made. Spare me, polluted by the stain of sin, especially capital sins, and do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight. Although we are weighed down by vices and the pleasures of the flesh, O God, nevertheless remember that we are flesh. Even the heavens are not pure in your sight; how much less are we earthly human beings, unclean like a menstrual cloth? We are unworthy, Lord Jesus Christ, to be alive; but you, who do not desire the death of a sinner, grant us pardon while we remain in the flesh, so that through the labors of repentance we may deserve to enjoy eternal life in heaven. Through you, Christ Jesus.”

Another prayer:

> “Almighty and eternal God, who have willed that I, a sinner, should stand at the sacred altars and praise the power of your holy name, grant, we beseech you, through the mystery of this sacrament, pardon for my sins, so that I may deserve to minister worthily to your Majesty. Through.”

Then, when he kisses the Gospel, let him say:

> “May the peace of Christ, which he delivered to us through his Gospel, strengthen and preserve our hearts and bodies unto eternal life. Amen.”

And when he places incense in the censer before the Gospel is read, let him say:

> “May the Lord kindle and fill our hearts with the fragrance of his heavenly inspiration, so that we may hear and fulfill the commandments of his Gospel. He who lives.”

Then, with the deacon inclined and asking for a blessing, making the sign of the cross, let him say:

> “May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips, so that you may duly proclaim the Gospel of peace.”

Another blessing:

> “May the blessing of God the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit descend upon you and open your mouth to pronounce his Gospel worthily and suitably.”

The deacon is to say:

> “Strengthen me, O King who holds the principate of the saints, and give a right and well-sounding word to my mouth.”

After the Gospel has been read, let him say:

> “Through these holy words of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, may he forgive us all our offenses.”

And when the deacon has given him the chalice with the offering, let the deacon say:

> “To you, Lord, my Creator, I offer this sacrifice for the remission of all my sins and of all your faithful.”

And the priest, receiving the offering, is to say:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, who on the cross of your Passion willed blood to flow from your side, from which you might consecrate the Church to yourself, receive this sacrifice which your servant offers to you; and most mercifully grant that, for our redemption and that of the whole world, it may rise before your divine Majesty with an odor of sweetness.”

Then, offering the libation in the chalice, let the deacon say:

> “May this sacrifice be acceptable to almighty God.”

And when the priest offers it, let him say:

> “Receive, most merciful Father, the sacrifices of appeasement and praise which I, your unworthy servant, offer to you for the glory and honor of your name, so that they may benefit the living for pardon and all the faithful departed for indulgence; and look favorably upon me as I seek forgiveness. You who live, etc.”

Then let him bless the sacrifice that has been placed there, making the sign of the cross, with these words:

> “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, may this sacrifice be marked, consecrated, and blessed.”

Over the offering:

> “Sanctify, we beseech you, O Lord, this offering, so that it may become for us the body of your only-begotten Son.”

Over the chalice:

> “Sanctify, we beseech you, O Lord, this chalice also, so that it may become for us the blood of your only-begotten Son.”

Then let him place incense in the censer, saying:

> “Through the intercession of the holy archangel Gabriel, who stands at the right of the altar of incense, and of all his elect, may the Lord deign to bless this incense and receive it as an odor of sweetness.”

And when he has released the smoke, let him say:

> “May this incense, blessed by you, ascend to you, O Lord, and may your mercy descend upon us.”

Likewise:

> “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.”

When incense is offered to each person, let this be said:

> “May the Lord kindle in us the fire of his love and the flame of eternal charity.”

For offering the gifts:

> “Receive, Holy Trinity, this offering which we offer to you in memory of the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ; and in honor of Mary, the perpetual Virgin, and of all your elect who have pleased you from the beginning of the world. May it benefit all for honor, but us for salvation; and may all those whose memory we commemorate on earth deign to intercede for us in heaven. Through the same one.”

For the dead:

> “Receive, Holy Trinity, this offering which I offer to you for the souls of your male and female servants, so that you may deign to grant them eternal rest among your elect, that in their company they may enjoy eternal life. Through Christ.”

Afterward let him turn, kiss the altar, and say:

> “Pray for me, sinful brothers and sisters, that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable to almighty God in his sight.”

And those standing around are to respond:

> “May all the saints and elect of God pray for you, and may the Lord hear you as you pray for the salvation of us all; and may he remember all your sacrifice. Offer a sacrifice of praise to God, and may almighty God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins. May the Lord God be in your heart and in your mouth, and may he receive from your hands a sacrifice acceptable to him for our salvation and that of all.”

Afterward let them say these psalms:

> “May he hear you.”  
> Psalm: “To you I have lifted up.”  
> Psalm: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to.”  
> Psalm: “God our refuge.”  
> Psalm: “He who dwells.”  
> Psalm: “To the Lord when I was in distress.”  
> A Song of Ascents up to “He who made heaven and earth.”  
> “Lord, have mercy,” with the Our Father and these prayers:  
> “Save your servant.”  
> Response: “My God.”  
> “You have granted him the desire of his heart.”  
> Response: “And the will.”  
> “He asked life from you, and you granted it to him.”  
> Response: “Length of days.”  
> “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.”  
> Response: “And his ears.”  
> “May your will be done upon us.”  
> Response: “As we have hoped.”  
> “Arise, O Lord; help us.”  
> Response: “And deliver.”  
> “O Lord, hear my prayer.”  
> Response: “And my cry.”

Collect for the priest:

> “May your servant rejoice, O Lord, in the benefits obtained; and to him to whom you have granted confidence in hoping for your mercy, graciously grant the effect of the mercy he desires. Through.”

Collect for all:

> “Incline your ears, we beseech you, O Lord, of your mercy to our prayers, and, as the knower of hidden things, graciously hear the prayers of your suppliants, so that, by your generosity, we may reach eternal life. Through.”

The Apostles’ Creed:

> “I believe in one God, the Father almighty,” etc.

The Prefaces follow.

[Note: That is, the prefaces for the Nativity of the Lord; the Epiphany of the Lord; the whole of Lent; the Resurrection of the Lord; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the Holy Cross; the Apostles; the Assumption of Saint Mary; and in honor of the Holy Trinity. Then there is one preface used on the remaining days, as in the printed editions. Before the final preface there appears an image of the Savior holding a book in his hand. After it another image of the same figure hanging from the cross is seen. It was customary to kiss both, or at least one of them. The kisses that were given have worn away some of the color.]

The Canon follows.

[Note: The Canon proceeds as in the printed editions. There one reads: “Together with your servant, our pope (name), and our king, and our bishop (name),” etc. “Cosmas and Damian, and all your saints, and also those whose triumph is celebrated today in the presence of your glory as a solemnity. By whose merits and prayers,” etc.]

> “Therefore, etc.”

Here incline slightly.

> “This offering, therefore, etc. May it become the body + and blood + of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Here he takes the offering from the altar.

> “Who, on the day before he suffered, etc. He blessed, + broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat from this, all of you. For this is my body.”

Here he takes the chalice.

> “In like manner, after supper had been eaten, etc.,” as in the customary canon.

Before the body is mixed with the blood:

> “May this most holy commixture of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be salvation of mind and body for all who receive it, and a saving preparation for attaining eternal life. Through the same one.”

Here the priest kisses the altar, saying:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your apostles, etc.”

Then let him say the peace:

> “Hold fast the bond of charity and peace, so that you may be fit for the most holy mysteries.”

The others are to say to one another:

> “May the peace of Christ and of the Church abound in our hearts. Amen.”

Before Communion let him say:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, etc.”

Then, holding the bread in his hand, let him say:

> “I will receive the heavenly bread and call upon the name of the Lord.”

Another:

> “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed.”

When he receives the body, let him say:

> “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be for me an everlasting remedy unto eternal life. Amen.”

When receiving the chalice, let him say:

> “What shall I repay to the Lord, etc.”

When drinking from the chalice, let him say:

> “May the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve me unto eternal life.”

After receiving the body and blood, let him say:

> “May the body of my Lord Jesus Christ, which I have received, and his blood, with which I have been given to drink, adhere to my inward parts, and grant that no stain of sin remain there where his sacraments have entered. He who lives with the Father, etc.”

[Note: How ancient this kind of prayer is, which is still repeated daily in the Roman liturgy, is shown by the Gothic Missal used before the year 800 of the Christian era. There, in the Sunday Mass, this Postcommunion is found: “May your body, O Lord, which we have received, and your chalice, of which we have drunk, adhere to our inward parts; grant, almighty God, that no stain remain where pure and holy sacraments have entered. Through.”]

And when he gives Communion to others, let him say:

> “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen.”

Another:

> “May the reception of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your soul unto eternal life. Amen.”

Postcommunion:

> “We have joyfully received the heavenly sacraments, O Lord. Through the intercession of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, Mother of God, together with all your saints, may they benefit us unto eternal life. Through the same one.”

Likewise let him say:

> “Go. The Mass is ended.”

When the Mass has been completed, let him kiss the altar and say:

> “Through the merits and intercessions of the most blessed Mary, ever-virgin, and of all the saints, may almighty God have mercy on us. He who lives, etc.”

Afterward, returning to the sacristy, let him say:

> “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord,” etc.

[Col. 0921A] Let these few excerpts from that Missal suffice. For anyone wishing to display to readers, without discrimination, every sort of ecclesiastical rite—whether legitimate or illegitimate—that was formerly practiced in sacred worship during barbarous times would be undertaking a task either of little usefulness or of diminished interest. Nor should you think that variations and additions in the celebration of Masses once stopped here. For since pious men were then restrained by no curb, and imagined that they could increase the devotion of the faithful through new inventions, they did not hesitate to introduce into the Mass itself new sequences—for that is what they called them—many of which were indeed elegant and pious, but some also consisted of absurdities, being products of simplicity.

Nor did the treasury of the Mass grow only through these sequences, sung after the reading of the Epistles; they also attached pious embellishments to the Kyrie eleison. I possess as a witness to this custom a very ancient parchment Antiphonary of the Church of Modena. The codex, badly treated by the injury of time, with its characters corrupted and obliterated in more than one place, may be judged to have been written in the tenth century, both from the form of its letters and from the number of its feasts, among which is the more recent feast of All Saints. It also presents antiphons used in Masses, with very small musical notes placed above them, by whose guidance the singers were then directed in the choir.

In most respects it agrees with the Antiphonary published by Cardinal Tommasi. On the other hand, it contains some things that are lacking in that work. I offer a specimen.

## At the Resurrection of the Lord

[Col. 0921C]

**Ant.** “I saw water flowing out of the temple on the right side. Alleluia. And all to whom that water came were saved, and they shall say: Alleluia, alleluia. On the day of my Resurrection, says the Lord: Alleluia. I shall gather the nations, assemble the kingdoms, and pour clean water over them. Alleluia.”

“When the King of glory entered to conquer the gates of hell, the choir of the saints, which was held captive in death, cried out in tearful voice: ‘You have come, O desired One, whom we awaited in the darkness, that you might lead us, bound as we are, out from our prisons. Our vows called upon you; abundant sighs sought you.’”

“The angel sat at the Lord’s tomb, etc.”

**Verse.** “Praise the crucified Lord, and glorify him who was buried for us; adore him who rose from the dead.”

[Col. 0921D]

**Response.** “Do not be afraid; I tell you, for he whom you seek as dead is already alive, and the life of human beings has risen with him.”

**Verse.** “Remember how he foretold that the Son of Man must be crucified and raised from the dead on the third day.”

“Kyrie eleison. O Theos … athanatos … ymas”—“O God … immortal … us.”

“Kyrie eleison. O gracious Father, seated above the wings of cherubim and seraphim, be merciful and kind to your servants on account of their debts.”

“Kyrie eleison. To you alone are due hymn, melody, song, symphony, and the voice of every kind of tongue. Kyrie eleison.”

“Christe eleison. Only-begotten of the Father, renew your nature within us.”

“Christe eleison, etc.”

“All together, with loud voices, we praise you, Three and One.”

“Whose harmonious unity and equality in the Trinity lives and reigns now and unto infinite ages of ages. Amen.”

“I rose, and I am still with you. Alleluia.”

Sometimes a hymn composed according to the ingenuity of those times was also added to such additions. Here is another example, containing appendices to the Kyrie eleison together with a hymn arranged in meter.

## Concerning the Kyrie eleison

“Kyrie eleison. Almighty Father, light and source of light;

“Kyrie eleison. By the command of the Word, you created all things from nothing;

“Kyrie eleison. For the human race, burdened beneath the weight of sin;

“Christe eleison. Sent into the filth of earth from the Father’s citadel;

“Christe eleison. You clothed yourself in flesh, born of the chaste Virgin;

“Christe eleison. You cleansed the world’s guilt by the blood you shed.

“Kyrie eleison. Benevolent Spirit, equal to the Father and the Son;

“Kyrie eleison. God, three in persons but one in divinity.”

“Kyrie eleison, etc.”

“Let us all sing

Praises in hymns,

Peacefully to God alone,

Who in his goodness saves

And always protects

Those who follow him forever, etc.”

John of John, the canon mentioned above, also reports that additions of this kind, sung to the Kyrie eleison, were used among the people of Palermo and Messina on the double feasts of the saints; indeed, he observes that the same additions are found in the Missals of other places, even in printed editions.

At the end of the most ancient Antiphonary of Modena there are also several hymns in which one sometimes finds neither meter nor rhythm. Similar hymns, though composed with greater care, were produced in the ninth and tenth centuries by the monks of St. Gall—Notker, Hartmann, Ratpert, and others—whose works we possess in Canisius (*Lectiones antiquae*). These hymns were sung at Mass in Modena on the more solemn feasts.

Here are the opening verses of the hymn customarily sung during the night of the Lord’s Nativity:

“Come, let us recall in pious praises the worthy songs

Of this day,

On which the most welcome One is born for us, etc.”

Another was sung at first light:

[Col. 0923A]

“Now let us all

Return thanks to the Lord God,

Who by his birth, etc.”

A third was used during the day at Mass:

“Born before the ages,

The invisible Son of God,

Through whom the universe is made, etc.”

Elegiac verses are also read at the Resurrection of the Lord:

“Hail, festal Day, revered throughout the whole world,

On which God conquered hell and holds the stars, etc.”

The wisdom of the Roman pontiffs is to be praised: having removed these foreign wares, with which the sacred liturgy had been burdened rather than adorned, they restored the Roman Mass to its former purity and moderation. But considerable severity will also be needed in the future. The human race reveals itself to be excessively inclined toward novelty, and unless it encountered barriers, it would introduce something new every day.

If better things can be brought forward to enlarge the kingdom of piety, it will certainly not be wrong to embrace them; indeed, at times it will be advantageous. But if the novelties proposed are wholly unfit either to nourish or to increase true piety, and have perhaps been devised secretly out of the ambition of some private person, or from a desire for preeminence or advantage, it is right to resist them and not permit them to come into use. But I must not proceed farther.

## CHAPTER VIII. What the non-Catholics have attempted against the Mass and the Eucharist; and a refutation of the Englishman Bingham, who brings out weapons worn out by repeated use

[Col. 0923C]

Among the other prerogatives that strongly commend the ancient liturgies—once diverse according to the variety of the Churches—this one certainly deserves the highest regard: that a rich mass of Catholic dogmas is found interspersed throughout them. For in so many prayers, rites, and ceremonies one repeatedly recognizes what the orthodox Church has believed for so many centuries concerning the unity and Trinity of God; concerning the divinity, incarnation, and other matters relating to the Son of God; likewise concerning the divinity and power of the Holy Spirit; the invocation and intercession of the saints; and other articles of the Catholic faith.

For this very reason Saint Augustine returned to this source when he was discussing the necessity of heavenly grace; and other Fathers did the same as occasion required. For the dogmas encountered there are not the opinions of one private teacher, but of that entire Church which used those same liturgies.

Among these liturgies, no one is unaware that the Roman liturgy has always held the first place. Just as, from its origins, it perpetually preserved the faith undefiled as the teacher of the others, so it had many other Churches following its rites. For, as Augustine himself teaches, the authority of public prayers is especially effective for learning the faith of the Church.

The books we call sacramentaries themselves sufficiently indicate by their very name that they chiefly contain Catholic teaching concerning the sacraments—that is, visible signs containing the invisible gift of God’s power and grace, through which, by divine institution, grace and sanctification are either conferred or increased in a person professing faith in Christ.

The matters belonging to the Church’s sacraments are indeed well known from the many works and books of theologians devoted to this subject, so that nothing new can be contributed to it, and anyone wishing to discuss them is compelled merely to repeat what others have long ago debated with the greatest diligence.

Nevertheless, I hope that an honest reader will forgive me if I undertake to examine what in the liturgy of the Roman Church concerns the Eucharist—both for the greater consolation and strengthening of orthodox believers and also, if possible, for the healing of some who may be willing to read these pages, whose weak minds and dim eyes do not see the true doctrine concerning the body and blood of Christ in the Mass, although it is evident and perfectly clear.

[Col. 0924B]

The Englishman Joseph Bingham prompted me to renew this discussion (*The Antiquities of the Christian Church*, Book XI). He treats the rites of the Mass of the faithful with considerable learning, but at the same time either conceals or condemns the chief Catholic dogmas contained in and constituting the tremendous sacrifice and sacrament of the Eucharist—this sacrament which, in substance, stands far above the others.

For he says nothing about the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass; he denies the real presence of the Lord’s body and blood in the Eucharist and the transubstantiation of the gifts; and he disapproves the worship due to Christ who is present. Remove these things from the Mass of the faithful, and its immense dignity is diminished in a remarkable way—indeed, it perishes.

Moreover, other heretics have denied that this sacrifice is propitiatory, so that the most august action in the Church of God is reduced almost to nothing. Finally, this position also spread among Luther’s followers, who completely abolished the Mass itself as a sacrifice, retaining only communion.

The things that Luther himself vomited forth against the Roman Mass are horrifying. He did not hesitate to confess that he had received this doctrine from the devil—and indeed while he was awake. Let none of us begrudge him and his followers so great a teacher.

What Zwingli and Calvin later established concerning the same Mass and Eucharist, and what was established by the Anglicans, Socinians, and others torn away from the bosom of the Roman Catholic Church, is sufficiently known to the learned.

It is also well known that these people devised a way of evading the clear testimonies not only of the most ancient sacred liturgy but also of the holy Fathers, who explicitly teach that through consecration bread and wine truly become the body and blood of the Lord. In the Eucharist they recognize or imagine nothing else but a figure of Christ seated at the right hand of the Father in heaven, together with a heavenly power infused into the bread and wine; and they deny both their conversion into the body and blood and the real presence of Christ in the same sacrament.

They also dispute with us concerning the name “transubstantiation,” as though it were an invention of more recent centuries, as if the liturgy and the Fathers had not designated the same reality by other names from the earliest centuries onward.

Bingham himself undertook to show that “the principal ancient Fathers declared as clearly as words can do so that the change effected in the elements of bread and wine through consecration is not a change of such a kind as to destroy their nature and substance, but merely changes their qualities and elevates them to a spiritual use, as happens in many other consecrations, where the qualities of things are changed without any real alteration of substance” (Bingham, Book XV, chapter 5, §4).

Once he has established this opinion, he immediately supposes that the real presence and adoration of the Eucharist have been eliminated.

Against this, Catholics insist that the judgment of the entire ancient Church concerning the real change of the sacred gifts in the Eucharist is clear and certain; that the Lord’s real presence in the sacrament is clear; and that from this very presence proceeds the efficacy and power of so august a sacrament, not from some figure or promise, of which there is no trace in sacred Scripture or among the holy Fathers.

Either we or they are grossly mistaken. And when these people reject and despise the Church—which Christ nevertheless established as the legitimate judge in religious controversies, the pillar of truth, and one that he declared would never fail—what end will there ever be to disputation?

We have here a truly lamentable proof of human misery, when we see men devoting great effort to sacred Scripture yet, in matters of the greatest importance, on which eternal salvation or damnation depends, obstinately and most stubbornly defending whatever false and absurd opinion each has absorbed from childhood and from school, trying everything lest, once defeated, he should ever surrender—even in matters surrounded by the clearest light.

Above all, God must be entreated to grant our brothers separated from the unity of the Church a sincere and peaceful disposition and a mind eager for truth and peace. Then they too will easily perceive that, on the one hand, the Mass has been rejected by men inflated not by the Spirit of God but by the spirit of pride, with inexcusable rashness; while, on the other hand, we retain and observe it with the most just religious devotion. They will also see that the Catholic Church’s doctrine concerning the Eucharist cannot be rejected without enormous wrongdoing.

Now it must be revealed with what love and concern for truth Bingham proceeded in this argument. He collected certain well-worn passages from Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom in his letter to Caesarius, Theodoret, Ephraem, bishop of Antioch, Tertullian, Augustine, Gelasius I, Roman pontiff, Facundus of Hermiane, and Isidore of Seville.

Then he refers the reader who desires more to the Calvinist Cosin’s *History of Transubstantiation* and to the book on the sacrament of the Eucharist by Albertinus, an adherent of Calvin. Having done this, the case is finished, and, as I judge, the Anglican writer has sung a triumph for himself and his Protestants.

But if this was the man’s conviction, how could he have thought that he had satisfied his own conscience when he brings forward only what the Sacramentarians commonly produce in support of their position, as though the arguments of Catholics were either nonexistent or of no weight, and as though there were no need to consider what Catholic men have contributed in confirmation of the truth of their dogma?

Certainly that man must be said to wish to deceive his reader who, undertaking to explain a controversy of such importance, conceals the strength of the opposing side and presents only the weapons of his own side as victorious.

In 1719 Bingham published this sixth volume of his work in London. Yet for more than half a century before that, a notable controversy concerning the Eucharist had already been pursued with the greatest zeal and effort—indeed, had been brought to completion—between the French writer Arnauld and the other authors of the books on the perpetual consensus of the Catholic Church, on the one side, and Claude, a member of the Calvinist flock, on the other.

The Catholic position was strengthened by such an abundance and force of arguments, and the quibbles and sophistries not only of Claude but also of Albertinus were refuted, that anyone exercising free judgment and sincerity must admit that those who deny the truth of the Lord’s flesh and blood in the Eucharist and dissent from the Catholic Church are guilty of the most evident crime.

If these matters were unknown to Bingham, he must be charged with gross ignorance. But if he knew them, who will excuse him before God when he presented this controversy to the common people and to his readers as though it had been settled by the arguments of the Calvinist sect alone?

How weak and worthless their arguments are when compared with those of the Catholics, although the labors of distinguished men have long since made this clear, I too shall demonstrate as briefly as I can.

Before I do so, I ask the reader to remember that however powerful a man may be in intellectual ability, he cannot always speak or write with complete precision, nor can he always express his thoughts in terms so clear and exact that they are free of all obscurity in every place—especially when the subject demands difficult metaphysical ideas. It is therefore possible for quibblers and sophistical minds to twist words and statements toward opinions contrary to those of the same author.

Sound reason, however, commands that we interpret and explain obscure matters from those that are clear and open elsewhere. For who but a fool would use darkness itself to cast obscurity over the light, instead of using light to drive away darkness?

Would that the Sacramentarians did not daily abuse this detestable method, when they do nothing but pluck out and press in the question of the Eucharist a few passages of the holy Fathers that are doubtful, obscure, and open to various interpretations, while at the same time rejecting what those same Fathers pronounce in explicit and unmistakable words on the very subject, by which the doctrine of the Catholic Church is most plainly revealed.

It is useful to begin with Facundus of Hermiane. It is remarkable how opportunely and inopportunely Protestants are accustomed to produce and repeat his words, as though the unshakable settlement of this controversy depended upon them.

The Englishman William Cave, in his *Ecclesiastical Writers*, when discussing Facundus, brought forward the same words, contrary to his usual practice and out of context, as though they were a chief monument of the Calvinist position.

Likewise John Fell, the Anglican bishop of Oxford, in his notes on Saint Cyprian’s *On the Lapsed*, chapter 10, introduces Facundus onto the stage and takes care to turn the readers’ eyes away from Saint Cyprian’s weighty and manifest words concerning the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, which we shall cite below.

I shall pass over the others and concentrate on Bingham, to whom it seems evident that Facundus excludes the real presence of the Lord in the ineffable sacrament of the altar.

Here are Facundus’s own words (Facundus, Book IX, chapter 5):

“Christ deigned to receive the sacrament of adoption both when he was circumcised and when he was baptized. And adoption may be called the sacrament of adoption, just as we receive his body and blood, the sacrament of which is in the consecrated bread and cup—not because the bread is properly his body and the cup his blood, but because it contains within itself the mystery of his body and blood.

“Therefore the Lord himself called the blessed bread and cup that he handed to the disciples his body and blood. Accordingly, just as Christ’s faithful are rightly said to receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, so Christ himself, when he had received the sacrament of the adoption of sons, could rightly be said to have received the adoption of sons.”

Anyone not held captive by partisan zeal will discover nothing in these obscure words that is manifestly opposed to Catholic doctrine. Once the reader remembers that by the word “sacrament” nothing other than a visible sign containing some invisible gift of divine power and grace is meant, he will have no difficulty understanding Facundus’s thought.

The bread and wine in the Eucharist are symbols and signs which, sanctified by God through the words of consecration, contain the true flesh and blood of Christ. Through consecration they do not cease to be symbols and signs, although the substance of the bread and wine is converted into the body and blood of the Lord.

Now ask whether the consecrated bread properly—that is, the species of bread—is the Lord’s body, and whether the cup is his blood. Facundus denies this, and not without reason. For although the symbols truly contain the body and blood, they are not themselves the body and blood; and although Christ’s faithful, when they receive the sacrament—that is, the symbols and signs—of his body and blood, are rightly said to receive Christ’s body and blood, nevertheless those same symbols are not properly Christ’s body and blood.

Does Facundus therefore deny that the Lord’s flesh and blood are truly received by the faithful, hidden beneath the sacrament, or beneath the symbols? Not at all. Indeed, if you weigh his words properly, they confess precisely this.

For what else does he mean when he says that the bread and cup contain within themselves the mystery of the body and blood? By the word “mystery,” the ancients meant something secret, hidden, or ineffable. Chrysostom (*Homily 19 on the Epistle to the Romans*) calls a mystery something unknown and secret, something exceedingly wonderful, unusual, and unexpected.

For this reason Saints Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Chrysostom, and other Fathers called the Eucharist itself a mystery or mysteries—life-giving, heavenly, awe-inspiring, holy, and divine.

In the post-communion collects, the Roman Church in particular used this word to signify the body and blood of the Lord that had been received. See below the Leonine, Gelasian, and Gregorian Sacramentaries. There one reads:

“Restored by the sacred mysteries.”

“Refreshed by the heavenly mystery.”

“We ask that the divine mysteries…”

“O God, by whose mysteries we are cleansed and nourished…”

“Be present, O Lord, to your people, whom you have instructed with heavenly mysteries.”

“Sanctified by the saving mystery.”

“Filled with saving mysteries.”

“May the heavenly mystery be for us the restoration of mind and body.”

I pass over the remainder.

It is as certain as anything can be that both now and in ancient centuries this designated a real, not figurative, reception of the Lord’s body and blood, as we shall show below.

You therefore now understand that Facundus’s statement is so far from conflicting with the Catholic position that it explicitly confirms it.

The same truth follows from the comparison with baptism that Facundus himself uses. Although baptism is merely the sacrament—that is, the visible sign—of adoption, and is not adoption itself, nevertheless baptism may be called adoption.

There is no doubt, moreover, that those who receive baptism receive a true, not figurative, adoption as children of God. Therefore, even if the sacrament—that is, the visible sign—of the Lord’s body and blood is not properly the Lord’s body and blood themselves, whoever receives the sacrament nevertheless receives the true, not figurative, flesh and blood of Christ, because the species of bread and wine truly contain within themselves the mystery—that is, the hidden and awe-inspiring presence—of the Lord’s body and blood. In the consecrated bread and cup we receive his flesh and blood, as Facundus explicitly testifies.

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that someone could infer from this passage of Facundus the so-called “impanation” of the Lutheran sect, as though in the Eucharist bread and wine, retaining their own substance, were joined with the reality of the Lord’s body and blood.

But this inference collapses when one notices the custom practiced throughout all the centuries and still occasionally retained by Catholics: namely, calling the bread the consecrated host and the chalice consecrated wine, even though they have always held and still hold that the bread and wine whose species remain were converted through consecration into the true and real body and blood of the Lord.

I proceed to Saint Augustine. It cannot be denied that the first fathers of the Sacramentarian sect—Berengarius, followed by Zwingli and Calvin—abused certain doubtful, obscure, and wrongly understood passages from Augustine’s works in order to remove the real presence of Christ the Lord from the Eucharist, contemptuously committing the enormous crime of disregarding the Church’s perpetual consensus on this matter.

But Augustine never dreamed that he held a different opinion here from the other Fathers of the Church. If ambiguous statements occur in his books, his meaning must be sought from other statements and words of his that are by no means ambiguous.

Facundus, whom we have just heard, speaks aptly on this matter and should be heard here as well:

“Just as it is characteristic of heretical slanderers to interpret badly, from doubtful and obscure passages, what is certain and manifest, so it is characteristic of Catholic prudence and truth to explain doubtful and hidden matters by what is certain and evident.”

Would that all who love truth more than their sect would use this prudent, indeed necessary, rule.

From Albertinus, Bingham selected, as though it were a fearsome battering ram for overthrowing the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist, a fragment of a sermon of Saint Augustine preserved for us by Saint Fulgentius.

Augustine says to the infants—that is, to the newly baptized:

“What you see on God’s altar you also saw last night. But what it was and what it signified, since it contains the sacrament of a great reality, you have not yet heard. What you see, therefore, is bread and a cup, as your own eyes also report to you. But what your faith, which must be instructed, demands is this: THE BREAD IS THE BODY OF CHRIST; THE CUP IS THE BLOOD OF CHRIST” (Augustine, Sermon 272, new Benedictine edition).

Then he introduces the infants asking “how,” since Christ has ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, “is the bread his body, and is the cup—or what the cup contains—his blood?”

Augustine replies:

“These things, brothers, are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance. What is understood has a spiritual fruit.

“But if you wish to understand the body of Christ, listen to the Apostle speaking to the faithful: ‘You are the body of Christ and members.’ If, therefore, you are the body of Christ and its members, your mystery is placed upon the Lord’s table; you receive your mystery. To what you are, you answer ‘Amen,’ and by answering you give your assent. For you hear: ‘The body of Christ’; and you answer: ‘Amen.’ Be a member of the body, so that your Amen may be true.”

He then goes on to show why Christ wished this sacrament to be made in bread and wine: namely, to commend charity and unity to his faithful, since both bread and wine are made from many grains.

From this sermon Bingham and others of his party infer that there is nothing on the altar but bread and wine; that Christ’s natural body is not there; and that only a representation of it, and also of his mystical body—that is, the Church—is present.

How readily we flatter ourselves in the things we want, feel, and love! Whoever carefully examines and weighs this sermon must admit that he finds there many obscurities and no coherent sequence of thought, to such an extent that Cardinal Perron suspected, not without reason, that something had dropped out here.

For it explicitly says: “The bread is the body of Christ; the cup is the blood of Christ.” Then the question is raised how Christ’s natural body and blood can be in the Eucharist when Christ is seated in heaven.

Augustine replies with the Apostle: “You are the body of Christ and members.”

The answer plainly appears absurd. For from it follows that the bread is not the body of Christ but the body—and the blood—of the faithful. Moreover, even outside the sacrament the Church is the mystical body of Christ.

How, then, are these words to be understood?

This much is certainly evident: the Calvinists cannot derive anything from this passage in support of their opinion. For although they do not admit Christ’s natural body in the Eucharist, they nevertheless acknowledge in it a figure of that same natural body. But here there is no word about a figure.

Either Augustine in this passage determines nothing as to whether the flesh and blood of the Lord’s natural body are truly present in the sacrament, or he expresses only the Catholic position when he says: “The bread is Christ’s body, and the cup is his blood.”

No one but a rash person will dare deny that in Augustine’s own time the Church also prayed in the liturgy that the bread “might become the body of Christ” and be changed into the Lord’s flesh through the Lord’s words and the descent of the Holy Spirit.

Thus the only conclusion that can be drawn from this passage is that Augustine did not undertake there to explain whether Christ’s flesh and blood are truly in the sacrament. He proposed only to explain why the sacrament itself had been instituted in bread and wine.

He says that this was done mystically to proclaim to the faithful the necessity of charity and union among themselves and with Christ—something he inculcates in so many other passages in order to turn his people away from the violent schism of the Donatists.

Nevertheless, even in this passage he plainly teaches the truth and reality of Christ’s body in the Eucharist when he says that the sanctified bread presented by the priest to the newly baptized is called “THE BODY OF CHRIST”—that is, “Behold the Lord’s body”—and that they themselves respond “AMEN,” meaning: “So I believe; so it is. I believe, I say, that this is the true body of Christ.”

Then Augustine adds: “Be a member of the body, so that your Amen may be true.”

That is: If you believe this to be the true body of Christ, then you too must act through genuine charity so that you may be a member of this true body. For if you act otherwise and lack charity, you do not say Amen from the heart; that is, you do not truly desire to be a member of the Lord’s body, who especially demands charity from those devoted to the Gospel.

Here another sermon of the same holy teacher to the infants, or newly baptized, must be brought forward:

“I remember,” he says, “my promise. For I promised you who have been baptized a sermon in which I would explain the sacrament of the Lord’s table, which you now also see and of which you became partakers last night.

“You ought to know what you have received, what you are about to receive, and what you ought to receive every day. That bread which you see on the altar, sanctified by the word of God, IS THE BODY OF CHRIST. That cup—or rather, what the cup contains—sanctified by the word of God, IS THE BLOOD OF CHRIST.

“Through these things the Lord Christ wished to commend his BODY and BLOOD, which he shed for us for the forgiveness of sins” (Augustine, Sermon 227, new edition; formerly 83).

As everyone understands, someone explaining the Calvinist opinion to newly baptized persons who were then learning for the first time what the Eucharist is would surely have spoken differently, lest anyone be deceived.

Such an explanation is appropriate only to one intending to hand on the judgment of the Catholic Church.

But Augustine explains what this body and blood are: namely, Christ’s natural body and natural blood, which he himself shed for us.

The bread, therefore, sanctified by the word of God—that is, by the words of consecration—is Christ’s natural body, not an imaginary body received by faith. For if the latter had been intended, Augustine would have said: “That bread which you see is a figure of Christ’s body”; he would not have said: “It is Christ’s body.”

In the same way he says that the wine sanctified by the word of God is Christ’s natural blood, and emphatically not a figure of it.

Augustine then continues in this sermon to teach the newly baptized what Christ requires for receiving his body and blood worthily and correctly: namely, charity and the union of the members with one another and with the head himself, the Lord Jesus.

“By this bread,” he says, “it is commended to you how you ought to love unity. ‘One bread, one body, we who are many,’ says the Apostle” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

Here Augustine follows Chrysostom (*Homily 24 on 1 Corinthians*). This sermon, therefore, must be explained in light of the other.

Each sincere follower of Calvin should at least acknowledge that the former sermon is shrouded in some obscurity and suffers from excessive confidence. Whoever contends that Calvin’s teachings are plainly contained there, and that many other passages of Augustine—which most clearly establish the position of the Catholic Church—must be explained from this and other obscure passages, is arguing with undue assurance. I select a few passages:

“We have said, brothers,” he says, “that the Lord commended this to us in the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood: that we should remain in him, and he in us, etc. What do we believe and have come to know? That you are Christ, the Son of the living God—that is, you are life itself, eternal life—and you give us in your flesh and blood nothing other than what you are, etc. Let us eat the flesh of Christ and drink the blood of Christ, not only in the sacrament, as many wicked people also do, but let us eat and drink unto participation in the Spirit, so that we may remain in the Lord’s body as members” (Augustine, *Tractate* 27 on John 6).

If Christ gives us what he himself is, then he gives himself—that is, his true flesh and blood united with his divinity. He also gives us the life of the Spirit, so that he remains in us and we remain in him, because Christ himself is eternal life.

Regarding his mother Monica, Augustine says:

“She desired that remembrance of her should be made at your altar, which she had served without interruption of a single day, knowing that there the holy victim was dispensed, by which the record that stood against us had been erased” (Augustine, *Confessions*, book 9, chapter 13).

Was bread of the sort that the Sacramentarians consider the Eucharist ever a holy victim that erased the record of our condemnation? Certainly not. This victim was, and is, the true body of Christ. Nor does Augustine say that a figure of that victim was dispensed, but the victim itself.

Again the same holy bishop writes:

“The Ecclesiastes says: ‘There is nothing good for a man except what he shall eat and drink.’ What can more plausibly be understood than that which pertains to participation in this table, which the priest himself, the mediator of the New Testament, presents according to the order of Melchizedek from his body and blood? For this sacrifice succeeded all those sacrifices of the Old Testament that were offered in the shadow of what was to come” (Augustine, *The City of God*, book 17, chapter 20).

If Christ is said to perform an unbloody sacrifice with his body and blood, then Augustine recognized in that sacrifice neither a figure nor a shadow of the Lord’s body and blood. Above all, in this passage and in so many others, he writes that the ancient sacrifices were figures, shadows, and signs of the one Christian sacrifice, and of Christ sacrificed daily upon the sacred altar. For, Augustine adds, “in place of all those sacrifices and offerings, his body is offered and administered to those who participate.”

Therefore, it is not merely bread, nor a figure of Christ’s body and blood, that is offered and sacrificed in the Mass, but Christ’s true body and blood.

Moreover, the same holy bishop writes:

“We receive with faithful heart and mouth the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gives us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink, although it seems more horrifying to eat human flesh than to kill it, and to drink human blood than to shed it” (Augustine, *Against the Adversary of the Law*, book 2, chapter 9).

That is, although the Lord said that he would give us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink, and actually does give them to us—which is indeed horrifying—nevertheless, trusting his words, we believe with the firmest faith that we receive and eat that same flesh with our mouths, and drink that very blood. These words would be utterly senseless according to Calvin’s position. What difficulty is there in believing, and what horror, if only a figure of Christ’s flesh and blood is received in the sacrament?

Finally, to omit other passages, which may be sought in Bellarmine and other controversial writers, especially in the author of *The Perpetuity of the Faith*, consider what Augustine says in a very famous passage:

“And he was carried in his own hands. But how this could happen in a human being, who can understand? For who is carried in his own hands? A person could be carried in the hands of others; no one is carried in his own hands. How this is to be understood literally in David, we do not find; but in Christ we do find it. For Christ was carried in his own hands when, commending his body, he said: ‘This is my body’; for that body was carried in his own hands” (Augustine, exposition of Psalm 33).

The Sacramentarians can indeed fish out their own opinion from Sacred Scripture and from innumerable passages of the holy Fathers where the Eucharist is discussed. Everywhere they can force the notion of a figure upon the text, interpret *est* (“is”) as *significat* (“signifies”), and turn what is altogether literal into a metaphor, deceiving themselves and others. For it could not have happened that, if the Fathers had shared Calvin’s view, they would at some point—indeed, often—have explained what “the body and blood of the Lord” signified in the Eucharist according to the Calvinist interpretation. Yet they abstained from doing so; indeed, they taught the opposite.

Augustine’s words recently quoted, however, are so clear that there is no room for escape. He says that, when instituting the Eucharist and saying of the bread, “This is my body,” Jesus carried himself in his own hands, and that this was fulfilled literally—that is, not metaphorically, not figuratively, and not merely through the imagination of those receiving the Eucharist. Augustine recognizes that, according to the natural order, it is impossible for any human being to carry himself in his own hands. But it was not impossible for God; he acknowledges that this prodigy was truly performed by the Lord in the institution of this ineffable sacrament.

Nothing extraordinary, however, would occur in a human being carrying an image or figure of himself in his own hands. Therefore, unless obstinate and blinded people can maintain that Saint Augustine was ignorant of or denied the real presence of the Lord’s body and blood in the Eucharist, these manifest passages must be used to explain the passages that are sometimes ambiguous and obscure in Augustine’s works, not the clear passages explained away by the obscure ones. No reasonable person understands so great a man to be guilty of contradictions. One should also consult his sermon 225, formerly 140, *On Time*, and sermon 372, formerly 54, *On Various Matters*, to pass over other passages.

I do not know what Bingham wishes to extract from Gregory of Nyssa, who writes:

“Bread likewise is bread at the beginning, common bread; but once the mystery has sanctified it, it is called Christ’s and becomes Christ’s body: Χριστοῦ λέγεται καὶ γίνεται—‘it is called Christ’s and becomes [his] body.’ So also the altar, the oil, and the priest are sanctified through blessing. The priest, although changed neither in body nor in form, but remaining, as regards outward appearance, the same person he was, bears within him an invisible soul transformed for the better by a certain invisible power and grace” (Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Baptism of Christ*).

Perhaps Bingham wishes to establish a comparison between the altar, the sacred oil, and priests, whose substance is not changed, and the Eucharist, in which Catholics assert that the substance of the bread and wine is changed. But it is astonishing that he does not see that Nyssa’s statement lends no support to Calvinism and, on the contrary, clearly confirms the Catholic position.
