What does blessing, or sanctification, accomplish in the altar, the oil, and the priests? It causes what was previously profane and common to begin, through the invisible effect of grace, to be holy and sacred, and to become worthy of veneration. The power of blessing truly and most truly accomplishes this, although, as regards outward appearance, no change occurs.

Again, for what purpose is blessing and sanctification applied to bread and wine on the sacred table? So that the bread may become the body, and the wine may become the blood, of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. This is what the Roman liturgy and the other liturgies of the West and East proclaim.

Through blessing and Christ’s words, the Church truly and most truly obtains this every day: what was previously common bread, as Nyssa testifies, becomes Christ’s body and is called so—not merely λέγεται, “is called,” but γίνεται, “becomes”—although outward appearance undergoes no change. Anyone who does not see this must be blinded in his understanding.

Here too I would gladly have asked Bingham whether he possessed a mind sincerely disposed to seek the truth, since he searched Gregory of Nyssa for what he wished to find, yet did not find it, while neglecting other passages in which the same holy teacher most clearly bears witness both to the real presence of the Lord in the Eucharist and to the change of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood. Gregory flourished in the year of Christ 380.

I would be excessive if I were to cite his entire discourse on the Eucharist from his *Great Catechetical Oration*. I shall be content with a few passages:

“The body of Jesus Christ, because it was inhabited by the Word of God, was changed into divine dignity. Therefore we rightly believe that the sanctified bread, through the Word of God, is the immaculate body” (Gregory of Nyssa, *Catechetical Oration*, chapter 37).

He then says that, just as bread and wine, natural foods, are converted into our substance, so the Lord has given us these gifts, “when the power of the sacred blessing changes and transforms the nature of visible things”—that is, bread and wine—“into his body.”

He also expressly teaches that, like leaven, Christ’s body enters into the body of the faithful, so that it may transfer the whole into itself and grant it immortality. Search here, if you can, for Calvin’s dreams. You will find nothing except the true doctrine of the Catholic Church.

From the catechesis of Saint Cyril, who governed the Church of Jerusalem in the year of Christ 360, Bingham extracted the following passage, in which the holy bishop speaks about sacred chrism:

“See that you do not think it is merely ointment. For just as Eucharistic bread, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, is no longer common bread, but is Christ’s body, so this holy ointment is no longer merely ointment, nor, so to speak, common, after it has been consecrated; rather, it is the charisma—or gift—of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, made effective by the presence of his divinity” (Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 21, or *Mystagogical Catechesis* 3).

But Bingham is still fighting with the air. Cyril clearly distinguishes the Eucharist from sacred chrism. Both the bread and the ointment are sanctified through the invocation of God; but the ointment remains what it was, possessing only the efficacy of imparting strength to the faithful.

What does Eucharistic bread receive through the invocation? It is no longer common bread, but becomes the living bread that came down from heaven. It is Christ’s body. Thus this passage too fights against the Sacramentarians.

I do not see how this class of men can consult their consciences before God when they scrape together passages that are either doubtful or altogether contrary to their own opinion, in order to persuade themselves and their hearers that the inventions of Berengarius and Calvin have been found, while they have clear passages before their eyes from which the doctrine of the ancient Church concerning the Eucharist most plainly emerges.

Catholics have opposed Cyril of Jerusalem a thousand times to the Calvinists. Why do they turn their faces away from his light and seek support only in obscure passages? They know that Cyril also has the following:

“Since Christ himself, therefore, has pronounced and said of the bread, ‘This is my body,’ who will dare henceforth to doubt? And since he himself has affirmed and said, ‘This is my blood,’ who will ever doubt, saying that it is not his blood?” (Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 22, or *Mystagogical Catechesis* 4).

Cyril then anticipates those who might still continue to doubt so great a miracle—namely, the conversion of bread into the body and of wine into blood—and says:

“Formerly he changed water into wine, which is akin to blood, at Cana in Galilee; and shall we consider him unworthy when he has changed wine into blood? When invited to bodily nuptials, he performed this astonishing miracle; and shall we not confess that he has given his body and blood to the sons of the bridal chamber for their enjoyment, all the more generously?”

Here you have the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation placed in full midday light, and Calvin’s dreams wholly cast down. What miracle can you show me in the Eucharist understood in the Calvinist manner, such that another miracle would be needed to confirm that a change has occurred there?

The position of the Catholic Church is presented to you in still greater light below, when the bishop of Jerusalem says:

“Therefore do not regard the bread and wine as bare and common elements: for they are the body and blood of Christ, according to the Lord’s affirmation. For even if your senses suggest this to you, let faith make you certain and firm. Do not judge the matter by taste, but by faith; without any doubt, be certain that you have been deemed worthy of the gift of Christ’s body and blood.”

These passages are available; Protestants read them. In them everyone is compelled to see what the ancient Church truly believed about the Eucharist. Nevertheless, they either do not see it or treat it as worthless. Indeed, they loudly present transubstantiation as a new invention, as though Catholics, by using a new term, were designating something new, whereas it is certain that the holy Fathers too transmitted the doctrine itself in other expressions with the same meaning, as we shall show more fully below.

## CHAPTER IX  
### What the ancient liturgies of the Roman Church teach concerning the Eucharist

Although no liturgy of either the Western or Eastern Churches survives that retains exactly the form it possessed in the first centuries of the Christian religion, it is nevertheless certain that even in those very centuries the unbloody sacrifice was always celebrated, and that prayers and rites—in other words, a liturgy—were employed in the action that embraces the most excellent of all mysteries.

Other prayers, orations, and rites were gradually added according to the variety of feasts and the differing piety and ability of the bishops. Yet it is clear from the very Fathers who illuminated the earlier centuries of the Church in their writings that what is principal in the Mass, and what belongs to the substance of the sacrifice, was always carefully preserved and never changed. Cardinal Bona and many other distinguished writers, both ancient and modern, have demonstrated this at length.

Therefore, what should be thought and believed concerning the Eucharist must be sought especially from this source. We possess the most ancient Sacramentaries of the Roman Church: the Leonine, Gelasian, and Gregorian, as well as codices written nearly a thousand years ago. The few additions found in them, made after Saints Gelasius and Gregory, do not prevent such liturgies from having proceeded from them.

Certainly, nothing was ever added to the Canon, in which the substance of the awe-inspiring mystery consists, that would alter the substance of the rite even in the slightest. The Canon is read in both the Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries.

Whatever is now found in the Roman Mass concerning the consecration of the offering, or offerings—that is, bread and wine—the Roman Church likewise employed in each preceding century. The priest says:

“May you, O God, we ask, deign to make this offering blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect, so that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

He then adds Christ’s words, through which Christ himself at the supper changed bread and wine into his own body and blood, and through which the consecration is actually effected.

There is some difference between the Roman and Eastern Churches. For the Greeks and various Christian groups in the East, after Christ’s words, also invoke the Holy Spirit, so that, entering into the sacred gifts, he may transform them and make them the body and blood of the Lord—that is, so that the transformation of the gifts, already accomplished through Christ’s words, may be completed and perfected.

The same practice is also known to have existed in the Mozarabic, Gothic, and ancient Gallican liturgies. There was no dispute about this among the ancients; only in recent centuries did a controversy arise among the Latins and Greeks as to whether the consecration occurs through Christ’s words, or simultaneously with them, or afterward through the invocation of the Holy Spirit.

Several Catholics—Goar, Chefontaine, Renaudot, Bruni, and more recently Father Cardon the Benedictine—have maintained that the Greeks and Syrians should not be troubled because, in their liturgies, the consecration of the gifts may not yet appear to have been sufficiently completed and perfected through the Lord’s words, since the Holy Spirit is invoked afterward to make those same gifts the body and blood of Christ.

But in recent years several Catholics have not shown such indulgence toward the Greeks and Syrians. With the gravest arguments they have demonstrated that the Greeks cannot be tolerated unless they openly acknowledge that complete transubstantiation follows from the Lord’s words alone—something they too seem to have admitted at the Council of Florence.

For if, in addition to those words, a subsequent invocation of the Holy Spirit is required for consecration, the Latins would have to be called *artolatroi*, or worshipers of bread. Accordingly, if we listen to these authors, the Greeks and Syrians must be judged to have improperly introduced into the ancient liturgies those prayers, or invocation, by which the power of the Lord’s words appears to be weakened.

I shall say briefly that the Catholics rightly established that the consecration depends solely upon Christ’s words. For this dogma is drawn from the ancient Fathers, especially John Chrysostom, Ambrose, and Augustine.

Only a few years ago Father Peter de Benedictis, in his notable edition of the works of Saint Ephrem, showed that the Syrians themselves acknowledged that the consecration is effected through those same words of Christ, and that the later invocation of the Holy Spirit contributes nothing to it—an invocation that is also absent from quite a few liturgies.

As for the Latin Churches, no suspicion of bread-worship remains. Even if prayers were required for the essence of the consecration—which is false—in the Latin liturgies they precede Christ’s words, so that, after those words have been pronounced, transubstantiation has certainly and absolutely been completed, and nothing is thereafter adored except the true body and true blood of the Lord.

As for the claim that the Greeks and Syrians adulterated the ancient liturgies, it is as easy to assert as it would be difficult to confirm with legitimate evidence. After the Nestorians and Eutychians separated from the Greeks and Latins, one must never suppose that they conspired with the Greeks to corrupt the ancient liturgy that had been common to both peoples in the fifth century of Christ.

“But they employ a later invocation,” you will say, “which seems to conflict with the efficacy of the Lord’s words.” Indeed they do; but we should not be angry with those who soften or accommodate the rites of the Eastern peoples, provided that they in no way doubt that the consecration rests upon the power of such words.

Moreover, there has never been any disagreement or dispute between the Churches of the West and East concerning the real presence of the Lord in the Eucharist, nor concerning the change or transubstantiation. All have always adhered, and continue to adhere, unanimously to these dogmas. We also possess the most certain Acts, especially those in which the Greeks condemn the new opinions of Luther and Calvin on this matter.

What the priests ask of God when they ask that the sacred gifts become the body and blood of the Lord is sufficiently revealed by the force of their words: namely, that bread and wine are not fictitiously or metaphorically, but really, changed into Christ’s body and blood.

For the petition rests upon the omnipotence of God, to whom this is possible, and upon Christ’s example, who accomplished the same thing at the supper when he said, “This is my body.” It also rests upon the Lord’s own command, by which he ordered priests to do the same in his memory.

If one of the saints were to ask God that “this rod become a serpent” or “this water become wine,” who would ever dream that anything other than what the verb “become” signifies in Latin—and what in the Italian language is expressed by *diventi*—was being requested?

Yet the Sacramentarians have dared to acknowledge no real change here. According to them, even after consecration, bread remains bread. Faith alone imagines the Lord in the sacrament.

But the Church teaches none of this. The liturgy reports none of the things they arbitrarily imagine. Indeed, they have twisted the very words of consecration—“This is my body”—into a new meaning, so that they signify nothing other than, “This signifies my body.”

Those who think this way should be asked to declare openly whether a person professing the Christian faith may shape, interpret, and virtually establish anew this most holy religion according to the dictates of his own brain and ingenuity, or whether it is rather fitting and necessary to receive and venerate it as it was handed down by the apostles to their successors during the first centuries of the Church.

If they choose the first option, they approve the temerity of the Socinian plague and must admit that the dreams of the British Locke and of others indifferent in religion are not to be despised. Then there will be as many opinions as heads; against the clear teaching of Christ there will no longer be one Church but many; and no one will thereafter be able to recognize which Church is the true and legitimate Church of God.

If they choose the second option, as one should hope—since they do not seem to despise at least the Fathers of the earlier centuries of the Church—they should once again be asked to lay aside their hatred of Catholics and their prejudiced opinions, and, inflamed by a single desire for truth, sincerely investigate what the doctrine of the ancient Church concerning the Eucharist was, not only in their own books but also in Catholic writings.

Then, with God extending his hand, they will easily understand that the position Catholics profess concerning the Eucharist has always been proclaimed by the ancient and universal Church as well.

Albertinus and Claudius, the chief champions of the Calvinists, constructed in their own minds a truly entertaining fable and easily persuaded their fellow tribesmen of it: namely, that Paschasius Ratbertus, abbot of Corbie, was the first, in the year of Christ 818, to introduce the reality of the Lord’s body and blood into the Eucharist, whereas previously the whole Church had been possessed by the Calvinist opinion; and that Rhabanus, Amalarius, Walafrid, Florus, Heribald, Lupus, and other writers of that century therefore rose up against Paschasius.

In recent times Bingham too has fearlessly brought this same fable onto the stage. This method of arguing provokes indignation, since everything Catholics—and especially the author of the books on *The Perpetuity of the Faith*—have brought forward to overthrow and scatter this badly stitched-together fiction is plainly concealed.

So far from finding the Church of his time opposed to him, Paschasius appealed, on behalf of his own position, to the agreement of all the Churches, and no one was found to contradict that agreement. He says:

“Nevertheless, no one is openly found who contradicts that this is what the whole world believes and confesses. Let him who wishes to oppose this consider what he is doing against the Lord himself and against the whole Church of Christ.”

It has also been demonstrated that none of the writers mentioned above opposed Paschasius with respect to the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist. If John Scotus is excepted, whose mind was doubtful, the others either did not attack Paschasius at all or expressly supported his position.

These are therefore mere mockeries. Whoever continues to serve up to unwary readers a fable long since worn out will not escape God’s punishment for this grave offense.

I return to the Roman liturgy, which was certainly in use before the time of Paschasius Ratbertus. The codices, or Sacramentaries, that I present here were also written before he composed his books.

The literal meaning of the Roman liturgy, when it says “may it become the body,” implies both the change of the sacred gifts and the real presence of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrament. Accordingly, when the priest afterward offers the consecrated host to God, he calls it the holy bread of eternal life, a name by which Christ himself is designated, and the chalice of salvation, an expression by which the Fathers indicate Christ’s own blood.

He then asks that all who have received from participation in this altar the most holy body and blood of your Son may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace. He does not say, “who have received a figure or image of the body and blood of your Son,” but “the body and blood themselves.”

Thus, when a particle of the consecrated host is placed into the chalice, the priest says:

“This commixture and consecration of the body and blood of the Lord,” etc.

In the Roman Order, written before the time of Charlemagne, as found in Mabillon, it was said: “May the commixture be made,” etc.

The prayers used in the most ancient Sacramentaries—the Leonine, Gelasian, and Gregorian—which belong to the Roman Church before the time of Paschasius Ratbertus, most clearly confirm this mind of the Church.

Thus in the Leonine and Gregorian Sacramentaries we read:

“Filled with the draught of the sacred body and precious blood, we ask you, our God, that through what we perform with pious devotion we may receive certain redemption.”

Likewise in the Leonine:

“Filled with the substance—and by no means merely the figure—of restoration and life, we ask you, Lord our God, that through these heavenly gifts which you deign to provide for us, you may grant us through these same gifts to cling to heavenly things.”

Likewise:

“Receiving the pledge of the heavenly mystery, and placed on earth, already satisfied with the bread from above,” etc.

In the Leonine and Gelasian:

“Once the shadows of carnal victims have been removed, we bring before you, supreme Father, in humble service, a spiritual victim, which by a wondrous and ineffable mystery is both always sacrificed and always offered; and it is at once the gift of the devoted and the reward of the one who bestows the recompense.”

In the Leonine, Gelasian, and Gregorian:

“Strengthened by the nourishment of the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, we humbly beseech you, our God, that through this singular remedy you may purify us from the contagion of all sins and protect us from the assaults of every danger.”

In the Leonine and Gelasian:

“We humbly beseech you, Lord our God, that we who receive the substance of the heavenly table may attain eternal life.”

In the same Sacramentaries:

“We humbly beseech your majesty, Lord, that just as you nourish us with the food of the most holy body and blood, so you may make us sharers in the divine nature.”

Finally, to omit other passages, the Leonine contains the following in its invitation to the fast of the tenth month:

“For it was fitting that, once the fruits of the earth had passed away, heavenly seed should arise—this refers to the Nativity of the Lord—and that, when the nourishment of mortal life had been completed, the germ of immortality should appear; and that, when carnal foods had been put aside, food for souls should wondrously be born. When the season of grain, wine, and oil had been completed, he who is eaten ineffably should be born, so that, as the children of God advance in the likeness of the angels, he might bring all this not only in substance but also in name, and provide eternal bread.”

In the Gelasian Sacramentary and in the most ancient Missal of the Franks, at the ordination of presbyters, God is asked that they preserve the pure and immaculate gift of his ministry, and that, through the service of his people, “they may transform the body and blood of your Son through immaculate blessing.”

Likewise, for the Wednesday after Easter:

“That we may be nourished unto eternal life by heavenly sacrifices, with his body and blood by which we have been redeemed from sins.”

In the Gelasian, Gregorian, and Frankish Missals, for the consecration of a paten:

“We consecrate and sanctify this paten for making in it the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who suffered the cross for the salvation of us all.”

One codex reads *ad conflingendum* (“for forming or fashioning”) instead of *ad conficiendum*.

In the Gelasian and Frankish Missals, for the consecration of the vessel in which the Lord’s body was kept for the sick:

“Let us pray that almighty God may deign to fill with blessing this ministry that carries the body of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Likewise:

“O inseparable Trinity, pour the help of your blessing into our hands, so that through our blessing this vessel may be sanctified and may be made, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the new tomb of Christ’s body.”

In the Gregorian, on the Sunday after Pentecost:

“Sanctify the gifts offered, Lord, so that they may become for us the body and blood of your Only-Begotten.”

In the Roman Mass the following prayer is now said before communion:

“May the reception of the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, which I, though unworthy, presume to receive,” etc.

This was also recited in ancient times, as is clear from the most ancient Mass edited by Matthias Flacius Illyricus.

In the Othobonian Codex of the ninth century, for the Fifth Sunday after the Epiphany, the following preface is found:

“Eternal God, and to offer you the victim of sacrifice, which is saving and the ineffable sacrament of divine grace. It is offered by many, and through the infusion of the Holy Spirit is perfected as one body of Christ. Each person receives Christ the Lord, and in each portion he is wholly present; he is not diminished among the individuals, but presents himself whole in each. Therefore we who receive communion of this holy bread and chalice become one body of Christ,” etc.

This same preface is found in the Ambrosian Sacramentary. Algerus produced it against Berengarius in the eleventh century (*On the Sacrament*, book 1), as though it were a work of Saint Ambrose. Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, also brought forward “this preface,” saying that “it is found throughout almost the whole Latin world” (Guitmund, *On the Truth of the Eucharist*, book 1).

Consider another preface taken from the previously praised Othobonian Codex, for the Tuesday after the First Sunday of Lent. It is also presented in the Ambrosian Sacramentary by Pamelius:

“Through Christ our Lord. In him the faith of those who fast is increased, hope is advanced, and charity is strengthened. For he is the living and true bread, which is the substance of eternity and the food of virtue. Your Word, through whom all things were made, is not merely the bread of human minds, but himself the bread of angels. You never cease to minister this bread to us, and you urge us to hunger for it without ceasing: as we are nourished by his flesh, we are strengthened, and as we drink his blood, we are cleansed.”

It is also useful to add a few passages from the most ancient Mass once published by Matthias Flacius Illyricus. Because it had emerged from the storehouse of a heretical man, Catholics in the sixteenth century were initially apprehensive about it. Gradually, however, they recognized that it was nothing other than the Roman Mass itself, burdened with many different prayers, whose use at that time was left to the discretion of priests. See Martène, volume 1, *On the Rites of the Church*.

There, after the offering of the bread, the priest says:

“Sanctify, Lord, this offering, so that it may become for us the body of your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And below:

“Sanctify, Lord, the chalice offered to you, so that it may become for us the blood of your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

When the body and blood are received, the following is said:

“Holy Lord, almighty and eternal God, grant that I may receive this body and blood of your Son in such a way that through it I may deserve to receive remission of all sins.”

In the same Mass are found the two prayers that Roman priests now recite after communion, and which are also found in the Dionysian Missal dating from the time of Charlemagne, as reported by the same Martène. They are:

“Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who by the will of the Father,” etc.,

and:

“Your body, Lord, which I have received, and the chalice which I have drunk,” etc.

The Mass of Illyricus then adds this other prayer:

“Grant, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, that we who eat and drink your own body and blood, given for us unworthy ones, may have them as salvation and an everlasting remedy for the redemption of all our sins.”

What we have presented thus far, extracted from the most ancient liturgies of the Roman Church, asks nothing else of the sincere reader, eager for the one truth, than that he understand what that same Church taught and believed about the Eucharist in those very ancient centuries. Namely, that a true conversion of the offerings into the body [Col. 0941C] and blood of the Lord takes place in the sacrifice; and that the faithful were wholly persuaded that, in the sacrament, they received Christ’s true flesh and his true and real blood. This conviction cannot possibly be reconciled with all those various formulas of speech with which the fiction of a figure was devised by Berengar and his followers.

If the ancients acknowledged nothing in the Eucharist except a shadow and figure of the Lord’s body and blood, how could they have expressed this view nowhere, while in so many places they expressed the truth and reality of that same body and blood? Certainly for no other reason than that this truth was perfectly clear to the faithful, and that formerly nothing other than what is now believed in the Roman Church was believed.

But so that every avenue of doubt and quibbling may be closed, hear Leo the Great, the most holy pontiff of that same Church, [Col. 0941D] who affirmed in his own sermon what the liturgy teaches—namely, around the year of Christ 450:

> “When the Lord says, ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,’ you ought to communicate at the sacred table in such a way that you have absolutely no doubt about the TRUTH OF THE BODY AND BLOOD. For what is received by the MOUTH is believed by faith; and those who dispute against what they receive answer AMEN in vain” (Leo the Great, Sermon 90, or 6 of the September collection).

It is very well known from the words of Augustine cited earlier—that is, in the preceding chapter—and from Cyril of Jerusalem, Ambrose (or the author of the books *On the Mysteries and Sacraments*), and other Fathers, that when the priest offered the consecrated Host [Col. 0942A] to communicants, he said, “The body of Christ”; while the communicant replied, “Amen,” by which word he signified: “I believe this; this is true.”

Such, then, was the faith concerning the Eucharist even in the age of Leo the Great. Read those words again and weigh them carefully. Does anyone seem to have doubted even then about so great a miracle—namely, whether the true body of Christ was contained and hidden in the Eucharist? What does Leo say? “When you receive the body of Christ, you say ‘Amen,’ which is the same as saying: ‘I believe that I am receiving the true and real body of the Lord.’ Therefore do not doubt the truth of the body and blood; for if you draw this into dispute, you appear to pronounce ‘Amen’ vainly and insincerely.”

You may see the same point repeated by the pontiff himself when he speaks against heretics who denied the reality of the flesh assumed by the Lord:

> “In what darkness of ignorance are they? In what sluggish torpor of indifference have they lain until now, that they have learned neither by hearing nor by reading what in the Church of God is so harmonious on everyone’s lips that the TRUTH OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST is not silent even on the tongues of infants amid the sacraments of communion?” (The same, Letter 46, formerly 23, to the clergy of the city of Constantinople).

For infants—as is well known, and as the Roman sacramentaries show—were given the sacrament of the Lord’s body after baptism.

Therefore it was not a figure, nor an imaginary flesh of Christ, that was then believed and received in the Eucharist, but the truth and substance of that most sacred body. Saint Leo confirms this still more forcefully when he adds:

> “Because in that mystical distribution of spiritual nourishment THIS IS IMPARTED, THIS IS RECEIVED”—that is, the true [Col. 0942C] body and blood of Christ—“so that, receiving the power of the HEAVENLY FOOD, we may pass into the flesh of him who became our flesh.”

The same pontiff also writes to Anatolius, bishop:

> “Although Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father, he nevertheless carries out the sacrament of reconciliation IN THAT SAME FLESH which he assumed from the Virgin” (Leo the Great, Letter 60, formerly 40, to Anatolius).

Read and weigh these words once more.

Let us hear another, and indeed a most celebrated, pontiff of that same Roman Church, Gregory the Great. Interpreting the Lord’s words, “I am the good shepherd,” he writes:

> “He did what he taught; he displayed what he commanded. The good shepherd laid down his life so that HE MIGHT TURN HIS BODY AND BLOOD INTO OUR SACRAMENT, and satisfy the sheep whom he had redeemed with the nourishment of HIS FLESH” [Col. 0942D] (Gregory the Great, Homily 14 on the Gospels).

Elsewhere the same holy pontiff writes:

> “We ought to offer daily sacrifices of CHRIST’S FLESH and BLOOD. For this singular victim saves the soul from eternal destruction: through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten, who is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. For THERE HIS BODY IS RECEIVED; HIS FLESH IS DISTRIBUTED for the salvation of the people; HIS BLOOD, no longer into the hands of unbelievers, but INTO THE MOUTHS OF THE FAITHFUL, IS POURED OUT” (the same, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 58).

Then he adds:

> “For what believer could doubt that at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened; that in the mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and the lowest are joined; that earthly things are united [Col. 0943A] with heavenly things; and that one reality is made from visible and invisible things?”

I pass over other passages of Gregory. For from those already cited it is most clearly evident what the Roman Church believed about the Eucharist in its most ancient sacramentaries—namely, what it still believes today. Nor was any change ever made in a dogma of such importance, as the sacramentary writers of recent times wrongly imagined.

## CHAPTER X. The Agreement of the Ambrosian Church with the Roman Church in the Doctrine of the Eucharist

There is no need to warn readers that the Church of Milan, or Ambrosian Church, both now and in ancient centuries, performed the sacred rites with ceremonies and prayers different from the custom of the Roman Church. Yet, as regards the canon and the principal parts of the unbloody sacrifice, the two Churches proceeded in agreement even in ancient times.

I asked the distinguished Joseph Anthony Saxius, prefect of the Ambrosian Library, to send me, out of his ancient goodwill toward me, the canon of the Mass taken from the most ancient Ambrosian missal. He consulted a parchment codex belonging to his own collection, whose antiquity he judged to reach back to the ninth or tenth century, as well as another of equal age preserved in the Ambrosian Library. From it he transcribed the canon as it is read in the Mass of the Lord’s Supper. It differs very little from the ordinary canon, except in certain matters specifically pertaining to that sacred day, the Thursday of Holy Week. The following passages occur there.

> **The ancient canon of the Ambrosian Mass for the Lord’s Supper**
>
> Therefore, most merciful Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, we humbly implore and ask you to regard as acceptable and bless + these gifts + these offerings + these holy and unblemished sacrifices. In the first place, those which we offer to you for your holy Catholic Church, which may you deign to pacify, guard, unite, and govern throughout the whole world, together with your servant and priest, that pontiff (N.), and your servant (N.), the emperor, and also all orthodox people and worshipers of the apostolic faith.
>
> Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women (N.), and all who stand around, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is recognized; for whom we offer you—or who offer you—this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all who belong to them, for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and safety. They render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God.
>
> In communion and celebrating this most holy day on which our Lord Jesus Christ was handed over: you, Lord, commanded us to be participants in your Son, sharers in your kingdom, inhabitants of paradise, and companions of the angels, provided that we preserve unharmed and undefiled the sacraments of heavenly service.
>
> Yet what can we despair of concerning your mercy, when we have received so great a gift that we have been deemed worthy to offer you such a victim—namely, the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, who for the redemption of the world gave himself over to that pious and venerable passion? Establishing the form of the sacrifice of eternal salvation, he first offered himself as a victim and first taught that he should be offered.
>
> We also venerate the memory, first, of the ever-glorious Virgin Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of your blessed apostles and martyrs Peter, Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, and Thaddeus; Sixtus, Lawrence, Hippolytus, Vincent, Cornelius, Cyprian, Clement, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian, Apollinaris, [Col. 0944B] Vitalis, Nazarius, Celsus, Protasius, Gervasius, Victor, Nabor, Felix, Calimerus, Eustorgius, Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0943D] In the Ambrosian Mass published by Pamelius in the first volume of his liturgical collection, the enumeration of the saints ends with the name of Dionysius. And rightly so. For here only martyrs are mentioned, not confessors. Why, then, were these names added through ill-considered piety and ritual?], Ambrose, Simplicianus, Martin, Eusebius, Hilary, and Julius, and of all your saints. By their merits and prayers, grant that we may be protected in all things by your help. Through Christ our Lord.
>
> Therefore, Lord, graciously regard this offering, which we offer to you for the fast of the Lord’s Supper, on which our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, instituted the rite of sacrifice under the new covenant, when he TRANSFORMED THE BREAD AND WINE which Melchizedek the priest had offered as a foreshadowing of the future mystery INTO THE SACRAMENT OF HIS BODY AND BLOOD. Grant that we may celebrate it, we ask, Lord, so that through many cycles of years we may be found safe and unharmed offering our gifts, Lord; order our days in your peace; rescue us from eternal condemnation; and command that we be numbered among your chosen flock. Through Christ our Lord.
>
> This offering, which we offer to your goodness, do you, God, we ask, deign in every respect to make + blessed + approved + ratified, and reasonable, so that it may become for us THE BODY AND BLOOD of your most beloved Son, our Lord and God Jesus Christ.
>
> He, on the day before he suffered for our salvation and that of all—namely, today—while reclining among his disciples, took bread, raised his eyes to heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, giving you thanks + blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying to them: “Take and eat from this, all of you. [Col. 0944D] For this is my body.”
>
> In like manner, after supper had ended, taking the cup, he raised his eyes to heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, likewise giving you thanks, blessed it, and handed it to his disciples, saying to them: “Take and drink from it, all of you. For this is the cup of my blood, of the new and eternal covenant, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.”
>
> He also commanded and said to them: “Whenever you do these things, you shall proclaim my death, announce my resurrection, and hope for my coming [Col. 0945A] from heaven to you again.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0945D] In the ordinary Ambrosian Mass, after the words “until I come,” and so forth, there follows: “Therefore we, your servants, and your people also, remembering you, Lord,” and “Remember also, Lord,” and “To us sinners also,” which prayer ends with Justina and Sabina. For many centuries, in the Ambrosian Mass, the breaking of the Host and the commingling in the chalice were expressed in these words: “YOUR BODY is broken, O CHRIST; the chalice is blessed; may YOUR BLOOD be for us always unto life and for the salvation of souls, our God.” But in the most ancient missals of the same Church these words are not found; only the following appears: “the commingling of the consecrated BODY AND BLOOD,” and so forth. Concerning this formula for the breaking of the Host, formerly added to the Ambrosian Mass, and its origin, the aforementioned Saxius published a letter rich in learning.]
>
> We do these things and celebrate them, observing your commands, Lord; and, for inviolate communion, we proclaim the Lord’s death in this very act by which WE RECEIVE THE BODY OF THE LORD. It is yours, almighty Father, to send us now your Only-Begotten Son, whom you willingly sent to those who sought him. Although you yourself are immeasurable and beyond valuation, you begot from yourself a God likewise immeasurable and beyond valuation, so that you may now grant us HIS BODY for salvation, by whose passion you bestowed the redemption of the human race. Through the same Christ our Lord.
>
> Through him, Lord, you always create all these good things + sanctify them + give them life + bless them, and generously bestow them upon us your servants, for the increase of faith and the forgiveness of all our sins.
>
> And to you, God the almighty Father, from him, and through him, and in him, belongs all honor, power, praise, glory, dominion, perpetuity, and authority throughout infinite ages of ages.
>
> Then the following prayer is said:
>
> It is his command, Lord, that we are carrying out, whose presence we now ask of you; grant the sacrifice its author, so that faith in the reality may be fulfilled in the sublimity of the mystery; so that, just as we carry out the truth of the heavenly sacrifice, so may we draw forth THE TRUTH OF THE LORD’S BODY AND BLOOD. Through the same Christ our Lord, saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” and so forth.

[Col. 0945C] Someone might meanwhile suppose that the more important parts of the Ambrosian canon were taken from the Roman canon; and since, after Charlemagne had recently taken possession of the kingdom of the Lombards, Pope Adrian I had endeavored to have the rites of the Roman Church adopted by the clergy and people of Milan, after the Ambrosian liturgy had been abolished, it might then have happened that the Roman canon was substituted for the Milanese.

But such claims are made without evidence. For there is no slight difference between the canon recently presented and the Roman canon. As you see, at the consecration of the bread alone it was said, “This is my body”; nor was there then added—as Pamelius and others think—the phrase “which will be broken for you.”

Moreover, if Saint Ambrose had certainly been the author of the books *On the Sacraments*, or at least if some Milanese bishop after him had been their author, it would be clear from chapters 5 and 6 of the fourth book that the Ambrosian canon proceeded in many respects in agreement with the Roman canon, even before the time of Charlemagne. Certainly those books were extremely widespread in the ninth century and are mentioned by Amalarius, Paschasius Radbertus, Hincmar, Florus, and other writers of that age, indeed under the name of Ambrose.

Furthermore, anyone who carefully weighs their style and diction, their divergence from the Vulgate version of Scripture, and the other arguments adduced by the Benedictines in their preface, must admit that, even if they were not written by Ambrose, they were composed at least by some bishop before the barbarian invasion had spread ignorance through the regions of Italy.

In the fourth and fifth centuries of the Christian era, we know that it was customary for bishops to instruct the newly baptized in the sacred mysteries, as is evident from Ambrose himself, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nyssa, Gaudentius of Brescia, and Augustine. Show me, if you can, that this custom was observed in subsequent centuries—yet it is observed in the books *On the Sacraments*.

We have seen the real presence and truth of the Lord’s flesh and blood in the Eucharist expressed in the Ambrosian canon. In those same books *On the Sacraments*, published under the name of Saint Ambrose, there are so many clear and indeed universally known testimonies by which the conversion and change—or, as we now say, transubstantiation—of the bread and wine into the same body and blood of Christ is confirmed, that anyone who dares deny it reveals himself to be utterly blind and obstinate.

Comparable evidence is found in the book *On the Mysteries*, which scarcely any learned person dares deny to be the work of Saint Ambrose. From it take the following brief passages. After the holy teacher has shown how much superior the flesh of Christ, given to us in the sacrament, is to the manna of the Jews—“For light is superior to shadow, truth to figure, the body of the author to manna from heaven”—he adds:

> “Perhaps you will say: ‘I see something else. How do you assert to me that I receive the body of Christ?’ Let us prove that this is not what nature formed—namely, bread—but what blessing consecrated; and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because BY BLESSING NATURE ITSELF IS ALSO CHANGED” (Ambrose, *On the Mysteries*, chapter 9).

Then, after assembling several miracles of divine power from the Old Testament, he adds:

> “If human blessing had such power that it could change nature, what shall we say of the divine consecration itself, where the very words of the Lord the Savior operate? The word of Christ, which could make from nothing what did not exist, cannot CHANGE THOSE THINGS THAT EXIST INTO WHAT THEY WERE NOT?”

I pass over the remainder, from which it shines more clearly than the midday sun that not the Calvinist figure but the truth [Col. 0946D] of the Lord’s body and blood, through the real change of the sacred gifts, must be affirmed in the Eucharist. These passages also explain what the same Ambrose writes elsewhere, in works unquestionably his:

> “Whenever we receive the sacraments, which through the mystery of the sacred prayer are TRANSFIGURED INTO FLESH and blood, we proclaim the death of the Lord” (the same, *On the Faith*, Book IV, chapter 10, no. 124).

He says something similar elsewhere:

> “I possess the venerable fellowship of the heavenly sacraments. I am already received to the honor of the heavenly table. Christ is food for me; Christ is drink for me; the flesh of God is food for me, and the blood of God is drink for me. I no longer await annual produce for my satisfaction. Christ is ministered to me daily.
>
> “Before, bread from heaven had been wondrous to me; for it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’ But that was not the true Bread, but a shadow of the future. The Father has preserved for me the true Bread from heaven” (the same, Sermon 18, no. 26, on Psalm CXVIII), and so forth.

Again the holy teacher says:

> “For even if you believe that true flesh was assumed by Christ, and that you OFFER THE BODY TO BE TRANSFIGURED UPON THE ALTARS” (the same, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 4), and so forth.

But what did “transfiguration” and “to be transfigured” mean to Ambrose? Certainly a substantial conversion and change of one thing into another.

Hear Suetonius writing:

> “He even attempted to transfigure the boy Sporus, after his testicles had been removed, into a woman’s nature” (Suetonius, *On Claudius Nero*, chapter 28).

Hear Pliny:

> “When the sun passes through the sign of Cancer, it is said that the body of crabs, when they have been dismembered, is transfigured into scorpions” (Pliny, Book IX, chapter 3).

The same Pliny considers it a fable that human beings are changed into wolves, that human beings are transfigured into wolves (the same, Book VIII, chapter 22).

But Tertullian explains the force and meaning of this word most clearly of all when he says:

> “Transfiguration, however, is the destruction of the former state. For everything that is transfigured into another ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not” (Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 27).

Do you see? Transfiguration is the same as transubstantiation. The name is different, but the reality is the same.

I ask that heterodox writers read and reread these passages with a calm mind, and finally understand how well it suits them to defend so stubbornly the doctrine of impanation and to insult transubstantiation on account of the novelty of its word. The Catholic Church can produce witnesses for its position from the whole of antiquity. Yet one distinguished pastor of the Milanese Church, Ambrose, is enough to overthrow all Protestant fictions on this matter.

Let the Sacramentarians continue, if they wish, to force upon similar words of the holy Fathers a figure invented by themselves, and to force upon them figurative expressions and a power supposedly flowing from their faith. Since, however, the Fathers had none of these things in their sermons when they spoke about the Eucharist, and since they never instructed their hearers that their statements were to be understood figuratively, such people may perhaps not realize that they have been deceived by this opinion and that they are attributing to the Fathers something that never entered the Fathers’ minds.

Yet two points will always remain, apart from others, which will accuse those who think differently from the Catholic Church of inexcusable rashness.

All Christians know that baptismal water is a sign of heavenly grace which washes away human sins, and that such great power is infused into it by the Holy Spirit. No one raises doubts about it or regards this as astonishing and scarcely credible. The same must follow if the Eucharist is nothing other than a figure and sign of the Lord’s body and blood, with a heavenly power infused into the bread and [Col. 0948A] wine.

Yet the Fathers present the Eucharist to us as a mystery exposed to many grave doubts. Why? For no other reason than that the mind recoils from believing in the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s real flesh and true blood. Although in the Eucharist it sees, touches, and tastes nothing except what resembles the appearance of bread and wine, it is nevertheless compelled to believe that Christ’s body and blood really exist in it, and that the body, always undivided and wholly intact, is daily divided among so many thousands of people.

Therefore the holy Fathers, preparing to arm the faithful against such doubts, invoked here the omnipotence of God, proclaimed the ineffable power of the Holy Spirit, and pressed the truthfulness of God, which no one but an impious person denies. For when instituting the Eucharist, Christ expressly affirmed that his body and blood were given there.

The Fathers then brought forward other great miracles performed by God, which we are commanded to believe, so that we might acknowledge that the great miracle of the Eucharist also must be believed. We have already seen what Cyril of Jerusalem and Ambrose wrote on this subject. To them must be added Gaudentius of Brescia (*Treatise 2 to the Newly Baptized*), Gregory of Nyssa (*Catechetical Oration*), Ephraem the Edessene, deacon (*Homily on the Nativity of God*), the author of the books *On the Sacraments*, Eutychius of Constantinople (*Book II on Leviticus*), Cyril of Alexandria (*Book IV on John*), and Epiphanius (*In the Anchoratus*).

I pass over the other Fathers who pursued the same purpose and add only one celebrated passage of Saint Hilary:

> “It is not by human judgment or by the sense of the world that we should speak about the things of God; nor should perversity be extorted from heavenly utterances by a violent and reckless proclamation, in opposition to sound and godly understanding. Let us read what has been written, understand what we have read, and then we shall fulfill the duty of perfect faith.
>
> “For concerning the natural truth of Christ in us, unless we have learned what we say from him, we have learned it foolishly and impiously. For he himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ THERE IS NO ROOM LEFT FOR DOUBT ABOUT THE TRUTH OF THE FLESH AND BLOOD. For now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, IT IS TRULY FLESH, AND IT IS TRULY BLOOD. [Col. 0948D] And once received and consumed, these make it happen that we are in Christ and Christ in us.
>
> “Is this not truth? Let it plainly be untrue for those who deny that Christ Jesus is the true God” (Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VIII, no. 14), and so forth.

If the enemies of the Catholic Church sincerely sought and weighed these things, they too would see what we see. Hilary says: “It is truly flesh”—not imaginary flesh. “It is truly blood”—not merely something taken according to opinion, or according only to the faith of the recipient.

But even if they seek, it is doubtful whether they truly desire to find.

There remains another irresistible argument among the Fathers for the truth of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist. Above we saw that the ancient Roman liturgies say that the true sacrifice of the new law—namely, the body and blood of the Lord—succeeded the shadows of the fleshly victims of the old law.

From the Apostle, the Fathers learned that the things presented in the old law were a shadow of the good things to come in the new law (Hebrews 10:1). Therefore the manna falling from heaven, the paschal lamb to be eaten at the table, and the bread and wine offered by Melchizedek were shadows, figures, and images of the truth to be fulfilled in the New Testament—that is, in the ineffable sacrament of the Eucharist.

Hence, when speaking of the unbloody sacrifice of the altar, the Fathers say that it was prefigured in what Melchizedek offered—as the Apostle had previously indicated—in the Paschal Lamb and in the other memorials of the Jewish covenant.

As we recently heard, Ambrose wrote that the manna was a shadow of the future; but that the true bread from heaven—namely, Christ’s [Col. 0949B] body and blood—is now eaten and drunk.

Hear Chrysostom also speaking about Melchizedek:

> “And observe, because of the honor bestowed upon the patriarch, how the sacrament is intimated. For there he brought forth bread and wine. Seeing the type, consider, I beg you, the TRUTH; and admire the precise care of the divine Scriptures, how in former ages and from the beginning these things were prefigured” (Chrysostom, Homily 35 on Genesis).

Other Fathers spoke in the same way. Since the matter is well known, I refrain from listing them.

How, then, can the fiction of the Sacramentarians ever stand—those who acknowledge nothing in the Eucharist except a figure, shadow, and image, and reject the truth of the Lord’s body and blood?

From the unanimous judgment of the holy Fathers we understand that the lamb before Passover was a figure [Col. 0949C] of the truth to be fulfilled at the Lord’s table—namely, the true flesh and blood of that Lamb himself who takes away the sins of the world, as all the Churches profess in the Mass.

Where is this truth on the altar and table of Christians, if even there nothing other than a type or figure is received, together with material bread prefiguring the true bread that descended from heaven?

I add nothing further. These matters have been widely explained by theological controversialists, who long ago exposed the quibbles of the Protestants concerning so evident a matter. I conclude the present chapter with the words of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, who wrote the following in the third century of the Christian era:

> “That ineffable mystery is called by him [Christ] the New Testament: GIVING HIMSELF TO US IN THE MYSTICAL SUPPER. It is not as formerly, when they placed on the altar the flesh of irrational animals, and so forth. Now it is not so. Rather, our Lord and God, the Savior of Israel, himself says: ‘Whoever eats me will live because of me.’
>
> “Therefore God DWELLS IN US according to the covenant which he established with us, saying, ‘Take and divide,’ and so forth. This is God’s self-emptying made for our use, SO THAT WE MAY BE ABLE TO RECEIVE HIM. For the Apostle calls this mystery fearful, because he emptied himself.
>
> “Nor does he DWELL IN US while abandoning the Father—away with such a thought! The Apostle calls this emptying himself, and the mystery of life being received by us—that is, the body and blood in the Eucharist—through his undefiled, incorruptible, and divine hands, SO THAT WE, who are his faithful, MAY RECEIVE HIM, and BECOME HIS DWELLING, RECEIVING HIM WHOLE” (Dionysius of Alexandria, *To Paul of Samosata).

## CHAPTER XI. The Agreement of the Other Western Churches with the Roman Church in the Dogma of the Eucharist

We owe the edition of the Gothic Missal to the venerable Cardinal Thomasius. This missal was once used in Narbonese Gaul, which was subject to the Goths ruling in Spain. The antiquity of this Gothic Mass belongs to the centuries preceding the kingdom and empire of Charlemagne; it seems to have ceased under his reign.

The same distinguished cardinal also gave us the Frankish Missal and the old Gallican Missal, which were used by the Churches of those regions before the liturgy of the Roman Church was introduced there under Pope Adrian I and King Charlemagne, to which the preceding liturgies yielded. The antiquity of those missals will also be confirmed by the form of their script, which Father Blanchini supplied to me.

It is now worthwhile to investigate in these obsolete and antiquated liturgies what those Churches believed and taught about the Eucharist so many centuries ago. Indeed, they taught precisely what Rome professed. For the diversity of rites did not prevent all the Churches of the West from proceeding in agreement in dogma.

Thus, in the Gothic Sacramentary, on the Feast of the Circumcision of the Lord, we read:

> “We humbly implore you to deign to receive, bless, and sanctify this sacrifice, so that it may become for us a legitimate Eucharist in the name of you, your Son, and the Holy Spirit, FOR THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, your Only-Begotten Son, through whom you create all things, bless what has been created, sanctify what has been blessed, and bestow what has been sanctified, O God.”

The same prayer is repeated on the Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, and after “your Only-Begotten Son” there is added:

> “So that, as we eat, it may bestow eternal life upon us, and, as we drink, an everlasting kingdom.”

For the Feast of the Epiphany:

> “Let us, dearest brothers, venerate the day of the Epiphany with solemn celebration, asking in pious supplication that he who then changed water into wine may NOW CHANGE THE WINE OF OUR OFFERINGS INTO HIS BLOOD; and that he who granted others satiety through the drinking of wine may sanctify us by the taste of his drink and by the infusion of the Spirit, the Paraclete.”

For the Feast of the Assumption of Saint Mary:

> “May the coeternal and co-working Paraclete of your blessing descend, Lord, upon these sacrifices, so that, with you sanctifying it, we may receive the offering which we present to you, made fruitful from your earth, with heavenly reward, SO THAT THE GRAIN MAY BE CHANGED INTO THE BODY AND THE CUP INTO BLOOD, and what we have offered for our offenses may advance us through its merits.”

At the beginning of Lent:

> “For he is the living and true bread”—namely, Christ, mentioned above—“who descended from heaven, and so forth. Deign, Lord, to minister to us during these forty days this bread which you continually urge us to desire, so that we may thirst for it. While we are nourished by HIS FLESH, sanctified by you yourself, we are strengthened; and while we drink HIS BLOOD as thirsty people who have drunk deeply, we are cleansed.
>
> “May this living and true bread, which descended from heaven to give food to the hungry, indeed, so that IT ITSELF MIGHT BE THE FOOD of the living, become for us the bread by which hearts are strengthened.” [Col. 0951A]

This same prayer is found in the old Gallican Sacramentary, which Mabillon published. There, after the *Sanctus*, we read:

> “May this living and true bread, which descended from heaven to give food to the hungry, indeed, so that IT ITSELF MIGHT BE THE FOOD of the hungry, become for us the bread by which hearts are strengthened.”

In the Gothic liturgy for the Lord’s Supper we find:

> “As we are about to receive the nourishment of the living bread and the gifts of the sacred blood, let us strengthen our minds and hearts through the Lord’s prayer.”

In the Mass of Saint Leodegar the martyr:

> “May your blessing descend upon this bread and cup IN THE TRANSFORMATION wrought by your Holy Spirit, so that by blessing these things you may bless them,” and so forth.

In the Sunday Mass, page 395, after the Secret, we read:

> “As the solemn rites of the sacred ceremonies are completed, according to the rite of Melchizedek, the supreme priest, we devoutly beseech you, eternal Majesty, that through the working of power we may receive THE BREAD CHANGED INTO FLESH and THE CUP CHANGED INTO BLOOD: him in the chalice who flowed from you on the cross from his side.”

After the Lord’s Prayer:

> “Deliver us from evil, Lord Christ Jesus. We EAT YOUR BODY, CRUCIFIED FOR US, AND DRINK YOUR BLOOD, POURED OUT FOR US. May your holy BODY be for us unto salvation, and your holy BLOOD for the forgiveness of sins.”

When we produce these and similar passages, the Innovators are accustomed to twist them into their own position, supplying from their own ingenuity the idea that Christ’s body is said to be eaten through faith and not really, and that his blood is drunk in the same way.

But who does not see that this class of people creates an obvious fraud for themselves and their hearers when they interpret the Fathers’ statements in this way—not seeking in them what the Fathers’ real meaning was, but what it ought to have been according to the principles and wishes of Berengar and Calvin?

There is nothing in the words of others that could not be twisted into ridiculous, false, and absurd meanings if we added a single word of our own. If the ancient Fathers had held what the Sacramentarians now believe, would they not have warned the people a hundred and a thousand times that, when it is said that Christ’s body is eaten and his blood drunk, these expressions must be understood figuratively and metaphorically, not literally, since this eating and drinking does not truly and really occur, but faith merely imagines it?

Let the Innovators produce, I ask, even one passage from the ancient books in which their opinion is explicitly and clearly taught. I do not think they will produce one. For it is certainly true that the ancients often taught that we do not eat Christ’s raw flesh according to the understanding of the people of Capernaum; but this does nothing to support their cause, as everyone knows.

On the contrary, the ancient Church was so far from teaching the inventions of the Calvinist school that it transmitted the Catholic position in clear formulas. A moment ago you saw “bread changed into flesh” and “the cup changed into blood.” You may often find the same statement repeated in the books of the ancients.

Either the Fathers were mistaken through excessive simplicity when they transmitted these statements without applying any other interpretation or correction, or the innovators of later centuries are being excessively deceived—and deceiving others—when they attribute to the ancient liturgies and writers of the Church what they themselves never dreamed of.

Here I appeal to the judgment of a sincere and learned people.

Meanwhile, let us sample a few passages from the most ancient Missal of the Franks. In its preface concerning the linens, we read:

> Deign to sanctify, bless, and consecrate these LINENS for the use of your altar, to hold and wrap the body and blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

In another preface:

> And may the BODILY PRESENCE OF THE MYSTERY of your Son Jesus Christ, who promised to be present with his faithful until the end of the age, not abandon those whom he redeemed.

Thus, in the very ancient Gallican Missal edited by Cardinal Thomasius, this collect is found after the Eucharist has been received:

> Receiving from the sacred altars the body and blood of Christ, our Lord and God . . . believing in the unity of the blessed Trinity, let us pray, etc.

> Look, Lord, upon the faithful whom you wish to feed on your body and to make your body; grant that what we have received may be for us the remission of sins.

> Having received spiritual foods, dearest brothers, and having tasted Christ’s blood, let us ask that he may possess our breasts, who has deigned to sanctify our mouths through these gifts.

On the Lord’s Supper, the same Gallican Mass contains in the canon the prayer that we cited above from the canon of the Ambrosian Mass, namely:

> Therefore this offering, which we present to you, etc., when he TRANSFORMED the bread and wine—which Melchizedek the priest had offered as a prefiguration of the mystery to come—INTO THE SACRAMENT OF HIS BODY AND BLOOD.

Likewise, in the very ancient exposition of the Gallican liturgy published by Father Martène, these few words are read:

> “The body of the Lord is therefore carried in towers”—concerning this word there will be further discussion below—“because the Lord’s tomb was hewn in rock in the likeness of a tower. The blood of Christ, however, is specially offered in a chalice because the mystery of the Eucharist was consecrated in such a vessel, etc. But the BREAD IS TRANSFORMED INTO THE BODY and the WINE INTO THE BLOOD” (Marten[e], *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* and vol. I of *De antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*).

The Britons boast that they received both the faith of Christ and the sacred liturgy from the Roman Church, when Saint Gregory the Great was pope, through Saint Augustine, the first bishop of Canterbury. Would that they had not cast away in these last centuries, through their lamentable schism, the doctrines and rites that they then received! They praise those two learned men of their nation and founders of their churches; yet, indirectly and silently, they portray them as deceivers and forgers, since they reject as impious merchandise some of the doctrines then handed down to them—especially those concerning the unbloody sacrifice and the real presence of the Lord in the Eucharist.

Yet it is evident and absolutely certain that Saint Gregory, together with the whole Church both of his own age and of preceding ages, believed and transmitted to the English what is now believed and taught in the Roman Church. Nevertheless, they repay this kindness to the most holy pontiffs by not merely abolishing but even condemning their teaching concerning the Mass. Whether the English have brought to light any of the most ancient Missals of their nation, I do not know. Perhaps they realized that its publication would in no way serve their opinions. Certainly, in those Missals they will find nothing else concerning the unbloody sacrifice than what the other liturgies of the West present, and what their most distinguished writers of the eighth century, Bede and Alcuin, proclaimed.

I have already published the very ancient Antiphonary of the celebrated monastery of Bangor in Ireland, written in the seventh, or at least the eighth, century of Christ. In the time of Charlemagne, the Scottish monk Dungal carried it to Ticinum and later gave it to the monastery of Bobbio (Murator[i], *Anecdota*, vol. IV). From it I have excerpted the following:

> A hymn for when the priests receive Communion:
>
> “Holy ones, come; receive the BODY of Christ, drinking the holy BLOOD by which you were redeemed.”

There follows, for Communion:

> “We have received the Lord’s body, and have been given drink from his blood. We shall fear no evil, because the Lord is with us.”

Further on one finds:

> “Receive for yourselves THIS SACRED BODY OF THE LORD AND SAVIOR for everlasting life. This is the living Bread that came down from heaven. Alleluia.”

Thus spoke the most devout monks of that age. They did not suppose that through faith they received in the Eucharist merely an imaginary body and blood of the Lord, or only the figure and power of an absent Christ. Rather, they most certainly believed that they were then receiving the real body and true blood by which we were redeemed—the same thing that the rest of the Church believed before Paschasius Radbertus.

Nor was the doctrine of the Mozarabic liturgy different, a liturgy that the churches of Spain used for so many centuries. On this subject, see the cardinals Bona and de Aguirre of the Holy Roman Church, Martène, Le Brun, Father Pinius of the Society of Jesus, and others. There, after the Lord’s Prayer, as among the Greeks, one reads:

> “Holy things for the holy. And may the union of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be for us who receive and drink them unto forgiveness,” etc.

The Fourth Council of Toledo, held in the year of Christ 633, states:

> “After the Lord’s Prayer and the joining of the bread and the chalice, let the blessing upon the people follow” (*Council of Toledo IV*, canon 18).

I wished to note this so that Protestants may learn not to misuse the names “bread” and “wine,” which many formerly used, and many Catholics still use, after their consecration—as though the consecrated gifts continued to be what they had been. What the Fathers of Toledo call “bread” and “chalice” on account of the appearances, their liturgy—and indeed the other liturgies as well—calls “the body and blood of the Lord” at the breaking, on account of the Eucharist’s inward substance.

The Mozarabic rite continues:

> “I shall receive the heavenly Bread from the table of the Lord,”

as in the Roman liturgy. By the name “heavenly Bread,” however, the Church has always designated the one Lord Christ, following the Lord himself, who said:

> “I am the living Bread who came down from heaven.”

It adds:

> “My Lord God, grant that I may receive the body and blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, so that through it I may deserve to receive remission of all sins.”

Then the priest, believing faithfully in the flesh and blood of Christ present, addresses the same flesh and blood, saying:

> “Hail forever, most holy flesh of Christ; forever, highest sweetness. Hail forever, heavenly drink, who are sweet to me before and above all things.”

A prayer is added:

> “May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve my body and soul unto eternal life.”

> “Refreshed by the body and blood of Christ, and likewise sanctified,” etc.

In the Mass of the Nativity of the Lord, this prayer is found after the names:

> “We, your unworthy and lowly servants, priests offering spiritual victims to your awesome Majesty, present to you, O God, an immaculate victim, whom a mother’s womb produced in undefiled virginity, whom modesty brought forth, whom sanctification engendered; and the immaculate victim lives, and while living is continually offered—the victim who alone is able to please God, because he is the Lord.”

Here you have the doctrine of the churches of Spain concerning the Eucharist. It is the same doctrine that Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville and doctor, transmitted when he wrote:

> “At first the disciples did not receive the body and blood of the Lord while fasting. But now throughout the universal Church it is always received by those who are fasting. For it pleased the Holy Spirit through the apostles that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should first enter the Christian’s mouth before any other food. For the bread that we break IS THE BODY OF CHRIST; he says: ‘I am the living Bread,’ etc. The wine, however, IS HIS BLOOD. These two things are visible; yet, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, they PASS OVER INTO THE SACRAMENT OF THE DIVINE BODY” (Isidore, *On the Offices of the Church*, book I, chapter 18), etc.

It is astonishing that Bingham cites some of Isidore’s words as though consecrated bread and wine were nothing other than signs of an absent Christ. They are indeed a sacrament and a visible sign of Christ, but of Christ really present in that same sacrament. Otherwise Isidore would not say that the Lord’s body enters the Christian’s mouth, that the apostles received the Lord’s body and blood, that the bread is Christ’s body, and that the wine is Christ’s blood.

He also says farther on:

> “How great is the difference between the loaves of the proposition and the body of Christ? What difference is there between body and shadow, between image and truth, between the patterns of future things and the very things represented by those patterns?”

# CHAPTER XII  
## On the Liturgies of the Eastern Churches in Agreement with the Roman Church. Other Feeble Weapons of Bingham the Englishman, or the Innovators, against the Doctrine of the Eucharist

For many centuries, most of the Eastern Churches have been separated from the Roman Church by a schism that cannot sufficiently be lamented. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that the disagreement of the Greeks with us was formed chiefly for rather slight reasons, while the remaining groups of Eastern Christians differ from the Latin Catholics in one or another doctrine. We also know for certain that there is no one of those groups that does not abhor the teaching of Luther, Calvin, Socinus, and the other innovators in the West.

Each of the Eastern groups has its own particular liturgies: among the Greeks living under the patriarch of Constantinople, those bearing the names of Saints Basil the Great and John Chrysostom; the Alexandrian Church had its own, distinguished by the name of Saint Mark; and the Antiochene and Jerusalem churches had one retaining the name of Saint James. There are also other liturgies among the Nestorians and Eutychians—that is, among the Syrians, Alexandrians or Copts, and Ethiopians.

Jacques Goar published and explained the principal liturgies of Basil and Chrysostom in a separate volume. Others published the remaining liturgies, especially Eusebius Renaudot of Paris, who collected and made them public in two books. Le Brun likewise published the liturgy of the Armenians (*Explanation of the Mass*, vol. III).

It is certain that the Eastern liturgies experienced the same fate as the Western ones. For just as no Codex now survives that preserves in its original form the very Latin liturgy which either Gregory I, Ambrose, or Saints Leander and Isidore—having received it in Spain from their predecessors—gave a new form, since subsequent centuries introduced some addition into all of them, so additions were gradually made to the Eastern liturgies, and, according to the diversity of the churches, a diversity of prayers prevailed in the Codices.

I say “of prayers,” because as regards the substance and canon of the unbloody sacrifice, the Eastern Christians—although for so many centuries divided into various groups and most of them separated from the unity of the Roman Church—have nevertheless always continued, and are found still to continue, in agreement on this point. If, therefore, we can demonstrate such agreement among all the Churches concerning the Eucharistic doctrine, and if we find that same doctrine expressed in a simple and literal style—for all the ancient liturgies were written in various languages in a style suited to the people’s understanding—what else will remain to be said except that the doctrine concerning the reality of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrifice of the altar flowed from one source, namely Christ through his apostles, into the whole Church?

For it could be conceived only by a damaged mind or an impudent man that so many Churches spread throughout the world could have conspired in corrupting the apostolic teaching on a matter of such importance—Churches some of which separated from the orthodox as many as thirteen hundred years ago.

We have already adduced so many passages from the liturgies of the Latin Churches in which the real presence and reality of the Lord’s body and blood in the Eucharist are openly taught that anyone acting sincerely can recognize that the mind of the ancient Church was no different from that which the Catholic Church established against Berengar and his more recent followers.

If Christ’s body is really present and received in the Eucharist, it necessarily follows that the bread and wine have been changed, as the Church has customarily required, into that same body and blood of the Lord. Among the Latins, after Berengar, this change necessarily began to be called “transubstantiation,” in order to exclude the quibbles and evasions by which the Sacramentarians try to elude the terms and words of the Church and the Fathers, terms and words that designated the same change throughout all the centuries preceding the attempt of the innovator Berengar.

Heretics attack the novelty of the word in vain, since what it signifies is by no means new. Once the conversion of the bread and wine into the body and blood of the Lord has been posited, the bread and wine must cease to be what they were in their substance, although nothing in their appearances is changed. For if they continue to be what they were, they cannot be said to have been converted and changed into the body and blood of the Lord.

How this sort of conversion occurs, and how Christ’s body exists in the Eucharist—and in its smallest particle, and at one time in many places—and other matters that seem contrary to philosophy, to the senses, and to our understanding, the ancient Fathers showed to be credible through God’s omnipotence. For who could deny that God can do innumerable things surpassing our understanding?

For this reason, in the sacred liturgies God is asked that the offering—that is, the bread and wine—may become Christ’s body and blood. In the Greek and Syriac liturgies, as we shall see below, the Holy Spirit is also invoked, so that, entering into the sacred gifts, he may transform them into the body and blood of the Lord.

But before I produce the words of those liturgies as well, it is useful to anticipate what the Englishman Bingham brought forward against the judgment concerning transubstantiation held by all the ancient Churches—not something exotic, certainly, but something extremely common and well worn.

He cites, namely, Chrysostom’s letter to Caesarius, where we read:

> “Just as, before it is sanctified, we call the bread ‘bread,’ but when divine grace has sanctified it through the priest, it has indeed been released from the designation ‘bread’ and has been deemed worthy of the designation ‘the Lord’s body,’ even though the nature of the bread remains in it, and not two bodies but one body of the Son is proclaimed; so also here, when the divine nature has entered—or flooded into—the body, these two have made one Son, one person.”

Next he brings forward the famous passage from Theodoret’s second dialogue, where the Eutychian Eranistes says:

> “Just as the symbols of the Lord’s body and blood are one thing before the priest’s invocation, but after the invocation are CHANGED and BECOME something else (*μεταβάλλεται, καὶ ἕτερα γίνεται*—‘are changed, and become other things’), so the Lord’s body after the ascension was changed into the divine substance.”

Theodoret replied:

> “You have been caught in the nets that you yourself wove. For the mystical symbols do not depart from their nature after sanctification; they remain in their former substance, figure, and form, and can be seen and touched just as before. But they are understood to be what they have been made, and are believed and adored as being what they are believed to be. Compare the image with the archetype, and you will see the likeness. For the figure must be like the truth. That body has its former shape and outline and, to put it in a word, the substance of a body; but after the resurrection it was made immortal and free from corruption, and, seated at the right hand, it attained to this state and is adored by every creature, because it is called the body of the Lord’s nature.”

Furthermore, Ephraem, bishop of Antioch, according to Photius, while proclaiming two natures in Christ, says:

> “Thus the body of Christ received by the faithful neither departs from sensible substance and remains undivided from intelligible grace. Baptism likewise, having become wholly spiritual and existing as one thing, preserves what belongs to sensible substance—namely, water—and does not lose what it was.”

Finally, Gelasius I, Roman pontiff, writes in his book *On the Two Natures*:

> “Certainly, the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord that we receive are a divine reality; through them also we are made partakers of the divine nature, and yet the substance of the bread and wine will not cease to exist.
