Certainly, the image and likeness of the body and blood of the Lord are celebrated in the rite. Therefore, what we should perceive in Christ the Lord himself is sufficiently evident from what we profess, celebrate, and receive in his image: just as in this image—that is, in the DIVINE SUBSTANCE—they PASS OVER, with the Holy Spirit perfecting the sacrament, while the nature remains in its own proper character, so that principal mystery itself—namely, the union in Christ of the divine and human nature—whose efficacy and power this represents for you, remains one Christ, since both remain whole in their proper existence.”

These passages were sharply debated between Catholics and Protestants. I have no intention of transcribing what Cardinals Bellarmine and Perronius, the authors of the books *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*, Natalis Alexander, and other Catholic writers have discussed at length. Nevertheless, I shall explain, to the best of my ability, what the attentive reader should observe here.

From these passages the Lutherans derive consubstantiation, or impanation, in the sacrament. They otherwise believe with Catholics in the real presence—that is, in the principal, indeed the greatest, constituent of the Eucharist, on which its awesome majesty, ineffable efficacy, power, and excellence above the other sacraments depend.

But how justly and solidly the Church has condemned the impanation, or consubstantiation, devised by Luther, you will easily see. One must observe that the force of the words used both by the liturgies of all the Churches and by the holy Fathers to designate the change effected in the bread and wine through the words of consecration—and ordinarily designated by the word “transubstantiation”—is so clear that it is utterly absurd to devise a surviving substance of those elements in the sacrament while admitting that their substance is converted into the body and blood of the Lord.

Indeed, the whole Church prays that the bread may become the Lord’s body and the wine his blood; that the Holy Spirit, entering into the sacred gifts, may make the bread a body, may change it, and may transform it. Therefore the mind of the Church can be no other than that the bread ceases to be bread and its substance is converted into Christ’s body.

The Churches never prayed that the Lord’s body might descend into bread and be united with it, which would have had to be asserted under the Lutheran hypothesis. The Fathers used the terms “change,” “trans-elementation,” “transfiguration”—the force of the latter word was shown above—and similar expressions, from which the doctrine of the Catholic Church is most clearly derived.

It is also well known that those same Fathers used similar examples of substantial change to confirm the same miracle, as we have noted more than once in this work. Therefore, if at some time, as may be hoped, merciful God inclines the hearts of the Lutheran people toward reconciliation with the Catholic Church, from whose maternal bosom they were unhappily torn away, they will easily perceive how rashly their ancestors departed from the judgment of that same Church in the matter of the Eucharist.

The Calvinists, therefore, using—or rather abusing—the passages cited above, wage war against Catholics and Lutherans alike, denying not only transubstantiation but also the real presence itself. Since, however, they do not dare to deny that a change is introduced into the bread and wine through the words of consecration, they maintain that this change is no different from what occurs with baptism and sacred oil: namely, the addition of a heavenly power to the symbols, which symbols exhibit not the reality and truth of the Lord’s body and blood but only a figure and type.

Let us see from the passages recently cited whether their argument is slippery or sound, beginning with the real presence. As for Chrysostom’s words, Father Montfaucon (*In the Edition of Chrysostom’s Works*) and Father Lequien (*In the Edition of Damascene’s Works*) brought forward much to prove that the letter to Caesarius should by no means be attributed to Chrysostom. I also know that Father Hardouin of the Society of Jesus and the Marquis Scipione Maffei disputed this letter, but I have not yet seen their studies.

Nor should Jacques Basnage be passed over. He printed the same letter again (*Canisius’s Lectures*, vol. I, p. 226), yet did not dare to draw anything from it against the Catholic position. Quite wisely. For even if it were not clear from many other passages how much troubled emotion leads the minds and pens of the Calvinists astray, this one passage alone could prove that they fight against us with their eyes firmly closed, without considering whether, while attempting to wound their enemy, they are simultaneously stabbing themselves most grievously.

Whoever the author of that letter may be, he is certainly ancient, and he speaks of the Eucharist in such a way that he may seem contrary to the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation. At the same time, however, he clearly condemns the error of the Calvinists, who deny the real presence of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist.

For two centuries now Calvin’s followers have hurled such a letter against us, although this weapon properly strikes and pierces their own breast. The author uses the example of the Eucharist to show the two natures united in Christ, neither confused nor mingled, against the Eutychian. Both natures truly converge in Christ through the hypostatic union—not figuratively or imaginatively. The same thing, therefore, must have been believed by that author concerning the Eucharist.

It follows clearly that the writer himself holds that the Lord’s body exists really in the Eucharist. For he would argue ridiculously—indeed, he would agree entirely with the dreams of the Eutychians—if he believed that there was nothing else in the Eucharist except a figure and image of the Lord’s body; indeed, he would not even place that figure in the sacrament itself, but only in the minds and imaginations of the faithful, as the Calvinists pretend.

Therefore this author too, in agreement with the whole Church, necessarily believed and taught that the Lord’s body exists really in the Eucharist after consecration.

But now the Calvinist, struck down, rises up and says that this passage at least favors, as they call it, the Lutheran impanation and opposes transubstantiation. What benefit, I ask, does this bring to the Calvinist cause? Yet the mind of this writer cannot even be opposed to transubstantiation.

Let me cite his words again:

> “Just as, before it is sanctified, we call the bread ‘bread’”—because it truly is bread—“but when divine grace sanctifies it, it is released from the designation ‘bread’”—because it is no longer bread and has become Christ’s body, as the prayer of the Church and priest required.

Since, however, the color, odor, friability, tangibility, and other qualities—or appearances—of bread remain after consecration, the nature of bread is therefore said to remain in the sacrament. For these qualities truly pertain to the nature of bread; they are not imaginary but real accidents of bread.

If, by sophistry, you insist that just as Christ’s body exists really in the Eucharist, so the body of bread must remain there also, we answer with the same author that not two bodies but ONE BODY OF THE SON is proclaimed of the Eucharist, because the substance of the bread has been converted into the Lord’s body by divine power. Therefore Christ’s body is there, together with the visible appearances—that is, invisibly and really hidden beneath the surviving nature of bread.

This, however, plainly reveals the perverse method of proceeding—if I may say so—and the obstinacy of the Calvinist people. In the case of a doubtful writer, and in the obscure and confused words of a single Latin translation, they seek a basis for excluding the Lord’s real presence from the Eucharist, while they have against them, in so many unquestionably authentic books of Chrysostom, his clear teaching concerning the sacrament of the altar.

Show me no one among the holy Fathers who spoke more brilliantly, magnificently, or openly than Chrysostom about this ineffable sacrament. We can overwhelm the heretics with numerous passages—as others have already done—in which that incomparable bishop, and therefore rightly called the doctor of the Eucharist, recognizes and proclaims the real flesh and blood in the sacrament.

Nor did he ever imagine, as the innovators do, that the Lord’s words, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink,” should be understood figuratively and metaphorically. Rather, explicitly condemning such interpreters, he wrote that Christ truly added these words:

> “So that they would not suppose that what had been said was an enigma and a parable, but would know that it was altogether necessary to eat the body:
>
> **Ὥστε μὴ νομίζειν αἴνιγμα εἶναι τὸ εἰρημένον, καὶ παραβολήν, ἀλλ’ εἰδέναι, ὅτι πάντως δεῖ φαγεῖν τὸ σῶμα**  
> ‘So that they would not think that what was said was an enigma and a parable, but would know that it is altogether necessary to eat the body’” (Chrysostom, Homily 46 on John 6).

If anyone desires more from Chrysostom, let him consult his homilies, or the polemical theologians, especially the books *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*. I too shall shortly bring forward some passages from him below.

As for Theodoret’s words, let anyone be blind who does not see that the real presence of the Lord in the Eucharist shines forth most clearly from that very passage. First, the Eutychian asserts that after consecration the symbols are called the body and blood of Jesus Christ, and that we become partakers of that same body and blood. Theodoret affirms the same thing.

The Eutychian proceeds to say that the symbols are changed through the invocation and become something else—that is, they are converted into the flesh and blood of the Lord—from which he later infers that Christ’s body after the ascension was converted into the divine nature, which was the error of the Eutychians.

What does Theodoret reply? He says that the symbols still retain their external form, so that they can truly be seen and touched. We, however, understand that beneath the form of the symbols there lies and exists that for which they are called the Lord’s body and blood, since in reality they have become Christ’s body and blood; and therefore we believe and adore that same body and blood there.

What I express in my own words Theodoret expresses more cautiously, according to the discipline of those times. For he had first said that these matters should not be discussed openly, lest someone not yet initiated into the Christian mysteries should hear them. Nevertheless, his meaning is perfectly clear to anyone when he says:

> “They are understood to BE WHAT THEY HAVE BEEN MADE, and are BELIEVED and ADORED as being what they ARE BELIEVED to be.”

What were the bread and wine made by the invocation? What are they? What are they believed to be? Clearly, the body and blood of the Lord, and for that reason they are ADORED. If there were nothing there except bread and wine, and if the Lord’s true body and blood were not there, they certainly would not be adored.

Further on, Theodoret adds that the Eucharist is called not only the body of Jesus Christ but also the bread of life:

> “As regards the body, we call it the DIVINE BODY, the life-giving body, the BODY OF THE LORD; by these expressions we signify that it is not the body of some ordinary human being, but THE BODY OF JESUS CHRIST, who is God and man.”

Here, therefore, you have a decisive argument against the Sacramentarians’ fabrications. Theodoret acknowledges that the bread has been made, through consecration, into a body—and indeed into Christ’s own body—which, because it is present in the sacrament, is consequently owed worship.

But since Theodoret’s preceding words seem to favor the opponents of Catholic transubstantiation, we shall discuss this matter again below.

Ephraem of Antioch, as we saw above, likewise testifies that Christ’s body is received by the faithful in the Eucharist. Nor was the mind of Gelasius I, Roman pontiff, any different, if the books *On the Two Natures in Christ* truly belong to him; this is still disputed. He says that the sacraments we receive are a divine reality—the body and blood of Christ. Then he adds that these PASS OVER INTO THE DIVINE SUBSTANCE, with the Holy Spirit perfecting the sacrament.

Here is precisely what was and still is requested of God in all the liturgies: that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood; that God convert and transform the sacred gifts into the flesh and blood of the Lord.

“But this author,” you will say, “no less than the writer of the letter to Caesarius, and Theodoret and Ephraem of Antioch, writes that the substance or nature of the bread and wine remains after consecration. Where, then, is transubstantiation?”

The Catholics Bellarmine, Perronius, Natalis Alexander, Arnauld, and others long ago observed that the terms “substance” and “nature” are equivocal and are not always taken with the strict meaning assigned to them by the Peripatetic school. They can also designate the properties of bodies, as those writers establish through many examples.

It is certain that the Eucharistic symbols remain after consecration with respect to their external appearance and form, just as they were before, and that they can be touched and seen; our senses do not err in this. Something, therefore, remains of the nature of the bread and wine—namely, what is exposed to our senses—so that it can truly be said that everything belonging to the bread and wine and to their nature does not pass into the substance and nature of Christ’s body. This was sufficient to blunt the arguments of the Eutychians, who maintained that Christ’s body and human nature had been entirely converted and changed into the nature and essence of divinity.

But as regards the inward substance and nature of the symbols after consecration, those same ancient writers sufficiently showed that they believed it to be converted into the substance of the Lord’s body and blood. Theodoret himself does not deny that a change occurs in the symbols through consecration, as we have seen. He likewise testifies that the symbols of bread and wine are symbols of Christ’s true body. When the Eutychian asks, “And do you believe that you receive Christ’s body and blood?” the orthodox Christian answers, “I believe so.”

Then he admits that the symbols have been made Christ’s body and blood when he says:

> “They are understood to BE WHAT THEY HAVE BEEN MADE, and are BELIEVED and ADORED as being what they ARE BELIEVED to be.”

That is, they are believed to be the Lord’s true body and blood. No other sense can legitimately be drawn from his words.

Gelasius teaches the same thing when he writes that the sacraments of the Eucharist are a divine reality, and that through them we become partakers of the divine nature—a doctrine that Saint Hilary and so many other Fathers had earlier transmitted in agreement. He says that they PASS OVER INTO THE DIVINE SUBSTANCE, with the Holy Spirit perfecting the sacrament.

These passages overthrow the Calvinists’ imaginings and leave no room for the Lutheran opinion. According to the Lutherans, there is no change of the gifts into Christ’s body, but only the addition of one substance to another. The Church, by contrast, has always acknowledged that the bread and wine are transmuted, converted, and pass over into the flesh and blood of the Lord.

Nor can the examples of baptismal water and sacred oil, as we said—as we said—be twisted into an evasion of the real change of the Eucharistic symbols. No one ever wrote that that water and oil pass over into the substance of Christ or of the Holy Spirit.

Finally, what can and must wholly disperse the darkness stirred up by the passages cited from the Fathers is this: throughout the preceding ten centuries, the Churches and Fathers always proceeded in agreement concerning the doctrine of the Eucharistic sacrament, and at that time no more than slight clouds arose against this ineffable mystery.

Therefore Theodoret, Gelasius, and Ephraem of Antioch must be understood to have meant the same as the other Fathers. As for Chrysostom, he alone can settle the entire controversy concerning the Eucharist; and anyone who denies that he most explicitly transmits here the doctrines of the Catholic Church must be blind or impudent.

We shall investigate what the Eastern Churches also thought concerning the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist and the transformation of the sacred gifts—or, as we now say, transubstantiation. But let the reader, I ask, always remember what we previously brought forward from Leo the Great against the Eutychians, and from Saints Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, and the other Fathers.

From those passages it is most clearly gathered that a marvelous change occurs through consecration in the sacred gifts—not through the faith of the Christian, but really and through God’s omnipotence—and that through his words the true body and blood of Christ come to be and are present in the sacrament.

Let us conclude this chapter with the words of Anastasius of Sinai, who, like Theodoret, was writing against the Eutychians, called Gaianites, around the year of Christ 620, or somewhat later, if you prefer. He introduces a Gaianite disputing with an orthodox Christian. The orthodox Christian asks:

> “Tell me, I beg you: is the most sacred Communion of the body and blood of Christ, which you offer and receive, truly the true body and blood of Christ, the Son of God, or merely bread such as is sold from door to door, or does it merely occupy the place of, and serve as a figure of, Christ’s body, like the sacrifice of the goat that the Jews offer?” (Anastasius of Sinai, *Hodegos*, or *The Guide of the Way*).

The Gaianite replied:

> “Far be it from us to say that the sacred Communion is merely a figure of Christ’s body or merely bread; rather, we receive THE VERY BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST, THE INCARNATE SON OF GOD, BORN OF THE MOST HOLY VIRGIN MARY.”

The orthodox Christian replied:

> “So we believe and confess,” etc. “Christ did not say, ‘This is a figure,’ or ‘something occupying the place of,’ my body and blood,” etc.

Behold what both heretics and orthodox Christians believed concerning the Eucharist in the seventh century of Christ.

# CHAPTER XIII  
## What the Liturgies of the Eastern Christians—whether Greeks or Syrians—Contain Concerning the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist and Transubstantiation
Let us now approach the liturgies which the faithful of Christ in the East have used from ancient times, so that we may perceive what their faith has been and is concerning the Eucharist. If it becomes clear that their view of the truth of the Lord’s body and blood [Col. 0962D] in the Eucharist, and of transubstantiation, has not been and is not other than that which has always been observed by the Roman Church, then Protestants—if they lend their eyes and ears to the truth—will at last understand, or will be able to understand, that the agreement of the entire ancient and present Church militates against them, and that no change has occurred in these articles of faith in any age, since the Eastern Christians too—some separated from the Roman Church seven hundred years ago, others thirteen hundred years ago—have always proceeded in agreement on this dogma.

For the disagreement between us and them concerning unleavened bread, concerning the communion of the people under both kinds, and concerning whether consecration is accomplished by the words of the Lord or by invocation, has no bearing at all on the argument presently before us. Let us see what is contained in the liturgy which for so many centuries has borne the name of Saint [Col. 0963A] John Chrysostom, and which is used by most of the Greeks, especially those subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople, as well as by the Russians, or Ruthenians, the Wallachians, and the Moldavians. Jacob Goar has illuminated it with a distinguished commentary.

There the priest, while the Cherubic Hymn is being sung, thus prays to Christ, saying: “Make me worthy, by the power of your Holy Spirit, etc., to stand before this holy table and to consecrate your holy and immaculate BODY and your precious BLOOD.” Again he prays to God in these words: “Send your Holy Spirit upon us and upon these gifts set forth. Make this bread the precious BODY of your Christ.” The deacon says: “Amen.” The priest adds: “And that which is in this chalice, make it the precious BLOOD of your Christ.” The deacon: “Amen.” Again the priest: [Col. 0963B] “TRANSFORMING it by your Holy Spirit.” The deacon: “Amen, amen, amen.” The priest: “So that it may become, for those who receive it, sobriety of soul, forgiveness of sins, and participation in the Holy Spirit, etc.”

After other prayers, the priest says secretly in prayer: “Attend, Lord Jesus Christ our God, from your holy dwelling and from the throne of the glory of your kingdom; and come to sanctify us—you who dwell with the Father on high and are invisibly present here with us also—and deign by your mighty hand to impart to us your immaculate body and precious blood, and through us to all the people.”

At the fraction: “The Lamb of God, the Son of the Father, is broken and divided; he is broken but not dismembered; he is always eaten and is not consumed, but sanctifies those who partake of him.”

The deacon says at communion: “Grant [Col. 0963C] me, Lord, the precious and holy body of the Lord, our God and Savior, Jesus Christ.”

The priest then takes the holy bread, bowing his head before the holy table, and prays in this manner: “I believe, Lord, and I confess that you are Christ, the Son of the living God, who came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first.” Then he says: “Lord, I am not worthy, etc.” But just as the Lord did not disdain to recline in a stable and to enter the house of Simon the Leper, so he asks that the Lord deign to enter the manger of his soul and his defiled body, etc. I pass over the many remaining passages.

Among these same Greeks there is also in use the Mass of Saint Basil, as well as another liturgy entitled *τῶν προηγιασμένων*—“of the Presanctified.” But since similar prayers occur there, I have judged that nothing need be extracted from them. Nor are the passages read in Book Eight of the *Apostolic Constitutions* concerning the Greek Mass dissimilar.

It could happen that some Calvinist, reading these things, would, according to the custom of his sect, find here not the true mind of the Greek Church but his own opinion, adding and supplying what neither the ancient nor the modern Greeks ever dreamed of. But those who deal sincerely with their teaching cannot fail to understand that the Greeks truly believe and confess the conversion and transformation of the gifts into the real body and blood of the Lord. Although these are invisible, they nevertheless believe them to be truly and really present in the sacrament, and truly—not through mere imagination—to be eaten [Col. 0964A] and drunk by the faithful.

They also openly testify to this belief in their confession, when, before the body of Christ is set forth, they say: “I believe, Lord, and I confess,” as quoted above. The Latins too, as we previously observed, once professed the same thing at communion; for when the priest said, “The body of the Lord,” the faithful replied, “Amen”—that is, “I believe it to be so.” This is also found in the *Apostolic Constitutions*.

There will also be some among the Sacramentarians who will deny that the aforementioned Masses should be attributed to Basil and Chrysostom, as though it were not known that a sacred liturgy was in use in the time of Saint Basil, and that Basil himself mentioned it (*On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27); or as though Proclus, Bishop of Constantinople, in the following century, the Council in Trullo (canon 32), Peter the Deacon around [Col. 0964B] the year of Christ 520, and Leontius Scholasticus (*Against Nestorius*, Book II), had not given us certain knowledge of liturgies restored by Basil and Chrysostom.

But what leaves no room for all quibbling is this: what else is contained in Chrysostom’s liturgy than what he so often and so plainly inculcated in his sacred homilies? Let me cite a few passages from the great abundance.

In his homily on Matthew he says:

> “These works are not the product of human power. What Christ did then at that supper, he now does and accomplishes. We occupy the rank of ministers; but he himself is the one who sanctifies and TRANSFORMS the gifts. Approach with confidence. ‘With my disciples,’ he says, ‘I celebrate the Passover.’ For this is not a different table; this table is in no respect inferior to that one. Christ did not make that table while some human being makes this one. [Col. 0964C] Rather, he himself makes both” (Chrysostom, Homily 83 on Matthew).

What follows from such a transformation he reveals everywhere, acknowledging in the sacrament the reality and truth of the Lord’s body and blood, although our proud mind—such as that of the Calvinists—and our senses may seem to resist so great a mystery.

Thus, in the same homily, and also in Homily 60, he says to the people:

> “Let us believe God everywhere and not oppose him, even if what he says appears absurd to our senses and thoughts. Let us act in this way especially in the mysteries, looking not only at what lies before us, but also holding fast to his words. For we cannot be deceived by his words; our senses, however, are easily deceived. Those words cannot be false. Since, therefore, he said, ‘This is my body,’ let us not be held by any doubt, but believe and perceive it with the eyes of the understanding.”

In another homily on Matthew the holy teacher says:

> “He who said, ‘This is my body,’ accomplished the reality together with the word. It is not merely a garment, but Christ’s body that is set before us—not merely so that we may touch it, but so that we may eat and be satisfied” (Homily 5 on Matthew).

In his homily on the betrayal of Judas:

> “For it is not a human being who makes the BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST from the offering set before us on the Lord’s table, but he who was crucified for us, Christ. The words are spoken by the mouth of the priest, but they are consecrated by the power and grace of God. ‘This is my body,’ he says. By this word the things set forth are consecrated.”

Here is the judgment of the Roman Church concerning the words of consecration, which certain little Greeks have dared to criticize.

In his homily on Saint Philogonius:

> “This table takes the place of the manger in which Christ was born. For here too the LORD’S BODY IS PLACED—not wrapped in swaddling clothes, as then, BUT CLOTHED ON EVERY SIDE WITH THE HOLY SPIRIT.”

When he discusses the priesthood, we read:

> “O miracle! O loving-kindness of God! He who sits above with the Father is, at that very moment, handled by everyone’s hands, and gives himself to those who desire to receive and embrace him” (Chrysostom, Book III *On the Priesthood*).

In another homily:

> “Remember that it is the BODY AND BLOOD OF HIM WHO DWELLS ABOVE THE HEAVENS, WHO IS DEVOUTLY ADORED BY THE ANGELS. I mean him who stands near the immortal power of God. Of HIS BLOOD we partake, and he has delivered his OWN BODY to us to receive” (the same, Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Ephesians).

I add no more. Would that those who, by the gravest crime, have robbed this ineffable sacrament and mystery of its first and principal weight of dignity and power—that is, those who have dared to deny the real presence of the Lord—would diligently and sincerely study Chrysostom’s writings, laying aside all hostility! There they will see, placed in broad daylight, the Roman Church’s teaching concerning the Eucharist, and will find many ceremonies of the Greek Mass, including the fraction of Christ’s body, to mention nothing else.

I said that the Greeks profess at communion their faith in the truth of the Lord’s body. I think this should be confirmed by the authority of Theodore the Studite, who writes in a dialogue between a heretic and an orthodox believer:

> “How,” says the orthodox believer, “do you call those things which are handled by the priest in the sacred liturgy and sacred hymns? An image or the reality? If an image, what absurdity! You rush from blasphemy into blasphemy. But if the reality, as it truly is—for while they receive them, the faithful CONFESS, by the authority of the divine word, that they are the very BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD—why do you trifle, reducing the mysteries of THE REALITY to figures?” (Theodore the Studite, *Antirrheticus* I against the Iconoclasts).

Thus he wrote around the year of Christ 796.

Nor did the Greek Fathers at the Second Council of Nicaea, in the year 787, think or speak otherwise, when they said against those same Iconoclasts:

> “No trumpet-like voice—that is, the voice of the holy apostles or of our illustrious Fathers—has ever called our unbloody sacrifice an image of Christ’s body” (Second Council of Nicaea, Act 6).

After the Savior’s words they add:

> “He did not say, ‘Take and eat the image of my body,’ etc.”

Therefore it has been clearly demonstrated that the Lord, the apostles, and the Fathers never called the unbloody sacrifice offered by the priest an image; rather, they called it THE VERY BODY AND THE VERY BLOOD.

Finally, concerning the Eucharistic bread and wine they say:

> “Before they are sanctified, they are called types; but after sanctification they are properly called, ARE, and ARE BELIEVED TO BE, the BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST.”

Add to this what John of Damascus—another Thomas Aquinas among the Greeks—wrote long before the Second Council of Nicaea concerning the Eucharist (*On the Orthodox Faith*, Book IV, chapter 13), wholly contrary to the Calvinists’ fictions. Since these passages are very well known, I pass them over. Add also the many other sacred Greek writers who, through succeeding centuries, remained in agreement on this dogma; their testimonies are gathered in the books *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*. In a word, no doubt remains that the belief of the Greek Churches concerning the Eucharist, both ancient and recent, has always been and still is the same as that which the Roman Church believes and proclaims.

At Jerusalem there was formerly in use a liturgy under the name of James, the brother of the Lord. It was first written in Greek and later in Syriac, because Syrians chiefly inhabited that city. It is certain, indeed, that the most ancient liturgies in the East were recorded in Greek letters. This liturgy was used both by the Jacobite Christians, who profess the Monophysite error, [Col. 0966B] and by the orthodox Melchites.

Those peoples also have other liturgies, which Renaudot has published. What we can observe especially amid such a multitude of liturgies is that, in what concerns the substance of the Eucharist and the unbloody sacrifice, they agree with the liturgies and teaching of the Roman Church and of the other Churches.

It is worthwhile now to hear the liturgy of the Syriac Jacobites. The variety of the prayers introduces only a superficial difference. There this hymn is found:

> “Your people, O Christ, blessed Christ, who built his Church upon Simon and chose priests to divide within it his body and blood. The priests stand with the deacons in great fear and distribute the body and blood of the Son of God. Your sheep, O Christ, stand at your door; they eat your body and drink your blood, and sing glory to your divinity.”

Below, the priest says:

> “I am the Bread of life, says our Lord, who descended from on high to the depths so that through me the world might live, etc.; and behold, the priests carry me in their hands upon the altars: alleluia.”

Then he says this concerning those who have already died:

> “Those who ate your holy body and tasted your blood, the cup of salvation, recline with Abraham at your table, O Lord.”

The priest, while breaking the host and while the body is in his hands, says this prayer, or profession of faith:

> “You are Christ our God, who on the summit of Golgotha in Jerusalem were pierced in your side for us. You are the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Spare our offenses and forgive our sins, [Col. 0966D] and place us at your right hand.”

While putting a fragment into the chalice, he says:

> “Father of truth, behold your Son, an offering pleasing to you. Receive him who died for me, and through him be gracious to me.”

Before communion he says:

> “Grant me, Lord, to eat you in holiness, so that through eating you all my evil desires may be driven away, etc.”

While receiving a fragment from the spoon, he says:

> “I hold you, who contain the ends of the earth; I have you in my hands, who rule the depths; you, O God, I place in my mouth, etc.”

The communicant says:

> “The propitiatory fragment of the body and blood of Christ is given to the infirm servant, etc.”

The person receiving communion says: “Amen.”

The priest, having returned to the altar, says:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, may your holy body, which we have eaten, and your propitiatory blood, which we have drunk, not become for us judgment or vengeance, but life and salvation.”

In the more ancient liturgy of Saint James, where the canon of the Mass is found, the priest, according to the custom of the Eastern Christians, says after the consecratory words of Christ:

> “Have mercy on us, God the Father almighty, and send your Holy Spirit, etc., so that, when he comes, he may make this bread a life-giving body, a saving body, a heavenly body, a body granting salvation to souls and bodies, the body of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life to those who receive it.”

The people say: “Amen.”

The priest continues:

> “And may that which is mixed in this chalice become the blood of the new covenant, etc., the blood of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, etc.”

Below he says:

> “We believe, we approach, we seal, and we break this Eucharist, the heavenly bread, the body of the Word of the living God in the cup of salvation, etc. May your holy body and blood become the way that leads to your kingdom.”

Below, the deacon says:

> “Bow your heads before the merciful God, before the propitiatory altar, and before the body and blood of our Savior, etc.”

To pass over other matters, this prayer is read there:

> “Mouths accustomed to food and produce acknowledge your grace, through which they have merited this heavenly gift, which is the body and blood of your only-begotten Son.”

In Renaudot, the liturgy of Saint Xystus, Roman pope, follows; it is used by these same Jacobites. I extract only a few passages from it.

The priest, while breaking the offering, says:

> “Grant, Lord, that with my weak hands I may approach and break your holy body, and divide it among the children of the holy Church, etc.”

While signing the fragments of the broken body and the chalice, he says:

> “The blood of our Lord is sprinkled upon his holy body, etc.”

When he is about to receive communion, he recites this prayer while bowing:

> “I carry you, Lord, in my hands and embrace you in my fist, Lord of the ages, whom creatures cannot contain; and I place you, Almighty, in my mouth. Grant me, Lord, to eat you in holiness, etc.”

In the two Jacobite liturgies which bear the name of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, similar statements are read concerning the invocation of the Holy Spirit to consecrate the offerings, so that he may make the bread Christ’s body and the wine his blood.

You will find similar passages in the liturgy of the Twelve Apostles, and in another of Saint John the Evangelist; [Col. 0967D] in that attributed to Saint Mark the Evangelist; and in others bearing the names of Saint Clement of Rome, Saint Dionysius, Bishop of Athens, Saint Ignatius, Saint Julius, Roman pope, and Saint John Chrysostom of Syria.

In the liturgy of Saint Maruta, also Syriac, the Holy Spirit is likewise invoked “to TRANSFORM THIS SIMPLE BREAD and MAKE IT THE VERY BODY that was sacrificed for us upon the cross,” etc., and “to TRANSFORM the mixed wine in this chalice and PERFECT IT AS THE VERY BLOOD that was poured out for us on the summit of Golgotha,” etc.

There are also liturgies bearing the names of Dioscorus, Patriarch of Alexandria, and of Philoxenus, Bishop. In the latter it is said of Christ:

> “He who mingled his body with our bodies and mixed his blood with our members.”

And in the Syriac liturgy of Matthew the Shepherd this prayer is found:

> “Christ, who gave your body for us to eat, so that it might be the leaven of life, etc.”

In the Syriac liturgy of blessed James of Edessa, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, this is said concerning the Lord’s body and blood:

> “So that, mingled with our souls and bodies, they may be for us unto pardon and not unto accusation, etc.”

In the Syriac liturgy of Dionysius Barsalibi, the Holy Spirit is invoked to make this bread the body of our God and to transform the mixture in the chalice into the blood of our God Christ. A similar formula occurs in the liturgy of Bishop Dioscorus.

I pass over the Syriac liturgies of the Nestorians. In all these Eastern liturgies the principal parts of the canon are the same: they begin with “Lift up your hearts,” the Seraphic Hymn, the consecratory words of the Lord, and the invocation of the Holy Spirit to accomplish the same consecration. The Lord’s Prayer follows, and then communion.

Here too, no learned person whose eyes are not wholly blinded can fail to see that the doctrine of the Roman and other Western Churches concerning the Eucharist is confirmed by the Eastern Christians. Here also real presence is established, here the true conversion of the gifts into the body and blood of the Lord, and here their true eating and drinking. Nor did those peoples, separated from the Roman Church for so many centuries, ever conceive the imaginary Calvinian presence of Christ, which depends upon the faith of the recipients and not upon the words of the Lord and the wondrous power of the Holy Spirit.

Nor did they ever dream that the change in the Eucharist—which even the Calvinists cannot deny—was anything other than the addition of a heavenly power and quality to the bread and wine. For all the Eastern Christians, in agreement with the Roman Church, acknowledge, believe, and confess that the offered gifts are changed into the very body and blood of the Lord.

In nearly all these liturgies one must also observe that after the words of invocation of the Holy Spirit the people respond, “Amen”—that is, “We believe it to be so.”

What these peoples have believed for so many centuries is the same as what holy men in those very regions believed and proclaimed in the fourth century of Christ, around the year of Christ 360—namely, Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem, and Ephraem, the Edessan deacon.

Let whoever thinks he can divert elsewhere the celebrated words of Cyril, in which he explains the doctrine of the Catholic Church and which we have already quoted above, do so without shame. We may add this:

> “In the type—or figure—of bread, the body is given to you; and in the type of wine, the blood is given to you, so that when you HAVE RECEIVED THE BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST, YOU MAY BECOME OF ONE BODY AND OF ONE BLOOD WITH HIM” (Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 22, or *Mystagogical Catechesis* 4).

Other Fathers likewise used this manner of speaking.

Cyril subsequently explains the liturgy, which in substance is not unlike the others recently mentioned. Concerning the invocation for consecration he speaks in these words:

> “We entreat the loving God to send the Holy Spirit upon the gifts set forth, so that he may MAKE THE BREAD THE BODY OF CHRIST AND THE WINE THE BLOOD OF CHRIST. For whatever the Holy Spirit touches, τοῦτο ἡγίασται καὶ ΜΕΤΑΒΕΒΛΗΤΑΙ—‘that has been sanctified and TRANSFORMED’” (*Catechesis* 23, or *Mystagogical Catechesis* 5).

Here you have transubstantiation.

Ephraem, as though he had undertaken to instruct the Sacramentarians who attack the faith of the Catholic Church with so many quibbles, writes as follows:

> “He who looks through the eyes of faith plainly and clearly beholds the Lord, and with full and firm faith eats the most holy body and drinks the most sacred blood of the immaculate Lamb, who is the only-begotten Son of the heavenly Father. He does not investigate the mysteries of the most holy and wholly divine faith with empty curiosity, etc. What Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, our Savior, accomplished for us surpasses all wonder, all thought, and all words, when, although clothed in flesh, he nourishes us with fire and Spirit, while he gives us HIS BODY TO EAT [Col. 0969B] AND HIS BLOOD TO DRINK” (Ephraem of Edessa, *Sermon on the Nativity of God: Do Not Investigate Curiously*).

Everyone understands how far those who have always regarded the Eucharist as ineffable and beyond human comprehension—as Catholics still believe it—were from the fictions of Berengarius and Calvin. Saint Ephraem says that we must use true faith, not curiosity, when contemplating that great miracle of divine omnipotence and love.

Meanwhile, we see how the liturgies shed light upon the holy Fathers, and how in turn the liturgies themselves receive their meaning from the Fathers. I could have introduced here the Armenian liturgy, fully incorporated by Father Le Brun into his liturgical books, in which anyone who does not deliberately wish to blind himself cannot fail to recognize the faith of those peoples also in Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist. But since those books are available in Italy as well, I refrain from extracting passages from the liturgy itself.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Agreement of the Dogma Concerning the Eucharist Confirmed by the Egyptian Liturgies, Both Greek and Coptic

Let us pass to Egypt, where the Alexandrian Church formerly held the first place after the Roman Church and traced its origin to Saint Mark the Evangelist. Several liturgies were and still are in use there, recorded either in Greek or in Coptic letters; we owe their publication to the diligence of the most distinguished Eusebius Renaudot.

They are used especially by the Coptic Jacobites, who for so many centuries have fallen into the error of the Monophysites. Since the Christian Ethiopians, a vast people, are subject to the Alexandrian patriarch and have been accustomed to receive from him their metropolitan, or *abuna*, it is not surprising that the ancient liturgies of those Churches also agree with the Coptic liturgies and foster the same error.

As far as our argument is concerned, however, divine Providence has brought it about that these same peoples have never professed or professed today any view concerning the unbloody sacrifice and the Eucharist other than that which has always been preserved in the Roman Church.

This will first be evident from the Greek liturgy to which the name of Saint Mark is prefixed. Before the consecratory words of the Lord, we read:

> “O God, grant that this sacrifice also may be full of your blessing through the coming of your most Holy Spirit.”

The words of Christ follow, pronounced aloud, to which the people respond: “Amen.” Nevertheless, according to the custom of the Eastern Christians, this is added afterward:

> “Send also upon us and upon these breads and chalices your Holy Spirit, so that, as almighty God, he may sanctify and consecrate them, and make the bread the body”—the people respond, “Amen”—“and the chalice the blood of the new covenant, of our Lord God and Savior and supreme King, Jesus Christ.”

In the Coptic liturgy of Saint Basil, the prayer of offering, or presentation, of the bread and chalice is expressed in these words:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, only-begotten Son, Word of God the Father, etc., we ask and beseech your goodness, O lover of humanity. [Col. 0970B] Show your face upon this bread and upon this chalice, which we have placed upon this, your priestly table. Bless them + sanctify them + and consecrate them. TRANSFER THEM, so that this bread MAY BECOME YOUR HOLY BODY, and this mixture in this chalice YOUR PRECIOUS BLOOD, so that they may be a protection for us all, etc.”

The liturgy then proceeds, followed by the anaphora, or canon. At the consecratory words over the bread, the people respond “Amen”; and at those over the chalice, “Amen”—that is, “It is so.”

Then follows the invocation of the Holy Spirit, that he may make this bread the holy body of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, which is given for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life to the one who receives it. The people respond “Amen.” The priest likewise asks that this chalice become the precious blood of your new covenant, of our Lord God and Savior, etc. The people repeat “Amen.”

At the fraction, as the rubric states, the priest takes the holy body in his right hand, places it in his left, and puts a finger upon the body at the side of the *Despotic*—that is, the larger fragment—at the place where it was broken, saying:

> “The holy body.”

He removes his finger from the body, puts it into the chalice, and dips the tip of his thumb into the precious blood. Then he withdraws his finger from the blood, again signs the blood in the form of the glorious cross, and says:

> “And the precious blood of Christ himself, our almighty Lord and God.”

After “Holy things for the holy,” the priest takes the third part in which the *Despotic* was located and divides it into three parts. If the pieces are large, he breaks them on the disk and places the three parts in his raised right hand, keeping his left within the disk, saying:

> “The holy BODY and the precious, pure, TRUE BLOOD of Jesus Christ, our God’s Son. Amen. The BODY and BLOOD of Emmanuel, our God, IN VERY TRUTH. AMEN. I believe, I believe, I believe, and I confess until the final breath of life THAT THIS IS the life-giving BODY of your only-begotten Son, our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, which he received from the Lady of us all, the God-bearer, etc.”

Before communion the priest says secretly:

> “Make us all worthy, Lord, to receive your holy body and your precious blood for the cleansing of our bodies and souls, etc.”

Whether this passage can be understood in terms of metaphors, types, figures, and the other Calvinist imaginations, those who calmly and sincerely consider these matters among them will easily be able to judge.

In the Coptic liturgy attributed to Saint Basil, the prayer of the fraction addressed to the Son is expressed in these words:

> “Blessed are you, Christ God, who through your incomprehensible incarnation prepared for us heavenly bread, THIS YOUR HOLY BODY in the mystery, holy in every respect. You mixed for us a chalice from the fruit of the true vine, which is your divine and immaculate side, from which, after you had given up your spirit, blood and water flowed for us, and purified the whole world.”

Then follows: “The holy body,” etc., and the profession of faith: “I believe, I believe,” etc.

In the liturgy of Saint Cyril the Holy Spirit is invoked upon this bread and upon this chalice, so that they may be purified and transferred, and so that he may make this bread the body of Christ, etc. There is also a prayer concerning the spoon with which the members of the holy body, which is the body of your Son, etc., are to be received.

Similar passages are read in the Greek Alexandrian liturgy of Saint Basil and in another of Saint Gregory—whoever he may have been, I do not know—in which the prayer of bowing the head contains these words:

> “Attend, Lord Jesus, etc., who sit above with the Father and are invisibly present here with us, etc., and deign by your mighty hand to make us partakers of your immaculate body and precious blood, and through us the whole people. For you are the one who is broken and who breaks, although unbroken, etc.”

There too occurs a profession of faith concerning the Lord’s body and blood: “I believe, I believe,” etc.

Nor should it be omitted that this liturgy of Saint Gregory is found written in ancient times in Greek, Coptic, and Arabic letters. Among its other prayers, special attention should be given to the prayer which follows the words of consecration.

The deacon says:

> “Worship God with fear and trembling.”

From the context it is clear that this is to be referred to Christ the Lord.

The priest continues:

> “YOU, LORD, BY YOUR VOICE TRANSFORM THESE THINGS which have been set forth”—namely, the bread and wine. “YOU, WHO ARE SET BEFORE US, perfect for us this ministry full of mysteries; send upon us the grace of the Holy Spirit, who may sanctify and TRANSFER THESE GIFTS set forth INTO THE BODY AND BLOOD of our salvation, and make this BREAD YOUR HOLY BODY, etc.”

And again:

> “Make this CHALICE THE PRECIOUS BLOOD of your new covenant, Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, etc.”

The Lord is asked to transform the sacred gifts by his voice—that is, by the voice which can accomplish all things—and for the Holy Spirit to transfer them into his body and blood as he descends upon them. Whoever does not recognize in such words and petitions the transformation of the gifts proclaimed by the ancients is not considering them with an open mind.

Renaudot had already shown by what futile and forced interpretation Claudius Salmasius attempted to evade and distort the clear meaning and faith of the Egyptian Church expressed in the words of this same liturgy.

No learned person is unaware of how many outstanding teachers once flourished in the Alexandrian Church. If Protestants were to seek in their books after laying aside their prejudices, they would easily find there everything that the recently cited liturgies present concerning the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist.

For what else does Origen teach us in the third century of Christ, when, speaking of the centurion’s boy, he writes:

> “When you receive the holy food and that incorruptible feast, when you enjoy the BREAD OF LIFE and the CUP, you EAT AND DRINK THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD; then the LORD ENTERS UNDER YOUR ROOF. Therefore, humbling yourself, imitate this centurion and say: ‘Lord, I am not worthy’” (Origen, Homily 4 on Various Gospel Passages), etc.

The words of Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, who flourished in the fifth century of Christ, are so clear on this matter that anyone who has tried to cast darkness over his meaning has always engaged in a futile game. Receive these few passages from among the many:

> “Why was the mystical blessing”—that is, the Eucharist—“instituted? What is its power, unless it is TO ENTER INTO US AND MAKE JESUS CHRIST DWELL IN US ALSO BODILY THROUGH THE PARTICIPATION AND COMMUNION OF HIS HOLY FLESH? Jesus Christ does not say merely that he will be within us by a union of benevolence and love, but also THROUGH A NATURAL COMMUNICATION” (Cyril of Alexandria, Book X on John II, chapter 15).

For this purpose he uses the example of two portions of wax which, melted by fire, are mingled together.

Elsewhere, arguing against Nestorius, he introduces Christ saying that he enters and is introduced into our bodies THROUGH HIS OWN FLESH. For it is not the Divinity, but THE PROPER BODY OF THE WORD, that is set upon the holy tables of the churches. “We celebrate in the churches the holy, life-giving, and unbloody sacrifice, believing that the body set before us upon the altar is not the body of an ordinary man or one like us; rather, we receive IT AS THE VERY BODY AND THE VERY BLOOD OF THE WORD, who gives life to all” (the same, Book IV *Against Nestorius*, chapter 5).

Elsewhere he says again that we receive “bodily and spiritually” the one who is the true and natural Son of God (Book XI on John, chapter 12). In many passages he likewise rebukes as blasphemers those who ask how it can be possible for Christ’s body and blood to be really present in the Eucharist, as though they were setting limits to God’s omnipotence (Book IV on John).

At the same time as Cyril of Alexandria—that is, in the middle of the fifth century of Christ—Isidore of Pelusium, his friend, also flourished. He writes to the monk Marathon:

> “It is the same Holy Spirit who, at the mystical table, makes the COMMON AND FAMILIAR BREAD that has been offered BECOME THE VERY BODY which the Son of God assumed in the Incarnation” (Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 109).

In another letter he says:

> “Just as Joseph of Arimathea wrapped the Lord’s body in linen and buried it in the tomb, etc., so, when we sanctify the offered bread upon linen, we find without doubt THE BODY OF JESUS CHRIST” (the same, Book I, Letter 123).

Behold how the holy Fathers of old also continued in agreement with the liturgies of their own people. If the Sacramentarians, through their misfortune or obstinacy, do not yet understand their speech, it will nevertheless be a consolation to Catholics to read these passages again here in confirmation of the faith and doctrine which they profess.

[Col. 0973A] It remains for us to adduce something also from the sacred liturgies of the Abyssinians, or Ethiopians. To this day, in the innermost regions of Africa, the king of the Abyssinians rules over many provinces; with his people he observes the religion of Christ, which was introduced there from the time of Saint Athanasius the Great, bishop of Alexandria. Since these peoples first received the doctrines of the faith from the Church of Alexandria, they have also been accustomed to receive the Catholic—that is, metropolitan—bishop from the patriarch of Alexandria. Hence it also happened that they adopted Dioscorus of Alexandria’s error concerning one nature in Christ, whether at that time or afterward. From the time when the Arabs took possession of Egypt in the seventh century after Christ, all intercourse with the Abyssinians was severed among the peoples of the West, indeed also of the East.

[Col. 0973B] But after the Portuguese penetrated into the East Indies toward the end of the fifteenth century, knowledge of that region began again to spread, and in the year of Christ 1530 the Portuguese priest Francisco Álvares, who had lived among them for six years, described their customs in a special book. It then became known, by God’s mercy, that a people scarcely known in the West for so many centuries, and separated from the Roman and Greek Churches, had steadfastly preserved the same doctrine concerning the Eucharist which both the Romans and the Greeks had always kept intact. For that entire people believes, professes, and proclaims the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist and the transformation of the gifts into his body and blood.

It is to be regretted that the attempt, made more than once, to unite those Churches with the Roman Church failed unhappily, although it had begun well. But because we demanded too much from those peoples, and judged certain rites intolerable which nevertheless could be tolerated with slight alteration, everything collapsed, so that now access to Abyssinia is closed not only to Romans, but to all Europeans.

As learned men have observed, Job Ludolf, a Protestant who rendered valuable service concerning the Ethiopian language and affairs, played a clever game when he asked an Ethiopian priest named Gregory whether the Abyssinians embraced the Catholics’ transubstantiation. Gregory replied that such a transubstantiation was unknown to the Abyssinians; that his fellow citizens were not so scrupulous, nor did they raise such thorny questions.

[Col. 0973D] If Ludolf had acted in good faith and earnestly desired to attain the truth, he should not have asked about transubstantiation, since none of the ancient Fathers used that word; rather, he should have asked whether the Abyssinians believed what Catholics signify by that word—namely, whether bread and wine are truly converted and changed by consecration into the real body and blood of the Lord. Without doubt that Abyssinian priest would have affirmed this; for it is established that this is the faith of that people, as their liturgies plainly testify.

These peoples, who profess the religion of Christ, have several liturgies, among which two are regarded as the most ancient. The first bears the name of the Apostles and is chiefly in use among them. Renaudot published it [Col. 0974A] (vol. I, *Liturgies*). The other is attributed to Dioscorus of Alexandria, the famous champion of the Monophysites; Wansleb of Erfurt made it publicly available. We must now consult them, in order to see what their doctrine concerning the Eucharist is.

In the liturgy published by Renaudot, which is common among the Ethiopian faithful of Christ and is called the universal canon, a prayer over the paten is recited, in which these words are read:

> Lord our God Jesus Christ, etc., extend your hand now over this paten; bless, sanctify, and purify it, so that upon it YOUR HOLY BODY MAY BE PERFECTED, etc.

The prayer over the chalice contains equivalent words. In the prayer over the spoon, by which the Lord’s blood was administered, its sanctification is requested so that it may administer the body and [Col. 0974B] blood of your only-begotten Son, etc.

The prayer of the mystical oblation is worded as follows:

> Prince Jesus Christ, etc., show your face over this bread and over this chalice, which we have set upon this, your spiritual altar. Bless, sanctify, and purify them, AND TRANSFORM THIS BREAD SO THAT IT MAY BECOME YOUR PURE BODY, and that which is mixed in THIS CHALICE, YOUR PRECIOUS BLOOD, etc.

After the priest has used the words of the Lord Christ in consecrating the bread, “This is my body,” etc. (for which the Gospel and the Apostle read, “This is my body”), the people respond:

> Amen, amen, amen. We believe, and we are certain. We praise you, Lord our God: THIS IS TRULY, and so we believe, YOUR BODY.

Likewise, when the priest has pronounced over the chalice, “This is the chalice,” etc., [Col. 0974C] the people respond:

> Amen. IT IS TRULY YOUR BLOOD. We believe.

I now appeal to the faith of the Protestants: is not the Abyssinians’ faith concerning the reality of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrament perfectly clear here? For at that point they do not testify that they believe merely in the human flesh assumed by the Word of God, nor do they imagine for themselves an imaginary and figurative body and blood in the mystery; rather, in explicit words and an inescapable profession they acknowledge that a conversion and transformation have taken place, saying: “This is truly your body. So we believe. It is truly your blood. We believe.”

Then, in order to complete and perfect this marvelous mystery, they add, as is especially customary among the Eastern Churches:

> We ask and beseech you, Lord, to send the Holy Spirit and power upon this bread and upon [Col. 0974D] this chalice, AND TO MAKE BOTH OF THEM THE BODY AND BLOOD OF OUR LORD AND SAVIOR JESUS CHRIST.

That the consecration is nevertheless carried out by Christ’s own words is made certain to us by the holy Fathers Cyprian, Gregory of Nyssa, the author of the books *On the Sacraments*, Chrysostom, Augustine, and others. Nor do the Eastern Churches deny this. Yet learned men, as we indicated above, have long shown that their addition of the invocation of the Holy Spirit—that is, the prayers which the Roman liturgy places before the words of consecration—does nothing to diminish the power of the Lord’s words, and that no dispute should for this reason be raised against the Easterners.

At the fraction, in the same liturgy, the subdeacon says together with the people:

> The armies of the angels of the Savior [Col. 0975A] of the world are before you

(as Chrysostom and other Fathers likewise testify, and as the Greek liturgy testifies to occur in the unbloody sacrifice),

> and they surround the body and blood of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ

—which are without doubt understood and believed to be present upon the sacred table.

> Let us approach before his face, and with faith let us venerate Christ.

Those who have turned away from the Roman Church may indeed practice quibbling here; but the Abyssinians’ faith is so clear in these words that anyone who dares to interpret them otherwise is abusing his own ingenuity.

The same faith shines forth even more clearly from what the priest professes in his own name and that of the people after the customary formula “Holy things for the holy,” and before communion. Holding the consecrated gifts in his hand and displaying them to the people, he makes this confession:

> The holy, precious, living, and true body of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which is given for the remission of sins and eternal life to those who receive it with faith. Amen.  
> The holy, precious, life-giving, and true blood of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which is given, etc. Amen.  
> This is the body and blood of Emmanuel, in the reality of the thing. Amen, amen, amen.  
> I believe, I believe, now and forever. Amen.  
> This is the body and blood of the Lord, etc., as above in the Egyptian Mass.

While the priest distributes communion to the people, he says:

> This is the bread of life, which descended from heaven, truly the precious body of Emmanuel our God. Amen.

The person who receives it says “Amen,” that is, “So I believe.” The priest adds:

> This is the chalice of life, which descended from heaven, which is the precious blood of Christ.

[Col. 0975C] The recipient says “Amen.” This is from the common liturgy of the Abyssinians.

In the other liturgy, published by Wansleb, the following ancient note is read after the words of consecration:

> Lest anyone among us should think that this body which he eats is a body without blood and soul, and that when he drinks this chalice it is blood alone without body and soul: it is body, and blood, and soul.

Below this appears the following prayer:

> Just as, Lord, you have implanted the body of your Son in our bodies, and just as you have mingled the blood of your Messiah with our blood, so also implant your fear in our hearts, etc.

Behold how, in those remotest regions of the world, God has preserved for so many centuries, uncorrupted, the true doctrine of the Roman Catholic Church concerning the Eucharist.

[Col. 0975D] The Roman Mass was celebrated by the priest Francisco Álvares, mentioned above, in the presence of the Abyssinian king and his nobles, before Luther’s heresy broke out. They praised it highly and consequently approved the adoration of the host and chalice, since it conformed to the faith of their own Church.

From the liturgies of so many different and ancient Churches that have been mentioned thus far, anyone who still does not understand that the dogma of the Lord’s real presence in the Eucharist, and of the transformation of the sacred gifts into the true body and blood of Jesus Christ, was spread by the apostles throughout the whole Church of Christ, must be doing violence to his own understanding; and he will be strictly judged by God for resisting manifest truth.

Once you have established that bread and wine become the body and blood of the Lord through consecration, and that they are transformed, there is no longer any dispute to be had about the word and meaning of transubstantiation. For we are immediately compelled to recognize that the things offered have ceased inwardly to be what they were, while retaining only their outward appearance and form, accessible to our senses.

If the human mind cannot grasp the manner of so great a thing, and if difficulties arise in our minds because of the many other marvels that follow from the Catholic position, the faith which we profess concerning divine omnipotence ought to wipe away every doubt, as so many holy Fathers have already warned us. For they themselves thought and believed as we do, and likewise acknowledged that the wondrous structure of this most sacred mystery surpasses our understanding. Therefore they required the same power of faith for the Eucharist that it is necessary to apply to the other difficult mysteries of the Christian religion.

And when they required this, who does not see that so many centuries ago they condemned the rashness of the sacramentarian flock, which leaves nothing difficult and nothing marvelous in the Eucharist or in the sacrifice of the altar, contrary to the consensus of all antiquity? From the liturgies of so many different Churches throughout the Christian world, belonging to the ancient centuries, is anything more needed to overthrow and crush the utterly ridiculous fable invented by the Calvinists—that Christ’s real presence was introduced into the Eucharist by Paschasius Radbertus in the ninth century after Christ?

In the midst of so much light, it is now to be hoped that those who lie in darkness, at evident peril to their souls, and do not sincerely seek the truth concerning a dogma of such importance, may advance.

## CHAPTER XV  
### What Samuel Basnage brought forward against the dogma of transubstantiation, refuted

Before I proceed to other matters, the reader will not begrudge learning with what weapons Samuel Basnage, a Calvinist, fought against transubstantiation at the beginning of this century (*Political-Ecclesiastical Annals*, year of Christ 33). He too, in order to keep his fellow sectarians in the faith, perhaps thought that he had sufficiently settled a question of such importance by producing, in a few words, passages from the holy Fathers who flourished during the first centuries of the Church, passages in which both the real presence and the substantial transformation of the sacred gifts seem to be denied.

But Catholics, having brought forward countless documents, have shown with the greatest clarity—especially in the most recent century—the Church’s perpetual consensus from its beginning concerning the Eucharist, and have shown that the very words of the Fathers which Basnage produced either favor this dogma or are in no way opposed to it. Yet Basnage, pretending not to have read these things or despising them, supposed that the Catholic ranks would be scattered by the few champions he had himself brought forward.

He objects to us Saint Justin Martyr, speaking about the most sacred synaxis, that is, a writer of the second century after Christ. Before we produce his words, let us oppose to Basnage an older writer, a disciple of the apostles themselves: namely Saint Ignatius of Antioch, [Col. 0977A] bishop and martyr, who wrote the following about certain heretics of his time, that is, the Gnostics and Ophites:

> They abstain from the Eucharist and prayer because they do not confess the Eucharist **to be the flesh of our Savior** (*σάρκα εἶναι τοῦ Σωτῆρος*), the flesh that suffered for our sins, which the Father in his goodness raised up (*Ignatius Martyr, Letter to the Smyrnaeans*).

The holy martyr does not say that the Eucharist signifies, as the sacramentarians wish, but rather that it **is the flesh** of Jesus our Lord. Do the heterodox understand the force of this word?

Let us now hear Saint Justin, who completed his life by martyrdom around the year of Christ 168. Describing the sacred synaxis, he says:

> Bread and a cup mixed with water and wine are offered to the priest. Having received them, he gives praise and glory to the Father of all, in the name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and gives thanks at length. When these things have been completed, the whole people present acclaim the prayers and thanksgiving with “Amen,” that is, “May it be so” (*Justin Martyr, Apology to Antoninus Pius Augustus*).

Then:

> Those who among us are called deacons distribute to each of those present, so that he may partake, the bread, wine, and water over which thanks have been given, and they carry them to the absent.

To this Basnage adds:

> By this it is clearly indicated what change befell the bread: namely, that, while its substance remained, it was consecrated.

So he says—but with an excessively hasty judgment, abusing the word “bread” as soon as he heard it, and forgetting the discipline of that period.

What this bread is must first be learned from Justin, [Col. 0977C] who continues:

> Moreover, this food is called Eucharist among us, and no one is permitted to share in it except one who believes that our teaching is true, etc. For we do not receive these things as common bread or common drink; but just as Jesus Christ our Savior, having become flesh through the Word of God, possessed flesh and blood for the sake of our salvation, **in the same way** we have been taught that the food over which thanks have been given through the prayer of the word proceeding from him—and from which our blood and flesh are nourished by transformation—is **the flesh and blood of that incarnate Jesus** (*Ἰησοῦ καὶ σάρκα καὶ αἷμα ἐδιδάχθημεν εἶναι*, “we have been taught it to be the flesh and blood of Jesus”).

Here also observe the word *εἶναι*, that is, “to be,” by which figure, type, and other Calvinist imaginings are driven out.

Then the holy man brings forward the words of consecration from the Gospel and the Apostle. Against these Basnage constructs his sophistries, saying:

> Of something that is not bread at all, it cannot properly and appropriately be said that it is common bread.

On the contrary, Justin distinguishes the Eucharist from common bread. Basnage adds:

> This language indicates that it is still bread, but something more worthy and holier than that which serves as nourishment.

This is contrary to the clear meaning and testimony of Saint Justin, who expressly writes that this food **is** Christ’s flesh and blood—that is, that the substance of bread is no longer present there. He confirms this by the words of the Lord himself: “This is my body.”

Indeed, he also proves it by another ineffable mystery of the Christian religion, namely, the flesh assumed by the Word of God. Just as the Word of God assumed true flesh, so we have been taught and believe that his true flesh is present in the sacrament.

“Finally,” Basnage adds,

> the bread, wine, and water could not have been carried to the absent by the ministry of the deacons if they had been expelled from the nature of things by the power of consecration.

This is said to deceive readers; for he himself knows that it was customary to carry only the consecrated bread, not the wine and water, to the absent.

Basnage wishes to say that if the substance of bread was changed into the Lord’s body, it could no longer be called bread; yet Justin calls it bread. But as far as Catholics are concerned, it is false that bread and wine were expelled from their nature; for their appearances and properties remain. Other Fathers, and we ourselves even now, continue to use the name “consecrated bread,” while firmly believing transubstantiation.

Thus, since Saint Justin so plainly acknowledges that bread and wine, consecrated by Christ’s words, are his body and blood, Catholics legitimately infer that their inner nature or substance has ceased to be what it was, having been changed into the Lord’s true body and blood. There are exceedingly numerous examples, both among the ancients and among more recent writers, of people continuing to call the Eucharist “bread,” although they believe and teach others the dogma of transubstantiation—not because it is still bread, but because it retains the form and visible properties of bread, and because it has become the heavenly bread, the bread of eternal life.

To this Basnage says:

> Bodily food cannot truly and properly be the blood and flesh of Christ—as Justin nevertheless asserts—since the difference in substances, whether in number or species, absolutely prevents it.

Basnage is not bringing a dispute against us, but against Justin himself and against Saints Irenaeus, Cyril of Jerusalem, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Alexandria, and others, who most clearly handed down the real presence of the Lord in the Eucharist and asserted, as Justin did, that the body and blood truly enter our bodies by way of food and drink.

Our writers have answered this old objection more than once: those ancient Fathers believed and taught that our body is not increased or restored from the Lord’s body in the manner of earthly food, but that through contact with it our corruptible body becomes incorruptible, so that in its proper time it will attain the blessed resurrection and eternal life, as the Lord said:

> Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day (John 6),

namely, he will raise that person’s body to blessed immortality.

Basnage has also brought Saint Irenaeus into the ranks against Catholics, quoting him as follows:

> How, then, will it be established for them—namely, the Marcionites and Valentinians, who deny that Christ truly had flesh or that it was formed from the same matter from which ours was formed—that the bread over which thanks have been given **is the body of their Lord**, and that the cup is **his blood**, if they do not say that he is the Son of the Maker of the world? (*Irenaeus*, book IV, chapter 34)

Basnage did not touch upon these words, from which it is clear that Saint Irenaeus acknowledged the Eucharist **to be the body** of the Lord, not a figure of it.

That holy bishop adds the following other words, which Basnage did indicate:

[Col. 0979A]

> How, then, do they again say that the flesh enters into corruption and does not receive life, when it is nourished by **the body and blood of the Lord**? Let them therefore either change their opinion or cease offering the things mentioned above. But our opinion agrees with the Eucharist, and the Eucharist in turn confirms our opinion. For we offer to him what belongs to him, proclaiming appropriately the communion and union of flesh and spirit. For just as bread from the earth, receiving God’s invocation, is no longer common bread but Eucharist, consisting of two realities, one earthly and one heavenly, so also our bodies, receiving the Eucharist, are no longer corruptible, possessing the hope of resurrection.

Again Basnage contends that the bread is not destroyed, but merely sanctified. I must once more say that these are mockeries. Basnage insists on this one point: that an earthly reality, namely bread, remains in the sacrament, so that unwary readers, even without his saying so openly, may infer that the bread is not changed into Christ’s body and that the real presence is excluded.

Yet Irenaeus had already stated most explicitly that the bread over which thanks had been given—that is, the sanctified bread—is the Lord’s body, a fact which Basnage pretends not to have seen. Therefore it is certain that the heavenly reality in the Eucharist is nothing other than the Lord’s own body and blood.

What, then, is the earthly reality? The appearances, properties, and external form of the bread and wine. These are not, as Basnage thinks, “bare and empty images of things,” since without deception they affect our senses. But the question of how these remain without their substance must not be asked of us, but of God, whose infinite power and truth are always to be adored. For this reason the Fathers so often declared that philosophical curiosity must not be employed here, but faith.

That this was truly Saint Irenaeus’s meaning is shown at greater length by the distinguished Benedictine Father Massuet (*Preliminary Dissertation to the Most Recent Edition of the Works of Irenaeus*). That illustrious bishop and martyr was refuting the inventions of Marcion and Valentinus, who denied not only that earthly things were created by God the Father, but also that Christ assumed true flesh from the most holy Virgin.

If the Lord’s flesh and presence in the sacrament of the altar were merely imaginary, as the Calvinists have supposed, with what solidity of reasoning, I ask, could Irenaeus have insisted repeatedly on the institution of the Eucharist in order to establish the truth of Christ’s flesh against the Marcionites?

The same opinion is confirmed by other words of Irenaeus:

> When, therefore, the mixed cup—that is, wine mixed with water, a mixture which those among the more recent heretics who have removed it oppose the primitive Church—and the bread, receiving the Word of God, become the Eucharist of the blood and body of Christ (in Greek it is: “the blood and body of Christ”), from which the substance of our flesh is increased and sustained, how do they deny that the flesh is capable of receiving God’s gift, which is eternal life, when it is nourished by **the blood and body of Christ** and is a member of him, etc.? And just as a cutting from the vine, planted in the earth, bears fruit in its season, and as a grain of wheat, etc., receiving the Word of God, **become the Eucharist, which is the body and blood of Christ**, so also our bodies, nourished by it and laid in the earth and dissolved in it, will rise in their own time, when the Word of God grants them resurrection (*Irenaeus*, book V, chapter 2).

Perhaps you will find it difficult to understand how our flesh is nourished by the Lord’s body and blood. Nevertheless, it remains unshaken that the apostolic Fathers taught that his most sacred body and blood truly enter our body through the Eucharist, not merely a figure of them; and that from this not only the soul but also the body receives God’s gift, which is eternal life. This is what we seek, and we see it plainly handed down by these apostolic men.

Another passage of the same Irenaeus may be added, where he discusses the magical tricks of a certain heretic named Marcus:

> For, pretending to consecrate a cup mixed with wine, and extending the words of the invocation at great length, he makes it purple and red, so that it may be thought that the grace which is above all things—namely, the woman whom he himself calls “the inconceivable”—causes her blood to drip through his invocation into that cup (*Irenaeus*, book I, chapter 13).

As the aforementioned Father Massuet observed, it follows from this that in the second century of Christ, when Irenaeus flourished, the conversion of wine into Christ’s true blood was an established belief—we now call it transubstantiation. For why would that heretic have so laboriously pretended that the wine was changed in the chalice, unless it had then been the opinion of all Christians that, once consecration had taken place, the wine did not remain but was converted into true blood?

And yet there are people who dare to set Saint Irenaeus against Catholics—an apostolic man from whom nothing is clearly handed down except what the Catholic Church teaches concerning the sacrament of the altar!

Nor shall I detain the reader long in examining Tertullian’s sufficiently controversial statement, which Basnage adduces as though many Catholics had not already shown that it does nothing to harm their dogma:

> Having taken bread and distributed it to the disciples, he made it his body, saying, “This is my body,” that is, “a figure of my body.” But there would not have been a figure unless there were a true body (*Tertullian*, book IV against Marcion, chapter 40).

Here we have one certain point: namely, that through the Lord’s words the bread becomes his body. The rest is obscure, [Col. 0980D] but Catholics nevertheless explain it.
