Tertullian’s meaning was that the bread had been a figure of Christ’s body in the books of the Old Testament. For in the same place he writes:

> Why, then, does he call bread his body, etc., if he does not understand that this was an ancient figure of Christ’s body, saying through Jeremiah: “Come, let us cast wood into his bread”—that is, the cross into his body.

Tertullian’s meaning, therefore, is this: “Having taken bread, he made it his body,” saying, “This”—that is, the ancient figure of my body—“has become my body.”

Nor can his words be explained otherwise. For the bread had previously been a figure of Christ’s body, as Tertullian himself admits. Therefore Christ, in consecrating the bread, did not make that figure become a figure of his body; rather, he made that bread his body—that is, what in the earlier Testament had been a figure was made by Christ in the New Testament to be his true body.

By these words he indicates that the ancient figure had now been fulfilled, and that beneath the type and qualities of bread the apostles received Christ’s true body.

Here also Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, a fourth-century writer, must be heard. In *Treatise 2 to the Newly Baptized* he says:

> Reasonably, a figure of Christ’s body is received in bread, because we know that from the multitude of the whole human race one body has been made.

Yet in the same sermon 2, as I shall show below in chapter 19, that same holy bishop teaches in the clearest words that this very figure, or bread, is truly made the Lord’s body through the words of consecration.

The same dogma is likewise inferred from other passages of Tertullian, for example when he writes:

> The flesh is washed so that the soul may be cleansed. The flesh is anointed so that the soul may be consecrated. The flesh is nourished by **the body and blood of Christ**, so that the soul may be fattened **from God** (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 8).

The Fathers never said that our flesh is nourished by a figure of Christ’s body, but rather by his very body and blood.

Then, against Marcion, he says:

> By the sacrament of bread and the chalice we have already proved **the reality of the Lord’s body and blood** (*Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 8).

Elsewhere he writes:

> At that time he also first receives a ring, by which, when questioned, he seals the pact of faith—that is, in baptism—and from then on **is nourished by the richness of the Lord’s body** (*On Modesty*, chapter 9).

This refers to the Eucharist, for at that time the Eucharist was given to the newly baptized. He repeats the point when he says:

> So that those who believed in his blood might be washed in water, and those who had washed in water might also **drink the blood** (*On Baptism*, chapter 16).

Then, in writing against those who had fallen into idolatry, he laments that they dared

> to lay hands upon **the body of the Lord**, hands which bring bodies to demons. Idol-makers are admitted into the ecclesiastical order. What a crime! Once the Jews laid hands upon Christ. These men daily assault **his body** (*On Idolatry*, chapter 7).

These things are sufficiently clear on our behalf. But the innovators pass over them and dwell on obscure passages.

Moreover, Basnage praises Saint Cyprian as a witness on his side because, while refuting certain heretics who used water alone for the sacrifice, he said:

> We find that it was wine which he called his blood. The Lord’s chalice is not water alone or wine alone, unless both are mixed together; just as the Lord’s body cannot be flour alone or water, unless both have been united (*Cyprian*, Letter 63).

One must be dreaming who thinks that a Calvinist position can be carved out of these words. Certainly there was previously wine, which Christ, consecrating it, said had become his blood. Nor is the Lord’s body made from flour alone, nor the blood from water alone or wine alone. Yet from these things, mixed together and consecrated, Christ’s body and blood are made.

But we can understand from this how ruinous this is to the Calvinists’ cause, since they beg some support from these words of Cyprian, while the same holy bishop and martyr, in order to overthrow their inventions, adds the following:

[Col. 0982A]

> Nor can it be thought that **his blood**, by which we were redeemed and given life, **is in the chalice**, when wine is absent from the chalice.

Below he says:

> Who is more truly the priest of the Most High God than our Lord Jesus Christ? He offered to God the Father the same sacrifice that Melchizedek had offered, namely bread and wine—**his own body and blood**.

Then he adds:

> The mention of wine [in Isaiah] is made so that **the Lord’s blood** may be understood, **and so that what was afterward manifested in the Lord’s chalice** may be understood.

Again he says:

> Nor could we **drink Christ’s blood** unless Christ had first been trodden and pressed in his passion, and had first drunk the chalice which he would offer—or by which he would give drink—to believers.

He then adds:

> Hence it is evident that **Christ’s blood** is not offered if wine is absent from the chalice.

He also adds the following:

> Just as the mind is relaxed by this ordinary wine, the soul is released, and all sadness is driven away, so, **when the Lord’s blood has been drunk**, and the saving cup or chalice received, the memory of the old man is removed, and the sorrowful heart, previously weighed down by enormous sins, is released in the joy of divine indulgence.

I pass over the remaining passages of that letter, mentioning only one, in which he praises the confessors whose sanctified mouths, **after receiving the body and blood** of the Lord—for at that time the faithful sought strength from the Eucharist in order to resist torments—spurned profane contaminations and the remains of idols, having been sanctified by heavenly foods (*Cyprian, On the Lapsed*).

Against others he inveighs:

> They return from the altars of the devil and approach **the Lord’s holy thing**—for so the Eucharist was called—with filthy and contaminated hands; still belching up the deadly foods of idols, they seize **the Lord’s body**—that is, the Eucharist—when divine Scripture confronts them and cries out, etc. Despising and rejecting all these things, violence is done to **his body and blood**; and now they sin against the Lord with their hands and mouth more than when they denied the Lord, etc.

From these words Basnage could have understood what Saint Cyprian’s view of the Eucharist was. As for his continued quibbling, and perhaps ridicule, concerning certain miracles accomplished through the Eucharist and narrated by that same holy bishop, there is nothing we need refute. Whether one judges such marvels true or false, it is sufficiently clear from them that Saint Cyprian believed and proclaimed the real presence of the Lord in the sacrament of the altar—especially when he describes someone who had sacrificed to idols. After the priest had celebrated the sacrifice, that man

> dared secretly to receive a portion of the Lord’s body,

in order to carry it home, as was then customary.

> But he could not eat or touch **the Lord’s holy thing**—that is, the body. He found that, when he opened his hands, he was carrying ashes. By the evidence of one event it was shown that **the Lord withdraws when he is denied**.

If the Lord withdrew, then he truly existed in the sacrament.

What surpasses every excess, Basnagius also brings forward Saint Cyril of Jerusalem as though he supported him, citing his passage, which begins with these words: “For just as the Eucharistic bread [Col. 0983A] (Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catechesis 3),” etc. We showed above, in chapter 8, that this passage plainly favors the Catholic position. Indeed, anyone who, setting aside the other passages of the same Saint Cyril in which the real presence and transubstantiation in the Eucharist are stated most explicitly, keeps his reader occupied with these words—which do not even help his case, but rather destroy it—must have cast off all shame.

With such trifling weapons Basnagius nevertheless continues the battle, among other things reporting the recovery of Saint Gorgonia’s health through the Eucharist. Her brother, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, relates the story:

“She, when every other aid had failed, at the dead of night falls before the altar in faith, and with a cry invokes Him who is honored upon it [Col. 0983B], etc.; and when she had mixed her tears with whatever portion of the precious BODY or BLOOD her hand had kept hidden—O wondrous deed!—she immediately feels herself freed from her illness” (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 11).

Everyone must infer from this the real presence of the Lord in the Eucharist. For although Nazianzenus calls it an *antitypon*—an “antitype” or representation—Elias of Crete and other Greeks taught that this did not conflict with the truth of the body and blood in the sacrament.

But what does Basnagius say? “Gorgonia’s deed ought rightly to be considered a crime if the Eucharist were Christ’s very body”; yet Gregory “not only does not condemn it, but even praises it.” These words, however, are spoken to mislead the Protestant populace and, if possible, certain unlearned Catholics as well. At that time faith [Col. 0983C] in the reality of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist was entirely certain. Basnagius, as an educated man, knew that laypeople were also permitted to handle the Eucharist, since it was given into the hands of communicants and was sometimes carried home. Where, then, did he invent the crime? Gorgonia did nothing other than either receive Communion or bring the holy body, drenched with tears, into contact with her own body.

On the contrary, from this very event an attentive reader will perceive what faith Nazianzenus and his sister then held concerning the Eucharist. The same holy man says that Gorgonia imitated the Gospel woman who, by touching Christ’s fringe, was freed from her flow of blood, as well as the other woman who once drenched Christ’s feet with her tears. Those women touched the true body of the Lord, whether mediately or immediately [Col. 0983D]. If Gorgonia imitated them, then it must likewise be said that she touched that same most sacred and true body in the sacrament.

Basnagius offers a second example from Saint Augustine’s work against Julian (Book III, chapter 162, formerly 146). A boy had been born with his eyes closed and, at five years of age, still had his eyelids joined together. A physician, however, offered to open them. “His devout mother did not permit this; rather, she accomplished it by applying a poultice made from the Eucharist.”

From this Basnagius concludes that the woman did not believe that the Lord’s body was contained in the Eucharist. We, on the contrary, say that because she believed that He who had given sight to the man born blind was contained there, she used His contact to heal her son. According to Saint Cyril of Jerusalem [Col. 0984A], the faithful received the sacred body in their hands at Communion and “sanctified their eyes by contact with the holy body.” This may have been the metaphorical poultice mentioned by Augustine. Even if the poultice was a real one, however, the woman’s act displays an excess of faith, which the Church nevertheless in no way approved.

If Basnagius reports other excesses of devout people of this kind, none of them harms the truth of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist. On the contrary, it is evident that Christians sometimes fell into such excesses precisely because they believed the Truth itself with unwavering conviction.

Meanwhile, it is not I but Christ who will ask Basnagius and his like at His judgment:

“Why did you fight by such methods against the awesome mystery of the Eucharist instituted by Me? Were you not guilty of monstrous crime when, from [Col. 0984B] a few obscure and doubtful passages of certain Fathers and from several popular incidents, you attempted to extract the inventions of Berengarius and Calvin, while neglecting the innumerable testimonies of My Church, from which it shines more clearly than midday what must be believed concerning the Eucharist?

“You despised sufficiently clear statements about this mystery. The writings of apostolic men who flourished in the first centuries of My Church lay before you. You were content to seize upon certain ambiguous expressions of theirs in support of your opinion and to press those alone upon the people and your unwary readers; the remainder, from which the true position is most plainly deduced, you either did not seek or despised.

“You saw that the Fathers of so many earlier centuries, especially those of the fourth and fifth centuries, agreed in asserting the real presence in the sacrament [Col. 0984C] of the altar; you saw that the liturgies of all the Churches bore witness to the same truth; and you saw that Catholics produced and emphasized the perpetual consensus of the whole Church on this matter down to the times of Berengarius, Zwingli, and Calvin. Was it not your duty carefully to consult these witnesses, sincerely to weigh them, and, submitting your judgment humbly, to embrace them, abandoning the many sophistries by which the sect of innovators has hitherto operated?

“What just excuse such innovators may offer, let them consider for themselves.”

## CHAPTER XVI  
### The true sacrifice confirmed in the sacred Mass from the most ancient liturgies of the Western Churches

After so many centuries, Luther was the first to abolish the sacrifice from the sacred Mass with murderous hatred burning against the Roman Church—and, as he himself confesses, instructed by the devil [Col. 0984D]—and he decreed that the consecration of the chalice should be performed with wine alone, without water. The practice of the primitive Church, the consensus of the Fathers, and especially of Justin, Irenaeus, Cyprian, and others were brought against him. But, as Cardinal Bellarmine reports, he replied in his book *On the Abolition of the Mass*:

“First of all, I declare against those who will cry out that I have taught something contrary to the rite of the Church and contrary to the ordinances of the Fathers: I will listen to none of this.”

He says similar things in his book against the King of England:

“Finally,” he says, “the king brings forward the statements of the Fathers in favor of the sacrificial Mass and laughs at my folly, because I alone wish to be wise above all others. This is what I said: that the Thomistic asses have nothing to produce [Col. 0985A] except a multitude of men and ancient custom.”

Thus he was accustomed to fight with such insults and contempt for everyone else. Then, in his book *On the Private Mass*:

“Here we are not concerned,” he says, “if the papists cry out: ‘The Church, the Church; the Fathers, the Fathers.’ For, as I have said, we care nothing about the sayings or deeds of men in matters of such great importance. We know that the prophets themselves fell, and therefore the apostles also. By the word of Christ we judge the Church, the apostles, and therefore even the angels.”

Finally, in his book *On the Babylonian Captivity*:

“If there is nothing,” he says, “that can be said, it is safer to deny everything than to concede that there is a sacrifice of the Mass.”

I have wished to report these words so that from Luther himself you may understand what his mind was like and how greatly it was inflated with pride. But what above all inspires horror is to hear him writing the following, as Bellarmine [Col. 0985B] reports, in the formula of the Mass for the Church of Wittenberg:

“There follows that entire abomination to which everything that preceded in the Mass was compelled to minister; hence it is also called the Offertory, and from this point nearly everything sounds and smells of offerings.”

And below:

“Therefore, after rejecting all those things that sound of offering, together with the entire canon, let us retain what is pure and holy.”

Such was Luther. Later Calvin and his flock more willingly rushed to abolish the sacrifice; the Anglicans joined them, since they excluded the real presence of Christ from the Eucharist. Calvin went so far that he was not ashamed to call the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass a most pestilential error.

Thus the most shameless men attack and wickedly trample underfoot not only the Catholic Church of our own time but also that of earlier [Col. 0985C] centuries, although it is absolutely certain that the apostolic men themselves and their successors, through five continuous centuries, acknowledged, as we do, the sacrifice of the new covenant in the Mass.

The more moderate followers of Luther and Calvin do not dare to deny such a sacrifice altogether, but they insist that it is not a true and proper sacrifice, since, as they suppose, the primitive Church did not offer the body and blood to God in the sacred mysteries. Catholics, however, teach that this was done in former times and is still done today. Samuel Basnagius, the Calvinist mentioned above, discussed this question in his *Political-Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 33 of the Christian era, chapter 67.

At nearly the same time—that is, at the beginning of the present [Col. 0985D] century—Johann Ernst Grabe, a fierce champion of the Anglican sect, published the works of Saint Irenaeus and adapted the opinions of that most holy man to the taste of his own people with all the strength he could command. Nevertheless, overcome by the excessive light of truth, he openly confessed that the Eucharist is the true sacrifice of the new law (Grabe, notes on Book IV, chapter 32 of Saint Irenaeus).

Indeed, he publicly declared that he wished that, “after many among the Protestants had recognized this error and blemish of Luther and Calvin,” and had perceived that their opinion concerning the sacrifice of the Mass had departed from apostolic teaching, the Mass might also be restored to use. For the most holy liturgical formulas of the unbloody sacrifice—by which the same sacrifice has been offered to God for so many centuries both in the Latin [Col. 0986A] and in the Greek Church—had been banned from Protestant assemblies, to the immense detriment of the honor owed to God.

Catholic readers will certainly be glad to hear Grabe’s words. In his notes on Book IV, chapter 32, of Saint Irenaeus, he writes:

“It is certain that Irenaeus, and all the Fathers whose writings we possess, whether contemporaries of the apostles or immediately succeeding them, regarded the holy Eucharist as the sacrifice of the new law. And it was not the private teaching and practice of one particular Church or doctor, but the public teaching and practice of the universal Church, which they received from the apostles, and the apostles from Christ Himself.”

He then reports the words of Saint Clement of Rome and indicates that other most ancient Fathers likewise bear witness to the same doctrine and truth. Finally, concerning [Col. 0986B] the sacrifice of the Eucharist, he says that there are not lacking “teachers of the Anglican Church, among whom I name one man distinguished both in doctrine and in piety, Joseph Mede, who, in a special treatise on the Christian sacrifice written in English, has admirably proved and explained this matter. It should therefore be carefully read by all students of theology, especially candidates for the sacred priesthood.

“I wholeheartedly subscribe not only to his opinion but also to the wish expressed at the end of chapter 8, and I desire that, after many pious and learned men among the Protestants have rightly recognized this error of Luther and Calvin and the true doctrine of the apostolic Church, they may also restore to use those most holy liturgical formulas by which this sacrifice is offered to God, formulas which they have wrongly proscribed from their assemblies [Col. 0986C], and may duly return this supreme honor to the divine Majesty.”

So writes Grabe. His words, just as they will bring consolation to Roman Catholics, can and ought to cause the consciences of Protestants in the future to reproach them severely. John Francis Buddeus, a public professor of theology at Leipzig, clearly understood how much such a confession and wish, proceeding from a most learned man who was by no means fighting in the Catholic ranks, could harm Luther and the honor and doctrines of the Lutheran communion. He therefore decided to enter the arena against Grabe.

Accordingly [Col. 0986D], as I learned from the *Acta Eruditorum* (*Acta Eruditorum*, Leipzig, 1713), by publishing a dissertation he perhaps achieved this much: he kept his countrymen, especially the mass of his fellow sectarians, within their allegiance. For in desperate causes it is sufficient to enter the arena so as to persuade an ignorant populace that victory at least remained doubtful.

If we believe Basnagius and Buddeus, no mention of sacrifice occurs in the time of Christ and the apostles, and even the word “Mass” was unknown. In Saint Justin, a second-century writer after the birth of Christ who wrote so carefully about the mysteries of Christians and descended to the smallest details, no trace of a sacrifice—and still less of a propitiatory sacrifice—appears; nor do the offerings he mentions contribute anything to this question, since offerings were also made from inanimate things, which nevertheless were not the matter of a true sacrifice. Nor, they say, can an argument be drawn from Justin’s dialogue with the Jew Trypho [Col. 0987A].

They assert the same concerning the third century of the Church. Although the offering for the dead became the principal prelude to the sacrificial Mass, and an excessive veneration of rites, ceremonies, and symbols—departing from apostolic simplicity and purity—was added, nevertheless, they say, no testimony can be produced from the earlier centuries, “down to the beginning of the seventh,” by which it could be proved that ancient Christians acknowledged a “propitiatory sacrifice” in the Mass.

At nearly the same time, Christoph Matthäus Pfaff, a Protestant theologian at Tübingen, also published another dissertation, which I have not seen, in which he discussed the ancient Eucharistic offering and consecration. There he claims to have shown that “in the liturgies celebrated before Gregory there existed various excellent features, especially features that could be urged against the repeated sacrifice of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, drawn from the Greek liturgies and later partly abolished” [Col. 0987B].

For my part, I do not undertake to enter that dense forest of interpretations, sophistries, and omissions which Protestants have hitherto employed to overthrow, if possible, the true and proper sacrifice of the Mass. Let anyone who desires fuller instruction on this matter consult the distinguished Cardinal Bellarmine and our other controversial writers.

Here I propose only two things: first, to show from the most ancient liturgies of all the Churches that the whole Church has always agreed concerning a true, not imaginary, sacrifice of the altar; and then, with as much brevity [Col. 0987C] as I can, to make clear how harmoniously the Fathers who flourished in the first centuries of the Church continue to agree with the sacred liturgies.

At the same time, the reader will be led to understand how great a crime before God is committed by one who peddled to his followers the doctrine that a propitiatory sacrifice did not arise before the seventh century of Christ—namely, that through it God is made favorable toward living and deceased believers and forgives their sins by the power of the sacrifice itself.

Alas!—we may exclaim—what devastation the innovators have inflicted upon the heavenly religion of Christians, when they abolished the real presence of Christ, that ineffable marvel of divine love toward us; and when, moreover, they cast out from the Church the true sacrifice, of which even the Jews were not deprived—that is, they overturned the daily [Col. 0987D] treasury of divine grace through which the most merciful of all Fathers gave us the power to redeem our sins!

But when we show that such doctrines descend from the apostles through the perennial consensus of the Catholic Church—not from some innovation made by the Church, as Protestants seem to contend was done in the fourth century, burdening the great Fathers of that time with disgrace—let those who made the innovation, not the Church, reflect that they will be brought before the tribunal of Christ. He will demand from them an account of the innovation made by them, with such disturbance of the Christian name and unity and with the deception of countless souls.

Come, then, let us see whether Pfaffius rightly brought the most ancient liturgies forward in defense of his opinion [Col. 0988A], and let us begin with the Leonine and Gelasian liturgies, which precede the Gregorian.

In the first, namely the Leonine, the divine sacrifice occurs: “A sacrifice of appeasement and praise.” “We offer sacrifice to You, Lord, for the anniversaries of the holy martyrs.”

Certainly, the word “sacrifice” is used in several senses in sacred writings, with its proper meaning transferred to various acts of piety. When Protestants find this sacrifice of praise in the Roman Mass, they go no further. But there they should also seek and will find a sacrifice of appeasement, which is likewise read in the Gelasian Sacramentary on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, at the feast of Saint Cecilia, as also in the Gregorian and Gothic books:

“This victim, Lord, of appeasement and praise.”

Likewise [Col. 0988B], in the Leonine they will find sacrifice being immolated in the Mass. Even pagan writers used the word “immolation” to designate a true sacrifice, as is demonstrated by their words, which it would be superfluous to quote. For *immolare* presupposes a living victim and sacrificial offering.

Again, the following preface occurs in the Leonine:

“It is truly fitting. For who could, or would dare, cease from praising You, when he considers the effects of Your wondrous dispensation: that from the substance of a sinful nature an immaculate victim should be born, by whose IMMOLATION You may be appeased for the guilt of that same nature?”

Here you have a victim immolated in an unbloody sacrifice, namely Christ, and indeed for the purpose of appeasing God toward us sinners. These words are not to be referred to the sacrifice of the Cross but, according to the usage of the liturgy, to the Sacrifice of the Mass.

Above, from the same [Col. 0988C] Leonine and Gelasian books and from the Frankish Missal, we produced the spiritual VICTIM which, through a wondrous and ineffable mystery, is always both IMMOLATED and always OFFERED.

In June, in the Leonine, at the feast of Saints John and Paul:

“We place VICTIMS OF APPEASEMENT upon Your altars, Lord.”

We find the same victims of appeasement in the Gelasian and Gregorian books. In July, the Leonine presents to us a “UNIQUE SACRIFICE” which “is both rendered and owed always to Your Majesty.” In it, and likewise in the Gregorian:

“We bring You, Lord, VICTIMS TO BE IMMOLATED,” etc.

“We humbly IMMOLATE VICTIMS to You, Lord”—that is, the living body and blood of the Lord existing under the appearances.

You may see this confirmed below, at the Nativity of the Lord, in these words:

“Look with favor, Lord, upon the offering of Your people, in which no foreign fire is brought upon Your altars, nor is the blood [Col. 0988D] of irrational animals poured out; but, through the working power of the Holy Spirit, our SACRIFICE is now the BODY AND BLOOD OF THE PRIEST HIMSELF, Christ our Lord.”

Behold transubstantiation and the true sacrifice.

In the same place, at the Nativity of the Lord:

“It is truly fitting, as we continually IMMOLATE THE VICTIM of Your praise, whose figure the righteous Abel established, which the legal lamb also displayed, which Abraham celebrated, which the priest Melchizedek presented; but which Christ, the true Lamb and eternal High Priest, born today, fulfilled.”

In the same place, at the Nativity of the Lord:

“With so many senses we celebrate today’s SACRIFICE, whose beginnings have been born for us as the beginnings of the sacrifice itself.”

In the same place, and in the Gelasian book for the fast of the tenth month:

“Receive, Lord, the SACRIFICE by whose IMMOLATION You have graciously willed to be appeased.”

In the Leonine, at Mass 3 in September [Col. 0989A]:

“Grant that THIS YOUR SACRAMENT may not be guilt leading us to punishment, but may become a saving intercession leading to forgiveness; may it be the abolition of sins,” etc.

The Roman Church still uses a similar prayer during Lent.

I now proceed to the Gelasian Sacramentary. At the Vigil of the Theophany it reads:

“Grant, we beseech You, Lord, that we may OFFER HIM in the SACRIFICES that are present and RECEIVE HIM whom the devout gifts of the coming solemnity proclaim beforehand.”

On the Monday after the Second Sunday of Lent, and in the Gregorian book on the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost:

“Grant us, we beseech You, Lord, to celebrate these mysteries frequently, because whenever the celebration of THIS VICTIM is commemorated, the work of our REDEMPTION [Col. 0989B] is carried out.”

On the Wednesday after Easter:

“Receive, we beseech You, Lord, the VICTIMS OF HUMAN REDEMPTION,” etc.

And in the preface:

“Surrounding Your altars with the powers, and rejoicing in the recognition of THE IMMACULATE LAMB HIMSELF, who offered Himself to be immolated for us, so that by His BODY AND BLOOD, by which we have been redeemed from sins, we may be nourished by HEAVENLY SACRIFICES unto eternal life.”

On the Third Sunday after the Octave of Easter:

“O God, who through the venerable exchange of THIS SACRIFICE have made us participants in the one supreme Divinity,” etc.

There, and in the Gregorian book at the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian:

“In the precious death of Your righteous ones, Lord, WE OFFER THIS SACRIFICE, from which every martyrdom took its beginning.”

On the Nones of October, at the feast of Saints Marcellus and Apuleius:

“May THIS VICTIM [Col. 0989C] TO BE IMMOLATED render Your Majesty appeased toward us, Lord,” etc.

In the Mass of the Lord’s Day:

“THE OFFERING TO BE IMMOLATED in Your sight, Lord,” etc.

“Being appeased by the SACRIFICES OFFERED, Lord,” etc.

There, as also in the Gregorian book:

“Being appeased, receive, Lord, the VICTIMS by which You willed to be appeased and to restore salvation to us by Your powerful mercy.”

In the same place:

“May the SAVING VICTIM, Lord, we beseech You, protect us, and may that WHICH IS IMMOLATED to the honor of Your name benefit us unto forgiveness.”

The Gregorian Sacramentary offers us parallel passages. On the Third Sunday of Lent it has:

“May THIS VICTIM, Lord, we beseech You, cleanse our offenses, and may THE SACRIFICE TO BE CELEBRATED sanctify the bodies and minds of Your subjects.”

On the Wednesday after Easter:

“We IMMOLATE SACRIFICES, Lord, amid the paschal joys, by which the Church is wonderfully both fed and nourished.”

On the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost [Col. 0989D]:

“O God, who established the distinction between the legal victims by the perfection of ONE SACRIFICE, receive the SACRIFICE from servants devoted to You,” etc.

On the Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost:

“May the SACRIFICES DEDICATED TO YOU, Lord, be returned to You, which You granted us to bring to the honor of Your name, so that You might make them remedies for us.”

On the Thirteenth Sunday:

“Look with favor, Lord, we beseech You, upon the VICTIMS which we present at the sacred altars, so that by granting us forgiveness they may give honor to Your name.”

In the special Mass for a priest:

“May the OFFERING OF THE PRESENT SACRIFICE, I beseech You, Lord, cleanse my sins, by which You willed the sins of the whole world to be forgiven.”

The liturgies have often inculcated what the holy Fathers also taught concerning a propitiatory sacrifice, so that it is astonishing that anyone should have been found among Protestants who was not afraid to write that, throughout the first six [Col. 0990A] centuries of the Church, no one believed that through the sacrifice of the altar God was made favorable to living and deceased believers.

The Gothic Sacramentary, edited by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius, presents the same doctrine concerning the unbloody sacrifice. There is the following preface in the tradition of the Creed:

“Come, then, we beseech You, O Christ, and stand among us; and You who then restored us through the Cross, restore us again, now fallen, THROUGH THIS IMMACULATE BREAD AND BLOOD, so that, sensing You coming into our hearts, we may go out to meet You,” etc.

At the Paschal Vigil:

“So that, as we receive THIS HOLOCAUST, we may have within us the peace for which we hope.”

And in the preface:

“It is fitting and just for us to give You praise and to IMMOLATE VICTIMS,” etc.

“We ask You to bless THIS SACRIFICE [Col. 0990B] with Your blessing and to drench it with the dew of Your Holy Spirit, so that it may be a lawful EUCHARIST for all.”

On Easter Day:

“Serving You with devoted mind, we ask through THE IMMOLATION OF THIS SACRIFICE,” etc.

On the Wednesday after Easter:

“For this is the LAMB OF GOD, Your only-begotten Son, who takes away the sin of the world; who, by offering Himself for us, does not cease to defend us before You through perpetual advocacy; who, though IMMOLATED, never dies, but, though slain, lives forever,” etc.

In the Sunday Mass:

“Let us pray that He may kindly accept these things that have been offered; may He never permit any of those for whom HOLOCAUSTS are broken to be excluded from His gift.”

Likewise:

“Great is this gift of Your mercy, by which You taught us to celebrate THE SACRIFICES OF OUR REDEMPTION, just as our Lord Jesus Christ offered Himself on earth.”

And in the preface:

“It is fitting and just, infinite God [Col. 0990C] and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, establishing the form of THE ETERNAL SACRIFICE, FIRST OFFERED HIMSELF TO YOU and FIRST TAUGHT THAT IT SHOULD BE OFFERED.”

In the most ancient Frankish Missal, also published by the aforementioned Cardinal Thomasius, we read:

“O God, after the variety of all sacrifices has come to an end, to whom we now offer A UNIQUE VICTIM.”

In the most ancient Gallican Missal, likewise found in Thomasius, the following is read on Holy Thursday:

“Therefore, this offering which we present to You on the day of the fast of the Lord’s Supper, on which our Lord Jesus Christ, Your Son, INSTITUTED THE RITE OF SACRIFICING IN THE NEW TESTAMENT, when He TRANSFORMED THE BREAD AND WINE which the priest Melchizedek had offered as a prefiguration of the future mystery INTO THE SACRAMENT OF HIS BODY AND BLOOD.”

As we saw above, the Ambrosian liturgy uses this same prayer.

Finally [Col. 0990D], in the Gregorian, Gothic, and Mozarabic books, on the sacred day of the Epiphany, this prayer occurs:

“Look favorably, Lord, we beseech You, upon the gifts of Your Church, by which now not gold, frankincense, and myrrh are brought forth, but that which is DECLARED BY THOSE GIFTS IS IMMOLATED AND RECEIVED.”

What was believed about this matter in Spain before the year 595 of the Christian era will be taught us by Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, who says:

“Certainly, animal sacrifices were offered for this reason: because they prefigured THE TRUE SACRIFICE, that is, the body and blood of Christ. The Truth came, and the shadow departed. THE TRUE SACRIFICE came, and the sacrifice of animals ceased” (Saint Leander of Seville, chapter 7 of *Rule on the Institution of Virgins*).

Thus far we have the ancient and clear testimonies of the Roman Church and of the other Western Churches concerning an unbloody and propitiatory sacrifice [Col. 0991A]. But before considering what benefit results from this survey, it is useful also to travel to the East and inquire what opinion so many Churches in those regions, even Churches divided from one another, hold concerning the same sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### The consensus of the Eastern Churches concerning the true and proper sacrifice in the Mass

The Roman Church has observed a twofold offering in the sacred mysteries: one, of the bread and wine offered before they were consecrated; and the other, after those gifts themselves had been changed into the body and blood of the Lord.

The Greeks and others among the Eastern peoples [Col. 0991B] appear to have used a threefold offering. The first occurs when the priest offers to God the bread and wine formerly offered by the people. He performs the second after the words of the Lord’s consecration. The third occurs after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, at which time the Greeks believe that the consecration is complete and perfect.

From what we have cited above it is certain—indeed absolutely certain—that, at least in this third offering, they firmly believe that they are not offering material bread and wine to God the Father, as the Calvinist sect supposes, but the very true, though invisible, body and blood existing under visible appearances: that victim and sacrificial offering which hung upon the Cross, though mystically and without blood slaughtered in the sacrament.

They called the sacrifice, or victim [Col. 0991C], *thysia* (Θυσία), and indeed *anaimaktos* (ἀναίμακτον), that is, “unbloody,” in order to show that the sacrifice of the altar is the same as the sacrifice of the Cross. The only difference was the visible blood with which the Cross was stained and which does not at all appear to the eyes of those present at the mystical immolation of the altar.

In the customary liturgy of Chrysostom, as found in Goar—a liturgy used extensively in the sacred worship of the Greeks, Russians, and other peoples—the priest says:

“Make us worthy to OFFER You prayers and supplications, AND UNBLOODY SACRIFICES,” that is, unbloody offerings and victims.

Addressing and entreating Christ the Lord below, he says:

“Make me worthy, clothed with the power of Your Holy Spirit and endowed with the grace of the priesthood, to stand before this Your holy table and to consecrate Your holy and immaculate body and precious blood. For You are [Col. 0991D] HE WHO OFFERS (*offers*) AND IS OFFERED (*offerris*, or, if preferred, *offereris*, “is offered”), WHO RECEIVES AND IS DISTRIBUTED, O Christ our God.””

From these words you understand what is truly offered in the sacrifice.

After the words of the Lord’s consecration, the priest says secretly:

“We offer You this rational, or spiritual, worship”—*latreia* (λατρεία), a name by which the Eucharist was also designated—and this worship is unbloody.

Again, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, in which He is asked to change the bread and wine so that they may become for those who receive them the means of forgiveness of sins—at which point there can be no doubt that the Greeks believe the body and blood of the Lord to be really present in the sacrament—the priest again says:

“We offer You this rational worship for those who have fallen asleep in Christ.”

Parallel passages [Col. 0992A] occur in the liturgy of Saint Basil, which is likewise celebrated among the Greeks. There, on the Saturday before Easter, after the sacred gifts have been consecrated, the priest says:

“The King of those who reign and the Lord of those who rule goes forth to be slaughtered and given as food to the faithful. Choirs of angels go before Him,” etc.

In the *Apostolic Constitutions*, whose author certainly appears to belong to the earliest centuries of the Church, a sacred liturgy is reported (Book VIII, chapter 12) in which the offering is mentioned both after the consecratory words of the Lord and again after the invocation of the Holy Spirit.

The same author, to show that the institutions of the ancient law were perfected by Christ, says:

“In place of the bloody sacrifice He instituted a RATIONAL, UNBLOODY, AND MYSTICAL sacrifice, celebrated in remembrance of His death through its symbols: THE SACRIFICE OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD” (Book VI, chapter 23).

The sacrifices [Col. 0992B] of the Jews were true and proper sacrifices, although they were only shadows of the sacrifice of the new law, in which the reality is present; nevertheless Protestants dare to call our sacrifice imaginary and improper.

But let us now turn to the remaining liturgies of the East, used by the Nestorians and the Syrian Eutychians—sects separated from the unity of the Catholic Church for thirteen hundred years. As we mentioned above, Renaudot published them in print.

In the Syriac, or Coptic, liturgy of Saint Basil, the priest says in the prayer after the reading of the Gospel:

“While we offer You THIS AWESOME AND UNBLOODY SACRIFICE.”

In other liturgies and among the Fathers as well, we find this sacrifice called “awesome.” This single word indicates the surpassing majesty of the Christian sacrifice and how far it surpasses the Jewish sacrifices.

In the prayer at the kiss of peace, the priest’s words are:

“These things You have graciously bestowed upon us sinners, so that we might administer them and be sanctified through them, when You presented to us the dispensation of Your Son and [Col. 0992C] handed down THE SACRED RITE OF THIS UNBLOODY SACRIFICE. For it is not the blood of the law or bodily righteousness, but A SPIRITUAL LAMB, and a rational and incorporeal sword, in THIS SACRIFICE which we offer to You.”

Here again is shown the true and ineffable offering in the sacrifice of the new covenant.

In the Syriac liturgy attributed to a certain Gregory, the priest says: “I OFFER YOU THIS SACRIFICE, RATIONAL AND BLOODLESS,” for the remission of my sins, the forgiveness of the offenses of your people, and the rest and refreshment of our fathers who have fallen asleep. [Col. 0992D] You may see this marvelous effect of the bloodless sacrifice proclaimed in other liturgies and among the holy Fathers; and yet there are those who dare to deny that this heavenly sacrifice is propitiatory.

Now consider what is contained in the Greek Alexandrian liturgy bearing the name of Saint Basil. There too it is repeated: “WE OFFER YOU THIS TREMENDOUS AND BLOODLESS SACRIFICE.” And below, the words we have recently seen: “You have given us THE RITE OF THIS SACRIFICE, in which there is not legal blood, nor the justification of flesh, but A SPIRITUAL LAMB,” and so forth. Further below, after Communion, the priest says: “Having been deemed worthy to minister at your holy altar, we have offered to you the spotless BODY and precious BLOOD of our great God and Savior JESUS CHRIST,” and so forth.

In the common liturgy of the Jacobite [Col. 0993A] Syrians, the priest prays as follows: “The one whom Moses saw in the bush and Ezekiel upon the chariot, HE IS PLACED UPON THE ALTAR, AND THE PEOPLES RECEIVE HIM, and live.” “O God, who through your mercy accepted the sacrifice of the ancient righteous, ACCEPT through your mercy OUR SACRIFICE.” Further on he says: “O God, YOU BECAME A SACRIFICE, AND A SACRIFICE IS OFFERED TO YOU. Accept this sacrifice for the soul of N.,” and so forth.

While washing his hands, he prays in these words: “That I may handle, without stain, your adorable and divine mysteries, and with a pure conscience OFFER YOU A LIVING SACRIFICE, pleasing to your Divinity, and MAY IT BE LIKE YOUR GLORIOUS SACRIFICE, Lord and our God.”

After the prayer of the fraction, the priest pronounces these words, especially worthy of consideration: “Thus truly did God the Word suffer in the flesh, and was sacrificed [Col. 0993B] and broken in the crucifixion,” and so forth. “Thus we believe and confess; and thus we proclaim: THAT THIS IS THE BODY OF THIS BLOOD, AND THAT THIS IS THE BLOOD OF THIS BODY.” Then he places in the chalice the pearl, or particle, which he has broken.

Another prayer of Saint James follows: “Father of truth: BEHOLD YOUR SON, AN OFFERING PLEASING TO YOU: receive HIM WHO DIED FOR ME, and through him BE PROPITIOUS.” “Accept THIS SACRIFICE from my hands, that you may be reconciled to me,” and so forth.

Behold the faith and doctrine of that people, which for so many centuries has had no communion with the Roman Church. Here there is no place for the imaginings, arbitrary supplements to words and meaning, by which the innovators of our time so often attempt to obscure the open, simple, neither figurative nor metaphorical meaning of the expressions in which liturgical writers and the holy Fathers have described for us the ineffable ordinance of the Eucharist and of the bloodless sacrifice. [Col. 0993C]

Further it is added: “Your pure and holy mouth, Lord, pronounced and said: Whoever eats,” and so forth. “Therefore, Lord, may it not be for judgment to us, who EAT YOUR HOLY BODY AND DRINK YOUR PROPITIATORY BLOOD,” and so forth.

Let us now examine what is contained in the liturgy attributed by the Copts to Saint James the Apostle, the brother of the Lord, and used at Jerusalem. There, before the kiss of peace, it is said: “Let us stand decorously, and pray, give thanks, and praise THE LIVING LAMB OF GOD, WHO IS OFFERED UPON THE ALTAR,” and so forth.

After the words of consecration the priest says: “WE OFFER YOU THIS TREMENDOUS AND BLOODLESS SACRIFICE, that you may wipe away our sins.” Again, after the invocation of the Holy [Col. 0993D] Spirit, he repeats the same offering, saying: “Therefore we offer you, Lord, this tremendous and bloodless sacrifice for your holy places,” and so forth. These words sufficiently reveal that the transformation of the gifts had already taken place through the very words of consecration, and that the Holy Spirit is invoked afterward so that he may perfect what has been accomplished, for the remission of sins and eternal life to those who receive the Lord’s body and blood.

This agrees with the Greek Mass of Chrysostom, in which, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, God is asked that the sacrifice may become, for those who receive it, a means of sobriety of soul, remission of sins, and so forth.

Again, in the Coptic liturgy, at the fraction, the priest says: “We break this Eucharist, the heavenly Bread, THE BODY OF THE WORD OF THE LIVING GOD,” and so forth. The people respond: [Col. 0994A] “Amen.” Then the deacon says in a loud voice: “Bless, Lord.” Again and again, he speaks of “THIS HOLY OFFERING AND PROPITIATORY SACRIFICE, which HAS BEEN OFFERED TO GOD THE FATHER, sanctified, completed, and perfected through the descent of the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

Before Communion the deacon says: “The powers of heaven stand with us in the midst of the sanctuary, and minister to THE BODY OF THE SON OF GOD, WHO HAS BEEN SACRIFICED BEFORE US.” Let the innovators twist this as they may, if they can.

In the Coptic liturgy attributed to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit these words occur: “Through THIS SACRIFICE, which is OFFERED TO YOU, Lord, by our sinful hands,” and so forth.

Likewise, in the liturgy called that of the Twelve Apostles, after the invocation we read: “WE OFFER you, almighty Lord, [Col. 0994B] THIS DIVINE SACRIFICE,” and so forth.

In the liturgy of Saint Baradatus the priest says: “WE OFFER HIM” — your Son — “to you as our intercessor, so that in him and through him we may be delivered from condemnation at the coming judgment,” and so forth.

And in the liturgy of John Psasorensis, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, the priest uses this prayer: “Your beloved Son,” and so forth. “HIMSELF WE OFFER TO YOU AS A SACRIFICE AND OFFERING, spotless and pure; and we make him himself our intercessor with you.” Further below he adds: “Since we have been deemed worthy of all these things and others of the same kind, and have in a certain manner made a well-trodden path for ourselves to heaven, and SEE THE LAMB SLAIN UPON THE ALTAR,” and so forth, “we beseech you, lover of mankind, Lord, TO BE PROPITIOUS toward our sins,” and so forth.

Similar statements are found in many other liturgies published by Renaudot, as also in [Col. 0994C] the liturgy of the Abyssinians. Father Le Brun made public the liturgy used by the Armenians, and in it, before the consecration, we read: “You have given us your only-begotten Son, debtor and debt, offering and anointed one, lamb and heavenly bread, high priest and SACRIFICE, BECAUSE HE IS ALWAYS DISTRIBUTED among us without being consumed,” and so forth.

After the consecration the choir sings these words: “SON OF GOD, who was sacrificed to the Father for reconciliation, you ARE DISTRIBUTED AMONG US AS THE BREAD OF LIFE,” and so forth. Further below it reads: “BE PROPITIOUS, Lord, to the souls of the departed, for whom WE OFFER THIS HOLY SACRIFICE.”

There too are many testimonies to the real presence and transubstantiation in the sacrament, and to the true and ineffable sacrifice of the altar, at once propitiatory and impetratory.

[Col. 0994D] When Protestants honestly consider such a rich harvest of testimonies and such agreement throughout the Christian world—that is, among all the Churches spread across the world, some of which have broken communion with the Roman Catholic Church for so many centuries—they will recognize that they have been excessively deceived by Luther’s and Calvin’s impious rashness. Those men did not hesitate to call the Roman Mass an abomination and a most pestilential error, although it is nothing other than the same rite observed throughout the entire world by Christians from the beginning of the Church.

Nor will they be able to deny that the sacrifice of the new law is a true and proper sacrifice, and incomparably more perfect than all the Jewish sacrifices. For whatever they say about the qualities and rites of the ancient sacrifices, offerings, and victims is mere quibbling once they acknowledge—and from all that has been brought forward thus far they are compelled to acknowledge—that Christ the Lord really exists in the sacrament after the consecration, and that not merely bread and wine are offered in the Eucharistic sacrifice.

He is the offering; he is the living victim placed upon the altar, mystically slain and offered to his heavenly Father for us, for the remission of our sins. He is also, in this most sacred mystery, the priest and high priest who offers and is offered, presenting himself to the Father as he hung upon the cross for us, so that he might apply to us the merit of his precious blood, which he poured out for sinners in his Passion.

Nor is this sacrifice something different from the sacrifice of the cross. Indeed, it is that very sacrifice, repeated by us at the command of Christ [Col. 0995B] in remembrance of him and so that we may proclaim his death. Thus, whenever the Fathers, in united testimony, called the Mass a sacrifice, and specifically a bloodless sacrifice, they sufficiently indicated that it is one with the true sacrifice of the cross, although the latter was accomplished with visible blood, whereas this is performed without visible blood.

For the true blood of Christ is not absent from our sacrifice; it is present there mystically—that is, secretly and inaccessible to our eyes. Finally, all quibbling disappears whenever the wondrous majesty and excellence of the Eucharistic sacrifice are considered and compared with the victims of the Jewish people, which become utterly insignificant by comparison.

Among the Jews, calves and lambs—earthly animals—were sacrificed to God. Here there is the mystical Lamb whom the paschal lamb of the Old Testament prefigured; here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world: here is the very Son of the Father, God and man, mystically sacrificed for us.

From every age the faithful of Christ have believed and professed that the efficacy of our sacrifice surpasses all the sacrifices of the Jews. Through it they expect not only the remission of sins; it is offered not only for the living but also for those who have died in the peace of Christ and of the Church, as all the liturgies testify. Indeed, through this heavenly Mystery every spiritual grace, together with many public and private benefits in temporal matters, can be obtained in times of need.

Do you dare call this an improper and unreal sacrifice, endowed with such excellence and such power? For this reason the Council of Trent rightly decreed [Col. 0995D] that not only “the saving power of that sacrifice is applied for the remission of the sins we commit daily,” but also that “by this offering the Lord, being appeased, grants the grace and gift of repentance and forgives even grave crimes and sins.” (Council of Trent, Session 22, chapters 1–2.)

As we read in the Life of Pope Gregory the Great, when he distributed the Eucharist to the faithful he said: “May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit you for the remission of all sins and for eternal life.” You find similar words in the Eastern liturgies.

But whenever we set before Protestants the agreement of the liturgies of the entire Christian world, they turn to suspicions, imagining that additions were gradually made to the liturgies, [Col. 0996A] and that from them it cannot be established what the ancient and primitive Church believed about the sacrifice of the Mass.

You will immediately recognize how entirely empty this escape is when you observe that whatever additions occur in the liturgies, as we have already said above, consist solely in prayers and supplications, which vary according to the diversity of the Churches. Since, however, the same faith and doctrine concerning the real presence and the Eucharistic sacrifice, both propitiatory and impetratory, is most consistently found in the liturgies of so many Churches—although often expressed in different words—it necessarily follows that this was not an addition, but rather a dogma diffused among all peoples who embraced the faith of Christ from the very birth of the Church, transmitted to later generations, and proclaimed without controversy.

For it is impossible—indeed, it cannot even be imagined—that if one of the Churches had fabricated a new dogma about the Eucharist, it could have advanced with such ease that it would enter all the Churches of the Christian world without anyone objecting and be accepted by all without difficulty. The sacred pastors rejected every novelty in doctrine, especially the Roman Church, in which the celebrated maxim prevailed: “Nothing is to be changed. What has been handed down must be preserved.”

But, to close every avenue here to Protestant suspicions, it remains to be shown that no other doctrine concerning the sacrament and sacrifice of the altar had a place in the liturgies of the fourth and fifth centuries than that which, in subsequent centuries, was handed down and observed by the Fathers of both the West and the East. [Col. 0996C]

## CHAPTER XVIII

The dogma concerning the true Christian sacrifice, unequivocally set forth and preserved in the liturgies of the Church’s earlier centuries, and confirmed by the holy Fathers.

Having considered what has been brought forward by the most learned Catholic writers—and what I too indicated in chapter 1—it is clear that, even in the earliest centuries of the Christian people, every Church used some liturgy for celebrating the Eucharist, as Christ the Lord had commanded it to be done.

I do not think that any Protestant will dare deny this, after even the Englishman Joseph Bingham, himself one of their number, confirmed the same point at length in his books. Moreover, we must hold that the Fathers of the fourth and fifth centuries understood the Eucharistic sacrifice in the same way as it was transmitted in the liturgies, and especially in the canon. Since this part of the Mass is always found to have remained stable in all the Churches, it is rightly believed to have come down from the institution of the apostles, as Pope Vigilius testified in his Letter to Eutherius, or Profuturus.

Let us therefore ask the Fathers of those times whether the Catholic belief concerning the true sacrifice of the altar, or the inventions of the Protestants, prevailed then in the Church.

Let us hear Saint Ambrose writing:

“We have seen the chief priest coming to us; we have both seen and heard him offering his blood for us. We follow the priests as best we can, so that we may offer a sacrifice for the people—weak indeed in merit, yet honored by the sacrifice. For although Christ is not now seen to offer, nevertheless HE IS OFFERED ON EARTH WHEN THE BODY OF CHRIST IS OFFERED. Indeed, HE IS SHOWN TO OFFER IN US, whose word sanctifies the sacrifice that is offered.” (Ambrose, Commentary on Psalm 38, no. 25.)

These final words indicate that the transformation of the gifts in the sacrifice takes place through the words of the Lord. In the liturgies we find that Christ is sacrificed whenever the tremendous sacrifice is celebrated.

Consider also what the same most celebrated holy Father teaches elsewhere:

“Would that, while we too burn incense at the altars and bring forward the sacrifice, an angel might stand beside us, indeed, might make himself visible to us, as he appeared to Zechariah when he was sacrificing. For do not doubt that an angel is present when Christ is present, WHEN CHRIST IS SACRIFICED.” (The same author, Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, book 1, no. 28.)

Here you have evidence that incense was used in the celebration of the mysteries already in the fourth century of Christ, and that Christ himself was sacrificed as a victim in the bloodless sacrifice. All the liturgies testify that remission of sins follows from the offering and reception of this heavenly victim.

Saint Ambrose proclaims the same thing when he says that the Eucharist must be received by those who are fasting. When the time arrives “for the celebration of the offering,” he says, “then stand ready, so that you may receive protection for yourself; so that you may EAT THE BODY OF THE LORD JESUS, IN WHICH THERE IS REMISSION OF SINS, the petition for divine reconciliation and eternal protection.” (The same author, Exposition of Psalm 118, no. 48.)

I pass over other passages of this holy bishop. In the same century, Saint Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, recalls this same teaching in the East, saying:

“After the spiritual sacrifice, the bloodless worship, we entreat God over that VICTIM OF PROPITIATION (ἐπὶ τῆς θυσίας ἐκείνης τοῦ ἱλασμοῦ, ‘over that sacrifice of propitiation’) for the common peace of the Church.” (Cyril of Jerusalem, Oration 23, or Mystagogical Catechesis 5, no. 8.)

He also affirms that we pray to God for the departed, “believing this to be the greatest assistance for those souls for whom the prayer is offered, while THE HOLY AND EXCEEDINGLY TREMENDOUS VICTIM lies before us.” And further: “We offer Christ who was slain for our sins.”

Do not the sacred liturgies repeat the same thing everywhere?

Saint Augustine likewise agrees when he writes:

“Was Christ not once sacrificed in himself, and yet IN THE SACRAMENT he is sacrificed for the people not only throughout all the solemnities of Easter, but EVERY DAY? Nor does the person who, when questioned, answers ‘he sacrifices’ speak falsely.” (Augustine, Letter 98, formerly 23, to Boniface.)

For this reason the same holy teacher calls the sacrifice of the new law “most true and unique.” (Book on the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 11.)

Let Optatus of Milevis also be heard. Around the year 365 of Christ he wrote:

“For what is so sacrilegious as to break, scrape away, or remove the altars of God, upon which you too once offered, and upon which the vows of the people and the members of Christ have been carried? From them many received the pledge of eternal salvation—that is, the Lord’s body—as well as the safeguard of faith and the hope of resurrection. FOR WHAT IS AN ALTAR, IF NOT THE SEAT OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST?” (Optatus of Milevis, Book 1 against the Donatists.)

We shall explain below what the name “altar” signifies.

[Col. 0998A] No one expressed more clearly than Saint John Chrysostom the nature of the sacrifice of the new law, in these famous words:

“We do indeed offer, but we recall his death to mind; and THE VICTIM IS ONE, not many. How is it one and not many? Because it was offered once; it was brought into the holy of holies. This is a figure of that, and this is that. For we always offer THE SAME ONE—not now one, and now another, but always the same one. Therefore THERE IS ONE SACRIFICE, for the same reason. Since Christ is offered in many places, are there many Christs? By no means, but ONE CHRIST EVERYWHERE, who is complete both here and there, ONE BODY.

How, then, is the one body offered in many places one and not many bodies? In the same way there is also one sacrifice. Our high priest is the one who offered that victim which cleanses us; we now offer THAT ONE, WHICH WAS THEN OFFERED, which cannot be consumed. This is done in remembrance of what was done then. For he says: ‘Do this in remembrance of me.’ We do not make another victim, as the high priest does, but we always make THE SAME ONE; or rather, we make a remembrance of the victim, that is, of the sacrifice.” (Chrysostom, Homily 17 on Hebrews 9.)

For this reason Chrysostom likewise judged the Christian priesthood “much better and more sublime” than the Jewish priesthood. (Oration 5 against the Jews.)

Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, and others may also be called as witnesses in this matter. But there is no need for more, if we are to grasp that the very doctrine concerning the Eucharistic sacrifice was the doctrine now read in the ancient liturgies and expounded to the people by the Fathers of the fourth and fifth centuries, and that it is wrong to fabricate a novelty in this matter within the liturgies themselves. [Col. 0998C]

Nevertheless, I do not think that the innovators will even then consider themselves defeated. They will construct a new but imaginary rampart behind which to retreat.

Luther, with impious rashness, professed that on this subject he would not listen to the holy Fathers, and demanded that the entire Christian world bow its forehead to his authority. He wished faith and Eucharistic practice to be sought solely from the books of the New Testament. Yet, he claimed, there is no mention there of a sacrifice, but only of a supper.

His disciple Buddeus, Samuel Basnage, Pfaffius, and others among the Protestants maintain that the doctrine of our sacrifice was unknown to the Fathers of the primitive Church; that later Fathers departed from the simplicity and purity [Col. 0998D] of the apostolic dogmas and imposed this new sacrifice upon us; and that it does not emerge from Saint Justin or the writers of earlier times.

Thus they sufficiently reveal what factional love can accomplish in men, when it does not hesitate to accuse of treachery and imposture so many pastors and writers of the Churches, distinguished no less by holiness of life than by doctrine, who governed and enlightened the Church of God in the fourth and fifth centuries and repeatedly declared that nothing other than what Christ and his apostles had handed down was to be believed and maintained.

And by what laws of logic, I ask, do the innovators dare to say these things? By illegitimate and detestable ones.

Even if we were to suppose that the apostles and Christian writers of the third century had said no word about the Eucharistic sacrifice, tell me, did any of them deny such a sacrifice? Was a law imposed upon them that whenever they mentioned the Eucharist they must also mention the sacrifice?

Moreover, the Apostle and Saint Irenaeus acknowledged that certain doctrines not written down had passed to later generations through tradition, and Protestants themselves embrace quite a few of these. Since the doctrine of the sacrifice is found diffused throughout the provinces of the Christian world already in the fourth century itself, it certainly follows that it was not then invented or fabricated, and that the holy men proclaimed it as they found it, namely, as proceeding from the preaching of the apostles.

But what removes every excuse from the Protestants in this matter is that Catholics have long since made it clear that the same doctrine concerning the ineffable sacrifice is not absent even from the divine books or from the writings of the primitive Church—the doctrine which the Fathers of the fourth century taught with one voice. [Col. 0999B]

Allow me to repeat this, so that our dissenting brothers may more clearly understand what moved the Briton Grabe to desire the restoration of the Mass among his own people, and with what rashness Luther and Calvin not only abolished the Mass but also shamelessly branded it with the mark of abomination and intolerable error.

As is clear from Psalm 109 and from the Apostle’s Letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews 7), Christ was High Priest and priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Whoever considers this truth and dogma sincerely, without human passions, cannot fail to understand [Col. 0999C] what we are seeking.

Among the Jews and among the gentiles alike, a priest or high priest is nothing other than a sacrificer. If you deny someone the right to sacrifice, you must also remove from him the name “priest.” Christ the Lord was certainly priest and victim upon the cross; but there he did not perform the sacrifice as a priest imitating Melchizedek.

He exercises this function only when, in imitation of Melchizedek, he offers bread and wine to God in the sacred mysteries. Since there is no sacrifice without a priest, no priest without a sacrifice, and since we can assign no other place where Christ exercises priesthood and sacrifice in the manner of Melchizedek than the consecration of bread and wine and their offering, it is necessary that we recognize this sublime action [Col. 0999D] as that other sacrifice of our Lord.

Bear this in mind while I place before you for consideration the words also of the prophet Malachi:

“I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept your sacrifices from your hands. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is glorified among the gentiles” — who, clearly, are foretold as believing in Christ — “and IN EVERY PLACE incense is offered to my name, καὶ θυσία καθαρά, ‘and a pure sacrifice,’ and A PURE VICTIM.” (Malachi 1:10.)

What was this pure victim or offering foretold by that prophet, or this sacrifice—for the ancients signified the same thing by the word θυσία—let us ask a writer of the primitive Church.

He will be Justin the Martyr, who around the year 150 of Christ, in his Dialogue with the Jew Trypho, after bringing forward the same words of Malachi, adds:

“Concerning the offerings, or victims, which are EVERYWHERE OFFERED to that same God by us who have turned from the gentiles, that is, concerning THE EUCHARISTIC BREAD AND THE CUP OF THE EUCHARIST, he spoke and foretold this beforehand.”

From these words you understand that it was the belief of Christians, before the century in which the apostles flourished had yet passed, that the victims and bloodless sacrifice of the Eucharist had succeeded the bloody victims of the Jews. And just as the Jewish sacrifices were true and proper sacrifices, although they were only figures of the sacrifice to be instituted by Christ, so afterward the sacrifice of the Christian religion was true and proper, and it is the one sacrifice in which God now takes delight.

You find the same thing repeated below by Saint Justin:

“We are the true priestly and sacerdotal race, as God himself also bears witness, saying that IN EVERY PLACE AMONG THE GENTILES VICTIMS ACCEPTABLE AND PLEASING TO HIM ARE OFFERED. Nor does God accept victims from anyone except his own priests.

Therefore all the SACRIFICES which Jesus Christ commanded to be made in his name—that is, THE EUCHARIST OF THE BREAD AND THE CUP, which Christians perform IN EVERY PLACE—God declares, by anticipation, to be pleasing to him. But those made by you and your priests he rejects,” and so forth.

That holy man, who afterward confirmed his doctrine by a glorious martyrdom, also mentions elsewhere Christ as priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

At the same time, around the year 168 of Christ, the Christian philosopher Athenagoras presented an apology for the Christians to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus. There can scarcely be any doubt that he too was referring to the Eucharist when he teaches that God has no need of bloody victims, but demands ἀναίμακτον θυσίαν, καὶ λογικὴν λατρείαν—“a bloodless sacrifice and rational worship.” For both the liturgies and the holy Fathers regularly designate the Eucharistic sacrifice by these terms in countless passages.

From this we understand how ancient this doctrine is within the liturgies themselves.

The words of Saint Justin are so clear and so irresistible that anyone who still does not see—and dares still to deny—that in the very age of the apostles the celebration of the Eucharist was regarded and believed to be a sacrifice, and one superior to the sacrifices of the Hebrews, must be completely disturbed, not to say blinded, by human passions. [Col. 1000D]

I appeal here to everyone’s eyes and mind. Since Justin calls Christians true high priests and priests, which Protestants dare deny that a true sacrifice is performed by them? And who would not condemn their detestable rashness, since they have removed both the office and the name of priests from the Church of God?

Nor do we have only Justin as a witness to this truth. Around the year 190 of Christ, the most glorious bishop and martyr of the people of Lyon, Irenaeus, wrote his books Against the Heresies. He too speaks of Christ in these words:

“But also giving his disciples counsel to offer the firstfruits to God from his own creatures, he took what is from creation, bread, and gave thanks, saying: ‘This is my body’; and likewise, confessing the cup to be HIS OWN BLOOD, he taught THE NEW OFFERING OF THE NEW TESTAMENT” — by which word the liturgies and the Fathers very frequently designate sacrifice — “which THE CHURCH, HAVING RECEIVED FROM THE APOSTLES, OFFERS TO GOD THROUGHOUT THE WHOLE WORLD. Concerning this Malachi thus prefigured it: ‘I have no pleasure in you,’ and so forth. Through these words it is most clearly shown that, although the people would cease to offer to God, A SACRIFICE IS OFFERED TO HIM IN EVERY PLACE, and this sacrifice is pure.” (Irenaeus, Book 4, chapter 17, no. 5, Benedictine edition.)

He adds afterward:

“Therefore THE OFFERING OF THE CHURCH, which the Lord taught to be offered throughout the whole world, IS REGARDED AS A PURE SACRIFICE BEFORE GOD.” (The same author, chapter 18.)

And further:

“There is an offering there” — that is, among the Jewish people — “but offerings here also” — namely, in the Church. Sacrifices among the people, SACRIFICES IN THE CHURCH; but only the form has been changed.”

We have already shown from Irenaeus himself above that the body and blood of Christ, really present, are offered to God in this tremendous sacrifice. This holy martyr, taught by the disciples of the apostles, states most explicitly that the sacrifice is now offered in every place by the faithful of Christ; he contrasts it with the sacrifices of the Jews and gives it precedence over them. Yet there are those so blind to such great light that they boldly sell to their people the claim that no mention of a Christian sacrifice is found among the primitive Fathers of the Church.

Let Tertullian, a writer of the same century, also be brought forward. He calls Christ “the priest of NEW SACRIFICES, who offers NEW SACRIFICES, and the chief minister of eternal sacrifices.” (Tertullian, Book against the Jews, chapter 6.)

But what does Tertullian mean by the word “sacrifices”? He explains it for us himself:

“Likewise, concerning the days of the stations, most people do not think that one should take part in the prayers of the sacrifices, because the station must be broken by RECEIVING THE BODY OF THE LORD. Does the Eucharist therefore release the service devoted to God, or does it rather bind one more firmly to God?” (The same author, On Prayer, chapter 14.)

Here is the bloodless sacrifice of the Mass, which was completed by numerous prayers. Rigaltius, a Calvinist—or at least one who often defected to the Calvinist camp—thrusts upon us here the claim that by the word “sacrifices” prayers are meant, as though Tertullian had not plainly distinguished sacrifices from prayers.

Above, he himself had separated prayers more clearly from sacrifice when he wrote:

“What prayer is complete with the separation of the holy kiss? What kind of sacrifice is one from which a person departs without peace?”

Thus, for Tertullian also, the Eucharist is a sacrifice, [Col. 1001D] a point he confirms in the following words by adding:

“After RECEIVING THE BODY OF THE LORD and reserving it, both things remain secure: participation in THE SACRIFICE and fulfillment of the duty.”

The meaning of these words is obvious to everyone. Nor should we omit what he adds:

“Will your station not be solemn if you also stand AT THE ALTAR OF GOD?”

The word “altar” itself makes us certain of the sacrifice. Yet Rigaltius, interpreting this word through Calvinist eyes, argued from the dialogue of Minucius Felix—and he could also have added from Origen against Celsus—that in those times the Christian people had neither altars nor temples, and therefore that the “altar” here was the table of Christ.

We know this refrain repeated by Samuel Basnage in his Annals and by others, who themselves wrote that the Lord’s table was called the altar metaphorically [Col. 1002A] by Tertullian, Cyprian, the Fathers of Elvira, in the Apostolic Canons, and elsewhere.

From the History of Socrates, Basnage reports the following. During the disturbance caused by the affair of Arius:

“Alexander the bishop shut himself alone in the church called Irene, and, going to the altar, prostrated himself face down upon the ground beneath the sacred table.” (Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 37.)

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, is likewise said by Rufinus to have taken his position beneath the altar while the empress Justina was raging.

“From these things,” Basnage says, “it appears that the sacred table and the altar were one and the same.”

And so indeed they were. Yet he adds: “It is unheard-of in all memory that a genuine altar should have been designated by the name ‘table.’ Let the annals of the gentiles and of the Jews be consulted.”

[Col. 1002B] I should call the Calvinist people wretched indeed—who would not call them so?—whom such empty documents nourish and instruct. This is not something to be sought among the pagans or the Jews, but rather the distinctive and singular privilege of the Christian religion: namely, that the same Eucharistic table also fulfills the function of an altar. It is a table because there the Lord’s sacred supper is renewed; it is an altar because there the sacrifice of the cross is mystically renewed. Catholics acknowledge both and use both names. This was likewise the custom of the Fathers of earlier centuries, since scarcely any one of them failed to call the sacred table an altar as well.

Basnage ought to have learned and could have learned this very thing from the passage he himself cited from Socrates; but, with his mind preoccupied by Calvinist fictions, he failed to see what lay plainly before him. Yet anyone will see it who observes [Col. 1002C] that the Fathers of every age, so often and with such complete agreement, called one and the same thing now a table, now an altar. He will understand that this could have happened for no other reason than that on that table the Lord’s supper and the true sacrifice of the new law, foretold by Malachi, were celebrated simultaneously. If this were otherwise, the Fathers would seem blameworthy for having so often misused the name “altar.”

Basnage could also and ought to have learned that the holy bishops Alexander and Ambrose went to the altar in the necessities of the Church so that beneath it—for at that time the wooden sacred table was hollow—they might implore divine assistance. This was done for no other reason than that upon the altar, or above the table, the Eucharist was kept in a ciborium, reserved as viaticum for the sick. This may rightly be inferred [Col. 1002D] from the Acts of Saint Gorgonia, mentioned above in Nazianzenus, her brother, and from the Life of Saint Ambrose written by Paulinus. Who would ever approach a merely Calvinist table, outside the supper, in order to pray to God?

In vain, however, the pagans are brought forward against us, as though they had once mocked Minucius Felix and Origen because Christians had no altars, no temples, and no recognizable images. No one is unaware what the pagans designated by the name “altar”: stone altars intended for bloody sacrifices and fleshly victims. Certainly the Christians of the earlier centuries lacked these, as well as magnificent temples; for this reason the pagans reproached them for their lack of such altars and temples, as though the Divinity could be appeased only by such victims.

Arnobius likewise writes [Col. 1003A] against the Gentiles:

> “You are accustomed,” he says, “to fasten upon us the greatest charge of impiety, because we build neither sacred shrines nor altars nor altars [aras]” (Arnobius, *Against the Gentiles*, book VI).

Arnobius wrote this about the year of Christ 303. Much later still, when the Christian religion itself was reigning, Julian the Apostate accused Christ’s faithful because they did not erect **βώμους καὶ θυσιαστήρια**, “altars and sacrificial altars.” See Cyril of Alexandria (*Against Julian*, book X). Since there was such a great difference between pagan and Christian altars, the slander arose that the Christian religion was destitute of altars.

Basnage might wish that Christians had replied that they too were not without an altar. But the ancient Christians needed no teacher such as Basnage to take care of their own affairs. Moreover, [Col. 1003B] there was too great a distinction between pagan altars and the wooden Christian altars, fashioned in the form of a table during the earlier centuries of the Church. Examples are found everywhere showing that Christians often refused to reveal their dread mysteries and expose them to pagan mockery.

But when they addressed the faithful, did they remain silent about the altars of our religion? Certainly not—not merely in the time of Arnobius and Cyril of Alexandria, but not even during the first three centuries of the Church. Indeed, we received this doctrine from the Apostle himself. For when writing to the Corinthians he mentions the Lord’s table; and likewise, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, he recognizes an altar in the Church:

> “We have an altar (**θυσιαστήριον**, that is, a place of sacrifice), from which those who serve the [Col. 1003C] tabernacle have no right to eat” (Hebrews 13:10);

that is, the Jews who still cling to the prescriptions of the Law. These words cannot be applied to an altar placed in heaven, since Paul explicitly says that it is to be eaten from; rather, they refer to our mystical altar, on which the Bread of Life is truly eaten—that is, the Lord’s body.

Receive the same testimony from the holy martyr Ignatius, the disciple of the apostles, who wrote the following in his authentic Epistle to the Philadelphians, before the time of Minucius and Origen:

> “Therefore take care to use one Eucharist.
