For there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ”—see what the Eucharist is; we saw it stated still more clearly by him above in his Epistle to the Smyrnaeans—“and one cup for the unity of his blood; **one altar** (**ἓν θυσιαστήριον**), just as there is one bishop,” [Col. 1003D] etc.

Origen too could have replied to Celsus that Christians were not without an altar. Indeed, elsewhere he himself confessed this when he wrote:

> “The priest who attends the **divine altars** uses other garments when he is **engaged in the ministry of sacrifices**” (Origen, *Homily 4 on Leviticus*).

Behold, then, according to Origen’s testimony, a divine altar and sacrifice in the Church of Christ. And what did I say—he could have replied? He did reply, when he used these words against that same Celsus:

> “Pouring out prayers to the almighty God of all things through his Only-Begotten Son, to whom we first offer them, we ask him—for he is the propitiation for our sins—that, as the high priest, to whom sacrifice pertains, he may present **both prayers and sacrifices** (**καὶ τὰς θυσίας**) and our conversations to him who is God over all” (the same author, *Against Celsus*, [Col. 1004A] book VIII).

Whoever establishes a sacrifice must also establish an altar. Ask Origen, moreover, whether this sacrifice is propitiatory. He will answer:

> “This is the sole commemoration that makes God propitious to human beings” (the same author, *Homily 13 on Leviticus*).

Let our prayer now proceed to the glorious light of Africa, the martyr Cyprian, so that from him we may learn what the Church’s judgment concerning the sacred Mass was in the third century of Christ, in which he himself flourished.

In the letter written to Caecilius around the year of Christ 253, the holy bishop is wholly occupied in refuting certain ignorant persons who used water, rather than wine, in the dread sacrifice (Cyprian, Letter 63 to Caecilius). That both were always used in the Church is shown by the earliest Fathers—Justin, Irenaeus, Clement of [Col. 1004B] Alexandria—and finally by Cyprian himself:

> “Since the Lord taught that the cup, following the example of his instruction, should be mixed with a combination of wine and water.”

Certainly those great men did not introduce this rite; they received it as handed down by the apostles. Nevertheless, with impious authority the innovators proscribed water from the supper. Who could tolerate such great audacity, which condemns, whether through ignorance or treachery, the Fathers of the primitive Church?

As for the Mass, Cyprian does not debate whether it should be called a “sacrifice.” He presents it as an established doctrine, one that no one in the Church of God had called into question:

> “Who is a priest of the most high God more than our Lord Jesus Christ? He **offered a sacrifice to God the Father**, and he offered the very thing that Melchizedek had offered, namely bread and [Col. 1004C] wine, that is, **his body and blood**.”

Whoever does not recognize, in words so clear, the true sacrifice of the Christian religion and the real presence of the Lord in the Eucharist proves himself guilty of inexcusable obstinacy.

A little later the most praiseworthy holy bishop adds:

> “For if Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, is himself both the supreme priest of God the Father and the first to **offer himself as a sacrifice to the Father**, and if he commanded **this to be done** in remembrance of himself, then that priest truly acts in the place of Christ who imitates what Christ did and **offers a true and complete sacrifice** to God the Father in the Church, if he begins to offer in this manner, according to what he sees Christ himself to have offered.”

Read these words again, and consider them carefully. Yet even in our own age, when learning [Col. 1004D] and the pursuit of truth are cultivated above all else, there have been people bold enough to defend the errors of Luther and Calvin concerning the sacred Mass—errors already recognized by many Protestants—and to continue persuading the ignorant populace that the unbloody sacrifice was unknown to the ancient Church, and that such an error, or abomination, must be attributed either to the corrupters of the Christian religion or to the Papists. When shall we learn, setting aside prejudiced opinions, to seek the one truth and, once we have found it, to acknowledge it?

Cyprian later shows that the Holy Spirit, in Proverbs 9, had mentioned the **Lord’s sacrifice**, the **immaculate victim** of bread and wine, as well as the **altar** and the apostles. He then adds:

> “It is evident that **the blood of Christ is not offered** [Col. 1005A] if wine is absent from the cup, and that **the Lord’s sacrifice is not celebrated with legitimate sanctification** unless **our offering and sacrifice correspond to the Passion**.”

Furthermore, that holy man, who later confirmed the Church’s teaching by his martyrdom, testifies that in the priest Melchizedek there had previously been established “an image of **the sacrifice of Christ**, namely, in bread and wine.” The Lord, “completing and fulfilling this,” offered bread and a cup mixed with wine; and he who is the fullness “fulfilled the **truth** of the prefigured image.”

Cyprian likewise mentions the **Lord’s sacrifices** (Cyprian, Letter 69); elsewhere he says:

> “When **in the sacrifices** we make prayer together with many others” (the same author, Letter 37).

Here Rigaltius is ridiculous, interpreting “sacrifices” once again as “prayers,” when the text most plainly distinguishes prayer from [Col. 1005B] sacrifices; and what sacrifices meant to Saint Cyprian shines forth from the passages cited, clearer than the midday sun.

There are also abundant other passages in which he mentions the altar, a word by which the idea of a true sacrifice is renewed in our minds. I shall mention one. Concerning a schismatic he says:

> “An enemy of the **altar**, a rebel against **the sacrifice of Christ**, etc., he dares to make another altar and another prayer in illicit words, and to profane **the truth of the Lord’s victim** by false sacrifices” (the same author, *On the Unity of the Church*).

But Cyprian must not be dismissed before we also learn from him whether, even then, Christians believed the sacrifice of the people to be propitiatory for the faithful who had fallen asleep in Christ. Writing to another Cyprian, he says that his episcopal predecessors had forbidden any [Col. 1005C] cleric to be employed as a guardian:

> “If anyone had done this, no offering would be made for him, nor would **a sacrifice for his repose** be celebrated” (the same author, Letter 1 to another Cyprian).

Therefore, when a certain Victor had disregarded this decree, he adds:

> “There is no reason that **an offering**—that is, a sacrifice—or any **supplication** should be made for his repose among you in the Church in his name.”

John Fell, Bishop of Oxford in England, thought that he could wrest this passage from Catholics as evidence of the efficacy of the divine sacrifice even for the assistance of the dead—leaving other innovators aside—by saying in his notes on Cyprian’s first letter that the martyrs too were commemorated in the sacred rites, and that sacrifices were offered for them, although Cyprian believed that they had already attained the crown. But he closed his eyes so as not to see.

[Col. 1005D] Read Cyprian’s words again:

> “Let no offering be made for his repose among you, nor any supplication be made in his name.”

Fell himself admits that no supplication was made for the martyrs. If supplication was made for the other faithful, then the Church must have believed that assistance was also provided to the dead through sacrifices and prayers. We have Tertullian, older than Cyprian, as a witness to the same doctrine (Tertullian, *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 11, and *On Monogamy*, chapter 10).

Since, then, the names of sacrifice, altar, and victim so often occur in the liturgies of Rome and the other Churches, you now hold in your hand the fact that Protestants vainly attempt to cast suspicion of novelty upon both the reality signified by these names and the thing itself, as though they had been unknown in the [Col. 1006A] first centuries of the Church and had gradually slipped into the prayers of the sacred mysteries.

You also have reason to understand why the Anglican Grabe thought that the Mass ought to be restored in England, and why he did not fear confessing Luther’s and Calvin’s errors in this matter. From the many testimonies of the ancients assembled here it is also evident that the sacrifice of the Catholic Church is neither imaginary nor improper. Everything Protestants devise to show that all the conditions and qualities found in the bloody sacrifices of the Jews do not occur in our sacrifice—and therefore that it should not be called a true and proper sacrifice—dissolves into mere empty ornament and caviling.

Catholics, on the contrary, demonstrate that all the marks of a true sacrifice converge in the Eucharistic sacrifice. But why waste time on [Col. 1006B] these superfluous disputes? He who instituted the Jewish victims also prescribed the Eucharist for the new people. Even if those sacrifices were bloody and this one unbloody, and even if we granted some difference between this sacrifice and those, was it not permissible for God to institute different yet genuine sacrifices? In the sacrifice of the cross, the victim, altar, and priest were not similar to those of the Jews. The Eucharistic sacrifice, however, is nothing other than the mystical renewal of that same sacrifice.

Yet what dispels every quibble is this: grant me that the true body and blood of the Lord are really contained in the Eucharist—a truth that the liturgies and Fathers have always proclaimed from the beginning of the Church, as we demonstrated above with the utmost clarity. Grant me further that in the mysteries we offer to God this divine victim, mystically [Col. 1006C] sacrificed each day and never ceasing, for the remission of sins. What further length can we add to the rope of contention? Does not the Son of God surpass creatures without reason? Can any victim more pleasing and effective than this be offered to the heavenly Father?

Thus we have in the Eucharist a new sacrifice, a singular sacrifice: “a sacrifice far superior” to the ancient sacrifices, as Eusebius writes (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, book II, chapter 10). Therefore, whoever believes in Christ yet dares to deny this wondrous benefit bestowed by him upon the Christian religion, against such a cloud of witnesses from both the earlier and later centuries of the Church, and who gives more faith and obedience to Luther and Calvin than to all the liturgies of the Christian world and the holy Fathers, should consider whether he has undertaken a matter of such magnitude rightly and sincerely [Col. 1006D], a matter to which every conscience feels itself bound.

The days will come, I hope, when so many peoples now separated from us by the most dreadful schism will return to the unity of the Catholic religion. Then they will be astonished that they and their ancestors were so long deceived by the sophisms and quibbles of the innovators. For the controversy concerning the Eucharist is not among those questions that, being obscure, torment the human mind and are difficult to extricate from every darkness. If a Christian professes to God, who speaks, the same submission of soul and mind that each of us professes when believing in the Trinity, the Incarnation of the Word, and the other mysteries of the Christian religion, I assert with complete confidence that he cannot fail to see [Col. 1007A] here the manifest light of truth: namely, that the doctrine of the real presence and the sacrifice of the Mass has been the perennial judgment of the Church throughout all the centuries, and that to depart from it is the greatest of crimes.

I am not speaking here of the Socinians, nor of other people of that kind, who either believe nothing or, with detestable authority, submit religion to their own intellects rather than their intellects to religion, and mock the credulity of the rest of Christians. In our age Jonathan Swift broke out among the Britons; he was the author of a little book translated into French and bearing the title *Le Conte du tonneau* [*A Tale of a Tub*], in which he did not hesitate to construct a comedy out of the sacrament of the altar. Only an impious man could dare such things—one who openly serves in the camp of Epicurus and the atheists. What I have gathered thus far does not concern this most pestilential class of [Col. 1007B] people.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Adoration of the Eucharist Confirmed by the Liturgies and the Fathers

As all learned Catholics acknowledge, after the heresy of Berengarius a rite became established in the Catholic Roman Church: namely, after the consecration, to raise or elevate the host and then the chalice, so that the people might adore the body and blood of the Lord. Hence the heterodox object to us that the rite is an innovation, and loudly proclaim that it originated from the opinion of transubstantiation, which they absurdly imagine to have arisen in the ninth century of Christ and to have first been devised by Paschasius Radbertus.

The Lutherans abolished this kind of adoration, although they acknowledged the reality of the Lord’s body in the sacrament [Col. 1007C]; the Calvinists, however, accuse us—if heaven approves—of idolatry on account of this custom. No one needs a particularly powerful intellect to recognize how absurd and childish this accusation is. If it is an absolutely certain dogma among Catholics that the whole Christ exists in the Eucharist by his real presence, who does not see and understand that it necessarily follows that he must be adored there, since wherever he is present he must be honored and obeyed in this way? Indeed, anyone who acted otherwise would be condemned.

A person would be equally—or rather, even more—ridiculous if from the rite of adoration, introduced after the year 1100 of Christ, he wished to infer that transubstantiation and the presence in the sacrament of the altar began to be believed around that time, when this dogma [Col. 1007D] was born with the Church and has always been preserved. and has always been preserved.

Nevertheless, to satisfy even the weak, it must be noted that it is astonishing for people who are not unlearned to bring this reproach against us on account of the adoration of the Lord’s body and blood at Mass when they are elevated. Let that elevation be new, if they wish; the adoration of the Eucharist certainly is not new. Indeed, it was always customary, as the polemical writers of the Catholic Church made clear long ago.

By “adoration” we mean the homage of inward humiliation that a servant offers to his master. It is divided into inward and outward adoration. Without doubt, the inward is superior to the other; indeed, the outward is scarcely anything without it. Outward adoration was devised so that a person might display the homage [Col. 1008A] situated in the heart. Our ancestors always regarded bending the knee, or falling upon one’s knees, as highly appropriate for expressing the servile reverence and humility of the inner person.

There is no doubt, however, that reverence and adoration toward God can also be rightly and perfectly performed and manifested by the heart alone, without prostration of the knees and body. Even a mere inclination of the head can provide this outward expression.

> “When they pray,” says Saint Augustine, “they make such use of the members of their body as is appropriate for those who are supplicating, when they bend their knees, stretch out their hands, or even prostrate themselves on the ground; and if they do anything else, although their visible will and the intention of their heart are known to God, and although he does not need these signs in order that the human mind may be disclosed to him” (Augustine, *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 5).

Apuleius reveals [Col. 1008B] what the pagans did when they wished to venerate temples or idols:

> “If Aemilianus passes by some shrine, he considers it a crime not to bring his hand to his lips for the sake of adoration” (Apuleius, *Apology* 1).

Therefore, although it is known from the Acts of the Apostles and from the Epistle to the Ephesians that the apostles were accustomed to pray while kneeling, nevertheless, according to Justin Martyr and Tertullian, “on the Lord’s Day and from Easter until Pentecost, it was unlawful to adore while kneeling.” You may also see this established by the Fathers of Nicaea (First Council of Nicaea, final canon). Was God therefore adored any less in prayer and in the mysteries? To vary and prescribe such a rite belongs to the Church.

It is certain that formerly the faithful, both in the East and in the West, [Col. 1008C] received the body and blood of the Lord standing. Now they receive them kneeling. The priests who still partake of the most sacred body and blood while standing undoubtedly adore just as those others did.

Since we possess no ancient sacramentary in which all the rubrics or rites used in the Mass are recorded, much light is consequently lacking for determining the adoration of former times in the sacred mysteries. Nevertheless, a sufficiently clear trace of this rite remains.

Consider the first Roman Order of the pontifical Mass, edited by Cassander, Hittorp, and Mabillon, whose antiquity predates the year 800 of Christ, since Amalarius mentions it. There we read:

> “With head bowed, the pontiff or deacon salutes [Col. 1008D] the holy things”—

that is, the Eucharist reserved from the preceding day, which was placed above the altar in order to elicit greater reverence for the new solemn sacrifice that was about to be celebrated.

We also have Gregory of Tours as a witness to this rite (*On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 85). In another Roman Order preserved by the same Mabillon, the same rite is repeated in these words:

> “The pontiff proceeds to the head of the schola and, on the higher step, with head bowed toward the altar, first adores the holy things.”

Moreover, Amalarius, who had one or another of these Orders at hand, says of the sacred ministers:

> “They remain standing behind, bowed down, until it is said: ‘But deliver us from evil’” (Amalarius, *On the Divine Offices*, book III, chapter 23).

That is, they continued their adoration [Col. 1009A] throughout the entire canon. In his *Eclogues*, written around the year 820 of Christ, he wrote:

> “When the bishop comes before the altar, he first adores the holy things” (the same author, in the *Eclogues*, edited by Baluze and Mabillon).

And below:

> “After the bishop has adored the holy things, he proceeds to the right side of the altar.”

All this was done before the books of Paschasius Radbertus.

In the most ancient of all, Order I, note the following, which agrees with Amalarius’s words:

> “When the Angelic Hymn, that is, the *Sanctus*, has been completed, the pontiff alone rises and enters the canon. The bishops, deacons, subdeacons, and priests, however, **remain bowed down in the presbytery**. And when he has said, ‘To us also, sinners,’ the subdeacons rise,” etc.

Behold the adoration that was continued in the divine mysteries throughout the whole duration of the canon.

Among the Greeks, the principal time for adoring the most sacred [Col. 1009B] body and blood of the Lord is when, after the Lord’s Prayer, they say *Holy things for holy persons*, and the elevation of the host and chalice takes place. Anastasius the Sinaite wrote:

> “After the consecration of that unbloody sacrifice, the priest raises the bread of life on high and displays it to all, etc. Then he immediately adds: ‘Holy things for holy persons’” (Anastasius the Sinaite, *Discourse on the Holy Synaxis*, volume I of Canisius).

In the customary Greek liturgy of Chrysostom, edited by James Goar, we find the following:

> “Then the priest and deacon adore where they are, secretly saying three times: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ The whole people likewise adore with devotion. When the deacon sees the priest extending his hands and touching the holy bread in order to perform the holy elevation, he cries out: ‘Let us attend.’ And the priest says: [Col. 1009C] ‘Holy things for holy persons.’ The choir: ‘One is Holy, one is Lord, Jesus Christ, in the glory of God the Father. Amen.’”

Then, approaching for Communion, the deacon:

> “Adoring once, says: ‘Behold, I come to the immortal King. I believe, Lord, and I confess.’”

When communicating the people, the deacon:

> “Adoring once, takes the holy chalice, etc., and displays it to the people, saying: ‘With fear,’” etc.

It is well known that the same Greeks are carried toward the Eucharist with such devotion that they seem to fall into excesses. For even while the sacred gifts are being carried to the altar with great ceremony, although they have not yet been consecrated, the people fall upon their knees as though they were going to adore them.

Not only the Greeks but also learned Latins judged that this rite should be tolerated rather than forbidden, provided that [Col. 1009D] the people were taught the distinction in mind and worship with which gifts not yet consecrated and gifts subsequently consecrated are to be received.

Nevertheless, there will be cavillers who, following their usual practice, will suspect novelty in the adoration of the Greeks when the priest cries out, “Holy things for holy persons.” I have a notable passage with which to silence them, namely, Theodore the Studite, who, around the year 796 of Christ, wrote the following in a dialogue between an Orthodox Christian and a heretic (Theodore the Studite, *Antirrheticus* II, chapter 31):

> **Orthodox:** “Among what things do you place the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ?”
>
> **Heretic:** “They are certainly holy things. For the priest says, ‘Holy things for holy persons.’”
>
> **Orthodox:** “Do you therefore judge that these things are also to be adored?”
>
> **Heretic:** [Col. 1010A] “Who could be so impious as not to confess that holy things are also to be adored?”
>
> **Orthodox:** “Are you not therefore saying things contrary to yourself? Earlier you said that whatever is holy is not immediately also to be adored; now you again affirm what you denied.”
>
> **Heretic:** “But I was not speaking about the mysteries—that is, about the Mass—when I spoke of these things, since everyone agrees about them, as I said.”

Saint Maximus likewise confirms the same point, saying:

> “The pontiff, raising the sacred bread, displayed the blessing, or sacrament, saying: ‘Holy things for holy persons’” (Saint Maximus, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy of Dionysius*).

Here we have the elevation of the Eucharistic body and blood, which is also attested by Symeon of Thessalonica (*Short Treatise on the Temple and the Mass*, in Canisius).

The same sacred practice also occurs in the Life of Blessed Luke the Younger, edited by Combefis, [Col. 1010B] among the short works of the Greeks. He flourished among the Greek ascetics in the tenth century of Christ and was living in solitude when the archbishop of Corinth came to visit him. Luke asked by what means those anchorites could receive “the dread mysteries.” The bishop replied that they should receive the Presanctified Gifts:

> “Then,” he says, “unfolding the smaller veil, you will place the sacred particles upon it; after lighting incense, you will sing the psalms of the Typica, or the hymn ‘Thrice-Holy,’ together with the Symbol of Faith. **Adoring with a threefold bending of the knees**, you will draw in your hands—in the form of a cross—and with your mouth receive the sacred and precious body of Christ our God, saying ‘Amen.’ Then you will gather the remaining particles again into the linen vessel, taking every care lest a pearl should fall [Col. 1010C] and be trampled underfoot.”

Behold how much reverence the Greeks formerly showed toward the dread body of Christ, whom, as you have seen, they adored as present. From these examples we learn what the Greek Church believed and practiced, even then, concerning the adoration due to the Lord’s body in the sacred mysteries.

The Syrians and Copts held no different view and followed no different practice. For, as Renaudot demonstrated, they too performed, and still perform, the elevation of the host and chalice—not immediately after the consecration, but after the Lord’s Prayer:

> “It is the custom of the whole East,” he says, “that the sacrament should not be elevated and displayed to the people before the words are said: ‘Holy things for holy persons.’ From this error it happened that many rashly asserted that the elevation [Col. 1010D] was unknown to the Eastern Churches.”

At that point the people adored the holy mysteries, and they still adore them, with a special devotion. In the Syriac liturgy attributed to Saint Gregory, after the consecration the deacon cries out:

> “Adore the Lamb, the Word,” etc.

What does it matter if the Roman Church performs the elevation and adoration of the divine mysteries immediately after the consecration, while the Eastern Churches perform it only before Communion? It is enough that we possess the constant doctrine and practice of all the Churches concerning the adoration due in the sacred mysteries to Christ the Lord, who is really present. For that reason the Latin Churches were permitted—indeed, deserve particular praise—for having gradually introduced and approved this act of our humiliation and homage immediately after [Col. 1011A] the consecration had been completed, and for continuing to perform it, so that we might render more visibly and earnestly to the divine Redeemer the honor that the Sacramentarians have withheld from him in the sacred rites.

But why seek further evidence, when many centuries ago the holy Fathers acknowledged that adoration was customary in the Church of God while the unbloody sacrifice was being offered? The words of Saint Ambrose are well known and widely circulated:

> “The flesh of Christ, **which we adore even today in the mysteries**, and **which the apostles adored in the Lord Jesus**” (Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, chapter 11).

A person would be completely dull-witted, or would possess a corrupted mind, if he did not see here how confidently the faithful at that time believed that Christ’s flesh was present in the mysteries, just as Jesus the Lord was certainly present to the apostles.

Saint Augustine speaks [Col. 1011B] no differently:

> “The Lord received earth from the earth, because flesh is from the earth, and he received flesh from the flesh of Mary. And because he walked here in that very flesh, **he gave us that very flesh to eat** for salvation. But no one eats that flesh **unless he has first adored it**. Thus it has been discovered how the Lord’s footstool is to be adored; and not only **do we not sin by adoring**, but **we sin by not adoring**” (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 98*, no. 9).

He then adds:

> “Therefore you bow and prostrate yourself before any earth”—that is, before any portion of the Eucharist, which is Christ’s flesh—“not as though you were looking upon earth”—that is, as though it were an earthly thing unworthy of any veneration—“but before **that [Col. 1011C] Holy One whose footstool it is that you adore**”—that is, the flesh. “For his sake you adore.”

As we saw above, in chapter 12, Theodoret likewise speaks of the sacred symbols of the Eucharist when he says:

> “They are understood to be what they have become, and they are believed and **adored**, since they are what they are believed to be.”

In the preceding fourth century, Saint Cyril of Jerusalem also handed down the rite by which the people at that time received the sacred body and blood of the Lord: standing, certainly, but with body or head inclined. For the word **κύπτων**, which he uses—meaning “bent forward” or “prostrate”—shows that this was then a sign of adoration established by the Church:

> “Approach,” he says, “and at the cup of blood do not extend your hands, but come **bent forward**, in the manner of adoration and veneration, [Col. 1011D] saying: ‘Amen.’”

And when receiving the body, he instructs that the left hand should be placed beneath the right “as a throne,” since it is about to receive the King. So great was their faith at that time: that the very body of Christ the Lord was received in the sacrament, not figuratively, but truly.

As the Bishop of Meaux, Bossuet—a truly great man—also observed in his *Explanation of the Mass*, not only was supreme veneration and the worship of *latria* offered by Christ’s faithful to the most sacred Eucharist in ancient centuries, but it was also extended to the sacred vessels of the awe-inspiring sacrifice. This worship, however, did not stop at the material objects, but was directed to the Lord himself, who was to be adored. Saint Jerome bears witness to this when he says:

“Let those who are ignorant learn, instructed by the testimonies of Scripture, with what veneration they ought to receive holy things and minister in the service of Christ’s altar, and let them learn that the sacred chalices, holy veils, and the other things belonging to the worship of the Lord’s Passion are not to be regarded as empty and senseless objects devoid of sanctity, but, through their association with the Lord’s body and blood, are to be venerated with the same majesty as his body and blood” (Jerome, letter prefixed to the letter of Theophilus of Alexandria, vol. V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*).

Jerome does not say that they are to be adored, but that they are to be venerated, or are worthy of veneration. Whether anyone who writes that the sacred chalices shared in the veneration due to Christ the Lord—because they had been sanctified through association or contact with his body and blood—believed in the Eucharist merely a figure of the Lord’s body, I leave to every fair-minded and perceptive reader to judge.

Finally, I ask you to read—leaving aside other passages—these words of Chrysostom concerning Christ:

“The Magi revered this body even as it lay in the manger, and with great fear and trembling they adored it. You do not see it in a manger, but upon the altar. Let us therefore show a far greater reverence than those barbarians” (Chrysostom, Homily 24 on 1 Corinthians).

And so on. Do you still doubt whether, in ancient times, worship was also rendered to Christ’s body in the sacred mysteries? The same Chrysostom said:

“He who sits above with the Father is held in everyone’s hands” (the same, Book III *On the Priesthood*),

namely, in the sacred assembly. This was proclaimed to the faithful; and do you still ask whether they adored so great a Lord present among them?

Meanwhile, if this little work of mine should have the great good fortune to reach the hands of Protestants, I beg them, by the bowels of Jesus Christ, if they love religion and desire the peace of the Churches—a peace from which no one but an impious person can shrink—that they carefully and impartially consider what necessarily follows from the adoration of the Eucharist.

No doubt can remain that Christ’s faithful, in the fourth and fifth centuries of the Christian era, directed their adoration to the Eucharist as present, whether by bending the knee or by inclining the head. If Ambrose, Augustine, and the other Fathers had thought, as Luther’s disciples now maintain, that in the sacrament the substance of bread and wine still remained together with Christ’s body and blood, they would have rejected adoration, lest the worship due to God alone should at the same time be rendered to a creature—as the Lutherans appear to think, though I do not inquire whether rightly.

If, however, as the Calvinists believe, those Fathers had thought that the Eucharist contained only bread and wine, they would not merely have refrained from it, but would have condemned it as idolatry. Yet we know for certain that the ancient Fathers approved such adoration and indeed judged that it could not be omitted without sin.

Do you not therefore understand that the ancient Church had no other judgment and faith concerning the Eucharist than that which is maintained, and has always been maintained, in the Roman Church? You must also admit that the Fathers thought nothing of bread and wine after consecration, but regarded the sacrament as containing one body, blood, and soul of Christ, worthy of adoration. For this reason they explicitly bore witness elsewhere to this truth, namely, the true transformation of the symbols.

[Col. 1013A] Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, a contemporary of Ambrose and Chrysostom, will also assure you that the Church’s faith was no different at that time. For he says:

“Therefore the Creator and Lord of natures himself, who brings forth bread from the earth, makes from bread again—because he both can and has promised to do so—his own body. And he who made wine from water makes from wine his blood, and so forth. Do not suppose that what has been made heavenly by him who passes into it, and makes it his own body and blood, is earthly” (Gaudentius of Brescia, Treatise 2 to the Newly Baptized).

Below he repeats the same point:

“Do not consider that sacrament common and earthly, but believe that, through the fire of the divine Spirit, that has been effected which was proclaimed. For what you receive is the body of that heavenly Bread—not a figure, not an image—and it is the blood of that sacred Vine, and so forth. Let us believe, I beg you, him in whom we have believed. Truth does not know falsehood.”

Thus, in those same times, Ambrose at Milan, Gaudentius at Brescia, Chrysostom at Constantinople, Cyril at Jerusalem, Theodoret in Syria, and Augustine in Africa—leaving aside the other Fathers—proclaimed with one voice what the Roman Church proclaims. Understand at last that this was formerly, and still is, the doctrine of the true Church, and that the innovators of the later centuries were its impious disturbers.

Those among them, however, who do not flee from the truth but love it, and who desire the peace of their conscience rather than the honor and defense of their sect, should, I beg them, consult the books on the Perpetuity of the Faith written in French. At least let them investigate, in the works of Saint John Chrysostom alone, what the judgment and faith of the universal Church once were concerning the Eucharist.

You have heard so many words of that holy bishop, yet I cannot restrain myself from drawing one more here from his treasury. Concerning the unbloody sacrifice he says:

“This mystery makes the earth heaven for you. For what is most precious and honorable there, that I shall show you placed upon the earth. Just as in a royal palace the most magnificent thing is not the walls or the golden roof, but the body of the king sitting upon the throne, so also in heaven it is the body of the King. But this you are now permitted to see upon earth. For I shall show you not angels or archangels, but their very Lord himself. Nor do you merely see him; you also touch him, you also eat him, and after receiving him you return home” (Chrysostom, Homily 24 on 1 Corinthians).

Whoever still does not understand these and similar statements, and tries to corrupt them by arbitrary Calvinist interpretations, should fear that dreadful declaration which the Apostle applied to the Jews:

“You will indeed hear with your ears, and you will not understand; and seeing, you will indeed see, and you will not perceive” (Acts 28:26).

## CHAPTER XX  
### Concerning Certain Rites of the Sacred Liturgy against Which the Innovators Bring Charges

After Luther and Calvin, or Zwingli—by an authority certainly not granted to them by God—had utterly disfigured the chief sacrament of the Christian religion, whether by abolishing the unbloody sacrifice or by removing from the Eucharist the real presence of the Lord’s body, they and their disciples never ceased attacking the Roman liturgy and even hunting for flies, so as to bring it into contempt among their followers. Whether justly, must now be examined.

In the Mass of the Roman rite, before the priest ascends to the altar, he first makes a general confession of his own sins and those of the people standing by. Although anyone who longs to receive Holy Communion is first commanded to wash away grave sins through the sacrament of penance, nevertheless, because through human weakness we fall into daily faults, these too must be removed; and for that purpose this preliminary confession and absolution were instituted before the beginning of Mass.

Saint Augustine seems to have inculcated this very point when he says:

“Enter his gates with confession. In the gates there is a beginning; begin with confession. Let confession be your gate—that is, your beginning. Hence it is said in another psalm: ‘Begin to the Lord with confession.’ And what then? Once we have entered, shall we not confess? Always confess; you always have something to confess. It is difficult in this life for a person to be so changed that nothing can be found in him deserving reproach. You must reproach yourself, lest he reproach you who is going to condemn” (Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm 99*).

Furthermore, it is established and confirmed by many ancient records that priests formerly used this same kind of confession, either before leaving the sacristy or at the foot of the sacred altar.

Since the oldest sacramentaries of the Roman Church lack the rubrics and ceremonies used in the Mass, it is not known whether this particular confession was in use in the ancient centuries. In the Mass published by Illyricus, which unquestionably bears the marks of great antiquity, a similar formula is found. Another, nearly identical, formula of confession is reported by the *Micrologus*, who wrote about liturgical matters toward the end of the eleventh century, as well as in the Roman Sacramentary published by Cardinal Bona from the Chisian Library.

The Missal of the canon of the cathedral of Modena, written six hundred years ago, is preserved; from it I previously displayed the Mass used at Modena in that period. In it, after the *Introibo* (“I will enter”) and *Judica me, Deus* (“Judge me, O God”), this rubric follows:

“When he [the priest] has reached the altar, let him say, humbly and with bowed face: ‘Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth.’ Let the response be: ‘And a door of restraint about my lips.’ And let him make his confession, as is customary. After the confession has been completed, let him say: ‘I have declared my life to you, O God,’” and so forth.

What is certain is that, in the Masses both of the Westerners and of the Easterners, priest and people alike were accustomed to implore divine mercy—not only at the very entrance, by crying out *Kyrie eleison*, *Christe eleison*, that is, “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy,” but also in other parts of the Mass. We see the same practice observed and repeated in the liturgies of the Easterners themselves, especially in the Mass of Chrysostom, before the priest communicates.

Certainly no one can fail to praise this most holy practice of ecclesiastical discipline.

Nevertheless, Bingham, a British writer (*On the Origin of the Church*, Book XV, chapter 1), finds something to criticize in the Roman liturgy: there the confession is made to Almighty God, the Mother of God, and all the saints, whereas, as he himself insists, formerly it was made to God alone.

On this point he recalls an old apology, or confession, from the Gallican rite. But what words this same confession was expressed in among the other Churches in ancient times, we cannot discover because of the absence of the rubrics, as I have said. What is sufficient is that there is nothing here inconsistent with the doctrine and discipline of the Catholic Church.

For the invocation of the saints rests upon legitimate reasons, as we shall indicate below, and in the Creed we profess their communion with us. We confess to God so that he may pardon us; to the saints only so that they may pray for us. The confession itself explicitly bears witness to this, since priest and people pray that all the saints may pray for me to the Lord our God.

This is a public confession. If it is made before the people, why not also before the saints? The holy men certainly stand before God in the heavenly homeland, and it is chiefly to him that the confession is directed.

For this reason, in the most ancient confession of the penitent, which Hittorpius presents from the Roman Order and Morinus reports, we read:

“I confess to you, O Lord, Father of heaven and earth, and to you, most gracious Jesus, together with the Holy Spirit, before the holy angels and before all the saints” (Morinus, appendix to the book *On Penance), and so forth.

Morinus extracted other similar formulas from ancient penitentials. By the same reasoning, the priest asks the people, and the people ask the priest, to pray for him or for them.

### Candles in the Unbloody Sacrifice

Candles are used in the unbloody sacrifice. There are not lacking heterodox writers, among them the Calvinist Johann Heinrich Ottius, who instituted an examination against Cardinal Baronius’s *Annals*, insulting Catholics on account of this rite and bringing against us Saint Jerome, who says the following against Vigilantius:

“We do not light candles in broad daylight, as you falsely accuse us, but so that by this consolation we may temper the darkness of night and keep watch by the light, lest we sleep with you, blind, in darkness.”

For this reason Father Le Brun thought that, in Jerome’s time, Christians did not use lights during daytime sacred services, but that this custom arose later, taken from the practice of carrying lights when the Gospel was read. Jerome himself adds:

“Throughout all the Churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, lights are kindled while the sun is already shining—not, of course, to drive away darkness, but to display a sign of joy.”

The discussion there concerned candles lit in honor of the martyrs. Nevertheless, since Jerome approves the use of lights “when the Gospel is to be read, as a sign of joy,” Father Le Brun thinks that Christ’s faithful, relying on this example, extended the custom of lights to the entire Mass.

As I believe I have already shown elsewhere (Murat, *Anecdotes*, vol. I, dissertation 16), it should not so readily be conceded that in Jerome’s time there were no daytime lights in churches or at the celebration of the sacraments. If this practice did not exist in Palestine, it could have flourished in other regions.

Candles were carried not only for the Gospel but also for baptism, as is clear from Cyril of Jerusalem and Gregory of Nazianzus. Nor were they used only by the newly baptized; others also used them in honor of so great a sacrament.

Mark the Deacon of Gaza, a contemporary writer, describes in the *Life of Saint Porphyry, Bishop*, the preparations for the day on which Theodosius II, the infant son of the Emperor Arcadius, was regenerated by holy baptism in the year of Christ 401—that is, while Saint Jerome was still alive and active. When the infant had emerged from the saving bath:

“Patricians, illustrious men, and every rank of dignity preceded him, together with the military formations, all carrying candles, so that one might have thought that stars were visible in the darkness.”

Moreover, Saint Paulinus of Nola, in the year of Christ 396, writes the following in his *Natalicius* 3, in honor of Saint Felix:

> Bright altars are crowned with dense lamps,  
> Fragrant lights burn in waxen reeds.  
> By night and day they shine. Thus night, and the splendor of day,  
> Gleam, and day itself, bright with heavenly honor,  
> Shines more brightly, multiplying its light through countless lamps.

Thus Paulinus wrote several years before Vigilantius; his words require no interpreter.

Saint Epiphanius likewise writes in his letter to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, that as he passed through a certain village he saw there “a burning lamp,” and, when he asked about it, learned that it “was a church.”

Saint Isidore of Seville recognized that candles were lit “when the Gospel was to be read or the sacrifice offered,” and he did not present this as something new, but as something already long customary. Venantius Fortunatus also, describing the feast of the Lord’s Ascension (*Book V, poem 5*), mentions burning candles and candelabra.

Even if we were to grant—and this should not be granted—that the custom of candles or lights for the entire sacrifice of the Mass was introduced only after Jerome’s time, it certainly would have been introduced for a commendable reason. If lights had previously been used at the Gospel to display joy, why could they not afterward be used for the entire Mass for the same reason?

But consider another and more important reason. The Mass presents the most sacred Supper of the Lord together with the sacrifice of the cross. Accordingly, you find there the equipment of a table: a chalice, a paten, cloths, and so forth, everything arranged in imitation and renewal of so great a work. The Savior’s final Supper was certainly not celebrated without lights. Who, then, would not approve the lights that we use in renewing that same Supper? Indeed, just as it was fitting to add them, so it would be unfitting to remove them, and it would be foolish to condemn them.

[Col. 1016D] We saw above, in chapter 16, how far the pride and fury of Luther had advanced when he did not blush to call the Offertory—and whatever had the appearance of an offering in the heavenly sacrifice of the Mass—an abomination, and decreed by an imperial edict that it should be entirely rejected together with the whole canon.

In this way he brought into contempt not merely the present Roman Church, and all the Churches of both West and East, which observe the rite of the sacred offering in their liturgies, as we have shown above with so many examples, but even the primitive Church itself.

How great that man’s inability to restrain himself and his rashness were, and how undeservedly some still enter the fray to defend his errors, can be taught us by the one holy Clement, Roman pontiff and martyr. He speaks in these words:

“We ought to perform in due order everything that the Lord commanded us to perform. He commanded that offerings and liturgies be completed at appointed times, and not done irregularly, but at fixed times and hours: ‘τάς τε προσφορὰς καὶ λειτουργίας ἐπιτελεῖσθαι’—‘that offerings and liturgies be performed.’ He also adds: ‘Οἱ οὖν τοῖς προστεταγμένοις καιροῖς ποιοῦντες τὰς προσφορὰς αὐτῶν, εὐπροσδεκτοί τε καὶ μακάριοι’—‘Those, therefore, who make their offerings at the appointed times are acceptable and blessed’” (Pope Clement I, Letter to the Corinthians, chapter 40).

When you hear Clement, consider that you are hearing the apostles themselves; for he flourished while the apostles were still alive and was their disciple.

Do not imagine here that the word “offerings” can mean gifts offered upon the altar for the use of the poor. The offerings here are nothing other than those by which the unbloody sacrifice was effected and offered to God. For this is what the Lord commanded to be performed, and at definite times and hours.

If we wish to listen to Johann Caspar Suicer, a Zurich Protestant—or Calvinist—professor, in his *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, the word *προσφορά*—“offering”—is “used of the sacred Supper.” Indeed, he should have said “of the sacrifice,” on account of which the offering is made; for the same offering does not pertain to the Supper as such.

He was afterward forced to admit this himself when he wrote that *προσφέρειν*, or “to offer,” when used absolutely, means *θυσίαν προσφέρειν*, that is, “to offer a sacrifice.”

Accordingly, in the sixth canon of the apostles you find this decree:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, after an offering has been made, does not communicate, let him state the reason.”

Learned men know how great is the antiquity of these canons, although in truth they cannot be attributed to the apostles.

Furthermore, we saw above, in chapter 18, that the holy Irenaeus and Cyprian proclaimed the offering and the true sacrifice in the Catholic Church. The character of these holy men is sufficiently known to the learned reader.

Tertullian likewise says of the devil, who imitates “the divine sacraments”:

“He marks his soldiers on their foreheads; he also celebrates the offering of bread” (Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 11).

Elsewhere he says:

“Women are not permitted to speak in the Church, nor to baptize, nor to offer [the sacrifice], nor to claim for themselves any part in a masculine function, much less in a priestly office” (the same, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 9).

The same point is confirmed by the canon of the celebrated First Council of Nicaea, held in the year of Christ 325:

“It has come to the attention of the holy and great council that in certain places and cities deacons distribute the grace of Holy Communion to presbyters; yet neither rule nor custom has handed down that those who do not have the authority to offer—‘τὴν ἐξουσίαν μὴ ἔχοντας προσφέρειν’—should receive the body of Christ from those who offer it” (Council of Nicaea I, canon 18).

Previously, at the Council of Arles in the year 314, it had also been forbidden “for deacons to offer”—understand, “the sacrifice” (Council of Arles, canon 15).

Who, then, would not shudder at Luther, who not only removed the Oblation and the Offertory from the Mass, but also dared to stain the primitive Church with the mark of “abomination” because it had used the Oblation in the sacred mysteries, and did not blush to defame the Council of Nicaea itself—whose dogmas, nevertheless, the universal Church throughout the world has always embraced with the highest veneration—as though those most holy Fathers had either rashly introduced or foolishly approved the liturgical offering, which had been practiced from the beginning of the Christian religion and therefore descended from Christ himself, its founder?

### The Response *Et cum spiritu tuo*

Cardinal Bona observed in his *Liturgics* that now “only the clergy or ministers respond in the Mass, ‘And with your spirit.’” Bingham seizes upon this as an occasion to insult the Roman Church, as though it had “entirely excluded the people from this part of divine worship,” and had therefore “fallen into error and depravity” (Bingham, *Origin of the Church*, Book XV, chapter 3).

He then adds:

“No other reason can be given for this than the magisterial authority of the Church, which assumes the right to prescribe to the people whatever it pleases, regardless of every rule or tradition of the ancient Church.”

But this accusation arose solely from the ignorance of a man who judged rashly, and it ought to have been reserved for Lutherans and Calvinists, who without any authority removed so much from the sacred liturgy, although it had been approved by the tradition of the ancient Church.

Let Bingham show me, if he can, any decree of the Church by which the people were forbidden to respond to the priest during sacred rites.

A single necessity gradually introduced this custom: in private Masses one cleric, and in solemn Masses the choir, responds on behalf of the people. The people ceased responding because they no longer understood the Latin language and were ignorant of the responses. It then became necessary, in a non-solemn Mass, to substitute one cleric who could supply the deficiency of the uneducated people and respond to the priest in their name. For whatever the cleric now responds, it is certain that he responds in the name of those standing by.

Even now, however, laypeople may perform the function of clerics by serving at private Masses. Laypeople who have been taught the rules of chant are not forbidden to join the clerical choir and respond. Indeed, in sacred confraternities the laymen alone respond, and nuns alone respond to the priest while Mass is sung.

Thus you can see how unjust Bingham’s accusation is. He goes on to make another claim, maintaining that “the words of Consecration were always pronounced in a loud voice,” and that the people responded “Amen.”

On this point he cites a novella of the Emperor Justinian, which commands that “the divine offering be made not in secret, but with such a voice as can be heard by the most faithful people, so that the people may add that holy Amen to the thanksgiving to God” (Justinian, Novella 137, chapter 6).

Bingham then adds:

“This makes a case for the Roman Church, because canon law is superior to civil law; otherwise so dreadful a violation of all divine and human laws would not have remained without punishment.”

The learned man was not ashamed to burst into so dreadful an outcry as to attribute to the Roman Church “the violation of all divine and human laws.” If Bingham despised the judgment of human beings when he was swept into this detestable slander, did he escape the judgment of God, who will certainly demand from him an account of why he dared to burden the Roman Church with so great an infamy?

As for his accusation against Cardinal Baronius, whom he says was indignant with Justinian on account of such a law, the only question to be put to him is whether emperors or bishops were placed in authority to govern the Church of God, which Christ acquired with his blood, and whether Saint Ambrose rightly said:

“The emperors are within the Church, not above the Church; to the emperor has been entrusted jurisdiction over public walls, not over sacred things” (Ambrose, Letter 20).

If the British writer should happen to confer this jurisdiction upon his king, he will show himself injurious both to divine law and to ecclesiastical discipline.

But what should be said about this rite? Cardinal Bona held the opinion that formerly “in the Western Church everyone heard the most holy and efficacious words by which Christ’s body is effected, and that afterward it was decreed that the canon should be recited in a subdued voice” (Bona, *On the Liturgy*, Book II, chapter 13).

He judged by conjecture that the ancient practice ceased in the tenth century of Christ. For this reason, some years ago people arose who would no longer recite the canon secretly, or who demanded that it be recited in a loud voice.

But Father Le Brun opposed those who desired this novelty with a very carefully prepared dissertation, and with many arguments and extensive learning maintained that secret recitation of the canon had always prevailed in the Western Churches and had never ceased.

It cannot, however, be denied that in all the Eastern Churches, as is clear from nearly all the Greek, Syriac, and Coptic liturgies, the words of consecration are heard by the people, who afterward respond, “Amen.”

Le Brun believes that this novelty was introduced into those regions after the recently mentioned law of Justinian, whereas previously the only rite observed there was the one always observed by the Westerners. I do not think that this has been sufficiently established. Whoever wants more information may consult his dissertation.

For the present, we must say that this rite is among those which are indifferent, and that whether it is performed in one way or another, it is supported by reason and authority. For this variation no controversy has ever arisen between Latins and Greeks, although they dispute about so many other matters; and it is right that each Church should retain its praiseworthy custom without contradiction from the other.

It must be established above all that no one may introduce a change here on his own authority. Even if the rites in question are ones that can be changed without harm to religion, the right to prescribe, retain, or alter them belongs only to the supreme pastors of the Church, not to us, according as their wisdom judges best.

### The Use of Latin in the Liturgy

Bingham did not omit to sing the old song of complaint that the Roman Church uses daily in sacred worship a language unknown to the people:

“This corruption,” he says, “is intolerable and contrary to the authority of the apostles, the rules of the ancient Church, the edification of the Christian people, and the common sense and reason of mankind.”

So he speaks, and indeed with cheeks puffed out.

But he failed entirely to reflect that there are countless customs and practices in the world concerning which we find, with Epictetus, two handles. If we look at them from one side, they appear useful and worthy of praise; if from the other, they are found to be useless, perhaps even deserving of condemnation.

Such is the condition of mortals that very often advantages and disadvantages arise from one and the same thing.

If Protestants commend their method—namely, the use in sacred worship of a language known to the people—they will certainly not lack arguments. But a person must be devoid of judgment to rush on this account into quarrels and insults against the Roman Church.

And what corruption can be charged against a Church that still retains the Latin language as it received it from the age of the apostles? Is it corruption to consider it a religious duty not to abandon what the ancient Church used?

Did the British nation act contrary to the common sense and reason of mankind when it preserved Latin in its sacred liturgies until the sixteenth century of Christ?

But, you will say, it would be better to depart from the ancient custom.

I hear you. But the Catholic Church too has reasons of her own: she should not change the institutions of venerable antiquity. You can observe the same thing among so many other Christian peoples who celebrate the liturgy either in Greek, Syriac, Ethiopic, Coptic, Armenian, or some other language, although they do not understand that ancient language.

Let the reader not expect me to report what learned men have said on this matter, for I have not undertaken to enter into every controversy relating to the sacred liturgy.

It is enough to observe that majesty is imparted to sacred things by the Latin language in which these rites were instituted; that the devotion of Catholic peoples does not grow cold even if they do not understand the Latin words or if the priest prays in secret; and that the Church permits the sacred prayers to be supplied in translation into the vernacular for those who desire to understand them.

For the same reason I refrain from reopening the question which Nicholas Cabasilas, a Greek writer, and others of his nation raised against the Latins. They maintained that the consecration of the gifts is effected not by the words of the Lord, but by the invocation of the Holy Spirit—that is, by the prayer which follows those same words in the various liturgies of the Easterners.

It is enough that I warned the reader about this matter in chapter 10. We should not be hostile to the Greeks, nor the Greeks to us, on account of this difference of rite, as Cardinal Bona has shown (*Book II of the Liturgy*, chapter 13), along with Renaudot (*Collection of Liturgies*), Martène (*On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, Book I, chapter 4, article 8), and especially Pierre Le Brun (*Explanation of the Mass*, vol. IV), who prepared a proper dissertation on this very subject and showed that the different customs of Westerners and Easterners concerning this matter do not conflict with one another.

As for the Roman liturgy, since the invocation or prayers, as I observed above, precede, and the efficacious words of Christ follow, no doubt remains that the consecration is then complete and perfected, and that the subsequent elevation and adoration of the Lord’s body and blood were legitimately instituted.

I said that the invocation precedes. It is performed not only when God is asked to make the offering for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord, and so forth, but also before the washing of the hands, when the priest says:

“Come, almighty and eternal God, sanctifier, and bless this sacrifice prepared for your holy name.”

In the Mass of the Mozarabs the same invocation occurs, and it is directed to the Holy Spirit. They say:

“Come, Holy Spirit, Sanctifier; sanctify this sacrifice prepared from my hands for you.”

In the most ancient of all the Sacramentaries, the Leonine, which we discussed above, the following prayer is found in the thirtieth Mass, in the month of July:

“Send, Lord, we ask, the Holy Spirit, who may make these gifts now present our sacrament for us, and purify our hearts for receiving it.”

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Concerning Other Rites of the Roman Mass, Unjustly Attacked by Protestants

The eminent Cardinal Bona (*Book I of the Liturgy*, chapter 23, § 11) observed learnedly and sincerely that the wafers now used in the Church arose only after the year one thousand from Christ’s birth. They are thin and formed to the shape and approximate size of a single coin, whereas formerly they were much larger.

From this Bingham the Englishman took occasion to declaim against the rite, as though the bread to be offered at the altar “had fallen into such an extreme state that it had almost lost the nature of a sacramental element, with something that could scarcely be called bread substituted for the common element” (Bingham, *Origin of the Church*, Book XV, chapter 2, §§ 5–6).

But who would fail to recognize in this the utmost itch for quibbling? A foolish declaimer would be one who dared to deny that the wafers, or hosts, which we now use are true and natural bread.

He would also be deranged if he derived a greater or lesser efficacy of the heavenly sacrament from the greater or smaller size of the bread.

Among the homilies published under the name of Eusebius of Gaul, in the fifth homily on Easter—which is attributed to Saint Isidore in manuscripts—we read:

“The invisible priest converts visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood by his word, through a hidden power.”

It then adds:

“The sacred reception of the Eucharist consists not in quantity but in power. What is the body, when distributed by the priest, is as much in the small portion as it is known to be in the whole.”

Certainly, in ancient times a large morsel was not thrust into the mouths of the faithful. Any fragment of the consecrated bread was sufficient, because Christians in former times believed that they received the whole body of Christ there no less than in larger fragments.

Bingham constructs another criticism, although he admits that it concerns “a minor matter” (the same, same work, chapter 3, § 35). He claims that formerly, after consecration, the bread was broken and divided into many portions for distribution to the faithful, whereas now in the Roman Church “a single wafer alone is divided into three particles, of which none is given out, merely so that the shadow of the ancient custom may be retained.”

He calls this practice “a departure from the simplicity of the ancient Church,” and indeed “blameworthy.”

He himself gives the reasons—reasonable ones—which our writers have offered for this minor change. He does not dare refute them, and nevertheless continues to chatter.

The change was made through a new arrangement to guard against the danger of the many fragments that could not be avoided in the ancient breaking of the bread. It is clear, however, that in such minor matters the Church has the power to vary the practice as she judges best.

Before consecration, as is probably believed, our Lord blessed and broke the bread. Nevertheless, the Church has always been accustomed to break it after consecration. How much more, then, was it permitted to break the priestly host into only three portions, to consecrate the bread previously divided into so many particles or wafers, and afterward distribute them to the faithful, removing, as far as possible, the inconvenience caused by fragments?

But let us proceed to more serious matters. There are some Protestants, and among them especially Bingham (Book XV, chap. 3, § 25), who thought they had discovered in the Roman canon certain statements contradictory to the doctrine of transubstantiation and the real presence of the Lord’s body and blood after the consecration of the gifts. Thus, it is written there:

“Upon which may you deign to look with a favorable and serene countenance and to accept them, just as you deigned to accept the gifts of your just servant Abel, and the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and that which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you: a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.”

To this Bingham adds:

“For how can the real body and blood of Christ be called these gifts? Or how can they be compared with the sacrifice of Abel, who offered animals? How can anyone pray—without injury to the Son of God—that God may permit the sacrifice of his only Son to be acceptable to him, just as Abel’s sacrifice was?” [Col. 1022B–C]

For this reason, he thinks that these words once had a sound meaning, when they were pronounced over bread and wine in order to consecrate them as a memorial and symbol of the Lord’s body; but now, as he continues, “they are absurd and contrary to the primitive intention.”

Because Bingham viewed these matters through Calvinist eyes, he failed to see what he ought to have seen. We call the Eucharistic sacrament “gifts” and “things given,” because the heavenly victim contained therein is an incomparable benefit bestowed upon us by God. We also acknowledge as a gift from God, the giver of every good thing, the bread and wine themselves, without which the sacrifice of the New Law could not be accomplished.

But what are these “gifts” and “things given” when the priest pronounces these words? They are gifts transformed into a divine reality: what before the words of consecration was bread and wine has now become the body and blood of the Lord. Why did Bingham not read, or carefully consider, the words immediately preceding them, in which the priest says in his own name and that of the people:

“We offer to your most excellent Majesty, from your gifts and things given, a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation. Upon which may you deign to look with a favorable countenance, etc.”?

Therefore it is no longer earthly bread, but the holy bread of eternal life, by which one flesh and the body of the Lord are given. Is there any Protestant who would suppose that this expression refers to the bread by which our bodies are nourished, when Jesus himself has taught us its true meaning in explicit words, saying: “I am the living bread” (John 6:48)? [Col. 1023A] This is expressed even more forcefully by the addition “eternal.” Material bread cannot give this life; only that divine bread can give it—that is, the body of the Lord Christ, of which he himself says: “Whoever eats this bread will live forever.”

The truth concerning Christ’s blood is likewise confirmed. The sacred table gives it to us under the appearances of wine, not figuratively but truly, when we see the chalice called “the chalice of everlasting salvation,” in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.”

This, then, is what the gifts are after consecration. To recognize this, nothing more is required than a mind freed from corrupt affections and prejudices.

Let us proceed to Bingham’s second question. [Col. 1023B] He found no comparison between the sacrifices of Abel, Abraham, and Melchizedek and the unbloody sacrifice of the altar, as Catholics understand it. Bingham should have been taught that the holy Fathers held that the sacrifices of the patriarchs, which pleased God in the Old Testament, pleased him because they prefigured the only-begotten Son of God, who was later to become a victim for us; and that those sacrifices were figures of the most excellent sacrifice of the cross and of the altar.

But leaving this consideration aside, two things must be considered in the present matter: the sacrifice and the thing sacrificed—that is, the one who performs the sacrifice and the victim offered to God. The Church never dreamed of asking God to accept that victim, namely, the body and blood of his Son, since no Christian has ever doubted that it is always supremely acceptable to his divine Father. Rather, she asks that the sacrifice offered by unworthy and sinful persons may please him; she asks that he receive with a gracious countenance the immaculate victim offered by those who present their vows and prayers.

In the preceding prayers of the same Roman Mass we pray:

“May our sacrifice today be made in your sight in such a way that it may please you, Lord God.”

“And may it become an acceptable sacrifice before God the almighty Father.”

Likewise, in the Liturgy of Saint Basil, we read:

“God, giver of grace, grant us that our sacrifice may be acceptable before you.”

Since, then, we have examples of God’s receiving with a gracious countenance certain sacrifices of the ancient Law, which prefigured the far more excellent sacrifice of the New Law, the Church uses them so that we too, although unequal and unworthy, may obtain what holy men secured through their offerings by their purity, faith, and devout disposition. [Col. 1023C–D]

The words that follow must likewise be understood in relation to this same intention, when the priest asks God to command that these offerings be carried by the hands of his holy angel into the presence of his divine Majesty. Bingham says:

“How can Christ, who sits at the right hand of the Father, need the ministry of angels to be carried to the Father upon the heavenly altar?”

Our Lord certainly has no need of such ministry. Chrysostom says of him:

“He who sits above with the Father is handled by everyone’s hands at that very moment, and gives himself to those who wish to receive him” (Chrysostom, Book III on the Priesthood).

But even if the Church’s meaning were what Bingham supposes, nothing unworthy of the majesty of the Son of God would follow if his most sacred body were said to be carried by angels from the earthly altar to the heavenly altar. For Christ exists in the sacrament bearing the appearance of a sacrificed victim, although he is always alive; and he presents himself to the Father for us as he hung upon the cross, humbled even unto death.

It is better, however, to understand the expression “command that these things be carried” in this way: the Church desires nothing other than that to the heavenly altar mentioned in the Apocalypse—or to the heavenly throne of God and the sanctuary of his divinity—the prayers, vows, and offering, that is, the sacrifice then being offered to God, may be conveyed by the angel who presides over the prayers of the faithful living and carries them to the Father, as is likewise read in the Apocalypse.

[Col. 1024B] For it cannot be supposed that the Church desires the body and blood of Christ actually to be carried from the altar into heaven, or from a lower place to a higher one, since this could not happen without a miracle, and indeed an everlasting one; whereas the heavenly gifts are seen every day not to be removed from the earthly altar.

We learn that this is the mind of the Church from the other liturgies, both Latin and Eastern, where the first offering is made of bread and wine. In the Roman rite we beseech God that the wine offered, still unconsecrated—that is, the chalice—may ascend into the presence of his divine Majesty with the odor of sweetness.

In the Liturgy of Saint Basil, as edited by Goar, we read:

“May we be worthy to offer you this rational and unbloody sacrifice for our sins and the people’s errors; and, having received it upon your holy, spiritual, and intellectual altar as an odor of sweetness, in return grant us the grace of your Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 1024C] We do not therefore ask that the bread and wine offered be physically raised by a miracle to the supercelestial altar, to the spiritual altar which, as other liturgies say, is higher than the heavens. Rather, we ask that the sacrifice to be performed—which embraces the prayers and hope of forgiveness conceived by those who offer it and depends upon their action—be presented in heaven before the divine Father.

For it is customary in the Church to contemplate God, although he is omnipresent, as seated and reigning especially upon the throne of his glory and the seat of his majesty. Thus, when the priest burns incense to God, he asks that it may ascend to God. In the Greek Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, edited by Goar, and in others that I pass over, incense is offered with the words:

“Receive, Lord, upon your holy, supercelestial, and spiritual altar, etc.” [Col. 1024D]

Certainly no one believes that the smoke and odor of incense will penetrate all the way to heaven. Rather, we hope that the prayers and affections of the priest and people, who offer worship to God through this sign, will reach there.

Accordingly, in the prayer mentioned above, the Church does not ask that the divine victim present on the altar be carried into heaven. She asks only, with Daniel, that our sacrifice may be made in the sight of God and please him (Daniel 3:40)—that is, that our prayer, action, and offering may be conveyed to God, and that what is performed on the earthly altar may be completed in heaven before God’s presence. Then, through the excellence of the heavenly victim and the acceptance of our sacrifice, every blessing may descend upon us.

The words that follow confirm this. [Col. 1025A] We desire our vows to ascend to God, so that all who have received the most holy body and blood of your Son by partaking of this altar may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.

The body and blood of the Lord are on the altar, and we must receive them from it. But his divine Father must be asked to receive mercifully the action of sinful human beings who offer so holy a victim. Only then may we hope that every heavenly blessing and grace will come to us from this heavenly banquet and sacrifice.

Finally, before the Lord’s Prayer, the canon contains these words:

“Through him”—that is, through Christ the Lord—“you always create, sanctify, enliven, bless, and bestow upon us all these good things, Lord.”

Here too Bingham and his followers become entangled. “By what manner of speech,” he asks, “can Christ be called ‘all these good things’? And indeed good things which God always creates, sanctifies, blesses, and bestows? Does God create, sanctify, enliven, and bless God Christ through Jesus Christ?”

Thus he constructs in his own mind a phantom that never existed in reality. These words are not spoken of Christ present in the sacrament; it would be exceedingly incongruous for the expression “all these things” to signify the Lord Christ. Rather, this expression signifies all the good things that divine mercy creates daily for our use; or merely the fruits of the earth, which on a certain day of the year were blessed with these words; or finally the bread and wine by which the sacrifice is accomplished.

God continually creates and produces these things each year through Jesus Christ his Son for our benefit. This benefit is exceedingly great, since these created things serve us not only for life but also for the greatest of all mysteries in the Church of God, and without them the ineffable sacrifice of the altar cannot be accomplished.

Afterward the Lord increases this benefit wonderfully, sanctifying the bread and wine and separating them from common use, and elevating them to such dignity that they can become the sacrament of his immaculate body and blood. This benefit rises still higher when Christ, through his words, gives life to the bread itself.

Bread and wine are inanimate things. How are they enlivened and given life? In no other way or for any other reason than through the omnipotence of God, who “transforms and trans-elementates” the gifts themselves into the body and blood of his Son, united with soul and divinity, as the holy Fathers and liturgies testify. He does so in the same way in which he enlivened Moses’ rod by turning it into a serpent; for the same Fathers also use this example to establish the real transformation of the gifts in the sacrament of the altar.

Thus what was previously earthly bread becomes that bread which says of itself: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” God blesses this bread, once it has been given life, so that through it every heavenly blessing and grace may at last be poured out upon his faithful communicants.

If Bingham had paid attention to these matters, he would have refrained from that ridiculous question.

From these observations you may also understand the words mentioned shortly before, which precede the consecration in the canon, when the priest says after the consecration:

“We offer to your most excellent Majesty from your gifts and things given a pure victim, etc., the holy bread of eternal life.”

The Greeks, in the Divine Mass attributed to Chrysostom, likewise say after the words of consecration:

“Your own gifts, from your own, we offer to you in all things and through all things”—

that is, the body and blood of your Son, formed from bread and wine, your creatures.

I do not know for what purpose the distinguished Leibniz noted in his *Miscellanies* that, according to Book XI of Apuleius’ *Metamorphoses*, after the rites of Isis had been completed the people were dismissed with the words: “The people’s dismissal.”

If he wishes to criticize us as though our people had received this rite from pagan initiates, the reader should be directed to Pamelius and the eminent Bona, who previously examined this very passage of Apuleius and also made it clear that this was an ancient Roman custom: whenever the people assembled for sacred rites or for a public assembly, they were dismissed at the end with a set formula.

Virgil writes:

“He purified the men and spoke the final words.”

That is, *Ilicet*, meaning “You may go,” as Servius explains.

The Senate, moreover, was dismissed with these words:

“We do not detain you, Conscript Fathers.”

The formula for dismissing the assembly was:

“If it pleases you, depart, Quirites.”

Tertullian and Cyprian likewise testify that the Christian people of their age were dismissed in this manner.

What, I ask, is there here that calls for criticism?

## CHAPTER XXII. On the invocation and commemoration of saints in the liturgy, disapproved or condemned by Protestants.

[Col. 1026C]

Learned persons know that the invocation of holy men departed from this life was condemned in the Augsburg Confession of the Lutherans. The remaining Protestants have joined in the same opinion. It is not my task to enter into this celebrated controversy, since it has been copiously treated by so many defenders of the Catholic Church, and recently by that most learned man John Chrysostom Trombelli, Bolognese abbot of the Regular Canons of the Savior, who, treating of the cult of the saints, seems above all others to have exhausted this subject in various books. Let me say a few things relevant to the present matter.

How ancient in the Church of God it is to venerate the saints translated to their heavenly country and to commend ourselves to their prayers is plainly demonstrated by the agreement of all the liturgies.
