What the Roman Church and the other churches of the West think concerning those blessed citizens of paradise, all the Eastern churches too, though divided from us and from one another for so many centuries, think: both honoring their memory on feast days and fleeing to their protection. This custom displeases Protestants, as though we inflicted an injury upon Christ, the Mediator of God and men. Bingham himself, the Englishman, as we said above, by no means approves of our invoking the saints in the general confession before Mass, that they may pray for us. He then endeavors to cavil at the commemoration of the saints made after the consecration in the Mass (Book XV, chap. 3, § 16), as though the ancient Church prayed to God for them just as for the other departed faithful, and not that they might pray to God for the living.

But would that Protestants more diligently investigated, and more fairly weighed, the teaching of the Catholic Church concerning the saints, which they have expressed in the Council of Trent. Namely: “It is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them, and, in order to obtain benefits from God through His Son Jesus our Lord, who alone is our Redeemer (and Savior), to have recourse to their prayers, help, and assistance” (Council of Trent, sess. 25). From this you have that we acknowledge and expect from God alone, the giver, whatever good and graces flow to us or are hoped for by us. You further learn that hope of obtaining is founded upon Christ the Lord; for even the saints in heaven pray to God through our Mediator. And just as, even by the confession of Protestants themselves, it is good and useful for us to commend ourselves to the prayers of living saints, and no injury is thereby inflicted upon Christ, so nothing is detracted from the dignity of our most holy Mediator if we have recourse to the prayers of the saints reigning with him in heaven. Consult the liturgy, therefore; there you will immediately understand the Church’s mind concerning the cult and invocation of the saints.

Accordingly, we honor and venerate the saints with religious worship; we celebrate feast days in their memory, and we also offer sacrifice in their honor—but above all so that God may be honored and glorified in them, by whose grace and gifts they lived a holy life or endured torments and death for Christ, and were made worthy of heavenly blessedness. In [Col. 1027C] the Leonine Sacramentary this preface occurs: “Truly worthy. For we admire, O Lord, your mighty works and your victories whenever the festivals of these days are celebrated in your Church, days which the conspicuous triumphs of your confessors and martyrs have consecrated for faithful peoples to perpetual remembrance and solemn joy.” In another one we read: “Truly worthy. You are wondrous in the power not only of your martyrs but also of your confessors.” Take another: “Truly worthy. For all your saints praise and bless you, to whom you have granted strength in confession and victory in suffering.” Below occurs another preface: “Truly worthy. For you grant us, while we venerate the triumphs of the blessed martyrs on the days which they marked with their blood, always to exult in your power and to rejoice, O Lord, in your honor.” Then another: “Truly worthy. Because you are glorious in the saints, to whom you have granted victory both in persecution and in suffering.” Many other passages occur there agreeing with the same sense.

Similar things are found in the Gelasian Sacramentary. Let us select a few. On the day before the Ides of June: “For the venerable blood of the saints Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius, we solemnly immolate offerings to you, O Lord, recounting your wonders, through whom such a victory was brought to completion.” On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July: “As gifts offered for the saints testify to the power of divine glory, so may they bestow upon us, O Lord, the effect of your salvation.” On the sixth day before the Kalends of July: “We present to your altars, O Lord, victims of propitiation, honoring your power in the suffering of your saints.” On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September: “May the precious merits of the holy martyr Agapitus protect us, O Lord, in which we proclaim the works of your Majesty,” etc. Nor do you find a dissimilar profession of doctrine in the Gregorian Sacramentary. On the Nones of February: “O God, who among the other miracles of your power granted victory in martyrdom even to the frail sex,” etc. On the fifth day before the Kalends of September: “O God, who strengthened your blessed martyr Hermes by the power of constancy,” etc. More is found in the Gothic Sacramentary and in the Missal of the Franks, but I do not wish to wander further. These things suffice for anyone to understand that those who condemn us because we glorify God in his saints and honor his gifts and triumphs in the blessed citizens of heaven are themselves to be condemned.

[Col. 1028B] We also flee to the protection of the saints, commending ourselves to their prayers. But in what manner? The sacred liturgy will tell you. They can confer nothing upon us. We ask God alone to pour out his benefits upon us through their prayers and intercession. We also believe that their very petitions can have efficacy only if they are presented and commended to the divine Father through Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and men. Therefore it is the Church’s custom to conclude with the usual formula the prayers which we address to God on their solemnities, as also on other occasions: “Through the Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. We cannot prevent Protestants from disapproving such recourse to the saints who have attained the kingdom of heaven, as an invention of pious persons resting on no support of sacred Scripture. Is that so? Yet we point out traces of this doctrine in the Apocalypse, where the prayers, προσευχαί, of the saints reigning with Christ in heaven are mentioned—saints who surely have no need to pray for themselves—and in the Second Epistle of Peter (II Pet. I, 15), and in the Second Book of Maccabees (II Macc. XIV, 11). We then trace the antiquity of this custom back almost to the times of the apostles, adducing as witnesses Irenaeus, Origen, Cyprian, and then the other Fathers of the fourth and fifth centuries. If they wish to denounce these competent witnesses as patrons of superstition or guilty of gross ignorance, and at the same time brand the primitive Church with apostasy, they do not lack rashness; especially after it has been clearly demonstrated that the cult and invocation of saints in no way impairs the holiness and teaching of the Christian religion.

But here, as I indicated above, the British Bingham rises up, wishing to persuade us that in the Church of earlier centuries there was also a custom of praying to God for the saints. He thinks that he can infer this from the Apostolic Constitutions (Book VIII, chap. 12), where after the consecration the priest says: “We offer to you for all the saints who have pleased you from the beginning of the world—patriarchs, prophets, righteous men, apostles,” etc., “laypeople, and all whose names you know.” He then adds: “That it was the universal practice of the Church to pray for all without exception is clear from the concordant testimony of all ecclesiastical writers.”

[Col. 1029A] Certainly, we answer, for all—but with a different intention on the Church’s part. Bingham himself does not dare deny this below, when he writes: “For martyrs they offered prayers, praises, and thanksgivings; for others, prayers principally.” Yet notwithstanding this, he later endeavors to show that the faithful once prayed “for all saints, not excluding the Virgin Mary herself,” as though they too needed the prayers of the living before God; and for this purpose he distorts certain words of the ancients. But, as we observed earlier, it was this writer’s custom, no less than that of others anxious about the honor of their own sect rather than the care of truth, not to seek the light that meets every eye, but to seek out only darkness, by whose aid they may, if possible, show that light is lacking there.

I ask: Did Bingham read, or did he not, what the same author of the Apostolic Constitutions has in the same book, where he gives a prayer for the dead? There we read: “Place him in the bosom of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all who have pleased you from the beginning of the world, where there is no sadness, pain, or groaning, but a peaceful place of the godly, and likewise the land of the upright and of those who therein behold the glory of your Christ” (ibid., chap. 41). Thus that author recognized two orders of the departed: those, namely, who have already attained their country, or paradise, where they see the glory of Christ seated at the right hand of the Father; and those who are still on the way and groan while excluded from paradise. Indeed, the author himself had previously distinguished these deceased persons; for the words cited by Bingham, namely, “We offer to you,” etc., concern an offering made to God in honor of the saints. Then in the following chapter a prayer is given for the faithful after the divine offering, and among other things it says: “For those who have fallen asleep in the faith, let us pray.” Here are the remaining departed faithful, distinguished from the saints already received into heaven, for whom prayers must be poured out to God that they may be released from sins. Whether Bingham has acted here in good faith, let the readers judge.

Yet he proceeds further, later writing: “Augustine indeed maintains a peculiar opinion in this matter of prayers for the dead. For he holds that one should not pray for martyrs in the same way as for other men, because they were admitted to the enjoyment of heavenly blessedness immediately after death.” Do you hear, “a peculiar opinion”? On the contrary, except for a few Millenarians, concerning whom I have dealt at length in the treatise on Paradise, this has always been the teaching of the Catholic Church; and Bingham, in being ignorant of this or pretending not to know it, most shamefully deceives his people. Who, unless he is senseless, would think that those who have died and have already been received into the heavenly country on account of their piety still need our prayers? Indeed, from her very beginning the Church has been accustomed to invoke them, that they may entreat God for us.

The things Bingham adds are absurd, namely, that in an old Greek and Latin edition of the Gregorian Sacramentary it is found written: “Remember, O Lord, all your servants, male and female, who have gone before us,” etc. “But in later,” as he adds, “reformed missals they changed it thus: ‘Remember, O Lord, your servants, male and female, N. and N., who have gone before,’ etc., lest they seem to pray for saints as well as for others who were in purgatory.” From this, I hope, readers will see that I did not unjustly apply above to Protestant polemical writers the words of Isaiah and the Apostle: “You will hear with your ears and not understand; and seeing you will see and not perceive.” Where, pray, were Bingham’s eyes when he wrote this? I pass over our denial of the change alleged by him; for manuscripts of the Gregorian Sacramentary remain, written almost a thousand years ago, in which the same words occur as are read in the reformed Missals. But what ought to have shamed Bingham: do not these words still follow in the Roman Missals? [Col. 1030B] “To them, O Lord, and to ALL who rest in Christ, grant, we beseech you, a place of refreshment, light, and peace”—words which everyone sees are said only for the departed who have not yet been endowed with heavenly glory.

Observe in passing, I ask, the venerable antiquity and doctrine of the Roman Liturgy; for there is the formula which the Church used in Tertullian’s age when praying for the dead. For indeed—these are Tertullian’s own words—“she prays also for his soul and asks refreshment for him” (Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, chap. 10). What is astonishing is that Bingham not only read, but copied word for word, the passage of the very Missal which we now use; and nevertheless, seeing that “all who rest in Christ,” he did not perceive that the imagined change was ridiculous, “lest we seem to pray for saints also.”

What is more, I do not know how he can escape the charge of bad faith when he suppresses the following words of the Roman canon, namely: “To us also, your sinful servants, hoping in the multitude of your mercies, deign to grant some share and fellowship with your holy apostles and martyrs, with John, Stephen,” etc., “and with all your saints; into whose company, we beseech you, admit us, not weighing our merits, but generously granting pardon.” Here you have the midday sun. For all faithful persons who have died in the peace of Christ and the Church and have now been released from the earthly prison, we ask from God a place of refreshment and forgiveness. Afterwards, speaking of the saints who have already attained the kingdom of heaven, we pray that merciful God may grant us fellowship and communion with them.

But Bingham does not yet lose heart and observes from Hincmar, a writer of the ninth century, that when the feast of Pope Saint Leo recurred, the prayer in the Roman Sacramentary was then framed in these words: “Grant us, O Lord, that this offering may benefit the soul of your servant Leo, through whom you granted, by immolating, the sins of the whole world to be remitted.” But, says Bingham, in more recent Sacramentaries it was changed thus: “Grant us, we beseech you, O Lord, that through the intercession of blessed Leo this offering may benefit us.” The reader may observe that not only is this prayer, as Hincmar read it, found on the fourth day before the Kalends of July in the most ancient Gregorian Sacramentary to be published below, but also that on the fourth day before the Ides of March the prayer on the feast of Pope Saint Gregory was expressed in precisely the same words.

[Col. 1031A] But what, pray, did that *prosit* (“may benefit”) formerly mean? Nothing other than “may benefit for honor”; for even now in the received liturgy we say: “Receive, O Holy Trinity, this offering which we offer to you,” etc., “and in honor of blessed Mary,” etc., “and of all the saints, that it may avail them for honor and us for salvation, and that they may deign to intercede for us in heaven,” etc. And that this, and no other, was the Church’s meaning is plainly inferred from two other prayers joined to it. In one of them we read: “O God, who have made blessed Leo the pontiff equal to the merits of your saints,” etc.; and in the other: “O God, who have bestowed the rewards of eternal blessedness upon the soul of your servant Leo” (and likewise Gregory), etc. Do you suppose that the Roman Church was so forgetful of herself that by her prayers she wished to assist in attaining eternal blessedness that pontiff whom she acknowledges already to have obtained possession of that great reward?

Nor should it be omitted that some Protestants have been accustomed, not only in their sermons but also in public books, to disparage the sacrifice of the Mass as a theatrical spectacle because of its many “The Lord be with you”s, genuflections, crosses, gestures, as they call them, and what not. Yet such criticism sufficiently reveals what an embittered mind, corrupted by turbulent passions, can do in them, when without any just reason and by mere arbitrariness they condemn with mockery what so many wise men composing the Catholic commonwealth, indeed other nations that have embraced the faith of Christ, approve as they perform the sacrifice from the Church’s earliest centuries with not a few rites devised for veneration of the mysteries. The eyes of enemies are faithless judges.

I remember hearing a Calvinist insult our priests as though they treated the Mass as a comic spectacle. I asked why he gave vent to this harsh criticism. “Because,” he replied, “with these very eyes I saw them carrying to the altar a box for taking snuff while they performed the sacred rites.” Then I said: “Alas! Pray tell, who ever persuaded you that any Catholic priest had fallen into such madness and irreverence toward the divine mysteries? It is perfectly clear that the box you saw contained not snuff but spectacles, which elderly priests commonly use to restore their failing eyesight.”

[Col. 1031D] Nevertheless, it can happen that through inexperience, haste, or languishing devotion, some priests handle the sacred mysteries improperly, whence contempt rather than reverence may be aroused in ill-disposed or insufficiently devout spectators. But the blame must be laid upon them, not upon the mysteries and rites themselves; and canons and all pious Catholic writers thunder with one voice against ministers of this kind, who do not build up but destroy. Therefore heterodox persons will find nothing theatrical, nothing mimetic, in the Mass of Catholics, provided that they guard themselves against the snares of inward hatred conceived against us. Certainly they have nothing to object to in its many prayers, readings both of the Old and New Testament, antiphons, gradual, etc., since these were instituted to implore God’s mercy and the other benefits to be expected from the one Father of mercies through our Lord Jesus Christ, and most of them are drawn from the divine Scriptures.

Hands joined before the breast or modestly raised accord with humility of heart and the disposition of those who pray. We have a copious witness to this most ancient custom—besides examples drawn from sacred Scripture—in Tertullian, who writes: “But by worshipping with modesty and humility, we more commend our prayers to God, with not even our HANDS raised too high, but RAISED MODERATELY AND PROPERLY” (Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chap. 17). The extension of the hands over the offerings, which in antiquity occupied much space on the altar, when we say, “Therefore this offering,” etc., is an imitation of the priests of the old Law, who, as is found in Leviticus, placed a hand upon the head of the victim (Lev. IV, 4).

The moving of the Missal to the other side of the altar in private Masses is believed by seekers after mysteries to contain mystical reasons. But it is nothing other than a certain imitation of the solemn Mass. Most Christian churches of old faced east. The ambo, or pulpit, was situated on the north side. After the readings had been recited on the south side, the deacon, having asked leave of the bishop, ascended the ambo, and there, turning toward the people, chanted the Gospel. From this arose in private Masses the custom of carrying the Missal to the other side of the altar, and likewise the custom by which the priest recites the Gospel not facing straight ahead, but with his face turned somewhat toward the people. [Col. 1032C]

Yet incense is used in solemn services.

That is so. This practice was abolished by the new enemies of the ancient rites and of the Church herself. But would they dare devise something theatrical in this rite? The Jews also used incense in worship at God’s command. Christians likewise learned the same practice from the Apocalypse, for an angel stood before the altar holding a golden censer, and “there were given unto him much incense,” etc. “And the smoke of the incense ascended from the prayers of the saints out of the angel’s hand before God” (Rev. 8:3). No learned person denies that the very ancient canons circulated under the name of the Apostles. There incense, or *thymiama*, is said to be offered “at the time of the sacred oblation” (*Apostolic Canons*, ch. 3). Therefore, as we saw above, Saint Ambrose reports that this was customary in the divine sacrifice in the fourth century of Christ, writing: “And would that, while we too burn incense upon the altars and bring forward the sacrifice, an angel might stand beside us” (Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel of Luke*, bk. 1, ch. 28), etc. Eusebius also mentions the same rite (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, bk. 1).

Many signs of the cross are likewise used by priests in the sacred liturgy, both over the offerings and over the very body and blood of the Lord. Saint Augustine had already given this warning concerning the sign of the Cross: “Unless it is applied to the foreheads of believers, or to the water itself by which they are regenerated, or to the oil with which they are anointed in chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these things is rightly accomplished” (Augustine, *Tractate 118 on John*).

From the time when Charles—truly “the Great”—in the eighth and following centuries of Christ roused his people to the study of letters, which had long been neglected, certain learned men undertook to explain and elucidate the divine Offices: Alcuin, Amalarius, Florus, Agobard, Walafrid Strabo, and others. It is remarkable how many allegories and mysteries they found in all manner of sacred rites. And indeed mystical meanings are not absent from them; most of those produced by these men, however—if I may say so—are fantasies of pious minds, easily dissolved into light air.

As for the very signs of the cross, the interpretation of the most learned Father Lebrun seems especially worthy of praise, in these words:

> “Before the consecration, these signs are used to obtain the graces that can be expected only through the merits of the cross of Christ the Lord. After the consecration, however, we merely offer. Thus, we make the signs of the cross at that point for no other purpose than to show that the gifts of the altar have already been changed into the Lord’s body. The Church omits nothing that might impress upon the hearts of priests and assistants that the sacrifice of the altar is the same as the sacrifice of the cross, and that Christ is present there as one sacrificed upon the cross” (Lebrun, *Literal Explanation of the Mass*, vol. 1, p. 3, art. 11).

We derive the use of the salutation—whether “The Lord be with you” or “Peace be with you”—from the books of divine Scripture. Uranius, a contemporary author, mentions it in his *Life of Saint Paulinus*, bishop who was called to the heavenly homeland in the year 431. There, writing about Saint John of Naples, he says: “He proceeded to the church, and after ascending the tribunal he greeted the people according to custom; and, having been greeted in return by the people, he gave the prayer.” That is, the people replied, “And with your spirit”; “may the Lord be [with you]” is understood.

Having before his eyes the Roman Order, composed long before the year 800 after the birth of Christ, Amalarius wrote in the ninth century:

> “When we say, ‘Peace be with you’—or rather, ‘Peace to you’—or ‘The Lord be with you,’ which is a salutation, we turn toward the people” (bk. 3, ch. 9).

And indeed at that time the priest turned toward the people. But in ancient times no turning was necessary for those who celebrated the sacred rites not at the front but at the rear of the altar, always facing the people. Traces of this practice still remain in certain places, especially at Rome in the patriarchal and other very ancient churches.

Certainly some deformity may sometimes enter this rite through the ministers’ defects, either because the turnings are performed by a rapid revolution of the body, like the movements of dancers, or because priests, whose eyes they are then commanded to keep lowered, cast them openly upon the faces of those standing around. But who does not see that this happens contrary to the Church’s intention and to the rules prescribed by her? The Ambrosian Church is free from such danger: except at the Gospel of the solemn Mass, it always recites or chants “The Lord be with you” facing the altar.

Indeed, even in the Roman rite the same salutation is performed four times without any turning of the body: before approaching the altar, before the Gospel in private Masses, before the Preface, and before the Gospel of John at the end of Mass. Why priests should then refrain from the same turning is asked by Amalarius, Durandus, and others; but they seem to me to bring forward foolish reasons. In any case, whether the turning takes place or not, provided that what the Rituals prescribe is observed, it is certain that nothing occurs which leaves room for censure.

Whoever would condemn singing in sacred worship would, I think, suffer from a lack of judgment, since he would oppose the Apostle, who wrote to the Ephesians: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord”—that is, with the heart consenting to the singing. You may see the same instruction repeated to the Colossians (Col. 3:16). Our Lord himself concluded the sacred Supper after singing a hymn. A hymn, by its very institution, requires singing.

That such a practice was already in use in the earliest centuries is attested by Tertullian when he describes sacred banquets, saying:

> “Each person is invited to sing publicly to God from the Holy Scriptures, or from his own ability, as he can” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39).

These words indicate that the faithful were then also permitted to use new hymns and songs.

Nor are musical instruments unfitting in sacred worship; we are instructed by the example of the Old Testament, and the royal Psalmist himself demonstrates this in more than one place. But would that no abuses or excesses were ever found in the lawful and praiseworthy use of sacred music! The Council of Trent warned that these must be avoided (Sess. 22, ch. 8), and the most devout Catholic writers have long lamented and condemned their intrusion.

Everyone should commend serious music and singing in the Church—namely, music that through a unison melody arouses both joy and devotion, such as Gregorian, Ambrosian, Benedictine, and any other music of that kind. You can also often observe tender devotional affections stirred by Gregorian figured chant, through sounds concordant in their discord. Moreover, the moderate and non-capricious playing of pneumatic organs has accustomed us to attain the same composure of mind. Yet the prudent music instituted or tolerated by the holy Fathers for use in the temple did not end there.

For many centuries men distinguished for piety and disciplined judgment have complained—and especially in our own times lament—that soft and effeminate music has crept into the house of God, and particularly into the very august sacrifice of the Mass. Even the philosophers of the pagans judged that such music ought to be expelled from the assemblies of the people, as a deaf corrupter of minds and morals.

I leave it to others to debate whether this music should be tolerated in theaters. But when it has been transferred from theaters into the most solemn mysteries of the holy Church, no one who considers the matter attentively and understands the mind of the Church can praise or wish to tolerate this kind of music. Whoever considers it, would he not immediately exclaim that whatever does not arouse or nourish devotion in the divine mysteries—and, what is more serious, turns the mind away from devotion—must be rejected?

I now appeal to experience. When the clamor of so many voices and instruments, and such ingenious—not to say luxurious—melody, resounds in churches, the entire attention of ears and minds is carried away to it. Everything is arranged for pleasure; nothing leads toward devotion. This is the time for gathering the mind and having our hearts lifted up to the Lord. Who does not see that by these things the mind is distracted and drawn away from contemplation of heavenly realities?

Yet, with the greatest thoughtlessness, we admire these things and applaud them. We then think that feasts and sacred Offices are celebrated with greater solemnity the more spectacles are presented to give extraordinary delight to the eyes and ears. Nor do we perceive that in these things we are not seeking God or uniting ourselves with him through the obedience of our mind and the affection of our heart, but only the pleasure of our senses.

What you may find astonishing is that these are not merely vices of our own times; they arose and were deplored already in the fourth century of the Christian era. These are the words of Jerome:

> “Let the servant of Christ sing in such a way that it is not the voice of the singer but the words being read that please; so that the evil spirit who was in Saul may be driven out by those who are similarly possessed by him, and may not be introduced into those who have made a theater of the house of God for the peoples” (Jerome, on Eph. 5).

Saint Augustine says:

> “When it happens to me that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I am sinning in a punishable way, and then I would prefer not to hear it” (Augustine, *Confessions*, bk. 10, ch. 33).

Similarly, Isidore of Pelusium condemns women because in churches they sang hymns “for dissolution and as an occasion of sin.” For, he says, “using the sweetness of song to provoke and stimulate lusts, they consider it no better than theatrical songs” (Isidore of Pelusium, bk. 1, ep. 90).

I shall not add the attacks of others upon such intemperance. Nor do I wish to dwell longer on these matters, since I am convinced that this discussion of mine will have little power to overcome the pleasurable music of our times or to recommend stricter conduct in the divine Offices.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On the preservation of Christ’s body after the sacred mysteries, and on heterodox writers’ misuse of the words of Hesychius of Jerusalem on this matter

It could not happen in the ancient centuries of the Church that, after the people’s Communion, some remnants of the consecrated bread would not occasionally remain. As learned men have observed—and the Englishman Bingham himself admits (*Ecclesiastical Origins*, bk. 15, ch. 7, § 2)—it was customary in the Alexandrian Church to distribute these remnants to clergy and faithful who had already communicated, so that they might eat and drink them. This is established by the seventh canon of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria (in Beveridge, vol. 2).

At Constantinople there was another custom, as Evagrius testifies:

> “Whenever a large quantity of the portions of the IMMACULATE BODY of Christ our God remained, young children who had not yet reached puberty were summoned to eat them” (Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. 4, ch. 36).

We learn from the Second Council of Mâcon (canon 6), held in the year 588, that the same practice had been customary in the Gallican Churches.

Bingham brings forward another custom as peculiar to the Church of Jerusalem, drawing it from Hesychius, who is said to have been a Jerusalemite priest and bishop in the fifth or sixth century. His words are taken from an ancient Latin translation—for this is the only one that survives:

> “He commanded that what remained of the flesh and bread be burned in the fire. This is what we now also see being done visibly in the church: whatever happens to remain unconsumed is handed over to the fire—not absolutely those things that have been kept for one day, or two, or many days” (Hesychius, on Leviticus, bk. 2, ch. 8).

Bingham took this from Albertinus, that famous patron of the Calvinist contrivance, trusting that sophism far too readily. He says that Albertinus observed:

> “It was not the custom of the Church of Jerusalem to reserve the Eucharist from one day to another; they did not believe that it was really, properly, and substantially the body of their Christ, but only typologically and symbolically. For how great an offense it would have been to Jews and pagans if they had learned that Christians handed over to the fire the living and glorified body of their Christ! Simple Christians too would have abhorred this as something dreadful.”

Bingham then inflates the matter further and bursts into these words:

> “If no other argument were available against transubstantiation and the worship of the Host, this one fact alone would be sufficient to persuade any rational person that such doctrines and practices were never proposed or defended by the ancient Church.”

Indeed, this one fact might suffice to prove that the man who so greatly flatters himself on the basis of this single passage of Hesychius was wholly without reason, and that he not only considers himself secure in Calvin’s position but also believes that the doctrine of all the Churches of the world concerning the truth and reality of Christ’s body in the Eucharist ought to be reformed and corrected.

For when could anyone legitimately infer from the fact that certain people once observed a rite which now seems wholly devoid of the reverence due to so august a sacrament that they were not at all persuaded that the true body of Christ existed there? So much light has been shed by learned men upon ecclesiastical and literary history concerning the Eucharistic dogma that no one can now rightly doubt that, both in our own age and throughout the preceding centuries, the Greek and other Eastern Churches and writers proceeded in agreement with the Roman Church in believing and affirming the real presence of Christ in the sacrament of the altar.

In the middle of the eleventh century Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, attacked the Greek Nicetas with an excessively sharp style for their irreverence, saying:

> “Breaking and receiving the bread, you do not care about the crumbs that fall here and there. For this usually happens when you disgracefully rub the sacred patens with palm leaves and pigs’ bristles. Many of you also store the BODY OF CHRIST so irreverently that you fill pyxes with it, and, lest it fall or overflow, press it down with your hand. You consume the remnants of the oblation like common bread, even to satiety. And if you are unable to consume them, you bury them or throw them into a well” (Humbert, *Against Nicetas*, vol. 18 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*).

If someone from the Calvinist flock wished to conclude from this that the Greeks of that time thought differently about the Eucharist from the way they think now, a cloud of ancient writers would readily be available to accuse him of falsehood. Moreover, if reverence toward the Lord’s body was lacking in some place, was it not observed in countless others?

Perhaps that custom was even limited to a few. For the same Humbert wrote concerning his own age:

> “If anything of the holy and venerable Eucharist remains in the Churches of Jerusalem, they neither burn it nor throw it into a pit, but store it in a clean pyx, and on the following day communicate the people from it, etc. But to bury or inter the holy Eucharist in the earth, as some are said to do, or to put it into a flask, or to pour it out, is great negligence and a lack of fear of God.”

I fear that Humbert may also have exaggerated these matters as a general custom. Perhaps no such abuse existed. He adds, drawing from a certain letter translated into Latin:

> “It is clearer than daylight that the holy Church of Jerusalem anciently observed the same rite of the divine sacrifice which the holy Roman Church has not ceased to observe to this day.”

Certainly those who once treated the Lord’s body so irreverently would have deserved no excuse, although perhaps they did not notice the excess because they knew that the Eucharistic species themselves are destroyed, while nothing thereby happens to the Lord’s body, which is incorruptible and does not consider it dishonorable to descend into the workshop of our stomach.

Let us now expose the vanity of the Binghamian—or rather Albertinian—argument. This sort of men, like Aesop’s dog, letting go of the real flesh and gaping only at its shadow, need to be warned so that they may recognize how greatly they deceive themselves and others.

They therefore suppose that, from the burning of the remnants of the unbloody sacrifice, they can infer that the truth and reality of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist was neither acknowledged nor believed. Meanwhile they do not ask—or rather they avoid seeing—that a clear profession of this truth prevailed in the very Church of Jerusalem.

We have already established this from Saint Cyril, bishop of that same holy Church. How great a reverence was shown there to the most sacred body and blood of the Lord, even after Mass had been completed, is evident from the *Life of Saint Mary of Egypt*, who died in Palestine. This work is attributed to Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem and a contemporary of Hesychius, or else it has an even earlier author. See Surius and the *Acts of the Saints* for 2 April.

The holy penitent says to the abbot Zosimas:

> “Take for me the sacred vessel of the life-giving body and blood of Christ, worthy of such great mysteries, and bring it, remaining entirely on that bank of the Jordan, etc. By all means bring me the saving and divine mysteries at the hour when the Lord made his disciples participants in that divine banquet.”

Thus you have evidence that the Lord’s body was customarily preserved after the sacred assembly with great veneration. The life-giving body and blood of Christ were believed to remain there—and truly and really, contrary to what the Calvinists think. Nor was that same reality removed after the Supper, as other Protestants maintain.

This dogma and this faith were professed not only by the Church of Jerusalem but also by the other Churches of the world; this has already been demonstrated by the authority of so many liturgies and holy Fathers. Can you suspect that Hesychius held another mind and another faith? Let him speak for himself. For he says:

> “The FLESH of CHRIST, which before the Passion was unfit to be eaten—for who desired to eat the flesh of God?—he MADE FIT FOR FOOD after the Passion. For if he had not been crucified, we would not eat the SACRIFICE OF HIS BODY at all. But now WE EAT FOOD, receiving his memory of the Passion” (Hesychius of Jerusalem, on Leviticus, bk. 1, ch. 2).

From these clear words—not from obscure ones—Hesychius’s faith and doctrine must be drawn. If Christ’s flesh was made fit for food, then we truly receive it as food, and not merely typologically and symbolically; for a type cannot be eaten.

On the words of Leviticus, “Whoever eats of the holy things through ignorance,” etc., he again writes:

> “The holy of holies are PROPERLY the mysteries of Christ, because it is HIS BODY, concerning which Gabriel said to the Virgin: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you,’ etc. For from this he prohibited not only foreigners, resident aliens, and hired servants of the sacrifice, but also commanded that no one should receive it through ignorance. He receives it through ignorance who does not know its power and dignity, WHO DOES NOT KNOW THAT THIS IS THE BODY AND BLOOD IN TRUTH; he receives the mysteries, indeed, but does not know the power of the mysteries” (the same, on book 6, concerning Leviticus, ch. 22).

The Calvinists will surely say: “We know and believe the power of the mysteries very well.” But let them answer, I ask, whether they know and believe that the body and blood of Christ are in the mysteries according to the truth. In their mind and brain, certainly—but not in the mysteries themselves. And why? Because, placing faith only in the senses—namely, sight, touch, and smell—they cannot conceive anything in the sacrament except mere bread and wine.

But Hesychius addresses such men, adding:

> “The word that was uttered by Christ himself concerning the Lord’s mystery—that is, the words of consecration—is the very word that frees us from ignorance and removes from us the notion that there is anything carnal or earthly in the holy things—namely, the notion that the bread and wine, which have been sanctified by Christ’s words, are still present as such—but commands that they be received divinely and spiritually. For the divine Spirit is within us—namely, the invocation of the Holy Spirit, as in the Greek liturgy—and the word that he delivered—namely, the Lord’s words—orders our senses. It leads not only our taste toward the mystery, but also our hearing, sight, touch, and smell, so that we suspect nothing in them that is akin to lesser reason and a feeble mind, concerning things that are exceedingly heavenly.”

The senses, and the reason and mind of the Calvinists, resist the truth and reality of Christ’s body in the Eucharist. But when one considers that the Holy Spirit enters into the offerings and that “This is my body” is pronounced by the priest at the Lord’s command, every resistance of the senses and reason must cease, and the truth of so great a miracle must be believed. Hesychius’s clear mind is evident here.

Do you still doubt? Hear what he adds:

> “For the sanctification of the mystical sacrifice, and the transfer or change from sensible things to intelligible things, must be attributed to him who is the true priest, namely Christ; that is, IT MUST BE BELIEVED AND ASCRIBED TO HIM THAT A MIRACLE HAS BEEN PERFORMED concerning them, because through his power, and through the WORD UTTERED BY HIM, the things that are seen have been sanctified in a manner surpassing every sense of the flesh.”

Tell me, if you can, what other miracle is found in the Eucharist against which the senses and reason rebel, except the transformation of the gifts into the flesh and blood of Christ.

Hesychius adds these further words:

> “For those who ascribe to Christ the sanctification of his mysteries, and add to themselves his word, which leads our senses toward higher things, do not defile the holy of holies, since they understand them as they ought. Nor do they bring upon themselves the guilt of sin—which happens to the Calvinists, who give more credence to the senses than to the efficacy of Christ’s words—by eating the holy of holies. For they do not approach as though to ordinary food, but as to something mystical, terrible, and heavenly.”

The Fathers and liturgies frequently call the sacrament of the altar awesome and terrible, for no other reason than that faith teaches us that beneath it and within it there exists—though invisibly, yet truly and really—the King of kings and Lord.

From these things, therefore, you may understand how rashly Albertinus and Bingham supposed that they could extort from the rite mentioned by Hesychius the conclusion that the real presence of the Lord’s body in the Eucharist was formerly not believed in Jerusalem.

We have in Hesychius himself a clear witness to the Catholic position; indeed, we have it in the very passage from which they took the occasion for their dreaming. Here are his words:

> “The holy place is the altar. For THERE THE HOLY OF HOLIES RESTS”—words utterly clear and wholly contrary to Calvinist imaginings. “How, then, should the wisdom of the Spirit not be admired in these matters? For he left no doubt whatsoever to this understanding. Therefore, commanding that flesh be eaten together with bread, he wished us to understand that the mystery spoken of by him is at once bread and flesh, like Christ, the living bread that came down from heaven. For this reason, according to the Septuagint edition, ravens carried flesh in the morning and bread in the evening to Elijah from above, prefiguring, by the Lord’s will, this mystery: that within the church, in the holy place—that is, at the altar—it must be cooked and eaten, and nowhere else, etc. Aaron and his sons rightly eat it. For unless Christ himself, when asked to be priest, comes, sanctifies the Supper, and initiates what is being done, it is in no way the Lord’s sacrifice, but merely what remains of the flesh,” etc.

The words cited above by Bingham follow. After them, Hesychius continues by explaining what it signifies to burn the remnants of the sacrifice:

> “Therefore, from what is performed visibly, a signification of some intelligible reality comes to those who pay attention. When, for example, we grow weak in consuming the sacrifice and cannot consume it whole, perhaps because the mind has grown weary or failed, no doubt should be left as to WHETHER THE THINGS THAT ARE SEEN OUGHT TO BE UNDERSTOOD AS THE BODY OF THE LORD, into which not even angels can look with their eyes; rather, they too must be handed over to the fire of the Spirit, so that it may consume what is inedible for us because of our weakness. But how does it consume it? When we consider that WHAT SEEMS IMPOSSIBLE TO US IS POSSIBLE TO THE POWER OF THE SPIRIT.”

Protestants, I ask you, open your eyes. In Hesychius you will see not what you dream, but what the Catholic faith teaches, although his language abounds in allegories and the ancient Latin translation, which alone we use, is not free from obscurity.

What is it that can trouble our minds in this ineffable sacrament and introduce doubts into them? It is this question: whether the bread and wine—which are still seen after the consecration as they were before—must be understood as the body of the Lord, into which the universal Church recognizes and proclaims that they have been transformed and changed. For this appears impossible to human reason.

But Hesychius says that such hesitations of mind must be burned away by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and that we must consider that those things which appear impossible to us are possible through the power of that same Spirit, invoked by the priest for this transformation.

He would be plainly ridiculous who wished to interpret these words of the Calvinist Supper. Every sincere mind is compelled to understand them as referring to the real presence of the Lord in the sacrament and to the substantial trans-elementation of the gifts—namely, the miracle performed daily from heaven in the unbloody sacrifice.

What Hesychius writes here will be explained for you by the words of John of Damascus. Speaking of the Eucharist, he says:

> “It is not that the body which was received into heaven descends, but that THE BREAD AND WINE ARE TRANSFORMED INTO THE BODY AND BLOOD OF GOD. If you ask how this occurs, let it be enough for you that it occurs through the Holy Spirit, just as the Lord assumed flesh for himself from the holy Mother of God. We know and understand nothing more than that the word of God is true and effective and can do all things. But the manner cannot be investigated at all” (John of Damascus, *On the Faith*, bk. 4, ch. 13).

Long before this, Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, around the year 395 of Christ, had taught the newly baptized in these words:

> “If anything of the mysteries should remain, to be revealed on the morning of that future Resurrection—things which we cannot now comprehend—these must be burned with fire; that is, they must be handed over to the divine Spirit, so that things whose meaning we do not now grasp may be consumed by the spirit of burning faith” (Gaudentius, *Treatise 2 on the Meaning of the Sacraments*).

There, as we also observed above in chapter 19, Gaudentius explains Catholic doctrine so clearly that anyone who fails to perceive it is guilty of willful blindness. He then concludes his reasoning, saying:

> “Receive with us, with all the eagerness of a devout heart, this Paschal sacrifice of the Savior, so that the inner parts of our bodies may be sanctified by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, WHOM WE BELIEVE TO BE PRESENT IN HIS SACRAMENTS.”

Gregory the Great also used the same reasoning, writing:

> “What remains of the Lamb we burn with fire when we reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot understand and penetrate concerning the mystery of his Incarnation, so that no one may presumptuously dare either to despise or to denounce what he does not understand. He hands it over to the fire when he reserves it to the Holy Spirit” (Gregory the Great, *Homily 22 on the Gospels*, bk. 2).

Yet I seem still to hear Bingham, astonished and asking: How could those who truly believed that the Lord’s body was really present in the sacrament afterward burn it? What would pagans have said? Would this not have been horrifying and scandalous to the faithful? Let us see whether the matter was really so.

Bingham himself asserts that the remnants of the sacrament were handed over to the fire, writing that “it was not the custom of the Church of Jerusalem to reserve the Eucharist from one day to another.”

Let us repeat the words of Hesychius:

> “What we now also see being done visibly in the Church is that whatever happens to remain unconsumed is handed over to the fire; not absolutely those things that have been preserved for one day, or two, or many. For, as is evident, the legislator did not command this, but commands that what remains be burned. He did not specify the days, so that whatever remains unconsumed for whatever reason—whether time is responsible or anything else—may become the work and object of the fire.”

Had the heterodox examined these words more carefully, they would not have imposed upon them their own opinion: namely, that in the Church of Jerusalem the remnants of the sacrifice, or Eucharist, were not preserved from one day to the next. On the contrary, the opposite follows from Hesychius’s words; for he mentions things left unconsumed “which have been preserved for one day, or two, or many.”

His meaning is that the Law indeed commands that the remnants of the sacrifice be handed over to the fire, but determines nothing about the day on which the burning is to occur. Hence you understand that it is falsely asserted that they were not preserved at all and were immediately burned.

What, then, was Hesychius’s meaning? It was the meaning that the Catholic Church once had and still has. The Eucharistic remnants, unless communicants or innocent children consumed them, were kept in the *pastophorium*, of which we shall speak below.

But because the species of consecrated bread may, after some or many days, acquire mold or a corrupt smell, or may be spoiled by water, moths, mice, or other accidents, the Church, believing that the body and blood of the Lord had thereby departed, lowers those remnants into a sacred subterranean place; others have customarily burned them.

You have this from Hesychius himself, when he says: “For whatever reason arises—whether time is responsible,” meaning that they have been kept longer than is proper, “or anything else—they are to be handed over to the fire.”

Here you should also hear Algerus, who flourished and wrote around the year 1130 of Christ. He says:

> “But when the sacramental species themselves are said to be handed over by religious persons to the fire and disappear there, this is not done as an insult to Christ, as though he were handed over to be burned by fires; that is impossible, since he is the God of all the elements. Rather, whenever some such indignity—which we have recently indicated—has happened carelessly to the sacrament, so that the sensible species themselves inspire horror at receiving them, those species which God in his highest wisdom willed to remain THERE AFTER THE CHANGE OF THEIR SUBSTANCE are handed over to the fire, to show that what belongs to them perishes and disappears without any foulness in that purest element, fire” (Algerus, *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*, bk. 2, ch. 1).

Hear also the Fourth Council of Orléans, held in the year 541, almost the same period in which Hesychius is believed to have flourished:

> “The offerings,” it says, “which are offered upon the altar are always to be renewed from one Saturday to the next, because the loaves of the Presence, which were changed upon the table of the Lord, should not become moldy from being kept too long; and, as some believe, they should be burned in the fire.”

Indeed, “the Eucharist was to be changed from the third day to the third day, lest, if it were kept longer, it should perhaps become moldy, God forbid,” as stated in the Council of Tours, preserved by Regino (*On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, bk. 1, ch. 7).

From what has been presented up to this point, Protestants may now understand, if they are willing, how unjustly they use Hesychius’s authority to attack the Catholic position concerning the Eucharist. Indeed, they are compelled by this same writer to learn what they should think of Berengar and Calvin, since Hesychius no less than the universal Church of the world has always handed down and believed doctrines plainly contrary to their fantasies.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the reverence shown to Christ’s body preserved after the sacrifice, and on its public exposition and procession in sacred supplications
[Col. 1042D] That the followers of Luther should still persist in teaching that the Eucharist vanishes outside the Supper, and that the most sacred body of Christ does not remain in the sacrament, is truly astonishing. For an educated people cannot fail to recognize that, even in the primitive Church, there was a practice of carrying the Eucharist home, sending it to the absent, and bringing it as viaticum to the sick in danger of death—to pass over other practices of which Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, the Acts of Saint Lucian the Martyr, Basil, Ambrose, and other Fathers are witnesses. The apostolic man Saint Irenaeus himself, as quoted by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 24), testifies that the Eucharist was sent to the presbyters of the Churches who observed Easter; this is also confirmed by Saint Justin Martyr, a writer of approximately the same period. Will the authority of Luther, a most turbulent man, if I may say so, count for more among rational men than the Church of earlier centuries? Would you dare merely to suspect—indeed, to assert—that the Church instructed by the apostles and their disciples corrupted apostolic doctrine?

The discipline of the Church concerning the preservation of the immaculate body of Christ after the sacred rites had been completed varied according to times and places. Nor should the practices of the ancients be blamed on that account, since they observed the same measure of reverence and service toward that heavenly pledge which the Catholic Church now observes with such devotion and praiseworthy custom. Formerly, as we have said, the faithful were permitted to carry the sacred [Col. 1043B] Eucharist to their own homes, so that they might receive communion there. It was placed in the hands of communicants; travelers sometimes carried it with them, and we know that it was occasionally entrusted even to laypeople so that they might take it to the sick. Yet all held the same faith and doctrine: namely, that the precious body and blood of the Lord existed in the sacrament. But the discipline of subsequent centuries abolished these religious practices.

Moreover, it was formerly a common rite that the remnants of the ineffable sacrifice, unless they were consumed by communicants or innocent children, should be brought into the sacrarium and kept there. We adduce as a witness to this very ancient practice the *Apostolic Constitutions* themselves, which even the Englishman Bingham held in such esteem. There we read:

“When all men and women have communicated, the deacons, taking what remains, shall carry it into the pastophorium” (*Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 13).

The pastophorium is believed to have been the sacrarium, or sacristy, situated not far from the principal altar. Saint Jerome calls it a chamber. There also seems to have been an altar and a tabernacle, or ciborium, in which the ancients were accustomed to deposit the most sacred Eucharist, especially for reservation for the sick. That there was formerly more than one altar in sacred buildings we learn from Saints Ambrose and Paulinus of Nola, when they mention altars in a single basilica. Optatus of Milevis likewise states that the Eucharist, thrown upon the altars by the Donatists, was devoured by dogs. And in the First Council of Tours, held in the year 567, it was decreed:

“Let the body of the Lord be placed upon the altar beneath the sign of the cross.”

Gregory of Tours and Venantius Fortunatus testify that it was then kept in golden or silver towers. Because the Holy of Holies rested upon the altar, holy bishops Alexander and Ambrose, as we saw above, offered private prayers beneath the altar itself in times of need. Gorgonia, too, the sister of Gregory Nazianzen, approached the altar at an untimely hour of the night and, having received the Lord’s body from it, obtained healing for herself.

Furthermore, according to the testimony of Paulinus the Deacon in the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, when that holy bishop was at the point of death, he received the most sacred viaticum of the Lord’s body during the night:

“For Honoratus, the priest—that is, the bishop—of the Church of Vercelli, having arranged himself to rest in the upper part of the house, heard the voice of one calling him for the third time and saying to him: ‘Rise, hasten, for he is now about to depart.’ He went down and offered the holy body of the Lord; having received it, and having swallowed it, he gave up his spirit, carrying with him a good viaticum.”

Here observe in passing that it was the Lord’s body, but not the blood, that was customarily administered to the sick, so that you may understand that the ancient Church too held that, under the species of bread alone, the whole Christ was contained and received by the faithful.

Further, if anyone asks what the Eucharist was called when it was reserved for the faithful of those times, you have already seen that it was called the Lord’s body. This doctrine clearly shows how greatly it opposes the disciples of Luther, who hold that the body of Christ is present only in the use of a single Supper; and even more greatly it opposes the followers of Calvin, [Col. 1044B] who do not acknowledge the true and real body of the same Lord even in the Supper itself. Certainly, the First Council of Nicaea decreed, according to the rule of the ancient law, that the sick were not to be deprived of viaticum. Therefore, even then it was customary to keep the sacred body of the Lord reserved for them.

A notable passage of Saint Cyril of Alexandria agrees with this truth. He says:

“I hear that there are some who dare to say that the Eucharist can confer no sanctity upon those who receive it if it is kept from one day to the next. Those who peddle such claims must surely be delirious. For Jesus Christ is not subject to any corruption, and his HOLY BODY undergoes no change whatsoever, so long as the species remain. Moreover, the power and efficacy of the blessing—that is, of the consecration—and the life-giving grace which the BODY OF JESUS CHRIST always contains within itself are perpetual and unchangeable” (Cyril of Alexandria, Letter to Calosyrius, *Against the Anthropomorphites*).

Why do those who everywhere dream up fantasies about Paschasius Radbertus not read these words? From a letter of Saint John Chrysostom to Pope Innocent I we also learn that the most sacred blood of Christ was spilled in a church by soldiers, although Mass was not then being celebrated.

If among the ancients you encounter certain practices in which you think reverence toward this ineffable sacrament was lacking, they must be attributed either to the simplicity or to the ill-considered piety of those times. Their faith in the truth and power of Christ’s body in the Eucharist was then so great that, when those who were at the point of death had been unable to receive this heavenly pledge, they presented it to them after death and considered the act beneficial. The Councils of Carthage and Auxerre abolished this practice.

There was also at times a custom of burying the Eucharist together with the bodies of bishops. Saint Gregory the Great likewise writes that, when the earth cast out the buried body of a certain little boy, the abbot Saint Benedict said:

“Go and place this dominical body upon his breast with great reverence, and then commit him to burial.” Then the earth held his body after it had been received, and no longer cast it out (Gregory the Great, book II, chapter 24).

It has been known for many centuries that these and other practices of private individuals, which I pass over, were little compatible with the institution and majesty of the Eucharist and were never approved by the universal Church, and that they have disappeared. Certainly, they arose from nothing other than firm and vigorous faith in the presence and power of Christ in the Eucharist.

Even in our own times the Greeks and other Eastern Christians preserve the Eucharist throughout the entire year, to be administered to the sick as viaticum, and do not replace it until the year has ended. To prevent it from corrupting, they dip it in the precious blood and bake it again in an oven, or dry it—a practice which even Arcudius, a Greek writer, disapproved. Moreover, they keep the host itself enclosed either behind the altar or in wooden or iron vessels, without a lamp. The Latins, seeing this, are astonished and reproach them for showing so little reverence toward the most sacred body of Christ. But they defend themselves by pleading poverty and Turkish tyranny; and, what is especially important, they nevertheless all unanimously confess and believe that the most holy body of Christ is really contained in the reserved Eucharist, as is most clearly evident from their published professions of faith and other records. It would now be impudent to doubt this faith and profession of theirs.

The Western Churches, however, and above all the Roman Church, teacher of them all, from the time when Berengarius attempted by an impious doctrine to diminish the dignity of the Eucharist, have considered nothing more important than to increase daily the worship and reverence shown toward the august sacrament of the altar. Hence arose the feast of Corpus Christi; hence its public exposition upon the altar outside the sacrifice; hence its carrying outside the church in sacred processions [Col. 1045C] and the imparting of blessing to the people through it.

We do not deny that these practices are new in the Church of God; for during the preceding twelve centuries no trace of them appears to us in the books of the ancients. The question has been raised whether Pope Urban IV, when he instituted the feast of Corpus Christi in the year 1264, also instituted the public procession in which the same body of the Lord is now carried. The stronger opinion appears to be the one written by the most eminent Cardinal Lambertini (*Book I, Instruction 5*): no institution of such a procession, or supplication, should be attributed to Urban, since the records of the ancients are entirely silent about it, and it is not the action of a prudent man to decide the truth of ancient matters without suitable witnesses.

Only in the year 1336, as Gualvaneus Flamma records in his history, “John Visconti, Bishop of Novara and protector of the Church of Milan, ordered the feast of Corpus Christi to be celebrated. The entire clergy was present, together with a certain marvelous procession of religious, such as Rome, left to itself, would not have been able to make” (G. Flamma, *On the Deeds of the Visconti*, volume XII of *Rerum Italicarum*).

You see that both the feast and the procession of Corpus Christi were then instituted for the first time at Milan. The very learned John de Joanne, a canon of Palermo, also observed (*On the Sicilian Divine Office*, chapter 33) that the feast of Corpus Christi is recorded in Sicilian Missals only from the year 1346. Father Martène likewise reports that Urban IV’s constitution was received later even in France itself (*On Ecclesiastical Rites*).

Nevertheless, even in the most ancient centuries some trace appears to us both of the carrying about and of the public exposition of the divine sacrament. Above, in chapter 19, from the Roman Order, which seems to have been written at least nine hundred years ago, we showed that the Eucharist was exposed upon the altar before the pontifical Mass began. We can learn from Gregory of Tours that it was taken from the sacrarium, or repository, where it had previously been placed, and carried in procession to the altar. Writing in the sixth century, he says:

“The time for offering the sacrifice arrived; and the deacon, having taken the tower—that is, the golden or silver vessel—in which the *ministerium* (‘ministration’) of the Lord’s body was contained—other manuscripts more correctly read *mysterium* (‘mystery’)—began to carry it toward the door. Having entered the church, as he was about to place it upon the altar, it slipped from his hands and was carried into the air” (Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I).

That Christ’s body was then carried with immense reverence is taught by the ancient Order of the Gallican Church, edited by the highly praised Martène and conjecturally attributed to Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris. There we read:

“Now, as the body of Christ proceeds to the altar, let the Church, not with irreproachable trumpets but with spiritual voices, sing in splendid melody the great deeds of Christ. The body of the Lord is carried in towers for this reason: because they represent the Lord’s tomb,” and so forth.

Earlier that author had said:

“With the clerics singing, the priest, in the likeness of Christ, proceeds from the sacrarium—as from heaven—in the Ark of the Lord,” and so forth.

The Greeks, too, have practiced the same thing from ancient centuries when the Liturgy of the Presanctified is celebrated. Then the presanctified gifts are carried from the sacrarium to the altar with the utmost reverence; and, according to the testimony of the very ancient author of the Paschal, or Alexandrian, Chronicle, in the fifth year of Olympiad 348, the people began to sing:

“Now the powers of heaven invisibly WORSHIP GOD WITH US. Behold, the KING OF GLORY comes forth. Behold, the mystical sacrifice is offered. Let us draw near with faith and trembling, that we may become partakers of eternal life. Alleluia.”

It is certain, however, that the practice of exposing the Lord’s body upon the altar, in a monstrance above an elevated throne, and of carrying it outside the sacred buildings with great pomp and beneath a canopy, as we now see done, was not introduced before the thirteenth century of Christ. It is no wonder that Protestants disapprove this rite, since it conflicts with their impious opinions concerning the Eucharist.

If we listen to Grotius, this practice, besides being new, “also differs from the custom of the ancients, who excluded noncommunicants from the very sight of the Eucharist” (Hugo Grotius, notes on Cassander’s consultation, article 10). Something must now be said about this.

Grotius is referring to the seventh canon—numbered ninth or tenth by others among those which we call apostolic—where, in the translation of Dionysius Exiguus, we read:

“All the faithful who enter the Church but do not remain in prayer and do not receive holy communion, as persons causing disturbances in the Church, ought to be deprived of communion.”

Likewise, in the Council of Antioch, held in the year 341, canon 2 is worded as follows:

“All who enter the church and hear the sacred Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer, or who, through some insolence, avoid participation in the holy Eucharist, must be expelled from the Church until, after confessing, showing fruits of repentance, and imploring pardon, they are able to obtain forgiveness.”

For this reason Bingham judged that, in former times, all the faithful who flocked to the Church “were required by the rules of the Church to come forward to receive the Eucharist under penalty of ecclesiastical censure” (Bingham, book XV, chapter 4, § 1).

But Grotius has vainly wrested this practice of the primitive Church against the more recent practice of the Roman Church, as though it were not permitted to behold the Eucharist outside the sacrifice. Tertullian himself testifies that the faithful were accustomed to complete their station, or sacrifice, “having received the body of the Lord” (Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chapter 19). At the same time, however, he notes that they were permitted to attend “the prayers of the sacrifices” and afterward to carry the received body of the Lord home with them.

It was certainly the same body of Christ Jesus that was consumed at home, carried to the sick, and received in the church. Therefore, what is now the real body of the Lord in the church, and what, as we have seen, was also worshiped there in ancient times, does not cease to be the true body of the Lord if it is carried outside the church, either to the sick or, for the sake of devotion and adoration, in public processions.

Whether, in the centuries of the primitive Church, those who attended the unbloody sacrifice but did not receive the Eucharist would have been struck with an anathema may well be doubted in view of such severity. Certainly, the penitents, who were called *consistentes*, attended the sacrifice and nevertheless did not communicate. In the Antiochene canon, however, those who are said to be expelled from the church are those who [Col. 1047C] “do not join the people in prayer”—perhaps because they departed before the Mass of the faithful—or who “avoid the Eucharist through some insolence,” or who “cause disturbance in the church.” They were a scandal to the faithful and for that reason were subjected to penance.

In the same century in which the Council of Antioch was held, Saint Ambrose and John Chrysostom acknowledge that frequent communion had fallen out of use; yet no one mentions a precept concerning this matter. Chrysostom indeed rebukes and criticizes those who attended Mass but did not communicate, regarding them as cold in devotion, but he never says that they should be struck with anathema. Balsamon the Greek himself, in his *Response to Mark, Bishop of Alexandria*, judged that the Antiochene canon by no means compelled all who attended the sacred rites to approach communion.

As is evident from the *Constitutions of the Apostles* themselves (canon 6), there were at times presbyters, deacons, and others from the ranks of the sacred orders who did not communicate. When they offered a legitimate reason for abstaining from communion, they obtained pardon.

In any event, it is futile to object to the novelty of the rite of publicly exposing the Lord’s body and carrying it in sacred processions. For once it has been demonstrated that the entire Church has always believed, by perpetual faith, in the real presence of Jesus Christ in the sacrament, both during Mass and outside Mass, whether it was received in the church or outside it, and that the faithful have always offered it adoration, then the rite which corresponds to that unshaken dogma must also be legitimate [Col. 1048C] and must flow from it.

The Jews also carried about the Ark of the Lord, which was merely a figure of the heavenly Eucharist. Why, then, should not the reality also be carried about, to increase the honor of our divine Savior and enlarge the devotion of his faithful?

[Col. 1049]

# THE GELASIAN SACRAMENTARY, OR BOOK OF THE SACRAMENTS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, BY SAINT GELASIUS I, POPE

Published at Rome in 1680 by Joseph Maria Thomasius, and annotated by Muratori.

(From Muratori’s edition entitled *The Ancient Roman Liturgy*.) (C)*

## To the Most Serene Christina Alexandra, Queen of the Swedes, Goths, and Vandals

Joseph Maria Thomasius, priest of the Congregation of Regular Clerics, sends greetings.

The manuscripts written several centuries ago which your munificence allowed me to publish I now return to you, most serene queen, enriched with their own examples. In doing so I congratulate you on two things: that you can now read them in this single volume without the inconvenience of their ancient script, and that you may rightly be regarded by all learned people as having deserved exceptionally well of sacred scholarship through them. Accept, therefore, this work, which is worthy of your distinguished wisdom and religion, and graciously receive in it the service of my profound respect for you.

## Preface

[Col. 1049A] As I was examining the finest libraries of the City, I conceived the idea of selecting from the many and varied manuscript codices with which they abound certain works to be shared for the public good—namely, four Sacramentary codices, which I judged would be worthy of recommendation both for their antiquity and for the knowledge they provide of ecclesiastical rites.

We now present these under the title of Sacramentaries. Everyone knows that among the most ancient Fathers of the Church the sacraments, by antonomasia, are called the body and blood of Christ when they are confected upon the altar during Mass. It is chiefly for this reason that Missal books have been called books of the Sacraments, although they also contain what pertains to the administration of the other sacraments.

Concerning these Sacramentary codices which we are publishing, reason itself requires that I offer the pious and studious reader a brief preliminary account, so that he may first learn where they were obtained, when they were written, and by whom they were compiled.

I divided the Sacramentary of the Roman Church into three books. The first concerns the cycle of the year, the second the feast days of the saints, and the third Sundays and various occasions. It now belongs to the exceptionally well-stocked library of the most serene Queen of Sweden, through whose kindness it has been possible to make it public.

The eminent Cardinal Bona, in his book *On Liturgical Matters*, and the very learned Jean Morin, in his book *On Penance and Sacred Orders*, saw it and frequently praised it. In the appendix of manuscripts to his commentary on Penance, published in 1651, in his note on the Gelasian Sacramentary, page [Col. 1050A] 52, Morin writes:

“The most ancient of all the codices which we have been able to obtain is the one which we have often called the Petavian in our work, after its owner, the most distinguished man Lord Petavius, an entirely upright senator of the Paris Parlement, who courteously allowed us to use it. Its script does not appear to be less than nine hundred years old; for it is written in large, square letters, which some call uncials. The scribe was not very skilled in Latin; for often, through ignorance rather than negligence or haste, he miswrites—*παραγράφει*. It was written in France, since the canon commemorates Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, as well as Hilary and Martin. Moreover, in the office of the Friday before Easter, when prayer is offered for the Roman Empire, it says: ‘Look favorably upon the Roman, or, more kindly, the Frankish, empire.’ It is divided into three books, and the beginning of each book is written with considerable artistic care and in large letters formed with a single stroke. This codex now belongs to that most celebrated and powerful queen of the Swedes and Goths, Christina,” and so forth.

Thus far he has spoken about the owners and qualities of the codex. Among other considerations, the following support its antiquity:

1. In the Creed recited at the scrutiny before Palm Sunday, the addition *Filioque* is absent. That addition was certainly made in Germany and Gaul—where the codex appears to have been written—in the seventh century, and in Rome only in the ninth century of Christ.

2. It does not contain the Masses for the five weekdays of Lent, which Saint Gregory II first instituted at the beginning of the eighth century, as Anastasius—or another writer—in the *Lives of the Popes* records, along with the preface placed under the name of Grimold before his Sacramentary in Pamelius, volume II of the *Liturgicon*. I say “under the name of Grimold” because the *Micrologus*, chapter 60, cites it as belonging to Albinus, the teacher of Charlemagne. We too have seen that preface in the most ancient manuscript of Saint Gregory’s Sacramentary in the library of the Queen of Sweden, but it bears no name.

3. It lacks many Masses which we know to have been used from the seventh century onward, such as those for the feast of the Dedication of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, in May, and for All Saints, in November. Boniface IV, who succeeded Gregory the Great after the intervening pontificate of Sabinian, was responsible for these at the beginning of the seventh century.

4. Fewer feast days of saints are listed here than in other Sacramentary books. Menardus correctly observed that this is an indication of antiquity, and J. Fronto, in his preliminary notes to the Roman Calendar, especially § 3, demonstrated the genuine reason: only those feasts of the saints were recorded in the Missal books on which assemblies of the people, or public Masses, were celebrated by the bishop together with the clergy and people.

5. In this codex the proper feasts celebrated are those of martyrs alone; moreover, in accordance with an ancient practice of the Church, Saint Felix in Pincis and Pope Marcellus, because they did not shed their blood, are called not martyrs but confessors.

There are also many other arguments for its greater antiquity which the reader will discover for himself in the codex. Accordingly, Morin rightly conjectures that it predates the year 700 (*On Penance*, book VII, chapter 1, no. 15).

As for the compiler of the codex, the same Morin considers him to have been Gelasius, although it was written after Saint Gregory: “or, to use his words in the passage cited, it contains the order of offices as it was used before Saint Gregory.” Cardinal Bona did not disagree, *On Liturgical Matters*, book II, chapter 5.

To lead the reader gradually, as it were by slow steps, toward attaining the truth we seek, it must first be repeated that, from the very beginning of the rising Church, certain fixed formulas of sacrifice and prayer were in use. The acts of the martyrs and the treatises of the Fathers teach us this, for they often report certain established and solemn words customarily recited in sacred assemblies.

As time went on, the bishops increased and revised these prayers, or once again abbreviated them; nevertheless, the Church always retained them and handed them down to later generations. We still possess them in our Missals, together with other offices newly instituted over time.

Among the other holy bishops, Saint Leo the Great clearly applied his hand with distinction to this work. His very style, which immediately reveals itself to anyone even slightly familiar with his writings, shows this openly. Nor does the distinguished Morin depart from the truth when he writes (*On Penance*, book IX, chapter 30, no. 2) that many of these ritual prayers are no later than the pontificates of Saints Sylvester and Julius, and that their phrasing and style unmistakably reflect the period before the Emperor Constantine.

Thus, concerning the highly eloquent speech of the archdeacon to the pope at the reconciliation of penitents—which you will find above, column 914—he makes its author at least contemporary with Constantine, although one or another expression may perhaps suggest a Gelasian recension.

I am not unaware that the learned Paschasius Quesnel attributes this very speech to Leo the Great, in volume I of that saint’s works. I readily agree with him, overcome by the Leonine pen which I seem to see there, either writing for the first time or revising the text almost in its entirety.
