Among the compilers of liturgical prayers, Saint Gelasius, pope from the year 492, is especially commended in the *Lives of the Popes*. There we read of him: “He also composed prefaces and prayers for the Sacraments in carefully considered language.”

From the new contribution of this holy bishop, the entire work of the Missal prayers began to be called the Gelasian Codex. Hence, toward the end of the sixth century, Saint Gregory prepared his own Sacramentary as though it were an abridgment and summary of that work, as is perfectly clear from John the Deacon’s *Life of Gregory*, book II, chapter 17. He says of it:

“Moreover, removing much from the Gelasian Codex concerning the solemn rites of the Mass, changing a little, and adding some things for the exposition of the Gospel readings, he compressed it into a single volume.”

From these words we learn in passing that the Gelasian Codex was indeed one work, but divided into several books, as is our own, which is divided into three books. This seems to me what John implies when, by way of contrast, he says that Gregory compressed his Sacramentary into a single book.

After Saint Gregory, all the popes who followed made the greatest use of that Gregorian work and introduced it into other nations, as is evident in Adrian, who gave it as a gift to Charlemagne. Yet I would not believe that the Gelasian Codex was entirely rejected, for the manuscript Antiphoner of the Angelica Library at Saint Augustine’s here in Rome, written before the middle of the eleventh century for the use of the Roman Church, contains much that agrees with it.

Gregorian copies are found everywhere, both manuscripts—in the Vatican Library, the Queen of Sweden’s library, and elsewhere—and printed editions: at Rome by Angelo Rocca, at Cologne by Pamelius, and at Paris by Hugh Menardus. Each of them proclaims his edition to be the genuine offspring of Gregory. Yet it is astonishing how much they disagree among themselves, making it difficult to settle the dispute. I can neither be nor wish to be the judge of such great men. Nevertheless, for the love of truth I must not conceal that I am more inclined to Pamelius than to the others.

I am moved by the agreement of the most ancient manuscript codices; I am moved by the omission in his edition of many feasts and Masses—provided, that is, that one carefully removes what Pamelius himself marked with quotation marks or noted as having been introduced from elsewhere; I am moved by its brevity, which seems more strongly to breathe the compression of Gregory according to John the Deacon’s account. Nor would I regard as less weighty the testimony of Grimold the abbot—or, according to the *Micrologus*, Albinus, the teacher of Charlemagne—in the highly praised preface which he attached to the Gregorian work.

After these authentic Sacramentary books of the Roman Church—the Gelasian and the Gregorian—there arose another, private compilation of a Missal made by Albinus from both. Thus we read in the *Chronicle of Centula*, book III, chapter 3, volume IV of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, in the catalogue of books listed in the year 831:

“The Gregorian and Gelasian Missal, arranged by Albinus in recent times.”

From this somewhat lengthy, though not entirely useless, account the reader can now discern for himself what sort of composition the codex we are publishing represents. It is clear that it does not belong to this Albinus, since it does not contain those prayers and Masses which at that time were widely found in the Gregorian Sacramentary. Why would he have omitted the Gregorian Masses if he had first arranged his Missal from Gregory? Nor does the title of this work allow for such a private arrangement, since it claims for itself the complete usage and authority of the Roman Church.

Anyone can easily persuade himself that it is not Gregorian by comparing it with our codex: they differ so greatly that, from the comparison itself, he will argue that this is the Gelasian Codex mentioned by John the Deacon. For it will become clear that:

1. Many things found in the Gregorian have been omitted here.

2. A few have been altered.

3. Some things have been added to the Gregorian which do not appear here.

To sum up, I would regard this as the Sacramentary Codex of the Roman Church which was formerly called Gelasian because of the additions made to the prayers by that holy pontiff. I say “was called,” for I would not have you attribute the entire work to him; it belongs in large part to Leo the Great and to his Roman predecessors in the episcopate.

Nor is this without good reason. I had begun comparing the Leonine phrases and sentences with this codex, and I found that not merely Leo’s style but his very words are recited here. Thus I became more certain and do not hesitate to assert this with some confidence. What lack of leisure has prevented me from pursuing, any diligent scholar can accomplish through his own observations.

I readily admit, however, that some things were added to this codex in a later century and do not bear the character of the compilers mentioned above. They are not numerous: fewer are found in the second book and very few in the first, while more occur in the third.

Nor should you therefore rightly reject it, just as the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory is not wholly rejected as spurious even though it contains the Mass for the Dedication of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, instituted several years after Gregory by Boniface IV. For it is clear that such sacred books are not written merely for the sake of scholarship, but chiefly for the use of the Churches; consequently, they must always admit new additions as the circumstances of custom and time require.

This also easily refutes the objection that Saint Gregory is named in the canon of this codex, that his words occur there—“And dispose our days in your peace”—and, more importantly, that an entire chapter from his *Register* is recited among the sacred ordinations. We willingly grant that the codex was written a considerable time afterward and therefore underwent some additions.

Again, it seems possible to infer without difficulty that this codex is older than Saint Gregory from the fact that it does not contain the Commemoration of Saint Paul on the day before the Kalends of July, and that on the third day before the Kalends of the same month it records a proper Mass for the feast of Saint Peter, while on that very day it has another proper Mass for the feast of Saint Paul.

The *Micrologus*, in agreement with Gregory’s Sacramentaries, makes Saint Gregory the author of this Commemoration. Before that time, on the same day for both apostles, just as there was a feast in the two churches—the Triumphal and the Ostian—so there was also a repeated Mass in the two basilicas, Saint Peter’s at the Vatican and Saint Paul’s outside the Three Gates, celebrated by the Roman bishop.

Prudentius, who flourished toward the end of the fourth century, beautifully expressed this in his hymn for the apostles:

> Behold, the Roman people divide through the two-branched streets:
>
> One light blazes in two feasts.
>
> Yet let us hasten with eager step toward both,
>
> And enjoy the hymns of each.
>
> We shall go farther along the road that leads across Hadrian’s Bridge;
>
> Then we shall seek the left bank of the river.
>
> First, beyond the Tiber, the watchful priest completes the sacred rites;
>
> Then he returns here and DUPLICATES his vows.

Our codex corresponds admirably to this ancient practice, since it prescribes two separate Masses on the same day of the apostles, besides a third common Mass for both apostles, to be recited in other churches of the City.

That this codex is Gelasian is clearly shown, if I am not mistaken, by the Toulouse Codex cited by Morin in the appendix to his commentary on Penance, page 55. For in that codex the office of Holy Saturday, when twelve readings are recited, is written as follows:

“The readings according to Gelasius follow. Prayer before the first reading is read, immediately after the blessing of the candle.”

After the twelve readings according to Gelasius have been set out, the rubric follows:

“Likewise, the readings according to Gregory. The first reading from Genesis: ‘In the beginning God created.’ Prayer: ‘O God, who wonderfully created man,’ and the rest, as above, according to Gelasius.”

From this we learn that in the Gelasian Codex the blessing of the candle is included, that a prayer precedes the first reading from Genesis, and that twelve readings are contained in it. None of these features is found in the Gregorian books, whereas all are fully displayed in our codex, except that here only ten readings are found, two having been omitted, as I conjecture, through the copyist’s carelessness.

No less favorable is the very ancient parchment manuscript Missal of the Oratorian Vallicellana Library, marked B. VIII. In it, on Sundays after Easter and Pentecost, an almost double Mass is recorded, one of them being titled:

“Likewise, another Mass.”

But on the Second Sunday after the Octave of Easter this second Mass is described as follows:

> “Another Mass of Saint Gelasius.
>
> Grant your people, O our God, a will pleasing to you, because then you will provide them with every prosperity when you have made them suited to your ordinances.
>
> **Over the Offerings**
>
> Through these mysteries, O Lord, may this be granted to us: that, by moderating earthly desires, we may learn to love heavenly things. Through.
>
> **At Communion**
The sacraments which we have received, we ask, O Lord, may both cleanse us with spiritual nourishment and protect us with bodily assistance. Through [Christ].

We read this same Mass of Saint Gelasius here on the same day. The only difference is that here two prayers are prescribed, whereas there one is prescribed. Yet that other prayer is found in the same Missal in the earlier Mass, which is Gregorian. Of the two Gelasian prayers, then, one was omitted, while Gregory retained the others; as has already been said, he removed much from the Gelasian book, altered a little, and added some material of his own.

Finally, let the reader not overlook the fact that in our Codex the Masses, prayers, and petitions are often given headings. I cite Vigilius as a witness to how well this title agrees with the Book of Sacraments used in the Roman Church before Saint Gregory. More than forty years before him—that is, in the year 538—Vigilius wrote an “Order of Prayers” in his letter to Eutherius, chapter 5:

> “In the celebration of Masses we indicate that at no time, on no feast, do we have the rite divided, but always consecrate the gifts offered to God according to the same order. Whenever, however, the feast of Easter, or of the Lord’s Ascension, or of Pentecost, or of the Epiphany, or of God’s saints is to be celebrated, we append individual sections suited to the days, by which we make commemoration of the holy solemnity or of those whose birthdays we celebrate; but the rest we continue according to the customary order. Therefore we have also sent below the text of the canonical prayer itself, which, by God’s favor, we have received from apostolic tradition. And so that your Charity may know at which points you should attach material suited to particular feasts, we have likewise added the Prayers of Easter Day.”

Thus far Vigilius. Here, too, he called the Mass prayers “sections,” following an ancient custom, as may be seen in the Mozarabic Breviary, in which several prayers are called sections. This indication concerning the first Book of Sacraments of the Roman Church will suffice.

These matters seemed necessary to place briefly before the diligent reader. We had indeed begun to illuminate these Books of Sacraments with more extensive notes; but since we had no leisure, we preferred to satisfy the desire of learned men quickly rather than labor for a still longer time in elucidating them. For the same reason, we could not continue at length what we had begun around the middle of the book, in the outer margins, by adding textual corrections from other codices, because the codices then available were not at hand.

Nevertheless, in place of our notes, those concerning the Books of Sacraments of the Roman Church may be found in the highly learned commentaries of the distinguished men Vicecomes, Pamelius, Rocca, Menard, Haller, Habert, Morin, and Cardinal Bona, to say nothing of the Roman Order, Alcuin, Amalarius, and the other ancient writers. For Gallican Missals, however, the Fathers who should chiefly be consulted are Augustine, Caesarius of Arles, Gregory of Tours, and the other ancient writers of Gaul, from whom we have observed that considerable light may be obtained.

What we could not accomplish by means of longer annotations, we have nevertheless attempted to provide, at least in some fashion. As far as could properly be done in haste, we took care to compare the Book of Sacraments of the Roman Church with other sacred books—for we had no other examples of Gallican Missals—so that corrections of the errors with which it abounds might be readily available. What could not easily be corrected from such books, we have left for the reader to amend.

We wish the reader to be aware that, with complete fidelity, as is proper, we have presented the manuscript copies themselves, removing only those errors—and not even all of them—which would produce tedium rather than confidence. Such errors include *medillam*, *concide*, *antestes*, and so forth. These are attributable not so much to the copyist as to the Latin language, which at that time was common and vernacular, but already defiled by the mixture of barbarian speech. The remaining barbarisms and solecisms, especially those that could be restored in many different ways, we have deliberately retained.

## Alpha and Omega. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, Savior, the Book of the Sacraments of the Roman Church begins: the Order of the Cycle of the Year.

## XVI. Order for Those Performing Public Penance

You receive him on Wednesday morning at the beginning of Lent, cover him with sackcloth, pray for him, and enclose him until the Lord’s Supper. On that same day he is presented in the bosom of the Church, and, with his whole body prostrate on the ground, the bishop offers a prayer over him for reconciliation on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, as is contained there.

We ask, almighty God, that we may be numbered among the members of him whose body and blood we share. Through.

[Note: Pamelius, on Saturday of the third week: “whose body and blood we share.”]

### For the people

Be merciful to your people, O Lord, and do not deprive them of temporal consolation, whom you will to strive toward eternal things. Through.

## Tuesday

Grant, O Lord, we ask, the saving effect of the observance of our fast, so that the bodily chastisement undertaken may pass into the strengthening of our souls. Through the Lord.

Kindly pour into our hearts, O Lord, we ask, that just as we abstain from temporal foods, so also we may withdraw our senses from harmful excess.

[Note: Read: “bodily foods.”]

### Secret

Receive, almighty Creator God, what we fasting bring from the abundance of your generosity, and, in your mercy, turn the temporal assistance granted to us toward eternal life. Through.

### Postcommunion

We have received the vowed sacraments of the annual celebration. Grant, we ask, that they may anticipate for us both the remedies of temporal life and those of eternal life. Through.

[Note: Menard: “may proceed.”]

### For the people

Look favorably, O Lord, upon your people, and absolve from all sins those whom you grant to advance through divine sacraments. Through our Lord.

[Note: Pamelius, on the following Wednesday: “whom you grant to advance.”]

[Column 1067D]

## Wednesday

We beseech you, almighty God, that, abstaining from transitory works, we may instead perform those by which both hope and ability may be given us to attain eternal joys. Through the Lord.

Grant us peace of mind and body, O Lord, we ask, so that through fasting the manifest enemies of our weakness may be subjected and the invisible ones excluded. Through.

[Column 1068A]

### Secret

May these sacrifices, O Lord, graciously save us, for they have been instituted through medicinal fasts. Through.

### Postcommunion

Through the generosity of your gifts, O Lord, raise us up both by temporal assistance and renew us for eternal things. Through.

### For the people

Grant, we ask, to Christian peoples both to recognize what they profess and to love the heavenly gift which they frequent. Through.

[Note: Pamelius, on the following Thursday: “and the heavenly.”]

## Friday.

Of this abstinence, grant us, we ask, O Lord, a measure, so that what we take away from the license of the flesh may gain for us the salutary fruit of the mind. [Col. 1068B] Through.

Grant us, we ask, almighty God, always to handle with magnificence and worthiness the mysteries of the sacrament of fasting, and suitably its beginnings. Through.

### Secret

Receive, we ask, O Lord, the offerings of your devoted servants, and purify those who serve your divine mysteries by your divine loving-kindness, by which you also justify those who are ignorant. Through the Lord.

### Postcommunion

Grant, we ask, O Lord, that we may be filled with spiritual joys. [Note: [Col. 1068D] Read: “spiritual.”] Thus may we pursue in mind what we perform in deed. Through.

### For the people

May your people, O Lord, we ask, receive the gift of holy blessing, through which it may both avoid every harmful thing and obtain what it desires. [Col. 1068C] Through.

## SEVENTH FERIA

O God, who by glorious remedies already make us, while we are still placed on earth, participants in heavenly things, govern us, we ask, in this life in which we live, so that you may lead us to that light in which you yourself are. Through our Lord.

May your providence and mercy always repair and renew our frailty. [Note: [Col. 1068D] In Pamelius, under the vacant Sunday, it reads: “of your mercy, which.”] May it protect and govern us amid the storms of the world and bring us into the harbor of perpetual salvation. Through.

### Secret

May these blessed mysteries, we ask, O Lord, which restore us, make us worthy through their own gift. [Col. 1068D] Through the Lord.

### Postcommunion

Pursue perpetually with favor, O Lord, those whom you refresh with the divine mystery; and accompany with saving consolations those whom you have instructed in heavenly teachings. Through.

### For the people

May the desired blessing strengthen your faithful, O Lord, so that it may never allow them to depart from your will and may always grant them to rejoice in your benefits. [Col. 1069A] Through.

## XIX. The following prayers are to be said on the first Saturday of the first month. PRAYERS AND PETITIONS IN THE TWELVE LESSONS OF THE FIRST MONTH

O God, who do not permit those who sin to perish until they turn and live, suspend, we ask, the punishment due for our sins, and graciously grant that concealment may not increase vengeance, but rather that amendment through fasting may contribute to pardon. Through our Lord.

Turn all our hearts to yourself, O Lord, we ask, and, abstaining from those things by which you are offended, may we experience not your anger but your mercy. [Col. 1069B] Through.

May the consecrated fasts gladden us, we ask, O Lord, so that help may be granted to our weakness and the desired inclination toward virtue may enter our minds. Through the Lord.

Be present, we ask, almighty God, and refresh our mind through bodily fasting with the works of your commandments. Through the Lord.

Grant us, O Lord, observance that is legitimate and perfected by devotion, so that, through restraint from bodily nourishment, we may please you by holy conduct. Through.

Almighty and eternal God, who by salutary self-restraint heal bodies and minds, we humbly implore your majesty: being appeased by the devout prayer of those who fast, grant us both temporal assistance [Note: [Col. 1069D] In the Roman Missal: “and eternal.”] and eternal things. Through.

## XX.

The order of the manner in which priests, deacons, or subdeacons are to be chosen in the church of the apostolic Roman See.

In the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months, on the Saturday, during the twelve lessons, at Saint Peter’s, where the Masses are celebrated. After they have said the antiphon at the entrance, the pontiff, having given the prayer, announces to the people, saying:

“With the help of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 1069D] Read: “He says again, again.”] He says again:

“With the help of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, we have chosen, for the order of deacon or presbyter, that subdeacon or deacon from that titular church. If anyone has anything against these men, let him come forward confidently and say so, for God and on account of God. Nevertheless, let him remember his communion.”

After a short interval, everyone immediately begins: “Kyrie eleison,” with the litany. When this has been completed, the elect themselves go up to the pontiff’s seat, and he by whom they have been called blesses them [Note: [Col. 1069D] In Menardus: “to which.”] and they descend. Having received the blessing, they stand in their proper orders. [Note: [Col. 1069D] These words and the rubric that follows have been wrongly transposed here; they ought to be restored after the prayer in the twelve lessons.] Through.

The prayer of blessing follows. Find it in the fourth or tenth month.

### For the ordination of priests

Let us pray, most beloved, to almighty God the Father, that he may multiply heavenly gifts upon these servants of his whom he has chosen for the office of the presbyterate, and that they may carry out, with his help, what they receive through his favor. Through the Lord.

Hear us, God our Savior, and pour upon these servants of yours the blessing of the Holy Spirit and the power of priestly grace, so that those whom we present before the sight of your loving-kindness for consecration may attain it through the perpetual abundance of your gift. [Note: [Col. 1069D] Other codices: “may you accompany.”] Through.

### Consecration

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, distributor of all honors and dignities that serve you [Note: [Col. 1070D] In Menardus: “author and distributor of all honors and dignities. Through whom, etc.”]. Through whom all things advance, through whom all things are established, as the growth of rational nature is always increased for the better, arranged in fitting order by harmonious reason.

Hence the priestly rank and the offices of the Levites, instituted through mystical sacraments, grew, so that when you had placed high priests over the governance of peoples, you might choose, for the assistance of their fellowship and work, men of the succeeding order and of the second dignity. [Note: [Col. 1070D] We have corrected this, since the exemplar reads incorrectly: “you will have chosen.”]

Thus, in the wilderness, you spread Moses’ spirit through the minds of seventy prudent men, [Col. 1070C] and, using these helpers among the people, he governed innumerable multitudes with ease. Thus also you poured into Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron, the abundance of their father’s fullness, [Note: [Col. 1070D] Other codices: “so that the merit of the priests might suffice for the salutary sacrifices and the more frequent office.” In Menardus: “So that it might suffice for the salutary sacrifices and the more frequent sacraments of the priestly office and ministry, etc.”] so that the merit of the priests might suffice for the offices of the saving sacrifice.

By this providence, O Lord, you added to the apostles of your Son teachers and companions in the faith, by whom they filled the whole world with secondary preachers. Therefore, we ask, O Lord, grant these aids also to our weakness, for the more fragile we are, the more greatly we need them. [Note: [Col. 1070D] “More abundantly.”]

Grant, we ask, almighty Father, the dignity of the presbyterate to these servants of yours. Renew within them the Spirit of holiness, so that, having received from you, O God, the office of a secondary rank, they may obtain it and, by the example of their conduct, make known the discipline of morals. Let them be prudent cooperators in our order; let the full form of justice shine forth in them, so that, when they must render a good account of the stewardship entrusted to them, they may obtain the rewards of eternal blessedness. [Note: [Col. 1070D] Delete.] Through.

### Completion of the priest

Let us have a common prayer, brothers, that those who are chosen for the assistance and benefit of your salvation may obtain, through the indulgence of the divine gift, the blessing of the presbyterate, so that they may receive the priestly gifts of the Holy Spirit through the privilege of virtues and may not be found in an inferior position. [Note: [Col. 1071D] Read: “so that they.”] Through his own.

### Likewise, a blessing

Author of every sanctification, whose consecration is true and whose blessing is complete: you, O Lord, pour the hand of your blessing upon these servants of yours whom we dedicate with the honor of the presbyterate, so that by the gravity of their actions and the discipline of their manner of life they may prove themselves elders, instructed in those disciplines which Paul set forth to Titus and Timothy.

As they meditate day and night on your law, O Almighty, may they believe what they have chosen, teach what they have believed, and imitate what they have taught. [Note: [Col. 1071D] Delete “and”; from other Orders, in Morinus.] May they display in themselves justice, steadfastness, mercy, and fortitude; may they confirm them by example and strengthen them by admonition, so that they may guard the pure and undefiled gift of your ministry and, through the service of your people, transform the body and blood of your Son with undefiled blessing.

May they fulfill this with inviolate charity, attaining mature manhood, the measure of the fullness of Christ, and, on the day of the judgment of eternal justice [Note: [Col. 1071D] From the same Orders, read: “of the eternal judgment.”], with pure constancy, full faith, and fullness of the Holy Spirit. Through.

## XXI. A chapter of Saint Gregory the pope

Just as one who, when invited, refuses, and, when sought, withdraws, must be removed from the holy altars, so one who seeks office on his own initiative or thrusts himself forward importunately must unquestionably be rejected. For one who strives to climb to higher things—what does he do except diminish by increasing? Why is it not understood that the blessing is turned into a curse for him, and that he is advanced in such a way as to become a heretic? Through.

## XXII. For the ordination of deacons

Let us pray, most beloved, to almighty God the Father, that he may mercifully pour the blessing of his grace upon these servants of his whom he deigns to call to the office of the diaconate, and graciously preserve the gifts of mature consecration.

Let us pray.

[Col. 1071D] The prayer follows.

Lord God, graciously hear our prayers, [Note: [Col. 1071D] Read: “so that what.”] so that you may kindly accompany with your help what is to be carried out through our service, and those whom, according to our understanding, we believe ought to be presented for the execution of sacred ministries, may rather be justified by your choice.

### Consecration

Be present, we ask, almighty God, giver of honors, distributor of ranks, and arranger of offices. Abiding in yourself, you renew all things, and, disposing all things through your Word, Power, and Wisdom, Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, you prepare them by eternal providence and distribute to each the temporal things suited to them. [Note: [Col. 1071D] “At the proper times.”]

You grant that the body of your Church, distinguished by the variety of heavenly graces, joined together by the ordered arrangement of its members, and united by the law of its whole marvelous structure, may grow and spread for the enlargement of your temple, establishing the service of the sacred ministry to serve your name through three grades of ministers. [Note: [Col. 1071D] Read: “serving.”] From the beginning you chose the sons of Levi, who, remaining in faithful watchfulness over the mystical operations of your house, might possess the inheritance of eternal blessing by an everlasting lot.

Look with favor also, we ask, O Lord, upon these servants of yours whom we humbly dedicate to serve your sacred altars in the office of the diaconate. [Note: [Col. 1071D] “To serve your sacred altars in the office of the diaconate.”]

We, indeed, as human beings ignorant of divine understanding [Note: [Col. 1071D] Thus we have corrected the text from Menardus, since the exemplar reads incorrectly: “ignorant of supreme reason.”], judge the life of these men as far as we can. But you, O Lord, are not unaware of what is unknown to us, nor are you deceived by what is known to you. You are the knower of hearts [Note: [Col. 1072D] “Of secrets.”], the searcher of souls; you can truly exercise heavenly judgment upon them and, as though they were unworthy, grant what we ask.

Send upon them, we ask, O Lord, the Holy Spirit, by whom they may be strengthened for the faithful execution of the work of the ministry through the sevenfold gift of your grace. [Col. 1072C] Let every form of virtue abound in them, modest authority, constant modesty, purity of innocence, and spiritual observance of discipline. [Note: [Col. 1072D] In Menardus: “Purity of innocence and spiritual…”]

Let your commandments shine in their conduct. [Note: [Col. 1072D] The source has “his conduct.”] Thus, by the example of their chastity, may they gain the imitation of the holy people, [Note: [Col. 1072D] “The holy people’s imitation.”] and, bearing before them a good testimony of conscience, may they persevere firm and steadfast in Christ. Through your grace may they deserve, by worthy advancement from the lower rank, to receive higher things. Through.

## XXIII. For completing the offices of the deacons

Let a common prayer accompany the common vow, so that these men, who are prepared for the ministry of the diaconate by the prayer of the whole Church, may shine with Levitical blessing [Note: [Col. 1072D] Add from other Orders, in Morinus: “may shine in rank.”] and, preeminent in spiritual conduct, may shine forth with the grace of sanctification. Through.

### The blessing follows

Lord, giver of holy hope, faith, grace, and advancement, who, having appointed the ministering angels everywhere in heavenly and earthly things, pour forth the impulse of your will through all the elements, graciously regard these servants of yours with your special attention. [Note: [Col. 1073D] So that the sentence is complete, read: “their names.”]

May they, freed for your service, grow as pure ministers at the sacred altars. [Note: [Col. 1073D] Read: “holy.”] By your indulgence, may they become purer, and may they prove worthy in their rank of those whom your apostles chose as a group of seven, with blessed Stephen as leader and forerunner, under the direction of the Holy Spirit. Instructed in all the virtues by which it is necessary to serve you, may they please you. Through.

## XXIV. Likewise, prayer and petition

### At Mass

Hear, O Lord, the prayers of your suppliants, and guard perpetually with your defense those who serve you with devoted heart, so that, hindered by no disturbances, we may always offer free service in your offices. [Col. 1073B] Through.

### Secret

Work through your mysteries, O Lord, we ask, so that we may offer these gifts to you with worthy minds. Through.

You graciously instruct the rational creature by your dispensation, so that, devoted to temporal goods, it may not strive toward eternal rewards. [Note: [Col. 1073D] This passage should be corrected from the Roman edition of the Gregorian Sacramentary, in the preface for the Sunday of Sexagesima: “So that, devoted to temporal goods, it may not fail to strive toward eternal rewards, you graciously instruct it by that dispensation, so that it may neither fail through correction nor grow insolent through prosperity, etc.”] May it neither fail through correction nor grow insolent through prosperity; but rather let this be its glorious devotion, by which, overwhelmed by no adversities, it may be overcome. [Note: [Col. 1074D] In the same Sacramentary: “Through Christ our Lord.”] Through him your majesty.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, this offering which we present to you for your servants whom you have deigned to advance to the ranks of the presbyterate or diaconate, we ask you, O Lord, graciously to receive; and what you have conferred upon them by the divine gift, graciously preserve in them as your own gifts. Through Christ our Lord. Quam.

### Postcommunion

Kindly raise up with your assistance those whom you refresh with the sacraments, O Lord, so that we may receive the effect of your redemption both in the mysteries and in our conduct. Through.

### For the people

Grant, we ask, O Lord, to the Christian peoples both to recognize what they profess and to love the heavenly gift that they frequent. Through. [Note: [Col. 1074D] Add: “the Lord.”]

## XXV. SECOND SUNDAY

[Col. 1073D]

### In Lent

Grant us, almighty God, that, since our mortality is subject to vices, your medicine may purify us and your power protect us. Through the Lord.

Grant us, merciful God, to implore your reconciliation with ready minds and, obtaining forgiveness of sins, to be freed from harmful assaults. Through.

### Secret

Graciously receive, O Lord, the gifts of your Church, which you mercifully granted to be offered and powerfully cause to pass into the mystery of our salvation. Through.

### Postcommunion

Refreshed, O Lord, with heavenly bread, may we be nourished, we ask, for eternal life. Through.

### For the people

Graciously enlighten your household, we ask, O Lord, so that, clinging to what pleases you, it may deserve to receive all good things. Through.

## SECOND FERIA OF THE SECOND WEEK

Be present, we ask, O Lord, to your suppliants, and amid the snares of worldly wickedness accompany our frailty with everlasting mercy. Through the Lord.

Accompany your Church, O Lord, with perpetual compassion, so that, established amid the storms of the age, it may breathe again in present joy [Note: [Col. 1074D] In Pamelius, on the Thursday after the Second Sunday of Lent, it reads: “and may receive eternal blessedness.”] and receive eternal blessedness. Through.

### Secret

Grant us, we ask, O Lord, to frequent these mysteries, because whenever the celebration of this sacrifice is commemorated, the work of our redemption is carried out. [Note: [Col. 1074D] Read: “whenever.”] Through.

### Postcommunion

May the holy things we have received help us, O Lord, and fill us with their teachings. Through.

[Col. 1074C] ### For the people

Turn your people to yourself with all their heart, O Lord, we ask, because those whom you defend even when they sin, you protect with greater mercy when they are devoted with a sincere mind. Through.

## THIRD FERIA OF THE SECOND WEEK

O God, who commanded bodies to be chastened by the devotion of fasting for the healing of souls, [Note: [Col. 1074D] In Menardus, in the preface for the aforementioned Thursday: “to be chastened.”] grant that our hearts may be able to practice the commands of your loving-kindness in such a way that we may always abstain from every sin. Through.

We implore your clemency, O Lord, that these divine aids of fasting, after cleansing us from vices, may prepare us for the coming festivals. Through.

[Col. 1074D] ### Secret

Sanctify our fasts by these present sacrifices, O Lord, so that what our observance professes outwardly may work inwardly. Through.

### Postcommunion

We desire the marvelous delights of the heavenly table, O Lord, by which, through fasting, we are more abundantly filled. Through.

[Col. 1075A] ### For the people

Grant, we ask, O Lord, to your faithful both to receive the Paschal mysteries without ceasing and eagerly to await what is to come, so that, remaining in the mysteries by which they have been reborn, they may be led by these works to new life. Through.

## FOURTH FERIA OF THE SECOND WEEK

O God, who wonderfully accomplish the reconciliation of the human race through your Word, grant, we ask, that through holy fasting we may be subject to you with all our heart and may be made harmonious with you in prayer. Through the Lord.

Grant us, O Lord, we ask, the help of your grace, so that, intent in a fitting manner upon fasts and prayers, [Col. 1075B] we may be freed from enemies of mind and body. Through.

### Secret

May the fasts dedicated to your name sanctify us, O Lord, through this present sacrifice, and may what our observance professes outwardly produce its effect inwardly. Through.

### Postcommunion

May your grace not abandon us, we ask, O Lord; may it make us devoted to sacred service and always obtain your help for us. Through.

### For the people

Be present to your servants, O Lord, and grant help to those who ask for it, so that you may restore in favor those who glory in having you as author and governor, and preserve what has been restored. [Note: [Col. 1075D] In Pamelius, on the Thursday, it reads: “and having been gathered.”] Through.

[Col. 1075C] ## SIXTH FERIA OF THE SECOND WEEK

For overcoming our enemies, grant, we ask, O Lord, that we may obtain your help through fasts pleasing to you and through good works. Through the Lord.

Almighty and eternal God, who by salutary self-restraint heal bodies and minds, we humbly implore your majesty: being appeased by the devout prayer of those who fast, grant us temporal assistance [Note: [Col. 1075D] Delete “and.”] and eternal things. Through.

### Secret

May this offering become pleasing, O Lord, we ask, through the solemn fasts, so that it may be more acceptable to you and that we, purified in mind, may be offered in sacrifice. [Note: [Col. 1075D] In Menardus, on the Thursday, it reads: “may be sacrificed.”]

### Postcommunion

[Note: [Col. 1075D] In the same source, on the Monday after Palm Sunday: “May they provide.”] May your divine holy things, O Lord, we ask, go before us with fervor, so that we may alike delight in their action and their fruit. Through.

Look favorably upon your people, O Lord, and do not abandon with temporal consolation those who strive toward eternal things. Through.

Come to the aid of your servants, O Lord, who continually groan over their own iniquity, and grant to unload our minds, weighed down by earthly attachments, through the medicinal fasts. [Note: [Col. 1076D] In the same source, in the preface for Saturday: “to be unloaded.”] Strengthen the affection of the body. Through the Lord.

O God, who, in profound counsel and by watching over mortals, instituted holy fasts by which the hearts of the sick might be healed beneficially, sanctify our soul and body, Savior of soul and body, kindly giver of eternal happiness. Through the Lord.

### Secret

Lord our God, in whose spiritual camp sobriety worthy of praise, fruitful abstinence, and the rich frugality of a chaste heart serve, graciously receive the vows of those who fast and, with your customary compassion, come to the aid of the faithful in their requests. Through.

[Col. 1076B] ### Postcommunion

May the tasting of the sacred table, O Lord, we ask, grant us both an increase of devout conduct and the continual help of your reconciliation. Through our Lord.

### For the people

## XXVI. THIRD SUNDAY

Celebrated for the scrutinies of the elect.

Grant, we ask, O Lord, that our elect may approach the confession of your praise worthily and wisely, so that through your glory they may be restored to the former dignity which they had lost through the transgression of original sin. [Col. 1076C] Through.

### Secret

May your mercy, O God, both fittingly precede your servants, we ask, in receiving these mysteries and lead them to them through devout conduct. Through.

“Remember, O Lord, your servants, men and women, who are to receive your elect into the holy grace of your baptism, and all who stand around you.” And you are silent. The names of the men and women who are to receive those infants are recited. And you enter: “Whose faith you know…”

We beseech you, O Lord, graciously to receive this offering, [Col. 1076D] which we present to you for your servants, men and women, whom you have deigned to count, choose, and call to eternal life and the blessed gift of your grace. [Note: [Col. 1076D] From the Roman Order, correct to: “the gift of your grace.”] Through Christ.

And the names of the elect are recited.

## SECOND FERIA OF THE THIRD WEEK

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that at the beginnings of the restoration of our abstinence we may go before it with fitting and worthy duties. Through.

### Secret

May these blessed mysteries, O God, make us fit to recount their beginnings. [Col. 1077B]

Within the Canon, as above.

It follows:

### Postcommunion

### For the people

Accompany us, almighty God, and grant that those whom you command to abstain from foods of the flesh may also cease from harmful vices. Through the Lord.

Grant, we ask, O Lord, eternal King of all, that, purified by sacred fasting, you may also bring us with sincere minds to your holy things that are to come. Through.

### Secret

### Postcommunion

### For the people

[Col. 1077D] Grant, merciful God, that your devoted people may always exist and unceasingly obtain from your clemency what benefits them. Through.

O God, who taught us the form of humility through fasting and prayer, in imitation of your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord, grant, we ask, that what he completed through the continual practice of fasts, we too may fulfill by stages throughout the days. Through.

Grant us, O Lord, we ask, observance perfected by legitimate devotion, so that, through restraint from bodily nourishment, we may please you by holy conduct. Through.

### Secret

O God, from whose dew of grace it comes that we approach your mysteries with purified senses, grant, we ask, that in solemnly honoring their tradition we may offer fitting service. Through.

### Postcommunion

Receiving the glorious mysteries, we give thanks, O Lord, because you grant that we, placed on earth, are already participants in heavenly things. Through.

### For the people

## SIXTH FERIA OF THE THIRD WEEK

Grant, we ask, O Lord, that, recalling the sacred observances with annual devotion, we may please you both in body and in mind. Through.

Grant, we ask, O Lord, sufficient assistance suited to our frailty, so that it may both acknowledge the effect of its restoration through devout conduct and receive it with exultation. Through.

### Secret

May the gifts of our fasting be acceptable to you, O Lord, we ask, so that by cleansing us your grace may make us worthy and lead us to eternal promises. Through.

### Postcommunion

Kindly raise up with your assistance those whom you refresh with the sacraments, O Lord, [Col. 1078C] so that we may receive the effect of your redemption both in the mysteries and in our conduct. Through.

### For the people

May abundant blessing descend upon your people, O Lord, we ask; may forgiveness come, consolation be granted, holy faith increase, and eternal redemption be made firm. Through.

## SEVENTH FERIA OF THE THIRD WEEK

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that the dignity of the human condition, wounded by immoderation, may be restored through the practice of medicinal restraint. Through the Lord.

### Secret

### Postcommunion

May we grasp in mind what we have taken with the mouth, O Lord, and may the temporal gift become for us an eternal remedy. Through.

[Col. 1079A] ### For the people

Be favorable, we ask, O Lord, to your people, so that, rejecting what does not please you, they may rather be filled with the delights of your commandments. Through the Lord.

## XXVII. FOURTH SUNDAY

### For the second scrutiny

Almighty and eternal God, multiply your Church with spiritual joy, so that those who are earthly by generation may become heavenly by regeneration. Through.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] In the margin: “Secret.”] [lacuna]

We offer, rejoicing, the gifts of eternal healing, O Lord, and humbly implore that you may perfect us so that we may both worthily venerate these same gifts [Note: [Col. 1079D] From the Roman Order, correct to: “worthily.”] and fittingly present them for those who are to be saved. [Col. 1079B] Through.

Within the Canon, as above.

It follows:

### Postcommunion

Always kindly raise up your household, O Lord; arrange it when corrected; graciously protect it when subject to you; govern it by perpetual goodness, so that it may be saved. Through.

### For the people

Kindly instruct your servants, we ask, O Lord, in good conduct; graciously infuse into them what pleases you, so that they may both be worthy and be able to earn your benefits. Through.

## SECOND FERIA OF THE FOURTH WEEK

May the fasts of sacred observance, O Lord, we ask, grant us both an increase of devout conduct and the continual help of your reconciliation. Through.

May the inclination toward devout devotion of the people dedicated to you advance, we ask, O Lord, so that, instructed by sacred actions, the more pleasing it is to your majesty, the more abundantly it may be increased with better gifts. Through.

### Secret

Graciously absolve us from every guilt and danger, we ask, O Lord, and grant that we may be participants in so great a mystery. Through the Lord.

### Postcommunion

Satisfied by the abundance of the divine gift, we ask you, Lord our God, to live always in participation in this. Through.

[Col. 1079D] ### For the people

May your right hand protect the people who entreat you, O Lord, and graciously instruct them when purified, so that through present consolation they may advance toward future goods. Through.

## THIRD FERIA OF THE FOURTH WEEK

Grant, Recreator of our highest condition, that we may always turn away from evils and pursue every good thing with ready will. Through the Lord.

May the venerable practice of the salutary fast dispose the hearts of your people, so that it may receive the Paschal mystery with worthy minds [Col. 1080A] and take up an increase of continuous devotion. Through.

### Secret

Purify us, merciful God, so that the prayers of your Church, which offers you pleasing gifts with devotion, may become more pleasing when offered by purified minds. Through.

### Postcommunion

Since we are receiving heavenly gifts, we ask, O Lord, do not permit us to come to judgment through what you have provided for your faithful as a remedy. Through.

### For the people

O God, founder and ruler of your people, drive away the sins by which they are attacked. [Note: [Col. 1079D] In Pamelius, on the Thursday of the fourth week of Lent: “by which they are assaulted.”] Thus may they always be pleasing to you and secure under your protection. Through.

[Col. 1080B] ## FOURTH FERIA OF THE FOURTH WEEK

Almighty and eternal God, who grant both rewards of merit to the just and, through fasting, forgiveness of their error to sinners, have mercy on your suppliants and spare those who sin, so that confession of our guilt may obtain forgiveness of sins. Through our Lord.

Grant, merciful God, that, just as you grant us to offer a solemn fast to you, so you may graciously provide us the help of your forgiveness. Through.

### Secret

May the offering of our devotion be acceptable to you, O Lord; through your working, may it sanctify our fast and obtain the forgiveness of your consolation. Through.

### Postcommunion

Satisfied with the blessing of the sacraments, we ask, O Lord, that through them we may always be cleansed from vices. Through.

### For the people

Grant your people, O Lord, the inclination toward devout devotion always, so that, rejecting what is depraved, it may be strengthened by holy conduct and, freed from sins, may not be crushed by any adversities. Through.

## SIXTH FERIA OF THE FOURTH WEEK

Grant, we ask, O Lord, that, instructed by salutary fasts and abstaining also from harmful vices, we may more easily obtain your reconciliation. Through.

Accompany, we ask, almighty God, the sacred mysteries of the fasts, and grant that those whom you command to abstain from foods of the flesh may also cease from harmful vices. Through.

[Col. 1080D] ### Secret

May these sacrifices, almighty God, after cleansing us by powerful virtue, make us come purer to their own beginning. Through.

### Postcommunion

[Note: [Col. 1080D] Read: “Holy things.”] May your sacred things, O Lord, we ask, both renew us by giving life and give us life by renewing us. Through.

### For the people

Be present, O Lord, to the peoples who have touched the sacred mysteries. [Note: [Col. 1080D] Read: “have received.”] May those who trust in you as their protector be afflicted by no dangers. Through the Lord.

[Col. 1081A] ## SEVENTH FERIA OF THE FOURTH WEEK

O God, author of all mercies and of every goodness, who showed that remedies for sins are found in fasts, prayers, and almsgiving, look favorably upon this confession of our humility, so that we who are bowed down by our conscience may always be raised up by your mercy. Through.

May your grace, O Lord, we ask, exercise us through venerable holy fasts and make us more suitable for the heavenly mysteries. Through.

### Secret

We offer you, O Lord, the gifts which you have given, so that they may both bear witness to the assistance of your creation toward our mortality and bring about the remedy of immortality. [Col. 1081B] Through.

### Postcommunion

May your sacraments, received by us, O Lord, provide assistance, so that our fasts may be pleasing to you and may benefit us as a remedy. Through the Lord.

### For the people

Restore your people, O Lord, we ask, inwardly and outwardly, whom you do not wish to be hindered by bodily delights; make them flourish in spiritual purpose, and so nourish them with passing things [Note: [Col. 1081D] Read: “transitory things”] that you may instead grant them to cling to what is everlasting. Through.

## XXVIII. FIFTH SUNDAY
Which is celebrated for the scrutiny.

Grant, Lord, to our elect that, instructed in the sacred mysteries [Note: Read: “holy”], they may both be renewed in the font of baptism and be numbered among the members of your Church. Through the Lord.

Secret.

Hear us, almighty God, and grant that your servants, whom you have imbued with the first beginnings of the Christian faith, may be cleansed through the working of this sacrifice. Through.

Within the canon, as above.

It follows:

Postcommunion.

May your people, Lord, we beseech you, come together and, subject to you with their whole heart, obtain that, secure from every disturbance, they may eagerly celebrate the joys of their salvation and kindly intercede for those who are to be regenerated. Through.

For the People.

[Col. 1081D] O God, who are always at work for the salvation of humankind, yet now multiply your people with more abundant grace: look favorably upon your chosen ones, so that, by the help of the Father’s protection, you may strengthen both those who are to be regenerated and those who have been reborn. Through.

MONDAY OF THE FIFTH WEEK.

O God, who give temporal things to those created in your image for this purpose, that you may bestow eternal things, multiply your Church by spiritual fruitfulness, so that those who are earthly by generation may become heavenly by regeneration. Through the Lord.

Help us, O God our Savior, and purify our minds in the sacrifice of fasts, so that you may grant us to come joyfully to recall the benefits by which you have deigned to restore us. Through.

Secret.

Hear us, almighty God, and grant that your servants, whom you have imbued with the first beginnings of the Christian faith, may be cleansed through the working of this sacrifice. Through.

Postcommunion.

May the mysteries we have received sanctify us, Lord, and grant us sufficient strength for the observance of Easter. Through.

For the People.

May blessing, Lord, we beseech you, descend abundantly upon your faithful, and may they generously obtain what they seek with submissive hearts. Through.

[Col. 1082B] TUESDAY OF THE FIFTH WEEK.

Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that, recalling the sacred observances with annual devotion, we may please you both in body and in mind. Through.

May the inclination of our devotion become fruitful through your grace, we beseech you, Lord, for the fasts we have undertaken will benefit us only if they are pleasing to your loving-kindness. Through.

Secret.

Grant us, we beseech you, Lord, that, when we are about to celebrate the sacred mysteries [Note: Read: “holy”], we may possess not only bodily abstinence but, what is more important, purity of mind. Through.

Postcommunion.

May the libation of your table always nourish and renew us, Lord; may it govern and protect our frailty and lead us into the harbor of everlasting salvation. Through.

For the People.

Deliver from sins and enemies, Lord, we beseech you, your people who beseech you; may those who live in holy conduct suffer no adversity. Through the Lord.

WEDNESDAY OF THE FIFTH WEEK.

May the fasts we carry out according to sacred ordinances, we beseech you, Lord, always free us from our guilt and make your justice favorable toward us. Through the Lord.

[Col. 1082D] Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that those whom vowed fasts chastise may also be gladdened by that same holy devotion, so that, with earthly desires quieted, we may more readily grasp heavenly things. Through.

Secret.

Grant, almighty God, that, appeased by the sacrifices of fasting, you may follow us with the pardon of your forgiveness. Through.

Postcommunion.

Be present to your faithful, Lord, and preserve from earthly dangers those whom you refresh with heavenly sacraments. Through the Lord.

[Col. 1083A] For the People.

Look favorably upon your flock, Good Shepherd, and do not allow the sheep whom you redeemed with the precious blood of your Son to be torn by the devil’s attack. Through.

FRIDAY OF THE FIFTH WEEK.

Grant us, we beseech you, Lord, forgiveness of sins, so that we may carry out the Easter observances with dispositions pleasing to you. Through.

Almighty and eternal God, we humbly implore your clemency: you always anticipate our evils with mercy; make us pleasing to you by expiating them through pious actions and salutary fasts. Through.

Secret.

[Col. 1083B] Sanctify us, we beseech you, Lord, by these gifts that are to be offered, and grant us sufficient strength for the observance of Easter. Through.

Postcommunion.

Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that the gift bestowed through so great a mystery may be not condemnation but healing for those who receive it. Through.

For the People.

Protect your people, Lord, and guide with perpetual defense those who trust in the patronage of your saints [Note: Read: “who confess”]. Through.

SATURDAY OF THE FIFTH WEEK.

Almighty and eternal God, who through salutary abstinence heal both our bodies and our minds [Col. 1083C], we humbly implore your Majesty that, appeased by the pious prayer of those who fast, you may grant us both present assistance and future blessings. Through.

Sanctify this fast [Note: It should be read: “and the hearts of your faithful.” Or, as in the printed editions: “Having sanctified this fast, illumine the hearts of your faithful,” etc.], merciful God; illumine the hearts of your faithful, and graciously grant a kindly hearing to those who beseech you, upon whom you bestow the disposition of devotion. Through.

Secret.

May these sacrifices, Lord, more fully restore us, since they have been instituted through medicinal fasts. Through.

Postcommunion.

We beseech you, Lord our God, that just as you feed us with the nourishment of the most holy body and blood of your Son, so also you may make us partakers of his divine nature. Through.

For the People.

Visit your people, we beseech you, Lord, and guard with watchful loving-kindness the hearts dedicated to the sacred mysteries, so that they may preserve, under your protection, the remedies of eternal salvation which they receive through your mercy. Through.

XXIX. ANNOUNCEMENT FOR THE SCRUTINY, WHICH IS INITIATED ON MONDAY OF THE THIRD WEEK IN LENT. [Note: [Col. 1083D] Thus we have emended it from the old manuscript Missal of Cardinal Sanctorius in the Barberini Library; in the exemplar it read: “initiarum.” In Vatican Codex 567 the same scrutiny is found, so that we understand that the Roman Church used it.]

[Col. 1084A]

Know, beloved brothers, that the day of the scrutiny is approaching, on which our elect are to be divinely instructed. Therefore, with conscientious devotion, be pleased to assemble on the following Monday, around the sixth hour of the day, so that, with God’s help, we may be able to carry out without blame the heavenly mystery by which the devil with his pomp will be destroyed [Note: The old manuscript Missal of the same cardinal reads: “is destroyed”] and the gate of the heavenly kingdom opened. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

When they have come to the church, the names of the infants are written down by the acolyte, and they are called in the church by name, just as they have been written. The boys are placed on the right side, the girls on the left, and the priest says a prayer over them.

XXX. PRAYER OVER THE ELECT, FOR MAKING A CATECHUMEN.

Almighty and eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, deign to look upon these servants of yours, whom you have deigned to call to the beginnings of faith. Drive every blindness of heart away from them; break all the snares of Satan by which they had been bound; open to them, Lord, the door of your loving-kindness [Note: Pamelius has: “that they may be marked with the sign”]. Imbued with the sign of your wisdom, may they be free from the foulness of every desire, and, rejoicing in the sweet fragrance of your commandments, may they serve you gladly in the Church [Col. 1084C]. May they advance from day to day, so that they may become fit to approach the grace of your baptism, having received the remedy [Note: Thus we have emended it from Pamelius, since the exemplar erroneously reads: “of the received medicine.”]. Through our Lord.

Mercifully hear our prayers, we beseech you, Lord, and guard these your elect by the power of the Lord’s cross, with whose impress we mark them [Note: Pamelius reads: “by the impress,” although the prayer speaks in the singular]. May they preserve the beginnings of the greatness of glory and, through keeping your commandments, deserve to reach the glory of regeneration. Through.

O God, who are the creator of the human race in such a way that you are also its reformer, be favorable to your adopted peoples and enroll the offspring of a new people in the new covenant, so that the children of promise may rejoice that they have received through grace what they could not attain by nature [Note: Thus corrected from Pamelius; the exemplar erroneously reads: “what they were unable”]. Through our Lord.

XXXI. BLESSING OF SALT TO BE GIVEN TO A CATECHUMEN.

I exorcise you, creature of salt, in the name of God the almighty Father, and in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the power of the Holy Spirit. I exorcise you by the living God and by the true God, who created you for the protection of the human race and commanded you to be consecrated by his servants for the people coming to faith. Therefore we beseech you, Lord our God, that this creature of salt may become, in the name of the Trinity, a saving sacrament for driving away the enemy. May you, Lord, sanctify it by sanctifying it, bless it by blessing it, so that it may become a perfect medicine for all who receive it, remaining in their innermost being, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

After this prayer, place salt in the infant’s mouth and say:

Receive the salt of wisdom; may it be propitious unto eternal life.

XXXII. BLESSING AFTER THE SALT HAS BEEN GIVEN.

[Col. 1085B]

God of our fathers, creator of all truth, we humbly implore you to look favorably upon this servant of yours, so that, having tasted this first nourishment of salt, you may not permit him to hunger any longer, but may fill him with heavenly food [Note: We have inserted this from Pamelius, because the exemplar incorrectly had: “so that he may not be filled”]. Thus may he always be fervent in spirit, rejoicing in hope, and always serving your name, Lord. Lead him to the washing of new birth, so that, together with your faithful, he may deserve to obtain the eternal rewards of your promises. Through the Lord.

XXXIII. HERE BEGIN THE EXORCISMS OVER THE ELECT, WHICH THE ACOLYTES ARE TO RECITE WITH THEIR HAND PLACED UPON THEM.

[Col. 1085C]

God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God who appeared to your servant Moses on Mount Sinai and led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, appointing for them an angel of your loving-kindness to guard them day and night: we beseech you, Lord, deign to send your holy angel, so that he may likewise guard these your servants and lead them to the grace of your baptism.

Therefore, accursed devil, acknowledge your sentence and give honor to the living and true God; give honor to Jesus Christ, his Son, and to the Holy Spirit; and depart from these servants of God. For God and our Lord Jesus Christ has deigned to call these persons to his holy grace and blessing and to the gift of the baptismal font [Note: Cardinal Sanctorius’s Missal omits “gift”]. By this sign of the holy cross, which we place upon their foreheads [Note: Read: “which we give them”; we have emended it from Pamelius. The exemplar is incorrectly written: “which we”], never dare, accursed devil, to violate them.

Likewise [Note: In the margin: “over the women.”].

God of heaven, God of earth, God of angels, God of archangels, God of prophets, God of martyrs, God of all who live well, God to whom every tongue of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth confesses: I call upon you, Lord, to deign to lead these your female servants to the grace of your baptism and to guard them. Therefore, accursed one, as above.

Likewise over the boys.

Hear, accursed Satan, adjured by the name of the eternal God and of our Savior, the Son of God. Defeated by your envy, depart trembling and groaning. Let nothing be shared between you and the servants of God, who already think of heavenly things and are about to renounce you [Note: Read: “those renouncing you.” — But Pamelius’s “about to renounce” is erroneous], together with your age [Note: Pamelius so reads. The exemplar incorrectly has: “your world”], and who are to live for blessed immortality [Note: The exemplar has incorrectly: “of the victor”]. Therefore give honor to the Holy Spirit who is coming, who, descending from the highest citadel of heaven, will make hearts cleansed by the divine font—that is, sanctified—a temple and dwelling place for God [Note: Read: “habitation.” — But this is erroneous]. Then, completely freed from all the harmful things of their former crimes [Col. 1086B] [Note: Pamelius reads: “faults”], the servants of God may always give thanks to the eternal God and bless his holy name forever and ever. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

Likewise over the girls.

God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God who instructed the tribes of Israel [Note: Pamelius has: “who freed Israel from Egyptian slavery through your servant Moses and admonished them concerning the keeping of your commandments”], and freed Susanna from a false accusation: I humbly implore you, Lord, to free these your female servants also and to deign to lead them to the grace of your baptism. Therefore, accursed one, as above.

Likewise over the boys.

I exorcise you, unclean spirit, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, that you may go out and depart from these servants of God. For he himself commands you, accursed and condemned one, who walked upon the sea with his feet and extended his right hand to Peter as he was sinking. Therefore, accursed one, as above.

Likewise over the girls.

I exorcise you, unclean spirit, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, that you may go out and depart from these female servants. For he himself commands you, accursed and condemned one, who opened the eyes of the man born blind and raised Lazarus, four days dead, from the tomb. Therefore, accursed one, as above.

The following is the prayer which the priest is to say.

I beseech your eternal and most just loving-kindness, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God of light and truth, over these your male and female servants, that you may deign to illumine them with the light of your understanding. Cleanse them and sanctify them. Give them true knowledge, so that they may become worthy to approach the grace of your baptism. May they hold firm hope, right counsel, and holy teaching, so that they may be fit to receive your grace. Through.

XXXIV. HERE BEGINS THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPELS FOR THE OPENING OF THE EARS OF THE ELECT.

[Col. 1087A]

First, four deacons come out of the sacristy with the four Gospels, preceded by two candelabra with incense burners [Note: From Cardinal Sanctorius’s Missal. The exemplar reads: “thurabula”], and they are placed at the four corners of the altar. Before any of them reads, the priest addresses them in these words:

When we are about to open the Gospels, dearest sons—that is, the divine deeds—we must first explain their order to you: what the Gospel is, from where it comes, whose words are set down in it, and why there are four who wrote these deeds, or who those four are whom the Prophet marked out when announcing them by the divine Spirit. Otherwise, without this explanation of order or reason, we might leave astonishment in your minds. And since you have come for this purpose, so that your ears may be opened and your understanding may not begin to grow dull, hear this.

“Gospel” properly means “good announcement,” and this announcement is certainly that of Jesus Christ our Lord. The Gospel derives its name from announcing and showing that the one who was speaking through the prophets has come in the flesh, as it is written: “I who was speaking—behold, I am here.” Having briefly explained what the Gospel is and who the four are who were previously shown through the Prophet, let us now assign their respective names to the individual signs.

For the prophet Ezekiel says: “And the likeness of their faces was as the face of a man, and the face of a lion on his right; and the face of a calf, and the face of an eagle on his left.” [Note: The exemplar incorrectly has: “These.”] There is no doubt that these four, bearing these figures, are the evangelists. The names of those who wrote the Gospels are these: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

And the deacon announces, saying:

Stand in silence and listen attentively.

And, beginning, he reads: “The beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew,” up to: “For he himself will save his people from their sins.”

After he has read, the priest addresses them in these words:

Dearest sons, so that we may not detain you any longer, let us explain what meaning and what figure each one contains, and why Matthew bears the figure of a man. At his beginning he does nothing other than narrate the Savior’s birth in the full order of his genealogy. For he begins in this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” You see that the persona of a man has rightly been assigned to him, since he begins with the birth of a man; and, as we have said, the persona of Matthew has rightly been assigned to this mystery.

Likewise the deacon announces, as above:

Stand in silence and listen attentively.

And he reads: “The beginning of the Gospel according to Mark,” up to: “I baptize you with water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

And the priest continues in these words:

The evangelist Mark, bearing the figure of a lion, begins from the wilderness, saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord.” [Note: You find these same words in the old Gallican Missal. Cardinal Sanctorius’s Missal reads: “Or because he reigns.”] Or because he reigns unconquered. We find many examples of this lion [Note: Read: “of many forms.” — But this is erroneous], so that that saying is not without purpose: “Judah, my son, a lion’s cub; from the shoot you have grown up for me; lying down, he slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub: who will rouse him?” [Note: Read: “who has roused him?”]

Likewise the deacon announces, as above.

And he reads: “The beginning of the Gospel according to Luke,” up to: “To prepare a perfect people for the Lord.”

[Col. 1088B] And the priest continues in these words:

The evangelist Luke bears the likeness of a calf, after whose pattern our Savior was sacrificed. For, about to speak of Christ’s Gospel, he began with Zechariah and Elizabeth, from whom John the Baptist was born in their advanced old age. And therefore Luke is compared with a calf, because it has two horns, the two Testaments, and four hoofed feet, the four Gospels, containing them within himself as though they were born with tender strength [Note: The old Gallican Missal placed below reads: “most fully.” Cardinal Sanctorius’s Missal omits “born”].

Likewise the deacon makes the announcement as above.

And he reads: “The beginning of the Gospel according to John,” up to: “Full of grace and truth.”

The priest again continues in these words:

John bears the likeness of an eagle, because he sought things exceedingly high. For he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.” And David says concerning the person of Christ: “Your youth will be renewed like that of an eagle”—that is, of Jesus Christ our Lord, who, rising from the dead, ascended into heaven.

Therefore, now that you have conceived [Note: Thus corrected from Cardinal Sanctorius’s Missal. The exemplar is corruptly written: “pregnant”], the pregnant Church rejoices, declaring that the whole celebration of her vows tends toward the new beginnings of the Christian law, so that, when the venerable day of Easter arrives, having been reborn through the washing of baptism, you may all, like the saints, deserve to receive from Christ our Lord the faithful gift of infancy. He lives and reigns forever and ever.

XXXV. HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE OF THE CREED FOR THE ELECT—that is, before you say the Creed, you shall continue in these words:

[Col. 1088D]

Dearest ones, since you are about to receive the sacraments of baptism and to be brought forth as a new creation in the Holy Spirit, conceive with your whole heart the faith by which you are to be justified as believers. Having changed your minds through a true way of life, draw near to God, who illumines our minds. Receive the sacrament of the evangelical Creed [Note: The manuscript Missal of Cardinal Sanctorius reads: “evangelical”], inspired by the Lord and established by the apostles [Note: In the same Missal: “by the Apostles”]. Its words are few indeed, but its mysteries are great.

For the Holy Spirit, who dictated these things to the teachers of the Church, established the saving faith in such speech and with such brevity that what you must believe and always keep before you can neither escape the understanding nor burden the memory. Therefore learn the Creed with attentive minds, and write what we hand on to you as we have received it—not on any material that can decay, but on the pages of your hearts. The confession of faith which you have received begins with this preface.

After this, the acolyte takes one of the male infants, holds him in his left arm, and places his hand upon his head. The priest asks him [Note: The exemplar reads: “asks him”]:

“In what language do they confess our Lord Jesus Christ?”

Response: “In Greek.”

Again the priest says:

“Announce their faith, how they believe.”

And the acolyte chants the Creed in Greek, holding his hand over the infant’s head, in these words: [Note: In Migne, the transliterated Greek version of the following text is printed as an interlinear translation of the Latin.]

I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages; light from light; true God from true God; begotten, not made; of one substance with the Father, through whom all things were made; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven; and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became human; was also crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered, and was buried; and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures; and ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; and will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead; his kingdom will have no end [Note: Read: “there will be no end of his kingdom”]. And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father; who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified; who spoke through the prophets. In one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. I await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

“Pisteuo” [I believe], “his hena” [in one], “Theon” [God], “Patera” [Father], “pantocratora” [almighty], “poietin” [maker], “uranu” [of heaven], “kae gis” [and earth], “oraton” [visible], “kae panton” [and all], “kae aoraton” [and invisible], “kae his ena Kyrion” [and in one Lord], “Ihm. Xpm.” [Jesus Christ], “ton yon tu theu” [the Son of God], “ton monogenin” [the only-begotten], “ton ec tu patros genitenta” [begotten from the Father], “pro panton ton eonon” [before all ages], “fos ec fotos” [light from light], “theon alithin ec theu alithinu” [true God from true God], “genithenta upyithenta” [begotten, not made], “omoysion tu patri” [of one substance with the Father], “didi’u tao panta egenonto” [through whom all things came to be], “ton di’himas tus anthropus” [who for us human beings], “kae dia tin himeteran soterian” [and for our salvation], “kateltonta ec ton uranon” [came down from heaven], “kae sarcotenta ec pneumatos agiu kae Marias tis parthenu” [and became incarnate from the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin], “kae inanthropisanta” [and became human], “staurothenta de yper imon epi Pontiu Pilatu” [crucified for us under Pontius Pilate], “kae pathonta” [and suffered], “kae pathenta” [and suffered], “kae anastenta ti triti himera kata tas Graphas” [and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures], “kae anelthonta his tus uranus” [and ascended into heaven], “kae katezomeno en dexia tu Patros” [and sits at the right hand of the Father], “kae palin ercomenon meta doxis crinein zontas kae necrus” [and will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead], “vtis basilias vc estin thelos” [whose kingdom will have no end], “kae his to Pneuma to agion” [and in the Holy Spirit], “ton Kyrion kae zoophyon” [the Lord and giver of life], “ton ec tu patros emporegomenon” [proceeding from the Father], “ton syn Patri kae yion synpros kynumenon kae syndoxazomenon” [who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified], “to talesan dia ton prophiton” [who spoke through the prophets], “His mian agian catholicin kae apostolocin Ecclesian” [in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church], “Omologo en baptisma his apesin amartion” [I confess one baptism for the remission of sins], “Prosdoko anastasin necron kae zoin tu mellontos aeonas” [I await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come]. “Amin” [Amen].

Dearest sons, you have heard the Creed in Greek; hear it also in Latin. And you say:

“In what language do they confess our Lord Jesus Christ?”

Response: “In Latin.”

“Announce their faith, how they believe.”

The acolyte places his hand over the infant’s head and chants the Creed in these words:

I believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages; light from light; true God from true God; begotten, not made; of one substance with the Father [Note: Read: “of the Father”], through whom all things were made [Note: Cardinal Sanctorius’s Missal has the following words in this form: “he descended, was incarnate, and became human, crucified, suffered, and was buried,” etc.]; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven; and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became human; was also crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered, and was buried; and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures; and ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; and will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead; his kingdom will have no end. And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father; who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified [Note: The same Missal has the words in this form: “is worshiped and glorified”]; who spoke through the prophets. In one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. I await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

When this has been completed, the priest continues in these words:

This is the summary of our faith, dearest ones; these are the words of the Creed, composed not in human eloquence of wisdom but arranged according to true divine reason. No one is unfit or incapable of grasping and preserving them. Here the one and equal power of God the Father and the Son is proclaimed. Here the Only-Begotten of God is shown to have been born according to the flesh from the Virgin Mary and the Holy Spirit. Here his crucifixion and burial, and his resurrection on the third day, are proclaimed. Here his ascent above the heavens and his confession at the right hand of the Father’s majesty are acknowledged, and he is declared to be coming to judge the living and the dead. Here the Holy Spirit is received as undivided in the same divinity as the Father and the Son. Finally, here the calling of the Church, the remission of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh are fully taught [Note: Read: “is brought to completion.” — But we have corrected it from the Missal cited above].

Therefore, dearest ones, you are being reformed from the old person into the new; from being carnal, you begin to become spiritual; from being earthly, heavenly. Believe with secure and steadfast faith that the resurrection which took place in Christ is also to be completed in all of us [Note: Thus we have emended it from the said Missal, since the exemplar reads: “is to be fulfilled”], and that what preceded in the Head will follow in the whole body.
