[Note: [Col. 1235D] In Menardus: “God, who among the apostolic priests …”] God, who caused your servant N., a bishop, to flourish in dignity among the apostolic priests, grant, we ask, that he may also be joined to their company [Note: [Col. 1235D] Menardus: “and to their perpetual company.”] forever. [Note: [Col. 1235D] In the margin: “Through him.”]

Hear favorably, Lord, we ask, our prayers which we offer at the burial of your servant N., so that he who faithfully carried out service in your name may rejoice in the perpetual fellowship of the saints. Through him.

### Secret

Receive, Lord, we ask, for the soul of your servant and priest N., the offerings which we present, so that to him to whom you gave episcopal merit you may also give its reward. Through the Lord.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, Lord, graciously regard this offering which we present to you for the burial of your servant and priest N. For it we pour forth humble prayers before your Majesty, so that you may cause him to be counted among the priests pleasing to you. Through him.

### Postcommunion

Show favor, Lord, to our supplications, and command that the soul of your servant N., the bishop, be joined to eternal joys in the land of the living. Through the Lord.

## XCIII. ANOTHER FOR A PRIEST

Grant, we ask, Lord, that the soul of your servant N., the bishop, whom, while he dwelt in this age, you adorned with sacred gifts, may always rejoice in a glorious heavenly seat. Through our Lord.

God, whose mercy has no number, receive our prayers for the soul of your servant N., the bishop, and grant him a share in the joy and light of the land of your saints. Through him.

### Secret

Receive, Lord, we ask, the offerings for the soul of your servant N., the bishop, so that to him to whom you gave the episcopal reward you may also give its merit. Through the Lord.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, Lord, graciously accept this offering of our service which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N., the bishop, and grant that, with the bishops of apostolic dignity, whose office he followed, he may have a share in everlasting blessedness; and our days …

### Postcommunion

Grant, almighty God, we ask, that you may command the soul of your servant N., the bishop, to be a companion of eternal blessedness in the congregation of the righteous. Through our Lord.

## XCIV. ANOTHER FOR A PRIEST OR ABBOT

[Col. 1236C] God, who both sanctify your servant N., priest and abbot, with the anointing of your mercy and have taken him up through a blessed completion, graciously receive our prayers and grant that, just as he is with you through his merits, so he may not depart from us through his example. Through the Lord.

Almighty eternal God, we humbly beseech your Majesty that you may grant your servant N., the abbot and priest whom you deigned to call to your rest, an honored seat and the fruit of everlasting blessedness, so that what he taught and did before our eyes may bring us not judgment but progress; and that, through him by whom we now rejoice in you on earth, we may deserve to exult with him in heaven. Through him.

### Secret

[Col. 1236D] Grant, we ask, almighty God, that through these holy mysteries the soul of your servant N., the abbot and priest, may always stand bright in your sight, the soul which faithfully ministered. Through him.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, Lord, graciously regard this offering which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N., the abbot and priest. For it we pour forth humble prayers before your Majesty, so that you may deign to enroll him among the number of your saints pleasing to you. [Note: [Col. 1236D] It should read: “pleasing to you,” as it appears in the following prayer within the canon, on the next column.] And our days …

[Col. 1237A] ### Postcommunion

May the mercy of your clemency, implored, benefit the soul of your servant N., the priest, so that, through your mercy, he may receive eternal fellowship with the one in whom he hoped and believed. Through the Lord.

## XCV. PRAYER AT MASS: ON THE FEAST OF SAINTS, OR FOR THE DEAD

Protect us, Lord, we ask, through the intercession of your blessed martyr N.; and join the soul of your servant N., the priest, to the fellowship of the saints. Through him.

Help us, Lord our God, entreated by the prayers of your blessed N., and establish the soul of your servant N., the priest, in the light of everlasting blessedness. Through him.

### Secret

[Col. 1237B] Receive, we ask, Lord, the offerings of appeasement and praise which we bring to you in honor of your holy martyr N., to be consecrated to your name, and which we humbly sacrifice to you for the rest of your servant N., the priest. Through him.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, Lord, graciously regard this offering which we offer to you in honor of your holy martyr N., or for the rest of your servant N., the priest. For it we pour forth prayers before your Majesty. [Note: [Col. 1237D] Read: “before your Majesty.”] Grant that you may deign to enroll it among the saints pleasing to you. This offering …

### Postcommunion

May our prayers ascend to you, Lord, and may eternal joys receive the soul of your servant N., so that, having made him a participant in adoption, [Note: [Col. 1237D] This should be corrected to: “of adoption.”] you may command him to be a companion of your inheritance. Through the Lord.

## XCVI. MASS FOR A RECENTLY BAPTIZED DECEASED PERSON

God, who open the entrance to the heavenly kingdom only to those reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, multiply your mercy over the soul of your servant N.; and to him to whom you granted a swift and undefiled passage after the sacrament of Baptism, grant also the fullness of eternal joys. Through him.

Another.

God, who anticipate every merit of those called by the gifts of your goodness, show favor to the soul of your servant N., which the wave of regeneration cleansed at the end of this life; and him whom you made not fear because of guilt, make rejoice because of grace. [Col. 1237D] Through him.

### Secret

Show favor, Lord, to our supplications for the soul of your servant N., for whom we offer you a sacrifice of praise, so that you may deign to join him to the fellowship of your saints. [Note: [Col. 1237D] Pamelius: “to associate him with the fellowship.”] Through him.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, Lord, graciously accept this offering which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N., and deign to insert him, cleansed in the font of regeneration and stripped of the dangers [Col. 1238A] of this life, among the number of blessed spirits. This offering …

### Postcommunion

Show favor, Lord, to the soul of your servant N., so that him whom you cleansed at the end of this life in the font of regeneration you may cause to reach the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom. Through him.

## XCVII. ANOTHER MASS

God, whose goodness has no number, since mercy is always the cause of your showing mercy, hear those who beseech you for the soul of that servant of yours, so that, just as your grace gave him to Baptism, so it may also give him to the kingdom. Through him.

God, who open the entrance to the heavenly kingdom only to those reborn, [Col. 1238B] increase upon the soul of your servant N. the gifts of your grace, so that, having been cleansed from all sins, it may be alien to none of what you promised. Through him.

### Secret

Graciously regard our offerings, Lord, we ask, which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N.; and to him to whom you gave the sacrament of Baptism, grant the fullness of eternal joys. Through him.

### Postcommunion

May our prayers ascend to you, Lord, and may eternal joys receive the soul of your servant N., so that, having made him a participant in adoption, you may command him to be a companion of your inheritance. Through him.

## XCVIII. PRAYER AT MASS FOR THE DEAD [Note: [Col. 1237D] In Pamelius it reads: “For the dead desiring repentance and not at all attaining it.”] For One Who Desired Repentance and Obtained It Only Minimally

[Col. 1238C]

If anyone, while asking for repentance, is deprived of the use of speech when the priest arrives, it has been established that, if suitable witnesses have said this [Note: [Col. 1238D] Pamelius: “have stated it.”] and he himself makes satisfaction by some movements, the priest should complete everything concerning the penitent, as is customary. [Note: [Col. 1238D] In the same source: “for the rite.”]

Another, for Masses.

Almighty and merciful God, in whose power human existence rests, we beseech you: absolve the soul of your servant N. from all sins, so that he may not lose the fruit of repentance which his will desired, overtaken by mortality [Note: The same editor has: “overtaken by death.”]. Through Christ.

### Secret

May the offering of this present sacrifice, we beseech you, O Lord, make satisfaction to you for the soul of your servant N., and may he find the forgiveness of sins which he sought; and what he could not fulfill by the ministry of his tongue, may he receive through the compensation of his desired repentance [Note: In the same source: “of the repentance desired.”]. Through the Lord.

### Within the Canon

May you graciously accept, we beseech you, this offering which your servant N. presents to you for the soul of your servant N., whose day of burial we commemorate; and in your ineffable mercy grant that, what he could not carry out by the ministry of his tongue because he was overtaken by mortal condition, he may deserve everlasting pardon, since the will to repent was not lacking in his mind. Which offering—

### Post-Communion

O God, from whom every good thing hoped for by the human body comes, grant, we beseech you, through these holy mysteries, that just as you granted the soul of your servant N. the will to repent, so in your mercy you may grant the forgiveness he desired. Through Christ.

## XCIX. PRAYER FOR LAY DECEASED  
### Also for one deceased person

Almighty and everlasting God, to whom no one supplicates without hope of mercy, be merciful to the soul of your servant N., so that, having departed this life in confession of your name, you may cause him to be numbered among your saints. Through Christ.

### Secret

Be merciful, we beseech you, O Lord, to the soul of your servant N., for whom we offer you sacrifices of reconciliation; and because he remained in the light of Catholic faith [Note: Pamelius: “in the light, in faith”], may his recompense be granted to him in the life to come.

[Note: Read: “within the canon.”]

### Secret

May you graciously accept, we beseech you, this offering which we present to you for the repose and soul of your servant N.; and in your mercy grant that, freed from the bonds of mortality, you may appoint him a portion among your faithful. Through Christ.

### Post-Communion

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that you may cause the soul of your servant N., received by the angels of light, to be led into the prepared dwellings of the blessed [Note: Thus corrected from Pamelius]. Through Christ.

## C. FOR THE CELEBRATION OF MASS FOR MANY

Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, everlasting mercy to the souls of your servants and handmaids, so that, released from mortal bonds, eternal light may possess them. Through Christ.

### Another

O God, to whom alone it belongs to provide healing after death, grant, we beseech you, that the souls of your servants and handmaids, stripped of all sins, may be gathered into the fellowship of your elect. Through Christ.

### Secret

We humbly bring you sacrifices, O Lord, seeking reconciliation, so that through these services of reconciliation the souls of your servants and handmaids may obtain perpetual mercy. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

Look favorably, we beseech you, O Lord, upon this offering which we present to you for the repose of the souls of your servants and handmaids; and grant that what you have deigned to prepare as a remedy for all the living may also benefit the dead for forgiveness. Which offering—

### Post-Communion

May the souls of all your servants and handmaids who rest in Christ, we beseech you, find a share in eternal light, since while placed in this light they obtained your sacrament. Through Christ.

## CI. ALSO ANOTHER MASS

O God, creator and redeemer of all the faithful, grant remission of all sins to the souls of your servants and handmaids [Note: Pamelius: “to the souls”], so that through devout supplications they may obtain the forgiveness which they have always desired. Through Christ.

We humbly beseech your majesty, O Lord, that the souls of your servants and handmaids, freed from all that they committed through human weakness, may be counted among the portion of your righteous. Through Christ.

### Secret

Graciously regard, we beseech you, O Lord, these sacrifices which we offer to you for the souls of your servants and handmaids [Note: The same source: “so that”], and grant those to whom you have given the merit of Christian faith also their reward. Through the Lord.

### Within the Canon

May you kindly accept, we beseech you, this offering which we humbly sacrifice to you in memory of the souls sleeping in peace; and in your mercy grant that this devotion may benefit us and obtain everlasting blessedness for them. Through Christ.

### Post-Communion

May the prayer of those who supplicate, we beseech you, O Lord, benefit the souls of your servants and handmaids, so that you may both free them from sins and make them sharers in your redemption. Through Christ.

## CII. ALSO ANOTHER MASS

Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, perpetual mercy to the souls of your servants and handmaids, so that what they hoped for and believed in you may benefit them forever. Through Christ.

### Secret

Graciously regard, we beseech you, O Lord, these gifts; and may what we offer while supplicating for the praise of your name benefit the dead for forgiveness. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

Graciously regard, we beseech you, O Lord, this offering which we reverently bring to you for the souls of your servants and handmaids; and in your favor grant that, freed from the bonds of death, they may deserve passage into life. Through Christ.

### Post-Communion

We pour out supplications, we beseech you, O Lord, for the souls of your servants, hoping that whatever they contracted through human conduct you may both mercifully forgive and establish them in the abode of your redeemed who rejoice. Through Christ.

## CIII. ALSO ANOTHER MASS  
### In cemeteries

O God, by whose mercy the souls of the faithful rest, graciously grant forgiveness of sins to your servants N. and N., or to all who rest here, so that, absolved from every guilt [Note: Pamelius: “freed”], they may rejoice without end. Through Christ.

### Another

Almighty and everlasting God, heed our prayers and grant what we ask; give to all whose bodies rest here a place of refreshment, the blessedness of rest, and the brightness of light. And to those who are weighed down by the burden of their sins, may the supplication of the Church commend them to you. Through Christ.

### Secret

Graciously receive, O Lord, the sacrifice offered for the souls of your servants N. and N., and of all who sleep here [Note: In the same source: “of them and them”]; and by this singular sacrifice may those freed from the bonds of dreadful death [Note: The same source: “stripped of”] deserve eternal life. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

May you graciously accept, we beseech you, O Lord, this offering which we present to you for the repose of your servants and handmaids N. and N., and of all faithful Catholic and orthodox Christians resting in Christ in this basilica, and of those who rest around this church of yours; so that through these aids to human salvation they may be counted among your redeemed in an everlasting portion—and our days—

### Post-Communion

O God, light of the souls of the faithful, attend to our supplications and give all whose bodies rest here a place of refreshment, rest, blessedness, and the brightness of light [Note: The same source: “of rest”]. Through the Lord.

## CIV. ALSO ANOTHER MASS

Attend, we beseech you, O Lord, for the souls of your servants and handmaids and of all who rest here, so that if any stains of the flesh have clung to them from earthly contagion, they may be wiped away by the forgiveness of your mercy. Through Christ.

Incline your ears, we beseech you, O Lord, to our prayers, by which we humbly implore your mercy, so that you may establish the souls of your servants and handmaids in a region of peace and light, and command that they be companions of the saints. Through Christ.

### Secret

May the gifts which we offer you, we beseech you, O Lord, for the repose and souls of all your servants and handmaids who rest in Christ, benefit them for redemption. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

May you graciously accept, we beseech you, O Lord, this offering which we present to you for the dead; and in the abundance of your mercy grant that by these sacrifices they may be cleansed from all that they drew upon themselves through earthly life. Through Christ.

### Post-Communion

Increase your mercy, O Lord, over the souls of your servants and handmaids; and to those to whom you granted the sacrament of baptism, give the fullness of eternal joys. Through Christ.

## CV. MASS AT THE BURIAL OF THE DECEASED, ON THE THIRD, SEVENTH, OR THIRTIETH DAY, OR AN ANNIVERSARY

Attend, we beseech you, O Lord, for the soul of your servant N., for whom we perform the office of commemoration on the day of his burial, so that if any worldly stain has invaded him or any earthly fault has infected him, you may forgive and cleanse it by the gift of your mercy. Through our Lord.

We beseech you [Note: In Menardus: “O Lord, [to your] servant.”], O Lord, to grant your servant, whose seventh day after death we commemorate, fellowship with the saints and elect [Note: Menardus: “and pour over him the enduring dew of your mercy”], and to infuse him with the enduring dew of your mercy. Through Christ.

O Lord, God of forgiveness, grant your servant N., whose anniversary of burial we commemorate, a place of refreshment, the blessedness of rest, and the brightness of light. Through Christ.

### Secret

Attend to our supplications, O Lord; and graciously and kindly receive this offering which we present to you for the seventh or thirtieth day of the burial of the soul of your servant N. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

May you graciously accept, O Lord, this offering which we present to you for the soul of your servant N., whose seventh or thirtieth day of burial we celebrate, since, having laid aside his body, he returned to you, the Creator, the soul which you had given him. For him we ask your divine clemency, that, freed from the bonds of death, he may deserve passage into life. Through Christ.

### Post-Communion

Almighty and everlasting God, deign to place the body, soul, and spirit of your servant N., whose seventh or thirtieth day we have celebrated, whether at his burial or otherwise, in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so that when the day of your recognition comes, you may command that he be raised among your saints and elect. Through Christ.

## CVI. ALSO A PRAYER AT MASS  
### For the salvation of the living

Extend your mercy, O Lord [Note: In Pamelius these two words, “your mercy,” are omitted], to your servants and handmaids, together with the right hand of heavenly assistance, so that they may seek you with all their heart and obtain what they rightly ask. Through Christ.

### Secret

Be merciful to our supplications, and kindly receive these offerings of your servants and handmaids—which [Latin quam, singular; Pamelius: quas, plural] we offer to you for their safety—so that no one’s vow may be fruitless and no one’s petition empty [Note: In the same source: “and so that”]. Grant, we beseech you, that what we faithfully ask we may effectively obtain. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

May you, O Lord, in your goodness and mercy, receive with a compassionate countenance this offering of your servants and handmaids, which we offer to you because of their devotion of mind; willingly protect them as they supplicate you, graciously hear them, and preserve them by eternal protection, so that, always rejoicing in your worship, they may persist steadfastly in the Catholic faith and confession of the Holy Trinity; and our days—

### Post-Communion

Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, steadfastness in your faith and sincerity to your servants and handmaids, so that, strengthened in divine charity, they may not be torn away from its integrity by any temptations. Through the Lord.

### Preface

Through Christ our Lord. Through him comes the salvation of the world, through him the life of all, through him the resurrection of the dead. Through him we humbly beseech you, O Lord, that you may deign to grant perpetual forgiveness to the soul of your servant N., whose day we celebrate, and, stripped of the contagions of mortality, restore it to a share in eternal salvation with the angels and archangels.

# HERE BEGINS THE RITE FOR IMPARTING PENANCE

You recite the whole of Psalm 6; then he again says: “Let us pray.” And, beginning Psalm 102, he continues to: “His youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.” Then you recite Psalm 50; after this the prayer follows.

Let us humbly beseech almighty and merciful God, who does not desire the death of sinners but that they should turn and live, dearest brothers, that in his mercy he may graciously grant forgiveness to his servant N., who has turned to the right path; and if there are any wounds from all his faults which he contracted after the waters of holy baptism, may his offenses be healed in this public confession in such a way that no further marks of scars remain upon him. Through our Lord.

O God, glory of the righteous and mercy of sinners, grant this servant of yours N. the full forgiveness of pardon; and, entreated in place of penance, mercifully forgive him, so that he who mourns his past sins may not experience future evils and may no longer commit deeds that must be mourned. Forgive him, O Lord, all his crimes, and in your mercy restore him to the paths of righteousness, so that, secure, he may thereafter deserve to run among your servants distinguished by good works and reach the rewards of eternal peace. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Lord God almighty and everlasting, who have placed the forgiveness of sins in swift confession, come to the aid of those who have fallen and have mercy on those who confess, so that your merciful compassion may release those whom the chain of offenses binds. Through the Lord.

[Col. 1243B] Here ends the Book of Sacraments. Thanks be to God.

As a harbor is sweet to sailors,

so the final verse is sweet to the scribe.

# IN THE UNCERTAIN SIXTH CENTURY, ARMENIUS AND HONORIUS, COMMONLY CALLED MONKS

[Col. 1243]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

Who these monks were is uncertain. I would readily believe that Theophilus, to whom the following confession of faith is addressed, was the patriarch of Alexandria, unless the title of illustrious man given to him were more suitable to a count than to a bishop. If, however, one preferred to interpret this as referring to Theophilus the patriarch, this confession could be attributed to the monk Ammonius and his brothers, whom they called the Long Brothers. For Theophilus of Alexandria was attempting to make their faith suspect. Nevertheless, the confession mentioned above seems more likely to be assigned to Latin monks than to Greek ones. But these are conjectures.

In the large and splendid Codex Augiensis this confession is found together with other confessions of the ancient Fathers and their expositions of the Lord’s Prayer. Among those confessions there is also the Brief of Faith which the Luciferian presbyter Faustinus addressed to the emperor Theodosius after the supplicatory petition published by Sirmond; the learned Quesnel published this Brief in the second volume of the works of Saint Leo.

[Col. 1243]

# HERE BEGINS THE CAREFUL WORK OF THE BLESSED MONKS ARMENIUS AND HONORIUS [Note: Perhaps “Ammonius”]

## ON THE CANONICAL BOOKS OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT, AND ALSO A CONFESSION OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH WHICH THEY ADDRESSED VERY BRIEFLY TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS THEOPHILUS (C)*

[Col. 1243D] Among other matters, and having been led to the place by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, we confess and venerate with devout faith the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as three co-eternal and co-equal persons, of one substance, one God. Since we read in the divine Scriptures of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, we confess this according to Catholic and apostolic doctrine. Far be from us and be driven far away the impiety of pagan error, lest we appear to profess three gods in the one divinity of the three persons. Far be this, far be it from us, and let it be excluded from the minds of the devout.

For, in accordance with the authority of holy Scripture—as we have shown—we make in the Trinity only a distinction of names and persons. But we confess one divinity, invisible, ineffable, incomprehensible, incapable of being contained, because the same and perfect divinity is in the Father, the same in the Son, and the same in the Holy Spirit. We do not call them three gods when we confess one divinity; nor have we forgotten the Scripture that says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one”; and again: “The Lord your God himself is in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him.”

Therefore, we neither count a plurality in the divinity with the pagans or heretics, nor deny the mystery of the Trinity with the Jews. Rather, we confess that the Father exists, the Son exists, and the Holy Spirit exists; believing and venerating the unity of the divinity in the distinct property of the persons, in the Trinity—that is, we confess that the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.

And therefore God is almighty because, before all beginnings, before all origins, and before all ages, he begot for himself an almighty Son, co-eternal with him, without any beginning whatsoever. For he begot him, he did not create or make him, since he is neither a work nor a creature, but the co-eternal and co-equal Son of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, as all Catholics confess.

But how he was begotten by that secret and ineffable counsel, no Catholic at all ought to proclaim or conceive in mind or in any thought, since the prophet, rebuking this very matter most openly, said: “Who shall declare his generation?”

God, therefore, is the Father. Christ is the Son of God, that is, the Anointed One, because in our age he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. Jesus, because he is the savior of all us believers. Lord, because he is the Lord of majesty, who was also crucified for us. Word, because the prophet speaks from the person of the Father: “My heart has uttered a good Word.” Power, because he himself spoke all things that are in heaven, on earth, and in the sea, and in all that is in them, and they were made; he himself commanded, and they were created. Wisdom, because all things were made in wisdom, and without him nothing was made. Light, because he came into this world, as he himself also said: “I am the light of the world.” Truth, because there is no falsehood in him. Way, because through him we have access to the Father. Life, because in him, made alive from the dead, we rise again in this flesh in which we now are. King, because he is the King of kings and Lord of lords. Priest, because he is priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Arm, because by his excellence and strength he freed us from the hand of death. Right Hand, because there is nothing left-handed in him. Nets, because, coming into the world as into the sea, he embraced and chose us by his majesty. Stone, because he was placed at the head of the corner and contains the two walls, the Old and the New Testament. Foundation, because he is our redemption and salvation, as the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” Eagle, because he returned from earthly lowliness to heavenly height. Lion, because he is the victor over the devil, as it is written: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” Calf, because he was voluntarily offered and sacrificed as a victim for us. Man, because, while both natures remain—that is, divinity and humanity—Christ Jesus is one man. Lamb, because, innocent, he was condemned, suffered, was crucified, and died for us; on the third day he rose again and took away the sins of the world. Giant, because there is a double substance in him, namely, of the Word and of flesh, and by his power and strength he traverses all things. Worm, because he was conceived without intercourse or seed and was born of a Virgin. Mirror, because he is without spot or wrinkle, being the image of divinity. Door, because through him we enter into eternal life. Bridegroom, because, born a virgin from a Virgin, he joined the immaculate Church to himself. Shepherd, because he separates the lambs from the goats and at the resurrection assigns each according to merit. Bread, because he himself is the living bread that came down from heaven. Vine, because we drink of his blood for the remission of sins. Form of God, because he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit in the divinity of the same substance. Spring, because he himself is the fountain of life, who granted us the fullness of grace in the rebirth of baptism. Fire, because he is the one who appeared to our fathers in the pillar of cloud and to Moses in the bush, and who set us aflame with his utterance.

Almighty triune power, God, most excellent Father of all things,

by whose begetting he was born without seed, time, or mother,

without origin, end, place, or limbs, afterward born as flesh,

permitting himself to be seen and likewise called by many names:

Hope, reason, way, life, salvation, wisdom, mind, mountain,

[Col. 1246D] Judge, door, giant, king, gem, prophet, priest,

Messiah (the Anointed One), Sabaoth (“Hosts”), Rabbi (“Teacher”), bridegroom, mediator,

Rod, dove, hand, rock, Son, Emmanuel (“God-with-us”), light,

Vineyard, shepherd, sheep, peace, root, vine, olive,

Spring, Etos [perhaps Greek ethos, “character”], bread, lamb, calf, lion, Jesus,

Word, man, net, stone, Lord, God—all things: Christ.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 540. SAINT CARILEFUS, PRIEST AND MONK, FIRST ABBOT OF ANISOLA

[Col. 1247]

# LIFE OF SAINT CARILEFUS, BY THE BLESSED SIVIARD, FIFTH ABBOT OF ANISOLA

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictines*, vol. I.)

## Author’s Prologue

[Col. 1247A] It is well established that it was the custom of the ancients to commend the men of their own time to posterity by monuments of their writings, and to commit their sayings or deeds worthy of remembrance either to letters or to painting; or at least to portray them in bronze or marble by laborious and impressive workmanship. Their purpose was that whatever was useful for knowledge, worthy of recognition, or considered worthy of imitation might through their industry be brought to the knowledge of their successors, so that they would appear neither negligent in their own time nor useless to posterity.

Since this is so, we too must fear lest we bury in the prison of silence the brave deeds and imitable trophies of Christ’s soldiers, by which they shone in our age; rather, we should commit them, even in a modest style, to the benefit of the coming generation. For the Lord assigned to our age one among the strongest warriors of Christ, named Carilefus [Note: The manuscripts have “Karileffus”], whose illustrious life, destined to benefit many, we have undertaken, with his help, to commit to writing.

And although we recognize ourselves unequal to so great a task, since we possess both scant eloquence and a very narrow supply of talent, we nevertheless judged it better either to speak feebly of what we know or to say a little than, like the lazy and negligent servant, to incur the penalty of silence over the money of the Lord that we have retained. The Lord also gives encouragement to speak: he commands us to open our mouths and promises that the grace of the Holy Spirit will fill them, so that they do not remain speechless.

He himself, therefore, must be entreated, so that he who was the helper of his servant in accomplishing the good works he commanded may also be our helper in narrating what he accomplished in him. Thus the more tender age, learning of the laborious struggles of Christ’s veteran soldiers for Christ, and the rewards they attained through their own labors, may, like the strongest athletes in a gymnastic contest, be made stronger for enduring the bitter conflicts against spiritual wickedness, anointed with the oil of paternal imitation.

All these things are referred to the glory of the Divinity, which grants such distinction of merit to its servants. By the hand of his admonition he also knocks upon sluggish hearts so that they may awaken, and so that they may be ashamed not to imitate those whom they know to have once been like themselves, since their flesh too was formed from the same material and their souls were likewise implanted with every good thing by God.

[Col. 1248B] But because, through the fault of our own laziness, we are made weak for following in their footsteps, let us at least recount, however inadequately, the wonders we have learned about them, so that in this way they may admit us to their fellowship if we are found to be, in however small a degree, narrators of the works of which they were the doers.

We undertake this work not by our own presumption but at the command of the bishops presiding over the holy Church. For we have been charged to describe in some fashion the Life of the aforesaid most blessed Carilefus, who flourished in the time of the most eminent king Childebert and, like a vigorous soldier in the camp of the holy Church, hurled darts of doctrine against the airy powers, protected by the shield of faith, and sent forth thunderbolts of miracles.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1247C] While the aforesaid prince and his brother Chlothar were governing the commonwealth of the Frankish kingdom, they divided the monarchy of their kingdom into two, as is customary in such affairs; yet in such a way that, while the unity of brotherly love remained, each possessed the portion of the kingdom handed over to him by the other.

Moved also by the desire of succession, they sought to enter into marriages. Chlothar took as his queen Radegund, a Thuringian by birth and distinguished for her pious character. After several years had passed in her marriage to him, she later went to Poitiers and made herself illustrious in the suburb of that city among souls desiring Christ. There, approaching as far as she was able the manner of life of those above, when the hour appointed for mortals summoned her, she left to the earth what belonged to it and sent her soul to join the company of the angels, with whom she had made herself a companion through long labors.

Leaving the watches of her body with sweat to those who still preside over earthly houses, eager to be mingled with the angelic gatherings, she abandoned mortal things and joined herself to the immortal Bridegroom, to whom she had long burned to be united.

The illustrious king Childebert, meanwhile, joined in marriage with Ultrogod, a queen venerable for her merits. At that time the aforesaid servant of Christ, Carilefus, was born in the territory of Auvergne to parents who were most illustrious according to worldly rank. Although they were distinguished by the titles of nobility, a spirit deeply devoted to the Lord’s service was added to this nobility, and, while the dignity of the world cast its shadow over them, it bestowed upon them a more excellent distinction.

They therefore received the servant of God entrusted to them and carefully raised him while he was still in his tender years. But when he reached the age suited to learning, he was sent for the sake of instruction to the monastery called Menat, where, with the Lord as his helper, he received both eloquence in letters and the rule of holy conduct.

For he saw the devoted servants of Christ in that place hastening to outdo one another in his love, each laboring to instruct him, one by word and another by example; and he himself was like good soil receiving the investment of the divine word, so that he might return the seed a hundredfold.

Although his age, still immature, promised the years of youth, his inner seriousness nevertheless restrained youthful impulses. And although he possessed sharpness of understanding and wisdom, he nevertheless behaved as though weak in everything, and, with humility as his teacher, sought counsel from his elders. Whatever he heard from their mouths, he strove with the utmost care to preserve, as though it were an oracle sent to him from heaven.

Meanwhile, after devoting himself for a long time to these exercises, as one trained in a heavenly gymnasium, he desired at last to entrust himself to the open field and fight the devil in single combat—that is, he sought the eremitical life, in which he could join right hands alone with the Alone and, with the Divinity as his ally, crush the insolent enemy with the weapons of humility.

While he pondered these things within himself for a long time and deliberated with due caution about how he should act, one day a man distinguished in life and praiseworthy in every respect, a monk of the same monastery named Avitus, came to him for a conversation.

The man of whom we speak, although less distinguished in ancestry according to the perishable dignity of the world, was nevertheless endowed with the distinction of the highest merits. As they exchanged suitable conversation and tasted the feasts of the divine word upon the palate of the mind, they opened a book containing the text of the holy Gospel and recited with their tongues and pondered in their minds the line that first met their eyes. It was this:

“Whoever loves father or mother or brothers or sisters more than me cannot be my disciple, and is not worthy of me.”

They therefore began, like clean animals, to chew this food with the tooth of discernment and to interpret how these words urged them to pursue the more difficult way of life: namely, freed from concern for their parents and separated from knowledge of their relatives, they could freely crush the vices of the flesh with the single arm of heavenly purpose and holy desire.

Accordingly, they immediately followed the apostle Peter, who, when he heard the voice of the one commanding him, at once left his nets and boat and followed the Lord’s paths. Blessed Avitus secretly placed the keys of the storeroom, bound together with his belt, beneath his abbot’s pillow. At that time he was in charge of the monastery’s grain stores and storerooms.

Thus, at last breaking through the delays of deliberation, they left the monastery and began the appointed journey on foot. After traveling not far from the monastery, they reached the bank of the Loire. They crossed it easily by boat, with Christ favorable to them, and arrived in the suburb of Orléans.

Having heard of the fame of the most excellent and God-beloved man Maximinus, who presided in those parts over the companies of monks living in the monastery of Miciacum, they hastened at once to visit him. This distinguished man Maximinus had received an estate through the generosity of King Clovis and his queen Clotild; there he had built a monastery for himself and his companions, and at that time was devoting himself to spiritual philosophy.

When he learned that the holy men had arrived and perceived their ardent devotion to the worship of God, he immediately granted them both the opportunity to live with him and fellowship with the brothers.

They themselves, however, by no means forgot the purpose of their resolve. They did not turn the ranks of their minds backward or give themselves over to tepidity or sloth; rather, as though laying their hands upon the Gospel plow, they fixed the eyes of their minds upon the prize of the heavenly calling. They chastised the senses of the body from corrupt affections and strove to make them beautiful through the display of holy deeds; it was their concern to make themselves conspicuous by their works and gracious in their speech.

Their works inspired wonder in those who saw them, and their speech brought delight through grace. Chastity made them flourish, faith made them invincible, purity of mind made them simple, and the splendor of their life made them praiseworthy. They placed the Lord above all things that can be loved and in no way placed their neighbor beneath their own self-love.

Their humility was not merely one of words or dress; their entire conduct was formed by truth, so that whoever saw them might think that the words of the Lord had been painted in their practices as in a spiritual picture: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

Meanwhile, the man of pious memory, Maximinus, when he learned that their efforts aspired to contemplation (theoria) [Note: Another reading: “theoriae,” “of contemplation”] and that through persistent prayer, continual vigils, and nights spent in supplication their life was aspiring to the heavenly assembly, sought to mark both of them with priestly dignity; by divine providence, the outcome favored his will.

But the most devoted servants of Christ, burning with excessive love and perceiving that their desire was not satisfied by these things, judged that they should seek a more remote dwelling. They were not driven to this by fickle lightness, but by the Lord’s will and by an insatiable desire to please Christ.

Their purpose was that, since they had already completed a long course in monastic life, they might deserve to undertake the anchoritic struggle [Note: Another reading: “singular”], so that no perfection indicated to them by the reading of the Fathers might be lacking.

Accordingly, they withdrew their feet from that place as well and sought the vast solitary regions of the forests of Perche. As they traveled through them, among the dark recesses of the woods and the most hidden lairs of wild beasts, a fertile place presented itself to their sight. It was then called Piciacus, but now it is known by the name of the Cell of Saint Avitus.

Truly, so that the delightful power of the Divinity might show that the stream of the Holy Spirit flowed most abundantly in their hearts, he opened for them a spring of living water, so that those who were inwardly refreshed by the grace of the Holy Spirit would not be burdened by outward necessity.

Blessed Carilefus surrounded this spring with a structure of earth, made by his own hand, so that it might retain the water; out of devotion to him, it is still covered by the faithful with a not unworthy lid. They embraced this place as chosen for them by the Lord’s providence, established their station there, and continued for many days in devotion to the Holy Trinity.

But as the periods of time devoted to divine study lengthened for them in that same place, and the fragrance of their reputation and deeds spread everywhere, the fame of the blessed Avitus reached the ears of the aforementioned king, confirming the truthful saying of the Savior: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.”

Therefore, at the command of that illustrious king, a basilica was built in the same place and endowed with royal resources; a monastery was also prepared, so that the lamp of the holy Church would not be hidden in dark shadows but would spread the rays of its light among all the sons of the holy Church.

Blessed Carilefus—just as it is customary for holy men to shun prosperity and seek adversity for the sake of their spiritual discipline—left Avitus, who was most dear to him, in those places, withdrawing bodily from his presence into the recesses of the desert, although in spirit he remained bound to him by bonds that could not be undone. For Divinity did not approve that two renowned leaders of its army should preside over a single fold, since either of them could suffice for many. Accordingly, taking with him his fellow soldier Daumerus, and likewise his fellow servant Gallus, he turned his steps toward the region of the city of Le Mans. At length he withdrew to a place called by the ancient name Casa-Gayani, situated in the parish of Labrocinus, near which the river Anisola flows; borrowing its name from that river, the place is still called by the same name. There he remained hidden for a considerable number of days. For the place was secluded from anyone’s approach, remote from the company of the living in the heights of the desert, yet pleasant because of the fertility of its soil.

There he also found a spring pouring forth a stream from a living vein, as well as the walls of an old building, worn by age but still displaying, through the traces of its construction, the dignity of its former work. A small vine also presented itself to his gaze. As he examined each of these things with attentive eyes, filled with immeasurable joy, he immediately prostrated himself upon the ground and offered countless thanks to the Lord’s mercy, as to one who had prepared these things for him. With all his strength he prayed that the One who had prepared the place for him would also command him to accomplish there the fruits of heavenly labor. After occupying the hours of night with prayers, on the following day he wove a dwelling-cell for himself and his brothers within the walls of the aforesaid building, using pliant wicker, and began on every side to devote himself to cultivation.

One day, then, while he was applying himself to the work he had begun, cultivating the vine he had found as an aid to his hope by digging around it and cutting away everything superfluous, he was compelled by the sweat of his labor to remove the garment called a cuculla and hang it on an oak tree. Meanwhile, a very small bird called a bitriscus [Note: [Col. 1251D] Alternative reading: bitericus], while wandering everywhere in all directions—as is its habit—and, following its familiar custom, inspecting every recess under the prompting of its curiosity, concealed itself in the garment and, departing, left behind an egg that it had laid.

But Carilefus, the devoted servant of Christ, having completed his daytime work, when the sun was already leaving the summit of the sky inclined toward its decline and, with its rays growing tepid, gave promise of the approaching sunset, went to the tree to retrieve his garment and found the bird’s egg. At the sight of it, immeasurable joy mingled with astonishment seized him, and he spent all the time in which the withdrawal of daylight left the earth in shadow praising God.

When Phoebus’ lamp had adorned the world with its radiance, and, the darkness of blind night having been suppressed, things hidden by the density of shadows had been made visible, he took his brother Daumerus with him and went to visit blessed Avitus, intending to consult him about what was hidden in his heart and at the same time to report the suitability of the place he had found. While, as is customary among holy men, they exchanged many matters beneficial to the welfare of many, the venerable man also reported to venerable Avitus, among other things, what had happened to him, wishing to discover whether Avitus had ever heard of such a novel event, or whether it appeared that anything might be signified by it.

The man of God Avitus confessed that he was moved by this, and, adding that it had not occurred without purpose or by chance, said:

“My most beloved Carilefus, whom no mortal should place second to anyone, persist in your labor. These things, whatever they may be, do not make insignificant promises; rather, the offspring produced by the bird portends great future increase for that place. Know, indeed, that the Lord’s flock of that place will in future be much larger than the one you now see dwelling here with us. Like excellent soldiers spending their lives in the exercises of the Lord, after triumphing over the labors of the flesh they will receive from the Lord the unfading fruits of their labors.”

They therefore passed that night without sleep, dedicating it entirely to the service of the Lord. At one moment they discussed the ordering of the present life; at another their conversation turned to future recompense. Sometimes the learned mind took part in the company of immortal spirits; at other times they considered the instruction and examples of holy men; and again the trained mind struck the sweet plectrum of the Psalter and played, producing a pleasing sound for the Lord. By such activities they relieved the darkness of the whole shadowed night. But when the shadows began to fade, Christ’s soldier Carilefus retraced his steps to the place from which he had come and withdrew into his beloved hut.

As has already been said, that place was secure from all external disturbance and accessible only to wild creatures familiar with the desert. For it was often visited by their arrival, so that in a certain sense the saying seemed to have been spoken specifically of it: “And the beasts of the earth shall be at peace with you.” It was a remarkable sight to see a buffalo—which is difficult to find in that province—coming among the other animals to him. You would see the creature that previously had thought itself obliged to hide only in the densest thickets now, having forgotten all its fierceness and laid aside its snarling and the obstinacy of its wild nature, presenting itself as gentle and tractable to the servant of God. Like one offering homage, it would incline its muscular neck, while the venerable man, free from every anxiety of fear, approached the beast and slowly furrowed its bristles with his fingernail between the horns; he also stroked its thick neck and dewlap, soothing it as though familiarly. And the wild creature, as though blessed by this touch, would return at full speed—as nature prompted it to do—to the vast solitudes.

Meanwhile Childebert Augustus, accompanied by his wife Ultrogoda and the whole multitude of his retinue, went into the region of the city of Le Mans and arrived at a villa called Madualis. While he was staying there, he was informed that not far away in the wilderness a buffalo, an animal unusual in those regions, lay hidden. The king, delighted with joy, ordered his hunters to prepare everything necessary for capturing the beast: namely, to sharpen the strength of the dogs and provide a sufficient supply of bows and arrows, since he wished to hunt it on the following day. All this was swiftly carried out.

On the following day, before blind night had yet fled, they entered the inner parts of the forest. Wherever they perceived a trace of the animal, as soon as the light appeared they searched the ground with attentive eyes. At length, after long investigating the signs of its path, they found them and released fierce mastiffs from their ropes to pursue it.

The wretched buffalo, now almost captured, ran to Saint Carilefus, as though flight had been denied it in every direction, and approached the man of God as its sole refuge. The hunters, following the signs of its movements and trusting also to the barking of the dogs, at length reached the place where the saint lived in a cell he had built with his own hands. There they saw the holy man, and behind him the aforesaid buffalo standing, as though complaining and trembling.

Then, disturbed by the extraordinary novelty of the event, they dared neither touch the beast nor cause the holy man any annoyance. Instead, when the king arrived, questioned them about the reason for their delay, and reproached them for their sluggishness and apathy, they replied:

“Behold, as we customarily do under the direction of experience and skill, we have carried out everything. We found the buffalo itself, but we have been struck by an extraordinary turn of events. In a certain hut we found a man unknown to us, and beside his dwelling the wild beast standing there, tamed despite its fierceness. Since it seemed to us that this same man was a servant of God—for savage animals are subjected to him—we dared neither disturb his peace nor attack the buffalo.”

But the king, moved to anger, said: “Let us go to the place of which you speak.”

They therefore went and reached the place where the servant of God, with the beast serving him, was beseeching the Lord.

When the king saw this miracle, he did not attempt to venerate the power of God in such things. Instead, moved by indignation, he began to utter these reproachful words:

“Whence comes to you, unknown persons, such arrogant presumption that you have dared, without anyone’s permission, to invade a forest under my jurisdiction, or by your intrusion in any way diminish the dignity of our hunt?”

But the holy man, by no means forgetting the saying of the Lord—“When you stand before kings and governors, do not prepare beforehand what you will say, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom”—said to the king with complete steadfastness and humble reverence:

“O good king, we whom you see here did not invade the haunts of wild beasts or occupy uninhabited places out of contempt for you or in order to disturb your hunt. Rather, we sought places inaccessible to human beings so that we might devote ourselves more intimately and earnestly to the service of the Lord, in the hope that, because we are separated here from the company of human beings, we may after the fall of mortal life deserve to enjoy the company of angels in heaven.”

But the king, filled with excessive bitterness, said:

“I command by our authority that you and your companions withdraw from here, and take care that none of you is ever found here again.”

Then venerable Carilefus, not in the least disturbed by the royal threats, turned to fulfill the command and said to the king:

“Most illustrious king, we your servants possess some wine produced by the small vine found and cultivated here. We ask your serene majesty to indulge for a little while in drinking from it, so that both your nobility and your companions may have greater strength to return to the palace.”

He did this in obedience to Scripture, which says: “If your enemy is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.” But that prince, obeying his excessive rage, not only quenched the coals of charity with the coldness of malice, but also struck his horse with the spurs and set out on the road to return to the palace.

But the Lord’s abundant mercy and inexhaustible power, which is accustomed to exalt his humble servants by breaking the power of the proud, displayed most fully how great before him was the one who had been despised. For when that same king, swollen with disordered pride, wished to hasten his return, his horse, suddenly seized by astonishment, came to an abrupt halt. Although wounded and bloodied on every side, it refused to carry the king forward.

Meanwhile astonishment mingled with fear seized everyone and compelled them all to consider what should be done. While they remained for a long time uncertain, one of them, who surpassed the others in wisdom, addressed the king:

“Excellent king, if suspicion does not deceive me, that man who was treated contemptuously and addressed insultingly by us is devoted to the service of God. The Lord has granted this power to his virtue: because you did not treat him as you ought, you too are being denied success in accomplishing what you desire.”

A messenger was therefore sent swiftly to the man of God, both to obtain pardon for what had happened and to bring the king his instruction concerning what should be done. The messenger reached the place where the man of God was with all speed, found him praying, and explained the king’s predicament.

The most devoted servant of Christ, hearing this, glorified the mercy of the Lord, honoring him, and humbly ordered the king to return to him, saying:

“Go, son, and tell the king to return.”

Since he had departed in anger without a blessing, he was to receive from the Lord, through his servant, a blessing, and thus return to the palace free from every injury.

The saint therefore applied himself most devotedly to prayer. The attendant, having received the command, returned to the king as quickly as possible. He found him immobile, just as he had left him, bound by spiritual bonds, and presented before him the words of his message:

“Excellent prince, the man of God, to whom your authority ordered me to go, commands you to return to him and greatly desires that you receive his blessing—the blessing of which you yourself deprived yourself in your anger.”

In a marvelous manner, as soon as the king, terrible in arms, singular in power, and accompanied by an almost inaccessible multitude of attendants, heard the words of the servant of God, the bonds by which he had been bound were loosed. He recognized that he had opposed the will of God dwelling in the holy man of God and had bound himself by resisting it. Therefore, once more obeying the saint’s command, he was freed from the straps that held him and hastened to fulfill what was ordered.

The once fearsome king, now trembling, quickly reached the man of God after his horse had been released. The eyes that earlier, because of the intensity of his anger, had been covered by a bloody cloud, he now washed with a contrite heart, drawing forth tears. The neck that pride had earlier made rigid humility now bent. He fell at the saint’s feet, repeatedly struck his breast with his right hand, confessed again and again that he was guilty, and sorrowfully begged to obtain from the holy man pardon for what he had committed in his arrogance.

Blessed Carilefus, urged by the humility that was congenial to him, approached the prostrate king and humbly and kindly raised him up. He instructed him most devoutly with words of admonition and warned him thereafter not to command such rash actions.

But the prince again submitting himself to the saint’s feet said that he would regard it as a great favor if, through the generosity of the blessed man, he might now drink the wine that earlier he had considered worthless. The saint, who had entirely renounced resentment and had persuaded himself that he must care solely for the king’s salvation, immediately ordered what was requested to be done, saying to one of his fellow soldiers:

“Quickly, my brother; let wine be brought here, together with a cup, so that we may comply with the king’s desire.”

The cup was brought at once. Saint Carilefus filled it with his own hand and offered the drink to the king. The king received what was offered with a willing spirit, valuing it more according to the dignity of the giver than according to its flavor; he kissed the saint’s hand, brought it to his lips, drained the cup, and gave thanks to Divinity. Each of his companions did the same.

It was marvelous to see the tiny vessel increase so greatly in abundance that the wine was poured generously for each person, yet suffered no diminution from scarcity until all had drunk sufficiently. It is therefore evident that blessed Carilefus, the hermit of our own time, was not inferior in merit to Elijah and Elisha, those prophetic hermits of old. One of them caused a small jar of flour to provide abundant food for himself and his hostess; the other, from a few barley loaves, removed the hunger of a hundred men.

When the king and his companions had drunk as much wine as they desired, while the vessel mentioned above suffered no loss through diminution, he again fell at the holy man’s feet and poured out this petition:

“I am certain, excellent among men, that you cling to the cultivation of the Lord, that you are the servant of the Lord, and that Divinity favors your prayers in all things. Therefore I ask you to grant your assent to my desire: namely, that, having accepted as much of this estate of Madualis as seems suitable to you, you should, with Christ’s assistance, build a monastery.”

Although the man of God resisted this request for a very long time, the king’s petition nevertheless prevailed, and he obtained permission for it to be done. Yet the man of God in no way agreed to accept a larger area than he could ride around in a day while seated on a donkey.

Having obtained this, the king returned to his own residence as though he had been granted a great reward, after asking for and receiving the saint’s blessing. When the queen, devoted to God, came to meet him as he returned and entered the inner chamber of the house, he related to her in order the story of all that had happened to him.

She replied:

“Brother, what I learn by hearing has brought great joy to my heart, mingled with fear. I fear for you, my lord king, lest on account of this affair you have incurred some offense before God or his servant. Yet I rejoice in your salvation, because in his great kindness God did not wish to avenge immediately the injuries done to him and to his servant. You must make an effort to follow what you have learned from him, lest perhaps by concealing your fault you be accused of disobedience and irreverence, and, while avoiding lighter punishments, be chastised with worse torments.”

Meanwhile the devoted servant of Christ did not rejoice, as those who long for earthly advantages are accustomed to do, in the abundance of rural estates that had been supplied to him. Rather, he praised the all-powerful generosity of divine mercy, which had granted him the means by which he could feed the poor and provide comfort to exiles and strangers.

Divine clemency also wished to increase its servant’s devotion more and more by sweetening his service. One day, when he had gathered the brothers who lived with him and was engaged in agriculture on the estate just mentioned, turning the earth with a rake—for they lacked the means to plow—blessed Carilefus, removing a clod of earth with a mattock, uncovered a hidden treasure, unknown until then to mortal people.

When he saw it, he summoned his brothers and explained how the mercy of the Lord was comforting them. He showed it to them and said:

“Behold, excellent fellow soldiers, observe how the mercy of our Creator ennobles our poverty with his gifts. It is not enough for him to enrich us with the benefits of human beings; he has now begun to bring forth for us the riches that have until now been hidden in the earth’s bosom. Let us therefore give him thanks and strive to praise him with the whole devotion of our hearts, since he has granted us greater things, and gifts befitting those who serve him, as is proper to him—although we are the lowest and most contemptible of his members.”

They therefore prostrated themselves upon the ground and for a very long time worshiped the Holy Trinity with hymns and songs of praise. At length they rose and carried the treasure they had found into the oratory that they had built earlier.

For the Son of the supreme Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, whose custom it is to show his servants dwelling in earthen habitations the good things that await them, so that they may strive to kindle themselves more abundantly in his love, and who had commanded them through the utterance of the Gospel to store up a treasure that remains in heaven, saying, “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust destroys nor moth damages, and where thieves do not break in and steal,” wished also, while they remained upon the earth, to invite them through an earthly treasure, so that they might weigh the value of the heavenly one, if a human treasure could be so valuable.

Perhaps no one will wonder less worthily at this also: that the dignity which we lost through the transgression of the first man was restored to this man by his obedience to the divine will—not indeed because he had yet been granted the habitation of paradise, but while he was still burdened with earthly heaviness.

For we know that our same ancestor was of such great wisdom that all the animals of field, sea, and air were believed to obey his commands, and, when called, did not refuse obedience; they accepted the names appropriate to them when he imposed them.

Does it not seem that this wisdom was restored to the holy man, to whom a savage beast learned to submit? The jaws that well-disposed men ordinarily flee from could now be seen clinging to his threshold like a servant; and, like a disciple continually wearing down the threshold of his teacher, as soon as it heard his commands, it would hasten into the remotest places.

It should also be considered that divine Majesty mercifully bestowed upon this man the commanding power destined to perish that had been assigned to the first human beings. For it was said to them when they were first created: “Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and the beasts.”

Therefore the outstanding Carilefus, because he had seen the one who seemed to rule royal scepters depart from human dignity, and because he had seen bestial ferocity enter instead into the human heart, did not forget the power of his own dominion. By the bridle of prayers he taught the king to impose a limit upon his anger and thereafter to treat himself humanely and civilly, lest it be said of him: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”

Meanwhile, I also see that the saint did not lack the ancient dignity. Just as the earth was commanded to provide the inhabitants of paradise with the yield of its fruits spontaneously, with all the sweat of labor suppressed, so the blessed man’s small supply of wine, when offered, learned to extend itself toward the satisfaction of many men.

Nor is it surprising that holy men should recover, even amid the labors of the present, by their own exertion what another’s negligence caused them to lose, since the Creator of all things has determined to restore those freed from the flesh to the places in which they would have remained without any loss of their condition, had transgression of the commandment not placed an obstacle in their way. And because these men burn with humility to carry out the divine commands, it is fitting that they should not be punished by the sentence of severity imposed upon transgressors; rather, even in the present life, they should be honored by divine generosity.

The man of God, therefore, seeing himself honored by such and so many benefits, grew more and more in the practice of various virtues. In the giving of alms he showed himself most generous; in fasts, ready; in vigils, vigorous; and in every fullness of virtue he proved himself an outstanding worker. Thus he seemed in some manner uniquely to have fulfilled the sentence spoken by David’s mouth: “The saints, without doubt, will go from strength to strength until they lay aside humanity and see the God of gods in the heavenly Jerusalem.”

Meanwhile, around the places of that desert which the holy man had occupied, seven men lived, sustaining a meager existence by rustic labor. Inspired by fear and love of God, and attracted at the same time by the novelty of the matter, they took care to visit the servant of God frequently and, as far as they were able, to relieve his needs.

They had been given by the man of God a portion of the treasure delivered to him from the earth’s depths, so that they might both lessen their own need through that assistance and become helpers in the building of the monastery. Mindful of their promise, they fulfilled in action what they had professed for as long as they remained among mortal affairs. Their descendants, too, are known to have followed the examples of their ancestors with the utmost devotion down to the present day.

Meanwhile, when Queen Ultrogoda, most noble in her devotion to the Lord, had learned through reliable messengers the nature of the man’s life—his frugality in food, his sleeplessness at night, the poverty of his clothing, and above all his renowned and steadfast devotion in the service of Christ—for it was also his custom to wrap his body in ashes and a hair shirt, and, whenever extreme exhaustion required him to rest, to stretch his body upon the bare ground—she sent some of her attendants to him to make her will known to the man of God. She spoke as follows:

“Rumor, my dearest ones, has reached our ears that this venerable man who inhabits the neighboring desert is most intimate with the Lord and that divine access is open to his mouth. Therefore I ask you to hurry to him with the greatest speed, make known to him the desire of my heart, and obtain through your earnest prayers that he satisfy it.

“For I greatly desire, if my will may be fulfilled, to deserve to enjoy the presence of his face, and through his intercession I wish to make my soul acceptable to divine mercy. If he agrees to my prayers, I will assign to him all the estates of the royal fisc in whose portion they reside, so that he may have the power to do with them whatever he wishes.”

The ministers, by no means tardy in carrying out their mistress’s command, quickly reached the venerable servant of Christ to disclose her will. He, however, after deliberating briefly, silently turned the following thought over in his mind:

“Why would the queen desire so greatly to see me, unkempt through the long-lasting colours of a chameleon [text uncertain] [Note: [Col. 1259D] Alternative reading: ‘unkempt through prolonged labors’], horrid with the squalor of fasts, rustic from rural labor, disfigured by the poverty of my rags, and degenerate through the weakness of my understanding? I know—indeed, I know—the poisonous cunning of the ancient enemy, by which he broke the strength of the man through feminine weakness in the delight of paradise.

“It is therefore right for me to beware of a woman’s gaze, lest I be caught in the snares of the enemy while inhabiting the squalid places of the desert, if the one who enjoyed paradise with the delight of life and even divine conversation was ensnared by his persuasions.”

He therefore quickly ended his deliberation and gave this reply to the queen’s messengers:

“Go, excellent young men, and report these words of mine to your mistress. If I have any power, I will pray for her. Let her nevertheless be certain that, as long as I remain in the body, I will never see the face of a woman, nor will this monastery, which I built at the Lord’s command, ever be open to the entrance of a woman.

“For it is not fitting that we, who are reckoned among the household of Christ, should sell our gaze to women or, in order to obtain land, prostitute our souls to the enemy of the human race. Therefore let her turn her mind away from this intention and assign a portion of her fisc to whomever she pleases.”

By God’s favor, this custom has remained unshaken in that monastery down to the present day.

The servants returned to their mistress with great haste, repeated the answer entrusted to them, and brought the queen deep sadness. Nevertheless, she did not press her request further to see the face of the man of God, both because she feared disturbing the holy man and because she judged that she had received a reasonable answer.

The devoted servant of God was so universally regarded with reverence that, as the merits of his works grew brighter, no one attempted to resist his will. His face appeared to shine with an almost angelic aspect; and, according to Scripture, his face revealed his mind. His conduct displayed a moderation weighed in an even balance; concerning the exercises of the Lord’s worship, he possessed the most devoted spirit and inexhaustible love. His words, whenever he spoke, could be seen to be seasoned with the salt of divine wisdom, and he communicated to everyone the fragrance of his own odor.

He had placed all these things upon the foundation of Christian faith in his heart, making Christ the perpetual foundation of his structure—Christ, who is the true rock upon which every structure established grows into a holy temple in the Lord.

Meanwhile he possessed great love for strangers and exiles, so that he supplied them with food and provided them with coverings no less than if they had been attached to him.

Pressed down by the foot of this heavenly desire, the love of the world collapsed; the almost unconquerable cunning of the ancient enemy trembled before it; and, too late, he lamented that the snares of his trifling deceptions had been leapt over. For Carilefus entered the contest of the struggle without attributing anything to his own strength; supported by the help of Christ and instructed by his example, he fought against Christ’s enemies under Christ as his leader.

The natural weakness of the flesh was strengthened in him by the inner ardor of charity, and the weakness of bodily powers was comforted by the abundance of spiritual gifts. The apostolic exhortation also strengthened him: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us”; and again: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.”

These and other teachings of Holy Scripture, like spiritual salt, dried up for him the fleeting joys and filth of the world and kindled his heart toward what would endure forever. This was his discipline; this was his continual struggle against the devil, until at last, after the course of his labor, the Lord granted him the desired rest and repaid him with the reward of his work.

While blessed Carilefus was thus sweating in the struggle in many ways [Note: [Col. 1260D] Alternative reading: “was sweating in struggles of this and similar kinds”], and, as an eager fighter with almost tireless determination, offered himself daily to the arrogant enemy for single combat, leaving to the monastic companies that flocked to him from every direction an invincible example of his virtues, the inevitable end that is the door of all mortals began to knock upon his little body. Thus his soul, beloved of God, long bound by prison chains, might finally break the bonds of servitude and meet its king, to be received into his joy.

His body was therefore seized by an acute fever, his marrow was scorched by a double fire, and the current of his blood was dried through every limb. Yet his spirit grew stronger as the strength of the flesh failed, and it was inflamed more and more to beseech the face of the Lord, so that, once the bond of the flesh had been dissolved, he might be freed as quickly as possible. He desired, according to the Apostle, “to depart and be with Christ.”

But Divinity, the helper of good prayers and gracious receiver of reasonable words, kindly admitted his prayers to itself and mercifully fulfilled what he earnestly requested.

At length, when his dissolution was near, with companies of monks standing around him and awaiting what was about to happen, he foretold to them shortly beforehand his approaching departure and, as far as his strength allowed, admonished them in these words to be mindful of themselves:

“My little sons, the irreversible hour of my end is at hand. Therefore I ask you, mindful of yourselves and also mindful of Christ, to preserve the right faith in him and not defile it with any adulterous mixture. Likewise, establish in your hearts and actions an obedience joined to charity as Christ’s singular imitation, so that you may not merely escape the punishments of Gehenna but, if the Lord grants it, also deserve to receive, like most devoted soldiers, crowns of triumph.”

With these and similar teachings he said his final farewell to the brothers and returned his heavenly spirit to heaven, where it was to be placed.

Now that he was departing, what tongue could explain, what style could recount the grief of those standing around him, the sobs of their anxious hearts, and the sighs that repeatedly struck their lungs? How could the greatness of their grief, interrupting their words midway, have prevented them from speaking when they wished to speak and attempting to pray?

Although they rejoiced that they were sending such a patron ahead to heaven, they could not nevertheless be separated from him without grief, since they had been accustomed to being encouraged by his words and continually increased in the love of the Lord by imitating him.

They performed funeral rites for his body, carefully prepared a coffin, and buried him in the basilica that he himself had built before his death. The Lord Jesus Christ has often chosen to ennoble that place by displays of wondrous works, demonstrating the favor he held toward his servant.

Neither the brevity of the work nor the capacity of my style is sufficient to recount how many blind people recovered their sight at his tomb after his departure, how many weak people were restored to health, how demons were driven from possessed bodies, and how very many benefits were bestowed upon mortals by the Lord through his intercession.

Thus the mirror of every good was buried on the Kalends of July, while the earth wept and heaven rejoiced, under the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1261]

THE EXEMPLAR OF THE DEED OF GIFT, OR TESTAMENT, OF SAINT CARILEFUS, PRIEST AND MONK

(Mabillon, *Ancient Analecta*)

[Col. 1261B] What follows is the exemplar of the deed of gift, or testament, which Saint Karileffus made, at the urging and exhortation of Saint Innocent, of the monastery of Anisola to the holy mother church of Le Mans, in the time and with the permission of King Hildebert and his queen Vuldrogoda.

It has therefore seemed appropriate to insert it here so that, if—which God forbid—through some negligence the authentic document should be lost or burned, its exemplar may be found here, by which it may be known how this was carried out, just as it is contained in the document itself.

While the frailty of the human race fears that the final moment of life will come by sudden transition, it is fitting that it should not find anyone unprepared, lest he depart from this world without any consideration of a good work. Therefore I, Carileffus, in the name of God, an unworthy priest and monk, reflected upon the Lord’s mercy as a remedy for my soul and for the forgiveness of my sins, so that I might deserve to obtain an eternal reward from the Lord [Col. 1261C] in the future. I had begun, with the Lord’s help, to build some cell and little monastery wherever I might find a suitable place.

While I was thinking and turning these matters over in my mind—where I could do this—and had begun going about in search of places, under the Lord’s guidance I reached the territory of Le Mans, in the district of Lavardin, at a certain place which the ancients called Casa-Gayana, above the river Anisola, now called Anisola after the name of that river. There Lord Turibius, bishop of that parish, had formerly built, on the property of the senior and mother church of the city over which he presided, a church in honor of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles.
