It had nevertheless been destroyed because of pressing necessities, although part of those walls still remained.

There, then, I, Carileffus, searching for a more remote place where, with the Lord’s help, I might build some cell for winning and saving souls, arrived and found part of the ancient walls. I built a sort of hut around them, as best I could, and began [Col. 1261D] to clear the ground. While I was engaged in this work and laboring at it, one day King Childebert, practicing his hunting, reached us. When he saw what was being done—although at first it displeased him—later, at the Lord’s prompting, he took counsel with his wife and advisers about providing me with some assistance from his treasury for completing the work.

He did so and granted me everything I could travel around in one day with my little donkey. Later I began to work and clear the land there with even greater labor and delight, and I was also enriched by other noblemen and free persons from their own property. While I was doing this and had begun to build the church, [Col. 1262B] Lord Innocent, bishop of that parish, came to me one day and severely rebuked me for daring to do this without his counsel or permission, and for undertaking such work on property where his predecessors had formerly built a church under their jurisdiction and dominion.

As soon as I recognized him, I humbled myself before him and disclosed what I had previously been considering inwardly: namely, that I wished to hand over to the senior church of the city and to that same bishop, Lord Innocent, both myself and the little souls whom I hoped to win for the Lord there, together with the property and everything that had been given or transferred to me from any source, or that I might deserve to acquire in future. Under his protection or defense, I wished both I myself and those properties and the people dwelling there to remain in future.

I willingly entrusted myself into his hands, together with certain monks who were with me, and I legally transferred and confirmed, by these written instruments, for him or his successors to possess forever, [Col. 1262C] with the permission, authorization, and consent of my benefactor, King Childebert, together with his envoy, Count Wiliricus, all the property I had been able to acquire or might be able to acquire in the future.

Indeed, from the property of his church—of Saint Mary and of Saints Gervasius and Protasius—the aforesaid Bishop Innocent greatly enriched me for the completion of this little monastery, and, supported by the assistance of that bishop, I was able to build a cell there. As has been said, at the command and urging of the aforesaid King Childebert, we handed it over and confirmed it to him or to his church see for perpetual possession, in such a way that in future monks living there regularly would always remain under the authority of the bishop.

We humbly beseech them before God, entrusting this to them, that it may be so—on the express condition and under this provision: that the granted property shall be freed from the authority of the bishop and from every ecclesiastical, episcopal, and public authority; no services [Col. 1262D] or exactions, no demanded or lavish banquets, no especially welcome or treacherous gifts, nor even the offspring of horses, transport services, compulsory carriage, or any other title of service that may be named by judicial authority, shall ever be exacted from the aforesaid property. Rather, under complete immunity, and with its little estate intact, just as it has until now been possessed by us, it shall, with God protecting and assisting it, remain in the right of the oratory of Saint Peter and Saint Martin and of the aforesaid holy apostles, under the right, authority, and dominion of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and of their rectors and bishops.

[Col. 1263A] Although it is not necessary to attach a penalty to transfers, nevertheless, for the sake of complete security, we have decided that the following should be inserted. If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, God forbid, or any of our heirs or heirs’ heirs, or any person moved by cunning or overcome by greed, should at any time attempt to violate or do anything against this written instrument of our transfer, which we resolved to make of our own free will for the Lord’s name and in veneration of that holy place, or should become evasive, let him be anathema, and let him render an account with the aforesaid saints before the tribunal of Christ. Moreover, let him be compelled by the treasury to pay to the church itself or its rectors, as a penalty of this world, 500 pounds of gold and 1,000 pounds of silver [Note: Perhaps read: “let him pay just penalties”], and let him in no way be able to reclaim what he seeks; but let this present transfer and our will remain inviolate at all times, supported by formal stipulation.

And so that this transfer may be held more firmly and preserved inviolate, we have confirmed it below with our own hand [Col. 1263B] and decreed that it be strengthened by the hands of other good men.

[Col. 1264A] Executed at the little monastery of Anisola. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the fourteenth year of the reign of King Childebert.

## Of Saint Carileffus, Priest and Monk: Concerning the Exemplary Copy of the Precaria Made for Him by Saint Innocent, Bishop

*(Mabillon, in the place cited.)*

[Col. 1263C] What follows is the exemplary copy of the precaria of Saint Innocent, bishop, which he made for Saint Karileffus, abbot of the monastery of Anisola. We have inserted its copy here for this reason: so that, if—God forbid—the same precaria should happen to be lost, its copy may be found inserted here, by which its recovery may be effected and it may be known how the matter was conducted.

To Lord Innocent, holy and venerable, [of] the apostolic see, bishop of the church of Le Mans, together with the holy congregation established in that city: I, Karileffus, in the name of God, an unworthy priest and monk, come before you as a petitioner.

Since I had made my request, and since your will decreed that the little monastery constructed in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Martin, situated on the territory of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, belonging to the senior and mother church of the city of Le Mans, in the territory of Le Mans, at a certain place formerly called by the ancients Casa-Gayana above the river Anisola—which is called [Col. 1263D] Anisola after the name of that river—where Lord Turibius, bishop of that parish, had formerly built, on the property of the senior and mother church of the city over which he presided, a church in honor of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, which had nevertheless been destroyed because of impending devastations, although part of those walls still remained there: I, the aforesaid man, with your permission and assistance, built it on your land through my own work, using your resources and those of other good men.

By your benefaction, you permitted me to hold it, with all the property belonging or pertaining to it, for the term of my life under a usufructuary arrangement, and to pay an annual census to the mother church of the city, to its bishops and rectors: namely, four pounds of wax for the church’s lights; one cambutta and two pairs of sandals for the bishop’s work; and, for the work of the canons [Col. 1264C] dwelling there in God’s service, two prepared little bottles filled with the best wine, and, on the Lord’s Supper, a full modius of eggs.

If I should appear negligent or late in paying this census, I shall provide a guarantee concerning it, and I shall not lose the little monastery during my lifetime. Nor shall I have the episcopal right to sell, give away, or alienate it anywhere, unless it remains under the right, authority, and dominion of Saint Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, or of their bishops and rectors.

After my departure from this life, when God commands it, you or your succeeding rectors shall, without the authorization of any judge or the opposition of our heirs, cause the aforesaid monastery, with all its integrity and with the property belonging or pertaining to it, to be recalled to your authority and dominion.

And so that the precariae, written in one tenor—one to be deposited in the treasury of the city church, and the other which I, Karileffus, may receive from you—may possess firmer validity, we have confirmed them below with our own hands and decreed that they be strengthened by the hands of good men.

[Col. 1264D] Executed publicly in the city of Le Mans. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourteenth year of the reign of King Childebert.

I, Innocent, although an unworthy bishop, have subscribed this precaria made by me.

I have been crucified with Christ; yet I live—not I, but Christ lives in me, 837. III, 16. It does not say, “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “and to your seed,” which is Christ, 112. Ibid., 27. As many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ, 196. Ibid., 28. There is neither male nor female, 345, 976. V, 14. The whole Law and the Prophets are summed up in this saying, namely: You shall love your neighbor as yourself, 811. Ibid., 16. Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh, 256, 754. Ibid., 17. The flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do whatever you wish, 678. Ibid., 21. For those who do such things go into torments, 579. VI, 3. Whoever considers himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself, 684. Ibid., 7. God is not mocked, 177. Ibid., 14. The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world, 244, 282.

## PAUL’S LETTER TO THE EPHESIANS

III, 14. For this reason I bend my knees to our God, 280. IV, 26. Let not the sun go down upon your anger, 50, 813. Ibid., 13. Into a perfect person, and into the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age, 287. V, 3. Let fornication and impurity, or any form of greed, not even be named among you, 665. Ibid., 18. Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, 573. VI, 12. Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places, 42, 795. Ibid., 13. Take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day, 52, 795. Ibid., 14. Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet with the preparation of the gospel of peace; in all things take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one, 795.

I, 23. I am constrained by the two alternatives, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is much better, 283, 940. IV, 7. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard, etc., 335.

I, 26. The mystery that was hidden from the ages and generations, 257. III, 3. For you have died to this world, and your life is hidden with Christ in God, 990.

V, 16, 17. Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything, 37, 751.

I, 11, 12. If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him, 336. II, 4. No one serving as a soldier for Christ entangles himself in secular affairs, 683. I, 3. He who is the splendor of glory and the truly subsisting Word, 282. IV, 12. ## A

**Abban:** wondrous abstinence, even from water, 813. He girds his loins with iron, ibid. Prefect of monks, ibid.

**Renunciation of possessions:** and the ancient teaching concerning it, 276. Complete renunciation necessary for monks, 596.

**Abenner:** king of the Jews devoted to idols, 243. He grieves that he has no children, ibid. He persecutes monks, 244, 294, 295. He persecutes Christians more severely, 246, 247. His son Josaphat is born, 247. On Josaphat’s birth he offers sacrifices, consults astrologers about his son, and learns that he will become a Christian, ibid. He strives to keep every trouble far from his son, ibid. The secretly Christian prince is craftily accused before him by his rivals, 248. He pretends before that same prince that he wishes to become a monk, ibid. He suppresses the anger aroused by the pious answer of the aforementioned prince, 249. He captures two monks, ibid. He orders them to be burned, 250. He summons the counselor Araches to him, 293. He detests relics, 295. He threatens the monks with death, ibid. He subjects seventeen monks to martyrdom, 296. His prayer concerning his son, 297. His threats against the same son, 298, 300. He is pierced with remorse but does not convert, 303. He proclaims a free public debate on the faith, ibid. He establishes the law of the debate, 304. His rhetors and priests fall silent, 309. From then on he is tormented by great anxiety of mind, 311. His answer to Theuda, 312. He sacrifices to the gods with Theuda, ibid. He asks Theuda for counsel and help, ibid. He visits his sick son, 316. He deliberates what should be done with his son, 322. He summons his son to share half the kingdom, ibid. He repents, 324. His letter to his son, ibid. He receives his son when he comes to him, 325. In the sight of everyone he worships the sign of the cross, 326. He overturns the idols, ibid. He builds temples for God, ibid. He is baptized, ibid. He performs penance with great humility, 327. He gives thanks to God and to his son, ibid. He dies, ibid. He is buried in a hair shirt, ibid.

**To abhor evils:** what this means, 519.

**Abibas:** continent and withdrawn from worldly affairs, 929. Rebuked by his father, he endures it patiently, ibid. His father records him as sole heir, ibid. He makes his brothers co-heirs, ibid. He distributes his share among the poor, ibid. He foreknows his death, ibid.

**Abiton:** disciple of Eusebius, 848.

**Self-denial and humility:** the tools of the soul, 625.

**Abraames:** an old man whom Marcian recalls from the error of celebrating Easter contrary to the usage of the Church, 809. — Abraames, both monk and bishop, 834. He disciplines his body by vigils, standing, and fasting, ibid. He assumes the role of a merchant in order to win others, ibid. He suffers various insults, ibid. He prays and gives surety for his adversaries, ibid. He is chosen governor by his adversaries, ibid. He builds a church, ibid. He is ordained a priest, 835. He becomes bishop of Carrhae, ibid. His manner of exhorting is sometimes gentle, sometimes harsh, as physicians customarily are, ibid. He abstains from bread and water, ibid. He sings forty hymns at night, ibid. His manner of life, ibid. He is generous toward guests, 835. His judgment is upright, and so is his justice, ibid. He is visited by the emperor, ibid. The emperor and empress attend his funeral, ibid. His garments, after his death, are precious to everyone, 836.

**Abraham the patriarch:** recognizes the Creator from created things, 250.

**A saying of Abbot Abraham:** 517, 597.

**Abrahamius:** mocked by demons because of his pride; believing that he had been ordained priest by God, 769. He is corrected by the elders through humility, ibid.

**Abram the hermit:** a second Abraham, 144. He preserved chastity from childhood, ibid. Born of wealthy parents, ibid. As a boy he became betrothed, ibid. As a young man he attended church, ibid. He was devoted to the word of God, ibid. He entered marriage, 145. Fleeing from the bridal chamber, he abandoned his bride, ibid. He blocked the entrance to his cell, ibid. Many people flocked to him, ibid. A discourse of wisdom was in him, ibid. He arranged for his rich inheritance to be distributed among the poor, ibid. His clothing was a cloak and hair shirt, ibid. His furnishings were a cup and a mat, ibid. He showed the same affection toward everyone, ibid. His speech was gentle, ibid. His face was an image of holiness, ibid. He persevered in his way of life for fifty years, ibid. He was ordained priest by the laying on of the bishop’s hand, 146. He built a church from his own patrimony, ibid. He prayed for the conversion of the Gentiles, ibid. He overturned the Gentiles’ altars, ibid. Though severely beaten, he paid no attention to the blows, ibid. Beaten again, he was left half-dead, ibid. He was beaten a third time, 147. Through his patience and charity the Gentiles were converted, ibid. He baptized all of them, six hundred in number, ibid. He was regarded as like an angel, ibid. He preached the word to the newly converted, ibid. After prayer he fled, out of love for solitude, ibid., and 148. He was diligently sought, ibid. He returned to his cell, ibid. He was tempted by a demon in the appearance of a good angel, ibid. He overcame the demon through humility, ibid., and by the name of Jesus, ibid. The demon attempted to destroy his cell with an axe and was defeated, ibid. He trod upon fire unharmed, ibid. The demon appeared to him in the form of a young man, ibid. He sang psalms, 149. It was driven away by prayer, ibid. It proclaimed itself defeated, ibid. He was undaunted against demons, ibid. He did not wash his face or feet, ibid. His face revealed the purity of his mind, ibid. His face was unchanged even in death, ibid. He did not change his hair-cloth garment for fifty years, 150. He taught his niece Mary the Psalter and the Scriptures, 368. He ordered her possessions to be distributed among the poor, 369. His vision concerning the fall of his niece Mary, ibid. He grieves over the lost sheep, 370. He goes dressed as a soldier to search for his niece, ibid. His comparison with Abraham the patriarch, ibid. He asks the stablekeeper for Mary’s presence, ibid. He who had not tasted bread for fifty years now eats meat, 371. He withdraws with his niece into a room, ibid. With tears he reveals himself to her and urges her to return to her former life, ibid. He consoles his confused niece, ibid. He dies at the age of seventy, after fifty years of conversion, 372. His encomia, 149, 372. His relics bring healing, 372.

**Perfect renunciation:** extending even to the removal of one’s clothing, 666. — The devil demands Christ’s and baptism’s renunciation, 156.

**Abrodianus:** husband of a woman from Assyria; he asks Saint Macedonius for help on behalf of his wife, 830.

**An apse:** inscribed by Alexander the Great, a guide to the road, 225.

**A monk who possessed property:** though dead and excommunicated, he is absolved and set free, 923.

Anaxanontus is content with very little food, 873. Antony uses only bread, salt, and water, 38. Likewise Palaemon, 105. Likewise Zacchaeus, 136. Likewise the monks living with Evagrius, 479. John abstains from provisions because the elder had not blessed them for him, 877. Macarius of Rome lives on herbs for three years, 230. A certain monk abstains from every drink, 542. Likewise another old man abstains from drink for forty days, 572. Paul of Galatia passes Lent on a measure of lentils and a small vessel of water, 666. Paul of Nazarba lives for fifty years on bread supplied as alms by the Church, 873. Peter Pyoni uses lukewarm water in place of wine, 570. Philoromus abstains from cooked food, 770. Pior lives on salt water, one biscuit, and five olives, 503, 570. Pityrion eats only twice a week, 760. Polychronius is accustomed to fast for seven days, 839. Posidonius abstains from bread for forty years, 761. Posthumius eats only water and vegetables, 235. Publius eats bread by weight, 814, 815. Romanus is content solely with bread, salt, and water, 826. The ancient Scetiotes never take food except for hospitality’s sake, 877. A certain elder, 492. Simeon Stylites takes food only on the seventh day, 170. Sisoi abstains from wine, and why, ibid. Likewise Elias, already a bishop, ibid. Sophronius lives on herbs for seventy years, 910. The remarkable abstinence of the boy Theodore, 125. A certain virgin eats only on Saturday and Sunday, 727. Likewise Elpidius, 769. Zacchaeus lives only on bread, salt, and water, 136. Zeno lives on bread and water, 827. Abstinence from drink, 542, 572; from wine, 570, 870; from bread, 761, 770; from water, 813; from bread and water, 835; from bread and wine, 866; from meat, 572, 780; from meat and wine, 724; from cooked food, 716, 770. Abstinence does not alter Abraham’s face, 150. Abstinence is necessary for monks, 511. Abstinence from food is proved by a miracle, 571. **Ammon of Tabenna, or Ammonas:** father of two thousand monks, 458, 746. — Ammon is divinely freed from a basilisk, 532. — Ammon the Egyptian, or Nitriote, founder of the Nitrian brothers, 113, 482. He is compelled to marry, 482, 713. He persuades his bride to preserve virginity, 743. He lives continently with his wife, 482. [Col. XVII] His practices, 713. Through prayer he overcomes temptations, ibid. At his wife’s advice he lives separately, ibid. He hastens to Mount Nitria, 714. He becomes the father of monks, and she of virgins, 482. By persuading the restitution of stolen property, he heals a boy bitten by a rabid dog, ibid., and 714. Through prophetic spirit he recognizes the theft, ibid. He refuses to let himself be seen naked, 51, 714. He is transported across the river by divine power, ibid. Antony sees his soul ascending to heaven, 51, 714. Whoever refuses him the service of a camel loses the camel, 714. He dies at the age of sixty-two, ibid. — Ammon, or Amun, places two dragons as guards at the monastery gate against robbers, 752. He treats the robbers humanely and converts them to God, 752. His prayer splits the dragon, ibid. With sacred oil he restores a deranged boy to himself, ibid.

**Ammona, or Piammon:** sick, he is healed by an angel, 759. While he offers at the altar, an angel marks those who receive Communion, 759. Those whom the angel passes over die within three days, 759.

**Sayings of Ammona:** 597, 584.

**Ammonas:** see *Ammon of Tabenna*.

**Ammonius’s brothers:** Eusebius, Euthymius, and Dioscorus, 715, 946. Ammonius yields his cell to a guest, 759. Among his brethren, cells for novices are secretly furnished with equipment, 379. **Love of Christ:** overcomes every difficulty, 331.

**Love:** casts out fear, 632. Impure love is conquered by divine love, 314. The force and power of divine love, 333. The demon of love, 97.

**Angelic appearance:** of monks, 924.

**Anuph:** is always attended and taught by a guardian angel, 754. The guardian angel is to be honored, 685.

**An angel:** restores Onuphrius’s strength, 99. He brings him bread and water every day, 102. An angel heals the sick Ammona, or Piammon, 759. At Ammona’s Mass an angel marks those receiving Communion; those whom he passes over die within three days, 759. An angel heals a certain gardener’s foot, which was already about to be amputated, by touching it, 584. He teaches the same man to trust not in money but in God, ibid. An angel counts laborious footsteps, 589. An angel sings psalms with interruptions of prayer, 543. From this comes the custom of singing psalms, ibid. An angel ministers to a certain sick man, 591. An angel instructs an old man concerning his error, 636. An angel rejoices over one who receives Communion worthily, 640. An angel heals a sick man’s liver, 655. An angel of temperance withdraws from a woman possessed by the spirit of pride, 735. An angel announces that someone’s repentance is pleasing to God, 745. An angel continually stands beside a consecrated altar, 864. An angel appears to an old man asking about burial, 916. Leontius sees an angel standing beside the altar, 864. Pachomius dies at the sight of an angel, 138.

**Angels:** carry Ammon’s soul to heaven, 51, 714. Likewise the soul of a certain brother, 130; of Anuph, 754; of Onuphrius, 103; of a certain pilgrim, 645; of a certain Protocomes, 756; of Silvanus, 129; of Simeon Stylites, 174. Angels serve saints and the just, 106. Angels lift Pachomius from the ground, 133. The protection of angels over those who pray, 529. — Angels protect human beings against demons, 638. Angels rejoice over the conversion of a sinner and, conversely, are saddened, 677. Angels stand to the right and left of the one offering sacrifice, 927. The orders of angels, 705. Antony sees angels as he dies, 59. Basil, while celebrating the sacrifice, is surrounded by angels, 155.

**A narrow way:** is to do violence to one’s own will, 605. — Why the narrow way is to be chosen, 647.

**The upright soul:** in what sense it is called so, 41.

**The soul:** when it can truly be called a Shunammite, 645. The penitent soul described by a beautiful apologue, 659. The soul is stained by vices, 681. The soul must always be armed, 682. The soul is unconquered unless one opens the gates of the senses, 796. — Poemen teaches that one should lay down one’s soul for a friend, 530. He lays down his soul for his neighbor who patiently bears grief, 633. — Those who receive the soul in vain, 712. The souls of the saints are carried to heaven by angels. See *Angels*. — Antony sees the various states of souls after death, 52, 675, 729.

**Animals:** obey the saints. See *Beasts*.

**The mind:** is to be separated from external things, 684. Care of the mind is required, 905.

**The years of a person:** from what time they are to be counted, 282.

**The anniversary of an abbot’s ordination:** a celebrated day, 364.

**Antigonus:** prefect of Lycia and father of Euphrasia, 351. His discourse to his wife Eufraxia concerning the vanity of the world, 351. He dies after having performed many acts of almsgiving, 351. A vision shows that he is in heaven, 354.

**Antioch:** became famous through various holy men, 831.

**Antiochus:** lives outdoors on a mountain, 845.

**The difference between the ancient and new law:** 266.

**Antony:** head and chief of monastic life, 113, 270. His life, 35. His remembrance is gain for Athanasius, 35. His perfect life is a road to virtue, 35. The history of his life is completely truthful, 36. At the sight of a hippocentaur he arms his forehead with the sign of the cross, ibid. He opposes the satyr with the shield of faith, ibid. He sees Paul’s soul ascending to heaven, ibid. He blesses dumb animals, ibid. On the solemn days of Easter and Pentecost he wore Paul’s palm-fiber tunic, ibid. His family and homeland, 36. His holy childhood, 36. His frequent attendance at church, 36. An attentive listener, 36. He sells his possessions, 36. He renounces the world, ibid. He imitates the better, 36, 37. He works with his hands, 36. He prays frequently, 37. He listens eagerly to Sacred Scripture, 37. He is called “God-loving,” ibid. He is harassed by the devil, 37. He overcomes him through prayer, ibid. He devotes himself to vigils and fasts, 37. He overcomes the allurements of the flesh by remembrance of death, ibid. He sees the spirit of fornication in a hideous form, ibid. He conquers it, ibid. His prayers, 38. His food: bread, salt, and water, 38. His bed: reeds and a hair shirt, 38. His clothing: hair cloth and a skin, 48. He is beaten by demons, 38. He is carried half-dead to a village, ibid. Returned to the desert, he reproaches the demons, ibid. The demons frighten him in various ways, 38, 39. He protects himself with the sign of the cross, 39. He is refreshed by a heavenly vision, 39. He asks for the desert, 39. He is tempted by a disk placed before him, 39. At the sight of gold he flees, ibid. He withdraws to the first mountain, ibid. Serpents flee from him, ibid. He lives in solitude for twenty years, 40. The beauty of his body always remains the same, 40. He heals the sick and demoniacs, 40. He crosses crocodiles unharmed, 40. He builds monasteries, ibid. He hands on precepts to his disciples, 40, 41. His address to his disciples, 40. He sees a demon in a terrible form, 42. He recounts the demon’s various ways of causing harm, 42, 43, 44. When tempted in various ways, what he answers the demon, 46. He spits upon the demon, ibid. The virtues of his disciples, 47. He attends to the body’s necessity with modesty, 47. By desiring martyrdom he strengthens martyrs, ibid. His fasts and vigils, 48. He heals a demoniac woman, 48, 54. He prepares to flee out of fear of glory, 48. He is divinely sent to the inner desert, 48. He withdraws to the second mountain, ibid. He obtains food for himself, ibid. He commands the beasts, 48, 49. At the instigation of demons he is attacked by beasts, 49. He drives away one beast’s form by the cross, 49. Defeated by the prayers of the brothers, he visits them, ibid. By prayer he obtains a spring, ibid. His sister becomes a teacher of girls, ibid. His various counsels, 49, 50. The memory of the saints is an incentive to virtue, 50. His deeds are to be examined day and night, ibid. Rash judgment is to be avoided, ibid. Offenses are to be recorded in a little book, ibid. Antony is always the same in face and mind, ibid. He frees various persons from the devil, 50, 52, 56. He frees a virgin from various illnesses, 50. He knows things while absent, 51, 52. He sees Ammon’s soul carried to heaven, 51. He predicts Ammon’s death, 51. In his absence he heals the virgin Polycratia, ibid. He sends everyone away from him rejoicing, 52. He alone perceives the stench of the demon, 52. He is carried aloft by angels, whom the demons vainly try to hinder, 52. He is accused by demons, ibid. He is God-taught (*theodidaktos*), ibid. He sees the states of souls after death, 52, 675, 729. He honors clerics, 53. He is recognized by the cheerfulness of his face, 53. He detests heretics and schismatics, 53. He openly condemns the Arians as forerunners of Antichrist, ibid. He strengthens the faith by miracles, 53. He converts pagans, 53, 54. His clever saying to the philosophers, 54. He instructs philosophers, 54, 55. He challenges the sophists to cast out demons, 56. Constantine writes to him, 56. He does not think highly of the matter, ibid. He sends back a salutary reply, ibid. He returns to his customary severity, ibid. He foresees the Church’s affliction, 57. He predicts peace after the storm, 57. He admonishes judges, 57. His letter to Balacius the Arian, 58. He bestows benefits on various people, 58. [Col. XIX] He predicts his own death, 58. His final counsels, 58, 59. He forbids funeral pomp, 59. He makes a will, ibid. He honors confessors of the faith with gifts, ibid. He sees angels as he dies, ibid. He is always even-tempered in his purpose, 60. Famous everywhere, 60.

Antony consoles the blind Didymus, 533. Antony teaches most beautifully what the vice of possessiveness does in a monk, 581, 582. Antony teaches the stages of patience, 667, 668. Antony warns that one must learn before teaching, 680, 681. — Antony is called “the Great,” 674, 728, 936. Antony divinely recognizes the presence of Eulogius, 674, 729. His prayer concerning Eulogius and the Elephantine, 675, 729. He reconciles the same men, 675, 729. Antony’s perfection, 626. Antony’s book is creation itself, 659. Antony’s solitude, 727. Antony’s vision concerning the souls of the just and the condemned, 675. — Antony is shown that work must be joined to prayer, 584. Who the Jerusalemite guests and who the Egyptian guests are in Antony’s account, 674, 728. — A certain Antony, author of the life of Simeon Stylites, 172.

**Anuph:** never lied, 763. He is nourished by the ministry of angels, 753. He is taught by his guardian angel, who is always beside him, 754. He always obtains from God what he asks, 754. He sees the glory of the saints and the torments of demons, 754. His soul is carried to heaven by angels with hymns, 754.

**Apelles, or Apellen:** an ironsmith and priest, 755. He drives away the devil, appearing in the form of a woman, with red-hot iron, ibid. Afterward he handles the red-hot iron with his bare hand, ibid.

**Aphraates:** of the race of the Persian Magi, 818. First an ascetic at Edessa, then at Antioch, ibid. He instructs people of every condition, 819. He accepts bread from only one person, 819. He does not even accept a Persian tunic from Anthemius, 819. He explains the matter through an excellent apologue, 819. Strong during persecution, he explains to the emperor by a comparison why he abandoned solitude, 820. A eunuch who threatens him is suffocated in a bath, 820. He heals the emperor’s sick horse with water and oil blessed by the sign of the cross, 821. He does not admit women inside his doors, 821. With holy oil he dissolves a malefice between husband and wife, 821. With blessed water he keeps locusts away from a field, ibid. He blesses Theodoret and his mother, ibid.

**Aphthonius:** Pachomius’s steward, 737.

**Apollinaris:** bishop of Alexandria, 899. Apollinaris, patriarch of Alexandria, assists a modest and poor young man with remarkable skill and charity, 923, 924.

**Apollo:** with bow, quiver, lyre, and flute, a god of the Gentiles, 307.

**Apollonius, or Apollo:** father of five hundred monks, 460, 747. At fifteen years of age he seeks the desert, 160, 747. When he prays to have the spirit of boastfulness removed from him, he is heard, 747. He prays one hundred times by day and one hundred times by night, 747. His clothing does not wear out, 747. On the Lord’s Day he invites his people to food as an act of charity, 747. He is imprisoned with others for military service, 748. The prison doors are divinely opened and he is freed, 748. He obtains whatever he asks from God, 748. He receives revelations, 748. Many come to him to become monks, 748. He loves cleanliness of clothing, ibid. He makes those carrying an idol’s image in procession for rain stand motionless, 749. He converts those freed through prayer to Christ, 749. He recalls a robber to a better life, 749. His vision, and that of the robber, ibid. He predicts the death of a contentious ruler, 749. He reconciles two quarreling villages, 749. He obtains for someone the grace of humility and gentleness, 750. Through prayer he multiplies loaves day by day, 750. [Col. XIX] He foretells the arrival of guests, 750. He worships guests, kisses them, and washes their feet, 750. His brothers receive Communion before food, 750. He recommends daily Communion, 751.

**Apollonius the deacon:** encourager of martyrs, 757. He suffers a curse from Philemon, 757. Through patience and gentleness he converts Philemon, 757. He is handed over to the fire with Philemon, 758. He remains unharmed with his companion, ibid. After the prefects of Alexandria, their officials, and guards are converted, miracles occur at their relics, 758.

**Apollonius, surnamed “From among the Merchants” (*Ex negotiatoribus*):** he serves the brothers as physician and pharmacist, 717, 948.

**The apologue of the nightingale:** by which idolaters are shown whom they resemble, 263, 262.

**Apologue:** see *Parable*.

**The apostles:** scattered into every part of the world, 243.

**Apparition:** of Astion to Vigilantius praying at his tomb, 219. Of Astion and Epictetus to their parents, 223. Of Christ to Macarius in a cave, 230. Of Barlaam to Josaphat, 337. Of Eugenia to her mother Claudia, 348. Of many saints to Sisoi at his death, 524.

**Apparitions:** are not to be trusted immediately, 628.

**Appetite:** remarkable restraint, by not tasting food that has been seen, 509. In an old man who silently uses rancid oil offered as honey, even while ill, 509.

**Aprion:** bishop of Tentyris, 123.

**Water:** of a well rises through the prayer of a certain brother, 502, 651. Water is made solid beneath the feet of Mary of Egypt, 391. Likewise beneath those of Besarion, 649. Seawater is sweetened through Besarion’s prayer, 532, 649. Likewise through Theodore’s prayer and the sign of the cross, 914. Excessive drinking of water generates fantasies, 479, 483. Water has wondrous power when given from the hands of holy men to heal the tempted, 634, 635. The power and efficacy of blessed water, 840. To drink water against obedience is a sin, 236. How drinking water is harmful, 708. The water of Simeon Stylites’ monastery frees a woman from a serpent, 173. A harmful leopard dies when water or dust from Simeon Stylites’ monastery is sprinkled upon it, ibid. Macarius the Egyptian drives away, with blessed water, an apparition seen as a woman transformed into a mare, 720. Macarius of Alexandria heals a demoniac with blessed water and holy oil, 724. Macedonius frees a woman from demonic gluttony with blessed water, 830. The same water cures madness, ibid. Drinking blessed water removes the danger of miscarriage, 831. Blessed water heals Aphraates’ imperial horse, 821. It keeps away locusts, ibid.

**Altar:** see *Altar*, 725.

**Julian:** builds an altar on Mount Sinai, 803.

**An altar:** when a boy is brought near it, he is healed by Maesyma, 832.

**Abraham:** demolishes the altars of the Gentiles, 146.

**Araches:** counselor, summoned to King Abenner, 293. He advises that Barlaam be sought, ibid. He searches for him, 294. He captures monks, ibid. He threatens them with death, ibid.

**A tree:** bends down in order to settle the holy Fathers’ controversy concerning fasting, 615.

**A bow:** is not always to be drawn, 596.

**Ardaborius:** master of soldiers, comes to the burial of Simeon Stylites, 174.

**Pastor:** ardor for learning, 610.

**To accuse oneself:** what this means, 1003.

**Arians:** openly condemned by Antony as forerunners of Antichrist, 53. The Arians falsely claim that Antony agrees with them, ibid. The elements detest Arianism, ibid.

**Weapons against the demon:** 44, 47.

**Weapons of the spirit:** are taught, 285.

**The armor of Christ’s soldiers:** 795.

**Possessed person:** see *Demoniac*.

[Col. XX]

**The arrogant and self-satisfied:** is abandoned by the angel of providence, 766.

**Arsenius:** received Arcadius and Honorius, the emperors, from the font of baptism, 506. He seeks the desert, ibid. As he had sought more costly things in the world, so in the desert he seeks cheaper clothing, 506, 620. His vision concerning three classes of people and their works, 506, 635, 681. He chastises the fragrances of the world with stench, 507. Concerned for his salvation, he is divinely warned, 528, 563. By his example he praises devotion to solitude and flight from human beings, 528, 564. He avoids the sight of the brothers so that he may continually look toward heaven, 528. He falls forward onto the ground so as not to see people, ibid. In church always after
sits after the column so as neither to see nor to be seen, 528, 621. He also avoids the rustling of reeds, 564. He laments the devastation of Scythia, ibid. He shuns the sight of women, 511, 564. As he was dying, he forbade his disciples to give anyone anything from his body as relics, 524, 621. He asks his disciples to make an offering for him after his death, 524. But he forbids the other offices of charity, 524, 569. His continual tears, 524. His remembrance of the judgment, 565. Having died to the world, he rejects wills, 582. His devotion to poverty, ibid. He teaches that God’s help against demons must be invoked, 620. He admits that he does not know the rustic alphabet, 621. He requests that even a very small *eulogia* be sent to the brothers, ibid. His disciples Alexander and Zoilus, ibid. He never wished to speak about questions concerning Scripture, ibid. Description of his appearance, ibid. A brief summary of his life, 621, 622. He appears entirely fiery, 635. Always fleeing and silent, 673. He explains beautifully why he avoids people, 680. He seizes an opportunity for an excuse lest he be seen by people, 680.

What Arsisius did and of what sort his deeds were, 713. Asclepion, abbot and father of many monks, 225. Asclepius, outstanding in the same discipline as Polychronius, both in civic and solitary life, 847. Asella establishes a community of men and women at Rome, 775. A donkey serves as a provider of provisions and, by itself, carries vegetables to the monks, 910. By his mere appearance Saint Ephraem teaches modesty, 168, 169. A young man is inflamed by the sight of a holy virgin, 878. The sight of a woman is a cause of temptation, 866. Rough clothing and conduct among monks, 244. Harshness of spirit is expelled after being turned into blood by vomiting, 568. An asp is handled harmlessly by religious boys, 539. A woman named Assyria is cured of madness through blessed water, 830. The young Asterius visits the old Julian to learn the manner of life, 802. He is tested by thirst, ibid. Julian obtains a spring for his consolation, 802. He practices the monastic life, 803. He visits the old Julian several times with little gifts, 803. Asterius, a bishop of heretics, abuses dialectic and eloquence in support of heresy, 803. He dies, struck down by divine power, ibid.

The young nobleman Astion hears Epictetus discussing the faith, 212. He is converted, 212. He is baptized, 213. He flees with Epictetus into Scythia, 214. He cures a demoniac by the sign of the cross, 215. He restores a half-dead man who had fallen to his former health, ibid., 215. After leaving without the old man’s command, he is afflicted by a shameful thought, ibid. He is cured by confession, 216. He is arrested by the commander Latronianus, ibid. His age and appearance, ibid. He is tortured in various ways, 216, 217, 218. He is beheaded, [Col. XXI] 219. His body shines, ibid. He appears to Vigilantius while the latter is praying at his tomb, ibid. Vigilantius receives his parents, ibid. His testament is the Lord’s cross and the holy Gospel, 220, 221. He appears to his parents, 223. He asks that his possessions be distributed to the poor, ibid.

The church as a place of asylum, 194. Athanasius comes to Tabennisi, 123. He is honored by Pachomius, ibid. He is received with hymns and psalms, ibid. Athanasius sets out for Rome, 709. As a boy, Athanasius, pretending to be a bishop on the seashore, baptizes catechumens, 927. See *Boys*. Athanasius is handed over to the Church together with his companions, priests and deacons, 927. He lives with Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, ibid. Athanasius hides for six years in Alexandria with a virgin, 776. He returns to his own people, ibid. Athanasius embraces Antony among Antony’s gifts, 59. Praise of Athanasius’s writings, 873. Praise of Athens, 153. Athenogenes, bishop of Petra, 900.

Pachomius’ attention while reading the Scriptures, 116. Antony is an attentive hearer in church, 36, 37. Contempt for gold. See *Contempt for gold and money*. At the sight of gold Antony flees, 39. A young goldsmith, out of piety and from his own funds, adds something to a golden cross, 928. For this act of piety he is adopted as a son by Patricius, 928. Austerity without charity is dangerous, 735. The austerity of life is to be undertaken secretly, 751. The remarkable austerity of life of Marana and Cyra, 855, 856. They live in the open air, ibid. The austerity of Simeon Stylites, 171. Divine help is present where human help has failed, 591. A miser, in order to enrich his friends, is stripped of heavenly goods, 741. The miserly are always poor, 284. The miserly resemble springs containing frogs, 766. When the miserly bishop Troilus reluctantly gives alms, he falls ill, 193. After the money is returned, he recovers, 194. The miser is described by a striking comparison drawn from dogs and hunting birds, 295. Avarice is punished by elephantiasis, 719. Avarice destroys what almsgiving had prepared, 194. Avarice is punished when Pachomius burns the mats, 131. Macarius teaches a virgin a good stratagem as a remedy for avarice and converts her, 711, 712. Isidore does likewise, 945. Rebuke of avarice, 295. Birds and ducks mourn the death of Simeon Stylites, 174. Avita serves God with her husband and daughter, 775. Avitus, brother of Saint Eugenia, 340. Avitus the monk visits Marcianus, 808. Azarias, guardian of the Holy Sepulchre, 876.

## B

Babylas the mime, having heard a Gospel saying, is converted to a better life, 364. Likewise his two concubines, ibid. He assumes the religious habit with them, ibid. Bacchus, master of drunkenness, 307. An old man’s staff, as proof of his chastity, puts forth leaves upon his grave, 500. A possessed woman is struck with an abbess’s staff to the terror of the devil, 359. Balacius the Arian, spitting upon Antony’s letter, is punished, 58. Basil’s baptism is confirmed by lightning and a dove, 155. Baptism, the root of the Christian faith, 258. What baptism accomplishes, [Col. XXI] 266. What must be avoided afterward, ibid. Baptism washes away all sins, 321. The baptism of martyrdom is the most excellent of all, 269. Baptism is not given to prostitutes unless they provide a surety, 578. Baptism was formerly customarily administered during Holy Week, 911. How many kinds of baptism there are, 915. Effects of baptism, 258. Fasting and prayer precede baptism, 285. After baptism the baptized are clothed in white, 379. A certain dying Jew asks for baptism, 915. Even a merely supposed baptism restores a person to health, ibid. Without baptism there can be no good hope, 258. A disputation concerning baptism administered to a certain Jew through sand, 915. The baptistery sweats at Epiphany, 933. Another baptistery is spontaneously filled from Easter to Pentecost, ibid. Abraham baptizes a thousand converts, 147. Basil is baptized in the Jordan, 155. Likewise Eubulus, ibid. The prefect of Alexandria is baptized with his household, 345. Astion’s parents are baptized by Evangelicus, 223. The baptized are healed of every illness, 323. Those who have not been baptized must above all be baptized, 803.

Barachias, a Christian, comes forward to dispute on behalf of Josaphat, 303. Josaphat offers him the kingdom, 328. He refuses, ibid. He is appointed king, 329. He is ordered to be informed of Josaphat’s death, 338.

He transfers the still incorrupt bodies of Barlaam and Josaphat to India with great pomp, ibid.

Baradatus confines himself in a cell narrower than his own stature, 854. He wears a hide, ibid. He reasons better than the Aristotelians, ibid.

Barbarism joined with zeal and truth is better than empty eloquence, 818.

The history of Barlaam and Josaphat was received from the Indians, 242. Barlaam, a monk and priest in the land of Sennaar, 252. At the divine prompting he sets out for India, ibid. He promises the king’s son that he will give him a precious stone, which, he asserts, can be seen only by a pure eye, 252. His speech to Josaphat, 253. He explains to whom pious doctrine should be preached, ibid. By a most beautiful example he teaches that religious persons, as heralds of death and of divine judgment, should be held in the highest honor, 254. He teaches that religious persons should be honored by the likeness of two chests, ibid. He instructs Josaphat in the faith, ibid. He exhorts him to repentance and baptism, 263. He teaches the transience of worldly things, 265. He terrifies him with punishments, ibid. He invites him with rewards, ibid. He discusses good works, ibid. On repentance, 267. On renunciation of all possessions, 276. He teaches by the example of the prodigal son that one must by no means despair because of sins, 267. Likewise by the example of the good shepherd, ibid. He explains why Peter was permitted to fall, 268. By the example of another king he instructs Josaphat, 278. He leads him to hope for his father’s conversion, 279. By a most beautiful parable he recommends the religious life, 279, 280. He prays for Josaphat’s salvation, 281. His food and clothing, 283. By the likeness of one wishing to redeem a captive from enemies, he explains why he has changed his clothing, 283. He teaches Josaphat, who wishes to accompany him, that this is not yet expedient, by a beautiful parable concerning a chosen doe; he advises concealment, 284. He refuses gifts, 284, 291. He declines clothing, 285. He catechizes Josaphat, 285. He baptizes him, 287. He celebrates a private Mass, ibid. After the baptism he exhorts Josaphat to good works, ibid. He asks Josaphat for permission to depart, 291. His final prayer for him, ibid. His prayer to God for Josaphat, 292. He is sought out by Arachis for counsel concerning punishment, 293. After being sought for two years by Josaphat, he is found, 332, 333. His abstinence and choice of foods, [Col. XXII] 333. His vigils and nocturnal prayers, ibid. His pursuit of virtue, ibid. He foretells his death, 334. Fearing purgatory, he asks for prayers, 334, 336. He impresses upon Josaphat the remembrance of death, ibid. He suggests a remedy against vainglory, 335. He celebrates Mass before his death, 336. His prayer while dying, ibid. He dies fortified by the sign of the cross, 336. Josaphat recites psalms over his body, ibid. He is buried, ibid. He rebukes Josaphat in a vision, 337. His incorrupt body is transferred to India by King Barachias, 338. It is received with honor, ibid. Many miracles occur during its translation, ibid.

Barnabas does not pull out a thorn embedded in his foot, 865.

Basianilla, daughter of the general Candianus, an ascetic woman, 775.

Basilicus, king of the Saracens, visits Simeon Stylites, 172.

The life of Basil was written by various authors, 152. Various praises of Basil, 152. Basil is entrusted to letters at the age of seven, ibid. At twelve he is a philosopher, ibid. Eubulus is his teacher, 153. His fellow students are Gregory Nazianzen, Julian, and Libanius, ibid. He devotes fifteen years to study, ibid. He learns astronomy and geometry, ibid. He is divinely admonished to read Sacred Scripture, ibid. He goes to Egypt to Porphyrius the archimandrite, ibid. He lives on water and vegetables, ibid. He tries to lead his teacher and fellow students to the faith, ibid. His teacher praises his intelligence, ibid. He disputes about the faith with his teacher Eubulus, 153. He teaches that the first definition of philosophy is meditation on death, ibid. By means of three tablets, as it were those of Cebes, he instructs the mind through parables, ibid. He teaches the resurrection, ibid. He enters into partnership with Eubulus, 154. They piously distribute their possessions, ibid. They reach Antioch, ibid. Basil dictates a composition for the child of their host Philoromus, ibid. Basil and Eubulus are invited by Libanius to an elegant banquet, 154. They reject luxury, ibid. They live on bread and water, ibid. He exhorts Libanius’s students to all honorable conduct, ibid. At Jerusalem he visits the holy places, ibid. They request baptism from the bishop, ibid. His baptism is confirmed by lightning and a dove, 155. Chrism and communion are given to both, 165. They return to Antioch, ibid. Basil is made a deacon by Meletius, ibid. He writes on Proverbs, ibid. He returns with Eubulus to Cappadocia, ibid. The bishop Eusebius of Caesarea learns of their arrival by divine revelation, ibid. They are received by him with honor, ibid. Basil is made bishop of Caesarea, 155. He celebrates Mass daily, ibid. Divinely instructed, he writes the Liturgy, ibid. He divides the sacred Host into three parts, ibid. While celebrating the sacrifice, he is surrounded by a brilliant light and angels, ibid. He keeps the Eucharist in a golden dove above the altar, 156. While he is celebrating, a little child appears in the Eucharist to a certain Jew, together with a chalice full of blood, ibid. He then baptizes the Jew, now believing, with his entire household, ibid. He brings back to a better mind Proterius’s servant, who had devoted himself to the demon by a written contract, 157. He confines him, marked with the cross, in the sacristy, ibid. He struggles with the demon on his behalf, 158. He wrests the written contract from the demon, ibid. He foretells that Anastasius is at home, 158. He heals a leper, 159. Through his prayers all the sins of a sinful woman, written and sealed on a document, are blotted out except one, 160. What is afterward thrown upon his bier is also blotted out, 160. He appears to Ephraem like a column of fire, ibid. In the same vision Ephraem sees a tongue of fire, 161. Ephraem receives him with a kiss, ibid. Through prayer he obtains for Ephraem the ability to speak Greek, 161.

Basilla seeks the company of Eugenia, 346. She is baptized by Pope Cornelius, ibid. God reveals to her the martyrdom that is impending, 347. She is betrayed by a maidservant, 347. She kisses the feet of Protus and Hyacinthus, ibid. She rejects a conversation with her betrothed Pompeius, ibid. The emperor Gallienus orders her either to accept Pompeius as her husband or to perish by the sword, 348. Because of her love of chastity, she is pierced through with a sword, ibid.

Bassus, superintendent of monasteries, 843.

Be, or Benus, wholly gentle, 458, 746. He commands a hippopotamus and a crocodile, 459, 746.

Delicacies given to Macarius, 733.

The ancient custom of blessing children, 799.

Blessing of garments, 127; of oil, ibid., 724; of animals, 20; of water, 724; of bread, 473; of bread and oil, 81. The blessing of monks is salutary, 524. Simeon Stylites considers priestly blessing to bear great fruit, 851. The Saracens ask for Hilarion’s blessing, 80. A guest who arrives asks the host who receives him for a blessing, 101. The barbarians seek Simeon Stylites’ blessing, even contending for it, 851. Theodoret asks for the blessing of Marana and Cyra, 856. Through Polychronius’s blessing, a flask is filled with oil, 847. When an old man withholds his blessing, a monk abstains from food, 877.

To do good is a likeness of the divine nature, 197.

The greatness of God’s benefits, 280.

Benjamin cures illnesses with sacred oil, 716, 947. He suffers from dropsy, ibid. In patience he is another Job, 717, 947. Since his inner person is healthy, he does not care about the body, 717, 948. Though himself ill, he heals others, ibid. He dies, ibid.

Kindness. See Forgetfulness of injuries.

People are corrected by kindness rather than by severity, 577.

Kindness toward the blind and poor, 845.

The monk Benus. See above, Be.

Besarion makes seawater fresh by prayer, 532, 649. He teaches that one must trust in God, ibid. He walks upon the waters, 649. The sun stands still at his prayers, 649. Without knowing it, he drives out a demon by a word, 518, 649, 671. He cures a paralytic, 518. He stands among thorns for forty nights without sleeping, 584. His saying, 594.

Besarion. See Bisarion.

Beasts obeyed man before sin, 894.

Beasts obey and serve the saints. Wild asses obey Antony, 49. A crocodile obeys Pachomius, 120. A dove obeys Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, 226. Lions likewise, 231. Lions obey Roman Macarius, 228. Also a wild ass, 229. A hippopotamus obeys Benus, 746. Likewise a crocodile, ibid. A crocodile obeys Helenus, 471. Two dragons obey Ammonas, 465, 752. A lioness obeys John, 502. A lion obeys a certain anchorite, 539. Lions obey Simeon Priscus, 816, 817. A lion obeys a certain old man, 651. A hyena obeys Macarius of Alexandria, 725. A lion obeys Gerasimus, 893. A lion obeys Julian’s disciple, 878. Likewise Sergius, 899; Paul the Helladic, 911. A dog obeys the abbot of the Syrian Subbaei, 910.

Beasts honor the saints. A lioness humbly throws herself at the feet of an anchorite, 540.

Beasts do not harm the saints but rather benefit them. Lions live with an old man in the same den, 863, 866. Hyenas surround Pachon, 732. Poemen lies naked beside a lion, 912. Serpents do not harm Paul, 650. Lions do not harm those who approach at the command of Roman Macarius, 228. A lion makes a path for John the anchorite, 917.

A bigamist is not admitted to the diaconate by John the Almsgiver either by prayer or by payment, 185.

Bisarion is content with one tunic and an outer cloak, 772. He clothes a dead man in the outer cloak, ibid. Meanwhile he himself remains naked, ibid. He sells the Gospel, 772.

Bisarion. See Besarion.

Blaesilla, daughter of Saint Paula, 402.

Araches teaches that one should proceed by blandishments rather than threats, 322.

Blasphemy against God is characteristic of heretics, 672.

Gaianus, who blasphemes against the Blessed Virgin, is miraculously punished by having his feet and hands cut off, 875.

Good companionship teaches the fear of God, 610.

Greater care should be given to a good life than to miracles, 45.

The crown of good works, 149.

Ecclesiastical goods: a consuming fire, 616.

The presbyter Bonosus makes Astion’s parents catechumens, 222.

Brochas alone lifts a massive beam given jokingly as alms, 922.

- How great is the dignity of the diaconate? 623.
- The first deaconess, a Roman by name, receives Pelagia from baptism, 379.
- Basil is ordained deacon by Meletius, bishop of Antioch, 155.
- An unworthy deacon standing beside a celebrant prevents the descent of the Holy Spirit, 907.
- He is removed from the altar, ibid.
- The deacon’s fall and true repentance are demonstrated by a miracle, 577.
- Diana, the ancient goddess of the hunt, 397.
- Didymus was deprived of his eyes, 711, 944, 986.
- How long he lived, ibid.
- He knew the Holy Scriptures although he had not studied them, ibid.
- The death of Julian the Apostate is revealed to him, ibid.
- The first day of conversion must always be preserved, 529.
- The difference between hermits and monks, 10[lacuna]6.
- The difference between God the Father and a carnal father, 212.
- The difference between the old law and the new, 266.
- There are many false gods, 264.
- The gods of the Egyptians: Isis, Osiris, numerous brute animals, onions, garlic, thorns, and so forth, 307.
- The gods of the Chaldeans: the elements and the stars, 305, 306.
- The gods of the Greeks: Saturn, Jupiter, Ganymede, Vulcan, Mercury, and Aesculapius, 306; Mars, Bacchus, Hercules, Apollo, Diana, and Venus, 307; Adonis, 307.
- The gods of the nations are not gods, and why, 308.
- Many gods in Egypt, and their origin, 748.
- The gods of the Persians: the sun, fire, and water, according to Milido, 585.
- He who had not freed a stranger from wild beasts is torn apart by them, 912.
- Delay of salvation is dangerous, 258.
- Cautious love, 96.
- Love of God, 237.
- The Flood, 255.
- Exposure to the sun and open air: Eusebius, 836; Cyra, 855, 856; Limnaeus for thirty-eight years, 845; Macarius of Alexandria for twenty days, in order to overcome sleep, 722; Macarius the Younger, a murderer, for three years in the desert, 718; Marana, 855, 856; Maro, 833.
- Diocles, from philosopher to monk, 767.
- Dionysius the priest rebukes Pachomius because he separates guests from the others, 126. —Dionysius, bishop of Seleucia, and what happened under him, 885.
- Eagerness to learn, 610.
- Macarius’s disciple is subjected to blows, 118.
- The disciple becomes a teacher through patience, 632.
- The disciple of Sisinnius rests in the same tomb with him when he is buried there, 889.
- Antony is tempted by a silver platter placed before him, 39.
- Abraham the hermit’s discernment in saving his niece’s soul while she freely ate meat, 371.
- Agathon’s discernment concerning clothing, 512, 687.
- John the Dwarf’s discernment in accepting water when others refused it, so that the giver would not be saddened, 599.
- Mathois’s discernment in preferring light and continuous work to heavy work that is quickly completed, 585.
- The discernment of a certain father who preferred prayer and abstinence to great labors, 580.
- Silvanus’s discernment saves the soul of a fallen monk, 605.
- Discernment is the ax that fells the tree, 602.
- Discernment in fasting: what it is and what kind, 603.
- Discernment teaches the royal road, 552.
- It is the mother and guardian of the virtues, ibid.
- Discernment is necessary in all works, 606.
- A singular example of discernment and prudence: a disciple restrains his teacher from anger and is afterward praised by the teacher, 501, 502.
- Through lack of discernment, a man deceived by the devil would have sacrificed his son had he not escaped by flight, 552, 553.
- Heron falls through lack of discernment, 532.
- Through lack of discernment, another monk circumcises himself, 553.
- Paul, who abhorred women, is taught discernment when he is forced to accept women’s service, 553.
- By discernment one is saved; another, unwilling to accept the food offered to him and waiting for it from God, dies, 552.
- Antony is distinguished by discernment of spirits, 45, 47.
- Dissensions must be avoided, 237.
- Distraction occurs easily, 606.
- Not to be distracted in prayer is a great thing; not to be distracted while singing psalms is greater, 609.
- If distractions are charged against us by God, who will be saved? 609.
- A certain distracted man was never distracted in prayer, 891.
- The demons’ diverse wickedness, 42, 43, 45.
- People walk in the Lord’s way in different manners, 565.
- The difference between the earlier and later monks, 637.
- The diversity of those who practice abstinence, 665.
- Divination must be despised, 44.
- Divine help is present to Macarius laboring and wearied on a journey, 532.
- The truly rich, 284.
- Riches are to be sent to heaven through the hands of the poor, 276.
- One who teaches but does not act is like a well, 601.
- Simeon Stylites has a teacher of salvation as his father, 170.
- Christian teaching takes its origin from Christ, 308.
- The power of evangelical teaching, 56.
- Wholesome lessons, 531.
- On Sunday an angel brings communion to Onuphrius, 102.
- Domnina continually weeps, 856.
- She urges the adornment of the temple, ibid.
- She lives on moistened lentils, ibid.
- She conceals her face, ibid.
- She encourages athletes, ibid.
- She supplies monks with necessities, 857.
- Her monasteries are scattered throughout the world, ibid.
- Domnion’s bed cures the sick, 762, 968.
- The various gifts found in holy men, 796.
- A man who nods off during a spiritual conversation is rebuked by divine intervention, 752.
- The arrangement of the dormitory, 237.
- Dorotheus lived in a cave for sixty years, 709, 943, 985.
- Palladius was entrusted to him for instruction, 709, 985.
- Likewise Heraclides, 943.
- He labors continually in order to afflict his body, 710, 943, 985.
- He provides his food by the work of his hands, 710, 943, 985.
- He overcomes sleep in a marvelous way, ibid.
- He overcomes poison by the sign of the cross, ibid.
- Dorotheus, enclosed, is the director of virgins, 735.
- Dorotheus despises money, 767.
- A dragon is burned by Hilarion, 84.
- A dragon worships Simeon Stylites, 173.
- A dragon is cured by Simeon Stylites, ibid.
- A dragon torments a woman, 226.
- A dragon is shattered by Amun’s prayers, 752.
- Holy men do not fear a huge dragon, 751.
- Cosmas passes unharmed through a dragon, 873.
- Dragons guard the entrance of Amun from robbers, 752.
- Dracontius, a bishop and confessor, 82.
- Two natures in Christ, 319.
- Two luxurious young men are tested by Macarius. See *Macarius*.
- Basil is a philosopher at the age of twelve, 152.
- God restores double to John the Almsgiver, 195.
- A harsh rebuke drives a monk to leave, 573.
- Hard things are sweet to holy men who are harsh toward the world, 796.
- A certain governor of Palestine is barred from entering the Holy Sepulcher by a ram because of the Severian heresy, 876.
- When he repents, he is admitted, ibid.

### E
Church of penitence at Antioch, 175. Church as a place of asylum, 194. Crystal church worthy of admiration, 227. Church dedicated by a bishop, [Col. XXXIV] 327. The largest church on Mount Nitria, 713. Antony foresees the affliction of the Church, 57. God protects the treasures of the Church, 184, 185. The money of the Church, when mixed with money unjustly acquired, causes both to perish, 183. Description of the Church as mother, from the Song of Songs, 223. Attendance at church by three and four thousand people, 478. Antony regularly attends church, 36. Abraham builds a church from his own resources, 146. A laborer who attends church becomes richer by not idling but always working, 202. The same man is promoted to the priesthood, ibid. Paul the Simple sees the various conditions of those entering a church, 525. Julian Sabas builds a church on Sinai, 803. Simeon warns Julian not to abandon the church, 890.

Demonic gluttony cured by Macedonius through the sign of the cross and holy water, 830. Monks eat beyond their usual custom for God’s sake, 527. John the Almsgiver properly corrects those leaving before Mass has ended, 201.

What election is, 277. Its beautiful variety is demonstrated by a pleasing comparison drawn from fountains, 278.

Eleemon is merciful toward everyone, 771. He helps a woman in childbirth, ibid. He sells books to help the poor, 772.

Almsgiving appears to Saint John the Almsgiver in the form of a virgin crowned with an olive branch, 182. The same almsgiving receives a dying person, 205. The almsgiving of Onuphrius, 103. The almsgiving of John, 147. Almsgiving prepares a palace in heaven, 194. Almsgiving given to the poor is received by Christ as though offered to him personally, 276. Almsgiving is most appropriately spent on the poor, 601, 602. Almsgiving should be given to non-relatives rather than to relatives, 607. Almsgiving should be given without measure, 616. Almsgiving is confirmed by a miracle involving genuine beggars, 616. Almsgiving should be given cheerfully, 766. The almsgiving of Eleemon, who sells his books to help the poor, 772. Almsgiving should be given to the poor not from natural affection but from piety, 809. An old woman gives to charity whatever she earns by her labor in the temple, 900. The lupins purchased with it become sweet, ibid. Almsgiving frees the emperor Zeno from punishment, 915. Almsgiving given to a wretched woman frees Moschus from prison, 920. Almsgiving. See Peter the Tax Collector and Serapion. Almsgiving ingeniously devised and given by Apollinarius to a modest and poor young man, 923, 924.

Defrauding almsgiving incurs compensation and erases the written record, 184. A fine example of secretly given alms, 199. The value of almsgiving should be entrusted to God, 715. The reward of almsgiving is recorded in a written document, 194. The method of obtaining alms from the rich, 189. An inheritance is usefully given to the poor in the name of almsgiving, 681. The virtue of almsgiving turns tin into silver, 183. When asked for alms, he silently gives a small silver cross, because he has nothing else, 180. God rewards almsgiving: John the Almsgiver experiences a hundredfold return, 182. A poor man who gives alms to monks becomes rich, 616. A beautiful parable teaches that alms should be sent ahead to heaven, through the example of a man who reigns for one year while meanwhile making provision for himself, 273, 274. Eupraxia praises almsgiving to her husband, and gives a notable example of generosity, 3[lacuna]1. When almsgiving is withheld, blessing is withheld, 887. The almsgiving of Josaphat to the poor, 324, 328, 331. Alms are offered for the dead, [Col. XXXV] 354. Olympias’s abundant almsgiving, 779. Blessed Leontius attributes his alms to the blessed Virgin Mary, 879.

The blessedness of John the Almsgiver’s soul is shown through various visions, 265. The son of the Almsgiver, who had chosen Christ as his physician, receives a rich daughter as his wife, by God’s providence, 928.

The elements detest Arianism, 53. The elements are not gods, 305.

A man suffering from elephantiasis is cared for very well by Eulogius for fifteen years, 673, 728.

The martyr Eleutherius punishes a lector who had often been warned and was living disgracefully, 905.

The elevation of the Eucharist, 155.

Elijah as an example of monastic life, 38. Onuphrius is inspired by his example to go into the desert, 1006. Elijah and John the Baptist, leaders of monastic life, 17, 811.

The community of Abbot Elijah, 594. Elijah lives in solitude for seventy years, 746. He fasts for entire weeks, 747. He is radiant with signs and healing when he is 110 years old, 747. Elijah builds a monastery for virgins, 735. The superior of thirty virgins is tempted by lust, ibid. He flees for fear of falling, 735. Angels cure him of the impulse, ibid. Elijah is hospitable; God multiplies his loaves, 770.

Elijah, archbishop of Jerusalem, wishes to ordain the monk John bishop, 863. Elijah the abbot overcomes a temptation of the flesh, terrified by a remarkable vision, 866. Elijah, bishop of Jerusalem, abstains from wine as he had done when he was a monk, 870. He is sent into exile, ibid. A saying of Elijah the solitary, 877.

Eulogies of Pope Nicholas, 178, 179.

An eloquent man of perverse life, an imitator of the devil, 766.

Elpidius lives in a cave, 769. For twenty-five years he eats only on Saturdays and Sundays, 769. He treads on a scorpion without harm, ibid. A shoot planted by him grows into a vine, ibid. He scarcely has flesh on his bones, ibid. He always faces east, ibid.

Emilis elicits an answer from a murdered man in order to save an innocent person, 630.

Possessed men and women are freed. See Demoniac and Demoniac woman.

Ephraem sees Basil in the spirit, like a column of fire, 160. Basil recognizes him by the spirit of prophecy, 161. He is disturbed when he sees Basil, ibid. In Basil he sees a fiery tongue, ibid. He speaks Greek through Basil’s prayers, ibid. He is ordained a priest, ibid. His homeland is Edessa in Syria, 167. His childhood, ibid. A vine seen by the child’s parents growing from his mouth and filling the whole region, ibid. He inhabits the desert, ibid. In another vision, he is shown what kind of fountain he will become, ibid. In another vision, another old man is taught how great Ephraem is, ibid. He thinks of Edessa, 168. He prays to meet someone with whom he may discuss the Scriptures, ibid. A prostitute meets him, ibid. The prostitute’s fine reply, ibid. A prostitute lies in wait for him, ibid. He replies cleverly: one must be more ashamed before God than before human beings, 168. He prudently corrects the shameless woman, 168, 598. He comes to Caesarea to see Basil, 168. He sees a dove dictating a sermon to Basil, ibid. He does not know how to become angry, ibid. By his mere appearance he teaches modesty, 169. He makes a testament, ibid. He dies, ibid.

Ephraem, companion of the monk Abraham, 369. He laments his misery, 372, 373. He demands an account from himself of his actions, 373. His prayer to God, ibid. Ephraem meets hungry people, 768.

Ephremius, patriarch of Antioch, challenges a heretic to trial by fire concerning the faith, 875. His stole remains unharmed in the fire, [Col. XXXV] ibid.

Ephremius, a count, repairs public buildings and later becomes a bishop, 871.

Epictetus, in the time of Diocletian, 211 and 223. Pious from childhood, 211. He performs miracles, ibid. He is ordained a priest, ibid. He heals a fifteen-year-old paralytic by anointing her, 211. He heals a demoniac who claims to be the father of many heretics, 212. By touching her eyes he restores sight to a blind woman, ibid. He converts the young man Astion, ibid. They flee to Scythia, 214. He heals, after fifteen years, a deaf, mute, and withered man, ibid. More than a thousand people are converted, 215. He spits three times into a boy’s mouth, ibid. He is arrested by the commander Latronianus, 216. His age and appearance, ibid. He is tortured in various ways, 216, 217, 218. He first offers the younger Astion to martyrdom as a precaution, 219. He is beheaded, ibid. His body shines, 219.

Evagrius receives communion on the feast of Epiphany, 764. On the feast of Epiphany, a baptistery in the city of the Coeanenses sweats, 933.

After abandoning the episcopate, Sisinnius embraces the solitary life, 889. Zosimas refuses the episcopate, 899.

A bishop dedicates a church, 323. A certain bishop serves the builders, 871. A column of fire appears above his head, ibid. He foretells the episcopate of the official Ephremius, ibid. The bishop of Rumella, falsely accused before Pope Agapetus, is handed over to prison, 907. His innocence is demonstrated by a vision, ibid. More than ten thousand men accompany Bishop Helenus, 341. Two dead bishops yield the middle place in the tomb to the dead John the Almsgiver, 203.

John the Almsgiver’s letter pierces the heart of Nicetas the patrician, who had taken away his treasure, 184. A sorcerer’s letter to the devil, 156. Leo’s letter, placed on the tomb of Saint Peter, is corrected by apostolic hand, 906.

A certain man by magic makes a woman appear to be a mare, 720. Aphraates heals the emperor’s sick horse with water and oil blessed by the sign of the cross, 821.

A hermit must be a teacher, 605, 675. Two naked hermits meet Macarius, 653. The strength of hermits, 1006. God is the protector of hermits, ibid. Angels are the helpers of hermits, 101.

Ero despises Macarius out of pride, 734. His astonishing abstinence for three months, except for Communion alone, ibid. His incredible memory, ibid. He falls into every kind of vice, ibid. He repents and dies, ibid. Ero. See Hero.

Worldly education delays the pursuit of virtue, 596. Food given out of charity does not break a fast, 508. Hunger overcomes the impulses of the flesh, 577.

Eubulus, Basil’s teacher, 153. His testimony concerning Basil, ibid. Basil converts him to faith in the Trinity, and he asks for baptism, 154. He forms a partnership with Basil, ibid. He piously distributes his possessions, ibid. They come to Antioch, ibid. Libanius invites them to an elaborate meal, 154. They reject luxury, ibid. They live on bread and water, ibid. They visit the holy places in Jerusalem, ibid. They ask the bishop of Jerusalem for baptism, ibid. They are baptized, 155. They are confirmed and receive holy Communion, ibid. They return to Antioch, ibid. Then they return to Cappadocia, ibid. Their arrival is divinely made known to Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, ibid. He receives them honorably, ibid.

The Eucharist is a heavenly mystery, 122. The Eucharist appears to a Jew in the form of a child, 156. The Eucharist is by nature the body of Christ, not a figure, 636. An old man who doubts this asks for a revelation, ibid. In the Eucharist Christ appears in the form of a little child, 636. Christ accommodates himself to human nature under the appearance of bread, ibid. The Eucharist is a fountain for the thirsty soul, 638. To those who receive it worthily it is light; to those who receive it unworthily it is consuming fire, 648. The Eucharist must be placed before all bodily food, 715. When the Eucharist of the Catholics is thrown into a boiling pot, it remains intact; the Severian bread is immediately consumed, 869. The Eucharist, thrown into mud by a Severian, flashes brightly, ibid. The Eucharist of the Catholic Church, sprouting stalks and ears of grain, converts the heretic Severian and many others, 885. Basil teaches the faith concerning the Eucharist, 155. Receiving the Eucharist on Sundays, 270. Its effects, ibid. Explanation of faith in the Eucharist, 286. Basil keeps the Eucharist in a golden dove above the altar, 156. A man who had devoted himself to the devil recoils from the Eucharist, 157. Saint Mary of Egypt receives the Eucharist in the church of Saint John the Baptist beside the Jordan, 388. Saint Mary of Egypt reverently asks that the Eucharist be brought to her in a sacred vessel, 389. Mary of Egypt receives the Eucharist before her death, 390. Mark receives the Eucharist from an angel, 726. Apollo always gives the Eucharist to the brothers before other food, 750. Through receiving the Eucharist we obtain remission of sins, 751. Theodoret celebrates the Eucharist in the hands of deacons in place of an altar, 837. An anchorite receives the Eucharist on Sunday, 887. Knowing that he is about to die, he likewise strengthens himself with it before death, ibid. John is nourished by the Eucharist alone, 755.

Saint Eugenia, virgin and martyr, 340. Her parents, ibid. She is taught philosophy, 340. She rejects marriage to the son of the consul Aquilius, ibid. She rejects the schools of the philosophers, 341. She arranges to have her hair cut in a man’s style, ibid. She asks to become a Christian, 342. Even after her change of dress she is recognized by Bishop Helenus, ibid. She is mourned in Alexandria as lost, 343. An image of her is made as though she were a goddess, ibid. A catalog of her virtues, ibid. She is compelled to preside over a monastery, 343. She performs the lowliest duties, ibid. She is especially devoted to the appointed hours of prayer, ibid. She cures Melanthia of quartan fever with sacred oil, ibid. Melanthia loves her with an incestuous passion, 344. She resists bravely, ibid. She is falsely accused of attempted rape, ibid. Bound in chains, she is brought before the prefect, 344. Her prudent response to the charges, ibid. She answers the false testimony, 345. She confounds all her accusers by revealing her sex, 345. Her parents recognize her, 345. She builds a monastery for virgins, 346. She gathers virgins in Rome, ibid. God reveals to her that martyrdom is imminent, 347. Her prayer to Christ, ibid. Her exhortation to virginity and martyrdom, ibid. Her splendid testimony concerning the chastity of the Church, 348. She is led to the temple of Diana, ibid. Her prayer, ibid. At her prayer the temple of Diana collapses, 348. The emperor orders her to be thrown into the Tiber, ibid. Though thrown in, she does not drown, ibid. She remains unharmed by the fire of the baths, ibid. Christ nourishes her in prison, ibid. She is struck with a sword, ibid. She appears after death to her mother Claudia and foretells her death, ibid.

Eulalius, out of humility, takes upon himself the offenses of the other brothers, 502. His chamber pot remains unharmed in the fire as testimony to his true humility, 503. To attain eternal glory, he flees temporal glory, ibid.

[Col. XXXVII] Eulogius the presbyter, disciple of John the archbishop, fasts for two days, 592; sometimes for an entire week, ibid. He lives on bread and salt, ibid.

Eulogius of Alexandria changes from a scholar into a monk, 673, 728. He accepts a mutilated man so that he may be restored, ibid. His remarkable kindness toward the mutilated man, 674, 728. He consults Antony about the mutilated man’s wickedness, 674, 728. Both die, 675, 727.

Eulogius the presbyter recognizes the dispositions of those receiving Communion, 472, 760. He announces them individually, ibid.

Eulogius of Alexandria, bishop, is commanded by a remarkable vision to build a church for the martyr Julian, 905, 906.

Eunomia, daughter of Avita, 775.

A eunuch who threatens Aphraates is suffocated in a bath, 820.

Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople, is driven into exile by Anastasius, 872.

Euphrasia, or Euphraxia, virgin, 351. Her parents, ibid. At the age of five she is betrothed to a wealthy senator, 352. With her mother she secretly goes to Egypt, ibid. The pious and religious desire of the little girl, 353. At seven she kisses an image of the Lord and devotes herself to Christ, ibid. She puts on monastic clothing, ibid. She is reclaimed by her fiancé, 354. Her letter to the emperor, ibid. She asks that her possessions be distributed among the poor, ibid. The emperor reads her letter to the senate, ibid. At twelve she undertakes pious exercises in the monastery, ibid. When she is tempted, the abbess strengthens her, 355. She discloses the temptation to the abbess, ibid. She fortifies herself through abstinence, ibid. She fasts for four days, ibid. She is tempted again at the age of twenty, ibid. She obeys simply even in difficult matters, ibid. She is exercised through work in the bakery, ibid. When idle, she is tempted again, ibid. Even when busiest, she neglects none of the divine offices, ibid.
