She is tempted again and strengthened by the abbess, 356. She fasts for the whole week, ibid. She is never seen sitting during the entire year, ibid. Her rival Germana disciplines her, ibid. She humbles herself before her rival, ibid. She begs the abbess on her behalf, ibid. The devil throws her into a well, ibid. She escapes through Christ’s help, ibid. She doubles her labor against the devil, ibid. She wounds herself accidentally, 357. Though injured, she completes her task, ibid. She is injured again at the devil’s instigation, ibid. She does not cease from her work, ibid. A demon throws her from an upper room, but she remains unharmed, ibid. Her face, splashed with boiling vegetable broth, is not injured, ibid. By the sign of the cross she heals a paralyzed, mute, and deaf boy, 358. She ministers to a possessed woman, ibid. She prevails over the possessed woman and threatens her with the abbess’s rod, ibid. She again assists Germana when she is being rivalrous, ibid. She ministers once more to the possessed woman, ibid. She receives power from God to expel a demon, 359. She strikes the possessed woman with a staff, ibid. She drives out the demon by prayer, ibid. She humbles herself still further, ibid. The abbess foresees her approaching death, ibid. The abbess sees a throne prepared for her in heaven, 360. Her profound humility, 360. She falls ill and is carried to the oratory, ibid. At the final hour she asks for the sisters’ prayers, 361. She gives up her spirit at the age of thirty, ibid. She is buried in her mother’s tomb, ibid. Many miracles occur at her tomb, ibid. Her abbess likewise falls asleep in the Lord, ibid.

Euphraxia, wife of Antigonus and mother of Euphrasia, 351. As a widow, she commends her daughter Euphrasia to the emperor, 352. She rejects a second marriage, 352. With her daughter she secretly goes to Egypt, ibid. She penetrates into the inner Thebaid, ibid. She offers gifts to monasteries, ibid. She offers incense and candles, 353. She asks for prayers for her deceased husband, ibid. Before an image of the Lord, she entrusts her daughter to the abbess, 353. Her sobriety and virtue, 354. The abbess foretells her death, ibid. As she is dying, she instructs her daughter, ibid.

Euphrosyna, virgin, 363. Her parents, ibid. Her mother is barren, ibid. She obtains a child through the abbot’s prayers, ibid. She is baptized at seven, ibid. Many seek her in marriage, 363. She is betrothed, ibid. Her father commends her to the abbot’s prayers, ibid. She is blessed by the abbot, ibid. She investigates the customs of the monastery, 364. A monk advises her to practice virginity and conceal her sex, ibid. She arranges for a monk from the monastery of Abbot Theodosius to be summoned, 364. She is instructed by the old monk, ibid. She is tonsured and clothed in the monastic habit, ibid. She pretends to be a eunuch and hastens to the monastery, 365. She is admitted, ibid. She calls herself Smaragdus, ibid. The devil tries to exploit her beauty, ibid. Solitude is prescribed for her so that she may not be a cause of scandal to others, 365. She prays that she not be exposed, and prevails, 366. She instructs and consoles her father with good words, ibid. She lives alone in a cell for thirty-eight years, 366. She reveals herself to her father, 367. She dies, ibid. She restores an eye to a one-eyed person, ibid.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, learns by divine revelation of the arrival of Basil and Eubulus, 155. He receives them honorably, ibid. He marvels at their understanding of the divine Scriptures, ibid. He dies, ibid.

Eusebius, imitator of Marcianus, 809. His austerity in binding his body with iron: at first twenty pounds, then he adds fifty, then eighty, ibid. His uncle Marcianus, 810. He remains perpetually enclosed, speaking to no one, 811. He undertakes care of the monastic flock, ibid. By his face alone he corrects the negligent, ibid. He observes fasts of three and four days, ibid. He teaches them to arrange each limb of the body, ibid. He guards his eyes, ibid. He restrains himself with an iron belt and collar so that his eyes will not wander, ibid. His spiritual struggle, 812. Julian’s successors submit themselves to him, ibid. His disciples are scattered throughout the world, 813.

Eusebius lives under the open sky, 836. He is clothed in a hide, ibid. He lives on chickpeas and beans, ibid. His remarkable mortification, ibid. He detests earthly association, 836. He blocks the entrance to his cell, ibid. He spends Lent on fifteen figs, ibid. He dies, ibid.

Eustathius the lector is falsely accused of rape, 777. He is removed from office, ibid. His prayer to God, 778. The woman who slandered him, suffering in childbirth, is compelled by divine judgment to clear him, ibid. Though innocent, he remains enclosed like a penitent, 778. The bishop goes to his cell, ibid. Through his prayers the slanderer gives birth, ibid.

Eustochium, daughter of Saint Paula, lives with fifty virgins, 775.

Eustochius, translator of the Life of Saint Pelagia, 376.

Evagrius asks Macarius a question, 596. His saying, 598. Evagrius the Origenist is made a lector by Basil, 763. He is ordained deacon by Gregory of Nyssa, ibid. He spends time with Nectarius of Constantinople, ibid. He is stirred by desire for a woman, ibid. A vision terrifies him away from love, ibid. An angel in the form of an intimate friend consoles him, 763. He swears that he will emigrate in order to avoid danger, ibid. He comes to Jerusalem and is received by Melania, ibid. He again attempts to return to the world, ibid. Illness recalls him, ibid. He puts on the monastic garb, 764. His manner of life and meager diet, ibid. He writes the *Contradictoria*, ibid. He breaks the assaults of demons, ibid. By the sign of the cross he opens a lock, ibid. He foretells the future, ibid. He lives on raw vegetables and water, ibid. He prefers to be a pilgrim rather than a bishop, [Col. XXXVIII] 630. He receives Communion on the feast of Epiphany, 764. He calls his father immortal, ibid.

A monk living in the cell of the heretic Evagrius hangs himself, 916.

Synesius tries to bring the philosopher Evagrius to the faith, 925. Evagrius hesitates concerning the resurrection, ibid. At last he is baptized with his household, ibid. Through the poor he lends gold to God, having accepted from Synesius a written pledge, ibid. He arranges to be buried with the written document, ibid. After his death he announces that Christ has repaid him, ibid. This is attested by the written pledge found in his hand in the tomb, 925. The miraculous written document is preserved, ibid.

Evangelicus, bishop of the Scythians, 218. He baptizes Astion’s parents, 223.

The evangelical counsel: renouncing one’s possessions, 276. The power, virtue, and endurance of the Gospel, 320. Serapion Sindonius sells the Gospel in order to help the poor, 191. Besarion sells the Gospel, 772.

Orentus teaches the overthrow of Sinai with an inverted saddlecloth, 899. The publication of a good work is punished, 197.

The Exaltation of the Holy Cross is celebrated in Jerusalem, 386.

Examination of conscience twice a day, 611. Examination of one’s actions, 373.

Those who castrate themselves are excommunicated, 625. Excommunication is the bond of priests, 838. A dead excommunicated monk is absolved and freed, 923.

We are drawn to the pursuit of virtue by examples rather than commands, 242. Religious exercises around the Jordan, 383. The temptation of fornication is overcome through exercises in virtue, 575. Basil’s exhortation to Libanius’s disciples, 154. Saint John the Almsgiver’s exhortation to almsgiving, through the example of Peter the Tax Collector, 191. The exhortation of a pious prince to King Abenner in favor of monasticism and flight from the world, 246.

Exorcism precedes baptism, 378. Through experience people become more approved, 601. The summary of Christian doctrine is expounded while Zardanes listens, 290. The gradual eradication of vices is taught through an excellent comparison, 596. Exsufflation drives out a demon, 119. Josaphat prays with outstretched hands, 329. While the outer person is afflicted, the inner person grows strong, 865. The well-guarded outer person guards the inner person, 612. People should not be judged by their outward clothing, 254.

## F

A cheerful face is an indication of a pure mind, 137. Abraham’s face indicates purity of spirit, 149. Abraham washed neither his face nor his feet, ibid. Abstinence does not alter the face, 150. The way to heaven is easy, 287. Deeds must correspond to words, lest we be like fountains that wash others, 527. Deeds teach, not words, 603.

Various forms of false religion, 255. A woman who falsely accuses Saint Marina is seized by a demon and freed beside the dead woman’s body, 394. God punishes the person who imposes a false charge on another, 623. The maidservant’s false testimony against Eugenia, 345.

Familiarity with an abbot should not be sought, 629. A handmaid of God refuses to see her brother, 504. [Col. XXXIX] A servant plotting his mistress’s death is prevented by the blessed Virgin Mary and kills himself, 883.

Disgust is the beginning of turning away from God, 603. Julian’s fever is driven away by prayer, 805. Abbot Felix says that he has nothing to say because he would not see any practical effect in others, 566.

A woman devoted to lust repents, 159. She offers Basil her sins written and sealed on a sheet of paper, ibid. A woman who publicizes Vitalis’s secret good work is possessed by a demon, 197. A woman is dangerous, 313. A woman must be avoided by a monk, 742. A woman must be fled, and one must not eat with her, 660. A certain woman, so as not to be a cause of scandal to a brother, avoids his sight, 930. By mentioning the uncleanness of women she drives temptation away from the brother, ibid. Love of a woman surpasses love of other things, 323. A phantom admitted in the form of a woman deceives a proud monk with flatteries, 454. Demons are called women, 303. Demons lie in wait in the form of women, 575. See Demon. Visiting female relatives with an old man, 124. Woman. See Female.

Three ruinous moneylenders: greed, gluttony, and lust, 761. Apelles drives away a demon appearing in the form of a woman with glowing iron, 755.

Jacob makes a barren mountain fertile through his dwelling there, 838. Demons flee from a person fervent in spirit as flies flee from a boiling pot, 531, 682. Simeon Stylites’ fervor: love of salvation and of the monastery, 170. The fervor of the novitiate must be preserved at all times, 596, 683. A certain brother takes up fervor before death, 864.

The feast of the Passion and Resurrection, 808. Maris celebrates the feasts of the martyrs, 837. Angels smell the stench of sin, 657. A monk conquers lust through the stench of a corpse, 576. Young men carrying figs prefer to die rather than eat them, 551.

The faithfulness of Philagrius, 583. One must trust God, 649, 651. Faith, hope, and charity are three precious stones, 149. Faith, hope, and charity should always be in the mind, 685. Faith from the Gospel, 259. Faith alone is not enough for someone to ascend to God, 245. Faith alone is not sufficient for salvation, 302. Faith preserves one who enters a burning furnace, 541. What faith is, 672. If faith is not sound, no virtues are of benefit, 868. Perverse faith is represented by a sooty dove, 893. Praise of the Christian faith, 318, 319. One reaches eternal glory by faith and works, 258. Fidosus, 492.

Presumption or overconfidence must be avoided, 596, 608. Saint John the Almsgiver’s confidence in God, 182. Theodore’s confidence, 585. Macarius’s confidence, 585. The confidence of an old man who does not fear a lion, 651. Sisoi’s confidence when he says to the Lord, “I will not let you go unless you heal him,” 651. Agathon’s confidence in God and contempt for worldly things, 667. The saints’ confidence against the dragon, 751. Apollo’s confidence during a famine, and his generosity, 750. Abraham the hermit teaches a fallen woman to have confidence in God, 371. A man who trusts in God is wonderfully refreshed in the desert, 655. Confidence enables Pachomius to tread on snakes and tame crocodiles, 120. Through confidence in God, an angel supplies bread to the hungry Hellenus, 755.

The daughter of Proterius is inflamed with love through the devil’s arts, 156, 157. The son of a good man is preserved from evil through the prayers of Saint John the Almsgiver, 193. Children are concerned for their parents in heaven, 229. The end distinguishes an action, 735.

A threefold scourge in the monastery, 713. Flavianus, bishop of Antioch, ordains Macedonius, without his knowledge, a priest, 829. He is sent into exile, 870. A certain old man weeps because he is not ill throughout the year, 523. Arsenius is accustomed always to weep, 621. A monk should weep, 566. A man digging a well is buried beneath it, 765.

The natural purity of the soul is the fountain of virtues, 41. Simeon Stylites obtains a spring, 178. Sisinnius prevents the desire to fornicate by providing daily food because of poverty, 903.

Fornication of the mind, 573. Fornication is death, 574. Fornication causes monks to deny God, baptism, and their profession, 579. The spirit of fornication in a hideous form, 37. The spirit of fornication attacks Josaphat, 313. The temptation of fornication is overcome by thoughts of death and torments, 577. Macarius wonderfully overcomes the spirit of fornication, 722. Isidore teaches Moses how the temptation of fornication is to be overcome, 726. The spirit of fornication tempts Pachon in the form of an Ethiopian woman, 732. A monk falls into fornication after abandoning his monastery under the pretext of humility, 580, 581. Evagrius teaches that fornication must be fled, 763. Elijah is warned by a vision, 866. A certain girl teaches this by her example, 916. A girl prudently recalls a certain monk from fornication, 872. A fornicator who enters a temple is pierced with remorse when he hears the sacred reading, 640. A fornicator going to a prostitute is struck with leprosy, 866. A fornicator returns to his senses through his brother’s affliction and prayers, 890.

The strong must be given strong commands, 617. A person who resists bravely is freed from the sting of the flesh, 574, 575. Abraham’s strength against demons, 149. The strength of Epictetus and Astion, who answer nothing other than that they are Christians, 216, 217, 218. A monk’s strength must be such that, like a statue, he is changed neither by praise nor by insult, 530. Jacob’s strength in despising the demon, 840, 842. Polychronius’s strength in illnesses, 847.

Salamanus inhabits a pit, 837. A dying brother asks Pachomius for a blessing, 130. Angels carry his soul into heaven, ibid. A brother converts his sister, a prostitute, by recalling eternal torment, 677. Fraud in distributing less than Saint John the Almsgiver had ordered is exposed by the erasure of the written document, 184.

A person frequented by human beings is not frequented by angels, 541.

Frontonius under Antony, 241. His prayer to the seventy brothers, 239. He goes with them into the desert, ibid. He confronts the brothers’ murmuring against the strictness of the rule, ibid. Seventy camels, sent by divine instruction through a certain man, are dispatched without a guide into an unknown place with provisions, 240. On the fourth day, angels lead them to him, 240. He rebukes those who murmur, ibid. He remits half, ibid. Every year thereafter this submission is made to him by the same man, 241.

A person who bears no fruit in a place is expelled from the place, 605. Pachomius’s remarkable frugality from adolescence, 114. The secure feast of frugality, 627, 665. Five measures of grain withheld from the poor; because of this, five thousand measures of wheat are lost, [Col. XL] 887. Julian’s granary is filled with grain through his merits, 869.

Flight from women, 735. Flight from fornication and women, 605. Flight from people. See Solitude. Flight from the monastery under the pretext of humility drives a monk into fornication, 580, 581. Flight from the world, 654. Flight from idleness, 607. The flight of the devout during persecution is proper, and why it is sometimes so, 249. Ammonius’s flight from the priesthood, 716. See Ammonius. Flight from worldly people, 236. Whoever wishes to be with God must flee from people, 632, 633. A society that causes harm must be avoided, 602. Antony flees honor, 48. A monk accustomed to be visited by the emperor flees honor lest he suffer a loss of humility, 498, 628. Poemen flees the company of great men lest he fall away from humility, 498. Cyriacus avoids the sight of his friends, 877. Five fugitive virgins are seized by a demon after fleeing the monastery, 903.

Simeon Stylites binds his whole body with a rope, 170. The cord of charity, 236. Antony forbids pomp and glory at his funeral, 59. John the Almsgiver willingly attends funerals, 192.

A thief must not be tolerated, though he may be very ill, 597, 598. Macarius helps a thief who is stealing from him, 631, 666. Gregory wipes out a furnace with his garment and emerges unharmed, 889. Theft must not be committed, remembering the torments, 569. Theft is divinely punished by lightning, 816. Theft is exposed through the prayer of Innocentius, 768. Vegetables stolen cannot be cooked, 753.

God alone knows the future, 44. The future is established from what precedes, 260.

## G

Gaddana lives without a roof, 770. The hand of a Jew who wished to strike him withers, ibid. Gaianus the mime, who blasphemes the blessed Virgin, is punished by having his hands and feet cut off, 875. Gaitan sends the Constantinopolitan bishops Euphemius and Macedonius into exile, 872. Whether Ganymede is a god, 306.

Gluttony is the source of the devil’s attack, 509. How a certain brother overcame gluttony, 493. Gelasia is gentle and forgives injuries, 780. A certain man throws gems into the sea so that he will not be killed because of them, 929. Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, is gentle, pure, and temperate, 905.

Poets convict the Gentiles of error, 320. The conversion of Gentiles, 147, 345. When one must kneel, and when one must cease kneeling, 544. Kneeling hollows out a board to a depth of four fingers, 919.

George, nephew of Saint John the Almsgiver, is upset because of an injury but is appeased, 187. George, an enclosed monk, foresees a great future disaster, 876. George is always undisturbed, restraining his eyes, ears, and tongue, 895. George, remaining in his cell, is found in the church so that he may receive Communion, 900. He worships the tomb of our Lord, ibid. He foretells his own death and that of the patriarch of Jerusalem, ibid.

Gerasimus removes a thorn from a lion’s paw, 893. The lion is grateful and obedient to him, ibid. Germana, a devout rival, rises up against Euphrasia, 356. Germana rises up again, not without punishment, 338.

John the Almsgiver builds homes for the elderly, [Col. XLI] 203. Worldly glory lacks heavenly fruit, 670. Pachomius is said to have seen the glory of the Lord with bodily eyes, 135. God must be glorified at all times, 607. The gods of the Greeks, 306, 307.

Three orders of people are pleasing to God, 562. God’s presence, the examples of the Scriptures, and stability of place make us pleasing to God, 516.

Grace, 121. Grace is greater where charity is greater, ibid. God’s grace appears to a certain person in the form of a virgin, 591. Grace is sometimes hidden in the saints, 527. Grace is lost because of a hateful word, 596. God’s grace makes the soul shine, 678, 679. The absence of grace results from a lack of charity, 679. Good things must not be attributed to free will rather than to God’s grace, 766.

Thanksgiving, 279, 280. The hyena’s gratitude: it brings Macarius a sheepskin because he had restored sight to its blind cub, 725. The gratitude of the lion that always accompanied Gerasimus because he had removed a thorn from its paw, 893. An example of gratitude. See Macarius.

Gregory the Cappadocian wipes the furnace with his garment and emerges unharmed, 889. Sergius foresees that Gregory, superior of the monastery of Pharan, will become patriarch, 895. Gregory’s virtues, ibid. Pope Gregory’s humility shown to John the Persian in greeting him, 907. Gregory the anchorite walks naked for thirty-five years, 882. Gregory, narrator of the Life of Onuphrius, 99. Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil’s fellow student, 153.

A ship’s pilot deceives many through his own error; so does one who governs the republic, 329.

Gluttony. See Serapion and Macarius. Gluttony is the source of the devil’s attack, 509. Gluttony is the worst moneylender, 761. Gluttony is conquered by the food set before one, 572. Gluttony inflames, 569, 570. Gluttony must be restrained, 665. Hor’s contempt for gluttony: he regards tasteless food as the best, 625. Victory over gluttony consists in eating bread and salt, 665. Likewise, in being content with what is present, ibid. Zeno’s victory over gluttony: the experience of torments overcomes his greedy thought of theft, 494. Gluttons are like muddy springs, 766.

## H
Dwelling of Jacob in the open air, 832. See *Dio*. Baradatus’s cramped dwelling, smaller than his own body, 854. Thalelaeus’s dwelling consisted of wheels suspended in the open air, 855. The monks’ habit is fixed, 271. The habit of the monks of Egypt, 543. The habit of virtue can scarcely be uprooted, 288. The habit of virtue proceeds spontaneously into action, 288. A woman with hemorrhage is healed by touching Pachomius’s hood, 127. Heresy is separation from God, 597. Heresy prevents a leader from entering the Holy Sepulchre, 876. Heresy arises from self-love, 882. Heresy is evil, 499. Agathon removes the charge of heresy from himself alone, ibid. Heresy as spiritual adultery is shown by a vision, 921. Heresy must be avoided, 330. Heresies grow through disputes, 538. A heretic woman is kept away from the Lord’s tomb by the blessed Virgin, 875. See *Cosmiana*. A heretic must be shunned, 563, 596. The flight of heretics, 865. Heretics falsely accuse the monk Julian of sharing their heresy, 804. Heretical books must be burned, 869. The books of heretics must be avoided and, following Pachomius’s example, sunk in water, 123. As he is dying, Pachomius warns that association with heretics must be avoided, 137. John the Almsgiver warns that communion with heretics must be avoided, 201. The devil professes himself the father of many heretics, 212. The dwellings of heretics must be avoided, 916. A man who lived in a heretic’s cell hangs himself, ibid. Even monks must resist heretics, 904. Pachomius teaches that heretics and their books must be shunned, 123. Pachomius smells heretics and recognizes them by their stench, 131. Pachomius teaches that heretical books must be sunk, 132. Generosity converts heretics, 771.

Abbot Hagiodulus, 865. He raises a dead brother so that he may give him the kiss of peace, ibid. He sees the twelve stones of Joshua son of Nun in the Jordan, ibid. A little child appears to a Hebrew in the Eucharist, 156. He is baptized, ibid. A certain dying Hebrew, requesting baptism, is baptized with sand, 915. He is also restored to health through a counterfeit baptism, 915.

Helenus, also called Hellen, bishop of Heliopolis, 341. His monastery, 311. While still a little child, he carries glowing coals in his unharmed garment, 341. More than ten thousand men accompany him with psalms, 341. He disputes with the magician Za[eus], 341–342. Protected by the sign of the cross, he remains unharmed in the fire as a testimony to the true faith, 342. His vision concerning Eugenia, 342. He recognizes her even when she has changed her clothing, ibid. He is divinely refreshed with miraculous foods, 755. An onager obeys him by carrying his burden, 754. He crosses a river riding upon a crocodile, 754. By divine power he knows and reveals the thoughts of the brothers and their hidden temptations, 754. His abstinence from food, lest his soul be harmed, 754. Helenus, Basilia’s cousin, 347.

Heliodorus, administrator of a monastery, 848. He entered the monastery when he was three years old and was exceedingly simple, 848–849. He fasts for an entire week, 849. He girds his loins with a palm-fiber cord, ibid. He chooses a dry cistern as his dwelling, ibid. He spends three years shut up in a small hut, 849. He fasts through the entire Quadragesima without food, ibid. He is refreshed by the Eucharist, ibid.

Helladius, Basil’s successor, 156. Helladius, Theodosius’s successor and later bishop of the Cilicians, 826. Heraclides’ letter to the prefect Lausus, 942. His humility, ibid. A monk is harmed by the power of unknown herbs, 541. Josaphat lives only on herbs, 331. See *Abstinence*. Why Hercules is not a god, 307. Hero falls through lack of discretion, 552. He fasts on Easter Day, 552. He throws himself into a well, ibid. Hero. See *Ero*.

Jerome governed the church at Bethlehem, 538. His encomium, ibid. Most learned in sacred law, ibid. By whom Jerome is hated and by whom he is loved, 538. He is accused of envy, 761. Hilarion the Luciferian, 632. He eats nothing that has been killed, 568. A cheerful face is an indication of a pure mind, 137. The usefulness of history, 794. A man one hundred cubits tall appears to Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, 226. Man is a sword to man, 592. Human beings must not be judged by their outward appearance, 254. Human beings are compared to the dove that flees the hawk, 275. Human beings must be corrected by human beings, not by angels, 928. A murderer is exposed when the murdered man is raised from the dead, and the man falsely accused through slander is released, 815, 881. How someone may consider himself lower than a murderer, [Col. XLII] 519. Murder and infanticide are punished in a marvelous manner. See *Maria, the infanticide*.

The honor due to priests, 122. Exceptional honor shown by a king to two religious men, 253. Honor is rejected by the saints and yet given by God, 833. The honor of the saints is greater after death, 835. Flight from and contempt for honor: in Julian, 803; in Philagrius, 583; in Pastor, 661; in a certain virgin, 639, 738. Honors sometimes change character for the better, 127. God honors the saints, 60. To be honored by human beings prevents one from being honored by God, and conversely, 517. Religious men must be honored because they are heralds of death and judgment, and because they are full of virtues; this is taught by the example of a king and the likeness of two chests, 254. Epictetus teaches that parents must be honored, 213. The honorific exception of Basil and Eubulus by Eusebius of Caesarea, 155. Hor never lied and never swore an oath, 653. Hor. See *Or*. At the sixth hour of prayer Josaphat prays with outstretched hands, 329. The canonical hours in monasteries, 356, 543; introduced by an angel, 543; their mysteries, 545. Barley ripening on the thirtieth day, 537. A certain Hertulanus is taught by an angel to trust not in money but in God, 584. The hermit of Cyrene gives an extraordinary meal, 537. The charity of an hospitable old man is revealed and proved by a tree divinely bent down, 605. The remarkable hospitality of Ammonius, 759; of Abraamis, 835. A certain hermit refreshes guests before the ninth hour, 549; the remarkable hospitality of Maesyma, 832; of a certain Protocomites, 755; of the poor Sisinnius, to the reproach of the rich, 770; that of Theodotus, patriarch of Jerusalem, is commended, 870; that of Zebina, 846.

Hospitality must be shown to a stranger, 237. Hospitality is the rule of charity, 615. Hospitality wins over a Manichaean through charity, 615–616. Hospitality must not become a cause of scandal, 606–607. A certain monk eats only for the sake of hospitality, 549, 559. The customary three days of hospitality in the desert, 607. For the sake of hospitality Moses relaxes the fast for travelers, 615. Eating for the sake of hospitality brings a double reward, 615. A contest in hospitality between Pambo and Pior, 716. Through the merit of hospitality a boy who has fallen into a well is preserved, 805. The reward of hospitality: an unfailing supply of grain and oil, 832. Hospitality is rewarded with miraculous refreshment in thirst, 866. Ungrateful guests are taught a lesson in the story of a remarkable old man, 493. Guests must sometimes be compelled to stay, 751. Guests must be received with joy, 614. The manner of receiving guests under Pachomius, 120, 126, 736. Theodosius entrusts the care of guests to gentle men, 825. Spiritual enemies, 795. Basil divides the sacred Host into three parts, 151. See *Eucharist*.

Human prudence dries a person up, 594. Humble things must be pursued, 592. Humble yourself, even if an angel appears, 628. It is found that one humbles and reproves oneself more often in the desert than in the world, 623. To humble oneself below every creature is a great thing, 626. The person who thinks himself perfect must be humbled, 626. The one who humbles himself is glorified, 627. The one who humbles himself burns the demons, 627. The one who humbles himself will be exalted, 669. A deceased monk is purified through humiliation and contempt, 130. A humble man, when commanding obedience, obtains it easily, 529. A humble man rejoices in being reproved, 592–593. The humble man repays evil with good, 627. The perfect humble man compares himself to a dog, 627. A humble word changes the wicked for the better, and conversely, as shown by the example of Macarius, 518–519. The glory of a humble man surpasses the glory of a king, 920. God appears to the humble, 627. Be humble like the publican and gentle like Moses, 626.

The humility of King Abenner, 327; of Abraham, who declined the office of preaching, 146; of Agathon, who pretended to be guilty of many sins, 499; of Aphthonius, who even as a bishop occupied himself with menial services for the brothers, 815; of Apollonius, who counted himself among the evangelical goats, 627, 501; various examples concerning Arsenius, 620–621; of Basil, who sent a certain penitent woman to Saint Ephraem, 160; of a certain leatherworker, who judged others worthy of heaven but himself worthy of hell, 519; of Daniel, who, after being ordained a priest, continued in the ministry of a deacon, 554; of Evagrius, 630; of Eugenia, who undertook the most menial tasks, 343; of Eulalius, who endured the brothers’ slanders with equanimity, 502, 629; of Eupraxia, who performed menial tasks, 354–355; of the same woman, who threw herself at the feet of her rival and begged forgiveness for her, 356; of the same woman when possessed, 359; of the same woman, wondrously, 360; of Eusebius, who declined the prefecture, 811. Likewise of Jacob, 812, and also of John, 863. Of a certain brother who, while being beaten because a lamp had been extinguished through the devil’s work, asked forgiveness from the brother, 497. Of a certain younger brother who appeased an angry old man, 501. Of a certain brother who offered the other cheek to a demoniac, 626. Of a certain brother who, in order to appease an angry man, acknowledged his fault, 934. Of Pope Gregory, shown in his greeting to John the Persian, 907. Of John the Almsgiver, who attributed all his deeds to God and to the faith of others, 193; of the same man, shown toward an obstinate cleric, 186; of the same man, who called himself the servant of servants, 181; of the same man, who attributed the cause of a shipwreck to himself, 194. Of John, 630. Of Isaac, who fled the priesthood, 680. Of Julian, who asked that a miracle performed while he was alive be kept secret, 802. Of Macarius of Egypt, 653; of the same man, who withdrew into a cave so that people would not know him, 720. Of Macarius, by which he conquers the devil, 518, 624, 670. Of Macarius, who fled the clerical office, 623. Of Macarius, who attributed the raising of the dead to another, 650. Of Mareus, who greeted his mother in torn clothing, 618. Of Mathois, also called Motcis and Muthuis, who, although ordained, declined to consecrate, 528, 624, 680. Of a certain noble monk who carried his baskets around for sale, 547. Of a certain monk visited by the emperor Theodosius, who fled lest he be honored, 627. Of another who judged himself unworthy of angelic visitations, 628. Of Moses, who accused himself of heresy in order to avoid vainglory, 593. Of Moses, who received rejection from the altar with the calmest spirit, 624. Of Nesteron, who compared himself to a donkey, ibid. Of the noble virgin Olympia, 779. Of Olympius, who every year brought his wages to his masters even when they refused them, 624–625. Of Pachomius, who submitted to his lord while agitated by various movements of the soul, 118; who served the brothers, 121–122; who hid himself among the monks so that Athanasius would not ordain him, 123. Of the dying Pambo, 716. Of Pastor, who healed the troubled spirit of a rival, 633; who avoided miracles, 650. Of Patricius, who resigned his leadership out of fear of danger, 890. Of Peter, concerning miracles, 823. Of Polychronius, who concealed his virtues, 846; who received visitors with the greatest self-abasement, 847; who asked for the prayers of a certain prefect, ibid. Of Pimen, who declined miracles, 671. Of Pinuphius, who fled the priesthood, 547; who cultivated the monastery garden, 548; who, when recognized a second time, fled lest he be honored, ibid. Of Poemen, who appeased the spirit of an angry old man, 514; who declined honor, 525–526. Of a certain old man who pretended to be foolish in order to avoid glory, 517, 661, 670. Of a certain old man who refused to cast out a demon, 651. Of a certain old man who preferred death to leadership and obtained it from God, 864. Of the monk Silvanus, who placed all the brothers above himself, 128–129. Of Simeon the Stylite, who revered as God an old man teaching the way of salvation, 170; who endured a rebuke with equanimity, 171; who attributed the honor of healings to God, 173; who sent a demoniac to Andrew to be healed, 897. Of Sisoes, 653; of the same man, who declined to perform miracles, 651. Of solitaries who avoided the performance of miracles, 622. Of Theodore, who refused to exercise the office of deacon, 623, 679–680. Of Theodotus, patriarch of Jerusalem, who yielded his litter to a cleric, 870. Of a certain virgin who pretended to be foolish, endured the insults of the others with the greatest patience, and finally fled glory, 639, 738. Of Zosima, who declined the episcopate, 899.

How humility is acquired, 526, 549, 620, 671. Humility overcomes the devil, 129, 497, 516, 624. It sets the devil on fire, 518, 628. It drives out the devil, 622. Humility is the soul’s salvation, 499. The rudder of the spiritual vessel, 518. The guardian of good works, 519. It escapes the devil’s snares, 519, 620. It is effective against fornication, 574. It generates charity, 671. It conquers vainglory, 618–619. It is better than bodily labors, 622. It causes one to abstain from courtly behavior, 623. The gate of God, ibid. It surpasses all virtues, ibid. The monk’s first virtue, 623. Unshakable humility, 627. Humility is a person’s progress, 617. It brings one near to God, 624, 628. It avoids intimacy with the abbot, 629. It preserves peace between two brothers, 630. It is the forerunner of charity, like John the Baptist of Christ, 518, 670. It is a tree of life growing upward, 671. It climbs the tree of life, 626. It is the earth on which God wishes sacrifice to be offered to him, 625, 671. It is human perfection, 671. It neither becomes angry itself nor permits others to become angry, ibid. It forgives before being asked, ibid.; it is like a veil that protects us, 671. The foundation of all virtues, 743. Humility is the occasion of continual tears for the monk Silvanus, 128. Humility is no less necessary to a person than breathing, 625. Humility commands what seventy weeks of fasting could not accomplish, 628. Humility is forgiving before one is asked, 627. Likewise, submitting oneself below irrational animals, 625. Likewise, judging oneself lower than a dog, 660. When it commands, humility obtains compliance, not authority, 627. Humility arising from temptation, 732. A contest of humility: which of the two will bless first, 385. Apollonius obtains the grace of humility for someone, 750. A notable example of humility, 500. A contest of humility, 539. Signs of humility, 549. Teachings on humility, 626. The necessity of humility, ibid. The way of humility, 629. Humility and self-denial are the tools of the soul, 625. By humility Abraham overcomes the devil’s praises, 148. John the Almsgiver teaches humility to the proud with great skill, 199–200. John the Almsgiver teaches humility in a most beautiful exhortation, ibid. Posthumius teaches his people humility, [Col. XLIV] 236. Zacharias teaches humility by trampling on his own hood, 513, 623, 668. Isidore teaches that pride must be conquered through humility, 516. A conversation of demons about humility converts a priest of idols, 497. Muthuis forestalls his adversary through humility, 514. A contest in humility between Zosima and Mary of Egypt, 385. Through humility it is better to be defeated than to conquer through pride, 627. The enemy must be overcome through humility, 629–630. The adversary is conquered through humility, 926.

The incursion of the Huns into the Roman world, 399. Hyacinthus, Eugenia’s servant, becomes a religious, 343. Hyacinthus is beheaded, 348. Hymns and psalmody at the burial of the saints, 219. Hymns at the ninth hour, 713. Miraculous hymn-singing beside the tomb of Saint John the Almsgiver, 205. The sayings of Hyperichius, 587, 603. Jacobus detests hypocrisy, 840.

## I

By the instruction of an ibis, a monk learns about harmful herbs, 541. Cruel idolaters reject the Gospel, 145. An instructive fable about a nightingale teaches what idolaters resemble, 263–264. The foolishness of idolaters, 264, 318. Fire from heaven punishes Melanthia’s slanders, 345. Fire consumes a woman’s body, 572. Fire and water are carried on a cloth through the merits of the saints, 868. Divine fire is kindled by tears, 566. Abraham tramples the fire sent by a demon, 148. Bodily fire extinguishes the fire of lust, 579. A hermit’s cave is illuminated by heavenly fire, 887. Ignorance of God is darkness of the soul, 263. The image of Christ must be honored, and why, 286. An image of the Lord in a monastery, 353. An image of the blessed Virgin Mary before the church of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem in the time of Mary of Egypt, 387. John venerates an image of the blessed Mary with the child, 917. A candle lit before an image of the blessed Virgin does not diminish miraculously, 917. The demon requires that its veneration be omitted so that he may desist from the temptation of fornication, 874. An image of Simeon in Rome, in workshops, for protection, 850. An image of the monk Theodosius, lowered into water, causes the water to gush forth, 886. Eupraxia kisses an image of Christ, 353. Images must be honored, 286.

Impatience under injury is theft from the soul, 513. One must command with humility, not authority, 627. The impiety of Thallelaeus, bishop of Thessalonica, is punished by God with suffocation in a latrine, 368. The misery of the impious, 302. The laying on of hands in catechization, 234. The life of the wicked has no true pleasure, 302. Christ’s incarnation shattered the devil’s strength, 136. Christ’s incarnation is affirmed, 256. Christ’s incarnation is beautifully described and defended, 319. Always consider yourself to be beginning, 684. A monk must always be beginning, 563. A person must always be beginning, 611. Excessive rebuke is sometimes harmful, 520. India is devoted to idols, 243. An eighty-day fast, 225. A seven-day fast, 226. A forty-day fast, 227. A hundred-day fast, ibid. Macarius of Alexandria’s twenty-day fast, 723. A barely born infant is designated a monk, 739. Infants are cared for in Eupraxia’s monastery, 357. Cyriacus, chief of the robbers, is rescued from danger through the intercession of the infants whom he had saved from death, 911. A monk who committed infanticide returns to the world so that he may expiate the crime by death, 912. The skull of an idolater instructs Macarius about the punishments of hell, 526. Double service must be rendered to an infirm brother, 635. One who serves a difficult sick man is regarded as an angel, 673. Eulogius patiently serves a leprous man for fifteen years, 673, 728. To render service to the sick is better than a six-day fast, 673. God protects the infirm from temptations, 596. The weaker person must not investigate higher things, but should speak of sufferings, not heavenly matters, 527. Bodily illness benefits the soul, 675. In illness the Lord must be blessed, 136. A salutary misfortune, 718, 949. Demonic gluttony is cured by the sign of the cross and blessed water, 830. All creatures reproach human ingratitude, 200.

The enemy must be forestalled through humility, 669. An injury must be forgiven, 330. To endure an injury and not return like for like is to lay down one’s life for one’s neighbor, 681. Endurance of injuries is the gate of heaven, 513, 659; the way of salvation, 513; the perfection of a monk, 592. A monk patient under injuries is an object of wonder to philosophers, 632. Sins are the cause of injuries, 668. To endure injuries, everyone must be insensible like a stone, 668, 683. This is taught by a beautiful example, 530, 622, 683. Forgetfulness of injuries, and its celebrated example, 870. Someone gives a three-year reward to those who injure him, 659. Innocent children handle an asp without harm, 539. Innocent Macarius is mocked, 623. The innocence of a monk who had fallen under suspicion of disgraceful conduct is wonderfully revealed, 191–192. The innocence of the people of Cyrene, 537. The innocence of an accused man is attested by one raised from the dead by Macarius, 507. Innocentius, a monk who had never married, 768. His remarkable power against the devil, 768. He heals a paralytic, ibid. He reveals a theft by prayer, ibid. The punishment of disobedience is fornication, 576. The pretext of heretics, 734. Its punishment, 131. Sleeplessness is obtained from God, 120. The intercession of the saints, 337–338. Through the intercession of the infants whom he had saved from death, the robber Cyriacus is rescued from danger, 611. The inner person flows into the outer, 913. Interior striving toward perfection, 116. Seruch, inventor of statues, 320. Envy is overcome through humility, 514. Likewise through remembrance of the tomb, 631.

The saints must be invoked, and why, 841. Ephraem invokes Saint Paula, 169; a certain abbot invokes Euphrosyna, 367. Theodoret invokes the saints, 798, 813, 815, 817, 818; Aphraates, 821; Peter the Galatian, 825; Theodosius, ibid.; Romanus, 827; Zeno, 828; Macedonius, 831; Maesyma, 832; Acepsimas, 833; Abraames, 836; Eusebius, ibid.; Salamanus, 837; Mareus, ibid.; Jacobus, 844; many others, ibid.; Simeon the Stylite, 854; Baradatus, ibid.; the saints, 855, 857, 886.

Anger must be overcome, 41, 237. Anger must be overcome by prayers, 584. Anger must be banished from the tribunal, 244. Anger is an impediment to prayer, 289. Anger must be overcome not in solitude but in company, 515. Anger pours itself out thoughtlessly, and God permits it to happen, 527. Anger disturbs the mind, 568. Anger, once defeated, puts the demons to flight, 569. Anger must be absent from one who rebukes, 570. Anger attacks even the solitary, 589. God’s anger against an evil deed, 645. Anger must sometimes be avoided by flight, 681. Anger excludes the soul from prayer, 682. Anger belongs to nature, not to our free choice, 813. The measure of anger, 4[lacuna]2. The four causes of anger, 512, 667. Four modes, 512, 567, 638. Degrees of anger, 667. The limit of anger, 813. The continual suppression of anger before sunset, 569. The occasion of anger must be avoided, 681. The demon of anger, 910. Saint John the Almsgiver causes a prince to lay aside his anger through a marvelous discovery at Mass, 199. Sisoes most beautifully calms anger by saying that we, who can take vengeance, no longer need God, 512, 631, 668. Epiphanius laid aside all anger before going to sleep, 568. Isidore restrains anger, 569. Ammonas asks God for fourteen years that he may overcome anger, 584. Agathon always laid aside anger before sunset, 633. John the Almsgiver and the patrician Nicetas lay aside anger before sunset, 186. The devil fears one who is free from anger, 569. An angry man must rebuke no one, 570. An angry man is not pleasing to God, even if he raises the dead, 597. The field of an angry farmer is burned as he had wished, and David’s prayer extinguishes the fire, 918. If someone wishes to separate you from God, that alone—not anything else—is a reason for anger, 501. The threefold diversity of angry people, 512. A certain monk was never angry, 539, 569. An angry farmer is appeased by the moderation of the monk Sergius and becomes a monk, 933–934.

Isaac, Antony’s interpreter, flees out of humility lest he become a priest, 500. Though hidden, he is remarkably exposed, ibid. By God’s will he accepts the priesthood, ibid. An angel teaches Isaac that judgment of one’s neighbor must be left to God, 520, 594. —Isaac the Theban considers that children should be sent away from the desert, 599. His vision, through which he learns that reconciliation with an enemy is necessary before communion, 910.

Isidore, the things from which he abstained, 709, 943, 984. His shadow is revered by pagans, 709, 943. His ecstasy at the time of refreshment, 709, 943, 984. Food of immortality comforts him when hungry, 709, 943, 984. He is honored at Rome, ibid. When dying, he leaves his sisters no wealth but commends them to Christ, ibid. Isidore weeps continually, calls himself the greatest sinner, and explains why, 869. —Isidore, also called Macarius, a priest and prefect of the poor, healed a certain virgin of greed, 945. How long he lived, ibid.

Isidore, father of one thousand monks, 759. His monastery abounds in everything, 759. Its enclosure, ibid. Whoever enters once never leaves, 759. No one there is sick, even at the time of death, 759. Everyone foreknows the day of his death, ibid. Isis, goddess of the Egyptians, 307. A dove shows the way, 226. The heavenly journey requires abundant provisions, 275. The difficulties of the journey, 226.

## J
- James the deacon, author of the *Life of Saint Pelagia*, 376. Travels from Antioch to Jerusalem, 380. Visits Pelagia, ibid.
- James the lame, endowed with profound knowledge, 765.
- James, born at Nisibis [Col. XLVI], 798. His cell, food, and clothing, ibid. Foresees the future, ibid. Because of some wanton girls, causes a spring to dry up, ibid. Also causes them to turn gray before their time, ibid. When asked, restores water to the spring, ibid. Performs miracles by the sign of the cross, ibid. Punishes an unjust judge by shattering a stone through a curse, ibid. Chosen bishop of Nisibis, 799. Cares for the poor, ibid. Raises a poor man who had been laid out as dead and was truly dead, 799. Takes part in the Council of Nicaea, ibid. By his prayers renders useless the siegeworks of the enemy against a besieged city, 800. When the wall is destroyed, he is a great wall for the citizens, ibid. Intercessor for the besieged, ibid. Obtains from God that a cloud of gnats be sent against the enemy, ibid. While invoking punishment upon the enemy, James remembers mercy, ibid. His body is carried away from Nisibis after it has been captured by the Persians, ibid.

- James the Persian, a monk, 802. Is ordered to follow Julian at a distance, lest he be distracted, ibid.

- James, disciple of Maron, similar in conduct to the great James, 838. Has the sky for a roof, ibid. Brings fertility to the mountain, ibid. Falls ill, ibid. His patience, ibid. Carries a weight of iron, 839. People rush together so that each may seize a piece of his body, ibid. Forbade himself the use of fire, ibid. Detests hypocrisy, 840. His food is soaked lentils, ibid. Does not shrink from a man who comes to him late, thinking him a demon, ibid. Is brought out covered with ice and snow, ibid. Cures diseases and blesses water, ibid. Raises a boy from the dead, ibid. Is a help against demons, ibid. Sees John the Baptist, 841; likewise Joseph the patriarch, 840. In greatness of spirit despises a demon, ibid. A demon in the form of an Ethiopian troubles him in various ways, but is overcome while repeatedly assuming different forms, 842, 843. Theodoret prepares a tomb for him while he is still alive in the Church of the Apostles, 843. His humility in choosing a tomb, ibid. Interrupts the time of prayer only with the greatest difficulty, ibid. Explains his saying through a remarkable extended parable, 844.

- James, enclosed in a little house according to the same discipline as Polychronius, 848. Uses neither fire nor lamplight, ibid. Speaks with those who come to him through a certain curved trench, ibid.

- Boasting empties virtues of their worth, 122.
- Boasting must be avoided, 452. It is twofold, ibid.
- The doorkeeper of nuns ought to be mature in age and character, 352.
- The door of the tongue must be shut, 615.
- One must fast with discernment, 708.
- The five-day fast of Adolius, 769.
- The three-day fast of Avitus, 808.
- The fast of Conon, who ate only once a week for thirty years, 867.
- The extraordinary fast of Cyra, 856.
- The two-day fast of David, disciple of Eusebius, 813.
- Elijah’s week-long fast in his youth, 747.
- Likewise that of Heliodorus, 849.
- The fast of Elpidius, who ate only on Saturdays and Sundays, 769.
- Eron’s three-month fast, except for Communion and, sometimes, wild sorrel, 734.
- The two-day fast of the presbyter Eulogius, 592; sometimes lasting a week, ibid.; sustained on bread and salt, ibid.
- Euphrasia’s three-day and four-day fast, 355. The same woman’s week-long fast, 356.
- An unnamed brother’s eight-day fast in the desert, 539.
- An unnamed brother’s fast throughout the whole week of Easter, 552.
- Eusebius’s three-day fast on some occasions and four-day fast on others, 811.
- Josaphat’s fast for his deceased father Abenner, 327.
- The remarkable fast of Macarius, 723.
- The extraordinary fast of Marana, 856.
- Mark’s fast, when he fasted for entire weeks, 865.
- The remarkable fast of Onuphrius, 99.
- Peter the Galatian’s fast on alternate days, 822.
- Polychronius’s seven-day fast, 839.
- The fast of Posthumius, 235.
- Serapion the Sindonite’s five-day fast aboard a ship, 762.
- Silvanus’s fast, including abstinence even from drinking water, 508, 570.
- The fast of the adolescent monk Theodore [Col. XLVII], 125.
- Theodore the layman’s fast until evening, for twenty-two years, except on Saturdays and Sundays, 909.
- The two-day fast of Theodosius the solitary, practiced for thirty-five years, 880.
- The daily fast of Theodulus, 867.
- Simeon Stylites’ seven-day fast, 170. The same man’s forty-day fast without food for twenty-eight years, 849, 850.
- Zachaeus’s two-day fast, 137.
- Fasting precedes Baptism, 234, 322.
- Fasting overcomes the passions, 509, 511. It weakens the internal enemy, 569. It is a bridle of sin, 571. It is the monk’s seasoning, ibid. It dries up the channels of pleasures, ibid. It elevates the mind, ibid.
- What sort of fasting makes the demon rejoice, 603.
- Weekly fasting in Scetis, 607.
- Fasting on the fourth and sixth days, 751.
- Fasting on Friday, 595, 599.
- The best measure of fasting, 601.
- The martyrs Epictetus and Astion are tormented by a thirty-day fast, 217.
- By seven days of fasting and prayer, Macarius the Egyptian drives out a demon, 721.
- Poemen disapproves of two-day and three-day fasts, 508.
- Weekly fasts, 587.
- Fasts and vigils humble the soul, 657.
- Moderate fasts under Pachomius, 763.
- Moderate fasts are better, 806.
- The bones of Jeremiah rest in the Tetraphylum at Alexandria, 883.
- Tallelaeus visits the holy places in Jerusalem, 888.
- Christopher travels to Jerusalem to adore the Cross, 892.
- Pilgrimage to Jerusalem, 771.
- When the name of Jesus is invoked, Antony cures a demoniac, 48.
- Demons dread the name of Jesus, 59.
- By the name of Jesus Abraham drives away a demon, 148.
- Julian kills a dragon by invoking the name of Jesus together with the sign of the cross, 802.
- John the Baptist appears to James, 841. He prays to God for the restoration of those who have gone astray, 842.
- John the Baptist frees Conon from the sting of the flesh, 864.

- John, Pachomius’s brother, joins him, 117. From the surplus of his work he assists the poor, ibid. Uses only one garment, ibid. Rebukes his brother Pachomius for enlarging the monastery’s enclosure, 118. Dies. Pachomius accompanies his funeral with hymns, an all-night vigil, psalms, and prayers, ibid. Is buried by him, ibid.

- John, a disciple of Pachomius, 121.

- John the Almsgiver (Saint): John and Leontius are the writers of his life, 179. The reasons why Leontius wrote his life, ibid. Menas the steward recounts his deeds to Leontius, 180. He never swore an oath, ibid. Calls the poor his masters, 181; and feeds more than 7,000 every day, ibid. Is consecrated patriarch, ibid. Forbids inequality in weights and measures, ibid. Prohibits officials from accepting gifts, ibid. Devises a way by which everyone can conveniently approach him, ibid. Weeps because no one comes to him wearing a cloak, ibid. Cherishes the wounded and sick, 182. Assists debtors more generously, ibid. Orders that nothing be refused to petitioners dressed in finer clothing, ibid. His trust in God, ibid. Mercy appears to him in the form of a virgin crowned with olives. He gives a poor man his own clothing, ibid. Tests God’s promise concerning the hundredfold return, ibid. Visits the sick two or three times a week, 183. When the same man asks a third time, orders that double be given him, saying, “Lest Christ test me,” ibid. Twice gives a boatman a notable alms, and the third time gives him an entire ship laden with grain, ibid. A ship is guided by John while he is absent, ibid. It arrives in Britain, ibid. Tin is changed into silver, ibid. By divine revelation he recognizes the fraud of his associates who were cheating the alms, 184. Nicetas the patrician, under the pretext of an imperial necessity, seizes his treasury, 184. By God’s providence other money is sent to him, ibid. His letter to Nicetas the patrician, ibid. Nicetas returns to him the money he had seized and received, with interest, 185. He becomes the godfather of Nicetas the patrician, ibid. He admits no bigamist to the diaconate, whether through entreaty or payment, ibid. Receives two ships laden with grain from Sicily, ibid. Through his efforts, the dispute that had arisen between John and Nicetas is settled before sunset, 186. He does good to the man who had offended his nephew, 187. Refuses Communion to the deacon Damian until he is reconciled, in the church, 187. His discourse consists of Holy Scripture and the teachings of the Fathers, 188. Excludes slander, ibid. Orders his monument to be built and wishes it to be announced on solemn days when it is to be completed, ibid. Sends gifts for the church of Jerusalem, ibid. His cheap blanket, ibid. His devotion to poverty, shown when he arranges for a more expensive blanket that had been offered to him to be sold, ibid., and 189. Does not accept an accusation against a monk, 191. Builds a hospice for monks, 192. Gladly attends funerals and the dying, ibid. Many offer him their possessions, ibid. Visits the poor, 193. Receives from Troilus, in a document, a written acknowledgment of the alms’ reward, 194. Great-hearted and patient in adversity: after thirteen ships are lost, God restores double to him, ibid. Gives two pounds of gold to his needy servant, 195. Cheerful in the loss of possessions, 193, 194. Lends money most readily, 195. By his readiness to lend, recovers the hundredfold that had been lost through another’s slowness to lend, 195. Promptly helps his son-in-law when he is troubled, ibid. Gently rebukes the man who treated his servants harshly, ibid. Advises a slave who has found an unmerciful master to flee, 196. In a marvelous way helps a boy who had chosen the Mother of God over money, ibid. Does not allow the alms of impostors to be punished, ibid. Teaches, through a remarkable deed, that rash judgment must be avoided, 197, 198. Orders a man who insults him to take as much alms as he wishes at his discretion, 198, 199. Asks almsgivers how they attained that grace, 199. Brings a prince who is nursing anger to reconciliation, ibid. Skillfully cures pride, ibid., and 200. Delivers a long and beautiful exhortation on humility, ibid. Skillfully corrects those who leave before the Mass is finished, 201. Forbids conversations in church, ibid. At all times observed the force of ecclesiastical discipline so strictly that he surpassed many monks, ibid. Maintains two orders of monks, ibid. Warns against communion with heretics, ibid. Condemns no one and rebukes those who condemn, ibid. Teaches by a beautiful example that even public sins should not be judged, ibid., and 202. Flees to Cyprus, ibid. Is summoned to God by an angel, 203. He reveals to Nicetas the patrician that he is being called out of this life, ibid. His testament, ibid. How much he gave to the poor, and how poor he died, ibid. Built hospices, homes for the elderly, and hospitals, ibid. Two bishops yield him the middle place in the tomb, dead to the dead, ibid. After death he obtains the erasure of a written sin, 204. His soul is seen by the monk Sabinus being received by Almsgiving, 205. He died on the day of Saint Menas, ibid. Another vision concerning the blessedness of his soul, ibid. His tomb exudes fragrant and healing ointment, ibid.

- John, counselor to John the Almsgiver, 195.

- John the abbot, at first a smith, 738. Lives near the city of Lycus, 738. Sees no woman, 739. Is endowed with the spirit of prophecy, 739. Foretells the outcome of the war to Theodosius [Col. XLVIII], 546, 739, 745. Appears in a dream to the tribune’s wife, 739. Foretells danger to the husband of an absent wife, ibid. Knows the secrets of the heart, ibid. Reveals the causes of God’s scourges, ibid. Cures the sick with oil blessed by him, ibid. With the same oil frees a woman from blindness, ibid. Drives away tertian fever with it, 741. Knows Palladius and where he comes from, 740. By divine revelation foresees his temptations, ibid. Reveals to him the condition of his parents, ibid. Foretells his bishopric, ibid. For forty years sees neither a woman nor money, ibid. Kisses a deacon’s hand, 741. His exhortations, ibid., and 742. John is fed by God for ten years, 745. Demons appear to him in the form of angels, ibid. Though absent, knows of Theodosius’s victory over Eugenius, 745. Foretells Theodosius’s death, ibid. Dies with his knees bent, ibid. Announces to Poemenia the danger of a fall, 745. John stands continuously for three years, 755. Lives by receiving only the Eucharist on Sunday, 755. Resists the devil disguised as a presbyter, ibid. His feet are torn by prolonged standing, ibid. Is healed by an angel and filled with divine knowledge, ibid. Makes straps for pack animals, ibid. A lame man is cured by touching a strap made by him, ibid. The sick are healed by bread blessed by him, ibid. Though absent, knows the conduct of the brothers, ibid.

- John the Short, or Dwarf, desires to live in the desert like an angel, 509, 598.
- John waters a dry piece of wood, 546.
- John attempts to move an enormous stone, 546.
- John cures paralytics and sufferers from gout, 759.
- John lives for twenty-five years on a rough rock, 845. Renounces every kind of recreation, ibid.
- John refuses the administration of a monastery, 863. Undertakes a pilgrimage to Mount Sinai, ibid. John the Baptist appears to him and promises him health, ibid.
- John abstains from food because an old man had not given him his blessing, 877. Cures various diseases, ibid. Frees a woman from cancer, 878.
- John cures all demoniacs, 886. By prayer releases a ship immobilized by incantations, ibid.
- John dies after being fatally struck by a serpent, 899. Is raised from the dead, ibid.

- John the Persian makes a pilgrimage to the tombs of the apostles, 907.
- John undertakes various pilgrimages, 917. A lion provides him with a route and removes obstacles, ibid. His cave is a spiritual marketplace: he gives and receives, ibid. John is extraordinarily hospitable even toward beasts, and despises everything while intent upon the future, 98. To one asking for a loan he gives money borrowed elsewhere, ibid. Helps a debtor repay a loan, ibid.

- The body of John the Humble is found, 887.
- The admonitions of John the Cilician, 897.

- Jonathan the robber flees to the column of Simeon Stylites as to an asylum, and there dies, 173.
- Josaphat is born in India as the son of King Abenner, 247. His father offers sacrifices on account of his birth, ibid. An astrologer predicts that he will become a Christian, ibid. Every annoyance is most carefully kept away from him so that he may abound in luxuries, 247. His studies, 250. He asks the reason why he is kept confined and is not allowed to go out, 250. He asks his father to be permitted to leave, 250; and obtains permission, 251. He sees a leper and a blind man, ibid. Asks the cause of diseases, ibid. Is astonished at a decrepit old man, ibid. Asks whether he is going to die, 251. Conceals from his father the sorrow brought on by meditation on death, ibid. Asks who might instruct him, ibid. Informed of the savage persecution against religious people initiated by his father, he is deeply distressed, 251, 252. Barlaam is admitted to him under the pretext of showing him a precious stone, 252, 253. He is seized by an incredible desire to hear about good things, 253. Receives the light of faith, 257. Inquires into the order of future events, 260. Asks what he ought to do, 263. Requests Baptism, 265. Asks whether renunciation of all possessions is an ancient institution, 276. Embraces renunciation of all possessions, 279. When he asks how many years Barlaam has, he receives an ingenious answer, 282. Begs him to show himself in his customary clothing, 283. Wishes to accompany Barlaam, 284. Offers him gifts, ibid. Is baptized, 287. His tutor Zardan warns him to send away Barlaam as a foreigner, 289. Tests Zardan’s mind and earnestly exhorts him to the faith, 290. Reluctantly grants Barlaam permission to leave, 291. Esteems Barlaam’s garment better than any purple robe, 291. Devotes himself to prayer after Barlaam’s departure, 292. Takes great care concerning himself so as to live well, ibid. God reveals everything to him, 296. His response to his father’s prayer, 297. Freely professes the faith, 297, 298, 299. Despises idols, 298. Earnestly admonishes his father, 299. His prayer to God, 300. Understands his father’s deceitful flattery, 301. Replies to his father, ibid. His prayer to Nachor, who is falsely representing Barlaam, 304. The beginning of the disputation between Nachor and Josaphat, 304. Requests Nachor as a companion from his father, 309. Takes Nachor away with him, ibid. Gives thanks that he stood for the truth, 310. Orders him to hope for forgiveness, ibid. By his discourses converts many from pagan errors and turns them away from the world, 311. Devotes himself to prayers and fasts, 311. Girls are brought in to him, 313. The spirit of fornication is sent against him, ibid. Sets divine love against illicit love, 314. Sets prayer against temptation, ibid. Receives consolation from God, ibid. Is tempted by a royal girl, 314. Is sought by her as a husband, but in vain, 314, 315. Says that he is bound by a vow of chastity, 315. Is enticed toward fornication, ibid. Demons bring torches against him, 315, 316. Overcomes the temptations of the flesh by prayer, 316. In a vision is led to pleasant places, ibid. Likewise to gloomy places, 316. Returns to himself, ibid. Falls ill, ibid. His father visits him, ibid. Earnestly admonishes his father, 317. Refutes Theuda’s arguments with distinction, ibid. Turns Theuda’s argument back against him, 320. Converts Theuda, 321. Obeys his parent when summoned to share in the kingdom, 322. Erects a cross at the beginning of his reign, ibid. Builds a temple for Christ, ibid. Draws everyone to himself, 323. Distributes money among the poor, 324. His household increases and his father’s decreases, ibid. Receives a letter from his converted father, 324, 325. Prostrates himself before the image of Christ, 325. Gives thanks to God, ibid. Travels to his converted father, ibid. His prayer to his father, ibid. Consoles his father, 327. Offers the kingdom to Barachias, 328. When Barachias refuses, he leaves a letter and secretly flees, 329. He is found completing the prayer of the sixth hour with outstretched hands, ibid. Is compelled to return, ibid. Appoints Barachias king, ibid. His prayer to Barachias, 329. Prays again, 330. Gives clothing to the poor, ibid. Wears only a hair shirt, ibid. Lives only on herbs, 331. Suffers from thirst, ibid. Is attacked by the devil’s temptations, ibid. Is harassed by apparitions, 332. Conquers them by the sign of the cross, ibid. Beasts meet him, ibid. Searches for Barlaam for two years, 332. At last finds him, 333. Barlaam blesses him, ibid. He relates his father’s conversion, 333. His vigils and nightly prayers, 334. His devotion to virtue, ibid. Desires to die with Barlaam, 335. Brings what is necessary for the sacrifice, 336. Commits the body of the deceased Barlaam to the tomb with psalms, ibid. His prayer to God, ibid. Prays that God may save him through the prayers of his servant Barlaam, 337. His vision, ibid. Sees two crowns, ibid. Wonders at his father’s crown, ibid. In the vision Barlaam rebukes him for murmuring, ibid. Spends thirty-five years in solitude, 337. Dies, 338. Is buried with Barlaam, ibid. By a vision these events are ordered to be announced in India to King Barachias, ibid. His body does not decay, ibid. It is received with honor, ibid. Miracles occur during its translation, ibid.

- Joseph the abbot teaches that temptations benefit some people but harm others, 599.
- Joseph the patriarch appears to James, 842.
- Jubinus, bishop of Ascalon, 779.
- A Jew, having seen the form of an infant in the Eucharist, is converted and baptized by Basil, 156.

- Julia, tutor of Euphrasia, instructs her, 355, 356, 357. Desires to die with her, 361. Dies on the fifth day after the death of blessed Euphrasia and is buried in the same tomb, 361.
- Juliana, Origen’s hostess, 786, 787.
- Julian, Basil’s fellow student, 153.
- Julian the Apostate is killed in Persia, at a place called Assia, by Saint Mercury, 225. His death is revealed to Didymus, 711. Likewise to Julian the monk, 803.
- Julian is called Sabas for the sake of honor, that is, “old man,” 800. His food is barley bread, salt, and water, 801. He always has Davidic hymns on his lips, ibid. Many gather around him, ibid. He prays far removed from the others, 801. The manner of his prayers, ibid. Orders James to follow him at a distance, lest he be distracted, 802. Asks that the miracle of the slain dragon be kept secret, ibid. Invoking Jesus by the sign of the cross, he kills the dragon, 802. The young man Asterius consults him as an old man about his way of life, ibid. Tests Asterius by thirst, ibid. Obtains a spring for him to quench his thirst, ibid. Attracted Acacius, later bishop of Beroea, to the ascetic life, 803. Asterius visits him several times with small gifts, ibid. Avoiding the crowds and honor of visitors, he withdraws to Mount Sinai, 803. There he builds a church and consecrates an altar, ibid. The death of Julian the Apostate is divinely made known to him, ibid. The heretics falsely accuse him of communion with their heresy, 804. He travels to Antioch to refute the heretics, 804. A boy who has fallen into a well is saved through his merits, 805. He turns aside to the retreat of blessed Paul near Antioch, ibid. Drives away a fever by prayer, ibid. A beggar with disabled feet is restored by touching his cloak, ibid. His presence confounds his adversaries, ibid. Cures the prefect of the East, ibid.

- Julian the Stylite cures a sick man by prayer, 869. A granary is filled with grain through his merits, ibid. Though absent, learns of the death of Simeon Stylites, struck by lightning, 878. Through a disciple orders a lion to depart, ibid.

- Julian, an old man of the Egyptian monastery, lives for seventy years in a cave in extreme poverty, 876. At night his cell is illuminated from heaven, ibid.

- Julian, bishop of Bostra, harmlessly drinks a poisoned cup after first making the sign of the cross, 889.

- Julian the Arab, who was blind, is warned not to separate himself from the Church, 890.
- A younger person accommodates himself to the will of an older person, 608.
- What sort Jupiter was, 306.
- Simeon Stylites forbids swearing by God, but permits swearing by oneself, 173.
- Evil and harmful oaths are not to be kept, 933.
- A certain brother clears himself of a crime by swearing an oath over the sacred chalice, 934.
- John the Almsgiver never swore an oath, 180.
- One must judge justly, 597.
- From love of justice, Poemen, or Pastor, gives nothing to the flesh and leaves everything to justice, 499, 593.
- The just man is likened to a palm tree, 645.
- The communicant appears with a bright face; the sinner with a dark one, 676.
- A young monk needs labors rather than words, 709.
- Two luxurious young men are tested by Macarius, 528, 652. They make progress, 529, 652. He visits them, ibid. They rise for prayer, ibid. They are protected by an angel, ibid. They sing twelve psalms, ibid. Fire comes out of their mouths, 529, 652. They die, ibid.

- Kitissefodo, the name of the place where the three boys Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael rest, 225.

- The perpetual tears of the Lady, 856.
- The gift of tears is the promised land, 567.
- The sword of tears must be sharpened against thoughts, 613.
- The power of tears, 682.
- Abraham the hermit weeps every day, 149.
- Pammon weeps for two reasons: the destruction of a well-adorned woman and his own negligence, 524.
- Arsenius weeps continually, 531.
- Spiritual joy conquers the demon, 47.
- Those who serve God ought to abound in joy, 751 [Col. LI].
- Euphrasia trains herself by carrying stones back and forth, 355.
- A merchant throws precious stones into the sea lest sailors kill him because of them, 929.

- The true repentance of a fallen deacon is demonstrated by miracles, 577.
- The demon rejoices at the fall of human beings, 556.
- Who can escape the devil’s snares? 551.
- The wantonness of girls is punished by the drying up of a spring and the graying of their hair, 798.
- Latoius, because he does not obey Maesyma’s admonitions, remains stuck with his cart, unable to move, 832. He is released by Maesyma’s prayers, ibid.
- The robber Jonathan flees to the column of Simeon Stylites as to an asylum and dies there, 173.
- A robber is converted by Apollonius, 749.
- A robber becomes a monk, 912. He returns to the world so that he may atone for the crime of infanticide by death, ibid.

- Latronianus, commander in Scythia, arrests Epictetus and Astion, 216. His cruelty toward the martyrs, 216, 217. He stiffens with terror when he sees them, 216. He is seized by a demon, 219. He is suffocated, ibid.
- Other people’s praise is commendable, 625.
- Praise of Antony, 58.
- Self-praise must be avoided, 591.
- Human praise is harmful and dangerous, 627.
- Praise of Athanasius’s writings, 873.
- Praises of Abraham the hermit, 149.
- Praises of Basil the Great, 161.
- Who Lausus was, 704.
- Lausus renounces everything, 789.
- More sumptuous foods at Easter, 115.
- After a spring constructed at a monastery bathhouse dries up, it flows again when the building is destroyed, 885.
- A lioness humbly prostrates herself at the feet of a hermit, 540.
- A hermit restores sight to a lioness’s blind cubs, 540.
- Simple obedience brings a bound lioness, 502.
- Antony’s bed is rushes and a hair shirt, or the bare ground, 38.
- Domnion’s bed cures the sick, 761.
- The difference between the old and the new law, 266.
- The laws of the nations punish the gods, 308.
- A man is punished for neglecting three lentils, 546.
- The humble and silent lion, etc., 896. To free others, he sells himself, 896. He suffers martyrdom, ibid.

When the donkey is stolen, he performs its service by carrying water, ibid. He brings the donkey back, 894. He mourns the death of the abbot Gerasimus, ibid. Unable to find consolation over Gerasimus’s death, he dies upon his tomb, ibid.
- A lion provides a route for John the hermit, 917.
- Sergius commands a lion, 899.

- Lions live with an old man in the same den, 863.
- They show the way to those who are lost, 816.

- Libanius, Basil’s fellow student, 153.
- Libanius invites Basil to an elaborate meal, 154.

- Sabbatius’s, 770.
- That of a certain old man, 865.

- See *Mercy*.

- Generosity toward the poor converts heretics, 771.
- Free will is affirmed, 121, 255.
- Free will makes it depend on us to attain virtue, though with the addition of God’s grace, 288.
- The definition of free will, 277.
- Lust lives even in old men, 578.
- The temptation of lust must be overcome by hardships, 533.
- The inflammation of lust is the punishment of a worse sin, 551.
- Demons kindle lust, 316.
- The three causes of lustful thoughts are the flesh, the movement of the mind, and the demon, 732.
- A dry branch planted by Elpidius grows into a vine, 769.
- Limnaeus, disciple of Thalassius, 844. Imposes silence upon himself, ibid. Is instructed by Maron, ibid. Cures the sick and demoniacs, 845. Lives in the open air, ibid. Cures colic pains by the sign of the cross, ibid. Likewise the bite of a viper, ibid. Is kind and generous toward the blind and the poor, ibid.
- The tongue and the belly must be restrained, 511, 562, 574, 865.
- Guarding the tongue, 607.
- The door of the tongue must be shut, 615.
- Unrestrained speech is a stable without a door, 567.

- He who restrains the tongue restrains the passions, 571.

- Maches burns unopened letters from his parents and friends so that he will not be distracted, 550.

- A place that harms salvation must be changed, 582.
- Stability of place bears fruit, 586.
- Stability of place must be maintained during temptation because of various circumstances, 589.

- The religious sites in Jerusalem are visited [Col. LII] by Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, 225.

- Lucius the abbot gives a more distinguished answer than Longinus to what is asked, 599.

- The gain of one’s brother is your fruit, 635.

- Light surrounds the dying Onuphrius, 103.
- Lust must be overcome by the clever invention of the potter who makes a wife and children for himself; this is taught skillfully, 496, 497.
- Luxury is a moneylender, 761.
- Thoughts of luxury must be overcome by hardships, 533.
- The demon kindles luxury, 156.
