## M
Macarius, father of fifty thousand monks, 235. — Life of Macarius the Roman and its authors, 234. His cave, 228. He protects himself with the sign of the cross, ibid. His appearance and dress, ibid. He asks what is happening in the world, ibid. He recounts whose property he is and how he came there, 228. Lions familiar to him, ibid. He flees from marriage, ibid. Raphael his guide on the journey, 229. When the angel disappears, he is directed on the road by a wild ass, ibid. He protects himself against the dragon with the sign of the cross, 229. By the cross he drives away various illusions of the devil, ibid. The devil appears to him in the form of a woman, 230. He is deceived, ibid. After committing sin, the lions flee from him, ibid. They return when he repents, ibid. Macarius stands buried in the earth up to his neck for three years, 230. He remains forty days and nights in the same place on bended knees, ibid. Christ appears to him in the cave, ibid. The blessed Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, guided by lions, return to the monastery and tell the brothers what they have seen, 231.

Macarius the Egyptian raises a dead man to confirm the faith, 720. He visits Antony, 585. Wonderfully industrious, 585. He conquers the demon by confidence and courage, 585. Exhausted, he is carried away by angels, 649. He heals a paralytic by a word, ibid. He examines a suggestion for five years, 653. He lived ninety years, sixty of them in solitude, 719. Because of his maturity he is called παιδαριογέρων, “child-elder,” ibid. At the age of forty he prevails against spirits and is endowed with the gifts of healing and prophecy, 719. He is ordained a priest, ibid. He foresees that the disciple John will be tempted by the spirit of avarice, ibid. Frequently in ecstasy, 720. By revelation he learns why a certain woman appears to the mare through amorous magic, ibid. By the power of blessed water he drives the apparition away from the woman, 720. To escape human notice, he digs tunnels, ibid. He recites twenty-four prayers while going and as many while returning, ibid. By prayer and a seven-day fast he drives out a gluttonous demon, 721.

— Macarius of Alexandria, priest of the Cells, 721. Antony teaches him not to desire anything, when the palm branches he had desired are miraculously scorched, ibid. In the desert he is tempted by the devil in the form of a camel loaded with food, 721. He drives away the apparition by prayer, ibid. His saying to the tribunes whom the world deceived, ibid. He tames his desire for food by sending to the brothers [Col. LIII] the grape that had been sent to him, ibid. Whenever he heard that another had done something admirable, he eagerly imitated it, ibid. For seven years he ate only raw food, ibid. He ate as much bread as his hand could extract from a narrow-mouthed flask, ibid. He calls that flask his “publican,” 722. He overcomes sleep by not entering a roofed building for twenty days, ibid. Tempted by the spirit of fornication, he exposes himself to the bites of gnats, ibid. He visits the tomb of Jannes and Jambres in order to contend with demons, 722. The demon removes the reeds he had fixed as markers along the road, ibid. He is not frightened when seventy demons confront him, ibid. He swears to the demons, ibid. He sets the name of the Lord against the devil’s drawn sword, ibid. While hungry, he is tempted by a twenty-day fast, 723. When the apparition of a girl carrying a water jar and apparently inviting him is presented to him, he endures another three days, ibid. He is suckled by a buffalo, ibid. The bite of the same asp does not harm him, ibid. He examines the austerity of the Tabennesiot monks, 723. His astonishing Lenten fast: on Sunday he eats nothing except a few raw cabbage leaves, and he always remains standing, 723. This amazes Pachomius’ monks, ibid. Pachomius recognizes him miraculously, ibid. He decides to stand continuously for five days in contemplation, 724. By what arguments he raised his mind to heavenly things, ibid. A demon in the likeness of a flame burns everything in his cell, ibid. He heals a priest suffering from cancer because, having been conscious of fornication, he had offered sacrifice; he does so after the priest’s confession of sin and promise of amendment, 724. His various cells, 724. He heals various demoniacs, ibid. He heals a paralyzed woman with holy oil, ibid. He heals a demon-possessed boy with oil and blessed water, ibid. He courageously resists vainglory, ibid. He imposes a wondrous burden upon himself, tormenting the flesh that torments him, ibid. With spittle he gives sight to a hyena’s cub, 725. The hyena brings him a skin as a gift, ibid. He adjures the hyena not to devour the poor men’s sheep thereafter, ibid. The hyena assents and nods its head, ibid. After baptism he does not spit upon the ground for sixty years, ibid. His appearance, ibid. When Palladius was tempted to depart because he sat idle in his cell, Macarius suggests that he reply that he guarded the walls of his cell for God’s sake, 725. He sees Mark receiving communion from an angel at the altar, ibid.

Macarius tests two luxurious young men, 528, 651. Macarius allows himself to be regarded as a fornicator, 515, 623. When the calumny is exposed, he flees to Scetis so that he will not be honored, 516, 624. Macarius raises a dead man so that he may indicate where he had been buried, 650. Macarius is neither satisfied with bread nor water nor sleep for twenty years, 660. When praised, Macarius remains silent; when despised, he speaks words of edification, 669. Macarius disciplines himself by abstaining from water for one cup of wine, 569. Macarius comforts a thirsty man with shade, 659. Macarius is miraculously transported across the river, 649. Macarius, priest and superintendent of the Ptochotrophium, by remarkable cunning drew a virgin away from avarice, 712. He lived to the age of one hundred, ibid. Macarius the younger enters solitude because of an involuntary killing, 718, 948. He remains three years in the desert without a roof, ibid. He spits at demons, ibid. Macarius devoted himself to a monastic substitute, 775.

— Macarius, archbishop of Jerusalem, 866.

Macedonius lives on mountain summits, 828. For forty-five years he lives standing in a pit under the open sky, ibid. His food is barley soaked in water, ibid. Unknowingly he is enrolled in the priesthood by Flavian, bishop of Antioch, 829. Great simplicity and purity of spirit are found in him, 829. He establishes a spiritual “hunt” for God, ibid. He is honored by the emperor’s commanders, ibid. He arranges that the emperor be told that living statues are superior to dead ones, ibid. He heals a woman of gluttony, 830. He drives out a demon brought in by magical arts through a girl, ibid. He silences a demon accusing several people, 830. He orders the chief culprits to be named, 830. He heals a madwoman by giving her a taste of water blessed with the sign of the cross, ibid. He is illumined by heavenly fire, ibid. He foretells something to Lupicianus by a prophetic gift, 831. He obtains a child for Macrius and Theodoretus, ibid. Blessed water averts the danger of miscarriage, 831. His exhortation to Theodoretus, ibid. He is buried near Aphraates and Theodosius, ibid.

Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, is driven into exile by Anastasius, 872.

Maches sleeps through slanders and idle words, 550. He burns unread the letters of his parents and friends so that he will not be distracted by them, ibid.

Macnus abstains from bread and wine, 866.

Maesymas, village priest, 832. Always content with a single tunic, ibid. Wonderfully hospitable, ibid. Always abounding in grain and oil, ibid. Famous for miracles, ibid. He heals a boy brought to the base of the altar, ibid. He renders immobile the chariot of one who despises him, 832. When asked, he releases it by his prayers, ibid.

Mafortes, the same as palliola, 543.

Magicians are driven out of Egypt, 340. Theudas burns magical books, 321.

Magistrianus, a handsome young man, preserves a virgin, 781. He becomes a martyr, ibid.

Magna exercises restraint in marriage, 776. Severe in appearance and respected by bishops, ibid. Generous toward the poor, ibid.

The magnanimity of Isidore, who always humbles himself and replies to demons: “Even if I am sent into torments, nevertheless I find you beneath me,” 669.

The greatness of God’s benefits, 280.

One must yield to elders and contemporaries, 628.

He who hates sins and loves everyone detests evils, 519.

Evils are to be attributed to us, good things to God, 668.

Nothing should be done with an evil purpose, even if it has the appearance of good, 766.

He is beautifully taught to suffocate the seeds of evil thoughts, 578.

Malchus and his fellow-servant mount the master’s camels, 95. They come to the Roman camp, ibid. He joins the monks again, ibid.

An amorous magical spell, 156.

Adolius awakens the brothers with a hammer, 769.

Observance of the commandments is necessary if one is to ascend to God, 245. Observance of the commandments is the guardianship of ourselves, 638.

Sol does not see a certain monk eating, 539, 569.

In the morning one should think about every virtue, 162. In the morning one’s resolutions should be renewed, 683, 684. God should be prayed to in the morning, 684.

A Manichaean priest is converted by the charity of an old man, 616. The Manichaeans are refuted concerning the two principles, 286.

Sinners should be gently admonished to repentance, 601.

Gentleness is a terror to demons, 513.

Saint John the Almsgiver beautifully commends gentleness toward servants, 195. The gentleness of John the Almsgiver toward an impostor seeking alms, 196. The same man orders that a poor person who had abused him be given as much as he wished to take, 198, 199. Apollonius converts the abusive Philemon, 476. Apollonius restores a distressed monk [Col. LIV] who was hastening back to the world to a sounder mind, 573. The shepherd prescribes repentance for one who has fallen, 601. The wonderful gentleness of Abbot Be, 746. Gelasia forgives an injury, 780.

Saint John the Almsgiver persuades an angry ruler to be gentle, 199. By gentleness Anus converts robbers, 752.

Gentleness. See Kindness, Forgetfulness of injuries, and Tranquility.

The hands of those wishing to kill Conon become stiff, 866. The same happens to a barbarian who attempts to kill Addas, 881. The same happens to the shepherd preparing to hurl a weapon at Acepsimas, 833.

Marana and Cyra, natives of Beroea, live under the open sky, 855. They are covered by a veil, 856. For forty-two years they carry heavy iron on their necks, loins, and hands, ibid. They patiently endure the harshness of the weather, ibid. They imitate the fasts of Moses and Daniel, ibid. They travel to Jerusalem, ibid. Likewise to Saint Thecla, ibid.

Marcellus remains thirty-five years in Scetis so that he will not receive a crown in the city, 908. The sayings and Life of Marcellus of Scetis, 908.

Marcianus, a nobleman from Cyrus, chooses solitude and shuts himself, with his small body, into a narrow cell, 806. He prays and reads the Scriptures, 806. His manner of life, ibid. Never satisfied, always hungry and always thirsty, 806. He builds two monasteries, ibid. His head is miraculously overshadowed by light, 807. A flask of oil is brought to his cell so that it may receive virtue, 807. He heals a demoniac by his prayers even when absent, ibid. Bishops gather around him, 808. Avitus visits him, 808. They celebrate the office of None together, ibid. Although absent in body, they see one another in spirit as well, ibid. He does not allow his sister to appear before him, 809. He refuses an alms from his sister’s sons because it was given out of regard for kinship, ibid. He attacks Arius, Sabellius, the Euchites, and the Manichaeans, ibid. Zealous for ecclesiastical decrees, ibid. He converts Abraames to celebrate Easter according to the custom of the Church, 809. While he is alive, oratories are erected for him, ibid. He strives to keep his burial place unknown, ibid. His relics are honorably preserved, 809.

Marcianus, the uncle of Eusebius, 810. He leads Eusebius and his brother to the monastic life, 811.

The Marcionites worshipped a serpent, 635.

Mark foretold his own death, 638. His remarkable obedience, 521, 617, 618. Mark was accustomed to receive the Eucharist from the hands of an angel, 725. He knows the Old and New Testaments by heart, ibid. His virtues, ibid. He disputes with himself and with the devil; in everything he humbles himself, ibid. Mark fasts for weeks, 865.

The sea is sweetened by the prayer of Besarion, 532. Two monks walk on foot across the Red Sea, 898.

The Blessed Virgin Mary appears to Cyriacus together with John the Baptist and the Evangelist, 878. The Blessed Virgin Mary refuses to enter Cyriacus’ cell because of Nestorius’ books, ibid. A certain boy chooses the Blessed Virgin Mary over money, 166. God provides for him in a remarkable manner, ibid. The Blessed Virgin Mary promptly aids Mary of Egypt, 389. Image of the Blessed Virgin Mary. See Image. A wife commended to the Blessed Virgin Mary by her husband when he is setting out elsewhere is preserved from death together with her daughter, 882.

Mary, Abraham’s niece, at the age of seven learns the Psalter and the Scriptures, 368. She lives with her uncle for twenty years, 369. The demon arms itself against her, ibid. She is violated by a monk, ibid. She mourns her sin privately, ibid. She leaves [Col. LV] her uncle and hires herself out to a stablekeeper, 369. She lives as a prostitute for two years, 370. Dressed as a prostitute, she appears unknowingly before her uncle Abraham, 370. She is moved to compunction, ibid. She returns with her uncle Abraham to the cell, 372. Shut up in the cell, she wears herself out in acts of repentance, ibid. God shows that her repentance is acceptable by granting her the gift of healing, 372. After completing five years of repentance, she dies, ibid.

Mary of Egypt, 382. Found by Abbot Zosimas in the desert, she flees, 384. She addresses Zosimas by name, although she had never seen him before, 385. They ask one another’s blessing, ibid. Taught by God, she knows that Zosimas is a priest, ibid. When adjured, she blesses him first, 385. They ask one another’s prayers, ibid. She prays suspended in the air, ibid. She corrects Zosimas when he suspects that she is a spirit, 385. She makes the sign of the cross, ibid. She recounts her former life to Zosimas, 386. Devoted to lust, she sails to Jerusalem, 386. She reviews her deeds on the ship, ibid. Even in Jerusalem she defiles herself with lusts, 387. Miraculously repelled, she is not admitted into the temple, 387. Understanding that her crimes prevent her from seeing the holy cross, she is moved to compunction, 387. She implores the intercession of the most blessed Virgin Mary, ibid. She resolves to amend her life, ibid. Through the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary she enters the temple freely, ibid. She kisses the pavement of the temple, 388. She gives thanks to the Mother of God, ibid. A voice sent from heaven teaches her what she must do, ibid. She miraculously receives three coins with which to buy provisions, 388. She enters the church of Saint John the Baptist near the Jordan and receives communion there, ibid. She spends forty-seven years in solitude, 388. For seventeen years she lives on three loaves of bread, ibid. She struggles with memories of her former luxury, ibid. She resists the memory of the origin of her conversion, 389. She continually experiences the prompt aid of the Blessed Mary, ibid. She is nourished by herbs, ibid. She is tormented by heat and cold, ibid. For forty-seven years she sees neither a human being nor an animal, 389. Alive and surviving, she wishes to remain hidden, ibid. She asks that the life-giving sacraments be brought to her honorably in a sacred vessel, ibid. She knows the secrets of the monastery from a distance, 390. Having made the sign of the cross, she walks upon the waters of the Jordan, 390. At the point of death she receives the most holy Eucharist, ibid. Zosimas finds her body lifeless, 391. A lion prepares her grave, 391.

Mary the prostitute approaches old men reading the Gospel, 869. She is converted from a shameful life to a better one, ibid.

Mary, the child-killer, is carried by ship, but the ship does not advance, 882. When she is thrown into a small boat and drowned, the ship completes its course, 883.

Mary of the lake, 712, 945.

Marina the virgin, 393. Her father is concerned for her salvation, ibid. Changing her clothing and name to Marinus, she enters a monastery of men, ibid. She is instructed by her father, ibid. Her father dies, 393. She is accused of having committed fornication with the daughter of an innkeeper, ibid. She acknowledges as though committed by herself the sin she had not committed, ibid. She is expelled from the monastery and repents at the gate, ibid. She is admitted into the monastery again, 394. She performs the most menial services, ibid. She dies, and her sex is discovered, 394. The abbot, because he had afflicted her unjustly, afflicts himself, ibid. Her calumniator, a fornicating woman, is seized by a demon, ibid. At Marina’s body the same woman is freed, ibid. Her holiness is confirmed by miracles, ibid.

Bishop Nonnus, formerly a monk of Tabennesi, comes to the Synod of Antioch, 376. He takes from a vice the spur toward virtue when he sees Pelagia, 377. He incites himself toward the beauty of the soul by contemplating Pelagia’s bodily beauty, 377. He foresees the conversion of the prostitute Pelagia, [Col. LX] 377. The people are pierced with compunction by his sermon, ibid. His reply to Pelagia’s letter, 378. He refuses to see Pelagia alone, ibid. He baptizes and confirms the converted Pelagia and refreshes her with the Eucharist, 378, 379. He rejoices at Pelagia’s conversion, drinks wine, and dines more generously, 379. He converts 30,000 Saracens, ibid. He does not allow anything acquired through disgraceful means to be transferred into the church, 379.
