The difference between the New and the Old Law, 266.

Remembrance of the last things, 565, 566, 609.

A three-year novitiate under Pachomius, 736.

The fervor of the novitiate must always be preserved, 683.

A novice complains to Pachomius that the porridge is uncooked, 131.

Novilius is admonished and excellently guided, 548, 549.

On entering the order, a novice should prepare himself for patience by saying, “I and the ass are one,” 624.

In the desert an angel, in the form of an eagle, leads a novice monk to a place filled with provisions, 587.

An angel consoles a patient novice, 632.

What the novices did according to the rule of Pachomius, 120.

Novices ought to return to the condition of children, 543.

In what novices ought especially to labor, 453.

Novices are tested by being commanded to do improper things, 599.

Novices sometimes serve as guides in virtue even to the old, 632.

The testing of novices before and after entry, 511, 515, 517. They renounce money, 546. They lay aside their clothing, ibid. Along with secular clothing, pride must also be laid aside, ibid. The clothing of novices is kept separately, 545. They live under the discipline of an elder, ibid. They serve guests, ibid. They are taught to renounce their own will, ibid. They receive the commands of their superiors as those of God, ibid. Readiness for work, ibid. No private property, 546.

Abbot Nupli flees from the sight of his mother, 523.

Saint Macarius flees from a wedding on the very night of the wedding, 228.

## O
Obedient Paphnutius drinks wine at a robber’s bidding and wins him and his companions over, 522, 633. The obedient person is a true confessor, and why, 618. The obedient person attends only to his superior’s command, 618. By his superior’s prayer, the obedient person escapes the danger of fornication, 619. The obedient person, in difficult circumstances, is not harmed by crocodiles, 619. The obedient person raises the dead, ibid. The obedient person is preferred to the solitary, 620. The perfect obedient person compares himself to a dog, 627. The order of the obedient is pre-eminent, 520. Alexander’s scrupulous obedience, 617. Athre, who, when summoned by Hor, left the knife in the fish he was gutting, 625. Euphrasia’s obedience in difficult circumstances, 355. John’s obedience: for a whole year he watered a dry piece of wood with water fetched from far away, 546. The same: his attempt over a long period to move a huge stone, 547. John, who tied up a lioness and brought her to the abbot, 502, 617. Mark, who left a letter unfinished, 521, 617, 618. Mutius, who threw his son into a river, 547. Paphnutius, who drank wine offered by robbers, 522, 633. Simeon’s obedience in obeying the bishop who advised that the chain be released, 850.

Obedience is the most eminent of all virtues, 146. Obedience toward superiors is taught by Posthumius, 236. Likewise toward equals, 236. The obedience [Col. LXI] of monks, 370. Obedience is the short road to perfection, 562. Obedience, superior to many virtues, raises the dead, 521. Obedience is the first virtue of monks, 538, 541. Obedience is taught in monasteries, 545. Blind obedience is pleasing to God, 547. Obedience victorious in war, 584. Obedience is preferred to other virtues because it casts down the will, 618. Obedience obtains everything from God, 618. It is preferred to continence, and why, ibid. Obedience to the Scriptures is required, ibid. Obedience is required of novices, 619. Obedience is necessary for a monk, 730. It is attacked in the manner of our heretics, 734. Neglect of obedience is punished in Saint Astion by a shameful thought, 215. By obedience a dry branch, watered in the third year, blossomed, 512, 617. The fruit of obedience is prophecy, 546. The aureole of obedience, 620. Eulogies of obedience, ibid. Pachomius strongly urges obedience, 122. Likewise Poemen, 522. Departing in obedience, he is rescued from the danger of fornication, 521. Out of obedience he enters a burning oven and emerges unharmed, 54. Out of obedience, when ordered to put his son into the furnace, he preserves him unharmed, 609, 620. Wishing to obey the abbot, he is ready to throw his own son into the river, 547, 618.

Offering of candles and incense, 353. The offering of sacrifice belongs only to the just, 528. Candida makes the loaves of the offering, 780. The Holy Spirit was once seen at the time of the offering, 867. A brother reciting the words of the offering over the bread sanctifies it wondrously, 867. Only one ordained should recite the words of the offering, 868. The form of the offering, corresponding to right faith, should be spoken, 927. Arsenius asks that an offering be made for the dead, 524.

Forgetfulness of bodily refreshment through spiritual conversation, 493, 571. Forgetfulness of sins, Satan’s forerunner, 612. Why forgetfulness of injuries is necessary, 681. The service of charity is praiseworthy, 672, 673. Observance of the commandments, in addition to faith, is necessary for ascending to God, 245. Observance of the commandments, our protection, 638. Those possessed by demons are not to be despised, 555. “Possessed.” See Demoniac. Obsis, a disciple of Pachomius, 121. Obstinacy is taught by the likeness of those who refuse to look at salt, 277. The slanderer eats the flesh of the brothers, 571.

The hands of those wishing to kill Conon grow stiff; he loosens them by his prayers, 856. The hand of one attempting to kill Addan grows stiff; he likewise restores it, 863. A Saracen attempting to kill the aged monk Antony is swallowed up by the earth, 891. The killer of a monk is punished by death from God, 867. Sighs should be secret, 670. Good works should be concealed, 592. The eyes are more trustworthy than the ears, 741. So that his eyes might not wander, Eusebius lowered his head with an iron collar, 911. What the guarding of the eyes should be for a perfect monk, 572. The guarding of the eyes practiced by Elladius, who for twenty years did not look upward toward the roof of his cell, 568. The guarding of the eyes practiced by Alexander when he went to Alexandria and looked at no one except the bishop, 571. The guarding of the eyes practiced by Sarah for sixty-five years, 587. The guarding of the eyes practiced by Silvanus, who covered his face so as not to see the trees he was watering, 510. See Continence of the eyes. A consecrated virgin tears out her eyes because a young man said that he had been chosen by them, 878.

The fragrance of abstinence is exceedingly sweet, 370. The dead body of a Stylite gives off a fragrance, 174. Arsenius teaches that perfumes should be corrected by stench, 568.

The Office of the Ninth Hour, 808. The Office of Burial, 913.

Simeon Stylites’ blessed oil is held by the queen of the Persians as a gift of the greatest value, 814. With sacred oil Amun restores a mentally deranged boy to himself, 752. Aphraates heals the emperor’s horse, 821. He restrains sorcery, ibid. Benjamin heals the sick, 716. Epictetus heals a fifteen-year-old girl, 211. Eugenia cures Melanthia of quartan fever, 343. John heals the sick, 739. He restores a woman’s sight, ibid. He drives away tertian fever, 741. Macarius of Alexandria cures a woman of paralysis, 724. Paul heals the sick, 555. Macarius of Alexandria frees a demoniac boy with holy oil and blessed water, 724.

Olympias, of noble birth, 779. A virgin in marriage, ibid. Generous in almsgiving, ibid. Flourishing in body and mind in complete humility, ibid. She honors the clergy, ibid. She practices various works of mercy, 780. She wears shabby clothing, ibid. She is dissolved in tears, ibid. A precious vessel of the Holy Spirit, ibid. Counted among the confessors, ibid.

Olympius the abbot teaches flight from heretics and continence of tongue and stomach, 866. Olympius endures present evils with a view to eternal things, 904. Complete renunciation is approved by Arsenius, 596.

A wild ass serves as guide on the road for Saint Macarius of Rome, 229. It carries Helenus’s burden, 370, 754. One must gradually become accustomed to burdens, 121.

Onuphrius the hermit, 99. Paphnutius is the author of his Life, ibid. Completely shaggy, he terrifies Paphnutius, 99. Paphnutius recognizes him through divine revelation, 100. He had seen no one for seventy years, ibid. Which monastery he belonged to, ibid. He is urged toward the desert by the example of Elijah and the Baptist, 100. He is led by his guardian angel, 101. He asks the hermit’s blessing, ibid. He is received with the kiss of peace, ibid. He is led into the interior of the desert, ibid. His guide dies, 102. His prayer to Paphnutius, ibid. Every day he receives bread and water from an angel, ibid. On Sunday he receives communion from an angel together with the other hermits, 102. They are carried up into heaven in a vision, ibid. He prays with Paphnutius, 102. He eats with him, ibid. He obtains from God that whoever offers sacrifice in his memory may be freed from every temptation, 103. As he is dying, he is surrounded by light, 103. He is carried into heaven to the singing of angels, ibid. His cave and palm trees collapse, ibid. He is buried, ibid. He died on 11 June, ibid.

Where the laborer may make progress, 605. Paul imposes daily tasks and a daily quota upon himself, 551. Antony is shown that work must be joined to prayer, 584. Three works acceptable to God, 563. Three operations of the soul, ibid. Antony works with his hands, 36. Even the elect must work in order to guard themselves, 521, 678. What must be done by those who hear the sermon, 566. A monk must work with his hands, 583. John the Dwarf is taught to work when he wished to be an angel, 509, 598. The worker is attacked by one demon, while the idle are assaulted by many, 551. John works with his mind fixed on God, 609. One who works for God is compared to a bee making honey, 679. Cheremon dies while at work, 765. God helps those who work, 905. Three kinds of people who work badly, and Arsenius’s vision concerning them, 506, 635, 681. The industrious Macarius, 585.

One who trusts too much in his own opinion is rarely converted to the Lord, 605. It is best to possess nothing, 582. What the monk’s work is, 562. What the monk’s work is not, 601. The principal work of the soul, and the work of the hands as an accessory, 598. What the work of the soul and of the hands is, 672. Constancy in work in the monasteries, 545. What we say must first be performed in deed, 592. What is said with the mouth must be fulfilled in deed, 593, 607. Doctrines must be fulfilled in deed, not preserved on paper, 608. The kingdom of God is acquired by work, not by memory or books, 682. External works, 117. Good works are necessary in addition to baptism, 265. Works performed out of a desire for human praise lack their reward, 270. Three good works are required after baptism, 562. Good works drive away the devil, 527. Works, not words, are necessary, 604. The good works of two married people, 652. Good works are the best teaching, not words, 705. Theodosius commends work with the hands, 825. The reward of works on the Day of Judgment, 261. The same is asserted from the story of Lazarus and the Rich Man, ibid.; from the parable of the king who made a wedding feast for his son, 262; from the parable of the ten virgins, ibid.; from the Scripture of the New Testament, 262; from the prophets, ibid. The necessity of manual work is asserted by Paul, 551. Similar merits in different works, 601. The rewards of good works and the punishments of evil ones, 646. They are most beautifully established by example and vision, 647.

Or, or Or the broom-maker, father of a thousand monasteries, 714. What his food was, ibid. An angelic apparition, with ten thousand destined to be saved through him, ibid. He himself builds cells, 715. He knows by divine revelation a brother’s deception, ibid. What is especially remarkable in him, ibid. and 916. Or. See Hor.

To pray is the greatest labor, 613. Posthumius prays continually, 233, 234, 235. Josaphat prays with outstretched hands, 329. Zosimas prays at fixed hours, 384. Arsenius prays from sunset until dawn, 531. A certain person prays while eating, 613. Christopher prays one hundred times at night on bended knees, 892. The parents of martyrs pray at the place of the martyrs, 222. Macarius teaches how one should pray, 531. Lucius always teaches how one should pray, 531, 614. One should always pray or sing psalms, 613. One should pray with a purified soul, because nothing can be seen in muddy water, 614. Macarius’s manner of praying, ibid. One who prays for another is not always heard, 495, 496, 575. Fire comes forth from the mouths of those who pray, 529.

Abraham’s prayer for the conversion of the Gentiles, 146. Add: he restores to health the hand of Barbarus, which had stiffened when he attempted to kill himself, 881. He frees Adelphus’s demoniac, 901. Apollo makes those worshiping an idol, together with their god, immobile, 749. He releases them, ibid. Antony overcomes the devil, 37. Astion and Epictetus pray even for their enemies, 218. Barlaam prays to God for Josaphat, 336. Basil heals a leper, 159. Besarion makes seawater sweet, 532. Besarion prays continually for fourteen days with his hands extended toward heaven, 613. Cyriacus obtains a cloud for a weary and overheated man, 877. He makes that same man invisible to the friends from whom he is fleeing, ibid. David extinguishes fire, 918. Jacob of Nisibis makes the enemies’ efforts fruitless, 900. John releases an enchanted ship, 886. Josaphat prays for his father’s soul, 327. The same, to God, 336. [Col. LXIII] Innocentius’s prayer reveals a theft, 768. Julian’s prayer drives away fever, 799. A certain soldier repeats his prayer seven times a day, 882. He obtains miraculous rain for a certain devout sailor, ibid. Nicholas saves one whom the Saracens are attempting to kill, 909. Pachomius prays for the evil monks who afflict him, 126. The same, remonstrating with God, 132. The same cures a scorpion’s sting, 136. Pior remedies the barrenness of a well, 765. Posthumius’s prayer drives away hosts of demons, 238. Publius stops Julian’s emissary devil, 650. An old man obtains rain, 614. Simeon Stylites obtains water, 173. Suri obtains a ship and a favorable wind, 753. The noble youth Theodore prays to God, 124. Theodosius obtains a spring from a rock, 885. Theon makes robbers immobile, 746. Zacchaeus averts plague from Caesarea, 902. Zebina’s continual prayer, 845.

Prayer with hands raised toward heaven, 114, 613, 853. Prayer with the hands extended in the form of a cross, 118. Prayer at the tombs of martyrs, 219. Prayer customarily made toward the East, 233. Posthumius commends frequent prayer, 236. Constant prayer quickly perfects the mind, 614. What true prayer should be said, 289. Prayer is conversation with God, 288, 811. A prelude to future blessedness, ibid. It is effective against the demon, 149, 910. A remedy against carnal temptations, 324, 316. It extinguishes shameful thoughts as water extinguishes fire, 531. It should be used against phantoms, 531, 637, 745. It quickly corrects the mind, 614. Medicine for the sick person on the way of God, 659. It overcomes temptations, 682. It makes armed men immobile, 736. It drives away barrenness, 831. Prayer without a good life is like a barren ear of grain, 766. What the “feathers” of prayer are, 289. The fervor of prayer makes one fiery, 613. The power of prayer binds and releases a slanderous woman in the pains of childbirth, 779. Anger is an impediment to prayer, 289. Jacob teaches and proves by many parables that interruption of prayer must be avoided, 844. Things that distract prayer must be driven away, 613. The devil tries to hinder prayer, ibid. By prayer Sisoes is carried into ecstasy, 614. John teaches by the likeness of climbing trees that temptations must be overcome through prayer, 531. By prayer the water of a well rises, 502, 651. By prayer and a seven-day fast, Macarius of Egypt drives out a gluttonous demon, 721. Through Theodore’s prayer and the sign of the cross, seawater becomes sweet, 914.

The prayers of Antony, 38. The prayers of the saints, 103. Short but more frequent prayers are praised, 544. Simeon Stylites offers very many prayers to God every day, 853. A virgin pours forth seven hundred prayers every day, 727. One hundred prayers by a person occupied with public affairs are no less valuable than three hundred by one doing nothing else, ibid. The prayers of the saints are a common remedy for every illness, 834. Simeon Stylites’ stationing himself with his hands extended toward heaven for entire nights on feast days, 833. Prayers lessen punishments, 874. The number of daily prayers prescribed to Pachomius and his monks by an angel, 120. Macarius says twenty-four prayers while going and the same number while returning, 720. Paul of Pherme recites three hundred prayers and uses the same number of pebbles, 727. Josaphat devotes himself to prayers, 311.

The prayer of King Abenner to the monk, 244, 245. Barlaam’s final prayer to Josaphat, 292. Josaphat’s prayer to his people, 328. The exhortatory prayer of the hermit Abraham to a fallen woman, 371. An oratory built over the relics of the saints, 888. Maro makes an oratory from a shrine of demons, 833.

The monk Abraham is ordained priest by the laying on of the bishop’s hand, 146. Three honorable orders in the sight of God, 562. Four orders of merit, 620. Orentus teaches the overthrow of Sina by means of an inverted cloak, 899.

Origen lodges with a virgin for two years, 780, 781. His books suffer controversy, 537. They are said to have been corrupted by heretics, ibid. Where he is good, no one has a better judgment; where he is bad, no one has a worse, ibid. He holds that the devil will at some time be redeemed, 537, 538. Pachomius announces eternal punishments to those who read Origen, 132. The origin of the oracles of demons, 44. Melania turns secular ornaments into ornaments of the Church, 774. Excessive adornment of clothing is censured by a beautiful comparison, 823. The adornment of the church moves the Gentiles, 146.

Orsesius, appointed superior after Petronius, 138. The mouth is the door of the heart, 610. The monk’s pilgrimage restrains the mouth, 571. Agiodulus raises a dead man so that he may give the kiss of peace, 865.

Idleness must be avoided, 544, 551, 607, 666, 678, 715. Antony is shown the flight from idleness, 584. The flight from idleness in monasteries, 545. Euphraxia is tempted while idle, 355. The idle person is harassed by many demons, while the worker is harassed by one, 551. The idle man is a fruitless tree, 605. An idle word is banished from Pachomius’s congregation, 506.

The city of Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid: integrity in the faith, ibid. Likewise hospitality, ibid. In it there are twenty thousand virgins and ten thousand monks, ibid.

Pachomius is converted from paganism to Christianity, 114. In his presence the demon falls silent, ibid. He tastes and vomits out the wine of the libation, ibid. He becomes a soldier, ibid. The charity of Christians attracts him, ibid. He prays with raised hands, ibid. He makes a vow, ibid. He loves chastity, ibid. He is discharged from military service, ibid. He is catechized, ibid. He is baptized, ibid. He visits the anchorite Palaemon, 115. He asks to become a monk, ibid. He is received, ibid. He exercises himself in various virtues, 116. He is divinely ordered to build a monastery, ibid. He receives the Rule from an angel, ibid. He reveals the revelation to Palaemon, 117. He goes with him to Tabennesi, ibid. He enters into an inseparable partnership with him, 117. From the surplus of his work he assists the poor, ibid. He uses only one garment, ibid. To humble his body he clothes himself in a hair shirt, ibid. Sitting in the middle of the cell, he takes a brief sleep, ibid. He enlarges the monastery, 117, 118. When reproved by a brother, he restrains himself meekly, 118. Agitated by various movements of the soul, he humbles himself before the Lord, ibid. Before teaching others, he desires to have mastered the passions of the flesh, ibid. He prays with his hands spread in the form of a cross, 118. He accompanies his brother’s funeral vigil with psalms and hymns, ibid. The memory of eternal punishments drives away harmful thoughts, ibid. Demons attempt to overthrow his dwelling, 119. He drives them away with prayers and the sign of the cross, ibid. The demons appear to him in the form of women, 119. He is beaten by the devil, ibid. He is strengthened by the monk Apollo, ibid. He celebrates Apollo’s funeral with psalms, hymns, and songs, ibid. He treads upon serpents unharmed, 120. With the help of crocodiles he crosses rivers, ibid. He asks God for sleeplessness, ibid. He is divinely called to be abbot, 120, 736. An angel appears to him and gives him the monastery’s Rule, ibid. He marks the monks’ hoods with a purple cross, 736. What his method of receiving guests was, [Col. LXIV] ibid. His way of eating and working, 120, 736. His manner of praying, 120, ibid. Likewise his manner of receiving Holy Communion, ibid. He diligently warns his monks about three things, 121. He serves the brothers, ibid. He commends psalms and the Gospel to his monks, ibid. His disciples, 121. He does not allow his priests to be ordained, 122. By a beautiful comparison he declares how harmful ambition is to monks, ibid. He orders priests to be held in honor, ibid. He professes that he sees Christ in them, 123. He entrusts the judgment of offenders to the ordinary authority, ibid. His charity toward everyone, 122. His prudence in governing, ibid. He strongly urges obedience, ibid. He takes the place of others in their duties, ibid. His zeal for souls, 122, 123. He performs the office of reader, 123. He receives Saint Athanasius with psalms and hymns, ibid. His humility, ibid. His judgment concerning Athanasius, ibid. He detests all heretics, and especially Origen, 123. He submerges Origen’s books in water, ibid. He avoids detractors, ibid. He refuses to see his sister, ibid. He orders a monastery to be built for his sister and appoints an old man named Peter as visitor, 124. He writes a Rule for the same monastery, ibid. He kindly receives the noble youth Theodore after his conversion, 125. He prays for unruly monks, 126. The presbyter Dionysius reproves him because he received guests separately from the others, 126. He gives the same man an account of his actions, ibid. A woman suffering from hemorrhage is healed by touching his hood, 127. By his prudence he saves a monk who desired the clerical state, ibid. He knows the hidden sins of others, 127. With blessed oil he frees from a demon a girl who had violated her vow, ibid. With blessed bread he frees a demoniac, 128. In all things he remains always the same and constant, ibid. He patiently bears it when God sometimes does not hear him, ibid. He brings Silvanus back to a better frame of mind, ibid. His testimony concerning Silvanus, 129. He is summoned by Bishop Varo of Panos to build monasteries in his diocese, ibid. He visits the monasteries, ibid. He orders the splendid garments of a deceased brother to be burned, and why, ibid. He sees the soul of another being carried into heaven by angels, 130. He shines with the gift of prophecy, 130. He is honorably received by Bishop Varo and builds monasteries, ibid. He reproves the cook for excessive and misplaced frugality, 131. He orders mats made through disobedience to be burned, ibid. From the stench of present things he detects heresy, ibid. He announces the punishments of hell to those who read Origen and adhere to him, 132. He is divinely informed about the condition of his monks, ibid. He remonstrates with God in prayer, ibid. Throughout the whole period of his conversion, he was never satiated by any creature, 132. He is lifted from the earth by angels, 133. The continuance of his posterity is promised by the Lord, ibid. His sermon exhorting his monks to perseverance and the pursuit of virtue, 133, 134. His sermon to his monks on perseverance, 133, 134. He returns to Tabennesi, 134. He orders the offering of bread to be made in silence, ibid. While absent, he recognizes a violation of silence, ibid. Reproved by a boy, he learns to weave mats, ibid. By the sign of the cross he drives away a demon appearing to him in the form of Christ, 135. He questions a demon appearing in the form of a very beautiful woman, ibid. He sees the glory of the Lord with bodily eyes, ibid. In the name of Christ he drives away a crowd of demons, 136. By his prayers he heals someone struck by a scorpion, ibid. He falls ill, 137. His face is always cheerful, ibid. He warns that the company of heretics must be avoided, ibid. He appoints Petronius as his successor in the superior office, ibid. As he is dying, he fortifies himself with the sign of the cross, 138. He dies after seeing an angel, [Col. LXV] ibid. His disciples celebrate his funeral with vigils, psalms, and hymns, ibid. In his monasteries there were seven thousand men, 737. Pachomius recognizes Macarius miraculously, 723.

Pachomius, a disciple of Pachomius, 121. Pachon reveals the demons’ extraordinary temptations, 732. Attacked by the spirit of fornication, he despairs, ibid. Hyenas lick him all around without harming him, 731. The spirit of fornication tempts him in the form of an Ethiopian woman, ibid.

The pact of partnership between Pachomius and Palaemon, 117. Paeesius and Isaiah, brothers of Apollo, aspire to solitude, 717, 942. They adopt different ways of life, 717. After their death there is a dispute over their blessedness because of their different ways of life, ibid.

Palaemon the hermit, stern in appearance, 115. His abstinence, vigils, and prayers, ibid. At first he refuses to receive Pachomius, who aspires to monastic life, but later consecrates him in the monastic habit, ibid. He teaches that sleepiness should be driven away by exercise, 115. In memory of Christ’s Passion he abstains from more sumptuous foods at Easter, ibid. He goes with Pachomius to Tabennesi, 117. He enters into an inseparable partnership with him, ibid. He is seized by illness, ibid. He does not relax anything of his former abstinence, ibid. He strengthens himself by the example of the martyrs, ibid. He dies, 117.

The school of the hermits, 100.

What Palladius the Galatian was like, 704. His humility, ibid. From whom he learned what he writes, 705. He was held by a desire to visit pious men, 707. He goes to Alexandria, 709. He is entrusted to Theodore for instruction, ibid. He consults Macarius about his thoughts and is taught to guard the walls for God’s sake, 725. He reveals the temptations of the flesh to Pachon, 732. He hastens to John, 740. Impatient of delay, he prepares a habit, ibid. He says that he is a “culinary bishop,” 740. He is made bishop in Bithynia, ibid. He slanders Saint Jerome, 775. His saying, 603. The dangers of his pilgrimage, 782. His companion possesses extraordinary virtues, ibid. He struggles with a demon, ibid. He is fed by an angel, ibid. He sympathizes with the wretched, 782.

Another Palladius, familiar with Saint Simeon, 818. His dwelling, fasting, and prayer, ibid. He raises a dead man so that he may declare the murderer whose crime had been falsely attributed to an innocent man, ibid. His tomb is famous for healings, ibid.

Palladius the abbot’s exhortations to patience, 882. His conversion, resulting from a vision of fire appearing divinely above the cell of the old man David, 881.

What the use of little cloaks among Egyptian monks was like, 543. Palm trees bearing fruit twelve times a year, 102.

Pambo the abbot, out of charity, gives his camel to another, 521. Pambo teaches that peace with one’s neighbor is the way of salvation, 602. Pambo, or Pammo, weeps because a theatrical woman had devoted more diligence to pleasing the world than he himself had devoted to pleasing God, 524, 566. From whom Pambo learned, 715, 946. He despises gold, ibid. He distributes gifts received among poor monks, 715, 940. He dies at the age of seventy, ibid. The words of the dying man: he had always been occupied, 715, 941. He declares that not even at death had he begun to live religiously, 716, 947. He deliberated before speaking, ibid. His dispute with Pior over hospitality, ibid.

Pammachius, praiseworthy in life and generous toward the poor, 399. Pammachius, a proconsul, renounces everything, 775.

Heaven-sent bread becomes inferior through the recipient’s remissness [the wording is uncertain], 744, 455. A demon recoils from blessed bread, 128. Candida makes the loaves of the offering, 780.

Paphnutius the monk and confessor, 50. Paphnutius, author of the Life of Saint Onuphrius, 99. While exploring the desert he undergoes many hardships, ibid. After consuming bread and water, he himself collapses, ibid. He is strengthened divinely, and an angel restores his strength, ibid. On seeing Onuphrius, he is terrified, ibid. He prays and eats food with him, 102. He is ordered to return to Egypt, 103. He buries Onuphrius, ibid.

Paphnutius of Alexandria obtains from God a daughter, Euphrosyne, 363. He commends her to the abbot’s prayers, ibid. Anxiously, he seeks his missing daughter, 365. He laments, ibid. He begs the abbot’s prayers, 366. He receives consolation from the abbot, ibid. Without knowing it, he is admitted to his daughter, ibid. He receives consolation, 366. He returns home happier, ibid. He visits Euphrosyne when she is ill, 367. His consternation when he recognizes his daughter, ibid. He becomes a monk and offers his possessions, ibid. He dies after ten years in the same monastery, ibid.

Paphnutius the abbot devotes himself to the conversion of Thais, a prostitute, 374. He converts her and encloses her in a small cell, ibid. He consults Abbot Antony about her, ibid. Paphnutius prays that it may be revealed to him whom he resembles, 756. He is equaled by a musician or flute-player, ibid. Likewise by a provincial governor or chief man of a district, 756. And also by an Alexandrian merchant, 757. He is summoned by an angel, 757. His soul is carried into heaven by angels, ibid.

Paphnutius Cephalas teaches that excessive reproach is harmful, 520. Taught by God, 765. He uses one garment for eighty years, ibid. Paphnutius, a disciple of Macarius, 725.

A Gospel parable establishing the twofold merits of good works, 262. Another parable demonstrating the folly of lovers of the world, 272. Another showing the vanity of the world, ibid. Another concerning good things sent ahead into heaven through almsgiving, 273. Another concerning one who embraces the religious life, 279. Another by which Barlaam dissuades Josaphat from accompanying him, 284. Another teaching us to care for our own affairs and not those of others, 658. Another beautifully describing a slanderer, 658. Another concerning a repentant soul, 659. Another teaching that prayer should not be interrupted, 844.

The earthly paradise, inaccessible, 228. In it the first man was placed by God, 155. Antony sees paradise and hell, 729.

Cosmas heals a paralytic, 872. One must always be prepared against thoughts of fornication, 574. Excessive frugality is reproved, 131.

The muleteer Pardus, because his mule killed a boy, repents extraordinarily, 891. He offers himself to be devoured by a lion, ibid. The lion spares him, ibid.

Epictetus teaches that parents should be honored, 213. The presbyter Bonosus catechizes Astion’s parents, 222. Vigilantius receives them, 219. Pior recoils from visiting his parents, 504.

Macarius teaches Palladius that “I guard the walls for Christ” should be the response to troubling thoughts, 723. Easter is the universal feast day of Christians, 115.

The passions do not die but are bound in the saints, 517, 597. Bodily passions must be restrained, 608, 660, 665. There are many bodily passions, 665. The origin of the passions is fourfold, 510. Remedies for the passions, [Col. LXVI] ibid. Poemen teaches that remedies for the passions should be sought, and that heavenly things should not be scrutinized, 527, 600. Cures for vicious passions, 598. Which passions must be overcome, 603. One intent upon God is not led by the passions, 609.

The feast of the Passion, 808.

Pastor the abbot says that there are three operations of the soul, 563. He advises that God must be served, ibid. He lists three operations pleasing to God, ibid. He shows who is free from this world, ibid. He refuses to see a judge, 593. He weeps when invited to food, 590. He grants nothing to the flesh but leaves everything to the law, ibid. He teaches that deeds must correspond to words, ibid. In this matter he compares the delinquent to a well, 601. He advises that the sins of others should be diminished and one’s own increased, 600. He behaves as a dead man, ibid. He scrutinizes humble and earthly things, not heavenly things, ibid. He is gentle in prescribing penance, ibid. Questioned about unclean and vain thoughts, he gives various answers, 601. He teaches how one should fast, ibid. Likewise, for what reason one should become angry, ibid. Likewise, that delinquents should not be forced into penance but aroused to it, ibid. He declares who is not a monk, ibid. He beautifully teaches that thoughts can be eluded rather than excluded, ibid. See Poemen.

An open door is not attacked, 612. By reciting the Lord’s Prayer three times in honor of Onuphrius, one is freed from every temptation, 103. A monk calls his father immortal, 562. Evagrius does likewise, 764. One must suffer for future glory, 102. To endure insult is a great thing, 629. The person who inflicts suffering gives the sufferer an opportunity for salvation, 668. An angel comforts a patient novice, 632. Pachomius patiently bears it when God sometimes does not hear him, 128. Marina patiently bears a false accusation of fornication, 393, 394. Macarius likewise, 515. Eustathius likewise, 777 and following. The person who looks upon another’s greater misery patiently bears his own, 591. The solitary Theodosius patiently bears having his cloak taken by robbers, 880.

The patience of Abban or Amman, varied and astonishing, 813. Abraham converts unbelievers, 835. The hermit Abraham converts Gentiles who do not care about his beatings, 146, 147. The patience of a certain youth in enduring insults, 513. Apollonius’s patience under curses, 758. Barnabas’s patience: he does not pull out a thorn lodged in his foot, 865. Benjamin’s patience while suffering from dropsy, 717. Besarion stands among thorns for forty nights while keeping vigil, 584. Eulogius cares for an elephantiasis sufferer for fifteen years, 673, 728. Euphraxia’s patience toward her rival, 356, 358. Eustathius’s patience in bearing a false accusation of fornication, 777, 778, 779. The patience of two brothers when their little garden was disturbed, 500. Gelasius’s patience in pretending not to notice a theft committed against him, 630. Jacob’s patience in enduring cold, 840. Saint John the Almsgiver’s patience in adversity, 194. The remarkable inner and outer patience of John the abbot, 514. John the younger of the Thebaid serves a difficult sick man for a long time, 523, 630, 673. Macarius assists a thief who was stripping his cell, 512. Marina, falsely accused of fornication, undergoes admirable penance, 393, 394. Maris does not change an unhealthy dwelling for thirty-seven years, 837. A monk slapped by a demoniac offers the other cheek, 622. A monk repeatedly approaches those by whom he has been injured, 631. Seven monks are tortured by Saracens, 530. Monks who, though ninety years old, trained themselves in the labors of youth, 813. A certain nun promptly serves an old man suffering from an incurable disease, 500. Moses’s patience under reproaches, 631. Myrogenes, suffering from dropsy, wishes to suffer from internal dropsy, 865. Olympius tolerates present evils with a view to eternal things, 904. Onuphrius’s marvelous patience in the desert, 102. Pachomius patiently bears his brother’s reproof, 118. The same man heals a theatrical monk who is failing, 128. Simeon Stylites’ varied and astonishing patience, 850. The same man’s patience in bearing a very grievous ulcer, 853. A certain sick old man says that he wishes to remain ill for thirty years, 572. A certain old man’s patience with bad-tasting food, 571, 572. Another old man complains that he has been abandoned because he had not been ill for one year, 599. An old man recalls thieves and offers them what they had left behind, 631, 926. An old man doubles his labors after a theft and kisses the thief’s hands, 632. An old man is compelled by his boy to fast for three days, 631. A certain old man sends gifts to those who slander him, 668. Several old men, 845. An old man pretends not to notice a theft committed against him, feeds the captured thief, and frees him from prison, 932. A blind old man drawing water, 912. The admirable Stephen, 733. Theodore and Zoilus, 913. Zacchaeus injures his hands through labor, 137.

Patience in illness is the greatest merit, 136. Patience receives a double reward, 195. Patience under injuries is the gate of heaven, 513, 639, 667. It is the way of salvation, 513, 624. Macarius tests the patience of two delicate young men, 528. Patience makes a dry branch, moistened for three years, grow green, 542. Patience and charity are commended among the monks of Scetis, 609. Patience is taught, 864. Patience makes one insensitive to injury like a stone, 668. Patience carries the living rather than the dead, ibid. Patience is taught by a fired stone thrown into a river, 669. A singular example of patience and gentleness: one who desires, for the sake of a modest virgin, someone whom she may train, 930. An example of patience. See Gentleness. The degrees of patience, 658, 659, 667, 668. Pachomius practices patience, 116. Macarius urges the thirsty man to patience because he enjoys shade, which many travelers and sailors lack, 659. A[.....]ub teaches us patience by means of a struck statue, 530, 622, 683. The man who committed a theft against Anastasius is pierced by Anastasius’s patience and humility, 503. Through patience temptation is overcome and provisions are miraculously sent down, 587. Patience is a work even in solitude, 589. A temptation lasting nine years is conquered by patience, 590. Isidorus cures those who are tempted through patience, 631. We grow in patience when we become accustomed to enduring greater things after lesser ones, 514, 631. Patience is a work, because evil does not overcome evil, 668.

Patricius, fearing danger, renounces the office of superior, 890. Josaphat becomes his father’s godfather when he receives him from the sacred font, 326. Paul, a disciple of Pachomius, 121.

Paul, a monk and disciple of Abbot Antony, sees a place prepared for Thais in heaven, 374. Paul the Deacon translated Theophilus’s penance into Latin, 381. He also wrote the deeds and constitutions of the pontiffs, ibid.

Paul the Simple is converted after his wife’s adultery, 730. He visits the blessed Antony, 730. He obeys simply, 730. From each person’s face he sees his thoughts, 676, 677. His perseverance in asking, 730; in praying, ibid.; in working, ibid. He perseveres in fasting for seven days, ibid. His extraordinary testing, ibid. By obedience and simplicity he merits the grace of casting out demons, 731. He himself heals a demoniac youth whom Antony could not heal, 731.

Paul imposes a daily quota upon himself, 551. Paul flees from a woman as from a lion, 555. He is compelled by a woman …

Having undertaken the ministry indiscreetly, he is punished for it, ibid. He heals the sick with oil, ibid. — Paul of Galata, abbot, spends Lent with a sextarius of lentils and a small vessel of water, 606. — Paul, a monk on Mount Pherme, 727. His eremitical life [reading uncertain], ibid. He recites 300 prayers and uses an equal number of pebbles for them, ibid. Paul lives for fifty years on alms-bread, speaking to no one, 873. — Paul the Heliadic feeds a lion daily, 911. He chastises the disobedient, ibid. Paulinus joined to Melania by blood, 436. A poor man substituted for a dead person truly dies and is raised by James of Nisibis, 799. Good counsel from a poor man is given to a prince, 249. The poor should frequently be visited, if progress can be made among them, 675. The poor and the sick are gems of great value, 712, 945. Pachomius and his brother John assist the poor from the surplus of their labors, 117. The hermit Abraham arranges for a rich inheritance to be distributed to the poor, 145. Astion asks that his possessions be distributed to the poor, 223. Astion’s parents distribute their possessions to the poor, ibid. An inheritance is best distributed to the poor, 601, 602. John the Almsgiver called the poor his masters, 181.

Voluntary poverty is an evangelical counsel, 276. John the Almsgiver’s poverty appears from his testament, 203. Agathon’s poverty, refusing to receive anything, 512. The poverty practiced by a certain abbess, who rejected greater things, 353. That of Aphraates, who accepted only what was strictly necessary from one person, 819. His refusal, by an excellent apologue, of a Persian tunic offered by Anthemius, 819. That of Arsenius, who accepted no clothing, 582. His begging even a single coin in necessity, ibid. That of the monks of Cyrene, 537. That of Dorotheus, who provided his food with his own hands, 710. His acceptance of only three coins from the five hundred sent to him, 767. That of John the Almsgiver, who arranged for an expensive blanket given to him to be sold, 188, 189. That of Julian, who possessed nothing except a hair shirt, a cloak, a small vessel, and a book, 876. That of Maesima, who used only one tunic, 832. That of a certain monk who refused money offered by John the Almsgiver, 192. Four monasteries in which not even a little vinegar was found for a sick man, 896. That of Myrogenes, who accepted nothing except [reading uncertain], 865. That of Paul at Pherme, who accepted nothing beyond what he could eat on the same day, 727. That of Serapion, 583. That of Serapion the Sindonite, who sold the Gospel and himself in order to assist the poor, 512, 582, 761. That of Silvanus, who wished to depart because his garden had been enlarged, 667. That of Theodora, who was in extreme need, 775. That of Zeno, who possessed no utensils, 827. His acceptance of individual books only on loan and return of them immediately after reading, 827, 828.

The poverty of religious persons consists in possessing nothing as one’s own, 124, 546. Perfect poverty is taught by Antony through an excellent doctrine and example, 511. Likewise by another, 512. Voluntary poverty is the soul’s rest, 526. Poverty makes souls white, 583. It is the monk’s treasure, ibid. It easily overcomes the devil, 660. Poverty pleasing to God, as Julian’s cell is illuminated from heaven at night, 876. Poverty. See Contempt of gold and money.

How peace of mind is acquired, 563. Peace with one’s neighbor is the way of salvation, 602. Agathon a lover of peace, 514. The best method of preserving peace is to be like a statue, [Col. LXVIII] 622. The enemy of peace alone is killed among them all, 750. Paysion commends good fellowship, 610.

The habit of sinning must be avoided, 287. The blindness of sinners, 612. The sinner should be encouraged, 594. John the Almsgiver, after his death, obtains the erasure of a great sin that had been written down, 204. Sin is the death of the soul, 282. Sin must be hated, 613. Fear of sin made us like lions, 866. The stench of sin is abhorrent to angels, 657. After sinning, lions flee from Macarius, 230. Sins should be noted in a little book, 50. Sins written on paper are erased through Basil’s prayers, 159, 160. The avoidance of lesser sins is beautifully taught, 288. Sins should be recounted so that we may be helped by the prayers of others, 386. Whoever mingles sins with good works does the same as one who draws water into a leaky vessel, 506. Our sins should be weighed more carefully than those of others, 594, 595. The sins of others should be diminished and our own magnified, 600. Adding sins to sins is compared with one who heaps a burden upon a burden, 506. Sins should be mourned, 658, 672. One’s own sins should be considered, 660. Sins are the cause of injuries, 668. There are various remedies for sins, as for diseases, 884.

Money unjustly acquired for the Church perishes with it [text uncertain], 183. Pecusius, a disciple of Pachomius, 121. — Pecusius the Elder visits the brothers, 125. Lice eat Zoilus, and he endures it patiently, 913. Pelagia, or Porphyria, the prostitute, is converted, 202. A sheep’s skin is brought to Macarius by a hyena in return for his illuminating its cub, 725. Olymptus, formerly a slave and later a hermit, annually delivers the rent to his masters, even against their will, 497, 625.

The pilgrimage of Leontius to the tombs of the holy martyrs Cyrus and John at Alexandria, 180. A pilgrimage to the church of Saint Cyrus, 192. A pilgrimage to Saint John the martyr, 195. Adolius’s pilgrimage to Jerusalem, 768. The pilgrimage of Basil and Eubulus to the holy places in Jerusalem, 154. That of Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, 225. A Roman and Jerusalem pilgrimage, 771. Peter’s pilgrimage to Mount Sinai, 891. His journey from there to Alexandria, to Saint Menas, ibid. His journey from there to Jerusalem, to Christ’s tomb, ibid. A pilgrimage to Mount Sinai, 913. A pilgrimage to the holy places, 930. John undertakes various pilgrimages, 917. The monk’s pilgrimage consists in restraining his mouth and keeping silence, 571, 626.

Perennius, prefect of Alexandria, persecutes the Church, 346. The degrees of perfection, 549. The dangerous delay of salvation, 258. A dangerous fall into sin, 268. It is no small danger to converse about the Scriptures, 610. The danger of the world must be feared, 619. The dangers of Palladius’s pilgrimage: marshes and thorns, ibid.; thirst, ibid.; the [reading uncertain], ibid.; the rising of the Nile, ibid.; robbers, ibid.; shipwreck, ibid.; a deserted island, 782; crocodiles, ibid. The persecution of Maximian, 47. The persecution of Christians under Valerian and Gallienus, 347. The Church grows through the persecution of tyrants, 113. Abraham the monk’s zeal grows through persecution, 147. King Abennet persecutes monks in India, 244.

One must labor perseveringly, 678. [Col. LXIX] Perseverance conquers demons, 743. The perseverance of the hermit Abraham for fifty years, 145. The perseverance of a certain person in prayer, which not even a scorpion’s fatal sting interrupts, 136. The perseverance of Paul the Simple in asking Antony to make him a monk, 730. His perseverance in prayer, 730. Arsenius’s perseverance in prayer, prolonging it from sunset until sunrise, 613. A monk’s perseverance should be like that of a hunting dog pursuing a hare, 589. The crown of perseverance and victory, 660.

Petronius succeeds Pachomius in the superintendence, 137. He dies, 138. Orsesius is appointed in his place, ibid. Peter of Alexandria, martyr, 113. Peter of Pachomius, 120, 121. — Peter is placed by Pachomius over the women, 124. — Peter the Tax-Collector throws wheaten bread to a poor man, 189. His deeds are weighed in a balance, and the fact that he gave the bread to the poor man while angry pleads in his favor, ibid. He becomes a distinguished almsgiver, ibid. He gives his undergarment to a poor man, ibid. Christ shows himself clothed in it, 190. He orders himself to be sold and the price distributed to the poor, ibid. The duties and pious works in which he exercised himself after being sold, ibid. He is restored to liberty, 190. He is regarded as a madman, ibid. Christ consoles him, ibid. He is recognized by his fellow countrymen, ibid. While fleeing, he obtains hearing and speech for a deaf-mute, ibid. — Why Peter was permitted to fall, 268. Peter is teacher of the world and holds the chief place, ibid. — Peter, disciple of Abbot Lot, 596. — Peter of Galata contended for ninety-two years, 822. His deeds were remarkable, ibid. He visits the holy places of Palestine, ibid. He eats only on alternate days, ibid. He uses a tomb in place of a house, ibid. He frees a demoniac, ibid. He blesses Theodoret, ibid. He heals the wife of the prefect of the East from an eye ailment by the sign of the cross, ibid. He censures Theodoret’s mother’s excessive adornment by means of an apt comparison, 823. His humility, ibid. He heals Theodoret’s mother of pain in her eyes by the sign of the cross, ibid. He frees a demoniac from a demon, 823, 824. He relieves the pain of cancer by his presence, 824. He raises Theodoret’s dying mother, ibid. His miraculous belt, ibid. He dies, 825.

Peter proceeds fasting to Mount Sinai in fulfillment of a vow, 891. Likewise to Alexandria, to Saint Menas, 821. From there to Jerusalem, to Christ’s tomb, ibid. The apparition of Peter the solitary, 889. The discovery of his body, ibid.

Prayer drives away phantoms, 531, 745. Pharaoh drowned, 256. Philagrius’s contempt for money and his fidelity, 383. Philip, prefect of Alexandria and father of Eugenia, 340. He drives the magicians out of Egypt, ibid. He orders Eugenia to be arrested, 344. He acts against Eugenia, his unknown daughter, ibid. Once his daughter is recognized, he is baptized with his household, 343. He is accused before the emperor at Rome, 345, 346. He is proscribed, 346. He distributes his possessions to the Church and the poor, ibid. He is elected bishop of Alexandria, ibid. He is struck with the sword, ibid.

Philoromus, a presbyter and intimate of Basil in Julian’s time, extinguishes the spirit of gluttony and fornication through abstinence, 770, 771. The training ground of monastic philosophy, 810. A philosopher is converted, 130, 131. Three questions proposed by him are resolved, 131. Philosophers send demons against Antony; when these are repulsed for the third time, they are converted, 556. Antony instructs philosophers, 54, 55. Photina, a virgin, is trained together with Melania the Younger, 775. Piammon, a presbyter, is scourged by demons and healed by angels, ibid. Piamun, a virgin, is granted the gift of prophecy, 736. By prayer she makes her adversaries stand motionless, ibid. What the Pichiti or Pygmies are like, 225, 227.

A certain man wishes the pursuit of piety to equal the pursuit of vanity, 905. A monk’s laziness is corrected by a vision, 567. Pinianus is trained together with thirty monks, 775. Pinuphius the presbyter flees honors, 547, 518. He is humbled, 548. He works secretly at night, ibid. He is recognized and honored, ibid. He flees again and is recognized, 548. He instructs a novice about many matters, 549. He teaches how humility is acquired, ibid. Likewise what must be observed in a community, 549. He enumerates the degrees of perfection, ibid.

Pior, a disciple of Saint Antony, drinks salt water, 503. He lives on one paximace and a few olives, ibid. He recoils from visits by his parents, 504. He vowed not to see his friends, 764. When his sister wished to see him, he allowed himself to be seen with his eyes closed, 501, 764. He competes with Pambo in hospitality, 716. By means of a sack full of sand, he teaches that our sins must be weighed more carefully than those of others, 520, 595. His garment is a sheepskin, 765. By his prayers he cures the sterility of a well, ibid. With what eagerness pious men should be approached, 707. A fish outside water is like a monk outside his cell, 563. Pithyrion, a disciple of Saint Antony, 759. Distinguished in discerning spirits, 760. He teaches how demons are to be expelled, ibid. He is accustomed to eat only once a week, 760. Plenthessus, a disciple of Pachomius, 121.

The danger of Poemen’s fall is foretold by John, 745. Poemen rejects the company of great men lest he fall from humility through vainglory, 498. He advises a monk not to betray robbers, 513. Poemen lies beside a lion naked, 912. He is devoured by beasts because he had not rescued a stranger from being torn apart by dogs, ibid. Poemen. See Pastor.

The punishment of the Arian who despised Antony’s admonitions, 48. The punishment of one who wished to mutilate Simeon Stylites’s body, 174. The punishment of unjust informers, 187. The punishment of the condemned, lacking the vision of God, is most severe, 260. The punishment of Christians in hell is more severe than that of pagans, 526, 656, 657. The terror of punishments, 265.

One must repent today, 524, 676, 895. A penitent must not be rejected but received, 594. The penitent soul is described by a beautiful apologue, 659. A repentant sinner appears to Paul the Simple with a radiant face, 525. God does not cast off penitents but receives them; this is established by a beautiful comparison, 660. It is impossible that God should not have mercy on penitents, 327. The repentance of Arsenius, who wept continually, 524. Fabiola’s public repentance, 397. Macarius’s repentance makes the lions that had fled from him return, 230. His remaining buried up to the neck for three years, 230. His remaining in the same place for forty days and nights on bended knees, ibid. Simeon Stylites’s repentance, binding his whole body with a rope, 170. His annual penance, which he imposed on his foot for hurrying too quickly, 172. Repentance in the Church, 267. How true repentance is to be practiced, [Col. LXX] 268. Repentance must not be postponed, 524, 612. How pleasing repentance is to God is shown by the gift of healing granted to Mary the penitent, 372. Repentance is more pleasing to God in a certain virgin than virginity, 777. Repentance is fruitless for no one, 755. Repentance is voluntary chastisement, 586. Repentance obtains water from the Nile, 576, 577. The repentance of two equal persons, one fulfilling it with sorrow and the other with joy, 578. Repentance is necessary for the young and the old, and why, 910. Repentance and confession enroll penitents among the divine number, 648. The true repentance of a fallen deacon is declared by a miracle, 577. Rigorous repentance, 584. The power of repentance is declared by a lamp kindled by divine agency, 581. The fruit of repentance and God’s goodness toward penitents, 525. One who performs repentance for the fallen man who did not repent obtains forgiveness, 577. Pastor describes repentance gently, 600. Wrongdoers must not be compelled to repent but stirred to repentance, 601. A bishop who fell during the persecution does penance for forty-nine years, 655. An angel announces that the repentance of the fallen is pleasing to God, 745. Repentance. See Mortification.

The pagan poets are convicted of error, 320. Nocturnal pollution that prevents communion, 758. The origin of pollution, 665. Polychronius fasts for seven days, 839. — Polychronius, a disciple of Zebinas, 846. He exercises himself in a nocturnal vigil, ibid. He conceals his virtues, ibid. He performs miracles, 847. Through his blessing a flask is filled with oil, ibid. He reverences those who arrive, ibid. He asks for prayers, ibid. He is hindered by no illnesses in the pursuit of virtue, 847. He rejects gold, ibid. He returns a cilicium more elegant than the one given to him, ibid. Polychronius, presbyter of the New Laura, 864. Antony heals the absent virgin Polycratia, 51.

Pompeius, Basilla’s fiancé, 347. Basilla avoids conversation with him, ibid. His slander against Christians, ibid. Saint John the Almsgiver forbids inequality in weights and measures, 181. The converted prostitute Porphyria is given the name Pelagia, 202. Basil visits Porphyrius the archimandrite in Egypt, 153. The gate of heaven is endurance of injuries, 513.

Posidonius is completely gentle, 760. When he lacked bread, he found by divine providence a basket full of grapes and figs, ibid. He heals a pregnant woman from an unclean spirit, ibid. He abstains from bread for forty years, 761. What is possible should be done, 609.

Posthumius, or Posthumianus, worships at the tomb of Saint Cyprian, 536. He remains seven days with an old man of Cyrene, 537; six months with Jerome, 538. After Alexandria he travels through the Thebaid, ibid. He remains in the desert for a full year and nearly seven months, 541. — Posthumius of Memphis, 233. A rope-maker, ibid. His various virtues, ibid. He is taught by an angel, 233. He prays kneeling toward the East, ibid. His first prayer, ibid. He is transported by an angel, 234. He is baptized by Priscus, ibid. He is adorned with various virtues, 235. His fasting, food, hair shirt, and vigils, ibid. He overcomes temptations through the protection of prayer, ibid. He never left the table satiated, ibid. He struggles bravely against illnesses, ibid. He prays continually, ibid. He seeks the secrets of the desert, 235. He becomes known to Macarius, 235. When dying, Macarius entrusts him with the governance of his own people, 236. He receives a rule from an angel and hands it on to his disciples, [Col. LXXI] 236, 237. By prayer he routs hosts of demons, 238.

Potamia, or Potamenia, is solicited by her master to submit to sexual violation, 710, 943, 985. She is moved neither by rewards nor punishments, 710, 943, 985. She is cruelly tortured, 710, 943, 944, 985. The wonderful power of expelling demons, 542. The drink of certain persons consists only of dew, 530. Abstinence from drink, 542, 572.

Antony hands down the precepts of the monastic life, 40. The prefect of a village is equated with Paphnutius, 735. See Protocomes. Peter is placed by Pachomius over the women’s monastery, 124. A superior is chosen while Pachomius is present and ill, 137. What a superior should be like, 683. The rewards of good works and the punishments of evil works are shown by an example and a vision, 646, 647. Barlaam attracts Josaphat to the faith by rewards, 265. Superiors should be chosen not by seniority but by moral excellence, 123. Pachomius foresees that through the negligence of superiors everything will decline for the worse, 132.

The present life is the devil’s hook, 302. Consideration of God’s presence, 685. Saint Ephraem corrects an immodest woman’s fornication through awareness of God’s presence, 598. The vanity and instability of present things, 246. The hospitable meal of the hermit of Cyrene, 537. The name and explanation of the name of the Spiritual Meadow, 862, 863. Anger must be overcome by prayers, 584. It is sometimes advantageous not to be heard, 128. See Prayer.

Eight presbyters serve the monks, 713. Primianus serves God together with his wife and daughter, 775. A certain prince of King Abennet becomes a monk, 244. He is sought at the king’s command, ibid. He appears before the king in his monastic habit, 244. The king’s address to him, ibid. His excellent reply, 244–246.

A prince who is secretly a Christian takes in a poor man crippled in one foot, 247, 248. He is accused by his rivals, 248. The king’s crafty address to him, ibid. His pious reply to the king, 248. Following the poor man’s advice, he appeases the king, 249. Subjects imitate their prince, 323. The beginning of victory is the disclosure of temptation, 574. Those who aspire to the religious life must be tested well, 903. Future things are tested by preceding things, 260. The remarkable testing of Paul the Simple by Antony, 730, 731. Macarius’s testing of two pleasure-loving young novices, 528. The testing of novices, 541. Testimonies to moral excellence, 709. The procession of the Holy Spirit must not be investigated curiously, 285.

Procopius Porphyreonites consults Abbot Zacchaeus about his sons living at Caesarea during a plague, 902. The fathers do not approve of prostrating oneself in prayer, 544. Progress must also be sought among the needy, 675. Profession benefits the negligent person nothing, 126. We can make progress in a single day, 609. Progress is made when charity grows less cold, 679. God’s promise to Pachomius of enduring posterity, 133. Readiness in a good work is beautifully taught both by a vision and by an example, 195. Pachomius possessed the gift of prophecy, 130. The resolve to repent is profitable, 677. A good resolve must always be maintained, 613. Possessiveness is detestable in a monk, 533. Antony teaches the vice of possessiveness in a monk through a most beautiful comparison, 581, 582.

Proterius’s servant falls in love with his master’s daughter, 156. He consults a magician, ibid. He renounces Christ and seeks the devil’s aid, 156. A letter is written to the devil, ibid. He is presented to the devil, ibid. He renounces Christ and baptism by giving a written contract to the demon, ibid. He is signed with the cross, strengthened by prayer, and shut up in a shrine, 157. He is harassed in various ways by demons, ibid. He is again strengthened by the sign of the cross and prayer, ibid. He is brought out after forty days, ibid. The clergy, monks, and people hold an all-night vigil for him, 158. Through Basil’s intercession he recovers the written contract he had given to the devil, ibid. The devil prevents Proterius’s daughter from entering a monastery, 156. She is inflamed with love for the servant, ibid. Her father grieves over her madness, 157. She urges her father to give her to him in marriage, ibid. The wicked marriage is completed, ibid. She invites her husband, who shuns the Eucharistic sacrament, to partake of it, ibid. Her husband reveals to her the crime he has prepared, 157. With her husband she asks Basil for help and obtains it, ibid.

The Protocomes is equated with Paphnutius, 755. He remains continent in marriage for thirty years, ibid. His hospitality and almsgiving, ibid. His sound judgment, 756. He renounces the world, 756. Paphnutius sees his soul carried into heaven by angels, ibid. Protus, Eugenia’s servant, becomes religious with her, 343. He is beheaded, 348.

By God’s providence Apollo and his companions miraculously provide abundant food at Easter, 750. God’s providence. See Divine providence. Isidorus sings psalms night and day without interruption, 609. An angel sings psalms with interruptions for prayer, 543. The practice of singing psalms comes from the angels, ibid. Ptolemy, despising everyone in his pride, falls into the miserable heresy that everything is carried along by chance and plunges into every vice, 734. Chastity as a wall against beasts, 96. Love of chastity is confirmed by a miracle, 51. See Continence. The presence of girls is dangerous to a man, threatening the overthrow of his mind, 313. A boy who had chosen the Mother of God over money is enriched in a marvelous way by John the Almsgiver, 193. Antony’s holy childhood, 36. Posthumius’s childhood, adorned with various virtues, 233.

Struggle is necessary, 965. Struggle together with endurance is salutary for the soul, 585. What a monk who endures no struggle is to be compared to, 612. A vision of spiritual struggle and God’s help granted to Theodosius, 879. The beauty of the body should, by the example of Bishop Nonnus, urge us toward the beauty of the soul, 377. The dangerous and temptation-prone nature of beauty is demonstrated in Euphrosyna, 365. A harmful leopard dies from the dust or water of Simeon Stylites’s monastery, 173. The killers of the martyrs at Milidone are punished, 586. Barlaam fears purgatory and therefore asks for prayers, 334. Purity of heart acquires knowledge of the Scriptures, 550. Purity of mind is to be preferred to ornate speech, 593. Purity of mind must be cultivated, 335. Even serpents are harmless toward the pure, 650. Cowardice is overcome by remembrance of death, 660. Cowardice is a disease of the soul, 911. The water of a well rises at the prayer of a certain brother so that he may draw it, 502, 651. What the Pygmies or Pichiti are like, 225, 227. The woman whom the other nuns considered insane—he prostrates himself before her and asks her blessing, 639, 738. The Pythagorean doctrine concerning the transmigration of souls is refuted, 54.

He enters the monastery of Saint Timothy, ibid. He communicates there daily, ibid. He eats only on the seventh day, ibid. He binds his whole body with a rope, ibid. Ordered to leave the monastery, he enters an abandoned well, ibid. His holiness is shown to the abbot in a vision, ibid. The monks search for him, ibid. He is found in the well, 171. People of various nations flock to him and are converted, 851. He considers the priestly blessing a great benefit, ibid. Barbarians contend for his blessing, 851. He heals a paralytic after the man renounces impiety, ibid. In one who violates a vow made in his presence, the flesh becomes stone, 852. He foretells famine and plague, ibid.; the invasion of locusts, ibid.; and the end of a lawsuit, ibid. He sees the invasion of the Persians and Scythians, 852. On public feast days he prays whole nights with his hands extended toward heaven, ibid. The word of God, heard frequently, softens Pimen’s heart, 679. The fruit of often-heard but not retained words of God is illustrated by the likeness of vessels frequently washed with water, 526. A sinner is pierced to the heart upon hearing the word of God, 677. An offensive word drives away grace, 596. Evil words must be avoided like thorns, 571. The truth of the Christian faith is proved because the weak overcame the stronger, 320. Truth is not found in rhetorical elegance, 7[lacuna]6. The clothing of Pachomius’ monks, 120. The clothing of Abraham the monk, 145. Olympias’ poor clothing, 780. Monastic clothing is the pledge of the heavenly bridegroom, 353. When monastic clothing is to be changed for secular clothing is taught by a beautiful comparison, 283. The clothing of the monks of Egypt, 543. The mystery of monastic clothing, 608. Paphnutius Cephala uses one garment for eighty years, 765. The old garments of monks, 583. The garments of the saints are to be held in esteem, 291. Excessive adornment of clothing is criticized by a beautiful comparison, 823. Agathon’s judicious use of clothing, 512. Barlaam brings sacred vestments necessary for the sacrifice to Josaphat, 336. The way to heaven is easy, 287. The heavenly journey requires much provisions, 275. Barlaam’s and his companions’, 283; that of seven monks, 530. The monk’s food, according to Sisoes: bread with salt and water, 508. Watchfulness against the devil, 685. Astion appears to him while he is praying at the tomb, 219. Vigils against the demon, 555. The vigils of Posthumius, 235; of Dorotheus, 710; of Stratigius, 892. They are commended to the monks of Posthumius, [Col. LXXXIII] 237. Antony is devoted to vigils and fasts, 37. Conquering oneself is the mark of a true monk, 513. The bonds of a captive are loosed while a sacrifice is offered for him, 192. God does not concern himself with one who wishes to avenge himself, 631. Vengeance must be left to God, 668. Achillas’ restraint of vengeance, 514. Sisoes’ beautiful rejection of vengeance, 512. Likewise another’s, 513. Ephraem sees a vine springing up on his tongue and spreading widely, 636. When someone violates his vow not to eat meat, the flesh turns to stone, 852. An energumen is restrained by a rod, 358, 359. A certain virgin is healed of avarice by Macarius, 712, and by Isidore, 945. A virgin possessed by the demon of pride is abandoned by the angel of temperance and falls shamefully, 735. A Corinthian virgin, despiser of the gods, is handed over to a brothel, 781. She mocks fornicators by a remarkable stratagem, ibid. Making the sign of the cross, she leaves clothed in a man’s garment by a young man, 781. A fallen virgin is despairing [source reading uncertain: “despe abunda”], 777. The prayer of that penitent, 777. She obtains from God the removal of the son of fornication, ibid. The same penitence is more pleasing to God than virginity, ibid. A virgin pours forth seven hundred prayers every day, 727. A virgin feigns foolishness for Christ, 639, 738. She is called “the monastery’s sponge,” dirty and performing every task, ibid. She remains silent when abused, ibid. She is preferred to Saint Ploterius or Pitirum, ibid. She fasts every day except Saturday and Sunday, 727. Regarded by everyone as insane, she is shown to be holier than all, 639, 738. She is called Amma as a mark of honor, ibid. Unable to bear glory and honor, she flees, ibid. A virgin who never goes out, 777. She asks for prayers as her final provision for the journey, ibid. She reads the work of Clement the Stromatean on Bishop Amos, ibid. A virgin gouges out her eyes because a young man claimed that he was captivated by them, 878. John the Almsgiver receives alms in the guise of a virgin, 205. The dangerous association of a sacred virgin, 654. Antony induces virgins to chastity by his mere appearance, 58. Seventy virgins exercise themselves with Isidore’s sisters, 709. ## Z

Zacchaeus the monk is afflicted with the royal disease, 136. He lived entirely on bread and salt [OCR: “con eutus”], ibid. His endurance in labors and pain of the hands, 136, 137. He makes the sign of the cross before going to bed, 137. His pain is increased by [unclear: “Nannum ejus”], 137. He weeps for an entire year, ibid. His two-day fasts, ibid. He dies, ibid. Zacchaeus the abbot foresees the future, 902. [Col. LXXXV] He averts a plague from Caesarea by his prayers, ibid. Zacharias, a disciple of John the Almsgiver, is very generous toward the poor, 180. Zacharias the abbot, 562. He considers one a monk who has subjected himself to necessities, ibid. Zacharias, a disciple of Moses, 513, 623, 668. By trampling on a pallium he declares a true monk, ibid. Zardan advises Josaphat to send away Barlaam, a foreigner, 289. In his hearing the substance of Christian doctrine is expounded, 290. Josaphat examines his mind and urges him to embrace the faith, 290. He departs from Josaphat, 292. He pretends to be ill, ibid. He approaches King Abenner and reveals to him everything that had happened to his son Josaphat, 293. Zareas is thought to have been sent by Christ, 341. He debates with Saint Helen at Heliopolis, ibid. As proof of his mission, he is challenged by the same man to enter the fire, 342. Reluctantly and unwillingly, he is handed over by the people to the fire, ibid. Half-burned, he is rescued by Saint Helen and driven from that region by the people, ibid. Zebinas, likewise an old man steadfast in his discipline, 845. Constant in prayer, ibid. Hospitable, 846. Various people are healed at his tomb, ibid. Pachomius’ zeal for souls: he induces Aprio, bishop of Tentyra, to build a church in a nearly deserted village and himself serves there as lector, 122, 123. Basil’s zeal, by which he strives to lead his teacher, fellow students, and others to the faith, 155. The zeal of a certain monk who hurries from the solitude to the city in order to convert his sister, a prostitute, 532. Where there is zeal against you, do not remain there, 601. The emperor Zeno, divinely destined to be punished for a grave crime, escapes punishment through almsgiving, 914, 915. —Zeno, a disciple of Basil, lives in a tomb, 827. He possesses no utensils, ibid. He lives on bread and water, ibid. He drinks no water unless it has been brought by his own labor, [Col. LXXXVI] 827. He is recognized by his modesty, ibid. Theodoretus asks a blessing from him, ibid. He has practiced monastic discipline for forty years, ibid. He is a diligent hearer of the word of God and a participant in the Lord’s Table, ibid. Through his prayer the eyes of the Isaurians grow dim and they are driven away by angels, 828. He arranges for his possessions to be distributed through Bishop Alexander, ibid. He dies happily, ibid. Zenon teaches that humble things should be pursued, 592. Likewise, that God alone is pure, 598. Zolius buys Peter the Publican for thirty coins, 190. The lector Zolius’ various exercises of piety, 913. Zosimas the monk in a monastery of the Palestinians, 382. His perfection, 382. He frequently sings psalms and meditates, and has visions, ibid. He is handed over to the monastery from his mother’s arms, ibid. He is tempted by pride in his perfection, ibid. He is divinely warned to leave, 383. At the divine warning he seeks the monastery situated by the Jordan, ibid. He is admitted by the abbot, ibid. He learns the customs of the monastery and the monks’ abstinence, 383, 384. During Lent he wanders through the desert, ibid. Resting from his journey at fixed hours, he prays, 384. At what he thought was the approach of an apparition, he makes the sign of the cross, 384. He pursues Mary of Egypt as she flees, ibid. They ask for a mutual blessing, 385. They request one another’s prayers, 383. Thinking Mary to be a spirit, he is corrected by her, ibid. He returns to the monastery, 390. He remains in the monastery when ill, ibid. After receiving the Eucharist, he hurries to Mary, 390. He goes to Mary for the third time, 391. He finds her body lifeless, ibid. —Zosimas the heretic, 382. Zosimus the Cilician, refusing the bishopric, returns to his cell, 899. By divine revelation it is indicated that the bishopric of Babylon is to be offered to him, ibid.

Valens persecutes the Church, 859. Basil silenced Valens, 163. When the emperor Valentinian reigned, 689. The lives of saints formerly appeared without the author’s name, 34. Whether one should say *Vita* or *Vitae Patrum*, VI. Whether these books should be entitled *Vitae Patrum* or *Vitas Patrum*, VIII. *Vitae Patrum*, the old title of these books, III. How it came about that this book was entitled *Vitas Patrum*, VIII, IX. The *Lives of the Augustinian Brothers*, IX. The *Lives of the Dominican Brothers*, VIII. The *Lives of the Fathers* should not be rejected because of their rougher style, LIV. Some books of the *Lives of the Fathers* formerly bore various titles, IV, VI: *Apophthegmata Patrum*, “Sayings of the Fathers,” V; *Interrogationes et responsiones Aegyptiorum Patrum*, “Questions and Answers of the Egyptian Fathers,” ibid.; *Responsa Patrum*, “Responses of the Fathers,” ibid.; *Sententiae Seniorum*, “Sayings of the Elders,” ibid.; *Sermones Patrum*, “Discourses of the Fathers,” ibid.; *Verba Seniorum*, “Words of the Elders,” IV.

The various Latin editions of the *Lives of the Fathers*, LVII. Three editions of uncertain place, printer, and year, ibid. Two Nuremberg editions, ibid. Three Venetian editions, LVIII. Two German editions of uncertain place and printer, ibid. Seven Lyons editions, ibid. Two Cologne editions, ibid. The Complutensian edition, ibid. The difference among all these editions is threefold, ibid. The first of them was printed at least before the year 69 after 1400, LIX. The second edition differs somewhat from the first, LXI. The third edition differs somewhat from the preceding editions, LXIV. The fourth edition, now newly issued, LXVI. Besides what was contained in the other editions, it includes Books VIII, IX, and X, and the appendix of Heraclides, Palladius, and Martin of Dumium, LXVIII, LXIX. Comparison of these four editions with one another, LXIX, LXX, LXXI, LXXIII. The various vernacular editions of the *Lives of the Fathers*, LXXIV. Two Italian editions, ibid. Four French editions, ibid. Three Flemish editions, LXXV. One German edition, ibid. An English edition, LXXV.

Manuscripts of the *Lives of the Fathers*: Affligemiensis, LXXVIII; Amandinus, LXXVII; Aquicinctinus, LXXVIII; Audomarensis, LXXVII; Bonae Spei, LXXIX; Camberonensis, LXXX; of the Brussels Carthusians, LXXXI; Claromarescanus, LXXX; Crispiniensis, LXXVIII; Saint Florian’s, LXXVI; Gemblacensis, LXXVIII; Saint James of Liège, LXXX; Ingolstadiensis, LXXVIII; Insulensis, LXXXI; Greater and Lesser Laetiensis, LXXVIII, LXXIX; Saint Mary of Bibrach, LXXX; Moretianus, LXXIX; Saint Peter’s at Münster, LXXXI; Rebdorffiensis, LXXX; Ruraemundanus, LXXXII; Greater and Lesser Holy Sepulchre, LXXXI; Sionius, LXXXII; Vedastinus, LXXVI.

The authority of the *Lives of the Fathers* is established: first, by the commendation of holy and very weighty men, III, IV, XLVI, XLVII; second, by the interpretation of very weighty men, XLVI. Heads bound with a fillet, 97, 98.
